title: Murakami’s Dream
text: # Murakami’s Dream This guide explains the retained results, their proofs, and the approaches that remain unfinished. The [current papers](../../papers/README.md) are organized by mathematical subject, with shared foundations cited by numbered statement. Their 21 drafts are provisional groupings, not a decision to publish 21 papers. The [manuscript guide](manuscript.md) describes the current 210-page reference and its relationship to the 21 subject papers, totaling 420 pages. The papers are separately readable accounts of overlapping results, not 21 prerequisites for one theorem. ## The question and the knots under consideration For a knot $K$ and an integer $N\geq2$, Kashaev’s invariant $K_N(K)$ is a complex number obtained by evaluating a finite sum at a root of unity. We use the reduced normalization, in which the unknot has value one. If the knot complement admits a complete hyperbolic metric of finite volume, the volume conjecture predicts that \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \] The left side measures exponential growth: a value of the form $N^a e^{NV/(2\pi)}$ has limit $V$, because the polynomial factor disappears after taking the logarithm and dividing by $N$. The right side is the volume of the knot complement. The knot remains removed from the three-sphere. This project studies the conjecture by cutting knot diagrams into tangles and keeping their finite evaluations and geometric face identifications together. One construction starts from a planar diagram encoded by a simple triangulation of the sphere. Other results treat **Conway algebraic, or arborescent, knots**, built by joining and turning rational tangles. The planar construction gives broad families after a specified finite decoration; the tree results also give explicit degree and twist bounds. The [manuscript](manuscript.md) contains completed proofs with their exact scope. This guide also explains the research approaches that have not yet produced a general theorem. Start with [the knot diagram and its finite evaluation](starting.md) for the definitions of tangles, filling, colors, and shared coefficients. Then [methods and approaches](methods.md) explains Fourier energy, weighted Cauchy, angle optimization, quantum recurrences, and torsors, with examples and literature references. The [algebraic approaches](algebraic.md) work through Hilbert 90, Koszul gluing, rigidity, and covers, including the tests that these proposals have not yet passed. The [notation chapter](notation.md) collects the symbols and normalizations. ## A general planar construction Choose a finite simple triangulation of the sphere, and pair adjacent triangles so that each triangle occurs once. The pairs specify crossing-circle tangles and their strand connections in the three-sphere. There is an explicit procedure that adds finitely many tangles on both sides of each original crossing circle. The numbers added are even, and the new pieces have odd crossing parity, so a chosen knot pairing is preserved. For every resulting decorated diagram, independently sufficiently long positive or negative twists at all original and added regions give the volume equality above. No tree decomposition of the tangle operations is required. The added tangles generally change the knot; the theorem does not remove them from its conclusion. The [construction and proof](results.md#decorating-a-planar-diagram) explain how a common circle packing determines the decoration and how its inequalities bound the full finite invariant. The geometric part constructs the smooth fillings of the auxiliary cusps while leaving the main knot cusp complete. ![A triangle is subdivided by an added circle, preserving the old matching edge and adding a new one.](../figures/balanced-terminal-fans.png) ## A criterion requiring no added tangles The [weak-balance theorem](results.md#an-unchanged-diagram-satisfying-weak-balance) applies directly to a matched spherical diagram when its complete packing satisfies explicit non-strict inequalities at every crossing region. If the original strand connections give one knot with no extra closed main component, independently long signed twists give the full volume equality. The proof changes the coefficient radii by a small common power: its entropy gain is linear in the perturbation, while the cost to the stationary complete action is quadratic. The condition is not asserted for every diagram. The linked explanation defines the potential, entropies, and precise inequality before deriving the estimate. ## The ordered-tree constructions For the specified construction with an integer braid at every vertex of an ordered tree with at least one edge, a [single twist threshold works for every finite tree](results.md#one-twist-threshold-for-arbitrarily-many-tangles): \[ |n_v|\ge2^{27}. \] The integer \(n_v\) counts signed half-twists. The actual endpoint pairing must form one knot, with no additional closed component. The threshold is independent of the size, depth and degrees of the tree. A more flexible sufficient condition lets each vertex have either this twist magnitude or degree \(d_v\ge2^{28}\). The entire diagram is still fixed before the quantum level grows. ## Stacking and turning the tree pieces A two-string tangle consists of two arcs in a ball, with four specified endpoints on its boundary. Draw the ball as a rectangle with two endpoints at the top and two at the bottom. There are two operations. To stack two tangles, put one above the other and join the adjacent pairs of endpoints without adding crossings. To turn a tangle, rotate its entire diagram through a quarter-turn. The order of the pieces matters. Start with an elementary box containing two strands with an integer number of half twists, and turn that box through a quarter-turn. Make finitely many such pieces, each with its own integer twist number. Repeated stacking and turning gives larger tangles. Finally, stack two such tangles and close the diagram by connecting the bottom-left endpoint to the top-left endpoint outside the box, and likewise on the right. This is the *cylindrical closure* used here. To decide whether the result is a knot, follow all strand connections and count any circles already closed inside intermediate boxes as well as those formed by the final closure. The construction can have arbitrarily many pieces and arbitrarily deep nesting. It is recorded by a finite ordered tree: its leaves are the elementary twist pieces, and its internal operations are stacking and turning. A tree in this description records a construction; it is not a drawing of the knot. The [manuscript guide](manuscript.md) gives drawings, worked examples, and the precise recursive class treated in the paper. The [results chapter](results.md) also explains the larger class covered by the companion theorem. ## The volume theorem and its quantifiers The [tangle-reduction paper](../../docs/papers/conway-reductions.pdf), Theorem 1.2, first simplifies the actual tangle diagram. Integral twist boxes that can be brought together are combined by adding their signed twist numbers. Moving a twist box past a tangle carries a specified half-turn of that tangle, which the reduction retains. The result is either an elementary two-strand braid closure or a presentation passing the strict angle-feasibility test described in the [results chapter](results.md). For each fixed input construction $\mathcal E$, the reduction partitions the original pieces into disjoint groups $B_1,\ldots,B_s$. Their surviving twist numbers are \[ W_j=\sum_{i\in B_j}n_i. \] The groups are determined before the integer weights are chosen. The order of some surviving pieces can depend on their parities. There is a finite threshold $B(\mathcal E)$ such that, on a non-elementary output, the conditions \[ |W_j|>B(\mathcal E)\qquad(1\leq j\leq s) \] and the requirement that the actual closed link be a knot imply hyperbolicity and \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N} \log|K_N(K_{\mathcal E}(\mathbf n))| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K_{\mathcal E}(\mathbf n)). \] The elementary output is the closure of a single two-strand braid, hence a torus link or knot; it is excluded from this positive-volume theorem. On a strict output the different net twists may have independent signs and incomparable magnitudes. Original weights within one group can cancel, so their individual largeness does not suffice. For example, two boxes with weights $a+2m$ and $-2m$ combine to the fixed weight $a$, however large $|m|$ becomes. Choose the entire construction and all twist integers first; then let $N$ grow through the positive integers. The threshold may depend on the construction, but is uniform over its finitely many parity choices. Neither the tree nor its weights grow with $N$. This covers arbitrarily large fixed compositions when their reduced twists satisfy the bound. It does not cover arbitrary short twists or classify every arborescent knot up to all possible presentation changes. The earlier chapters of the TeX manuscript prove an included family; the companion strict-tree estimates and exact tangle reduction give this extension. A further manuscript chapter proves the quantitative circle-tree result below. The [manuscript page](manuscript.md) distinguishes those scopes. The same paper's Theorem 1.3 also permits cap closures, which join each upper and lower endpoint pair, and twist sums that vanish exactly. Removing these zero sums can split the diagram into connected-sum factors. If the input is hyperbolic and every surviving strict factor has long net twists, the proof shows that just one strict factor remains and all others are unknots. The original knot is isotopic to that covered factor. The [results chapter](results.md#cap-closures-and-exact-cancellations) gives the precise criterion, including a sufficient condition on the original subset sums. ## Numerical conditions for trees of crossing circles In this construction every product junction contains an integer two-strand braid. To describe its geometry, place a crossing circle around that braid and retain its parity as a half twist. Let \(d_v\) be the number of incident tree edges and \(n_v\) its signed crossing power. The [directed subtree theorem](../../notes/actual_all_circle_directed_volume.md) proves the actual hyperbolic knot-volume equality when, independently at each vertex, \[ |n_v|\ge2^{27}\quad\text{or}\quad d_v\ge2^{28}, \] and the original strand pairing gives one knot. Its more detailed finite criterion assigns a separate decay bound to each subtree; the displayed condition is a simple consequence of that criterion. The degree alternative allows short and zero powers. For example, start with any fixed ordered core whose strand pairing is a knot. At an existing product slot at each vertex, insert an even stack of \(B\ge2^{28}\) new terminal pieces, each with an odd power of magnitude at least \(2^{27}+1\). The stack has the same endpoint pairing as two straight strands and creates no internal circle. The resulting knot satisfies the theorem. This is a way to construct new covered knots; it generally changes the knot represented by the original core. The [summed criterion](../../docs/papers/circle-tree-volume.pdf) gives a different sufficient test: \[ \sum_v\frac{d_v}{d_v^2+n_v^2}\le2^{-25}. \] For a tree with \(E\) edges, every \(|n_v|\ge8192\sqrt E\) suffices. This can be numerically better for a particular diagram. The earlier local condition is also retained in its original note. All these theorems keep the tree and the twist integers fixed while \(N\) grows through both parities. Both the finite-sum estimate and its geometric interpretation are proved. The original octahedral pieces deform with their marked filling curves, and the final metric is smooth on the original knot complement. The main knot cusp remains unfilled. The [results chapter](results.md) gives the exact scope and the [manuscript guide](manuscript.md) locates the full proofs. ## Why the proof has both an analytic and a geometric part After the exact tangle reduction, the analytic and geometric proof begins by removing the surviving long twists and placing an auxiliary circle around the two strands in each twist region. The resulting *augmented link* remembers where the twists will be restored. Assigning integer labels, called colors, to these auxiliary circles produces a finite evaluation depending on those labels. The notes call this evaluation the *source*. At each level $N$, the source is an exact finite sum. Its leading exponential growth is described by a real function of the summation indices divided by $N$. Maximizing that function produces angles for ideal hyperbolic cells. The geometric part of the proof shows that these cells fit together with precisely the face identifications of the augmented link complement. This establishes which manifold supplies the volume. Restoring the twists requires another finite sum over the auxiliary colors. Its terms have complex phases, so their absolute values alone do not determine its growth. The analytic part proves a nonzero leading contribution and bounds the rest of this whole sum. It also follows the chosen geometric structure through the fillings that restore the twists. Filling an auxiliary crossing circle means removing that auxiliary cusp by attaching a solid torus with the specified slope. The cusp belonging to the knot is left unfilled. Consequently the final critical value is the volume of the resulting **knot complement**, rather than the volume of the augmented link used at the beginning. ![Exact tangle reduction, finite-sum estimates, and identification of the knot complement volume.](../figures/research-map.png) The [mechanism chapter](mechanism.md) develops the finite sum and its estimates. The [geometry chapter](geometry.md) explains the ideal cells, peripheral curves, and the volume comparison. These two parts are both needed: constructing a hyperbolic metric does not by itself estimate the quantum invariant, and estimating a finite sum does not by itself identify its exponential rate with the volume of a particular complement. ## The quantum A-polynomial formulation There is also a recurrence formulation. A quantum A-operator is a finite difference operator annihilating the color-dependent invariant. Its coefficients depend on the quantum parameter and a peripheral variable; a shift changes the color. An operator alone generally has more than one solution. Initial values and the prescribed behavior at singular specializations select the solution corresponding to the knot invariant. The [pointed quantum A-period theorem](../../notes/actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) gives an exact reconstruction of $K_N(K)$ from this operator and finite initial data, retaining the peripheral factors. For the knots covered above, this reconstructed value therefore has the same hyperbolic volume limit. The theorem also gives a positive determinant expression whose exponential rate is the volume. For every covered strict long-filling presentation, the [geometric longitude proof](../../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf) identifies the whole selected curve with the preferred meridian--longitude deformation of the knot complement. Junctions without crossing circles may have arbitrary valence and adjacency. The earlier summed circle-tree theorem and the local theorem with bound \(2^{-120}\) also have the required geometric identification and full expansion. The selected complex geometric irreducible factor therefore divides the first nonzero classical symbol of every genuine all-level annihilator of the reduced invariant. This does not identify the other factors, their multiplicities, or the full recurrence ideal. The actual meridian state imposes a concrete constraint: its complete value has volume growth, but its value one quantum shift away is exactly one. The [nearby-zero theorem](../../notes/actual_ado_complete_meridian_zero_accumulation.md) proves that zeros approach completeness at distance $O(1/N)$. A nonvanishing scalar asymptotic for the unchanged state therefore cannot hold on a fixed neighborhood. There is now a uniform volume limit on smaller disks \(M=q_N^s\), \(|s|\le R<1\), for every fixed strict Conway tree with independently sufficiently long signed twists. Product junctions can have arbitrary fixed valence and adjacency. The ratio to the complete value tends to \(\sin(\pi s)/(\pi s)\); after division by the exact finite sine quotient, its first correction is determined by the preferred cusp shape. The [moving-meridian theorem](results.md#the-volume-limit-while-the-meridian-varies) states the normalization, the threshold and the whole-sum comparison. The same intrinsic volume, nonvanishing, cusp and selected-factor conclusions pass through the net-twist and closure reductions under their stated hypotheses. Their ambient isotopies preserve the entire zero-framed meridian family and the preferred peripheral curves. The comparison may use the reduced strict diagram to compute its factors; it does not identify the auxiliary augmented links of different presentations. The disk still stops before the ordinary-color resonances. Continuation through them and coverage of other knot classes remain further questions. ## Reading and checking the arguments Use [the results chapter](results.md) to choose a theorem whose hypotheses fit the diagram under consideration. Then follow its [paper and numbered imports](../../papers/README.md). The [dependency graph](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html) shows which foundational statements that argument uses; it is not a requirement to read the entire collection. The [manuscript guide](manuscript.md) locates the current and earlier accounts, and the [notation chapter](notation.md) explains their conventions. The [closing assessment](../../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) records the review of the retained results. The [reproduction chapter](audits.md) distinguishes finite computations, compiled mathematical implications, and written analytic and geometric proofs. No complete knot-family theorem is claimed as an end-to-end Lean formalization. The [research library](../library.html) organizes the supporting notes by question. It keeps the Fourier, weighted Cauchy, torsor, cube and other retained approaches, with their hypotheses and limits. Superseded proofs are cited through the current papers. Useful obstructions remain explained in the methods chapters; obsolete diagnostic histories belong to the source snapshot in Git. The [figure gallery](../figures.md) explains what each diagram represents and links to editable sources. The general volume conjecture remains open.

title: From a knot diagram to a volume limit
text: # From a knot diagram to a volume limit This chapter introduces the objects used in the guide. It explains what is being constructed, what is being summed, and what a volume theorem must prove. The [results chapter](results.md) then states the families covered by the arguments. The [methods chapter](methods.md) develops the estimates and the alternative approaches. There is no need to read the reference manuscript from beginning to end. After these definitions, choose a construction in the results chapter and use the [dependency graph](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html) to find the statements its proof imports. The graph distinguishes an exact finite formula, an estimate, and a geometric conclusion. The invariant originates in Kashaev’s [1994 construction using cyclic quantum dilogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9411147). His [1995 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9504020) gives the crossing-matrix formulation, and his [volume paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9601025) proposes the exponential comparison with the hyperbolic complement. We use the finite crossing formulation and keep its normalization explicit. The later relation to the colored Jones polynomial is a separate identification. ## Knots, complements, and tangles **Definition (knot and exterior).** A knot \(K\) is a smoothly embedded circle in the three-sphere \(S^3\), considered up to ambient isotopy. An ambient isotopy moves the circle continuously through embeddings; it does not let one strand pass through another. Removing the interior of a small solid-torus neighborhood of \(K\) gives its compact exterior \(X_K\). Its boundary is a torus. The interior of \(X_K\) is homeomorphic to \(S^3\setminus K\), the knot complement. A link has several circle components. Its exterior has one boundary torus for each component. This distinction matters whenever a tangle construction is closed: a well-defined scalar for a link does not make that link a knot. **Definition (hyperbolic knot).** A knot is hyperbolic when \(S^3\setminus K\) admits a complete metric of constant curvature \(-1\) and finite volume. The notation \(\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K)\) means the volume of this metric. The metric has an end, or cusp, corresponding to the removed knot. The knot itself is not a subset of hyperbolic space whose volume is being measured. **Definition (two-string tangle).** Take two disjoint arcs properly embedded in a three-ball, with their four endpoints at four specified points on its boundary. Properly embedded means that only the endpoints meet the boundary. Such a pair is a two-string tangle. We draw the ball as a box with two upper and two lower endpoints. The endpoint positions and their order are part of the description. Stacking two boxes joins the lower endpoints of the upper box to the upper endpoints of the lower box. A quarter-turn rotates a box and its endpoints into the new input and output positions. A closure joins the four remaining endpoints by specified arcs outside the box. Different closures can give different links. A rational tangle is obtained from the trivial pair of arcs by a finite sequence of twists of adjacent boundary endpoints. Conway's algebraic, or arborescent, constructions compose rational tangles along a tree of such operations. In this project “algebraic knot” has this tangle meaning. A convenient reference for the basic conventions and rational tangle classification is [Kauffman and Lambropoulou, *On the classification of rational tangles*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0311499). The repository's particular stacking, turning, and closing conventions are specified in Chapter 1 of the manuscript. Following the arcs gives a finite test for the number of components. This test must count circles already closed inside an intermediate box as well as components formed by the final closure. The knot hypotheses in the theorems refer to that full test. ## Half twists, full twists, and auxiliary circles Write \(R\) for the chosen positive crossing of two strands, including the interchange of their endpoints. The tangle \(R^n\) has signed half-twist count \(n\in\mathbb Z\). Its inverse crossing is \(R^{-1}\). Two successive crossings form a full twist. Thus changing \(n\) by an even integer preserves the endpoint permutation; changing its parity interchanges the two endpoints. This is why the theorems separate the parity pattern from the long twist parameters. A parity pattern can ensure that the strands form one knot. Increasing the number of full twists then preserves that pairing, although it generally changes the knot type. A **crossing circle** is an auxiliary circle bounding a disk pierced by the two strands in a twist region. To augment a diagram, remove its full twists, keep the specified residual half twist, and add the crossing circle. Do this at every designated region. The result is an augmented link with auxiliary components as well as the main strands. **Definition (Dehn filling).** On one boundary torus of a link exterior, choose a primitive closed curve, called a slope. Glue in a solid torus so that this curve bounds a meridian disk of the solid torus. This operation is Dehn filling. “Primitive” means that the curve represents an indivisible element of the integral first homology of the boundary torus. **Definition (meridian and longitude).** The meridian of a link component is an essential simple closed curve on its boundary torus that bounds a disk in the removed tubular neighborhood. Essential means that it does not contract to a point within the boundary torus. A longitude runs once parallel to the component. In the three-sphere, the preferred longitude is the parallel curve with linking number zero with that component. After orientations are chosen, the meridian and preferred longitude give a basis of the torus's first integral homology. A slope is then specified by a coprime integer pair in this basis; reversing both integers leaves the unoriented slope unchanged. For a crossing circle, choose the meridian \(\mu_e\) and disk longitude \(\lambda_e\) with the orientations used in the proof. The subscript \(e\) labels the twist region. In the manuscript's convention, filling the slope \(\mu_e+p_e\lambda_e\) restores the signed count \[ n_e=\epsilon_e-2p_e, \] where \(p_e\in\mathbb Z\) and the retained half twist \(\epsilon_e\in\{-1,0,1\}\) is fixed in advance. The minus sign records the chosen disk orientation; it is not a universal sign convention for every diagram. Only these auxiliary tori are filled in the knot-volume theorems. The main knot cusp remains complete and unfilled. There are therefore two different volumes during the argument: \[ \operatorname{Vol}(Y_D) \quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K_{\boldsymbol p}). \] Here \(D\) is the fixed augmented diagram, \(Y_D\) is its link complement, and \(K_{\boldsymbol p}\) is the knot after the auxiliary fillings. The geometric proof must reach the second volume. ## What the finite invariant contains At level \(N\ge2\), put \[ q_N=e^{\pi i/N},\qquad Q_N=q_N^2=e^{2\pi i/N}. \] In the finite representation used here a main strand carries an \(N\)-dimensional complex vector space \(V_N\), with a chosen basis \(v_0,\ldots,v_{N-1}\). A crossing acts on \(V_N\otimes V_N\). A cup creates two endpoints, a cap joins them, and each internal wire means summation over its basis index. These maps, the closing correction, the framing, and the reduced normalization together specify the scalar \(K_N(K)\). The word **color** specifies a representation carried by a strand or auxiliary circle. Complete color in this guide means the \(N\)-dimensional representation. An internal basis index is not a second color. Here is the elementary matrix rule behind a stacked tangle. If \(A\) and \(B\) act on \(V_N\otimes V_N\), write \[ A(v_i\otimes v_j) =\sum_{a,b=0}^{N-1}A^{ab}_{ij}\,v_a\otimes v_b. \] Then \(B\) followed by \(A\) has entries \[ (AB)^{ab}_{cd} =\sum_{i,j=0}^{N-1}A^{ab}_{ij}B^{ij}_{cd}. \] The four indices \(a,b,c,d\) remain on the outside. The two internal indices \(i,j\) are summed, with the same values used in both factors. ![Stacking two linear maps joins their two internal wires. The lower map B acts first, and both copies of each internal index are summed together.](../figures/finite-contraction.svg) The actual crossing matrices, cup and cap entries, and closing functional appear in Chapter 2 of the manuscript. Kashaev's [original matrix construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9504020) is the starting definition. The normalization comparison in Appendix A is a separate finite calculation. An arbitrary choice of local matrices does not define a knot invariant merely because it has an interesting large-\(N\) limit. The **source** of a calculation means this specified finite expression: its local maps, summation ranges, closure, and all scalar factors. An exact source identity rewrites that expression without changing its value. The guide uses “source” in this concrete sense. ## Why polynomial coefficients appear Polynomials can record the entries of a finite tensor contraction. For instance, fix a nonnegative integer \(d\) and write \[ A(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jz^j,\qquad B(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}b_jz^j, \] then \[ [z^d]A(z)B(z) =\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jb_{d-j}. \] The notation \([z^d]\) asks for the coefficient of \(z^d\). It enforces one shared constraint on the two indices. In the face description of a knot diagram, each projection region has one variable \(L_f\). The subscript \(f\) labels the region. Every local factor touching that region uses that same variable. A product of local polynomials followed by a specified coefficient extraction then enforces all face constraints at once. In the marked construction two designated face variables are set to zero; these are the **protected faces**. Their zero exponents come from the original cut, not from a later choice of an estimate. For positive real numbers \(r_1,\ldots,r_s\), the elementary multivariable Cauchy formula gives \[ |[z_1^{k_1}\cdots z_s^{k_s}]P| \le \frac{\displaystyle\sup_{|z_f|=r_f}|P(z_1,\ldots,z_s)|} {\displaystyle\prod_{f=1}^{s}r_f^{k_f}}. \] Here \(P\) is a polynomial and the \(k_f\) are nonnegative integer target exponents. To see the formula, integrate \(P(r_1e^{i\theta_1},\ldots,r_se^{i\theta_s}) e^{-i\sum_f k_f\theta_f}\) over all \(\theta_f\in[0,2\pi]\), divide by \((2\pi)^s\prod_f r_f^{k_f}\), and use Fourier orthogonality. Taking the absolute value gives the inequality. Each occurrence of a face must have the same radius in this integral. That requirement is what the phrase “shared radii” means. When the geometric construction interprets \(L_f\) as a circle curvature, its circle radius is \(1/L_f\). The integration radius \(r_f\) is a weight in a coefficient estimate; the two meanings of “radius” should not be confused. ## What has to converge Kashaev's volume question asks for the exponential rate of the **whole scalar**: \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \] Its formulation comes from [Kashaev's volume paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9601025). The [Murakami–Murakami relation to colored Jones polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9905075) gives another formulation of the invariant. It does not by itself prove the volume limit for a new knot. The quantifiers in a long-twist theorem have the following order: 1. Choose one permitted finite diagram and any finite decoration required by the theorem. 2. Find a threshold \(T\) for that diagram. 3. Choose every filling integer \(p_e\), with \(|p_e|>T\), and fix these integers permanently. 4. Let \(N\) tend to infinity for the resulting fixed knot. Allowing arbitrarily many tangles means that step 1 permits diagrams of arbitrarily large finite size. It does not let the number of tangles increase during step 4. A degree-and-twist criterion may give an explicit \(T\); an existence theorem need not do so. To understand the analytic issue, consider \[ Z_N=e^N+\bigl(-e^N+1\bigr)=1. \] Both summands have exponential size, but their sum does not. Thus finding a critical point with the expected volume, or bounding a positive sum of absolute values, is only part of an argument. A successful decomposition writes \(K_N=G_N+R_N\), where \(G_N\) is a specified contribution and \(R_N\) is the remaining sum. For example, let \(S\in\mathbb C\) and suppose \[ G_N=a_Ne^{NS},\qquad \frac{\log|a_N|}{N}\longrightarrow0,\qquad |R_N|\le e^{N(\operatorname{Re}S-\eta)+o(N)},\quad\eta>0. \] The amplitude \(a_N\) is nonzero for sufficiently large \(N\). The notation \(o(N)\) denotes an error whose ratio to \(N\) tends to zero. These assumptions imply \(R_N/G_N\to0\), so the full scalar has rate \(2\pi\operatorname{Re}S\). A separate geometric argument must show that this number is the volume of the intended knot complement. This explains the different conclusions found in the guide: | Result | What it establishes | | --- | --- | | Finite identity | Two expressions evaluate to the same number at each level. | | Upper estimate | The specified quantity cannot grow faster than the stated rate. | | Nonzero geometric contribution | One specified part has the stated nonzero asymptotic. | | Full volume equality | The entire invariant has the rate of the actual hyperbolic knot complement. | The manuscript includes completed arguments at these different levels of strength. In particular, its geometric-contribution theorem for an unchanged matched spherical diagram remains a partial result. The [methods chapter](methods.md) explains which techniques supply each step, and the [results chapter](results.md) records the exact hypotheses under which all steps have been completed.

title: A guide to the volume reference
text: # A guide to the volume reference [Read the reference PDF](../../manuscript/build/main.pdf) · [Source and build instructions](../../manuscript/README.md) · [Papers organized by subject](../../papers/README.md) The reference begins with the volume theorem for strict Conway compositions, proved through the pure auxiliary source. It includes the same proof files as the [19-page Conway paper](../../papers/conway-asymptotics/README.md). The rest of the volume reference retains independent circle-tree and planar constructions with their own hypotheses. The companion manuscripts are from the same project. The Conway paper uses five directly and one further geometric prerequisite, as explained in the [collection guide](../../papers/README.md#the-conway-paper-and-its-supporting-proofs). They reorganize the shared mathematical material; the long reference also contains results outside this seven-paper route. The [exposition audit](../../repro/CONWAY_SERIES_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) describes the corrections and expanded explanations. The seven-paper series has 160 pages in total; it is the complete prerequisite collection for the 19-page Conway result. The [collection-wide audit](../../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) extends that revision to all fourteen remaining papers and this 210-page reference. Its logical comparison records exactly which statements Lean proves and which application lemmas retain written proofs. The signed local calculation used for the separate recurrence problem is proved in the [quarter-index paper](../../papers/quarter-index-asymptotics/README.md). Standalone meridian, longitude and recurrence papers remain [available separately](../../papers/README.md#reading-routes-and-retained-boundaries). The guide's other methods chapters keep the history of alternative approaches; this chapter describes the current volume proofs. Readers new to the invariant can begin with [the first-reading chapter](starting.md). The [results chapter](results.md) gives the complete family-by-family scope. ## The question and the fixed data At level \(N\), let \(K_N(K)\) be the reduced Kashaev invariant of a knot \(K\), normalized to be one on the unknot. For a hyperbolic knot, the volume conjecture asks whether \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \] The volume is that of the complete knot complement. In every theorem described here, the finite diagram, its strand connections, disk framings and integer powers are fixed before \(N\) grows. The limit includes all sufficiently large integer levels, not just primes or one parity. The auxiliary crossing circles are filled; the main knot cusp remains complete. A crossing circle bounds a disk pierced by two strands. Filling its primitive slope \(\mu_\ell+p_\ell\lambda_\ell\) inserts the recorded twists, where \(\mu_\ell\) is its meridian and \(\lambda_\ell\) its disk longitude. With retained half twist \(\epsilon_\ell\in\{0,\pm1\}\), the crossing power is \[ n_\ell=\epsilon_\ell-2p_\ell. \] The factor two distinguishes full twists from individual crossings. The strand connections, including any component closed inside a box, must give one knot. ## The strict construction A two-strand tangle is drawn in a box with four ordered endpoints. Stacking joins the adjacent endpoints without changing their order. A quarter-turn carries the entire tangle and its crossing disks. Cylindrical closure joins bottom-left to top-left and bottom-right to top-right outside the last box. The elementary leaf is the clockwise quarter-turn of an augmented crossing-circle box; the turn carries its disk and endpoint labels. Every occurrence has its own crossing circle. The strictness test assigns a real label to every exposed output: | Operation | Constraint | | --- | --- | | Elementary leaf | \(0<a<1/2\) | | Quarter-turn | \(x\mapsto1-x\) | | Product with inputs \(x,y\) and output \(z\) | \(\max(x,y)<z<x+y<1\) | | Final closing pair | The two outputs sum to one; its forced product is omitted | An expression is strict when these finitely many constraints have a solution. An elementary closing child is allowed. A leaf at the stationary value \(1/4\) is allowed as well; the proof does not require separated roots of a signed leaf recurrence. For example, \(C((h_1h_2)(h_3h_4))\) is strict when every leaf has label \(3/10\) and the two product outputs have label \(1/2\). Then \(3/10<1/2<3/5<1\). Retained crossing parities \((0,1,1,1)\) give a knot: tracing the elementary endpoint pairings through the stacks and the outside arcs gives one component and no internally closed component. For each fixed strict expression with at least two leaves and an admissible parity pattern, there is a threshold \(P_0\). Every fixed tuple with \(|p_\ell|>P_0\) at every auxiliary circle has the volume limit. Signs and ratios are unrestricted. The tuple does not grow with \(N\). The assignments covered by this condition have natural density one in \(\mathbb Z^b\), where \(b\) is the fixed number of circles. Among integer tuples in \([-R,R]^b\), at most \[ b(2\lfloor P_0\rfloor+1)(2R+1)^{b-1} \] have a bounded coordinate. Their proportion tends to zero, but these excluded slabs are still infinite. Different assignments may describe the same knot. The theorem is not a density claim for distinct knots ordered by crossing number or a result for every short filling. ## Five steps in the pure-source proof The finite source is the evaluation of the augmented diagram as a function of its auxiliary colors. A color is an integer representation label; a circle is a component of the diagram. Summing colors and filling a circle are different operations. The pure source uses no retained half twists on the auxiliary circles. Its core Newton coefficients are positive. The complementary-color terms, called aliases, remain part of the physical invariant and need separate estimates. The proof proceeds as follows. 1. **Keep the exact integer sum.** The finite Newton calculus gives product, turn and closing coefficients, including derivatives at repeated spectral roots. Turns substitute \(r\mapsto N-1-r\); the closing constraint has coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\). Solving these equations leaves a lattice of cell volume one, with every bounded integer offset retained. 2. **Interpolate the positive pure core exactly.** The canonical factorial \(G_N\) has precisely the finite sine-factorial values. Its complex expansion applies at the unique strict positive maximum. One lattice contour lemma gives the nonzero local Gaussian coefficient. This argument also works at a quarter-index leaf; no signed recurrence estimate is used. 3. **Pay for the physical and Fourier complements.** The source-bound theorem controls the full physical remainder and every macroscopic color deficit. A second use of the lattice lemma evaluates the color Fourier sum. A separate contour estimate bounds the rest of the Fourier torus. A local Taylor expansion alone would not supply that global estimate. 4. **Perform each full crossing power.** Fourier–Hermite inversion expands every positive or negative integer power, including odd powers, in ordinary colored circles. The whole filling-sum theorem retains all Fourier charges and endpoint currents and proves that their leading coefficient is nonzero. 5. **Identify the same action geometrically.** The marked classical shear restores the retained half twist and the original integer filling slope. The geometric theorem proves the metric on the specified filled exterior, its primitive cusp completion and the absolute action–volume equality. The [Conway source guide](../../papers/conway-asymptotics/README.md#proof-inputs) lists each numbered companion import. The proof requires all five steps. A positive auxiliary sum alone does not control a signed closing. ## What orthogonality does, and what it does not do The reference opens with explicit linear-algebra propositions used by the proof. They explain where exact simplification is available. ### Transport the coefficient pairing Let \(B:\mathbb C^m\to V\) send coefficients \(c\) to a vector \(Bc\) in a finite-dimensional inner-product space \(V\). Its Gram matrix is \(G=B^*B\), with \(^*\) the adjoint. Then \[ \|Bc\|^2=c^*Gc,\qquad \ker G=\ker B. \] Thus the form becomes positive definite on the quotient by coefficients representing zero. Under a coordinate change \(c=Sd\), it becomes \(S^*GS\). It can be replaced by the identity only when those coordinates are orthonormal. A closing row \(\ell:V\to\mathbb C\) is additional data. The estimate \(|\ell(Bc)|\le\|\ell\|\sqrt{c^*Gc}\) is an upper bound. A large nonzero vector can still lie in \(\ker\ell\). The volume proof must therefore estimate the specified closing, not replace it by a norm. A linear corridor is a sequence of prescribed linear maps. Replacing it by their matrix product is exact. A product with one fixed input can be part of such a corridor; a product with two independently summed inputs cannot be treated as one prescribed map. ### Use all shifted Fourier characters For a real shift \(\alpha\), set \(w_k=e^{2\pi i(k+\alpha)/N}\), \(0\le k<N\). The coefficients \[ H_a=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}f_kw_k^{-a}, \qquad 0\le a<N, \] satisfy \[ f_k=\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}H_aw_k^a,\qquad \sum_a|H_a|^2=\frac1N\sum_k|f_k|^2. \] The shift contributes only unit phases to the complete character basis. The filling calculation uses \(\alpha=1/2\), so \(w_k^N=-1\). The repeated spectral roots require normal data as well as values. For the crossing power \(n\), the value data \(h_k\) have modulus one and the normal data are \(d_k=n(k-(N-1)/2)h_k\). Parseval controls both vectors. Their exact coefficient reconstruction gives \[ \sum_j|\beta_j| \le2\sqrt N\left(1+\frac{|n|}{\sqrt{12}}\right), \] where the \(\beta_j\) are the coefficients of the full power in the ordinary-circle basis. Discarding the derivatives would reconstruct a different element of the nonsemisimple algebra. The estimate is a polynomial filling cost; it does not prove a lower bound. For the full closing, let \(j\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^r\) range over every color tuple and let \(D_N(j)\) be the original source error. The exact identity and its subsequent bound are \[ E_N=\sum_j\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^r\beta_{N,\ell,j_\ell}\right)D_N(j), \qquad |E_N|\le \left(\prod_{\ell=1}^r\sum_k|\beta_{N,\ell,k}|\right)B_N \quad\text{if }|D_N(j)|\le B_N\text{ for every }j. \] The sum remains coherent until the triangle inequality is applied. For fixed powers and a fixed number of circles, the coefficient product grows only polynomially. The Lean module [ConwayAssembly](../../formal-real/ConwayAssembly.lean) derives this whole-error estimate from the proved Fourier–Hermite bound. ### Eliminate stationary variables with their Hessian Let \(F(y,t)\) be a holomorphic phase. Suppose \(F_y(y_0,0)=0\) and \(F_{yy}(y_0,0)\) is invertible. There is then a local stationary solution \(y_*(t)\). For \(\Phi(t)=F(y_*(t),t)\), \[ \Phi_{tt}=F_{tt}-F_{ty}F_{yy}^{-1}F_{yt}. \] This is stationary elimination, not an exact contraction of the finite sum. The displayed matrix is its Schur complement. In the pure source, color evenness makes the mixed block vanish at zero. The critical value \(\Phi(0)\) must also be retained: derivatives alone do not determine the additive constant needed for volume. ## The final complex implication The reference proves the final logarithmic step directly. Suppose the exact invariant has the form \[ K_N=u_N\left(N^\rho a_Ne^{NS_N}+E_N\right),\qquad |u_N|=1, \] with fixed real \(\rho\), complex sequences \(a_N\to a\ne0\) and \(S_N\to S\), and \[ \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log|E_N|<\Re S. \] Here \(E_N\) is the **entire** remainder, not one selected tail. The leading term has rate \(\Re S\), so the remainder divided by it tends exponentially to zero. The reverse triangle inequality makes \(K_N\) eventually nonzero and gives the ordinary limit \(N^{-1}\log|K_N|\to\Re S\). If the marked geometric proof identifies \(2\pi\Re S\) with the knot-complement volume, the desired volume limit follows. A factor \(1+O(N^{-1})\) belongs to the leading amplitude \(a_N\); it need not have a smaller exponential rate. Also \(S_N\to S\) permits the logarithmic conclusion without asserting \(e^{NS_N}/e^{NS}\to1\). The accompanying cost lemma is zero-safe. If nonnegative budgets and costs satisfy \(B_N\) of upper rate at most \(b\), \(C_N\) of upper rate at most zero, and \(|E_N|\le C_NB_N\), then the remainder has upper rate at most \(b\). Upper rate means \(\limsup N^{-1}\log(\cdot)\), with \(\log0=-\infty\). In particular a nonnegative polynomial cost does not change that upper rate. No division by a possibly zero budget is needed. ## Other volume families retain their own hypotheses The ordered circle-tree construction has a crossing circle at every vertex. An edge is a prescribed quarter-turn attachment, and the cyclic order and strand frame are retained. For vertex degree \(d_v\) and signed crossing power \(n_v\), the summed criterion is \[ \sum_v\frac{d_v}{d_v^2+n_v^2}\le2^{-25}. \] A separate directed criterion has the simple sufficient consequence \(d_v\ge2^{28}\) or \(|n_v|\ge2^{27}\) at each vertex. The degree alternative permits fixed short or zero powers. The graph remains fixed, and the component test must give one knot. The [circle-tree paper](../../docs/papers/circle-tree-volume.pdf) proves the two analytic routes separately. Its [geometric companion](../../docs/papers/circle-tree-geometry.pdf) constructs the metric under \(L_v=\sqrt{d_v^2+n_v^2}\ge630\); that geometric criterion alone does not establish a quantum asymptotic. The local ratio test \(\max_v d_v/(d_v^2+n_v^2)\le2^{-120}\) is now a direct corollary of the directed theorem. A short numerical implication supplies its degree-or-twist alternative, so no separate local quantum induction remains. The summed proof still gives its explicit first microscopic meridian correction. The directed and local statements give the centered ratio \(1+O(N^{-1})\), without claiming that sharper correction. For planar constructions, begin with a finite simple triangulated sphere and a perfect matching of its dual triangles. Each matched pair determines one crossing-circle region. There are several different sufficient hypotheses: | Construction | What supplies the full remainder bound | | --- | --- | | Terminal decoration | Explicit finite insertions give strict shared packing inequalities. | | An unchanged matched sphere | Weak balance, including the stated small-defect extension. | | Protected triangular sums | Certificates for all locally allowed noncentral strings in each input. | | Ordinary triangular insertion | Certified pieces and small positive boundary ratios at every chosen witness. | The terminal decoration preserves its chosen strand pairing but can change the knot type. Its theorem fills all original and added circles sufficiently long. The ordinary insertion also has a fixed-boundary geometric minimization and retains the old coefficient demands. None of these statements asserts a general remainder bound for every unchanged sphere. The [results page](results.md) gives the conditions and diagrams. The reference keeps their complete proofs in the corresponding chapters and appendices, rather than importing the strict Conway conclusion into a different diagram class. ![Supporting tangents used to control an attachment over its entire allowed state region.](../../manuscript/build/figures/attachment-tangents.png) The supporting-tangent certificates are exact finite parts of specified inequality proofs. Their rational points, domain cover and outward bounds establish those inequalities; numerical optimization is not part of verification. The figure is available as a [vector PDF](../../manuscript/build/figures/attachment-tangents.pdf) and [editable TikZ source](../../manuscript/figures/attachment-tangents.tex). ## Two useful conclusions that are not full volume theorems The uniform filling appendix starts with a polynomial \(S_N\) of separate degree at most \(N-1\) in \(r\) spectral variables. For fixed crossing powers \(n_e\), its filled contraction satisfies \[ |Z_N|\le\prod_{e=1}^r(1+|n_e|/2) \,\|S_N\|_{[-2,2]^r}. \] The constant is independent of \(N\), and the functional retains the derivatives at repeated roots. A strict estimate for the shared norm remains a separate premise of any volume application. The matched-sphere geometric-contribution appendix evaluates one specified central contribution of the original invariant. It proves a nonzero asymptotic at the actual filled volume rate. Without a complementary-source bound it does not prove that the whole invariant has that rate. The restricted planar theorems above supply the missing bound under their own conditions. ## Reading and reproducing the argument For the strict result, read the conceptual chapter, then the shared Conway proof. Its main export is Theorem \(\texttt{ca:main}\). The standalone paper numbers the pure-source theorem as 3.1 and the Fourier proposition as 3.2. Its [input list](../../papers/conway-asymptotics/README.md#proof-inputs) names the finite Newton algebra, strict optimizer, physical source bound, whole filling theorem and marked geometry separately. The [dependency graph](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html) records these named uses; it does not prove the statements at its vertices. The finite algebra and exact certificates can be replayed with: ```sh python3 -I papers/conway-asymptotics/check.py python3 repro/verify.py --output repro/results ``` For the registered paper checks: ```sh python3 repro/check_paper_algebra.py --output repro/results/paper-collection/finite ``` The output records each bounded scope. Finite samples do not prove uniform analytic estimates, a contour deformation or a primitive metric completion. The [reproduction guide](../../repro/README.md) lists the requirements and individual check groups. Build the reference and guide with: ```sh python3 tools/build_manuscript.py python3 tools/build_book.py python3 tools/check_book.py ``` The [source guide](../../manuscript/README.md) explains the outputs. Typesetting and navigation checks are separate from mathematical proofs. The [formal code](../../formal-real/README.md) proves the retained Gram form and closing upper bound, shifted Parseval and full Hermite coefficient mass bound at \(N\ge2\), complex bilinear Schur block algebra, and direct complex rate transfer. ConwayAssembly uses the actual coherent color sum to derive the whole remainder bound. The analytic stationary germ, source contours, nonzero whole packet and marked geometric equality remain written inputs. The [coverage map](../../formal/coverage.json) records the exact manuscript statements and remaining written contour/geometric inputs. Earlier tracked versions remain in Git history. Historical approaches are explained in [methods](methods.md) and [algebraic approaches](algebraic.md), outside the current proof.

title: Volume equalities: the families and the hypotheses
text: # Volume equalities: the families and the hypotheses The results on this page compare a finite quantum invariant with the volume of the knot or link complement that the diagram actually constructs. For a knot $K$, the principal conclusion is $$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). $$ Here \(K_N\) is the reduced Kashaev invariant at \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\), with the unknot normalized to one and the framing convention fixed in the theorem. The knot is held fixed while the positive integer level \(N\) grows. The statements below include both even and odd levels unless a smaller scope is explicitly stated. The planar construction below begins with a triangulated sphere and adds specified tangles to its planar diagram. Separate results give explicit twist and degree bounds for ordered tangle trees, as well as net-twist reductions preserving an existing knot. These hypotheses differ. Each section states the knot it constructs, the estimates it uses, and which parameters are held fixed. For the basic diagram, color and filling conventions, begin with [the first-reading chapter](starting.md). Three kinds of conclusions occur below. A **full filled-invariant theorem** proves the displayed limit for the resulting knot. An **augmented-link theorem** leaves its crossing circles present and computes that larger complement's rate. A **selected-contribution theorem** evaluates only the specified part of an exact finite formula. The latter can be a completed theorem even when the remaining part of the invariant has not been bounded. The local identities and conditional estimates near the end of this chapter are stated with those smaller conclusions. For the current proof texts, use the [papers by subject](../../papers/README.md) and their [statement dependencies](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html). The current reference and subject papers retain their own hypotheses. Superseded proof notes are cited through the corresponding paper. The [collection-wide audit](../../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) records which proof requirements were checked for the retained results. The following table separates the principal conclusions. The subsequent sections define each construction and give its proof and restrictions. | Diagram or input | Additional hypothesis | Conclusion | | --- | --- | --- | | Recursive ordered tangles | The stated construction rule and sufficiently long surviving twists | Full knot-invariant volume limit | | Ordered circle trees | A summed, local, or directed degree-and-twist criterion | Full volume limit; the simple directed twist bound is independent of tree size | | Matched spherical diagrams after terminal insertions | The prescribed finite decoration, knot pairing, and long twists at every old and new circle | Full volume limit for the decorated knot | | Unchanged matched spherical diagrams | Knot pairing without extra main components, weak balance or its quantified variant, and long twists | Full volume limit for the unchanged diagram | | Insertion at ordinary triangular faces | A fixed finite list of certified pieces, sufficiently small positive boundary ratios at the core witnesses, and long twists | Full volume limit; explicit cores supply the required boundaries | | A general unchanged matched spherical diagram | The stated geometric construction and long twists | Nonzero geometric contribution with the actual volume rate; the remaining contribution still needs a separate estimate | | A genuine fixed quantum recurrence | The stated initial values, peripheral factors, and regularized evaluation | Exact reconstruction of the invariant; a volume limit follows in the covered knot classes | ## Decorating a planar diagram The [planar decoration theorem](../../docs/papers/terminal-decorations.pdf) starts from a more general diagram than a tree of tangle operations. Its input can be given entirely by finite combinatorial data: take a simple triangulation of the sphere with at least four vertices, and pair its triangles across selected edges so that each triangle belongs to exactly one pair. “Simple” means that there are no loops or repeated edges. The cyclic orders belong to the sphere embedding. Each paired pair of triangles specifies a crossing-circle tangle. Contracting the pair gives a four-ended box; the other edges specify the connections between boxes. Drawing the prescribed strands and placing an auxiliary circle around each pair constructs an actual link in the three-sphere. The proof gives a parity choice for the crossings that makes the main strands one knot. The theorem then adds finitely many terminal tangles on both sides of each original box. Each side receives an even number, and the added pieces have odd crossing parity. These insertions preserve the chosen endpoint pairing and create no internal closed component. They usually change the knot itself. **Conclusion.** For each such decorated diagram there is a finite threshold \(T\). Choose every original and added filling integer \(p_e\) independently with \(|p_e|>T\), retaining the chosen half twist \(\epsilon_e\), so that the signed number of crossings is \(n_e=\epsilon_e-2p_e\). The resulting knot is hyperbolic and satisfies the volume limit at the top of this page. Both signs and arbitrarily different magnitudes are allowed. The diagram, decoration, and all integers are fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity. This covers arbitrarily large planar arrangements without a tree hypothesis. It does not cover the unchanged core knot, arbitrary short powers at the original boxes, or a diagram growing with \(N\). The threshold may depend on the decorated diagram. ### How the number of added tangles is chosen The proof first constructs the complete circle packing of the original sphere by maximizing a strictly concave angle function. Normalize the two circles beside the marked strand to parallel lines. Their curvatures are zero; every other circle has positive curvature. At one crossing circle, the two triangles have vertices \((x,b,y)\) and \((x,c,y)\). Here the letters denote the curvatures of the corresponding circles. The edge \(xy\) is the selected pairing edge, and \(b,c\) are its opposite vertices. Put \[ A=x+y>0,\qquad P=xy. \] Inserting a circle in the first triangular gap replaces \(b\), as seen from the retained crossing circle, by \[ b_1=b+A+2\sqrt{Ab+P}. \] The original circles remain in place. The new circle has curvature \(b_1\); the new matching edge joins it to the old circle \(b\). ![Inserting w subdivides one triangle, retains the matched edge xy, and creates the matched edge bw. The two-sided drawing uses two insertions on each side; any even counts preserve the four-endpoint pairing.](../figures/balanced-terminal-fans.png) After \(j\) insertions on this side, \[ b_j=b+2j\sqrt{Ab+P}+j^2A. \] There is the same formula for \(c_k\) on the other side. Choose even nonnegative \(j,k\) so that \[ U=\frac{\sqrt{Ab+P}}A+j,\qquad V=\frac{\sqrt{Ac+P}}A+k,\qquad U,V\ge4,\quad |U-V|\le1. \] Such a choice always exists: even increments let the two numbers be brought within one, after which adding the same even increment makes both large enough. Repeating this finite procedure at every original crossing circle gives the required decoration. ### Why this proves an equality for the full invariant The exact finite evaluation is a coefficient of a product of local polynomials. All factors use the same face variables and the original marked coefficient. The proof divides each local polynomial into three explicit sums. One gives the geometric contribution. The two others must be bounded on the entire spectral interval, including its endpoints. The required weight is explicit. For nonnegative curvatures \(w=(w_1,w_2,w_3)=(x,b,y)\), with at least two positive entries, set \[ \Delta_w=\sqrt{w_1w_2+w_2w_3+w_3w_1},\qquad \alpha_i=\arctan(w_i/\Delta_w), \qquad \Lambda(t)=-\int_0^t\log|2\sin u|\,du. \] The angles satisfy \(\sum_i\alpha_i=\pi/2\). The source-normalized triangle action is \[ F(w_1,w_2,w_3)=\frac1\pi\sum_{w_i>0} \left\{\Lambda(\alpha_i)+ \Lambda\!\left(\frac\pi2-\alpha_i\right) +\alpha_i\log w_i\right\}. \] If only one weight \(w_i\) is positive, define \(F(w)=\tfrac12\log w_i\). A triangle with all weights zero does not occur at a crossing region in this marked simple-sphere construction. This is the function denoted \(Q(w)=Q_b(0)\) in the [triangle-action theorem](../../docs/papers/planar-certificates.pdf), §1, with the explicit evaluation in the [shared-radius theorem](../../notes/general_anchored_shared_radius_filling_volume.md), §5. It is the limiting logarithmic growth, divided by \(N\), of the positive triangle polynomial evaluated at these weights. In particular \(F(tw)=F(w)+\tfrac12\log t\); its additive constant is fixed by the finite source. The name *triangle action* refers to this weighted source expression, not to a separately inserted component of the link. At a crossing circle the condition needed for the two one-sided sums is \[ F(x,b,y)+F(x,c,y)>\log b,\qquad F(x,b,y)+F(x,c,y)>\log c, \] with a condition omitted when its middle curvature is zero. At a zero middle the corresponding finite sum vanishes exactly. The two-sided construction proves these strict inequalities at every retained crossing circle. Every newly added circle satisfies them as well. Because the packing is shared by the entire diagram, the local losses combine into a bound for the original coefficient, including all its coupled summation variables. The complete Fourier calculation then retains all charges and boundary terms and proves a nonzero geometric leading term. The remainder is exponentially smaller for sufficiently long fixed twists. The value of that leading term is identified geometrically. Its peripheral equations use the actual crossing disks and their primitive meridians. The unit Fourier charge gives angular period \(2\pi\), so each auxiliary end completes to a smooth solid torus on the prescribed filling slope. The main cusp remains complete. The regulator’s boundary correction cancels the filling terms, leaving precisely \(\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K)\). The finite checks replay the recurrence, rational gap bound, oriented triangle subdivision, parity extension, and endpoint pairing. The written proof supplies the uniform estimates and metric completion; those conclusions are not inferred from numerical examples. ## An unchanged diagram satisfying weak balance The [weak-balance theorem](../../docs/papers/planar-certificates.pdf), proved in Appendix P of the manuscript, gives a condition under which no terminal tangles need to be inserted. Start with the same simple triangulated sphere, matching, and marked strand as above. Let \(w_f^*\) be the curvature of its complete packing circle at vertex \(f\). The two protected vertices have curvature zero. All other curvatures are positive. At a matching edge, write the two triangles as \((x,b,y)\) and \((x,c,y)\), using their curvatures as arguments. Use the triangle potential \(F\) defined in the preceding section and set \[ X_e=F(w_x^*,w_b^*,w_y^*)+F(w_x^*,w_c^*,w_y^*). \] The **weak balance condition** is \[ X_e\ge\log w_b^*\quad(w_b^*>0),\qquad X_e\ge\log w_c^*\quad(w_c^*>0) \] at every matching edge \(e\). A condition with zero middle curvature is omitted because the corresponding part of the finite polynomial vanishes. Equality is allowed. These inequalities concern the actual complete packing; the theorem does not claim that all packings satisfy them. **Conclusion.** Fix a retained half-twist pattern whose strand connections give one knot. Under weak balance, independently sufficiently long signed twists at the existing crossing circles give the full Kashaev volume limit for that knot. The limit runs through all integer levels. The diagram and all twist numbers remain fixed. The threshold may depend on the diagram and its packing. The theorem has no bound on the number of crossing circles and requires no tangle-tree decomposition. ### Why equality in the local condition is enough Cauchy’s coefficient inequality allows any positive radius for each ordinary face variable. These radii need not themselves be circle packing curvatures. This freedom is useful when a balance inequality holds with equality: the complete packing supplies the reference geometry, and a nearby choice of coefficient radii supplies a strict bound. Put \(q_f=\log w_f^*\) at ordinary vertices, and define \[ f(a)=\frac{\Lambda(\pi a)+\Lambda(\pi/2-\pi a)}{\pi}, \qquad 0\le a\le\tfrac12. \] For each original triangle \(\tau\), let \(I_\tau\) be its set of ordinary vertices. Its potential in logarithmic coordinates is \[ Q_\tau(q)= \max_{\substack{a_i\ge0\ (i\in I_\tau)\\ \sum_{i\in I_\tau}a_i=1/2}} \sum_{i\in I_\tau}\{f(a_i)+a_iq_i\}. \] Thus \(Q_\tau(q)\) is the same function as \(F\), with the weights written as exponentials. A zero-curvature corner is removed from the simplex of allowed \(a_i\). It is never replaced by a small positive number. The complete action is \[ P(q)=\sum_\tau Q_\tau(q)-\sum_{f\ \mathrm{ordinary}}q_f, \qquad P(q)=\Phi_D=\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(Y_D)}{2\pi} \] at the complete packing. Here \(Y_D\) is the augmented link complement. The subtracted sum is the cost of taking the original shared coefficient. The packing equations give \(\nabla P(q)=0\). For \(0<t<1\), replace every ordinary coefficient radius by \((w_f^*)^{1-t}\), leaving the protected radii zero. The full increase in the action obeys \[ 0\le P((1-t)q)-P(q)\le\frac{t^2}{2}\mathcal E, \qquad \mathcal E=\frac1{4\pi} \sum_\tau\sum_{\{i,j\}\subset I_\tau}(q_i-q_j)^2. \] The inner sum is over unordered pairs of distinct ordinary vertices in that triangle. Shared edges are counted once for each incident triangle. This defines the constant \(\mathcal E\) completely; it is finite for the fixed packing. Let \(a_{\tau i}\) be the maximizing loads in \(Q_\tau(q)\). Define its entropy by \[ E_\tau=\sum_{i\in I_\tau}f(a_{\tau i}). \] For a surviving left term, use the triangle \((x,c,y)\); for a surviving right term, use \((x,b,y)\). Each of these triangles has at least two ordinary corners, so its entropy is positive. Let \(h_*\) be the smallest of these finitely many positive entropies. The local estimates show that each surviving one-sided term loses at least \(t h_*\) relative to the central term under weak balance. Every noncentral choice contains at least one such term. Its shared coefficient therefore has rate at most \[ \Phi_D+\frac{t^2}{2}\mathcal E-t h_*. \] If \(\mathcal E>0\), take \(t=\min\{1/2,h_*/\mathcal E\}\). The last expression is at most \(\Phi_D-t h_*/2<\Phi_D\). If \(\mathcal E=0\), take \(t=1/2\). If there are no surviving one-sided terms, the complementary polynomial is already zero and no minimum \(h_*\) is needed. ![The linear entropy gain and quadratic action cost for illustrative constants h*=1 and E=1. Their positive difference is the strict remainder gap.](../figures/weak-balance-gain.svg) The horizontal variable is the fixed coefficient-weight perturbation \(t\), not the quantum level. The figure uses \(h_*=\mathcal E=1\) solely to display the two orders of vanishing; the proof computes these constants from the original packing. The finite filling bound transfers this strict gap to the filled remainder. The geometric-contribution theorem supplies a nonzero term whose real action tends to \(\Phi_D\) as the fixed twist magnitudes become large.
