Weighted Cauchy and finite Parseval are proved explicitly above. 4. **Cross-level asymptotics:** Taylor's Tauberian notes. Compare the cumulative conclusion with the additional source-transport condition in the local criterion. 5. **Recurrences:** Wilf–Zeilberger for multisum elimination, then the colored-Jones and ADO papers for the objects and conventions concerned. Keep the classical A-curve and the proposed characteristic comparison separate. 6. **Regulators and peripheral geometry:** Neumann–Zagier for the local deformation potential, Neumann for logarithmic regulator data, and the explicit torsor definitions for any claimed group action. 7. **Local asymptotics versus a whole knot period:** Costantino's \(6j\)-volume result and the Nahm-sum comparison illustrate related problems with different normalizations and limiting regimes. The complete-source estimates and contour arguments remain the additional work in this project. The [comparison of volume statements](results.md#comparing-the-result-with-other-volume-statements) separately records which invariant and knot or link family occur in related results. In particular, a theorem for a local recoupling coefficient, a partially projected source, or a different three-manifold invariant should not be read as the same assertion as a full Kashaev limit for the original knot. The literature search is a coverage and attribution check. It does not turn an external paper into an unchecked proof input, or turn a local calculation into a theorem about an arbitrary knot. The manuscript states the actual hypotheses and supplies the arguments used for its conclusions.

title: Algebraic approaches and the tests they must pass
text: # Algebraic approaches and the tests they must pass The algebraic approaches in this project try to retain an entire quantum state and its relations, rather than estimate every summand separately. They ask whether gluing, changes of coordinates, and evaluation at roots of unity can determine the volume contribution. Several of these constructions give exact identities. Their implications for the growth of the original knot invariant require additional arguments, specified below. The [methods chapter](methods.md) introduces the finite invariant, weighted estimates, Fourier transformation, and geometric optimization. Here we explain the algebra behind some earlier proposals. This chapter also retains an unsuccessful model: knowing why it fails as an exact state is useful even when its volume rate is correct. These proposals are not premises silently added to the manuscript's volume theorems. The retained operator result has a separate, precise scope in [Meridian expansions and classical symbols of quantum recurrences](../../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf). It assumes a genuine fixed annihilator and the stated expansions of the actual source, then derives a nonzero classical symbol and its selected geometric factor. It neither constructs a universal operator nor proves the general volume conjecture. The proposals below should be compared with those hypotheses, rather than treated as substitutes for them. ## A positive factorial model and a change of triangulation Fix an integer \(N\ge2\), and put \[ \zeta_N=e^{2\pi i/N},\qquad S_N(k)=\prod_{j=1}^k2\sin(\pi j/N),\qquad S_N(0)=1. \] The index satisfies \(0\le k<N\), so these products are positive. The finite quantum factorial \[ (\zeta_N;\zeta_N)_k=\prod_{j=1}^k(1-\zeta_N^j) \] has the exact expression \[ (\zeta_N;\zeta_N)_k =(-i)^k\exp\!\left(\frac{\pi i k(k+1)}{2N}\right)S_N(k). \] Indeed, each factor is \(1-e^{2\pi i j/N}=-2i\,e^{\pi i j/N}\sin(\pi j/N)\). Thus the positive model retains the magnitudes of familiar quantum factorials. Removing their phases changes a sum of such terms. A triangulated model must also be compared under changes of its triangulation. In a \(2\leftrightarrow3\) move, two tetrahedra sharing a face are replaced by three tetrahedra surrounding an interior edge. The boundary triangulation is unchanged. An exact identity must compare the two evaluations with the same boundary data and with every internal summation measure included. ![Two triangulations of a triangular bipyramid. The left shares the face ABC; the right shares the edge PQ. The five boundary vertices and six boundary triangles are unchanged.](../figures/bipyramid-move.svg) In the drawing, \(P,Q\) are the apices and \(A,B,C\) the equatorial vertices. The two tetrahedra are \(PABC\) and \(QABC\). The three are \(PQAB\), \(PQBC\), and \(PQCA\). The shaded face on the left and the highlighted edge on the right are internal. For the symmetric test in the [comparison of the custom definitions](../../notes/custom_literature_equivalence.md#21-the-factor-eight-test-has-a-measure-scale-asymptotic), take \(6\mid N\). The two bare evaluations are \[ B_{2,N}=S_N(N/3)^{-6}, \qquad B_{3,N}=S_N(2N/3)^{-3} \sum_{p=1}^{N/3-1} \bigl[S_N(p)S_N(N/3-p)\bigr]^{-3}. \] The sum is over the additional internal label on the three-tetrahedron side. At \(N=6\), \[ S_6(1)=1,\quad S_6(2)=\sqrt3,\quad S_6(4)=6,\quad B_{2,6}=\frac1{27},\quad B_{3,6}=\frac1{216}. \] The ratio is eight. More generally, the calculation in the linked note gives \(B_{2,N}/B_{3,N}\sim N\) along \(6\mid N\). Consequently the two expressions have the same logarithmic rate, since \(\log N/N\to0\), while their finite values differ. Multiplying one side by \(N\) fixes the leading scale, but already fails to give equality at \(N=6\). This test does not decide whether a model with additional boundary factors could satisfy an exact move law. For example, a product of three factors \(1+M^{a_j}\), with integers \(a_j\), equals eight at \(M=1\). To use such an explanation, one must construct the generic boundary state, derive its multiplier, and verify compatibility under successive moves. A numerical ratio at one boundary value does not determine that multiplier. The completed positive variational result is retained. Equivalence of this positive model with the original Kashaev invariant remains unproved. For the literature origin of the quantum pentagon relation, see [Faddeev and Kashaev, *Quantum Dilogarithm*](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9310070). Their operator identity and the bare positive sum above are different objects. ## Hilbert 90 solves a transport equation Let \(E/F\) be a finite cyclic extension of fields, of degree \(r\), and let \(\sigma\) generate its Galois group. This means that the field automorphisms fixing \(F\) are \(1,\sigma,\ldots,\sigma^{r-1}\), that \(\sigma^r=1\), and that their common fixed field is \(F\). The notation \(E^\times\) means the nonzero elements of \(E\), under multiplication. For \(a\in E^\times\), its norm is \[ \operatorname{Nm}_{E/F}(a)=\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}\sigma^j(a). \] Hilbert's theorem 90 says that norm one is equivalent to \[ a=\frac{b}{\sigma(b)} \quad\text{for some }b\in E^\times. \] The norm of such a quotient is one by cancellation of consecutive factors. The converse is the substantive assertion. See [Milne, *Fields and Galois Theory*, version 4.22, Corollary 5.24](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT422.pdf). This has a direct interpretation for a scalar difference equation. If \(\sigma(y)=a\,y\) and \(a=b/\sigma(b)\), then \(\sigma(by)=by\). Multiplication by \(b\) removes the coefficient from the equation. In this setting a *gauge* is precisely such an invertible change of the dependent variable. Reversing the convention for the equation reverses the quotient. The theorem gives existence of \(b\); it does not estimate its absolute value under a chosen complex embedding. It also allows multiplication of \(b\) by any element of \(F^\times\). A comparison of quantum periods must retain the normalization selecting a particular gauge and control the sizes of that gauge and its inverse as \(N\) grows. There is an explicit warning within the original source calculations. The [primitive gauge calculation](../../notes/actual_hilbert90_gauge_dilogarithm_action.md) works in the nilpotent algebra \(\mathbb C[z]/(z^N)\). Put \(Q_N=e^{2\pi i/N}\). In that algebra it constructs the unique unit \(g_N\) with constant term one satisfying \[ \frac{g_N(Q_Nz)}{g_N(z)} =\frac1{(1-z)(1-Q_Nz)}. \] Both denominators are units because their constant terms are one. This is a concrete cyclic transport equation in a ring with nilpotents, not a direct application of the field theorem above. A unit is an element with a multiplicative inverse. A nilpotent element has a power equal to zero; here \(z^N=0\). In particular \((1-z)^{-1}=1+z+\cdots+z^{N-1}\) in this ring. Choose the unique polynomial representative of degree less than \(N\). On \(|z|\le1/4\), the calculation proves \[ g_N(z)= \exp\!\left(\frac{2\operatorname{Li}_2(z)}{h_N} +O(N^{-1})\right), \qquad h_N=\frac{2\pi i}{N}. \] Here \(\operatorname{Li}_2(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}z^k/k^2\) on this disk. The proof estimates the finite polynomial itself, including its truncation error. For complex \(z\), the real part of its leading exponent can have size proportional to \(N\). Exact trivialization of the transport can therefore carry an exponential cost. The [polynomial companion construction](../../notes/pointed_companion_source_and_polynomial_hilbert90.md) provides another exact change of coordinates, retaining the original input vector and output row. Its residual spectral polynomial has not thereby been identified with the knot's geometric A-polynomial. Both constructions are useful algebraic results with stated remaining comparison problems. ## Why a Koszul complex appears Suppose \(R\) is a commutative ring of coefficients and the gluing conditions are \(H_1=\cdots=H_s=1\), where \(H_i\in R\). Write \(f_i=1-H_i\). The quotient \(R/(f_1,\ldots,f_s)\) imposes these equations. A Koszul complex also records relations between the equations. A **chain complex** has modules \(C_i\) and maps \(d_i:C_i\to C_{i-1}\) with \(d_{i-1}d_i=0\). Its homology \(H_i(C)=\ker d_i/\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}\) records elements killed by one map, modulo those already supplied by the preceding map. An \(R\)-module allows addition and multiplication by coefficients in \(R\), as a vector space does over a field. Below \(R^k\) is the free module of \(k\)-tuples. For one equation its entire definition is the two-term sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow R \xrightarrow{\ f_1\ } R\longrightarrow0. \] For two equations it is \[ 0\longrightarrow R \xrightarrow{\ c\mapsto(-f_2c,f_1c)\ } R^2 \xrightarrow{\ (a,b)\mapsto f_1a+f_2b\ }R \longrightarrow0. \] The composite map is zero. Its degree-zero homology is \(R/(f_1,f_2)\). The degree-one homology is the set of relations \(f_1a+f_2b=0\), modulo the relations \((a,b)=(-f_2c,f_1c)\) already supplied by the first map. For \(s\) equations one takes the tensor product of the corresponding two-term complexes. The sign rule is \[ d(x\otimes y)=d(x)\otimes y+(-1)^p x\otimes d(y), \qquad x\in C_p. \] It makes the two mixed terms in \(d^2\) cancel. This is the [standard Koszul construction](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0621). There is a particularly concrete reason for it in the finite translation calculation. Let \(V\) have basis \(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1}\), and define \[ Te_j=e_{j+1}\quad(j<n-1),\qquad Te_{n-1}=H e_0. \] Then \(T^n=H I\). The cokernel of \(1-T\) identifies all the \(e_j\), and its final relation is \((1-H)e_0=0\). More precisely, separate changes of basis in the domain and codomain, using no division, reduce \(1-T\) to \[ \operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,1-H). \] The [finite translation proof](../../notes/rational_period_pushforward.md#4-the-algebraic-gluing-support-is-a-koszul-reduction) gives those bases explicitly. This is a reduction of a linear map, not conjugation of \(T\) by one basis change. Each diagonal entry one gives a two-term complex \(R\xrightarrow{1}R\), whose homology is zero. It can be removed by an explicit **contracting homotopy**: send its degree-zero copy of \(R\) back to degree one by the identity map \(h\), and set \(h=0\) elsewhere. Then \(dh+hd=1\). This identity supplies the contraction, rather than merely observing that the quotient is zero. The remaining complex is \(R\xrightarrow{1-H}R\). For several commuting translations on separate tensor factors, tensoring these reductions gives a chain equivalence with the Koszul complex of the equations \(1-H_i\). It preserves homology without asserting that the original and reduced complexes have equal dimensions. A sequence is *regular* if its generated ideal is proper and each \(f_i\) is a non-zero-divisor after the preceding equations have been imposed: multiplication by \(f_i\) is injective on \(R/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})\). For such a sequence the higher Koszul homology vanishes; see [Stacks Project, Lemma 15.31.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/062F). With redundant equations it can remain. For example, in \(R=\mathbb Q[x]\), the sequence \((x,x)\) has degree-one homology \(R/(x)\): every relation is \((a,-a)\), and the boundaries are exactly those with \(a\) divisible by \(x\). By contrast, the single equation \(x^2\) has zero higher homology although its quotient has a nilpotent element. Singularity or nonreducedness alone does not establish a failure of Koszul exactness. This construction describes simultaneous algebraic constraints. It does not select an integration cycle, prove a nonzero quantum evaluation, or determine a regulator constant. Those are additional data and arguments. ## What cyclotomic rigidity can determine The elementary model of a rigidity argument is a polynomial \(P(q)\in\mathbb Q[q]\) which vanishes at infinitely many distinct roots of unity. It must be zero: a nonzero polynomial has at most its degree many roots. The polynomial is fixed throughout this argument. Compare the level-dependent polynomials \(P_N(q)=q^N-1\). Each vanishes at \(\zeta_N\), but none is the zero polynomial. Moreover, \[ \left.q\frac{d}{dq}P_N(q)\right|_{q=\zeta_N}=N. \] Thus knowing the root values does not give their transverse derivatives. A *jet of order \(k\)* at a point means its Taylor coefficients through order \(k\), or equivalently its derivatives of orders \(0,\ldots,k\). Values are only jets of order zero. The cyclotomic polynomial \(\Phi_n(q)\) is the monic polynomial whose roots are the primitive \(n\)-th roots of unity. In characteristic zero, divisibility by \(\Phi_n(q)^{k+1}\) means vanishing of all these derivatives through order \(k\) at every primitive \(n\)-th root. There is a more concrete finite-jet statement for the meridian coefficients of a fixed operator. A Laurent polynomial is a finite sum \[ p(M)=\sum_{m\in E}c_mM^m, \qquad E\subset\mathbb Z\text{ finite},\quad c_m\in\mathbb C. \] Negative exponents are allowed. Substituting \(M=e^u\) gives the formal power series \(\mathcal E(p)=\sum_{m\in E}c_me^{mu}\). If the allowed exponent set \(E\) has \(k\) elements, its coefficients through degree \(k-1\) determine every \(c_m\). Indeed, \[ n!\,[u^n]\mathcal E(p)=\sum_{m\in E}c_m m^n, \qquad 0\le n<k. \] Here \([u^n]\) means the coefficient of \(u^n\). After ordering the distinct exponents as \(m_1,\ldots,m_k\), these equations have the Vandermonde matrix \((m_j^n)_{0\le n<k,\,1\le j\le k}\). Its determinant is \(\prod_{i<j}(m_j-m_i)\ne0\), so the system has a unique solution. This proves that \(p\mapsto\mathcal E(p)\) is injective. The identity \(e^{mu}e^{nu}=e^{(m+n)u}\) also proves that it preserves multiplication. The exponent restriction is essential. For any prescribed jet order \(r\), the nonzero polynomial \((M-1)^{r+1}\) becomes \((e^u-1)^{r+1}\), whose coefficients through degree \(r\) vanish. Thus a finite jet gives uniqueness within a specified finite-dimensional space; no fixed jet order works for every Laurent polynomial. For a polynomial in a second variable \(L\), the same argument applies to each coefficient while \(L\) remains an independent variable. Subsequently setting \(L=\ell(u)\) can kill a nonzero polynomial: \(L+1\) vanishes at \(\ell(u)=-1\). Vandermonde injectivity applies here to a fixed operator with a fixed finite exponent set. The [meridian-expansion paper](../../papers/meridian-expansions/README.md) states the further all-orders and operator hypotheses used for its classical-symbol consequence. It assumes a specified nonzero all-level annihilator; it does not construct one. The finite argument above is a written proof. Its scope is distinct from the retained Lean statements listed in the [coverage report](../../repro/PAPER_FORMAL_COVERAGE.md). There is also an established uniqueness theorem for a different, precisely specified class. Habiro's cyclotomic completion is \[ \widehat{\mathbb Z[q]} =\underset{n}{\lim_{\leftarrow}}\mathbb Z[q]/I_n,\qquad I_n=\bigl((1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^n)\bigr). \] An element is a compatible system of polynomial residue classes, not an arbitrary list of values at different levels. Each root of unity gives an evaluation because the displayed product eventually vanishes there. The full Taylor series at one root determines an element of this completion; its values at all roots also determine it. These are injectivity statements in [Habiro, *Cyclotomic completions of polynomial rings*, Theorems 5.4 and 6.3](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0209324). The integer coefficient ring and the specified completion matter. These statements neither put an arbitrary level-dependent state in that completion nor estimate its size. A proposed regulator comparison would first have to be constructed in the same class. The [whole algebraic comparison theorem](../../notes/whole_period_cyclotomic_rigidity.md) works with a fixed algebraic presentation, bounds on its possible comparison maps, and the required quantum jets. Its reconstruction argument uses separation of exponents and finite linear algebra. The [rank-one descent theorem](../../notes/full_rank_one_cyclotomic_descent.md) likewise has a fixed rational coefficient and whole cyclic transport identities as hypotheses. Neither theorem manufactures an algebraic comparison with the geometric period from isolated numerical values. The geometric distinction is equally important. Nondegenerate gluing equations with a fixed meridian can select algebraic tetrahedron shapes \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\). If these shapes realize the specified oriented hyperbolic triangulation of \(Y\), with its required peripheral completion, its volume is the regulator value \[ \operatorname{Vol}(Y)=\sum_{j=1}^t D(z_j),\qquad D(z)=\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Li}_2(z) +\log|z|\arg(1-z), \] with the orientations retained and the continuous Bloch–Wigner interpretation of \(D\). An arbitrary algebraic gluing solution has not yet been shown to realize that metric. Algebraicity of the shapes does not make this dilogarithm evaluation algebraic. More importantly, it does not show that the original finite quantum evaluation has this exponential rate. The [selected-period analysis](../../notes/cyclotomic_rigidity_selected_period.md) tests exactly this distinction. In the figure-eight example, the same state has exponential growth at the complete meridian and bounded values on fixed ordinary-color sequences approaching that meridian. A proposed uniform comparison must retain the derivative data and the correct domain. Uniqueness of an algebraically specified object does not prove that a proposed regulator period satisfies its equations. ## Regge symmetry and nilpotent transport A Regge involution fixes a pair of opposite tetrahedral edges. If the other four edge lengths are \(a,b,c,d\), put \(s=(a+b+c+d)/2\) and replace them by \[ s-a,\quad s-b,\quad s-c,\quad s-d. \] For a tetrahedron in Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic space, the geometric Regge theorem identifies the transformed dihedral angles and proves equality of volume; see [Akopyan and Izmestiev, *The Regge symmetry, confocal conics, and the Schläfli formula*, Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04929). This is a specific transformation of one tetrahedron, not an arbitrary change of a knot's triangulation. At ideal vertices the edge lengths are infinite, so the ideal discussion below uses angles and logarithmic shapes instead of substituting into this finite-length formula. For an ideal tetrahedron, opposite dihedral angles agree. The angle data are a triple \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) with sum \(\pi\). The [Regge and period calculation](../../notes/regge_period_covers_and_a_curves.md) shows that the faithful finite action on these angle data reduces to their permutations. Logarithms of the shapes retain additional translations and a central period coordinate. The elementary model for the latter is the Heisenberg group \[ H(a,b,c)= \begin{pmatrix}1&a&c\\0&1&b\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. \] Multiplication gives \[ H(a,b,c)H(a',b',c') =H(a+a',b+b',c+c'+ab'). \] Every commutator has \(a=b=0\), so it is central; commutators with a further group element are the identity. This is the meaning of *two-step nilpotent*. The linked note constructs a specific lattice of this type for the lifted classical period, together with the finite permutation action. The full group need not be nilpotent merely because a finite-index subgroup is. Nilpotence can simplify a differential equation. If \(A(t)\) is a strictly upper-triangular \(3\times3\) matrix and \(U'=A(t)U\), \(U(0)=I\), then products of three such matrices vanish. The exact solution at \(t=1\) is \[ U(1)=I+\int_0^1A(t)\,dt +\int_{0<s<t<1}A(t)A(s)\,ds\,dt . \] Differentiating the analogous formula with upper endpoint \(t\) verifies the equation. The integrals themselves can still be transcendental. The classical logarithmic construction therefore offers a tractable transport problem, but it does not place the entire quantum knot state in this three-dimensional system. That further representation and its selected solution have to be constructed. ## Passing to a cover and descending Two different kinds of cover occur. Labeling the vertices of a tetrahedron removes a finite ordering ambiguity in its shape. A finite covering map \(p:Y'\to Y\) of hyperbolic manifolds changes the manifold. These operations have different consequences. In the ideal-shape calculation, reordering four vertices gives six possible cross-ratios, \[ z,\quad\frac1{1-z},\quad\frac{z-1}{z}, \qquad 1-z,\quad\frac1z,\quad\frac{z}{z-1}. \] The twenty-four vertex orderings give each cross-ratio four times. Away from shapes with a stabilizer, the six cross-ratios form a sixfold cover of the unordered shape space. At a symmetric shape, including the regular ideal tetrahedron, some of them coincide: the stabilizer and the chosen logarithmic data must still be recorded. Orientation matters even away from those points. The first three Bloch–Wigner values equal \(D(z)\), and the last three equal \(-D(z)\), so their unweighted sum is zero. Retaining the orientation sign is necessary to descend the volume; simply averaging over the orderings would erase it. The [explicit period calculation](../../notes/regge_period_covers_and_a_curves.md#2-the-explicit-twist-on-the-logarithmic-period) derives these signs and the logarithmic transformations. For an orientation-preserving manifold cover of degree \(D\), the pulled-back metric gives \[ \operatorname{Vol}(Y') =D\,\operatorname{Vol}(Y). \] Choose a torus boundary component upstairs and compatible peripheral bases. Suppose its meridian and longitude map to \[ \mu'=\mu^a\lambda^b,\qquad \lambda'=\mu^c\lambda^d,\qquad ad-bc>0 . \] For simultaneously selected eigenvalues of a restricted representation, this gives the monomial map \[ M'=M^aL^b,\qquad L'=M^cL^d. \] The determinant is the degree of that boundary-torus cover. It need not equal \(D\) when there are several boundary components upstairs. The [cover calculation](../../notes/regge_period_covers_and_a_curves.md#4-what-a-finite-manifold-cover-does-to-the-geometric-a-curve) uses these equations to eliminate the downstairs variables from a marked geometric A-curve. It keeps track of possible multiplicities and the distinction between one and several cusps. Representations upstairs need not extend downstairs, so this restriction construction alone does not recover every component of the upstairs character variety. Descent of the quantum invariant needs more: a relation between the actual finite states, their boundary evaluations, and their normalizations. Volume multiplication supplies no such relation. A cover can simplify the classical geometry or remove a branch ambiguity while leaving this quantum comparison unresolved. ## How to read these results together | Construction | Established output in the linked argument | Additional step for the unrestricted volume conjecture | |---|---|---| | Positive factorial model | A variational volume rate for its specified positive sum | Exact comparison with the original invariant, including phases and move factors | | Hilbert-90 gauge | An invertible change solving the specified algebraic transport | Bounds for that change and the original boundary evaluation | | Koszul reduction | Simultaneous gluing constraints and their relations | The contributing cycle, normalization, and nonvanishing | | Cyclotomic reconstruction | Uniqueness within the stated fixed algebraic class | Construction of a regulator comparison inside that class | | Regge and nilpotent transport | Explicit changes of the lifted classical tetrahedral period | A compatible transport of the whole quantum knot state | | Finite manifold cover | Volume multiplication and peripheral restriction | A source-preserving quantum descent formula | The [results chapter](results.md) gives the separate full volume theorems already proved for specified knot constructions. The [frontier chapter](frontier.md) explains which estimates are missing for the unchanged general source. The exact algebraic results here remain useful without being treated as substitutes for those estimates.

title: Why the limiting action is the actual knot volume
text: # Why the limiting action is the actual knot volume The volume theorem has two geometric tasks. First, construct the hyperbolic metric on the complement of the link drawn by the specified diagram. Second, identify the normalized source action with that metric's volume. Face labels, orientations and peripheral curves enter both tasks. The current proof accounts are [marked geometry of strict Conway compositions](../../docs/papers/strict-conway-geometry.pdf), [circle patterns and primitive fillings of augmented links](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf), and [positive octahedra for trees of crossing circles](../../docs/papers/circle-tree-geometry.pdf). They treat different constructions and thresholds. The [dependency graph](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html) records which geometric theorem each asymptotic argument uses; a metric construction alone does not supply the quantum remainder estimate. Throughout this chapter \(D\) is a fixed diagram. Its **augmented exterior** \(Y_D\) is obtained by surrounding each recorded twist region with an auxiliary crossing circle and retaining its specified half twist. Filling those auxiliary cusps with the recorded integer slopes restores the signed twist powers and produces the **filled exterior** \(S^3\setminus K_{\boldsymbol p}\) when the main strands form a knot. The knot cusp is left unfilled. The complete augmented action is \[ \Phi_D=\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(Y_D)}{2\pi}. \] A filled quantum contribution has the form \(a_Ne^{NS_{\mathrm{fill}}}\), where \(S_{\mathrm{fill}}\) is its complex critical action and the amplitude satisfies \(\log|a_N|=o(N)\). The geometric conclusion is \[ 2\pi\operatorname{Re}S_{\mathrm{fill}} =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K_{\boldsymbol p}). \] Thus the logarithmic growth rate is the filled volume divided by \(2\pi\), rather than the complete augmented value \(\Phi_D\). Here \(N\) denotes the quantum level; all diagram and filling data are fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity. For the [strict Conway tree theorem](../../docs/papers/conway-asymptotics.pdf), the geometric construction, nonzero quantum contribution and bound on the remaining terms are all proved. The planar constructions below also establish their specified complements and marked deformations. For a general planar source, proving that the complementary terms are smaller than the geometric contribution remains a separate estimate. The [results](results.md) and [frontier](frontier.md) chapters keep those scopes distinct. The [first-reading chapter](starting.md) defines the diagram, its twist boxes and the coefficient extracted from the finite source. Here the emphasis is on the geometric objects represented by those variables. The real part of a source action determines the exponential rate of the specified contribution once its amplitude is controlled. Interpreting that rate as volume requires the geometric realization and the factor \(2\pi\) in the displayed normalization. ## The geometric objects and the required checks Start with the augmented diagram: each twist region has an auxiliary crossing circle around its two strands. Cutting along the projection sphere and the original crossing disks divides its exterior into pieces with labeled faces. The labels remember exactly how to glue the pieces back. They also remember which curves on each torus end are the original meridian and longitude. An **ideal vertex** lies at the boundary at infinity of hyperbolic space. A small horosphere about it cuts a Euclidean polygon from each adjacent cell. These polygons are the vertex links. In a complete link complement, the polygons around each end glue to a Euclidean torus. This torus is a cross-section of a **cusp**, the noncompact end of the manifold. Checking only that the dihedral angles sum to \(2\pi\) does not establish cusp completeness; the horospherical polygons must also match with the correct translations. An **angle structure** assigns positive dihedral angles to the proposed cells while satisfying their internal angle relations and the sum around every glued edge. Its volume is the sum of the cell volumes. The angles still retain the actual incidence equations: two copies of one manifold edge are not independent variables. At an interior maximum, variation in every allowed direction gives the shape-matching equations. The proof must then show that these equations produce the original face pairings and complete ends. A **developing map** places the lifted cells in hyperbolic space. Following a based closed path compares its initial and final placements by an isometry. These isometries form the **holonomy representation** of the fundamental group. In matrix formulas an orientation-preserving isometry is represented by a determinant-one complex \(2\times2\) matrix, up to sign. A **peripheral eigenflag** is the common invariant line selected for the commuting meridian and longitude matrices at a torus end. The face maps must transport that line together with the based paths. A **marked** construction retains the chosen peripheral curves and their basepaths. This matters after filling. The equation that closes a meridian disk depends on a primitive pair of curves on the torus, not just on an unlabeled complex cusp shape. Replacing a primitive longitude by twice that curve would change the filling problem. The geometric identification has three parts. The cut identifies the manifold and its boundary curves. The positive shapes and their return maps identify a metric on that manifold. Finally, comparison with the finite source fixes the numerical factor and additive constant in the action. None of these statements says how much of an oscillating quantum sum comes from that metric. That last question requires the nonzero leading term and remainder estimates stated in the analytic theorems. ## The circle packing for a general planar core A **simple white triangulation** is a triangulation of the projection sphere with no loop or repeated edge. Its vertices label white faces of the cut diagram. The **dual graph** has one vertex for each triangle and one edge for each shared triangle side. It is cubic because each triangle has three sides. A **perfect matching** chooses one dual edge at every dual vertex. Its pairs of triangles become the crossing disks. The four-sided boundary of a pair records the surrounding strand ends in cyclic order. The circles bounding the two shaded planes become concentric, with radii \(\rho_b,\rho_c>0\). Their ordered pairing is \[ C(w)=R_0w,\qquad R_0=\rho_c/\rho_b, \] \[ C_1\longmapsto C_0,\qquad C_2\longmapsto C_3. \] The radii \(\rho_b,\rho_c\) belong to the transformed shaded circles; they are different quantities from the original white radii \(1/b,1/c\). ![The crossing-disk collar in the exact configuration x=y=b=c=1 and delta=1/10. Dashed circles bound the shaded planes and are orthogonal to the white circles on their side. The displayed Möbius coordinate turns the prescribed contact pairing into a dilation.](../figures/deformed-circle-collar.svg) The [primitive collar theorem](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) also follows the based meridian path through this map. The auxiliary meridian uses \(C^{-1}\), so its pure similarity logarithm is \(-\operatorname{Log}R_0\). The disk-longitude product selects the eigenpoint \(P_-\), with determinant-one eigenvalue \(J=-e^{-2\pi i\delta}\). A retained signed half twist \(\epsilon\in\{0,\pm1\}\) therefore gives \[ U=-\operatorname{Log}R_0+2\pi i\epsilon\delta,\qquad V=-4\pi i\delta. \] The logarithms vanish at the complete point and are continued on the prescribed branch. At \(\delta=0\), \(R_0=1\) but the matrix limit of the side map is a nontrivial parabolic translation in the original coordinate. The theorem retains that limit and also treats the zero-curvature marked lines. The [global geometric assembly](../../notes/actual_complete_core_geometric_deformation.md) checks these maps against the full link-group relations, including their translations. It identifies the complete-image core's action with the marked geometric deformation. For complex peripheral parameters it retains the boundary correction \(\tfrac12\sum_i\operatorname{Re}U_i\operatorname{Im}V_i\); for real external deficits that correction vanishes. The local calculation and the group assembly establish the geometric contribution. Bounding the remaining reflected-color terms is the additional step needed for the full invariant; the [results](results.md) chapter states the families for which that step is proved. An identity smoothing replaces a specified crossing-disk operator by the identity and retains the remaining face identifications. The result discussed here concerns the certified flat-plat source: the smoothing is connected and untwisted, and the original two marked faces remain distinct. Under these hypotheses, the [block capacity theorem](../../notes/actual_smoothed_source_capacity_blocks.md) removes the need to assume an attained positive-radius minimum. Here capacity is the infimum of the positive weighted expression used for a coefficient bound. The theorem splits degenerate angle problems along two-edge cycles and constructs each simple block's actual polyhedron. The [block representation and volume theorem](../../notes/actual_smoothed_block_representation_volume.md) then retains the original face pairings and realizes their volume sum as a regulator of the original group. Its deleted meridians lie in the kernel, so the [classical strict-kernel argument](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/general_representation_volume_kernel_strictness.md) proves strict loss for every nonempty connected untwisted smoothing with finite capacity. Loop-infeasible cases already have an arbitrarily low capacity bound. The chain argument uses a controlled finite degeneration: cut corners have a common horospherical height and mutual distance $O(T^{-1})$. A uniform short-edge tetrahedron estimate makes the added volume vanish. Arbitrary ideal vertices merely approaching one another would not justify this step. The [near-maximal-volume corollary](../../notes/general_representation_volume_peripheral_gap.md) also gives uniform gaps from fixed marked peripheral trace conditions; applying those gaps to the remaining quantum color complement is still a source-estimate problem. Here **representation volume** means the oriented hyperbolic volume assigned to a homomorphism from the original manifold group to \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)\), using an equivariant map and the prescribed treatment of its cusp ends. It can be defined when the homomorphism is not discrete or faithful. At geometric holonomy it equals the metric volume; maximal-volume rigidity restricts when equality can occur. See [Francaviglia's construction for cusped manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0305275) and [Francaviglia–Klaff's volume-rigidity theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411050). To use such a theorem for a source term, the source equations must first produce a representation of the same group with the same peripheral words. An absolute-value coefficient envelope has no such interpretation merely because its variables resemble shapes. ## A local tetrahedron is a genuine geometric result The [local hyperideal theorem](../../notes/actual_four_port_hyperideal_angle_volume.md) uses six internal representation labels \(j_e\), one for each edge of a tetrahedron. The exact half-shifted coordinates are \[ a_e=\frac{j_e+1/2}{N},\qquad \alpha_e=\pi-2\pi a_e. \] In the strict geometric domain, \(0<a_e<1/2\) and the three \(a_e\)'s at each vertex sum to more than one. Equivalently, the three positive dihedral angles \(\alpha_e\) there sum to less than \(\pi\). Such a vertex is **hyperideal**: its polar plane cuts off the end and leaves a geodesic truncation triangle. The source in this local statement is a positive Racah scalar \(W_N\) with its four face-normalization factors retained. If \(\Psi=\lim N^{-1}\log W_N\), the theorem proves \[ \operatorname{Vol}(\text{tetrahedron})=\pi\Psi. \] Squaring \(W_N\) doubles its logarithmic action. The proof constructs the Gram matrix of outward face normals in Lorentz space, recovers the edge lengths, checks the volume differential and fixes the constant at an ideal configuration. Boundary values are continuous volume extensions. Here Lorentz space is four-dimensional real space with a bilinear form of signature \((3,1)\). Its hyperboloid model realizes hyperbolic three-space, and the Gram matrix records the pairwise Lorentz inner products of the face normals. This is how the algebraic matrix determines the cell's metric. ![A truncated tetrahedron in a combinatorial projection. Blue triangles indicate polar truncation faces; the hyperbolic metric comes from the Gram matrix.](../figures/truncated-tetrahedron.png) This is stronger than observing that a factorial action resembles a dilogarithm. It is also local: a collection of such tetrahedra does not automatically form the knot complement. ## The global angle slice carries the topology An actual ideal triangulation specifies which faces are glued, which tetrahedron edges belong to each manifold edge, and which peripheral curves represent meridians and longitudes. Its angle constraints must retain this incidence. At a candidate maximum, stationarity must hold in every allowed angle direction. The corresponding shape and length equations must make adjacent cells agree. The resulting developing map must have the intended winding and end behavior. Complete cusps, or the specified filled peripheral equations, are part of the certificate. The [source-volume certificate](../../notes/source_volume_casson_rivin_certificate.md) keeps these requirements explicit. An algebraic critical point can be isolated and still belong to the wrong component or have the wrong peripheral marking. ## A general certificate through volume maximization For an ideal tetrahedron, its three positive dihedral angles \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\), one for each pair of opposite edges, have sum \(\pi\), and its volume is \[ \Lambda(\alpha)+\Lambda(\beta)+\Lambda(\gamma),\qquad \Lambda(t)=-\int_0^t\log|2\sin u|\,du. \] An ideal triangulation imposes additional linear sums \(2\pi\) around the manifold edges. These equations define its angle polytope. Casson and Rivin's variational method recovers the nonlinear shape equations by differentiating the sum of these volumes. [Rivin's 1994 paper](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1994/139-3/p02) is a primary source for the volume method; the [proof by Futer and Guéritaud, Theorem 1.2 and §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.0440) explains the completeness implication in terms of angle variations. Their formulation concerns a fixed ideal triangulation of an orientable manifold with torus boundary. The maximum on the closed angle polytope can lie on its boundary; an interior critical point must therefore be established for the triangulation being used. For an actual marked ideal triangulation with torus vertex links, the [positive gluing criterion](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) gives a direct proof of the Casson–Rivin equivalence: an interior critical point of the ideal-tetrahedron volume function is exactly a complete positive gluing. Strict concavity makes it the unique maximum, including over the closed angle polytope, and its value is the actual complement volume. The proof keeps the geometry explicit. Lagrange multipliers prescribe one truncated length for each global edge. These lengths determine compatible corner horospheres; the face maps then match them, giving complete flat cusp tori. Conversely, compatible horospheres make the geometric volume stationary under all allowed angle variations. There is a finite algebraic certificate using positive upper-half-plane phases and positive multiplier variables. The unique optimum has algebraic shapes. Neither its dilogarithm volume nor the original quantum period is asserted to be an algebraic number. Existence of an interior optimum on a proposed triangulation, and selection of its period by the quantum source, remain distinct questions. For fixed critical shapes, choosing a horosphere at one cusp and then rescaling it changes the decoration but leaves the hyperbolic metric unchanged. With \(c\) cusps these independent choices form a torsor for \((\mathbb R_{>0})^c\): there is one and only one tuple of scales taking one decoration to another. This accounts for the decoration freedom in the algebraic certificate. It does not yet determine the quantum period, and extending the action to complex scalars requires retaining its sign kernels. For augmented plats, the [actual matching-graph construction](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) is one way to supply this certificate: a positive labeled right-angled polyhedron gives the marked complete exterior and an explicit positive ideal triangulation. The general gluing criterion does not require that particular polyhedral decomposition or a bound on bridge width. ## The general endpoint action has the actual volume normalization The original augmented-plat coupon now has an [exact local critical-character map](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_local_critical_character_map.md). It preserves the whole ordered meridian product, recovers the actual crossing-circle transport and retains both physical degree charts and signed half twists. On a correctly marked stationary branch, the original Fourier coupling gives $d(2\pi i\phi)=\tfrac12\sum_i V_i\,dU_i$ in its specified peripheral convention. A [generic-framing theorem](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_regular_geometric_phase_chart.md) places the complete geometric representation in regular charts for every coupon simultaneously. It also solves the unrestricted integral degree-lifting problem. It does not put that candidate into a contributing physical support chamber or choose a contributing Poisson sector. The [endpoint regulator theorem](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_endpoint_regulator.md) fixes the absolute constant. The fully normalized q-Hahn action and the original crossing-circle diagram have the same rational wedge. Their Bloch–Wigner regulators agree at a real point and hence throughout the connected regular chart. The original diagram cycle has degree one on each cusp, so its regulator is the actual augmented-link volume. Writing $Y_D$ for the actual augmented-link exterior of the fixed diagram $D$, the full stationary-action identity gives $$2\pi\operatorname{Re}\phi(0)=\operatorname{Vol}(Y_D).$$ This holds at a regular, correctly marked full geometric critical point; the fixed endpoint channel has purely imaginary logarithm and introduces no residual real contribution. The theorem fixes the geometric candidate's value. A quantum cycle coefficient, a nonzero amplitude and bounds for other contributions remain separate parts of the general conjecture. The same marked matrices now determine the [channel Hessian](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_channel_hessian.md), without assuming a deformation theorem. If the endpoint transport is $I+b_iH_i$ with $H_i^2=0$, the actual primitive cusp shape is $\tau_i=(b_i-\epsilon_i/2)^{-1}$. Let $\xi_i$ be the scaled channel variables, $y$ the remaining magnetic variables, and $F$ the full local phase. After the two internal q-Hahn variables are eliminated on their marked critical sheets, $$\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial\xi_i\partial\xi_j}=-\delta_{ij}\frac{4\pi i}{\tau_i},\qquad \frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial\xi_i\partial y}=0.$$ Since $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i>0$, this channel block has negative real part. Eliminating those channels gives the color Hessian $\pi i\operatorname{diag}(\tau_i)$, with the factor of two in the transfer convention retained. The [marked multi-cusp rigidity theorem](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) supplies a direct deformation proof from an actual positive ideal gluing certificate. Positive polarization makes the marked gluing Jacobian invertible; the developing-map inverse retains exact peripheral eigenflags, including infinitesimal data. The [actual critical-scheme theorem](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_critical_scheme.md) then reconstructs the whole ordered representation from the stationary magnetic variables and conversely. The magnetic Hessian has exactly two null directions, both from framing. After taking a transverse slice, there is a nearby holomorphic geometric stationary branch, with the displayed peripheral differential and absolute volume anchor. This classical existence statement is general in plat width under the certificate. Selecting it from the original quantum sum is a separate analytic requirement, now met for the specifically proved families but not asserted for every plat. There is now an explicit [physical framing test](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_physical_framing_criterion.md) for the domain of the joint kernel theorem. One rank-one projector records the common frame; traces of the original prefix words give finite strict inequalities for every input and output. The theorem distinguishes these inequalities from mere avoidance of algebraic chart poles. The [local sheet test](../../notes/actual_q_hahn_joint_complex_amplitude.md) then checks which characteristic root the finite source selects. Neither test asserts that a common solution or a contributing global cycle always exists. The [right-angled framing obstruction](../../notes/actual_right_angled_selected_framing_obstruction.md) now rules out an all-central selected common frame for the certified right-angled plats. In the Lorentz model, the white face normals form a convex polyhedron whose facets correspond to the original shaded triangles. Under the oriented geometric strip conditions, the two flags determine a line through its interior. At each facet crossed by that line, a nonnegative relation among the three actual prefix diagonals violates strict physical support. Generic flags cross exactly two facets, so the obstruction involves exactly two local factors at every bridge width. Any two distinct facets can be prescribed, including the pair incident to the original marked physical edge. The [selected-factor corollary](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_selected_factor_localization.md), using the [full physical packet](../../notes/actual_q_hahn_full_physical_complex_packet.md), now proves that every other ordinary factor is physical and source-selected. The selected square root is continued from the original source; the old pointwise principal-root test is not assumed outside the central domain. The completed contraction and global quantum cycle remain unresolved. ![A schematic section of the white-normal convex polyhedron: the polarization line crosses two facets, locating the two strict physical-support failures.](../figures/two-exceptional-factors.png) For the complete-circle source, the pair at a crossing-circle matching edge now has an [exact rewrite with four external representation factors](../../notes/actual_matching_edge_marked_four_port_block.md). Its four outside objects are all physical, so the [positive scalar estimate](../../notes/actual_matching_edge_racah_positive_scalar.md) applies to every target channel, independently of bridge width. The original row measure cancels its exponential factorial gauge. In this unrestricted-plat method, the target tensor, the remaining network and the original integration contour still require control; geometric localization alone does not estimate them. The [finite selected-critical certificate](../../notes/actual_augmented_plat_selected_local_certificate.md) combines the positive gluing, common-frame and local-sheet tests, retaining the original logarithmic characters. When supplied, it identifies the geometric stationary germ with the source-selected local principal phase. At completeness the sheet tests also have an exact interpretation as oriented regions between the two actual disk circles. For other geometric realizations, existence of that simultaneous certificate remains open. For an unrestricted plat, this test alone does not show that the geometric point contributes to the original integration contour. The same deformation coordinates give a [geometric long-filling corollary](../../notes/general_augmented_plat_long_filling_quantifiers.md) without a quantum input. Write $V_i(U)=U_i t_i(U)$ and set $e_i=1/p_i$ at filled cusps, $e_i=0$ at unfilled ones. The equations $V_i(U)+e_iU_i=-2\pi i e_i$ have an invertible Jacobian at completeness and a solution in one fixed polydisk. Their exact factorization bounds each $|U_i|$ by a constant times $|e_i|$. The existing geometric completion argument therefore applies to all independently long signed slopes. This proves the geometric threshold, while the volume-limit threshold still requires the quantum estimates. ## The local maximum can be the wrong global maximum The four face-support inequalities alone are insufficient. In the local hyperideal theorem, differentiating the normalized action with respect to a color gives the corresponding edge length. Increasing every color preserves those support inequalities and pushes the maximum to an octahedral boundary configuration. A manifold saddle therefore requires the actual global edge constraints or additional boundary contributions. This is a concrete obstruction to deriving the complement volume by multiplying separately maximized local estimates. There is now an exact [geometric interpretation of a native magnetic energy](../../notes/actual_native_magnetic_energy_local_geometry.md). At the folded color, the highest-weight degree block gives four positive ideal tetrahedra forming a convex ideal octahedron, whose maximum is $v_8$. The full boundary operator has the larger rate computed in the [Plancherel theorem](../../notes/actual_matching_edge_magnetic_energy_profile.md). Away from the fold the normalized summands require a signed face term. These are local comparison geometries; placing their cells in the actual complement and matching the remaining phase equations still requires proof. The [positive radial Fourier obstruction](../../notes/actual_positive_fourier_radial_geometric_obstruction.md) makes the phase issue concrete for the general certified right-angled source. Its retained cycle congruences close particular local momentum characters, including the cup signs and marked charge. They do not supply the real magnetic-coordinate matching equations carried by the discarded coefficient phases. An all-ordinary strict radial reconstruction would contradict the common-frame theorem above. This excludes that proposed geometric assembly, without asserting a strict gap between positive and coherent exponential rates. ## Shared cores explain the cube test For the certified augmented graph geometry, the actual volume has the form $$4b\,v_8+2\operatorname{Vol}(Q),$$ where \(Q\) is the supplied positive ideal right-angled central polyhedron and \(b\) counts the prescribed octahedral pieces in that construction. The exact cut, face, and cusp identifications are checked in its theorem. The core is shared by the graph; it is not a sum of independent vertex constants. The cube is a useful nontrivial example of this phenomenon. Its projected quantum calculations recover the shared core contribution. Extending those estimates to the full source is still a quantum problem, even after the geometric complement has been constructed.

title: What remains to be proved
text: # What remains to be proved The current papers prove volume limits for specified diagram classes under explicit sufficient conditions. The central open problem in this project is to remove the requirement that every surviving filling be long. The question is about the original reduced Kashaev invariant and the volume of the complete knot complement. The [results chapter](results.md) gives the established hypotheses. The [research status](../../notes/research_finite_exceptions_progress.md) records the separate extension project. The manuscripts are frozen at their stated results; exploratory lemmas are not added to their premises. ## The established long-filling result Fix a finite strict Conway construction, its auxiliary crossing circles and a half-twist pattern whose strand connections form one knot. Let \(r\) be the number of auxiliary circles. Write \(\boldsymbol p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)\in\mathbb Z^r\) for the primitive integer filling coefficients and \(K(\boldsymbol p)\) for the resulting knot. All this data is fixed before the quantum level \(N\) grows. The [Conway theorem](../../docs/papers/conway-asymptotics.pdf) supplies a threshold \(P\), depending on the fixed construction, such that every fixed assignment with \(|p_j|>P\) for all \(j\) has \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N} \log|K_N(K(\boldsymbol p))| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K(\boldsymbol p)). \] The signs and relative magnitudes of the coefficients are unrestricted. The strictness and knot-component tests remain part of the theorem. The [ordered-reduction result](../../docs/papers/conway-reductions.pdf) extends its use to presentations whose surviving net twists satisfy these conditions. A large written exponent can cancel against another one, so the hypothesis must be checked after that reduction. For this fixed parameter lattice, long assignments have natural density one. The excluded set is contained in a union of slabs \(\{|p_j|\le P\}\). Each slab is infinite when \(r\ge2\). This does not give finitely many exceptional assignments, or a density statement for distinct knots ordered by crossing number. Other papers permit some short powers under different conditions. The [circle-tree criterion](../../docs/papers/circle-tree-volume.pdf) uses summed or directed degree-and-twist inequalities. Planar weak balance, terminal decorations and certified triangular gluings have their own hypotheses. Those results do not prove the arbitrary-short-filling extension of the Conway theorem. ## The desired statement after partial filling Choose a proper subset \(S\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and fix an arbitrary integer tuple \((p_j)_{j\in S}\). These coefficients may be short, zero or have mixed signs. The proposed extension asks for a threshold \(P_S\), allowed to depend on the construction and every already fixed coefficient, such that all assignments satisfying \[ |p_j|>P_S\qquad(j\notin S) \] and producing hyperbolic knots have the same original-invariant volume identity. The partially filled exterior need not satisfy the positivity conditions used at the unfilled augmented point. It must be analyzed with its actual remaining boundary data. This is stronger than proving another collection of isolated short-word examples. The [partial-filling formulation](../../notes/research_finite_exceptions_under_partial_fillings.md) keeps these quantifiers explicit. The proposed statement remains open. If it were established for every proper subset and every fixed tuple, a finite branching argument would give finitely many exceptional assignments for each original template. At the first stage, an assignment outside the long region has some bounded coordinate. There are finitely many choices of that coordinate and its bounded value. Fix one such choice and apply the proposed theorem to the remaining coordinates. Repeat. There are at most \(r\) stages and finitely many branches at each stage, so only finitely many fully bounded leaves remain. A threshold at a later branch may depend on all earlier choices; no uniform threshold over every partial filling is required. Assignments and knot types must still be distinguished. Different tuples can represent the same knot. In particular, zero fillings and exact cap reductions can turn an apparently long twist into removable curls. The remaining scalar is then the unresolved core invariant, up to its known phase. Such padding shows why a general partial-filling theorem can be substantially stronger than a collection of long-slope estimates. A covering shortcut also needs care. If a finite unbranched cover extends over a filled solid torus, a primitive meridian upstairs maps to the primitive meridian downstairs, up to sign. In the pulled-back drilled metric its length is unchanged, while a degree-\(d\) boundary cover multiplies horotorus area by \(d\). Its normalized slope length therefore becomes \(\mathcal L/\sqrt d\). This does not turn a fixed short filling into a geometrically long one. The current research status explains this restriction; a quantum descent theorem would be additional work. ## What a different orthogonality can simplify Let \(B\) synthesize a physical boundary vector from coefficients: \(v=Bc\). In a positive Hermitian pairing, \[ \|v\|^2=c^*B^*Bc. \] The matrix \(B^*B\) is the Gram matrix of the spanning vectors. It annihilates directions that represent zero. Replacing it by the identity is valid for orthonormal coordinates, or after proving a suitable comparison for the actual matrix. Squaring unrelated expansion coefficients separately can otherwise count contributions that cancel when the boundary states are assembled. The [conceptual chapter](../../manuscript/sections/02-exact-concepts.tex) and [formal statement guide](../../repro/PAPER_FORMAL_COVERAGE.md) make this distinction precise. The original closing row remains part of the data. A norm upper bound does not supply a lower bound for that one matrix coefficient. For the full color-orbit transform, Fourier orthogonality is already exact. Arrange the complete value and ordinary colors as \(c_N=(K_N,C_1,\ldots,C_{N-1})\), and use a unitary discrete Fourier transform. If \(u_N\) is the transform of its first coordinate vector, then \[ \widehat c_N=K_Nu_N+e_N,\qquad e_N\perp u_N,\qquad \|\widehat c_N\|^2=|K_N|^2+\|e_N\|^2. \] The [ordinary-color estimate](../../notes/ordinary_color_plancherel_bound_audit.md) bounds \(\|e_N\|^2\) polynomially in \(N\), with the diagram fixed. The missing geometric growth of the actual norm is not changed by choosing another orthonormal basis. A better basis may nevertheless make that norm accessible. Internal tangle coordinates raise a different question. Repeated Casimir roots require both values and derivatives. The [local Hermite frame](../../notes/actual_tame_c0_hermite_source_frame.md) retains both directions, and the [ordinary-cap tree identity](../../notes/actual_cap_tree_angle_energy.md) gives a positive normalized pairing for its specified trees. Arbitrary interior crossings and overlapping gluings still require their own compatibility argument. A channel invisible to one closing row can become visible after another crossing; it cannot be discarded early. ## A fixed-degree minimum for the original source The [normalized Conway formulation](../../notes/research_convex_normalized_conway_source.md) turns exact packet equations into a positive least-squares problem. At each proper vertex, let \(x_v\) be the full boundary packet, including its repeated-root directions. After the stated normalization, a leaf, turn or product has a prescribed map \(\Phi_v\), and \(L\) is the original normalized closing row. The energy is \[ E_N(x)=\sum_{v\text{ proper}} \|\Phi_v((x_c)_{c\text{ child of }v})-x_v\|^2 +|Lx_{\mathrm{top}}|^2. \] The variables lie in a product of unit packet balls. Each product is bilinear, so the energy has polynomial degree at most four. Its degree is fixed as \(N\) grows; its number of coordinates is not. The full Newton packet has dimension \(N\). The note proves uniform strong convexity for this specifically normalized problem, an interior minimizer, and the comparison \[ B_{\mathrm{tot}}^2e_N\le |K_N|^2 \le\frac{197}{196}B_{\mathrm{tot}}^2e_N, \qquad e_N=\min E_N. \] The known budget \(B_{\mathrm{tot}}\) contains all local normalization costs. It can contribute to the exponential rate and must be retained. These inequalities include source zeros. Positivity of the energy does not assert that its minimum is positive for every assignment. The [orthogonal elimination](../../notes/research_conway_orthogonal_linear_elimination.md) chooses one child packet at each binary product and retains those variables as \(u\). The other variables, denoted \(z\), enter the residual linearly: \[ E_N(u,z)=\|A(u)z+b(u)\|^2. \] The original normalized maps make the relevant linear solve uniformly nondegenerate and its solution feasible. Thus the inner minimization can be performed exactly: \[ \min_z E_N(u,z) =b(u)^*\left[I-A(u)(A(u)^*A(u))^{-1}A(u)^*\right]b(u). \] The bracket is an orthogonal projection. Its Gram factors remain in the formula; they have not been replaced by independent coefficient costs. An equivalent boundary formulation has a Gram matrix between \(I\) and \((226/225)I\). The original scalar observation is retained. Elimination removes linear variables, although the resulting rational or expanded polynomial expression need not still have degree four. The unresolved step is to evaluate this minimum at the geometric rate after arbitrary fixed partial fillings. By the displayed comparison, this would require two-sided exponential estimates for \(B_{\mathrm{tot}}^2e_N\) at rate \(\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K)/\pi\). In particular a lower bound is needed. Substituting a trial configuration into a minimization problem gives an upper bound. It does not prove that every admissible configuration has energy at the desired scale. Strong convexity does provide a useful lower certificate. With the real Euclidean gradient, the same note proves \[ D_N(x):=E_N(x)-\tfrac12\|\nabla E_N(x)\|^2 \le e_N. \] This polynomial has degree at most six. A configuration with \(D_N(x)>0\) gives the genuine lower bound \(B_{\mathrm{tot}}^2D_N(x)\le |K_N|^2\). For a geometric argument, one would need configurations whose energies have the desired rate and whose gradient defects are small relative to those energies. An absolute error bound is insufficient when the energy itself is exponentially small. Producing such a controlled positive certificate for every fixed short partial filling is still open. ## Geometry and noncancellation are separate inputs Casson--Rivin optimization concerns the volume on an angle-structure domain. At a positive interior critical point, the permitted variations supply the geometric gluing equations. The actual face identifications, primitive peripheral slopes and absolute volume normalization remain essential. The [geometry chapter](geometry.md) and [marked-filling paper](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) explain those steps for their stated constructions. For an oscillatory quantum sum, a geometric critical point must also occur with a nonzero coefficient in the original contour or discrete sum. Competing contributions must not cancel it at the same exponential scale. The [whole filling theorem](../../docs/papers/oscillatory-fillings.pdf) provides this conclusion from explicit local and global source hypotheses. Extending those hypotheses across an arbitrary short component remains part of the proposed partial-filling theorem. ## The external-color route and its exact cancellations An external color is an auxiliary representation label used to expand a crossing-circle operation. The full finite formula can contain complementary colors, or aliases, in addition to the selected central expression. A small-color term can cancel an alias of a complete-color term. Estimating the latter alone changes the expression being bounded. ![The small-color region and its complementary source terms.](../figures/external-color-corridor.png) The [finite spectral paper](../../docs/papers/filling-bounds.pdf) retains the derivative channels and the full closing functional. The [Conway source estimates](../../docs/papers/conway-source-bounds.pdf) control the required physical and Fourier complements for their stated strict constructions. The [Casimir-source paper](../../docs/papers/casimir-source-asymptotics.pdf) evaluates the central contribution for its broader planar setting. Its conclusion is distinct from an unrestricted bound for every complementary source term. A positive local majorant or one small-color corridor is therefore not a full source theorem. ## Direct twist transport and the classical operator question The alternative operator approach keeps a signed power inside its original tangle and follows the resulting quantum relations. Its local classical spectral variables are not automatically the preferred meridian and longitude of the closed knot. The gluing and closing maps must identify the peripheral curve with its original marking. The [meridian-expansion paper](../../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf) derives a selected classical factor under its stated hypotheses, including a fixed nonzero annihilating operator and the needed source expansions. It does not construct a universal operator from an arbitrary local polynomial. The [torsor discussion](algebraic.md) explains the coordinate and descent questions separately. The present finite-exception target still concerns the original scalar invariant, whether its proof uses Fourier sums, a variational minimum or operator relations.

title: Notation and conventions
text: # Notation and conventions The calculations in this guide pass through three kinds of object: a finite quantum expression, a function describing its large-level growth, and a geometric structure on a specified link complement. A symbol does not acquire a geometric meaning merely because it occurs in a critical-point equation. The proof must identify the relevant matrix, path, or gluing map. This chapter gives the conventions needed to read those identifications and to compare the different approaches in the [mechanism](mechanism.md) and [geometry](geometry.md) chapters. For a first reading, [From a knot diagram to a volume limit](starting.md) defines the topological objects, writes out a finite contraction, and derives the coefficient estimate. This chapter is a reference for the notation used after those definitions. Letters are reused in the papers and retained research notes. In particular, a tangle turn, a crossing matrix, and a shift of a meridian variable are different operations. Local definitions take precedence when a note uses another convention. Each [current paper](../../papers/README.md) defines its own notation and identifies the numbered statements it imports. When moving between papers, compare those definitions and hypotheses before substituting a formula. The [dependency graph](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html) locates the imported statement; it does not identify two symbols merely because their names agree. ## The invariant and the order of limits Fix the diagram, its ordered tangle construction, its integer twist powers, and any finite certificate used by a theorem. Then let the integer quantum level \(N\) tend to infinity. Statements for arbitrary finite trees or spheres allow arbitrarily large fixed diagrams; they do not allow the diagram to grow with \(N\). A universal sufficient twist bound and a uniform error estimate over all diagrams are different assertions. | Symbol | Meaning | | --- | --- | | \(N\ge2\) | Quantum level. Unless a theorem states otherwise, the limit includes both parities and composite levels. | | \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q_N=q_N^2\) | The chosen root and its square. The methods chapter also writes \(\zeta_N=Q_N\). A large summand or a large sum of absolute values supplies no lower bound for that scalar. “Independently sufficiently long” means that a fixed presentation has a threshold and each surviving twist exceeds it in absolute value, with either sign and without a bound on ratios between twist lengths.
