The [results chapter](results.md) states the separate long-filling, degree-and-twist, and decorated-planar hypotheses. ## Finite sums, colors and derivatives A **color** specifies a representation on a physical strand or auxiliary circle. An internal **channel** is a representation label introduced by a decomposition of tensor products. A **head index** specifies a basis vector inside a representation. These are different finite indices. The ordinary auxiliary color is \(j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), and its highest weight is \(j-1\). Complete color means \(j=N\), with highest weight \(d\). Its external deficit is \(h=N-j\), and the corresponding scaled deficit is \(\chi=h/N\). Some older formulas use \(n\) for this color; their \(n\) must not be confused with a crossing power \(n_i\). An internal polynomial or head index \(r\in\{0,\ldots,d\}\) often gives a scaled variable \(x=r/N\). A different formula may use the half-shifted channel variable \[ a_j=\frac{j+1/2}{N},\qquad c_j=2\cos(2\pi a_j). \] For the folded spectral coordinate, set \[ \delta_j=\frac12-a_j,\qquad c_j=-2\cos(2\pi\delta_j). \] On the representative half of the spectrum, the continuous variable \(\delta\) near zero describes the internal endpoint near \(-2\); it is not the external color deficit \(\chi\). At odd levels the endpoint \(\delta=0\) is an actual simple node. At even levels the nearest representative has \(\delta=1/(2N)\). Those finite offsets are retained in the interpolation. The choice \(r/N\), \(r/(N-1)\), or \((r+1/2)/N\) must remain visible. They have the same interior leading limit in suitable regimes, but different exact endpoints and first corrections. For example, \(r_1+r_2\le d\) becomes \(x_1+x_2\le1-1/N\) when \(x_i=r_i/N\). Replacing it by a closed limiting inequality is an estimate, not an exact source identity. A **normal** is a derivative in a specified direction. At a repeated Casimir node \(c\), a polynomial operator can depend on both \(p(c)\) and \(p'(c)\); evaluating only \(p(c)\) loses its nilpotent part. This is the reason for Hermite data. A derivative in the generic parameter \(\zeta=q_Ne^t\), with \(N\) fixed, is another operation. A factor that vanishes at \(t=0\) can have a nonzero derivative there. Neither derivative is the next coefficient of an \(N\to\infty\) expansion. The [physical polynomial compiler](../../docs/papers/meridian-tangles.pdf) records the finite Casimir algebra and its repeated-root data. The [homogeneous face source](../../docs/papers/filling-bounds.pdf) records how its polynomials become original matrix entries. Root-only identities must not be differentiated in a generic parameter without that additional source calculation. For the complete Newton basis, the convention used in the moving-meridian bounds is \[ e_r(z)=\frac{\prod_{a=0}^{r-1}(c_a-z)}{S_r^2}, \qquad 0\le r\le d,\qquad e_0=1. \] “Low” means \(r\le\lfloor d/2\rfloor\), and “high” means \(r>\lfloor d/2\rfloor\). These are ranges of an internal polynomial index, not small or large physical colors. A high basis polynomial vanishes at the complete spectral nodes but may have nonzero derivatives there. For a polynomial \(F\), the coefficient trace in an equal-color channel with \(M=q_N^s\) is \[ \phi_s(F)=(-1)^dN^2[z^d]\operatorname{rem}_{P_s}F,\qquad P_s(z)=\mathsf T_N(z)+2\cos(2\pi s), \quad \mathsf T_N(u+u^{-1})=u^N+u^{-N}. \] Here \(\operatorname{rem}_{P_s}F\) is the unique remainder of degree less than \(N\) after polynomial division. This retains the full repeated-root data. The normalized polynomial \(\mathsf T_N(z)\) is \(2T_N(z/2)\) in the convention \(T_N(\cos\theta)=\cos(N\theta)\). Opposite-color channels use the constant quotient \(P_0\), with their original reference maps retained. The compiler fixes which channel occurs; one cannot move every quotient in a diagram indiscriminately. Changing coordinates, changing the quotient product, and applying a physical turn are three different operations. In particular, an entry of a moving multiplication tensor need not be bounded by its complete value at the same indices. The [same-index obstruction](../../notes/actual_main_meridian_same_index_obstruction.md) disproves that estimate. The [reflected-trace bound](../../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) compares the change in the tensor with a different index and keeps the neighboring source profiles. Neither statement concerns a counterexample to a knot-volume limit. ## Source polynomials, sectors and the invariant The **source** is the full prescribed expression: physical matrices, their index ranges, cups, caps, the marked cut, and every scalar factor. A **coupon** is one specified operator inserted in a tangle box. A source polynomial is a way of storing the matrix entries of such an operator or the coefficients of a whole contraction. A **simple triangulated sphere** is a finite graph embedded in the two-sphere with triangular complementary faces, with no loops or multiple edges. Its dual has a vertex for each triangle and an edge for each shared side. Every dual vertex has degree three. A **perfect matching** of that dual chooses one incident edge at every dual vertex, pairing all the triangles. Each pair gives one ordered four-face crossing region. If there are \(R\) pairs, the sphere has \(2R\) triangles, \(3R\) edges and \(R+2\) vertices: the first edge count follows by counting three sides per triangle twice, and the vertex count then follows from Euler's formula. The marked main edge is an original strand edge, not one of the white edges selected by this matching. Its two endpoints \(u,v\) are the protected white vertices. Thus the same graph vocabulary can refer to two different edges: a matched diagonal describes a crossing region; a nonmatching marked edge records the cut in a main strand. The cyclic orders and the terminal strand pairing remain part of the source data. A matching alone does not establish that the resulting link has one component. A **Morse presentation** draws the original strands with respect to a height function whose local maxima and minima are isolated and nondegenerate. A horizontal slice between events has a fixed number of strand intersections. A cup increases that number by two, a cap decreases it by two, and a crossing acts on the strands present at its height. A flat plat puts all upper cups and lower caps outside one braid region; a general Morse presentation can have cups and caps between crossing regions. The general source identity retains these intervening maps. It does not replace the diagram by a flat plat without proving such a transformation. The face construction uses three successive operations. First multiply the local polynomials, then extract one shared face coefficient, then apply the functionals that insert the prescribed twists. The variables have different roles at these stages: | Symbol | What varies, and what is done with it | | --- | --- | | \(L_f\) | A formal variable for projection face \(f\). Its prescribed coefficient is extracted once from the whole product. | | \(\rho_f>0\) | The radius of the integration circle \(\lvert L_f\rvert=\rho_f\) in a Cauchy coefficient estimate. It is a freely chosen weight for a bound. | | \(\sigma_e\) | A spectral variable retained at crossing region \(e\) after the face extraction. | | \(\mathcal L_N^{n_e}\) | A linear functional on the polynomial in \(\sigma_e\); it inserts the fixed signed crossing power \(n_e\). | | \(S_N(\boldsymbol\sigma)\) | The polynomial after the common face coefficient has been taken. It is not yet the filled scalar. | Thus the final step has the form \[ Z_N(\boldsymbol n)= \left(\mathcal L_N^{n_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes \mathcal L_N^{n_R}\right)S_N. \] Each functional acts on its own spectral variable. The exact source identity specifies the exterior and framing factors relating \(Z_N\) to \(K_N(K)\). A bound for a polynomial before coefficient extraction, a bound for \(S_N\), and a bound for \(Z_N\) are therefore three distinct statements. In the homogeneous face description, a box has ordered faces \((x,b,c,y)\): \(b,c\) are its middle faces and \(x,y\) its outer faces. Its polynomial \(H_e(x,b,c,y)\) has total degree \(d\). For a diagram with \(R\) boxes, the product has degree \(Rd\). With two protected faces \(u,v\), the original marked contraction is expressed by \[ \left[\prod_{f\ne u,v}L_f^d\right]\! \left.\prod_{e=1}^R H_e(L_{x_e},L_{b_e},L_{c_e},L_{y_e}) \right|_{L_u=L_v=0}. \] The brackets mean coefficient extraction, not substitution of face radii. There are \(R\) ordinary targets, each of degree \(d\), and two protected targets of degree zero. A shared face has one variable wherever it occurs. Giving separate occurrences unrelated values would change the problem. For physical coupons this coefficient formula gives the original scalar with its stated exterior normalization. If \(H_e\) is instead a spectral numerator depending on a variable \(\sigma_e\), the extracted result \(S_N(\boldsymbol\sigma)\) is still a polynomial in those spectral variables. The original trace and filling functional remain to be applied. The [general Morse source theorem](../../notes/research_matched_sphere_morse_source.md) keeps the turns, mark, primitive face grid, and both level parities in this description. Several decompositions of the source are used: | Term | Exact meaning | | --- | --- | | Complete-color source | The original contraction with every designated auxiliary color equal to \(N\). | | Color core | The term retaining the complete-circle part of each exact external-color identity. It can be an entire function of \(\chi\). | | Color alias | A complementary small-color term in that identity. Its exponential smallness is a theorem to be proved, not part of its definition. | | central sector | The specified central-cut support in a local continuant/cofactor spectral numerator. | | left or right sector | One of the complementary one-sided supports in that same numerator. | | All-central contraction | The coefficient or period obtained by selecting central at every box, while retaining the shared face targets and original trace. | | Full contraction | The sum over all the prescribed sector choices, with their signs and normal data. | These sector names describe finite subsets of the recurrence paths; central does not mean a physical crossing matrix. A color core and an all-central projection arise from different decompositions and must not be identified by their names. A nonzero all-central period with the correct geometric rate does not by itself prove the full invariant's rate: the other sectors might contribute or cancel it. The [cofactor theorem](../../docs/papers/filling-bounds.pdf) defines that projection, and the [balanced planar theorem](../../docs/papers/terminal-decorations.pdf) explains a sufficient comparison with the remaining sectors. A **finite-sector cover** groups genuine central/left/right choices for estimates. A branch has one full shared face-weight vector; it does not assign unrelated weights to the two occurrences of a face. The maxima inside a scalar upper bound are comparison terms, not additional quantum sectors. This combinatorial use of “cover” is different from a covering space of a link complement. The [methods chapter](methods.md#refining-the-coefficient-estimate-by-genuine-sectors) gives the cost and the remaining coverage question. ## Norms used in the estimates The same notation for a norm can hide different mathematical objects. These are the main choices in the guide: | Expression | Definition and object being bounded | | --- | --- | | \(\|H\|_{[-2,2]^R}\) | \(\sup_{\boldsymbol\sigma\in[-2,2]^R}|H(\boldsymbol\sigma)|\), for the complex spectral polynomial after the shared face coefficient has been extracted. | | \(\|v\|_2^2\) | \(\sum_j|v_j|^2\), for a specified finite vector and basis. | | \(\|A\|_{2\to2}\) | \(\sup_{v\ne0}\|Av\|_2/\|v\|_2\), the largest singular value of the matrix in that basis. | | \(\|v\|_G^2\) | \(v^*Gv\), where \(G\) is a specified positive definite Hermitian matrix. | | \(\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|\boldsymbol\rho^\alpha\) | The absolute coefficient sum of \(P(\boldsymbol L)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\boldsymbol L^\alpha\), evaluated at positive radii \(\boldsymbol\rho\); it is an upper bound on the face torus, not the original signed evaluation. | In the last row, \(\alpha\) is a tuple of nonnegative integers and \(\boldsymbol\rho^\alpha=\prod_f\rho_f^{\alpha_f}\). A star on a vector or matrix denotes conjugate transpose. A nonunitary change of basis changes matrix norms, even when it preserves an exact contraction. The physical cup/cap pairing and the Frobenius coefficient trace are also not automatically positive Hermitian inner products. Their endpoint costs must be proved when a positive norm is introduced. The [weighted-Cauchy section](methods.md#weighted-cauchy-and-the-cost-of-joining-pieces) shows those costs explicitly. ## Tangles and geometric variables A tangle box has four ordered endpoints. A product stacks compatible boxes in their specified order. A **physical quarter-turn** bends an incoming strand into an outgoing one and changes the input/output presentation. Its evaluation includes the original duality maps. The cylindrical closure joins lower endpoints to upper endpoints outside the box; the cap closure joins the two upper endpoints and the two lower endpoints respectively. These closures can have different topology. The knot test counts both components formed at final closure and any circles already closed inside a tangle. The guide usually writes \(R\) for a checked crossing operator, including the interchange of its two tensor factors, and \(T\) for a tangle turn. Some older notes call a turn \(R\). The shift called \(T\) in a quantum difference equation below is a third operation. A construction tree records products and turns; it is not a knot projection. A **circle-marked junction** contains a crossing-circle operator. A **bare junction** is a maximal consecutive group of products without one. Resolving a high-valence product into binary products introduces internal bookkeeping variables, not new physical quarter-turn edges. For a vertex \(v\), \(d_v\) is its graph degree, including the specified boundary attachments. It has no relation to the quantum top index \(d=N-1\). In strict-tree geometry, a physical turn edge has a normalized polynomial label \(x_e\). When exposed as the ordinary output of a rooted branch, that output angle is \(1-x_e\). The set \(\mathcal E_T\) in the longitude formulas consists of the original physical turn edges; hidden binary-resolution edges are excluded. The [strict-tree geometric theorem](../../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf) explains this convention and the case \(x_e=1/2\). A geometric gluing face may be a quadrilateral with four ordered ideal vertices. “Ideal” means that its vertices lie on the sphere at infinity of hyperbolic space. The vertex order specifies the face identification. An external representation factor is different from a geometric gluing face. The older word “port” was used for both and is avoided in this guide. ## Circle packings, shapes and geometric actions In the face-source geometry, a positive real \(L_f\) is the **curvature**, or inverse radius, of a finite white circle. A protected value \(L_u=0\) denotes a straight line, not a circle of radius zero. Sending the marked tangency to infinity gives two parallel protected lines. The remaining circles lie in their common strip. Shared positive radii used in a Cauchy estimate are choices of weights; only a separately proved stationary identification makes them the geometric packing. A complex number \(z_\Delta\) attached to an ideal tetrahedron is its ordered cross-ratio shape. Its branch and orientation matter; a coordinate with positive imaginary part gives a positively oriented tetrahedron in the usual vertex convention. The same letter \(z\) can instead be a formal polynomial variable, a spectral variable, or the microscopic meridian coordinate below. These uses are unrelated. The real factorial rate uses \[ J(x)=\int_0^x\log(2\sin\pi t)\,dt,\qquad 0\le x\le1, \] with the integrable endpoint limits. The Lobachevsky function is \[ \Lambda(\theta)=-\int_0^\theta\log|2\sin u|\,du. \] Thus \(J(x)=-\Lambda(\pi x)/\pi\) on that real interval. Complex continuations require a specified logarithm and path; the absolute value in the real definition of \(\Lambda\) is not a holomorphic prescription. **Definition (triangle potential).** For three nonnegative weights \(w_1,w_2,w_3\), not all zero, put \[ \begin{aligned} f(t)&=\frac{\Lambda(\pi t)+\Lambda(\pi/2-\pi t)}{\pi}, &&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\ Q(w_1,w_2,w_3) &=\max_{\substack{\alpha_j\ge0\\\sum_j\alpha_j=1/2}} \sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(f(\alpha_j)+\alpha_j\log w_j\bigr). \end{aligned} \] When \(w_j=0\), require \(\alpha_j=0\) and assign the corresponding product \(\alpha_j\log w_j\) the value zero. The \(\alpha_j\) are normalized angle variables in this maximization. This definition fixes the additive constant: for example, \(Q(w,0,0)=\tfrac12\log w\) for \(w>0\). Scaling all three weights by \(c>0\) adds \(\tfrac12\log c\), because their normalized angles sum to \(1/2\). The **complete local rate** at an ordered quartet \((x,b,c,y)\) is \(Q(x,b,y)+Q(x,c,y)\). A **capacity bound** sums these local rates, subtracts the logarithmic cost of the required face powers, and minimizes over one positive weight per ordinary face. Its value at the stationary packing and its value at arbitrary trial weights have different roles. The [methods chapter](methods.md#refining-the-coefficient-estimate-by-genuine-sectors) gives the one-sided rates and explains the strict comparison needed to control the remainder. The function \(Q\) is unrelated to the quantum root \(Q_N=q_N^2\). For a positive complete source, \(\Phi_D\) or \(F_0\) often denotes its maximal limiting action. Once the original geometry has been proved, its normalization is \[ 2\pi\Phi_D=\operatorname{Vol}(Y_D), \] where \(Y_D\) is the complete **augmented** exterior. A filled critical action is generally complex. Its real part is converted to the filled volume only after the original primitive peripheral equations and the regulator boundary correction have been checked. A **boundary profile** maximizes an open tangle's action with one output index fixed. It retains that boundary constraint and its original joining terms. It is not an independent volume budget that can be added arbitrarily to a neighboring profile. ## Packets, gaps and finite actions A **packet** is a local asymptotic formula which includes the critical action, its nonzero amplitude, and a controlled remainder. A typical notation is \[ \mathcal I_N =N^\beta a_N e^{NS_N}(1+O(N^{-1})). \] Here \(\mathcal I_N\) is the specified integral or sum, \(\beta\) is its level exponent, \(a_N\) is the amplitude, and \(S_N\) is the finite-level critical value. A nonzero lower asymptotic needs control of \(a_N\) and all contributions outside the packet. Merely knowing \(S_N\to S\) does not permit replacing \(e^{NS_N}\) by \(e^{NS}\) with relative error tending to zero. A strict **exponential gap** at rate \(\Phi\) means an estimate such as \[ |\mathcal E_N|\le N^C e^{N(\Phi-\gamma)}, \qquad \gamma>0, \] uniformly on the parameter set stated in that theorem. A polynomial factor \(N^C\) does not change the rate. The constants and starting level may depend on the fixed diagram, fixed twists, compact domain, and derivative order. Uniformity through a complex neighborhood is stronger than a bound at physical integer samples. A Hessian records second derivatives of the relevant phase. The face Cauchy integral and the spectral filling integral use different Hessians and different determinant branches. “Primitive lattice” means the retained integer summation coordinates have no hidden finite-index multiplicity. “First charge” refers to the unit Fourier magnitudes in the exact filling transform; other charges and endpoint currents remain part of the original period until estimated. An estimate \(r_N(s)=O_C(N^{-k})\) on a compact parameter set \(C\) means that one constant \(B_C\) bounds \(|r_N(s)|\le B_CN^{-k}\) for every \(s\in C\) and all sufficiently large \(N\). A statement to all asymptotic orders supplies such a remainder after every prescribed finite truncation; it need not give a convergent infinite series. The notation \(o(N)\), uniform on \(C\), means that its supremum in absolute value divided by \(N\) tends to zero. The relevant compact set and any derivative order belong to the statement. ## Augmented and filled complements; peripheral coordinates An **augmented exterior** \(Y_D\) is the complement of the main strands together with the auxiliary crossing circles. Filling an auxiliary cusp attaches a solid torus along the prescribed primitive slope and restores the twists. The resulting knot exterior is \(S^3\setminus K_{\boldsymbol p}\). Its volume generally differs from \(\operatorname{Vol}(Y_D)\). The main knot cusp remains unfilled. On each auxiliary torus, \(\mu_i\) goes once around its crossing circle and \(\lambda_i\) is the recorded disk longitude. They form a primitive integral basis. Choose the specified matrix eigenline. Let \(m_i\) and \(\ell_i\) be the corresponding determinant-one eigenvalues divided by their values \(\pm1\) at completeness, so that both normalized eigenvalues equal \(1\) there. Continue their logarithms from that point and write \[ U_i=2\operatorname{Log}m_i,\qquad V_i=2\operatorname{Log}\ell_i . \] These are logarithms of **similarity multipliers**, equivalently twice the normalized eigenvalue logarithms. For example, if the chosen auxiliary longitude matrix in the Morse collar has eigenvalue \(J_i=-1\) at completeness, then \(\ell_i=-J_i\) and \(V_i=2\operatorname{Log}(-J_i)\). At the smooth unit-charge filling saddle the convention is \[ U_i+p_iV_i=-2\pi i. \] The equation is an equality of the continued logarithms. Its exponential alone would allow a wrong winding, and at a parabolic longitude could permit a nontrivial filling holonomy. The [primitive collar calculation](../../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) fixes the paths; the [metric completion theorem](../../notes/general_source_regulator_hyperbolic_equality.md) checks the actual log-link periods and the smooth solid torus. Two useful descriptions of the auxiliary deformation are \[ U_i=-2\pi i\chi_i \quad\text{in the external-color coordinate},\qquad V_i=-4\pi i\delta_i \quad\text{in the internal spectral coordinate}. \] They belong to the same selected branch only after the stationary equations and the marked geometric adapter identify them. In the angular circle-tree chart one instead writes \(V_i=2i\tau_i\). The angle \(\tau_i\) is therefore not a cusp shape. For the main cusp, normalize a horospherical Euclidean coordinate so that the positive meridian translates by \(1\). The preferred longitude follows the knot once with zero linking number; its translation is the **cusp shape** \(\tau_K\). If \(U_K=2\log M\) and \(V_K=2\log(-L)\) are centered at the complete lift, then \(dV_K/dU_K=\tau_K\) there. The sign \(-L\) centers the negative-unipotent preferred longitude lift \(L=-1\). Under surgery on the auxiliary circles, the image of the augmented main longitude need not remain preferred. If \(k_i=\operatorname{lk}(K,C_i)\) is the integer linking number with the \(i\)th crossing circle, the stated disk convention gives \[ \lambda_{\mathrm{fill}} =\lambda_{\mathrm{aug}}\, \mu_K^{\sum_i p_i k_i^2}. \] This shear changes the marked basis on the filled cusp. The [preferred-longitude proof](../../docs/papers/preferred-longitudes.pdf) tracks it independently of the quantum asymptotic. ## The main-meridian quantum \(A\)-period The raw unrolled highest-weight coordinate is \(x=q_N^\alpha\). The marked meridian coordinate is \[ M=-q_Nx. \] Thus complete weight \(\alpha=d\) gives \(M=1\), and quotient color \(\alpha=j-1\) gives \(M=-q_N^j\). For the reduced, zero-framed ADO family \(F_N(M)\), \[ F_N(1)=K_N(K),\qquad F_N(-q_N^j)=C_j(q_N). \] The ordinary reduced \(j\)-color period is \(C_j(q)\). This notation is distinct from a color core also called \(C_N\) in some notes. The [pointing theorem](../../notes/kashaev_ado_pointing.md) fixes these equalities and the component convention. The microscopic variable is \(s\), defined by \[ M=q_N^s=e^{z/(2N)},\qquad z=2\pi i s. \] Bounded \(s\) describes an \(O(1/N)\) neighborhood of \(M=1\); it is not a fixed meridian neighborhood. The proved strict-tree profile uses \(|s|\le R<1\), before the first ordinary-color resonances at \(s=\pm1\). In particular \(F_N(q_N)=1\) even when \(F_N(1)\) has positive volume growth. The exact finite sine factor and scalar in that profile are \[ H_N(s)=\frac{\sin\pi s}{N\sin(\pi s/N)},\quad H_N(0)=1, \qquad A_N^{\mathrm{sc}}(s)=q_N^{a(D)s^2/2}, \quad a(D)=-w(D)-\sum_i n_i. \] Here \(w(D)\) is the oriented writhe. The superscript “sc” distinguishes this scalar from a finite critical action also often called \(A_N\). Its exponent uses the actual checked-crossing powers and framing convention. It is retained exactly even though it tends to one. The full modified-trace invariant is another normalization: \[ \mathcal N_N(M)=d_N(M)F_N(M),\qquad d_N(M)=i^{N+3}\frac{M-M^{-1}}{M^N-M^{-N}}. \] Evaluating the entire germ gives \(d_N(1)=i^{N+3}/N\) and \(d_N(q_N^s)/d_N(1)=H_N(s)^{-1}\). Thus its normalized profile cancels the reduced sine factor exactly. One must not set the numerator and denominator separately to zero. For the covered moving-meridian knots, the first correction in the zero-framed convention is \[ \frac{F_N(q_N^s)}{F_N(1)H_N(s)} =1+\frac{\pi i s^2\tau_K}{2N}+O(N^{-2}) =1+\frac{\tau_K z^2}{8\pi iN}+O(N^{-2}). \] The exact scalar contributes to this coefficient. The [scalar proof](../../docs/papers/meridian-tangles.pdf) and [geometric cusp proof](../../docs/papers/preferred-longitudes.pdf) are separate arguments. Their combination is the [filled profile theorem](../../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf), with its stated domain and fixed-presentation hypotheses. ## Difference operators, classical curves and selected solutions A quantum \(A\)-operator is a specified finite difference operator \[ P(q,M,T)=\sum_{j=0}^{r}a_j(q,M)T^j,\qquad (TF)(M)=F(qM),\qquad TM=qMT. \] Here \(r\) is the operator order, fixed independently of \(N\); it is not the top color index \(d\). The \(a_j\) are fixed rational functions in the formal quantum and meridian variables. A **genuine all-level annihilator** satisfies \(P(q_N,M,T)F_N(M)=0\) as an identity of meridian functions at every sufficiently large root level, with the original state and normalization. The finite-source theorem constructs such operators; the selected-factor theorem applies to any operator satisfying these hypotheses. Choosing a new ratio of two evaluated values at each level does not meet them. The associated **Ore ring** is the ring of these difference operators with the multiplication rule \[ T\,a(q,M)=a(q,qM)\,T. \] For example, \(T(MF)(M)=qM\,F(qM)\), which proves \(TM=qMT\) directly from the action. The **annihilator left ideal** is the set of operators killing the specified state. It is closed under addition and under applying another operator on the left. The side matters because the operators do not commute. An equation \(PF=0\) does not select its solution by itself. The **pointed period** also retains a fixed vector \(c_0(q)\) of small-color Laurent polynomials and the prescribed companion transport row \(r_N(q)\). At a root pole its value is \[ K_N(K)=\operatorname{CT}_{t=0} \bigl[r_N(q_N(1+t))c_0(q_N(1+t))\bigr]. \] The constant term is taken after multiplying the entire Laurent germs. The parameter \(t\) here is a local evaluation variable, not the geometric deformation \(M=e^{\pi it}\) used in another note. The [pointed operator theorem](../../notes/actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) explains the finite initial data and its volume statement. To form a classical symbol, first clear the specified rational denominators and remove the common power of \(q-1\), then take the first nonzero specialization and replace the commuting shift variable by \(L\). The **geometric \(A\)-curve** records the meridian and preferred-longitude eigenvalues of the selected geometric representations of the knot group. An arbitrary eliminated source equation can contain other components or points excluded from its original chart. A **germ** records a function or curve only in a neighborhood of the specified point, with two representatives identified if they agree on a smaller neighborhood. A **jet of order \(k\)** retains only the derivatives through order \(k\); it is less information than a germ. A selected irreducible Laurent factor is a polynomial in \(M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}\) which vanishes on the chosen algebraic curve and does not split into two nonconstant factors over the stated coefficient field. Multiplication by a nonzero constant or a monomial does not change its zero set in \((\mathbb C^\times)^2\). The field matters: a factor irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\) can split over \(\mathbb C\). Thus the assertion that the selected geometric factor divides a classical symbol is a statement about one component. It does not specify the symbol's other factors or their multiplicities, and it does not identify the whole noncommutative annihilator ideal. Scalar gauges, denominator factors and the selected longitude lift are retained before making that comparison. In the geometric convention, \(M\) is the eigenvalue of the positively oriented main meridian and \(L\) is the preferred-longitude eigenvalue on the same line. The word “positively” specifies the orientation of the curve; \(M\) is a nonzero complex number, not necessarily a positive real number. The source cut selects the \(M^{-1}\) line, so \(L\) is the inverse longitude eigenvalue there. At the complete filled knot, \(M=1\) and \(L=-1\). On the covered strict-tree germ, \[ L_{\mathrm{geom}}(M) =-M^{a(D)} \prod_{e\in\mathcal E_T} \frac{M^2-X_e(M)}{1-M^2X_e(M)}, \qquad X_e=e^{2\pi ix_e}. \] The [full strict-tree longitude theorem](../../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf) identifies these source variables and paths, including bare product junctions. This replaces the earlier circle-tree-only identification. Its operator corollary, and the [directed all-orders theorem](../../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf), specify when the selected geometric irreducible factor divides the first nonzero classical symbol. Such divisibility does not identify every factor, its multiplicity, or the complete quantum recurrence ideal. ## What a torsor records A **torsor** is a space with a free and transitive action of a group, without a preferred origin. Choosing one point identifies it with that group, but a formula using the chosen coordinate must record the choice. Several different torsors occur in the retained approaches. For auxiliary holonomy, a half-longitude eigenvalue satisfies \(\ell^2=e^V\), and the logarithm of \(\ell\) has integral-period ambiguity. The actual collar and complete anchor select the sheet and logarithm. A retained half twist changes \[ U^\epsilon=U^0-\frac{\epsilon}{2}V^0, \qquad V^\epsilon=V^0. \] On the selected double cover this is an integral monomial change of peripheral coordinates. It does not authorize a half-integer substitution into the pure-link filling formula. For a regular quantum difference module at a root of order \(m\), a chosen scalar frame can satisfy a cyclic norm equation \[ \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\sigma^j(a)=v, \] where \(\sigma\) is the prescribed cyclic field automorphism and \(v\) a central eigenvalue. Replacing the frame by \(f\) changes \(a\) to \(a\,\sigma(f)/f\). This algebraic norm is not the absolute value of the knot invariant, nor an operator norm. The [intrinsic norm-torsor construction](../../notes/intrinsic_quantum_a_norm_torsor.md) states the additional hypotheses needed to compare its selected period with a regulator. The gauge factor has cyclic product one: \[ \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac{\sigma^{j+1}(f)}{\sigma^j(f)} =\frac{\sigma^m(f)}{f}=1. \] This explains why the algebraic norm is unchanged. It gives no bound for the complex absolute value of \(f\) or its inverse. The [Hilbert-90 discussion](algebraic.md#hilbert-90-solves-a-transport-equation) shows an actual finite gauge with exponential operator cost. A third local example is the [Casimir transport conic](../../notes/actual_crossing_casimir_torus.md): after choosing a spectral sheet and a reference point, crossing powers act multiplicatively on its regular fibers. The endpoint fibers degenerate, and the original excluded divisors and boundary targets remain part of the problem. An abstract norm torus or a local conic does not by itself identify a knot's geometric longitude or prove a nonzero source asymptotic. These distinctions explain why the guide keeps the operator, regulator, relative-cycle, and full-source methods separate. Each technical route states which object is constructed and which comparison is still required. The [algebraic approaches chapter](algebraic.md) defines Hilbert 90 transport, Koszul differentials, cyclotomic root data and jets, and nilpotent groups with triangular transport. It distinguishes these algebraic structures from bounds on the original quantum state.

title: Reproducing the arguments and calculations
text: # Reproducing the arguments and calculations The papers contain written proofs, exact finite certificates and a partial Lean formalization. Each has a different role. A rational certificate can establish the inequality it encodes. A Lean proof establishes its stated proposition. A numerical sample can expose an incorrect formula, but cannot establish a uniform asymptotic estimate. Building a PDF checks its presentation and references. Start with the [collection-wide audit](../../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) and the [reproduction instructions](../../repro/README.md). The [seven-paper Conway audit](../../repro/CONWAY_SERIES_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) records the earlier revision of the Conway theorem and its prerequisites. The current subject papers give the detailed statements and proofs; the reference supplies a unified account of overlapping material. ## Following the proof's dependencies The [dependency graph](../../docs/papers/dependencies.html) records named mathematical results and the places where later proofs use them. An arrow runs from a prerequisite to its consumer. The detailed view shows the source statement, its direct prerequisites and the reason for each use. Selecting a result gives a reading route in which shared prerequisites occur once. The current inventory has 154 statement entries and 348 recorded uses, organized into 16 components and 21 subject papers. The statement, component and article graphs are acyclic. These are checks on the recorded dependencies. An omitted premise would still be a mathematical error even if the resulting graph were acyclic. A separate proof-logic record distinguishes the original diagram class, its knot-component test, its filling hypothesis and the conclusion to which each argument applies. For example, evaluating a nonzero central contribution is a different statement from bounding the rest of the invariant. The latter premise cannot be removed from the final volume argument. Replay that structural check with: ~~~sh python3 repro/check_manuscript_logic.py --output repro/results/manuscript-and-lean/manuscript-logic ~~~ The current record checks 49 declared steps and rejects 23 deliberately invalid substitutions. It detects errors in those recorded implications; it does not turn their written analytic or geometric inputs into formal proofs. ## Separating the strict Conway proof The [Conway application](../../docs/papers/conway-asymptotics.pdf) uses five companion papers directly and one further geometric prerequisite. The [paper guide](../../papers/README.md#the-conway-paper-and-its-supporting-proofs) lists that route. Its seven papers form a fixed, dated edition so that their cited theorem numbers can be used together. The standalone article and reference include the same Conway proof files. The proof keeps the original coherent color contraction, uses the pure auxiliary source, and restores each full signed crossing power by its exact finite coefficients. The whole Fourier remainder estimate and the nonzero leading coefficient are both needed. A local critical-point calculation alone would supply neither conclusion. After building the papers, check their actual inputs, compiled statement labels, published PDFs and companion references with: ~~~sh python3 tools/build_papers.py python3 tools/build_dependency_graph.py python3 tools/check_paper_collection.py ~~~ The [collection record](../../repro/results/paper-collection/summary.json) covers all 21 current papers. Its source and PDF hashes describe the edition checked. They identify files; they do not verify their proofs. ## Checking the implications in Lean The [formal coverage guide](../../repro/PAPER_FORMAL_COVERAGE.md) explains the relationship between the written arguments and the retained Lean code. There are 76 selected manuscript statements in 28 modules. For each one, a correspondence record states the symbol dictionary, hypotheses, conclusion and any step that remains written. The records distinguish four relationships. Fifteen are exact matches with the cited abstract statement. Ten specialize a more general formal theorem. Forty-one verify a specified component of a longer proof. Ten prove a conditional implication whose application hypotheses must be supplied by the written arguments. An exact scalar lemma still needs a written application identifying its sequence with the knot invariant. Each selected statement has an independent expected-type contract: an anonymous Lean example first spells out the proposition and then proves it using the selected theorem. This catches a mismatch in hypotheses or conclusions that checking only a theorem name would miss. The mathematical interpretation of the symbols is also read against the manuscript; Lean does not translate the prose automatically. The formalization retains the full coefficient pairing, including its Gram matrix and null directions. It checks the normalized shifted Fourier transform, derivative data at repeated roots, and the finite crossing coefficient bound. The stationary calculation uses an ordinary transpose for a holomorphic Hessian. The scalar asymptotic argument keeps a strict exponential gap for the entire remainder and permits the finite-level action to vary with the level. The final Conway implication assumes the written physical source identity, contour estimates, nonzero limiting amplitude and marked geometric action-volume comparison. Those are visible hypotheses. The fixed-boundary variational modules likewise require the diagram's written support and cut calculations before their generic balance results apply. Run the complete formal replay with: ~~~sh python3 repro/check_lean.py --output repro/results/manuscript-and-lean/lean ~~~ The runner uses the pinned Lean and Mathlib versions, clears only local generated build directories, and compiles the active modules and all 76 contracts. It also inventories all 534 public declarations and checks their axiom dependencies. Admitted proofs and extra axioms are rejected. The [formal setup](../../formal-real/README.md) gives the dependency installation instructions for a fresh checkout. Three compiler controls test substantive distinctions. Removing the factor \(1/N\) from Parseval gives the wrong norm already for a constant array at level two. Replacing the holomorphic mixed-block identity by a conjugate-transpose identity fails over \(\mathbb C\). Replacing a strict remainder gap by a nonstrict one permits complete cancellation of the leading term. The valid control sources compile; the altered types are rejected. These controls check the intended interfaces, rather than a numerical volume limit. ## Exact certificates and finite checks The [registered finite suite](../../repro/check_paper_algebra.py) collects the checks needed by the current papers. It runs each program in a separate process with assertions enabled and stops on a failure: ~~~sh python3 repro/check_paper_algebra.py --output repro/results/paper-collection/finite ~~~ Its 20 groups include finite spectral and Newton identities, both parity conventions, primitive peripheral coordinates and the rational constants used by the stated volume families. Some groups invoke retained component checks. The saved record identifies the scripts, data and manuscript sources by their hashes. The planar certificate verifiers use outward bounds and explicit series remainders on a finite domain cover. The written argument explains why those cells cover the required continuous region. In particular, a list of sampled radii would not replace that cover. The Conway attachment certificates are exact rational checks for their stated domains; their analytic interpretation is proved in the source-bound paper. The small certificate suite can also be run without the optional scientific Python packages: ~~~sh python3 repro/verify.py --output repro/results ~~~ Numerical matrix comparisons, Gaussian samples and selected-level tests have a narrower purpose. They check formulas and conventions. They do not prove analytic continuation, uniform error estimates, survival of a geometric contribution or completion of a hyperbolic metric. ## Running a named group The [research runner](../../repro/run_research_checks.py) is separate from the publication suite. It groups the retained exploratory checks so that one need not copy a long sequence of individual commands. Use its help and group listing to select the desired calculation. A research record describes its own scope; it is not another prerequisite for the Conway theorem merely because it has been computed successfully. ## Rebuilding this guide and its figures The guide is built from the retained chapter, figure and note sources: ~~~sh python3 tools/build_book.py python3 tools/check_book.py ~~~ The second command checks local links, fragments, image descriptions, search coverage and rendered formulas. A typesetting or link check has no mathematical proof content. After editing a native TikZ drawing, regenerate its exports with `python3 tools/render_figures.py` before rebuilding the guide. See the [guide source instructions](../../book/README.md) for the required software. Obsolete working notes, duplicated reports and failed diagnostic outputs are absent from the maintained collection. Their source snapshot remains in Git history. The current library contains the retained arguments and research questions; it is not a second archive of every intermediate calculation.

title: Figure gallery
text: # Figure gallery ## Joining two certified matched spheres ![Two triangles incident to the protected edge are removed, and their former partners become one matched pair.](figures/protected-triangular-sum.svg) The vertices \(u,v\) have protected source variables zero. The ordinary vertices \(a,c,B\) carry positive weights. Only the two orange triangle interiors are removed; the rest of each sphere and the marked vertex \(v\) survive. Write \(q_B=\log B\), \(Q_a=Q(0,a,B)\), and \(Q_c=Q(0,c,B)\), where \(Q\) is the triangle potential. The new local rate loses \(q_B\), while the two old copies of the ordinary \(B\)-target become one. These changes cancel in the shared action. The [results chapter](chapters/results.md#joining-diagrams-with-a-shared-weight-certificate) explains the complementary sectors and the exact certificate requirement. ## Changing the interior triangulation of a bipyramid ![Two tetrahedra share the interior face ABC on the left; three share the interior edge PQ on the right.](figures/bipyramid-move.svg) The five vertices are \(P,Q,A,B,C\). Both drawings have the same six boundary triangles. The move replaces \(PABC,QABC\) by \(PQAB,PQBC,PQCA\); only the interior triangulation changes. The [algebraic approaches chapter](chapters/algebraic.md#a-positive-factorial-model-and-a-change-of-triangulation) uses this example to distinguish equality of volume rates from an exact identity of finite evaluations, with measures and boundary factors retained. [Editable SVG](figures/bipyramid-move.svg) ## Summing the indices shared by two tangles ![The lower map B acts first. Its two output indices i and j become the input indices of A and are summed together.](figures/finite-contraction.svg) Each box represents a linear map on \(V_N\otimes V_N\), where \(V_N\) has dimension \(N\). The outside indices \(a,b,c,d\) are fixed; the two internal indices \(i,j\) run from \(0\) to \(N-1\). Thus the drawing represents \((AB)^{ab}_{cd}=\sum_{i,j}A^{ab}_{ij}B^{ij}_{cd}\). The [introductory chapter](chapters/starting.md#what-the-finite-invariant-contains) explains how the crossing, cup, and cap matrices use this same rule. [Editable SVG](figures/finite-contraction.svg) ## The requirements of a volume proof ![An exact decomposition, a nonzero geometric contribution, a strict remainder bound, and an identification of the critical value with hyperbolic volume are separate parts of the proof.](figures/methods-proof-map.svg) Here \(K_N\) is the original invariant, \(G_N\) is the selected contribution, and \(R_N\) is the remaining signed sum. The two analytic estimates determine the growth rate of \(K_N\). The geometric argument identifies that rate with the volume of the actual knot complement. The arrows record logical dependencies; they do not assert that all these steps hold for every knot. The [methods chapter](chapters/methods.md) defines the quantities and proves the elementary implication. [Editable SVG](figures/methods-proof-map.svg) ## Adding terminal tangles on both sides ![One stellar subdivision preserves the old matching edge xy and creates the new matching edge bw. The last panel shows two insertions on each side.](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.png) The vertices in this diagram label white projection regions. They also label circles in the complete packing; the drawing itself records their adjacencies, not their radii. The two triangles beside the blue edge \(xy\) specify the original crossing circle. Insert a new vertex \(w\) in the triangle \(xby\). The new triangles have cyclic orders \(xbw\), \(byw\), and \(yxw\). Pair the first two across the amber edge \(bw\); the old blue edge and its crossing circle remain. In the final panel, \(b_0=b\) and \(c_0=c\) are the original opposite vertices. The vertices \(b_1,b_2\) and \(c_1,c_2\) are the two successively inserted circles on each side. The blue triangles nearest \(xy\) belong to the retained crossing circle, and each amber edge specifies an added crossing circle. The general construction uses any suitable even counts \(j,k\), chosen by the curvature recurrence in the [results chapter](chapters/results.md#decorating-a-planar-diagram). Giving the new tangles odd crossing parity makes an even stack preserve the four outside endpoint connections. [SVG](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.svg) · [PDF](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/balanced-terminal-fans.tex) The drawings below explain the constructions used in the guide. Some show actual circle configurations in the boundary plane of hyperbolic space. Others show only incidence, algebraic composition, or the sequence of a proof. Each caption states which kind of drawing it is, defines the important labels, and explains the result for which it is used. The volume theorem applies to the stated ordered Conway compositions with sufficiently long net twists and to several separately certified plat families. A remaining question attached to a local method is not an unresolved step in those theorems. The diagrams below explain the proved constructions and their remaining scope. ## Evaluating one subtree and keeping its attaching variable ![The parent angle u is joined to the current vertex angle t by the complete edge kernel. Child subtrees have already been evaluated as polynomials in t; the crossing trace acts only on t.](figures/tree-boundary-message.png) The triangles stand for child subtrees of the construction tree, not for ideal tetrahedra. Their evaluations are the displayed functions \(M_{w_j,N}(t)\). Multiply these functions by the full kernel on the parent edge, then take the crossing trace at vertex \(v\). This leaves the parent angle \(u\) free and gives \(M_{v,N}(u)\). Only the edge kernel contains \(u\), so the result has trigonometric degree at most \(N-1\), however many vertices lie below \(v\). The [local volume proof](../docs/papers/circle-tree-volume.pdf) shows that its value at \(u=0\) is nonzero. Dividing by that exact value keeps the child's completed contribution outside the next estimate. The crossing and orientation factors remain in this denominator; they are not discarded. [Vector drawing](figures/tree-boundary-message.svg) · [PDF](figures/tree-boundary-message.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/tree-boundary-message.tex) ## Attaching an octahedron in the original tangle cut ![An octahedron attaches to a projection half along a shaded disk triangle. The parent and child circle vertices are O_v and O_w; the four equatorial vertices are the corresponding strand ends.](figures/octahedral-page-attachment.svg) The blue triangle on the left is a boundary face of the existing projection half. The blue triangle on the right is glued to it with the opposite boundary orientation. Equal labels specify the vertex identifications. The new vertex \(O_w\) belongs to the inserted child crossing circle, while \(O_v\) belongs to its parent. The other three crossing-disk triangles are listed in the [decomposition proof](../docs/papers/circle-tree-geometry.pdf). The same attachment is made in the other projection half. This is the local attachment used in the induction over the tree. The [geometric chapter](chapters/geometry.md#the-geometric-proof-for-the-explicit-degree-and-twist-bound) explains the positive hyperbolic realization and the filling path. Download the [vector PDF](figures/octahedral-page-attachment.pdf) or the [TikZ source](figures/octahedral-page-attachment.tex). ## Established results and remaining scope ![The reduction to long net twists, the full quantum invariant and knot volume, with quantum A-operator formulations and the remaining questions.](figures/research-map.png) Fix an ordered Conway composition with the prescribed cylindrical closure. Reduce it by the explicit twist slides and combinations, excluding an elementary two-strand braid output. Then choose sufficiently long net twists for which the actual closed diagram is a knot. The reduction identifies this knot with one covered by the strict-tree estimates. The three upper boxes describe the proved argument for that knot: reduce the tangle by exact isotopies, control the whole signed quantum sum while keeping a nonzero geometric contribution, and identify its growth with the volume of the actual knot complement. Only the auxiliary crossing-circle cusps are filled; the knot cusp remains unfilled. The lower blue box gives two other exact formulations of the same invariant: a selected period of a quantum difference operator and a positive ratio of Gram determinants. These also have the stated volume limits. The amber box concerns arbitrary short net twists, more general knot families, and extension of the selected geometric-factor theorem beyond trees of crossing circles. The geometric factor is identified for the covered trees; the full recurrence ideal remains a separate question. It does not leave the full-sum estimate open for the covered class. See the [results chapter](chapters/results.md) for the precise hypotheses. [SVG](figures/research-map.svg) · [PDF](figures/research-map.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/research-map.tex) ## Varying the figure-eight meridian near completeness ![The reduced figure-eight invariant approaches a sine profile on the imaginary parameter axis, while its centered regular part approaches one.](figures/figure-eight-meridian-profile.png) Keep the quantum parameter at \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\) and write the meridian eigenvalue as \(M=e^{it/(2N)}\). The left panel plots the reduced invariant divided by its complete value at levels \(N=24,47,80\). Its limiting curve is \(2\sin(t/2)/t\), with value one at zero. The right panel shows the error after subtracting the polynomial interpolating the ordinary colors, dividing by \(1+Y+\cdots+Y^{N-1}\), and applying the centering displayed below the axes. Here \(Y=M^2\). At the marked nonzero multiples of \(2\pi\), numerator and denominator both vanish; the dots use the removable derivative values. The logarithmic vertical scale makes the small errors visible. The [profile theorem](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) proves convergence on every fixed complex compact set, including these points, and identifies the first correction with the preferred cusp shape \(2\sqrt3\,i\). Its proof uses the positive finite figure-eight sum. A separate criterion states the estimate needed to extend the argument to signed sums for other knots. [Vector figure](figures/figure-eight-meridian-profile.svg) · [PDF](figures/figure-eight-meridian-profile.pdf) · [Reproduction script](../experiments/plot_figure_eight_meridian_profile.py) ## Products of tangle polynomials as the meridian varies ![Two triangles distinguish the Newton products that are nonzero at completeness from those that can become nonzero after changing the meridian.](figures/moving-newton-products.png) A two-strand tangle operator is expressed in the normalized Newton basis \(e_0,\ldots,e_{N-1}\) of its Casimir polynomial algebra. Joining two boxes requires multiplying their polynomials. Here \(i,j\) are the indices of two basis elements; the axes show \(x=i/N\) and \(y=j/N\). At the complete meridian \(s=0\), the product \(e_i e_j\) is zero whenever \(i+j\ge N\). For a generic displacement \(M=q_N^s\), those products become nonzero. The [multiplication theorem](../docs/papers/meridian-tangles.pdf) gives every coefficient and explains the special displacements where some coefficients vanish again. This is a picture of multiplication in a specified basis. The basis also changes with \(s\); its motion accounts for the nonzero first derivatives of the new coefficients. Keeping the complete basis fixed makes the first derivative of multiplication zero. Neither description by itself estimates the knot invariant, which also requires turns, summation over shared indices, and closure. [Vector figure](figures/moving-newton-products.svg) · [PDF](figures/moving-newton-products.pdf) · [Reproduction script](../experiments/audit_main_meridian_newton_algebra.py) ## Reflecting an index and combining two product junctions ![Three diagrams show a trace-difference bound, its reflected complete pairing, and the fused product junction with all five exterior branches retained.](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.png) The vertices represent multiplication and trace operations on tangle polynomials. In the left panel, a physical quarter-turn joins two equal indices \(h\). The left trace is the difference \(\delta\phi_s=\phi_s-\phi_0\) between its moving-meridian and complete values. The [Fourier estimate](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) bounds this difference after replacing \(h\) at that endpoint by \(r=N-1-h\). All other branches, denoted collectively by \(F\) and \(G\), remain attached. The middle panel therefore has complementary labels \(r+h=N-1\). Summing this positive complete pairing gives exactly the single trace \(\phi_0(FG)\), shown on the right. The three branches from the first junction and two from the second give the five displayed branches. Their order is inherited from the original ordered products. The first arrow is an upper estimate; the second is an algebra identity. Deleting the turn in this comparison can change the represented link. The [pressure theorem](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) proves that the new positive maximum is no larger than the original one, and a strict Fourier estimate controls the case of equal maxima. The invariant and the hyperbolic volume in the final theorem still belong to the original diagram. This comparison is what allows the [general component proof](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) to treat junctions of arbitrary valence. [SVG](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.svg) · [PDF](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/main-meridian-reflected-turn-fusion.tex) ## A separated example of the product tree ![Two product junctions are connected through a third junction carrying the original crossing-circle operator p_0. Each connecting edge applies a quarter-turn.](figures/separated-product-junctions.png) The four lower boxes represent the tangle operators \(h_1,\ldots,h_4\). The left junction multiplies \(h_1h_2\), and the right junction multiplies \(h_3h_4\). Apply the indicated quarter-turn \(T\) to each result, multiply them with the original operator \(p_0\), and take the prescribed closing trace. The formulas below the drawing define each leaf and retain its half-twist and auxiliary-circle color. This is a simple instance of the general theorem above. The two outer junctions carry no unturned crossing-circle operator; the central junction does. The [source growth theorem](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) allows any fixed finite tree with this separation property: whenever two product junctions are adjacent, at least one carries such an original operator. Their degrees and the size of the tree may be arbitrary. The largest source value over the allowed colors and a small neighborhood of the complete main meridian has exponential growth equal to the volume of the augmented complement. The crossing circles remain unfilled in this statement. [Vector figure](figures/separated-product-junctions.svg) · [PDF](figures/separated-product-junctions.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/separated-product-junctions.tex) ## The operations that build the knot diagram ![Three panels show the actual connections for stacking two four-ended tangles, rotating a tangle by a quarter-turn, and taking the cylindrical closure.](../manuscript/build/figures/tangle-construction.png) Each box contains a tangle whose internal strands have been suppressed. The black dots are its four ordered boundary endpoints. In the left panel, the product \(FG\) joins the two upper endpoints of \(F\) to the two lower endpoints of \(G\) in the displayed order. In the middle panel, the entire tangle rotates clockwise, carrying its endpoint labels with it. This is a geometric operation, not a renaming of an internal summation index. The right panel adds the two exterior arcs defining the cylindrical closure \(C(FG)\). These arcs determine the final endpoint pairing and hence whether the result is a knot or a link. The picture introduces the [manuscript's construction](chapters/manuscript.md); the theorem then imposes its explicit recursive and knot-pairing conditions. [PDF](../manuscript/build/figures/tangle-construction.pdf) · [TikZ source](../manuscript/figures/tangle-construction.tex) ## Moving a twist box and combining signed twists ![An integral twist box moves past a tangle with a specified half-turn; adjacent twist boxes then combine by addition.](figures/net-twist-reduction.png) Products are read from bottom to top. In the upper row, moving the integral box $R^a$ past $F$ replaces $F$ by $\rho^a(F)$, where $\rho$ is the half-turn about the stacking axis. An even $a$ leaves $F$ unchanged; an odd $a$ retains that half-turn. The four outside endpoints stay fixed. Rotating the inner tangle and interpolating through the empty end collars gives the isotopy proved in the [net-twist theorem](../docs/papers/conway-reductions.pdf). The lower row combines adjacent integral boxes: their signed weights add. Each surviving twist in the general reduction is the sum over a disjoint group of original boxes. The example $(a+2m)+(-2m)=a$ explains why large original magnitudes alone cannot supply the theorem's size condition. The condition is imposed on the final sums. The marked point and any ribbon framing are transported through the moves. [SVG](figures/net-twist-reduction.svg) · [PDF](figures/net-twist-reduction.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/net-twist-reduction.tex) ## Splitting a cap-closed stack ![A sphere around the lower tangle and its bottom cap meets the two interface strands. Cutting produces the cap closures of both boxes, with the summing arcs marked in amber.](figures/conway-cap-splitting.png) The product places $F$ below $G$. The sphere $S$ encloses $F$ and its lower cap; its only intersections with the link are the two marked points. Cutting along $S$ and capping on each side gives $D(F)$ and $D(G)$. The amber arcs specify how to reconstruct the original stack by a connected sum. When a factor is a link with several components, these specified arcs determine which components are joined. The [closure theorem](../docs/papers/conway-asymptotics.pdf) uses this operation after removing exact zero twist sums and when processing an initial cap closure. For a hyperbolic input with long surviving strict weights, the decomposition contains one strict factor and otherwise only unknots. To obtain the preferred longitude, add \(\sum_i p_i\ell_i^2\) meridians, where \(p_i\) is the filling coefficient and \(\ell_i\) is the linking number with crossing circle \(i\). The drawing uses one coefficient \(p=1\) and \(|\ell|=2\), so the orange vector differs by four meridians. The [longitude proof](../docs/papers/preferred-longitudes.pdf) derives this correction in the homology of the actual filled complement. [Vector drawing](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.svg) · [PDF](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/main-cusp-longitude-shear.tex) ## Connected trees of trivalent product junctions ![A path and a branching tree, each with degree three at every bare junction and with circle-operator attachments shown.](figures/trivalent-bare-components.svg) The open vertices are product junctions without a crossing-circle operator. Each has three incident branches, counting the attachments to the filled vertices. These graphs record tangle operations: consecutive unturned products have already been grouped, and every displayed edge is a physical quarter-turn. A fixed tree of any size is allowed by the [trivalent meridian theorem](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf). This is a retained special case: the [general component theorem](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) now also permits arbitrary higher-valence junctions and arbitrary mixtures of these valences. [Vector drawing](figures/trivalent-bare-components.svg) · [PDF](figures/trivalent-bare-components.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/trivalent-bare-components.tex) ## Turning weak balance into a strict remainder estimate ![A linear entropy gain exceeds the quadratic action cost at a small positive perturbation. The example constants in this plot are h*=E=1.](figures/weak-balance-gain.svg) The parameter \(t\) replaces each ordinary coefficient radius \(w_f\) by \(w_f^{1-t}\). The blue line is the lower bound \(t h_*\) for entropy loss in a noncentral term. The amber curve is the upper bound \(t^2\mathcal E/2\) for the cost to the full action. Their difference is positive for a sufficiently small fixed \(t>0\). The constants in the drawing illustrate the estimate; the [weak-balance theorem](chapters/results.md#an-unchanged-diagram-satisfying-weak-balance) defines them from the complete packing and proves the bounds. [SVG](figures/weak-balance-gain.svg) · [PDF](figures/weak-balance-gain.pdf) · [TikZ source](figures/weak-balance-gain.tex) ## Inserting a disk at an ordinary triangular face ![Two oppositely oriented attaching faces are removed; their retained partners form the new matched pair along ub.](../manuscript/build/figures/triangular-boundary-insertion.png) The boundary vertices are \(u,v,b\). The core's retained triangle has potential \(Q_c=Q(u,c,b)\), and the inserted disk's retained triangle has \(Q_a=Q(u,a,b)\). The removed face has potential \(T=Q(u,v,b)\). The final matched pair therefore has central rate \(Q_a+Q_c\). The disk's other triangles are suppressed in the drawing. The core retains the sole coefficient demands at \(u,v\); the proof accounts separately for the duplicated demand at \(b\). [The construction and proof](chapters/results.md#inserting-a-piece-at-an-ordinary-triangular-face) · [Vector PDF](../manuscript/build/figures/triangular-boundary-insertion.pdf) · [TikZ source](../manuscript/figures/triangular-boundary-insertion.tex) ## An ordinary face with small curvature ratios ![Two stellar subdivisions inside a triangle and the three matching edges in blue. The terminal face has vertices u, v and b2.](../manuscript/build/figures/ordinary-triangular-zigzag.png) The original boundary circles have curvatures \(u=2,v=1,b_0=2\). Insert \(b_1\), then \(b_2\), into the indicated successive faces. The labels \(A_j,B_j,F_j\) name triangles, while \(b_j\) names both a vertex and its curvature. The thick edges specify the pairs \(A_1\) with the old partner, \(B_1\) with \(B_2\), and \(F_2\) with \(A_2\). Repeating the construction at even length \(n\) gives \(b_n=3n^2+4\sqrt2\,n+2\), hence small terminal ratios \(u/b_n,v/b_n\). The protected mark lies outside this disk. [Vector PDF](../manuscript/build/figures/ordinary-triangular-zigzag.pdf) · [TikZ source](../manuscript/figures/ordinary-triangular-zigzag.tex)

title: Finite quantum invariants and hyperbolic volume
text: # Finite quantum invariants and hyperbolic volume The manuscripts are organized by the mathematical results they establish and the results they use. The dependency graph records those relations before assigning paper boundaries. A finite spectral theorem should be citable independently of an asymptotic theorem; a geometric filling construction should state precisely the information needed to compare its volume with a quantum action. The first reference edition collected finite quantum algebra, geometric constructions, asymptotic estimates, several volume families, and meridian and longitude results in 374 pages. Earlier tracked versions remain in Git history. The active [volume reference](../manuscript/README.md) now follows the same pure-source Conway proof as the 19-page application paper, using the same proof files. It retains the independent tree and planar volume families; standalone meridian and recurrence developments remain in their separate papers. The reference incorporates its [errata](../manuscript/ERRATA.md). Its length is not the length of one proof. The working limit of 30 pages per subject paper is an editorial constraint, not the principle for grouping results. ## The Conway paper and its supporting proofs These are manuscripts from the same project. They reorganize and expand the material developed in the reference; they are not independent external sources confirming its results. The division follows mathematical prerequisites. It is not a division of the reference into five equal parts. The reference also contains other volume families. The 19-page [Conway application](conway-asymptotics/README.md) uses five companion papers directly. Its geometry paper uses one further geometric result, so the complete reading route has six supporting manuscripts: | Supporting paper | What the Conway proof uses | | --- | --- | | [Finite spectral evaluation](filling-bounds/README.md) | The original invariant, its normalization, and full repeated-root crossing data. | | [Newton calculus](newton-calculus/README.md) | Exact tangle algebra, the primitive lattice and the strict stationary maximum. | | [Conway source bounds](conway-source-bounds/README.md) | The whole physical-source and complementary-source estimates. | | [Oscillatory fillings](oscillatory-fillings/README.md) | The nonzero whole filling asymptotic from the verified local and global source hypotheses. | | [Strict Conway geometry](strict-conway-geometry/README.md) | The marked knot complement, primitive fillings and absolute action-volume comparison. | | [Circle patterns and primitive fillings](marked-fillings/README.md) | The general completion and volume-differential results used by strict Conway geometry. | The first five are cited by the Conway paper; the last is used through strict geometry. The long reference is another account of overlapping material, rather than an additional seventh prerequisite. The collection check below verifies that the source files, compiled exports, PDFs and this reading route belong to the same current edition. The [exposition audit](../repro/CONWAY_SERIES_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) records the notation errors corrected, definitions added and duplicated argument removed in this revision. The seven manuscripts total 160 pages; the Conway article itself is 19 pages. Their mutual citations refer to one [fixed series edition](conway-series.json), so its theorem numbers can be used together. The [collection-wide revision](../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) covers the other fourteen papers and the 210-page reference. All twenty-one subject papers have now been revised; together they have 420 pages. The report explains the mathematical corrections and the statement-by-statement comparison with Lean. Build and check the collection from the repository root: ~~~sh python3 tools/build_papers.py python3 tools/build_dependency_graph.py python3 tools/check_paper_collection.py ~~~ The last command checks actual TeX inputs, published PDFs, compiled theorem labels and companion links. The [current record](../repro/results/paper-collection/summary.json) lists the six supporting manuscripts and their versions. These are consistency checks; the proofs remain in the papers themselves. [Explore the dependency graph](../docs/papers/dependencies.html). Each statement lists the results it uses, the reason for each use, and the exact place where the statement or proof can be found. Arrows run from prerequisites to their consumers. The overview groups related results; the detailed view retains the individual statements. The components are finer than the eventual papers. They are not a proposal for one paper per box. Overlapping arguments belong in the same article: the broader Conway source estimate has been incorporated into the existing source paper, with its earlier local estimates retained as separate exports. For example, finite spectral algebra and exact diagram evaluation now form one article, with the global contraction and normalization calculations included. The graph keeps them as separate components because the abstract norm theorem does not use that contraction argument. For a particular theorem, expand **The recorded proof route** in the graph. It lists that theorem and its earlier prerequisites in dependency order, with each shared result appearing once and its paper identified. This makes it possible to follow one argument without working through every subject in the collection. The route follows the named uses in the inventory; it does not automatically include every result from an article that supplies one lemma. The Casimir-source proof defines its finite action directly from the exact cofactor polynomial. The strict Conway volume argument uses only the pure source. The separate quarter-index paper proves the signed local result needed for its recurrence theorem. Three other distinctions determine the division. The classical filling construction does not need a nonzero quantum asymptotic; their comparison comes later, through the same marked critical equations. A nonzero geometric contribution does not bound the rest of the invariant. Finally, weak balance, protected triangular gluing, ordinary triangular insertion and the three-braid comparison provide different sufficient estimates for that remainder. Protected gluing does not require weak balance. The ordinary-insertion estimate has a separate proof; the construction of a common core for several inserted diagrams also uses protected gluing. ## The current drafts The twenty-one current drafts are organized by mathematical subject, not a decision to make twenty-one separate deposits. Each states its results, gives their proofs and identifies its numbered companion imports. Superseded editions have been removed after their necessary checks were moved into the current papers. Earlier tracked versions remain in Git history. The reading routes below identify which papers a result uses. The aggregate page count is not a measure of compression: separate papers repeat their conventions and references, and some supply arguments only sketched in the reference. The Newton, circle-tree and Casimir mergers state their common arguments once. The Conway application uses only the pure-source argument and states the Fourier, stationary-elimination and cost comparisons explicitly. The aim is to make each proof independently readable and citable while giving every shared argument one home. The [current audit](../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) records the completed review of these retained results. It distinguishes written analytic and geometric proofs, compiled internal implications, and finite diagnostics. The general volume conjecture remains open. Editorial consolidation and broader research do not enlarge the scope of the reviewed theorems. **Finite spectral evaluation and uniform filling bounds.** 28 pages. [TeX source](filling-bounds/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/filling-bounds.pdf) This paper asks how a fixed twisting operation acts on a polynomial of degree less than the root-of-unity level. It defines the functional at simple and repeated spectral roots, proves its norm bound, and explains why the canonical polynomial representative matters. It then proves the exact coefficient formula for a marked planar diagram constructed from a matched triangulated sphere. The proof includes the face variables, the integer support, the shifted grids at even levels, the cups and caps, and the single reduced cut. A finite Fourier and matrix calculation compares the result with the reduced Kashaev invariant, including the framing factor. These results supply the finite formulas used by later papers. They do not estimate the large-level invariant or identify an exponential rate with volume. **Newton calculus and stationary profiles of Conway tangles.** 28 pages. [TeX source](newton-calculus/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/newton-calculus.pdf) The paper develops the finite tangle algebra and the variational problem that it defines. Values and first derivatives are retained at repeated spectral roots. Exact formulas describe multiplication, a physical quarter-turn, marked closure, colored crossing circles and retained half twists. Their positive integer supports determine which ordered expressions admit a strict real state. For every such expression, the paper proves that the complete positive source has a unique interior maximum with negative definite Hessian. It derives the positive-source limit at both level parities by a uniform factorial estimate and an admissible integer approximation to that maximum. Fixing an exposed output gives a boundary profile; the paper calculates these profiles, their additive constants and their harmonic response law. Every original stationary leaf is at least one quarter. The completed-root subclass retains its stronger, strict two-sided bound. This account replaces the separate 18-page finite-calculus paper and 14-page strict-profile paper in the current reading route. The support, lattice, concavity and boundary arguments are now proved once. Both illustrations and the stronger special-case result remain. The paper proves a positive-source limit; estimates for signed fillings and a geometric interpretation of the limiting action are separate inputs. **Exact Newton calculus for tangles with a moving meridian.** 16 pages. [TeX source](meridian-tangles/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/meridian-tangles.pdf) The parameter of the main strand now varies while the quantum level stays fixed. The paper starts with the physical representation matrices and computes the partial trace before identifying its polynomial form. It proves all six oriented quarter-turn formulas and keeps the derivatives needed when spectral roots coincide, including at the additional collisions away from the complete meridian. The closing scalar and crossing phases are retained. The resulting tree formula sums every index and gives the same contraction regardless of the order in which vertices are eliminated. These are exact finite identities; they do not show which part of the sum dominates as the level grows. The comparison with Kashaev's original normalization imports the finite spectral paper at levels at least three; the algebraic identities hold from level two. **Spectral estimates for Conway tangle sources.** 30 pages. [TeX source](conway-source-bounds/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/conway-source-bounds.pdf) An auxiliary circle has an integer color between one and the quantum level. The theorem bounds the whole source uniformly over all these colors. It proves a strict exponential loss when any color stays a fixed fraction below the level, and also bounds the entire difference between the source and its central part. Theorem 1.1 treats any fixed strict expression with at least three leaves; Corollary 9.1 proves the two-leaf case separately. All retained half-twist signs and both level parities are included. The proof uses the value and first derivative at every repeated spectral root. An exact Fourier formula controls a colored circle followed by a turn, including its endpoint terms. Products between such turns are bounded by positive sums with their shared indices retained. Two rational supporting-plane inequalities and the absolute boundary profiles propagate these bounds through the whole expression. The older signed recurrence estimates remain available as local results; they are not premises of this global argument. The conclusion is a bound before filling, with no claim here about a nonzero filled invariant or its volume. **Marked geometry of strict Conway compositions.** 23 pages. [TeX source](strict-conway-geometry/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/strict-conway-geometry.pdf) This paper extends the geometric construction to every fixed expression passing the strict-state test. Four separate boundary-edge labels record which shaded triangles have already been attached. Tracking them through each product and turn proves convexity and identifies the assembled polyhedron with the original projection cut. The complete metric is therefore on the specified augmented link complement, with the original meridians and primitive disk longitudes. The complex face maps then give a marked deformation with complete main cusps. Solving the primitive filling equations in one neighborhood permits independently long twists of either sign. Smooth completion and a comparison of the same oriented fundamental chain identify the absolute filled volume. The local cell construction is included: supporting planes, dihedral angles, tetrahedron volumes and the entire ordered face maps are derived explicitly. The paper also computes the original collar translations and their deformed multipliers. The two earlier geometry papers are no longer prerequisites. The remaining companion imports are the stationary-profile theorem and the general primitive completion and volume differential.
