There is no quantum asymptotic premise. **Holomorphic source asymptotics and volume limits for strict Conway compositions.** 19 pages. [TeX source](conway-asymptotics/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/conway-asymptotics.pdf) This paper proves the nonzero asymptotic of the whole reduced invariant for every fixed strict Conway expression with at least two leaves, provided its actual strand pairing gives a knot and all signed twist powers are independently sufficiently long. The expression and the powers are fixed before the level tends to infinity. The exact expansion of each full crossing power in ordinary colored circles permits the analytic calculation to use the pure source. Canonical factorial interpolation agrees exactly with its finite coefficients, including at a quarter-index leaf. Summing over the original wire lattice gives a nonzero local Gaussian term. A second finite Fourier sum has a real local phase and a strict bound away from its maximum. The source bounds control the original physical error before the whole-period filling theorem is applied. Its nonzero amplitude supplies the lower bound needed for a volume limit. An explicit classical shear then identifies the quantum action with the primitive filling action on the actual retained half-twist partner. The calculation keeps its additive constant and the integer slope; odd powers are not treated as half-integral surgery on another partner. The canonical factorial lemma, exact pure leaf, primitive wire offsets, gate density, physical remainder and complex color bound are all stated on this one proof path. The pure source is Theorem 3.1 and its Fourier estimate is Proposition 3.2. The reference includes these same proof files. The separate quarter-index paper proves its own signed local source statements. Its recurrence theorem is not a premise of the volume result. **Moving-meridian source estimates for strict Conway tangles.** 21 pages. [TeX source](moving-meridian-sources/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/moving-meridian-sources.pdf) The exact moving-meridian formulas describe a finite sum. This paper proves which part of that sum dominates for a fixed strict expression, including connected groups of product junctions without crossing circles. The main meridian is $M=q_N^s$, where $q_N=e^{\pi i/N}$ and $s$ stays in a fixed disk $|s|\le R<1$ or a fixed compact subset of the upper half-plane. All original turns, crossing powers and shared indices remain in the calculation. A high Newton index at a deformed junction cannot always be bounded by the complete junction at the same index. The proof reflects that index and joins the two adjacent tensors using their exact pairing. It then compares the maximum of the positive action, called its pressure, for the whole connected group, retaining the constants supplied by its attached branches. Simultaneous high indices are treated together. This gives an exponentially smaller error before any filling contour is moved. Theorem 1.1 constructs the remaining primitive wire sum, proves its nonzero holomorphic Gaussian term and bounds it on the whole real angular domain. Theorem 1.2 evaluates all original filling traces for independently long fixed signed powers. It retains every Fourier charge, endpoint term and repeated-root derivative, and proves that the joint first charge is nonzero through both level parities. The estimates hold on the fixed translated nonreal parameter sets needed by a recurrence. Its imports are the finite moving-meridian calculus, the positive Newton product, the strict stationary profiles, Source Bounds Lemmas 2.1 and 7.2, and the canonical factorial of Conway Asymptotics Lemma 2.1. The signed quarter-index expansion is not required. The conclusion is an analytic source theorem; it makes no additional volume or longitude claim. **Ordered tangle reductions and long net twists.** 15 pages. [TeX source](conway-reductions/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/conway-reductions.pdf) Large written twists can cancel. This paper determines the signed sums that survive an ordered tangle construction before applying a long-twist theorem. It proves the actual collar isotopy that slides a twist box past a tangle, retaining the resulting rotation. An unrooted tree records which original labels fuse. The net blocks are independent of crossing parities, although their order and the recorded rotations can depend on those parities. A vanishing net weight needs a separate treatment: the turned zero box is a cup and a cap. Deleting it changes the closure, and a sphere through two connecting strands can split a cap-closed product. The proof tracks every component and shows that the resulting reduction terminates. For sufficiently long surviving strict weights, an elementary meridian-centralizer argument shows that a hyperbolic input has exactly one strict terminal factor and only unknot factors beside it. The input is isotopic to that strict knot, so the strict companion's volume limit applies. The paper gives a criterion on terminal factors and a sufficient condition on all nonzero subset sums. It supplies no numerical universal twist threshold and makes no claim about all short-twist arborescent knots. **Asymptotics of signed Newton coefficients near the quarter index.** 14 pages. [TeX source](quarter-index-asymptotics/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/quarter-index-asymptotics.pdf) At one quarter of the level, the two roots of the signed leaf recurrence have equal modulus. The earlier high-index contraction no longer applies across that point. This paper first reduces the actual matrix recurrence on a fixed complex domain, then chooses a short propagation interval whose relative action cannot amplify the exponentially small remainder. Both initial components come from the original finite sum. The resulting holomorphic interpolation retains the same nonzero amplitude and absolute shear action. A local Gaussian consequence states its wire-window and lattice hypotheses explicitly. These are local analytic results for use in broader Conway arguments; they do not bound a whole complementary source or prove a further knot-family volume theorem. **Spectral bounds and asymptotics of Casimir sources.** 26 pages. [TeX source](casimir-source-asymptotics/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/casimir-source-asymptotics.pdf) This paper studies one finite Casimir face polynomial and the coefficients obtained by sharing its variables across a diagram. Theorem 1.1 bounds its central and two one-sided degree sectors uniformly over the entire real spectral interval and all face phases. The proof retains the signed recurrence, both unused spectral products, the endpoint optimization, both level parities and variables fixed exactly at zero. These are local upper bounds; the one-sided conclusions do not assert coefficientwise domination. Theorem 8.1 considers the shared central coefficient on a simple triangulated sphere with a dual perfect matching and a marked nonmatching edge. Given stationary positive radii for the ordinary faces, it proves a nonzero holomorphic Gaussian expansion and a strict spectral gap away from the complete point. Its finite action comes directly from the exact cofactor polynomial. Positive matrices control the complementary face phases, and the proof uses one common radius vector and the primitive ordinary phase lattice. The two figures illustrate the local path partition and a shared coefficient on a tetrahedral sphere. Section 14 supplies the exact normalized input to the oscillatory filling theorem. The local estimates and the central expansion now use one set of definitions and a single proof of the common nodal comparison. The former 14-page local-bound paper and 12-page central-source paper remain combined in this account. A bound on the other degree sectors and a geometric identification of the action are still separate inputs to a volume theorem. **Oscillatory filling sums with independently long twists.** 12 pages. [TeX source](oscillatory-fillings/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/oscillatory-fillings.pdf) This paper addresses cancellation in the complete Fourier filling sum. Theorem 1.1 assumes a nonzero holomorphic expansion near the complete point and a strict bound for the shared source away from it. It then proves a nonzero asymptotic for the entire sum, including every nonzero integer Fourier charge and the original endpoints. The twist integers are fixed, independently signed and sufficiently large; their ratios are unrestricted. The proof estimates the infinite tail before localizing the remaining finitely many integrals. An elementary polynomial example verifies both hypotheses explicitly. For a knot source, construction of those hypotheses and identification of the critical action with volume remain separate theorems. **Circle patterns and primitive fillings of augmented links.** 20 pages. [TeX source](marked-fillings/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/marked-fillings.pdf) This is the classical geometric foundation. Starting from the marked matched sphere, the paper constructs its complete augmented exterior and one common deformed circle pattern. It calculates the peripheral paths through each original crossing disk, including retained half twists. The critical equations then specify a primitive filling slope. The proof constructs the smooth complete metric and compares its volume with the absolute critical action using the same fundamental chain. Theorem 1.1 holds for independently sufficiently long signed fillings; it does not assume a quantum asymptotic. Two drawings explain the single disk pairing and the logarithmic torus periods. The final corollary states the exact action comparison used by the quantum applications. **Positive octahedra and primitive fillings for trees of crossing circles.** 15 pages. [TeX source](circle-tree-geometry/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/circle-tree-geometry.pdf) For an ordered tree with an original crossing circle at every vertex, this paper builds the actual two-octahedron block for each edge and retains its ordered disk pages, half twists and primitive curves. With $d_v$ the vertex degree and $n_v$ the signed crossing power, the condition $\sqrt{d_v^2+n_v^2}\ge630$ at every vertex gives a positive cone path ending at a smooth complete filling, together with an absolute action-volume identity and quantitative core-length and volume-loss bounds. A more flexible criterion uses different radii at the vertices. The theorem allows zero power at a sufficiently high-degree vertex. Its only specialized companion import is the geometric foundation's local peripheral-volume differential, not that paper's long-filling existence theorem. It supplies geometry for subsequent asymptotic applications; it does not select a nonzero contribution to a quantum invariant. **Nonparabolic holonomy of trees of crossing circles.** 23 pages. [TeX source](nonparabolic-tree-geometry/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/nonparabolic-tree-geometry.pdf) This paper allows the main meridian holonomy to move away from its complete parabolic value. It constructs matrices for the original augmented-link group and proves the ordered conjugacy relations used to join the pieces. Selected eigenlines, half twists and primitive peripheral curves are followed through that construction. Agreement of matrix traces alone would not suffice. A second argument proves local rigidity on a positive ideal triangulation: one primitive peripheral logarithm per cusp gives local coordinates. The proof computes the edge-row rank, uses positivity to prove that the gluing Jacobian is invertible, and constructs inverse maps between shape parameters and decorated representations. With the auxiliary filling slopes fixed, the remaining coordinate is the main meridian. The circle-tree geometry paper supplies the actual positive filling point; the present paper identifies its coordinates and markings. These results neither determine the preferred longitude nor estimate a quantum source. **Preferred longitudes of Conway tree complements.** 30 pages. [TeX source](preferred-longitudes/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/preferred-longitudes.pdf) For each physical quarter-turn edge, the formula contributes $(M^2-X_e)/(1-M^2X_e)$, where $M$ is the meridian eigenvalue and $X_e$ is the edge shape coordinate. The proof first shows that the ratio between this product and the actual longitude depends only on $M$. It then constructs regular representations at every nonzero meridian value, excluding additional zeros and poles. The remaining factor is a monomial. A direct cusp-path calculation determines its exponent, including the writhe and surgery correction; a Seifert-surface frame argument fixes the determinant-one sign. The final section treats junctions without crossing circles. Inserting an identity box inside an auxiliary circle and filling that circle's meridian restores the original tangle. The proof follows the group words through this operation and eliminates the added angular variable from the classical action, including at the allowed half-label singularity. It imports finite Newton identities and the exact Fourier trace, but no quantum asymptotic. The conclusion identifies a geometric longitude germ. Applying it to a recurrence requires a separate all-orders expansion and an actual annihilating operator, as specified in the following paper. **Meridian expansions and classical symbols of quantum recurrences.** 14 pages. [TeX source](meridian-expansions/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/meridian-expansions.pdf) Theorem 1.1 proves every prescribed inverse-level order of the normalized meridian state. It covers three alternatives: strict Conway sources with independently long fixed powers, circle trees satisfying the summed criterion, and circle trees satisfying the directed criterion. These conditions are not imposed simultaneously. The directed proof keeps each subtree divided by its exact zero-parent value, so its constants and error margins survive the induction to higher orders. The permitted high-degree, zero-power cases remain included. The expansion holds for $M=q_N^s$ on fixed microscopic parameter sets and their required integer translates. At order $N^{-r}$, the logarithmic coefficient is an even polynomial in $s$ of degree at most $r+1$. Its highest-degree term is determined by the same stationary action on the original physical edges. The proof needs the nonzero source theorem and its full error bounds; a volume limit or a first-order meridian profile alone would not supply these estimates. Theorem 1.2 begins with a specified fixed nonzero operator that annihilates the **whole reduced meridian function at every sufficiently large integer level**. It retains the exact reduced/full meridian divisor and sign, recovers a two-variable formal identity from all the microscopic coefficients, and proves that the first nonzero classical symbol vanishes on the selected analytic germ. Corollary 8.1 identifies that germ with the preferred longitude by importing the separate nonparabolic and longitude theorems. For strict sources it uses the larger of the analytic and classical filling thresholds. These are distinct steps: the moving-source paper controls the entire finite sum and its errors; this paper constructs all orders and uses them in an operator identity. It does not prove that such an operator exists, identify the full A-polynomial or its multiplicities, or prove the full AJ conjecture. The expansion remains microscopic; it is not an asymptotic at a fixed meridian value different from one. **Volume asymptotics for trees of crossing circles.** 27 pages. [TeX source](circle-tree-volume/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/circle-tree-volume.pdf) For a fixed literal ordered tree of crossing circles, the paper proves two sufficient conditions for the volume limit of the whole reduced invariant. Both start from the same finite Newton contraction, keeping all first derivatives at repeated spectral roots. Sections 2–5 develop the common polynomial bounds, complex edge sum and exact Fourier trace. The diagram must close to one knot, with no component already closed inside an intermediate tangle. Its powers are fixed before the level tends to infinity. Theorem 1.1 assumes that the sum of $d_v/(d_v^2+n_v^2)$ is at most $2^{-25}$. Its proof estimates the joint Fourier integral, retaining all charges, endpoints and connecting contours. Other variables remain on real integrals or their physical grids while each infinite tail is bounded. The first charge has a nonzero coefficient at both level parities. Theorem 1.2 gives the explicit first centered microscopic meridian correction under this same summed condition, with the physical framing factor retained. Theorem 1.3 instead uses a finite directed criterion. It evaluates the contraction one vertex at a time and divides each subtree polynomial by its exact value at zero before taking the next trace. A conditional kernel estimate and a renewed real-domain bound close the induction without an exponential loss proportional to the depth. One consequence requires, independently at every vertex, degree at least $2^{28}$ or absolute signed crossing power at least $2^{27}$. Large-degree vertices may keep zero power. This proof gives a centered meridian ratio $1+O(N^{-1})$; the sharper correction in Theorem 1.2 is not assigned to it. The uniform local ratio condition $\max_v d_v/(d_v^2+n_v^2)\le2^{-120}$ is a direct corollary of the directed theorem: the elementary implication to the degree-or-twist alternative is written out in the reference's [local criterion](../manuscript/sections/08b-local-circle-messages.tex). There is no third quantum induction for that corollary. Each proof checks the hypotheses of the positive-octahedra companion, which identifies its selected action with the volume of the original knot complement. The two earlier 15-page asymptotic papers are combined here, with their shared definitions and Fourier calculation given once. Their separate sufficient conditions, proof arguments and three illustrations remain. The all-orders meridian and longitude results require the separate companion theorems. **Shared face estimates and triangular gluing for planar link diagrams.** 15 pages. [TeX source](planar-certificates/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/planar-certificates.pdf) The first criterion bounds every noncentral sector using one weight for all occurrences of each face. At the complete packing, non-strict balance suffices: convexity gives a linear local gain under a common change of weights, while stationarity bounds the total action cost quadratically. The second theorem joins two marked triangular faces and transports a certificate for every locally allowed sector string. It counts the shared boundary target once. A fully specified seventeen-region example and rational certificates show that this gluing theorem applies beyond weak balance. The full volume conclusion imports the five numbered foundation results; the source estimates and their transport are proved here. **Balanced circle packings from terminal tangle decorations.** 13 pages. [TeX source](terminal-decorations/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/terminal-decorations.pdf) Starting from a simple marked matched sphere, the paper gives an explicit finite number of terminal insertions on both sides of each original crossing circle. It proves their literal endpoint connections, constructs the packing extension while fixing all old circles, and solves the curvature recurrence. The resulting inequalities establish strict balance at every original and added region. Even stacks of odd terminal tangles preserve a chosen knot pairing, while generally changing the knot type. The strict-balance criterion in the planar paper then gives the full reduced Kashaev volume limit after independently sufficiently long fixed signed powers at all regions. The exact source, central asymptotic and primitive volume inputs are named foundation results; the insertion and all-length balance arguments are proved here. **Triangular insertion and volume limits for augmented diagrams.** 17 pages. [TeX source](triangular-insertion/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/triangular-insertion.pdf) This paper permits insertion at an ordinary triangular face, where all three boundary weights are positive. Its geometric theorem minimizes the disk action with those weights fixed and proves that the result is the removed triangle's potential plus a constant. It proves existence, uniqueness and the joint limit when two boundary weights vanish. The coefficient estimate then distinguishes a wholly central inserted piece from every other sector string, keeping each old face target once. Explicit circle chains supply small boundary ratios for any fixed finite list of certified inputs. The proof includes the exact recurrence and all-length inequalities; interval arithmetic checks the finitely many constants and certificate inequalities used in the example. **Volume limits for long alternating-generator three-braids.** 14 pages. [TeX source](three-braids/main.tex) · [PDF](../docs/papers/three-braids.pdf) This application concerns the ordinary closure of $$ \sigma_2^{n_0}\sigma_1^{n_1}\cdots \sigma_2^{n_{m-2}}\sigma_1^{n_{m-1}},\qquad m\ge6\text{ even}. $$ For each fixed number of factors, the signed powers are independently sufficiently large in magnitude, and their permutation must give a knot. The generators alternate; the crossing signs need not alternate. The braid axis is not a component. The paper develops the diagram, its circle packing and the estimates that control the entire remainder. It imports three explicitly stated results: the exact source identity, the uniform local coefficient estimates, and the nonzero geometric filling contribution with its absolute volume calibration. Those dependencies are substantial. The finite input and local upper bounds are proved in the finite spectral and Casimir-source papers. The filling-sum paper proves the analytic implication once its local expansion and global gap are supplied. The Casimir-source paper constructs that expansion and gap under its stated stationary-radius hypothesis. The circle-pattern paper supplies the marked geometric volume comparison. The application now cites numbered statements in these companion papers, and checks their common normalization and hypotheses. ## Reading routes and retained boundaries The volume-limit and recurrence arguments use different outputs of the shared foundations. For a strict Conway volume limit, follow the finite Newton calculus and stationary profiles, the complete-source estimates, the strict marked geometry, and the strict volume theorem in Conway Asymptotics. For a meridian expansion, the moving finite calculus leads instead to the moving-source comparison and its nonzero joint filling term. Meridian Expansions then supplies every inverse-level order. Its final geometric-factor corollary adds the nonparabolic and preferred longitude results; its analytic expansion does not depend on them. For the circle-tree alternatives, read the common finite and edge estimates in Sections 2–5 of **Volume asymptotics for trees of crossing circles**, then follow Section 6 for the summed condition or Section 7 for the directed condition. Each route checks its own geometric threshold before invoking the primitive circle-tree filling theorem. The directed criterion is not inferred from the summed one, and neither requires the strict Conway long-power hypothesis. Both routes supply the source estimates used by Meridian Expansions. The dependency graph retains their separate assumptions and theorem uses within the combined article. The local ratio test uses the directed route. The summed route keeps its explicit first microscopic correction; the directed and local statements give the centered ratio $1+O(N^{-1})$. The separate $L_v\ge630$ theorem constructs the positive filled metric and is not a quantum source estimate. For the matched-sphere applications, **Spectral bounds and asymptotics of Casimir sources** gives the local sector estimates in Sections 1–7. Sections 8–13 prove the shared central expansion and spectral gap, and Section 14 passes their normalization to the oscillatory filling theorem. The circle-pattern paper supplies stationary radii and the marked volume comparison. The planar certificate, terminal-decoration, triangular-insertion and three-braid papers prove their own sufficient estimates for the full complementary source. A central Gaussian alone does not supply those estimates. The reference manuscript and the 19-page application now share the same strict pure-source proof. An elementary closing child and a leaf at one quarter are allowed. The theorem retains strict feasibility, the knot component test and independently long fixed fillings. A further topological reduction can change the written expression before this theorem is applied. The tangle-reduction paper supplies that step: large written twists may cancel to a small net twist, and a vanishing net twist may change the closure or produce additional components. The proof of those isotopies is distinct from the strict asymptotic theorem. For a citation between papers, the exporting paper must state a numbered theorem with its normalization, degree restrictions, level parity and uniformity assumptions. The importing paper must name that theorem and check those hypotheses. A reference to a folder of calculations is not a substitute. The current drafts include the strict Conway volume theorem, the summed and directed circle-tree criteria, the local quarter-index expansion, and the moving-source, all-orders and preferred-longitude arguments, together with their finite and geometric foundations. The conditional operator conclusion retains its all-level hypothesis. Neither it nor the restricted volume theorems resolve the complementary source estimate for every unchanged planar diagram. The illustrated guide retains broader approaches and unsuccessful comparisons in its methods chapters. Its manuscript chapter describes the current volume proofs. Earlier tracked editions remain in Git history. ## Lean statements used by the current volume account The [active formalization](../formal-real/README.md) proves the following retained statements. [CoefficientGram](../formal-real/CoefficientGram.lean) proves the synthesis Gram form, kernel and closing upper bound; [FourierHermite](../formal-real/FourierHermite.lean) proves shifted reconstruction, Parseval and the full value/normal coefficient mass bound at $N\ge2$; and [StationaryElimination](../formal-real/StationaryElimination.lean) proves the complex bilinear Schur block algebra. [ConwayAssembly](../formal-real/ConwayAssembly.lean) uses the actual crossing coefficients to bound the entire coherent color error, then applies [RealTransfer](../formal-real/RealTransfer.lean) to a nonzero complex packet with its finite action retained. The exact source identity, contour estimates, nonzero packet and marked volume equality remain explicit inputs. The [coverage map](../formal/coverage.json) records the manuscript anchors and the [manuscript and logic audit](../repro/MANUSCRIPT_AND_LOGIC_AUDIT_2026-11-25.md) records the replay. ## Building and reproducing the papers With TeX Live or MacTeX, `latexmk`, Python and PyMuPDF installed, run from the repository root: ```sh python3 tools/build_papers.py ``` Use a directory name to build just one paper, for example `python3 tools/build_papers.py filling-bounds`. The command checks the page limit, unresolved references and overfull boxes, then copies the PDFs and their source-hash records to `docs/papers/`. Add `--no-publish` to keep the outputs in each paper's `build/` directory. These are typesetting checks, not mathematical verification. Rebuild the dependency graph with: ```sh python3 tools/build_dependency_graph.py ``` Its source is `papers/dependencies.json`. The command verifies the named source locations, checks statement, component and article graphs for cycles, and refuses a recorded completed result that imports an open result. Each article import has a path through named theorem uses; the builder checks that path and its declared ownership. Acyclic statements can become circular when grouped into papers, so this is a separate check. It generates the interactive graph, vector overview and source-hash record in `docs/papers/`. These checks validate the declared dependency record, not the proofs at its nodes or the completeness of the inventory. The article-cycle and witness controls run with `python3 -I tools/test_dependency_graph.py`. Replay the papers' finite identities and rational certificate constants with one command: ```sh python3 repro/check_paper_algebra.py --output repro/results/paper-collection/finite ``` The finite check runner requires SymPy, python-flint and NumPy. It saves a separate record and log for each registered check group, and stops on failure. The planar certificate groups retain their supporting interval records in separate subdirectories. The Newton group compares physical matrix turns, traces, circle coefficients and crossing normals with the stated formulas over exact finite fields. The terminal group checks symbolic curvature identities, oriented insertions and literal pairing graphs; its finite count examples supplement the written construction for every length. The circle-tree group checks rational seam and peripheral identities and the displayed numerical bounds. The constant verifier uses outward rational bounds with explicit series remainders. The argument for every even number of braid factors is written in the three-braid paper; it is not inferred from computations for finitely many braid lengths. The finite checks complement the written proofs of the analytic estimates and geometric constructions. The moving-source group checks full Fourier traces, Newton Laurent coefficients, reflected pairings, fusion and the odd-node projector. The meridian-expansion group checks the exact reduced/full gauge, rational sine identities and recovery of formal coefficients, with controls showing what a finite jet cannot determine. These calculations do not prove uniform analytic remainders, existence of an annihilator, or a geometric identification from sampled levels. The combined Casimir-source and filling-sum checks can also be run separately: ~~~sh python3 papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/check.py --output repro/results/casimir-source-asymptotics python3 papers/oscillatory-fillings/check.py --output repro/results/oscillatory-fillings.json ~~~ These require SymPy. They check finite polynomial identities and algebraic normalizations, with their exact scope recorded in the output. They do not replace the written uniform estimates, contour arguments or asymptotic proofs.

title: Corrections to the first reference edition
text: # Corrections to the first reference edition These corrections apply to the 374-page [1 November reference PDF](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/e3c75b2903498cc87c7465eb8e2047e527113276/docs/papers/conway-composition.pdf), whose SHA-256 is `e5b384c8fd103c1e1e7209ac97b3862b71abe227f8dc82e49dc0465bf4ae5437`. That PDF and its TeX sources are available in the linked Git commit. The 25 November expository revision incorporates both corrections below. This record continues to identify the version to which earlier page references apply. ## Appendix D: the derivative of the filling equations In Section D.4.3, printed page 127 (page 140 of the PDF), the Jacobian of the equations \[ V_\ell(\chi)+r_\ell U_\ell(\chi)=-2\pi i r_\ell \] with respect to \(\chi\), at \(\chi=r=0\), is \[ -2\pi i\,\operatorname{diag}(\tau_\ell), \] not the printed \(-4\pi i\,\operatorname{diag}(\tau_\ell)\). Here \(U_\ell=-2\pi i\chi_\ell\), \(V_\ell=-2\partial_{\chi_\ell}\Phi_\varepsilon\), and \(\tau_\ell=2ic_\ell/(1-\varepsilon_\ell ic_\ell)\), where \(c_\ell=\cot(\pi a_\ell)\). Direct differentiation of the leaf potential gives \[ \partial_{\chi_\ell}^2\Phi_\varepsilon(0) =\frac{-2\pi c_\ell}{1-\varepsilon_\ell ic_\ell} =\pi i\tau_\ell. \] The mixed derivatives between an internal edge variable and a leaf deformation vanish at the complete point. Eliminating the internal stationary variables therefore leaves this diagonal Hessian unchanged. Differentiating \(V=-2\nabla\Phi_\varepsilon\) yields the corrected Jacobian. This also agrees with the complete Hessian in equation (B.41). The matrix remains invertible because each \(\operatorname{Im}\tau_\ell\) is positive. The implicit-function argument and its conclusion about independently sufficiently long signed filling slopes are unchanged. This correction concerns that classical deformation argument; it supplies no estimate for the quantum invariant. ## Appendix R: the unchanged matched pair in the explicit core In Section R.8, printed page 356 (page 369 of the PDF), immediately after equation (R.39), the sentence “The other unchanged region has positive outer weights” describes the wrong support. The outer weights are \((2,0)\), and the two middle weights are \((1,1)\). This is the pair of triangles \(T_3,Z_3\), whose common edge is \(v_3v_0\). Equation (R.36) assigns curvatures \(v_3=2\), \(v_0=0\), and \(P=S=1\). The required strict inequalities still hold, with quantitative bounds. To see this directly, use the triangle potential \(Q\) defined in equation (R.3), and write \[ f(t)=\frac{\Lambda(\pi t)+\Lambda(\pi/2-\pi t)}{\pi}, \qquad g=f(1/4), \qquad \Lambda(s)=-\int_0^s\log(2\sin r)\,dr. \] For weights \((2,1,0)\), the admissible loads \((1/4,1/4,0)\) give \[ Q(2,1,0)\ge 2g+\tfrac14\log2. \] Both triangles have those weights, so their complete rate satisfies \(X=2Q(2,1,0)\ge4g+\tfrac12\log2\). Each overloaded middle has weight \(h=1\). Its pure-middle comparison is therefore \(X-\log h=X\), and its mixed comparison satisfies \[ Q(2,h,0)-\tfrac12\log h \ge 2g+\tfrac14\log2>\frac3{50}. \] The last inequality follows already from the stronger comparison \(2g-\tfrac34\log2>3/50\) in (R.39). Thus this correction preserves the stated uniform core gap and the insertion theorem. It changes neither the matching nor the protected zero weight. The corrected description and its branch bounds appear in Section 9 of [the triangular-insertion paper](../papers/triangular-insertion/main.tex), after equation (9.5) and in the table following (9.10).

title: A-polynomials, selected periods and the volume problem
text: # A-polynomials, selected periods and the volume problem 25 November 2026. This page distinguishes the algebraic objects in the research program. The [papers](../papers/README.md) state the proved results and their hypotheses. ## A classical branch does not select a quantum solution An algebraic gluing curve records possible peripheral eigenvalues \((M,L)\). A recurrence relates consecutive terms of a sequence. Neither datum alone specifies the scalar obtained by the original knot evaluation. Initial values, the prescribed closing, normalization and derivative data at singular steps can all be needed to select it. The [all-level period note](actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) explains these additional data in its recurrence formulation. Recovering the same invariant transfers an already established limit for a covered knot. It does not prove a volume theorem for every quantization of a classical curve. The [meridian-expansion paper](../papers/meridian-expansions/README.md) proves classical-symbol divisibility under a specified genuine annihilating operator. It does not construct that operator. The [preferred-longitude paper](../papers/preferred-longitudes/README.md) supplies the geometric peripheral comparison under its stated conditions. A selected irreducible factor and a full recurrence ideal are different conclusions. ## Why the period and torsor viewpoint remains useful A change of coordinates can preserve an algebraic equation while changing a scalar factor, a boundary functional or a chosen section. Those data must be retained. The [initialized coideal period](research_coideal_normalized_marked_period.md) constructs a source and marked observation with explicit commuting unipotent changes between neighboring-height presentations. It is finite algebra at the prescribed level; it does not identify a knot peripheral germ or geometric integration cycle. The [coideal Fourier compiler](research_coideal_full_fourier_crossing.md) retains the crossing and cup source in orthogonal coordinates. The [cyclic Hardy comparison](research_cyclic_atom_hardy_head_comparison.md) controls actual scalar functions and their finite coefficient projections. A lower bound for the original marked closure still requires a further argument. ## The unresolved implication To cross arbitrary short partial fillings, one must show that the original selected source has the required geometric exponential rate, with its prescribed closing and cancellation retained. A local algebraic critical point, nonzero abstract solution or positive ambient norm is insufficient. The [research status](research_finite_exceptions_progress.md) states the remaining theorem and the orthogonal variational reduction. The previous page mixed dated source constructions with changing progress reports. Its complete text is in the [pre-cleanup snapshot](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/a_polynomial_torsor_status.md). The illustrated [algebraic approaches](../book/chapters/algebraic.md) give the broader conceptual discussion and references.

title: Zeros of the ADO meridian state approach the complete point
status: Nearby zeros, the required boundary factor and exact regularization
text:
# Zeros of the ADO meridian state approach the complete point 31 October 2026. For a knot whose Kashaev invariant has positive exponential growth, the reduced ADO meridian state takes exponentially different values at two points separated by order $1/N$. Its value at the complete point is the Kashaev invariant, whereas its value one quantum shift away is exactly $1$. The state is a Laurent polynomial whose degree grows at most linearly with $N$. Together these facts force actual zeros within order $1/N$ of the complete point. This note proves an explicit bound on that distance, retaining the marked meridian coordinate and the full modified-dimension factor. The obstruction to a uniform nonzero scalar asymptotic expression across the two points was already described in the [formal A-curve period discussion](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/formal_a_curve_period_torsor.md#the-actual-peripheral-normalization-includes-a-difference-constant) and the [regular-period construction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/regularized_kashaev_period.md). The quantitative zero bound below makes that obstruction precise for the actual knot state. It does not identify a classical A-polynomial factor. The canonical regular remainder, defined by subtracting the ordinary-color polar data, remains a separate candidate for such a comparison. ## 1. The actual state and its two nearby values Fix a zero-framed knot $K$ for which the actual all-level volume limit is known. Write $K_N(K)$ for its reduced Kashaev invariant, with the unknot normalized to $1$, and assume \[ q_N=e^{\pi i/N},\qquad \lim_{N	o\infty} rac1N\log|K_N(K)| =v= rac{V}{2\pi}>0. 	ag{1} \] For example, this applies to the fixed long-twist knots covered by the [strict Conway-tree theorem](../papers/conway-asymptotics/README.md) and the [ordered net-twist theorem](../papers/conway-reductions/README.md). In either application, the knot and its integer twist weights are fixed before $N$ tends to infinity. The argument below otherwise uses no restriction on the knot presentation. Let $F_N(M)$ be its reduced ADO state. It is the zero-framed cut-tangle scalar, equivalently the full modified-trace invariant divided by the modified dimension. The relation between the unrolled color parameter $\alpha$, its exponential $x$, and the marked meridian eigenvalue $M$ is \[ x=q_N^\alpha,\qquad M=-q_Nx. 	ag{2} \] Thus $\alpha=N-1$ gives $M=1$. The exact [ADO normalization](kashaev_ado_pointing.md) and [integer-color specialization](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/root_orbit_pointing.md) give \[ F_N(-q_N^j)=C_j(q_N)\quad(1\le j\le N),\qquad F_N(1)=K_N(K),\qquad C_1(q)=1. 	ag{3} \] Here $C_j$ denotes the reduced $j$-dimensional ordinary quantum-group invariant of the same knot. In particular, its one-dimensional value is $1$. The [squared-meridian descent](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/even_meridian_norm_descent.md) proves the exact identity \[ F_N(-M)=F_N(M) \qquad(N\ge2). 	ag{4} \] There is no even-level exception in (4). To recall why the normalization introduces no sign, choose a $b$-strand braid of writhe $w$ closing to $K$. Its closure has one component, so the braid permutation is a $b$-cycle and $w\equiv b-1\pmod2$. The integer $\kappa_D=w-b+1$ is therefore even. In the exact meridian-shift insertion, all crossing factors depend on $Y=M^2$. Their product over the $N$ shifts $Y\mapsto q_N^2Y$ is $1$: the numerator and denominator products cancel by $\prod_{r=0}^{N-1}(1-q_N^{2r}z)=1-z^N$. The remaining framing factor has cyclic product $q_N^{-N\kappa_D}=1$. After $N$ shifts, $M$ has become $-M$, proving (4). At a vanishing numerator or denominator this is the cancelled rational identity, not a quotient of separately evaluated zeros. Equations (3) and (4) now imply, exactly at every level, \[ F_N(q_N)=F_N(-q_N)=1. 	ag{5} \] For sufficiently large $N$, (1) also gives $K_N(K)
e0$. Consequently \[  rac{F_N(q_N)}{F_N(1)}= rac1{K_N(K)},\qquad \lim_{N	o\infty} rac1N \log\left| rac{F_N(q_N)}{F_N(1)}ight|=-v. 	ag{6} \] The shift in (6) is the actual meridian shift $M\mapsto q_NM$. Writing $F_N(M)=f_N(Y)$ and $Q_N=q_N^2$, its squared-coordinate form is $Y\mapsto Q_NY$, with $f_N(Q_N)=1$. ## 2. A two-value estimate for Laurent polynomials The following elementary estimate explains why a degree bound matters. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial $P(z)=\sum_{j=m}^{n}a_jz^j$ with $a_ma_n
e0$, call $D=n-m$ its exponent spread. Multiplication by a Laurent monomial changes neither this spread nor the nonzero roots. **Two-value lemma.** Suppose $z_0,z_1
e0$ have equal modulus, $P(z_0)P(z_1)
e0$, and \[ A=\left| rac{P(z_0)}{P(z_1)}ight|>1,\qquad \delta=|z_1-z_0|. 	ag{7} \] Then $D>0$, and some nonzero root of $P$ lies at distance at most \[  rac{\delta}{1-A^{-1/D}} 	ag{8} \] from $z_0$. To prove this, factor the ordinary polynomial obtained by removing the lowest Laurent monomial: \[ z^{-m}P(z)=a_n\prod_{j=1}^{D}(z-\zeta_j). 	ag{9} \] Its constant coefficient is nonzero, so all $\zeta_j$ are nonzero. If $D=0$, the equal moduli of $z_0$ and $z_1$ would give $A=1$. For $D>0$, put $r=\min_j|z_0-\zeta_j|$. If $r\le\delta$, (8) already follows. Otherwise, the Laurent monomial has modulus ratio $1$, and the triangle inequality gives \[  egin{aligned} -\log A &=\sum_{j=1}^{D}\log  rac{|z_1-\zeta_j|}{|z_0-\zeta_j|}\ &\ge D\log\left(1- rac{\delta}{r}ight). \end{aligned} 	ag{10} \] Solving (10) for $r$ proves (8). The proof retains root multiplicities and requires no information about their angles or simplicity. A larger upper bound for $D$ may replace $D$ in (8), giving a weaker valid bound. ## 3. The finite crossing matrices give a linear degree bound Fix any braid presentation of $K$ with $b$ strands and $L$ crossings. Let $L_+$ and $L_-$ count the positive and negative crossings, so $L=L_++L_-$ and $w=L_+-L_-$. Put $d=N-1$. The [finite cut-state construction](finite_sum_annihilator.md) retains all indices in $\{0,\ldots,d\}$. The explicit [positive and negative crossing entries](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/relative_octahedral_period.md#exact-formulas-for-both-actual-crossings) make their color dependence particularly transparent. After stripping the common Cartan scalar, the positive entry with input indices $(a,b)$ and shift $k$ is an $x$-independent coefficient times \[ x^{-a-b-k}(Qx^2/Q^a;Q)_k, \qquad 0\le k\le\min(a,d-b),\qquad Q=q_N^2. 	ag{11} \] Here $(u;Q)_k=\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}(1-uQ^r)$. The negative entry is an $x$-independent coefficient times \[ x^{a+b-k}(Qx^2/Q^b;Q)_k, \qquad 0\le k\le\min(b,d-a). 	ag{12} \] These are the actual checked crossings; the two shift cutoffs are different and have both been retained. Expanding the finite products in (11) and (12) gives the respective exponent intervals \[  egin{aligned} [-a-b-k,-a-b+k]&\subset[-2d,0],\ [a+b-k,a+b+k]&\subset[0,2d]. \end{aligned} 	ag{13} \] For example, in the positive case $k\le d-b$ bounds $a+b+k$ by $2d$, while $k\le a$ bounds $-a-b+k$ by $0$. The negative case uses $k\le d-a$ and $k\le b$. The factorial denominators depend only on $q_N$, are nonzero for their actual indices below $N$, and introduce no color denominator. The common Cartan scalars cancel against the zero-framing twist correction. What remains of that correction is $x^{wd}$. Each of the $b-1$ pivotal traces contributes $x^{-d}$ times an $x$-independent factor. Thus the common remaining monomial is $x^{d(w-b+1)}$. Products and finite sums cannot enlarge the exponent interval. After including this monomial, the support of the actual reduced state lies in \[ [-d(L+b-1),\ d(L-b+1)]. 	ag{14} \] The substitution $x=-q_N^{-1}M$ only multiplies coefficients by nonzero constants. It leaves (14) unchanged. In particular the actual Laurent spread, after any cancellations, satisfies \[ D_N\le2L(N-1),\qquad D_N^Y\le L(N-1). 	ag{15} \] The second bound is for $f_N(Y)$: exact evenness (4) divides every actual exponent and its spread by two. These estimates hold at both parities and do not require a bound on the number of summands. For the knots in (1), $L>0$ and both spreads are positive for sufficiently large $N$, because a Laurent monomial cannot satisfy (6). ## 4. A quantitative zero bound at the complete point Let \[ r_N=\min\{|z-1|:z
e0,\ F_N(z)=0\},\qquad \delta_N=|q_N-1|=2\sin rac{\pi}{2N}. 	ag{16} \] For all sufficiently large $N$, the two-value lemma applied at $1$ and $q_N$ gives \[ r_N\le  rac{\delta_N}{1-|K_N(K)|^{-1/D_N}} \le rac{\delta_N} {1-|K_N(K)|^{-1/[2L(N-1)]}}. 	ag{17} \] In particular, \[ \limsup_{N	o\infty}Nr_N \le rac{\pi}{1-\exp(-V/(4\pi L))}. 	ag{18} \] The squared-meridian coordinate improves the constant. Apply the same lemma to $f_N$ at $1$ and $Q_N$. Its spread is at most $L(N-1)$, and $|Q_N-1|\sim2\pi/N$. Hence it has a zero $\zeta_N$ with \[ \limsup_{N	o\infty}N|\zeta_N-1| \le rac{2\pi}{1-\exp(-V/(2\pi L))}. 	ag{19} \] Choose the square root $z_N$ of $\zeta_N$ that tends to $1$. It is a zero of $F_N$, and $|z_N-1|=|\zeta_N-1|/|z_N+1|$, where $|z_N+1|	o2$. We obtain the stronger estimate \[  oxed{\displaystyle \limsup_{N	o\infty}Nr_N \le rac{\pi}{1-\exp(-V/(2\pi L))}.} 	ag{20} \] Every fixed braid presentation supplies a valid $L$. This is a bound on zeros of the actual reduced knot state, not an auxiliary polynomial chosen to have the same complete value. It does not give their number in the shrinking disk, their limiting directions, or a classical geometric interpretation of their factors. ## 5. Consequences for shift ratios and the full normalization There is no fixed complex neighborhood of $M=1$ on which all sufficiently large $F_N$ are nonvanishing. Moreover, (6) directly rules out a finite nonzero limit of $F_N(q_NM)/F_N(M)$ at $M=1$. These are distinct assertions: a zero of $F_N$ need not be a pole of that quotient, because a shifted numerator zero may cancel it. For example, a scalar WKB expression on a fixed neighborhood of $1$ would require a holomorphic action $S$ and nonvanishing amplitudes $a_N$ converging locally uniformly to a nonzero holomorphic function, with \[ F_N(M)=c_N e^{NS(M)}a_N(M),\qquad c_N
e0. 	ag{21} \] Such an expression would imply $F_N(q_N)/F_N(1)	o\exp(\pi iS'(1))
e0$, contradicting (6). It is also incompatible with (20). This does not exclude expressions on domains omitting the complete point, or with level-dependent divisors explicitly retained. A scalar normalization independent of $M$ changes neither the roots nor the ratio in (6). A fixed rational or algebraic gauge, on a branch that is holomorphic and nonzero near $(q,M)=(1,1)$, also cannot remove the roots and has ratio tending to $1$ between the two points. Gauges with moving poles or zeros require separate analysis. The actual full modified-trace state is an important example of the latter case. Its exact factor is \[ \mathcal N_N(M)=d_N(M)F_N(M),\qquad d_N(M)=\eta_N rac{M-M^{-1}}{M^N-M^{-N}},\qquad \eta_N=i^{N+3},\qquad d_N(1)=\eta_N/N. 	ag{22} \] At $M=q_N$ the denominator in (22) has derivative $-2Nq_N^{-1}$. Since $F_N(q_N)=1$, the full state has the uncancelled simple pole \[ \operatorname{Res}_{M=q_N}\mathcal N_N(M) = rac{\eta_N(1-q_N^2)}{2N}
e0 \qquad(N\ge2). 	ag{23} \] Its value at $M=1$ is nevertheless the regular whole-germ value $\eta_NK_N(K)/N$. Thus the full normalization does not supply a holomorphic nonzero scalar packet across these points either. For sufficiently large $N$, its shift quotient has a pole at $M=1$, consistent with the exact normalization gauge \[  rac{d_N(q_NM)}{d_N(M)} =-q_N^{-1} rac{q_N^2M^2-1}{M^2-1}. 	ag{24} \] ## 6. The canonical regular remainder is a different object The [regular-period construction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/regularized_kashaev_period.md) subtracts prescribed polar data, rather than applying a nonzero scalar normalization. Let $P_N^{\mathrm{ord}}$ be the unique polynomial of degree at most $N-2$ taking the values $C_j(q_N)$ at $Q_N^j$ for $1\le j<N$. Define \[ S_N(Y)= rac{Y^N-1}{Y-1},\qquad R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}(Y) = rac{f_N(Y)-P_N^{\mathrm{ord}}(Y)}{S_N(Y)}. 	ag{25} \] All roots of $S_N$ are simple ordinary-color points. The numerator vanishes there, so $R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is Laurent polynomial. In the full state this gives the exact separation \[ \mathcal N_N(M) =\eta_NM^{N-1}R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}(M^2) +\eta_NM^{N-1} rac{P_N^{\mathrm{ord}}(M^2)}{S_N(M^2)}. 	ag{26} \] The second term contains all finite nonzero polar principal parts. The ordinary-color bound in the same construction gives $|P_N^{\mathrm{ord}}(1)/N|=O_K(N^{b-1})$. Therefore \[ R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}(1) = rac{K_N(K)-P_N^{\mathrm{ord}}(1)}{N},\qquad \lim_{N	o\infty} rac1N\log|R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}(1)|=v. 	ag{27} \] Its first shifted value is not the ordinary anchor $1$. It is instead \[ R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}(Q_N) = rac{f_N'(Q_N)-(P_N^{\mathrm{ord}})'(Q_N)}{S_N'(Q_N)}. 	ag{28} \] Thus the two-value obstruction proved for $F_N$ does not automatically apply to $R_N^{\mathrm{reg}}$. Nor does (27) prove a neighborhood asymptotic or a shift-ratio limit for this remainder. A specified actual all-level annihilator gives the existing affine equation for the regular remainder, after its fixed rational gauge and denominator clearing. Its inhomogeneous term has fixed Laurent support and polynomially bounded coefficients. One possible next theorem would provide a locally uniform, nonzero shift-ratio limit for this actual regular state together with a locally uniform exponential lower bound. On a domain avoiding the fixed coefficient poles, such bounds would make the inhomogeneous term negligible after division by the state. The limiting ratio would then satisfy the homogeneous classical symbol. Its identification with the preferred geometric longitude would still require the marked geometric comparison. The complete scalar volume theorem and the [pointed quantum A-period and Gram formulas](actual_conway_pointed_quantum_a_volume.md) remain valid. What changes is the proposed neighborhood statement: the reduced state has the exponential one-step drop and nearby zeros proved above, and the full state has a nearby pole. The canonical regular remainder must be studied with its own affine equation and its ordinary-color subtraction intact. ## 7. The boundary factor of every polynomial annihilator The same ordinary-color bounds give an exact algebraic restriction on the recurrence. The squared-meridian version is the necessity theorem in [the peripheral normal-period note](peripheral_normal_period.md#2-a-nonzero-complete-column-forces-polynomial-growth). For the positive-volume knots in (1), its hypothesis is now established. Here is the corresponding statement without requiring an even operator. Let \[ P=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_i(q,M)T^i,\qquad TM=qMT,\qquad a_i\in\mathbb C[q^{\pm1},M^{\pm1}] 	ag{29} \] be any fixed genuine all-level annihilator of the reduced state, after clearing its rational denominators. Then \[ (q^{2i}M^2-1)\mid a_i(q,M)\quad(0\le i\le d),\qquad P=B(M^2-1) 	ag{30} \] for a polynomial quantum-torus operator $B$. This conclusion concerns all annihilators in the specified integral ring, not just a chosen minimal generator. Fix $i$ and evaluate the exact annihilation equation at $M=\pm q_N^{-i}$, with $N>d$. The $i$th term contains $F_N(\pm1)=K_N(K)$. Every other term is an ordinary-color value. If $k=j-i>0$, evenness and (3) give $F_N(\pm q_N^k)=C_k(q_N)$. If $k<0$, use $q_N^N=-1$ to obtain $F_N(\pm q_N^k)=C_{N+k}(q_N)$. All these indices lie between $1$ and $N-1$. The fixed-braid bound is uniform over that entire range: $|C_r(q_N)|\le(N/2)^{b-1}$. The fixed Laurent coefficients in (29) are bounded on these unit-circle trajectories. Hence the annihilation equation gives \[ |a_i(q_N,\pm q_N^{-i})|\,|K_N(K)|\le C_PN^{b-1}. 	ag{31} \] If the Laurent polynomial $a_i(q,\pm q^{-i})$ were nonzero, its finite vanishing order $
u$ at $q=1$ would give a lower bound $cN^{-
u}$ at $q_N$ for all sufficiently large $N$. Equation (31) would then bound $|K_N(K)|$ by a polynomial, contradicting (1). Thus both trajectory polynomials vanish identically. Their kernels are the relatively prime ideals generated by $M-q^{-i}$ and $M+q^{-i}$, proving the divisibility in (30). Finally, $T^i(M^2-1)=(q^{2i}M^2-1)T^i$, which proves the displayed order of multiplication. The finite exceptional levels of the annihilator do not affect this argument. For a polynomial annihilator in the squared-coordinate ring $Y=M^2$, with shift $\mathsf S Y=q^2Y\mathsf S$, the statement is $P_Y=B_Y(Y-1)$. An arbitrary unsquared operator need not itself have even coefficients. It splits as $P_0(q,Y,\mathsf S)+M P_1(q,Y,\mathsf S)$; evenness of the state makes the two parts separate annihilators, and the argument applies to each. Thus the squared polynomial annihilator ideal is contained in the left ideal generated by $Y-1$. Its cyclic module has the boundary quotient \[ \Delta=\mathcal R/\mathcal R(Y-1),\qquad \mathcal R=\mathbb C(q)[Y^{\pm1},\mathsf S^{\pm1}]. 	ag{32} \] The commutation rule above is understood in this ring. Localizing to $\mathbb C(q,Y)$ makes $Y-1$ invertible and kills this quotient. The boundary information must therefore be retained in a meridian lattice alongside the localized recurrence. This is a normalization factor of shift order zero; it is not the sought geometric factor involving the longitude variable. One must also keep the change of state when removing the factor: $B$ annihilates $(M^2-1)F_N(M)$, whose value at completeness is zero. The knot invariant is its normal derivative, \[ K_N(K)=\left. rac12 rac{d}{d\log M}  igl[(M^2-1)F_N(M) igr]ight|_{M=1}. 	ag{33} \] The peripheral normal-period note develops the corresponding affine lifting equation and states the additional rank condition under which its first normal derivative determines the period. Neither (30) nor the nearby-zero bound proves that rank condition or identifies the remaining classical characteristic factor with the geometric longitude. They specify boundary data that such a comparison must retain.

title: Volume limits from the degree and twist at each circle
status: Directed subtree criterion; uniform twist bound and independent degree alternative
text: # Volume limits from the degree and twist at each circle The [directed all-orders extension](../papers/meridian-expansions/README.md) proves the full expansion on the shifted microscopic meridian charts for every certificate below, identifies its preferred-cusp correction, and supplies the selected geometric-factor conclusion for genuine all-level annihilators. Start with a fixed finite ordered tree of two-strand integer braids, with at least one edge and one crossing circle at every vertex. Turn each child tangle through its specified quarter-turn before stacking it at the parent, and use the original cylindrical closure. The [literal construction and strand test](../papers/circle-tree-volume/README.md) retain the endpoint frames and require one closed main knot, with no component closed inside an intermediate tangle. Write \(d_v\) for the degree of vertex \(v\), and \(n_v\) for its signed number of half-twists. A sufficient condition for the volume limit is \[ \boxed{\qquad d_v\ge2^{28}\quad\text{or}\quad |n_v|\ge2^{27} \qquad\text{at every vertex}.\qquad} \] The alternative can be chosen separately at each vertex. High-degree vertices may retain any fixed signed powers, including zero and small nonzero powers. If the strand test gives a knot \(K\), its original complement is hyperbolic and \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \] Both level parities are included. The tree, powers and degrees are fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity. The constants are coarse sufficient bounds; they make no claim about the shortest possible twists. The more general criterion below assigns a real-decay bound to each subtree polynomial. Dividing by that polynomial's exact value at zero retains its complex scalar and isolates the contribution of the next trace. Different edges may use different bounds. The final vertex has no outgoing polynomial, so it need not pay the extra loss needed to send one to a parent. This distinction also gives a short-power star outside both the earlier summed and uniform local tests. Section 8 explains how to retain arbitrarily many prescribed short powers: add an even stack of sufficiently long terminal tangles at every vertex of a fixed ordered knot core. Their endpoint pairing preserves the knot condition, although the resulting knot type can change. The proof estimates the actual finite invariant throughout; it does not assume that a proposed global critical point dominates. ## 1. The directed criterion Put \[ a_0=\frac1{2\pi},\qquad k_0=2^{-16},\qquad R_0=\frac18,\qquad b_0=2^{-11},\qquad r_0=\frac1{16},\qquad t_0=2^{-14},\qquad \chi=1-\cos r_0. \tag{1} \] The parent-variable rectangle is \[ \mathcal R=\{u:|\Re u|\le R_0,\ |\Im u|\le b_0\}. \tag{2} \] Choose any vertex as root and direct all edges toward it. For every nonroot vertex choose a number \[ 0<c_v<k_0, \qquad \delta_v=\min\left\{\frac{b_0}2, \frac{c_v\chi}{4(1+c_v)}\right\}. \tag{3} \] These are parameters of the criterion. They can differ at every edge. They are not asymptotic quantities to be inferred from the invariant. Write \(q_v=1\) at a nonroot vertex and \(q_v=0\) at the root. If \(\mathrm{Ch}(v)\) is the set of children, define \[ \begin{aligned} a_v&=\frac{d_v}{2\pi},& b_v&=\frac{n_v}{2\pi},& D_v&=a_v-i b_v,\\ A_v&=\frac2{\pi^2} \left(q_vk_0+\frac12\sum_{w\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}c_w\right),& B_v&=16q_v+|\mathrm{Ch}(v)|,& C_v&=B_v+\frac{b_v^2}{4A_v}. \end{aligned} \tag{4} \] There is at least one incidence at every vertex, so \(A_v,B_v\) are positive. Let \[ \delta_v^{\mathrm{in}} =\min\bigl(\{b_0\}\cup \{\delta_w:w\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)\}\bigr) \tag{5} \] and set \[ y_v=\min\left\{ \frac{\delta_v^{\mathrm{in}}}2, \frac{t_0|D_v|}{4C_v}, \frac{A_v\pi^2}{8(\pi|b_v|+t_0|D_v|)}, \sqrt{\frac{A_v\pi^2}{8B_v}} \right\}. \tag{6} \] Finally define two action quantities \[ \beta_v=\frac{210}{361}\frac{a_v}{|D_v|^2}, \qquad \eta_v=\min\left\{ \frac12t_0|D_v|y_v, \frac12A_v\pi^2, A_vr_0^2, \frac18a_vr_0^2 \right\}. \tag{7} \] The criterion consists of the strict inequalities \[ \boxed{\quad t_0|D_v|\ge2,\qquad \beta_v<\frac{\eta_v}{2}\quad \text{at every vertex},\quad} \tag{8} \] and, only at nonroot vertices, \[ \boxed{\qquad \beta_v<(k_0-c_v)\chi.\qquad} \tag{9} \] It is a finite elementary test in the degrees, signed powers, root and positive numbers \(c_v\). It uses no value of an unknown quantum invariant and no assumed dominance of a global saddle. Its quantities are local: \(A_v\) and the available strip depend on the child budgets, while the exact child scalar will be divided out rather than estimated. Use the original reduced-state normalization \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(M=-q_Nx=q_N^s\), and \(F_N(1)=K_N\). The raw highest-weight parameter \(x\) here is distinct from a normalized wire coordinate. The [pointing theorem](kashaev_ado_pointing.md) fixes this ADO invariant and its zero framing. **Theorem.** If (3), (8), and (9) hold, the actual reduced state has \[ \frac{F_N(q_N^s)}{F_N(1)A_N(s)H_N(s)} =1+O_{\mathcal T,\mathbf n,R}(N^{-1}), \qquad |s|\le R<1, \tag{10} \] where \[ H_N(s)=\frac{\sin\pi s}{N\sin(\pi s/N)},\qquad A_N(s)=q_N^{a(D)s^2/2},\qquad a(D)=-w(D)-\sum_vn_v. \tag{11} \] Its complete values are nonzero for all sufficiently large levels and \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \tag{12} \] Both level parities and the original normal channels are retained. The proof identifies the same original filled critical value as the marked geometric completion. It does not use a sum of independent subtree volumes. ## 2. An actual conditional kernel on a rectangle The fixed Newton polynomials are \[ \begin{gathered} d=N-1,\qquad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N),\qquad S_k=\prod_{r=1}^k2\sin(\pi r/N),\\ e_k(z)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{j<k}(c_j-z),\qquad 0\le k<N. \end{gathered} \tag{N1} \] Let \(\mathcal T_N(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(N\theta)\), and put \(P_\sigma(z)=\mathcal T_N(z)+2\cos(2\pi\sigma)\). The normalized polynomial trace is \[ \phi_\sigma(F)=(-1)^dN^2[z^d]\operatorname{rem}_{P_\sigma}F, \qquad \phi_\sigma(e_i e_j)=\mathbf1_{i+j=d}. \tag{N2} \] The remainder has degree less than \(N\). This is the full polynomial functional, including its derivative values when roots coalesce. The [typed turn theorem](../papers/moving-meridian-sources/README.md) retains the paired factors \[ W_k(s)=\prod_{r=1}^k \left(1-\frac{\sin^2(\pi s/N)}{\sin^2(\pi r/N)}\right). \tag{N3} \] After lowering the pairing (N2), a physical turn gives the equal-index weight \(\gamma_e(s)H_N(s)/W_k(s)\). The factor \(\gamma_e\) is the original scalar prescribed by that edge's orientation type. It stays in the exact scalar ledger. For the edge action write \[ \begin{gathered} J(x)=\int_0^x\log(2\sin\pi v)\,dv,\qquad g(x)=J(2x)-4J(x),\qquad G_0=g(1/4),\\ b(x,t)=\int_0^x\log(2\cos(2\pi v)+2\cos t)\,dv-2J(x),\\ \psi(t,u)=\operatorname{stat}_x[b(x,t)+b(x,u)], \qquad\psi(0,0)=2G_0. \end{gathered} \tag{N4} \] The logarithms and stationary branch are continued from \(x=1/4,t=u=0\). The finite factorial interpolation, the actual edge contour and this phase are proved in [the all-circle finite-sum theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_all_circle_curvature_filling_limit.md). Its polynomial estimates use [the full Newton bounds](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/all_circle_uniform_newton_bounds.md). Use the exact full kernel \[ K_N(t,u;s)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} e_k(-2\cos t)e_k(-2\cos u)\frac{H_N(s)}{W_k(s)}. \tag{13} \] The definitions of \(e_k,W_k\) and the fixed anti-diagonal trace metric are unchanged. It is a polynomial of degree at most \(N-1\) in each of \(-2\cos t\) and \(-2\cos u\), hence has trigonometric degree at most \(N-1\) in either angle. The paired factors and their inverses are bounded for fixed \(|s|\le R<1\). Every inequality below permits a polynomial factor in N. The [full-kernel real estimate](../papers/circle-tree-volume/README.md) is \[ |K_N(t,u;s)|\le C_RN^{A_R} e^{N\{2G_0-k_0[(1-\cos t)+(1-\cos u)]\}}, \qquad t,u\in[-\pi,\pi]. \tag{14} \] The new estimate needed here is \[ |K_N(t+iy,u;s)|\le C_RN^{A_R} e^{N\{\Re\psi(0,u)-k_0(1-\cos t)+16y^2\}}, \quad u\in\mathcal R,\quad t\in[-\pi,\pi],\quad |y|\le b_0. \tag{15} \] Thus the parent compact is a long, thin rectangle, rather than the old disk of radius \(2^{-12}\). The constant term is the actual conditional phase \(\psi(0,u)\), not its upper bound \(2G_0+O(|u|^2)\). Here is a proof from the original finite kernel. Split the indices into \(I=[1/5,3/10]\) and its complement. The complementary full polynomial has the established single-edge loss \(\eta_K=\pi/200\), including high indices and their complete derivatives. Its ellipse bound is \[ C_RN^{A_R} e^{N\{2G_0-\eta_K+|y|+|\Im u|\}}. \tag{16} \] The exact edge phase has, on the radius 1/4 bidisk, \[ |\psi_{tt}+a_0|\le a_0/50, \quad |\psi_{uu}+a_0|\le a_0/50, \quad |\psi_{tu}|\le a_0/50, \quad \psi_t(0,u)=\psi_u(t,0)=0. \tag{17} \] In particular \(|\psi(0,u)-2G_0|\le |u|^2/10\). Hence (16) is smaller than (15): the sum \(b_0+b_0+(R_0^2+b_0^2)/10+2k_0\) is less than \(\eta_K/2\). All these constants are independent of the tree. For the retained indices write \(u=a+ib\). Their factors at \(a\) are positive. If \(r_j=\cos(2\pi(j+1/2)/N)\), then \(r_j>-1/3\) and \(r_j+\cos a>253/384\). Along \(|a|\le1/8,\ |b|\le2^{-11}\), the denominator \(r_j+\cos(a+ib)\) has modulus greater than \(3/5\), and \[ \left|\frac{d^2}{du^2}\log(r_j+\cos u)\right| =\left|\frac{-r_j\cos u-1}{(r_j+\cos u)^2}\right|<9. \tag{18} \] The first derivative at real a is real. Integrating vertically therefore gives the actual finite-product estimate \[ |e_k(-2\cos(a+ib))| \le e_k(-2\cos a)e^{5Nb^2},\qquad k/N\in I. \tag{19} \] At the other end retain the original product bound \[ |e_k(-2\cos(t+iy))| \le e^2e_k(-2)e^{N[-\alpha\sin^2(t/2)+11y^2]}, \qquad \alpha>1/250. \tag{20} \] The positive retained sum at \((0,a)\) is bounded by a polynomial times \(\exp(N\psi(0,a))\), uniformly for real \(|a|\le1/8\). This is the original one-edge positive Laplace estimate: its unique critical wire is \[ \tan^2(\pi x)=\frac1{1+\tan^2(a/2)}, \tag{21} \] which stays in the interior of \(I\). Its second derivative stays negative on this fixed real compact. Equations (19)–(20), and the second bound in (17), consequently give \[ |K_{N,I}(t+iy,u;s)|\le C_RN^{A_R} e^{N\{\Re\psi(0,u)-\alpha\sin^2(t/2)+11y^2+6b^2\}}. \tag{22} \] For \(|t|\ge1/8\), \[ 6b_0^2<\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin^2(1/16),\qquad 2k_0<\alpha/2. \tag{23} \] For example \(\sin(1/16)>1/(8\pi)\), \(\pi^2<10\) and \(\alpha>1/250\) already prove the first inequality. This proves (15) in this range. For \(|t|\le1/8\), the [canonical wire contour](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_all_circle_curvature_filling_limit.md) gives the exact nonzero edge asymptotic on the 1/4 bidisk. Both \(u\) and \(t+iy\) lie strictly inside that disk. Integrating the first bound of (17) gives (15) there. The original lattice currents and (16) are exponentially smaller. In particular the full kernel, uniformly on this smaller rectangle product, retains \[ K_N(t,u;s)=N^{-3/2}a_e(t,u)e^{N\psi(t,u)} (1+O_R(N^{-1})), \tag{24} \] with the original nonzero holomorphic leading amplitude and midpoint normalization. The outside physical edge gamma is not included in \(a_e\). ## 3. The exact recursion may be rooted anywhere Lower the fixed Frobenius pairing at every vertex of the original closed source. Every physical turn then identifies equal Newton indices and retains its factor \(\gamma_e H_N/W_k\). The resulting finite scalar is a sum over the original edge indices of a product of the original vertex trace tensors. Choosing a root merely specifies the order of these finite contractions. It does not move a cut through a tangle, commute open operators or change a framing. Consequently the [exact recursions](../papers/circle-tree-volume/README.md) hold for any chosen root: \[ M_{v,N}(u)=\gamma_{e_v}(s)\, \mathcal D_{n_v,\sigma_v,N}^{(t)} \left[K_N(t,u;s)\prod_{w\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}M_{w,N}(t)\right] \tag{25} \] at a nonroot vertex, and \[ Z_N=\mathcal D_{n_o,\sigma_o,N}^{(t)} \left[\prod_{w\in\mathrm{Ch}(o)}M_{w,N}(t)\right] \tag{26} \] at the root. The [original global closing, framing and reference factors](../papers/meridian-tangles/README.md), and the original single reduced cut \(H_N\), remain outside (26). Edge gammas are counted once. The exact normal value \(\sigma_v=0\) and the moving values \(\pm s\) retain their actual orientation types. Each message is an even trigonometric polynomial of degree at most \(N-1\) in \(u\), regardless of the subtree. There is no discarded-source error in (25)–(26). ## 4. The phase class and the variable envelopes The inductive analytic class is \[ h_v(0)=h'_v(0)=0,\qquad h_v(-u)=h_v(u),\qquad |h_v''(u)+a_0|\le a_0/20,\quad u\in\mathcal R. \tag{27} \] The leading normalized amplitude \(\alpha_v(u)/\alpha_v(0)\) is holomorphic and nonzero on a neighborhood of the required smaller compact. Exact subtree constants are retained: \[ \frac{M_{v,N}(u)}{M_{v,N}(0)} =\frac{\alpha_v(u)}{\alpha_v(0)}e^{Nh_v(u)}(1+O(N^{-1})), \quad u\in\mathcal R. \tag{28} \] As usual a slightly smaller rectangle can be used for fixed derivative estimates; the strict margins permit an initially slightly larger one. The global assertions attached to \(c_v\) are \[ \left|\frac{M_{v,N}(t)}{M_{v,N}(0)}\right| \le CN^A e^{-Nc_v(1-\cos t)}, \quad t\in[-\pi,\pi], \tag{29} \] \[ \left|\frac{M_{v,N}(t+iy)}{M_{v,N}(0)}\right| \le CN^A e^{N[-(c_v/2)(1-\cos t)+y^2]}, \quad |y|\le\delta_v. \tag{30} \] The real sup norm, full canonical polynomial norm and complete derivative norm differ by polynomial factors at the required fixed multiples of N. No estimate drops the repeated-root normal data. For completeness, (30) follows from (28)–(29) and exact degree. The Poisson estimate for a Laurent polynomial of degree less than \(N\) is \[ |M_{v,N}(t+iy)/M_{v,N}(0)| \le CN^A e^{N[-c_v(1-\cos t)+(1+c_v)|y|]}. \tag{31} \] For \(|t|\ge r_0\) use (3). For \(|t|<r_0\) use the rectangle expansion and \[ \Re h_v(t+iy)\le -\frac{19a_0}{40}t^2+\frac{21a_0}{40}y^2. \tag{32} \] Both arguments give (30), without a conjectured quadratic estimate for an individual high Newton basis element. Assume the children satisfy (27)–(30). At a nonroot vertex set \[ A_v^{\mathrm{loc}}(t,u)=\psi(t,u)+\sum_wh_w(t), \quad C_{v,\ell}(u)=\operatorname{stat}_t \{A_v^{\mathrm{loc}}(t,u)+ib_vt^2/2-i\ell t\}. \tag{33} \] At the root omit \(\psi\) and \(u\). There are \(d_v\) incidences in \(t\). Hence \[ A_v^{\mathrm{loc}}(t,u)=\psi(0,u)-a_vt^2/2+E_v(t,u), \quad |E_{v,tt}|,\ |E_{v,t}/t|\le a_v/20. \tag{34} \] The root constant in this formula is zero. For \(0\le\ell\le L_v=\lfloor t_0|D_v|\rfloor\) the equation \(D_vt=-i\ell+E_{v,t}\) contracts in \(|t|\le b_0\). Indeed \(t_0+b_0/20<b_0\). The actual solutions lie in the smaller disk \(|t|\le t_0/(19/20)\), leaving room for the translated contours. The same elementary calculation as in the original proof gives \[ \frac{380}{441}\frac{\ell a_v}{|D_v|^2} \le-\Im t_{v,\ell}\le \frac{420}{361}\frac{\ell a_v}{|D_v|^2}, \tag{35} \] also for complex parent \(u\). No child phase is asserted to be real on the real axis. Its nonlinear derivative is \(t\) times a function bounded by \(a_v/20\), so the real part of the denominator remains positive. The normalized phase \(h_v=C_{v,1}(u)-C_{v,1}(0)\) satisfies \[ h'_v=\psi_u(t_{v,1},u),\qquad h''_v=\psi_{uu} -\frac{\psi_{ut}^2}{A_{v,tt}^{\mathrm{loc}}+ib_v}. \tag{36} \] Using (17) and \(|A_{v,tt}^{\mathrm{loc}}+ib_v|\ge(19/20)|D_v|\ge(19/20)a_0\) proves (27), since \(1/50+20/(19\cdot2500)<1/20\). This is uniform on the rectangle. Charge ordering and the current-vertex drop are \[ \Re C_{v,\ell}(u)\le\Re C_{v,1}(u) -\frac{190}{441}\frac{a_v}{|D_v|^2}(\ell^2-1), \quad 0\le\Re\psi(0,u)-\Re C_{v,1}(u)\le\beta_v. \tag{37} \] At the root again replace \(\psi(0,u)\) by zero. ## 5. Actual trace tails with the directed budgets Divide every child by its exact nonzero value \(M_{w,N}(0)\). The induction uses those complex constants exactly; it never estimates them by their complete-source magnitudes. Equations (15) and (30) imply \[ |\text{normalized trace input}(t+iy,u)| \le CN^A e^{N[\Re\psi(0,u)-A_vt^2+B_vy^2]}, \quad |y|\le\delta_v^{\mathrm{in}}. \tag{38} \] The root constant is zero. The factor \(2/\pi^2\) in (4) is exactly the inequality \(1-\cos t\ge2t^2/\pi^2\) on the original interval. The [exact finite translated-grid trace](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_main_meridian_direct_crossing_trace.md), with its endpoint currents, has charge coefficients \[ c_{\ell,N}(\sigma)=(-1)^{(N-1)(\ell-1)} U_{\ell-1}(\cos2\pi\sigma),\qquad c_{1,N}=1. \tag{39} \] For \(\ell>L_v\), moving the single-grid rectangle by \(y_v\) costs, after maximizing the chirp term in the real variable, at most \(C_v y_v^2\). Since \(\ell>L_v\) implies \(\ell>t_0|D_v|\), (6) gives a tail loss at least \[ t_0|D_v|y_v-C_vy_v^2\ge\frac12t_0|D_v|y_v. \tag{40} \] Successive charges have the additional factor \(\exp(-Ny_v)\). The exact fixed-compact growth of (39) is absorbed for all sufficiently large N. This starting level may depend on the fixed vertex. At an original endpoint \(\pm\pi\), the chirp and finite-charge connectors cost at most \[ (\pi|b_v|+t_0|D_v|)y_v+B_vy_v^2 \le A_v\pi^2/4. \tag{41} \] Thus their loss is at least \(A_v\pi^2/2\). This includes the original zero-mode current. Nothing is inferred by dropping the endpoint terms of the nonperiodic chirp. For a retained charge, restrict its real integral to \([-r_0,r_0]\). Its complement loses \(A_vr_0^2\) by (38). Translate the retained interval to \(\Im t_{v,\ell}\). Its endpoints remain in the analytic rectangle. The original local Young inequality, now on this larger real interval, is \[ \begin{aligned} \Re\{A_v^{\mathrm{loc}}(t-iz,u)+ib_v(t-iz)^2/2-i\ell(t-iz)\} &\le\Re\psi(0,u)-a_vt^2/8\\ &\quad+\left[\frac{21}{40}a_v+ \frac{2b_v^2}{(14/5)a_v}\right]z^2-\ell z. \end{aligned} \tag{42} \] For \(0\le z\le-\Im t_{v,\ell}\), the last line after its quadratic term is at most \(-\ell z/8\), since \((420/361)\max(21/40,5/7)=300/361<7/8\). Every such connector therefore loses at least \(a_vr_0^2/8\). The translated horizontal saddle has negative real quadratic part at most \(-(19/20)a_v\). The physical sine factor is nonzero at \(t_{v,\ell}\). Equations (40)–(42) prove an absolute conditional error bounded by \(CN^A\exp N[\Re\psi(0,u)-\eta_v]\). Nonminimal charges are their saddle terms plus this absolute error; no relative approximation is asserted at a much lower nonminimal action. Conditions (8) and (37) put the whole conditional error strictly below the first charge. Equation (39) gives its nonzero coefficient for both parities. This establishes (28) and nonvanishing of the exact \(M_{v,N}(0)\). For the child inputs, their exact analytic logarithms differ from the limiting phases by \(O(N^{-1})\), with fixed derivatives on the required smaller compact. The finite product of those corrections is retained in the amplitude, or moves the saddle by \(O(N^{-1})\). As the tree is fixed, it spends no new exponential budget. The leading amplitude is a product of nonzero edge, child and Gaussian factors. All N-dependent physical crossing and carrier phases remain in \(M_{v,N}(0)\); its normalized leading amplitude does not conceal such phases. The full physical trace and the first-charge approximation are holomorphic in the formal meridian variables. As in the original proof, first take parameter circles avoiding collisions and then apply the maximum principle to their whole difference. This covers every actual \(\sigma_v=0,\pm s\), including normal limits. No isolated divided current is declared removable without its companions. ## 6. Regenerating the outgoing real bound The [canonical polynomial bounds](../papers/moving-meridian-sources/README.md), equations (D9)–(D14), retain the full source. For real \(u\), (14), the polynomial real sup bounds of the normalized children, the actual fixed-power crossing polynomial, Chebyshev folding in the correct quotient, and the full top-coefficient functional give \[ |M_{v,N}(u)|\le CN^A \left|\prod_wM_{w,N}(0)\right| e^{N[2G_0-k_0(1-\cos u)]}. \tag{43} \] This retains repeated-root derivatives and all fixed normals. Dividing by the nonzero first-charge value at zero costs at most \(\beta_v\). For \(|u|\ge r_0\), (9) absorbs that cost and yields (29). For \(|u|<r_0\), (28) and (32) give the stronger estimate, since \(c_v<k_0\ll19a_0/20\). Equation (30) follows by Section 4. Thus the induction closes with the selected directed budgets, rather than a common decay constant. There is no outgoing real bound at the final root. Imposing (9) there would be an unnecessary restriction. Its only normalization comparison is the conditional trace estimate (8). ## 7. Original action, geometry, and scope Restore the exact subtree constants successively. Stationary elimination in (33) gives the original joint equations \[ \sum_{e\sim v}\psi_{e,\tau_v} +\frac{in_v\tau_v}{2\pi}=i. \tag{44} \] The constants telescope to the original critical value \[ \mathcal C(\mathbf1)=\operatorname{stat}_{\boldsymbol\tau} \left[\sum_e\psi_e+ \frac{i}{4\pi}\sum_vn_v\tau_v^2-i\sum_v\tau_v\right]. \tag{45} \] Back-substitute from the final root: its first-charge angle belongs to the rectangle, so each child's selected parent value does also, and the same statement continues down the finite tree. Every restored angle has modulus at most \(1/[(19/20)|D_v|]\). Thus the vector satisfying (44) lies inside the full simultaneous small-angular uniqueness polydisk, not just the conditional disks used during elimination. The existing contraction identifies it with the same branch as the marked positive charge path. Indeed (8) implies \[ \sqrt{d_v^2+n_v^2}=2\pi|D_v|\ge 2\pi\,2^{15}>630. \tag{46} \] The [vertexwise geometric theorem](../papers/circle-tree-geometry/README.md) applies with no sum condition. Its original ordered two-octahedron cut, odd seam, primitive periods and calibrated action identify \(2\pi\Re\mathcal C(\mathbf1)\) with the volume of the actual filled knot complement. This is a geometric input, not a deduction from the quantum saddle alone. There are \(|E|\) edge Gaussians \(N^{-3/2}\) and \(|V|\) trace Gaussians \(N^{3/2}\); \(|V|=|E|+1\) leaves the original \(N^{3/2}\) power with nonzero amplitude. The exact first Fourier coefficient is one. The retained edge insertion has leading value one, and the scalar ledger remains precisely (11). This proves (10)–(12), with the original peripheral and framing factors. The criterion allows different strip and real-decay budgets and a different choice of final vertex. It is not the assertion that arbitrary capped short-twist islands can be substituted as black-box messages. Such an island requires a multi-boundary version of the conditional normalization proved here for an actual edge. The pointwise source estimates on the older tiny disk alone do not supply that extension. ## 8. A uniform twist corollary, with no degree sampling The directed criterion has the following simple consequence: \[ |n_v|\ge2^{27}\quad\text{at every vertex} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{(10)--(12)}. \tag{47} \] This sufficient constant is independent of the number of vertices, their degrees and the choice of root.
