From (2), \[ \mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,w+1) =\frac{1-\rho A^N e^{c_0Nw}}{1-\rho e^{c_0Nw}} \mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,w). \tag{14} \] The right side of the rectangle is upward, and the left side is downward. The residue theorem and (14) give the exact current \[ \boxed{\begin{split} \mathcal S_N(A,B;c)-\mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,y) ={}&\frac{1-A^N}{2\pi i} \int_{\Re w=-a/N}^{\uparrow} \mathcal K_N(y,w) \frac{\rho e^{c_0Nw}}{1-\rho e^{c_0Nw}} \mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,w)\,dw. \end{split}}\tag{15} \] Both Fermat factors remain: the other is \(B^N-1\) in (12). In particular the infinity cancellation is between two actual sides of one strip; neither side is independently discarded. ## 3. Uniform factorial estimates on complete vertical strips We record the uniformity needed in (15), directly from F's convergent Gamma product. For fixed \(b>0\), \(\delta>0\), uniformly on \[ b/N\le\Re z\le1-\delta, \qquad \Im z\in\mathbb R, \tag{16} \] one has, with the same logarithmic marks as F, \[ F_N(Nz)=\sqrt{iN(1-e^{c_0z})}\,e^{NI(z)}e^{O_{b,\delta}(1)}. \tag{17} \] The \(O(1)\) is a bound for a holomorphic logarithmic error, and therefore bounds the reciprocal as well. If the real part is also bounded below by a fixed positive constant, the error in (17) can be replaced by \(\pi\cot(\pi z)/(12N)+O(N^{-3})\), uniformly for all imaginary heights. For precision, apply Stirling through its \(1/(12Z)\) term to F's Gamma arguments \(Nz\), \(N(k+z)\), and \(N(k-z)\). Their real parts are positive. The remainder is bounded by \(C|Z|^{-3}\) throughout the closed right half-plane, as follows from the integral Bernoulli remainder used in F. The first remainder is at most \(Cb^{-3}\); the sum of the others is bounded by \[ CN^{-3}\sum_{k\ge1} \bigl((k+b/N)^{-3}+(k-1+\delta)^{-3}\bigr). \tag{18} \] These estimates are independent of \(\Im z\). The same sine-product summation as in F gives \(NI(z)\), the marked half logarithm, and \(\pi\cot(\pi z)/(12N)\). Since \(|\cot\pi z|\le C_{\delta}(1+1/\Re z)\), the last term is bounded on (16). This proves (17). On a fixed smaller vertical strip every remainder is \(O(N^{-3})\), proving the stronger assertion. Thus no compact-height estimate has been used at unbounded height. For \(\beta\) in the stated disk the same product at bounded argument gives \[ F_N(\beta)=(-c_0/N)^\beta\Gamma(1+\beta) (1+O(N^{-1})), \qquad \Log(-c_0)=\log(2\pi)-i\pi/2. \tag{19} \] For example the logarithm of the infinite Gamma-product correction is \(O(N^{-2})\) uniformly on this disk; the explicit Gaussian factor has a uniform \(O(N^{-1})\) correction. In particular this factor and its reciprocal have polynomial size in \(N\). Here also is the promised horizontal-end justification. On a fixed real substrip of the basic factorial strip, (17), with its bounded reciprocal, shows that \(F_N(z)\) and \(F_N(z)^{-1}\) are bounded as \(\Im z\to+\infty\), for fixed \(N\). This follows because \(e^{c_0z/N}\to0\), so both the displayed square root and \(I\) have finite limits. Literal shifts in (2) give the same conclusion on each bounded real interval needed for numerator arguments. Near the left edge, shift once before using (17); the shift factor tends to one. Consequently \(\mathcal B(x,w)\) is bounded at the upper horizontal end, whereas \(\mathcal K(y,w)=O_N(e^{-2\pi T})\). At the lower end use the reflection in (2), and these upper bounds and reciprocal bounds. For \(w=t-iT\), uniformly over the fixed real interval in (13), it gives \[ |\mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,w)| \le C_{N,x,\beta}e^{2\pi N(\Re x)T}, \qquad |\mathcal K_N(y,w)|\le C_{N,y}e^{-2\pi NT}. \tag{20} \] Indeed the ratio of the two reflected quadratic exponentials is a constant times \(e^{c_0Nxw}\); the remaining upper-height factorial ratios are bounded. Since \(\Re x<1\), this end also vanishes. These are fixed-\(N\) end limits establishing the exact current. The uniform estimate for that current is proved next. ## 4. The paired current has polynomial size Let \(x,y\) range in arbitrary fixed compact subsets of \(0<\Re x,\Re y<1\). We claim that there are constants \(C,p\) independent of \(N\) such that \[ \boxed{\quad |\mathcal S_N(A,B;c)-\mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,y)| \le CN^p|1-A^N|\,|1-B^N|. \quad}\tag{21} \] This bound holds wherever (3) is defined; numerator zeros are harmless. Only sufficiently large \(N\) is required on the fixed compacts. First prove the necessary estimate on the left side. Put \[ w=(-a+iv)/N,\qquad z=w+(\beta+1)/N. \tag{22} \] Then \(\Re z\in[1/4,3/4]/N\). A single factorial shift gives exactly \[ \mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,w)= \frac{F_N(N(x+z))}{F_N(Nz)} \frac{1-e^{c_0z}}{1-e^{c_0(x+z)}} \frac{F_N(\beta)}{F_N(Nx+\beta)}. \tag{23} \] All the denominator factors in this formula are nonzero on the stated domains. Apply (17) to \(z,x+z,x+\beta/N\), and (19). The half-logarithms in (23) combine into a bounded multiple of \[ N^{-1/2}|F_N(\beta)| \left|\frac{1-e^{c_0z}} {(1-e^{c_0(x+z)})(1-e^{c_0(x+\beta/N)})}\right|^{1/2}. \] This is polynomially bounded uniformly for all real \(v\). The ratio involving \(z\) is bounded also at large negative height, where its numerator and denominator have the same exponential growth; the real part of \(x+z\) stays away from both strip edges. Since \(N(I(x+\beta/N)-I(x))=O(1)\), it follows that \[ |\mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,w)| \le CN^p e^{N\Re\Phi(x,z)}. \tag{24} \] The endpoint displacement in (22) costs only \(O(\log N)\) in the exponent, uniformly for all \(v\): \[ N|\Phi(x,z)-\Phi(x,iv/N)|\le C(1+\log N). \tag{25} \] To see this, use \(\partial_z\Phi=\Log(1-e^{c_0(x+z)})- \Log(1-e^{c_0z})\). First move horizontally from \(iv/N\) to \(r+iv/N\), \(r=\Re z\), then vertically by \(i\Im\beta/N\). Near zero the only singularity is an integrable logarithm; its integral over a segment of length \(O(1/N)\) is \(O((1+\log N)/N)\), uniformly in the starting height. On bounded sets away from zero the derivative is bounded. At large positive height both logarithms tend to zero. At large negative height their linearly growing logarithms cancel, and their difference tends to \(c_0x\), uniformly on the compact \(x\)-set. This proves (25), including \(|v|\gg N\); bounding the two large logarithms separately would not prove it. There is a strict argument gap for the remaining phase. Choose \(\delta>0\) with \(\delta\le\Re x\le1-\delta\). For every \(r>0\), the strip branch satisfies \[ -\pi+2\pi\delta\le \Arg(1-r e^{c_0\Re x})\le\pi-2\pi\delta. \tag{26} \] For \(t>0\), taking the boundary value from \(\Re z>0\), \[ \partial_t\Re\Phi(x,it) =-\Arg(1-e^{c_0x}e^{-2\pi t}). \] For \(t<0\) the denominator logarithm has argument \(-\pi\), so the same derivative is the preceding expression minus \(\pi\). Since \(\Phi(x,0)=0\), integration gives \[ \Re\Phi(x,it)\le(2\pi-2\pi\delta)|t|. \tag{27} \] This uses only the real part of \(x\) in (26); its imaginary part changes the positive modulus \(r\). Combining (24)--(27), for some fixed \(\epsilon_0>0\), \[ |\mathcal B_{N,\beta}(x,(-a+iv)/N)| \le CN^p e^{(2\pi-\epsilon_0)|v|}. \tag{28} \] On this line \(V=e^{c_0w}\) has \(V^N=-e^{-2\pi v}\). For the small \(\beta\)-disk, \[ \left|\frac{\rho V^N}{(V^N-1)(1-\rho V^N)}\right| \le C e^{-2\pi|v|}. \tag{29} \] Also \(B/V-1\) is uniformly bounded away from zero: the argument of \(B/V\) is \(2\pi(\Re y+a/N)\), a fixed distance from \(2\pi\mathbb Z\). The modulus of \(B/V\) can vary with \(v\) without spoiling this lower bound. Substitute (28)--(29) in (15), with \(|dw|=dv/N\). The remaining integral is bounded by \(C\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\epsilon_0|v|}\,dv\). This proves (21), absolute convergence of the paired current, and local holomorphy in all scalar and scaled meridian parameters. ## 5. The positive triangle and the selected coefficient On a compact complex subdomain with \(x,y,x+y\) in the strip, F's uniform expansion and (19) give \[ F_N(Nx+\beta)= \sqrt{iN(1-e^{c_0x})}\, (1-e^{c_0x})^\beta e^{NI(x)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{30} \] Insert (30) and (19) into (3). The identity \[ (-c_0)\frac{1-e^{c_0(x+y)}} {(1-e^{c_0x})(1-e^{c_0y})}=\Lambda(x,y) \] and the marked square roots give precisely the leading term in (8) for the exact ratio, with a nonzero amplitude. For real \(0<x,y,x+y<1\), write \(J(t)=\int_0^t\log(2\sin\pi s)\,ds\). Then \[ \Re\Phi(x,y)=H(x,y):=J(x+y)-J(x)-J(y)>0, \qquad \Im\Phi(x,y)=\pi xy. \tag{31} \] For completeness, \(H\) is zero on the three boundary edges: \(J(1)=0\) and \(J(1-t)=-J(t)\). Its Hessian has negative first diagonal entry \(\pi(\cot\pi(x+y)-\cot\pi x)\) and determinant \(\pi^2\). It is strictly concave in the triangle. Strict positivity in (31) follows by comparing an interior point with the endpoints of a boundary-to-boundary segment through it. Thus \(H\) has a positive minimum on \(K\). Choose a fixed complex neighborhood \(U\) sufficiently small that \(\Re\Phi\) remains positive and \[ 2\pi\{(-\Im x)_++(-\Im y)_+\}<\tfrac12\Re\Phi(x,y) \quad\hbox{on }U. \tag{32} \] The two Fermat factors in (21) are bounded by \(4\exp(2\pi N\{(-\Im x)_++(-\Im y)_+\})\). The amplitude of (3) and its reciprocal are polynomially bounded on \(U\times\{|\beta|\le\beta_0\}\). Equations (21),(30)--(32) give (5), with a fixed exponential relative gap. The coefficient of the exact ratio is \(+1\), fixed by the source-pole residue in (12), not chosen by a saddle or by a positive replacement array. At grid source values the contour formula was initially obtained by separating poles. Both sides of (15) extend holomorphically, and the paired integral is uniformly convergent on the compact scalar domains. Thus (15), (21), and (5) continue to those values as well. Cauchy on slightly larger fixed neighborhoods gives all stated derivatives of the normalized errors. ## 6. Actual normals and the remaining source question The entire proof keeps \(c=M^{-2}Q\) before specialization. On the root, at fixed \(x,y\), the true \(\mu=\Log M\) derivative is \[ \left.\partial_\mu\Log\mathcal S_N\right|_{\mu=0} =\frac{2N}{c_0} \{\log N+\gamma_E-\Log\Lambda(x,y)\}+O(1). \tag{33} \] Indeed \(\partial_\mu=-(2N/c_0)\partial_\beta\), and \(\Gamma'(1)=-\gamma_E\). Fixed higher scaled normal derivatives of the relative reconstruction error are exponentially small; converting to fixed \(\mu\)-derivatives introduces the corresponding powers of \(N\). No moving-root normal is asserted. C's upper-carry array and its first normal have not been omitted: they are present in (9)--(11), and therefore in the exact strip current. Likewise (15) explicitly retains the infinity complement through its paired sides. A fixed-height estimate of just one side could have the positive rate \(-\Re I(x)\); it is (14) and the orbit weight (29) that prove the cancellation needed here. For the actual operator one still has C's ordered evaluation \(\mathcal A_N=H_dK^d\mathcal S_N(u,v;c)\), symmetric in \(u,v\), followed by its original routed factors and source closure. This note does not replace those commuting matrix/Jordan arguments by arbitrary scalar \(x,y\), bound their conditioned evaluation, or put a geometric opposite-polarization kernel into \(U\). Moving arguments, the outer \(H_dK^d\), quotient, turnover, central normalization, pivots, and marks retain all their own normal terms. A nonzero scalar coefficient on this fixed chart is not a nonzero original closed source. ## Complete proof directs * C: notes/research_balanced_gauss_cyclic_divisor_source.md, SHA256 c15668d7dff95346d72801b721bf95970b661e5b17d125aaadd7e0dc38905b00. * F: notes/exact_factorial_interpolation_and_complex_contours.md, SHA256 1f34f65437dfe0bfb4062a7a74840beae1676353cf13bb8a86f8849a8a36bc72. Both complete directs and the entire final were read nontruncated in this author sequence; every used implication and all matching pins were checked. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. Frozen and public files were not edited.

title: The original edge kernel on complex angular rectangles
text:
# The original edge kernel on complex angular rectangles Research proof, 3 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. Theorem 3 in Section 6 proves the full original kernel expansion on \(|\Re t|,|\Re u|\le\pi/2\), \(|\Im t|,|\Im u|\le3/10\), including both level parities and ordinary boundary derivatives. Section 5 proves the intermediate width-one rectangle; the earlier thin-rectangle proof is retained as well. The wider proofs separate the constant and nonconstant parts of the cotangent contour, retain every original Newton index, and control all endpoint integrals. The final extension uses a rigorous fixed-patch endpoint certificate together with analytic bounds for the other regions. It proves the coefficient of the finite sum; the classical Hessian alone would not establish that coefficient. Put \[ \mathcal B_0=\{t:|\Re t|\le1,\ |\Im t|\le1/200\},\qquad I=[9/50,3/10],\qquad h=1/500, 	ag{1} \] and use the original normalization \[ K_N(t,u)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e_k(-2\cos t)e_k(-2\cos u),\qquad e_k(z)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{j<k}(2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N)-z). 	ag{2} \] The functions \(J,b,A,\psi\) below have their original branches: \[  egin{split} J'(x)&=\Log(2\sin\pi x),\qquad J(0)=0,\ b(x,t)&=-J(1/2-x+t/(2\pi))-J(1/2-x-t/(2\pi))-2J(x),\ A(x,t,u)&=b(x,t)+b(x,u),\qquad \psi(t,u)=A(x_*(t,u),t,u),\quad x_*(0,0)=1/4. \end{split} 	ag{3} \] All arguments in (3) have real part strictly between zero and one on the wire rectangle used below. These are ordinary holomorphic branches there, including at zero angular height. **Theorem 1.** On a neighborhood of \(\mathcal B_0^2\), the full original kernel has the uniform expansion \[ K_N(t,u)=N^{-3/2}a_e(t,u)e^{N\psi(t,u)}(1+O(N^{-1})), \qquad a_e(t,u)= rac{\sqrt{2\pi}} {4\sin^2(\pi x_*)\sqrt{-A_{xx}(x_*,t,u)}}. 	ag{4} \] The amplitude is holomorphic and nonzero. The square root is positive at \((t,u)=(0,0)\), where \(a_e=1/4\). The normalized error is holomorphic, has an expansion to every fixed inverse-power order, and retains all fixed parameter derivatives on a smaller neighborhood. In particular (4) holds through both level parities with every ordinary free-boundary normal retained. It implies eventual nonvanishing uniformly on the displayed compact box. ## 1. The saddle lies inside one uniform wire rectangle Write \(c=\cos t=a+ib\), \(d=\cos u=a'+ib'\), and \[ C= rac{1-cd}{2+c+d},\qquad x_*=(2\pi)^{-1}\arccos C. 	ag{5} \] Throughout (1), elementary Taylor bounds give \[ 27/50<a,a'<10001/10000=:a_1,\qquad |b|,|b'|<1/190=:b_1. 	ag{6} \] Let \(p=2+a+a'\), \(e=b+b'\), and \(n_0=1-aa'\). The real comparison \(n_0/p\) lies between \(-1/20000\) and \(23/100\), since it decreases in each of \(a,a'\). Direct division in (5) shows \[ \left|\Re C- rac{n_0}{p}ight| \le b_1^2\left( rac13+ rac{4a_1}{9}+ rac4{27}ight) < rac1{30000}. 	ag{7} \] Here \(p>3\) and \(|n_0|<1\) were used; the estimate keeps the quadratic imaginary correction, rather than an absolute first-order complex bound. Also the exact imaginary numerator is \[ \Im C=- rac{b|1+d|^2+b'|1+c|^2}{|2+c+d|^2}, \qquad |Im C|\le rac{2b_1((1+a_1)^2+b_1^2)}9< rac1{200}. 	ag{8} \] Thus \(-1/1000<\Re C<231/1000\). If \(2\pi x_*=	heta+i
u\), the principal inverse cosine has \(0<	heta<\pi\), \(\cos	heta=\Re C/\cosh
u\), and \(|\sinh
u|=|\Im C|/\sin	heta\). Consequently \(\sin	heta>9/10\) and \[  oxed{\quad 21/100<\Re x_*<251/1000,\qquad |\Im x_*|<1/1000. \quad} 	ag{9} \] For the real bounds, use \(\cos(21\pi/50)>\cos(33/25)>6/25\) and \(\cos(251\pi/500)=-\sin(\pi/500)<-1/1000\). For the imaginary bound use \(\operatorname{arsinh}s\le s\) and \(\pi>3\). The exponential of \(A_x\) at (5) equals one algebraically. All the factors remain nonzero in the regular factorial strips, and the parameter box is connected. Hence the logarithmic equation is exactly \(A_x(x_*,t,u)=0\), as at the complete point; there is no unrecorded \(2\pi i\) charge. The derivative calculation of the [original edge packet](../papers/circle-tree-volume/edge-packet.tex) therefore identifies this phase with the same calibrated edge phase \(\psi_t=-\pi^{-1}\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(t/2)\cos(u/2))\). ## 2. Uniform curvature and the exact cotangent contour On \(x\in I+i[-h,h]\), differentiation gives \[ A_{xx}=-\pi\left[ \sum_{v=t,u}\{	an(\pi x+v/2)+	an(\pi x-v/2)\} +4\cot(\pi x)ight]. 	ag{10} \] Every real tangent argument belongs to \([9\pi/50-1/2,3\pi/10+1/2]\subset(0,\pi/2)\); its cosine exceeds \(1/8\), and its imaginary part has magnitude less than \(9/1000\). The real part of \(\pi x\) has sine greater than \(1/2\). The exact formulas for the real and imaginary parts of tangent and cotangent now imply \[  oxed{\qquad \Re A_{xx}<-20,\qquad |\Im A_{xx}|<8,\qquad |A_{xx}|<128. \qquad} 	ag{11} \] Here are explicit estimates sufficient for all three constants. For each tangent argument \(r+iv\), \(\Re	an(r+iv)>(99/100)	an r\), \(|\Im	an(r+iv)|<3/5\), and \(|	an(r+iv)|<8\). For \(a+iy=\pi x\), the corresponding bounds are \(\Re\cot(a+iy)>(99/100)\cot a\), \(|\Im\cot(a+iy)|<13/500\), and \(|\cot(a+iy)|<2\). For example the real-part attenuation denominators are \(1+\sinh^2v/\cos^2r<1+64/10000<100/99\) and \(1+\sinh^2y/\sin^2a<1+4/10000<100/99\). Convexity of tangent on \((0,\pi/2)\) gives each paired real tangent sum at least \(2	an a\). Thus its total with the cotangents is at least \((99/100)4(	an a+\cot a)\ge(99/100)8\). The imaginary and modulus bounds follow respectively from \(\pi(4\cdot3/5+4\cdot13/500)<8\) and \(40\pi<128\). Taylor's formula at the actual saddle gives, for \(X=\Re(x-x_*)\), \(Y=\Im(x-x_*)\), \[ \Re(A(x,t,u)-\psi(t,u)) \le-10X^2+8|XY|+64Y^2. 	ag{12} \] On each vertical side of the wire rectangle, \(|X|\ge3/100\), \(|Y|\le3/1000\), so the right side is at most \(-7704/10^6<-7/1000\). On either horizontal side its maximum over real \(X\) is at most \[ (64+64/40)(3/1000)^2=369/625000<1/1000. 	ag{13} \] This is strictly smaller than the nonconstant-cotangent penalty \(2\pi h>12/1000\), leaving a gap greater than \(1/100\). Use the exact canonical factorial interpolation \[ B_N(x,t)= rac{N} {G_N(N(1/2-x+t/(2\pi))-1/2) G_N(N(1/2-x-t/(2\pi))-1/2)G_N(Nx)^2}. 	ag{14} \] It equals \(e_k(-2\cos t)\) at \(x=k/N\), as an ordinary polynomial identity in the boundary variable. On the rectangle all scaled factorial real parts stay in a fixed compact subinterval of \((0,1)\); the smallest is greater than \(1/5-1/(2\pi)>1/30\). Therefore the original factorial theorem gives \[ B_N(x,t)B_N(x,u) = rac{e^{NA(x,t,u)}}{4N^2\sin^2(\pi x)}(1+O(N^{-1})), 	ag{15} \] uniformly and holomorphically, with every fixed further order. Enclose exactly the retained integers by the residue kernel \(\pi N\cot(\pi Nx)\), using vertical half-grid sides at distance \(O(N^{-1})\) from the ends of \(I\), and heights \(\pm h\). The strict inequalities above persist on these slightly displaced sides. On the vertical sides the cotangent has modulus at most one. On the horizontal sides it is \(\mp i+O(e^{-2\pi Nh})\). Equations (12)--(13) therefore bound every vertical current and every nonconstant cotangent mode strictly below the selected rate. The two constant horizontal terms have total coefficient \(+N\) times the wire integral. Move each to the horizontal through \(x_*\). The endpoint connectors retain the bound (12). On this line (11) gives a unique real maximum at the saddle and a uniform negative second derivative. The ordinary holomorphic Laplace expansion yields the coefficient (4); its powers are \(N\cdot N^{-2}\cdot N^{-1/2}=N^{-3/2}\). This argument proves the coefficient of the actual retained finite sum, rather than just the existence of a critical point. ## 3. All omitted original indices The exact consecutive-product relation is \[ e_{k+1}(-2\cos t)=e_k(-2\cos t)  rac{2\cos((2k+1)\pi/N)+2\cos t}{4\sin^2((k+1)\pi/N)}. 	ag{16} \] Below \(k/N=9/50+O(N^{-1})\), the multiplier has modulus uniformly greater than one. Indeed its limiting real numerator is greater than \(2(2/5+1/2)\), and its denominator is less than \(4\cdot3/10\), giving a ratio greater than \(3/2\). Above \(k/N=3/10+O(N^{-1})\), up to the last low index \(\lfloor(N-1)/2floor\), its modulus is uniformly less than one: \[  rac{|\cos^2(\pi(k+1/2)/N)-\sin^2(t/2)|} {\sin^2(\pi(k+1)/N)} \le rac{7/20+6/25+o(1)}{13/20+o(1)} \longrightarrow	ext{a value at most }59/65<1. 	ag{17} \] The bounds \(\cos^2(3\pi/10)<7/20\), \(\sin^2(3\pi/10)>13/20\), and \(|\sin^2(t/2)|<6/25\) were used. Inequality (16) is applied multiplicatively, so a Newton zero is retained and introduces no division by a vanishing term. Both omitted low-index tails are therefore bounded by a polynomial times their endpoint terms. Formula (15) at the real endpoints and (12) give their strict gap below \(\Re\psi\), uniformly on \(\mathcal B_0^2\). For high indices, the [complete Hermite estimates](../papers/circle-tree-volume/finite-bounds.tex) give \(\|e_k\|_{\mathcal J}\le CN^a\). Full Hermite Fourier interpolation gives the same polynomial bound on the entire real angular period. The trigonometric Bernstein inequality consequently gives, for every such \(k\), \[ |e_k(-2\cos t)e_k(-2\cos u)| \le CN^a e^{N(|\Im t|+|\Im u|)} \le CN^a e^{N/100}. 	ag{18} \] To compare this with the selected phase, the [edge Hessian bound](research_edge_hessian_and_phase_response.md), Corollary 6, makes \(\Re\psi\) convex along every imaginary segment in the larger box \(|\Re t|\le1,|\Im t|\le1/3\). Its first derivative on the real slice vanishes. Real evenness and \(-\psi_t(t,u)\le\pi^{-1}	an(t/2)\le2t/(3\pi)\) for \(0\le t,u\le1\) imply \[ \Re\psi(t,u)\ge\psi(\Re t,\Re u) >M_\infty- rac2{3\pi} > rac{112}{99}- rac29= rac{10}{11}. 	ag{19} \] Here \(G>8/9\), \(3<\pi<22/7\), and \(\sec^2(1/2)<4/3\) suffice. Thus the entire high half is exponentially negligible, including both parities and all its zeros. This finishes the full-kernel proof. All estimates have strict reserve on compact sets. They persist on a slightly enlarged parameter rectangle and wire rectangle, which justifies the claimed neighborhood and the differentiated remainders by Cauchy's estimate. At the simple odd boundary root, no artificial normal is inserted into a quotient: (2) and (14) are the original ordinary boundary polynomials from the start. ## 4. The original bounded meridian insertion For a fixed \(R<1\), the same proof permits the original edge insertion \(H_N(s)/W_k(s)\), uniformly for \(|s|\le R\). Its exact interpolation is \[ I_N(x,s)= rac{G_N(Nx)^2}{G_N(Nx-s)G_N(Nx+s)} =1- rac{\pi s^2}{N}\cot(\pi x)+O_R(N^{-2}). 	ag{20} \] The original finite estimates bound this insertion uniformly at every omitted index, including its inverse. On the retained contour it is holomorphic with (20). Thus the inserted kernel divided by the bare kernel is \[ 1- rac{\pi s^2}{N}\cot(\pi x_*(t,u))+O_R(N^{-2}). 	ag{21} \] Any separately prescribed physical-turn scalar is retained outside this ratio. The insertion statement does not change a meridian, replace a first normal, or assert an asymptotic for a subsequent multi-vertex contraction. It supplies the uniform original edge packet on the explicit domain (1). The [scalar checker](../experiments/check_bare_kernel_thin_rectangle_constants.py) verifies 33 strict inequalities above using exact fractions and Taylor-series remainder bounds. Its [record](../repro/results/research-bare-kernel-thin-rectangle.json) contains every rational margin and the script and note hashes. It checks the numerical constants in the proof; it is not a sampled test of the uniform kernel assertion. ## 5. The expansion at imaginary heights up to three tenths The small imaginary height in (1) is unnecessary. In this section put \[ \mathcal B_1=\{t:|\Re t|\le1,\ |\Im t|\le3/10\},\qquad a=1/10,\quad b=3/10,\quad h=3/100. 	ag{22} \] The letters \(a,b\) in this section denote endpoints of the wire interval; \(b(x,t)\) still denotes the phase in (3). **Theorem 2.** The expansion (4), with its original nonzero amplitude and normalization, holds uniformly on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal B_1^2\). It has all the holomorphic remainder and derivative properties stated in Theorem 1. This is a theorem about the complete finite edge sum (2). In particular, it estimates the kernel on the horizontal and vertical trace contours whose real angles have magnitude at most one. It does not cover angles between one and \(\pi/2\), and does not by itself establish a whole-path source theorem. ### 5.1. The critical point stays in one regular factorial strip Write \(c=\cos t\), \(d=\cos u\), \(U=1+\Re c\), \(V=1+\Re d\), \( eta=\Im c\), and \(\delta=\Im d\). On \(\mathcal B_1^2\), \[ 27/50<\Re c,\Re d<523/500,\qquad | eta|,|\delta|<129/500. 	ag{23} \] For the quantity \(C\) in (5) there are useful exact identities: \[  egin{split} \Re C&=1- rac{UV}{U+V} - rac{(V eta-U\delta)^2} {(U+V)((U+V)^2+( eta+\delta)^2)},\ \Im C&=- rac{ eta|1+d|^2+\delta|1+c|^2} {|2+c+d|^2}. \end{split} 	ag{24} \] The correction on the first line is nonnegative and is less than \((129/500)^2/(77/25)\). For the second line use \[  rac{|1+c|^2+|1+d|^2}{|2+c+d|^2} = rac12+ rac{|c-d|^2}{2|2+c+d|^2} < rac12+  rac{(253/500)^2+(129/250)^2}{2(77/25)^2}. \] It follows that \[ -9/200<\Re C<23/100,\qquad |\Im C|<7/50. 	ag{25} \] If \(2\pi x_*=	heta+i
u\) on the principal inverse-cosine branch, then \(\cos	heta=\Re C/\cosh
u\) and \(|\sinh
u|=|\Im C|/\sin	heta\). Thus \(\sin	heta>97/100\) and \[ 21/100<\Re x_*<13/50,\qquad |\Im x_*|<23/1000<h. 	ag{26} \] For the last inequality use \(|
u|<14/97\) and \(\pi>157/50\). On the real parameter square the stronger bounds \(1/5<x_*\le1/4\) follow immediately from \(0\le C<23/100\). Throughout the wire rectangle \([a,b]+i[-h,h]\), the factorial arguments \(1/2-x\pm t/(2\pi)\) have real parts in a fixed compact subinterval of \((0,1)\). The same holds for \(x\). Consequently (15) holds uniformly on this rectangle for every parameter in \(\mathcal B_1^2\), through every fixed order. The logarithmic critical equation is \(A_x(x_*,t,u)=0\): its exponential is one by (5), and continuation from \(t=u=0\) fixes its integer logarithmic charge on the connected box. ### 5.2. Endpoint gaps on the real wire Put \(r=\Re t\), \(s=\Re u\). On the real parameter square, \[ A_{xx}(x,r,s)\le-8\pi,\qquad a\le x\le b. 	ag{27} \] Indeed the cosine denominators in the paired tangent formula are positive, and \(	an(\pi x+r/2)+	an(\pi x-r/2)\ge2	an\pi x\). The cotangent terms in (10) then give (27). At a real wire point, a vertical change in a parameter has quadratic cost at most \[ \Re b(x,r+iH)-b(x,r) \le C_x(r)H^2,\qquad C_x(r)= rac{\sin(2\pi x)} {4\pi(\cos(2\pi x)+\cos r)}. 	ag{28} \] To see this, differentiate twice in \(H\). The real part of each squared secant is at most its modulus, and that modulus is at most the squared secant at real part \(r\). The first real derivative at \(H=0\) vanishes. This proves (28) with the displayed half of the real second derivative. For \(a\le x\le b\) and \(|r|\le1\), \(C_x(r)\le C_b(r)\). The inequality \(\cos r\ge1-r^2/2\), followed by the chord bound for the resulting convex reciprocal function of \(r^2\), gives \[ C_b(r)\le rac{11}{100}+ rac{29}{100}r^2< rac25. 	ag{29} \] The endpoint constants used here are \[  rac{	an(3\pi/10)}{4\pi}< rac{11}{100}, \qquad  rac{\sin(3\pi/5)} {4\pi(1+\cos(3\pi/5)-1/2)}< rac25. \] The edge Hessian estimate on the larger box \(|\Re t|\le1,\ |\Im t|\le1/3\), cited in Section 3, also gives \(\Re\psi(t,u)\ge\psi(r,s)\). Equations (28)--(29) therefore imply on the entire real wire \[ \Re A(x,t,u)-\Re\psi(t,u)<9/125. 	ag{30} \] There is a strict gap at each endpoint. At \(a\), (27) and the real critical-point bounds give a real gap greater than \(4\pi/100\). Subtracting the cost \(9/125\) leaves more than \(1/25\). For \(b\), let \(D(r,s)=\psi(r,s)-A(b,r,s)\), \(T_b=	an(3\pi/10)\). The exact edge derivative gives, for \(0\le r,s\le1\), \[ D_r= rac1\pi\left[ \operatorname{atanh}(T_b	an(r/2)) -\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(r/2)\cos(s/2))ight] \ge rac{T_b-1}{2\pi}\,r. 	ag{31} \] All the arguments of \(\operatorname{atanh}\) are below one. The last inequality uses \(\operatorname{atanh}z\ge z\), \(\operatorname{arsinh}z\le z\) for \(z\ge0\), and \(	an(r/2)\ge r/2\). Since \(D(0,0)\ge\pi/100\), separate evenness yields \[ D(r,s)\ge rac{\pi}{100} + rac{T_b-1}{4\pi}(r^2+s^2). 	ag{32} \] Now \(T_b>11/8\), so the coefficient of \(r^2+s^2\) on the right is greater than \(261/10000\), the corresponding coefficient in the height cost from (29). The constant terms leave more than \(1/100\). In particular \[ \Re A(a,t,u)<\Re\psi-1/25,\qquad \Re A(b,t,u)<\Re\psi-1/100. 	ag{33} \] ### 5.3. Separating the constant cotangent terms Two bounds hold throughout the entire wire rectangle: \[ \Re A_{xx}<-6,\qquad |\Im A_x|<7/2. 	ag{34} \] Here are elementary estimates establishing them. Each real tangent argument in (10) lies between \(\pi/10-1/2\) and \(3\pi/10+1/2\). A tangent with negative real part has real part greater than \(-1/5\); a tangent with nonnegative real part has nonnegative real part. Also \(\Re\cot(\pi x)>7/10\) on the rectangle. The bracket in (10) is consequently greater than \(4(7/10)-4/5=2\), proving the first inequality. For the second use \[ A_x=\sum_{v=t,u} \Log rac{\cos(2\pi x)+\cos v}{2\sin^2(\pi x)}. \] Each numerator has real part greater than \(11/50\) and imaginary part of magnitude less than \(9/20\). Its argument therefore has magnitude less than \(9/8\). Furthermore \(|\arg\sin(\pi x)|<3/10\). All these are the branches continued from the positive real factors. Their sum has magnitude less than \(2(9/8)+4(3/10)=69/20<7/2\). The elementary endpoint comparisons follow, respectively, from \[  egin{split} \cos(3\pi/5)\cosh(3\pi/50)+\cos1&>11/50,\ \sinh(3\pi/50)+\sin1\,\sinh(3/10)&<9/20,\ \arctan\!\left(\cot(\pi/10)	anh(3\pi/100)ight)&<3/10. \end{split} \] Let \(f_N(x)=B_N(x,t)B_N(x,u)\). Choose vertical sides \(a_N,b_N\) on half-grid lines, with \(a_N=a+O(N^{-1})\), \(b_N=b+O(N^{-1})\), enclosing exactly the retained indices. The residue formula is \[ \sum_{a_N<k/N<b_N}f_N(k/N) = rac N{2i}\oint f_N(x)\cot(\pi Nx)\,dx. 	ag{35} \] Split the cotangent into its constant part \(-i\,\operatorname{sgn}(\Im x)\) and the remainder. The constant parts, including the vertical segments on their respective half-rectangles, give exactly \(N\int_{a_N}^{b_N} f_N(x)\,dx\), by Cauchy's theorem. On a horizontal side the remainder is \(O(e^{-2\pi Nh})\); on a vertical half-grid side its modulus is at most \(2e^{-2\pi N|\Im x|}\). The second bound in (34) gives \[ \Re A(x+iy,t,u) \le\Re A(x,t,u)+	frac72|y|. 	ag{36} \] Thus every vertical remainder has the endpoint gap (33). Every horizontal remainder has rate, relative to \(\Re\psi\), at most \[  rac9{125}-(2\pi-	frac72) rac3{100}<- rac1{100}. 	ag{37} \] Rounding the half-grid endpoints retains a smaller fixed positive gap for all sufficiently large \(N\). This controls the actual nonconstant lattice modes even though the unsplit vertical contour need not itself have a gap. ### 5.4. The leading integral and the omitted indices Move the real integral in (35) to the horizontal segment through \(x_*\). The first inequality in (34) gives a strict maximum at \(x_*\), with Gaussian curvature bounded away from zero. At either endpoint on this horizontal line the rate is strictly smaller than \(\Re\psi\), by (26) and (34). Along the connecting vertical segment the real phase is convex: its second derivative is \(-\Re A_{xx}>6\). Both of its endpoints have a gap, one by (33), the other by horizontal concavity. Convexity bounds the whole connector by the larger of those endpoint values. No endpoint integral is therefore lost in the translation. The local Gaussian calculation is now exactly the one in Section 2. Its coefficient is \(+N\) times the wire integral, and (15) gives the nonzero amplitude in (4). It remains to restore every omitted original index. Below \(a_N\), the consecutive multiplier (16) has modulus uniformly greater than one: its real numerator has a positive lower bound already at \(x=a\). Above \(b_N\), through the last low index, it has modulus uniformly less than one, since \[ \cos^2(3\pi/10)<7/20,\quad \sin^2(3\pi/10)>13/20,\quad |\sin^2(t/2)| =\sin^2(r/2)+\sinh^2(\Im t/2)<13/50. 	ag{38} \] The limiting upper ratio is at most \((7/20+13/50)/(13/20)=61/65<1\). Their finite sums are therefore bounded by a polynomial times their endpoint terms, whose gaps are (33). This uses the multiplicative recurrence and remains valid at an exact Newton zero. On the high half the full Hermite estimate and trigonometric Bernstein inequality give rate at most \(|\Im t|+|\Im u|\le3/5\). Equation (19), valid on the larger phase box, gives \(\Re\psi>10/11\). Thus the entire high half is also exponentially smaller. All steps hold for both level parities. Every comparison has a strict reserve on a compact set, so it persists on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal B_1^2\). The normalized holomorphic remainder and its fixed ordinary-color derivatives follow by Cauchy's estimate, including at ramified angular endpoints. This proves Theorem 2. \(\square\) The [large-height scalar check](../experiments/check_bare_kernel_large_height_constants.py) verifies the endpoint comparisons used in this section with outward interval arithmetic and exact rational arithmetic. Its [saved record](../repro/results/research-bare-kernel-large-height.json) contains the margins and dependency hashes. The contour identities, uniform estimates and reconstruction of the finite sum are the written arguments above. ## 6. The full rectangle through real angle pi over two Put \[ \mathcal B_2=\{t:|\Re t|\le\pi/2,\ |\Im t|\le3/10\}, \qquad a=1/10,\qquad h=1/25. 	ag{39} \] **Theorem 3.** The original full kernel has expansion (4) on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal B_2^2\), with the same nonzero amplitude, normalization, both level parities, and all fixed holomorphic remainder orders and ordinary boundary derivatives. In particular it satisfies \[ |K_N(t,u)|\le CN^{-3/2}e^{N\Re\psi(t,u)} \quad(t,u\in\mathcal B_2) 	ag{40} \] for all sufficiently large levels. No term of the original finite sum is replaced by a positive surrogate in this assertion. We use the following three parameter patches. By evenness and interchange of the two arguments, it suffices to take \(r=\Re t\ge0\), \(s=\Re u\ge0\), with either sign of each imaginary part: \[  egin{array}{c|c|c|c} 	ext{patch}&r&s&b\ \hline 0&[0,23/20]&[0,23/20]&3/10\ 1&[11/10,7/5]&[0,7/5]&27/100\ 2&[27/20,\pi/2]&[0,\pi/2]&49/200. \end{array} 	ag{41} \] The patches and their interchanges cover the whole square. Their right endpoints satisfy \(b+\max(r,s)/(2\pi)<1/2\), with margin at least \(1/200\). Thus every factorial argument in (14) is in its regular real-part strip throughout \([a,b]+i[-h,h]\), for all parameters in its patch. ### 6.1. A common critical strip and phase lower bound Write \(c=\cos t,d=\cos u\), and retain the exact critical quantity \(C=(1-cd)/(2+c+d)\). On this larger box, \[ 0\le\Re c,\Re d<523/500, \qquad |\Im c|,|\Im d|<31/100. 	ag{42} \] Use the harmonic-mean identities (24), now with \(1\le U,V<1023/500\). Their nonnegative real correction is less than \((31/100)^2/2\). For the imaginary part use \[  rac{|1+c|^2+|1+d|^2}{|2+c+d|^2} \le rac12+  rac{(21/20)^2+(31/50)^2}{8}. \] Consequently \[ -3/40<\Re C\le1/2,\qquad |\Im C|<3/14. 	ag{43} \] If \(2\pi x_*=	heta+i
u\), its principal inverse cosine therefore has \(\sin	heta>6/7\), \(|
u|<1/4\), and \[ 1/6\le\Re x_*<53/200, \qquad |\Im x_*|<1/(8\pi)<h. 	ag{44} \] For the real upper bound use \(\sin(3\pi/100)>3/40\). Thus the saddle is below the right endpoint on patches 0 and 1. On patch 2 one also has \(\cos r<11/50\), hence \(U<5/4\), whereas \(V<41/20\). The same exact real identity gives \[ \Re C>1- rac{205}{264}- rac1{20}> rac16. \] As \(\cosh
u<11/10\), this implies \(\cos	heta>5/33>\sin(\pi/25)\), and therefore \(\Re x_*<23/100<49/200\). These estimates locate the critical point inside the regular factorial strip before using its critical action. The exponential critical equation is one by its defining algebra. All critical factorial arguments have positive real part by (41) and (44). Connected continuation from the complete point therefore fixes its logarithmic charge to zero and identifies its critical value with the original \(\psi\). The phase-only accretivity lemma on the wide rectangle, Lemma 5 of [the mixed-current note](research_path_mixed_trace_currents.md#9-vertical-current-monotonicity-at-powers-of-at-least-seven), uses the exact edge Hessian, independently of any finite-kernel expansion. It gives imaginary convexity and hence \[ \Re\psi(t,u)\ge\psi(r,s)\ge\psi(\pi/2,\pi/2) >M_\infty- rac{4(1-1/\sqrt2)}\pi> rac{19}{25}. 	ag{45} \] For the middle inequality decrease both real arguments to their largest values. Along the diagonal, \(d\psi(v,v)/dv=-2\operatorname{asinh}(\sin(v/2))/\pi\). Integrating \(\operatorname{asinh}z\le z\) proves the next inequality. The last uses \(M_\infty>29/25\), \(1/\sqrt2>7/10\), and \(\pi>3\). ### 6.2. Real-wire endpoints and the maximum between them The fixed-patch [endpoint lemma](research_bare_kernel_wide_endpoint_gaps.md) proves for each right endpoint in (41) \[ \Re A(b,t,u)<\Re\psi(t,u)-1/10000. 	ag{46} \] Its outward certificate treats 48 products of parameter-boundary sides. Separate harmonicity of \(\Re(A-\psi)\) proves the inequality inside each full complex parameter rectangle; this is not a sampled test of four real parameters. The phase branches and critical factorial strip are checked in that lemma. The left endpoint has an elementary bound. On the real regular wire interval, the paired tangent formula gives \(A_{xx}\le-8\pi\). The real critical point is at least \(1/6\), so the real left endpoint loses at least \(4\pi/225\). At a fixed real wire point, the vertical parameter cost is (28). At \(a=1/10\), \[ C_a(r)\le rac{	an(\pi/5)}{4\pi}< rac1{4\pi} \qquad(0\le r\le\pi/2). \] Both parameter heights together cost less than \(9/(200\pi)\). Equation (45) and \(\pi>3\) give \[ \Re A(a,t,u)<\Re\psi(t,u)-23/600. 	ag{47} \] For the nonconstant cotangent modes we need a bound between the endpoints, not only (46)–(47). We claim \[ \max_{a\le x\le b}\Re A(x,t,u)-\Re\psi(t,u)<3/50. 	ag{48} \] If the maximum is at an endpoint, (46)–(47) suffice. Otherwise put \(q=\cos(2\pi x)\) at an interior maximum. Its derivative equation is exactly \[ |q+c|\,|q+d|=(1-q)^2. 	ag{49} \] Let \(C_0=\cosh(3/10)<523/500\). For \(-1\le q<0\), convexity in \(v=\cos r\in[0,1]\), and monotonicity in \(|\Im t|\), give \[ |q+\cos t|^2\le \max\{(q+C_0)^2,\ q^2+C_0^2-1\}. 	ag{50} \] Both terms are strictly smaller than \((1-q)^2\) if \(q<(1-C_0)/2\). For the second term use \(C_0^2<11/10\); for the first, \(q+C_0>0\) on this interval. Equation (49) therefore forces \(q>-23/1000\). Write \(X=q+\cos r\), \(Y=q+\cos s\). The exact identity for the height increment gives \[ |q+c|^2-X^2 =2q\cos r\{\cosh(\Im t)-1\}+\sinh^2(\Im t) < rac{1+|q|}{10}, \qquad |q+d|\le |q|+523/500. 	ag{51} \] For \(-23/1000\le q\le1/4\), (49) implies \[ X^2>  rac{(3/4)^4}{(1/4+523/500)^2}- rac18> rac1{16}. \] Since \(X\ge q>-1/4\), this gives \(X>1/4\); the same holds for \(Y\). For \(q>1/4\) these inequalities are immediate. Thus the real wire point is in the regular real-parameter chamber, and the vertical parameter costs satisfy \[ C_x(r)+C_x(s) = rac{\sqrt{1-q^2}}{4\pi} \left( rac1X+ rac1Yight)< rac2\pi< rac23. 	ag{52} \] At this same point \(A(x,r,s)\le\psi(r,s)\) by real regular concavity. The height cost is at most \((3/10)^2\{C_x(r)+C_x(s)\}<3/50\), whereas \(\Re\psi(t,u)\ge\psi(r,s)\). This proves (48). ### 6.3. The exact lattice modes Every numerator \(\cos(2\pi x)+\cos t\) has positive real part on the complex wire rectangle of its patch. On patches 0 and 1, where \(\cos(2\pi b)<0\), a lower bound is \(\cos(2\pi b)\cosh(2\pi h)+\cos R\), where \(R\) is the patch's largest real parameter. Use, respectively, \[ \cos(23/20)>2/5,\quad -\cos(3\pi/5)<31/100, \qquad \cos(7/5)>1/6,\quad \sin(\pi/25)<22/175, \] together with \(\cosh(2\pi/25)<26/25\). On patch 2 use \(\cos(2\pi b)+\cos R>0\) instead: both real terms are nonnegative, and the first is bounded away from zero. Also throughout the rectangle \(|\arg\sin(\pi x)|<3/8\): use \(\cot(\pi/10)<31/10\), \(	anh(\pi/25)<22/175\), and \(	an(3/8)>39/100\). The exact logarithmic derivative therefore obeys \[ |\Im A_x|<\pi+3/2. 	ag{53} \] These are the continued original branches: the numerators remain in the right half-plane and \(\Re\sin(\pi x)>0\). The horizontal curvature has a uniform bound as well. In (10) at most one tangent in each pair has negative real part. Its real argument is greater than \(-3\pi/20\), so its real part exceeds \(-3/5\). All other tangent real parts are nonnegative because their arguments have real part less than \(\pi/2\). Moreover \(\Re\cot(\pi x)>7/10\) on this rectangle. For the latter comparison the minimum is at \(x=3/10+ih\); use \(\sin(3\pi/5)>19/20\) and the bounds just listed. It follows that \[ \Re A_{xx}<-8\pi/5. 	ag{54} \] Use the exact half-grid residue contour (35), with sides tending to \(a,b\) and heights \(\pm h\). Split its cotangent as in Section 5.3. Its constant pieces, including their portions of the vertical sides, are exactly \(N\int_{a_N}^{b_N}f_N(x)\,dx\). Every vertical remainder retains its endpoint gap, by (46), (47), (53), and the penalty \(2\pi|\Im x|\). Every horizontal remainder has upper rate, relative to \(\Re\psi\), less than \[  rac3{50}-(\pi-3/2) rac1{25}<- rac1{200}. 	ag{55} \] Here \(\pi>25/8\). Half-grid rounding preserves smaller fixed gaps at all sufficiently large levels. Move the remaining real integral to the horizontal through \(x_*\). By (44) the saddle lies inside that rectangle, and (54) gives its unique strict real maximum and nonzero Gaussian curvature. At each horizontal endpoint the rate is lower by horizontal concavity. The vertical connecting segment is bounded by its two endpoints, because its second height derivative is \(-\Re A_{xx}>0\). One endpoint has (46) or (47), and the other has the horizontal concavity gap. Thus no connector is lost. The coefficient remains exactly \(+N\) times the wire integral, and the original factorial expansion (15) gives amplitude (4). ### 6.4. Every original omitted index Below \(a_N\), the real numerator in each consecutive multiplier (16) is uniformly positive and its modulus exceeds one, since \(\Re c,\Re d\ge0\) and \(\cos(\pi/5)>4/5\). Their omitted sum is bounded by its endpoint at polynomial cost, and (47) supplies the gap. Above the right endpoint, use the product multiplier rather than bound its two factors separately. For real \(q\in[-1,1]\) set \[ P(q)=(1-q)^4-|q+c|^2|q+d|^2. 	ag{56} \] The quartic terms cancel. Its cubic, quadratic and linear coefficients satisfy \[ a_3\le-4,\qquad -3/5<a_2\le6,\qquad a_1\le-4. \] These follow from \(\Re c,\Re d\ge0\) and \(|c|^2,|d|^2<11/10\). Hence \[ P'(q)\le-14/5 \quad(-1\le q\le1/10). 	ag{57} \] At each patch endpoint \(q_b=\cos(2\pi b)\), the limiting product multiplier is strictly less than \(3/5\). Here are bounds sufficient to verify this independently of the endpoint phase certificate. On patch 0, convexity in \(\cos r\in[0,1]\) shows \(|q_b+c|,|q_b+d|<3/4\), so the ratio is at most \(225/676<3/5\). On patch 1, \(-3/20<q_b<-1/10\), and \(\cos r<1/2\) for the first parameter. Convexity gives \(|q_b+c|<11/20\), while \(|q_b+d|<6/5\), giving ratio at most \(66/121<3/5\). On patch 2, \(0<q_b<1/25\) and \(\cos r<1/4\). Thus \(|q_b+c|<9/20\), \(|q_b+d|<109/100\), and the ratio is less than \((9/20)(109/100)/(24/25)^2<3/5\). In each calculation the modulus squared is a convex quadratic in \(\cos r\); its maximum height is \(3/10\). Since \(q_b<1/10\), these bounds imply \(P(q_b)>(16/25)(9/10)^4\). Equations (56)–(57) and \((1-q)^4\le16\) then give, for all \(q\le q_b\), \[  rac{|q+c|^2|q+d|^2}{(1-q)^4} <1- rac{6561}{250000}<\left( rac{99}{100}ight)^2. 	ag{58} \] The actual finite recurrence has midpoint and endpoint offsets \(O(N^{-1})\), with denominator bounded away from zero on this range. Its product multiplier is therefore less than \(199/200\) uniformly for all sufficiently large levels. The omitted low-index tail, through \(\lfloor(N-1)/2floor\), is bounded by a constant times its endpoint term. Equation (46) supplies its gap. This multiplicative argument also retains an exact Newton zero; there is no division by a vanishing Newton polynomial. Finally the complete radical Fourier bound gives the whole high half, including its first normals, at rate at most \(|\Im t|+|\Im u|\le3/5\). Equation (45) supplies a strict gap greater than \(4/25\). Every original index has now been restored. The full Gaussian expansion follows through both parities. All inequalities have strict reserves on a finite compact cover; the same argument works on a neighborhood of the box. Holomorphy, separate evenness and Cauchy's estimates give every fixed ordinary-color derivative, including the ramified angles. This proves Theorem 3. \(\square\) The exact scalar margins in this section are checked by [check_bare_kernel_wide_rectangle.py](../experiments/check_bare_kernel_wide_rectangle.py), with the [saved record](../repro/results/research-bare-kernel-wide-rectangle.json). The independent endpoint interval certificate is linked in (46). The scalar checks and the endpoint certificate have distinct scopes; the written cotangent decomposition proves the original-sum coefficient.

title: The full original edge kernel on a three-fifths angular disk
text: # The full original edge kernel on a three-fifths angular disk Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The full same-index kernel has its original nonzero geometric expansion on the complex disk of radius \(3/5\) in each angle. This extends the available height range near completeness. The proof uses the existing split-cotangent contour mechanism, with new disk-specific phase, omitted-index and lattice-mode estimates. No numerical certificate is used. This is an edge-source theorem; an angular complement estimate for a subsequent network contraction is separate. ## 1. Statement and the original interpolation Put \(D=N-1\), \(N\ge2\), and \[ S_j=\prod_{a=1}^j2\sin(\pi a/N),\qquad e_j(z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{a<j} \{2\cos((2a+1)\pi/N)-z\}, \] \[ K_N(t,u)=\sum_{j=0}^{D}e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos u), \qquad r=3/5. \tag{1} \] An index is low when \(2j<N\), and high otherwise. Keep the canonical sine primitive and the complete edge branch \[ J'(z)=\Log(2\sin\pi z),\quad J(0)=0, \] \[ \begin{aligned} b(x,t)&=-J(1/2-x+t/(2\pi))-J(1/2-x-t/(2\pi))-2J(x),\\ A(x,t,u)&=b(x,t)+b(x,u),\\ C(t,u)&=\frac{1-\cos t\cos u}{2+\cos t+\cos u},\qquad x_* =\frac{\arccos C}{2\pi},\\ \psi(t,u)&=A(x_*,t,u),\qquad \psi(0,0)=M_\infty=4G/\pi. \end{aligned} \tag{2} \] All branches continue from \(t=u=0,x_*=1/4\). **Theorem.** Uniformly on a neighborhood of \(\{|t|\le3/5,\ |u|\le3/5\}\), the full original sum satisfies \[ K_N(t,u)=N^{-3/2}a(t,u)e^{N\psi(t,u)} (1+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-1})), \qquad a(t,u)=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}} {4\sin^2(\pi x_*)\sqrt{-A_{xx}(x_*,t,u)}}\ne0. \tag{3} \] The square root is positive at completeness, where \(a=1/4\). Every fixed further expansion order and every fixed ordinary boundary-color derivative is retained, at both level parities. This includes the ramification of \(-2\cos t\) at \(t=0\). The exact interpolation used in the pinned original-kernel proof is \[ B_N(x,t)=\frac{N} {G_N(N(1/2-x+t/(2\pi))-1/2) G_N(N(1/2-x-t/(2\pi))-1/2)G_N(Nx)^2}. \tag{4} \] It equals \(e_j(-2\cos t)\) at \(x=j/N\), as an ordinary polynomial identity in the color. On every compact strict factorial strip it has the original all-fixed-order expansion \[ B_N(x,t)B_N(x,u)= \frac{e^{NA(x,t,u)}}{4N^2\sin^2(\pi x)} (1+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-1})). \tag{5} \] We use (4)--(5), including the actual offsets \(-1/2\), from the original kernel source; we do not replace its interpolation. ## 2. The disk phase and the entire high half For \(|t|,|u|\le r\), define the removable function \[ f(t,u)=\frac{2\operatorname{asinh}(\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2))}{t}-1. \] The following elementary estimates hold on this disk: \[ \begin{aligned} |\tan(t/2)|&\le13|t|/25,& |\tan(t/2)-t/2|&\le |t|^3/20,\\ |\cos(u/2)|&<21/20,& |\cos(u/2)-1|&\le21|u|^2/160,\\ |\operatorname{asinh}z-z|&\le |z|^3/5 &&(|z|\le1/3). \end{aligned} \tag{6} \] The Taylor coefficients of \(\tan z\) are nonnegative, as follows recursively from \((\tan z)'=1+\tan^2z\). Thus \(|\tan z|\le\tan|z|\), and \(\tan a/a\) is increasing for \(0<a\le3/10\). The alternating sine and cosine estimates give \[ \tan(3/10)\le \frac{3/10-(3/10)^3/6+(3/10)^5/120}{1-(3/10)^2/2} <\frac{39}{125}=\frac{26}{25}\frac3{10}. \] Therefore \(|\tan z|\le(26/25)|z|\) on that disk. Integrating \(\tan^2z\) along the radial segment gives \(|\tan(t/2)-t/2|\le(26/25)^2|t|^3/24<|t|^3/20\). The positive cosh series proves the cosine estimates; the binomial derivative bound proves the asinh estimate by integration. The asinh argument has modulus at most \(819/2500<1/3\). Consequently \[ |f(t,u)|\le \left\{\frac{21}{200}+\frac25(273/500)^3\right\}|t|^2 +\frac{21}{160}|u|^2 <\frac13\max(|t|,|u|)^2. \tag{7} \] The calibrated derivative is \(\psi_t=-t(1+f(t,u))/(2\pi)\), and similarly in \(u\). Radial integration therefore gives \[ \psi(t,u)=M_\infty-\frac{t^2+u^2}{4\pi}+E(t,u), \qquad |E(t,u)|\le\frac{r^2(|t|^2+|u|^2)}{24\pi}. \tag{8} \] Write \(H=|\Im t|, L=|\Im u|\). Since \((\Re t)^2\le r^2-H^2\), and similarly for \(u\), \[ \begin{aligned} \Re\psi-H-L &\ge M_\infty-\frac{r^2}{2\pi}-\frac{r^4}{12\pi} +\frac{H^2+L^2}{2\pi}-H-L\\ &\ge M_\infty-2r+\frac{r^2}{2\pi}-\frac{r^4}{12\pi} >\frac{94}{6875}>\frac1{100}. \end{aligned} \tag{9} \] The second line minimizes the two decreasing quadratics on \([0,r]\). For the last inequality use \(3<\pi<22/7\) and \(M_\infty>29/25\). A rational proof of the latter is \(G>8/9+24/1225+40/9801>8207/9000>319/350\), from the first six alternating Catalan terms. The pinned full-radical Fourier estimate, which retains every double-root normal and the odd simple root, gives \[ \left|\sum_{2j\ge N}e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos u)\right| \le C N^a e^{N(H+L)}. \tag{10} \] Thus the entire high half has the strict gap (9). This is an estimate on the actual high polynomials, not their distinct-node values. ## 3. Uniform low-index tails For imaginary arguments put \[ A_{H,L}(x)= \int_0^x\log\{2\cos(2\pi v)+2\cosh H\}\,dv +\int_0^x\log\{2\cos(2\pi v)+2\cosh L\}\,dv-4J(x). \tag{11} \] The exact positive Laurent coefficients of every low polynomial give \[ |e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos u)| \le e_j(-2\cosh H)e_j(-2\cosh L). \tag{12} \] Uniform midpoint comparison of the numerator products and the sine factorials gives the upper estimate \[ e_j(-2\cosh H)e_j(-2\cosh L) \le C N^a e^{NA_{H,L}(j/N)}, \quad 2j<N,\quad 0\le H,L\le r. \tag{13} \] This includes \(H=0\) or \(L=0\). One can see the uniformity directly: the numerator logarithm is monotone on \([0,1/2]\); every included last midpoint and terminal integration endpoint is at distance at least a constant times \(N^{-1}\) from its possible zero at \(1/2\). The endpoint logarithmic errors are consequently \(O(\log N)\), uniformly in the nonnegative height. The usual two endpoint logarithms for the sine factorial give the same error. These are the same comparisons as in the pinned Fourier source. The unique maximum of (11) has \[ q_*:=\cos(2\pi x_*)= \frac{1-\cosh H\cosh L}{2+\cosh H+\cosh L}, \qquad -1/10<q_*\le0,\quad 1/4\le x_*<4/15. \tag{14} \] Here \(\cosh r<6/5\); monotonicity in the two coshes proves the \(q_*\) bound. The final bound follows from \(\sin(\pi/30)>1/10\). The derivative of (11) changes sign only at (14): after exponentiating it, the difference between numerator and denominator is linear in \(q=\cos(2\pi x)\). On \(1/10\le x\le2/5\), its curvature satisfies \[ -A_{H,L}''(x)\ge4\pi\sqrt3. \tag{15} \] Indeed, with \(q=\cos\theta,\theta=2\pi x,C=6/5\), \[ -A_{H,L}''\ge 4\pi\frac{(1+C)\cot(\theta/2)}{q+C}. \] For \(q\ge0\), the last factor is at least \(11/6>\sqrt3\), using \(\sqrt{(1+q)/(1-q)}\ge1+q\). For \(q=-v\le0\), one has \(0\le v<5/6\). Its square exceeds three because \[ 13-49v+105v^2-75v^3>0: \quad p'(v)=-(15v-7)^2,\qquad p(5/6)=121/72. \] Outside that interval the monotonicity around (14) suffices. It follows that every \(x\notin(3/20,7/20)\) loses at least \[ \frac{\pi\sqrt3}{72}>\frac{17}{240} \tag{16} \] relative to \(\psi(-iH,-iL)=\max A_{H,L}\). On the other hand (8) gives \[ \psi(-iH,-iL)-\Re\psi(t,u) \le D_r:=\frac{r^2}{2\pi}+\frac{r^4}{6\pi} <\frac{42}{625}. \tag{17} \] Thus every omitted low index has a gap greater than \(17/240-42/625=109/30000>3/1000\) below \(\Re\psi\). The same comparison gives, on the retained real wire interval, \[ \Re A(x,t,u)\le\Re\psi(t,u)+D_r. \tag{18} \] For (18), the continuum modulus inequality follows from (12), (5) at real wire points, and dense sequences \(j/N\to x\). All factorial arguments here are in strict strips. ## 4. The exact lattice modes and the nonzero coefficient Use the fixed wire rectangle \[ \mathcal R=[3/20,7/20]+i[-1/25,1/25]. \tag{19} \] Every \(x\) and \(1/2-x\pm t/(2\pi)\), and the corresponding arguments for \(u\), has real part strictly between zero and \(1/2\), uniformly on (19) and the parameter disks. Thus (5) holds throughout. In particular \[ \Re A_{xx}<0 \tag{20} \] uniformly: \( -A_{xx}/\pi\) is the sum of the four cotangents at those factorial arguments and \(4\cot(\pi x)\), all with strictly positive real part. The saddle is strictly inside (19). In fact \(|\cos t-1|<1/5\) implies \(|C|<11/90\), and \[ |x_*-1/4|\le \frac{|C|}{2\pi\sqrt{1-|C|^2}}<\frac{11}{534}<\frac1{25}. \tag{21} \] The logarithmic critical equation is exactly \(A_x(x_*)=0\): its exponential is one algebraically, and connected continuation from completeness in these strict strips fixes the integer branch. This also calibrates (2) and the derivative used in (8). There is a uniform bound on the imaginary derivative: \[ |\Im A_x|<23\pi/20. \tag{22} \] To prove it put \(q=\cos(2\pi x)\), \(c=\cos t\). On (19), \[ |\Re q|<78/125,\quad |\Im q|<13/50,\quad \Re c\ge41/50,\quad |\Im c|<24/125. \] Here \(\cos(3\pi/10)<3/5\), \(\cosh(2\pi/25)<26/25\), \(\sinh(2\pi/25)<13/50\), \(\sinh(3/5)<16/25\), and \(|\Re t\Im t|\le9/50\) suffice. Hence \[ \frac{|\Im(q+c)|}{\Re(q+c)}<\frac{113}{49}<1+\sqrt2, \qquad \frac{|\Im(1-q)|}{\Re(1-q)}<\frac{65}{94} <\tan(\pi/5). \] The first argument has magnitude below \(3\pi/8\), and the second below \(\pi/5\). Apply the exact continued identity \[ A_x=\Log(q+\cos t)+\Log(q+\cos u)-2\Log(1-q) \] to obtain (22). All three quantities remain in the right half-plane; no branch is reset in this calculation. Choose vertical sides \(a_N,b_N\) on half-grid lines tending to \(3/20,7/20\), and let \(f_N=B_N(x,t)B_N(x,u)\). The exact residue identity is \[ \sum_{a_N<j/N<b_N}f_N(j/N) =\frac N{2i}\oint f_N(x)\cot(\pi Nx)\,dx. \tag{23} \] Split the cotangent into \(-i\operatorname{sgn}\Im x\) and its remainder, including on the vertical sides. As in the pinned original proof, the constant pieces give exactly \(N\int_{a_N}^{b_N}f_N(x)\,dx\). The vertical remainder has modulus at most \(2e^{-2\pi N|\Im x|}\); (22) therefore preserves the real endpoint gap (16)--(17). On the horizontal sides its rate relative to \(\Re\psi\) is at most \[ D_r-(2\pi-23\pi/20)/25 <42/625-51/500<-3/100. \tag{24} \] All these gaps survive the half-grid rounding. Translate the constant real integral to the horizontal through \(x_*\). By (20) this line has its unique strict real maximum at \(x_*\); its endpoints have a uniform gap. The real endpoints have (16)--(17). Along each connecting vertical segment, the real phase is convex because its second vertical derivative is \(-\Re A_{xx}>0\). The larger of its two endpoint values therefore bounds the entire connector strictly below the saddle. This controls the actual constant-piece connectors, not just the lattice-mode remainder. Ordinary holomorphic Laplace expansion of this translated integral, with (5), proves (3). Its exact coefficient is \(+N\); the powers are \(N\cdot N^{-2}\cdot N^{-1/2}=N^{-3/2}\). Sections 2--3 restore every omitted original index with a strict exponential gap. All inequalities have strict reserves on compact sets, so the proof works on a slightly enlarged parameter neighborhood. Cauchy estimates retain every fixed angular derivative. Separate evenness of the actual sum and of the uniquely continued phase and amplitude gives holomorphic descent to the ordinary colors near the ramified complete angles; away from ramification it is immediate. Ordinary-color Cauchy estimates give all fixed spectral derivatives. No artificial odd-level normal is introduced. This completes the theorem. ## 5. Scope and pinned direct sources The existing rectangular kernel theorem, its exact interpolation, normalization and split-cotangent mechanism are prior coverage. The contribution here is the larger angular disk, with fully written uniform estimates for its high half, low tails and lattice modes. The disk contains the small positive saddles relevant to a possible degree-twelve network extension, but the theorem does not bound the whole angular complement or prove that network extension. Direct source versions: - `research_bare_kernel_thin_rectangle.md`, SHA-256 `04797c52fca87548857482461a470c46f70d3cb476b5f18249920527b733d847`: exact factorial interpolation, original phase/amplitude calibration, all-fixed-order strict-strip expansion and split-cotangent identity. - `research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md`, SHA-256 `1faa5d2e02edf0a1462cc43b243e0ab4403bf56e9f1af0befb6b492441d9dd03`: complete high-index Fourier bound, including both parities and normals. - `research_zero_power_subtree_fourier_bound.md`, SHA-256 `9c7e71319ba9f416f5ea510dee472e481894396d0c8a3cebf6ff9cce05816c58`: exact positive low Laurent coefficients and uniform elementary factorial/product comparison; the height-zero uniformity used here is explicitly checked after (13).

title: Right endpoint gaps for the full wide edge box
text: # Right endpoint gaps for the full wide edge box Research proof, 4 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. This note proves a uniform real-wire endpoint inequality for the original edge phase on \[ |\Re t|,|\Re u|\le\pi/2,\qquad |\Im t|,|\Im u|\le3/10. \tag{1} \] It is one input to the finite-kernel contour proof, not a kernel asymptotic by itself. ## 1. Three fixed wire endpoints Keep the original sine primitive and complete normalization \[ \begin{split} J(z)&=\frac{\pi^2/6-\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iz})}{2\pi i} +\frac{i\pi z(1-z)}2,\qquad 0<\Re z<1,\\ b(x,t)&=-J(1/2-x+t/(2\pi))-J(1/2-x-t/(2\pi))-2J(x),\\ A(x,t,u)&=b(x,t)+b(x,u),\\ c&=\cos t,\quad d=\cos u,\quad C=\frac{1-cd}{2+c+d},\quad x_*=\frac{\arccos C}{2\pi}, \qquad x_*(0,0)=1/4 . \end{split} \tag{2} \] The phase is \(\psi(t,u)=A(x_*,t,u)\), continued from \(\psi(0,0)=M_\infty\). The dilogarithm in (2) is its principal branch: the exponential of the open strip avoids its cut. By separate evenness and interchange of the parameters, it suffices to use the following three rectangles. In every row both imaginary parts range over \([-3/10,3/10]\). \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{patch}&\Re t&\Re u&b\\ \hline 0 &[0,23/20]&[0,23/20]&3/10\\ 1 &[11/10,7/5]&[0,7/5]&27/100\\ 2 &[27/20,\pi/2]&[0,\pi/2]&49/200 \end{array} \tag{3} \] If the larger absolute real angle is at most \(23/20\), use patch 0. Otherwise interchange the angles so that it is the first. Values up to \(7/5\) lie in patch 1, and the rest lie in patch 2. Thus these patches cover (1). Their interiors overlap. Each \(b\) is strictly below its largest real factorial wall: \(1/2-b-\max\Re t/(2\pi)>0\). **Lemma 1.** On every patch in (3), \[ \Re\{\psi(t,u)-A(b,t,u)\}>\frac1{10000}. \tag{4} \] The bound persists, with a smaller positive gap, on a neighborhood of each closed patch. ## 2. Analytic branches and the harmonic reduction The critical coordinate in (2) is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the whole box (1). Here is an elementary check of its inverse-cosine branch. Put \(a=1+c\), \(a'=1+d\). Their real parts are at least one and less than \(41/20\), and their imaginary parts have magnitude less than \(31/100\). The parallel-sum identity gives \[ \Re\frac{aa'}{a+a'}\ge\frac12,\qquad \Re\frac{aa'}{a+a'} \le\frac{\Re(a+a')}4+ \frac{\{\Im(a-a')\}^2}{4\Re(a+a')} <\frac{41}{40}+\frac{961}{20000}. \tag{5} \] The first inequality follows either by direct division or by completing the square. For the second use \(aa'/(a+a')=(a+a')/4-(a-a')^2/[4(a+a')]\) and \(\Re(z^2/w)\ge-(\Im z)^2/\Re w\) when \(\Re w>0\). Since \(C=1-aa'/(a+a')\), (5) places \(\Re C\) strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\). Thus the chosen inverse cosine never meets its cuts. For each patch, the certificate below also proves that \[ x_*,\quad 1/2-x_*\pm t/(2\pi),\quad 1/2-x_*\pm u/(2\pi) \quad\hbox{have real parts in }(0,1). \tag{6} \] These real parts are separately harmonic functions of \(t,u\). It therefore suffices to verify (6) on products of their parameter rectangle boundaries. The certified intervals verify it there; two applications of the minimum and maximum principles give it throughout each patch. Consequently the expression for \(\psi\) in (2) is holomorphic throughout their connected union. The algebraic identity \((C+c)(C+d)=(1-C)^2\) gives \(e^{A_x(x_*)}=1\). All the logarithms in \(A_x\) are the strip branches, and at \(t=u=0\) their sum is zero. Connected continuation therefore gives \(A_x(x_*)=0\) and the original zero logarithmic charge everywhere. Differentiation gives the calibrated edge derivative \(\psi_t=-\operatorname{asinh}(\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2))/\pi\). This is also the branch of the [wide phase rectangle](research_path_mixed_trace_currents.md#9-vertical-current-monotonicity-at-powers-of-at-least-seven). Thus (2) has the original phase and complete constant, rather than an independently reset saddle action. For a fixed patch and its fixed real \(b\), write \[ D_b(t,u)=\psi(t,u)-A(b,t,u). \tag{7} \] The real part of (7) is separately harmonic. Its minimum on the closed product rectangle is therefore attained on a product of two rectangle boundaries. There are \(4\cdot4=16\) such faces per patch. Each is parameterized affinely by \((s_1,s_2)\in[0,1]^2\). This reduces (4) to 48 two-dimensional inequalities. ## 3. Exact interval certificate The checker [certify_bare_kernel_wide_endpoint_gaps.py](../experiments/certify_bare_kernel_wide_endpoint_gaps.py) uses rational patch endpoints, outward Arb balls for \(\pi\), and outward complex balls for the trigonometric functions and dilogarithms. It evaluates \(D_b\) at each rational cell center. On the entire cell it encloses the exact derivatives \[ (D_b)_t= \frac{\operatorname{atanh}(\tan(\pi b)\tan(t/2)) -\operatorname{asinh}(\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2))}{\pi}, \qquad (D_b)_u=(D_b)_t(u,t). \tag{8} \] There is no missing derivative of \(x_*\), since \(A_x(x_*)=0\). The inverse functions in (8) have their principal branches. For the first, an argument on a real cut would require \(\Im t=0\); the strict factorial-wall inequality in (3) then gives \(|\tan(\pi b)\tan(t/2)|<1\). For the second, throughout (1) one has \(|\Re\tan(t/2)|\le1\), \(|\Im\tan(t/2)|<3/10\), \(\Re\cos(u/2)<51/50\), and \(|\Im\cos(u/2)|<11/100\). Hence the imaginary part of its argument has magnitude less than \(11/100+(3/10)(51/50)<1\). The original branches are therefore precisely the principal analytic branches. The checker additionally rejects any interval evaluation whose enclosing argument box meets an inverse-function cut. For a cell with center \(s^0\) and half-widths \(h_1,h_2\), the real mean-value formula gives the outward enclosure \[ \Re D_b(s)\in \Re D_b(s^0)+[-h_1,h_1]\, \Re\{(D_b)_t\,\partial_{s_1}t\} +[-h_2,h_2]\, \Re\{(D_b)_u\,\partial_{s_2}u\}. \tag{9} \] Every accepted cell has the lower endpoint of (9) greater than \(1/10000\), and satisfies (6). Otherwise the checker bisects its longer parameter side and repeats. All subdivisions and coverage data use exact rational numbers. A separate rational sweep verifies that the accepted rectangles cover each full unit square exactly, without gaps or overlaps. The [saved certificate](../repro/results/research-bare-kernel-wide-endpoint-gaps.json) records every accepted cell, its outward lower bound and strip margin, all 48 faces, precision and source hashes. Thus it certifies the full boundary faces, not a collection of samples. The harmonic argument in Section 2 then proves (4) on the entire complex parameter box. Strict compact margins prove the final neighborhood assertion. \(\square\) The lemma does not discard any finite Newton term or cotangent current. Those are separate parts of the original finite-kernel proof. Its purpose is to supply the real-wire endpoint gap that permits moving the constant cotangent integral to its saddle.

title: Holomorphic phase transport on the original Hermite jet quotient
text: # Holomorphic phase transport on the original Hermite jet quotient Fix \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), and \[ P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2,\qquad \chi_N=q^{d^2/4},\qquad \eta=(-1)^d . \tag{1} \] Fractional powers of \(q\) always mean their displayed exponential, not a newly chosen root of its numerical value. The finite algebra, Newton normalization, original trace, and signed crossing data are those of [C]. We construct norms on this same full algebra, retaining its repeated-root derivatives. ## 1. The domain and the full jet map Choose \(R>2\) and the fixed slit disk \[ D=\{z:|z|<R\}\setminus[2,R). \tag{2} \] Its physical double nodes are \(c_a=2\cos((2a+1)\pi/N)\), \(0\le a<\lfloor N/2\rfloor\). For odd \(N\), there is also the simple node \(-2\). Let \(J_N f\) list \(f(c_a),f'(c_a)\) at every double node and the odd simple value. Its target is the \(N\)-dimensional algebra \[ \mathcal Q_N=\prod_a\mathbb C[\epsilon_a]/(\epsilon_a^2) \quad\text{with an additional \(\mathbb C\) if \(N\) is odd}. \tag{3} \] This is precisely \(\mathbb C[z]/(P_N)\), by Hermite interpolation. In particular, the product on (3) retains the derivative product rule. All nodes lie in \(D\), and their distances to its boundary satisfy \[ \operatorname{dist}(c_a,\partial D) \ge \min\{R-2,\,4\sin^2(\pi/(2N))\}\ge c_R N^{-2}. \tag{4} \] The same bound holds for the odd simple node. An arbitrary bounded domain containing the nodes need not satisfy (4); the explicit choice (2) is used for the polynomial estimates below. For \(s\) traced variables use \(D^s\) and the full tensor jet map \(J_N^{(s)}\). At a product of double nodes it retains every mixed derivative \(\partial^\alpha\), \(\alpha_v\in\{0,1\}\); a simple-node slot has only \(\alpha_v=0\). The target has dimension \(N^s\). Tensor products of the one-variable Hermite polynomials prove surjectivity on holomorphic functions. ## 2. Minimal weighted representatives Let \(\Phi\) be any holomorphic function on \(D^s\). Define \[ \mathcal H_{\Phi,N} =\left\{f\in\mathcal O(D^s): \|f\|_{\Phi,N}^2 :=\int_{D^s}|f|^2e^{-2N\operatorname{Re}\Phi}\,dV<\infty \right\}. \tag{5} \] Multiplication by \(e^{-N\Phi}\) is an onto isometry from this space to the unweighted Bergman space \(\mathcal H_0=A^2(D^s)\). Indeed its inverse is multiplication by \(e^{N\Phi}\). The latter assertion does not require the weight to be bounded. The unweighted space is complete: local mean-value bounds turn an \(L^2\)-Cauchy sequence of holomorphic functions into a locally uniformly convergent sequence with the same \(L^2\) limit. The holomorphic functions with zero full jets form a holomorphic ideal \(\mathcal I_N\subset\mathcal O(D^s)\): the mixed Leibniz rule proves this assertion. Its intersection \[ I_{\Phi,N}=\mathcal I_N\cap\mathcal H_{\Phi,N} =\ker J_N^{(s)} \tag{6} \] is a closed Hilbert subspace. We do not treat \(\mathcal H_{\Phi,N}\) as an algebra or assert that an unbounded product stays in it. Evaluations and the indicated derivatives are continuous by local mean-value and Cauchy estimates after the gauge in (5). The restricted jet map in (6) is onto. Given a target jet \(u\), multiply it in the finite jet algebra by \(J(e^{-N\Phi})\), choose its Hermite polynomial \(p\), and take \(e^{N\Phi}p\). This belongs to (5), since \(D^s\) is bounded and \(p\in A^2(D^s)\). It has jets \(u\). Consequently the quotient norm \[ |u|_{\Phi,N} =\inf\{\|f\|_{\Phi,N}:Jf=u\} \tag{7} \] is a positive Hilbert norm on the entire original algebra \(\mathcal Q_N^{\otimes s}\). Here and below \(J=J_N^{(s)}\). Let \[ G_0=JJ^*,\qquad S_0=J^*G_0^{-1},\qquad P_0=S_0J \tag{8} \] in the unweighted space. Surjectivity makes \(G_0\) positive definite. Orthogonal decomposition by \(\ker J\) proves that \(S_0u\) is the unique least-norm lift and that \(P_0\) is its orthogonal projection. Put \(\Gamma_\Phi=M_{J(e^{N\Phi})}\), multiplication in the jet algebra. It is invertible, including all mixed normal entries. The weighted section and projection are exactly \[ \begin{split} S_\Phi u&=e^{N\Phi}S_0\Gamma_\Phi^{-1}u,\\ P_\Phi f&=e^{N\Phi}P_0(e^{-N\Phi}f),\\ G_\Phi&=\Gamma_\Phi G_0\Gamma_\Phi^*,\qquad |u|_{\Phi,N}^2=u^*G_\Phi^{-1}u . \end{split} \tag{9} \] These formulas prove existence, uniqueness, jet preservation, and projection norm one, rather than selecting a new polynomial source. If \(\Phi(z,\lambda)\) and \(u(\lambda)\) depend holomorphically on ordinary exterior parameters, the first formula (9) is holomorphic in \((z,\lambda)\). It uses the fixed finite section \(S_0\) and the holomorphic matrix \(\Gamma_\Phi^{-1}\). Thus exterior derivatives are retained without differentiating a varying orthogonal basis. The exterior variables are not themselves quotiented. ## 3. Exact crossing transport The function \[ \tau(z)=\arccos(-z/2)^2 =4\arcsin\!\left(\sqrt{(z+2)/4}\right)^2 \tag{10} \] is the single holomorphic continuation on \(\mathbb C\setminus[2,\infty)\) that is real nonnegative on \([-2,2)\). The square removes the apparent branch at \(-2\): the last expression has a power series in \(z+2\) there. Away from that point, if \(t=\arccos(-z/2)\) in its local branch, \(\tau'=t/\sin t\); this also extends at \(-2\). For any signed integer \(n\), set \[ \theta_n(z)=\frac{in}{4\pi}\tau(z),\qquad m_{n,N}(z)=\chi_N^n e^{N\theta_n(z)} . \tag{11} \] This is a nowhere-zero holomorphic function. It represents the original \(R^n\) in the full algebra. To check that claim directly, at the listed double nodes let \(t_a=\pi(d-2a)/N\). Then \[ \begin{split} m_{n,N}(c_a) &=\kappa^n(-1)^{na}q^{na(a+1)},\qquad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\\ \frac{m_{n,N}'(c_a)}{m_{n,N}(c_a)} &=\frac{in(d-2a)}{4\sin((2a+1)\pi/N)} . \end{split} \tag{12} \] For the first equality, use \([d^2+(d-2a)^2]/4=d^2/2+a(a+1)-Na\). For the second use \(dt/dz=1/(2\sin t)\). These are exactly [C, (5), (21)]. For odd \(N\), \(t=0\) at the simple node and (12)'s value formula is \(\chi_N^n\); there is no derivative condition at that node. It follows pointwise from (5) that multiplication by \(m_{n,N}\) is an onto isometry \[ \mathcal H_{\Phi,N}\longrightarrow \mathcal H_{\Phi+\theta_n,N},\qquad \|m_{n,N}f\|_{\Phi+\theta_n,N}=\|f\|_{\Phi,N}. \tag{13} \] It maps the zero-jet subspaces onto each other, with inverse \(m_{-n,N}\). Hence the actual finite operator \(M_{R^n}\) is an exact isometry between the quotient norms in (7), and \[ P_{\Phi+\theta_n}(m_{n,N}f)=m_{n,N}P_\Phi f . \tag{14} \] For \(s\) variables this holds with any signed powers \(n_v\), the multiplier \(\prod_v m_{n_v,N}(z_v)\), and phase increment \(\sum_v\theta_{n_v}(z_v)\), even when \(\Phi\) is not separable. The original Jordan blocks have been retained. Equation (13) changes the norm and does not make them unitary in one fixed positive metric. Nor does (11) claim equality to the canonical polynomial off its jets. More generally, if \(b=e^{N\Theta}a\) is holomorphic and \(\|a\|_\infty\le B\), multiplication gives \[ |J(b)u|_{\Phi+\Theta,N}\le B|u|_{\Phi,N}. \tag{15} \] Apply the ambient bound to the least-norm representative. An inverse bound follows when \(a^{-1}\) is holomorphic and bounded. This states the needed product hypothesis; arbitrary holomorphic spectators need not be bounded multipliers. ## 4. Evaluation bounds and the original closing For \(g=e^{-N\Phi}f\), product disks of radius comparable to \(N^{-2}\) at the nodes, the mean-value inequality and Cauchy's formula give, for each fixed multi-index \(\alpha\), \[ |\partial^\alpha g(c)|\le C_{\alpha,s,R}N^{2|\alpha|+2s}\|f\|_{\Phi,N}. \tag{16} \] Thus the gauge-covariant evaluations have polynomial cost, including the first mixed normals and the endpoint nodes. Ordinary evaluations extract \(e^{N\Phi(c)}\); ordinary derivative bounds also contain the explicit derivatives of that gauge. For arbitrary holomorphic \(\Phi\) those derivatives are not asserted polynomial. For (11) they are polynomial at the nodes for fixed derivative order and fixed \(n\): near \(2\), \(\tau^{(k)}=O(|2-z|^{1/2-k})\), and away from \(2\) they are bounded. In particular \(N\theta_n^{(k)}(c)=O_n(N^{2k})\) for \(k\ge1\). Here is the actual original trace, not an arbitrary evaluation. For a holomorphic germ \(f\) at all nodes, its full Hermite class has \[ \phi_N(f)=\eta\sum_a\{(4-c_a^2)f'(c_a)-c_af(c_a)\} +\mathbf1_{N\ {\rm odd}}f(-2). \tag{17} \] Indeed [C, (1)--(2)] imply that \(\phi_N\) extracts the \(e_d\) coefficient. The polynomial \(e_d\) has leading coefficient \(\eta/N^2\), since \(\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}2\sin(\pi j/N)=N\). The leading coefficient of the Hermite interpolant is the sum of residues of \(f/P_N\). The Chebyshev differential equation gives, at a double node, \[ P_N''(c_a)/2=N^2/(4-c_a^2),\qquad P_N'''(c_a)/(3P_N''(c_a))=c_a/(4-c_a^2). \] At the odd simple node \(P_N'(-2)=N^2\). These identities give (17), and also the exact Cauchy expression \[ \phi_N(f)=\frac{\eta N^2}{2\pi i} \int_{\Gamma_N}\frac{f(z)}{P_N(z)}\,dz, \tag{18} \] where \(\Gamma_N\subset D\) is the positive union of small circles around every distinct physical node. Products with attachments and the Gaussian (11) retain their full derivatives in this formula. Tensor products give the corresponding original multi-trace. Write any specified original closing, with its attachment and powers, as a row \(\ell\) on these full jets. The exact norm of that row is \[ \boxed{\ \|\ell\|_{\Phi,N,*}^2=\ell G_\Phi\ell^* =\ell\Gamma_\Phi G_0\Gamma_\Phi^*\ell^*.\ } \tag{19} \] The entries of \(G_0\) are the appropriate holomorphic and antiholomorphic derivatives of the unweighted Bergman kernel at the physical nodes. Formula (19) follows either from (9) or by applying the weighted adjoint of \(J\) to \(\ell^*\). It retains cross terms between all physical rows and all their normal components. Under (13), the inverse-dual row \(\ell_{\rm new}=\ell M_{R^n}^{-1}\) has exactly the old dual norm and pairs with the transported source to give the same scalar. This is bilinear source/co-source transport, not replacement of the original closing by a Hermitian positive expectation. The finite source compiler [C] can therefore be represented exactly on these least-norm ranges: an original finite operation \(A\) becomes \(S_\Psi A J\), and a closing remains \(\ell J\). Composition is exact because \(JS_\Phi=I\) at each intermediate stage; no estimate for that composition is being assumed. At a fully traced variable any replacement with the same full jets preserves the scalar, including arbitrary original attachment products and all mixed normals. A free exterior variable remains ordinary. Bounds for turns or general compositions do not follow from the crossing isometry alone. In particular, (19) does not estimate the fixed original row in a geometric phase norm, prove nonzero overlap, or assemble independently repaired spectral windows into a global holomorphic representative with controlled norm. The original exterior and seam terms in (18) must still be transported or estimated. All statements here concern an exact phase-adapted representation of the same finite invariant. ## Direct source [C] [Exact source compilation with arbitrary crossing powers](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_arbitrary_power_source_compilation.md), SHA256 55e2de84870cfd20dac5922791dbc2bed54909439dfbf4663f17c70a1089445f. The Gaussian jet calculation, Hilbert-space quotient, and residue derivation used here are given explicitly above.

title: A positive geometric presentation for negative chains of twos and threes
text: # A positive geometric presentation for negative chains of twos and threes A negative chain made from powers minus two and minus three, with power minus two at both ends, has an exact marked replacement by a positive chain whose magnitudes are at least three. One positive crossing remains at each outside boundary. The established geometric theorem therefore gives a positive decomposition of the same partially filled exterior, without assuming positivity of its old cells. There is also an exact identity in the full original quantum algebra. It gives another finite presentation of the same source. When the runs of twos satisfy the bounds in Section 6, the established long-power theorem applies to the replacement. This gives a full pendant boundary asymptotic and, after a sufficiently long closing twist, the volume conjecture for the resulting knot. The argument does not require identifying stationary points in the old presentation. ## 1. The complementary continued fraction Write the negative magnitudes as \[ \mathbf b=(2^{r_0},3,2^{r_1},3,\ldots,3,2^{r_k}), \qquad r_0,r_k\ge1,\quad r_1,\ldots,r_{k-1}\ge0. \tag{1} \] Here \(k\) counts the threes, \(2^r\) denotes a string of \(r\) twos, and \(m=k+\sum r_j\) is the path length. Adjacent threes are allowed. If there are no threes, write \(\mathbf b=(2^m)\). Set \[ \mathbf c= \begin{cases} (m+1),&k=0,\\ (r_0+2,r_1+3,\ldots,r_{k-1}+3,r_k+2),&k\ge1. \end{cases} \tag{2} \] There are \(\ell=k+1\) complementary entries. All are at least three, except for the single original vertex \(\mathbf b=(2)\), whose complement is \((2)\). When \(k=1\), there are no middle entries in the second line of (2). **Lemma 1.** For the negative continued fraction \[ \alpha=[b_1,\ldots,b_m]_- =b_1-\frac1{b_2-\dfrac1{\cdots-1/b_m}}, \] one has \[ \alpha/(\alpha-1)=[\mathbf c]_-. \tag{3} \] **Proof.** If a tail has value \(\beta>1\) and complementary value \(d=\beta/(\beta-1)\), then \[ \frac{2-1/\beta}{(2-1/\beta)-1}=d+1,\qquad \frac{3-1/\beta}{(3-1/\beta)-1}=2-\frac1{d+1}. \tag{4} \] Prepending a two increments the first complementary coefficient. Prepending a three inserts a two and increments the previous first coefficient. The last two has complement two. Induction from the right gives (2). \(\square\) Examples are \((2,3,2)\mapsto(3,3)\), \((2,3,3,2)\mapsto(3,3,3)\), and \((2,2,3,2,2)\mapsto(4,4)\). The proof holds at every length. The arithmetic is the elementary complementary continued-fraction operation; no novelty is claimed for it. ## 2. Both outside attachments and their markings Use the original crossing \(R\), clockwise turn \(T\), and their supported affine pillowcase lifts \[ \widetilde R^{\,n}(x,y)=(x+ny+n/2,y),\qquad \widetilde T(x,y)=(-y,x+1/2). \tag{5} \] Their linear parts are \[ A_n=\begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}. \] These are the actual maps proved in [the marked degree-two moves](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_marked_degree_two_tangle_moves.md). Put \[ W_-=TR^{-b_1}T\cdots TR^{-b_m}T,\qquad W_+=TR^{c_1}T\cdots TR^{c_\ell}T. \tag{6} \] **Proposition 2.** For every attached tangle \(F\), there is a specified proper half-turn \(H\), possibly the identity, such that \[ W_-(F)\simeq R\,W_+(R\,H(F)). \tag{7} \] Both boundaries remain present.
