The isotopy carries all marks, outside branches and ribbons. **Proof.** After its deck sign, the negative word has matrix \[ G=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}, \quad 0<A,D<C,\quad AD-BC=1,\quad C/A=\alpha, \tag{8} \] by the [rational normal-form theorem](research_definite_rational_corridor_normal_form.md). Conjugate by \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) and take a deck sign. The result is \[ \begin{pmatrix}-A&B\\C&-D\end{pmatrix}. \] Its two integral normalizing twists are minus one; its normalized diagonals are \(C-A,C-D\). The negative continued fraction is \(C/(C-A)=\alpha/(\alpha-1)\), which Lemma 1 identifies as \(\mathbf c\). Mirror this complete matrix identity back to obtain \[ S A_{-b_1}S\cdots A_{-b_m}S =A_1 S A_{c_1}S\cdots A_{c_\ell}S A_1 \quad\text{in }\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z). \tag{9} \] Thus the comparison is of full two-boundary maps, not just slopes. To specify \(H\), let \(B=R W_+R\), compute the actual affine maps using (5), and write \[ \widetilde B^{-1}\widetilde W_-(z)=\epsilon z+v, \quad \epsilon\in\{1,-1\},\quad \delta=\epsilon v\bmod\mathbb Z^2. \tag{10} \] The retained proper rotation is \[ \begin{array}{c|cccc} \delta&(0,0)&(1/2,0)&(0,1/2)&(1/2,1/2)\\ \hline H&1&\rho&K&T^2. \end{array} \tag{11} \] This is a finite integer and half-integer calculation for any word. The supported collar isotopy proves (7), with this rotation still acting on \(F\). \(\square\) For a pendant chain with through tangle \(I\), the identity is \[ TR^{-b_1}T\cdots TR^{-b_m}(I) \simeq R\,TR^{c_1}T\cdots TR^{c_\ell}(I). \tag{12} \] The relative linear map of the two sides, acting on the right, is \[ S A_1S^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix} \tag{13} \] up to the deck sign. The actual turn-and-cap isotopy of the normal-form theorem shows that it fixes \(I\); the remaining half-lattice translation is a proper half-turn of \(I\) and also fixes the cap. This does not erase \(H\) on an arbitrary spectator in (7). Each outside crossing changes the remaining original power by \(n\mapsto n+1\). Collecting it at that outside vertex uses the original twist-sliding isotopy, carrying the rotations and the orders of any intervening branches. The immediate carrier changes from \(\eta\) to \(\eta+1\), with its disk-filling coefficient \(p\) unchanged. If the carrier is normalized to \(\eta'=1-\eta\), with \(\eta\in\{0,1\}\), the exact bookkeeping is \[ p'=p-\eta,\qquad \lambda\longmapsto\lambda',\qquad \mu\longmapsto\mu'-\eta\lambda'. \tag{14} \] This is the disk-cut transfer of a full twist in Section 5 of the marked degree-two note. It sends the original primitive filling curve to \(\mu'+(p-\eta)\lambda'\). Normalizing the carrier without this basis change would lose the original marking. ## 3. The exact original source Let \(M\) multiply by the original crossing in the full Newton algebra \(\mathcal A_N\), let \(J\) reverse its coefficients, and put \[ \kappa_N=\exp\frac{\pi i(N-1)^2}{2N}. \tag{15} \] Repeated spectral roots retain their first normal derivatives. The identities \(J^2=1\) and \(JMJ=\kappa_NM^{-1}JM^{-1}\) imply the modular representation generated by \(J,\kappa_N^{-1/3}M\), with the displayed logarithm. The sums of the original and complementary magnitudes are \(2m+k\) and \(m+2k+1\). Comparing crossing exponents in (9) gives \[ JM^{-b_1}J\cdots JM^{-b_m}J =\kappa_N^{-(m+k+1)} M\bigl(JM^{c_1}J\cdots JM^{c_\ell}J\bigr)M. \tag{16} \] Indeed the exponent difference is \(-(2m+k)-2-(m+2k+1)=-3(m+k+1)\). Let \(\mathcal P_{\mathbf b,-,N}\) and \(\mathcal P_{\mathbf c,+,N}\) denote the full two-boundary sources. Their coefficient matrices are respectively \(JM^{-b_1}\cdots JM^{-b_m}\) and \(JM^{c_1}\cdots JM^{c_\ell}\). Multiply (16) by \(J\) and use \(JMJ=M^T\). The tensor identity is \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \mathcal P_{\mathbf b,-,N} =\kappa_N^{-(m+k+1)} (R\otimes R)\mathcal P_{\mathbf c,+,N}.} \tag{17} \] This is an equality in \(\mathcal A_N\otimes\mathcal A_N\). Both variables are canonically reduced; it is not an equality of unreduced products at arbitrary complex arguments. For the pendant coefficient columns, \[ \boxed{\displaystyle F_{\mathbf b,-,N} =\kappa_N^{-(m+k)}R F_{\mathbf c,+,N}.} \tag{18} \] Apply (16) to \(Je_0\), and use \(JMJ e_0=M^{\mathsf T}e_0=\kappa_Ne_0\). Thus \(MJ e_0=\kappa_NJe_0\), and the right side of (16) becomes \(\kappa_N^{-(m+k)}M F_{\mathbf c,+,N}\). The additional cap factor is exactly \(\kappa_N\), as also follows from the stabilizer (13). These equalities retain all normal data and their exact unit scalars. The physical rotation in (11) has the separate marked justification; the tensor formula is not an assertion of rotation invariance for an arbitrary attached tangle. ## 4. The positive geometric presentation **Theorem 3.** Let a selected path in an original circle tree have the powers (1), at least one complete outside end, and all other auxiliary circles complete. Its partially filled exterior has the positive circle-tree decomposition associated with (7), or (12) for a pendant path. Its outside primitive curves are carried by (14), and its original main-component condition is unchanged. **Proof.** Every new magnitude is at least three, except the single vertex \((2)\). The [negative-corridor geometry theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md), Theorem 15, also gives positive powers: replace a negative solution \(t_v\) by \(-\overline{t_v}\). Its returns become \(-\overline{r_{v,e}}\), its full unit charges have the positive sign, its core imaginary parts remain negative, and the inequality \(\Re q>\sqrt{(\Re a)^2+(\Re b)^2}\) is unchanged. The isolated-vertex theorem supplies the exceptional single positive power two. Retain the outside crossings in their carriers and disk frames. Their periods vanish when the outside angles are zero. The original annular attachments, with the proper rotations transported, are therefore the marked attachments of the new circle-tree presentation. The [pointwise marked-completion theorem](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md) gives its smooth hyperbolic filling. The tangle isotopy identifies this with the original partially filled exterior. It preserves the main strands and every outside component, so the same original knot or link condition applies. \(\square\) The absolute volume is the positive stationary action of the new whole presentation: \[ 2\pi\Re\left\{ \sum_{\text{new edges }e}\psi(t_{e^-},t_{e^+}) +\frac{i}{4\pi}\sum_{\text{new selected }v}c_vt_v^2 -i\sum_{\text{new selected }v}t_v \right\}. \tag{19} \] Every new edge is included, including complete outside edges. This uses the marked-completion theorem's absolute normalization. Equations (17)--(18) supply an exact finite source with this positive geometric presentation. They do not identify an old stationary cycle with a new one. No equality between individual old and new stationary actions is inferred from a finite operator identity. A full asymptotic for arbitrary adjacent powers at least three, or a proof of the required cycle transport, is still needed for a volume-conjecture conclusion in that generality. Section 6 gives the consequence when the complementary powers satisfy an already proved asymptotic theorem. For counting, the path (1) is fixed. Remaining powers undergo fixed integer translations, with permutations and rotations retained. This map is injective: no free powers are merged. Several disjoint fixed paths add their fixed shifts at a shared outside vertex. Thus the replacement has no infinite-fiber loss. It supplies a geometric family containing mixed short powers, not cofinite coverage of all assignments. ## 5. Reproducing the finite identities Run the [checker](../experiments/check_binary_negative_corridor_reexpression.py) with python3 experiments/check_binary_negative_corridor_reexpression.py \ --output repro/results/research-binary-negative-corridor-reexpression.json The default run checks all 2,048 binary words through length twelve whose end entries are two. Rational arithmetic checks the complementary fractions, full affine maps, retained rotations, pendant stabilizers, and scalar exponents. All four proper-rotation possibilities occur. Seven displayed words are also tested in the original full Newton matrices at levels two through eight, giving 49 two-boundary matrix comparisons and 49 pendant-column comparisons at 100 decimal digits. Those matrix comparisons are diagnostics; the modular-group argument proves (16)--(18) at every level. The [saved output](../repro/results/research-binary-negative-corridor-reexpression.json) records the exact examples, every matrix residual, and the SHA256 hashes of the checker and its dependencies. An independent run can write to a different output path. ## 6. Pendant boundary asymptotics and a long closing twist Read the coefficients in (1) and (2) from the outside boundary towards the terminal cap. Thus the positive pendant word is \[ F_{\mathbf c,+} =T\bigl(R^{c_1}T(R^{c_2}\cdots T(R^{c_\ell})\cdots)\bigr). \tag{20} \] Its terminal power is \(c_\ell\). The other coefficients are the successive turns to which the long-power theorem applies. Let \(B_*\) be the integer threshold in Section 6 of [the fixed-domain long-power theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_fixed_domain_long_power_turns.md). Enlarge it to at least three if necessary. Let \(B_{\rm cl}\) be the closing threshold in Section 7 of that same note; its equation (36) gives sufficient inequalities in the common analytic constants. Both thresholds are independent of the length of the fixed word. Use the initial common disk inside the marked geometric charts, as in that theorem, and include its stated final geometric enlargement in these thresholds. This is a single choice before any word is selected. **Theorem 4.** Suppose \[ c_j\ge B_*\quad(1\le j<\ell),\qquad c_\ell\ge2. \tag{21} \] Then the canonical original pendant source for the negative binary word has a nonzero full boundary asymptotic on a fixed complex disk, and a Gaussian angular bound on a fixed strip. More precisely, write the positive word's proved expansion as \[ F_{\mathbf c,+,N}(u) =\varepsilon_{\mathbf c,N}A_{\mathbf c}(u) e^{N W_{\mathbf c}(u)}(1+O_{\mathbf c}(N^{-1})). \tag{22} \] Here \(u\) is the original remaining boundary angle, the phase is even and holomorphic, and the holomorphic amplitude has no zero on the chosen closed disk. Then \[ \boxed{\displaystyle F_{\mathbf b,-,N}(u) =\kappa_N^{-(m+k)} C_{N,1}\varepsilon_{\mathbf c,N} A_{\mathbf c}(u) \exp N\left\{W_{\mathbf c}(u)+\frac{i u^2}{4\pi}\right\} (1+O_{\mathbf b}(N^{-1})),\qquad C_{N,1}=\exp\!\left(\frac{\pi i(N-1)^2}{4N}\right).} \tag{23} \] The disk and strip can be chosen independently of the word length and coefficients satisfying (21). Polynomial prefactors, amplitude sizes, error constants and the starting level may depend on the entire fixed word. Both level parities and all original first normal derivatives are included. **Proof.** Start with the terminal power \(c_\ell\), then apply the fixed-domain theorem to \(c_{\ell-1},\ldots,c_1\), in that order. Its Section 6 gives (22), a common phase bound and positive curvature, and a common bound \[ |F_{\mathbf c,+,N}(x+iy)| \le C_{\mathbf c}N^{d_{\mathbf c}} \exp N\{\Re W_{\mathbf c}(0) -\gamma(1-\cos x)+C y^2\}, \qquad |x|\le\pi,\quad |y|\le h, \tag{24} \] with \(\gamma,h>0\). In (18), multiplication by \(R\) is multiplication in the full original Hermite quotient, followed by its canonical representative; it is not multiplication by an arbitrary analytic interpolant. Apply Theorem 1 of [boundary crossing preservation](research_boundary_crossing_packet_preservation.md) with the fixed power \(+1\). That theorem gives (23) and preserves a bound of the form (24) on a possibly smaller common disk and strip. Its family statement gives the asserted uniformity. The exact scalar in (18) has modulus one and introduces no further error. \(\square\) The run-length conditions in this theorem are explicit. If \(k=0\), there is a single complementary terminal power \(m+1\); (21) imposes no lower bound on the length \(m\ge1\). If \(k\ge1\), (21) says \[ \begin{split} r_0&\ge\max(1,B_*-2),\\ r_j&\ge\max(0,B_*-3)\qquad(1\le j<k),\\ r_k&\ge1 . \end{split} \tag{25} \] In particular the final run, adjacent to the cap, need not be long. There may be arbitrarily many threes, provided each preceding run has the indicated length. All lengths and powers are fixed before the level \(N\) tends to infinity. **Corollary 5.** Assume (21). Give the remaining original circle a fixed signed closing power \(a\), and suppose \[ |a+1|\ge B_{\rm cl}. \tag{26} \] Under the original knot and framing conditions, the cylindrical closure of this negative pendant word satisfies the volume conjecture. Its complete source has a nonzero asymptotic \[ \begin{split} Z_{\mathbf b,a,N} &=\phi_N(R^a F_{\mathbf b,-,N})\\ &=\kappa_N^{-(m+k)} \phi_N(R^{a+1}F_{\mathbf c,+,N})\\ &=\kappa_N^{-(m+k)}\varepsilon_{\mathbf c,N}C_{N,a+1} N^{3/2}D_{\mathbf c,a+1} e^{N\mathcal V_{\mathbf c,a+1}} (1+O_{\mathbf b,a}(N^{-1})), \qquad D_{\mathbf c,a+1}\ne0 . \end{split} \tag{27} \] The invariant is the original zero-framed knot invariant, up to the unit normalization already retained in the original source convention. Consequently \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N(K)| =2\pi\Re\mathcal V_{\mathbf c,a+1} =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \tag{28} \] **Proof.** The middle line of (27) is the exact quotient identity (18), contracted with the original trace. Section 7 of the fixed-domain theorem applies with the closing power \(c_0=a+1\). It proves the last line of (27), including its nonzero coefficient, both parities and every trace normal. Its phase is \[ \mathcal V_{\mathbf c,a+1} =W_{\mathbf c}(s_*)+ \frac{i(a+1)s_*^2}{4\pi}-is_*, \qquad W_{\mathbf c}'(s_*)+ \frac{i(a+1)s_*}{2\pi}-i=0, \tag{29} \] on its selected small branch. The pendant isotopy (12), followed by the original closure, gives the same marked knot as this positive word with closing power \(a+1\). The peripheral shear is exactly (14); neither the original meridian nor the disk longitude is silently reset. The marked geometric part of the closing theorem identifies \(2\pi\Re\mathcal V_{\mathbf c,a+1}\) with the absolute volume of this knot complement. All displayed scalar factors have modulus one, so (28) follows. \(\square\) The original component test is essential: the closure must have one main component and satisfy the original exclusion of internal closed components. It is transported by the literal tangle isotopy. A sufficient condition for (26) is \(|a|\ge B_{\rm cl}+1\); (26) is the precise translated condition. For each fixed negative binary word satisfying (21), the map of remaining assignments is the injection \(a\mapsto a+1\). Thus the conclusion includes all sufficiently long signed closing assignments on that stratum, with no identification of distinct free parameters. For a path with two free outside boundaries, (17) is still an exact identity with both variables and all normal data. The one-boundary theorem used above does not by itself give a joint two-boundary asymptotic. Such a replacement can be made inside a whole marked tree and the existing tree theorem applied if the *transformed whole tree* satisfies its hypotheses, with all outside shifts and rotations retained. No standalone joint packet for an arbitrary complementary chain is asserted here. ## 7. What repeated complementation can reach The complementary fraction is defined for every finite list \(\mathbf b=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\) with \(b_j\ge2\). Let \(D(\mathbf b)\) be the unique list with entries at least two and \[ [D(\mathbf b)]_-=\frac{[\mathbf b]_-}{[\mathbf b]_--1}. \tag{30} \] The ceiling algorithm in the [definite rational normal form](research_definite_rational_corridor_normal_form.md), Section 2, proves uniqueness. Since \(x\mapsto x/(x-1)\) is an involution, so is \(D\). **Proposition 6.** The list \(D(\mathbf b)\) has every entry at least three if and only if \(\mathbf b\) is a binary list with both end entries two, other than the singleton \((2)\). With the original outside frames, the only uniform-sign chain forms with magnitudes at least two, allowing integral twists at the two ends and the retained proper rotations, are the negative form \(\mathbf b\) and the positive form \(D(\mathbf b)\). The same assertion holds for a pendant word with its original outside frame and cap. **Proof.** For a one-entry list \((a)\), \[ D((a))=(2^{a-1}). \tag{31} \] If the complementary list for a tail is \((d_1,d_2,\ldots)\), prepending \(a\ge2\) to the original list changes it to \[ (2^{a-2},d_1+1,d_2,\ldots). \tag{32} \] Here an empty string is omitted. Equation (32) follows from (4): prepending two increments the first entry, and each further unit in \(a\) inserts a two at the front. In this recursion, only the first entry of an existing list can ever increase. If the final entry \(b_m\) is at least three, (31) initially has a two that can never be increased. If any other \(b_j\ge4\), (32) inserts at least two leading twos; the second of them can never be increased. If \(b_1\ge3\), the final application of (32) leaves a leading two. Thus absence of twos in the complement requires entries in \(\{2,3\}\) and both ends two. Formula (2) proves sufficiency, except that the singleton two has itself as complement. For the statement with two boundaries, write the normalized matrix of the original negative word as \[ \begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}, \qquad 0<A,D<C,\qquad C/A=[\mathbf b]_- . \tag{33} \] Integral end twists do not change \(A,D\) modulo \(C\), and the proper rotations have identity linear part on the pillowcase. A uniform-negative chain with entries at least two already has its diagonals in this normalized range, so uniqueness of the ceiling expansion forces its list to be \(\mathbf b\). For a uniform-positive chain the normalized diagonal residues are the complementary ones \(C-A,C-D\). Its list is therefore uniquely \(D(\mathbf b)\), with the two end twists \(+1\). The full affine comparison retains the appropriate rotation as in (10)--(11). For a pendant word, its normalized slope is \(x=1/[\mathbf b]_-\in(0,1)\). A negative chain preceded by an integer twist has slope \(r+1/[\mathbf d]_-\); equality to \(x\) forces \(r=0\) and \(\mathbf d=\mathbf b\). A positive chain has slope \(r-1/[\mathbf d]_-\); equality forces \(r=1\) and \(\mathbf d=D(\mathbf b)\). The established cap stabilizer supplies the literal isotopy and does not enlarge either list. \(\square\) Consequently the all-magnitudes-at-least-three geometric theorem, combined only with repeated marked complementation and end twists, covers exactly two types of negative lists: those already having all entries at least three, and the binary lists of Proposition 6. The separately proved isolated power two is an additional elementary case. For example, \[ (3,2,3)\longleftrightarrow(2,4,2) \tag{34} \] has a two in both normalized forms. This is an obstruction to that particular reduction strategy, not to a positive subdivision of the actual filled manifold. Local replacements may produce a mixed-sign chain, but if their eventual result is a uniform-sign chain in the same outside frames, the same uniqueness argument still applies. No conclusion here permits a quarter-turn of an outside attachment while leaving its primitive curves untouched. Such a move changes the retained boundary frame and would require a separate geometric attachment argument. The fixed integer end shifts and proper rotations already allowed preserve the injective assignment bookkeeping of Section 2.

title: A binomial cut and its polynomially bounded framing density
text: # A binomial cut and its polynomially bounded framing density Private written proof, 18 November 2026. A single cut occupation near the middle of the physical module has an exact normal-residue description, but its coefficients at the two framing endpoints can grow exponentially with the level. A binomial average of cut occupations avoids that cost. It gives the same original unmarked knot invariant, and its entire density on the compact real framing interval has polynomial norm. The density is a Legendre polynomial evaluation kernel. The construction below keeps the original marked-current defect. It does not select a geometric contribution to the invariant. The complete proof sources are **C**, the actual normal-residue and cut-moment map; **D**, its whole-clock extension; and **I**, the exact change of physical cut. Their pins are listed below. The orthogonal-polynomial calculations are proved here. ## 1. The cut and its exact relation to the original scalar Fix \(N\ge2\), put \(d=N-1\), and use the factorial basis \(e_0,\ldots,e_d\) of I. Let \(T_a=e_ae_a^*\) be the diagonal coordinate projection. Define \[ \pi_{N,a}=2^{-d}\binom da,\qquad P_N^{\rm cut}=\sum_{a=0}^{d}\pi_{N,a}T_a . \tag{1} \] The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Positivity here is in the stated finite basis metric; no unitary structure on every quantum-group representation is assumed. For the actual unmarked one-cut endomorphism, I proves \(C_N(M)=F_N(M)I\), with the original framing and reduced scalar normalization. Therefore, exactly at every level, \[ \operatorname{Tr}(P_N^{\rm cut}C_N(M)) =F_N(M)=\operatorname{Tr}(T_0C_N(M)). \tag{2} \] At \(M=1\) this is the original Kashaev scalar. In particular no factor such as \(2^{-d}\) is being added to the invariant after its evaluation; it is part of a trace-one cut probe in (1). For an arbitrary marked endomorphism the comparison has a defect. Use I's actual raising coefficients and currents, \[ \epsilon_r(M)=M Q^{-r-1}-M^{-1},\quad Q=e^{2\pi i/N}, \qquad B_{N,a}=-\sum_{r<a}\epsilon_r(M)^{-1}E_{r+1,r}. \] Set \(B_N^{\rm cut}=\sum_a\pi_{N,a}B_{N,a}\). Then \[ [\mathcal E,B_N^{\rm cut}]=P_N^{\rm cut}-T_0,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}((P_N^{\rm cut}-T_0)C) =\operatorname{Tr}(B_N^{\rm cut}[C,\mathcal E]). \tag{3} \] Its subdiagonal coefficients are \(-\Pr(A>r)/\epsilon_r(M)\), where \(A\) has probabilities \(\pi_{N,a}\). Their numerators have absolute value at most one. The complete bounds of I consequently give \[ \|B_N^{\rm cut}\|\le N/3 \quad\left(|M-1|\le\frac1{4N}\right),\qquad \|\partial_M^j B_N^{\rm cut}\|\le C_jN^{j+1} \quad\left(|M-1|\le\frac1{8N}\right) \tag{4} \] for each fixed \(j\). The same physical tail pivots and marked word are retained on the right side of (3). ## 2. What a framing density must reproduce For any finite matrix \(C\), write its diagonal coherent polynomial as \[ \overline f_C(T)=\sum_{a=0}^{d}C_{aa}B_{a,d}(T),\qquad B_{a,d}(T)=\binom da T^a(1-T)^{d-a}. \tag{5} \] This polynomial has degree at most \(d\). It is the angular average of the full actual coherent symbol in C and D, including when \(C\) has off-diagonal entries. The exact Toeplitz row is \[ [\mathcal T_N(P)]_a =N\int_0^1P(-T)B_{a,d}(T)\,dT . \tag{6} \] The corresponding normal-residue pairing is \[ \frac1N\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal T_N(P)C) =\int_0^1P(-T)\overline f_C(T)\,dT . \tag{7} \] This is a normalized ordinary trace on arbitrary matrices. As in C and D, its equality with the prescribed average cut uses diagonality of the actual position-conserving cut arrays. It is not an equality with that average on arbitrary off-diagonal Ward matrices. Equation (3) retains the physical comparison. The density needed for (1) must therefore evaluate all degree \(\le d\) polynomials at \(T=1/2\): \[ \int_0^1p_N(T)q(T)\,dT=q(1/2). \tag{8} \] Indeed (8) applied to \(B_{a,d}\) gives \(\mathcal T_N(P_N^{\rm nor})=N P_N^{\rm cut}\), where \(P_N^{\rm nor}(b)=p_N(-b)\). The factor \(N\) is required by the original normalization (7). ## 3. An elementary construction of the evaluation kernel Let \(\mathsf L_k\) denote the ordinary Legendre polynomial, to distinguish it from the physical circle operators. Define it by \[ \mathsf L_k(x)=\frac1{2^kk!} \frac{d^k}{dx^k}(x^2-1)^k . \tag{9} \] Integration by parts \(k\) times shows that it is orthogonal to every polynomial of degree below \(k\) on \([-1,1]\). All boundary terms vanish because \((x^2-1)^k\) has a zero of order \(k\) at both endpoints. Its leading coefficient is \(2^{-k}\binom{2k}{k}\), and the same integration by parts, using \[ \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^k\,dx =\frac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^2}{(2k+1)!}, \] gives \(\int_{-1}^1\mathsf L_k^2\,dx=2/(2k+1)\). The displayed integral follows by the substitution \(x=2u-1\) and the elementary factorial beta integral. Thus \(\sqrt{2k+1}\mathsf L_k(2T-1)\) is an orthonormal polynomial basis for Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\). Set \[ p_N(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}(2k+1)\mathsf L_k(0) \mathsf L_k(2T-1). \tag{10} \] Expanding \(q\) in this orthonormal basis proves (8), without an approximation or an asymptotic passage. Consequently \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \operatorname{Tr}(P_N^{\rm cut}C) =\int_0^1p_N(T)\overline f_C(T)\,dT =\overline f_C(1/2).} \tag{11} \] The polynomial density can have either sign. The positive object in (1) is the physical cut matrix, not its contravariant density. There is also an exact compact contour presentation. The full coherent symbol of C and D is \[ f_C(v,T)=\sum_{i,j=0}^{d}C_{ij}\binom dj v^{i-j}T^j(1-T)^{d-j}. \] Taking its angular constant coefficient gives \[ \operatorname{Tr}(P_N^{\rm cut}C) =\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|v|=1}f_C(v,1/2)\,\frac{dv}{v}. \tag{11a} \] Thus the compact polynomial density can be integrated out exactly to an interior latitude circle, for every finite matrix \(C\). This circle is a co-source presentation; it has not been identified with the remaining geometric centralizer quotient. Here are the elementary bounds used next. Formula (9) gives \[ \mathsf L_{2m+1}(0)=0,\quad \mathsf L_{2m}(0)=(-1)^m c_m,\quad c_m=4^{-m}\binom{2m}{m},\quad \mathsf L_k(1)=1,\quad \mathsf L_k(-1)=(-1)^k. \tag{12} \] It also gives \(|\mathsf L_k(x)|\le1\) for real \(|x|\le1\). For completeness, its generating series, obtained by expanding (9), is \((1-2xz+z^2)^{-1/2}\). The same series is obtained by summing the geometric series under \[ \frac1\pi\int_0^\pi \bigl(x+i\sqrt{1-x^2}\cos\varphi\bigr)^k\,d\varphi. \] Indeed the normalized integral \(\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\) of \((1-zx-iz\sqrt{1-x^2}\cos\varphi)^{-1}\) is \(((1-zx)^2+z^2(1-x^2))^{-1/2}\); the substitution \(\tan(\varphi/2)\) verifies it near \(z=0\), with branch one there. Each base in the integrand has modulus at most one. Comparison of coefficients proves the bound. ## 4. Exact endpoint and norm formulas Put \(m_*=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\) and \(A_N=(2m_*+1)c_{m_*}>0\). Then \[ \boxed{\displaystyle p_N(0)=p_N(1)=(-1)^{m_*}A_N,\qquad \|p_N\|_{L^2(0,1)}=A_N.} \tag{13} \] Here is a direct verification. The endpoint sum is \(\sum_{m=0}^{m_*}(4m+1)(-1)^m c_m\). The ratio \(c_m/c_{m-1}=(2m-1)/(2m)\) shows by subtraction that its partial sum is \((-1)^{m_*}(2m_*+1)c_{m_*}\). Orthogonality gives \[ \|p_N\|_2^2=\sum_{m=0}^{m_*}(4m+1)c_m^2 =(2m_*+1)^2c_{m_*}^2. \] The last equality telescopes by the same ratio. Induction on that ratio proves \(c_m^2\le1/(m+1)\). Hence \(A_N\le2\sqrt N\), including \(N=2\), and \[ \|p_N\|_{L^1(0,1)},\ \|p_N\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le2\sqrt N, \qquad \|p_N\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\le N A_N\le2N^{3/2}. \tag{14} \] The supremum bound follows from Cauchy--Schwarz in (10): the evaluation vector at \(T\) has squared norm at most \(\sum_{k=0}^{d}(2k+1)=N^2\), while that at \(1/2\) has norm \(A_N\). All fixed real derivatives also have polynomial bounds: \[ \|p_N^{(r)}\|_\infty \le(2N^2)^r N A_N . \tag{15} \] To see this without importing a derivative inequality, expand \(\mathsf L_k'\) in the Legendre basis. Integration by parts and (12) give coefficient \(2\ell+1\) at every \(\ell<k\) of parity opposite to \(k\), and zero otherwise. Their sum is \(k(k+1)/2\le N^2\). Repeating this expansion at each derivative and using the factor two from \(2T-1\) proves (15). Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the original coefficient sum in (10) by \(N A_N\). In particular, on the complex distance-\(\delta\) neighborhood of \([0,1]\), Taylor's finite formula gives \[ |p_N(T)|\le N A_N\exp(2N^2\delta). \tag{16} \] This supplies a polynomial bound on collars of width \(O(N^{-2})\), not on a fixed complex neighborhood. ## 5. The actual normal residue and its retained current In the normal framing coordinates of C and D, \(b_N=-a/\eta\), \(T=va\), and \[ \nu_{\rm cut}=-\frac{d\eta}{\eta}\wedge \frac{\Omega}{1-\eta v}. \] The exact finite residue is \[ \operatorname{Res}_E [P_N^{\rm nor}(b_N)\nu_{\rm cut}] =-p_N(T)\Omega . \tag{17} \] With the original compact-cycle normalization, pairing (17) against the actual coherent source gives (11). The compatible south representative remains \(P_N^{\rm nor}(b_S-1)\). No change of the affine clutch or deletion of \(1-\eta v\) before the residue is made. The degree is \(2m_*\), so the normal pole order is \(2m_*+1\): it is \(N\) at odd levels and \(N-1\) at even levels. The polynomial compact residue bounds do not turn this into a bounded normal jet or identify the off-divisor source with its residue. The two density endpoints in (13) agree, but the full current does not consequently vanish. For arbitrary diagonal \(C\), the actual integration-by-parts map is \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \frac1N\operatorname{Tr} (\mathcal T_N((P_N^{\rm nor})')C) =(-1)^{m_*}A_N(C_{00}-C_{dd}) +\overline f_C'(1/2).} \tag{18} \] Indeed the endpoint formula in C gives the first term and the remaining integral is \(\int_0^1p_N(T)\overline f_C'(T)\,dT\). Here \(\overline f_C'\) has degree at most \(d-1\), so (8) evaluates that integral exactly. Explicitly \[ \overline f_C'(1/2) =d\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}2^{-(d-1)}\binom{d-1}{a} (C_{a+1,a+1}-C_{aa}). \] This includes \(N=2\). For \(C=I\) both terms vanish; for a marked source neither is to be omitted. The product-current correction of C is still present before pairing. ## 6. Scope of the new presentation The cut probabilities are concentrated near the middle occupation. Precisely \[ \Pr(|A-d/2|\ge\varepsilon d) \le2e^{-2\varepsilon^2d}. \tag{19} \] An elementary proof uses \(\mathbb E e^{t(A-d/2)}=\cosh(t/2)^d\le e^{dt^2/8}\) and exponential Markov inequality with \(t=4\varepsilon\). The hyperbolic-cosine bound follows by integrating \(\tanh x\le x\). The estimate describes the probe weights; discarding their tails in a marked contraction also needs a bound on that contraction's matrix entries. Equation (11) gives a fixed interior latitude evaluation of the angularly averaged coherent source. In I's existing classical cut-position chart, the central occupation has the noncentral complete parameter \(s=-2\). This does not prove that the full new quantum source has just the old geometric critical point or the same stationary equations. An exponentially varying matrix kernel can shift a saddle in a binomial sum. Its entropy and all remaining variables must be retained in a new source analysis. What is settled is a source-preserving choice of cut with a polynomially bounded compact framing density and exact current. The remaining centralizer coordinate, off-divisor normal transport, transverse source map, and geometric cycle coefficient are not supplied by this calculation. No new volume-conjecture filling case is claimed. ## Coverage and complete proof-source pins The polynomial evaluation kernel and its orthogonality belong to classical orthogonal-polynomial theory; see [DLMF, Section 18.2(v)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.2#v) and [the classical normalizations](https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.3). No novelty is claimed for them. The proof above derives the identities needed for the particular physical cut. The literature was consulted for coverage, not as a substitute for those derivations. * C: notes/centralizer_normal_residue_and_actual_cut_moments.md, SHA256 b040461ba07902277ae2964515060e4927322f30c0be81772bed7f2d3da72a1a. * D: notes/dual_clock_normal_cut_source.md, SHA256 73191e0560d48789aaacebb44c1c768f66f4c3c3f3ecf8af3faf1380d69eafa3. * I: notes/research_fixed_interior_cut_source.md, SHA256 93b2887527e0b5c9cb93f4da77702c996f0524e0a93f0c0032909345efdbd1b2. All three complete directs were read nontruncated in the author sequence, their used implications checked, and their matching pins renewed. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used; frozen/public files are unchanged.

title: Boundary multiplication preserves concentrated original sources
text: # Boundary multiplication preserves concentrated original sources Multiplication by a fixed crossing power preserves a boundary asymptotic when the original boundary polynomial has a strict angular decay bound. The multiplication is performed in the full Hermite quotient. Its canonical polynomial is exponentially close, on the real physical period and on a smaller complex disk, to the product with the original Gaussian representative of that crossing. The angular decay assumption is essential. The crossing polynomial by itself has exponentially large band-edge terms on a complex strip, as shown in the [polynomial crossing calculation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_polynomial_crossing_fourier_trace.md). The proof here suppresses those terms using the decay of the factor being multiplied. An unrestricted analogous assertion for the quarter-turn is false; Section 7 gives an original-source counterexample. ## 1. Statement for the original quotient Let \[ D=N-1,\qquad \eta=(-1)^D,\qquad \mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2),\qquad z(t)=-2\cos t. \tag{1} \] The Chebyshev polynomial has its ordinary normalization. Every double root retains its first derivative; at odd levels the root \(-2\) is simple. Write \(\operatorname{can}\) for the representative of degree less than \(N\), and let \(R\) be the original crossing. Suppose \(F_N(t)=f_N(-2\cos t)\), where \(\deg f_N<N\), is an original boundary source. Assume that there are constants \(c,b>0\), \(B\ge0\), \(C>0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(M\in\mathbb R\), independent of \(N\), such that \[ |F_N(x+iy)|\le C N^d \exp N\{M-c(1-\cos x)+B y^2\}, \qquad |x|\le\pi,\quad |y|\le b. \tag{2} \] Polynomial prefactors and the starting level may depend on the fixed source. For a fixed signed integer \(n\), define \[ \begin{split} P_{n,N}(t)&=\operatorname{can}(R^n f_N)(-2\cos t),\\ C_{N,n}&=\exp\left(\frac{\pi i nD^2}{4N}\right),\\ g_{n,N}(t)&=C_{N,n}\exp\left(\frac{inNt^2}{4\pi}\right)F_N(t). \end{split} \tag{3} \] Negative powers in the first line are taken in \(\mathcal A_N\), before choosing the representative. The scalar in the second line has the displayed logarithm convention, not a principal fractional power of another numerical scalar. **Theorem 1.** Under (2), there are \(\delta>0\), \(r>0\), and fixed polynomial prefactors such that \[ \sup_{|t|\le\pi,\ t\in\mathbb R} |P_{n,N}(t)-g_{n,N}(t)| \le C_nN^{d_n}e^{N(M-\delta)}, \tag{4} \] and \[ \sup_{|t|\le r}|P_{n,N}(t)-g_{n,N}(t)| \le C_n'N^{d_n'}e^{N(M-\delta/2)}. \tag{5} \] The constants \(\delta,r\) can be chosen using only \(c,B,b,n\). Both estimates preserve all physical first normals and hold at both parities of \(N\). Suppose in addition that on a fixed complex disk \[ F_N(u)=\epsilon_N N^\alpha A(u)e^{NW(u)}(1+O(N^{-1})),\qquad |\epsilon_N|=1, \tag{6} \] uniformly, where \(W\) is even and holomorphic, \(A\) is holomorphic and nonzero, \(\Re W(0)=M\), and \(-\Re W''(0)>0\). Then, on a possibly smaller fixed disk, \[ \boxed{\displaystyle P_{n,N}(u)=\epsilon_N C_{N,n}N^\alpha A(u) \exp N\left\{W(u)+\frac{in u^2}{4\pi}\right\} (1+O(N^{-1})).} \tag{7} \] It also satisfies a bound of the form (2), with positive constants \(c',b'\) and a finite \(B'\). Thus the class of these concentrated original boundary sources is closed under every fixed signed boundary crossing multiplication. No uniformity as \(n\) grows with \(N\) is asserted. A family with common constants in (2), a common disk for the full expansion (6) on which every amplitude is nonzero, common bounds on the normalized phases \(W-W(0)\), and a common positive curvature bound has common output constants for each fixed finite set of powers \(n\). Amplitude sizes, error constants and starting levels may still depend on the individual source. ## 2. Exact Hermite folding of a smooth periodic function The physical angles are \[ \tau_j=\frac{\pi(D-2j)}N, \qquad j=0,\ldots,D. \tag{8} \] The original crossing has the value and angular derivative of \(C_{N,n}e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)}\) at these angles. Therefore the canonical product in (3) has exactly the values and angular derivatives of \(g_{n,N}\) there. At the odd simple angle zero, the angular derivative vanishes by evenness and adds no spurious condition. Let \(f\) be an even smooth periodic function with Fourier coefficients \(a_\ell\), with enough decay that its value and first derivative series converge absolutely. Let \(p(t)=\sum_{|m|<N}b_me^{imt}\), \(b_{-m}=b_m\), be its full physical Hermite interpolant. Sampling on (8) gives \[ V_m=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\eta^k a_{m+kN},\qquad W_m=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(m+kN)\eta^k a_{m+kN}. \tag{9} \] For \(1\le m<N\), the two band coefficients in this residue class obey \(V_m=b_m+\eta b_{m-N}\) and \(W_m=mb_m+\eta(m-N)b_{m-N}\). Hence \[ b_m=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(k+1)\eta^k a_{m+kN}. \tag{10} \] At \(m=0\), the derivative sample mean is zero by evenness, and \[ b_0=\sum_k\eta^k a_{kN} =a_0+2\sum_{k\ge1}\eta^k a_{kN}. \tag{11} \] The same expression (10) also gives (11), after pairing \(k\) and \(-k\). This includes every alias and the repeated-root derivatives. The term \(k=-1\) in (10) is zero. All other terms apart from \(a_m\) have \(|m+kN|\ge N\). Summing their absolute values, and including the discarded original Fourier coefficients, gives \[ \|p-f\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)} \le C_0\sum_{|\ell|\ge N} (1+|\ell|/N)|a_\ell|. \tag{12} \] Here \(C_0\) is absolute. This is the general version of the exact two-mode calculation in the polynomial crossing note. In particular, value interpolation alone would not prove (12). ## 3. The endpoint cutoff and the complete Fourier tail We suppress the subscript \(n,N\) temporarily. Since \(1-\cos x\ge2x^2/\pi^2\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\), completing a square gives \[ \frac{|nxy|}{2\pi} \le\frac c2(1-\cos x)+\frac{n^2y^2}{16c}. \] Thus the analytic function \(g\) satisfies \[ |g(x+iy)|\le C N^d \exp N\{M-(c/2)(1-\cos x)+B_*y^2\},\qquad B_*=B+\frac{n^2}{16c}. \tag{13} \] Choose an even smooth cutoff \(\chi_N\) which is one on \(|t|\le a_N=\pi-3\pi/(4N)\), zero on \(|t|\ge b_N=\pi-\pi/(4N)\), and whose fixed derivatives are bounded by \(C_jN^j\). Such cutoffs are obtained by rescaling one fixed smooth function. The last physical angle is \(\pi-\pi/N<a_N\), so \[ f(t)=\chi_N(t)g(t) \tag{14} \] has exactly the same values and first derivatives at every physical angle. Extending it periodically gives an even smooth function. Its Hermite interpolant is consequently exactly \(P_{n,N}\), not a new model for that polynomial. Choose a fixed height \(h>0\) so small that \[ h<b/4,\qquad B_*h\le1/4,\qquad B_*h^2\le c/8. \tag{15} \] Conditions containing \(B_*\) are vacuous if it is zero. Cauchy's estimate on disks of radius \(1/(10N)\), with a slightly larger height bound if needed, shows that each fixed derivative of \(g\) costs only a fixed power of \(N\) in (13). These disks stay inside the original real window at every point used in the cutoff and central contour. Errors of size \(O(1/N)\) in the exponent are absorbed in the constant. Integrate the Fourier coefficient of (14) by parts four times. There are no endpoint terms because the cutoff is zero near the ends of the period. Terms with a derivative of \(\chi_N\), and the part of \(\chi_Ng^{(4)}\) outside \([-a_N,a_N]\), lie in the endpoint layers. On those layers \(1-\cos x\ge1\), so their total contribution before the factor \(|\ell|^{-4}\) is bounded by \(C_nN^{d+4}e^{N(M-c/4)}\). For the remaining integral of \(g^{(4)}e^{-i\ell t}\), move \([-a_N,a_N]\) to height \(-\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)h\). This is an ordinary holomorphic deformation on this central rectangle. Its horizontal part is bounded by \[ C_nN^{d+4}e^{N(M+B_*h^2)-|\ell|h}. \] Both vertical sides have \(1-\cos a_N\ge1\). Equations (13),(15) bound them by \(C_nN^{d+4}e^{N(M-c/4)}\); the Fourier factor decreases along each vertical side. In particular those sides have been estimated, not discarded. Altogether, for \(|\ell|\ge N\), \[ |a_\ell|\le \frac{C_nN^{d+4}}{|\ell|^4} \left[e^{N(M+B_*h^2)-|\ell|h}+e^{N(M-c/4)}\right]. \tag{16} \] Since \(B_*h^2\le h/4\), summation gives \[ \sum_{|\ell|\ge N}(1+|\ell|/N)|a_\ell| \le C_nN^{d+1}e^{N(M-\delta)},\qquad \delta=\min(h/2,c/8)>0. \tag{17} \] Increasing a polynomial prefactor does not affect the fixed gap. Equations (12),(17), together with the exponentially small difference between \(f\) and \(g\) in their endpoint layers, prove (4). The cutoff is used solely to estimate Fourier coefficients. It is not continued to a complex domain, and it does not replace the original finite source in any subsequent trace. ## 4. Local complex comparison Set \(E_N=P_{n,N}-g_{n,N}\). This is analytic near the whole real window. The real bound (4) holds, whereas (2)--(4) also give the crude bound \(\sup_{\mathbb R}|P_{n,N}|\le C_nN^{d_n}e^{NM}\). Each of its Fourier coefficients is therefore bounded by the latter quantity. Its band \(|m|<N\) implies \[ |P_{n,N}(x+iy)|\le C_nN^{d_n+1}e^{N(M+|y|)}. \tag{18} \] Fix \(a<\min(b/2,\pi/2)\). On the semicircle \(|z|=a\), (13),(18) give \[ |E_N(z)|\le C_nN^{d_n'}e^{N(M+C_a)},\qquad C_a=\max(a,B_*a^2). \tag{19} \] On its real diameter the exponent is \(M-\delta\). In the upper half-disk, the harmonic measure of the curved boundary is explicitly \[ \omega(z)=\frac2\pi\arg\frac{a+z}{a-z}. \] For \(|z|\le a/2\), it is at most \(16\Im z/(3\pi a)\). The two-constants inequality for the subharmonic function \(\log|E_N|\) therefore gives exponent \[ M-\delta+(\delta+C_a)\omega(z). \] The lower half-disk has the identical estimate with \(|\Im z|\). Choose \[ r\le\min\left(a/2,\frac{3\pi a\delta}{32(\delta+C_a)}\right). \tag{20} \] Then (5) follows. This argument uses the analytic function \(E_N\), not the smooth Fourier periodization. Under (6), shrink this disk once more so that \(\Re(W(u)+inu^2/(4\pi))\ge M-\delta/4\) there. The amplitude is bounded away from zero on a smaller closed disk. The error (5) is then exponentially small relative to the main term, proving (7). The same argument works uniformly for a family with the common phase bounds stated after the theorem. No common positive lower bound on the amplitudes is required: each fixed source has its own starting level. ## 5. Recovering a whole-period Gaussian strip bound On the real period, (4) and (2) immediately imply \[ |P_{n,N}(x)|\le C_nN^{d_n} e^{N\{M-c_1(1-\cos x)\}},\qquad c_1=\min(c,\delta/2)>0. \tag{21} \] Near zero the new phase in (7) has exactly the old real curvature: \[ -\Re\left(W''(0)+\frac{in}{2\pi}\right)=-\Re W''(0)>0. \] Its evenness and a fixed bound on its higher derivatives give, on a small fixed complex disk, \[ \Re\left(W(x+iy)+\frac{in(x+iy)^2}{4\pi}\right) \le M-a x^2+B_1y^2 \tag{22} \] for some \(a>0\), \(B_1<\infty\). For example, bound the mixed term from the imaginary quadratic coefficient by completing a square, then absorb higher terms by shrinking the disk. Formula (7) gives the same bound for the source, with a polynomial prefactor. For clarity, the far-angle strip can be obtained without continuing the exponentially small interpolation error. Fix a small \(r_0>0\) inside this local disk. The spectral interval \(J=[-2\cos(r_0/2),2]\) corresponds to real angles \(r_0/2\le|x|\le\pi\). On \(J\), (21) has a fixed gap \(\Delta=c_1(1-\cos(r_0/2))\). Expanding the degree-\(D\) polynomial in rescaled Chebyshev polynomials bounds its complex value by \[ 2N\sup_J|P_{n,N}|\,e^{NG_J(z)}, \] where \(G_J(z)=\log|\zeta+\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}|\) is zero on \(J\), \(\zeta\) being the affine coordinate taking \(J\) to \([-1,1]\), and the exterior branch is used. This elementary Chebyshev estimate is the interval Bernstein--Walsh bound used in the earlier source proofs. Continuity of \(G_J\) makes it at most \(\Delta/4\) on \(z=-2\cos(x+iy)\), \(r_0\le|x|\le\pi\), for a fixed sufficiently small \(|y|\le b'\). This remains true at the endpoint \(z=2\). Thus the far-angle strip retains a fixed gap. Combine it with (22), choosing \(c'>0\) smaller than both the local quadratic constant and \(\Delta/8\), and taking \(B'\ge B_1\). This proves the asserted bound (2) for the canonical product on one fixed whole-period strip. All choices are uniform under common input constants and local phase bounds; there is no iteration over the level. The same proof also handles a fixed finite product of concentrated boundary sources. More precisely, if \(F_{j,N}\), \(1\le j\le s\), satisfy (2),(6), then \[ \operatorname{can}\left(R^n\prod_{j=1}^s f_{j,N}\right)(-2\cos u) =C_{N,n}\left(\prod_j\epsilon_{j,N}\right) N^{\sum_j\alpha_j}\left(\prod_j A_j(u)\right) \exp N\left\{\sum_jW_j(u)+\frac{inu^2}{4\pi}\right\} (1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{22a} \] This canonical product also has a whole-period Gaussian bound. To verify the claim directly, use the analytic function \(C_{N,n}e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)}\prod_jF_{j,N}(t)\) in Sections 2--4. Its input constants are \(M=\sum M_j\), \(c=\sum c_j\), and \(B=\sum B_j\). The input product need not have degree less than \(N\): only the output Hermite interpolant needs that band, and its physical jets are exactly those of the original quotient product. The local real curvatures add, so Section 5 applies as well. The number of factors and their powers are fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity. This proves closure under multiplication and fixed crossings; it still makes no assertion about the turn. ## 6. Actual families to which the theorem applies The hypotheses are already proved for every terminal source \(H_{p,N}\), \(|p|\ge2\), with common phase, angular and strip constants in the [uniform terminal-family theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_uniform_terminal_family_and_star_fillings.md). They are also proved for the one-boundary pieces in the [recursive high-valence theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_recursive_high_valence_source.md). Consequently arbitrary fixed boundary crossing powers can be attached to any of those actual pieces without losing its full boundary asymptotic or its strict angular bound. A useful application concerns a pendant chain of \(k\ge1\) vertices, all of power \(2\sigma\), \(\sigma=\pm1\). Its exact quotient identity is proved in the [marked chain reduction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_repeated_two_crossing_chain_reduction.md): \[ F_{k,\sigma,N}=\kappa_N^{\sigma k} R^{-\sigma}H_{-\sigma(k+1),N},\qquad \kappa_N=\exp\frac{\pi iD^2}{2N}. \tag{23} \] Apply Theorem 1 to its canonical representative. On a common fixed disk, for each fixed \(k\), \[ \boxed{\displaystyle F_{k,\sigma,N}(u)= \kappa_N^{\sigma k}C_{N,-\sigma}\epsilon_{-\sigma(k+1),N} A_{-\sigma(k+1)}(u) \exp N\left\{W_{-\sigma(k+1)}(u) -\frac{\sigma i u^2}{4\pi}\right\} (1+O_k(N^{-1})).} \tag{24} \] The common real angular gap, complex strip and normalized phase bounds can be chosen independently of \(k\): the terminal family is uniform and the new boundary multiplier is only \(R\) or \(R^{-1}\). The amplitude and its error constant may depend on \(k\). This strengthens the earlier quotient reduction to an asymptotic of the actual canonical free-boundary polynomial. The existing marked tangle identity still supplies the geometric interpretation after attachment. Formula (24) does not identify the turn of an arbitrary packet, solve a general low-valence connected region, or justify discarding any current in a subsequent trace. Those operations still need their own estimates. ## 7. Why unrestricted closure under turns is false The turn problem cannot be solved by proving that every concentrated source stays concentrated. For any fixed \(|p|\ge2\), the actual terminal source is \[ H_{p,N}=T(R^p). \] It satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 1. But the original turn is the Newton reversal, so \(T^2=I\) in the full algebra and \[ T(H_{p,N})=R^p. \tag{25} \] Let \(r_{p,N}(t)=\operatorname{can}(R^p)(-2\cos t)\). Its exact physical values are \[ r_{p,N}(\tau_j)=C_{N,p}e^{ipN\tau_j^2/(4\pi)}, \qquad |r_{p,N}(\tau_j)|=1. \tag{26} \] This excludes concentration of the kind used here, regardless of the rate one attempts to assign to it. Indeed choose a physical angle \(t_N\) nearest zero: it is zero at odd levels and has magnitude \(\pi/N\) at even levels. If a nonzero local asymptotic (6) existed for this polynomial, its even phase and nonzero amplitude would give \[ 0=\log|r_{p,N}(t_N)| =N\Re W(0)+\alpha\log N+\log|A(0)|+O(N^{-1}). \tag{27} \] Dividing by \(N\) forces \(M=\Re W(0)=0\). In particular a positive rate is incompatible with the nonzero local expansion. A negative rate is already incompatible with (2) at these same near-zero nodes. Now fix any \(t_0\in(0,\pi)\), and choose physical nodes \(s_N\to t_0\). At rate zero, a real angular bound (2) with \(c>0\) would require \[ 1=|r_{p,N}(s_N)|\le C N^d e^{-Nc(1-\cos s_N)}, \tag{28} \] whose right side tends to zero. This is a contradiction at both parities. Thus a source in the proved class can leave that class after a single turn. A useful next theorem must therefore control the actual composed source and its relevant hyperbolic, nondegenerate geometry, with hypotheses that exclude this example. It cannot assert closure under all turns. This counterexample does not disprove a volume identity for a hyperbolic closure; it identifies a false unrestricted intermediate claim. Neither hyperbolicity alone nor a local geometric critical point has been shown here to supply the missing global source estimate. ## 8. Reproducing the finite normalization checks Run ```sh python3 experiments/check_boundary_crossing_packet_preservation.py \ --precision 120 \ --output repro/results/research-boundary-crossing-packet-preservation.json ``` The [script](../experiments/check_boundary_crossing_packet_preservation.py) compares multiplication by the original triangular Newton crossing matrices with the Hermite Fourier reconstruction from the Gaussian values and all angular derivatives. It uses the full bare-edge source and the two actual terminal sources of powers \(2,-3\), at every level \(2\le N\le12\), for multiplying powers \(-3,-1,1,2\). The 132 level/source/power cases agree at 120-digit precision; the largest relative physical-jet discrepancy is below \(3.0\cdot10^{-117}\), and the largest off-grid reconstruction discrepancy is below \(2.4\cdot10^{-119}\). The [saved output](../repro/results/research-boundary-crossing-packet-preservation.json) also records 24 comparisons of the actual canonical product with the chirped source at levels \(16,17,32,33,64,65\), on sampled real angles and two complex angles. These include the two signs of the pendant chain with two power-two vertices. Those finite comparisons check the normalization and illustrate the off-grid error. The exponential estimate, its uniformity, and the whole-source conclusions follow from the proof above, not from these samples.

title: An all-transfer logarithmic collar for the actual boundary Ward source
text: # An all-transfer logarithmic collar for the actual boundary Ward source Written research proof, 23 November 2026. The complete boundary Ward sum is one coefficient of an actual Euler matrix times a finite logarithmic derivative. No inverse of a nilpotent lowering operator is needed. On a coefficient circle approaching the unit circle at distance of order \((\log\log N)/N\), that logarithmic derivative has only its original vacuum kernel. After one literal lowering shift and its explicit scale of order \(N\) are extracted, the remaining matrix and its inverse have logarithmic and bounded norms. A diagonal gauge with polylogarithmic conditioning extends inverse control to the full unit activity disk. The physical degree grading then extracts every Ward coefficient by a unitary Fourier projection, with no small-activity hypothesis and no additional coefficient-contour loss. This controls an entire normal factor before geometric evaluation. The original factorial, Euler matrix, crossing, marked co-source and coefficient integral remain. No lower bound for that coefficient or for the closed scalar is inferred. ## 1. The complete original Ward sum Fix the original root and head count \[ N\ge2,\qquad d=N-1,\qquad q=e^{\pi i/N},\qquad Q=q^2, \qquad m=r+1\ge2,\qquad x_0=-q^{-1}. \tag{1} \] All norms below use the original physical Euclidean occupation basis \(|a\rangle\), \(0\le a\le d\), and its tensor products. In particular the actual first-remaining-head shift is \[ L|a\rangle=|a-1\rangle\quad(a>0),\qquad L|0\rangle=0, \qquad L^N=0,\qquad \|L\|=1. \tag{2} \] It acts as the identity on the other remaining heads. The ordered remaining lowering coproduct is denoted by \(E\); its one-head coefficient is \(Q^{-a}-1\), with the original bottom zero. Write \(b=b_{\sigma_1}\) for the actual reduced positive boundary crossing, including its crossing scalar. No framing factor is changed. Let \(1\le t<N\) and let the actual physical weight satisfy \(\lambda_0^2=Q^{-t}\). Put \(a=\lambda_0/x_0\); then \(|a|=1\). Source [W, (19)--(20)] gives its complete flattened first-normal arrow defect, with the fixed-root meridian derivative, as \[ \begin{split} \mathfrak D_t &=\sum_{n=1}^{t}\omega_{t,n}(\lambda_0)x_0^{-n} E^{t-n}bL^n,\\ \omega_{t,n}(\lambda_0) &=2m(-1)^{n-1}\lambda_0^n{t\brack n}_Q F_{n-1}, \qquad F_j=(Q;Q)_j,\quad F_0=1. \end{split} \tag{3} \] This is an equality of the original finite matrices, restricted to the indicated input weight when defining the Ward arrow. We can also form the displayed sum on the whole occupation space. Its order is always \(E^{t-n}\), then \(b\), then \(L^n\). In particular no commutation between these three operators is assumed. Every factorial in (3) has index below \(N\). Its scalar coefficient simplifies exactly to \[ \omega_{t,n}(\lambda_0)x_0^{-n} =2m(-1)^{n-1}a^n \frac{F_t}{F_{t-n}(1-Q^n)} =2m(-1)^{n-1}a^n \frac{(Q^{t-n+1};Q)_n}{1-Q^n}. \tag{4} \] There is no division by \(F_N\), and no transfer term has been replaced by a fixed-\(n\) asymptotic. For a nonself reciprocal pair, use its two physical orders \(t=s\) and \(t=N-s\), at their corresponding input weights. The two defects recover all four normal blocks of [W, (23)--(24)]. The construction below acts on those complete defects before the original word-source formula [W, (27)] is applied; its off-diagonal normal couplings remain. ## 2. A single coefficient and its finite logarithmic derivative Define the native Euler polynomial and its logarithmic derivative \[ \mathcal E_N(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\frac{z^j}{F_j},\qquad \ell_N(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{d}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}z^n}{1-Q^n}. \tag{5} \] Multiplication of finite polynomials, using (4), proves \[ \boxed{\quad \mathfrak D_t=2mF_t[\xi^t]\, \mathcal E_N(\xi E)\,b\,\ell_N(a\xi L). \quad} \tag{6} \] Indeed its term of degree \(\xi^t\) uses \(j=t-n\) and is exactly the corresponding term of (3). This is also a homogeneous polynomial in the commuting left- and right-multiplication operators \(P(B)=EB\) and \(R(B)=aBL\). Neither \(E^{-1}\) nor \(L^{-1}\) appears. For completeness the logarithmic identity is finite algebra. In \(\mathbb C[z]/(z^N)\), the Euler recurrence is \[ \mathcal E_N(Qz)=(1-z)\mathcal E_N(z),\qquad \log\mathcal E_N(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{d}\frac{z^n}{n(1-Q^n)}. \tag{7} \] The first formula follows by comparing coefficients. For the second, take the formal logarithm with zero constant term: its degree-\(n\) coefficient is determined by \((Q^n-1)c_n=-1/n\). The Euler derivative \(z\partial_z\) preserves the ideal \((z^N)\). Hence, with its sign specified, \[ \ell_N(z)=-z\partial_z\log\mathcal E_N(-z) =z\mathcal E_N'(-z)\mathcal E_N(-z)^{-1} \pmod {z^N}. \tag{8} \] Evaluation at \(z=a\xi L\) makes (7)--(8) exact matrix identities. The inverse is a finite polynomial because \(L^N=0\). No analytic logarithm or branch choice has been added. The same finite Euler logarithm is covered by [C]; the new use here is (6) and the uniform collar estimate below. For any actual linear co-source \(\Lambda\) on this insertion, fixed in \(\xi\), (6) gives the exact contraction formula \[ \Lambda(\mathfrak D_t)=\frac{2mF_t}{2\pi i} \oint_{|\xi|=\rho} \Lambda\!\left(\mathcal E_N(\xi E)b\ell_N(a\xi L)\right) \frac{d\xi}{\xi^{t+1}},\qquad \rho>0. \tag{9} \] The contour extracts a coefficient of a finite polynomial. Its value is independent of its positive radius. The input weight restriction can be retained inside \(\Lambda\) throughout, as can the original marked closing, exterior tensors and prescribed scalar lines when this normal insertion occurs in them. ## 3. Normalizing the q-log factor For \(T^N=0\), factor (5) exactly as \[ \ell_N(T)=\frac{1}{1-Q}\,T U_N(T),\qquad U_N(T)=\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}(-1)^{n-1}r_{N,n}T^{n-1}, \quad r_{N,n}=\frac{1-Q}{1-Q^n}. \tag{10} \] The constant term of \(U_N\) is one. In particular it is invertible at every nilpotent \(T\), but that observation alone would not bound its inverse. Compare it to the finite resolvent integral \[ V(T)=\int_0^1(I+sT)^{-1}\,ds =\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}T^{n-1}}n. \tag{11} \] The term of degree \(N-1\) in (11) is retained; it is not present in \(U_N\). There is an absolute constant \(C\) such that \[ |r_{N,n}-1/n|\le C/N\quad(1\le n\le N/2), \qquad |r_{N,n}|\le\frac{C}{\min(n,N-n)}\quad(1\le n<N). \tag{12} \] To prove the first bound, let \(g(s)=(e^{2\pi i s}-1)/(2\pi i s)\), continued by \(g(0)=1\). It is continuously differentiable on \([0,1/2]\), and \(|g(s)|\ge2/\pi\) there. Since \(r_{N,n}=g(1/N)/(ng(n/N))\), the mean value bound gives \(|r_{N,n}-1/n|\le C(n-1)/(nN)\le C/N\). The second bound follows from \(\sin(\pi n/N)\ge2\min(n,N-n)/N\) and \(\sin(\pi/N)\le\pi/N\). Consequently, for \(T^N=0\), \(\|T\|\le\rho\) and \(0<\rho<1\), one has \[ \|U_N(T)-V(T)\| \le \frac{C}{N(1-\rho)} +C\rho^{N-1}\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor} \frac{\rho^{-k}}k +\frac{2\rho^{N/2-1}}{N(1-\rho)} +\frac{\rho^{N-1}}N. \tag{13} \] For the lower half of the sum use the first bound in (12) and a geometric series. In the upper half put \(k=N-n\), so \(|r_{N,n}|\le C/k\), and bound the remaining \(1/n\) by \(2/N\). The last term in (13) is precisely the last term of (11). This proves the estimate for the complete polynomials, without dropping a high-degree tail. Choose the explicit collar \[ \rho_N=\exp(-4\log\log N/N) =(\log N)^{-4/N}. \tag{14} \] For all sufficiently large \(N\), writing \(v_N=4\log\log N/N\) gives \(v_N/2\le1-e^{-v_N}\le v_N\). Thus \(1-\rho_N\) is comparable to \((\log\log N)/N\). To estimate the second term of (13), put \(K=\lfloor N/\log N\rfloor\). For \(k\le K\), \(\rho_N^{-k}\le C\) and the harmonic sum is at most \(C\log N\). For \(K<k\le N/2\), use \(1/k\le C\log N/N\), at most \(N\) terms, and \(\rho_N^{-k}\le(\log N)^2\). Since \(\rho_N^{N-1}=\rho_N^{-1}(\log N)^{-4}\), the second term of (13) is bounded by \(C\{(\log N)^{-3}+(\log N)^{-1}\}\). The third term is at most \(C/\{(\log N)^2\log\log N\}\); the last is at most \(C/\{N(\log N)^4\}\). The first is at most \(C/\log\log N\). Therefore, uniformly for every \(T^N=0\) with \(\|T\|\le\rho_N\), \[ \|U_N(T)-V(T)\|\le C/\log\log N. \tag{15} \] ## 4. Accretivity and the genuine remaining endpoint If \(\|T\|\le\rho<1\), the resolvent in (11) satisfies \[ \operatorname{Re}(I+sT)^{-1}\ge\frac{I}{1+s\rho}, \quad 0\le s\le1, \qquad \operatorname{Re}V(T)\ge\frac{\log(1+\rho)}\rho I \ge(\log2)I. \tag{16} \] At \(\rho=0\) use the continuous value. Here is an elementary operator proof of the first inequality. Put \(B=I+sT\) and \(v=s\rho<1\). Then \[ (1+v)\operatorname{Re}B-B^\dagger B =vI-(1-v)s\operatorname{Re}T-s^2T^\dagger T\ge0, \] using \(\operatorname{Re}T\le\rho I\) and \(T^\dagger T\le\rho^2I\). Congruence by \(B^{-1}\) gives \((1+v)\operatorname{Re}B^{-1}\ge I\). Integration proves (16). Also the Neumann resolvent estimate gives \[ \|V(T)\|\le\frac{-\log(1-\rho)}\rho. \tag{17} \] Combining (15)--(17), there are absolute constants \(C,N_0\) such that for all \(N\ge N_0\) and all \(T^N=0\) with \(\|T\|\le\rho_N\), \[ \boxed{\quad \operatorname{Re}U_N(T)\ge\tfrac12\log2\,I,\qquad \|U_N(T)^{-1}\|\le2/\log2,\qquad \|U_N(T)\|\le C\log N. \quad} \tag{18} \] Indeed accretivity bounds \(\|U_N(T)v\|\) below by \((\log2)\|v\|/2\); in finite dimension this bounds the inverse. All constants in (18) are independent of the number of tensor heads. Now take the literal \(T=zL\). The factors in (10) commute, so \[ \ker\ell_N(zL)=\ker L,\qquad \operatorname{im}\ell_N(zL)=\operatorname{im}L\quad(z\ne0). \tag{19} \] These statements retain the original vacuum direction; no quotient of the source is being taken. On \((\ker L)^\perp\), the shift \(L\) is an isometry. Equations (10),(18) therefore bound the nonzero singular values of \(\ell_N(zL)\) between \(c|z|/|1-Q|\) and \(C|z|\log N/|1-Q|\). More generally, for any compatible rectangular matrix \(B\), either the physical operator norm or the Hilbert--Schmidt norm obeys \[ \frac{c|z|}{|1-Q|}\|BL\| \le\|B\ell_N(zL)\| \le\frac{C|z|\log N}{|1-Q|}\|BL\|, \qquad 0<|z|\le\rho_N, \tag{20} \] for \(N\ge N_0\). For the lower operator bound, write \(BL=(BLU_N)U_N^{-1}\). For the Hilbert--Schmidt bound use the least singular value of the right factor \(U_N\). The upper bounds follow by multiplication. Thus every matrix on the left is retained, including arbitrary exterior factors already placed there. No analogous lower bound for an arbitrary scalar co-source is asserted. On \(|z|=\rho_N\), the elementary inequalities \(4/N\le|1-Q|\le2\pi/N\), together with \(\rho_N\to1\), show that the interval for nonzero singular values is \([cN,CN\log N]\). This statement has no parity or primality restriction. ## 5. Polylogarithmic conditioning on the full unit disk The near-unit collar can be transported to unit activity by a stated physical diagonal gauge, whose cost is polylogarithmic. On the head where \(L\) acts put \[ S_\rho|j\rangle=\rho^{-j}|j\rangle,\qquad S_\rho L S_\rho^{-1}=\rho L,\qquad \|S_\rho\|\|S_\rho^{-1}\|=\rho^{-d}. \tag{21} \] Tensor with identities on all other heads. This is only a comparison of the indicated matrix factors; no source or cap is changed. With \(\rho=\rho_N\), one has \(\rho_N^{-d}=(\log N)^{4d/N}\le(\log N)^4\). Polynomial functional calculus in (21), followed by the inverse bound of (18), proves the inverse bound below. Its upper bound is even simpler: (12) gives \(\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}|r_{N,n}|\le C\log N\), so the triangle inequality proves it directly on the full unit disk. Thus \[ \boxed{\quad \|U_N(zL)\|\le C\log N,\qquad \|U_N(zL)^{-1}\|\le C(\log N)^4, \qquad |z|\le1,\quad N\ge N_0. \quad} \tag{22} \] Thus there is no small physical activity assumption in this estimate. At \(|z|=1\), equations (10),(19),(22) show that the nonzero singular values of \(\ell_N(zL)\) lie in \([cN/(\log N)^4,CN\log N]\). For every compatible left matrix \(B\), in either the physical operator norm or the Hilbert--Schmidt norm, \[ \frac{cN}{(\log N)^4}\|BL\|\le\|B\ell_N(zL)\| \le CN\log N\,\|BL\|, \qquad |z|=1,\quad N\ge N_0. \tag{23} \] Its kernel and image are still exactly (19). The same proof as (20) applies, now using the bounds of (22). The gauge has not introduced an unknown metric inverse or an exponential conditioning factor. ## 6. Physical Fourier extraction at unit activity Let \(\mathsf n\) be the total integer occupation on the remaining \(r\) heads and \(D_\theta=e^{-i\theta\mathsf n}\). The operators \(E\) and \(L\) both lower that degree by one. The literal reduced crossing \(b\) preserves it: each original crossing and every term of the prefix and its inverse preserve total occupation, and the first-head zero extraction retains the remaining degree. Therefore \[ D_\theta E D_\theta^{-1}=e^{i\theta}E,\qquad D_\theta L D_\theta^{-1}=e^{i\theta}L,\qquad D_\theta bD_\theta^{-1}=b. \tag{24} \] All these diagonal matrices are unitary in the original Euclidean basis. Set \(F(\xi)=\mathcal E_N(\xi E)b\ell_N(a\xi L)\). Equation (24) gives the exact operator identity \[ F(e^{i\theta})=D_\theta F(1)D_\theta^{-1},\qquad [\xi^t]F=\mathsf P_tF(1),\quad \mathsf P_tB=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-it\theta}D_\theta BD_\theta^{-1}\,d\theta. \tag{25} \] The map \(\mathsf P_t\) keeps precisely the entries whose output degree is the input degree minus \(t\). Its operator norm as a map on operator norm is at most one, by unitary averaging and the triangle inequality. In Hilbert--Schmidt norm it is an orthogonal projection: the different degree differences are disjoint matrix-entry supports. In particular they obey Parseval on this full matrix space. This projection is not an assertion about a selected geometric window. Combining (6),(23),(25) proves the uniform actual Ward estimate \[ \boxed{\quad \|\mathfrak D_t\| \le C m|F_t|N\log N\, \|\mathcal E_N(E)bL\|, \qquad 1\le t<N,\quad N\ge N_0, \quad} \tag{26} \] in either of the two stated physical norms. Thus all transfers are resummed before estimation, and extraction has norm at most one. The same unit-activity q-log factor estimate (23) permits any left exterior inside the norm, while the extraction identity (25) is applied before such an exterior unless it respects the degree action. The factorial \(F_t\), which can carry exponential size, is explicitly retained. Terms of \(F\) with degree at least \(N\) can occur; (25) projects them out for the specified observation and does not replace the full matrix \(F(1)\) by a low-degree truncation. The equality (9) keeps the original co-source on this normal insertion. Its contour can have cancellation, and its arbitrary co-source can annihilate a nonzero matrix. Consequently (23) does not give a lower bound after coefficient extraction or for the marked scalar. The full-activity Euler matrix, the crossing factor and their geometric contour remain separate analytic objects. The small-activity factorization [C] and coherent chart [F] are not being extended to unit activity by (26). The exact negative-boundary and word cocycle laws of [W, (21)] may be applied to (6), retaining their actual inverse matrices and every normal insertion. No bound for those inverses or a general word's remaining co-source is supplied by (18). All identities are at fixed quantum root; no quantum-normal derivative or identification of an off-circle geometric clock with a physical weight is used. ## Complete sources and coverage * W, complete proof direct: notes/research_actual_word_normal_cocycle_and_source.md, 458 lines, SHA256 db453e02bc349e7740b2718b25819e9aa8ad1a71b86044fb7128524bea292106. * C, complete proof direct: notes/research_root_capped_euler_coproduct_factorization.md, 360 lines, SHA256 e11f5f827f226ee93505e00aed3885a33abdbfc15ee71e023a67c048c9c17720. * F, complete coverage: notes/research_actual_coupled_euler_coherent_flow.md, 498 lines, SHA256 a7d3d29f4381f669fd3f6e72a6c637fa259e650757bd39a517e47c0419692def. All three complete texts were read untruncated in the author sequence. The finite logarithm itself and small-activity Euler bounds are prior coverage. The all-transfer Ward coefficient, normalized q-log collar, accretivity estimate and uniform extraction cost are proved above. The complete matching final is to receive independent whole-text and whole-source review. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used; earlier frozen files were not changed.

title: A positive Toeplitz Gram controls the full boundary Ward factor
text: # A positive Toeplitz Gram controls the full boundary Ward factor Written research proof, 23 November 2026. The entire actual boundary Ward sum is one finite Euler coefficient. Its logarithmic factor has exactly the original lowering vacuum as kernel. After that literal shift and an explicit factor of order \(N\) are extracted, the remaining matrix has logarithmic norm and a bounded inverse on the full unit activity disk, at every level \(N\ge2\). The inverse bound follows from a positive Toeplitz Gram, obtained by ordinary Fourier orthogonality on an auxiliary finite cycle. No activity collar, diagonal conditioning gauge or parity restriction is needed. The physical occupation grading extracts the Ward coefficient by a unitary Fourier projection. This gives an \(O(N\log N)\) normal-factor cost before the retained Euler matrix and original factorial. The marked co-source, all normal blocks and the final coefficient remain; no scalar lower bound or geometric-cycle selection is asserted. ## 1. The literal Ward sum and its ordered resummation Fix \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2, \quad m=r+1\ge2,\quad x_0=-q^{-1},\quad F_j=(Q;Q)_j. \tag{1} \] Use the original physical Euclidean occupation basis on the remaining \(r\) heads. The operator \(E\) is their ordered lowering coproduct, with one-head coefficient \(Q^{-a}-1\) and the original bottom zero. Let \(L\) be the first-remaining-head unit lowering shift, tensored with identities on other heads: \[ L|a\rangle=|a-1\rangle\ (a>0),\quad L|0\rangle=0, \qquad L^N=0,\quad \|L\|=1. \tag{2} \] Write \(b=b_{\sigma_1}\) for the actual reduced positive boundary crossing, including its scalar. For a physical Ward order \(1\le t<N\), input weight \(\lambda_0^2=Q^{-t}\), and \(a=\lambda_0/x_0\), one has \(|a|=1\). The complete first-normal arrow defect [W, (19)--(20)] is \[ \mathfrak D_t=2m\sum_{n=1}^{t}(-1)^{n-1}a^n \frac{F_t}{F_{t-n}(1-Q^n)}E^{t-n}bL^n. \tag{3} \] The actual Ward arrow restricts this matrix to its indicated input weight. The displayed finite sum can also be formed on the full occupation space. The factor order is part of the formula. Equation (3) follows from W by the exact cancellation \({t\brack n}_QF_{n-1}=F_t/[F_{t-n}(1-Q^n)]\). No denominator has index \(N\). Define \[ \mathcal E_N(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\frac{z^j}{F_j},\qquad \ell_N(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{d}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}z^n}{1-Q^n},\qquad U_N(T)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-2}(-1)^j \frac{1-Q}{1-Q^{j+1}}T^j. \tag{4} \] Finite coefficient multiplication proves the exact ordered identity \[ \boxed{\quad \mathfrak D_t=2mF_t[\xi^t]\, \mathcal E_N(\xi E)b\ell_N(a\xi L),\qquad \ell_N(T)=\frac{T}{1-Q}U_N(T)\quad(T^N=0). \quad} \tag{5} \] Left multiplication by \(E\) and right multiplication by \(aL\) commute as operations on matrices; \(E,b,L\) need not commute. Thus (5) never divides by either nilpotent operator. The logarithmic sign and normalization are also finite algebra. In \(\mathbb C[z]/(z^N)\), the Euler coefficient recurrence gives \[ \mathcal E_N(Qz)=(1-z)\mathcal E_N(z),\qquad \log\mathcal E_N(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{d}\frac{z^n}{n(1-Q^n)},\qquad \ell_N(z)=-z\partial_z\log\mathcal E_N(-z) =z\mathcal E_N'(-z)\mathcal E_N(-z)^{-1}. \tag{6} \] Indeed the logarithm has constant term zero, and its degree-\(n\) coefficient satisfies \((Q^n-1)c_n=-1/n\). The Euler derivative preserves the ideal \((z^N)\). Evaluation at a nilpotent matrix makes these identities exact, with finite polynomial inverses. This finite logarithm is prior coverage in [C]. For any original linear co-source \(\Lambda\) on the normal insertion, fixed in \(\xi\), the full contraction is exactly \[ \Lambda(\mathfrak D_t)=\frac{2mF_t}{2\pi i} \oint_{|\xi|=1}\Lambda\!\left( \mathcal E_N(\xi E)b\ell_N(a\xi L)\right) \frac{d\xi}{\xi^{t+1}}. \tag{7} \] The original weight restriction, exterior, marked closing and scalar lines stay inside this contraction. On a reciprocal pair, its two physical Ward arrows recover all four normal blocks of [W, (24)]. In particular the off-diagonal couplings of W's original source formula (27) are not dropped by (5) or (7). ## 2. The exact positive Toeplitz Gram Put \(\theta=\pi/N\). For \(0\le j\le N-2\), set \[ a_j=\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin((j+1)\theta)}>0, \qquad \frac{1-Q}{1-Q^{j+1}}=q^{-j}a_j. \tag{8} \] For the moment let \(N\ge3\) and put \(p=N-2\ge1\). The exact integral representation is \[ a_j=\frac{N\sin\theta}{\pi} \int_0^1\frac{x^j+x^{p-j}}{1+x^N}\,dx, \qquad 0\le j\le p. \tag{9} \] Here is a direct normalization proof. Integrate \(z^j/(1+z^N)\) around a sector of angle \(2\pi/N\), with positive orientation. The small and large circular arcs vanish, respectively as \(O(\epsilon^{j+1})\) and \(O(R^{j+1-N})\). The sole pole is \(e^{\pi i/N}\), so \[ (1-e^{2\pi i(j+1)/N}) \int_0^\infty\frac{x^j}{1+x^N}\,dx =-\frac{2\pi i}{N}e^{\pi i(j+1)/N}. \tag{10} \] This gives the integral \(\pi/[N\sin((j+1)\theta)]\). Substitute \(x\mapsto1/x\) in its part above one. The exponent becomes \(N-j-2=p-j\), proving (9), including its endpoints. For each \(0<x<1\), the matrix \[ C(x)_{ij}=x^{|i-j|}+x^{p-|i-j|},\qquad 0\le i,j\le p, \tag{11} \] is positive semidefinite. To verify this using finite Fourier orthogonality, start with the \(p\)-cycle circulant whose row is \(c_\ell=x^\ell+x^{p-\ell}\), \(0\le\ell<p\). Its Fourier eigenvalues are the positive numbers \[ \sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}c_\ell e^{-2\pi i k\ell/p} =\frac{(1-x^p)(1-x^2)} {1-2x\cos(2\pi k/p)+x^2},\qquad 0\le k<p. \tag{12} \] Summing the two finite geometric series proves the equality. It also holds for \(p=1\), when its single value is \(1+x\). The map taking basis vector \(e_j\), \(0\le j\le p\), to \(e_{[j]_p}\) pulls this positive circulant back to (11): its indices zero and \(p\) are duplicates, exactly as required by \(c_p=c_0\). Hence (11) is a positive Gram, without an alias assumption on a physical color. Integrating (11) with the positive weight in (9) proves \[ T_a=(a_{|i-j|})_{i,j=0}^{p}\ge0. \tag{13} \] This is an auxiliary cycle Gram. It neither changes the original physical quantum root nor replaces any Hermite boundary variable. ## 3. A uniform inverse on the full physical unit disk Work first on the one physical head where the shift acts. Its range is \(R=\operatorname{span}\{|0\rangle,\ldots,|N-2\rangle\}\). For \(|z|=1\), let \(\eta=-q^{-1}z\) and \(D_\eta|h\rangle=\eta^{-h}|h\rangle\). This is a physical diagonal unitary and \(D_\eta L D_\eta^{-1}=\eta L\). Equations (4),(8) give \[ U_N(zL)=D_\eta\left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-2}a_jL^j\right)D_\eta^{-1}. \tag{14} \] Restrict to the invariant space \(R\), of dimension \(p+1\). The Hermitian part of the middle matrix in (14) is exactly \((I+T_a)/2\): its diagonal is one and its upper diagonals are \(a_j\). Therefore (13) proves \[ \operatorname{Re}(U_N(zL)|_R)\ge\tfrac12 I_R, \qquad \|(U_N(zL)|_R)^{-1}\|\le2, \qquad |z|=1. \tag{15} \] For \(|z|<1\), apply the harmonic minimum principle to each quadratic form \(\operatorname{Re}\langle v,U_N(zL)v\rangle\), \(v\in R\). The same inequalities hold on the full closed disk. In the orthogonal decomposition \(R\oplus\mathbb C|d\rangle\), the whole one-head matrix has the form \[ U_N(zL)=\begin{pmatrix}U_R(z)&v(z)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \|v(z)\|^2\le\sum_{j=1}^{N-2}a_j^2\le\pi^2, \quad |z|\le1. \tag{16} \] For the last bound use \(a_j\le\pi/[2\min(j+1,N-j-1)]\). Each positive denominator occurs at most twice, and \(\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}\le2\). Block inversion and (15) now give \(\|U_N(zL)^{-1}\|\le2+2\pi\). Also \(\sum_{j=0}^{N-2}a_j\le C\log N\), by the corresponding harmonic-sum estimate. Thus, with absolute constants, \[ \boxed{\quad \|U_N(zL)\|\le C\log N,\qquad \|U_N(zL)^{-1}\|\le2+2\pi,\qquad |z|\le1, \quad N\ge2. \quad} \tag{17} \] For \(N=2\), the argument is completed directly by \(U_2=I\); there is no zero-length cycle to interpret in (12). Tensoring with identities preserves every bound. All estimates are in the stated physical Euclidean basis, not a binomial-gauged norm. ## 4. The exact endpoint and arbitrary left contexts Since \(U_N(zL)\) commutes with \(L\) and is invertible, (5) gives \[ \ker\ell_N(zL)=\ker L,\qquad \operatorname{im}\ell_N(zL)=\operatorname{im}L\quad(z\ne0). \tag{18} \] The shift is an isometry from \((\ker L)^\perp\) onto its range. Using both orders \(LU_N=U_NL\), the nonzero singular values of \(\ell_N(zL)\) lie between \(c|z|/|1-Q|\) and \(C|z|\log N/|1-Q|\). For any compatible rectangular left matrix \(B\), either the physical operator norm or the Hilbert--Schmidt norm satisfies \[ \frac{c|z|}{|1-Q|}\|BL\| \le\|B\ell_N(zL)\| \le\frac{C|z|\log N}{|1-Q|}\|BL\|, \qquad 0<|z|\le1,\quad N\ge2. \tag{19} \] The upper bound is multiplication by (17). For the lower bound, write \(BL=(BLU_N)U_N^{-1}\); the same argument uses the least singular value of the right factor in Hilbert--Schmidt norm. In particular \(4/N\le|1-Q|\le2\pi/N\) proves, at \(|z|=1\), \[ \boxed{\quad cN\|BL\|\le\|B\ell_N(zL)\| \le CN\log N\,\|BL\|. \quad} \tag{20} \] The nonzero singular values lie in the same interval \([cN,CN\log N]\). The vacuum kernel has not been removed from the original source. These bounds allow any matrix already on the left, without a condition number for it. They are not a lower bound for an arbitrary scalar co-source applied to the resulting matrix. ## 5. Unitary extraction of every physical Ward order Let \(\mathsf n\) be total remaining integer occupation and put \(D_\phi=e^{-i\phi\mathsf n}\). Both \(E\) and \(L\) lower degree by one. The actual \(b\) preserves degree, because every original crossing, each prefix term, and first-head zero extraction have that property. Thus \[ D_\phi ED_\phi^{-1}=e^{i\phi}E,\quad D_\phi LD_\phi^{-1}=e^{i\phi}L,\quad D_\phi bD_\phi^{-1}=b. \tag{21} \] The matrices \(D_\phi\) are unitary in the physical basis. For \(F(\xi)=\mathcal E_N(\xi E)b\ell_N(a\xi L)\), one consequently has \[ F(e^{i\phi})=D_\phi F(1)D_\phi^{-1},\qquad [\xi^t]F=\mathsf P_tF(1),\quad \mathsf P_tB=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-it\phi}D_\phi BD_\phi^{-1}\,d\phi. \tag{22} \] This is the exact projection onto entries of degree difference \(-t\). It is contractive in operator norm, by unitary averaging, and an orthogonal projection in Hilbert--Schmidt norm, where different degree differences have disjoint matrix-entry supports. In particular the full family satisfies Parseval; it is not a geometric-window projection. Combining (5),(20),(22) proves the all-transfer estimate \[ \boxed{\quad \|\mathfrak D_t\|\le C m|F_t|N\log N\, \|\mathcal E_N(E)bL\|, \qquad 1\le t<N,\quad N\ge2, \quad} \tag{23} \] in both of the stated physical norms. All constants in the factor estimates are independent of the number of heads; the displayed \(m\), factorial and remaining Euler-crossing product are retained. Terms of \(F\) of degree at least \(N\) can occur; exact projection selects the specified order without replacing \(F(1)\) by a truncated matrix. An arbitrary exterior is not commuted through \(\mathsf P_t\). It can always remain in (7), while (19)--(20) apply when it is already on the left of the logarithmic factor. There is no lower bound after \(\mathsf P_t\) or the original marked closing: both can annihilate nonzero matrices. The full-activity Euler matrix and its geometric period remain to be controlled. The small-activity results of [C] are not extended to unit activity by (23). The exact negative-generator and word cocycle laws in [W] retain their actual inverse matrices and normal insertions when applied to (5). No bound for those remaining factors is inferred. All quantum parameters remain at the original root.
