Combining (8), (9), and (12)--(14) proves the lower bound in (5). The excess is strictly positive by a direct derivative identity. It is continuous at zero with \(\chi(0)=0\), and \[ \begin{split} \chi'(u) &=2f'(u/2)-2f'(u)-2\log(2\cos(\pi u))\\ &=2\log\frac{1+\cos(\pi u)}{2\cos^2(\pi u)}>0 \qquad(0<u\le1/4). \end{split} \tag{15} \] Indeed if \(c=\cos(\pi u)\), then \(1+c-2c^2=(1-c)(2c+1)>0\). At \(u=1/4\), reflection in (14) also gives \(k(1/4)=f(1/4)\), recovering the special value \(\chi(1/4)=4f(1/8)-3f(1/4)>0\). No rational or numerical evaluation of special values is required. On each compact subinterval of \((0,1/4]\), (15) gives a positive lower bound for this excess; no uniform positive bound as \(u\downarrow0\) is asserted. The constant-tensor component \(\langle F(-tu),1\otimes1\rangle\) is the signed coefficient divided by \(U_0\). The large component used in (8) lies instead in the orthogonal direction \(P_n\otimes1\). Its growth cannot be removed from the positive norm, but it contributes zero to that constant-tensor expectation. More explicitly, if \(F_{N,n}(-tu)=\sum_{a,b}d_{a,b}P_a(t)P_b(u)\), then \[ d_{n,0}=(-1)^n C_{n,0}w_n/\kappa_n,\qquad d_{0,0}=S_{N,n}/U_0. \] Since \(g_n\) has zero exponential rate, the same proof gives \(\liminf N^{-1}\log(U_0|d_{n,0}|/D_{N,n})\ge\chi(u)>0\). Thus even a single coefficient defeats a polynomial comparison with the absolute coefficient sum or Euclidean coefficient norm in this fixed explicit basis. This is not a claim about every possible basis, and supplies no lower bound for the distinct coefficient \(d_{0,0}\). Consequently this proof explains precisely why a bare Cauchy step can lose exponential information. It leaves open a cancellation-aware operator identity or estimate for the original signed expectation. It does not show that any actual shared coefficient exceeds its endpoint rate, nor does it change the original source or its cutoffs. ## Proof inputs and validation scope The single-factor tensor construction and norms (6)--(7) are also derived in [actual continuant and cap tensor metric](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_cap_demand_continuant_jacobi_interface.md), §§6--7; the algebra needed here is stated explicitly above. The new inputs are the single-component lower bound (8), the elementary maximization (11), and their consequence (5). No finite numerical sampling is used to prove the asymptotic obstruction.

title: A stable exterior controls the whole protected spectral interval
status: Uniform real cap bound; odd exterior
text:
# A stable exterior controls the whole protected spectral interval This note proves a strict bound for one left contribution of the original finite source. All neighboring crossing regions retain their actual central numerators at spectrum \(-2\), while the selected spectrum ranges over the entire real interval \([-2,2]\). Section 3 states sufficient pressure hypotheses for a strict gap. Checking those hypotheses for a given diagram remains a separate task. This is not a bound for all source sectors or a new knot-volume theorem. Here a *source* is the polynomial obtained from the literal finite crossing operators before its original face coefficients and filling functionals are applied. The central contribution contains paths through the middle degree; the left contribution contains paths below it. The original main mark sets two adjacent face variables to zero. These are called the *protected* variables. At the selected crossing the ordered arguments are \((C,0,A,0)\). Removing this one crossing and extracting every other ordinary face coefficient leaves a homogeneous polynomial in the two remaining face variables \(A,C\). This polynomial is the *exterior* of the selected crossing; no additional tangle or manifold is inserted. The proof has two parts. A sine-Cauchy Gram matrix bounds the exact protected spectral functional. Log-concavity then controls the alternating truncated exterior on an unbounded integration interval. The original cutoff leaves enough room for its squared moment to exist. The full polynomial squared would exceed that moment range, and is never substituted for the truncation. ## 1. The original protected functional and its spectral metric Fix an integer level \(N\ge2\), corresponding to the original root \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\). Write \[ d=N-1,\qquad M=\lfloor N/2floor-1,\qquad 	heta=\pi/N,\qquad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)	heta),\qquad s_j=2\sin(j	heta),\qquad S_j=\prod_{r=1}^j s_r. 	ag{1} \] The real variable \(\sigma\) is the Casimir spectral parameter of the selected crossing. Its protected left numerator has the following exact coefficients, including all spectral factors from unused matrix rows: \[ v_j(\sigma)=(-1)^j S_j^2\prod_{r=j+1}^{d}(\sigma-c_r), \qquad 0\le j\le M. 	ag{2} \] Thus every spectral row, repeated node, and parity endpoint remains present. Put \(U_0=\csc^2(	heta/2)\) and \[ g_j(\sigma)=(-1)^jv_j(\sigma)/U_0,\qquad C_{ij}= rac{\sin	heta}{\sin((i+j+1)	heta)} =\alpha_N\int_0^\infty rac{t^{i+j}}{1+t^N}\,dt, \qquad \alpha_N= rac{N\sin	heta}{\pi}\le1. 	ag{3} \] All the integrals used here have degree at most \[ 2M=N-2\quad(N	ext{ even}),\qquad 2M=N-3\quad(N	ext{ odd}). 	ag{4} \] In particular \(C\) is a positive-definite Gram matrix. Its last diagonal entry is especially useful: \[ C_{MM}=  egin{cases}1,&N	ext{ even},\ (2\cos	heta)^{-1},&N	ext{ odd},\end{cases} \qquad C_{MM}\le1. 	ag{5} \] The exact sine-Cauchy spectral calculation gives \[ \sup_{-2\le\sigma\le2}g(\sigma)^T C^{-1}g(\sigma) \le rac{\pi^5}{16}(M+1)^2. 	ag{6} \] For completeness, take the lower bidiagonal matrix \(A\) with diagonal \(c_j\) and subdiagonal \(s_j^2\). The sine subtraction identities give \(AC=CA^T\), so \(A\) is self-adjoint in the \(C^{-1}\) metric. Here \(T_N\) is the Chebyshev polynomial defined by \(T_N(\cos u)=\cos(Nu)\), and \(e_0\) is the first coordinate vector. With \(\chi_N(z)=2(T_N(z/2)+1)\), the original recurrence in (2) gives \[ g(\sigma)=U_0^{-1}  rac{\chi_N(\sigma)-\chi_N(A)}{\sigma I-A}\,e_0. 	ag{7} \] The quotient denotes a polynomial divided difference, including at every spectral node. Since \(\chi_N(A)=0\), \(|\chi_N'|\le N^2\) on the real interval, and \((C^{-1})_{00}\le\pi(M+1)^2\), its spectral theorem proves (6), using \(U_0\ge4N^2/\pi^2\). The last evaluation bound follows by expanding degree-\(M\) polynomials in shifted Legendre polynomials on \([0,1]\), where the density in (3) is at least \(1/\pi\). The matrix notation in (7) is local to this spectral calculation. In the binary polynomial below, \(A,C\) denote the two remaining face variables. If the original extracted exterior is \[ P(A,C)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}p_j A^jC^{d-j},\qquad Q_M(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{M}(-1)^j p_jt^j, 	ag{8} \] then the original remaining targets give precisely \[ S_N(\sigma)=\sum_{j=0}^{M}v_j(\sigma)p_j. 	ag{9} \] There is no extra degree target. Cauchy--Schwarz in (3), followed by (6), therefore proves \[ \sup_{\sigma\in[-2,2]}|S_N(\sigma)| \le  rac{\pi^{5/2}}4\,U_0(M+1)\,\|Q_M\|_C, \qquad \|Q_M\|_C^2=\alpha_N\int_0^\infty  rac{|Q_M(t)|^2}{1+t^N}\,dt. 	ag{10} \] The prefactor is polynomial in \(N\). Both parities are included in this finite spectral statement. ## 2. A finite alternating-section estimate A real polynomial is called *real stable* when it does not vanish if every variable has positive imaginary part. A homogeneous binary real-stable polynomial with nonnegative coefficients factors into positive linear factors. For the finite estimate we use that explicit factorization: suppose the nonzero exterior has \[ P(A,C)=P(1,1)\prod_{r=1}^{d}[(1-\lambda_r)C+\lambda_r A], \qquad 0\le\lambda_r\le1,\qquad P(1,1)>0. 	ag{11} \] Write \(P(t)=P(t,1)\), and define \[ 
u= rac1d\sum_r\lambda_r,\qquad k= rac1d\sum_r\lambda_r(1-\lambda_r),\qquad a=1-
u-k,\qquad b=
u-k. 	ag{12} \] Here \(k\) is a finite polynomial response, not the protected spectral dual norm. For any fixed \(T\ge1\), put \[ R_T=\max\{a,b,1-4k,a/T+bT-2k\}. 	ag{13} \] The following inequality is completely finite: \[  oxed{\quad \|Q_M\|_C\le \sqrt{1+\log T}\,P(1,1)R_T^{d/2} +\max\{P(T)/T^M,(d+1)p_M\}+p_M. \quad} 	ag{14} \] It requires no lower bound for any coefficient, no bound for a coefficient ratio, and no moment of the full squared polynomial. First, the coefficients in (11) have contiguous support and are log-concave. This follows directly by multiplying successively by positive linear factors. If \((c_j)\) is log-concave and \(q_j=u c_j+v c_{j-1}\), then \[  egin{aligned} q_j^2-q_{j-1}q_{j+1} ={}&u^2(c_j^2-c_{j-1}c_{j+1}) +v^2(c_{j-1}^2-c_{j-2}c_j)\ &+uv(c_jc_{j-1}-c_{j-2}c_{j+1})\ge0. \end{aligned} 	ag{15} \] The last inequality follows from the ordering of consecutive ratios; endpoint zeros follow by continuity. Monomial factors merely shift the support. Assume first \(p_Mp_{M+1}>0\), and let \[ t_0=p_M/p_{M+1}. 	ag{16} \] For \(t\le t_0\), the terms \(p_jt^j\) decrease from \(j=M+1\) onwards. The alternating omitted tail is therefore bounded by its first term, which is at most \(p_Mt^M\). For \(t\ge t_0\), the terms up to \(M\) increase, and pairing successive terms from the last term bounds the alternating prefix by its last term. Thus \[ |Q_M(t)|\le  egin{cases} |P(-t)|+p_Mt^M,&0\le t\le t_0,\ p_Mt^M,&t\ge t_0. \end{cases} 	ag{17} \] At \(t=t_0\), the terms of index \(M,M+1\) are largest in the entire coefficient sequence, so \[ P(t_0)/t_0^M\le(d+1)p_M. 	ag{18} \] The function \(\log P(e^z)-Mz\) is convex: its second derivative is the variance of the exponent under the positive coefficient weights. If \(t_0>T\), its maximum on \([\log T,\log t_0]\) is at an endpoint. Consequently (17)--(18) give, on the whole unbounded interval \(t\ge T\), \[ |Q_M(t)|\le(K_T+p_M)t^M, \qquad K_T=\max\{P(T)/T^M,(d+1)p_M\}. 	ag{19} \] If \(t_0\le T\), this follows directly from the second line of (17). If the support lies above \(M\), the section is zero. If the support ends at or below \(M\), the section is the full polynomial and \(P(t)/t^M\) is nonincreasing for \(t>0\), proving (19) with the first term in \(K_T\). These cases include every zero coefficient possibility. In particular no division by a zero coefficient has occurred. It remains to estimate \(P(-t)\) only on the bounded interval \([0,T]\). The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality applied to the squared factors in (11) gives, for \(0\le t\le1\), \[ |P(-t)|\le P(1,1)\max\{a,1-4k\}^{d/2}. 	ag{20} \] Indeed the average square is \(1-2(1+t)
u+(1+t)^2(
u-k)\), a convex quadratic whose two endpoint values are \(a\) and \(1-4k\). For \(1\le t\le T\), divide each squared factor by \(t\). This gives \[  rac{|P(-t)|^2}{t^d} \le P(1,1)^2 igl(a/t+bt-2k igr)^d \le P(1,1)^2 R_T^d. 	ag{21} \] The final step uses convexity of \(a/t+bt-2k\) on \((0,\infty)\). All factors are squared before averaging, so real zeros cause no exception. By (17), (20), and (21), the contribution on \([0,T]\) is bounded pointwise by the sum of \(p_Mt^M\) and the function \[ P(1,1)R_T^{d/2}  egin{cases}1,&0\le t\le1,\t^{d/2},&1\le t\le T.\end{cases} 	ag{22} \] The squared \(C\) norm of the latter function, restricted to this bounded interval, is at most \(P(1,1)^2R_T^d(1+\log T)\): use \(\alpha_N\le1\) and \(t^d/(1+t^N)\le1/t\) for \(t\ge1\). Combine (19) with Minkowski's inequality and \(\|t^M\|_C=\sqrt{C_{MM}}\le1\). This proves (14). The use of \(t^M\), rather than \(t^{d/2}\), on the unbounded interval is essential. It retains the original one-row cutoff margin and makes the tail integrable with a norm at most one. No estimate for \(\log t_0\) is needed. ## 3. A general original-target rate criterion Consider a fixed original source and a sequence of levels on which its extracted exterior satisfies (11). Let \(\Phi\) denote its complete augmented action, so that \(2\pi\Phi\) is the original augmented volume. Suppose, for one fixed \(T\ge1\), \[  egin{aligned} \limsup_N N^{-1}\log P_N(1,1)&\le F_0,\ \limsup_N N^{-1}\log igl(P_N(T,1)/T^{d/2} igr)&\le F_T,\ \limsup_N N^{-1}\log p_{N,M}&\le\Phi-\gamma, \qquad\gamma>0,\ 
u_N\longrightarrow
u,\qquad k_N&\longrightarrow k. \end{aligned} 	ag{23} \] All coefficients and limits in (23) concern the same original extracted polynomial. Since \(d/2-M\) is \(1/2\) or \(1\), replacing \(T^{d/2}\) by \(T^M\) changes only a bounded factor. Equations (10) and (14) prove \[  oxed{\quad \limsup_N rac1N\log\sup_{\sigma\in[-2,2]}|S_N(\sigma)| \le\max\{F_0+	frac12\log R_T,\ F_T,\ \Phi-\gamma\}. \quad} 	ag{24} \] In particular, if the first two entries are strictly below \(\Phi\), this is a strict source gap on the entire real cap spectral interval. Polynomial prefactors may depend on the fixed diagram; none changes (24). For the original odd central exterior, stability is not an additional comparison assumption. At \(N=2m+1\), each actual central endpoint numerator is \[ N^2D_m(x,b,y)D_m(x,c,y),\qquad D_m(x,b,y)=\det igl(bI+xH_-/2+yH_+/2 igr), 	ag{25} \] with the actual positive-definite Hermitian matrices \(H_-,H_+\). Each determinant in (25) is nonzero when its surviving arguments have positive imaginary parts: the imaginary part of its matrix is positive definite. Products and identification of shared variables preserve this property. For differentiation, fix the other variables in the upper half-plane and apply the one-variable Gauss--Lucas argument; specialization at a real boundary value follows by taking a limit from the upper half-plane. These operations preserve stability or give the zero polynomial. Coefficient extraction is differentiation followed by such a specialization. Thus the nonzero extracted binary polynomial has exactly (11), with all original factors \(N^2\) retained. If it is zero, the bound is automatic. Borcea and Brändén's [study of stability-preserving operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.0401) provides general background for these closure operations. The quantitative finite inequalities used here are proved in sections 1--2. The cutoff coefficient in (23) comes from the same omitted-tail capacity as in the original fixed-cap argument. Let \(R(s)\) be the residual complete triangle capacity with the two unextracted loads \(s,1-s\). The strict complete optimizer gives \[ \max_{1/2\le s\le1}R(s)\le\Phi-\gamma_D, \qquad \limsup_N N^{-1}\log p_{N,j_N}\le R(s) \quad	ext{if }j_N/d\longrightarrow s. 	ag{26} \] The second assertion is the closed coefficient upper bound, including boundary loads. Since \(M/d	o1/2\), it proves the third line of (23) with \(\gamma=\gamma_D\), even though \(M\) lies just below the first omitted index. This uses no lower estimate and no asymptotic rounding. ## 4. Normals, exact scope, and proof inputs The scalar in (9) is a polynomial of degree at most \(d\) in \(\sigma\). The complex-coefficient Markov inequality on \([-2,2]\) therefore gives \[ \|S_N'\|_{[-2,2]}\le rac{d^2}{2}\|S_N\|_{[-2,2]}. 	ag{27} \] To see that complex coefficients cause no problem, rotate the derivative at a point to a positive real number and apply the real Markov inequality to the real part of the rotated polynomial. Consequently the normalized first normal \(N^{-2}S_N'\) has the same strict rate. Alternatively the exact finite full-Hermite filling functional in this one cap variable has norm at most \(1+|n|/2\) for fixed signed \(n\), so it too preserves the strict rate. All other spectra remain fixed at \(-2\) in these statements. Applying their filling functionals would require estimates not supplied here. The actual even central exterior is not known to satisfy (11), and its positive stable comparator cannot replace it in a signed estimate. Accordingly the actual-source specialization of (24) is odd-level only. The finite theorem (14), the local spectral metric (6), and the parity cutoff (5) themselves hold at both parities. The proof does not bound the beta-square spectator energy by \(e^{2N\Phi}\); it proves the desired spectral functional bound using the separate valid sine-Cauchy norm. It makes no assertion about multiple noncentral regions, varying neighboring spectra, an all-sector remainder, or a new actual knot-volume equality. The proof uses the following exact source results. - [The coupled protected spectral functional](research_protected_cap_coupled_norm.md), sections 1--2, gives the unused-row vector, sine-Cauchy metric, and spectral divided difference. Its subsequent comparison with the beta-square measure is not needed here. - [The original cap and its two negative-axis intervals](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_global_cap_negative_axis_and_mahler_bound.md), sections 1--4, gives the original exterior targets and the closed boundary capacity (26). - [Factorization of the central cofactor](../papers/filling-bounds/README.md), section 3, and [the boundary model and its curvature](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_q_hahn_boundary_model_curvature.md) give the actual odd central determinant pencils and their scalar normalization. - [The exterior response criterion](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_global_cap_effective_response_criterion.md), sections 1--3, and [the common-axis mean and response bound](research_cap_common_axis_bound.md), sections 3--5, give the positive coefficient packet, its differentiated pressure, and the original complete-flow normalization. - [Restoring the omitted cap triangles](research_cap_dirichlet_response_region.md) gives a geometric sufficient response region. Its final section combines that region with the finite section estimate proved here; all neighboring spectra stay fixed. - [The finite filling supremum bound](../papers/filling-bounds/README.md) gives the optional one-variable full-Hermite consequence following (27). The finite inequalities (6), (10) and (14) hold without a diagram-specific certificate. A strict source rate follows only after the actual pressure, response and cutoff bounds in (23) have been established. The old 54-region numerical application is omitted from this general account.

title: The capped Gauss scalar near the complete meridian
text: # The capped Gauss scalar near the complete meridian 23 November 2026. The meridian parameter is scaled as \(M=\exp(v/\sqrt N)\). The actual capped Gauss initializer admits a scalar-relative asymptotic on the meridian scale \(M=\exp(v/\sqrt N)\). Its ordinary quantum-dimension zeros are retained and divided removably. The remaining transport factor has an explicit nonzero Gaussian limit, jointly with the original binomial cap on its complex Gaussian activity collar. The quantum root and the physical Fourier frames are fixed throughout. This is a statement about the specified initialized period, not the original marked knot closing or an arbitrary Conway exterior. ## 1. Actual source and the statement Use the adopted whole-meridian terminal row of (MC1)--(MC7). Put \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad x_0=-q^{-1}, \qquad \ell=d-T\ge1,\quad t=N-2\ell>0,\quad \alpha_N=\ell/N\in I\Subset(0,1/2). \tag{PC1} \] The limit is through these admissible levels. On the physical degree \(T\) basis \(|a,T-a\rangle\), \(0\le a\le T\), let \(A(M)\) be the actual capped operator \(q_F(M)E_\Sigma(M)^di_d\). In particular its meridian family includes the original lowering coefficients \(E(M)w_a=(MQ^{-a}-M^{-1})w_{a-1}\), with bottom zero, and all its ordered Cartan factors. This is not a generic lift chosen from \(A(1)\). Write \(A_0=A(1)\), \(a_*=\lfloor\ell/2\rfloor\), and \[ \begin{gathered} D_{aa}=x_0^a q^{-Ta},\qquad (F_c)_{ab}=N^{-1/2}Q^{(a-T/2)(b-T/2)},\\ \beta_b=\binom db\binom d{T-b},\qquad c_T(z)=\sum_{b=0}^T\beta_bz^b|b,T-b\rangle,\\ \mathscr S_N(u,z) =e_T^{\mathsf T}\bar D A(e^{u/N})\bar D F_c c_T(z),\\ f_N(u)=\frac{A(e^{u/N})_{T,a_*}}{(A_0)_{T,a_*}},\qquad d_N(u)=\frac{\sinh u}{N\sinh(u/N)} . \end{gathered} \tag{PC2} \] Values at zero are removable. The bars in \(\bar D\) refer to the fixed root frame; neither \(D\) nor \(F_c\) is differentiated. In particular \(\beta_b\) are the ordinary capped binomials, without square roots or a new gauge. For \(0<\alpha<1/2\), define \[ \begin{gathered} A_\alpha=\pi\cot(\pi\alpha/2),\qquad V_\alpha=(1-\alpha^2)/8,\qquad H_\alpha=A_\alpha+2\pi^2V_\alpha,\\ \kappa_\alpha =2+i\{\cot(3\pi\alpha/2)-2\cot(\pi\alpha/2)\},\\ \mathcal E_\alpha(v,\zeta)= \exp\left\{\frac{\kappa_\alpha^2v^2}{4H_\alpha} +\frac{i\pi V_\alpha\kappa_\alpha v\zeta}{H_\alpha}\right\}. \end{gathered} \tag{PC3} \] Here \(A_\alpha,V_\alpha,H_\alpha\) are positive real numbers. For every fixed \(0<V,Z<\infty\), the following quotient is holomorphic after removal of its ordinary zeros, for all sufficiently large admissible levels: \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{\mathscr S_N(\sqrt N\,v,\, q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})} {f_N(\sqrt N\,v)\, \mathscr S_N(0,q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})} =\mathcal E_{\alpha_N}(v,\zeta)+o_{I,V,Z}(1), \qquad |v|\le V,\quad|\zeta|\le Z . \quad} \tag{PC4} \] Convergence is uniform on these complex disks. It holds with every fixed derivative on smaller disks. In particular the divided quotient is nonzero there for large \(N\). Its scale is \(\mu=v/\sqrt N\); an order-\(j\) original \(\mu\)-derivative carries the factor \(N^{j/2}\). No relative error rate beyond \(o(1)\) is asserted. ## 2. Exact meridian products and the cap phases The literal root terminal row, including its support, is \[ (A_0)_{Ta}=c_*q^{a^2}{\ell\brack a}_Q =c_*q^{\ell a}B_a,\quad B_a=\frac{S_\ell}{S_aS_{\ell-a}}>0\quad(0\le a\le\ell), \qquad (A_0)_{Ta}=0\quad(a>\ell), \tag{PC5} \] where \(S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j2\sin(\pi h/N)\) and \(c_*=(-1)^{\ell+1}Nq^{2\ell^2+\ell+1}\). This is the evaluated terminal column followed by the actual generic transpose adapter, not differentiation of root symmetry. For \(a\le\ell\), set \(R_a(u)=A(e^{u/N})_{Ta}/(A_0)_{Ta}\). The exact row product (MC6) gives \[ \begin{split} R_a(u)&=d_N(u)g_a(u),\\ g_a(u)&= e^{u[\,2d-3(T-a)\,]/N} \prod_{j=T+1}^{T+a}\frac{1-e^{-4u/N}Q^j}{1-Q^j} \prod_{j=T-a+1}^{T}\frac{1-Q^j}{1-e^{-2u/N}Q^j}. \end{split} \tag{PC6} \] Thus \(f_N=d_Ng_{a_*}\). On any disk \(|u|\le C\sqrt N\), all factors of \(g_{a_*}\) are units for sufficiently large \(N\): their indices remain a fixed fraction of \(N\) from zero modulo \(N\). The same holds for \(g_a\) on \(\ell/4\le a\le3\ell/4\). Logarithms there are continued from \(u=0\). Let \(k=t-1=T-\ell\), \(x_a=(a-\ell/2)/\sqrt N\), and put \[ H_N(w)=\sum_{b=0}^T\beta_b \exp\{w(b-T/2)/\sqrt N\},\qquad C_N=\frac{c_*\bar D_{TT}}{\sqrt N} q^{(T^2-\ell T)/2}. \tag{PC7} \] The part of the actual period with \(a\le\ell\) is exactly \[ C_Nd_N(u)e^{\zeta T/(2\sqrt N)} \sum_{a=0}^\ell B_ag_a(u)H_N(\zeta+2\pi i x_a), \qquad z=q^ke^{\zeta/\sqrt N}. \tag{PC8} \] Indeed \(q^{\ell a}\bar D_{aa}=1\), since \(q^{\ell+T}\bar x_0=q^d\bar x_0=1\). The remaining Fourier phase is \[ Q^{(a-T/2)(b-T/2)}q^{kb} =q^{(T^2-\ell T)/2} \exp\{2\pi i(a-\ell/2)(b-T/2)/N\}. \tag{PC9} \] The expression (PC8) has a separate \(a>\ell\) tail when \(u\ne0\). That tail is estimated below, not set to zero. At \(\zeta=0\), the head weights in (PC8) are positive and even about \(\ell/2\): the palindromic negative-root polynomial (NR3) has positive centered character at \(\theta=(2a-\ell)\pi/N\), \(|\theta|<\pi\). The proof below uses the exact complex-\(\zeta\) expression (PC8) and proves its needed nonzero Gaussian limit directly. ## 3. The two actual Gaussian limits Choose \(a_*=\lfloor\ell/2\rfloor\). Uniformly on \(I\), the root sine-binomial ratios give \[ \frac{B_{a+1}}{B_a} =\frac{\sin((\ell-a)\pi/N)}{\sin((a+1)\pi/N)},\qquad \frac{B_a}{B_{a_*}}\le C_Ie^{-c_Ix_a^2},\qquad \frac{B_a}{B_{a_*}}\longrightarrow e^{-A_\alpha x^2} \tag{PC10} \] when \(x_a\to x\) and \(\alpha_N\to\alpha\). For completeness the derivative of the logarithm of this ratio is negative with magnitude at least \(c_I/N\) on the entire index interval, by sine addition. At the center that derivative is \(-2A_\alpha/N+O_I(N^{-2})\). Summation proves both claims, including half-integer centers. Also \(B_{a_*}\ge e^{c_IN}\) for large \(N\): its logarithm divided by \(N\) tends to \(J(\alpha)-2J(\alpha/2)>0\), where \(J(s)=\int_0^s\log(2\sin\pi y)\,dy\). Strict positivity follows from strict convexity of \(J\) on \((0,1/2)\). The original binomials have a second, different Gaussian limit: \[ \frac{H_N(w)}{H_N(0)} \longrightarrow \exp(V_\alpha w^2/2), \tag{PC11} \] locally uniformly for complex \(w\), uniformly on \(I\). Here is an elementary justification. Their exact consecutive ratio is \[ \frac{\beta_{b+1}}{\beta_b} =\frac{(d-b)(T-b)}{(b+1)(\ell+b+1)}. \tag{PC12} \] The coefficients \(\beta_b\) are symmetric about \(T/2\). Summing the central logarithmic expansion gives \(\beta_b/\beta_{\lfloor T/2\rfloor}\to \exp[-y^2/(2V_\alpha)]\), \(y=(b-T/2)/\sqrt N\). The four linear factors in (PC12) give a global upper bound \(C_Ie^{-c_Iy^2}\). These estimates normalize the Riemann sums, give convergence of every exponential moment on compact \(w\)-sets, and prove (PC11). In particular, for real \(x\) and \(|\zeta|\le Z\), \[ |H_N(\zeta+2\pi ix)|\le C_{I,Z}H_N(0). \tag{PC13} \] This bound controls all real \(x\), not merely a fixed central interval. The meridian ratio has the matching local limit \[ \frac{g_a(\sqrt N\,v)}{g_{a_*}(\sqrt N\,v)} \longrightarrow \exp(\kappa_\alpha vx) \tag{PC14} \] for bounded complex \(v\) and bounded \(x_a\to x\). In fact the exact logarithmic consecutive quotient from (PC6) is \[ \frac{3u}{N} +\log\frac{1-e^{-4u/N}Q^{T+a+1}}{1-Q^{T+a+1}} -\log\frac{1-e^{-2u/N}Q^{T-a}}{1-Q^{T-a}} . \tag{PC15} \] For \(u=\sqrt N\,v\) its first term in \(u/N\), at \(a=\ell/2+O(\sqrt N)\), has coefficient \(3-4/(1-e^{i\pi\alpha})+2/(1-e^{3i\pi\alpha}) =\kappa_\alpha\). The quadratic remainder per step is \(O_{I,V}(N^{-1})\); the variation of the first coefficient over \(O(\sqrt N)\) steps is \(O_{I,V}(N^{-1/2})\) after summation. This proves (PC14). On the whole central fraction one also obtains \[ \left|\frac{g_a(\sqrt N\,v)}{g_{a_*}(\sqrt N\,v)}\right| \le C_{I,V}e^{C_{I,V}|x_a|}. \tag{PC16} \] All logarithms used for these estimates are of actual central units. ## 4. Growing ordinary zeros and the remaining coordinates We justify division before taking the head limit. The Laurent row formula (MC7), with \(k_a=T-a\), has, apart from a unit monomial and a nonzero constant, the factors \[ (M^{-2}Q;Q)_{k_a} (M^{-2}Q^{T+1};Q)_\ell (M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a . \tag{PC17} \] At \(M=q^{-j}\), \(1\le j\le\ell\), the middle factor vanishes. At \(M=q^j\), \(t\ge3j+1\), either \(k_a\ge j\) and the first factor vanishes, or \(k_a<j\) and \(T+a\ge2T-j+1=N+t-j-1\ge N+2j\), so the last factor vanishes. It contains \(1-M^{-4}Q^{2j}\), hence the simple divisor \(1-M^{-2}Q^j\). These statements apply to every physical row entry. Since \(\ell,t\) grow proportionally to \(N\), they cover every \(u=i\pi j\), \(|u|\le C\sqrt N\), for any fixed \(C\), at large \(N\). Thus division by \(d_N(u)\), and then by the central unit \(g_{a_*}(u)\), is holomorphic on each such disk. Here are uniform bounds for the omitted indices. Choose radii \[ R_N=\pi(k_N+1/2),\qquad R_N/\sqrt N\longrightarrow V+1 . \tag{PC18} \] Every point of \(|u|=R_N\) is at distance at least \(\pi/2\) from \(i\pi\mathbb Z\). On these circles, any interval product of the nonzero-root factor ratios in (PC6), or their needed inverse denominator ratios, is at most \(\exp[C_{I,V}\sqrt N\log(N+1)]\). Indeed numerator ratios are bounded by \(1+C_V\sqrt N/\min(j,N-j)\). For inverse ratios, the \(O_V(\sqrt N)\) indices nearest the endpoints are bounded individually by a polynomial in \(N\), using the circle separation. On all other indices the relative perturbation is small; summing its harmonic bound gives the same estimate. Moreover \[ |d_N(u)|^{-1}\le C_V\sqrt N,\qquad |g_{a_*}(u)|+|g_{a_*}(u)|^{-1}\le e^{C_{I,V}\sqrt N} \quad (|u|=R_N). \tag{PC19} \] The first follows from the separated zeros of \(\sinh u\); the second follows by expanding only the central unit products. For \(a\le\ell\) outside the central fraction, (PC10) has an exponential loss relative to \(B_{a_*}\). It absorbs all the losses above. For \(a>\ell\), extract the unique zero factor \(1-M^{-4}\) in (PC17). The exact first-normal tail (MC10)--(MC11) bounds the remaining root product by a polynomial in \(N\). Comparison of its nonzero factors with their root values therefore gives only \(\exp[C_{I,V}\sqrt N\log(N+1)]\), times a polynomial. The factor \(|1-e^{-4u/N}|\) is \(O_V(N^{-1/2})\) on the circle. After division by (PC19), this is still exponentially smaller than the root scale \(B_{a_*}\). The original tail is fully retained here. Multiplication by the cap costs no new relative exponential: \(\|c_T(q^{t-1}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N})\|_2 \le C_{I,Z}e^{\operatorname{Re}\zeta\,T/(2\sqrt N)}\|\beta\|_2\), by the Gaussian bound from (PC12). The frozen Fourier matrix is a compression of a unitary matrix, and \(\bar D\) is unitary. Also \(\|\beta\|_2/H_N(0)\) is polynomially bounded by (PC12). Consequently, after the common normalization in (PC8) and division by \(g_{a_*}\), both omitted parts are \(\exp[-c_IN+C_{I,V}\sqrt N\log(N+1)]\) on the circles, up to fixed powers of \(N\). Their divided expressions are holomorphic by (PC17). The maximum principle, for each fixed \(\zeta\) and uniformly on its disk, gives the same vanishing bound on \(|u|\le V\sqrt N\). No path bypasses an ordinary zero and no cap coordinate is removed. ## 5. Evaluation of the relative limit Apply (PC10)--(PC16) to the central part of (PC8). The Gaussian bound times \(e^{C_V|x|}\) is integrable, uniformly on the stated complex parameter disks. Dominated Riemann sums give \[ \frac{1}{\sqrt N B_{a_*}H_N(0)} \sum_{a=0}^\ell B_a\frac{g_a(\sqrt N\,v)}{g_{a_*}(\sqrt N\,v)} H_N(\zeta+2\pi ix_a) \longrightarrow I_\alpha(v,\zeta) :=\int_{\mathbb R} e^{-A_\alpha x^2+\kappa_\alpha vx +V_\alpha(\zeta+2\pi ix)^2/2}\,dx . \tag{PC20} \] The omitted-coordinate estimates make this the limit of the entire divided actual period, with the same normalization. The convergence is uniform for \(\alpha=\alpha_N\in I\), by the same uniform estimates or compactness in \(\alpha\). The real quadratic coefficient is \(H_\alpha>0\), so direct completion of the square, continued holomorphically in \(v,\zeta\), yields \[ I_\alpha(v,\zeta)= \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{H_\alpha}}\, \exp\left\{\frac{V_\alpha\zeta^2}{2} +\frac{(\kappa_\alpha v+2\pi iV_\alpha\zeta)^2} {4H_\alpha}\right\}. \tag{PC21} \] In particular \(I_\alpha(0,\zeta)\) never vanishes and is uniformly bounded away from zero on each compact parameter set. At \(u=0\) there is no \(a>\ell\) tail. Division of (PC20) by its actual root counterpart therefore proves (PC4), since \[ \frac{I_\alpha(v,\zeta)}{I_\alpha(0,\zeta)} =\mathcal E_\alpha(v,\zeta). \tag{PC22} \] This also directly proves the needed nonzero root cap on the Gaussian activity collar, with the original phases and binomials. The quotient in (PC4) is holomorphic on slightly larger fixed disks, including every removable ordinary zero. Cauchy gives all fixed \(v,\zeta\) derivatives on smaller disks. Since the limiting exponential is nonzero, the quotient is a unit there for large \(N\). The only zeros of the actual period in this growing scaled-\(u\) domain are consequently the simple ordinary zeros \[ v_j=i\pi j/\sqrt N,\qquad j\ne0,\quad |v_j|\le V, \tag{PC23} \] with the evident restriction to the chosen disk boundary. Their divided normals are obtained by differentiating the retained factor \(f_N(\sqrt N\,v)\); they are not deleted by normalization. The gain over (QD11) is the genuine meridian scale \(N^{-1/2}\), with an explicit nonconstant joint transport factor and all its fixed scaled jets. A fixed meridian disk is still outside the result. All outer routing factors, their meridian derivatives, further crossings, turns, external scalars and the marked closing remain as in the original source. No assertion about their noncancellation, the degree of the original quantum cycle, or arbitrary short fillings is made. ## Complete inputs and coverage The adopted complete proof sections used are (MC1)--(MC23), (FH1)--(FH21), and their exact source conventions in notes/research_finite_exceptions_progress.md. The complete (QD1)--(QD12) and (NR1)--(NR12) were also read; the growing-zero and Gaussian-cap arguments needed here are written above. At author freeze the complete ledger SHA256 is b7ba8e8229e4317029df825660b25466ede91f3f274756dd836610f09e91cb30. Its preceding fixed-jet section is comparison coverage only. The complete original-source proof texts were retained whole at their renewed matching pins: C549 b4fb801a1482316aebb4799f1d0b80d5b43ced39138d903c04cfde811ca166b0; F428 7589bb0f796a874608b9e558aac1f78699884f0003da4a73ba52778c1edba66e; G489 42e6d6c3a5039859c241a2832de56301eff49d749db86d67868f3534c89aaaaa; O639 d52c6dd8e62f575a262fc7af460e258f7cb0e40b5a9c037ac46dd8d151002d44; I623 abd8009aa0e0e729efe82450a4f838fe1bdf250574cedf82a7c84a51e2e1de8e; M482 bf9bd5c282d478c9cfff7c93da5546a76177315724292c33dea528d5e1dd729f; L487 7f8c7c0be05331e7c0679c5a26374bbcb4b38b817c36a1f4ac4e16d4c1739095; complementary640 9ebdf4611802b9091a1c3dc3194e6529ed867933008c3c3d0851212325673b19; negative-root259 b697a6c47257c534ff08ca093a94f2a5a8a6c71cd46c2e823b00436a13032689. Their exact filenames are those in the adopted MC/FH source footers. Complete comparison texts retained matching are first-column415, coherent-sector599, collective532, physical-row288, coherent-boundary383, coefficient218, vacuum449, and meridian-frames506, at the exact pins listed after (MC23). The root-capped Euler coproduct360 was freshly read whole at e11f5f827f226ee93505e00aed3885a33abdbfc15ee71e023a67c048c9c17720: its \(N^{-1/2}\) meridian estimate concerns fixed-denominator Euler operators on a small activity disk, not this shifted-denominator capped period. The complete factorial162, filling-Gram240, and quantum-jet241 coverage has pins 17fbb46d17b9678e35b9800e1c67cca24f846e8b5ccbcc540d360ec3189e1b18, 9345e275c4c086b5f18ff2ded0f78e41e700a58b601bebd4b5e953f64e1b0d88, and aa338e19460ceaaac9aef7c387b5b2fb88ddfc0de706a5a6f6a937342628dde0. Those texts do not give the scalar-relative limit (PC4). Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used.

title: Whole-meridian transport of the capped Gauss row through a physical crossing
text:
# Whole-meridian transport of the capped Gauss row through a physical crossing Private written proof, 23 November 2026. The actual terminal Gauss row times one positive physical crossing is exactly a reflected copy of the whole meridian row with an explicit clock multiplier. This identity retains every coordinate and normal tail. It gives a scalar-relative, nonzero transport theorem for the original capped initializer at \(M=\exp(v/\sqrt N)\), without applying a large crossing matrix to an asymptotic approximation. The result concerns one physical generator. No closure under arbitrary signed words, original turns, or an exterior marked closing is asserted. ## 1. Actual matrices, with the full crossing scalar Keep the fixed root and the actual balanced meridian family: \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad M
e0,\quad x=-M/q,\quad F_j=(Q;Q)_j,\quad g_j(M)=(M^{-2}Q;Q)_j . 	ag{CT1} \] On a physical degree \(0\le T\le d\), write \[ C=Q^{-T-1},\quad K_T=M^2C,\quad H_d=(-1)^dM^dg_d,\quad A(M)=q_F(M)E_\Sigma(M)^di_d,\quad r(M)=e_T^{\mathsf T}A(M). 	ag{CT2} \] The restriction to degree \(T\) is understood. The source \(A\) is the actual capped Gauss operator of G489 and (MC1), with the original ordered coproduct. Its lowering coefficient is \(E(M)w_a=(MQ^{-a}-M^{-1})w_{a-1}\), with bottom zero. Let \(R_{m full}(M)\) be the actual positive checked crossing on these two equally colored heads. Use its original unrolled logarithm: \[ \alpha(M)=d+ rac{N}{\pi i}\Log M,\qquad \varkappa(M)=q^{\alpha(M)^2/2},\qquad B(M)=\varkappa(M)^{-1}R_{m full}(M). 	ag{CT3} \] The branch is continued from \(M=1\). All displayed \(q\)-powers mean their indicated exponentials. The stripped matrix \(B\) is Laurent polynomial in \(M\); the full scalar remains in (CT3). For input \((a,b)\), output \((b+h,a-h)\), and \(0\le h\le\min(a,d-b)\), its complete coefficient is \[ B_{b+h,a-h;\,a,b} =x^{-a-b-h}M^{2h}Q^{ab-(b+1)h}  rac{g_a(M)}{g_{a-h}(M)}  rac{F_{b+h}}{F_bF_h}. 	ag{CT4} \] The quotient \(g_a/g_{a-h}\) is the finite interval product, so this formula has no meridian poles. To check the generic family, the original preflip factorization is \(D P_N(e_xf)\), with the full Cartan \(D=q^{\mathsf h_\alpha\otimes\mathsf h_\alpha/2}\). The actual \(h\)-fold lowering coefficient is \(x^{-h}(M^2Q^{-a};Q)_h\). Reflection of its factors gives \[ (M^2Q^{-a};Q)_h =(-1)^hM^{2h}Q^{-ah+h(h-1)/2}\,g_a/g_{a-h}. \] Combining this with the finite Euler coefficient \((-1)^hQ^{h(h-1)/2}/F_h\), the raising coefficient \(F_{b+h}/F_b\), and the Cartan ratio \(x^{-a-b}Q^{(a-h)(b+h)}\), proves (CT4). Thus no complete-only coefficient has been differentiated. ## 2. An exact row reflection, before any asymptotic The whole terminal row formula (MC6), with \(k_a=T-a\), is \[ r_a(M)=H_dK_T^d x^{-k_a}M^{-2k_a}Q^{Tk_a}  rac{F_T}{g_T}  rac{g_{k_a}}{F_{k_a}}  rac{(M^{-4}Q^{T+1};Q)_a}{F_a}. 	ag{CT5} \] Its proved finite summation has length at most \(T<N\) and does not require the upper-chamber restriction. Apparent denominators are first interpreted near \(M=1\); the cleared entries are Laurent polynomials, as in (MC7). The exact transport identity, for every \(0\le j\le T\), is \[  oxed{\qquad (r(M)B(M))_j=x^{-T}(M^4C)^j r_{T-j}(M). \qquad} 	ag{CT6} \] Here both rows have all \(T+1\) physical coordinates. We give the entire finite cancellation. Put \(P=M^{-4}Q^{T+1}\) and \(J_0=H_dK_T^dF_T/g_T\). The contribution of output row coordinate \(T-b\) and input first occupation \(j\) has transfer \(h=j-b\), with \(0\le b\le j\). Substitution of (CT4)--(CT5) cancels \(g_b\) and \(F_{T-b}\), leaving \[  egin{split} (rB)_j={}&J_0x^{-T-j}M^{2j}Q^{-j}  rac{g_j}{F_{T-j}}\ &{}	imes\sum_{b=0}^j  rac{M^{-4b}Q^{(2T-j+1)b}(P;Q)_{T-b}} {F_bF_{j-b}} . \end{split} 	ag{CT7} \] Set \(D=P Q^{T-j}\). The last sum is \[  rac{(P;Q)_{T-j}}{F_j} \sum_{n=0}^j{j rack n}_Q D^{j-n}(D;Q)_n = rac{(P;Q)_{T-j}}{F_j}. 	ag{CT8} \] For an elementary proof of the equality to one, apply Gaussian Pascal \({j+1 rack n}={j rack n-1}+Q^n{j rack n}\). The two sums combine, term by term, through \((D;Q)_{n+1}+DQ^n(D;Q)_n=(D;Q)_n\). Induction starts at \(j=0\). Only factorials with index below \(N\) occur. Finally \(M^2/(Qx)=x\), so (CT7) becomes \[ (rB)_j=J_0x^{j-T}  rac{g_j(P;Q)_{T-j}}{F_jF_{T-j}}. 	ag{CT9} \] Comparison with (CT5) at \(T-j\), using \(C=Q^{-T-1}\) and \(Qx^2=M^2\), proves (CT6). The proof is on a generic neighborhood only to allow the displayed ratios; Laurent continuation proves every exceptional meridian value. In particular the nonzero first-normal tail is transported, not omitted using the root support. As a quantitative whole-row consequence in the original flat occupation norm, \[  egin{split} \min(|M|^{-T},|M|^{3T})\|r(M)\|_2 &\le\|r(M)B(M)\|_2\ &\le\max(|M|^{-T},|M|^{3T})\|r(M)\|_2 . \end{split} 	ag{CT10} \] This is just the exact diagonal modulus in (CT6), followed by reflection. At \(|M|=1\) it is equality. For \(M=e^{v/\sqrt N}\), \(|v|\le V\), the two comparison factors lie between \(e^{-3V\sqrt N}\) and \(e^{3V\sqrt N}\). For the full physical crossing both sides retain the multiplier \(|\varkappa(M)|\). No claim about the crossing on arbitrary rows is inferred from (CT10). ## 3. Exact transport with the original cap Now impose the upper-chamber conditions of PC405: \[ \ell=d-T\ge1,\quad t=N-2\ell>0,\quad \alpha_N=\ell/N\in I\Subset(0,1/2),\quad a_*=\lfloor\ell/2floor,\quad k=t-1=T-\ell. 	ag{CT11} \] Keep exactly the root-frozen \(D,F_c\), original \(c_T(z)\), period \(\mathscr S_N\), central entry \(f_N(u)\), and constants \(V_\alpha,H_\alpha,\kappa_\alpha\) of (PC2)--(PC3). Thus \(D_{aa}=q^{\ell a}\) and \( eta_b= inom db inom d{T-b}\). The different symbols \(\varkappa\) and \(\kappa_\alpha\) mean, respectively, the physical crossing scalar and the Gaussian tilt. Define the actual stripped crossed period \[ \mathscr S_N^+(u,z) =e_T^{\mathsf T} ar D A(M)B(M) ar D F_c c_T(z), \qquad M=e^{u/N}. 	ag{CT12} \] For bookkeeping only, let \(\mathscr S_N^{[w]}(u,z)\) mean the same uncrossed period with the additional diagonal \(w^a\) between \(A(M)\) and the following \( ar D\). This diagonal is not a new closing functional. The finite row identity gives the cap-preserving identity \[  oxed{\quad \mathscr S_N^+(u,z) =D_{TT}x^{-T}M^{4T}z^T \mathscr S_N^{[M^{-4}]}(u,z^{-1}). \quad} 	ag{CT13} \] This is first an identity for \(z
e0\), and is polynomial after clearing the displayed inverse argument. Indeed \(D_{T-a,T-a}=D_{TT} ar D_{aa}\), \((F_c)_{T-a,b}=(F_c)_{a,T-b}\), and \( eta_{T-b}= eta_b\). Reindex \(j=T-a\) in (CT6), then \(b\mapsto T-b\) in the actual cap, to obtain (CT13). Every Fourier phase and the whole binomial cap have been retained. The natural central crossed normalizer is itself a literal entry ratio: \[ f_N^+(u) := rac{(r(M)B(M))_{T-a_*}} {(r(1)B(1))_{T-a_*}} =M^{3T-4a_*}f_N(u). 	ag{CT14} \] Its denominator is nonzero by (PC5)--(CT6). For the full crossing, replace \(f_N^+\) by \(\varkappa(M)f_N^+/\varkappa(1)\). ## 4. A relative asymptotic through the actual generator For every fixed complex disks \(|v|\le V\), \(|\zeta|\le Z\), with \(V,Z>0\) independent of \(N\), put \(z_N^+(\zeta)=q^{-k}e^{\zeta/\sqrt N}\). Then \[  oxed{\quad  rac{\mathscr S_N^+(\sqrt N\,v,z_N^+(\zeta))} {f_N^+(\sqrt N\,v)\, \mathscr S_N^+(0,z_N^+(\zeta))} =\exp\left\{  rac{ ar\kappa_{\alpha_N}^{\,2}v^2}{4H_{\alpha_N}} + rac{i\pi V_{\alpha_N} ar\kappa_{\alpha_N}v\zeta} {H_{\alpha_N}}ight\} +o_{I,V,Z}(1). \quad} 	ag{CT15} \] The bar conjugates the constant \(\kappa_\alpha\), not \(v\) or \(\zeta\). Quotients at ordinary zeros are interpreted removably. The statement and its holomorphic derivatives are uniform on smaller fixed disks. In original meridian \(\mu=v/\sqrt N\), order \(j\) differentiation retains the factor \(N^{j/2}\). Here is why this follows from the actual estimates in PC405, rather than an unproved stability of a remainder under \(B\). In (CT13), \(z^{-1}=q^ke^{-\zeta/\sqrt N}\). After extraction of \(M^{-4a_*}\), the extra diagonal contributes \[ M^{-4(a-a_*)} =\exp\{-4v(a-a_*)/\sqrt N\}. 	ag{CT16} \] On the central occupation scale \(y=(a-\ell/2)/\sqrt N\), its limit is \(e^{-4vy}\). Thus the head Gaussian integral (PC20) has tilt \(\kappa_\alpha-4\) and cap variable \(-\zeta\). Its domination remains a Gaussian times \(e^{C_V|y|}\). For off-central coordinates, (CT16) costs at most \(e^{C_V\sqrt N}\); this is absorbed by the same \(e^{-c_IN+C_V\sqrt N\log(N+1)}\) estimates as in PC405. The true \(a>\ell\) tail obeys exactly the same conclusion. All shared ordinary zeros and the maximum-principle removal from (PC17)--(PC19) remain valid after a nonzero diagonal multiplier. Consequently the divided auxiliary period has relative limit \[ \exp\left\{ rac{(\kappa_\alpha-4)^2v^2}{4H_\alpha} - rac{i\pi V_\alpha(\kappa_\alpha-4)v\zeta}{H_\alpha}ight\}. 	ag{CT17} \] In (CT13) the remaining meridian monomial, relative to its root value, is \(M^{-T+4T-4a_*}=M^{3T-4a_*}\), exactly (CT14). Finally \(\operatorname{Re}\kappa_\alpha=2\), so \(\kappa_\alpha-4=- ar\kappa_\alpha\). This proves (CT15), including every scalar in (CT13). At the root, (CT13) reduces to \[ \mathscr S_N^+(0,z) =D_{TT}x_0^{-T}z^T\mathscr S_N(0,z^{-1}), 	ag{CT18} \] which is nonzero on the stated activity collar for large \(N\) by PC405. The right side of (CT15) is also nonzero on every fixed compact parameter set. Hence the divided crossed period is a holomorphic unit there for large \(N\). Its only meridian zeros are the same simple ordinary zeros \(v=i\pi j/\sqrt N
e0\); their divided normals are retained. All fixed scaled jets follow by Cauchy from slightly larger disks. For the full physical period, multiply (CT12) by \(\varkappa(M)\), and use the full normalizer following (CT14). Explicitly, on the retained logarithm, \[  rac{\varkappa(e^{u/N})}{\varkappa(1)} =\exp\left\{ rac{du}{N}+ rac{u^2}{2\pi iN}ight\}. 	ag{CT19} \] This factor is not replaced by a unit-modulus bound. Other external framing or meridian factors remain in their original positions and their own derivatives are not included in (CT15). The advance is an exact whole-family physical crossing step and its scalar-relative capped estimate. An inverse crossing from the resulting family can of course undo the same exact step; this does not assert closure for arbitrary successive signs or native turns. Such compositions must still transport the full graded kernel, the complement, and the actual exterior covector. No filled-knot or arbitrary-short-component lower bound follows here. ## Complete proof inputs and coverage The adopted PC405 was freshly read whole, at SHA256 81cf79171ed28c3a5cdd6da93de78bebad83d82049a27b9cafecb3798bf150d3: notes/research_capped_gauss_parabolic_meridian_collar.md. The complete adopted MC430 and its source conventions were retained whole at the current ledger pin b7ba8e8229e4317029df825660b25466ede91f3f274756dd836610f09e91cb30. All nine original proof texts and their complete comparison texts listed in PC405 remain whole/current at their renewed matching pins. The complete actual crossing inputs are notes/actual_shared_quantum_flags_and_charged_exchange.md (459 lines), dcab795cc141e2e1db726998cf7b1141dd03c681eaae9076387f90581f53a7d9, and notes/research_real_meridian_krein_transport.md (310 lines), caf18090cb75a0527ffccdf4a3217fe422876d683271eda8e3e6d591259e92dc. The full unrolled Cartan and generic meridian coefficients used in (CT3)--(CT4) are precisely those of the latter's (2),(6). Complete comparison coverage was checked: notes/research_gauss_physical_crossing_factorization.md (383 lines), 54d1b6c1e200cab6ca6e5affc49c98fe57d7c395a542d5f8afe502345884486f, proves an operator identity at the root and explicitly retains its uncomputed meridian defect. The present result evaluates a terminal row on the whole meridian family; it is not an extension of that whole-operator equality. The whole meridian-frame506, 6f58fba195ba5e8208e1d5180a1d684b933f9f5d50eb28efc56609580fe29976, was also checked; its exact diagonal crossing gauges do not give the capped scalar-relative result (CT15). No mathematical program, test, build or git operation was used.

title: Exponential coherent decay of the actual carry-projector Ward currents
text:
# Exponential coherent decay of the actual carry-projector Ward currents Private written proof, 19 November 2026. The low/high pair-degree projectors have exact threshold Ward currents. Their normalized ordinary-binomial coherent kernels are exponentially small on the explicit \(\Gamma<1\) chamber of S. The estimate holds at resolved zero coordinates as well as on nonzero-coordinate charts, and retains every fixed true meridian derivative. This is a kernel estimate for the projector currents themselves, not an operator-norm estimate or an estimate after composition with an unspecified crossing or word. ## 1. Literal arrows, kernels, and the exact currents Fix \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), and \(M=e^\mu\), \(x=-M/q\). The quantum root is held fixed. F supplies the finite physical arrows \[ Ew_a=(MQ^{-a}-M^{-1})w_{a-1}\quad(a>0),\quad Ew_0=0,\qquad Fw_a=(1-Q^{a+1})w_{a+1},\qquad Kw_a=xQ^{-a}w_a . 	ag{1} \] The upper \(F\) arrow is zero, since \(1-Q^N=0\). On two heads put \[ E_{m p}=E_1K_2+E_2,\qquad F_{m p}=F_1+K_1^{-1}F_2,\qquad J=J_1+J_2,\qquad \Pi_0=\mathbf1_{J\le d},\quad \Pi_1=I-\Pi_0. 	ag{2} \] All thresholds are exact integer occupations. Direct degree counting, including the endpoint zeros in (1), gives S(18a--b): \[ [E_{m p},\Pi_0]=-E_{m p}\mathbf1_{J=N},\qquad [F_{m p},\Pi_0]=F_{m p}\mathbf1_{J=d}. 	ag{3} \] The high-projector currents have the opposite signs. In particular, for a scalar mark \(\zeta\), \[ [E_{m p},\Pi_0+\zeta\Pi_1] =(\zeta-1)E_{m p}\mathbf1_{J=N},\qquad [F_{m p},\Pi_0+\zeta\Pi_1] =(1-\zeta)F_{m p}\mathbf1_{J=d}. 	ag{4} \] There is no approximation in these identities or their meridian jets. For a two-head matrix \(A\), use the actual input-binomial convention \[ K_A(z,w)=\sum_{a,b,c,e=0}^{d} A_{(c,e),(a,b)} inom da inom db z_1^cz_2^e w_1^aw_2^b . 	ag{5} \] Put \(v_i=z_iw_i\) and \(I_N=K_I=(1+v_1)^d(1+v_2)^d\). Only \(1+v_i
e0\) is required to define the normalized kernels \[ \mathcal E_N= rac{K_{E_{m p}\mathbf1_{J=N}}}{I_N}, \qquad \mathcal F_N= rac{K_{F_{m p}\mathbf1_{J=d}}}{I_N}. 	ag{6} \] The symbols \(\mathcal E_N,\mathcal F_N\) here denote currents, not external framing lines. At \(z_1z_2
e0\), the exact finite formulas are \[ \mathcal E_N= rac1{I_N}\sum_{a+b=N}  inom da inom db v_1^av_2^b \left[ rac{xQ^{-b}(MQ^{-a}-M^{-1})}{z_1} + rac{MQ^{-b}-M^{-1}}{z_2}ight], 	ag{7} \] \[ \mathcal F_N= rac1{I_N}\sum_{a+b=d}  inom da inom db v_1^av_2^b \left[z_1(1-Q^{a+1}) +z_2x^{-1}Q^a(1-Q^{b+1})ight]. 	ag{8} \] All indices in these sums remain between zero and \(d\). In (7) the threshold forces \(a,b\ge1\); thus the displayed divisions by \(z_i\) are removable in the original polynomial kernel. In (8) the factors \(1-Q^N\) kill precisely the forbidden upper arrows. No occupation cap has been extended. ## 2. Exact shell bounds, including zero coordinates Write \(X=|v_1|\), \(Y=|v_2|\), and \[ \Gamma(v_1,v_2) = rac{(\sqrt X+\sqrt Y)^2}{|1+v_1|\,|1+v_2|},\qquad S_\ell(X,Y)=\sum_{a+b=\ell} inom da inom db X^aY^b . 	ag{9} \] For any \(R>0\), positivity of the coefficients gives \[ S_\ell(X,Y)\le R^{-\ell}(1+RX)^d(1+RY)^d. 	ag{10} \] If \(XY>0\), choose \(R=(XY)^{-1/2}\). Since \((1+RX)(1+RY)/R=(\sqrt X+\sqrt Y)^2\), this proves \[  rac{S_{d+1}}{|I_N|}\le\sqrt{XY}\,\Gamma^d,\qquad  rac{S_d}{|I_N|}\le\Gamma^d . 	ag{11} \] Neither inequality requires \(XY<1\) or \(XY>1\). At \(XY=0\), the first shell vanishes and the second inequality holds by continuity, including \(X=Y=0\). A second estimate removes the \(z_i^{-1}\) factors in (7). The polynomial \(S_{d+1}(X,Y)\) is divisible by \(XY\). Reindexing \(a'=a-1\), using \( inom da=(d/a) inom{d-1}{a-1}\le d inom{d-1}{a-1}\), and applying (10) to degree \(d\), gives \[  rac{S_{d+1}(X,Y)/X}{|I_N|} \le  rac{d\,\Gamma^d}{1+RX}\le d\Gamma^d,\qquad  rac{S_{d+1}(X,Y)/Y}{|I_N|}\le d\Gamma^d . 	ag{12} \] The first displayed denominator uses the same optimizing \(R\); the second follows by exchanging the heads. The final bounds extend continuously to \(XY=0\), since the quotients are polynomials. This argument estimates the absolute coefficients of the divided shell, so it applies unchanged with the unit \(Q\)-phases in (7). Fix a finite \(\eta>0\) and restrict to \(|N\mu|\le\eta\). Every coefficient in the brackets of (7)--(8), after removing the displayed coordinate factors, has a uniform bound \(C_\eta\). Indeed \(|Q|=1\), \(|M|^{\pm1}\le e^{\eta/2}\), and \(x=-M/q\). Equations (7)--(12) therefore prove \[ |\mathcal E_N| \le C_\eta d(|w_1|+|w_2|)\Gamma^d,\qquad |\mathcal F_N| \le C_\eta(|z_1|+|z_2|)\Gamma^d . 	ag{13} \] These inequalities hold at all coordinates with \(1+v_i
e0\), including \(z_i=0\). In deriving the first one, \(z_i^{-1}v_i=w_i\) is used before taking that zero value. On the smaller chart \(z_1z_2
e0\), the sharper alternative is \[ |\mathcal E_N|\le C_\eta (|z_1|^{-1}+|z_2|^{-1})\sqrt{XY}\,\Gamma^d . 	ag{14} \] When \(v_i=0\) because \(z_i=0\) but \(w_i
e0\), the \(E\)-current need not vanish. Formula (13), rather than division by that zero coordinate or differentiation of the factor \(\sqrt{XY}\), is the appropriate statement. ## 3. Genuine meridian and coherent jets At fixed \(z,w\), every fixed meridian derivative satisfies the same bounds (13)--(14), with \(C_\eta\) replaced by \(C_{\eta,k}\), uniformly in \(N\). To see this directly, the first coefficient of (7) is \[ xQ^{-b}(MQ^{-a}-M^{-1}) =-q^{-1} ig(M^2Q^{-a-b}-Q^{-b} ig). 	ag{15} \] The other coefficient uses only \(M,M^{-1}\), while (8) uses only constants and \(M^{-1}\). Thus \(\partial_\mu^k\) multiplies these finitely many Laurent monomials by powers of \(0,\pm1,2\); one may take \(C_{\eta,k}\le C_\eta(1+2^k)\). The identity kernel is meridian independent. No \(N^k\) loss is needed for these fixed-coordinate currents. Let \(\mathcal K\) be any compact subset of \[ \mathcal U=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^4: 1+z_iw_i
e0,\ \Gamma(z_1w_1,z_2w_2)<1\}. 	ag{16} \] There is a fixed complex neighborhood of \(\mathcal K\), with bounded coordinates, nonzero incidence denominators, and \(\Gamma\le\gamma<1\). Apply (13) and its meridian derivatives on that neighborhood, and then use the ordinary multivariable Cauchy estimate. For every fixed coordinate multi-index \(\alpha\) and fixed \(k\ge0\), \[ \sup_{\substack{(z,w)\in\mathcal K\|N\mu|\le\eta}} \left( |\partial_{z,w}^{\alpha}\partial_\mu^k\mathcal E_N| +|\partial_{z,w}^{\alpha}\partial_\mu^k\mathcal F_N| ight) \le C_{\mathcal K,\alpha,k,\eta}\,d\,\gamma^d . 	ag{17} \] In particular every such jet is exponentially small as \(N	o\infty\). The exponent uses the buffered \(\gamma\); it is not a claim that coordinate derivatives preserve the pointwise factor \(\Gamma(v)^d\). The conclusion includes resolved zero coordinates in \(\mathcal K\). It applies to both projector currents by (3), and to (4) for \(\zeta\) in a fixed compact set. Fixed integer powers of the physical \(K_1,K_2\) placed on either side of these currents preserve the same conclusion: they only multiply each occupation coefficient by a unit \(Q\)-phase and a fixed Laurent power of \(M\). Their fixed meridian derivatives change the constants. This assertion does not include arbitrary moving factorial gauges or coordinates. ## 4. Meaning and limitation This proves local almost-intertwining in the specific sense of normalized binomial coherent kernels on (16). The exact finite operators (3) are still present; no exponentially small operator norm is asserted. Even the exact identity \([E_{m p},R(\Pi_0+\zeta\Pi_1)] =R[E_{m p},\Pi_0+\zeta\Pi_1]\) does not turn (17) into a kernel estimate for that product by pointwise multiplication of normalized symbols. A contracting coherent chain, its remaining density, and its boundary currents require separate estimates before (17) bounds an inserted current in an original source. No membership of an arbitrary geometric point in (16), localized source/axis correspondence, geometric cycle coefficient, or lower bound for a closed period is inferred. ## Complete proof directs * S: notes/research_crossing_wall_degree_sectors.md, 532 lines, SHA256 638e7feb66eeb4671775f6df57f3994b4139f5be95263247956dece538cb0636. * F: notes/research_actual_meridian_source_frames.md, 506 lines, SHA256 6f58fba195ba5e8208e1d5180a1d684b933f9f5d50eb28efc56609580fe29976. Both complete directs were whole-read nontruncated in this active author/review sequence, every used implication was checked, and their matching pins are retained. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used; frozen and public files were not edited.

title: The full output of two centered coherent inputs
text: # The full output of two centered coherent inputs Written research proof, 22 November 2026. The product of two specified centered geometric-series packets has an exact positive norm sum. On every compact complex input bidisk this sum has one positive nondegenerate Laplace maximum. It gives a uniform norm asymptotic, concentration of the entire output, and a complex Gaussian approximation in the full Newton coefficient norm. The proof uses the actual finite wall products, including both endpoint rows. It is a forward estimate for this family of two inputs. It is not a theorem for arbitrary packets or an arbitrary Conway component. ## 1. Inputs, wall products, and the exact output Use the full original algebra and centered basis of the [compiler](research_centered_fourier_conway_compiler.md): \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \eta=(-1)^d,\quad\kappa=q^{d^2/2},\quad \mathcal H_N=\mathbb C[s]/(2T_N(s/2)+2). \tag{1} \] Here \(T_N\) is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. The positive norm makes both the original Newton basis \(e_j\) and the centered basis \(f_a\) orthonormal. It is not the uniform physical Hilbert--Schmidt metric. All spectral first normals remain in \(\mathcal H_N\). For \(t\in\mathbb D=\{|t|<1\}\), put \[ Z_N(t)=\sum_{a=0}^d|t|^{2a},\qquad u_N(t)=Z_N(t)^{-1/2}\sum_{a=0}^d t^af_a,\qquad w_N(y,z)=u_N(y)u_N(z). \tag{2} \] Thus the inputs have norm one. These are centered coefficient packets, not the binomial coherent states of the physical head representation. Write \[ C_{abc}=\phi(f_af_bf_c),\qquad \mathcal C_N(x,y,z)=\sum_{a,b,c=0}^dC_{abc}x^ay^bz^c, \quad D_N(t)=1-\eta t^N,\quad X_j=-qQ^j. \] The original Frobenius pairing is \(\phi(f_af_b)=\delta_{ab}\), so these are the actual multiplication coefficients. The complete [wall-source theorem](research_centered_tensor_wall_cauchy_source.md) gives, at every level and \(0\le j<N\), \[ \mathcal C_N(X_j,y,z) =\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N}D_N(y)D_N(z)H_{N,j}(y,z), \quad H_{N,j}= \frac{(Q;Q)_j(Qyz;Q)_j} {(-qy;Q)_{j+1}(-qz;Q)_{j+1}}. \tag{3} \] Every factor is nonzero for \(y,z\in\mathbb D\). The points \(X_j\) are distinct Fourier sampling points, not a replacement of the full Casimir algebra by distinct-root values. Let \(w_{N,c}\) be the centered coefficients of \(w_N\). Its generating polynomial is \(\mathcal C_N(x,y,z)/\sqrt{Z_N(y)Z_N(z)}\). Finite Fourier Parseval therefore gives the exact positive energy \[ \boxed{\quad \|w_N(y,z)\|^2 =\frac{|D_N(y)D_N(z)|^2}{N^2Z_N(y)Z_N(z)} \sum_{j=0}^d|H_{N,j}(y,z)|^2. \quad} \tag{4} \] Indeed its degree in \(x\) is less than \(N\), and multiplication of the \(N\)-th-root grid by \(-q\) preserves Fourier orthogonality. There is a stronger exact interpretation of the samples. If \(\alpha_{N,j}\) are the Newton coefficients of the output, the compiler matrix gives \[ \boxed{\quad \alpha_{N,j} =\frac{\kappa(-q)^j}{\sqrt{N Z_N(y)Z_N(z)}} \mathcal C_N(X_j,y,z) =\frac{\kappa^2(-q)^jD_N(y)D_N(z)} {N\sqrt{Z_N(y)Z_N(z)}}H_{N,j}. \quad} \tag{5} \] In fact \(U_{ja}=\kappa(-q)^jX_j^a/\sqrt N\). Thus the concentration proved below concerns the full actual output vector, up to an explicitly given unitary change of coordinates. ## 2. The rate has exactly one maximum Put \(v=e^{2\pi iu}\), \(0<u<1\), and define \[ \mathcal R(v;y,z)= \frac{(1-v)(1-yzv)}{(1+yv)(1+zv)},\qquad E(u;y,z)=2\int_0^u\log|\mathcal R(e^{2\pi is};y,z)|\,ds . \tag{6} \] Its endpoint logarithms are integrable. In particular \(E\) extends continuously to \([0,1]\). All assertions below are uniform on \(|y|,|z|\le r<1\). There are exactly two solutions of \(|\mathcal R(v)|=1\) on the unit circle. Their parameters satisfy \[ 0<u_-<u_*<1,\qquad E'<0\text{ on }(0,u_-),\quad E'>0\text{ on }(u_-,u_*),\quad E'<0\text{ on }(u_*,1). \tag{7} \] Both crossings are simple. Moreover \[ E(0)=E(1)=0,\qquad E_*:=E(u_*)>0,\qquad a_*:=-E''(u_*)>0. \tag{8} \] Here is an elementary proof valid for complex \(y,z\). Set \(a=(1+y)(1+z)\), \(D(v)=(1+yv)(1+zv)\), and \[ K=|a|^2-2\Re\{a(\bar y+\bar z)\},\qquad L=a+\bar a\,yz. \] Since \((1-v)(1-yzv)=D(v)-av\), on \(|v|=1\) one has \[ |D(v)|^2\bigl(|\mathcal R(v)|^2-1\bigr) =K-2\Re(Lv). \tag{9} \] At \(v=1\) this is \(-|a|^2<0\). On the other hand, \[ \int_0^1\log|\mathcal R(e^{2\pi iu})|\,du=0. \tag{10} \] For the three regular factors this follows by integrating their convergent logarithm series; the same identity for \(1-v\) follows by an integrable boundary limit, or the elementary log-sine integral. The logarithm is negative on a nonempty interval near \(v=1\), so it must be positive somewhere else. Thus the single cosine in (9) has negative and positive values. It has precisely two simple zeros, with one positive arc which does not contain \(v=1\). This proves (7), and (10) proves the two endpoint values in (8). The last decreasing interval forces \(E(u_*)>E(1)=0\); the downward simple crossing gives \(E''(u_*)<0\). The roots, \(E_*\), and \(a_*\) depend continuously on the complex parameters viewed as real coordinates. Compactness then gives uniform separation of the two roots from each other and from \(0,1\), a positive lower bound for \(E_*,a_*\), and uniform derivative bounds near \(u_*\). For every fixed \(\epsilon>0\), uniqueness also gives a uniform gap between \(E_*\) and \(E(u)\) on \(|u-u_*|\ge\epsilon\). ## 3. Bulk amplitude and the full norm asymptotic Use midpoint labels \(u_j=(j+1/2)/N\), and put \[ B(u;y,z)=[(1-yz)(1+ye^{2\pi iu})(1+ze^{2\pi iu})]^{-1/2}, \qquad b(u;y,z)=|B(u;y,z)|^2. \tag{11} \] Branches are one at \(y=z=0\). In particular \(B\) is nonzero and all its required bulk derivatives are uniformly bounded. The wall-source theorem, including its original complex phase, implies on each fixed bulk interval \[ |H_{N,j}|^2 =N\,b(u_j;y,z)e^{NE(u_j;y,z)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{12} \] One can also read the rate directly from (3). If \(J(u)=\int_0^u\log(2\sin\pi s)\,ds\), it is \[ \frac{E(u)}2=J(u)+ \int_0^u\log\left| \frac{1-yze^{2\pi is}} {(1+ye^{2\pi is})(1+ze^{2\pi is})}\right|ds . \tag{13} \] This proves agreement with (6), with no adjustable additive constant. We need global control before applying a local Laplace estimate. The exact same products give \[ \bigl|\log|H_{N,j}|-\tfrac N2E(u_j)\bigr| \le C_r\log N \quad(0\le j<N). \tag{14} \] For a direct endpoint-uniform justification, \(\log(2\sin\pi s)-\log s-\log(1-s)\) has a continuously differentiable extension to \([0,1]\). Integral comparison for the two logarithms and the bounded Riemann-sum error for the remainder show \(\log|(Q;Q)_j|=NJ(j/N)+O(\log N)\), uniformly even at \(j=0,d\). Moving \(j/N\) to \(u_j\) costs another \(O(\log N)\). All other logarithms in (3) have uniformly bounded first derivatives on the entire interval for \(|y|,|z|\le r\); their sum errors are bounded. This proves (14), retaining both finite endpoints. Let \(B_*=B(u_*;y,z)\). The full output norm is \[ \boxed{\quad \|w_N(y,z)\|^2= \frac{|D_N(y)D_N(z)|^2}{Z_N(y)Z_N(z)} |B_*|^2\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{a_*N}}\, e^{NE_*}(1+O_r(N^{-1})). \quad} \tag{15} \] In particular \(N^{-1}\log\|w_N\|\to E_*/2>0\), uniformly on compact input bidisks. For proof, the global gap and (14) make all rows outside one fixed bulk neighborhood exponentially small compared to \(e^{NE_*}\), with at most a polynomial factor. Inside, substitute (12). Uniform real Laplace expansion gives \[ \int b(u)e^{NE(u)}\,du =b_*\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{Na_*}}e^{NE_*}(1+O_r(N^{-1})). \tag{16} \] The usual error estimate follows by Taylor expansion on a symmetric fixed neighborhood of \(u_*\): the terms of odd Gaussian degree integrate to zero and the next even terms have relative order \(N^{-1}\). All derivatives and Gaussian bounds are uniform by Section 2. The midpoint sum has the same relative error. Insert a smooth cutoff equal to one near every possible \(u_*\). For \(f_N=b e^{NE}\) times this cutoff, midpoint quadrature gives \[ \left|\frac1N\sum_j f_N(u_j)-\int f_N(u)\,du\right| \le C N^{-2}\int|f_N''(u)|\,du \le C_rN^{-3/2}e^{NE_*}. \tag{17} \] The first inequality follows by integrating the second-order Taylor remainder on each mesh cell. The second follows from \(|E'|\le C|u-u_*|\), \(E\le E_*-c|u-u_*|^2\) near the maximum; the cutoff derivatives lie in a fixed gapped region. Comparison with (16) proves a relative \(O(N^{-1})\) error. Finally combine the extra factor \(N\) in (12), the factor \(N\) from summation, and \(N^{-2}\) in (4). This proves (15). ## 4. Concentration and an actual complex Gaussian output The entire output probability in Newton coordinates is exactly \[ \mu_{N,j}=\frac{|\alpha_{N,j}|^2}{\|w_N\|^2} =\frac{|H_{N,j}|^2}{\sum_h|H_{N,h}|^2}. \tag{18} \] For each fixed \(\epsilon>0\), (7), (14), and (15) give \[ \sum_{|u_j-u_*|\ge\epsilon}\mu_{N,j} \le C_{r,\epsilon}e^{-c_{r,\epsilon}N}. \tag{19} \] Polynomial factors have been absorbed by decreasing the positive exponential gap. In the scale \(s_j=(j+1/2-Nu_*)/\sqrt N\), the limiting density is \[ \sqrt{\frac{a_*}{2\pi}}e^{-a_*s^2/2}. \tag{20} \] For example, the discrete local probabilities are this density times \(N^{-1/2}(1+o(1))\), uniformly for bounded \(s_j\). The original complex phase also gives a full-vector approximation. Define its fixed branch on \(0<u<1\) by \[ \begin{split} \mathcal F(u;y,z)={}&J(u)+\frac{i\pi}{2}(u^2-u)\\ &+\int_0^u\{\log(1-yze^{2\pi is}) -\log(1+ye^{2\pi is})-\log(1+ze^{2\pi is})\}\,ds . \end{split} \tag{21} \] The regular logarithms use their power-series branches. Thus \(2\Re\mathcal F=E\), with the exact factorial phase retained. The complex wall theorem is, equivalently, \[ H_{N,j}=\sqrt N\,\xi_N B(u_j;y,z)e^{N\mathcal F(u_j;y,z)} (1+O_r(N^{-1})),\qquad \xi_N=e^{i\pi/4-\pi i/(8N)} \tag{22} \] on fixed bulk intervals. This is the already calibrated midpoint phase, not an inference from the absolute-value formula. Put \(\delta_j=j+1/2-Nu_*\), \(\vartheta_*=\Im\mathcal F'(u_*)\), and \(F_{2,*}=\mathcal F''(u_*)\), so that \(\Re F_{2,*}=-a_*/2<0\). The explicit unit vector \[ g_{N,j}=\mathcal Z_N^{-1/2}(-q)^j \exp\left\{i\vartheta_*\delta_j+ \frac{F_{2,*}\delta_j^2}{2N}\right\}, \qquad \mathcal Z_N=\sum_{j=0}^d e^{-a_*\delta_j^2/(2N)} \tag{23} \] satisfies \[ \boxed{\qquad \left\|\frac{(\alpha_{N,j})_j}{\|w_N\|} -\lambda_N(g_{N,j})_j\right\|_{\ell^2} =O_r(N^{-1/2}),\qquad} \tag{24} \] where the known unit phase is \[ \lambda_N= \frac{\kappa^2D_N(y)D_N(z)\xi_N B_*} {|\kappa^2D_N(y)D_N(z)\xi_N B_*|} e^{iN\Im\mathcal F(u_*)}. \tag{25} \] To prove (24), use (5) and (22) in a bulk neighborhood. The real part of \(\mathcal F'(u_*)\) is zero. Taylor expansion therefore gives the linear and quadratic terms in (23), with error \(O(|\delta_j|^3/N^2)\) in the exponent and \(O(|\delta_j|/N)\) in \(B/B_*\). On \(|\delta_j|\le N^{1/2+\gamma}\), \(0<\gamma<1/6\), the squared error is bounded by \(C/N\) times a fixed polynomial in \(|s_j|\) against a uniform Gaussian. Summing these Gaussian moments gives the \(O(N^{-1/2})\) norm error. The intervening bulk tails are \(e^{-cN^{2\gamma}}\), and (14) controls the remaining full interval with a fixed gap. The same Gaussian sum shows \(\mathcal Z_N=\sqrt{2\pi N/a_*}(1+o(1))\). Normalizing the approximating vector and the actual output changes the estimate by at most the same norm error, and fixes its phase as (25). This proves the assertion with all finite rows retained. ## 5. Exact endpoints, scope, and coverage Both original closing functionals are explicit. The compiler gives \(m(e_j)=\delta_{j0}\) and \(\phi(e_j)=\delta_{jd}\). Using the two exact wall endpoints in (3) yields \[ \boxed{\begin{aligned} m(w_N)&=\frac{\kappa^2D_N(y)D_N(z)} {N\sqrt{Z_N(y)Z_N(z)}(1+qy)(1+qz)},\\ \phi(w_N)&=\frac{\sum_{a=0}^d(yz)^a} {\sqrt{Z_N(y)Z_N(z)}}. \end{aligned}} \tag{26} \] The second identity also follows directly from \(\phi(f_af_b)=\delta_{ab}\). These closings remain bounded on compact bidisks while the internal output norm has the positive exponential rate in (15). Consequently the norm and Gaussian approximation do not supply a scalar closing lower bound. The result estimates the actual forward product of the two packets (2) in the original centered/Newton coefficient metric. It does not put an arbitrary incoming packet, a geometric short component, or every physical binomial coherent input into this family. No uniform positive conditioning of the full multiplication map or its \(MM^*\) factor is proved. Composition through arbitrary further turns and branching, or a filled-knot geometric action, remains outside the theorem. The complete proof directs are: | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Exact wall source and complex bulk amplitude, 366 lines](research_centered_tensor_wall_cauchy_source.md) | 3cda6a170c46abf27a1c8c15b110780ebcb6017a5aa18758a4e51ba0a271892c | | [Centered compiler and original closures, 405 lines](research_centered_fourier_conway_compiler.md) | 0edbabe42280d70e4d5dcbcb55b188a3e773c14b99fbd212eb0fe8c5b176a413 | Both complete matching texts were read. The full crossing-covariance note and the centered prism-transport notes were also checked for coverage; they concern different inputs or scalar source evaluations, not this whole-output norm and its single-cosine Laplace maximum. General bilinear and Poisson kernels for Al-Salam--Chihara polynomials are standard; see Ismail--Stanton, [Classical Orthogonal Polynomials as Moments, Section 4](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~stant001/PAPERS/opmom.pdf), Theorem 4.2 and equation (4.7), for primary coverage. No generic orthogonality theorem or root-of-unity specialization from that paper is a premise. Parseval, Laplace asymptotics, and Gaussian concentration are standard methods. The source-specific assertion here is the compact-complex full-output estimate for the original finite tensor, with its phases, endpoints and full Hermite algebra retained. Only written mathematics and text operations were used. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged.

title: A centered Fourier basis for the original Conway gluing
text: # A centered Fourier basis for the original Conway gluing 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. A single unitary change of Newton coordinates makes the original bilinear gluing diagonal and makes both signed crossing coupons coordinate vectors. Every multiplication then uses one symmetric three-index tensor. The tensor is explicit, but its phases cannot all be removed while keeping this diagonal gluing and the full repeated-root algebra. This is an exact compiler for the original finite source. It neither truncates a packet to a Gaussian window nor proves a geometric lower bound after short fillings. ## 1. The algebra and the two original closures Fix \(N\ge2\), and put \[ d=N-1,\qquad q=e^{\pi i/N},\qquad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad S_r=\prod_{j=1}^r2\sin(\pi j/N),\quad S_0=1. \tag{1} \] Powers of \(q\) in this note mean \(q^a=e^{\pi ia/N}\), including half-integer exponents. This fixes the phases at even levels. The original algebra and its normalized Newton basis are \[ \mathcal H_N=\mathbb C[z]/P_N(z),\quad P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2,\quad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N),\quad e_r=S_r^{-2}\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}(c_j-z). \tag{2} \] Here \(T_N(\cos t)=\cos Nt\). Work in the entire quotient, including the first derivatives at its double roots. The original Frobenius closing \(\phi\), the ordinary marked closing \(m\), the genuine turn \(J\), and coefficient reflection \(a^\sharp(z)=\overline{a(\bar z)}\) satisfy \[ \phi(e_re_s)=\delta_{r+s,d},\qquad \phi(e_r)=\delta_{r,d},\qquad m(e_r)=\delta_{r,0}, \qquad Je_r=e_{d-r},\qquad e_r^\sharp=e_r. \tag{3} \] The positive Newton norm is \(\|\sum_r\alpha_re_r\|^2=\sum_r|\alpha_r|^2\). The actual signed crossing elements are \[ R^+=\kappa\sum_{r=0}^d(-q)^re_r,\qquad R^-=\kappa^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^d(-q)^{-r}e_r,\qquad R^+R^-=1. \tag{4} \] These identities, including the original cups, caps and Cartan scalar, are the direct inputs from the Newton source theorem. ## 2. Diagonal bilinear gluing and exact signed modes For \(0\le a\le d\), set \[ k_a=a-d/2,\qquad U_{ra}=N^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i}{N}k_a(r-d/2)\right), \qquad f_a=\sum_{r=0}^dU_{ra}e_r. \tag{5} \] If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the Newton and Fourier coefficient columns of the same element, then \(\alpha=U\beta\). **Proposition 1.** The basis in (5) is Hermitian orthonormal in the positive Newton norm. It also satisfies the bilinear identities \[ \boxed{\quad \phi(f_af_b)=\delta_{ab},\qquad Jf_a=f_{d-a},\qquad f_a^\sharp=f_{d-a}. \quad} \tag{6} \] The two signed crossings are exactly \[ R^+=\sqrt N\,f_0,\qquad R^-=\sqrt N\,f_d . \tag{7} \] **Proof.** The differences \(k_b-k_a=b-a\) are integers. The finite geometric sum in \(\sum_r\overline{U_{ra}}U_{rb}\) therefore gives \(U^*U=I\), at both parities. Moreover \[ U_{d-r,b}=\overline{U_{rb}},\qquad U_{r,d-a}=\overline{U_{ra}}. \tag{8} \] Combining the first equality with (3) proves \(\phi(f_af_b)=\sum_rU_{ra}\overline{U_{rb}}=\delta_{ab}\). The two reversal assertions follow from (8). Since \(r\) is an integer, \[ (-q)^r=e^{-\pi idr/N},\qquad \sqrt N\,U_{r0}=\kappa(-q)^r,\qquad \sqrt N\,U_{rd}=\kappa^{-1}(-q)^{-r}. \tag{9} \] Thus (4) proves (7) with no remaining phase factor. \(\square\) The distinction between bilinear and Hermitian pairing remains essential. If \(A=\sum_aA_af_a\) and \(B=\sum_aB_af_a\), then \[ \phi(AB)=\sum_aA_aB_a , \tag{10} \] without conjugating either input. A physical turn on an attaching edge still inserts the reversal \(a\mapsto d-a\). The original closure rows are not discarded. Define \[ \omega_a=N^{-1/2}e^{\pi ik_ad/N}. \tag{11} \] Then \[ \phi(f_a)=\omega_a,\qquad m(f_a)=\overline{\omega_a},\qquad 1=\sum_{a=0}^d\omega_af_a . \tag{12} \] These formulas follow by taking the \(e_d\) and \(e_0\) coefficients in (5), or by pairing the unit with \(f_a\). Both closure rows retain dual norm one. For example \(\phi(1)=\sum_a\omega_a^2=0\), whereas \(m(1)=\sum_a|\omega_a|^2=1\). Thus the diagonal gluing has not erased the original source's exact zero or its marked closure. ## 3. One symmetric multiplication tensor Define the real symmetric Newton tensor \[ \tau_{ijk}=\phi(e_ie_je_k). \tag{13} \] Its exact support and coefficients are \[ \tau_{ijk}= \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{S_{i+j}S_{i+k}S_{j+k}} {N S_iS_jS_kS_{i+j+k-d}}, &i+j,\ i+k,\ j+k\le d,\quad i+j+k\ge d,\\[6pt] 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \tag{14} \] All factorial indices in the nonzero case lie between \(0\) and \(d\); every displayed coefficient is strictly positive. To derive (14), the actual positive multiplication theorem gives \[ e_ie_j=\sum_{\ell=\max(i,j)}^{i+j} \frac{S_{i+j}S_\ell} {S_iS_jS_{\ell-i}S_{\ell-j}S_{i+j-\ell}}e_\ell \quad(i+j<N), \tag{15} \] and gives zero when \(i+j\ge N\). By (3), only \(\ell=d-k\) contributes to (13). Its permitted range is equivalent to the four inequalities in (14). Finally use \(S_rS_{d-r}=N\) in its three complementary factorials. This proves the symmetric formula without evaluating only at the distinct Casimir roots. In the Fourier basis put \[ C_{abc}=\phi(f_af_bf_c) =\sum_{i,j,k=0}^dU_{ia}U_{jb}U_{kc}\tau_{ijk}. \tag{16} \] Thus \(C\) is an explicit centered three-dimensional finite Fourier transform of (14). Equivalently the summand's phase is \[ \exp\!\left\{\frac{2\pi i}{N} [k_a(i-d/2)+k_b(j-d/2)+k_c(k-d/2)]\right\}, \tag{17} \] with the common factor \(N^{-3/2}\). The tensor is symmetric in all three legs, and (6) gives \[ f_af_b=\sum_{c=0}^dC_{abc}f_c . \tag{18} \] It retains the conjugation rule \(\overline{C_{abc}}=C_{d-a,d-b,d-c}\). In particular multiplication by the two actual signed crossings has matrices \[ (A_+)_{cb}=\sqrt N\,C_{0bc},\qquad (A_-)_{cb}=\sqrt N\,C_{dbc},\qquad A_-A_+=I. \tag{19} \] These matrices retain their repeated-root Jordan directions. They have not become diagonal phase multipliers. ## 4. The actual Casimir becomes tridiagonal The tensor in (16) also satisfies finite three-term equations. For \(0\le a\le d\), put \[ A_a=Q^{-a-1}-1,\qquad B_a=2q^{-1}Q^{-a},\qquad D_a=Q^{-a}-1,\qquad Q=q^2. \tag{20} \] Then multiplication by the actual Casimir coordinate has the form \[ zf_a=A_af_{a+1}+B_af_a+D_af_{a-1}. \tag{21} \] The \(f_{a+1}\) and \(f_{a-1}\) terms are absent at \(a=d\) and \(a=0\), respectively: \(A_d=D_0=0\). There is no cyclic endpoint arrow. Here is a direct verification, including the endpoints. In Newton coordinates \[ ze_r=c_re_r+b_{r+1}e_{r+1},\qquad b_r=Q^r+Q^{-r}-2, \tag{22} \] with the absent term at \(r=d\) and \(b_0=0\). Set \(x=q^d=-q^{-1}\). In the output row \(r\), the coefficient of \(zf_a\) is \[ U_{ra}\{c_r+b_rxQ^{-a}\}. \tag{23} \] Using \(c_r=qQ^r+q^{-1}Q^{-r}\) and \(Q^{\pm r}U_{ra}=x^{\pm1}U_{r,a\pm1}\) gives (21). One may temporarily extend \(f_{a+N}=(-1)^df_a\) in this calculation, but the coefficients \(A_d,D_0\) kill both wrap terms in the final identity. Since \(f_0=R^+/\sqrt N\) and \(R^+\) is invertible, (21) gives unique polynomials \(p_a(z)\) of degree \(a\) such that \[ f_a=N^{-1/2}R^+p_a(z),\qquad p_0=1 . \tag{24} \] For \(a<d\), solve (21) for \(p_{a+1}\); its denominator \(A_a\) is nonzero. The monic rescaling \[ \mathcal P_a=(-1)^a(Q^{-1};Q^{-1})_a p_a,\qquad (Q^{-1};Q^{-1})_a=\prod_{j=1}^a(1-Q^{-j}), \tag{25} \] satisfies, for \(0\le a<d\), with \(\mathcal P_{-1}=0\), \[ z\mathcal P_a=\mathcal P_{a+1} +2q^{-1}Q^{-a}\mathcal P_a +(1-Q^{-a})^2\mathcal P_{a-1}. \tag{26} \] This is the Al-Salam--Chihara recurrence with argument \(z/2\), base \(Q^{-1}\), and both parameters \(q^{-1}\); compare [Koornwinder (2004), equation (5)](https://staff.fnwi.uva.nl/t.h.koornwinder/art/informal/ASC.pdf). The comparison only names a standard recurrence. Its specialization here was derived above. Only \(0\le a\le d\) is rescaled in (25); its factorial is nonzero on that range. No rescaling by the vanishing factor \((Q^{-1};Q^{-1})_N\), positive measure, or generic-parameter orthogonality theorem is used. The original complex linear functional \[ \psi(g)=\phi((R^+)^2g)/N \tag{27} \] obeys \[ \psi(p_ap_b)=\delta_{ab},\qquad C_{abc}=N^{-1/2}\psi(R^+p_ap_bp_c). \tag{28} \] These are bilinear identities; \(\psi\) is not asserted to be a positive measure. They follow by substituting (24) in (6) and (16). Finally, moving \(z\) among the three factors in \(\phi(zf_af_bf_c)\) proves \[ \begin{aligned} A_aC_{a+1,b,c}+B_aC_{abc}+D_aC_{a-1,b,c} &=A_bC_{a,b+1,c}+B_bC_{abc}+D_bC_{a,b-1,c}\\ &=A_cC_{a,b,c+1}+B_cC_{abc}+D_cC_{a,b,c-1}. \end{aligned} \tag{29} \] Every endpoint in these equations retains its zero coefficient. Thus the universal multiplication tensor comes with explicit finite difference equations, not only its Fourier sum. ## 5. The exact source compiler Every specified finite Conway source can now be evaluated using: * the single tensor \(C\) for each multiplication; * reversal \(a\mapsto d-a\) for each genuine turn; * the vectors \(\sqrt N\,\delta_0\) and \(\sqrt N\,\delta_d\) for signed crossing coupons; * the unit and the two original closing rows in (12). A power \(R^n\) is a product of \(|n|\) signed unit crossings, or the unit for \(n=0\). Consequently \(J(R^+)=\sqrt N f_d\) and \(J(R^-)=\sqrt N f_0\). An arbitrary fixed short filling can be retained exactly by this finite algebraic expansion. These auxiliary multiplication vertices are not new crossing circles or new independent twist parameters. There is no assertion that the expanded diagram is a new strict filling template, or that turns may be moved through products. The source identity follows by induction on the original expression, using (6), (12), and (18) at its actual attachments. Open outputs are retained as full \(N\)-component columns. No Casimir value or first derivative has been removed, because \(U\) is invertible on the entire algebra. The same change is unitary for the positive Newton packet norm. It preserves every vector norm, operator Hilbert--Schmidt norm, and multiplication-tensor Hilbert--Schmidt norm. For the latter, the ordinary output/input coordinate formula is \(U^*M(U\otimes U)\); equations (3) and (8) identify it with (16). Thus a previously recorded norm budget is unchanged if the same algebraic tree is written in these coordinates. In particular a normalized signed leaf is an exact endpoint mode, rather than an approximation obtained by deleting its other Newton coordinates. ## 6.
