title: A forced Rogers connection for the original multiplication tensor
text:
# A forced Rogers connection for the original multiplication tensor 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The original centered multiplication tensor satisfies three exact inhomogeneous quantum difference equations. A finite telescoping identity proves their forcing term, including the initialized normal which would be lost by evaluating the hypergeometric sum only at the root. No infinite Rogers sum is substituted. On the full finite boundary coefficient space, a known cyclic dilogarithm product removes the homogeneous part of the connection. The remaining additive equations are compatible and have an explicit finite Fourier solution. One universal scalar fixes their constant. That scalar also has a direct finite factorial initializer. These identities preserve the complete tensor and hence its original assembled source. They do not prove noncancellation after arbitrary short fillings. ## 1. The original source and its scalar factors Fix \(N\ge2\), and put \[ d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \eta=(-1)^d,\quad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad D_N(t)=1-\eta t^N . 	ag{1} \] All fractional powers mean the indicated exponential. Use the original full Casimir algebra \(\mathcal H_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2)\), its positive crossing \(R\), and its original Frobenius functional \(\phi\). Here \(T_N(\cos	heta)=\cos(N	heta)\). The finite source theorem fixes \[ \mathcal C_N(x,y,z)= \sum_{a,b,c=0}^{d}C_{abc}x^ay^bz^c =N^{-3/2}\phi\!\left( R^3G_N(x;\cdot)G_N(y;\cdot)G_N(z;\cdot)ight). 	ag{2} \] The arguments \(x,y,z\) in this note are boundary generating variables; the dot in (2) is the Casimir variable. In particular \(\mathcal C_N\) is the entire original three-boundary tensor, not an absolute-value envelope. Define the analytic function in the open unit polydisk \[ \widehat{\mathcal C}_N(x,y,z)=  rac{\mathcal C_N(x,y,z)}{D_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z)},\qquad  eta_N= rac{(-1)^{N+1}\kappa^3}{N^{3/2}} . 	ag{3} \] For \(i=x,y,z\), let \(T_i\) multiply that one argument by \(Q\). For example \(T_xF(x,y,z)=F(Qx,y,z)\). Write \[ a_x=(1-Qxy)(1-Qxz),\qquad b_x=(1+qx)(1+qxyz),\qquad r_x= rac{x}{1+qx}, 	ag{4} \] and define the other two triples by permutation. **Theorem 1.** The exact original source satisfies \[  oxed{\qquad a_xT_x\widehat{\mathcal C}_N-b_x\widehat{\mathcal C}_N = eta_N rac{x}{1+qx}, \qquad} 	ag{5} \] and the two permuted equations. Equivalently, its polynomial version retains every original norm factor: \[ a_xT_x\mathcal C_N-b_x\mathcal C_N = eta_ND_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z) rac{x}{1+qx}. 	ag{6} \] The right side has a removable denominator since \(1+qx\) divides \(D_N(x)\). ## 2. A finite telescoping certificate and its initialized normal This proof uses the auxiliary generic parameter \(\xi\) from the finite source theorem. Put \(B=\xi^2\), and let \[  egin{split} 	au_j(\xi;x,y,z) ={}& rac{1-\xi^{4j+2}}{1-\xi^2}(-\xi)^j\ &{}	imes \prod_{t\in\{x,y,z\}}  rac{\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}(t+\xi^{2h+1})} {\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}(1+\xi^{2h+3}t)},\qquad S_N(\xi)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}	au_j(\xi). \end{split} 	ag{7} \] Empty products are one. This canceled definition is regular at zero boundary arguments. In a fixed closed unit subpolydisk it is holomorphic for \(\xi\) sufficiently close to \(q\). The complete finite source theorem proves, with all root Hermite data calibrated, \[ S_N(q;x,y,z)=0,\qquad \widehat{\mathcal C}_N= K_N^{m loc}  rac{\dot S_N(q;x,y,z)} {(1+qx)(1+qy)(1+qz)},\quad K_N^{m loc}=  rac{(-1)^N(q-q^{-1})\kappa^3}{2N^{5/2}} . 	ag{8} \] Here the dot is \(\xi\partial_\xi\) with boundary arguments fixed. The notation \(K_N^{m loc}\) denotes only the displayed known local constant; it is not a knot invariant. For the \(x\)-equation define \[ g_\xi(u)=  rac{(1+\xi^3x)\xi x(1-u)(1+\xi yu)(1+\xi zu)} {(1-Bu^2)(u+\xi x)} . 	ag{9} \] For generic parameters the following rational identity holds: \[  egin{split} &(1-Bxy)(1-Bxz)	au_j(\xi;Bx,y,z) -(1+\xi^3x)(1+\xi xyz)	au_j(\xi;x,y,z)\ &\hspace{25mm}= 	au_{j+1}(\xi;x,y,z)g_\xi(B^{j+1}) -	au_j(\xi;x,y,z)g_\xi(B^j). \end{split} 	ag{10} \] Products on the right are canceled before specialization. This matters when the well-poised factor vanishes at an odd-level middle index. Here is a direct check, independent of an infinite summation. Set \(u=B^j\). The two needed ratios are \[  rac{	au_j(\xi;Bx,y,z)}{	au_j(\xi;x,y,z)} = rac{u(1+\xi x)(1+\xi^3x)} {(u+\xi x)(1+\xi^3xu)}, 	ag{11} \] \[  rac{	au_{j+1}}{	au_j} =-\xi rac{1-B^3u^2}{1-Bu^2} \prod_{t\in\{x,y,z\}} rac{t+\xi u}{1+\xi^3tu}. 	ag{12} \] Substitute (9) into (12), cancel the \(y,z\) denominators, and use \(Bu+\xi x=\xi(x+\xi u)\). The remaining identity, after multiplication by its denominators, is \[  egin{split} &\xi x igl[ (1-Bu)(y+\xi u)(z+\xi u)(u+\xi x)\ &\hspace{23mm} +(1-u)(1+\xi yu)(1+\xi zu)(1+\xi^3xu) igr]\ &=(1-Bu^2) igl[ (1+\xi xyz)(u+\xi x)(1+\xi^3xu) -(1-Bxy)(1-Bxz)u(1+\xi x) igr]. \end{split} 	ag{13} \] Expansion verifies this polynomial identity, proving (10). Since \(g_\xi(1)=0\), summing (10) gives exactly \[  egin{split} &(1-Bxy)(1-Bxz)S_N(\xi;Bx,y,z) -(1+\xi^3x)(1+\xi xyz)S_N(\xi;x,y,z)\ &\hspace{35mm}=	au_N(\xi;x,y,z)g_\xi(B^N). \end{split} 	ag{14} \] The boundary at \(j=N\) has not been discarded. At the root its canceled value is \(	au_N(q)=-1\). Indeed the well-poised prefactor equals one, \((-q)^N=\eta\), and each of the three product ratios in (7) equals \[  rac{t^N-\eta}{1-\eta t^N}=-\eta . 	ag{15} \] At \(u=B^N\), only the factor \(1-u\) in (9) contributes to its first derivative at the root. Thus \[ \left. rac{d}{d\log\xi}\{ 	au_N(\xi)g_\xi(B^N)\}ight|_{\xi=q} =  rac{2N(1+q^3x)qx(1+qy)(1+qz)} {(1-Q)(1+qx)} . 	ag{16} \] The numerator \(2N\) is the derivative of the finite endpoint, with the sign from (15). Differentiate (14). Derivatives of its scalar coefficients multiply \(S_N(q)=0\). The chain term from the moving argument \(B x\) is \(2Qx\,\partial_xS_N(q;Qx,y,z)=0\) for the same reason: \(S_N(q;\cdot)\) is identically zero. Consequently (16) is an equation for the specified initialized \(\dot S_N\), with no extra parameter current. Inserting (8) and canceling the three linear factors gives (5), because \[ K_N^{m loc} rac{2Nq}{1-Q}= eta_N . 	ag{17} \] The relation \(D_N(Qx)=D_N(x)\) then gives (6). All canceled identities extend to zero boundary arguments. Permutation proves the other equations. ## 3. The finite coefficient space and its homogeneous unit The connection will now be solved on the full boundary coefficient space \[ \mathscr R_N= \mathbb C[x,y,z]/(x^N,y^N,z^N). 	ag{18} \] Each element has a unique representative of degree below \(N\) in each variable. Thus it records all \(N^3\) entries of the original tensor. This quotient concerns the auxiliary generating powers, not a semisimple quotient of the physical Casimir module. In particular all original repeated-root directions are retained. The norm defect of the homogeneous connection is explicit: \[ \prod_{h=0}^{N-1}T_x^ha_x-\prod_{h=0}^{N-1}T_x^hb_x =\eta x^ND_N(y)D_N(z). 	ag{19} \] For example the two products are \((1-x^Ny^N)(1-x^Nz^N)\) and \((1-\eta x^N)(1-\eta x^Ny^Nz^N)\). Consequently the cyclic product of \(b_x/a_x\) is one in (18), though the off-quotient norm defect is nonzero. For any nilpotent monomial \(u\) with \(u^N=0\), define \[ \mathsf e_N(u)= \exp\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}  rac{u^n}{n(1-Q^n)}ight). 	ag{20} \] The exponential is a finite operation in the nilpotent ideal. Its constant is one and \(\mathsf e_N(Qu)/\mathsf e_N(u)=1-u\), by the finite logarithm of \(1-u\). Define the known unit \[  oxed{\qquad H=  rac{\mathsf e_N(-qx)\mathsf e_N(-qy) \mathsf e_N(-qz)\mathsf e_N(-qxyz)} {\mathsf e_N(Qxy)\mathsf e_N(Qxz)\mathsf e_N(Qyz)} . \qquad} 	ag{21} \] Every numerator and denominator has constant one. Using (20) gives exactly \[ a_iT_iH=b_iH\quad(i=x,y,z). 	ag{22} \] This is the finite cyclic-dilogarithm version of the homogeneous Rogers product, derived here by a finite logarithm. ## 4. Compatible forcing and an explicit Fourier potential Put \(\delta_i=T_i-I\), and define three known elements of \(\mathscr R_N\): \[ f_x= rac{x}{(1+qx)^2(1+qxyz)H},\qquad f_y,\ f_z	ext{ by permutation}. 	ag{23} \] All inverses exist because their constants are one. Dividing (5) by \(b_xH=a_xT_xH\) reduces its additive part to \[ \delta_i(\widehat{\mathcal C}_N/H) = eta_N f_i . 	ag{24} \] The forcing is compatible independently of the already known source. Indeed \[ a_y-(1+qy)(1+qQxyz)=-qy(1+qx)(1+qz). 	ag{25} \] Apply \(T_y\) to (23), use (22), and subtract. This gives \[ \delta_yf_x= - rac{qxy(1+qz)} {(1+qx)(1+qy)(1+qxyz)(1+qQxyz)H} =\delta_xf_y . 	ag{26} \] The other two identities follow by permutation. These identities can be integrated with no unspecified coefficient. Write \(x^\alpha=x^{\alpha_1}y^{\alpha_2}z^{\alpha_3}\) for \(0\le\alpha_i<N\), and \(f_i=\sum_\alpha f_{i,\alpha}x^\alpha\). For a nonzero multiindex put \[ d_{i,\alpha}=Q^{\alpha_i}-1,\qquad \lambda_\alpha=\sum_i|d_{i,\alpha}|^2>0 . 	ag{27} \] Define a zero-constant polynomial \(A\) by the explicit diagonal formula \[  oxed{\qquad A_0=0,\qquad A_\alpha=  rac{\sum_i\overline{d_{i,\alpha}}\,f_{i,\alpha}} {\lambda_\alpha}\quad(\alpha
e0). \qquad} 	ag{28} \] The bar in this formula conjugates the known root-of-unity scalar. It is not conjugation of a generating variable. To prove \(\delta_iA=f_i\), take coefficients in (26). They say \(d_{j,\alpha}f_{i,\alpha} =d_{i,\alpha}f_{j,\alpha}\). For \(\alpha
e0\), choose an index \(j\) with \(d_{j,\alpha}
e0\). All \(f_{i,\alpha}\) are then \(d_{i,\alpha}\) times the same scalar, and (28) recovers that scalar. At \(\alpha=0\), every \(f_i\) is zero because its numerator contains its own variable. This proves the equations. It also proves uniqueness with \(A_0=0\): common invariance under \(T_x,T_y,T_z\) leaves only the constant coefficient. For clarity the finite Fourier inverse has a polynomial norm bound. Give coefficients in the displayed monomial basis their Euclidean norm, and give triples the sum-of-squares norm. The \(T_i\) are unitary for this particular norm. Equation (28) and compatibility give \[ \|A\|\le rac{\|(f_x,f_y,f_z)\|}{2\sin(\pi/N)} \le rac N4\|(f_x,f_y,f_z)\|. 	ag{29} \] Indeed every nonzero multiindex has \(\lambda_\alpha\ge4\sin^2(\pi/N)\); equivalently, \(\sum_i\|\delta_iA\|^2 \ge4\sin^2(\pi/N)\|A\|^2\). This is only a bound for the additive Fourier inverse. Multiplication by \(H\) or \(H^{-1}\) need not be polynomially conditioned in this norm. ## 5. One scalar anchor and its finite initializer **Theorem 2.** Let \(a_N=\mathcal C_N(0,0,0) =N^{-3/2}\phi(R^3)\). In \(\mathscr R_N\), \[  oxed{\qquad \mathcal C_N=a_NH+ eta_NHA . \qquad} 	ag{30} \] More generally, the complete set of solutions of the three forced equations (5) in this finite coefficient space is \(aH+ eta_NHA\), with one arbitrary constant \(a\in\mathbb C\). In fact \(D_N=1\) in this quotient, so \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_N=\mathcal C_N\). Equation (24), the defining equations of \(A\), and the common-invariant observation after (28) prove the assertion. The physical constant is exactly \(a_N\), since \(H(0)=1\) and \(A(0)=0\). No knot-dependent scalar is used to define the tensor. The universal anchor itself has the following finite initializer. Set \[ F_0=1,\qquad F_r=(Q;Q)_r=\prod_{h=1}^r(1-Q^h) \quad(1\le r<N). 	ag{31} \] Then \[  oxed{\qquad a_N=- rac{ eta_N}{q} \sum_{r=0}^{N-1}F_r . \qquad} 	ag{32} \] Here is a proof using the terminal coefficient, rather than an infinite sum. Set \(y=z=0\) in the polynomial equation (6): \[ \mathcal C_N(Qx,0,0)-(1+qx)\mathcal C_N(x,0,0) = eta_N\sum_{a=1}^{N}(-q)^{a-1}x^a . 	ag{33} \] Write \(\mathcal C_N(x,0,0)=\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}v_ax^a\). The coefficients below \(N\) give \[ (Q^a-1)v_a-qv_{a-1}= eta_N(-q)^{a-1} \quad(1\le a<N). 	ag{34} \] Iteration, starting with \(v_0=a_N\), yields \[ v_a= rac{(-q)^a}{F_a} \left(a_N+ rac{ eta_N}{q} \sum_{r=0}^{a-1}F_right). 	ag{35} \] The terminal coefficient of (33) is \(-qv_{N-1}= eta_N(-q)^{N-1}\). Using \(F_{N-1}=N\) in (35) proves (32). Thus the anchor is initialized by a known finite factorial sum, with its full original phase. The sum in (32) is the root-of-unity value of the classical Kontsevich--Zagier series \(\sum_{r\ge0}(Q;Q)_r\); see [Zagier (2001), introduction and equation (1)](https://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/zagier/files/doi/10.1016/S0040-9383(00)00005-7/fulltext.pdf). That citation identifies the familiar series only. No radial-limit, strange-identity, modularity or asymptotic theorem from it is used. The forcing cannot be absorbed into a scalar normalization of \(H\). For example (5) gives the universal first-coefficient identity \[ (Q-1)C_{100}-qC_{000}= eta_N
e0 . 	ag{36} \] A pure homogeneous product would give zero on its right. This is an exact source obstruction, not an estimate based on a small selection of knots or levels. ## 6. Exact use in the original Conway assembly Equation (30) gives every original tensor entry by taking the unique representative of degree below \(N\) in each variable. Alternatively, choose any nonnegative-power Taylor sections for its right side agreeing with that representative modulo \((x^N,y^N,z^N)\). Use coefficient-conjugate sections for the conjugate vertices. The complete generating-section theorem proves the required whole-source rule: first reverse the finite indices along a Conway tree so every internal contraction is anti-diagonal. With the original leaves, turns and both actual closing arrays retained, the scalar is the coefficient \[ [\,\prod_e t_e^{N-1}\,]\prod_v V_v . 	ag{37} \] Every vertex section has nonnegative powers on every incident edge. Replacing a vertex by (30) changes it by a sum of terms containing an incident \(t_e^N\). Such a term cannot contribute to (37). Telescoping the replacements over the finitely many vertices therefore preserves the original scalar exactly. This order is essential. Reverse the finite tensors before choosing their Taylor extensions. A reversed untruncated series or a ratio of edge variables may introduce negative powers and does not satisfy the rule. No physical meridian power or Casimir normal is declared invisible. The final coefficient functional has not been replaced by a norm, and no physical source direction is discarded. The result reduces the universal tensor to a finite cyclic product, a completely specified additive potential, and the universal initializer (32). It does not estimate the coherent coefficient (37) at a geometric contour. In particular the small prefactor \( eta_N\), the Fourier bound (29), or the one-constant description does not supply a lower bound after arbitrary short fillings. Contributions from the homogeneous and forced terms may still cancel in the assembled source. ## Complete proof sources and coverage Both complete proof texts were read at the matching pins: | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Initialized finite tensor source](research_centered_tensor_finite_6phi5_source.md) | 238b5fd4daeca0293ae705d1a4c1189824129a0278e086e250207e8d51ed3f53 | | [Full-degree generating section](research_full_degree_centered_generating_section.md) | 6fbef2085aca79503518745a08d3466ec84cd337ec8131944e2aebb9c95c2f6b | The first supplies the complete physical source and its calibrated initialized normal. The second supplies the exact full-tree coefficient rule. The finite telescoper, forcing compatibility, Fourier potential and terminal initializer are proved above. The existing generating-section theorem already has a homogeneous finite cocycle for a single leg. No novelty is claimed for telescoping, cyclic dilogarithms, finite Fourier inversion, or the classical factorial series. No infinite Rogers summation or unverified root limit is an assumption here. Only written mathematics, text/hash operations and the stated primary-source lookup were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build, git operation or earlier-final edit was performed.

title: A geometric source block and a bounded current on the prism tube
text: # A geometric source block and a bounded current on the prism tube 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The original centered tensor is an explicit nonzero geometric block plus an absolutely bounded correction on the whole strict prism-angle tube, with independent moduli up to the unit boundary on its three legs. Wherever the geometric height is nonnegative this gives its nonzero leading asymptotic. In particular it transports the initialized packet along every strict positive-prism radial path, on compact families away from the origin. The coefficient is determined by the original finite source. The proof uses a canonical Gamma interpolation of its exact wall residues. A norm-corrected finite rectangle removes both outer pole families before any estimate. Its moving Cauchy pole gives an explicit nonzero geometric term. The remaining complete vertical current is uniformly bounded after its stated normalization. No absolute gap between the geometric action and an outer-facet action is assumed. This is a theorem about one universal multiplication tensor. It does not move the assembled Conway coefficient cycle or prove a knot volume identity after arbitrary short fillings. ## 1. The source, the paths, and the result Fix \(N\ge2\), and set \[ d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \eta=(-1)^d,\quad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad D_N(t)=1-\eta t^N . \tag{1} \] All fractional powers of \(q\) use this exponential. Let \(\mathcal C_N(x,y,z)\) be the entire initialized centered three-boundary source, with its original Frobenius closing and full Casimir first normals. Write a strict prism shape as \[ a,b,c>0,\quad a+b,a+c,b+c<1,\quad S=a+b+c>1. \tag{2} \] Permute the three legs, if necessary, so that \(a\) is a largest angle. Then \[ 0<b,c<1/2. \tag{3} \] The tensor is symmetric, so this does not change its value. For independent \(0<r_x,r_y,r_z\le1\), put \[ x=-r_x e^{-2\pi ia},\qquad y=-r_y e^{-2\pi ib},\qquad z=-r_z e^{-2\pi ic},\qquad \ell_i=-\frac{\log r_i}{2\pi}\ge0 . \tag{4} \] Use the initialized action and amplitude \[ \begin{split} \Psi(x,y,z)={}&-\frac{\pi}{12} +\frac1{2\pi}\bigl[ \operatorname{Li}_2(-x)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-y) +\operatorname{Li}_2(-z)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-xyz)\\ &\hspace{33mm} -\operatorname{Li}_2(xy)-\operatorname{Li}_2(xz) -\operatorname{Li}_2(yz)\bigr],\\ B(x,y,z)={}&[(1-xy)(1-xz)(1-yz)]^{-1/2}. \end{split} \tag{5} \] Their branches are fixed by power series at zero and their continuous limits at the stated strict angular boundary. **Theorem.** Let the shapes vary in a compact subset of (2), and let all three moduli vary independently in \([r_0,1]\), where \(r_0>0\). There is an explicit nonzero canonical Gamma quotient \(\mathcal G_N\), defined in (24) below, and an explicitly prescribed current \(\mathcal I_N\), such that \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal C_N(x,y,z)=\mathcal G_N(x,y,z) -\frac{\kappa}{N}D_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z)\mathcal I_N(x,y,z), \qquad |\mathcal I_N|\le C . \quad} \tag{6} \] The source identity is exact. The bound is uniform on these compact families for all sufficiently large \(N\). Moreover \[ \mathcal G_N= \kappa e^{\,i\pi/4-\pi i/(2N)} B(x,y,z)e^{iN\Psi(x,y,z)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{7} \] Consequently, on the portion of such a family where \(-\operatorname{Im}\Psi\ge0\), \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal C_N= \kappa e^{\,i\pi/4-\pi i/(2N)} B(x,y,z)e^{iN\Psi(x,y,z)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \quad} \tag{8} \] On that nonnegative-height portion, the original source is therefore nonzero for all sufficiently large levels, including both parities and composite levels. The common-radial subfamily \(r_x=r_y=r_z\) always has strictly positive height, by the prism radial theorem. Positivity is not asserted for arbitrary independent moduli. The estimate includes all level-dependent approaches to \(r_i=1\). In fact, if any \(D_N(t_i)=0\), then \(\mathcal C_N=\mathcal G_N\) exactly. No assertion is made uniformly as a modulus tends to zero or an angular shape meets a prism face. ## 2. The canonical interpolation and the exact wall sum Use the original canonical factorial \[ G_N(w)=\left(\frac{2\pi}{N}\right)^w\Gamma(w+1) \prod_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{\Gamma(Nm+w+1)} {\Gamma(Nm-w)(Nm)^{2w+1}}, \qquad -1<\Re w<N , \tag{9} \] with positive-base powers using their real logarithms. Define \[ F_N(w)=e^{\,\pi i w(w+1)/(2N)-\pi iw/2}G_N(w). \tag{10} \] Its normalization and shifts are fixed by this product, not by a choice of a periodic solution: \[ \begin{gathered} F_N(0)=1,\qquad F_N(j)=(Q;Q)_j\quad(0\le j<N),\\ F_N(w+1)=(1-Q^{w+1})F_N(w),\qquad F_N(w+N)=(1-e^{2\pi iw})F_N(w),\\ F_N(w)F_N(d-w)=Nq^{w(w-d)} . \end{gathered} \tag{11} \] Here \((u;Q)_j=\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}(1-uQ^h)\), with empty product one. The last two identities extend meromorphically. The first positive zero block of \(F_N\) consists of simple zeros at the integers \(N,\ldots,2N-1\). Its negative poles begin at \(-1\). These statements follow either from (9) or from its normalized shift and reflection. Set \[ A=N(1-b)-\tfrac12+iN\ell_y,\qquad B_0=N(1-c)-\tfrac12+iN\ell_z,\qquad C=N(1-b-c)+iN(\ell_y+\ell_z) . \tag{12} \] The name \(B_0\) distinguishes this shift from the amplitude in (5). Their exact balance and clock values are \[ A+B_0-C=d,\qquad Q^A=-q^{-1}y,\quad Q^{B_0}=-q^{-1}z,\quad Q^C=yz . \tag{13} \] Define the meromorphic weight \[ W_N(s)= \frac{F_N(s)F_N(s+C)F_N(A)F_N(B_0)} {F_N(C)F_N(s+1+A)F_N(s+1+B_0)} \tag{14} \] and the moving Cauchy factor \[ K_N(s)=\frac1{1+q^{-1}Q^{-s}x}. \tag{15} \] The two \(+1\)'s in (14) are part of the original source. Dropping them would remove two boundary factors. The exact wall theorem proves \[ \mathcal C_N(-qQ^j,y,z)= \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N}D_N(y)D_N(z)W_N(j) =\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N}D_N(y)D_N(z) \frac{(Q;Q)_j(Qyz;Q)_j} {(-qy;Q)_{j+1}(-qz;Q)_{j+1}} . \tag{16} \] The canonical lattice shifts in (11)--(13) verify this interpolation exactly. The finite Cauchy representation is therefore \[ \mathcal C_N(x,y,z)= \frac{\kappa}{N^{3/2}}D_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z) \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}W_N(j)K_N(j). \tag{17} \] No generic-\(q\) source, value-only interpolation, or periodic gauge has replaced the original tensor. ## 3. A finite rectangle with all outer poles canceled For this contour derivation assume first that all three moduli are strictly less than one. The final canceled formula will extend to the closed moduli in Section 6; the auxiliary differential need not be defined at a sample collision. Put \(t=e^{2\pi is}\). Equation (11) gives exactly \[ \frac{W_N(s+N)}{W_N(s)} =\Lambda(t):= \frac{(1-t)(1-y^Nz^Nt)} {(1-\eta y^Nt)(1-\eta z^Nt)} . \tag{18} \] In particular \[ \Lambda(t)-1= -\frac{tD_N(y)D_N(z)} {(1-\eta y^Nt)(1-\eta z^Nt)}. \tag{19} \] The variable \(t\) must remain in this monodromy. Consider the sample-preserving differential \[ \Omega_N(s)= 2\pi i\, \frac{(1-\eta y^Nt)(1-\eta z^Nt)} {D_N(y)D_N(z)(t-1)} W_N(s)K_N(s)\,ds . \tag{20} \] Its residue at an integer \(j\) is exactly \(W_N(j)K_N(j)\). We use a rectangle with vertical sides \(\Re s=-1/2\) and \(\Re s=N-1/2\). Here is its complete pole count. The numerator factorials have no poles in this strip: \(F_N(s)\)'s negative poles lie to the left, and \(\Re C>0\) puts those of \(F_N(s+C)\) farther left. The arguments \(s+1+A\) and \(s+1+B_0\) have real parts strictly between zero and \(2N\). Their zeros, if present, are therefore in the first simple block from (11). At a zero of the first denominator, \[ s=d-A+k,\qquad e^{2\pi is}=e^{-2\pi iA} =\eta y^{-N}, \tag{21} \] so the factor \(1-\eta y^Nt\) in (20) cancels it. The \(z\)-family cancels in exactly the same way. When the families coincide, the two numerator zeros cancel the two denominator zeros with matching multiplicity. Thus these outer families contribute no residues. No estimate of their separate action is used. Besides the \(N\) integer samples, the only remaining pole is the moving Cauchy pole \[ s_x=N(1-a)-\tfrac12+iN\ell_x . \tag{22} \] It lies strictly between the vertical sides. Its imaginary part is positive, so it does not collide with an integer sample. Both horizontal sides vanish as their heights tend to infinity. For completeness, the exact canonical factorial formula gives, for fixed \(N\), a nonzero constant limit of \(F_N(s)\) as \(\Im s\to+\infty\), uniformly on bounded real intervals. Reflection in (11) then gives the lower asymptotic \[ F_N(s)\sim c_-(N)\exp\{\,i\pi(s^2-ds)/N\,\}. \tag{23} \] These limits also follow from the finite cotangent formula for its logarithmic derivative; its quadratic phase is fixed by (9). Using the actual offsets \(0,C\) minus \(1+A,1+B_0\), the \(s\)-dependent lower factor in \(W_N\) is \(\exp[-2\pi i(1+1/N)s]\), since their offset difference is \(-N-1\). The norm factor in (20) grows only like \(e^{2\pi|\Im s|}\) below; \(K_N\) tends to one there. Thus the lower horizontal integral decays as \(O_N(e^{-2\pi|\Im s|/N})\). Above, \(W_N\) tends to a constant and \(K_N\) supplies that same decay. This establishes the limiting rectangle for the canonical weight itself. Define the nonzero geometric quotient \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal G_N= \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N} \frac{F_N(s_x)F_N(s_x+C)F_N(A)F_N(B_0)} {F_N(C)F_N(s_x+1+A-N)F_N(s_x+1+B_0-N)} . \quad} \tag{24} \] All seven arguments are in the original nonzero canonical strip. The scaled real labels in its numerator are \[ 1-a,\quad 2-S,\quad 1-b,\quad 1-c, \tag{25} \] with half-shift \(-1/2\); those in its denominator are \[ 1-b-c,\quad1-a-b,\quad1-a-c, \tag{26} \] without that shift. Their imaginary parts are the corresponding nonnegative sums of \(N\ell_x,N\ell_y,N\ell_z\). Strict prism support proves every assertion here. To check its exact residue normalization, \(K_N\) has residue \(N/(2\pi i)\) at \(s_x\), and \(e^{2\pi is_x}=\eta x^N\). The residue of (20) is therefore \[ -\frac{N(1-(xy)^N)(1-(xz)^N)} {D_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z)}W_N(s_x). \tag{27} \] Shifting the two denominator factorials in \(W_N(s_x)\) down by \(N\) using (11) produces precisely the factors \(1-(xy)^N\) and \(1-(xz)^N\). They cancel those in (27) before any asymptotics. This gives (24). The exact side difference is \[ \Omega_N(s+N)-\Omega_N(s) =-2\pi i\,\frac{t}{t-1}W_N(s)K_N(s)\,ds . \tag{28} \] Both vertical lines are oriented upwards when taking this difference. The residue theorem, (17), and (27) now give (6) with the prescribed normalized current \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal I_N= \frac1{\sqrt N}\int_{-1/2-i\infty}^{-1/2+i\infty} \frac{e^{2\pi is}}{e^{2\pi is}-1} W_N(s)K_N(s)\,ds . \quad} \tag{29} \] The minus sign in (6) is the sign of (28). ## 4. Canonical estimates on complete vertical strips Let \(J\) be the analytic primitive of \(\log(2\sin\pi w)\) on \(0<\Re w<1\), real on the real interval and normalized by \(J(0)=0\). Put \[ f(w)=J(w)+\frac{i\pi}{2}(w^2-w),\qquad h(w)=\sqrt{2\sin\pi w}\,e^{i\pi w/2}. \tag{30} \] These branches are fixed by their real-interval values. One has \[ f'(w)=\operatorname{Log}(1-e^{2\pi iw}),\qquad h(w)^2=i(1-e^{2\pi iw}). \tag{31} \] For \(0<\Re w<1\), the argument in (31) avoids the negative real logarithmic cut. The canonical Gamma-product proof gives, uniformly on the **entire** vertical strip \(\epsilon\le\Re w\le1-\epsilon\), \[ \log G_N(Nw)=NJ(w)+\tfrac12\log(2N\sin\pi w) +\frac{\pi\cot\pi w}{12N}+O_\epsilon(N^{-3}). \tag{32} \] Here is why its usual compact-strip proof is uniform at arbitrarily large imaginary part as needed in (29). Every Gamma argument \(Nw,N(k+w),N(k-w)\) stays in a closed right-half-plane sector. The sum of its Stirling remainders is at most \[ CN^{-3}\left[ |w|^{-3}+\sum_{k\ge1} (|k+w|^{-3}+|k-w|^{-3})\right] \le C_\epsilon N^{-3}. \tag{33} \] All paired main terms still converge pointwise and define analytic functions on the whole strip; their identities with \(J\) and the sine product follow there by analytic continuation. They need not be bounded term by term. The cotangent and its fixed derivatives are bounded on this full strip. This proves (32), with fixed derivatives on slightly smaller strips, directly from the same Gamma product. In particular, uniformly on such complete vertical strips, \[ \begin{split} F_N(Nw)&=\sqrt N\,h(w)e^{Nf(w)}(1+O_\epsilon(N^{-1})),\\ F_N(Nw-\tfrac12)&= \sqrt N\,\xi_Ne^{Nf(w)}(1+O_\epsilon(N^{-1})), \qquad \xi_N=e^{i\pi/4-\pi i/(8N)} . \end{split} \tag{34} \] Bounded derivatives of \(\log(2\sin\pi w)\) on the full strip justify the half-shift expansion, including unbounded imaginary parts. The one unshifted endpoint factor in the current has an exact formula instead of a strip approximation: \[ \boxed{\qquad |F_N(-1/2+iT)|^2 =\frac{N}{1+e^{-2\pi T}} \quad(T\in\mathbb R). \qquad} \tag{35} \] Indeed every Gamma ratio in (9) has modulus one on this line, as does its corresponding positive-base power. The remaining factor is \[ |G_N(-1/2+iT)|^2= \frac{N}{2\pi}|\Gamma(1/2+iT)|^2 =\frac{N}{2\cosh\pi T}. \tag{36} \] The exponential in (10) multiplies this by \(e^{\pi T}\). This proves (35) with the original canonical normalization. ## 5. The complete vertical current is uniformly bounded Write \(s=-1/2+iNY\). Introduce the scaled arguments \[ \begin{gathered} a_Y=1-b+i(Y+\ell_y),\qquad b_Y=1-c+i(Y+\ell_z),\\ c_Y=1-b-c+i(Y+\ell_y+\ell_z),\\ Q_0(Y)=f(c_Y)-f(a_Y)-f(b_Y) +f(a_0)+f(b_0)-f(c_0). \end{gathered} \tag{37} \] The notation \(Q_0\) is a function, not the root \(Q\). Every real part in (37) stays in a fixed strict substrip on the stated shape compacts. Applying (34) to all shifted factors of (14) gives \[ \frac{W_N(s)}{F_N(s)}= \frac{\xi_N^3}{h(c_0)h(a_Y)h(b_Y)} e^{NQ_0(Y)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{38} \] Its amplitude is bounded uniformly for all \(Y\in\mathbb R\). For example, because \(0<b,c<1/2\) stay in fixed compact intervals, \(|1-v e^{-2\pi ib}|\) and \(|1-v e^{-2\pi ic}|\) have positive lower bounds for every \(v\ge0\). They also grow at infinity. Equation (31) applies this observation to \(h(a_Y)\) and \(h(b_Y)\); \(h(c_0)\ne0\) is a fixed compact-parameter factor. Define the real rate \[ R_0(Y)=\Re Q_0(Y)+\pi\min(Y,0),\qquad R_0(0)=0. \tag{39} \] Equations (35) and (38) prove the actual quantum bound \[ |W_N(-1/2+iNY)|/\sqrt N \le C e^{NR_0(Y)}. \tag{40} \] It remains to bound this explicit rate on both halves of the line. Put \(v_y=r_y e^{-2\pi Y}\), \(v_z=r_z e^{-2\pi Y}\), and \(v_0=r_yr_z e^{-2\pi Y}\). Use the continuous arguments specified by (31). Differentiation gives \[ \begin{split} T(Y)={}&\arg(1-v_y e^{-2\pi ib}) +\arg(1-v_z e^{-2\pi ic}) -\arg(1-v_0 e^{-2\pi i(b+c)}),\\ R_0'(Y)&= \begin{cases} T(Y),&Y>0,\\ \pi+T(Y),&Y<0. \end{cases} \end{split} \tag{41} \] These are original-strip arguments, not a freely adjusted logarithmic lift. For \(Y>0\), all three \(v_y,v_z,v_0\) are less than one. Every argument in the first line of (41) lies between \(-\pi/2\) and \(\pi/2\). Hence \[ T(Y)<3\pi/2 . \tag{42} \] For \(Y<0\), the first two arguments in (41) are positive because \(0<b,c<1/2\). If \(b+c\ge1/2\), the third argument is nonpositive, and therefore \(T(Y)>0\). If \(b+c<1/2\), the function \(\arg(1-t e^{-2\pi i(b+c)})\) increases with \(t>0\). Let \(k=\min(v_y,v_z)>0\). Then \(v_0\le k\), and the first two arguments also increase with their radii. It therefore suffices to prove \[ \arg(1-k e^{-2\pi ib})+\arg(1-k e^{-2\pi ic}) -\arg(1-ke^{-2\pi i(b+c)})>0. \tag{43} \] For a direct proof put \(\theta=2\pi b\), \(\varphi=2\pi c\). The ratio \[ Z_k=\frac{(1-ke^{-i\theta})(1-ke^{-i\varphi})} {1-ke^{-i(\theta+\varphi)}} \tag{44} \] has strictly positive imaginary part: multiply by the conjugate denominator to obtain numerator \[ 2k(1+k)\sin\frac{\theta+\varphi}{2} \left(\cos\frac{\theta-\varphi}{2} -\cos\frac{\theta+\varphi}{2}\right)>0. \] Here \(0<b,c<1/2\) and \(b+c<1\). Its continuous argument, starting at zero as \(k\to0\), lies in \((0,\pi)\). This is precisely (43). We have proved \[ R_0(Y)\le \begin{cases} 3\pi Y/2,&Y\ge0,\\ \pi Y,&Y\le0. \end{cases} \tag{45} \] On the same half-step line \(t=-e^{-2\pi NY}\), so \[ \left|\frac{t}{t-1}\right| =\frac1{1+e^{2\pi NY}} \le \begin{cases} e^{-2\pi NY},&Y\ge0,\\ 1,&Y\le0. \end{cases} \tag{46} \] Also \(K_N(s)=(1+x e^{2\pi Y})^{-1}\) exactly. The estimate \[ |1-r_x e^{2\pi Y}e^{-2\pi ia}| \ge \sin(\pi a)(1+r_x e^{2\pi Y}) \tag{47} \] makes this Cauchy factor uniformly bounded on the strict shape compacts. Finally \(ds=iN\,dY\). Combining (29), (40), and (45)--(47) gives \[ |\mathcal I_N| \le CN\left[\int_{-\infty}^0e^{\pi NY}\,dY+ \int_0^\infty e^{-\pi NY/2}\,dY\right] \le C . \tag{48} \] Both halves of the same canonical current have now been controlled. No bound from a different periodic interpolation was transferred. ## 6. The initialized geometric residue and the growing branch For the seven strict-strip arguments in (24), use (34). The four numerator factors have half-shift \(-1/2\); the three denominator factors have shift zero. Their powers of \(N\), including the prefactor \(\kappa/\sqrt N\), cancel. Since \(h(w)=e^{i\pi/4}(1-e^{2\pi iw})^{1/2}\) on the upper part of the original strip, the remaining amplitude and phase are \[ \kappa e^{\,i\pi/4-\pi i/(2N)} [(1-xy)(1-xz)(1-yz)]^{-1/2}. \tag{49} \] The clocks of the four numerator arguments are \(-x,-xyz,-y,-z\); those of the denominators are \(yz,xy,xz\). On this upper strip \[ f(w)=\frac{i}{2\pi} \operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iw}) -\frac{i\pi}{12}. \tag{50} \] The sum of four numerator phases minus three denominator phases is exactly \(i\Psi(x,y,z)\). This proves (7), with its coefficient fixed by the actual moving-pole residue. We now include the unit boundary. All factors of (24) remain regular and nonzero when any \(\ell_i=0\): their real parts stay in the same strict canonical strips. In (29), the shifted factorials and the Cauchy factor remain regular for all real \(Y\). The lower bounds for \(h(c_0),h(a_Y),h(b_Y)\), (42), the inequality \(v_0\le\min(v_y,v_z)\), and (47) are uniform for \(r_x,r_y,r_z\in[r_0,1]\). The integrable majorant in (48) is therefore uniform up to that boundary. Dominated convergence extends the final canceled identity (6), and its bound, from \(r_i<1\) to \(r_i\le1\). This step extends neither the uncanceled differential (20) nor a pole count through a collision. In particular, whenever \(D_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z)=0\), \(\mathcal C_N=\mathcal G_N\) exactly. All level-dependent approaches to these norm walls are included in the same estimate. Equations (6) and (48) bound the full correction by \(O(N^{-1})\) on the whole closed-moduli tube. On any portion where \(-\Im\Psi\ge0\), (7) has modulus bounded away from zero; thus (8) follows uniformly there. For the common-radial subfamily, the prism radial theorem proves \(-\Im\Psi>0\) for every strict shape and \(0<r\le1\). Its minimum is positive on the compact families in the theorem, so the current is then exponentially small relative to \(\mathcal G_N\). Symmetry covers the initial permutation choosing the two smaller angles. No sign of the height has been assumed elsewhere in the tube. The result concerns the actual universal local source. A global Conway theorem still needs to place all geometric attachments in compatible source charts and control the assembled coefficient cycle and competing contributions. Nothing here identifies arbitrary vertex evaluations with that whole period. The \(r_i\to0\) layers and angular prism-face collisions remain outside the stated uniform estimate. ## Complete proof sources All four complete proof texts were read at the matching pins: | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Exact original wall and Cauchy source](research_centered_tensor_wall_cauchy_source.md) | 3cda6a170c46abf27a1c8c15b110780ebcb6017a5aa18758a4e51ba0a271892c | | [Strict prism action and radial growth](research_centered_tensor_prism_radial_bridge.md) | 892dfc5ef5e0774d45ccc44bc4f5122e7137d6185fe9191997e1b43d79003776 | | [Canonical factorial, exact phase and ends](research_exact_cyclotomic_factorial.md) | 0f989261f53747266ac62dba40ca7548138012b266521e98a03bd94b450c657b | | [Canonical Gamma interpolation and Stirling proof](../papers/conway-asymptotics/factorial.tex) | fa05557505927ae81f005b90edbd3d0946288e7eacf2363f070d9753db632fe1 | The exact wall source and radial growth were already established. The source-specific additions are the completed canonical rectangle, its exact removal of the outer families, the uniformly bounded full current in the two-small-angle chamber, and the resulting actual transport of the initialized tensor. No novelty is claimed for Gamma reflection, residue calculus or Stirling's method. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build, git operation or earlier-final edit was performed.

title: The positive prism boundary and its growing radial path
text: # The positive prism boundary and its growing radial path 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The dilogarithmic action of the initialized centered tensor has an exact boundary interpretation in the already constructed ideal prism. Its imaginary part is the negative Newton prism action; its real part is a specified linear phase. Moreover the entire radial segment from the origin to every strict positive prism boundary point lies on the growing side of this action. There is also an exact finite-source interpretation of the physical boundary grid. A centered generating packet on that grid selects one Newton basis vector. Three such packets therefore recover the positive Newton tensor, including its full repeated-root algebra and original Frobenius closing. These statements connect the geometric boundary symbol to the initialized source near the origin. They do not prove transport of its asymptotic through the whole disk or uniformly onto the unit boundary. ## 1. The strict prism domain and its original face labels Let \[ \mathcal P=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3: x_i>0,\quad x_i+x_j<1\ (i\ne j),\quad S:=x_1+x_2+x_3>1\}. \tag{1} \] Then \(x_i<1\) and \(1<S<3/2\). Define \[ L(u)=\int_0^u\log(2\sin\pi v)\,dv\quad(0<u<1), \qquad \tau(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i<j}L(x_i+x_j) -\sum_iL(x_i)-L(S-1). \tag{2} \] All arguments in this formula lie strictly between zero and one. The original directed Newton multiplication has action \[ m(a,b,c)=L(a+b)+L(c)-L(a)-L(b) -L(c-a)-L(c-b)-L(a+b-c). \tag{3} \] Set its two input labels to \(a=x_1,b=x_2\) and its output label to \(c=1-x_3\). Conditions (1) are exactly its strict support conditions. The reflection identity \(L(1-u)=-L(u)\) gives \[ \tau(\mathbf x)=m(x_1,x_2,1-x_3). \tag{4} \] The ideal-prism theorem constructs a convex ideal triangular prism with these directed, ordered quadrilateral faces and proves \[ \operatorname{Vol}(\operatorname{Prism}_{\mathbf x}) =\pi\tau(\mathbf x). \tag{5} \] The complement \(1-x_3\) is required by the original Frobenius pairing of an output with the third leg. It is not an unrecorded permutation or mutation of the ordered prism faces. ## 2. The complete action on the unit boundary Use the initialized centered action \[ \Psi(\mathbf t)=-\frac{\pi}{12} +\frac1{2\pi}\left[ \sum_i\operatorname{Li}_2(-t_i) +\operatorname{Li}_2(-t_1t_2t_3) -\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Li}_2(t_it_j)\right]. \tag{6} \] Its branches start from the power series on the unit polydisk. For \(\mathbf x\in\mathcal P\), put \[ t_i(r)=-r e^{-2\pi i x_i},\qquad 0\le r\le1. \tag{7} \] None of the dilogarithm arguments at \(r=1\) is one: this follows from \(0<x_i,x_i+x_j<1\) and \(1<S<3/2\). Thus (6) has the indicated continuous, locally analytic boundary value. **Theorem 1.** With the branches in (6)--(7), \[ \boxed{\quad i\Psi(\mathbf t(1)) =\tau(\mathbf x)+i\pi(1-S). \quad} \tag{8} \] In particular \[ -\operatorname{Im}\Psi(\mathbf t(1))=\tau(\mathbf x), \qquad -2\pi\operatorname{Im}\Psi(\mathbf t(1)) =2\operatorname{Vol}(\operatorname{Prism}_{\mathbf x}). \tag{9} \] The factor two in the latter equation has not been absorbed into the prism volume. **Proof.** The elementary unit-circle dilogarithm formula is \[ \operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iu}) =-2\pi L(u)\quad(0<u<1). \tag{10} \] It follows by differentiating the absolutely convergent Abel series, using \(\operatorname{Re}\log(1-e^{2\pi iu})=\log(2\sin\pi u)\), and fixing the value at zero. At (7), the three types of arguments in (6) are \[ e^{-2\pi i x_i},\qquad e^{-2\pi i S},\qquad e^{-2\pi i(x_i+x_j)} . \] Reflection in (10), and periodicity for \(S\), prove \(\operatorname{Im}\Psi=-\tau\). The real part follows from \[ \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iu}) =\pi^2B_2(u),\qquad B_2(u)=u^2-u+\tfrac16,\qquad 0\le u\le1. \tag{11} \] One may derive (11) by integrating the Fourier series \(\sum_{n\ge1}\sin(2\pi nu)/n=\pi(1/2-u)\); its constant is \(\sum n^{-2}=\pi^2/6\). The required Bernoulli combination is \[ \sum_iB_2(x_i)+B_2(S-1)-\sum_{i<j}B_2(x_i+x_j) =-2S+\tfrac{13}{6}. \] Including the constant \(-\pi/12\) in (6) therefore gives \(\operatorname{Re}\Psi=\pi(1-S)\), proving (8). \(\square\) The logarithmic momenta retain a corresponding sign: \[ R_i(\mathbf t)= \frac{(1-t_it_j)(1-t_it_k)} {(1+t_i)(1+t_1t_2t_3)},\qquad R_i(\mathbf t(1))=-e^{\partial_{x_i}\tau}, \quad \{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}. \tag{12} \] In fact the logarithm continued along (7) has the precise boundary value \[ \partial_{x_i}\{i\Psi(\mathbf t(1))\} =\partial_{x_i}\tau-i\pi . \tag{13} \] To check the sign directly, write every \(1-e^{-2\pi iu}\) as \(2i e^{-\pi iu}\sin(\pi u)\). The three pair arguments are in \((0,1)\), whereas \(S\in(1,3/2)\) has \(\sin(\pi S)=-\sin(\pi(S-1))\). The phases cancel except for this minus sign. The radial logarithms give the lift \(-i\pi\), agreeing with (8). These momenta also recover the actual ordered face metrics. In the directed prism theorem, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{in},1}=e^{-\partial_a m}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{in},2}=e^{-\partial_b m}\), and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{out}}=e^{-\partial_c m}\). The complemented output in (4) therefore gives \[ \kappa_{\mathrm{in},1}=-R_1^{-1},\qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{in},2}=-R_2^{-1},\qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{out}}=-R_3 . \tag{13a} \] All three are positive on the prism boundary. Thus the signs and the output complement identify these particular source momenta with the old prism's ordered quadrilateral metrics, rather than only with unmarked trace squares. ## 3. The entire strict prism has a growing radial path **Theorem 2.** For every \(\mathbf x\in\mathcal P\), \[ \operatorname{Im}\Psi(\mathbf t(r))<0 \qquad(0<r\le1). \tag{14} \] The inequality is uniform away from zero on compact subsets of \(\mathcal P\times(0,1]\). **Proof.** Define the real radial Clausen function \[ F_a(u)=-\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Li}_2(ae^{-2\pi iu}), \qquad 0<a\le1. \tag{15} \] It is periodic, \(F_a(1-u)=-F_a(u)\), and \(F_a(0)=F_a(1/2)=0\). On \(0<u<1/2\) it is positive and strictly concave. For \(a<1\), direct differentiation gives \[ F_a''(u)= -\frac{4\pi^2a\sin(2\pi u)} {1-2a\cos(2\pi u)+a^2}<0. \tag{16} \] Concavity and the endpoint zeros imply positivity. The same conclusions at \(a=1\) follow by continuity or direct differentiation on this open angle interval. There is also convexity in the logarithmic radius: \[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial(\log a)^2}F_a(u) =\frac{a\sin(2\pi u)} {1-2a\cos(2\pi u)+a^2}>0 \quad(0<u<1/2). \tag{17} \] Consequently \[ F_r(u)+F_{r^3}(u)\ge2F_{r^2}(u). \tag{18} \] In these terms the quantity to prove positive is \[ -2\pi\operatorname{Im}\Psi(\mathbf t(r)) =\sum_iF_r(x_i)+F_{r^3}(S-1) -\sum_{i<j}F_{r^2}(x_i+x_j). \tag{19} \] If every \(x_i\le1/2\), each pair \(x_i+x_j=S-x_k>1/2\). All pair terms on the right are therefore nonnegative after their minus sign, all single terms are nonnegative, and \(0<S-1<1/2\) supplies a strictly positive term. This proves (14) in this part of the domain. Otherwise exactly one angle is large. Relabel it \(x_1=1-\delta>1/2\), and put \[ b=x_2,\quad c=x_3,\quad u=b+c-\delta,\quad p=\delta-b,\quad q=\delta-c,\quad s=b+c . \tag{20} \] Here \[ 0<u<b,c<\delta<1/2,\qquad p,q>0,\qquad b+c=\delta+u,\qquad s=2u+p+q<1. \tag{21} \] By strict concavity, the pair \((b,c)\), with its fixed sum, lies strictly between the more separated pair \((u,\delta)\). Thus \[ F_r(b)+F_r(c)-F_r(\delta)>F_r(u). \tag{22} \] Reflection rewrites (19) as \[ \begin{aligned} &F_r(b)+F_r(c)-F_r(\delta)+F_{r^3}(u)\\ &\hspace{20mm}+F_{r^2}(p)+F_{r^2}(q)-F_{r^2}(s). \end{aligned} \tag{23} \] The first line is strictly larger than \(2F_{r^2}(u)\), by (18) and (22). If \(s\ge1/2\), then \(F_{r^2}(s)\le0\) and all other displayed terms needed for the bound are positive. If \(s<1/2\), concavity with \(F_{r^2}(0)=0\) gives subadditivity on this interval. Applying it repeatedly gives \[ 2F_{r^2}(u)+F_{r^2}(p)+F_{r^2}(q) \ge F_{r^2}(2u+p+q)=F_{r^2}(s). \tag{24} \] The strict inequality in (22) makes (23) positive in this case too. This proves (14) on the whole domain. Uniformity on the stated compact sets follows from continuity and strict positivity. \(\square\) ## 4. The unit boundary is an exact positive source grid The preceding action calculation has a finite counterpart. At level \(N\ge2\), put \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(\kappa=q^{d^2/2}\), and \(D_N(t)=1-(-1)^dt^N\). All fractional powers mean these displayed exponentials. Write \(s_j=\prod_{h=1}^j2\sin(\pi h/N)\), \(s_0=1\), and \(T_N(\cos\theta)=\cos(N\theta)\). The full algebra is \(H_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2)\), with its original Frobenius row \(\phi\), normalized Newton basis \(e_j=s_j^{-2}\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}(2\cos((2h+1)\pi/N)-z)\), and centered basis \(f_a\). Its original generating tensor is \[ \mathcal C_N(\mathbf t)= \phi\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^3\sum_{a=0}^{d}f_a t_i^a\right). \tag{24a} \] For \(0\le j\le d\), put \[ x_{j,N}=\frac{j+1/2}{N},\qquad t_{j,N}=-e^{-2\pi i x_{j,N}},\qquad \gamma_{j,N}=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\pi i d}{N}(j-d/2)\right]. \tag{25} \] Let \(e_j\) be the normalized full Newton basis and \(f_a\) the centered basis. The exact centered Fourier matrix gives \[ \boxed{\qquad \sum_{a=0}^d f_a t_{j,N}^{\,a} =\sqrt N\,\gamma_{j,N}e_j . \qquad} \tag{26} \] Indeed the coefficient of \(e_\ell\) on the left is \(N^{-1/2}e^{-\pi i d(\ell-d/2)/N}\) times \(\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ia(\ell-j)/N}\). The latter is \(N\delta_{\ell j}\). For a triple \(\mathbf j=(j_1,j_2,j_3)\), let \(T_{N,\mathbf j}=\phi(e_{j_1}e_{j_2}e_{j_3})\). Consequently the original complete tensor obeys \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal C_N(t_{j_1,N},t_{j_2,N},t_{j_3,N}) =N^{3/2}\left(\prod_i\gamma_{j_i,N}\right)T_{N,\mathbf j}. \quad} \tag{27} \] There is no unknown closing coefficient in this identity. The exact positive tensor is \[ T_{N,\mathbf j} =\frac{s_{j_1+j_2}s_{j_1+j_3}s_{j_2+j_3}} {N s_{j_1}s_{j_2}s_{j_3}s_{j_1+j_2+j_3-d}}, \qquad s_a=\prod_{h=1}^a2\sin(\pi h/N), \tag{28} \] when each pair sum is at most \(d\) and the total is at least \(d\), and is zero otherwise. These are the full-algebra coefficients; no Casimir first normal was removed. Every grid point \((x_{j_1,N},x_{j_2,N},x_{j_3,N})\in\mathcal P\) satisfies the positive support conditions in (28). The half-step offsets in (25) are important. The Newton indices divided by \(N\) are \(x_i-1/(2N)\). The centered directed output paired with \(j_3\) is exactly \((d-j_3+1/2)/N=1-x_3\). Uniformly on compact subsets of \(\mathcal P\), \[ \frac1N\log T_{N,\mathbf j} =\tau(\mathbf x_{\mathbf j,N}) +O(\log N/N). \tag{29} \] In fact the original packet has a sharper boundary estimate. Let \(B\) be the branch in the complex source theorem, and put \(L_N=(-1)^N\kappa^3e^{-3\pi i/(4N)}\). Uniformly on the same strict compact sets, \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal C_N(\mathbf t_{\mathbf j,N})= L_Ne^{i\pi/4}B(\mathbf t_{\mathbf j,N}) e^{iN\Psi(\mathbf t_{\mathbf j,N})}(1+O(N^{-1})). \quad} \tag{30} \] Here the displayed \(B\) is the product \(\prod_{i<j}(1-t_it_j)^{-1/2}\), continued radially. There is no factor \(\prod_iD_N(t_i)\) in (30). To prove both estimates with their normalization, use the uniform interior sine-factorial formula \[ s_{Na-\gamma}= \sqrt N(2\sin\pi a)^{1/2-\gamma}e^{NL(a)} (1+O(N^{-1})), \tag{31} \] when the subscript is an integer, \(a\) stays in a closed interior interval, and \(\gamma\in\{0,1/2,1\}\). Its constant can be checked without a singular endpoint summation. The exact identities \(s_js_{d-j}=N\) give the middle normalization: for odd \(N\), \(s_{d/2}=\sqrt N\); for even \(N\), \(s_{N/2}=\sqrt{2N}\). Apply the ordinary trapezoidal Euler--Maclaurin estimate, with error \(O(N^{-1})\), to \(\sum\log(2\sin(\pi h/N))\) between that middle and \(Na-\gamma\). This interval stays away from zero and one. Since \(L(1/2)=0\), its integral and two endpoint half-weights give exactly (31), with the stated middle constant. In (28) the three numerator factorials have arguments \(N(x_i+x_j)-1\), hence \(\gamma=1\). The four denominator factorials have arguments \(Nx_i-1/2\) and \(N(S-1)-1/2\), hence \(\gamma=1/2\). Formula (31) therefore gives \[ N^{3/2}T_{N,\mathbf j} =\prod_{i<j}(2\sin\pi(x_i+x_j))^{-1/2} e^{N\tau(\mathbf x)}(1+O(N^{-1})) =|B(\mathbf t_{\mathbf j,N})|e^{N\tau(\mathbf x)} (1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{32} \] It also proves (29). For the phases, put \(\Gamma_N=\prod_i\gamma_{j_i,N} =e^{-\pi i d(S-3/2)}\). The radial branch has \(\arg B=\pi S-3\pi/4\), and (8) gives \(\operatorname{Re}\Psi=\pi(1-S)\). Direct substitution yields \[ \frac{L_Ne^{i\pi/4}(B/|B|) e^{iN\operatorname{Re}\Psi}}{\Gamma_N} =e^{3\pi i/(4N)}. \tag{33} \] This known phase is \(1+O(N^{-1})\). Combining (27), (32), and (33) proves (30), retaining every original scalar. In particular the physical-grid rate is \(2\pi\tau=2\operatorname{Vol}\). Every coordinate in (25) has \(D_N(t_{j,N})=0\). The full polynomial in (27) is regular there, whereas expressions divided by the norm factors need cancellation before evaluation. An interior asymptotic with a displayed factor \(\prod_iD_N(t_i)\) cannot simply be evaluated on this grid. ## 5. What has been connected Near the origin, the proved complex source connection supplies its initialized nonzero growing packet wherever \(\operatorname{Im}\Psi\le0\). Every compact family of the radial paths (7) begins in that neighborhood. Theorem 2 shows that its classical saddle height stays strictly positive for every \(r>0\); Theorem 1 identifies its boundary height with the already constructed ordered prism volume. Independently, (27) initializes the actual positive source on the physical boundary grid. These facts do not prove that the source asymptotic is transported through the entire intervening disk, or uniformly into a level-dependent layer approaching \(r=1\). They also do not move the assembled Conway coefficient cycle to these local evaluations. Estimates for that source transport and the global marked geometric gluing are still required for arbitrary short fillings. No new volume-identity knot family or finite-exception theorem is asserted. ## Complete proof sources and coverage All three complete proof sources were read at their matching pins: | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Centered full source compiler](research_centered_fourier_conway_compiler.md) | 0edbabe42280d70e4d5dcbcb55b188a3e773c14b99fbd212eb0fe8c5b176a413 | | [Actual ordered ideal prisms](../papers/strict-conway-geometry/README.md) | c29321805df39a49854665df1255db1ec7180397a5dd689f19289d61335871c9 | | [Initialized complex source connection](research_centered_tensor_complex_source_connection.md) | 9b72f6d538a828bbbf2dd0be32828a5488b91865fa93fdcedee4d0b2fb556b0c | The complete positive Newton multiplication theorem was also read at pin 543b5be6035ecec349ce8e78ee47085345ceefe4fc51e5f2005b802d999805bb. It already proves positivity in the full physical algebra. The new bridge here is the exact centered unit grid, the fully normalized boundary action, and the growing radial path for the whole strict prism domain. No novelty is claimed for the dilogarithm Fourier formulas, finite Fourier orthogonality, or concavity inequalities. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build, git operation or earlier-final edit was performed.

title: The original three-boundary source on the real unit cube

# The original three-boundary source on the real unit cube 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The centered multiplication tensor has a nonzero leading asymptotic on every compact subset of the real cube \((-1,1)^3\). Both its phase and amplitude are explicit. This is an estimate of the entire original three-boundary source, with its first Casimir normals and original closing retained. The source selects two unit Fourier charges. Their contributions add. The zero-charge integral vanishes exactly, and all remaining charges, including their endpoint terms, have a summable uniform bound. No geometric cycle coefficient is assigned by hand. The result concerns real generating parameters. It does not assert a fixed complex neighborhood, a connection across Stokes regions, or a volume identity after arbitrary short fillings. ## 1. Statement with the original scalar factors Fix \(N\ge2\), and set \[ d=N-1,\quad \eta=(-1)^d,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad D_N(t)=1-\eta t^N . 	ag{1} \] All powers \(q^\alpha\) mean \(e^{\pi i\alpha/N}\). Use the original full algebra \(\mathcal H_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2)\), the positive crossing \(R\), and the original Frobenius row \(\phi\). Here \(T_N(\cos	heta)=\cos(N	heta)\). The initialized centered source is \[ \mathcal C_N(\mathbf t) =\sum_{a,b,c=0}^{d}C_{abc}t_1^at_2^bt_3^c =N^{-3/2}\phi\!\left(R^3 \prod_{
u=1}^3G_N(t_
u;z)ight). 	ag{2} \] This is the same polynomial as in the finite \({}_6\phi_5\) source identity. In particular its closing is \(\phi\), rather than a norm or an ordinary spectral trace. For real \(|t_
u|<1\), define \[  egin{aligned} \Psi(\mathbf t)=- rac{\pi}{12} + rac1{2\pi}\left[ \sum_{
u=1}^3\operatorname{Li}_2(-t_
u) +\operatorname{Li}_2(-t_1t_2t_3) -\sum_{\mu<
u}\operatorname{Li}_2(t_\mu t_
u)ight],\ B(\mathbf t)= \prod_{\mu<
u}(1-t_\mu t_
u)^{-1/2}. \end{aligned} 	ag{3} \] Every square root is positive. The dilogarithm is the real analytic function obtained from \(\operatorname{Li}_2(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n^2\) on \((-1,1)\). Thus \(\Psi\) is real and \(B>0\) throughout this cube. **Theorem.** For every \(0<ho<1\), uniformly for \(\mathbf t\in[-ho,ho]^3\), \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal C_N(\mathbf t)= (-1)^N\kappa^3 e^{\,i\pi/4-3\pi i/(4N)} \left[\prod_{
u=1}^3D_N(t_
u)ight] B(\mathbf t)e^{\,iN\Psi(\mathbf t)} (1+O_ho(N^{-1})). \quad} 	ag{4} \] The sequence includes both parities and composite levels. Consequently the actual polynomial is nonzero on that entire real compact cube for all sufficiently large \(N\). The normalizing factors \(D_N\) and the crossing phase have been displayed rather than reset. ## 2. A smooth interpolation with calibrated physical normals Put \(p=Q^{-1}\), and write \(W_n(z)=2T_n(z/2)\). The full generating-section theorem supplies the explicit unit \[ U_N(t,z)=\exp\left\{\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}  rac{(-1)^{n+1}(W_n(z)-2q^{-n})}{n(p^n-1)}\,t^night\}. 	ag{5} \] At every physical node \(c_j=2\cos	heta_j\), \(	heta_j=(2j+1)\pi/N\), it proves \[ \left|G_N/U_N-1ight| +\left|\partial_z(G_N/U_N)ight| \le C_ho N^2ho^N . 	ag{6} \] The derivative is required at double nodes; at the odd simple node \(-2\) only the value is used. Every quantity in (6) is evaluated at the actual finite polynomial's physical data. Its proof includes the central correction in the root equation. For use between sampling points, define \[  egin{aligned} b(t,z)&=1+zt+t^2,\qquad A(t,z)=b(t,z)^{-1/2},\ \Phi(t,z)&= rac{ \operatorname{Li}_2(-wt)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-w^{-1}t) -2\operatorname{Li}_2(-t)}{2\pi i}, \qquad z=w+w^{-1}. \end{aligned} 	ag{7} \] The branches are analytic at \(t=0\), with \(A(0,z)=1\). On real \(t\) and \(z=2\cos	heta\), the expression for \(\Phi\) is independent of choosing \(w=e^{i	heta}\) or \(w^{-1}\), is purely imaginary, and \(A(t,2\cos	heta)>0\). We need control of (5) at all real angles, rather than an unproved continuation of (6) away from the nodes. The logarithm of \(U_N\) below means its displayed exponent in (5), and the other logarithms are anchored at \(t=0\). **Lemma 1.** For every fixed integer \(k\ge0\), uniformly for real \(|t|\leho\), \[ \left\|\log U_N(t,2\cos	heta) -N\Phi(t,2\cos	heta)-\log A(t,2\cos	heta) ight\|_{C^k([0,2\pi])} \le C_{ho,k}/N . 	ag{8} \] **Proof.** At \(z=2\cos	heta\), \(W_n(z)=2\cos(n	heta)\). For \(n\le N/2\), expand the scalar denominator in (5): \[  rac1{e^{-2\pi in/N}-1} =- rac{N}{2\pi in}- rac12+O(n/N). 	ag{9} \] Together with \(q^{-n}=e^{-\pi in/N}\), this gives the coefficient identity \[  rac{(-1)^{n+1}(2\cos n	heta-2q^{-n})} {n(p^n-1)} =(-1)^n\left[  rac{N(2\cos n	heta-2)}{2\pi i n^2} + rac{\cos n	heta}{n}ight] +E_{N,n}(	heta), 	ag{10} \] where \(\|\partial_	heta^kE_{N,n}\|_\infty \le C_k(1+n)^k/N\). The expansions are uniform up to \(n=N/2\), since their next denominator pole is at \(2\pi\). For \(N/2<n<N\), use \[ |p^n-1|\ge c(N-n)/N . 	ag{11} \] The \(k\)-th angle derivatives of those coefficients are bounded by \(C_kN^k/(N-n)\). Their \(t^n\) tails are exponentially small, up to a polynomial in \(N\), on \(|t|\leho\). The same is true for the missing tails \(n\ge N\) of the two main series in (10). Summing (10) therefore has \(C^k\) error \(O(N^{-1})\). Its two main series are exactly \(N\Phi\) and \(\log A\), by the power series for \(\operatorname{Li}_2\) and the logarithm. This proves (8). \(\square\) For \(\mathbf t\in[-ho,ho]^3\), set \[ A_N(	heta)= \prod_{
u=1}^3U_N(t_
u,2\cos	heta) \exp\left\{-N\sum_{
u=1}^3 \Phi(t_
u,2\cos	heta)ight\}. 	ag{12} \] For every fixed \(k\), Lemma 1 gives \[ A_N(	heta)=A_*(	heta)+O_{C^k,ho}(N^{-1}),\qquad A_*(	heta)=\prod_{
u=1}^3 (1+2t_
u\cos	heta+t_
u^2)^{-1/2}. 	ag{13} \] All these amplitudes have uniform \(C^k\) bounds. They are exactly invariant under \(	heta\mapsto2\pi-	heta\). ## 3. The source itself removes the zero Fourier charge For any polynomial \(f\), the paired residue formula for the original Frobenius source is equivalently \[ \phi(f)=(-1)^N\sum_{j=0}^{d} \left. rac d{d	heta} \{\sin	heta\,f(2\cos	heta)\} ight|_{	heta=	heta_j}. 	ag{14} \] Indeed each paired node gives \((-1)^N[c f(c)+(c^2-4)f'(c)]\). At odd \(N\), the point \(	heta=\pi\) contributes \(f(-2)\), as required. Thus (14) includes the odd simple node. Introduce the smooth angular interpolation \[ \chi_N=q^{d^2/4},\qquad r_N(	heta)=\chi_N e^{\,iN(	heta-\pi)^2/(4\pi)} . 	ag{15} \] At every \(	heta_j\), its value is the actual \(R(c_j)\). At the double nodes its first derivative also gives the actual Casimir derivative: \[ R(c_j)=\kappa(-1)^jq^{j(j+1)},\qquad  rac{R'(c_j)}{R(c_j)} = rac{i(d-2j)}{4\sin	heta_j}. 	ag{16} \] The second identity is required only when \(\sin	heta_j
e0\). The odd simple node uses its value alone. This verifies the interpolation at the full Hermite data. It is not asserted that (15) equals the canonical crossing polynomial between the sampling points. We may factor the scalar \(\prod_
u D_N(t_
u)\) out of (2) exactly. Replacing each \(G_N/D_N\) by \(U_N\) in the remaining physical Hermite data has exponentially small source error. To check the scale, (6), \(D_N=1+O(ho^N)\), and the generating-section normal estimate give, uniformly at the nodes, bounded values of \(U_N\) and derivatives \(O_ho(N)\). The crossing has unit nodal values and first derivatives \(O(N^2)\) by (16). A product difference therefore has value error \(O_ho(N^2ho^N)\) and derivative error \(O_ho(N^4ho^N)\). Formula (14), or its paired version, bounds its source by \(O_ho(N^5ho^N)\). Define the real phase \[ \sigma(	heta)= rac{3(	heta-\pi)^2}{4\pi} + rac1i\sum_{
u=1}^3\Phi(t_
u,2\cos	heta) 	ag{17} \] and the amplitude \(a_N(	heta)=\sin	heta\,A_N(	heta)\). Equations (12)--(17) consequently reduce the actual source to \[ \mathcal C_N= \left[\prod_
u D_N(t_
u)ight] N^{-3/2}(-1)^N\chi_N^3 \sum_{j=0}^{d} \left. rac d{d	heta} \{a_N(	heta)e^{iN\sigma(	heta)}\} ight|_{	heta=	heta_j} +O_ho(N^4ho^N). 	ag{18} \] Put \(L_N(	heta)=a_N(	heta)e^{iN\sigma(	heta)}\). Its endpoint values are zero. Its first derivatives agree at \(0\) and \(2\pi\), since \(A_N\) is reflection-even and \(\sigma(0)=\sigma(2\pi)\). Hence \(L_N'\), regarded as a periodic continuous function, has absolutely summable Fourier coefficients: two integrations by parts give the usual \(O(m^{-2})\) bound, allowing the jump of its first derivative at the seam. This justification is for each fixed \(N\). The finite midpoint sampling identity is therefore exact: \[ \sum_{j=0}^{d}L_N'(	heta_j) = rac{N}{2\pi}\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^\ell \int_0^{2\pi}L_N'(	heta)e^{-i\ell N	heta}\,d	heta = rac{iN^2}{2\pi}\sum_{\ell
e0}(-1)^\ell\ell I_{\ell,N}, 	ag{19} \] where \[ I_{\ell,N}=\int_0^{2\pi} a_N(	heta)e^{iN(\sigma(	heta)-\ell	heta)}\,d	heta . 	ag{20} \] The last equality integrates by parts using \(L_N(0)=L_N(2\pi)=0\). In particular the zero-charge integral is zero exactly. No physical node, including the odd simple node, was deleted. These Fourier labels come from the midpoint sampling formula; they are not filling coefficients or peripheral charges. ## 4. All nonunit charges have a summable endpoint bound The argument of \(1+te^{i	heta}\) is chosen continuously from its positive value at \(	heta=0\). For real \(|t|<1\), its real part stays positive. Differentiating (17) gives \[  egin{aligned} \sigma'(	heta) &= rac{3(	heta-\pi)}{2\pi} - rac1\pi\sum_
u\arg(1+t_
u e^{i	heta}),\ \sigma''(	heta) &= rac1{2\pi}\sum_
u  rac{1-t_
u^2}{|1+t_
u e^{i	heta}|^2}>0. \end{aligned} 	ag{21} \] Thus \(\sigma'\) increases from \(-3/2\) to \(3/2\). On a fixed real compact cube, its second derivative is bounded above and below by positive constants, and every fixed higher derivative is uniformly bounded. For \(|\ell|\ge2\), set \(v_\ell=\sigma'-\ell\). Then \(|v_\ell|\ge|\ell|-3/2\). The endpoint values of \(a_N\) vanish, and \[ a_N'(0)=a_N'(2\pi)=A_N(0). 	ag{22} \] Two integrations by parts in (20) give a second boundary term proportional to \[  rac{A_N(0)e^{iN\sigma(0)}}{N^2} \left\{(3/2-\ell)^{-2}-(-3/2-\ell)^{-2}ight\}. 	ag{23} \] Its size is \(O_ho(N^{-2}|\ell|^{-3})\); the leading \(|\ell|^{-2}\) terms cancel because (22) and the endpoint phases agree. For completeness, after the first integration the new amplitude is \((a_N/v_\ell)'\). After the second, the remaining integral has amplitude \(((a_N/v_\ell)'/v_\ell)'\). One more integration bounds its boundary and integral by \(C_ho N^{-3}|\ell|^{-3}\), using the uniform \(C^3\) amplitude bounds and bounded phase derivatives. Consequently \[  oxed{\qquad |I_{\ell,N}| \le C_ho N^{-2}|\ell|^{-3} \qquad(|\ell|\ge2). \qquad} 	ag{24} \] The source-weighted complement \(N^2\sum_{|\ell|\ge2} |\ell I_{\ell,N}|\) is therefore \(O_ho(1)\). This estimate keeps the endpoint terms; it does not assume they vanish separately. ## 5. The two unit contributions add with a nonzero coefficient Define \[ h(	heta)=3	heta-2\sum_
u\arg(1+t_
u e^{i	heta}). 	ag{25} \] It has positive derivative, \(h(0)=0\), and \(h(\pi)=3\pi\). There is a unique \(	heta_*\in(0,\pi)\) with \(h(	heta_*)=\pi\). It is the stationary point of \(\sigma(	heta)+	heta\). The stationary point of \(\sigma(	heta)-	heta\) is \(2\pi-	heta_*\). Both stay a fixed distance from the endpoints on a compact parameter cube. Since \(A_N\) and \(\sigma\) are reflection-even while \(\sin	heta\) is reflection-odd, \[ I_{-\ell,N}=-I_{\ell,N} 	ag{26} \] exactly, with no complex conjugation. The factors \(\ell\) in (19) therefore make the two unit contributions add. The one-dimensional stationary-phase estimate, uniform in this compact family, is \[ I_{1,N}= -\sin	heta_*\,A_*(	heta_*)\, e^{\,iN(\sigma(	heta_*)+	heta_*)+i\pi/4} \sqrt{ rac{2\pi}{N\sigma''(	heta_*)}} +O_ho(N^{-3/2}). 	ag{27} \] The phase at \(2\pi-	heta_*\) differs by \(-2\pi\); its exponential is unchanged because \(N\) is an integer. The minus sign is its actual sine amplitude. Here the standard stationary-phase calculation is elementary and uniform: on a fixed neighborhood of the critical point use the signed square root of twice the phase difference as coordinate. The phase becomes \(y^2/2\), and the transformed amplitude has uniform derivatives. Its constant term integrates to \(e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt{2\pi/N}\), by the Gaussian integral with positive damping removed. The odd linear term vanishes under an even cutoff, and the quadratic remainder costs \(O(N^{-3/2})\). For the latter bound, integrate its \(y^2\) factor once using \(\partial_y e^{iNy^2/2}=iNy e^{iNy^2/2}\); the remaining smooth quadratic-phase integral is \(O(N^{-1/2})\), as follows by splitting at \(|y|=N^{-1/2}\) and integrating by parts outside. Away from that neighborhood, two integrations by parts give \(O(N^{-2})\), retaining the zero endpoint values of \(a_N\). Equation (13) permits replacing \(A_N\) by \(A_*\) at the critical point with an additional \(O(N^{-3/2})\) error. All coordinate and cutoff bounds are uniform by (21). Substituting (24), (26), and (27) into (18)--(19) gives \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal C_N={}&(-1)^N i\chi_N^3 e^{i\pi/4} \left[\prod_
u D_N(t_
u)ight] K(\mathbf t)\, e^{\,iN(\sigma(	heta_*)+	heta_*)} (1+O_ho(N^{-1})),\ K(\mathbf t)&=  rac{2\sin	heta_*\,A_*(	heta_*)}{\sqrt{h'(	heta_*)}}>0 . \end{aligned} 	ag{28} \] The higher charges contribute \(O(N^{-3/2})\) after the normalization in (18); the stationary error is \(O(N^{-1})\). The positive coefficient \(K\) is bounded away from zero on every compact real cube. ## 6. Eliminating the implicit saddle Write \(s_1=\sum_
u t_
u\), \(s_2=\sum_{\mu<
u}t_\mu t_
u\), \(s_3=t_1t_2t_3\), and put \(A_0=1+s_3>0\). At \(w=e^{i	heta_*}\), exponentiating (25) gives \[ \prod_
u(w+t_
u)+\prod_
u(1+t_
u w) =(w+1)\{A_0(w^2-w+1)+(s_1+s_2)w\}=0 . 	ag{29} \] Since \(w
e-1\), \[ z_*:=2\cos	heta_* =1- rac{s_1+s_2}{1+s_3}. 	ag{30} \] In particular \(z_*\in(-2,2)\) throughout the real cube. Let \(b_
u=1+t_
u z_*+t_
u^2\). Direct substitution gives \[ b_
u=  rac{(1+t_
u)(1-t_
u t_\mu)(1-t_
u t_\lambda)} {A_0},\qquad 4\sin^2(	heta_*/2)= rac{\prod_
u(1+t_
u)}{A_0}, 	ag{31} \] where \(\{
u,\mu,\lambda\}=\{1,2,3\}\). Differentiate the polynomial in (29) on the unit circle at its root. Equivalently differentiate the Blaschke product in (25). Taking absolute values gives \[ h'(	heta_*)\sqrt{\prod_
u b_
u} =4A_0\cos(	heta_*/2)\sin	heta_* . 	ag{32} \] Using (31)--(32) in \(K^2\) proves \[ K^2=\prod_{\mu<
u}(1-t_\mu t_
u)^{-1}. 	ag{33} \] Since \(K>0\), this is the amplitude \(B\) in (3). The stationary action without its fixed constant is \[ \Psi_*=\sigma(	heta_*)+	heta_*- rac{3\pi}{4}. 	ag{34} \] Its envelope derivative is \[ \partial_{t_
u}\Psi_*=  rac{\log b_
u-2\log(1+t_
u)}{2\pi t_
u}. 	ag{35} \] All arguments of these real logarithms are positive. At \(t_
u=0\), the quotient is interpreted by continuity. Substituting (31) into (35) and integrating gives precisely the dilogarithm expression in (3). Its constant is fixed at \(\mathbf t=0\): \(	heta_*=\pi/3\) and \(\Psi_*=-\pi/12\). Finally the exact level-phase identity \[ i\chi_N^3 e^{\,3\pi iN/4} =\kappa^3e^{-3\pi i/(4N)} 	ag{36} \] turns (28) into (4). This completes the proof. ## 7. Scope and complete proof sources The theorem estimates one universal joint source, not its absolute-value envelope. Its nonzero coefficient comes from the prescribed finite source after its zero-charge cancellation, unit-charge addition and endpoint control. The proof uses real phase and positivity of (21). For complex generating parameters, endpoint terms can have a different exponential scale. No fixed complex neighborhood, global zero-free domain, or continuation of the asymptotic through such a connection is proved. The estimate does not place the generating variables of an arbitrary short-filled geometric component in this real cube. title: Exact wall values and a Cauchy representation of the centered source
text: # Exact wall values and a Cauchy representation of the centered source 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. Fixing one generating leg at any physical norm-wall point gives an explicit product for the entire original three-boundary source. This product is nonzero at every level when the other two arguments lie in the open unit disk. Partial fractions then give a canonical finite Cauchy representation of the full source, without a derivative of a hypergeometric sum. In the bulk of that wall, the product has a uniform asymptotic with the initialized dilogarithmic action and a known nonzero amplitude. The other two arguments may range over arbitrary compact complex subsets of the disk. This is additional actual source control; transport from this wall representation through the whole interior still requires a separate estimate. ## 1. The original tensor and its forced connection Fix \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \eta=(-1)^d,\quad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad D_N(t)=1-\eta t^N . \tag{1} \] Powers of \(q\) mean the displayed exponential, including fractional powers. Put \(\mathbb D=\{t\in\mathbb C:|t|<1\}\). Write \(\mathcal C_N(x,y,z)=\sum_{a,b,c=0}^{d}C_{abc}x^ay^bz^c\) for the initialized centered tensor. It is the original full source \[ \mathcal C_N(x,y,z)= N^{-3/2}\phi\!\left( R^3G_N(x;\cdot)G_N(y;\cdot)G_N(z;\cdot)\right). \tag{2} \] Here \(R\) is the original positive crossing and \(\phi\) the original Frobenius closing on \(\mathcal H_N=\mathbb C[w]/(2T_N(w/2)+2)\), where \(T_N(\cos\theta)=\cos(N\theta)\). Every first derivative at a double Casimir root remains present. The dot in (2) is the Casimir argument, not another generating leg. The forced Rogers theorem proves the polynomial identity \[ \begin{split} &(1-Qxy)(1-Qxz)\mathcal C_N(Qx,y,z) -(1+qx)(1+qxyz)\mathcal C_N(x,y,z)\\ &\hspace{22mm} =\beta_ND_N(y)D_N(z)\frac{xD_N(x)}{1+qx}, \qquad \beta_N=\frac{(-1)^{N+1}\kappa^3}{N^{3/2}} . \end{split} \tag{3} \] The quotient on its right is a polynomial. The exact phase identities \[ \kappa^2=(-1)^Nq,\qquad \beta_N=-\frac{q\kappa}{N^{3/2}} \tag{4} \] will simplify the wall initializer. They follow directly from \((N-1)^2=N^2-2N+1\). For \(a\in\mathbb C\) and an integer \(j\ge0\), use \[ (a;Q)_j=\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}(1-aQ^h). \tag{5} \] Empty products equal one. Define the wall points \[ X_j=-qQ^j,\qquad 0\le j<N . \tag{6} \] They are precisely the distinct zeros of \(D_N(x)\). ## 2. Every wall slice is an explicit nonzero product **Theorem 1.** For every \(0\le j<N\) and \(y,z\in\mathbb D\), \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal C_N(X_j,y,z)= \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N}D_N(y)D_N(z) \frac{(Q;Q)_j(Qyz;Q)_j} {(-qy;Q)_{j+1}(-qz;Q)_{j+1}} . \quad} \tag{7} \] In particular each of these wall slices is nonzero on the whole \(\mathbb D^2\), at every level and for both parities. **Proof.** Evaluate (3) at \(x=-q^{-1}=X_d\). Its second term vanishes. Since \[ \frac{D_N(x)}{1+qx} =\sum_{h=0}^{N-1}(-qx)^h, \qquad \left.\frac{D_N(x)}{1+qx}\right|_{x=-q^{-1}}=N, \tag{8} \] equations (3)--(4) give the exact initial slice \[ \mathcal C_N(-q,y,z)= \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N} \frac{D_N(y)D_N(z)}{(1+qy)(1+qz)} . \tag{9} \] For \(0\le j<N-1\), the forcing in (3) is zero at \(X_j\); its displayed denominator is nonzero there. The remaining equation is \[ \frac{\mathcal C_N(X_{j+1},y,z)} {\mathcal C_N(X_j,y,z)} =\frac{(1-Q^{j+1})(1-Q^{j+1}yz)} {(1+qQ^{j+1}y)(1+qQ^{j+1}z)} . \tag{10} \] Starting with (9) proves (7). All divisions in this argument are valid inside \(\mathbb D^2\): the linear factors involving \(y,z\), and those involving \(yz\), cannot vanish there. Also \((Q;Q)_j\ne0\) for \(j<N\), and neither \(D_N(y)\) nor \(D_N(z)\) vanishes. This proves the nonvanishing assertion. \(\square\) The two ends have simple checks in the original source: \[ \mathcal C_N(X_0,y,z)= \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt N} \frac{D_N(y)D_N(z)}{(1+qy)(1+qz)},\qquad \mathcal C_N(X_d,y,z)= \kappa\sqrt N\,\frac{1-(yz)^N}{1-yz}. \tag{11} \] The second follows from \((Q;Q)_d=N\) and the complete cyclic products in (7). It is regular when \(yz=1\) by its finite geometric-sum interpretation, although that point is outside \(\mathbb D^2\). These are the marked and unit end slices; the intervening products retain all original boundary directions. The last wall step must not be made homogeneous. Extending the product in (7) formally to \(j=N\) would insert \((Q;Q)_N=0\), although \(X_N=X_0\) and (9) is nonzero. The nonzero forcing at the step \(X_d\longmapsto X_0\) is exactly what restores the original slice. Thus a periodic interpolation of the factorial weights cannot silently erase this missing cyclic arrow. ## 3. A canonical derivative-free Cauchy period For \(x,y,z\in\mathbb D\), put \[ \widehat{\mathcal C}_N= \frac{\mathcal C_N}{D_N(x)D_N(y)D_N(z)} . \tag{12} \] The exact finite representation is \[ \boxed{\quad \widehat{\mathcal C}_N(x,y,z)= \frac{\kappa}{N^{3/2}(1+qy)(1+qz)} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \frac{(Q;Q)_j(Qyz;Q)_j} {(-q^3y;Q)_j(-q^3z;Q)_j} \frac1{1+q^{-1}Q^{-j}x}. \quad} \tag{13} \] For a proof, \(\mathcal C_N(x,y,z)\) has degree below \(N\) in \(x\). Consequently its quotient by \(D_N(x)\) is proper rational with simple poles at \(X_j\). Since \(D_N'(X_j)=-N/X_j\), its partial fractions are \[ \widehat{\mathcal C}_N(x,y,z)= \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \frac{\mathcal C_N(X_j,y,z)} {N D_N(y)D_N(z)}\,\frac1{1-x/X_j}. \tag{14} \] Insert (7) and separate the first factor in each denominator to get (13). Thus the wall residues and the complete finite Cauchy period are prescribed, rather than fitted to an unknown source. Every pole in (13) has nonzero residue when \(y,z\in\mathbb D\). The full polynomial \(\mathcal C_N\) is regular at these points; one must use (7), not evaluate (12) without canceling its norm factor. Multiplication by all three \(D_N\)'s recovers the original source inside the disk. No derivative, scalar phase, or first Casimir normal has been omitted in passing from (3) to this representation. ## 4. A uniform complex packet on the bulk wall Use the initialized action \[ \Psi(x,y,z)=-\frac{\pi}{12} +\frac1{2\pi}\left[ \operatorname{Li}_2(-x)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-y) +\operatorname{Li}_2(-z)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-xyz) -\operatorname{Li}_2(xy)-\operatorname{Li}_2(xz) -\operatorname{Li}_2(yz)\right] \tag{15} \] and amplitude \[ B(x,y,z)= [(1-xy)(1-xz)(1-yz)]^{-1/2}. \tag{16} \] Both branches start from their power series in \(\mathbb D^3\). At \(x=-e^{2\pi iu}\), \(0<u<1\), continue radially in \(x\). The only unit-circle dilogarithm argument is \(e^{2\pi iu}\ne1\); all other arguments lie strictly inside the disk. These boundary values are locally analytic in \(u,y,z\), and \[ B(-e^{2\pi iu},y,z)= [(1+ye^{2\pi iu})(1+ze^{2\pi iu})(1-yz)]^{-1/2} \tag{17} \] is the branch equal to one at \(y=z=0\). **Theorem 2.** Fix \(0<\delta<1/2\) and \(0<\rho<1\). Uniformly for indices with \[ u_j=(j+1/2)/N\in[\delta,1-\delta], \qquad |y|,|z|\le\rho, \] the actual original wall source obeys \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal C_N(X_j,y,z)= \kappa e^{\,i\pi/4-\pi i/(8N)} D_N(y)D_N(z)\,B(X_j,y,z) e^{\,iN\Psi(X_j,y,z)} (1+O_{\delta,\rho}(N^{-1})). \quad} \tag{18} \] The error is a complex value estimate, relative to the nonzero displayed source. No real restriction on \(y,z\) is imposed. It gives, in particular, uniform two-sided bounds for its modulus by constant multiples of \(e^{-N\operatorname{Im}\Psi}\) on these sets. **Proof.** Write \(u=u_j\) and \(w=e^{2\pi iu}\). Let \(s_j=\prod_{h=1}^j2\sin(\pi h/N)\). The middle-calibrated sine-factorial estimate gives \[ s_j=\sqrt N\,e^{NL(u)} (1+O_\delta(N^{-1})), \quad L(u)=\int_0^u\log(2\sin\pi v)\,dv, \tag{19} \] because \(j=Nu-1/2\). Its normalization follows from \(s_js_{d-j}=N\) and trapezoidal Euler--Maclaurin between the middle and a strict interior label, as proved in the prism bridge. The exact phase of the complex factorial is \[ \begin{split} (Q;Q)_j &=(-i)^jq^{j(j+1)/2}s_j\\ &=\sqrt N\, e^{\,i\pi/4-\pi i/(8N)} \exp\left\{N\left[L(u)+ \frac{i\pi}{2}(u^2-u)\right]\right\} (1+O_\delta(N^{-1})). \end{split} \tag{20} \] For \(|a|<1\), put \[ I_a(u)=\int_0^u\log(1-ae^{2\pi iv})\,dv =-\frac{\operatorname{Li}_2(ae^{2\pi iu}) -\operatorname{Li}_2(a)}{2\pi i}. \tag{21} \] The logarithms are anchored at \(a=0\). Their derivatives on the real \(v\)-interval are bounded uniformly for \(a\) in a closed interior disk. Ordinary Euler--Maclaurin, with the indicated half-step offsets, gives \[ \begin{aligned} \log(Qyz;Q)_j &=NI_{yz}(u)-\tfrac12\log(1-yz)+O_{\delta,\rho}(N^{-1}),\\ \log(-qy;Q)_{j+1} &=NI_{-y}(u)+\tfrac12\log(1+yw) +O_{\delta,\rho}(N^{-1}), \end{aligned} \tag{22} \] and the same formula for \(z\). The first sum samples \(h/N\), \(1\le h\le j\); the second samples \((h+1/2)/N\), \(0\le h\le j\). Expanding their upper integration limit about \(u=(j+1/2)/N\) yields precisely the endpoint half-weights in (22). Substituting (20)--(22) in the exact product (7) gives amplitude \[ [(1-yz)(1+yw)(1+zw)]^{-1/2} =B(-w,y,z) \tag{23} \] and exponent \[ L(u)+\frac{i\pi}{2}(u^2-u) +I_{yz}(u)-I_{-y}(u)-I_{-z}(u). \tag{24} \] The unit-circle dilogarithm identities \[ \operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iu})=-2\pi L(u), \qquad \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iu}) =\pi^2(u^2-u+\tfrac16) \tag{25} \] turn (24), using (21), exactly into \(i\Psi(-w,y,z)\). The powers \(\sqrt N\) in (7) and (20) cancel. This proves (18), with its full scalar phase. All error bounds are uniform for the stated complex \(y,z\), since every regular factor in (22) stays away from zero. \(\square\) ## 5. What the wall data do and do not control Equation (13) is an exact, initialized Cauchy representation of the whole universal tensor. Equation (18) gives a known nonzero geometric principal amplitude on every strict bulk wall slice, even for arbitrary compact complex values of the other two legs. The result is not obtained by assigning a saddle coefficient. It does not justify inserting only (18) term by term in (13) and then discarding cancellation among its \(N\) terms. The two endpoint layers \(j\) near zero or \(d\) are outside the stated uniform wall asymptotic. A contour interpolation of the factorial weights must retain their finite initialization and the forced last arrow described after (11). An unchecked periodic quantum-gamma interpolation could change the source. In particular no estimate here transports the growing packet along an arbitrary interior radial path. Nor does it move the assembled Conway coefficient cycle or prove a lower bound after general short fillings. Those questions require estimates for the complete Cauchy period and the original global gluing. ## Complete proof sources and coverage Both complete proof sources were read at the matching pins: | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Forced original Rogers connection](research_centered_tensor_forced_rogers_connection.md) | 0d2ed84d814c892754f87dcda16d50167dc50acb845538720aa9e6abb9e3d8d7 | | [Prism boundary and radial bridge](research_centered_tensor_prism_radial_bridge.md) | 892dfc5ef5e0774d45ccc44bc4f5122e7137d6185fe9191997e1b43d79003776 | The first supplies the exact physical connection with its nonzero forcing. The second supplies the initialized action and the middle-calibrated sine-factorial estimate. The wall initializer, residue products, Cauchy representation and uniform complex two-leg wall packet are proved above. No novelty is claimed for partial fractions or Euler--Maclaurin summation. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build, git operation or earlier-final edit was performed.

title: Central resolvent, inverse Jacobian, and compact source symmetry
text: # Central resolvent, inverse Jacobian, and compact source symmetry Private written proof, 18 November 2026.
