title: A strongly convex minimum for the complete Conway source
status: Fixed-degree variational source; geometric rate open
text:
# A strongly convex minimum for the complete Conway source 21 November 2026. This note concerns the original reduced Kashaev source of a fixed literal Conway construction. Previous final notes and public manuscripts remain unchanged. After an explicit normalization of its local tensors, the source admits an unweighted quartic minimum on a product of unit balls. Its real Hessian lies between \(I\) and \(3I\), uniformly in the quantum level and the number of vertices. The minimum has a unique interior point, and the corresponding value satisfies \[ |K_N|^2\le Q_N\le\gamma|K_N|^2,\qquad \gamma= rac{197}{196}. 	ag{1} \] This includes zeros. An explicit degree-six polynomial gives an exact lower-certificate maximum for the minimum. These statements concern the original marked source; no reference coordinate or ordinary-color sum is introduced. Their geometric volume rate remains to be proved. ## 1. The physical boundary data and its normalization Fix \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), and \[ s_r=\prod_{j=1}^r2\sin(\pi j/N),\quad s_0=1,\qquad H_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2). \] Here \(T_N\) is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. Use the Euclidean Hermitian norm in the normalized Newton basis \[ b_r= rac{\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}(q^{2j+1}+q^{-2j-1}-z)}{s_r^2}, \qquad 0\le r\le d. 	ag{2} \] This is the full \(N\)-dimensional boundary algebra, including the first derivatives at its double roots. Its physical operations are the product \(M(f,g)=fg\), the turn \(Jb_r=b_{d-r}\), and the signed packets \[ R^{\pm1}=\kappa^{\pm1}\sum_{r=0}^d(-q)^{\pm r}b_r, \qquad \kappa=q^{d^2/2}. 	ag{3} \] Fractional powers mean the displayed exponentials. These are the actual complete packets. The formulas and original source conventions are in the [Conway compiler](research_conway_full_boundary_quotient_gram.md) and [Newton source theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_newton_turn_positive_gram.md). Take a fixed literal expression built from prescribed leaves, products and turns. Its ordered closure is assumed to give one knot, with the original reduced marking and zero-framing convention. There are \(m\ge2\) vertices, including the closing root, whose unique child is \(v_0\). Put \(s=m-1\). Let \(f_v\in H_N\) be the true open packet of the proper subtree at \(v\), and let the exact original closing row be \(\ell_N\). Thus \[ K_N=\ell_Nf_{v_0}. 	ag{4} \] The known framing phase and any recorded fixed power of \(N\) remain in this row. Neither original closing row is replaced by a norm or an ordinary cap. For each local physical tensor \(T_v\), including leaves and the root, choose the known budget \[ b_v=16\max(1,\|T_v\|_{m HS}),\qquad \sigma= rac1{16}. \] The squared Hilbert--Schmidt norm is the sum of the squared absolute values of all its coefficients. For a proper vertex \(v\), let \(B_v\) be the product of the budgets in its proper subtree, and put \[ B_{m tot}=\prod_vb_v. \] All these numbers are positive and algebraic at each level. Write \(a_v=f_v/B_v\). The exact normalized recursion is \[ a_v=\Phi_v((a_c)_{c	ext{ child of }v}),\qquad L=\ell_N/b_{m root},\qquad k_N=K_N/B_{m tot}=La_{v_0}. 	ag{5} \] At a leaf, \(\Phi_v=f_v/b_v\) is a prescribed constant. At a turn, \(\Phi_v=J/b_v\); at a product, \(\Phi_v=M/b_v\). Every normalized leaf and every normalized linear or bilinear map has norm at most \(\sigma\), as does \(L\). Induction gives \(\|a_v\|\le\sigma\). This normalization retains all phases, markings, and physical boundary directions. Its total scalar is kept explicitly in (5). ## 2. An unweighted quartic objective Use one trial packet \(x_v\in H_N\) at each proper vertex and put \[ \mathcal D_N=\prod_{v
e\mathrm{root}}\{x_v:\|x_v\|\le1\}, \qquad \mathcal R_v(x)=\Phi_v((x_c)_c)-x_v. \] Let \(G(x)=(\mathcal R_v(x))_v\). Define \[ E_N(x)=|Lx_{v_0}|^2+\|G(x)\|^2,\qquad  oxed{\quad Q_N=\gamma B_{m tot}^2 \min_{x\in\mathcal D_N}E_N(x).\quad} 	ag{6} \] There are \(2Ns\) real variables and the degree is at most four, independently of \(N\) and \(s\). This is the ordinary sum of squared local recursion errors, together with the original closing term. There are no depth weights or penalties depending on the quantum level. The feasible set is nonempty and compact, and all coefficients and ball radii are algebraic at each level. All differential statements use the real inner product \(\langle u,vangle_{\mathbb R}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_vu_v^*v_v\). The gradient includes every real and imaginary Newton coefficient. ## 3. Uniform convexity **Lemma.** On \(\mathcal D_N\), the real Hessian satisfies \[ I\le D^2E_N\le3I. 	ag{7} \] **Proof.** The derivative of the full residual map is \(DG=-I+A(x)\). A block of \(A\) from child \(c\) to parent \(v\) is \(D_c\Phi_v\), with norm at most \(\sigma\). This uses the unit-ball bound on the other input of a product. Each row has at most two child blocks, and each child occurs in at most one parent row. Therefore \[ \|A(x)\xi\|^2\le2\sigma^2\sum_v\|\xi_v\|^2,\qquad \|A(x)\|\le\sqrt2\sigma\le rac18. \] Consequently \[  rac78\|\xi\|\le\|DG(x)\xi\| \le rac98\|\xi\|. 	ag{8} \] Only product vertices contribute a second derivative to \(G\). At such a vertex, the residual-curvature term in the half-Hessian of \(\|G\|^2\) is \[ 2\operatorname{Re} \langle\mathcal R_v,\Phi_v(\xi_L,\xi_R)angle. \] Since \(\|\mathcal R_v\|\le1+\sigma\), its absolute value is at most \[ 2\sigma(1+\sigma)\|\xi_L\|\|\xi_R\| \le\sigma(1+\sigma)(\|\xi_L\|^2+\|\xi_R\|^2). \] Sibling pairs belonging to different parents are disjoint. Thus the total has absolute value at most \(\sigma(1+\sigma)\|\xi\|^2=17\|\xi\|^2/256\), and hence at most \(\|\xi\|^2/8\). The closing term adds at most \(\sigma^2\|\xi\|^2\) to the half-Hessian, and adds no negative term. Using (8), this proves the more explicit bounds \[  rac{41}{32}\|\xi\|^2 \le D^2E_N(x)[\xi,\xi] \le rac{357}{128}\|\xi\|^2. \] They imply (7). \(\square\) It follows that \(E_N\) has a unique minimizer on its feasible set. The Hessian assertion concerns this product of balls; convexity on the whole real coordinate space is not asserted. ## 4. Comparison with the original source Integrating \(DG=-I+A\) along a segment in the convex set \(\mathcal D_N\) gives \[ \|G(x)-G(y)\|\ge rac78\|x-y\|. 	ag{9} \] Indeed the difference is \(-(x-y)\) plus a vector of norm at most \(\|x-y\|/8\). The true normalized field \(a=(a_v)_v\) is feasible, with \(G(a)=0\). Since \(\|L\|\le1/16\), (9) implies \[ |k_N-Lx_{v_0}| \le rac1{16}\|x-a\|\le rac1{14}\|G(x)\|. 	ag{10} \] Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the two terms on the right gives \[ |k_N|^2\le\left(1+ rac1{196}ight) (|Lx_{v_0}|^2+\|G(x)\|^2). \] At the true field, \(E_N(a)=|k_N|^2\). Taking minima therefore proves \[  rac{|K_N|^2}{\gamma} \le B_{m tot}^2\min E_N\le|K_N|^2, 	ag{11} \] and hence (1). No step assumes \(K_N
e0\) or divides by it. A zero minimum forces every residual and the closing term to vanish, so \(Q_N=0\) precisely when \(K_N=0\). ## 5. An explicit local contracting iteration The gradient uses only local residuals and their actual adjoints: \[ g_v=-2\mathcal R_v +2(D_v\Phi_u)^*\mathcal R_u +\mathbf1_{v=v_0}\,2L^*Lx_v. 	ag{12} \] The middle term is present only if the parent \(u\) is proper. Define \[ T(x)=x- rac12
abla E_N(x). 	ag{13} \] No projection is necessary. At a nontop vertex, \(T_v=\Phi_v-(D_v\Phi_u)^*\mathcal R_u\), so \(\|T_v\|\le\sigma+\sigma(1+\sigma)=33/256\). At the top, \(T_{v_0}=\Phi_{v_0}-L^*Lx_{v_0}\), with norm at most \(\sigma+\sigma^2=17/256\). Thus \[ T(\mathcal D_N)\subset  rac{33}{256}\mathcal D_N. 	ag{14} \] The Hessian averaged between two feasible points is self-adjoint with eigenvalues in \([1,3]\), so \(I-H/2\) has norm at most \(1/2\). Consequently \(T\) is a contraction on the complete set \(\mathcal D_N\). Its iterates converge: successive displacements are bounded by a geometric series. The limit is a fixed point \(x_*\), and contraction makes it unique. Equation (13) gives \(
abla E_N(x_*)=0\). Strong convexity then identifies \(x_*\) as the unique minimum. It is strictly interior by (14), and \[ \|T^j(x)-x_*\|\le2^{-j}\|x-x_*\|. 	ag{15} \] Starting at zero gives the bound \(\|x_*\|\le\sqrt{s}\), independent of \(N\) for a fixed expression. The iteration needs no dense global Hessian. Uniform conditioning does not by itself give relative precision when \(\min E_N\) is exponentially small. No numerical iteration has been run here. ## 6. An exact polynomial lower certificate For any feasible field, define \[ D_N(x)=E_N(x)- rac12\|
abla E_N(x)\|^2. 	ag{16} \] This is a real polynomial of degree at most six. The lower Hessian bound gives \[ D_N(x)\le\min E_N\le E_N(x). 	ag{17} \] Indeed, for feasible \(y\), \[ E_N(y)\ge E_N(x)+\langle
abla E_N(x),y-xangle_{\mathbb R} +	frac12\|y-x\|^2. \] The minimum of this quadratic over the whole real coordinate space is \(D_N(x)\), by completing the square. This argument uses convexity only on the feasible balls. At \(x_*\) the gradient is zero, so \[ \min_{\mathcal D_N}E_N =\max_{\mathcal D_N}D_N. 	ag{18} \] The polynomial \(D_N\) need not be concave. Combining (11) and (17) gives, at every feasible trial field, \[  oxed{\quad B_{m tot}^2\max(0,D_N(x))\le|K_N|^2 \le\gamma B_{m tot}^2E_N(x). \quad} 	ag{19} \] This lower certificate includes every real and imaginary boundary coordinate, including the physical normal directions. For example, suppose feasible fields \(x_N\) satisfy \[ \|
abla E_N(x_N)\|^2\le2(1-\eta_N)E_N(x_N),\qquad 0<\eta_N\le1,\qquad \log\eta_N=o(N). 	ag{20} \] Then \(D_N(x_N)\ge\eta_NE_N(x_N)\). If also \( rac\pi N\log(B_{m tot}^2E_N(x_N))	o V>0\), (19) proves \[  rac{2\pi}N\log|K_N|\longrightarrow V. \] Thus a single controlled geometric trial field would suffice for a volume lower bound. Neither moment stationarity nor angle stationarity alone establishes (20), which uses the full real gradient. No geometric trial field with the required estimates is supplied here. ## 7. Scope and an optional exact reduction All coefficients come from the complete original source. For a fixed literal construction, \(\log B_{m tot}=O(N)\); the sine-factor bounds, crossing norms and closing normalization are recorded in Section 7 of the [earlier quartic note](research_anchored_conway_positive_variational_period.md). Two exact presentations have logarithmic \(Q_N\) values differing by at most \(\log\gamma\) whenever \(K_N
e0\), and both values vanish at every zero. Fixed short proper subtrees may be contracted with their full open boundary packets before applying this construction. There is an optional variable-projection reduction. Retain one child variable for each binary product and eliminate every other variable. Sibling pairs are disjoint, so if \(n_	imes\) is the number of product vertices this retains exactly \(n_	imes\) packets. Every residual is jointly affine in the eliminated variables when the retained ones are fixed. Their inner minimization is therefore a strictly convex quadratic problem on a product of balls. Its interaction graph consists of linear corridors: every eliminated vertex has at most one eliminated child and one parent. Its minimizer exists uniquely. Partial minimization preserves strong convexity in the retained variables: interpolate the two inner minimizers, then apply the original strong-convexity inequality and drop the nonnegative squared displacement of the inner variables. This gives an exact reduction to \(2Nn_	imes\) outer real variables. The reduced objective need not be polynomial. Finally, the fixed comparison factor in (1) makes the exponential rate of \(Q_N\) equivalent to that of the original source. Convexity has provided a unique finite minimum, a uniformly contracting iteration, and a lower witness at one trial field. Its asymptotic comparison with hyperbolic volume remains necessary, including after the fixed short partial assignments in the finite-exception program. ## Complete direct sources The following complete matching texts were read. The first records the earlier quartic formulation and source growth bounds; the others give the actual full boundary operations and markings. The normalization, convexity, source comparison, iteration and certificates are proved above. | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Earlier complete-source quartic](research_anchored_conway_positive_variational_period.md) | e83c35d16c79faa13ac6556db78b9b57da2a2371d3fc04c4673ecd74e1d336f7 | | [Complete Conway compiler](research_conway_full_boundary_quotient_gram.md) | debe56dbad8151b90d44d0fccbf0dcf33dafb780370e01c8acdadbd2939dc077 | | [Actual Newton turn and source](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_newton_turn_positive_gram.md) | d8b21fa8db909120035e86e997a0e02cb84f8dce2dcf6fb244bb5c85c17e28a3 | Only written mathematics and text operations were used. No mathematical program, test, build, numerical iteration, git operation or public-document edit was performed.

title: Analytic gap estimates for Conway tangle sources
text: # Analytic gap estimates for Conway tangle sources 23 November 2026. Research proof; frozen papers and earlier notes remain unchanged. The two scalar comparisons used in the Conway source bound admit analytic proofs with their original margins: \(1/100\) for each two-leaf alias comparison and \(1/2500\) for a proper single attachment. No finite comparison table is a proof input here. In the attachment argument we use its actual proper parameter region. We do not assert the stronger auxiliary comparison on the entire artificial slope square. The result replaces the finite comparison checks needed by those two lemmas. It supplies no new filled-source lower bound or volume identity. ## 1. Functions, domains and the assertions Put \[ J(t)=\int_0^t\log(2\sin\pi u)\,du,\quad 0\le t\le1, \qquad J(1-t)=-J(t),\quad J(0)=J(1/2)=J(1)=0, \] \[ g(x)=J(2x)-4J(x),\quad 0\le x\le1/2,\qquad \widetilde g(x)=g(\max(x,1/4)),\qquad k(x)=-2J(x/2). \tag{1} \] For completeness, substitution \(t\mapsto\pi/2-t\) and the double-angle identity give \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\log\sin t\,dt=-(\pi/2)\log2\). This proves the stated zero values of \(J\); reflection then proves \(J(1-t)=-J(t)\). The domain of \(k\) is \([0,1]\). The original product action is \[ \begin{split} m(x,y,z)={}&J(x+y)+J(z)-J(x)-J(y)\\ &-J(z-x)-J(z-y)-J(x+y-z),\\ D={}&\{x,y\ge0:\max(x,y)\le z\le x+y\le1\}. \end{split} \tag{2} \] All maxima below include their indicated closed domains. The convention for \(\operatorname{arccot}\) has values in \((0,\pi)\). For \(1/2\le X\le1\), define \[ a=\operatorname{arccot}X/\pi,\quad b=\operatorname{arccot}(X-1/(2X))/\pi,\quad \lambda=2\log(2X^2),\quad P_2(\lambda)=2g(a)+m(a,a,b)-\lambda b . \tag{3} \] The two seed assertions are \[ \begin{split} P_2(\lambda)-\max_{D,\ y\le1/2} \{k(x)+\widetilde g(y)+m(x,y,z)-\lambda z\}&>1/100,\\ P_2(\lambda)-\max_D \{k(x)+k(y)+m(x,y,z)-\lambda z\}&>1/100 . \end{split} \tag{4} \] Thus (4) includes the full closed slope interval \([-\log4,\log4]\). For the attachment, suppose \[ \frac12<X<1,\quad Y=\sqrt{1+B^2-X^2},\quad S=X+B>0,\quad Y_p=Y/S,\qquad 0<Y,Y_p<1 . \tag{5} \] Set \(a=\operatorname{arccot}X/\pi\), \(b=\operatorname{arccot}B/\pi\), \(c=\operatorname{arccot}(X-1/S)/\pi\), and \[ \begin{split} \mu=2\log(X/Y),\qquad \lambda=2\log(X/Y_p),\\ P(\mu,\lambda)=\max_{D,\ x\le1/2} \{g(x)+m(x,y,z)+\mu y-\lambda z\},\\ Q(\mu,\lambda)=\max_D \{k(x)+m(x,y,z)+\mu y-\lambda z\}. \end{split} \tag{6} \] We prove \[ P(\mu,\lambda)-Q(\mu,\lambda)>1/2500. \tag{7} \] Replacing \(g\) by \(\widetilde g\) in the pure maximum in (6) does not change it. Its maximum is at \((a,b,c)\). These statements and the identification of (3) as the pure seed maximum are proved below. ## 2. Concavity, strict maxima and elementary constants Direct differentiation gives \[ g'=2\log\cot\pi x,\quad g''=-4\pi/\sin(2\pi x),\qquad k'=-\log(2\sin(\pi x/2)),\quad k''=-\frac\pi2\cot(\pi x/2). \tag{8} \] In their open domains both second derivatives are negative. The plateau in \(\widetilde g\) joins \(g\) with derivative zero. It is therefore concave and continuously differentiable on \((0,1/2)\). For \(A+B+C=1\) put \(V(A,B,C)=-\pi[J(A)+J(B)+J(C)]\). On the positive angle triangle its negative Hessian in \(A,B\) is \[ \pi^2\begin{pmatrix} \cot\pi A+\cot\pi C&\cot\pi C\\ \cot\pi C&\cot\pi B+\cot\pi C \end{pmatrix}. \tag{9} \] The diagonal entries are positive and its determinant is \(\pi^4\): use \(\cot\pi A\cot\pi B+\cot\pi B\cot\pi C+ \cot\pi C\cot\pi A=1\). Thus \(V\) is strictly concave inside. For \(p=z-x,q=z-y,r=x+y-z,w=1-x-y\), direct substitution gives \[ \pi m=V(y,x,w)+V(p,q,2r+w)+V(p+q,r,r+w). \tag{10} \] Every triple has nonnegative entries summing to one on \(D\). Continuity proves concavity on all of \(D\). At a strict gate the first atom detects both input variations; with them zero, the second detects the output variation. Hence the full gate Hessian is negative definite at every strict point. We record why constrained maxima used below are strict when required. At a nonvertex flat atom, an inward segment has derivative \(+\infty\), since \(-J(t)=-t\log t+O(t)\) at zero. At a vertex atom the singular terms cancel to a finite derivative: \[ V(t\alpha,t\beta,1-t(\alpha+\beta)) =\pi t[(\alpha+\beta)\log(\alpha+\beta) -\alpha\log\alpha-\beta\log\beta]+O(t^2). \tag{11} \] No atom contributes a negative infinite derivative toward a strict gate. For a fixed output \(0<z<1\), every product face has a nonvertex flat atom: \(w=0\) gives \((y,x,0)\), \(r=0\) gives \((z,0,1-z)\), \(p=0<q\) or \(q=0<p\) gives one zero in the second atom, and \(p=q=0\) gives \((0,z,1-z)\) in the third. An input endpoint either belongs to these faces or gives \((0,z,1-z)\) in the first atom. Each is nonvertex for interior \(z\). The extra leaf terms \(k,\widetilde g\) have no negative infinite inward derivative; at \(y=1/2\), \(\widetilde g\) has positive infinite derivative in the inward direction. Consequently the AC and AA fixed-output maxima are strict and unique: their slices contain a strict point \(x=y\in(z/2,\min(z,1/2))\). Their profiles are continuously differentiable by uniqueness and the envelope formula, including across the continuously differentiable plateau seam. Continuity at endpoint outputs follows by compactness and interpolation with any strict state. The same argument gives unique strict one-variable core responses whenever the fixed \(x,z\) slice contains a strict gate. All numerical constants needed here have short analytic bounds. The series for \(\log((1+t)/(1-t))\), at \(t=1/3\), gives \[ \frac23<\log2< \frac23+\frac23\frac{1/27}{1-1/9} =\frac{25}{36}<\frac7{10}. \tag{12} \] The upper bound replaces every denominator in the tail by \(3\). Alternating arctangent series and \(\arctan(1/2)+\arctan(1/3)=\pi/4\) give \[ \arctan(1/2)>\frac{11}{24},\qquad \pi>4\left(\frac{11}{24}+\frac{26}{81}\right) =\frac{505}{162}>\frac{31}{10}. \tag{13} \] Polynomial division and integration give the independent upper bound \[ 0<\int_0^1\frac{t^4(1-t)^4}{1+t^2}\,dt=\frac{22}{7}-\pi . \tag{14} \] Write \(\operatorname{Ti}(u)=\int_0^u\arctan(t)\,dt/t\). Integration of its alternating series yields \[ \operatorname{Ti}(1/2)>\frac{35}{72},\qquad \operatorname{Ti}(2/3)> \frac23-\frac{(2/3)^3}{9}+\frac{(2/3)^5}{25} -\frac{(2/3)^7}{49} =\frac{1708762}{2679075}. \tag{15} \] Finally, \(k\) has its maximum at \(x=1/3\). Strict concavity of sine on \([0,\pi/6]\) gives \(\sin\pi u>3u\) for \(0<u<1/6\). Therefore \[ J(1/6)>\int_0^{1/6}\log(6u)\,du=-1/6,\qquad \max k<1/3 . \tag{16} \] ## 3. Stationary points and the attachment response At a strict gate let \(U=\cot\pi x,V=\cot\pi y,Z=\cot\pi z\) and \(D_0=1-UV+Z(U+V)\). Sine addition gives \[ e^{m_x}=\frac{(U+V)(U-Z)}{D_0},\quad e^{m_y}=\frac{(U+V)(V-Z)}{D_0},\quad e^{-m_z}=\frac{(U-Z)(V-Z)}{D_0}. \tag{17} \] Here \(U+V,U-Z,V-Z,D_0\) are positive. For (3), \(D_0=X^2\), \(m_x=m_y=-2\log X\), and \(m_z=\lambda\). Thus concavity proves that (3) is the pure two-leaf maximum. The same supporting plane applies to \(\widetilde g\), since \(a\ge1/4\). For the attachment point in (5), take \(U=X,V=B,Z=X-1/S\). Then \[ U+V=S,\quad U-Z=1/S,\quad V-Z=Y^2/S,\quad D_0=X^2 . \tag{18} \] These inequalities give a strict gate, and (17) gives \(m_x=-2\log X,m_y=-\mu,m_z=\lambda\). Concavity proves the assertion about the pure maximum in (6), also with \(\widetilde g\). Notice also \[ |B|<X,\quad B>\frac1{2X}-X,\quad Y_p^2=1+(X-1/S)^2-X^2 . \tag{19} \] The first two follow separately from \(Y<1\) and \(Y_p<1\). We need an explicit inner maximum, including its feasible branch. For any \(p,r>0\), put \(\mu=-2\log p,\lambda=-2\log r\) and \[ F_{\mu,\lambda}(x)=\max_{y,z:(x,y,z)\in D} \{m(x,y,z)+\mu y-\lambda z\}. \tag{20} \] For \(0<x<1\), let \[ A=p^2+r^2+p^2r^2,\quad U=\cot\pi x,\quad D_1=\sqrt{A+(A+1)U^2},\quad T=\frac{p^2(U+D_1)}A,\quad V=T-U,\quad Z=U-\frac{r^2}{p^2}T . \tag{21} \] These formulas give its unique strict maximizer \(y=\operatorname{arccot}V/\pi,z=\operatorname{arccot}Z/\pi\). Here is a direct check of feasibility, rather than a choice of a squared stationary branch. We have \(D_1>|U|\), so \(T>0\) and \(U-Z>0\). Put \(\Gamma=(1+r^2/p^2)T-2U=V-Z\). For \(U\le0\), it is positive immediately. For \(U>0\), write \(s=p^2+r^2,t=p^2r^2\); then \[ s^2D_1^2-(s+2t)^2U^2 =A[s^2+(p^2-r^2)^2U^2]>0 , \tag{22} \] which proves \(\Gamma>0\). The quadratic for \(T\) gives \[ AT^2-2p^2UT-p^4(1+U^2)=0,\qquad D_0=T\Gamma/p^2>0 . \tag{23} \] Thus \(x+y<1,z>x,z>y\); the sine-addition expression for \(D_0\) then gives \(x+y-z>0\). All gate inequalities are strict. Equations (17),(23) give \(e^{m_y}=p^2,e^{-m_z}=r^2\). Strict concavity proves global maximality and uniqueness. The profile is smooth for \(0<x<1\), concave, and continuous at the endpoints by compactness and interpolation. Suppose now \(p,r\ge1\) and \[ p^2<2r,\quad r^2<2p,\quad R=\sqrt{1+p^2+r^2},\quad X=\frac{R-1}{pr}. \tag{24} \] The corresponding pure parameters are \(B=p/r-X,\ C=X-r/p,\ Y=pX,\ Y_p=rX\). Indeed \(pX<1,rX<1\) are exactly the two inequalities in (24). The identity \(1+B^2-X^2=p^2X^2\) and \(X+B=p/r>0\) give the proper identities in (5). Since \(p\ge1\), \(pX<1\) gives \(X<1\); the two inequalities in (19) give \(X>1/2\). At the pure input \(U=X\), (21) gives \(T=p/r\), and \[ \begin{split} T_{UU}&=p^2(A+1)/D_1^3>0,\\ 1-T_U&=\frac{(1+p^2)r(r-pX)}{A-prX}>0,\\ 1-\frac{r^2}{p^2}T_U &=\frac{(1+r^2)p(p-rX)}{A-prX}>0 . \end{split} \tag{25} \] The denominator equals \(prD_1\) at that point and is positive. Since \(T_U\) increases with \(U\), the last two strict inequalities continue to every \(U\le X\). Hence as \(x>a\), the optimized input \(y(x)\) decreases and the optimized output \(z(x)\) increases. For \(a\ge1/4\), \(X=\cot\pi a\le1\), and \[ k'(a)-g'(a)=-\log[2X^2\sin(\operatorname{arccot}X/2)]>0 . \tag{26} \] For example \(2X\sin(\operatorname{arccot}X/2)<1\), as follows by squaring and using \(1+X^2+X\sqrt{1+X^2}>2X^2\); multiplying by \(X\le1\) proves (26). The concave alias profile \(k+F_{\mu,\lambda}\) therefore has its unique global maximum at some \(x_*>a\). It may be an endpoint: (25) still gives, by continuity, \(y_*<b,z_*>c\). Consequently the continuous gap \(\Delta=P-Q\) has envelope derivatives \[ \Delta_\mu=b-y_*>0,\qquad \Delta_\lambda=z_*-c>0 . \tag{27} \] There is no assumption that the full alias maximum is interior. Uniqueness gives the envelope formula even at an endpoint: compare the value at the old maximizer with the new maximum and pass to the limit using compactness. The same argument gives continuity of these derivatives. The inequalities in (24) imply \(1\le p,r<2\). Increase the smaller of \(p,r\) until they agree, then increase both to \(2\). For instance, if \(p\ge r\), increasing \(r\) to \(p\) preserves \(p^2<2r\), while \(r^2\le p^2<2p\). The balanced path is proper until its limiting endpoint. Moreover \[ X_p=\frac{pX-r}{p^2R}<0,\qquad X_r=\frac{rX-p}{r^2R}<0 . \tag{28} \] Each increase decreases \(\mu\) or \(\lambda\), so (27) decreases the gap. Continuity of the maxima on their compact domains proves \[ \Delta(p,r)\ge\Delta(2,2). \tag{29} \] In particular a starting condition \(X\le2/3\) is preserved. For the actual proper attachment with \(X\le2/3\), (19) gives \(Y,Y_p>X\), so \(p=Y/X,r=Y_p/X>1\), and (24) applies. ## 4. An analytic corner bound At \(p=r=2\), let \(\ell=\log2\) and \[ F(x)=\max_{y,z:(x,y,z)\in D} \{m(x,y,z)-\log4\,y+\log4\,z\}, \qquad a_0=\arctan(2)/\pi . \tag{30} \] The involution \((x,y,z)\mapsto(x,1-z,1-y)\) preserves \(D\), \(m\), and the displayed linear term, by \(J(1-t)=-J(t)\). Uniqueness of the inner maximum therefore gives \(z=1-y\). Writing \(U=\cot\pi x,D_2=\sqrt{24+25U^2}\), its stationary equation and profile derivative are \[ B=\cot\pi y=\frac{D_2-5U}{6},\qquad F'(x)=f(U)=\log\frac{2(D_2+U)}{D_2-5U}. \tag{31} \] These also follow by setting \(p=r=2\) in (21). Thus \(F'(a_0)=\log4,F'(1/2)=\ell\). Direct differentiation gives \[ h(U)=(1+U^2)f_U=U+\frac{6+5U^2}{D_2},\qquad h'(U)=1+\frac{90U+125U^3}{D_2^3}>0\quad(U\ge0). \tag{32} \] Hence \(F'''(x)=\pi^2(1+U^2)h'(U)>0\) on \([a_0,1/2]\). The derivative \(F'\) is convex there, so its integral lies below its endpoint trapezoid: \[ F(1/2)-F(a_0)\le(1/2-a_0)\frac32\ell . \tag{33} \] The global concave tangent of \(F\) at \(1/2\) gives \[ Q(-\log4,-\log4) \le F(1/2)-\ell/2+\max_{0\le x\le1}\{k(x)+\ell x\} =F(1/2)+\ell/2 . \tag{34} \] The last maximum is \(\ell\): its derivative is \(-\log\sin(\pi x/2)\ge0\), and \(k(1)=0\). The pure maximum is \(g(a_0)+F(a_0)\), since \(g'(a_0)+F'(a_0)=-\log4+\log4=0\) and both terms are concave. For use here and below, integration of \(g'\), with \(g(1/2)=0\), gives, for \(u=\cot\pi a\), \[ g(a)=\frac2\pi[\operatorname{Ti}(u)-\arctan(u)\log u], \quad g(a)+(1-a)g'(a)=\frac2\pi\operatorname{Ti}(u)+\log u . \tag{35} \] Indeed substitute \(a=1/2-\arctan(u)/\pi\) and integrate by parts. Since \(a_0=1/2-\arctan(1/2)/\pi\), (33)--(35) give \[ \begin{split} \Delta(2,2)&\ge g(a_0)-(5/4-3a_0/2)\ell\\ &=\frac{4\operatorname{Ti}(1/2) -(\pi-\arctan(1/2))\ell}{2\pi}\\ &>\frac{329}{5040}\frac7{44} =\frac{2303}{221760}>\frac1{100}. \end{split} \tag{36} \] For the numerator use (12)--(15): \(35/18-(22/7-11/24)(7/10)=329/5040\). Equations (29),(36) prove the attachment assertion for \(X\le2/3\). ## 5. The analytic large-\(X\) attachment bound For \(1/4\le a<1/2\) define the whole-interval deficit \[ I(a)=\min_{0\le u\le1}\{g(a)+g'(a)(u-a)-k(u)\}. \tag{37} \] Put \(a_*=\arctan\sqrt2/\pi\). For \(a\ge a_*\), \(g'(a)\le-\log2=k'(1)\), so the minimum is at \(u=1\), and \(I(a)=g(a)+(1-a)g'(a)\). For \(1/4\le a\le a_*\) the minimizer is \[ u(a)=\frac2\pi\arcsin\frac{\tan^2(\pi a)}2 . \tag{38} \] It exceeds \(a\). To see this, put \(t=\pi a\): the needed inequality is \(\tan^2t>2\sin(t/2)\). It holds at \(\pi/4\); its derivative \(2\tan t\sec^2t-\cos(t/2)\) is positive thereafter. The envelope derivative is therefore \(I'(a)=g''(a)(u(a)-a)<0\). On the other branch it is \((1-a)g''(a)<0\). Thus \(I\) decreases throughout the relevant interval. For \(X\ge2/3\), \(a=\operatorname{arccot}X/\pi\) lies between \(1/4\) and \(\operatorname{arccot}(2/3)/\pi>a_*\). Using (35), (15), and \(\pi<22/7\), we obtain \[ I(a)\ge \frac2\pi\operatorname{Ti}(2/3)-\log(3/2) >\frac7{11}\frac{1708762}{2679075}-\frac{177391}{437500} =\frac{57269}{136687500}>\frac1{2500}. \tag{39} \] The logarithm bound here is elementary: \[ \log(3/2)\le 2\left(\frac15+\frac1{3\cdot5^3}+\frac1{5\cdot5^5}\right) +\frac2{7\cdot5^7(1-1/25)} =\frac{177391}{437500}. \tag{40} \] It is the positive logarithmic series at \(1/5\), with all remaining denominators replaced by \(7\). Add the tangent plane of \(m\) at the strict pure point to \(k(x)\le g(a)+g'(a)(x-a)-I(a)\). The \(x,y,z\) coefficients cancel by (18). This proves \(Q\le P-I(a)\), and hence (7) for the remaining parameters. The attachment proof is complete on (5). ## 6. Seed gaps increase with the output slope For \(0<b<1\), define the fixed-output profiles \[ H_{AC}(b)=\max_{D,\ z=b,\ y\le1/2}\{k(x)+\widetilde g(y)+m\}, \qquad H_{AA}(b)=\max_{D,\ z=b}\{k(x)+k(y)+m\}. \tag{41} \] Their strictness, uniqueness, continuous derivatives and endpoint continuity were proved using the atoms in Section 2. In the AC fixed-output problem, fix \(x=a\) first. Its unique maximizing core input is \(y=a\), by the pure stationary equations and concavity. The derivative of the resulting optimized \(x\) profile there is \(k'(a)+m_x=k'(a)-g'(a)>0\), by (26). Concavity therefore puts its maximizing alias input strictly above \(a\). For AA, symmetry and uniqueness give equal maximizing inputs. The derivative along their diagonal at \(a\) is \(2(k'(a)-g'(a))>0\), so their common value also exceeds \(a\). Here is the full AC response calculation, including the plateau. Fix \(Z=\cot\pi b\), optimize the core input \(y\), and put \(U=\cot\pi x,V=\cot\pi y\). On the \(g\) branch, \(g'(y)+m_y=0\) and (17) give \[ D_0=V^2,\qquad U=\frac1{V-Z}-V,\qquad m_z=\log\frac{V^2}{1+Z^2-V^2}. \tag{42} \] For example the stationary equation factors by \(1+V^2\); it is equivalent to \((U+V)(V-Z)=1\). Here \(dU/dV=-1/(V-Z)^2-1<0\), while \(m_z\) strictly increases with \(V>0\) on its feasible branch. On the plateau, \(m_y=0\). With \(w=V-Z>0\), it gives \[ D_0=(1+V^2)/2,\quad U=\frac{1+Z^2-w^2}{2w},\quad \frac{dU}{dV}=-\frac{1+Z^2}{2w^2}-\frac12<0,\quad m_z=\log\frac{1+V^2}{1+2Z^2-V^2}. \tag{43} \] The last slope again strictly increases with \(V\). Indeed \(2U(V-Z)=1+2VZ-V^2\) derives the middle formula directly. At a feasible seam \(V=1\), both (42),(43) give \(U=Z/(1-Z)\) and the same output slope. Uniqueness and these derivatives continue the response from the pure input to the alias optimum. Increasing \(x\) decreases \(U\), increases \(V\), and strictly increases \(m_z\). Consequently \(H_{AC}'(b)>\lambda\). For AA the maximizing inputs are equal. At fixed \(Z\), \[ m_z=\log(2UZ-U^2+1)-2\log(U-Z),\qquad \frac{\partial m_z}{\partial U} =-\frac{2(1+Z^2)}{(2UZ-U^2+1)(U-Z)}<0 . \tag{44} \] Its maximizing input exceeds \(a\), so \(H_{AA}'(b)>\lambda\) as well. These arguments require only strict fixed-output maxima; they make no interior assumption about later conjugate maxima. Let \(A_J(\lambda)=\max_{0\le z\le1}\{H_J(z)-\lambda z\}\) for \(J=AC,AA\). Concavity and the strict derivative inequality at the pure output \(b(\lambda)\) imply that every maximizing output of \(A_J\) is greater than \(b(\lambda)\), including when that maximum occurs at \(1\). The conjugates are Lipschitz. At almost every slope their derivatives are \(-z_J(\lambda)\), where \(z_J\) is a maximizing output; this follows by comparing maximizers at nearby slopes and using compactness. Since \(P_2'(\lambda)=-b(\lambda)\), their gaps obey \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda}(P_2-A_J) =z_J(\lambda)-b(\lambda)>0 \quad\hbox{almost everywhere}. \tag{45} \] Lipschitz continuity and integration prove that both gaps are nondecreasing on the entire closed slope interval. It remains to bound them at \(\lambda=-\log4\). ## 7. The two seed endpoints At that endpoint \(a=a_0=\arctan2/\pi\), and the pure output is \(1-a_0\). The tangent of \(\widetilde g\) at \(a_0\) has slope \(-\log4\). Thus the AC conjugate is at most \[ g(a_0)+a_0\log4+Q(-\log4,-\log4), \tag{46} \] whereas \(P_2=g(a_0)+a_0\log4+P(-\log4,-\log4)\). The AC endpoint gap is therefore greater than \(1/100\) by (36). For AA, symmetry and concavity allow its two inputs to be equal: averaging them cannot decrease either the two \(k\) terms or \(m\). Write \[ F_2(s)=\max_z\{m(s,s,z)+\log4\,z\},\qquad 0\le s\le1/2. \tag{47} \] For \(0<s<1/2\), set \(U=\cot\pi s>0,D_3=\sqrt{1+5U^2}\). The unique feasible critical branch and its derivatives are \[ Z=\cot\pi z=5U-2D_3,\qquad F_2'(s)=2\log\frac{4U}{D_3-2U},\qquad F_2''(s)=-2\pi\left(\frac1U+\frac2{D_3}\right). \tag{48} \] Indeed \(m_z=-\log4\) is the quadratic \(Z^2-10UZ+5U^2-4=0\); only its displayed root has \(Z<U\). It has \(U-Z>0,D_0=(U-Z)^2/4>0\), proving every strict gate inequality. Differentiating the inner logarithm gives \(1/[UD_3(D_3-2U)]\), which proves (48). The pure value is \(P_2=2g(a_0)+F_2(a_0)\). The concave AA profile \(2k+F_2\) has positive derivative at \(a_0\), by (26), so its global maximum has \(s>a_0\). On that interval \(U\le1/2\), and (48) gives \(F_2''\le-4\pi\). Since \(F_2'(a_0)=4\log2\), continuity at \(s=1/2\) yields \[ F_2(s)\le F_2(a_0)+4\ell(s-a_0)-2\pi(s-a_0)^2 \le F_2(a_0)+2\ell^2/\pi . \tag{49} \] Using (16), the AA endpoint gap is strictly greater than \(2g(a_0)-2/3-2\ell^2/\pi\). The elementary bounds in Section 2 give \[ g(a_0)>\frac7{11} \left(\frac{35}{72}+\frac{11}{24}\frac23\right) =\frac{133}{264},\qquad \frac{2\ell^2}{\pi}<\frac{49}{155}. \tag{50} \] Consequently \[ P_2(-\log4)-A_{AA}(-\log4)> \frac{133}{132}-\frac23-\frac{49}{155} =\frac{169}{6820}>\frac1{100}. \tag{51} \] Equations (45),(46),(51) prove both seed assertions (4). ## 8.
