Its knot-volume consequence is restricted to graphs and markings coming from the original ordered circle-tree construction. An arbitrary graph sum is not declared to be a knot invariant. Frozen manuscripts and public documentation are unchanged. ## 1. The source and the statement Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless graph, allowing repeated edges. Choose a nonempty set \(I\subseteq V\), and let \(d_v\ge1\) be the original incidence degree of each \(v\in I\), including edges to unselected vertices and all multiplicities. Suppose the fixed integers \(n_v\) obey \[ |n_v|\ge\max\{8,4d_v\}. 	ag{1} \] Unselected angles are zero. With the original Newton kernel, crossing and full Hermite trace, define \[ Z_{\Gamma,I,N}= \left(\prod_{v\in I}\phi_N^{(t_v)}R(t_v)^{n_v}ight) \prod_{\{v,w\}\in E}K_N(t_v,t_w), \qquad t_w=0\quad(w
otin I). 	ag{2} \] This notation means that all edge factors are multiplied before taking the traces. Only traced variables are reduced; any unselected variables retain the literal polynomial representative in (2). Every shared edge occurs once, and every first normal at a double spectral root is retained. Use the calibrated edge phase and amplitude \(\psi,a_e\) of [the full wide-rectangle theorem](research_bare_kernel_thin_rectangle.md#6-the-full-rectangle-through-real-angle-pi-over-two). Thus \(\psi(0,0)=M_\infty=4G/\pi\). Put \[ \Phi_\lambda(t)=\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E}\psi(t_v,t_w) +\sum_{v\in I} rac{i n_vt_v^2}{4\pi} -i\sum_{v\in I}\lambda_vt_v, \qquad \Phi=\Phi_{\mathbf1}. 	ag{3} \] Complete edges outside the selected set remain in this sum; they contribute their original constant. **Theorem 1.** Under (1), \(\Phi\) has a unique critical point \(t^*\) in the box \(|\Re t_v|\le1,|\Im t_v|\le1/3\). It satisfies \[ |t_v^*|<9/10,\qquad 0<-\Im t_v^*<3/10, \qquad \operatorname{sgn}\Re t_v^*=\operatorname{sgn}n_v. 	ag{4} \] Write \(m=|I|\), \(e=|E|\), and \(\mathcal H=-\Phi''(t^*)\), with derivatives only in selected variables. Along all integer levels, \[ Z_{\Gamma,I,N}= \left(\prod_{v\in I}e^{\pi i n_v(N-1)^2/(4N)}ight) N^{3(m-e)/2}\mathcal A_{\Gamma,I} e^{N\Phi(t^*)}(1+O(N^{-1})), 	ag{5} \] where \[ \mathcal A_{\Gamma,I}= \left( rac{i}{\pi}ight)^m(2\pi)^{m/2}  rac{\displaystyle\prod_{v\in I}\sin t_v^* \prod_{\{v,w\}\in E}a_e(t_v^*,t_w^*)} {\sqrt{\det\mathcal H}}
e0. 	ag{6} \] The square root is the Gaussian branch for matrices with positive Hermitian real part. The expansion continues to every fixed inverse power of \(N\). It extends holomorphically to a neighborhood of the complete unselected colors, with all fixed ordinary spectral derivatives. Constants may depend on the fixed graph and powers; there is no claim about a simultaneous growth of the graph with \(N\). ## 2. The complete charge cube on a branching graph For an oriented incidence put \[ r_{vw}(t)=\operatorname{asinh} \{	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)\}. 	ag{7} \] All branches are continued from zero. The exact equations are \[ n_vt_v+2i\sum_{w\sim v}r_{vw}=2\pi\lambda_v. 	ag{8} \] Multiplicity is retained in the sum. The following argument uses only local degrees, not the order of vertices on a path. On \(\mathcal B=\{z:|\Re z|\le1,|\Im z|\le1/3\}\), the elementary calculations in Section 2 of [the partial-charge proof](research_positive_path_partial_charge_bounds.md#2-the-exact-return-map-is-a-contraction) give \[  egin{split} |	an(z/2)|&<3/5,& |\Im	an(z/2)|&<1/4,\ |\Re r_{vw}|&<123/200,&|\Im r_{vw}|&<7/20,\ |K_{vv}|+|K_{vw}|&<86/45,&|K_{vv}-1|&<2/5, \end{split} 	ag{9} \] where \(K=-2\pi\psi''\). These are estimates for one edge on the displayed box. They do not assume a source expansion or an existence theorem for this graph. Rewrite (8) as \[ \mathcal T_v(t)= rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{n_v} - rac{2i}{n_v}\sum_{w\sim v}r_{vw}(t). 	ag{10} \] For real \(\lambda\in[-1,1]^I\), (1) and (9) give \[ |\Re\mathcal T_v|<\pi/4+7/40<1, \qquad |\Im\mathcal T_v|<123/400<1/3. 	ag{11} \] The derivatives of one return are \(\partial_{t_v}r_{vw}=K_{vv}/2\) and \(\partial_{t_w}r_{vw}=K_{vw}/2\). Therefore the supremum-norm Jacobian row bound is \[  rac{d_v}{|n_v|} rac{86}{45} \le rac{43}{90}< rac12. 	ag{12} \] Repeated neighbors merely add their incidences to this row; complete outside variables contribute no derivative columns. Banach's theorem on the finite product box proves existence and uniqueness. It also proves a common holomorphic extension to charges within \(1/100\) of \([-1,1]^I\): the two bounds in (11) increase by at most \(\pi/400\), still inside the box, and (12) is unchanged. The removable quotient \[ Q_v=\sum_{w\sim v} rac{r_{vw}}{t_v} = rac12\sum_{w\sim v}\int_0^1 K_{vv}(\sigma t_v,t_w)\,d\sigma \] obeys \(|Q_v-d_v/2|<d_v/5\). Thus the exact equation factors as \[ t_v= rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{n_v+2iQ_v}. 	ag{13} \] For \(0\le\lambda_v\le1\), zero charge gives exactly zero angle. At positive charge the real angle has the sign of \(n_v\), while its imaginary part is negative. Also \[ |t_v|\le rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{|n_v|-2d_v/5} \le rac{5\pi}{18}\lambda_v< rac9{10}. 	ag{14} \] Write \(H_v=-\Im t_v\). The same quotient gives the componentwise bound \[ 0\le H_v\le U_{|n_v|,d_v}\lambda_v, \qquad U_{n,d}=  rac{14\pi d/5}{(n-2d/5)^2+(7d/5)^2}. 	ag{15} \] Indeed, for \(Q_v=A+iB\), \(H_v=4\pi\lambda_vA/[(n_v-2B)^2+4A^2]\). On \(3d/10<A<7d/10,|B|<d/5\), its maximum is at the upper \(A\)-corner and the \(B\)-corner with the sign of \(n_v\). The required monotonicity uses \(|n_v|>9d_v/5\), which follows from (1). For \(d\ge2\), the worst allowed power is \(n=4d\), and \(U_{n,d}\le70\pi/(373d)\). For \(d=1\), use \(n\ge8\) to obtain \(U_{n,1}\le70\pi/1493\). Consequently \[ U_{n,d}\le rac{35\pi}{373}< rac3{10}, \qquad  rac{U_{n,d}}{2d}\le rac{35\pi}{1492}< rac3{40}. 	ag{16} \] These prove (4), throughout the entire nonnegative charge cube. Let \(M(\lambda)=\Re\Phi_\lambda(t(\lambda))\). Stationarity gives \(\partial_{\lambda_v}M=-H_v\). For \(0\le\lambda\le\mu\le1\), integrate (15) to obtain \[ 0\le M(\lambda)-M(\mu) \le rac12\sum_v U_{|n_v|,d_v}(\mu_v^2-\lambda_v^2) < rac3{40}\sum_vd_v(\mu_v^2-\lambda_v^2) 	ag{17} \] when at least one coordinate changes. In particular, completing a set of selected vertices costs less than \(3/40\) per incidence. The vertices and all their original edges stay in the graph; only their charges and angles are set to zero. ## 3. Every mixed vertical current Choose the largest physical midpoint \(T_N\le\pi/2\). For all sufficiently large levels, \(3/2\le T_N\le\pi/2\). At a horizontal vertex use \(t_v=x_v-iH_v\), \(-T_N\le x_v\le T_N\). At a vertical vertex use \(t_v=\sigma_v T_N+ih_v\), \(-H_v\le h_v\le H_v\), where \(\sigma_v=\operatorname{sgn}n_v\). For a vertical subset \(J\), the exact exponential modulus is \[ \mathcal E_J= \Re\left\{\sum_e\psi(t_v,t_w)+ \sum_{v\in I} rac{i n_vt_v^2}{4\pi}ight\} -\sum_{v
otin J}H_v-\sum_{v\in J}|h_v|. 	ag{18} \] The degree sum is taken over the original graph even after some coordinates have been completed. Hold the other coordinates fixed. At a vertical vertex, \[ \partial_{h_v}\mathcal E_J = rac1\pi\sum_{w\sim v}\Im r_{vw} - rac{|n_v|T_N}{2\pi}-\operatorname{sign}h_v. 	ag{19} \] This is the derivative of the original phase and its folded vertical trace penalty. No Fourier coefficient has been discarded. The one-edge estimates in the [vertical-current proof](research_path_mixed_trace_currents.md#9-vertical-current-monotonicity-at-powers-of-at-least-seven) apply with either sign of \(\sigma_v\). For \(h_v\le0\), \(\Im	an(t_v/2)\le0\), \(|\Re	an(t_v/2)|\le1\), \(\Re\cos(t_w/2)>7/10\), and \(|\Im\cos(t_w/2)|<4/35\). A positive imaginary return therefore satisfies \(\Im r_{vw}<5/42\). The asinh argument stays in the right half-plane for \(\sigma_v=1\) and the left half-plane for \(\sigma_v=-1\); the original branch has \(|\Im r|<\pi/2\) in either case. For \(h_v<0\) and \(d_v\ge2\), equations (1) and (19) give \[ \partial_{h_v}\mathcal E_J \le1+ rac{5d_v}{42\pi}- rac{3d_v}{\pi} =1- rac{121d_v}{42\pi}<- rac56<- rac45. 	ag{20} \] For \(d_v=1\), use \(|n_v|\ge8\) to bound it by \(1-247/(42\pi)<-4/5\). For \(h_v>0\), the bound \(\Im r<\pi/2\) gives \[ \partial_{h_v}\mathcal E_J <d_v/2-3d_v/\pi-1<-1. 	ag{21} \] Both one-sided comparisons hold at zero. Thus each vertical height can be decreased to its bottom endpoint, with a loss of at least \((4/5)(h_v+H_v)\) in the original direction of integration. This estimate is valid while other vertices lie anywhere on their horizontal or vertical segments. On the whole wide rectangle the phase-only edge Hessian obeys \(\Re[-2\pi\psi'']\succeq I_2/10\). Summing it over edges gives, at every bottom horizontal point, \[ \Re\Phi(\mathbf x-i\mathbf H) \le M(\mathbf1)- rac1{40\pi} \sum_{v\in I}d_v(x_v-\Re t_v^*)^2. 	ag{22} \] For a vertical vertex, \(|\sigma_vT_N-\Re t_v^*|>3/5\), by (14). Combining (19)–(22) proves, for every nonempty \(J\), \[ \mathcal E_J<M(\mathbf1)- rac1{400}\sum_{v\in J}d_v - rac45\sum_{v\in J}(h_v+H_v). 	ag{23} \] The same proof applies to any partial-charge source whose nonzero charges are one. Zero-charge vertices are fixed at zero, with all incident edge factors retained. No estimate introduces a factor proportional to the total number of vertices. ## 4. The exact finite trace and its discarded rows Apply the original derivative-sampling formula (12) and midpoint identity (13) of [the path-source assembly](research_uniform_path_trace_assembly.md#3-a-nonzero-coefficient-in-the-original-trace) to each selected variable. These are one-variable identities in the full Frobenius algebra and place no restriction on its degree in the graph. Interchanging them is an operation on finitely many sums and ordinary derivatives. For the retained rows, the identity is a sum over every subset of vertical vertices. A negative-side vertical contour retains its extra factor \(-1\); the exact sign of a subset is their product. The lower horizontal factor always has principal charge \(+1\), with coefficient exactly one, for either sign of the crossing power. The full wide-kernel theorem converts (23) into a bound for these actual finite integrands and all their original normals. The all-horizontal phase has its unique maximum at \(t^*\) and \[ \Re\mathcal H\succeq  rac1{20\pi}\operatorname{diag}(d_v)>0. 	ag{24} \] At each fixed graph all positive depths \(H_v\) are fixed. The higher charges of the rational trace denominators are therefore exponentially smaller. The original edge amplitudes and sine factors are nonzero at the saddle. The Gaussian calculation is exactly (6): there are \(N^{2m}\) from the trace prefactors, \(N^{-3e/2}\) from all original edges, and \(N^{-m/2}\) from the Gaussian. This gives the power in (5), with no new normalization depending on the degree. Odd Gaussian moments vanish, giving the stated \(O(N^{-1})\) error and all further fixed orders. It remains to retain the rows outside the midpoint interval. Let \(S
e\varnothing\) be the set of vertices at those physical rows. Keep their exact crossing values and first normals, and set their analytic charges to zero. The full centered-incidence bounds in Section 8 of the [mixed-current note](research_path_mixed_trace_currents.md#8-a-stronger-centered-loss-for-a-removed-incidence) give an exponent loss \(21/200\) for each incidence at a removed vertex. An edge with both endpoints removed retains both losses. The comparisons hold for all ordinary mixed spectral derivatives. Their strict reserve permits the \(O(N^{-1})\) midpoint change from \(\pi/2\), at both parities. For the remaining exact traces choose the stationary heights of the partial-charge solution. Their exponents are the original partial-charge phase, with the removed coordinates zero, minus \((21/200)\sum_{v\in S}d_v\). The wide-kernel theorem and (23) apply to all of their horizontal and vertical terms. The crossing values at removed real rows have modulus one; their derivatives and all finite sampling weights cost powers of \(N\) only. Distributing a first normal over arbitrarily many incident factors is a finite product-rule expansion at a fixed graph. It changes polynomial prefactors, not exponential rates. By (17), the rate of the entire outside-row contribution is \[ <M(\mathbf1) -\left( rac{21}{200}- rac3{40}ight) \sum_{v\in S}d_v =M(\mathbf1)- rac3{100}\sum_{v\in S}d_v. 	ag{25} \] If no trace remains, the same comparison retains the complete-edge constants and needs no integral. There are finitely many subsets and product-rule terms, so none can cancel the leading Gaussian. This proves (5) for the complete outside colors. The removed-incidence lemma already controls its other endpoint throughout the complex wide rectangle. It therefore applies directly to a small complex perturbation of an unselected angle near zero; no inference from bounds only at its physical values is needed. On every retained edge the full kernel bound and phase are holomorphic on a fixed neighborhood of the contour. All the current and removed-row comparisons have strict gaps, and there are finitely many subsets for the fixed graph. A sufficiently small outside neighborhood preserves them, while the implicit function theorem continues each required stationary point inside the local kernel domain. The holomorphic Gaussian expansion follows there. Separate evenness descends the phases, amplitudes and normalized errors to ordinary spectral colors near the ramified complete point; Cauchy's estimates then give all asserted ordinary outside derivatives. This completes the analytic proof of Theorem 1. \(\square\) ## 5. The original circle-tree geometry Now suppose \(\Gamma\), its page ordering and carriers arise from an original ordered circle-tree exterior. Retain its disk longitudes, meridians, every main component and every marked annular interface. Choose the original integer fillings \(p_v\) with \[ n_v=\eta_v-2p_v 	ag{26} \] satisfying (1). The angle solution just constructed supplies the hypotheses of [the positive marked-completion theorem](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md). To see positivity directly, put \(w_v=	an(t_v^*/2)\). By (9), the sum of squared imaginary parts at either edge is less than \(1/8\). On the branch \(q_e=\sqrt{1+w_v^2+w_w^2}\), \[ (\Re q_e)^2\ge 1+(\Re w_v)^2+(\Re w_w)^2 -(\Im w_v)^2-(\Im w_w)^2 >(\Re w_v)^2+(\Re w_w)^2. 	ag{27} \] This is positivity of all eight original tetrahedra on that edge. The selected heights are strictly negative, and (8) at unit charge is exactly the original full logarithmic period equation \(\sum r_{vw}=i n_vt_v/2-\pi i\). There is no change of peripheral basis or replacement of a slope by its absolute value. The marked-completion theorem therefore proves \[ \operatorname{Vol}Y(\mathbf p) =2\pi\Re\Phi(t^*). 	ag{28} \] Every main cusp and unselected auxiliary cusp remains complete. **Corollary 2.** If all auxiliary vertices are filled, the original strand tracing gives one main component and no internal closed component, and (1), (26) hold, the resulting knot satisfies the original full-level Kashaev volume conjecture: \[ \lim_{N	o\infty} rac{2\pi}{N} \log|\langle Kangle_N| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). 	ag{29} \] Its complete asymptotic has the nonzero leading coefficient (6), with only the already retained unit carrier and zero-framing factors. This conclusion uses the original circle-tree source identification and the literal component test. No knot interpretation is attached to an arbitrary graph in the analytic theorem. It also does not imply finite exceptions in every original parameter template: assignments with a short power at a fixed vertex remain outside (1), even when other powers grow without bound. The scalar margins are reproduced by [check_degree_controlled_network_source.py](../experiments/check_degree_controlled_network_source.py), with the [saved record](../repro/results/research-degree-controlled-network-source.json). These exact checks verify constants used above; the graph-independent source decomposition and the marked geometry have written proofs.

title: Dimension independent covariance and stable fixed-degree extraction
text: # Dimension independent covariance and stable fixed-degree extraction Private written proof, 23 November 2026. The existing positive Conway recursion has a stronger covariance estimate when the full tensor normalization is used. Its covariance lies between \(\varepsilon I\) and \(2\varepsilon I\) for every \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), independently of the physical dimension and tree size. Fixed-degree extraction can consequently use evaluation points independent of \(N\), with uniformly conditioned full messages. Chebyshev--Lobatto points also reduce its absolute extrapolation amplification to less than four, independently of the number of leaves. The original complex source, closing row and budget remain unchanged. These are bounds for the auxiliary evaluation and extraction, not relative-precision bounds for an exponentially small selected scalar. ## 1. The full normalized tensors Use the complete literal expression tree in [C] and positive recursion in [P]. At level \(N\ge2\), every boundary is the full \(N\)-dimensional Newton space \(H_N\), with its fixed coefficient Hermitian metric. Repeated-root value and derivative directions are both retained. Write \[ \sigma=\frac1{16},\qquad b_v=16\max(1,\|T_v\|_{\mathrm{HS}}),\qquad B_N=\prod_vb_v\ge1 . \tag{1} \] The budgets include the actual root tensor. Let the normalized leaf vectors be \(a_v\), unary maps \(A_v\), product maps \(M_v\), and original closing row \(L\). The true normalized packets obey \[ a_v=A_va_c\ \text{or}\ M_v(a_l\otimes a_r),\qquad \|a_v\|\le\sigma,\quad\|A_v\|\le\sigma,\quad\|L\|\le\sigma, \qquad B_NLa_{\mathrm{top}}=K_N . \tag{2} \] Here \(K_N\) is the original reduced marked invariant, including its recorded phases, powers of \(N\), and framing normalization. The point needed below is stronger than a bound only on decomposable bilinear inputs. Normalization (1) gives \[ \|M_v:H_N\otimes H_N\longrightarrow H_N\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le\|M_v\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\sigma . \tag{3} \] Indeed the Hilbert--Schmidt norm in [C] sums every coefficient of the full tensor. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds its linearization on the whole Hilbert tensor product by that same norm. For real \(\varepsilon>0\), keep exactly the deterministic recursion \[ \begin{array}{ll} S_v=a_va_v^\dagger+\varepsilon I,&v\text{ a leaf},\\ S_v=A_vS_cA_v^\dagger+\varepsilon I,&v\text{ unary},\\ S_v=M_v(S_l\otimes S_r)M_v^\dagger+\varepsilon I, &v\text{ binary}, \end{array} \qquad F_N(\varepsilon)=B_N^2LS_{\mathrm{top}}L^\dagger . \tag{4} \] There is no fresh error at the closing root. All adjoints use the full original normalized maps, not separate absolute coefficients. Only the leaf vectors are needed to evaluate (4); the true internal packets enter the covariance proof, not its input data. ## 2. A covariance bound in operator order Set \(V_v=S_v-a_va_v^\dagger\). Expanding (4), or using its independent centered errors, gives exactly \[ \begin{array}{ll} V_v=\varepsilon I,&v\text{ a leaf},\\ V_v=A_vV_cA_v^\dagger+\varepsilon I,&v\text{ unary},\\ V_v=M_v(a_la_l^\dagger\otimes V_r+ V_l\otimes a_ra_r^\dagger+V_l\otimes V_r)M_v^\dagger +\varepsilon I,&v\text{ binary}. \end{array} \tag{5} \] Every term is positive semidefinite. Thus the covariance and its lower floor are genuine matrix statements, with all cross-channel coherence retained. For every \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), induction proves \[ \boxed{\quad \varepsilon I\preceq V_v\preceq2\varepsilon I,\qquad \varepsilon I\preceq S_v \preceq(\sigma^2+2\varepsilon)I . \quad} \tag{6} \] The leaf case is exact. The unary upper bound is \((1+2\sigma^2)\varepsilon I\prec2\varepsilon I\). At a binary vertex use (3) and the induction hypothesis in (5): \[ V_v\preceq \{\varepsilon+4\sigma^4\varepsilon +4\sigma^2\varepsilon^2\}I \preceq\varepsilon(1+4\sigma^4+4\sigma^2)I \prec2\varepsilon I . \tag{7} \] This closes without multiplying a constant for the number of vertices. The second assertion of (6) follows from \(\|a_v\|\le\sigma\). In particular \[ \operatorname{cond}_2S_v(\varepsilon) \le2+\sigma^2/\varepsilon . \tag{8} \] At \(\varepsilon=1\), this is \(2+\sigma^2\), independent of both \(N\) and the tree. The trace need not be dimension independent: the fresh floor has trace \(N\varepsilon\). Bounding the operator covariance rather than its trace removes that unnecessary factor from the original rank-one closing observation. ## 3. The calibrated additive error At the unchanged closing, \[ \varepsilon B_N^2\|L\|^2 \le F_N(\varepsilon)-|K_N|^2 =B_N^2LV_{\mathrm{top}}L^\dagger \le2\varepsilon B_N^2\|L\|^2 . \tag{9} \] For \(0<\theta\le1\), the improved choice \(\varepsilon=\theta/B_N^2\le1\) therefore gives \[ 0\le F_N(\theta/B_N^2)-|K_N|^2 \le\theta/128 . \tag{10} \] The earlier trace proof used \(\theta/(NB_N^2)\) for this same additive bound. The new choice removes \(N\), but can still be exponentially small because the known budget \(B_N\) can be large. The fixed-degree extraction below does not require that small choice. If errors are added only at leaves, omit the internal \(\varepsilon I\) in (5). The same induction gives \(0\preceq V_v\preceq\varepsilon I\), because its binary upper bound is \(\sigma^2(2\sigma^2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)I \preceq\varepsilon I\). The resulting closing error at \(\theta/B_N^2\) is at most \(\theta/256\). Internal matrices in this leaf-only version may be singular; the conditioning guarantee (8) uses fresh errors at every proper vertex. ## 4. Fixed evaluation points with bounded extrapolation cost Let \(l\ge1\) be the number of leaf occurrences. The existing positive-coefficient induction in [P] gives \[ F_N(\varepsilon)=|K_N|^2+ \sum_{j=1}^{l}c_{N,j}\varepsilon^j,\qquad c_{N,j}\ge0 . \tag{11} \] This degree counts auxiliary errors, not physical colors. The interpolation identities below are standard polynomial identities; the new input is (6), which permits constant evaluation points with conditioning independent of \(N\). For example, equally spaced points \(j/(l+1)\), \(1\le j\le l+1\), already give the existing forward-difference formula with weights \((-1)^{j-1}\binom{l+1}{j}\). Equation (8) improves their message condition bound to \(2+\sigma^2(l+1)\). Their absolute weight sum is \(2^{l+1}-1\). A better choice for absolute extraction is \[ \begin{gathered} a=(l+1)^{-2},\qquad x_j=\cos(j\pi/l),\\ \varepsilon_j=(1+a)/2+(1-a)x_j/2,\quad 0\le j\le l,\qquad x_*=-\frac{1+a}{1-a},\\ w_j=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{x_*-x_k}{x_j-x_k}. \end{gathered} \tag{12} \] The nodes are distinct and lie in \([a,1]\); zero corresponds to \(x_*\). Lagrange interpolation of the polynomial (11) proves \[ \boxed{\quad |K_N|^2=\sum_{j=0}^{l}w_jF_N(\varepsilon_j),\qquad \operatorname{cond}_2 S_v(\varepsilon_j) \le2+\sigma^2(l+1)^2 .\quad} \tag{13} \] There is no \(N\)-dependent or budget-dependent evaluation point. All matrices still have their full physical dimension \(N\). For completeness, the absolute amplification has an explicit bound. Since \(x_j\) decrease and \(x_*<-1\), the numerator in \(w_j\) has \(l\) negative factors and its denominator has \(j\). Thus \(\operatorname{sign}w_j=(-1)^{l-j}\). Using \(T_l(x_j)=(-1)^j\) in the same interpolation identity gives \[ \begin{split} \sum_{j=0}^{l}|w_j| &=(-1)^lT_l(x_*)=T_l((1+a)/(1-a))\\ &=\cosh\!\left(2l\,\operatorname{atanh}\frac1{l+1}\right) \le\cosh2<4 . \end{split} \tag{14} \] Here \(\operatorname{atanh}t\le t/(1-t)\) for \(0<t<1\), as follows by integrating \(1/(1-s^2)\le1/(1-s)^2\). This also checks \(l=1\), where the two nodes are \(1\) and \(1/4\). The weight sum in (14) is optimal for real nodes constrained to \([a,1]\). Any linear reconstruction exact through degree \(l\) can be tested on \(T_l((2\varepsilon-1-a)/(1-a))\), whose modulus is at most one on that interval. Its value at zero forces the weight sum to be at least \(T_l((1+a)/(1-a))\), attained in (14). No novelty is claimed for this classical interpolation fact. ## 5. What the improved conditioning does and does not control If each evaluated scalar \(F_N(\varepsilon_j)\) has absolute error at most \(\delta\), (13)--(14) give reconstruction error below \(4\delta\). If instead the normalized observations \(LS_{\mathrm{top}}L^\dagger\) have absolute errors at most \(\delta\), the guaranteed error is below \(4B_N^2\delta\). The original budget factor must remain in this statement. The signed scalar sum may vanish or be exponentially smaller than its positive summands. Uniformly conditioned messages and bounded absolute extrapolation therefore do not imply fixed relative precision, a nonzero constant Fourier mode, or a geometric lower bound. They also do not make the full correlated phase Gram uniformly positive in every auxiliary mode. The quantitative improvement is (6), its calibration (10), and the constant-point conditioning in (13), combined with the absolute amplification (14). Fourier filtering, fixed-degree extraction and elimination of the auxiliary minimization were already proved. Every original cap, complex phase and Hermite direction is retained. The full source value and its volume rate still require their own estimate after arbitrary fixed short partial fillings. ## Complete sources and coverage The two complete proof directs are [P], [Positive Conway recursion](research_orthogonal_error_positive_conway_recursion.md) (407 lines), SHA256 5506f489642f2ec118c4fef25cccc0485fecdc32ffccf09c700ac923c9da98dd; and [C], [Normalized complete compiler](research_convex_normalized_conway_source.md) (329 lines), SHA256 6b89b4c6a67ef7a32cc41a5966c650f32de65d284ae7b70d94a71bddba21df3c. Both were freshly read whole; the stronger use of their full Hilbert--Schmidt normalization is written explicitly above. Complete comparison sections in notes/research_finite_exceptions_progress.md were read at ledger pin cec7924dbd6e6d0eeb365ea7bd8d73d364ad1254cb77b2ae4cbebbeffa7c9d39: “Keeping the error degrees separately,” “A finite Fourier projection removes the auxiliary minimization,” and “Fixed degree removes the small error parameter.” These are complete individual sections, not a claim to have read the entire ledger as one proof source. The older finite-difference nodes there were \(j/[(l+1)N]\); their covariance trace estimate supplied conditioning of order \(N\). Only written mathematics and source-text/hash operations were used.

title: Persistence of a dominant saddle and the conditions it needs
text: # Persistence of a dominant saddle and the conditions it needs Research note, 2 November 2026. This note proves a continuation principle for a controlled holomorphic period. It also gives an explicit counterexample to replacing dominance along the path by dominance at its two endpoints. It does not establish the required global hypotheses for arbitrary short fillings. The useful object is a one-dimensional relative homology group: after contours supported at lower real action are discarded, the selected saddle supplies one remaining generator. Transport preserves its coefficient. Ordinary Stokes changes only add lower generators to this one. ## 1. What the period and its leading coefficient mean Let \(X_t\) be a complex manifold of dimension \(d\), depending smoothly on \(t\in[0,1]\). Any poles or branch divisors have been removed; alternatively, a specified covering has been chosen on which the phase is single valued. Consider \[ I_N(t)=\int_{\Gamma_t}e^{Nf_t(z)}\omega_{N,t}(z), \qquad N\longrightarrow+\infty. \tag{1} \] Here \(f_t\) is holomorphic, \(\Gamma_t\) is an oriented real \(d\)-cycle with permitted decaying ends, and \(\omega_{N,t}\) is a holomorphic \(d\)-form on all chains used in the argument. The cycle must be transported as a relative homology class. Replacing it at each parameter by a convenient real contour without recording crossed poles is a different operation. Write \(h_t=\operatorname{Re}f_t\). Suppose \(p(t)\) is a nondegenerate critical point. Choose continuous local Morse coordinates and the corresponding orientation so that \[ f_t=f_t(p(t))-\frac12(w_1^2+\cdots+w_d^2). \tag{2} \] Near \(p(t)\), suppose \[ \omega_{N,t}= \bigl(a_t(w)+O(N^{-1})\bigr)\,dw_1\cdots dw_d, \qquad a_t(0)\ne0, \tag{3} \] uniformly with the derivatives needed for the local integral. In arbitrary original coordinates, \(a_t(0)\) includes the chosen square root of the inverse Hessian determinant. Continuous transport can change its orientation sign around a loop, but cannot make it zero. The integer multiplying the local descending cycle is denoted \(k(t)\). It is distinct from \(a_t(0)\): the former comes from the integration cycle, the latter from the integrand. Both must be nonzero to obtain the usual nonzero leading term. ## 2. A precise controlled-transport hypothesis A statement merely saying that the critical points remain finite does not control the ends of a contour. The following are the specific topological and analytic assumptions used below. Choose continuous regular levels \(c(t)\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[ h_t(p(t))\ge c(t)+2\delta, \qquad h_t(q)\le c(t)-2\delta \quad\hbox{for every other critical point \(q\)}. \tag{4} \] Put \(A_t=\{h_t\le c(t)\}\), together with the permitted exit ends. Require the following facts. For homology, truncate each decaying end once it lies in \(\{h_t<c(t)\}\); the remainder must be a finite chain whose boundary lies in \(A_t\). Thus \(H_d(X_t,A_t;\mathbb Z)\) below means ordinary relative homology of these truncated chains, with the vanishing tail integrals restored afterwards. No infinite formal sum of contours is included without a separate convergence argument. **Morse deformation above the cutoff.** Lowering \(h_t\) deforms the region above \(A_t\) to \(A_t\) with one real \(d\)-handle, the handle at \(p(t)\). There are no additional handles from finite boundaries, deleted divisors, or infinity. The deformation and this handle identification are uniform in \(t\). This condition has a concrete flow formulation. Outside a small Morse neighborhood, the normalized negative gradient has \(dh_t/ds=-1\). Every part of a chain above the cutoff must follow this flow until it reaches \(A_t\) or the Morse neighborhood, without reaching a pole or escaping to infinity at finite height. This must hold uniformly on finite height intervals. Inside the Morse neighborhood, the quadratic model (2) attaches exactly its descending \(d\)-disk. The corresponding parameter transport of the level boundary and exit ends must also exist without an escape. A proper Morse cobordism is one sufficient way to verify these requirements. For a noncompact period, they are facts to prove, not consequences of nondegeneracy. **Transport of the original cycle.** The family of pairs \((X_t,A_t)\) and the original admissible cycle classes have compatible continuous identifications along the path. In particular no pole is crossed, no unrecorded residue cycle is added, and no integration boundary passes through the upper region. **Bounds on the lower chains.** The deformations of the original cycle give lower chains \(R_t\) supported in \(A_t\), with weighted integrability bounded by a power of \(N\). One precise sufficient estimate is, for a fixed \(N_0>0\), \[ \int_{R_t} e^{N_0h_t}\lvert\omega_{N,t}\rvert \le C N^b \tag{5} \] uniformly in \(t\). The portions of the selected descending cycle outside its local Morse neighborhood satisfy the corresponding estimate, with a fixed drop from \(h_t(p(t))\). All Stokes deformations have vanishing boundary integrals at the permitted ends. Polynomial volume growth and uniform exponential decay at those ends can establish (5), but must be checked for the particular period. These hypotheses explicitly exclude a critical contribution at an end whose real action is as large as that of \(p(t)\). An exact cancellation showing that such an end represents no cycle can also remove it; an upper bound on finite critical values alone cannot. ## 3. The persistence theorem **Theorem 1.** Under (2)--(5) and the controlled transport hypotheses of Section 2, the selected cycle coefficient \(k(t)\) is constant after its local orientation is transported. If \(k(0)\ne0\), then \[ I_N(t)= k(0)\left(\frac{2\pi}{N}\right)^{d/2} a_t(0)e^{Nf_t(p(t))} \bigl(1+O(N^{-1})\bigr), \tag{6} \] uniformly on the compact parameter path. In particular the leading coefficient never vanishes. **Proof.** The Morse deformation identifies \[ H_d(X_t,A_t;\mathbb Z)\simeq\mathbb Z. \tag{7} \] Indeed, outside the one critical neighborhood the normalized flow lowers the height to the cutoff. In the quadratic model, the change from the lower sublevel to the upper sublevel is the attachment of one \(d\)-disk with its boundary already in the lower sublevel. Its relative homology in degree \(d\) has one generator. The no-escape condition ensures that this procedure has not missed another component at a divisor, finite boundary, or infinity. The selected descending cycle \(J_t\) projects to that generator. The original cycle projects to \(k(t)[J_t]\). The identifications of pairs transport both classes continuously. The integer \(k(t)\) is consequently locally constant, and hence constant on the interval. This argument uses the group (7), not a choice of a complete thimble basis for all lower critical points. Subtracting \(k(0)J_t\) from \(\Gamma_t\) gives a cycle whose image in (7) is zero. Its integral therefore equals the integral of a lower chain \(R_t\), up to boundaries on which Stokes' theorem applies. The form \(e^{Nf_t}\omega_{N,t}\) is closed: it is a holomorphic top-degree form. There are no residue terms because the deformations stay in \(X_t\). For \(N\ge N_0\), (5) gives \[ \left|\int_{R_t}e^{Nf_t}\omega_{N,t}\right| \le C N^b e^{(N-N_0)c(t)}. \tag{8} \] The selected cycle outside its local neighborhood has the same type of exponentially smaller estimate. Inside it, use (2), rescale \(w=N^{-1/2}v\), and integrate the Taylor expansion in (3) against the real Gaussian. Odd terms integrate to zero; the first relative error is \(O(N^{-1})\). The leading integral is \((2\pi/N)^{d/2}a_t(0)\). Uniform nondegeneracy and compactness of the parameter interval give a common neighborhood and common constants. The strict gap (4) makes (8) exponentially smaller than this nonzero term, proving (6). \(\square\) This formulation separates the topological conclusion from the analytic estimates. A proof of a relative homology identification alone does not supply (5); a critical-value inequality alone supplies neither. ## 4. Why ordinary Stokes walls do not remove a dominant term There is an elementary equivalent description when the descending cycles form a finite basis. A downward gradient trajectory preserves \(\operatorname{Im}f\) and strictly decreases \(\operatorname{Re}f\). An ordinary Stokes event is a connection from one saddle \(p_h\) to another \(p_l\), with \[ \operatorname{Im}f(p_h)=\operatorname{Im}f(p_l), \qquad \operatorname{Re}f(p_h)>\operatorname{Re}f(p_l). \tag{9} \] Assume this is an isolated connection, all critical points remain nondegenerate, and no pole, boundary, or end event occurs at the same parameter. Cut the connecting descending cycle just before it enters a Morse neighborhood of \(p_l\). On the two sides of the wall, the two ways of continuing the cut differ by a local descending disk at \(p_l\). Continuing that disk downwards gives the lower descending cycle. Thus, with consistent orientations, \[ J_h^+=J_h^-+mJ_l^-, \qquad J_l^+=J_l^-, \tag{10} \] where \(m\) is the signed count of the connections; at a single transverse elementary event it is \(1\) or \(-1\). Cycles not involved in the event are unchanged. This is a cut-and-paste description of the usual Picard--Lefschetz change, with its direction fixed by the decreasing real action. Writing the same transported cycle in the two bases gives \[ k_h^+=k_h^-, \qquad k_l^+=k_l^- -m k_h^-. \tag{11} \] It is the coefficient of the **lower** saddle that can change. A strictly dominant saddle is never the lower endpoint, so its coefficient survives every such wall. The filtered proof in Section 3 avoids any difficulty caused by several changes among lower saddles. There is a useful weaker test: a selected coefficient can change only when it receives a term from a higher saddle whose coefficient is nonzero. One could prove persistence by excluding these particular connections, without proving that the selected saddle has the largest real value among all critical points. If every critical branch has one fixed strict real ordering along a path, all these matrices preserve the same triangular filtration. Their off-diagonal parts are nilpotent. By contrast, knowing that each individual wall matrix is unipotent is insufficient. Matrices \[ \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix} \tag{12} \] are individually unipotent, but their product has eigenvalues \((3+\sqrt5)/2\) and \((3-\sqrt5)/2\). A common ordering, or a common invariant one-dimensional quotient, is the relevant extra property. ## 5. Endpoint dominance is insufficient: an entire cubic example Let \(\Gamma\) run from infinity on the ray \(\arg z=-\pi/3\) to the origin, then from the origin to infinity on the ray \(\arg z=\pi/3\). Put \[ I_N(\lambda)=\int_\Gamma \exp\left[N\left(\frac{z^3}{3}-\lambda z\right)\right]\,dz, \qquad \lambda=e^{i\theta},\quad \frac{2\pi}{3}\le\theta\le2\pi. \tag{13} \] The contour is fixed. Its ends have uniform cubic decay for all these \(\lambda\). The integrand is entire, and its two critical points are distinct and nondegenerate throughout the path. Continue the selected branch by \[ p(\theta)=e^{i\theta/2}, \qquad f_\theta(p(\theta)) =-\frac23e^{3i\theta/2}. \tag{14} \] At **both endpoints**, its critical value is \(2/3\); the other critical value is \(-2/3\). Thus the selected point is uniquely dominant at each endpoint, with the same fixed gap \(4/3\). At the first endpoint, substitute \(z=e^{i\pi/3}w\). Then \[ f_\theta(z)=-\frac{w^3}{3}+w. \tag{15} \] The transformed contour consists of an incoming ray of argument \(-2\pi/3\) and the positive real axis. On the incoming ray \(w=re^{-2\pi i/3}\), \(\operatorname{Re}f=-r^3/3-r/2\), so its integral is \(O(N^{-1})\). On the positive real axis, the unique maximum is at \(w=1\), with value \(2/3\) and second derivative \(-2\). Ordinary real Gaussian estimation gives \[ I_N(e^{2\pi i/3})= e^{i\pi/3}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{N}}\, e^{2N/3}\bigl(1+O(N^{-1})\bigr). \tag{16} \] At the final endpoint \(\lambda=1\), deform the contour to the vertical line \(z=1+it\), oriented upwards. This deformation is legitimate because the integrand is entire. In the coordinate \(w=z-1\), the joining arcs have \(\pi/3\le|\arg w|\le\pi/2\); both \(\operatorname{Re}w^3\le0\) and \(\operatorname{Re}w^2\le-\lvert w\rvert^2/2\) there, so the large joining integrals tend to zero. On the vertical line, \[ \frac{(1+it)^3}{3}-(1+it) =-\frac23-t^2-\frac{i t^3}{3}. \tag{17} \] Rescaling \(t=N^{-1/2}s\) gives \[ I_N(1)= i\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{N}}\, e^{-2N/3}\bigl(1+O(N^{-1})\bigr). \tag{18} \] The selected branch at this endpoint is \(p=-1\), with value \(2/3\), but its coefficient is zero. The integral comes from the other saddle \(p=1\). There is no pole, amplitude zero, critical collision, or change of the decaying ends in this example. The missing hypothesis is precisely dominance along the path: \(\operatorname{Re}f_\theta(p(\theta))<0\) for \(\pi<\theta<5\pi/3\). At the interior ordinary Stokes wall \(\theta=4\pi/3\), the selected saddle is the lower one and its coefficient can change as in (11). The endpoints lie on ordinary Stokes rays, but the real gap and the displayed leading coefficients are unambiguous. Small perturbations of the endpoints into their adjacent sectors give the same example with endpoints off those rays. ## 6. Other hypotheses that cannot be dropped Nonzero cycle coefficient does not guarantee nonzero leading amplitude. For example, \[ \int_{\mathbb R}(t+z)e^{-Nz^2}\,dz =t\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{N}} \tag{19} \] has one nondegenerate saddle and fixed decaying ends, but vanishes at \(t=0\). Here the local amplitude vanishes. Poles can contribute a rate not represented by any critical point. For \(f(z)=-z^2\), a small positively oriented circle around \(z=i\) gives \[ \int_{|z-i|=\varepsilon} \frac{e^{-Nz^2}}{z-i}\,dz=2\pi i e^N. \tag{20} \] The only finite saddle has critical value zero. A description using that saddle alone has omitted the pole cycle. Moving poles or finite integration boundaries require their corresponding terms to be tracked just as explicitly. Equal real actions also require a separate argument. Two local Gaussian contributions with actions \(M\) and \(M+i\pi\) and equal coefficients have sum \[ \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{N}}\,e^{NM} \bigl(1+(-1)^N\bigr). \tag{21} \] Each local coefficient is nonzero, but the sum vanishes at every odd integer level. One can realize (21) on two components of a holomorphic period. The example is relevant when different logarithmic lifts or periodic aliases correspond to the same geometric representation. A volume bound on representations does not distinguish those lifts. Finally, a family with \(N\)-dependent divisors, phase branches, or cycles requires uniform versions of all the hypotheses. The identity of its classical limiting phase does not supply them. If a common top relative homology line exists at every level, its coefficient must be shown nonzero at every sufficiently large level, with subexponential normalization; a computation at one level is insufficient. ## 7. What representation-volume rigidity would supply The papers of [Francaviglia--Klaff](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0411050) and [Francaviglia--Savini](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.07347) state rigidity results for representations of the fundamental group of a **fixed complete finite-volume hyperbolic manifold**. The latter also treats sequences whose volumes approach the maximum. These are relevant coverage references, not proofs imported into Theorem 1. Even if those statements are independently verified, applying them at an integer hyperbolic filling first requires that every competing critical solution define an actual representation of that filled group, and that its real action equal the correctly normalized representation volume. An exponential meridian equation alone may not kill the full meridian matrix. Uncalibrated action constants and logarithmic lifts must also be accounted for. After those checks, rigidity can help order the real critical values **at that endpoint**. A compactness statement for representations near maximal volume can help exclude character-variety ends there. Neither statement proves dominance along a deformation, as the cubic example shows. Nor does character compactness prove properness of a chosen quantum chart: decoration coordinates or logarithmic lifts may escape while the represented character stays bounded. For a primitive cone deformation, the meridian equation is \[ U+pV=-2\pi i\lambda, \qquad 0<\lambda<1. \tag{22} \] Such a representation generally belongs to the unfilled exterior group; it does not factor through the ordinary filled manifold group. Complete representation-volume rigidity for the integer filling therefore does not apply at these intermediate parameters. Rigidity for the complete parent would give the parent's volume as an upper bound, whereas the geometric cone branch has already decreased below that value. This does not compare a competitor with the cone branch itself. One would need a relative or cone-angle maximality statement, with the same primitive constraints and the correct boundary correction, or another proof excluding incoming Stokes contributions to the selected branch. In addition, the geometric branch must remain nondegenerate along the chosen path. Hyperbolicity of the final integer filling supplies neither assertion. The completed adjacent two-crossing calculation is a useful warning. Its escaping alias has the same real action as the finite geometric saddle, as proved in [the Bloch identity](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_adjacent_alias_bloch_identity.md). The successful proof removes that end by the [exact full-circle cancellation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_adjacent_pair_full_circle_bound.md). It does not obtain a strict inequality between those two critical values. A general period-continuation approach must allow this kind of exact removal before claiming that the remaining top relative group is one-dimensional. ## 8. Attribution and the resulting research target The Stokes interpretation by relative cycles and intersection numbers is established asymptotic analysis. A directly relevant reference, including integration boundaries, is [Delabaere--Howls, *Global asymptotics for multiple integrals with boundaries*, Duke Mathematical Journal 112 (2002), 199--264](https://doi.org/10.1215/S0012-9074-02-11221-6). Its [institutional record](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/29213/) describes its treatment of generalized Picard--Lefschetz changes and boundary contributions. The arguments in Sections 3--5 were written directly here; no theorem from that article is needed for them. For the knot problem, the potentially useful general theorem is now precise: construct the **actual** period of the restored finite source, prove that its top relative homology quotient is a transported line after the genuine lower or null end cycles are removed, and prove a nonzero local amplitude with uniform subexponential normalization. A starting nonzero coefficient would then survive by Theorem 1. This could replace many separate contour certificates. It has not yet been established for arbitrary short fillings. Endpoint volume rigidity, or unipotence of individual Stokes matrices, does not by itself supply the missing transported line. ## 9. An exact analytic coupon family and the proved initializer The [small-charge source theorem](research_small_charge_path_source.md) now supplies an actual nonzero initial source on a fixed small positive charge box. Its scope includes the original positive paths, and the specified same-index finite graph sums treated there. This does not initialize the source at charge zero. The following interpolation makes the finite parameter family precise without asserting that its top relative quotient has been controlled. Fix \(N\), put \(D=N-1,\ \eta=(-1)^D\), and use the original physical angles and spectral variables \[ \tau_a=\frac{\pi(D-2a)}N,\qquad c_a=-2\cos\tau_a . \tag{23} \] For a complex parameter \(\chi\), let \(\mathcal C_{N,\chi}\) be the unique polynomial of degree less than \(N\) with the following full physical data. At a double root, choose either of its angles \(\tau\ne0\) and set \[ \begin{split} \mathcal C_{N,\chi}(-2\cos\tau) &=\cos\bigl(N(1-\chi)\tau\bigr),\\ \mathcal C_{N,\chi}'(-2\cos\tau) &=-\frac{N(1-\chi)\sin\bigl(N(1-\chi)\tau\bigr)} {2\sin\tau}. \end{split} \tag{24} \] The two choices \(\tau,-\tau\) agree. At the simple odd-level root \(-2\), prescribe the value one and no derivative. Finite Hermite interpolation proves existence, uniqueness, and entire dependence of every polynomial coefficient on \(\chi\). At integral charges it gives the exact old coupons: \[ \mathcal C_{N,j/N} =\operatorname{rem}_{\,2T_N(w/2)+2}T_{N-j}(-w/2) \quad(0\le j\le N),\qquad \mathcal C_{N,0}=\eta,\quad \mathcal C_{N,1}=1 . \tag{25} \] For the endpoint at zero, use \(\cos(N\tau_a)=\eta,\ \sin(N\tau_a)=0\); the odd simple root also has \(\eta=1\). Insert \(\mathcal C_{N,\chi_v}\) at each original traced vertex, keeping the fixed original integer crossing powers. The resulting finite source is entire in all the parameters. The [exact trace contour](research_exact_complete_trace_contour.md) continues to hold with angular representative \(\cos(N(1-\chi_v)t_v)\). Its derivation uses only the full physical jets and the oddness of the function being sampled; it does not require this angular representative to be periodic. Consequently, for each \(N\), the surrounding rectangles and their grid-pole divisors can be chosen independent of \(\boldsymbol\chi\). All vertical currents remain included. This is an exact analytic family in the original algebra, not a new assertion about a topological invariant at a nonintegral charge. In particular the all-zero-charge source equals \(\eta^m\) times the uninserted source, where \(m\) is the number of traced vertices. It is not a known complete bare-edge value. At that endpoint the formal zero-charge central phase is even in every selected angle, while each trace contributes its odd factor \(\sin t_v\). Its symmetric local Gaussian observation vanishes. The already proved initializer is instead a box bounded away from zero. There is no analogous cancellation from the companion at the other endpoint. On a lower contour the exact scalar kernel is \[ \frac{e^{-iNt}\cos(N(1-\chi)t)} {(1-\eta e^{-iNt})^2} =\frac12e^{-iN\chi t} \frac{1+e^{-2iN(1-\chi)t}} {(1-\eta e^{-iNt})^2}. \tag{26} \] At \(\chi=1\) the numerator becomes two, restoring the coefficient one of the original unit-charge trace. More quantitatively, on a compact neighborhood with \(|\Re t|\le A,\ -\Im t\ge h_0>0\), the numerator is uniformly nonzero for real \(0<\chi\le1\), at every \(N\). Indeed put \(s=N(1-\chi)\ge0\). For \(A>0\), set \(s_0=\pi/(4A)\). If \(s\le s_0\) the exponential \(e^{-2ist}\) has nonnegative real part, so the numerator has modulus at least one. If \(s\ge s_0\), its modulus is at least \(1-e^{-2s_0h_0}>0\). The case \(A=0\) is immediate. Every fixed derivative in \(t\) is uniformly bounded, using \[ \sup_{s\ge0}s^k e^{-2s h_0}<\infty . \tag{27} \] The denominator in (26) and its derivatives are likewise uniformly controlled on this neighborhood. The transition layer \(1-\chi=O(N^{-1})\) must nevertheless retain its \(N\)-dependent factor \(1+e^{-2ist}\). It does not have one \(N\)-independent limiting amplitude uniformly through \(\chi=1\). The local proof of Theorem 1 has the following direct variant: one may replace \(a_t\) in (3) by \(a_{N,t}\) if its spatial holomorphic derivatives are uniformly bounded and \(|a_{N,t}(0)|\) has a uniform positive lower bound. The same Gaussian Taylor proof gives (6) with \(a_{N,t}(0)\), with the same relative \(O(N^{-1})\) error. No derivative bound in the external parameter is required for this local estimate. Formula (26) satisfies this local amplitude requirement wherever the remaining actual source factors do. Thus an exact analytic finite family and a nonzero starting observation are now available. The Stokes conclusion of Sections 3--4 is unchanged: a flat top relative line keeps its coefficient through ordinary lower-saddle Stokes events, without a scalar almost-invariance defect estimate. What is still missing for general charge continuation is a uniform identification of that line for the actual \(N\)-dependent quantum period. In particular one must control all competing cycles, including divisor and infinity cycles, and verify the lower-chain bounds of Section 2. The finite edge kernels cannot simply be placed in a subexponential amplitude on an unproved global geometric contour. Fixed grid poles in the trace representation do not settle the other ends or aliases of a factorial-wire representation. Analyticity of the coupons and strict positivity of the geometric critical point alone do not discharge these conditions.

title: The edge Hessian and the response of a composed phase
text:
# The edge Hessian and the response of a composed phase Research note, 3 November 2026. This note recalls the determinant-one edge Hessian and its exact positivity criterion from [the edge-Hessian note](research_cone_chamber_accretivity.md). The equivalent tangent-coordinate criterion is also part of [the positive-edge theorem](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md) and Section 2 of [marked completion](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md). Those earlier results already give a graph comparison on convex domains and global uniqueness throughout the positive geometric domain, respectively. The additional conclusions here are an explicit quadrant strip and horizontal rectangles that can be used for contour bounds, a fractional-linear curvature response with a quantitative contraction estimate, and exact accounting for a peripheral shear. Their algebra does not require a large-power approximation. Section 7 locates the actual selected geometry of every fixed positive path with powers at least eight in one common complex box, independently of its length. The exact kernel asymptotic and the remaining original contour estimates on this larger domain are not proved here. Arbitrary smaller or mixed short powers also remain outside this conclusion. ## 1. Branches and the exact edge matrix Let \(\psi(t,u)\) be the phase of the original complete edge kernel. Its branch at the complete point satisfies \[ \psi_t(t,u)=- rac1\pi\operatorname{arsinh}  igl(	an(t/2)\cos(u/2) igr), \qquad \psi_u(t,u)=\psi_t(u,t). 	ag{1} \] This is the phase used in [the fixed-domain turn theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_fixed_domain_long_power_turns.md) and [the uniform terminal theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_uniform_terminal_family_and_star_fillings.md). Continue it from \((0,0)\), retaining its specified logarithms. Work on a branch domain with no poles of the tangents and put \[ w=	an(t/2),\qquad v=	an(u/2),\qquad s=\sqrt{1+w^2+v^2},\qquad \Re s>0. 	ag{2} \] In particular, \(1+w^2+v^2\) avoids the nonpositive real axis. All continuations considered below retain this square-root branch. The formulas apply on any local phase chart reached from the complete chart with these choices. The Hessian is unaffected by an additive period in the phase; choosing a different square-root sheet is not permitted. As in Section 1 of the earlier edge-Hessian note, differentiating (1) gives \[ K(t,u):=-2\pi\psi''(t,u) = rac1s  egin{pmatrix}1+w^2&-wv\-wv&1+v^2\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{3} \] For example, writing \(a=\cos(t/2)\), \(b=\cos(u/2)\) and \(D=\sqrt{a^2+b^2-a^2b^2}\) on the continued branch gives \[ -\psi_{tt}= rac{b}{2\pi aD},\qquad -\psi_{uu}= rac{a}{2\pi bD},\qquad \psi_{tu}= rac{\sin(t/2)\sin(u/2)}{2\pi D}. 	ag{4} \] Here \(D=a\,b\,s\) on the chosen chart, which proves (3). Direct multiplication shows \[ \det K=1,\qquad \operatorname{tr}K=s+s^{-1}. 	ag{5} \] For a complex symmetric matrix, \(\Re K\) denotes its entrywise real part, equivalently its Hermitian part. Positive definiteness of \(\Re K\) is the horizontal concavity condition for the complex edge phase. ## 2. An exact positivity criterion **Lemma 1 (recalled criterion and an explicit strip).** On the branch domain (2), \[ \Re K\succ0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |\Im(w\overline v)|<\Re s. 	ag{6} \] If \(w=x+iy\), \(v=z+i	au\), and \(x^2+z^2>0\), the exact criterion is equivalently \[ (yz-x	au)^2<x^2+z^2. 	ag{6a} \] In particular every pair in the quadrant strip \[ \Re w,\Re v>0,\qquad -1<\Im w,\Im v<0 	ag{6b} \] satisfies it. Another sufficient condition, with no signs imposed, is \[ (\Im w)^2+(\Im v)^2<1 	ag{7} \] on the stipulated branch. **Proof.** Write \(\alpha=\Re s>0\). Equation (5) gives \[ \operatorname{tr}(\Re K)=\alpha(1+|s|^{-2})>0. 	ag{8} \] For \(K=\left( egin{smallmatrix}A&C\C&E\end{smallmatrix}ight)\) with \(AE-C^2=1\), \[ \det(\Re K)= rac{1+\Re(A\overline E)-|C|^2}{2}. \] Substituting (3) and expanding the numerator gives \[  oxed{\displaystyle \det(\Re K)=  rac{\alpha^2-\{\Im(w\overline v)\}^2}{|s|^2}.} 	ag{9} \] Indeed \(1+\Re(w^2)+\Re(v^2)=\Re(s^2)\), while \(\Re((w\overline v)^2)-|w\overline v|^2 =-2\{\Im(w\overline v)\}^2\). Combining these identities with \(|s|^2+\Re(s^2)=2\alpha^2\) proves (9). A real symmetric two-by-two matrix with positive trace is positive definite exactly when its determinant is positive. Equations (8)--(9) prove (6). To obtain (6a), write \(X=(x,z)\), \(Y=(y,	au)\), \(R=|X|^2>0\), \(T=|Y|^2\), \(d=X\cdot Y\), and \(q=(yz-x	au)^2=RT-d^2\). The number \(\alpha^2\) is the positive root of \[ P(Z)=Z^2-(1+R-T)Z-d^2. \] At \(Z=q\), direct factorization gives \[ P(q)=(q-R)(q+T). 	ag{9a} \] If \(T>0\) and \(q>0\), the nonpositive second root of \(P\) shows that \(q<\alpha^2\) is equivalent to \(P(q)<0\), hence to \(q<R\). If \(q=0\), then \(\alpha^2>0\) and \(R>0\) make both inequalities true. If \(T=0\), this same direct argument applies. This proves (6a). For (6b), put \(y=-a\), \(	au=-b\), with \(0<a,b<1\). Since \(x,z>0\), \[ |az-bx|\le\max(az,bx) \le\max(a,b)\sqrt{x^2+z^2}<\sqrt{x^2+z^2}. \] Also \(\Im(s^2)=-2(ax+bz)<0\), so the square root with positive real part exists throughout that strip. For (7), use the same \(X,Y\) and put \(S=|Y|^2<1\). Then \[ \Re(s^2)=1+|X|^2-S>0,\qquad \alpha^2\ge1+|X|^2-S, \] and the two-dimensional determinant identity gives \[ \{\Im(w\overline v)\}^2 =|X|^2S-(X\cdot Y)^2. \] Consequently \[ \alpha^2-\{\Im(w\overline v)\}^2 \ge(1-S)(1+|X|^2)+(X\cdot Y)^2>0. 	ag{10} \] This proves (7). \(\square\) The case \(X=0\), excluded from (6a), is harmless but distinct. On the stipulated branch, \(s^2=1-|Y|^2\) must then be positive, so (7) applies. The strict inequality in (6a) should not be imposed at that point. The exact criterion depends on the relative arguments of the neighboring tangent variables, not just their individual imaginary parts. In particular, if \(w=v\) and \(\Re s>0\), then \(\Im(w\overline v)=0\), so (6) holds even when (7) fails. This is why a domain that controls differences between neighboring angles may be more useful than a rectangular bound on every angle separately. On a compact subset of (6), the lower eigenvalue is bounded away from zero. An explicit lower bound at each point is \[ \lambda_{\min}(\Re K) \ge  rac{\alpha^2-\{\Im(w\overline v)\}^2} {\alpha(|s|^2+1)}. 	ag{11} \] This follows from \(\lambda_{\min}\ge\det/\operatorname{tr}\) for a positive two-by-two matrix. The entire quadrant strip (6b) gives pointwise positivity, not a uniform positive lower bound. Such a bound still requires compactness or quantitative control in (11). ## 3. Eliminating one internal variable Let \(W(t)\) be an input phase and \(n\ge3\) a fixed positive crossing power. Consider \[ \mathcal F(t,u)=W(t)+\psi(t,u)+ rac{in}{4\pi}t^2-it. 	ag{12} \] Suppose \(t=t_*(u)\) is a holomorphic stationary branch, \(\mathcal F_t(t_*(u),u)=0\). Put \[ h=-2\pi W''(t_*),\qquad K(t_*,u)= egin{pmatrix}A&C\C&E\end{pmatrix},\qquad S(u)=\mathcal F(t_*(u),u). 	ag{13} \] The Schur-complement argument for preserving positive curvature already appears in Section 5 of [the fixed-domain turn theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_fixed_domain_long_power_turns.md). The determinant identity (5) makes its scalar response explicit. **Lemma 2.** If \(\Re h\ge0\) and \(\Re K\succeq\lambda I\) at this point, with \(\lambda>0\), then the stationary denominator is nonzero and \[  oxed{\displaystyle h_{m out}:=-2\pi S''(u) =E- rac{C^2}{h+A-in} = rac{E(h-in)+1}{h+A-in}.} 	ag{14} \] In addition, \(\Re h_{m out}\ge\lambda\). **Proof.** The negative normalized Hessian of (12) is \[ H= egin{pmatrix}h+A-in&C\C&E\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{15} \] Its Hermitian part is \(\Re K+\operatorname{diag}(\Re h,0)\), hence is at least \(\lambda I\). In particular \(\Re(h+A-in)>0\), so its first diagonal entry does not vanish. Implicit differentiation of the stationary equation gives the first equality in (14). The second uses the exact identity \(AE-C^2=1\). For \[ \xi=\left(- rac{C}{h+A-in},1ight)^T \] one has \(H\xi=(0,h_{m out})^T\). Therefore \[ \Re h_{m out} =\xi^*(\Re H)\xi \ge \lambda\|\xi\|^2 +(\Re h)\left| rac{C}{h+A-in}ight|^2 \ge\lambda. 	ag{16} \] This proves the claim. \(\square\) The same algebra is valid for any real \(n\); positivity of the crossing powers is relevant to the still unproved task of locating an invariant geometric domain, rather than to the Schur-complement calculation itself. There is also a contraction statement at a fixed edge point. Hold \(A,C,E,n\) fixed and regard (14) as a function \(f(h)\) on \(\Re h>0\). It maps that half-plane into itself and \[ f'(h)= rac{C^2}{(h+A-in)^2}. \] For the half-plane metric \(|dh|/\Re h\), its infinitesimal contraction factor satisfies \[  rac{|f'(h)|\Re h}{\Re f(h)} \le rac{\Re h}{\Re h+\lambda}<1. 	ag{17} \] To prove this, set \(r=|C/(h+A-in)|\) in (16). The left side is at most \((\Re h)r^2/\{\lambda(1+r^2)+(\Re h)r^2\}\), which gives (17). If \(\Re h\le H_0\), the factor is at most \(H_0/(H_0+\lambda)\). For \(C=0\), the map is constant. This is a curvature map at fixed \(t_*,u\). Changing the input phase also moves \(t_*\), and therefore changes \(A,C,E\). Equation (17) alone is not a contraction theorem for the complete phase-composition operator. ## 4. A peripheral shear does not change the effective filling The exact original operation is \[ F\longmapsto T(R^nF). 	ag{18} \] For any fixed integer \(r\), replace \(F\) by \(R^rF\) and the outside power by \(n-r\). The full original quantum operator in (18) is unchanged. This identity holds in the canonical quotient with all first normals. When the existing boundary-multiplication theorem applies, the new input phase is \[ W_r(t)=W(t)+ rac{ir}{4\pi}t^2. 	ag{19} \] Its unit scalar is retained separately. The phase in (12), its stationary equation and its critical value are unchanged, because \[ W_r(t)+ rac{i(n-r)}{4\pi}t^2 =W(t)+ rac{in}{4\pi}t^2. 	ag{20} \] Likewise \(h_r=h-ir\), so \[ h_r+A-i(n-r)=h+A-in. 	ag{21} \] A large apparent crossing power obtained solely by this change of frame is cancelled by the input's imaginary quadratic term. Thus this shear cannot satisfy a genuine large-power hypothesis that failed for the original source. The exact original parameter translation and primitive basis change are recorded in Section 3 of [the marked rational-piece criterion](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_marked_rational_pendant_admissibility.md). ## 5. What an invariant-domain proof would still require For a positive chain, indexed from its terminal end, write \(t_{k+1}=u\). Its critical equations are \[ n_jt_j+ 2i\left[ \operatorname{arsinh} igl(	an(t_j/2)\cos(t_{j+1}/2) igr) +{ f1}_{j>1} \operatorname{arsinh} igl(	an(t_j/2)\cos(t_{j-1}/2) igr) ight]=2\pi. 	ag{22} \] All branches and original powers are retained. The terminal vertex has one incident edge; every later filled vertex has its incoming and outgoing edge. Lemmas 1--2 suggest a precise next step: find a domain of these marked solutions, stable under every \(n_j\ge3\), in which each adjacent pair satisfies (6) with a uniform margin, and in which the amplitudes and branches stay regular. The quadrant strip (6b) supplies the needed edge positivity, but it is not itself preserved by the selected terminal filling, even at power three. A smaller invariant subset or the larger correlated domain (6a) is needed. Here is an exact counterexample to invariance of that entire strip. For a power-three terminal, write \[ k=\cos(t/2),\qquad y=\cos(u/2),\qquad P_3(k)=4k^3-k. \] The original stationary equation gives \(P_3(k)=iy\). Theorem 1 of [the terminal trace-domain note](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_terminal_intrinsic_trace_domain.md) identifies its selected branch as the inverse with lifted root-factor argument between zero and \(\pi\). Choose the internal tangent on the boundary of (6b): \[ w=	an(t/2)=1-i,\qquad k^2= rac1{1+w^2}= rac{1+2i}{5}, \qquad \Re k,\Im k>0. 	ag{22a} \] Here \(\Re k>1/2\). Put \(y=-iP_3(k)\). Direct calculation gives \[ P_3(k)^2= rac{-31-142i}{125},\qquad v^2:=y^{-2}-1= rac{-138-142i}{169}. 	ag{22b} \] The factors \(k\) and \(4k^2-1=(-1+8i)/5\) show that \(P_3(k)\) has negative real and positive imaginary part. Its square in (22b) then gives \(\pi/2<\arg P_3(k)<3\pi/4\). Thus \(y\) is in the first quadrant, with \(0<\arg y<\pi/4\). Take the square root \(v=x-ia\) of (22b) with \(x,a>0\). It lies strictly inside the proposed strip, since \[ a^2= rac{\sqrt{138^2+142^2}+138}{338}<1, \qquad 138^2+142^2=39208<40000=200^2. 	ag{22c} \] For the canonical angle \(u=2\arctan v\), the number \(\cos(u/2)\) is exactly \(y\), not its negative. Moreover \(k\) is the selected power-three root: all three factors \(k-r_
u\), for \(r_
u\in\{-1/2,0,1/2\}\), have arguments in \((0,\pi/2)\). Their sum is less than \(3\pi/2\). Its value modulo \(2\pi\) is the displayed argument of \(P_3(k)\), so it is that value and belongs to \((0,\pi)\). The trace-domain theorem therefore retains the full original logarithmic equation, rather than just its exponentiation. The edge is strictly positive at this point. Indeed the criterion (6a) is \[ (x-a)^2<1+x^2, \] which follows from \(0<a<1\) and \(x>0\). Now replace \(w\) by \(1-i(1+\epsilon)\) with a sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\), and define \(k,y,v\) by the same analytic formulas. The input \(v\) remains strictly in (6b), the edge stays positive, and the selected-root conditions persist. The internal tangent \(w\) has left the strip. This proves the asserted failure of invariance. This example concerns the selected terminal map at a complex outside angle. It does not assert that a complete finite chain with every power at least three leaves the strip. A theorem restricted to those realized neighboring angles remains possible; stability on the entire strip cannot be its proof. Even that classical result would still need a theorem for the full original source. The selected saddle must belong to the original integration cycle with a nonzero leading coefficient, and the other currents and real source bands must be controlled. The finite-current compiler gives an exact way to state those remaining estimates. Positive curvature of a geometric branch does not replace them. ## 6. Joint concavity for a finite graph of edges Theorem 3 of [the earlier edge-Hessian note](research_cone_chamber_accretivity.md) already controls arbitrary connected sets on convex domains. The result below supplies particular horizontal rectangles on which its edge hypotheses hold automatically, together with a degree-weighted bound. It does not require successive elimination of the vertices. Let \(G\) be a finite loop-free graph with a set \(I\) of internal vertices and a set \(B\) of boundary vertices. Every internal vertex must have at least one incident edge. Fix the boundary angles at zero. For real numbers \(n_v,\lambda_v\), define the analytic phase \[ \Phi(t)=\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E(G)}\psi(t_v,t_w) +\sum_{v\in I} \left( rac{i n_v t_v^2}{4\pi}-i\lambda_v t_vight), \qquad t_w=0\quad(w\in B). 	ag{23} \] Edges between two boundary vertices contribute only a constant. The branches of each edge phase are those of Section 1. This is the joint phase of the original edge contraction when its trace variables and charges are retained. The assertions below concern this phase; an asymptotic formula for the entire quantum contraction is an additional conclusion that still needs proof. Choose negative heights \(h_v<0\), and put \[ T_v=\arccos(-e^{h_v})\in(\pi/2,\pi),\qquad {\cal R}_h=\prod_{v\in I}(0,T_v),\qquad t_v=r_v+i h_v . 	ag{24} \] **Theorem 3.** On \({\cal R}_h\), the real function \(\Re\Phi(r+i h)\) is strictly concave, for every choice of the real powers \(n_v\) and charges \(\lambda_v\). The complex Hessian \(\Phi''\) is invertible at every point. More quantitatively, let \(P\) be a closed rectangle contained in \({\cal R}_h\). There is a \(\kappa>0\), obtained by taking the minimum of (11) over its finitely many edge images, such that \[ \Re[-2\pi\Phi''(r+i h)] \succeq \kappa\,\operatorname{diag}_{v\in I}(\deg v) \succeq \kappa d_{\min} I,\qquad r\in P, 	ag{25} \] where \(d_{\min}=\min_{v\in I}\deg v\ge1\). If \(r_*+i h\), with \(r_*\in P\), is a critical point of the full complex phase, then it is the unique maximum on \({\cal R}_h\), and for every \(r\in P\), \[ \Re\Phi(r+i h)\le \Re\Phi(r_*+i h) - rac{\kappa d_{\min}}{4\pi}\|r-r_*\|_2^2 . 	ag{26} \] **Proof.** For \(t=r+i h\), elementary trigonometry gives \[ 	an(t/2)=  rac{\sin r+i\sinh h}{\cos r+\cosh h}. 	ag{27} \] If \(0<r<T=\arccos(-e^h)\) and \(h<0\), its real part is positive. Its imaginary part is negative and greater than \(-1\), since \[ -\sinh h<\cos r+\cosh h \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \cos r>-e^h . \] Thus every internal edge joins two points of the quadrant strip (6b), and Lemma 1 applies. For an edge with one boundary angle zero, \(v=0\) and \[ K(t,0)=\operatorname{diag} \left(\sqrt{1+w^2},\, rac1{\sqrt{1+w^2}}ight). \] Here \(\Re(1+w^2)>0\), because \(|\Im w|<1\). Both diagonal entries have positive real part. Hence these boundary edges also have strictly positive real curvature. These are the branches continued from completeness. Along \(t_v(ho)=ho(r_v+i h_v)\), \(0<ho\le1\), one has \(ho r_v<r_v<T_v\le\arccos(-e^{ho h_v})\). Thus every tangent remains in the same quadrant strip. For an internal edge the imaginary part of \(1+w^2+v^2\) is strictly negative; for an edge ending at zero its real part is positive. The square root consequently stays on the sheet with positive real part, and the original logarithms are continued along this nonsingular path. The rectangle itself is simply connected, so these choices give a consistent phase chart there. A compact subrectangle has a complex neighborhood on the same chart. The quadratic filling terms contribute only the imaginary matrix \(-i\,\operatorname{diag}(n_v)\) to \(-2\pi\Phi''\), and the charges contribute nothing. The real part of the full normalized Hessian is therefore the sum of the embedded positive edge matrices. On the compact rectangle \(P\), each edge has a common positive lower eigenvalue \(\kappa\). For a vector \(\xi\) on the internal vertices, extend it by zero at the boundary. Each edge then contributes at least \(\kappa(|\xi_v|^2+|\xi_w|^2)\). Summing proves (25). The same argument is pointwise positive throughout \({\cal R}_h\). An accretive matrix with positive definite Hermitian part has trivial kernel: if \(H\xi=0\), then \(\Re(\xi^*H\xi)=0\), contradicting positivity for \(\xi
e0\). Thus \(\Phi''\) is invertible. Its restriction to real variations is the Hessian of \(\Re\Phi\), proving strict concavity. At a complex critical point the horizontal gradient vanishes. Concavity on the convex rectangle \({\cal R}_h\) proves uniqueness of its maximum. Integrating (25) twice along the segment from \(r_*\) to \(r\), which remains in \(P\), gives (26). \(\square\) For \(m=|I|\), (25) also gives \[ |\det[-2\pi\Phi'']|\ge(\kappa d_{\min})^m \qquad(r\in P). 	ag{28} \] Indeed its smallest singular value is at least \(\kappa d_{\min}\). Consequently the local Gaussian determinant cannot vanish on this domain, irrespective of the number of vertices. A nonzero analytic amplitude therefore gives a nonzero local Gaussian integral. Theorem 3 supplies a global comparison on the principal horizontal rectangle once the selected critical point lies there. It does not establish that such a point exists for every short filling, or that every other part of the original contour has smaller action. In particular it does not discard the other Fourier charges or the boundary currents of a finite contour deformation. For a selected solution \(t_v^*=r_v+i h_v\), with \(0<r_v<\pi\) and \(h_v<0\), its membership in this rectangle is exactly the additional inequality \[ \cos r_v>-e^{h_v}, \qquad	ext{equivalently}\qquad \Re(e^{it_v^*})>-1 . 	ag{29} \] Theorem 15 of [the corridor variational theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md), followed by mirroring, proves existence of the actual positive geometry for every finite positive path whose powers are at least three, with the stipulated complete outside ends. It gives the signs of \(r_v,h_v\) and positivity of every original edge. Its conclusion does not include (29). That additional location estimate is the precise requirement for applying this particular horizontal rectangle to the whole class. **Corollary 4.** For the original finite paths covered by that geometric existence theorem, suppose every selected positive power satisfies \[ n_v\ge2(d_v+2), 	ag{30} \] where \(d_v\) is its original degree, including complete outside incidences. Then its actual marked geometric critical point belongs to the rectangle (24) at its own imaginary heights. Consequently it has the principal-horizontal comparison and nonzero Gaussian determinant of Theorem 3. The thresholds in (30) are six at an original terminal vertex and eight at a vertex of degree two, independently of path length. **Proof.** Existence, positivity and the signs \(0<r_v<\pi\), \(h_v<0\) follow from the cited geometric theorem and mirroring. On the canonical positive edge branch, every original return obeys \[ |\Im r_{v,e}|<\pi/2 \] by equation (21) of the positive-edge theorem. Taking imaginary parts in the full original unit-charge equation \(\sum_e r_{v,e}=i n_vt_v/2-\pi i\) gives \[ n_v r_v/2-\pi =\sum_{e
i v}\Im r_{v,e}<d_v\pi/2. \] Thus \(n_vr_v<(d_v+2)\pi\). Under (30), this implies \(r_v<\pi/2<T_v\), proving the assertion. \(\square\) This corollary locates the geometric saddle and compares the action on one horizontal rectangle. It supplies neither the original-cycle coefficient nor the bounds on all other currents of the finite source. ## 7. A common complex box for paths with powers at least eight The geometric saddle can be located more precisely when all selected powers are at least eight. The resulting box also allows independent changes of the imaginary heights; it is therefore useful for estimates on the sides of a contour. **Proposition 5.** Consider any of the original finite positive paths in Corollary 4, with every integer power \(n_v\ge8\). Its selected marked solution satisfies \[ 0<\Re t_v< rac{7\pi}{24},\qquad - rac13<\Im t_v<0 \quad	ext{at every selected vertex.} 	ag{31} \] These constants do not depend on the length of the path or on its individual powers. The mirrored negative path satisfies the same bounds with \(0<-\Re t_v<7\pi/24\). **Proof.** Write \(t_v=	heta_v-iH_v\), where the existing geometric theorem gives \(H_v>0\). Corollary 4 gives \(0<	heta_v<\pi/2\). The original degrees \(d_v\), including complete outside incidences, are at most two. Put \(H_*=\max_v H_v\), and set \(H_w=0,	heta_w=0\) at a complete outside endpoint. The elementary formulas for the tangent and cosine give \[ \left|	an(t_v/2)ight|<1,\qquad \left|\cos(t_w/2)ight|\le\cosh(H_*/2). 	ag{32} \] For a return \(r=\operatorname{arsinh}z\) on the original positive branch, \(\Re r\le\operatorname{arsinh}|z|\). Indeed \(e^r=z+\cosh r\), so \(|e^r|\le |z|+\sqrt{1+|z|^2}\). Also \[ \operatorname{arsinh}(\cosh x)\le x+\operatorname{arsinh}1 \qquad(x\ge0); \] the derivative of the left side is less than one, and the two sides agree at zero. Taking real parts in the filling equation gives \[ n_v H_v=2\sum_{e
i v}\Re r_{v,e}. 	ag{33} \] At a vertex attaining \(H_*\), (32)--(33) imply \[ 8H_*\le2H_*+4\operatorname{arsinh}1,\qquad H_*\le rac23\operatorname{arsinh}1< rac35. 	ag{34} \] There is now a better real-angle bound. For an incidence put \(z=	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)\). The tangent has positive real part and negative imaginary part, whereas the cosine has positive real part and nonnegative imaginary part. Hence \[ \Im z\le \Re	an(t_v/2)\,\Im\cos(t_w/2) < rac{\sinh(3/10)}{\sqrt2}< rac14 . 	ag{35} \] The canonical return satisfies \(|\Im r|<\pi/2\), and \(\Im z=\cosh(\Re r)\sin(\Im r)\). If \(\Im r\) is positive, this proves \(\Im r<\arcsin(1/4)<\pi/12\); for a nonpositive imaginary part the same upper bound is immediate. The imaginary part of the filling equation consequently gives \[ n_v	heta_v =2\pi+2\sum_{e
i v}\Im r_{v,e} <2\pi+ rac{d_v\pi}{6} \le rac{7\pi}{3}. 	ag{36} \] Thus \(	heta_v<7\pi/24<1\). One more use of (33) improves the height. For \(	heta<1\), \(H<3/5\), \[ \left|	an((	heta-iH)/2)ight|^2 = rac{\sin^2(	heta/2)+\sinh^2(H/2)} {\cos^2(	heta/2)+\sinh^2(H/2)} < rac{3265}{8657}< rac{25}{64}. 	ag{37} \] Here \(\sin(1/2)<12/25\) and \(\sinh(3/10)<31/100\) give the first rational bound; the ratio increases with both squared quantities on this range. Since \(\cosh(3/10)<21/20\), every incidence now has \(|z|<21/32\), and therefore \(\Re r<21/32\). Equation (33) gives \[ H_v< rac{2d_v}{n_v} rac{21}{32} \le rac{21}{64}< rac13. 	ag{38} \] For explicit bounds on the positive Taylor tails one may use \(\sinh x\le x/(1-x^2/6)\) and \(\cosh x\le1/(1-x^2/2)\) at the displayed arguments; these follow from \((2j+1)!\ge6^j\) and \((2j)!\ge2^j\). The sine bound uses its alternating series. Also \(\operatorname{arsinh}1<9/10\) follows from \(\sinh(9/10)>9/10+(9/10)^3/6>1\), and \(\sin(\pi/12)>1/4\) follows from the exact half-angle formula. Mirroring conjugates the original phases and reverses the real angles, proving the last assertion. \(\square\) **Corollary 6.** On the full complex box \[ {\cal B}=\{t:|\Re t|\le1,\ |\Im t|\le1/3\}, 	ag{39} \] every edge pair satisfies \[ \Re K(t,u)\succeq rac15 I . 	ag{40} \] In particular all the saddles in Proposition 5 lie in one fixed convex region on which the joint phase has uniformly positive real negative Hessian. This includes all choices of signs for the imaginary heights within the box, not only the selected heights. **Proof.** The same tangent formula gives, on \({\cal B}\), \[ |	an(t/2)|< rac35,\qquad |\Im	an(t/2)| \le rac{\sinh(1/3)}{\cos1+\cosh(1/3)} < rac14 . 	ag{41} \] For the first inequality use \(\sin(1/2)<12/25\), \(\sinh(1/6)<17/100\); for the second use \(\sinh(1/3)<7/20\), \(\cos1>1/2\) and \(\cosh(1/3)\ge1\). In the notation of Lemma 1 this gives \[ S=(\Im w)^2+(\Im v)^2< rac18,\qquad |s|^2=|1+w^2+v^2|< rac{43}{25},\qquad \alpha=\Re s< rac43 . 	ag{42} \] The real part of \(s^2\) is positive, so the branch is holomorphic throughout the box and agrees with the complete branch. Equations (10)--(11) imply \[ \lambda_{\min}(\Re K) > rac{7/8}{(4/3)(68/25)} = rac{525}{2176}> rac15 , 	ag{43} \] proving (40). Summing the embedded matrices as in Theorem 3 proves the asserted joint bound. \(\square\) These are bounds for the actual geometric solution and the analytic edge phase. They provide a common domain for a possible uniform quantum-kernel and contour estimate. They do not assert such a kernel estimate, or the nonzero coefficient of the original global period.

title: Bulk Fourier coefficients of one original endpoint kernel
text: # Bulk Fourier coefficients of one original endpoint kernel Private written proof, 16 November 2026. For one microscopic endpoint color, the upper half of the original kernel's Fourier coefficients has an exact checkerboard sign and a positive finite sum. On every fixed degree interval strictly between zero and the fold, a short prefix of that sum is an analytic unit of order \(N^{-1}\). Its relative error at the physical degree nodes is exponentially small. A localized sinc correction gives one exact analytic interpolant on a fixed complex strip, with the same leading coefficient and no extensive phase after the checkerboard is removed. This is a statement about the ordinary original kernel, including its full spectral normals. It is not a bound for a whole interface integral. The checkerboard, its complex growth, the two degree endpoints, and all other source factors remain. ## 1.
