For the quantitative assertion, the normal formula (9) implies \[ |U_N'(c_a)|\le\frac{N^2-1}{12}. \tag{17} \] Indeed \(\sin((2a+1)\theta)\ge\sin\theta\) at the double nodes, and \(\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}\csc^2(r\theta)=(N^2-1)/3\). Consequently \[ \mathsf D_j:=\partial_{w_j}\mathsf D =2\sigma\,\operatorname{diag}(m_{vj}U_N'(c_{a_j})), \qquad \|\mathsf D_j\|\le M_j(N^2-1)/6. \tag{18} \] Every mixed derivative of \(\mathsf D\) in two distinct boundary variables is zero. Its possibly nonzero pure higher derivatives are never used by (13). Choose any local logarithm \(h=\log\det\mathsf D\) near the assignment. For a nonempty set \(J\) of \(r\) distinct variables, the expansion of \(\operatorname{tr}\log(I+\mathsf D^{-1}\Delta\mathsf D)\) gives \[ \partial_J h =\frac{(-1)^{r-1}}r \sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(J)} \operatorname{tr} (\mathsf D^{-1}\mathsf D_{\pi_1}\cdots \mathsf D^{-1}\mathsf D_{\pi_r}). \tag{19} \] Only terms linear in each distinct increment contribute. By (7), (10), and the dimension \(m\), \[ |\partial_Jh| \le m(r-1)!\,\delta_N^{-r} \prod_{j\in J}\|\mathsf D_j\|. \tag{20} \] The repeated product rule for \(e^{-h}\) is \[ \partial_J e^{-h} =e^{-h}\sum_{\mathcal P\ {\rm partition\ of}\ J} \prod_{C\in\mathcal P}(-\partial_Ch). \tag{21} \] The sum of the corresponding absolute combinatorial weights is \[ \sum_{\mathcal P}m^{|\mathcal P|} \prod_{C\in\mathcal P}(|C|-1)!=(m)_r. \tag{22} \] For positive integer \(m\), the left side counts permutations of \(J\) with one of \(m\) colors on every cycle. Adding the next element either starts a colored singleton in \(m\) ways or inserts it after one of the previous elements; this gives the displayed rising product. The empty-set case has value one. Now \(|\det\mathsf D|^{-1}\le\delta_N^{-m}\) by (7). Multiply (21) by the constant \((B_E\sigma^m)^{-1}\) and use (18)--(22). This gives (14). Finally \(\delta_N\ge2\), \(Ns_1=2N\sin(\pi/N)\ge4\), and \(|n_v|\ge1\) for every even current. Since \(r\le b\) and the graph is fixed, (15) follows. \(\square\) Thus multiplication by the current is injective on the *full* boundary algebra, not merely on its semisimple quotient. For any boundary state \(f\), the ordinary product rule and (15) give \[ \|f\|_{\mathcal J,B} \le 2^b C_{G,S}N^{2b} \|\mathcal E_{S,N}f\|_{\mathcal J,B}. \tag{23} \] For fixed powers the forward multiplier also has polynomial Hermite norm: the Ward coupon in (9) has values \(O(1+\log N)\) and first normals \(O(N^2)\), and (3) has a fixed number of factors. Consequently current multiplication preserves the exponential rate of this boundary norm in both directions for fixed powers. ## 4. What this does and does not control The theorem applies to the specified simultaneous one-step endpoint currents in their original slots. It does not identify an arbitrary relative-contour remainder with those currents. Shared outside variables, all unchosen edges, the retained boundary polynomial, and the original exterior contraction remain exactly where (3) places them. In particular, for the prescribed exterior functional \(\Lambda_N\), \[ \Lambda_N(\mathcal E_{S,N}f) \tag{24} \] may vanish even though \(\mathcal E_{S,N}\) is a unit and \(f\ne0\). Equations (11), (15), and (23) do not supply a scalar lower bound for (24), a nonzero original contour intersection, or a certificate for the ideal of all geometric scalar coefficients. The pointwise complex criterion is exactly the sufficient condition \(\Re x_v>0\) used in (6). No positive-period hypothesis was needed to prove it on the physical grid. It has not been deduced for the canonical boundary polynomial at an arbitrary complex geometric evaluation. Agreement of a different representative's physical Hermite data does not establish its equality as an ordinary polynomial at that evaluation, or a zero-free inverse throughout an entire complex physical window. Section 3 of the earlier grouped-current note treats a different question: when the complete exterior contour and all its currents are already controlled, the logarithmic Ward representative gives a nonzero leading matching coefficient relative to that exterior packet. The present exact finite unit and uniform inverse-normal bound do not assume that result's contour hypotheses, and do not remove them from its scalar conclusion. ## 5. Direct sources and written verification The proof uses the following two direct sources. Their complete written proofs were read; their recorded computational checks are not used here. | Source | Direct implication | SHA256 | |---|---|---| | [Grouped endpoint currents](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_grouped_endpoint_current_matchings.md) | Equations (2)--(10): actual simultaneous current, incidence monomers, positive edge weight, exact full-boundary matching identity; Section 3 for the stated prior scope | \(\texttt{4047782f665e9e6631e73aac42d55057d6f3cd5ae1e813d89111a0a5caaa21bb}\) | | [Signed Gaussian Ward packet](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_signed_gaussian_ward_endpoint_packet.md) | Equations (21)--(23): exact physical values, confluent first normals, odd simple node and quadratic normal bound | \(\texttt{6bdced1b01917e41631386a24b337b60dfe5b04d35d70007cb56badc511a0191}\) | All deductions above are written algebra and estimates. No mathematical execution, numerical evidence, or tests are used.

title: A nonzero microscopic endpoint insertion at a nonreal local saddle

# A nonzero microscopic endpoint insertion at a nonreal local saddle Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The explicit sharp endpoint baseline has the actual Gamma connection coefficients, uniformly on each prescribed fixed-height rectangle. At a genuinely nonreal point the two conjugate modes have unequal absolute values. This gives a polynomial lower bound, uniformly for bounded real endpoint parameters including zero, despite their oscillation in \(\log N\). The exact designated-half representatives inherit that bound. The last section applies this insertion to a supplied nonzero local Gaussian saddle contribution. It neither supplies the geometric cycle of the original closing nor estimates its other currents. ## 1. Actual normalization and the tall connection formula Write \[ h=N^{-1},\qquad C_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi h),\qquad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha h),\qquad B_N(x,\alpha)=K_N(w_N(\alpha),C_N(x)). 	ag{1} \] The endpoint kernel is the original canonical polynomial. Fix a real parameter bound \(|\alpha|\le A\), a target \(x_0\in(0,1/2)\), and a sufficiently small buffered real interval about \(x_0\). Fix arbitrary finite upper and lower heights. The resulting rectangles, including all buffers below, have real parts strictly between \(0\) and \(1/2\). Let \(V_N\) be the particular two-value-normalized baseline of the reflected sharp connection theorem. Thus its cutoff, mode pair and actual physical anchor are fixed as in that theorem. In particular, at a physical anchor \(x_{j_*}=j_*/N\) in its fixed right buffer, \[ V_N(x_{j_*})=B_N(x_{j_*}),\qquad V_N(x_{j_*}-h)=B_N(x_{j_*}-h). 	ag{2} \] The anchor remains a fixed distance from both endpoints and the fold. No arbitrary homogeneous solution is added to this normalization. Put \[ 
u=\alpha/\pi,\qquad \ell(x)=\Log\sin(\pi x),\qquad L_N=\log(N/\pi),\qquad S_N(x)=(N/\pi)\sin(\pi x). 	ag{3} \] The logarithm is the continuation of the real logarithm. Indeed, \(\Re\sin(\pi x)>0\) on \(0<\Re x<1/2\), so this logarithm is single-valued on every rectangle under consideration. For real \(
u

u)\cos(
u(L_N+\ell(x))) +C_1(
u) rac{\sin(

u\), this is equivalently \[ g_\alpha(S_N(x)) =k_+S_N(x)^{-1+i
u}+k_-S_N(x)^{-1-i
u}. 	ag{7} \] **Theorem 1.** On every smaller buffered rectangle of the prescribed fixed height there is \(\epsilon_0>0\) such that, for every fixed spatial derivative order \(k\), \[ \partial_x^k V_N(x,\alpha)= \partial_x^k g_\alpha(S_N(x))+O_k(N^{-1-\epsilon_0}). 	ag{8} \] Constants are uniform for real \(|\alpha|\le A\), at both parities of \(N\), and also for \(N\)-dependent real parameters in this compact interval. The exponent does not decrease merely because the prescribed height is larger; the constants and required buffers may depend on it. No endpoint-parameter derivative version of (8) is asserted. **Proof.** The archived actual value connection theorem gives, at the anchor in (2), \[  inom{B_N(x_{j_*})} {N(B_N(x_{j_*})-B_N(x_{j_*}-h))} =  inom{g_\alpha(S_N(x_{j_*}))} {\partial_x g_\alpha(S_N(x_{j_*}))} +O(N^{-1-\epsilon}). 	ag{9} \] Its error is uniform through the coalescence \(\alpha=0\) and at both parities. In particular the second entry is an actual two-value quantity; we have not replaced an independent spectral normal by a derivative. Let \(H_{0,N},H_{1,N}\) be the coalescence-safe mode pair used to define \(V_N\), and let \[ \psi_0(x)= rac{\cos(
u\ell(x))}{\sin(\pi x)},\qquad \psi_1(x)= rac{\sin(
u\ell(x))}{
u\sin(\pi x)}. 	ag{10} \] The sine-factor estimates in the reflected theorem give \[ H_{i,N}=\psi_i+O_{\mathrm{hol},x}(h) 	ag{11} \] on the whole prescribed fixed-height rectangle, uniformly on the real parameter compact. This follows there from the sharper centered estimate at \(x+h/2\). The same estimate holds for all fixed spatial derivatives on buffered rectangles. Consequently the balanced frame \[ \mathcal Y_N(x)=  egin{pmatrix} H_{0,N}(x)&H_{1,N}(x)\ [H_{0,N}(x)-H_{0,N}(x-h)]/h& [H_{1,N}(x)-H_{1,N}(x-h)]/h \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix}\psi_0&\psi_1\\psi_0'&\psi_1'\end{pmatrix} +O(h) 	ag{12} \] is uniformly invertible at the real anchor. The limiting determinant is \(\pi\cos(\pi x)/\sin^3(\pi x)\), independently of \(
u\). The divided-color frame in the reflected theorem and (12) are related at the anchor by an invertible row scaling; hence they define exactly the same coefficient vector \(\mathbf a_N\) for \(V_N\). Define the explicit leading coefficients \[ a_{0,N}^{\,0}= rac{\pi}{N} \left\{C_0\cos(
u L_N)+C_1 rac{\sin(
u L_N)}{
u}ight\}, \qquad a_{1,N}^{\,0}= rac{\pi}{N} \left\{-
u C_0\sin(
u L_N)+C_1\cos(
u L_N)ight\}. 	ag{13} \] The addition formulas give exactly \[ (\psi_0,\psi_1)\mathbf a_N^{\,0}=g_\alpha(S_N(x)),\qquad (\psi_0',\psi_1')\mathbf a_N^{\,0}=\partial_x g_\alpha(S_N(x)). 	ag{14} \] Uniformly on the real parameter compact, \[ c/N\le|\mathbf a_N^{\,0}|\le C(1+\log N)/N. 	ag{15} \] Here \(|\sin(
u L_N)/
u|\le L_N\), including its value at zero. For the lower bound at nonzero real \(
u\), the two entries of \(N\mathbf a_N^{\,0}/\pi\) are \(2\Re(k_+e^{i
u L_N})\) and \(-2
u\Im(k_+e^{i
u L_N})\). Their Euclidean norm is at least \(2|k_+|\min(1,|
u|)\), uniformly bounded below on the real compact because the Gamma function has no zeros and \(|
u k_+|	o1/\pi^2\). At zero the second entry is \(C_1(0)\). Combining (9), (12) and (14) proves \[ \mathbf a_N-\mathbf a_N^{\,0} =O(N^{-1-\epsilon})+O((1+\log N)/N^2) =O(N^{-1-\epsilon_0}), 	ag{16} \] where one may take \(\epsilon_0=\min(\epsilon,1/2)\). In particular this is also a relative vector estimate \(|\mathbf a_N-\mathbf a_N^{\,0}|/|\mathbf a_N^{\,0}| =O(N^{-\epsilon_0})\); no lower bound for either separate coalesced coordinate is required. Multiplying these coefficients by the bounded explicit modes and using (11) proves (8), including its derivatives. This proof transports two actual coefficients in an explicit global mode frame; it is not analytic continuation of a small real-axis error. \(\square\) ## 2. A uniform nonreal lower bound Let \(\mathcal K\) be a compact subset of the prescribed rectangle with \(\Im x
e0\), and reserve a slightly larger such compact neighborhood. Then \[  eta(x):=\Im\ell(x),\qquad \inf_{x\in\mathcal K}| eta(x)|= eta_0>0. 	ag{17} \] Indeed, for \(x=a+iy\) in this strip, \(\Im\sin(\pi x)=\cos(\pi a)\sinh(\pi y)\), which is nonzero exactly when \(y
e0\). **Theorem 2.** For all sufficiently large \(N\), uniformly for \(x\in\mathcal K\) and real \(|\alpha|\le A\), \[  rac{c}{N}\le |V_N(x,\alpha)|\le rac{C(1+\log N)}N. 	ag{18} \] Every fixed spatial derivative has the upper bound \(C_k(1+\log N)/N\). Moreover \[  rac{V_N(x,\alpha)}{g_\alpha(S_N(x))} =1+O(N^{-\epsilon_0}). 	ag{19} \] The denominator is nonzero throughout this compact neighborhood. **Proof.** For real \(
u
e0\), \(k_-=\overline{k_+}\). The reverse triangle inequality in (7), with \(\Log S_N=L_N+\ell(x)\), gives \[ |g_\alpha(S_N(x))| \ge  rac{2\pi |k_+(
u)|}{N|\sin(\pi x)|} |\sinh(
u eta(x))|. 	ag{20} \] This inequality eliminates the phase \(e^{i
u\log(N/\pi)}\). The Gamma function is nonzero, and its expansion at zero gives \[ |
u|\,|k_+(
u)|\longrightarrow1/\pi^2. 	ag{21} \] Thus the right side of \(N\) times (20) has the strictly positive continuous limit \[  rac{2| eta(x)|}{\pi|\sin(\pi x)|}. 	ag{22} \] At zero itself, (5)--(6) give \[ g_0(S_N(x))=  rac{2}{\pi N\sin(\pi x)} \{\log(N/\pi)+\ell(x)+\gamma_E+4\log2\}. 	ag{23} \] The imaginary part of the expression in braces proves the lower bound (22) directly. Compactness therefore makes (20)--(23) uniform for the entire real parameter interval, including sequences \(\alpha=\alpha_N	o0\). This proves \(|g_\alpha|\ge c_0/N\). The coalescence-safe formula (6) and its fixed spatial derivatives are bounded by \(C_k(1+\log N)/N\); the real parameter restriction prevents growth of its \(L_N\)-dependent oscillations. Now (8) proves (18)--(19) and the derivative assertions. \(\square\) The restriction to a nonreal compact is essential to this argument. No lower bound is asserted on the real interval, where the two conjugate terms may interfere with equal absolute values. ## 3. Exact physical representatives and shared insertions Choose either sign \(\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}\). Use the sharp one-sided assembly on the same window, with any fixed positive error rate \(\gamma\) below its local sharp rate. It gives \[ H_N^\sigma=V_N+C_N^\sigma 	ag{24} \] with exactly the original physical values and first spectral normals, and, for every fixed spatial derivative, \[ |\partial_x^k C_N^\sigma|\le C N^p e^{-N\gamma} \quad	ext{when }\sigma\Im x\ge0. 	ag{25} \] Therefore (8), (18) and (19) also hold with \(H_N^\sigma\) in place of \(V_N\) on every nonreal compact in its designated half. This is a lower bound for an exact local full-jet representative, not for the canonical polynomial evaluated away from its physical nodes. Nor is it a lower bound for its original closed trace. For a fixed number \(r\) of factors, let \(x_i(z)\) be fixed holomorphic functions near a point \(z_*\in\mathbb C^d\). Require that their images of a common compact neighborhood lie in the designated nonreal compacts just described. Let all \(\alpha_i\) be real and bounded, and set \[ \mathcal B_N(z)= \prod_{i=1}^r H_{i,N}^{\sigma_i}(x_i(z),\alpha_i). 	ag{26} \] Then uniformly on a smaller neighborhood, \[ |\mathcal B_N(z_*)|\ge cN^{-r},\qquad |\partial_z^\lambda\mathcal B_N(z)| \le C_\lambda\left( rac{1+\log N}{N}ight)^r. 	ag{27} \] The same statement holds with any or all factors replaced by their baselines. It follows directly from the product and chain rules. Repeated/shared colors are allowed: their physical first normals are retained by the ordinary product rule, not independent sampling. Endpoint-parameter derivatives or normal derivatives of the insertion are not asserted to have a nonzero lower bound. ## 4. Conditional local stationary-phase consequence The following hypotheses describe an already supplied local saddle contribution. They are not conclusions about the original global integration cycle. Let \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{loc}}\) have a fixed real \(d\)-dimensional parameterization \(z=z(u)\), with \(z(0)=z_*\) and \(|z(u)-z_*|\le C|u|\), contained in the neighborhood of (27). Suppose its bare amplitude and integration density satisfy a uniform absolute bound \(|a_N(z(u))\,d\mu|\le C\,du\), and its phase obeys \[ \Re(\Phi(z(u))-\Phi(z_*))\le-c|u|^2. 	ag{28} \] Suppose the bare local integral has its specified nonzero asymptotic \[ I_N^0:=\int_{\Gamma_{\mathrm{loc}}}e^{N\Phi(z)}a_N(z)\,d\mu =e^{N\Phi(z_*)}N^{-d/2}\{A_*+o(1)\},\qquad A_*
e0. 	ag{29} \] Uniform versions use uniform constants in (27)--(29) and \(\inf|A_*|>0\). A common scalar carrier may be factored out of both integrals without changing the assertion. **Corollary.** Under these supplied local hypotheses, \[ \int_{\Gamma_{\mathrm{loc}}}e^{N\Phi(z)} a_N(z)\mathcal B_N(z)\,d\mu =\mathcal B_N(z_*)\,e^{N\Phi(z_*)}N^{-d/2} \{A_*+o(1)\}. 	ag{30} \] In particular the endpoint insertion does not annihilate this already specified nonzero local coefficient, even when its own coefficient oscillates in \(\log N\). **Proof.** By (27) and the mean-value estimate along short paths in the fixed neighborhood, \[ |\mathcal B_N(z(u))-\mathcal B_N(z_*)| \le C|u|\left( rac{1+\log N}{N}ight)^r. 	ag{31} \] Equations (28) and the absolute amplitude bound show that subtracting \(\mathcal B_N(z_*)I_N^0\) from the integral in (30) has modulus at most \[ C e^{N\Re\Phi(z_*)}N^{-(d+1)/2} \left( rac{1+\log N}{N}ight)^r. 	ag{32} \] After division by \(|\mathcal B_N(z_*)e^{N\Phi(z_*)}N^{-d/2}|\), this is \(O((1+\log N)^r/\sqrt N)=o(1)\), by (27). Equation (29) proves (30). \(\square\) The exact one-sided trace construction still retains its real interface, both exterior half-contours, their vertical sides, all grid aliases, the original crossing, all shared spectators, and all physical rows outside the window. Nothing in (30) estimates these other terms or rules out cancellation between distinct local cycles in their closing. In particular it does not identify the original geometric cycle coefficient or prove a whole-source lower bound or a parent-volume comparison. ## 5. Coverage and direct sources The earlier [fixed-strip endpoint asymptotics](research_endpoint_fixed_strip_asymptotics.md) already continue the connection formula to a narrow strip and prove a local multiplier consequence for parameters of size \(1/\log N\). That coverage is not used as a proof dependency here. The new point is the actual two-coefficient transport in the explicit tall mode frame, followed by the nonreal reverse-triangle estimate uniformly for all bounded real parameters. The local Gaussian comparison above is included in full to specify the remaining cycle hypothesis. All three complete direct sources were read at these matching final pins, and the directly used anchor, uniform coalescence, physical normal and repair implications were checked: * [Actual value connection and growing overlap](research_endpoint_value_connection_and_overlap.md), SHA256 87801bd8baca255a86fdbcd5170662fd9f2b366f983507f776d5676fd8a324da. * [Reflected sharp full-normal connection](research_reflected_endpoint_sharp_normal_connection.md), SHA256 a8a379d7b492d7d2487de3c1397408478f66242f153ac0cab8eb3d224f226916. * [Sharp one-sided physical-window assembly](research_sharp_endpoint_one_sided_window_assembly.md), SHA256 163d4cf2fc98648c0739152dbb463f2ad8f19d58b34b31d9184469847e60e541. # The actual endpoint normal defect and its coherent bulk sine primitive Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The full first normal of a microscopic endpoint kernel is not obtained by differentiating an arbitrary interpolation of its physical values. This note gives the exact difference, including its original trace current. The difference is a sum of the derivative of the physical-value interpolant and a sine transform of the actual high Fourier coefficients. The checkerboard cancels inside this transform. On a fixed bulk frequency interval, the transform has an explicit discrete primitive with exponentially small remainder. Its two terminal terms remain. The separate value/normal interpolation theorem supplies polynomially bounded analytic representatives of both channels. It does not make their difference zero. No filled-action estimate, contour cancellation, or source nonvanishing follows here. ## 1. Original values, normals, and the exact radical Fourier split Put \[ N\ge2,\quad D=N-1,\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\quad 	heta=\pi/N, \quad m=\lfloor N/2floor,\quad J=\lfloor(N-1)/2floor, \] \[ c(j)=2\cos((2j+1)	heta),\quad 
u_j=(2j+1)	heta,\quad 	au_j=\pi-
u_j,\quad x_j=j/N, \] \[ c'(j)=-4	heta\sin
u_j,\qquad w=2\cosh(\alpha/N),\qquad B_N(Z)=K_N(w,Z). 	ag{1} \] The prime on \(c\) is the derivative in its unscaled index. Explicitly, the original normalization is \[ c_0=c(0),\quad s_r=2\sin(r	heta),\quad S_j=\prod_{r=1}^j s_r,\quad S_0=1,\quad e_j(Z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{r<j}(c(r)-Z),\quad K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{D}e_j(w)e_j(Z),\quad P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2. \] Define \[ F_j=B_N(c(j)),\qquad G_j=B_N'(c(j)),\qquad B(t)=B_N(-2\cos t) =b_0+\sum_{k=1}^{D}b_k(e^{ikt}+e^{-ikt}). 	ag{2} \] All identities in this section are ordinary polynomial identities in \(w\). In particular they retain every other free variable and normal. Let \(L_N(Z)\) be the unique polynomial of degree at most \(J\) taking the values \(F_j\) at the distinct physical nodes \(c(0),\ldots,c(J)\). Write \(L(t)=L_N(-2\cos t)\). For \(1\le s<N/2\), set \[ \mathcal R_s(t)=2\cos((N-s)t)-2\eta\cos(st). 	ag{3} \] At every physical angle, \(e^{iN	au_j}=\eta\), so these polynomials vanish at every distinct physical node. For even \(N=2m\), the polynomial \(2\cos(mt)\) also vanishes there. Consequently \[  oxed{ B(t)=L(t)+ \sum_{1\le s<N/2}b_{N-s}\mathcal R_s(t) +\mathbf1_{N\ {m even}}\,2b_m\cos(mt). } 	ag{4} \] Indeed subtract the displayed terms from \(B\). Every frequency above \(J\) has been removed, and the resulting degree-\(J\) spectral polynomial has precisely the original values. Uniqueness of ordinary interpolation proves (4). At odd levels the simple node \(-2\) is among these values. At \(N=2\), \(J=0\) and only the middle term occurs. Direct differentiation gives \[ \mathcal R_s'(	au_j)=2N\eta\sin(s	au_j). 	ag{5} \] Use a prime on a sum over \(1\le s\le m\) to mean weight one, except weight \(1/2\) at \(s=m\) when \(N\) is even. Then (4)--(5) imply \[ B_t(	au_j)=L_t(	au_j) +2N\eta\sum_{s=1}^{m}{}'b_{N-s}\sin(s	au_j). 	ag{6} \] The half weight gives exactly the derivative \(-Nb_m\sin(m	au_j)\) of the even middle term. The bulk Fourier source proves, for real \(\alpha\), \[ b_{N-s}=\eta(-1)^{s-1} eta_{s,N}(\alpha),\qquad  eta_{s,N}(\alpha)>0,\qquad 1\le s\le m. 	ag{7} \] Define \( eta_{s,N}\) by the same algebraic relation for any other parameter where an exact identity is wanted. Positivity is asserted only for real \(\alpha\). Since \(\sin(s	au_j)=(-1)^{s+1}\sin(s
u_j)\), the actual checkerboard cancels, with no parity sign left: \[  oxed{ B_t(	au_j)=L_t(	au_j) +2N\sum_{s=1}^{m}{}'  eta_{s,N}\sin(s
u_j). } 	ag{8} \] This cancellation is within one coherent transform. It does not permit replacing the transform by a sum of absolute coefficient values. ## 2. The true derivative defect and its original trace Let \(I\) be a fixed compact interval in \((0,1/2)\), and let \(f_N(x,\alpha)\) be any holomorphic function on a neighborhood of \(I\) such that \[ f_N(x_j,\alpha)=F_j(\alpha) \quad(x_j\in I). 	ag{9} \] No difference equation or relation to \(G_j\) is assumed. Its derivative-compatible spectral normal at these nodes would be \[ G_j^{\,f}= rac{\partial_x f_N(x_j)}{N c'(j)}. 	ag{10} \] The denominator is a unit on this fixed bulk interval. Define the true scaled defect \[ \Delta_j=Nc'(j)G_j-\partial_xf_N(x_j). 	ag{11} \] As \(Nc'(j)=-4\pi\sin
u_j\) and \(B_t(	au_j)=2\sin
u_j\,G_j\), equation (8) yields \[  oxed{ \Delta_j=-2\pi L_t(	au_j) -4\pi N\sum_{s=1}^{m}{}' eta_{s,N}\sin(s
u_j) -\partial_xf_N(x_j). } 	ag{12} \] This formula compares the actual normal to the derivative of the specified value interpolation. The common-index derivative of a Jacobi determinant with fixed initial data is a different object; its homogeneous remainder is not automatically (11). Here is the exact source effect. Let \(A_N(Z;\mathbf u)\) denote the actual remaining spectator, including any original crossing, coupon, kernel, shared trace variable, and ordinary outside parameter. At the double nodes the original trace is \[ \phi_N(B_NA_N)= \eta\sum_{m double\ j}  ig\{(4-c(j)^2)[G_jA_N(c(j))+F_jA_N'(c(j))] -c(j)F_jA_N(c(j)) ig\} +\mathbf1_{N\ {m odd}}B_N(-2)A_N(-2). 	ag{13} \] Replace only \(G_j\), for \(x_j\in I\), by (10), keeping all values and every other row unchanged. If \(\mathcal T_N^f\) is the resulting finite expression, then \[  oxed{ \phi_N(B_NA_N)-\mathcal T_N^f =- rac{\eta}{\pi}\sum_{x_j\in I} \sin
u_j\,\Delta_j A_N(c(j);\mathbf u). } 	ag{14} \] Indeed \(G_j-G_j^f=-\Delta_j/(4\pi\sin
u_j)\). The spectator derivative disappears only from this difference, because the values have not changed. It remains in \(\mathcal T_N^f\). The odd simple-node contribution in (13) is unchanged. If \(A_N=R^n\widetilde A_N\), the exact original factor \(R(c(j))^n\) remains in (14), together with its original carrier. No Gaussian sheet or crossing phase has been changed. Equation (14) is a consumed-normal physical-value current. It is not asserted to vanish. It is coefficientwise in all uncontracted variables, so their fixed normal operators and subsequent original traces commute with the identity. For finitely many endpoint factors, choose exact value interpolants \(f_i\) separately and write \[ F_{m prod,j}=\prod_iF_{i,j},\qquad G_{m prod,j}=\sum_iG_{i,j}\prod_{\ell
e i}F_{\ell,j}. \] The true product defect is exactly \[  oxed{ \Delta_{m prod,j} =Nc'(j)G_{m prod,j} -\partial_x\!\left(\prod_i f_iight)(x_j) =\sum_i\Delta_{i,j}\prod_{\ell
e i}F_{\ell,j}. } 	ag{15} \] No value is divided out. Thus zeros of physical rows cause no exception. Every occurrence of one shared physical color remains the same color in all incident factors. ## 3. A controlled primitive for the actual analytic bulk transform Fix a frequency interval \(J_0=[a,b]\Subset(0,1/2)\), a real parameter bound \(|\alpha|\le A\), and use the exact interpolant from the pinned bulk Fourier theorem on a slightly larger interval. After reserving its fixed buffer, there are \(d>0\) and \(C\) such that \[ \mathfrak b_N(s/N,\alpha)= eta_{s,N}(\alpha),\qquad \|\mathfrak b_N\|_{\Omega_d(J_0)}\le C/N,\qquad \Omega_d(J_0)=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,J_0)<d\}. 	ag{16} \] Take \(d\) smaller if necessary so that this tube is inside the source rectangle. The exact equality is required at every frequency node used below. All constants are uniform for the real parameter interval. Let the physical row angle \(
u\) range over a fixed compact interval \(\mathcal V_0\Subset(0,\pi)\). Choose a small complex neighborhood \(\mathcal V\) of it and constants \(\mu>0,\Lambda\ge1\) such that, for both signs, \[ z_\pm=e^{\pm i
u},\qquad |1-z_\pm|\ge\mu,\qquad \left| rac{z_\pm}{1-z_\pm}ight|\le\Lambda \quad(
u\in\mathcal V). 	ag{17} \] Put \(h=1/N\), \(T_hg(x)=g(x+h)\), and \[ P_\pm= rac{z_\pm}{1-z_\pm}(T_h-I),\qquad 0<a_*<\min\{d/4,d/(16\Lambda)\},\qquad K_N=\lfloor a_*Nfloor . 	ag{18} \] For sufficiently large \(N\), define \[ \mathcal A_{\pm,N}(x,
u,\alpha) = rac1{1-z_\pm}\sum_{r=0}^{K_N-1} P_\pm^r\mathfrak b_N(x,\alpha). 	ag{19} \] This is a finite holomorphic formula. It keeps the actual frequency sampling, rather than replacing that sampling by an integral. The exact operator identity is \[ (I-z_\pm T_h)\mathcal A_{\pm,N} =\mathfrak b_N-P_\pm^{K_N}\mathfrak b_N. 	ag{20} \] It follows from \(I-z_\pm T_h=(1-z_\pm)(I-P_\pm)\) and the finite geometric sum. In particular, for \(p=\lceil Naceil\), \(q=\lfloor Nbfloor\), \[  egin{split} \sum_{s=p}^{q} eta_{s,N}e^{\pm is
u} ={}&e^{\pm ip
u}\mathcal A_{\pm,N}(p/N,
u,\alpha)\ &-e^{\pm i(q+1)
u} \mathcal A_{\pm,N}((q+1)/N,
u,\alpha)\ &+\sum_{s=p}^{q}e^{\pm is
u} (P_\pm^{K_N}\mathfrak b_N)(s/N,\alpha). \end{split} 	ag{21} \] There is no omitted endpoint term in this summation by parts. For completeness, the exponential estimate follows from a fixed analytic buffer. Use \(K_N\) nested tubes losing radius \(\delta=d/(2K_N)\) at each step, from \(\Omega_d(J_0)\) to \(\Omega_{d/2}(J_0)\). If \(g\) is bounded on the larger tube, a segment of length \(h\) from a point in the next tube leaves Cauchy radius at least \(\delta/2\), since \(h\le\delta/2\) for large \(N\). Therefore \[ \|(T_h-I)g\|\le rac{2h}{\delta}\|g\| = rac{4K_N}{Nd}\|g\|. 	ag{22} \] The choices in (18) imply \(4\Lambda K_N/(Nd)\le1/4\). Iterating on the nested domains and using (16) gives \[ \|\mathcal A_{\pm,N}\|_{\Omega_{d/2}(J_0)} \le rac{4C}{3\mu N},\qquad \|P_\pm^{K_N}\mathfrak b_N\|_{\Omega_{d/2}(J_0)} \le  rac{C}{N}4^{-K_N}. 	ag{23} \] The point \((q+1)/N\) is within this tube for large \(N\). For real \(
u\), the final sum in (21) is thus at most \(C4^{-K_N}\). For an explicit common smaller exponent put \[ \kappa=a_*\log2/4. 	ag{24} \] Since \(K_N\ge a_*N/2\) eventually, (21)'s remainder is \(O(e^{-4\kappa N})\) on the real angle interval, after increasing a constant. On a smaller fixed complex neighborhood, it is \(O(e^{-2\kappa N})\) provided \[ b|\Im
u|\le\kappa 	ag{25} \] and that neighborhood stays inside \(\mathcal V\). The extra factor \(N\) in the actual normal transform still leaves an \(O(e^{-\kappa N})\) error. Fixed derivatives in \(x\) or \(
u\) have the same type of estimate on smaller domains, by Cauchy. Taking the difference of the two signs divided by \(2i\) gives the analytic sine identity \[  egin{split} \sum_{s=p}^{q} eta_{s,N}\sin(s
u) = rac1{2i} ig[& e^{ip
u}\mathcal A_{+,N}(p/N,
u,\alpha) -e^{i(q+1)
u}\mathcal A_{+,N}((q+1)/N,
u,\alpha)\ &-e^{-ip
u}\mathcal A_{-,N}(p/N,
u,\alpha) +e^{-i(q+1)
u}\mathcal A_{-,N}((q+1)/N,
u,\alpha) ig] +\mathcal E_N(
u,\alpha), \end{split} 	ag{26} \] where \(\mathcal E_N\) has the just-stated exponential bounds. Using a difference, rather than complex conjugation, preserves holomorphic spectator and parameter identities wherever the same uniform input domain is available. The terms in square brackets are unremoved terminal primitives. They have size \(O(N^{-1})\) on the real angle interval; multiplying by the normal factor \(N\) in (12) need not make them small. If the frequency interval is subdivided and the same function (19) is used, adjacent terminal terms cancel exactly, with their phases. The two external terminal terms remain. The frequency bands near \(s=0\) and \(s=N/2\), the even middle term, and the separate \(L_t\) term in (12) have not been estimated or discarded by this argument. All estimates here are for the amplitude itself. Multiplying (21) or (26) by an unestimated graph spectator does not provide a bound for that spectator or for its subsequent coherent trace. ## 4. Two bounded channels and the remaining compatibility equation The pinned two-channel theorem gives, on each fixed bulk interval, jointly holomorphic functions \(\mathcal F_N(x,\alpha)\) and \(\mathcal G_N(x,\alpha)\), exact at the original value and normal nodes, with polynomial bounds on a fixed strip. It permits every bounded complex \(\alpha\)-disk and fixed parameter derivatives on smaller disks. Therefore \[ \mathcal D_N(x,\alpha) =Nc'(Nx)\mathcal G_N(x,\alpha) -\partial_x\mathcal F_N(x,\alpha) 	ag{27} \] is a polynomially bounded analytic representative of the true defect (11), when \(f_N=\mathcal F_N\). This statement does not divide by \(\mathcal F_N\), and it does not assert \(\mathcal D_N=0\). The exact identities (12)--(15) apply to its nodal values. The precise recurrence adapter is also useful. Use \[ A(r)= rac{s_{r+1}^4}{s_{2r+1}s_{2r+2}},\qquad C(r)= rac{s_r^4}{s_{2r}s_{2r+1}},\qquad C(0)=0, \] \[ q_N(x)= rac{C(Nx)}{A(Nx)},\quad d_N(x)= rac{c_0-w}{A(Nx)},\quad T_N(x)= egin{pmatrix}1+d_N(x)&q_N(x)/N\ Nd_N(x)&q_N(x)\end{pmatrix}. \] Write the original bulk transfer as \[ X_{j+1}=T_N(x_j)X_j,\qquad Y_{j+1}=T_N(x_j)Y_j+T_N'(x_j)X_j, \] \[ X_j= inom{F_j}{N(F_j-F_{j-1})},\qquad Y_j= inom{Nc'(j)G_j} {N^2[c'(j)G_j-c'(j-1)G_{j-1}]}. 	ag{28} \] The derivative \(T_N'\) is in normalized degree \(x\). For any scalar value interpolant \(f_N\), on a buffered interval where the preceding node is also included, define \[ X_f(x)= inom{f_N(x)}{N[f_N(x)-f_N(x-h)]},\qquad E_f(x)=X_f(x+h)-T_N(x)X_f(x). 	ag{29} \] At every indicated grid point, \(X_f=X_j\) and \(E_f=0\). Differentiating the off-grid definition (29), then subtracting (28), gives the exact defect recurrence \[  oxed{ D_{j+1}=T_N(x_j)D_j-E_f'(x_j),\qquad D_j=Y_j-X_f'(x_j). } 	ag{30} \] Its first component is (11). A separately bounded interpolation of \(Y_j\) does not remove the initial \(D_j\). For \(f_N=\mathcal F_N\), the residual \(E_f\) and its derivatives are polynomially bounded on a slightly smaller fixed strip. The residual \(E_f\) vanishes at every interior grid node. The disk Blaschke estimate proved in the two-channel source consequently gives, after reducing the strip height and real interval by fixed buffers, \[ E_f,\ E_f'=O(N^p e^{-cN}) 	ag{31} \] for some \(p,c>0\). To check this implication directly, choose fixed concentric disks around each point of the smaller real interval. The larger disk lies in the analytic strip; a fixed central real subinterval contains \(c_1N\) grid zeros. On the smaller disk every associated Blaschke factor is at most some \(q<1\). Their product is at most \(q^{c_1N}\); Cauchy on another smaller disk controls the derivative. A finite cover gives (31). Thus the true defect is homogeneous up to exponentially small forcing in the buffered bulk. This does not set its actual initial coefficient to zero. Those initial normals are part of the original source. For example, put \(Q_N(w)=G_0(w)\), and use the just-defined unscaled coefficients. At the first regular step, \[ U_0=c'(0)Q_N(w),\qquad U_j=c'(j)G_j, \] \[ U_1=F_1U_0 - rac{(c_0-w)A'(0)}{A(0)^2} + rac{c'(0)P_N(w)}{N^2s_1^2A(0)}. 	ag{32} \] This formula is used only where that step is regular, in particular for \(N\ge3\). It follows by differentiating the original off-grid kernel equation at zero, using \(C(0)=C'(0)=0\) and \(e_D'(c_0)=\eta/s_1^2\). The last term is the literal endpoint source. For a microscopic real endpoint, \(P_N(w)=4\cosh^2(\alpha/2)\), so it cannot be dropped. Equation (32), or its propagation to a chosen bulk anchor, supplies actual normal data; it is not a choice of integration constant. Neither (32) nor the common-index Jacobi decomposition alone decides whether (27) is small for the chosen global value interpolant. ## 5. Scope and direct-source readbacks The note isolates the exact scalar compatibility question. It adds no claim that a polynomially bounded pair of channels is a single moderate scalar Hermite representative. The bulk sine primitive removes no external connector, physical endpoint, fold band, odd simple value, original crossing, or spectator. In particular it does not give a filled-action estimate for the joined endpoint current. title: Two source constants for the true bulk endpoint normal defect
text:
# Two source constants for the true bulk endpoint normal defect Private written proof, 16 November 2026. On a buffered physical-index interval, the true scalar normal defect is intrinsic up to exponentially small errors among polynomially bounded analytic value interpolants. Its exact discrete transport is determined, to that accuracy, by two actual anchor coefficients. The transport has an explicit two-dimensional continuum limit, regular also at the coalescing parameter \(\alpha=0\). No coefficient is set to zero or assumed small. This reduces the compatibility question to two source constants; it does not answer that question or estimate a filled source. ## 1. Source data and the true defect Fix nested closed intervals \[ I_0\Subset\operatorname{int}I_1,\qquad I_1\Subset\operatorname{int}I_2,\qquad I_2\Subset(0,1/2), 	ag{1} \] and an anchor \(x_*\in\operatorname{int}I_0\). The notation means positive distance from each indicated boundary. Let \(h=N^{-1}\), \(x_j=j/N\), \(	heta=\pi/N\), and use the original data \[ c(r)=2\cos((2r+1)	heta),\quad c'(r)=-4	heta\sin((2r+1)	heta), \quad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N), \] \[ F_j(\alpha)=K_N(c(j),w_N(\alpha)),\qquad G_j(\alpha)=\partial_zK_N(c(j),w_N(\alpha)). 	ag{2} \] Here \(K_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e_k\otimes e_k\) is the original Newton kernel and the original physical relation is \(P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2\). Explicitly, \(S_k=\prod_{r=1}^k2\sin(r	heta)\), \(S_0=1\), and \(e_k(Z)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{r<k}(c(r)-Z)\). All quantities are holomorphic in \(\alpha\). An admissible value interpolation for this note is a function \(f_N(x,\alpha)\), jointly holomorphic on a fixed complex neighborhood of \(I_2\) and on a larger bounded complex parameter disk, such that \[ f_N(x_j,\alpha)=F_j(\alpha)\quad(x_j\in I_2),\qquad \|f_N\|\le C N^p. 	ag{3} \] The pinned two-channel theorem supplies one such family. Its separate normal interpolation is not used to define the derivative in (3). All statements below are uniform on a fixed smaller parameter disk. Constants and strip widths may depend on the intervals, parameter disks, and the bounds in (3), but not on \(N\). Define the original value and common-index normal vectors \[ X_j= inom{F_j}{N(F_j-F_{j-1})},\qquad Y_j= inom{Nc'(j)G_j} {N^2[c'(j)G_j-c'(j-1)G_{j-1}]}. 	ag{4} \] For the chosen scalar interpolation put \[ X_f(x)= inom{f_N(x)}{N[f_N(x)-f_N(x-h)]},\qquad D_j^f=Y_j-X_f'(x_j). 	ag{5} \] The prime on \(X_f\) is in the normalized index \(x\). The first component of \(D_j^f\) is exactly \[ Nc'(j)G_j-\partial_xf_N(x_j). 	ag{6} \] Every node used in (4)--(5) lies inside \(I_2\) for large \(N\), when \(x_j\in I_1\). Use the original coefficients \[ A_N(r)= rac{s_{r+1}^4}{s_{2r+1}s_{2r+2}},\qquad C_N(r)= rac{s_r^4}{s_{2r}s_{2r+1}},\qquad s_r=2\sin(r	heta), \] \[ q_N(x)= rac{C_N(Nx)}{A_N(Nx)},\quad d_N(x)= rac{c(0)-w_N(\alpha)}{A_N(Nx)},\qquad T_N(x)= egin{pmatrix}1+d_N&q_N/N\Nd_N&q_N\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{7} \] The full source equation and its common-index derivative give at bulk physical nodes \[ X_{j+1}=T_N(x_j)X_j,\qquad Y_{j+1}=T_N(x_j)Y_j+T_N'(x_j)X_j. 	ag{8} \] Their endpoint forcing vanishes to the required order at these nodes only; it remains in the actual initial data (2), (4). Let \[ E_f(x)=X_f(x+h)-T_N(x)X_f(x). \] The source adapter proves the exact identity \[ D_{j+1}^f=T_N(x_j)D_j^f-E_f'(x_j). 	ag{9} \] Thus it is the derivative of the scalar residual, not an arbitrarily chosen homogeneous normal channel, that measures the forcing. ## 2. Intrinsic defect and exact discrete transport **Theorem 1.** For all sufficiently large \(N\), the following hold uniformly in the fixed parameter disk. 1. On a fixed complex neighborhood of \(I_1\), after shrinking its width if needed, \[ E_f,\ E_f'=O(N^P e^{-cN}) 	ag{10} \] for some \(P,c>0\). 2. If \(\widetilde f_N\) is any other family satisfying (3), then on \(I_1\)'s physical nodes \[ D_j^f-D_j^{\widetilde f} =O(N^P e^{-cN}). 	ag{11} \] Its constants may use the two common analytic neighborhoods and the larger of their polynomial bounds. 3. Choose a grid index \(j_*(N)\) nearest \(Nx_*\), and write \(x_{*,N}=j_*/N\) and \(\mathbf d_N^f=D_{j_*}^f\). Let \(\mathcal U_N(j,j_*)\) be the exact ordered product of the matrices \(T_N(x_r)\) from \(j_*\) to \(j\), using inverse products for \(j<j_*\). Then \[ D_j^f=\mathcal U_N(j,j_*)\mathbf d_N^f +O(N^P e^{-cN}),\qquad x_j\in I_0, 	ag{12} \] \[ \|\mathcal U_N(j,j_*)\|+ \|\mathcal U_N(j,j_*)^{-1}\|\le C,\qquad \|\mathbf d_N^f\|\le CN^P. 	ag{13} \] These are two actual source coefficients, intrinsic up to (11). They are not adjustable integration constants. *Proof.* Cauchy estimates from (3) control all fixed derivatives on smaller fixed domains. In particular \[ N[f_N(x)-f_N(x-h)]=\int_0^1f_N'(x-th)\,dt \] has the same polynomial bound there; so do \(X_f,E_f\) and their fixed derivatives. At every interior physical node, \(X_f(x_j)=X_j\), hence \(E_f(x_j)=0\) by (8). We recall the precise dense-zero argument. A fixed disk about a real point of \(I_1\), lying in the analytic neighborhood of \(I_2\), contains at least \(c_1N\) grid nodes in a smaller central real interval. A bounded holomorphic function with those zeros is bounded on a still smaller disk by its original bound times \(q^{c_1N}\), \(q<1\): divide by the associated disk Blaschke factors and apply the maximum principle. The factor bound is uniform because both the zeros and the smaller disk lie strictly inside the original disk. Cauchy's formula on one more smaller disk gives the same exponential type for fixed derivatives. Finitely many such disks cover \(I_1\), with a common smaller strip. Applying this to \(E_f\) proves (10). The same argument applied to \(f_N-\widetilde f_N\), which vanishes at all nodes in \(I_2\), proves exponential bounds for this difference and its first two derivatives on a buffered neighborhood of \(I_1\). Equation (5), including its difference quotient, then gives (11). No comparison with the ordinary off-grid kernel is made here. The source theorem gives polynomial bounds for the actual \(F_j,G_j\) on bounded complex parameter disks. Together with (3)--(5), this gives the last assertion in (13). On a fixed neighborhood of \(I_1\), \[ T_N=I_2+O(N^{-1}),\qquad T_N^{-1}=I_2+O(N^{-1}), 	ag{14} \] uniformly in the parameter. Multiplying \(O(N)\) such matrices along the real buffered interval gives the first bounds in (13). Variation of constants in (9) then bounds the error in (12) by \(O(N)\) times (10) times these product bounds. Absorb that factor into \(N^P\). Backward transport uses the same inverse bounds. This proves the theorem. \(\square\) Thus the unknown bulk defect is, to exponential precision, a two-dimensional source datum. The theorem says nothing about the size of that datum beyond its polynomial upper bound. ## 3. Explicit continuum modes and a uniform finite-step comparison The first-order expansion of the exact transfer is \[ T_N(x)=I_2+ rac1N B(x,\alpha)+O(N^{-2}), \] \[ B(x,\alpha)=  egin{pmatrix} 0&1\ -(\pi^2+\alpha^2)\cot^2(\pi x)& -\pi\{3\cot(\pi x)+	an(\pi x)\} \end{pmatrix}. 	ag{15} \] All fixed derivatives have the same uniform remainder on smaller bulk domains. To verify it directly, the exact quotient in (7) is \[ q_N(x)= \left( rac{\sin(\pi x)}{\sin(\pi x+\pi/N)}ight)^4  rac{\sin(2\pi x+2\pi/N)}{\sin(2\pi x)}. \] Hence \[ q_N(x)=1- rac{\pi}{N} \{3\cot(\pi x)+	an(\pi x)\}+O(N^{-2}), \] where \(2\cot(2u)=\cot u-	an u\). Also \[ A_N(Nx)=	an^2(\pi x)+O(N^{-1}),\qquad c(0)-w_N(\alpha)=-(\pi^2+\alpha^2)N^{-2}+O(N^{-4}). \] Substitution in (7) proves (15). Choose the holomorphic branch \[ \ell(x)=\log\sin(\pi x) \] that is real on the real bulk interval, shrinking its complex neighborhood once if necessary. Put \(a_\alpha=\alpha/\pi\) and \[ f_0(x,\alpha)= rac{\cos(a_\alpha\ell(x))}{\sin(\pi x)},\qquad f_1(x,\alpha)= rac{\sin(a_\alpha\ell(x))} {a_\alpha\sin(\pi x)}. 	ag{16} \] The second expression uses its removable value \[ f_1(x,0)= rac{\log\sin(\pi x)}{\sin(\pi x)}. \] These are entire in \(\alpha\), including at zero. Direct differentiation shows that both solve \[ f''+\pi\{3\cot(\pi x)+	an(\pi x)\}f' +(\pi^2+\alpha^2)\cot^2(\pi x)f=0. 	ag{17} \] For \(\alpha
e0\), equivalently use \(\sin(\pi x)^{-1\pm i\alpha/\pi}\); (16) keeps the coalescence at zero regular. Define \[ \Phi(x,\alpha)=  egin{pmatrix}f_0&f_1\ \partial_xf_0&\partial_xf_1\end{pmatrix}. \] Its Wronskian is exactly \[ \det\Phi(x,\alpha) = rac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{\sin^3(\pi x)}. 	ag{18} \] Indeed the common factor is \(\sin(\pi x)^{-1}\), while the Wronskian of \(\cos(a_\alpha\ell)\) and \(\sin(a_\alpha\ell)/a_\alpha\) is \(\ell'\). The determinant is independent of \(\alpha\) and is a unit on the chosen bulk domain. Thus \(\Phi,\Phi^{-1}\) are uniformly bounded on fixed compact parameter sets. They solve \(\Phi'=B\Phi\). **Theorem 2.** Uniformly for \(x_j\in I_0\), \[ \mathcal U_N(j,j_*)= \Phi(x_j,\alpha)\Phi(x_{*,N},\alpha)^{-1}+O(N^{-1}). 	ag{19} \] Consequently, with the actual mode coefficients \[ \mathbf a_N^f(\alpha) =\Phi(x_{*,N},\alpha)^{-1}\mathbf d_N^f, \] one has \[  oxed{\quad D_j^f=\Phi(x_j,\alpha)\mathbf a_N^f(\alpha) +O\!\left(N^{-1}\|\mathbf a_N^f(\alpha)\| +N^P e^{-cN}ight). \quad} 	ag{20} \] All constants are uniform in the fixed complex parameter disk. The coefficients are holomorphic in that parameter and independent of the moderate value interpolant up to exponential errors. *Proof.* Taylor's formula for the continuum fundamental matrix gives \[ \Phi(x+h)\Phi(x)^{-1}=I_2+hB(x,\alpha)+O(h^2). \] Its difference from \(T_N(x)\) is \(O(h^2)\) by (15). A telescoping comparison of the two ordered products has \(O(N)\) terms, each \(O(h^2)\), with their surrounding products uniformly bounded. For the discrete products this is (13); for the continuum products it follows from the bounded fundamental matrix and its inverse. The result is \(O(Nh^2)=O(N^{-1})\). The same argument with inverses works to the left of the anchor. Combining this with (12) proves (20). Holomorphic parameter dependence follows from all exact formulas; (11) and the bounded inverse in (18) prove its final intrinsic assertion. \(\square\) The error in (20) is relative to the norm of the two coefficients, not to a potentially vanishing individual scalar component. At \(\alpha=0\) the displayed logarithmic basis is required; no division by \(\alpha\) is left. ## 4. Physical-parameter calibration and an exact cosh factor There is actual source information about these two coefficients at fixed imaginary parameters. Choose a fixed enlarged radius \(R_\alpha\) whose boundary contains no zero of \(\cosh(\alpha/2)\), and construct the admissible interpolation on a parameter disk strictly larger than \(\{|\alpha|\le R_\alpha\}\). A desired bounded real interval can be contained in a smaller disk \(|\alpha|\le A<R_\alpha\). Every zero in the enlarged disk has the form \[ \zeta=\pm i(2b+1)\pi,\qquad b\ge0, 	ag{21} \] and there are finitely many such zeros, independent of \(N\). At this parameter, exactly \[ w_N(\zeta)=2\cos((2b+1)\pi/N)=c(b). \] For all sufficiently large \(N\), \(b\) is in the distinct physical range. Since \(e_k(c(b))=0\) for \(k>b\), the ordinary kernel reduces before any quotient to the degree-\(b\) polynomial \[ K_N(c(b),Z)=P_{b,N}(Z):=\sum_{k=0}^{b}e_k(c(b))e_k(Z). 	ag{22} \] The coefficients \(e_k(c(b))\) are \(O_b(1)\): the exact difference-of-cosines product is \[ e_k(c(b))= rac{S_{b+k}}{S_{b-k}S_k^2}. \] All indices in this expression are fixed, and cancellation of their powers of \(N^{-1}\) gives that bound. On any fixed complex spectral compact, \(e_k(Z)=O_b(N^{2k})\), directly from its \(k\) factors and \(S_k^{-2}=O_b(N^{2k})\). Thus \[ p_{b,N}(x):=P_{b,N}(c(Nx)) \] and all its fixed derivatives have polynomial bounds on a fixed bulk neighborhood. This is an ordinary scalar value interpolation with its actual compatible normal, not a selected solution of (17). In fact at \(\alpha=\zeta\), ordinary differentiation of (22) gives \[ p_{b,N}'(x_j)=Nc'(j)G_j(\zeta),\qquad X_{p_b}'(x_j)=Y_j(\zeta). 	ag{23} \] For the second component, the equality is explicitly \[ N[p_{b,N}'(x_j)-p_{b,N}'(x_j-h)] =N^2[c'(j)G_j(\zeta)-c'(j-1)G_{j-1}(\zeta)]. \] Therefore its true two-component defect is exactly zero. The difference \(f_N(\,\cdot\,,\zeta)-p_{b,N}\) has polynomial analytic norm and vanishes at every physical node in \(I_2\). The dense-zero argument in Theorem 1 controls its first two derivatives exponentially on \(I_1\). Equations (5), (23), and the bounded inverse of \(\Phi\) imply, for every zero (21), \[ \mathbf a_N^f(\zeta) =O(N^P e^{-cN}). 	ag{24} \] The finitely many \(b\)'s permit common constants and exponent. Here is an exact divisible version of this calibration. List all the zeros inside \(|\alpha|<R_\alpha\) as \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_q\). If there are none, use the empty correction. Otherwise let \[ L_
u(\alpha)=\prod_{\mu
e
u}  rac{\alpha-\zeta_\mu}{\zeta_
u-\zeta_\mu}, \qquad \mathbf r_N(\alpha)=\sum_{
u=1}^{q} \mathbf a_N^f(\zeta_
u)L_
u(\alpha). 	ag{25} \] These are fixed-degree Lagrange polynomials. By (24), \(\|\mathbf r_N\|_{|\alpha|\le R_\alpha} \le CN^Pe^{-cN}\). Every zero of \(\cosh(\alpha/2)\) in the disk is simple, and the numerator in \[ \mathbf h_N(\alpha)=  rac{\mathbf a_N^f(\alpha)-\mathbf r_N(\alpha)} {\cosh(\alpha/2)} 	ag{26} \] vanishes at all of them. Thus all these apparent poles are removable. There are no zeros on the disk boundary. The polynomial bound for \(\mathbf a_N^f\), the positive minimum of \(|\cosh(\alpha/2)|\) on that fixed boundary, and the maximum principle give a polynomial bound for \(\mathbf h_N\) throughout the disk. Consequently \[  oxed{\quad \mathbf a_N^f(\alpha)=\cosh(\alpha/2)\mathbf h_N(\alpha) +\mathbf r_N(\alpha),\qquad \|\mathbf h_N\|\le CN^P,\quad \|\mathbf r_N\|\le CN^Pe^{-cN}. \quad} 	ag{27} \] The equality is exact; only the bound on its correction is asymptotic. Fixed parameter derivatives retain the same estimates on smaller disks by Cauchy's formula. This calibration uses genuine low-degree physical kernels at every zero (21). It does not infer a factor by analytic continuation from finitely many approximate zeros without a correction: (25) is that correction. On the real parameter axis \(\cosh(\alpha/2)\) never vanishes. The quotient \(\mathbf h_N\) remains unknown, so (27) does not establish nonvanishing, smallness, or a leading coefficient for real microscopic endpoint parameters. ## 5. Exact criterion for a moderate scalar Hermite representative The two coefficients characterize, rather than merely accompany, the missing local scalar interpolation. All intervals in this statement retain fixed buffers about the anchor; a smaller fixed strip is allowed. Exponential estimates may include a polynomial factor in \(N\). **Corollary 3.** The following are equivalent: * The actual anchor vector \(\mathbf a_N^f\) is exponentially small. * On a fixed smaller bulk interval containing the anchor there is a polynomially bounded holomorphic scalar \(h_N(x,\alpha)\) matching both physical channels: \[ h_N(x_j,\alpha)=F_j(\alpha),\qquad \partial_xh_N(x_j,\alpha)=Nc'(j)G_j(\alpha). 	ag{28} \] For the forward implication, (28) can be imposed at every node of \(I_0\). For the converse it suffices to have (28) on any fixed neighborhood of the anchor, with an analytic strip and a polynomial bound there. Uniformity in a fixed parameter set is retained when the hypotheses are uniform on a larger parameter neighborhood. The condition is independent of the chosen admissible \(f_N\) in the exponential sense of (11). *Proof of necessity.* On the given neighborhood, \(h_N-f_N\) is polynomially bounded, holomorphic, and zero at every physical value node. Dense zeros therefore make its derivatives exponentially small near the anchor. By (28), \(X_h'(x_j)=Y_j\), including the second component formed from the preceding node. Consequently \[ \mathbf d_N^f =X_h'(x_{*,N})-X_f'(x_{*,N}) =O(N^P e^{-cN}). \] Multiplication by the bounded inverse of \(\Phi\) proves the first condition. The finite difference in component two costs at most a polynomial factor, or may be bounded by the second derivative. *Proof of sufficiency.* Exact transport (12), not just the continuum approximation, makes all \(D_j^f\) exponentially small for \(x_j\in I_0\). Let \(\Delta_j\) denote their first components. On a fixed smaller strip define the finite correction \[ h_N(x,\alpha)=f_N(x,\alpha)+ \sum_{j:\,x_j\in I_0} \Delta_j(\alpha)(x-x_j)\operatorname{sinc}^2(Nx-j), \qquad \operatorname{sinc}z= rac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}. 	ag{29} \] At its own node, each summand has value zero and derivative \(\Delta_j\). At every other grid node its sinc square has a double zero. Thus (29) gives both equalities (28) exactly. There are \(O(N)\) nodes, \(|x-x_j|\) is uniformly bounded on the fixed strip, and \[ |\operatorname{sinc}^2(Nx-j)|\le e^{2\pi N|\Im x|}. \] If \(|\Delta_j|\le CN^P e^{-cN}\), the correction is at most \[ CN^{P+1}e^{-cN+2\pi N|\Im x|}. \] Choose a fixed strip height less than \(c/(4\pi)\), also inside the analytic domain of \(f_N\). The correction is exponentially small there, and \(h_N\) has polynomial norm. Holomorphic parameter dependence and fixed derivative bounds follow directly and by Cauchy on smaller domains. This proves sufficiency. \(\square\) On a sufficiently narrow bulk strip the map \(x\mapsto c(Nx)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi/N)\) is one-to-one with nonzero derivative. Indeed the two possibilities for equality of cosines require either \(x-y\in\mathbb Z\) or \(x+y+1/N\in\mathbb Z\). The first gives \(x=y\) in this rectangle; the second is impossible because its real part lies strictly between zero and one for large \(N\). Its local inverse converts (28) to an actual scalar spectral Hermite representative there. This equivalence does not prove its smallness premise for real \(\alpha\). It supplies no full-period representative or endpoint extension, and no boundary current has been discarded. ## 6. Scope and direct sources The first component of this transported defect is the actual missing spectral normal, multiplied by \(Nc'(j)\). Its contribution to the original trace is the exact current in the pinned normal-defect source, with the original crossing, remaining spectator, shared colors, and all other traces retained. A polynomial upper bound for the two coefficients is not a filled-action bound for that current. Neither transport theorem says that \(\mathbf a_N^f\) is nonzero, zero, exponentially small, or of a specified algebraic order at real parameters. Section 4 gives only its physical-parameter calibration and divisible correction. Establishing its actual real leading coefficients remains a separate source calculation. The common-index determinant's homogeneous remainder is not substituted for the true defect (5). The endpoints of the physical interval, all external connectors, the odd simple node, and the full-period interface are outside this buffered bulk transport. A scalar moderate Hermite representative follows only under the equivalent smallness condition of Corollary 3. No completed contour follows merely from the two-mode reduction. A coverage search of the endpoint and physical-row notes found the exact prolonged recurrence and the true residual adapter, but not this intrinsic two-constant reduction with explicit Euler comparison. Both complete direct source proofs were read at the following unchanged versions, and their used implications and hashes checked: * [True endpoint normal defect and bulk primitive](research_endpoint_normal_defect_bulk_primitive.md), SHA256 60abb9d3e569fae7cd088a752d5f07211a1eeb444ffbd494b376470074ccfec7: true defect, its exact residual recurrence, the retained trace current, and the distinction from the common-index initial channel. * [Moderate two-channel bulk interpolation](research_microscopic_endpoint_two_channel_interpolation.md), SHA256 44f6db0f8afdf1205ab8b0935b95b8a4fd9fa16c6414be2467b8b40a123c0ffe: actual prolonged transfer, polynomial initialization, the analytic value interpolant, and the quantitative dense-zero proof. Only written mathematics, source-text reads, and file hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, or build was run. Adopted notes and public manuscripts remain unchanged.

title: The two-ended limit of the original microscopic endpoint normal
text: # The two-ended limit of the original microscopic endpoint normal Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The first normal at the original physical endpoint has a limit after division by \(N^2\). Both ends of its Newton sum contribute. A uniform inverse-square bound controls the intervening indices and justifies the limit on every bounded complex parameter disk, including the apparent zeros of the complementary formula. The resulting function is entire and strictly positive on the real parameter axis. This is the original endpoint normal constant. It is not either of the two bulk scalar-compatibility coefficients, and does not determine their cancellation with the coefficient-shift channel. ## 1. Exact endpoint normal and complementary identity Use \[ N\ge2,\quad D=N-1,\quad \theta=\pi/N,\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\qquad s_r=2\sin(r\theta),\quad S_i=\prod_{r=1}^i s_r,\quad S_0=1, \] \[ c_r=2\cos((2r+1)\theta),\quad e_i(Z)=S_i^{-2}\prod_{r=0}^{i-1}(c_r-Z),\quad K_N(Z,w)=\sum_{i=0}^{D}e_i(Z)e_i(w), \] \[ P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2,\qquad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N),\qquad Q_N(\alpha)= \left.\partial_ZK_N(Z,w_N(\alpha))\right|_{Z=c_0}. \tag{1} \] The polynomials and derivative are the ordinary original ones, before any quotient or free-boundary replacement. For \(1\le i<N\), the difference-of-cosines identity gives \[ c_r-c_0=-s_rs_{r+1}\quad(1\le r<N-1),\qquad e_i'(c_0)=\frac{(-1)^i}{s_1s_i}. \tag{2} \] Indeed only the factor \(c_0-Z\) is differentiated, and the remaining product is \((-1)^{i-1}S_{i-1}S_i/s_1\). Thus exactly \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{Q_N(\alpha)}{N^2} =\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}q_{i,N}(\alpha),\qquad q_{i,N}(\alpha)= \frac{(-1)^i e_i(w_N(\alpha))}{N^2s_1s_i}. \quad} \tag{3} \] For real \(\alpha\), every summand is strictly positive. Put \(E_{i,N}(\alpha)=(-1)^i e_i(w_N(\alpha))\). The full physical polynomial and the sine product give \[ S_{N-1}=N,\qquad P_N(w_N(\alpha))=4\cosh^2(\alpha/2), \] \[ \boxed{\quad E_{N-m,N}(\alpha) =\frac{P_N(w_N(\alpha))} {N^2s_m^2 E_{m,N}(\alpha)} \qquad(1\le m<N). \quad} \tag{4} \] At a zero of a denominator, (4) means its removable entire continuation. To verify it, the last \(m\) roots in the full product for \(P_N\) are \(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1}\) in reverse order and \(S_{N-m}=N/S_{m-1}\). Therefore \[ E_{N-m,N} =\frac{P_N(w_N)S_{m-1}^2} {N^2\prod_{r<m}(w_N-c_r)} =\frac{P_N(w_N)}{N^2s_m^2E_{m,N}}. \] This is an identity of ordinary functions, not an omitted high sector. ## 2. Uniform inverse-square tails at both ends Let \(d_i=\min(i,N-i)\). For each fixed \(A<\infty\), there is \(C_A\) such that \[ \boxed{\qquad |q_{i,N}(\alpha)|\le \frac{C_A}{d_i^2} \quad(1\le i<N,\ |\alpha|\le A,\ N\ge2). \qquad} \tag{5} \] Here is a proof uniform through the middle of the original list. At \(\alpha=0\), set \(a_{i,N}=E_{i,N}(0)=|e_i(2)|\). Directly \[ a_{i,N} =\prod_{r=0}^{i-1} \left(\frac{\sin((r+1/2)\theta)} {\sin((r+1)\theta)}\right)^2. \tag{6} \] For \(1\le i\le N/2\), split the sine into its argument and \(f(v)=\sin v/v\), with \(f(0)=1\). This function decreases on \([0,\pi/2]\), so \[ 1\le \prod_{r<i}\frac{f((r+1/2)\theta)}{f((r+1)\theta)} \le \frac1{f(i\theta)}\le\frac{\pi}{2}. \tag{7} \] For the middle inequality, the logarithm is the integral of \(-(\log f)'\) over disjoint half-step subintervals of \([0,i\theta]\). The remaining rational product is \((1/2)_i/i!\). The elementary central-binomial bounds therefore give absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that \[ \frac{c}{i+1}\le \left(\frac{(1/2)_i}{i!}\right)^2 \le a_{i,N}\le \frac{\pi^2}{4}\left(\frac{(1/2)_i}{i!}\right)^2 \le\frac{C}{i+1}. \tag{8} \] Equation (4) at \(\alpha=0\) gives \[ a_{N-m,N}=\frac4{N^2s_m^2a_{m,N}}. \tag{9} \] For \(m\le N/2\), \(4m/N\le s_m\le2\pi m/N\). Equations (8)--(9) show \[ a_{i,N}\le C/d_i \quad(1\le i<N). \tag{10} \] The same bound controls every bounded complex parameter disk. The power series for cosh gives \[ |w_N(\alpha)-2| \le2\cosh(A/N)-2\qquad(|\alpha|\le A). \tag{11} \] Each \(2-c_r\) is positive. Hence \[ \frac{|e_i(w_N(\alpha))|}{|e_i(2)|} \le\prod_{r<i} \left(1+\frac{2\cosh(A/N)-2}{2-c_r}\right) \le\prod_{r=0}^{N-1} \frac{2\cosh(A/N)-c_r}{2-c_r} =\cosh^2(A/2). \tag{12} \] The last equality uses the literal \(P_N\), with all repeated roots and the odd simple root included. Finally \(s_1\ge4/N\) and \(s_i=s_{d_i}\ge4d_i/N\). Substitution of (10)--(12) in (3) proves (5). In particular, for every integer \(L\ge1\) with \(2L<N\), \[ \sup_{|\alpha|\le A} \sum_{L<i<N-L}|q_{i,N}(\alpha)|\le C_A/L. \tag{13} \] This is the uniform middle-tail control needed before passing either end to a limiting series. ## 3. The limiting entire function Define the entire polynomials \[ \mathsf E_m(\alpha) =\frac{(1/2+i\alpha/(2\pi))_m (1/2-i\alpha/(2\pi))_m}{(m!)^2} =\prod_{r=0}^{m-1} \frac{(r+1/2)^2+(\alpha/(2\pi))^2}{(r+1)^2}. \tag{14} \] For fixed positive \(i\), the ordinary sine products in (1) give locally uniformly in \(\alpha\) \[ E_{i,N}(\alpha)\longrightarrow\mathsf E_i(\alpha),\qquad q_{i,N}(\alpha)\longrightarrow \mathsf L_i(\alpha):=\frac{\mathsf E_i(\alpha)}{4\pi^2i}. \tag{15} \] For the other end, (4) gives, for fixed positive \(m\), \[ q_{N-m,N}(\alpha)\longrightarrow \mathsf H_m(\alpha):= \frac{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)} {4\pi^4m^3\mathsf E_m(\alpha)}. \tag{16} \] The apparent poles in \(\mathsf H_m\) are removable. Every zero of \(\mathsf E_m\) is a simple zero among \(\alpha=\pm i(2r+1)\pi\), \(0\le r<m\), whereas \(\cosh^2(\alpha/2)\) has a double zero there. Thus \(\mathsf H_m\) denotes an entire function. The locally uniform limit in (16), including those zeros, also follows directly from the exact unit factorization in the next section. Passing the uniform finite bound (5) to each fixed end yields \[ \sup_{|\alpha|\le A} (|\mathsf L_m(\alpha)|+|\mathsf H_m(\alpha)|) \le C_A/m^2. \tag{17} \] Consequently the function \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal Q(\alpha)= \frac1{4\pi^2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mathsf E_i(\alpha)}{i} +\frac{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)}{4\pi^4} \sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac1{m^3\mathsf E_m(\alpha)} \quad} \tag{18} \] is interpreted by the entire summands in (16), and both sums converge normally on every bounded complex disk. It is an even entire function. For real \(\alpha\), all summands in both series are strictly positive, so \[ \mathcal Q(\alpha)>0. \tag{19} \] **Theorem.** Uniformly on every bounded complex parameter disk, \[ \frac{Q_N(\alpha)}{N^2}\longrightarrow\mathcal Q(\alpha). \tag{20} \] Every fixed parameter derivative converges uniformly on smaller disks. In fact the quantitative estimate \[ \sup_{|\alpha|\le A} \left|\frac{Q_N(\alpha)}{N^2}-\mathcal Q(\alpha)\right| \le C_A N^{-1/2} \tag{21} \] holds for all sufficiently large \(N\). The same rate holds for each fixed \(\alpha\)-derivative, after using a larger fixed parameter disk. Even without the quantitative argument, (20) follows by retaining the first \(L\) terms at each end, using (15)--(16), and then using (13),(17) before sending \(L\) to infinity. No unbounded Newton range is replaced by its fixed-index limit without this tail control. ## 4. Quantitative comparison through the apparent zeros Write \(\operatorname{sinhc}z=\sinh z/z\) and \(\operatorname{sinc}z=\sin z/z\), with their removable values one. There is an exact entire factorization \[ w_N(\alpha)-c_r =\frac{\alpha^2+(2r+1)^2\pi^2}{N^2} \operatorname{sinhc}\!\left(\frac{\alpha+i(2r+1)\pi}{2N}\right) \operatorname{sinhc}\!\left(\frac{\alpha-i(2r+1)\pi}{2N}\right). \tag{22} \] It is the identity \(2\cosh u-2\cos v =4\sinh((u+iv)/2)\sinh((u-iv)/2)\). Dividing the exact finite product by its sine denominators gives \[ E_{i,N}(\alpha)=\mathsf E_i(\alpha)\,\mathsf U_{i,N}(\alpha), \] \[ \mathsf U_{i,N}(\alpha)= \prod_{r=0}^{i-1} \frac{ \operatorname{sinhc}((\alpha+i(2r+1)\pi)/(2N)) \operatorname{sinhc}((\alpha-i(2r+1)\pi)/(2N))} {\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(r+1)/N)^2}. \tag{23} \] This identity holds at zeros of \(\mathsf E_i\); it is not obtained by dividing pointwise there. Let \(L=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). For \(|\alpha|\le A\) and \(i\le L\), all factors in (23) are units in one fixed neighborhood of one for large \(N\). Taylor's formula and their logarithms give \[ \left|\log\mathsf U_{i,N}(\alpha)\right| \le\frac{C_A}{N^2}\sum_{r<i}(r+1)^2 \le C_A N^{-1/2}, \] \[ \mathsf U_{i,N}^{\ \pm1}=1+O_A(N^{-1/2}) \qquad(i\le L). \tag{24} \] The logarithms here are the branches near one, chosen for individual unit factors; no logarithm of \(\mathsf E_i\) is taken. The sine denominators likewise give, uniformly for \(i\le L\), \[ \begin{split} q_{i,N} &=\mathsf L_i\,\mathsf U_{i,N} [\operatorname{sinc}(\pi/N) \operatorname{sinc}(\pi i/N)]^{-1},\\ q_{N-i,N} &=\mathsf H_i\,\mathsf U_{i,N}^{-1} [\operatorname{sinc}(\pi/N) \operatorname{sinc}(\pi i/N)^3]^{-1}. \end{split} \tag{25} \] The second equality follows first where \(\mathsf E_i\ne0\) from (4), then everywhere by removable continuation. Both displayed unit multipliers are \(1+O_A(N^{-1/2})\). For each fixed \(i\), (23)--(25) prove the locally uniform limits (15)--(16), justifying the earlier use of (5) to obtain (17). For sufficiently large \(N\), the two ranges \(1\le i\le L\) and \(1\le N-i\le L\) are disjoint. Sum (25), using (17): \[ \sup_{|\alpha|\le A} \left|\sum_{i=1}^{L} [q_{i,N}+q_{N-i,N}-\mathsf L_i-\mathsf H_i]\right| \le C_A N^{-1/2}. \tag{26} \] The remaining finite and infinite tails are \(O_A(L^{-1})\) by (13),(17). Since \(L^{-1}=O(N^{-1/2})\), this proves (21). Apply the estimate on a larger disk and then Cauchy's formula to obtain its derivative assertion. ## 5. Meaning for the original normal data In the unscaled original index coordinate, \(c'(0)=-4(\pi/N)\sin(\pi/N)\). Thus the actual initial common-index normal satisfies \[ c'(0)Q_N(\alpha) =-4\pi^2\mathcal Q(\alpha)+O_A(N^{-1/2}), \tag{27} \] uniformly on the same bounded complex disks. For real \(\alpha\), its limiting value is strictly negative. This fixes an actual endpoint datum in the original differentiated recurrence. The second series in (18) is indispensable: every fixed \(i=N-m\) contributes at the same \(N^2\) scale as a fixed low index. In particular a terminating fixed-degree value limit does not by itself determine (27). Nothing here compares (27) to the derivative of a chosen moderate bulk value interpolant. The true bulk defect also includes the coefficient-shift and propagated endpoint-source contributions. Its two anchor coefficients, the original trace current, the external connectors, and any filled-action comparison remain separate questions. No source coefficient is inferred from the positive real endpoint constant. ## 6. Direct-source readbacks Both complete direct sources were read at the displayed unchanged versions, with the used implications and hashes checked: * [Original bulk Fourier and complementary Newton identities](research_endpoint_bulk_fourier_interpolation.md), SHA256 4f92c6081bf67646a14181bb753a903cf615d16adcd8d56d1534842303adb7eb: the ordinary kernel normalization, full physical polynomial, and complementary-index identity underlying (4). * [True endpoint normal and its source placement](research_endpoint_normal_defect_bulk_primitive.md), SHA256 60abb9d3e569fae7cd088a752d5f07211a1eeb444ffbd494b376470074ccfec7: the original endpoint normal datum, its retained source term, and the distinction from scalar bulk compatibility. The uniform two-ended tail bound, entire limiting series and quantitative comparison are proved above. Only written mathematics, source-text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or build was run. Frozen notes and public manuscripts were not changed.

title: Decay of the actual omitted endpoint rows
text:
# Decay of the actual omitted endpoint rows Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The omitted high Newton band has an additional physical-row penalty, beyond its previously proved polynomial norm. This estimate applies before any remaining coupled trace is bounded. It concentrates the uncontrolled weights near the angular endpoint on the square-root level scale. A final proposition explains why the local low/high cancellation exponent cannot generally be improved to half the imaginary height for the same truncated kernel. ## 1. Original tail weights and their exact lowering products Put \[ D=N-1,\quad m=\lfloor N/2floor,\quad k_0=N-m,\quad 	heta=\pi/N,\quad\eta=(-1)^D,\quad c_a=2\cos((2a+1)	heta),\quad 	au_a=(D-2a)	heta. 	ag{1} \] Use the original Newton polynomials \(e_j(Z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{h<j}(c_h-Z)\), with \(s_j=2\sin(j	heta)\), \(S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j s_h\), the kernel \(K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{D}e_j(w)e_j(Z)\), and full closing \[ \phi_N(h)=\eta\sum_{a<m} \{(4-c_a^2)h'(c_a)-c_ah(c_a)\} +\mathbf1_{N\ {m odd}}h(-2). 	ag{2} \] Let \(w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N)\). For \(0\le L\le m-1\), set \[ P_{N,L}(\alpha,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k_0+L}e_j(w_N(\alpha))e_j(Z), \qquad O_{N,L}=K_N(w_N(\alpha),Z)-P_{N,L}(\alpha,Z). 	ag{3} \] Thus \(O_{N,L}\) is the omitted high band, not a value-only replacement of the kernel. With \(r_*=m-L-2\), its exact contraction is \[ \phi_N(O_{N,L}f)=\sum_{a=0}^{r_*}\omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha)f(c_a), \qquad \omega_{a,N,L}=\sum_{r=a}^{r_*}e_{D-r}(w_N(\alpha))b_{ra}, 	ag{4} \] \[ b_{ra}=(-1)^{r+a}  rac{s_{2a+1}S_r^2}{S_{r-a}S_{r+a+1}}, \quad s_j=2\sin(j	heta),\quad S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j s_h. \] An empty sum is zero. The surviving rows have \[ 	au_a\ge  egin{cases} (2L+3)	heta,&N\ {m even},\ (2L+4)	heta,&N\ {m odd}. \end{cases} 	ag{5} \] The radical value is zero at every physical node. Consequently the original normal in (2) differentiates \(O_{N,L}\), and no spectator normal remains in (4). The odd simple-node contribution is zero. For \(p_a=m-1-a\), introduce \[ (A_j,B_j)=  egin{cases} ((j+	frac12)	heta,(j+1)	heta),&N=2m,\ ((j+1)	heta,(j+	frac32)	heta),&N=2m+1, \end{cases} \] \[ ho_{j,N}(\alpha,t)=  rac{[\cos^2A_j+\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))] [\sin^2(t/2)-\sin^2A_j]}{\cos^4B_j}, 	ag{6} \] \[ T_{0,N}(\alpha,t)=  egin{cases} \displaystyle  rac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}N\sin t,&N=2m,\[3pt] \displaystyle  rac{\cosh(\alpha/2)\cosh(\alpha/(2N))} {N\cos^4(	heta/2)}\sin t\sin(t/2),&N=2m+1. \end{cases} 	ag{7} \] The exact lowering identities in the pinned sources give \[  oxed{\quad \omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha)= \eta(-1)^a T_{0,N}(\alpha,	au_a) \sum_{l=L+1}^{p_a}\prod_{j=0}^{l-1} ho_{j,N}(\alpha,	au_a). \quad} 	ag{8} \] Indeed \(r=m-1-l\), and for real \(\alpha\) the sign of \(e_{D-r}(w)b_{ra}\) is the common factor \(\eta(-1)^a\). The exact signed identity extends to complex \(\alpha\) because all its expressions are entire in that parameter. The last actual term is \(l=p_a\). The next ratio has \(\sin^2(	au_a/2)=\sin^2 A_{p_a}\), so the chain terminates exactly. No ratio with a vanishing denominator is used. ## 2. A uniform physical-row penalty **Theorem 1.** For every fixed \(A<\pi\), there is \(C_A\) such that, at both parities, for \(|\alpha|\le A\), every \(0\le L\le m-1\), and every row in (4), \[ |\omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha)| \le C_A\min\left\{N^{3/2}, N^4 igl[\sin^2(	au_a/2) igr]^{L+1}ight\}. 	ag{9} \] The second bound in fact holds on every bounded complex \(\alpha\)-set, without \(A<\pi\). The stricter parameter condition will be used for shared full-kernel values in Section 3. *Proof.* Fix a physical row and write \(z=\sin^2(	au_a/2)\). For \(j<l\le p_a\), all factors are before physical termination, and \[ 0\le z-\sin^2A_j\le z\cos^2A_j,\qquad |\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))|\le C_A/N^2. \] Therefore \[ \left|\prod_{j<l}ho_{j,N}ight| \le z^l \left(\prod_{j<l} rac{\cos A_j}{\cos B_j}ight)^4 \prod_{j<l}\left(1+ rac{C_A}{N^2\cos^2A_j}ight). 	ag{10} \] All cosines in this inequality are positive. Since \(B_j=A_j+	heta/2\) and \(A_{j+1}=A_j+	heta\), the intervals \([A_j,B_j]\) are disjoint and contained in \([0,B_{l-1}]\). Integrating \(	an u\ge0\) gives \[ \prod_{j<l} rac{\cos A_j}{\cos B_j} \le rac1{\cos B_{l-1}}\le rac1{\sin	heta}\le rac N2. 	ag{11} \] For the middle inequality, \(l\le p_a\le m-1\) gives \(B_{l-1}\le\pi/2-	heta\) at both parities. The case \(l=0\) is the empty product and needs no such estimate. Likewise \(A_j\le\pi/2-3	heta/2\), and the distances \(\pi/2-A_j\), read backwards, increase in steps of \(	heta\). Using \(\sin u\ge2u/\pi\) for \(0\le u\le\pi/2\), \[ \sum_{j<l}\sec^2A_j \le rac{N^2}{4}\sum_{q=0}^{\infty}(q+	frac32)^{-2} \le C N^2. 	ag{12} \] Thus the last product in (10) is at most a constant depending only on the bounded parameter set. Equations (10)--(12) imply \[ \left|\prod_{j<l}ho_{j,N}ight|\le C_A N^4 z^l. 	ag{13} \] The base (7) is \(O_A(N^{-1})\) uniformly over the physical grid. There are at most \(N\) terms in (8), and \(0\le z\le1\). Summing (13) for \(l\ge L+1\) proves the second bound in (9). The finitely many small levels can be absorbed in the constant; at \(N=2\) the omitted band is empty. The first bound in (9) is the full-radical Fourier bound already proved in the central-band source, whose parameters may be any bounded complex set. Both estimates concern the same coefficient, so their minimum is valid. \(\square\) For \(L=\lfloor\delta Nfloor\), \(0<\delta<1/2\), the pointwise exponential penalty in (9), after polynomial factors, is \[ -\delta\log igl(\sin^2(	au/2) igr). 	ag{14} \] It is strictly positive on every fixed physical angular compact away from \(\pi\). Its loss at \(	au=\pi\) has an explicit scale. Since \[ \sin^2(	au_a/2)=\cos^2\!\left( rac{\pi(a+1/2)}Night), \qquad \log\cos x\le-x^2/2\quad(0\le x<\pi/2), \] one obtains \[ |\omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha)| \le C_A N^4 \exp\left[- rac{\delta\pi^2(a+1/2)^2}{N}ight]. 	ag{15} \] This describes the weights on the \(\sqrt N\) endpoint scale. It is not a bound on a whole row after multiplying by its remaining coupled source. ## 3. Shared coupons and all surviving traces At one traced vertex take a fixed number \(r\) of endpoint coupons, \[ B_i(Z)=K_N(w_N(\alpha_i),Z),\quad P_i(Z)=P_{N,L}(\alpha_i,Z),\quad O_i=B_i-P_i, \qquad |\alpha_i|\le A<\pi. 	ag{16} \] The root-disk bound in the cancellation source gives \(|B_i(c_a)|\le1\) at every distinct physical node for all sufficiently large \(N\), uniformly in the indicated complex disk. The product of two \(O_i\)'s has zero values and first normals. Thus the exact full-normal product rule is \[ \phi_N\!\left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^r B_i-\prod_{i=1}^r P_iight)fight] =\sum_{a\le r_*}\Omega_a f(c_a),\qquad \Omega_a=\sum_{i=1}^r\omega_{a,N,L}(\alpha_i) \prod_{j
e i}B_j(c_a). 	ag{17} \] No \(B_j'\) or \(f'\) term is missing: in every surviving product-rule term the single normal has already fallen on the zero-valued factor \(O_i\). The odd simple value is zero. Consequently \[ |\Omega_a|\le C_A r \min\left\{N^{3/2},N^4[\sin^2(	au_a/2)]^{L+1}ight\}. 	ag{18} \] Here is a coefficientwise form for the original coupled graph. Let \(S\) be its traced vertices and \(T\subseteq S\) the vertices with such shared endpoint products. Retain every original edge, any joint polynomial spectator, and all original crossing and charge coupons. Let \(Z_B\) be the resulting full trace and \(Z_P\) the trace with every indicated product \(\prod_iB_i\) replaced by \(\prod_iP_i\). For \(\varnothing
e U\subseteq T\), define \(\mathscr Z_U(\mathbf a)\) by setting \(z_v=c_{a_v}\) at \(v\in U\), retaining all original kernel and spectator factors at these shared colors, using the partial endpoint products at \(T\setminus U\), and taking the full original traces at \(S\setminus U\). Omit the designated endpoint products at \(U\): their contribution is already in \(\Omega_{v,a_v}\). Keep any original charge coupon at an evaluated vertex in \(\mathscr Z_U\); keep its crossing value explicitly below. Expansion of (17) at distinct vertices gives \[ Z_B-Z_P= \sum_{\varnothing
e U\subseteq T}\ \sum_{0\le a_v\le r_*} \left[\prod_{v\in U}\Omega_{v,a_v}R_{n_v}(c_{a_v})ight] \mathscr Z_U(\mathbf a). 	ag{19} \] This is an identity for the original source. In particular an edge joining two evaluated vertices remains \(K_N(c_{a_v},c_{a_w})\); an edge to a surviving vertex remains its original physical-boundary kernel. The remaining traces retain all normals, carriers and their coherent sums. For real powers \(n_v\), the crossing values have modulus one. Writing \[ W_{N,L}(	au)= \min\{N^{3/2},N^4[\sin^2(	au/2)]^{L+1}\}, \] (18)--(19) give the actual weighted bound \[ |Z_B-Z_P| \le\sum_{\varnothing
e U\subseteq T} \prod_{v\in U}(C_A r_v) \sum_{\mathbf a} \left[\prod_{v\in U}W_{N,L}(	au_{a_v})ight] |\mathscr Z_U(\mathbf a)|. 	ag{20} \] Fixed derivatives in free spectator variables independent of the designated \(\alpha_i\)'s satisfy the same formula with those derivatives applied to \(\mathscr Z_U\). No bound for \(\mathscr Z_U\) at the filled geometric action is assumed or proved. The new penalty is retained before that separate source-estimation problem. ## 4. A sharp restriction on the partial-kernel cancellation rate The exact forcing of the adopted low/high cancellation equation also gives a limit on a proposed stronger bound. This concerns the same partial kernel (3), not a synthetic solution of its equation. Fix \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), set \(a_\delta=\sin^2(\pi\delta)\), and suppose \(H>0\) satisfies \[ b:=\sinh^2(H/2),\qquad b+2a_\delta<1. 	ag{21} \] This is exactly the condition that \(-iH\) belong to the general-domain contraction set. At \(\alpha=0\), let \[ E_N(t)= rac{P_{N,\lfloor\delta Nfloor}(0,-2\cos t)} {Q_N(-2\cos t)}, \] where \(Q_N\) is the monic distinct-node polynomial, and put \[ I_\delta(H)= -\int_0^\delta \log rac{b+\sin^2(\pi x)}{\cos^2(\pi x)}\,dx>0. 	ag{22} \] **Proposition 2.** There is a constant \(c>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\) at either parity, \[ \max_{j=-1,0,1}|E_N(-iH+2j\pi/N)| \ge cN^{-2}e^{-NI_\delta(H)}. 	ag{23} \] If also \(H\ge\log3\), then \[ I_\delta(H)\le\delta H<H/2. 	ag{24} \] Consequently no neighborhood-uniform estimate \(|E_N(t)|\le C N^C e^{-N|\Im t|/2}\) can hold near this point. The proposition does not give that lower bound at the center \(-iH\) alone. *Proof.* The exact gauged equation in the cancellation source is \[ M_NE_N+\widetilde A_N(E_N(t-2	heta)-E_N(t)) +\widetilde C_N(E_N(t+2	heta)-E_N(t))=\mathcal F_N, \] \[ \mathcal F_N=(c_{k_*}-2) eta_N(0) \prod_{l=0}^{L-1}ho_{l,N}(0,t), \quad L=\lfloor\delta Nfloor,\quad k_*=k_0+L. 	ag{25} \] The three left-hand coefficients are uniformly bounded near \(-iH\): the source proves \(M_N	o4\cot^2(t/2)\) and \(\widetilde A_N,\widetilde C_N	o\cot^2(t/2)\) there. At this point every ratio in the product is negative, and its absolute value is \[  rac{\cos^2A_l\,[b+\sin^2A_l]}{\cos^4B_l}. 	ag{26} \] All factors are bounded away from zero and infinity over the fixed interval \(0\le l/N\le\delta\). Their logarithms differ uniformly by \(O(N^{-1})\) from \(\log[(b+\sin^2(\pi l/N))/\cos^2(\pi l/N)]\). A Riemann-sum estimate therefore gives \[ \sum_{l<L}\log|ho_{l,N}(0,-iH)| =-NI_\delta(H)+O(1). 	ag{27} \] Moreover \( eta_N(0)\) is bounded above and below by positive constants times \(N^{-2}\), and \(c_{k_*}-2\longrightarrow-2(1+\cos(2\pi\delta))
e0\). Thus \(|\mathcal F_N|\ge c_1N^{-2}e^{-NI_\delta(H)}\). Taking absolute values in (25) proves (23). Finally \(b\ge e^{-H}\) is equivalent to \(H\ge\log3\): \[ b-e^{-H}= rac{(e^H-3)(e^H+1)}{4e^H}. \] The ratio inside the logarithm in (22) is at least \(b\), so \(-\log[(b+\sin^2(\pi x))/\cos^2(\pi x)]\le H\). This proves (24). All three points in (23) have imaginary height \(-H\) and approach the same center. The asserted uniform half-height estimate would contradict (23)--(24). \(\square\) The forcing obstruction does not contradict the positive, generally smaller exponential constant in the adopted cancellation theorem. Nor does it make the restored full kernel homogeneous: the original full kernel has its own nonzero highest-index forcing. Equations (19)--(20) and the retained vertical currents remain part of any comparison with the filled action. No whole-source upper bound or geometric coefficient follows from this note. ## 5.
