Direct sources The three complete direct sources were read at the following versions, their directly used identities checked, and hashes verified. * [Exact central band and original omitted weights](research_endpoint_central_band_half_charge_source.md), SHA256 a10186ce0d172eba2021d145b3eb5ced5c68f595397f47f3abac53429c6587da: full closing, radical weights and support, polynomial bound, original crossing values and coefficientwise graph placement. * [General endpoint amplitude domain](research_endpoint_radical_general_domain.md), SHA256 600ae0d78f29946272ed54b600cb1f5fdf170965985a08d6e3d9201303722074: exact bases, both-parity lowering products and physical termination. * [Actual low/high exponential cancellation](research_endpoint_low_high_exponential_cancellation.md), SHA256 594bd802439d08e3dfe32f6cfa1027d291b36c502061dc7723fd0a8734527f5d: root-disk bound, shared-coupon full-normal identity, exact gauged forcing equation and the distinction from the full kernel. Only written mathematics, text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or compilation was run. Adopted notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: A divided-difference module for original endpoint products
text: # A divided-difference module for original endpoint products Private written proof, 16 November 2026. An exact six-channel divided-difference module for one original endpoint kernel gives a fixed-dimensional module for every fixed ordinary product. All source aliases are retained. A polynomial change of channels gives a controlled-degree matrix equation whose bounded-variable principal determinant has only the terminal and microscopic factors. Its original-turn transport is literal. The result is algebraic. It supplies neither a whole-source rate nor a nonzero characteristic coefficient. In particular it does not identify the rate of a turned product with the terminal rate. ## 1. Exact half-shift calculus and the original operator Put \[ N\ge2,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad \kappa=q^{(N-1)^2/2}, \quad s=q-q^{-1},\quad a=\frac{q+q^{-1}}2,\quad c_0=2a,\quad \zeta=q^2+q^{-2}, \] \[ z(v)=v+v^{-1},\quad z_\pm=z(q^{\pm1}v),\quad \delta=z_+-z_-=s(v-v^{-1}),\quad Z=z(v). \tag{1} \] For an ordinary spectral polynomial \(f\), define \[ \mathcal Df(Z)=\frac{f(z_+)-f(z_-)}{\delta},\qquad \mathcal Sf(Z)=\frac{f(z_+)+f(z_-)}2. \tag{2} \] Both expressions are ordinary polynomials in \(Z\). Indeed the two spectral arguments have sum \(2aZ\) and product \(Z^2+s^2\); the symmetric difference quotient has the same polynomial property. These definitions also act on rational functions where their denominators do not vanish. Set \[ U_1=(a^2-1)Z,\qquad U_2=(a^2-1)(Z^2-4)=\delta^2/4. \] The exact identities are \[ \begin{split} \mathcal D(fg)&=(\mathcal Df)(\mathcal Sg) +(\mathcal Sf)(\mathcal Dg),\\ \mathcal S(fg)&=(\mathcal Sf)(\mathcal Sg) +U_2(\mathcal Df)(\mathcal Dg),\\ \mathcal D\mathcal S&=a\mathcal S\mathcal D+U_1\mathcal D^2,\\ \mathcal S^2&=I+U_1\mathcal S\mathcal D+aU_2\mathcal D^2. \end{split} \tag{3} \] The first two follow by expanding the two half shifts. For a complete check of the last two, put \(\delta_\pm=s(q^{\pm1}v-q^{\mp1}v^{-1})\). Then \[ \delta_+=a\delta+2U_1,\qquad \delta_-=a\delta-2U_1. \tag{4} \] Compare the coefficients of \(f(z(q^2v))\) and \(f(z(q^{-2}v))\) in the last two identities of (3). For the third identity the needed coefficients are \((a/2+U_1/\delta)/\delta_+=1/(2\delta)\) and \((-a/2+U_1/\delta)/\delta_-=-1/(2\delta)\). For the fourth they are \((U_1/2+a\delta/4)/\delta_+=1/4\) and \((-U_1/2+a\delta/4)/\delta_-=1/4\). The middle coefficients then agree because the operators annihilate constants in the third identity and preserve constants in the fourth. This proves (3) as rational identities, with their polynomial removable continuations. Let \(\mathcal L\) be the original ordinary Askey--Wilson operator from the pinned source. Define \[ \sigma(Z)=(2a^2-1)Z^2-4aZ+8-4a^2,\qquad \tau(Z)=2aZ-4. \tag{5} \] Then exactly \[ \mathcal L=c_0+s^2 \{\sigma\mathcal D^2+\tau\mathcal S\mathcal D\}. \tag{6} \] Here is a direct normalization check. The forward and backward coefficients of \(\mathcal L-c_0\) are \(-A(v),-B(v)\), where \[ A(v)=-\frac{(qv-1)^4}{q(v^2-1)(q^2v^2-1)},\qquad B(v)=-\frac{(v-q)^4}{q(v^2-1)(v^2-q^2)}. \] The coefficients of \(\mathcal D^2,\mathcal S\mathcal D\) are determined by \[ s^2\sigma=-\frac{\delta}{2}(A\delta_++B\delta_-), \qquad s^2\tau=-A\delta_++B\delta_-. \tag{7} \] Substitution gives (5). The middle coefficient follows by applying both operators to \(1\). In particular \[ \sigma\longrightarrow(Z-2)^2,\qquad \tau\longrightarrow2(Z-2) \quad\hbox{as }N\longrightarrow\infty. \tag{8} \] No division by \(Z+2\) occurs in this presentation. ## 2. Six actual polynomial channels, with both source aliases Retain the original kernel \(f_i(Z)=K_N(w_i,Z)\), and put \[ p(Z)=P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2,\qquad \lambda_i=\frac{w_i-c_0}{s^2},\qquad \gamma_i=-\frac{P_N(w_i)}{N^4s^2},\qquad r_i(Z)=\frac{\gamma_i}{Z-c_0}. \tag{9} \] The original forcing is equivalent to the ordinary rational identity \[ \sigma\mathcal D^2f_i+\tau\mathcal S\mathcal Df_i -\lambda_i f_i=r_i p. \tag{10} \] The product \(r_i p\) has its prescribed ordinary removable continuation. The signs and powers of \(N\) follow from \((w_i-\mathcal L)f_i=P_N(w_i)p/[N^4(Z-c_0)]\). Since \(q^N=-1\), the aliases satisfy exactly \[ \mathcal Dp=0,\qquad \mathcal Sp=4-p, \qquad \mathcal D1=0,\quad\mathcal S1=1. \tag{11} \] Thus the channel \(1\) must accompany \(p\). Applying a half shift after prematurely setting \(p=0\) would lose (11). Use the actual ordinary polynomial vector \[ Z_i=(f_i,d_i,h_i,t_i,p,1)^{\mathsf T}, \quad d_i=\mathcal Df_i,\quad h_i=\mathcal Sf_i,\quad t_i=\mathcal S\mathcal Df_i. \tag{12} \] The following formulas explicitly construct rational matrices \(\mathbf D_i,\mathbf S_i\) with \(\mathcal DZ_i=\mathbf D_i Z_i\), \(\mathcal SZ_i=\mathbf S_i Z_i\). All scalar operations \(\mathcal D,\mathcal S\) on coefficients below have the definition (2). Write \(X_i=\mathcal D^2f_i\), \(Y_i=\mathcal D^3f_i\), \(Z_i^{(2)}=\mathcal S\mathcal D^2f_i\), and define \[ X_i=\frac{\lambda_i f_i-\tau t_i+r_i p}{\sigma}, \] \[ A=\mathcal S\sigma+U_1\mathcal S\tau+aU_2\mathcal D\tau, \qquad B=\mathcal D\sigma+a\mathcal S\tau+U_1\mathcal D\tau, \] \[ u_i=(\mathcal Dr_i)(4-p)+(\lambda_i-\mathcal D\tau)d_i, \qquad v_i=(\mathcal Sr_i)(4-p)-(\mathcal S\tau)d_i+\lambda_i h_i. \tag{13} \] Applying \(\mathcal D\) and \(\mathcal S\) to (10), with (3), gives exactly \[ \begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ U_2B&A\end{pmatrix} \binom{Y_i}{Z_i^{(2)}}=\binom{u_i}{v_i}. \tag{14} \] For example the coefficient of \(\mathcal D^3f_i\) in the first row is \(\mathcal S\sigma+U_1\mathcal S\tau+aU_2\mathcal D\tau\); in the second it is \(U_2B\). The remaining lower terms are precisely the two terms in \(d_i,h_i\) displayed in (13). This determinant has an exact factorization. Put \(b=2a^2-1=\zeta/2\). Directly from (5), \[ A=(2b^2-1)Z^2-4bZ+8-4b^2,\qquad B=4a(bZ-2), \] \[ \Delta:=A^2-U_2B^2=(Z-2b)^4=(Z-\zeta)^4. \tag{15} \] To check the last equality, substitute \(U_2B^2=4(b^2-1)(Z^2-4)(bZ-2)^2\) and expand; the coefficients are \(1,-8b,24b^2,-32b^3,16b^4\). In particular \(\Delta\) is never the zero polynomial. The explicit solution of (14) is \[ Y_i=(Au_i-Bv_i)/\Delta,\qquad Z_i^{(2)}=(-U_2Bu_i+Av_i)/\Delta. \tag{16} \] The matrices are now completely specified by the six rows \[ \mathcal DZ_i= (d_i,\ X_i,\ at_i+U_1X_i,\ aZ_i^{(2)}+U_1Y_i,\ 0,\ 0)^{\mathsf T}, \] \[ \mathcal SZ_i= (h_i,\ t_i,\ f_i+U_1t_i+aU_2X_i,\ d_i+U_1Z_i^{(2)}+aU_2Y_i,\ 4-p,\ 1)^{\mathsf T}. \tag{17} \] Each entry on the right is the indicated linear form in (12). Here is an explicit common denominator: \[ d_0(Z)=\sigma(Z)(Z-c_0)(Z-2)(Z-\zeta)^5. \tag{18} \] Indeed \[ (z_+-c_0)(z_--c_0)=(Z-2)(Z-\zeta), \] \[ \mathcal Dr_i=-\frac{\gamma_i}{(Z-2)(Z-\zeta)},\qquad \mathcal Sr_i=\frac{\gamma_i(aZ-c_0)} {(Z-2)(Z-\zeta)}. \tag{19} \] Equations (13)--(17) prove the denominator assertion. For \(N\ge5\), \(d_0\) has degree \(9\), and \[ d_0(Z)\longrightarrow(Z-2)^9. \tag{20} \] The rational module itself is valid for every \(N\ge2\); the degree and principal statements below use \(N\ge5\). All denominators mean rational identities first, followed by clearing; they are not inverted in the physical quotient. ## 3. Exact ordinary products and a polynomial channel gauge Fix \(r\ge1\). Tensor the six-channel vectors: \[ \mathcal Z=Z_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Z_r,\qquad d_r=6^r. \tag{21} \] Its first component is the actual ordinary product \(\prod_i K_N(w_i,Z)\). For a subset \(I\) of the \(r\) indices let \(T_I\) be the ordered tensor of \(\mathbf D_i\) at indices in \(I\) and \(\mathbf S_i\) at the others. The product rules give the explicit matrices \[ \mathbf D=\sum_{|I|\ {\rm odd}}U_2^{(|I|-1)/2}T_I,\qquad \mathbf S=\sum_{|I|\ {\rm even}}U_2^{|I|/2}T_I, \] \[ \mathcal D\mathcal Z=\mathbf D\mathcal Z, \qquad \mathcal S\mathcal Z=\mathbf S\mathcal Z. \tag{22} \] One proof expands each half-shift as \(\mathcal S\pm(\delta/2)\mathcal D\) before multiplying; the even and odd terms give (22). In particular this is ordinary multiplication, not multiplication transported by the physical turn. A degree gauge is useful before converting back to \(J\). Give the six channels in (12) the weights \[ (0,-1,0,-1,1,1). \tag{23} \] Weights here describe rational coefficient degrees at infinity; they are not the actual degrees of \(p\) or \(f_i\). Inspection of (13)--(17) gives \[ \deg_\infty(\mathbf D_i)_{ab}\le w_a-w_b-1,\qquad \deg_\infty(\mathbf S_i)_{ab}\le w_a-w_b. \tag{24} \] For completeness, \(X_i\) has weighted degree \(-2\); the right sides \(u_i,v_i\) have weighted degrees \(-1,0\); since \(\deg A\le2,\deg B\le1,\deg\Delta=4\), (16) gives weighted degrees \(-3,-2\) for \(Y_i,Z_i^{(2)}\). These bounds prove every row of (24), using \(\deg U_1=1,\deg U_2=2\). They hold for \(N\ge5\); vanishing scalar coefficients do not worsen them. For tensor channels, add the weights, writing \(w_a\in[-r,r]\). Each term of (22) then has the same bounds (24): its powers of \(U_2\) exactly compensate all but one of the degree losses from the odd number of \(\mathbf D_i\), or all of them in the even case. Put \[ a_a=r-w_a\in\{0,\ldots,2r\},\qquad P(Z)=\operatorname{diag}((Z-2)^{a_a}),\qquad \mathcal W=P\mathcal Z. \tag{25} \] This is a polynomial change of actual channels, not an inverse in the quotient. Its exact rational matrices are \[ \widetilde{\mathbf D} =\{(\mathcal SP)\mathbf D+(\mathcal DP)\mathbf S\}P^{-1}, \] \[ \widetilde{\mathbf S} =\{(\mathcal SP)\mathbf S+U_2(\mathcal DP)\mathbf D\}P^{-1}. \tag{26} \] Here \(P^{-1}\) is used only in the rational calculation. The entrywise degree bounds become \[ \deg_\infty\widetilde{\mathbf D}_{ab}\le-1,\qquad \deg_\infty\widetilde{\mathbf S}_{ab}\le0. \tag{27} \] For example the first term in the first formula has degree at most \(a_a+w_a-w_b-1-a_b=-1\); the other three terms are checked the same way. A common denominator for both matrices is \[ e(Z)=d_0(Z)^r(Z-2)^{2r}. \tag{28} \] It has degree \(11r\), with limit \((Z-2)^{11r}\). Thus their numerators can be taken of degrees at most \(11r-1\) and \(11r\), respectively. ## 4. A controlled-degree \(C,J\) matrix and its principal determinant For a polynomial \(g\), define its half-shift norm \[ \mathcal N_qg(Z)=g(z_+)g(z_-). \tag{29} \] It is polynomial. If \(g\) has degree \(k\) and leading coefficient \(g_k\ne0\), its degree is \(2k\), with leading coefficient \(g_k^2\). This follows from \(z_+z_-=Z^2+s^2\). For a rational function \(f/g\), both \(\mathcal S(f/g)\) and \(\mathcal D(f/g)\) have denominator \(\mathcal N_qg\): their numerators are the symmetric sum and divided antisymmetric difference of \(f(z_+)g(z_-)\) and \(f(z_-)g(z_+)\). Their numerator degrees are at most \(\deg f+\deg g\) and \(\deg f+\deg g-1\), respectively. Apply \(\mathcal D,\mathcal S\) entrywise to matrix coefficients. Equations (3),(6),(26) give exactly \[ \mathcal L\mathcal W=c_0\mathcal W+s^2\mathbf H(Z)\mathcal W, \] \[ \begin{split} \mathbf H={}&\sigma\{(\mathcal S\widetilde{\mathbf D}) \widetilde{\mathbf D} +(\mathcal D\widetilde{\mathbf D}) \widetilde{\mathbf S}\}\\ &+\tau\{(\mathcal S\widetilde{\mathbf D}) \widetilde{\mathbf S} +U_2(\mathcal D\widetilde{\mathbf D}) \widetilde{\mathbf D}\}. \end{split} \tag{30} \] Matrix multiplication order in this formula is literal. Define \[ d(Z)=e(Z)\mathcal N_qe(Z),\qquad E(Z)=d(Z)\mathbf H(Z). \tag{31} \] These are a scalar polynomial and a polynomial matrix, and the exact degree bounds are \[ \deg d=33r,\qquad \deg E_{ab}\le33r. \tag{32} \] Indeed write \(l=11r\). The numerators of \(\mathcal S\widetilde{\mathbf D}\) and \(\mathcal D\widetilde{\mathbf D}\) have degrees at most \(2l-1,2l-2\) over \(\mathcal N_qe\). Combining with (27), and then the degrees \(2,1,2\) of \(\sigma,\tau,U_2\), bounds every numerator in (30) by \(3l=33r\). Every entry of \(\mathcal W\) is an ordinary polynomial. Clearing (30) therefore gives an ordinary polynomial identity, and then the exact full-algebra relation \[ \boxed{\quad \{d(C)(J-c_0)I-s^2E(C)\}\, \operatorname{can}\mathcal W=0. \quad} \tag{33} \] Canonical reduction is componentwise. Neither \(d(C)\) nor \(P(C)\) is inverted. Now assume \(w_i=2\cosh(\alpha_i/N)\), with all \(\alpha_i\) in fixed bounded complex sets. Then \(\lambda_i\) is bounded and has a limit, and \(\gamma_i=O(N^{-2})\). All rational matrix coefficients above have bounded limits on compact sets avoiding \(Z=2\). Entrywise half-shift divided differences of fixed-degree coefficient polynomials converge to their derivatives, so they introduce no uncontrolled \(s^{-1}\) coefficient. The cleared polynomial coefficients in \(E\) remain bounded as well. Moreover \[ d(Z)\longrightarrow(Z-2)^{33r}. \tag{34} \] Thus the commuting, bounded-variable principal matrix of (33) is precisely \[ (X-2)^{33r}(Y-2)I_{6^r}, \] and its determinant is \[ (X-2)^{33r\,6^r}(Y-2)^{6^r}. \tag{35} \] This is a characteristic containment statement for the specified matrix presentation. It is not a claim that the minimal scalar characteristic has these exact multiplicities or that every displayed component participates. In particular it establishes no separate \(X=-2\) factor in this controlled presentation; no such factor was discarded by an assumption about the solution. ## 5. Original turns, recovery, and the physical leading order Retain \(V_n=\kappa^nTR^{-n}T\), \(D_n=V_nCV_{-n}\) and \(V_nJ=JV_n\). Applying the original turn componentwise to (33) gives exactly \[ \boxed{\quad \{d(D_n)(J-c_0)I-s^2E(D_n)\}\,\mathcal F=0,\qquad \mathcal F=V_n\operatorname{can}\mathcal W . \quad} \tag{36} \] Every original ungauged channel is retained by the forced recovery equations \[ (D_n-2)^{a_a}\,\mathcal Y_a=\mathcal F_a,\qquad \mathcal Y_a=V_n\operatorname{can}\mathcal Z_a. \tag{37} \] In particular the turned original product is the first component of \(\mathcal Y\), whose recovery exponent is \(r\). Equation (37) is never solved by dividing by \(D_n-2\). Its actual homogeneous directions and anchors are part of the original source. Let \(x_n,y\) be the physical commuting symbols of \(D_n,J\) in the pinned operator/transfer convention. The principal determinant of (36) is \[ (x_n-2)^{33r\,6^r}(y-2)^{6^r}. \tag{38} \] Recovery adds only factors \(x_n-2\). There is also a useful exact leading-order fact, beyond merely taking this determinant. For fixed \(n\ne0\), put \(m=|n|\), \(k=33r\). The physical difference order of the first term \(d(D_n)J\) is \(km+1\) in each direction. Its two extreme coefficients are scalar multiples of the identity matrix and are nonzero on every buffered compact physical interval for all sufficiently large \(N\). This follows from the exact two extreme coefficients of \(D_n\), their shifted products, and the nonzero extreme coefficients of \(J\) in the bulk-transfer source. The leading coefficient of \(d\) tends to \(1\). All other terms in (36) have physical shift order at most \(km\), by (32). Hence the \(s^2E(D_n)\) correction cannot create a new highest-order recurrence coefficient. On a compact physical interval the normalized block-companion coefficients converge to the scalar leading matrix times the channel identity, whose determinant is (38). For \(n=0\), the separate equation has the usual first physical shift order of \(J\), with coefficient \(d(C)\), which is a unit on such an interval for large \(N\). This leading-order statement still supplies no transfer estimate. The multiple roots, the coupled channels, the forced recovery, and all actual initial directions remain to be estimated. Even a compact transfer upper bound would not by itself make the initial channels polynomially small after turning. No equality with a terminal growth budget is asserted here. Both (33) and (36)--(37) hold in the original \(\mathbb C[Z]/(P_N)\), so all double-root first normals, the odd simple values, shared spectators and original crossing phases remain. More explicitly, their ordinary polynomial residuals are \(P_N\) multiples. In the physical scaled coordinate \(c_N(u)=2\cos(2\pi u+\pi/N)\), one has \(P_N(c_N(u))=4\sin^2(\pi Nu)\). Therefore the value and first \(u\)-derivative equations hold exactly at every regular physical row. Differentiating them includes every coefficient derivative and gives the original normal system; it does not differentiate a quotient identity off the physical grid. The operations \(\mathcal D,\mathcal S\) themselves were applied to the ordinary polynomials before canonical reduction. They need not preserve the ideal \((P_N)\), as (11) already shows. Ordinary outside parameters are never quotiented, and their fixed mixed derivatives can be retained throughout the explicit matrix identities. ## 6. Direct sources and scope Both complete direct sources were read at their matching hashes, with their directly used implications checked: * [Original operator and branching source](research_unit_turn_finite_band_branching_operator.md), SHA256 31d9f574c7dc3aaac07e4eb50c131b3328be46b3c2a2ef46f9dae7f0c4ddb9cb: exact ordinary AW equation, source normalization, ideal preservation, and ordered original-turn conjugation. * [Exact physical terminal operator](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_terminal_twist_bulk_transfer_bound.md), SHA256 fca96865315f21dc9961be89061cc6c3a292b2b563e7ded756e86c3438ef5bde: physical shift convention, extreme coefficients and ordinary-residual justification of full normal equations. The six-channel closure, polynomial tensor gauge, denominator list and controlled degree are proved above. The earlier source-retaining tensor annihilator supplies complementary generic elimination; it is not used to infer (35) or (38). The gauge was checked independently in collaboration with the coefficient reviewer. No product-rate or arbitrary short-component theorem is claimed. Only written mathematics and source-text/hash reads were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or build was run. Adopted notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: An explicit general domain for the endpoint half-character amplitude
text: # An explicit general domain for the endpoint half-character amplitude Private research note, 16 November 2026. Written proof only. The analytic interpolation of the original endpoint's entire high coupon extends to an explicit complex domain. Its exact physical-row identity and its domain of uniform asymptotics remain different assertions. No original low coupon, spectator, or contour side term is discarded. The sole direct proof source is [the endpoint half-character amplitude theorem](research_endpoint_radical_half_character_amplitude.md), SHA256 85c866a031d1293a1cc896a172ab465a52f469a19a4326219856d52ed3970ac8. Its entire proof was read at this version. The adopted file is unchanged. ## 1. The exact interpolation with a general cutoff Retain the source's notation \[ D=N-1,\quad m=\lfloor N/2\rfloor,\quad\eta=(-1)^D,\quad \theta=\pi/N,\quad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N), \qquad \tau_a=(D-2a)\theta. \tag{1} \] Thus, with the original local normal consumed exactly, \[ \phi_N(B^{\rm high}_{N,\alpha}f) =\eta\sum_{a=0}^{m-1}(-1)^a \gamma_{a,N}(\alpha)f(c_a). \tag{2} \] Fix \(0<\delta<1/2\), put \(L_N=\lfloor\delta N\rfloor\), and take \(N\) large enough that \(L_N<m\). Define \[ (A_l,B_l)= \begin{cases} ((l+\tfrac12)\theta,(l+1)\theta),&N\ {\rm even},\\ ((l+1)\theta,(l+\tfrac32)\theta),&N\ {\rm odd}, \end{cases} \] \[ \rho_{l,N}(\alpha,t)= \frac{[\cos^2 A_l+\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))] [\sin^2(t/2)-\sin^2 A_l]}{\cos^4 B_l}, \qquad H_N^\delta(\alpha,t)= \sum_{l=0}^{L_N}\prod_{j=0}^{l-1}\rho_{j,N}(\alpha,t). \tag{3} \] All denominators are nonzero. With the exact base factor \[ T_{0,N}(\alpha,t)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}N\sin t,&N\ {\rm even},\\[3pt] \displaystyle \frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)\cosh(\alpha/(2N))} {N\cos^4(\theta/2)}\sin t\sin(t/2),&N\ {\rm odd}, \end{cases} \qquad \Gamma_N^\delta=T_{0,N}H_N^\delta, \tag{4} \] one has, for each fixed \(b<2\pi\delta\) and all sufficiently large \(N\), \[ \Gamma_N^\delta(\alpha,\tau_a)=\gamma_{a,N}(\alpha) \qquad(0<\tau_a\le b). \tag{5} \] This holds for every complex \(\alpha\). Indeed the actual lowering chain stops at \(p_a=m-1-a\), where the next ratio contains the zero \(\sin^2(\tau_a/2)-\sin^2 A_{p_a}\). Here \(p_a=(N\tau_a/\pi-1)/2\) at even levels and \(p_a=N\tau_a/(2\pi)-1\) at odd levels. The strict window bound gives \(p_a<L_N\), so every extra product vanishes exactly. No analytic estimate is used in (5). ## 2. The exact limiting contraction domain Put \[ a_\delta=\sin^2(\pi\delta),\quad c_\delta=\cos(2\pi\delta),\quad z=\sin^2(t/2), \] \[ \mathcal D_\delta =\{t:|z-a_\delta|<1-a_\delta\} =\{t:|\cos t-c_\delta|<1+c_\delta\}. \tag{6} \] Equivalently \(\Re\sec^2(t/2)>1/[2\cos^2(\pi\delta)]\): write \(w=1-z\), square \(|w-(1-a_\delta)|<1-a_\delta\), and divide by \(|w|^2\). In particular the displayed domain excludes \(w=0\). In the exponential coordinate \(\zeta=e^{it}\ne0\), this is the explicit real algebraic inequality \[ |\zeta^2-2c_\delta\zeta+1|^2 <4(1+c_\delta)^2|\zeta|^2. \tag{7} \] The limiting ratio indexed by \(v\in[0,a_\delta]\) is \(r_v(z)=(z-v)/(1-v)\). The disks \(\{|z-v|<1-v\}\) are nested. More precisely \(r_v(z)=1+(z-1)/(1-v)\) traverses the straight segment from \(z\) to \((z-a_\delta)/(1-a_\delta)\). Therefore \[ \max_{0\le v\le a_\delta}|r_v(z)| =\max\left\{|z|,\frac{|z-a_\delta|}{1-a_\delta}\right\}. \tag{8} \] This maximum is less than one exactly on (6). The criterion is sharp for contraction of the individual limiting ratios; its failure does not rule out another description of the finite sum. **Theorem 1.** On every compact \(\mathcal K\Subset\mathcal D_\delta\) and every compact set of complex \(\alpha\)'s, there are \(q<1\) and \(N_0\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_0\), \[ |\rho_{l,N}(\alpha,t)|\le q\quad(0\le l<L_N),\qquad H_N^\delta(\alpha,t)=\sec^2(t/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2}). \tag{9} \] Every fixed derivative in \(\alpha,t\) has the same error bound on compact subsets. The exact factors \(H_N^\delta\) are eventually nonzero on these compacts. *Proof.* Write \(v_l=\sin^2 A_l\). For \(l<L_N\), \(0\le A_l\le\pi\delta\), \(B_l=A_l+\theta/2\), and \(\cos B_l\) is uniformly bounded away from zero. Uniformly in \(l\), \[ \rho_{l,N}=\frac{z-v_l}{1-v_l}+O(N^{-1}). \tag{10} \] This includes the denominator shift and the \(O(N^{-2})\) term \(\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))\). Equation (8) proves the contraction bound in (9), also with \(|z|\le q\) after increasing \(q<1\). The stronger elementary estimate \[ |\rho_{l,N}-z|\le C(l+1)^2N^{-2} \tag{11} \] follows by expanding the sine and cosine factors at zero, with their denominators bounded away from zero and \(A_l,B_l=O((l+1)/N)\). Telescoping products gives \[ \left|\prod_{j<l}\rho_{j,N}-z^l\right| \le C N^{-2}l^3q^{l-1}. \tag{12} \] Summing this bound and the exponentially small geometric tail beyond \(L_N\) proves (9), since \(\sum z^l=(1-z)^{-1}\). Cauchy's formula on slightly larger compact neighborhoods proves the derivative assertion. Finally \((1-z)^{-1}\) is nonzero and bounded away from zero on each compact, proving eventual nonvanishing. A bound \(q<1\) alone would not prove this last assertion when \(q\) is close to one. \(\square\) Consequently the exact amplitudes have the normalized profiles \[ \Gamma_N^\delta(\alpha,t)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}N\sin t [\sec^2(t/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2})],&N\ {\rm even},\\[3pt] \displaystyle\frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}N\sin t\sin(t/2) [\sec^2(t/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2})],&N\ {\rm odd}. \end{cases} \tag{13} \] Derivatives are controlled after factoring the displayed exact zeros. The whole amplitude is a unit only where those factors are nonzero; in particular \(\cosh(\alpha/2)=0\) is an exact obstruction. Bounds and identities allow arbitrary bounded complex \(\alpha\)-sets, including these zeros. Evenness in \(\alpha\) also retains the source's \(O(N^{2j})\) cost for \(j\) ordinary derivatives in the microscopic endpoint color \(w\). Equation (5) holds throughout its physical window, whereas the estimates require the angles also to lie in a compact subset of (6). In particular \(0\in\mathcal D_\delta\) if and only if \(\delta<1/4\). A larger exact cutoff need not give symbol control near the complete angle. ## 3. A useful closed rectangle Take \(\delta=1/8\), so \(c_\delta=1/\sqrt2=:c\). Then \[ \mathcal R=\{t:|\Re t|\le\pi/4,\ |\Im t|\le\log3\} \Subset\mathcal D_{1/8}. \tag{14} \] Indeed put \(C=\cos(\Re t)\in[c,1]\) and \(u=\cosh(\Im t)\in[1,5/3]\). One has \[ |\cos t-c|^2=C^2+u^2-1-2cCu+c^2. \tag{15} \] This increases in \(u\) and is convex in \(C\). Its maximum is at \(u=5/3\), \(C=c\) or \(1\). These values are \(10/9\) and \((5/3-c)^2<10/9\), respectively. Thus \[ \frac{|z-a_\delta|}{1-a_\delta} \le\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3(1+c)}<\frac23,\qquad |z|=\frac{\cosh(\Im t)-\cos(\Re t)}2 \le\frac{5/3-c}{2}<\frac12. \tag{16} \] The limiting ratios are uniformly below \(2/3\); for bounded complex \(\alpha\), the finite ratios are at most \(3/4\) on \(\mathcal R\) for large \(N\). All conclusions of Theorem 1 hold on a neighborhood of this closed rectangle. Exact physical termination still uses \(0<\tau_a\le b<\pi/4\). This is an analytic scale statement, not a geometric existence theorem or a claim about a new knot class. ## 4. Exact contour identity versus uniform estimates Choose positive midpoints \(b_N\le b<2\pi\delta\) with \(e^{iNb_N}=-\eta\), and let \(H>0\). For any even spectator representative \(F\), holomorphic near the closed rectangle \([-b_N,b_N]+i[-H,H]\), put \[ A_N(t)=\Gamma_N^\delta(\alpha,t)F(t),\qquad \mathcal S_N=\eta i^{-D} \sum_{0<\tau_a<b_N}A_N(\tau_a)e^{iN\tau_a/2}. \tag{17} \] For large \(N\), (5) makes this the actual central high-coupon sum. The exact identity is \[ \begin{split} \mathcal S_N={}&\frac{N i^{-D}}{2\pi} \int_{-b_N-iH}^{b_N-iH} \frac{A_N(t)e^{-iNt/2}}{1-\eta e^{-iNt}}\,dt\\ &+\frac{\eta N i^{-D}e^{iNb_N/2}}{4\pi i} \int_{-H}^{H}\frac{A_N(b_N+ih)}{\cosh(Nh/2)}\,dh. \end{split} \tag{18} \] The source's residue proof applies unchanged: \(\Gamma_N^\delta\) is entire in \(t\), has parity \(\eta\), and vanishes at the odd zero-angle node. The residue-one kernel \(iN\eta/(e^{iNt}-\eta)\), reflection, and the midpoint phase give (18), with no contraction assumption on the rectangle. Uniform use of (13) along the contours, in contrast, requires them to lie in a common compact subset of \(\mathcal D_\delta\). For example \(\delta=1/8\), fixed \(b<\pi/4\), and \(0<H\le\log3\) meet that condition. The horizontal aliases, paired vertical integral, noncentral physical rows, low coupon, and original spectator all remain. Neither (18) nor the larger symbol domain proves a gap for their combined contribution.

title: The actual endpoint radical has a regular half-grid character amplitude
text: # The actual endpoint radical has a regular half-grid character amplitude Private research note, 16 November 2026. Written proof only. This note groups the entire radical part of the original endpoint coupon before estimating it. Near the complete physical color its alternating weights have an exact analytic interpolation, with the parity required for a full-grid Fourier argument. The interpolation also handles endpoint heights of order \(N^{-1}\). The low part of the coupon and the original spectator remain present; no filled-source rate or integration-cycle assertion is made. Half-charge sampling contours are already used for the distinct-node Cauchy observation in [the odd-level observation note](research_odd_half_charge_observation.md), Sections 1--2, and its [even-level counterpart](research_complete_source_pick_observation.md), Section 5. Those sections were checked for coverage. The new input here is the exact analytic amplitude of the actual endpoint's entire high coupon, including its microscopic-height normalization and terminating physical-row interpolation. Section 5 derives its own contour formula; the older observation theorems are coverage references, not additional proof dependencies or assertions about this different coupon. ## 1. Original coupon and surviving normal Use \[ D=N-1,\quad m=\lfloor N/2\rfloor,\quad k_0=N-m,\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\quad\theta=\pi/N,\qquad N\ge2, \] \[ s_j=2\sin(j\theta),\quad S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j s_h,\quad c_a=2\cos((2a+1)\theta),\quad e_k(z)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{h<k}(c_h-z). \tag{1} \] The original algebra and closing are \[ \mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[z]/(P_N),\quad P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2, \qquad\phi_N(f)=\eta N^2[z^D]\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}f. \tag{2} \] At the microscopic endpoint put \[ w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N),\qquad B_{N,\alpha}(z)=K_N(w_N(\alpha),z) =\sum_{k=0}^D e_k(w_N(\alpha))e_k(z). \tag{3} \] Its high part is \[ B^{\rm high}_{N,\alpha} =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}e_{D-r}(w_N(\alpha))e_{D-r}(z), \qquad B^{\rm low}_{N,\alpha}=B_{N,\alpha}-B^{\rm high}_{N,\alpha}. \tag{4} \] The two complete direct sources, read at the versions listed below, are the full-radical contraction theorem and the coherent endpoint kernel theorem. In particular the first gives, for every original spectator \(f\in\mathcal A_N\), \[ \phi_N(e_{D-r}f)=\sum_{a=0}^r b_{ra}f(c_a),\qquad b_{ra}=(-1)^{r+a} \frac{s_{2a+1}S_r^2}{S_{r-a}S_{r+a+1}}. \tag{5} \] This is the actual first-normal residue: the radical vanishes at every physical value, its normal consumes the local derivative, and the derivative of the spectator drops out by the product rule. At odd levels the extra simple node \(c_m=-2\) contributes zero. Thus (5) is not a values-only replacement for the original trace. For \(0\le a<m\) define the even entire function of \(\alpha\) \[ \gamma_{a,N}(\alpha)= \sum_{r=a}^{m-1}(-1)^{D-r}e_{D-r}(w_N(\alpha))\,|b_{ra}|. \tag{6} \] Absolute values in (6) apply only to the fixed real numbers \(b_{ra}\). The endpoint factor is its displayed signed polynomial, so complex continuation of (6) is unambiguous. For real \(\alpha\), all its summands are strictly positive. Equation (5) gives the exact identity \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \phi_N(B^{\rm high}_{N,\alpha}f) =\eta\sum_{a=0}^{m-1}(-1)^a \gamma_{a,N}(\alpha)f(c_a).} \tag{7} \] It is coefficientwise in arbitrary joint spectators and ordinary free-boundary variables. Original crossings of any power for which their physical class is specified can be included in \(f\). The source of (5) states \(N\ge3\); at \(N=2\), \(e_1=-z/4\), \(b_{00}=1\), and the same identity follows directly from (2). ## 2. Exact last term and lowering ratios Write the positive physical angle as \[ \tau_a=(D-2a)\theta,\qquad c_a=-2\cos\tau_a, \qquad p_a=m-1-a. \tag{8} \] The sum in (6) is most useful in the order \(r=m-1-l\), \(0\le l\le p_a\). Let its summand be \(T_l(\alpha,\tau_a)\). The first summand is exactly \[ T_0(\alpha,\tau)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}{N}\sin\tau, &N=2m,\\[4pt] \displaystyle \frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)\cosh(\alpha/(2N))} {N\cos^4(\theta/2)} \sin\tau\sin(\tau/2),&N=2m+1. \end{cases} \tag{9} \] Here is a direct normalization check. The sine products give \(S_m^2=2N\) at even levels and \(S_m^2=N\) at odd levels. Also \(P_N(w_N(\alpha))=4\cosh^2(\alpha/2)\). Factoring its double roots, and its odd simple root when present, yields \[ (-1)^{k_0}e_{k_0}(w_N(\alpha))= \begin{cases} \cosh(\alpha/2)/N,&N=2m,\\ \cosh(\alpha/2)\cosh(\alpha/(2N)) /(N\cos^2(\theta/2)),&N=2m+1. \end{cases} \tag{10} \] These are polynomial identities after substitution, fixed by their positive values at \(\alpha=0\), rather than a choice of a square-root branch. The same sine products in (5) give \[ |b_{m-1,a}|= \begin{cases} \sin\tau_a,&N=2m,\\ \sin\tau_a\sin(\tau_a/2)/\cos^2(\theta/2),&N=2m+1, \end{cases} \tag{11} \] proving (9). In particular the even central endpoint coefficient is exactly \(1/N\), not merely of polynomial size. Define \[ (A_l,B_l)= \begin{cases} ((l+\tfrac12)\theta,(l+1)\theta),&N=2m,\\ ((l+1)\theta,(l+\tfrac32)\theta),&N=2m+1, \end{cases} \] \[ \rho_{l,N}(\alpha,\tau)= \frac{[\cos^2 A_l+\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))] [\sin^2(\tau/2)-\sin^2 A_l]}{\cos^4 B_l}. \tag{12} \] For \(l<p_a\), the next summand satisfies \[ T_{l+1}=\rho_{l,N}T_l. \tag{13} \] Indeed, in the original \(r\) notation the ratio is simply \[ \frac{T_{r-1}}{T_r} =\frac{(w_N(\alpha)-c_r)(c_a-c_r)}{s_r^4}. \tag{14} \] The first factor follows by adding one Newton factor; the second follows by dividing (5) at consecutive \(r\). Substitution of \(r=m-1-l\) gives (12). At \(l=p_a\), its numerator has the exact factor \(\sin^2(\tau_a/2)-\sin^2 A_{p_a}=0\). At a zero of a summand, the ratio statements mean their multiplicative identities, obtained first for real \(\alpha\) and then by analytic continuation. The ratios are even entire functions of each of \(\alpha,\tau\) where their constant denominators are nonzero. These denominators become small late in the full lowering process; the next section avoids that part of the continuation. ## 3. Exact local interpolation and its nonzero symbol For \(N\ge100\), put \(L_N=\lfloor N/20\rfloor\) and define \[ H_N(\alpha,\tau)= \sum_{l=0}^{L_N}\prod_{j=0}^{l-1}\rho_{j,N}(\alpha,\tau), \qquad \Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau)=T_0(\alpha,\tau)H_N(\alpha,\tau). \tag{15} \] An empty product is one. Formula (15) is a finite analytic interpolant, not an asymptotic substitution for the summands. **Theorem 1.** At every physical double-node angle \(0<\tau_a\le1/10\), \[ \Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau_a)=\gamma_{a,N}(\alpha) \tag{16} \] for all complex \(\alpha\). On the fixed bidisk \(|\alpha|\le1, |\tau|\le1/5\), \[ |\rho_{j,N}|<\tfrac14\quad(0\le j<L_N),\qquad |H_N-1|\le\tfrac13, \tag{17} \] and \[ H_N(\alpha,\tau)=\sec^2(\tau/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2}). \tag{18} \] Here \(O_{\rm hol}\) means a holomorphic function with the indicated uniform bound on this bidisk; every fixed derivative has the same bound on a strictly smaller bidisk. Consequently \[ \Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}{N}\sin\tau [\sec^2(\tau/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2})],&N\ {\rm even},\\[4pt] \displaystyle\frac{\cosh(\alpha/2)}{N}\sin\tau\sin(\tau/2) [\sec^2(\tau/2)+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2})],&N\ {\rm odd}. \end{cases} \tag{19} \] The bracketed factors are nonzero for all sufficiently large \(N\). More directly, the exact factors \(H_N\) in (15) are nonzero by (17). The interpolation is odd in \(\tau\) at even levels and even in \(\tau\) at odd levels. The latter has its prescribed double zero at \(\tau=0\); this is not a lost normal at an odd simple node. *Proof.* From (8), \(p_a=(N\tau_a/\pi-1)/2\) at even levels and \(p_a=N\tau_a/(2\pi)-1\) at odd levels. Thus \(0\le p_a<L_N\) in (16). The factor at \(j=p_a\) in (12) annuls every later product in (15), so (13) proves the exact identity. For \(j<L_N\), \(0\le A_j<1/6\) and \(0<B_j<1/5\). Hence \(\cos^4 B_j>(49/50)^4>9/10\). For the complex arguments in the stated bidisk, \(|\sin(\tau/2)|\le\sinh(1/10)<1/9\), and \(|\sinh(\alpha/(2N))|<1/100\). Inserting these bounds and \(\sin^2 A_j<1/36\) in (12) proves the first inequality in (17), with room to spare. Summing the geometric majorant proves the second. These elementary bounds also apply on a slightly larger open neighborhood of the closed bidisk for each level. Put \(z=\sin^2(\tau/2)\). On the same bidisk, Taylor estimates for the real numbers \(A_j,B_j\), whose denominators stay away from zero, give \[ |\rho_{j,N}-z|\le C(j+1)^2N^{-2},\qquad |z|<1/4. \tag{20} \] Telescoping the product, using (17) for all its other factors, gives \[ \left|\prod_{j<l}\rho_{j,N}-z^l\right| \le C N^{-2}l^3(1/4)^{l-1}. \tag{21} \] The sum over \(l\) is \(O(N^{-2})\); the omitted geometric tail \(\sum_{l>L_N}z^l\) is \(O(e^{-cN})\). Since \((1-z)^{-1}=\sec^2(\tau/2)\), this proves (18). Cauchy's formula on smaller bidisks proves the derivative assertion. The odd extra factor in (9) satisfies \(\cosh(\alpha/(2N))/\cos^4(\theta/2)=1+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-2})\), which proves (19) and its parity statements. \(\square\) Equivalently the leading profiles in (19) are \[ \frac{2\cosh(\alpha/2)}N\tan(\tau/2),\qquad \frac{2\cosh(\alpha/2)}N \frac{\sin^2(\tau/2)}{\cos(\tau/2)}, \tag{22} \] respectively. At \(\alpha=0\), these start as \(\tau/N\) and \(\tau^2/(2N)\). All fixed angular and microscopic-height derivatives are controlled by (19) after the displayed zeros are factored out. Since every factor is even in \(\alpha\), the same interpolant descends analytically to \(\alpha^2\). Moreover \(N^2(w_N(\alpha)-2)=\alpha^2+O(\alpha^4/N^2)\) is a uniformly invertible local coordinate in \(\alpha^2\). On smaller fixed disks, each fixed ordinary derivative in the endpoint color \(w\) therefore costs at most \(C_aN^{2a}\), including at \(w=2\). ## 4. The actual character, both parities, and the retained low part At a physical angle one has exactly \[ (-1)^a=i^{-D}e^{iN\tau_a/2}. \tag{23} \] Thus the portion of (7) with \(\tau_a\le1/10\) is \[ \eta i^{-D}\sum_{\tau_a\le1/10} e^{iN\tau_a/2}\Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau_a)f(c_a). \tag{24} \] For an even angular spectator \(F(\tau)=f(-2\cos\tau)\), the central summand has an exact even holomorphic continuation obtained by replacing its character-amplitude product by \[ \begin{cases} i\sin(N\tau/2)\Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau)F(\tau),&N\ {\rm even},\\ \cos(N\tau/2)\Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau)F(\tau),&N\ {\rm odd}. \end{cases} \tag{25} \] It agrees with the product in (24) at every positive physical angle in the window. Both expressions in (25) are even; their values at the reflected grid points consequently agree too. The odd-level zero angle contributes zero because \(\Gamma_N(\alpha,0)=0\). The sum (24) can therefore be written as half its symmetric central grid sum, with no unaccounted half-grid endpoint at zero. The trigonometric factors in (25), before multiplication by \(F\), are in fact polynomials in \(\cos\tau\). At even levels this follows from \(\sin(m\tau)\sin\tau=(1-\cos^2\tau)U_{m-1}(\cos\tau)\). At odd levels use \(2\cos(\tau/2)\cos((m+1/2)\tau) =\cos(m\tau)+\cos((m+1)\tau)\), together with the factor \(\sin\tau\sin(\tau/2)\) in (9). The remaining factor \(H_N\) is a polynomial in \(\sin^2(\tau/2)\). This parity is essential. A half-charge cosine alone vanishes on the even physical grid; its normal data cannot simply be dropped. Equations (7) and (25) instead start with the full original trace, consume the radical normal exactly, and only then express its surviving values as a half-grid character. They do not assert an identity between full Hermite coupons by matching values alone. For completeness the noncentral part has only a polynomial weight cost. The radical source proves \(|e_{D-r}(-2\cos t)|\le\sqrt{N-1}e^{D|\Im t|}\). At \(t=\pi-i\alpha/N\), this and \(|b_{ra}|\le2\) imply, uniformly for \(|\alpha|\le1\), \[ |\gamma_{a,N}(\alpha)|\le C N^{3/2}. \tag{26} \] Hence the complete exact decomposition is \[ \begin{split} \phi_N(B_{N,\alpha}f) ={}&\phi_N(B^{\rm low}_{N,\alpha}f) +\eta i^{-D}\sum_{\tau_a\le1/10} e^{iN\tau_a/2}\Gamma_N(\alpha,\tau_a)f(c_a) +\mathcal R_N(f),\\ |\mathcal R_N(f)|\le{}& C N^{5/2} \max_{\tau_a>1/10}|f(c_a)|. \end{split} \tag{27} \] An empty maximum has value zero. Joint exterior variables and their ordinary derivatives remain in \(f\) throughout these identities. The local amplitude in (24) is controlled and carries an actual nonzero Fourier frequency. This removes the artificial zero-frequency description obtained by replacing the endpoint radical with an arbitrary positive radical weight. The following exact contour formula makes that frequency explicit without suppressing its side currents. ## 5. An exact central block with all aliases and both side currents For \(N\ge100\), choose a positive grid midpoint \(b\le1/10\), so \(e^{iNb}=-\eta\), and \(0<H\le1/10\). Suppose \(F(t)\) is even and holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed rectangle \([-b,b]+i[-H,H]\). An original physical spectator, including a real-power chirp, may use any such representative with its exact physical values; its normal has already been consumed in (5). Put \[ A_N(t)=\Gamma_N(\alpha,t)F(t),\qquad \mathcal S_N=\eta i^{-D} \sum_{0<\tau_a<b}A_N(\tau_a)e^{iN\tau_a/2}. \tag{28} \] Then \[ \boxed{\begin{split} \mathcal S_N={}&\frac{N i^{-D}}{2\pi} \int_{-b-iH}^{b-iH} \frac{A_N(t)e^{-iNt/2}}{1-\eta e^{-iNt}}\,dt\\ &+\frac{\eta N i^{-D}e^{iNb/2}}{4\pi i} \int_{-H}^{H}\frac{A_N(b+ih)}{\cosh(Nh/2)}\,dh. \end{split}} \tag{29} \] Both the midpoint phase and the second integral are part of the identity. No endpoint or vertical term has been discarded. To prove it, use the residue-one grid kernel \[ J_N(t)=\frac{iN\eta}{e^{iNt}-\eta},\qquad J_N(-t)=-J_N(t)-iN. \tag{30} \] The residue theorem on the counterclockwise rectangle sums all physical grid points inside. The full sum is twice the sum in (28), because \(A_N(-t)=\eta A_N(t)\) and \(e^{-iN\tau/2}=\eta e^{iN\tau/2}\) on the grid. The odd-level zero point has zero residue since \(A_N(0)=0\). Reflecting the top side onto the bottom, and the left side onto the right, gives in each case the same paired integrand \[ J_N(t)A_N(t)e^{iNt/2} -J_N(-t)A_N(-t)e^{-iNt/2} =\frac{2iN\eta A_N(t)e^{-iNt/2}} {1-\eta e^{-iNt}}. \tag{31} \] On the right side \(t=b+ih\), the midpoint relation changes (31) times \(dt=i\,dh\) into \(N e^{iNb/2}A_N(b+ih)\,dh/\cosh(Nh/2)\). Multiplying the whole residue formula by \(\eta i^{-D}/2\) proves (29), including its orientation and normalization. On the lower side the denominator in (29) has its absolutely convergent expansion \[ \frac{e^{-iNt/2}}{1-\eta e^{-iNt}} =\sum_{j\ge0}\eta^j e^{-iN(j+1/2)t}. \tag{32} \] Thus the first effective charge is exactly \(1/2\), and every alias is retained. The formula has no zero-charge horizontal term. It does not establish an exponential bound on its vertical integral, or combine the result with the low term in (27). In particular no rate below the selected filled action follows without estimating those terms and the actual spectator. The theorem concerns an exact central block of the original high coupon, not a substitute closing. ## 6. Direct source versions Both files below were read in full for this proof; the directly used identities and their original trace normalization were checked. * [Exact full-radical contraction](research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md), SHA256 `1faa5d2e02edf0a1462cc43b243e0ab4403bf56e9f1af0befb6b492441d9dd03`. Equations (2)--(6), (10)--(12), (17), and (34)--(36) give the original algebra, surviving normal, signs, parity split and Fourier bound used here. * [Coherent endpoint kernel bounds](research_full_period_endpoint_kernel_reduction.md), SHA256 `a1d67ac803c0160bbfdacaa96a6fde9dc1ffae06fc39eb94f0416dcf2ecef76e`. Equations (1)--(6) and (15) fix the actual endpoint coupon and distinguish its low interpolation from its full normal data. Its polynomial bounds do not already provide the local amplitude or character in (19)--(25).

title: Sine-factor endpoint modes with the sharp truncation rate
text:
# Sine-factor endpoint modes with the sharp truncation rate Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The normalized factorial interpolation gives exact first-order sine-ratio factors for the unturned endpoint equation. Their ordinary lowering relation produces a finite approximate homogeneous basis. On a buffered bulk rectangle of any fixed height this basis is bounded, and its optimally truncated residual has the sharp real product rate \(J_*\). Its two coefficients can be fixed by an actual physical value packet. The independent normal packet is retained separately; no sharper source-normal compatibility is inferred. ## 1. The normalized first-order factors Put \(h=N^{-1}\), \(	heta=\pi h\), and \[ s_\zeta=2\sin(\pi h\zeta),\qquad c_\zeta=2\cos(\pi h(2\zeta+1)),\qquad c_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi h). 	ag{1} \] The ordinary source operator is \[ \mathscr J_N f=(c_0+A_N+B_N)f-A_Nf(x+h)-B_Nf(x-h), \] \[ A_N(x)= rac{s_{Nx+1}^4}{s_{2Nx+1}s_{2Nx+2}},\qquad B_N(x)= rac{s_{Nx}^4}{s_{2Nx}s_{2Nx+1}}. 	ag{2} \] We use the factorial source's specified zero-free interpolation \[ G_N(t)=\left( rac{2\pi}{N}ight)^t\Gamma(t+1) \prod_{k\ge1}  rac{\Gamma(Nk+t+1)} {\Gamma(Nk-t)(Nk)^{2t+1}}, \qquad -1<\Re t<N. 	ag{3} \] Its logarithm is fixed by the positive real normalization. The convergent product proves, without a periodic multiplier, \[ G_N(t+1)=2\sin(\pi(t+1)/N)G_N(t),\qquad G_N(0)=1. 	ag{4} \] Define \[ \mathcal F_{\zeta,N}(x) =4^{-\zeta} rac{G_N(Nx+\zeta)}{G_N(Nx-\zeta)}. 	ag{5} \] The power of \(4\) uses its real logarithm. For bounded \(\zeta\) and any fixed compact subset of \(0<\Re x<1\), (5) is holomorphic and nonzero for all sufficiently large \(N\). Its exact ratio is \[  rac{\mathcal F_{\zeta,N}(x+h)}{\mathcal F_{\zeta,N}(x)} = rac{\sin\pi(x+(\zeta+1)h)} {\sin\pi(x+(1-\zeta)h)}=:R_{\zeta,N}(x). 	ag{6} \] On the same compact sets, the factorial source proves \[ \log G_N(Nx) =N\mathcal J(x)+	frac12\Log(2N\sin\pi x) + rac{\pi\cot\pi x}{12N}+O_{m hol}(N^{-3}), \quad \mathcal J'(x)=\Log(2\sin\pi x). 	ag{7} \] The logarithm is continued from \(0<x<1\). Substituting \(x\pm\zeta h\) in (7) gives \[ \mathcal F_{\zeta,N}(x) =(\sin\pi x)^{2\zeta} \{1+\zeta\pi h\cot\pi x+O_{m hol}(h^2)\} =(\sin\pi(x+h/2))^{2\zeta}\{1+O_{m hol}(h^2)\}. 	ag{8} \] All fixed parameter and spatial derivatives have the corresponding bounds on smaller compact sets. The exact function in (5), rather than its asymptotic, is used below. ## 2. Ordinary lowering and finite cancellation The original rational sine identity for the Newton lowering rule continues in its index \(\zeta\). Substitution of (6) and its backward ratio in (2) gives \[  rac{\mathscr J_N\mathcal F_{\zeta,N}}{\mathcal F_{\zeta,N}} =c_\zeta-  rac{s_\zeta^4}{s_{Nx+\zeta}s_{Nx-\zeta+1}}. 	ag{9} \] This can also be checked by the source's denominator-cleared identity, with its variable \(q^{2k}\) replaced by \(q^{2\zeta}\). By (4), \[  rac{\mathcal F_{\zeta-1,N}}{\mathcal F_{\zeta,N}} = rac4{s_{Nx+\zeta}s_{Nx-\zeta+1}}. \] Consequently the exact ordinary lowering equation is \[  oxed{\quad \mathscr J_N\mathcal F_{\zeta,N} =c_\zeta\mathcal F_{\zeta,N} - rac{s_\zeta^4}{4}\mathcal F_{\zeta-1,N}. \quad} 	ag{10} \] No quotient or restriction to physical values occurs in this identity. Fix \(A<\infty\) and \(0<\epsilon<\pi\), and take the parameter set \[ |\Re\alpha|\le A,\qquad |\Im\alpha|\le\pi-\epsilon,\qquad z_\pm=-	frac12\pm rac{i\alpha}{2\pi},\qquad w=2\cosh(\alpha h)=c_{z_\pm}. 	ag{11} \] Slightly larger parameter sets of the same kind are reserved for derivatives. In particular \(-1<\Re z_\pm<0\), with uniform margins. For either \(z=z_\pm\), let \[ a_0(z)=1,\qquad  rac{a_k(z)}{a_{k-1}(z)} = rac{s_{z-k+1}^4}{4(c_{z-k}-c_z)} = rac{s_{z-k+1}^4}{4s_k s_{2z+1-k}}, \qquad U_{m,N}(z,x)=\sum_{k=0}^m a_k(z)\mathcal F_{z-k,N}(x). 	ag{12} \] For \(m\le\delta N\) with fixed \(\delta<1/2\), these denominators are nonzero for all large \(N\), uniformly on (11). Indeed \(k\ge1\) and \(\Re(2z+1)\) stays strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\). The finite sum telescopes under (10): \[  oxed{\quad (\mathscr J_N-w)U_{m,N}(z,x) =- rac{a_m(z)s_{z-m}^4}{4}\mathcal F_{z-m-1,N}(x). \quad} 	ag{13} \] The individual mode construction is not extended here across its other complex-index resonances. Coalescence at \(\alpha=0\) is regular and is handled in section 4. ## 3. The sharp product estimate at arbitrary fixed height Fix \(x_0\in(0,1/2)\), and put \[ \delta=\delta(x_0) = rac1\pi\arcsin rac{\sin(\pi x_0)}{\sqrt2},\qquad m=\lfloor\delta Nfloor. 	ag{14} \] Thus \(0<\delta<x_0\). Choose a sufficiently small real interval \([a,b]\) about \(x_0\), with larger fixed buffers, such that \(\delta<a<b<1/2\). The interval will be shrunk once below. The imaginary coordinate may range over any fixed bounded interval, with additional buffers for derivatives. Since \(\delta<a\) and \(b+\delta<1\), all arguments \(Nx\pm(z-k)\), \(0\le k\le m+1\), remain in the zero-free strip of (3) for large \(N\). Thus every function in the finite sum and its final lowering term is defined there by the same normalization. Write \(T_k=a_k(z)\mathcal F_{z-k,N}(x)\). The exact summand ratio is \[  rac{T_k}{T_{k-1}} = rac{s_{z-k+1}^4} {s_k s_{2z+1-k} s_{Nx+z-k+1}s_{Nx-z+k}}. 	ag{15} \] For \(0\le v<X<1/2\), define \[ \mathcal I_v(X)= \int_0^v\log rac{\sin^2(\pi X)-\sin^2(\pi u)} {\sin^2(\pi u)}\,du. 	ag{16} \] The logarithmic singularity at zero is integrable. For \(x=X+iY\), the unshifted spatial denominator has the exact bound \[  egin{split} &|\sin\pi(X-v+iY)\sin\pi(X+v+iY)|^2\ &\quad= [\sin^2\pi(X-v)+\sinh^2\pi Y]\, [\sin^2\pi(X+v)+\sinh^2\pi Y]\ &\quad\ge[\sin^2(\pi X)-\sin^2(\pi v)]^2. \end{split} 	ag{17} \] Both spatial sine factors are uniform units when \(v\le\delta\) on the chosen rectangle. Their bounded \(z h\) shifts change their product by a factor bounded by \(e^{Ch}\). Uniformly for \(1\le k\le m\), the first two denominator factors in (15) give \[ \left| rac{s_{z-k+1}^4}{s_k s_{2z+1-k}}ight| \le s_k^2(1+C/k). 	ag{18} \] For large fixed \(k\), this follows from the sine mean-value estimate, \(s_k\ge c k/N\), and bounded \(z\). The finitely many smaller \(k\) are covered by the nonresonance margins in (11), increasing \(C\). Equations (15)--(18) imply \[ \left| rac{T_k}{T_{k-1}}ight| \le (1+C/k)e^{Ch}  rac{\sin^2(\pi k h)} {\sin^2(\pi X)-\sin^2(\pi k h)}. 	ag{19} \] The base term \(\mathcal F_{z,N}\) and its reciprocal are uniformly bounded on every chosen fixed-height rectangle. The logarithm of the last ratio is \(2\log u\) plus a smooth function on \(0\le u\le\delta\). Summing \(2\log(k/N)\) using the elementary factorial bounds, and using a Riemann sum for the smooth part, yields uniformly for \(0\le k\le m\) \[ |T_k(x)|\le C N^p\exp\{-N\mathcal I_{kh}(X)\}. 	ag{20} \] The floor, the product of \(1+C/k\), and the endpoint factorial error cost only powers of \(N\). The integrand in (16) decreases through zero once, at \(v=\delta(X)\). Therefore \(v\mapsto\mathcal I_v(X)\) first increases and then decreases. At \(X=x_0\), its value at \(v=\delta\) is strictly positive. Shrink the real interval so that \(\mathcal I_\delta(X)>c>0\) throughout it. It follows that \(\mathcal I_v(X)\ge0\) for every \(0\le v\le\delta\). Equation (20) bounds the whole finite sum polynomially. In fact, \[ U_{m,N}(z,x)=\mathcal F_{z,N}(x) +O_{m hol}(h^2). 	ag{21} \] To prove this stronger statement, choose a small fixed \(ho>0\) below every \(\delta(X)\) in the real interval. The first summand ratio is \(O(h^2)\); for \(k\leho N\), the exact ratios are bounded by \(C(k+C)^2/N^2\), and hence by a fixed \(q<1\) after reducing \(ho\). This part of the sum is \(O(h^2)\). For \(ho\le kh\le\delta\), (16) has a uniform positive lower bound, so (20) makes the rest exponentially small. Apply Cauchy's formula on larger fixed rectangles and parameter sets to obtain every fixed derivative in (21). The multiplier relating the last term in (13) to \(T_m\) is \[  rac{s_{z-m}^4}{s_{Nx+z-m}s_{Nx-z+m+1}}, 	ag{22} \] which is bounded on those same rectangles. Consequently, for all fixed nonnegative \(r,s\), \[  oxed{\quad |\partial_x^r\partial_\alpha^s [(\mathscr J_N-w)U_{m,N}(z_\pm,x)]| \le C_{r,s}N^{p_{r,s}} e^{-N\mathcal I_\delta(\Re x)}. \quad} 	ag{23} \] For spatial derivatives, apply the preceding bounds on disks of radius \(c/N\). The rate in (16) is smooth on the real buffer, so its variation on such a disk costs only a bounded factor. Parameter derivatives use a larger fixed set as in (11). This preserves the displayed exponential rate. At the target real part, the exponent is exactly the archived optimized product rate: \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal I_{\delta(x_0)}(x_0) =J_*(\pi-2\pi x_0). \quad} 	ag{24} \] For a direct verification, let \(I(X)=\mathcal I_{\delta(X)}(X)\). The endpoint term in its derivative is zero. Substitution \(y=	an(\pi u)\) gives \[ I'(X)=2\operatorname{atanh}  rac{\cos(\pi X)}{\sqrt{1+\cos^2(\pi X)}} =2\operatorname{asinh}(\cos\pi X). 	ag{25} \] Also \(I(X)	o0\) as \(X\downarrow0\), by scaling \(u=Xv\) in its integrable logarithm. The pinned diagnostic has \[ J_*(t)= rac1\pi\int_t^\pi\operatorname{asinh}(\sin(s/2))\,ds, \] which proves (24), including its constant. ## 4. A basis regular at the parameter coalescence Let \(
u=\alpha/\pi\), and use the same cutoff for both signs: \[ H_{0,N}= rac{U_{m,N}(z_+,x)+U_{m,N}(z_-,x)}2,\qquad H_{1,N}= rac{U_{m,N}(z_+,x)-U_{m,N}(z_-,x)}{2i
u}. 	ag{26} \] The second expression is defined by its removable value at zero. The functions are jointly holomorphic. Equations (8) and (21) give \[ H_{0,N}= rac{\cos(
u\log\sin\pi x)}{\sin\pi x}+O_{m hol}(h), \qquad H_{1,N}= rac{\sin(
u\log\sin\pi x)} {
u\sin\pi x}+O_{m hol}(h). 	ag{27} \] The sine quotient has its logarithmic value at \(
u=0\). Cauchy's formula in \(\alpha\) proves the uniform removable bounds in (27) and (23). Since both modes have the same \(w\), their residuals still obey (23). The limiting Wronskian is \[ W(H_{0,N},H_{1,N}) = rac{\pi\cos\pi x}{\sin^3\pi x}+O_{m hol}(h), 	ag{28} \] which is a uniform unit on each of the fixed rectangles above. The corresponding balanced frame \[ \mathcal Y_N(x)=  egin{pmatrix} H_{0,N}(x)&H_{1,N}(x)\ h^{-1}(H_{0,N}(x)-H_{0,N}(x-h))& h^{-1}(H_{1,N}(x)-H_{1,N}(x-h)) \end{pmatrix} 	ag{29} \] and its inverse are uniformly bounded on smaller rectangles. This gives two genuine, explicitly normalized analytic approximate modes. No diagonal Floquet eigenline, periodic scalar continuation, or exact homogeneous correction is being asserted. ## 5. An actual two-value connection and the retained normal packet Let \(F_j=K_N(w,c_j)\) on the physical bulk, and put \[ X_j=(F_j,h^{-1}(F_j-F_{j-1}))^t. 	ag{30} \] Choose a right physical anchor \(j_*\) in the real buffer and define the actual coefficients and scalar comparison by \[ \mathbf a_N(\alpha)=\mathcal Y_N(x_{j_*})^{-1}X_{j_*}, \qquad V_N(x,\alpha)=(H_{0,N}(x),H_{1,N}(x))\mathbf a_N(\alpha). 	ag{31} \] The original physical-row bounds give \(\|\mathbf a_N\|\le CN^p\), uniformly on (11); these coefficients are holomorphic there. Both values \(F_{j_*}\) and \(F_{j_*-1}\) are matched exactly. For clarity, the balanced original transfer and forcing vector are \[ T_N= egin{pmatrix}1+d_N&h q_N\d_N/h&q_N\end{pmatrix}, \quad q_N=B_N/A_N,\quad d_N=(c_0-w)/A_N,\quad b_N=A_N^{-1}(1,h^{-1})^t. 	ag{32} \] Thus \(X_f(x+h)=T_N(x)X_f(x)-b_N(x)(\mathscr J_N-w)f(x)\). On the buffered real interval, \(T_N^{\pm1}=I+O(h)\). The actual physical values satisfy the homogeneous recurrence, whereas \(V_N\) has residual \(r_V=(\mathscr J_N-w)V_N\) bounded by (23) with a polynomial loss from (31). Backward variation of constants from the exact two-value anchor gives \[  oxed{\quad \|X_j-X_{V_N}(x_j)\| \le CN^p e^{-N\mathcal I_\delta(x_j)} \qquad(x_j\in[a,b],\ j\le j_*). \quad} 	ag{33} \] Indeed the balanced propagators are bounded, there are \(O(N)\) forcing terms, and \(\mathcal I_\delta(X)\) is increasing in \(X\) for \(\delta<X<1/2\), directly from (16). The corresponding first-normal statement retains additional data. Use the ordinary \(x\)-derivative of the full kernel for the actual normal state, and set \(Z_f=(X_f,\partial_xX_f)^t\). At bulk physical rows the ordinary kernel source and its first derivative vanish. With \[ \mathcal T_N= egin{pmatrix}T_N&0\T_N'&T_N\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathcal R_N(r)= inom{b_Nr}{b_N'r+b_Nr'}, \] the exact difference \(E=K_N(w,c_N(\cdot))-V_N\) therefore obeys \[ Z_E(x_j)=\Phi_{j,j_*}Z_E(x_{j_*}) -\sum_{l=j}^{j_*-1}\Phi_{j,l+1}\mathcal R_N(r_V)(x_l). 	ag{34} \] Here \(\Phi_{j,k}\) is the homogeneous propagator of \(\mathcal T_N\), with inverse products for \(j<k\); all neighboring arguments stay inside the fixed real buffer. Its first two anchor entries vanish by (31); its last two entries are the actual independent normal mismatch. Consequently \[ \|Z_E(x_j)\|\le C\|Z_E(x_{j_*})\| +CN^p e^{-N\mathcal I_\delta(x_j)}. 	ag{35} \] Division by the bulk unit \(c_N'(x_j)\) translates this to spectral normals. Formula (35) neither resets nor estimates its normal anchor. It also does not control the actual fractional-grid packet of a separately normalized baseline. In particular (23), (33), and (35) do not supply that baseline's optimized full-normal Green budget. All currents, endpoint rows, shared spectators, and source coefficients outside these stated comparisons remain unchanged. There is no filled-action estimate, scalar noncancellation claim, or assertion that the approximate basis has the full physical jets. ## 6. Coverage and direct sources The continuum sine-power modes and their leading value connection constants were already known. The exact factorial interpolation was also available. The additional step here is its ordinary descending index expansion (12), the uniform tall-rectangle estimate for that specific finite sum, and the identity of its optimal residual rate with \(J_*\). The actual two-value normalization (31) retains the normal datum that the sharp residual alone does not determine. The following complete source texts were read, with their used identities and final pins checked: * [Normalized factorial interpolation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/exact_factorial_interpolation_and_complex_contours.md), SHA256 1f34f65437dfe0bfb4062a7a74840beae1676353cf13bb8a86f8849a8a36bc72. * [Ordinary edge-kernel lowering and source](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_edge_kernel_difference_and_endpoint_bound.md), SHA256 5d0d07d4d97d82cca66e0e0c3bf2cecad8e5f58ef8329178278b297cf0d6c5da. * [Actual complex baseline and optimized product diagnostic](research_unturned_endpoint_complex_baseline_and_window.md), SHA256 9d233d9bb11c2842e62d5523f97e9621a3bd22532e3b527ceaab8125782c1cc1. * [Retained full-normal Green budget](research_partial_endpoint_green_boundary_budget.md), SHA256 a1bbfaa8f64abca96d2b97078a9d87fbc60877b4f4791612b1e8e2d822be286e. Only written mathematics, source-text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build or compilation was run. Existing adopted and public notes are unchanged.

title: Two half-plane representatives and the exact endpoint-product interface
text:
# Two half-plane representatives and the exact endpoint-product interface Private written proof, 16 November 2026. Every fixed product of full microscopic endpoint kernels, at an original traced vertex, has an exact pair of representatives with polynomial bounds on their respective half-planes. Each preserves all angular Hermite jets. Using the lower representative below the real axis and the upper representative above it leaves an explicit holomorphic interface current. The original Gaussian, all spectators, and every vertical side remain. The projection and Fourier folding are archived identities. The new assembly applies them to the actual full shared endpoint product, with a polynomial coefficient bound and the complete relative contour. No intermediate Newton cutoff is introduced. ## 1. Full endpoint products and a polynomial coefficient bound Use \[ N\ge2,\quad D=N-1,\quad\eta=(-1)^D,\quad c_a=2\cos((2a+1)\pi/N),\quad P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2, \] \[ e_j(Z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{a<j}(c_a-Z),\quad S_j=\prod_{a=1}^j2\sin(\pi a/N),\quad S_0=1,\quad K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^D e_j(w)e_j(Z). 	ag{1} \] Fix \(r\ge0\) and \(A<\infty\), independent of the level. For complex parameters \(|\alpha_i|\le A\), set \[ w_i=2\cosh(\alpha_i/N),\quad Q_N(Z)=\prod_{i=1}^rK_N(w_i,Z),\quad C_N(Z)=\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}Q_N(Z). 	ag{2} \] The empty product is one. Reduction in (2) occurs only in an originally traced variable, after its endpoint kernels have been multiplied. It preserves every double-root value and first normal, and the odd simple-root value. All other factors remain untouched. There are constants \(C,p\), depending only on \(A,r\), such that \[ \sup_{Z\in[-2,2]}|Q_N(Z)|+\|\widehat C_N\|_1\le CN^p,\qquad C_N(-2\cos t)= eta_0+ \sum_{k=1}^D eta_k(e^{-ikt}+e^{ikt}), 	ag{3} \] where \(\|\widehat C_N\|_1=| eta_0|+2\sum_{k=1}^D| eta_k|\). To prove this for arbitrary bounded microscopic parameters, choose a fixed integer \(b\ge0\) with \((2b+1)\pi>A\). For sufficiently large \(N\), \[ |w_i-2|\le2-c_b . 	ag{4} \] The endpoint source proves the physical-row factorization \[ F_{j,N}(w)=K_N(c_j,w) =\prod_{
u=1}^j rac{r_{j,
u}-w}{r_{j,
u}-c_0}, \qquad r_{j,
u}>2. \] Thus, for every distinct physical row, \[ |F_{j,N}(w_i)|\le F_{j,N}(c_b) =F_{b,N}(c_j)\le F_{b,N}(-2)\le C_bN^{2b}. 	ag{5} \] The last inequality follows directly from its exact positive formula \[ F_{b,N}(-2)=\sum_{k=0}^b  rac{S_{b+k}}{S_{b-k}S_k^4}\prod_{h<k}(c_h+2). 	ag{6} \] For fixed \(b,k\), the factorial quotient is \(O_b(N^{2k})\); the remaining factors are at most four. The preceding inequality in (5) also follows from the root product. The low kernel is the ordinary degree-\(J\) interpolant of these values, where \(J=\lfloor(N-1)/2floor\). Its real-interval norm is at most \(N\max_j|F_{j,N}(w_i)|\), by the endpoint source's exact cosine interpolation bound. The remaining radical polynomials satisfy \[ |e_{D-a}(-2\cos t)|\le\sqrt{N-1}\,e^{D|\Im t|} \quad(0\le a<\lfloor N/2floor). 	ag{7} \] Use \(t=\pi-i\alpha_i/N\) in their first color and a real angle in the second. The at most \(N/2\) terms cost at most \(N^2e^A\). Hence each full kernel, and then \(Q_N\), has polynomial real norm. The finitely many smaller levels, including \(N=2\), are absorbed in the constant. The Laurent degree of \(Q_N(-2\cos t)\) is at most \(rD\). Its Fourier coefficient sum is therefore at most \(2rD+1\) times its real-period norm. Exact full-Hermite Fourier folding gives \[ \widehat C_N(m)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z} (\ell+1)\eta^\ell\widehat Q_N(m+\ell N), \qquad 1\le m<N, 	ag{8} \] together with its even zero-frequency formula. Only \(O_r(1)\) alias blocks occur; all their weights are \(O_r(1)\). Consequently folding increases the coefficient norm by at most a constant depending on \(r\), proving (3). All identities are holomorphic in the parameters. Fixed parameter derivatives retain polynomial bounds on smaller sets by Cauchy's formula on a larger bounded parameter set. ## 2. Two exact representatives with their full normals Put \(z=e^{-it}\), and abbreviate \(C(t)=C_N(-2\cos t)\). Define \[  egin{split} C_-(t)&= eta_0+\sum_{k=1}^D eta_k \{z^k+2\eta z^{N-k}-z^{2N-k}\},\ C_+(t)&=C_-(-t),\ A_-(t)&=\sum_{k=1}^D eta_k z^{N-k},\qquad A_+(t)=A_-(-t). \end{split} 	ag{9} \] The archived one-sided identity is \[ z^{-k}\equiv2\eta z^{N-k}-z^{2N-k} \pmod{(z^N-\eta)^2}. 	ag{10} \] It proves that each \(C_\pm\) separately has all angular values and first derivatives of \(C\) on the physical grid \[ 	au_j=\pi(D-2j)/N,\qquad z_j^N=\eta . 	ag{11} \] At double spectral roots these are the original spectral jets. At the odd simple root \(t=0\), (10) preserves the value and the zero angular derivative of the original even function. No extra spectral normal is imposed there. The representatives need not be even off the grid; no ordinary spectral descent is claimed for them. The algebraic proof of (10) works also at \(N=2\). Every exponent in \(C_-,A_-\) is nonnegative. Equation (3) therefore gives \[ \sup_{\Im t\le0}(|C_-|+|A_-|) +\sup_{\Im t\ge0}(|C_+|+|A_+|)\le C'N^{p'}. 	ag{12} \] Each fixed angular derivative adds only a power of \(N\). For the original double-pole grid kernel \[ W_N(t)= rac{z^N}{(1-\eta z^N)^2}, 	ag{13} \] direct subtraction gives the exact identities \[  oxed{\qquad CW_N=C_-W_N+A_-=C_+W_N+A_+. \qquad} 	ag{14} \] In particular the correction after multiplication by the grid kernel is holomorphic, with no remaining grid pole. ## 3. The original contour and its oriented interface Let \(\Gamma_H\), \(H>0\), be the counterclockwise rectangle with corners \(\pm\pi\pm iH\). Its lower exterior half \(E_-\) runs from \(-\pi\) down the left side, across the bottom from left to right, and up the right side to \(\pi\). Its upper exterior half \(E_+\) runs from \(\pi\) up the right side, across the top from right to left, and down to \(-\pi\). Thus every vertical half-side is included. Let \(F(t;\mathbf u)\) be the actual remaining even spectator, holomorphic on a neighborhood of this closed rectangle. It may retain every other trace variable, edge kernel, coupon, and ordinary free boundary parameter jointly. For the original integer crossing power \(n\), set \[ g(t)=\sin t\,e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)}F(t;\mathbf u),\qquad \mathfrak c_{N,n}=\exp\{\pi i nD^2/(4N)\}. 	ag{15} \] The original full derivative-residue formula is \[ \phi_N(R^nQ_NF)= - rac{N^2\mathfrak c_{N,n}}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma_H}CW_Ng\,dt . 	ag{16} \] Here \(F\) on the left means the original spectral spectator or its trace-compatible analytic angular representative. Reduction (2) preserves the full jets before the residue formula is applied. For the normalization, at each \(	au_j\) the kernel has expansion \(W_N(t)=-\eta/[N^2(t-	au_j)^2]+O(1)\), with no simple-pole term. Thus (16) is exactly the original derivative sum \(\eta\mathfrak c_{N,n}\sum_j(Cg)'(	au_j)\). At the odd zero angle the derivative of \(\sin t\) supplies the simple spectral value; this check also covers \(N=2\). **Theorem.** With these conventions, \[  oxed{ egin{split} \oint_{\Gamma_H}CW_Ng\,dt ={}&\int_{E_-}C_-W_Ng\,dt+\int_{E_+}C_+W_Ng\,dt\ &+\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(A_--A_+)g\,dt . \end{split}} 	ag{17} \] The exterior amplitudes obey (12); the interface amplitude is polynomially bounded on its real path. Every original normal, Gaussian factor, spectator, and vertical side remains. *Proof.* Apply the first expression in (14) on \(E_-\) and the second on \(E_+\). Holomorphy gives \[ \int_{E_-}A_-g\,dt=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}A_-g\,dt,\qquad \int_{E_+}A_+g\,dt=-\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}A_+g\,dt. 	ag{18} \] Indeed the lower half-rectangle's positive real boundary runs from \(\pi\) to \(-\pi\); the upper one's runs oppositely. Adding proves (17). The corrections have no grid poles, so zero at odd levels causes no exception. \(\square\) The interface is explicitly a finite sum of continuous Fourier integrals: \[  egin{split} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(A_--A_+)g\,dt =-i\sum_{k=1}^D eta_k\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} &\{\cos((N-k-1)t)-\cos((N-k+1)t)\}\ &	imes e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)}F(t;\mathbf u)\,dt . \end{split} 	ag{19} \] These are ordinary integrals, not substituted finite charged traces. Their frequencies include zero at \(k=D\); no separate exponential smallness is asserted. Both \(A_--A_+\) and \(g\) are odd, so their product is even and generally does not integrate to zero. Moving this interface back to the exterior halves restores (14); it does not cancel an endpoint current for free. ## 4. Shared graph placement and scope All identities are coefficientwise in uncontracted variables. At every traced vertex multiply its full endpoint coupons first, take the full-Hermite remainder, and then apply (9)--(17). Operations in distinct variables commute. Their tensor product gives the finite sum of exterior-half and interface integrals for a fixed graph, retaining every shared edge and all remaining original traces. Outside mixed derivatives commute with the identities. The spectator itself is not replaced by a value-only interpolant. There is no canonical reduction in an ordinary free variable. If the unreduced product \(Q_N\) is retained on separate contour sides, its difference from \(C_N\) has an additional holomorphic current after multiplication by \(W_N\); that current must remain. In (16), full quotient reduction has already been performed inside the exact closed original trace. The construction uses only full endpoint products. It is independent of a low/high truncation or a central physical window. It avoids a globally even moderate representative by using two angular representatives with the explicit interface. It supplies no bound for their Gaussian-spectator product at the filled action and no general inserted-descendant estimate. ## 5. Coverage and direct sources Projection (10), the full derivative-residue normalization, and Fourier folding are existing results. The additional assembly is their cutoff-independent use for all fixed shared microscopic endpoint products, with the polynomial bound and the fully oriented relative interface (17). The following complete sources were read at unchanged versions; their directly used implications and final hashes were checked: * [One-sided Hermite projection](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_one_sided_hermite_projection.md), SHA256 efa82935ada9aa9e06dcbd5d20d5e05357859986896b0b73a93eb78a4bb81cf4: exact angular projection, full derivative-residue trace, and transferred contour terms. * [Boundary crossing packet preservation](research_boundary_crossing_packet_preservation.md), SHA256 a2f9cadf0fd6f23889ea7d20b469055fe33cb9df4d971668a2923666983cfec8: full-Hermite Fourier folding with all aliases and odd ramification. * [Full-period endpoint kernel reduction](research_full_period_endpoint_kernel_reduction.md), SHA256 a1d67ac803c0160bbfdacaa96a6fde9dc1ffae06fc39eb94f0416dcf2ecef76e: actual row root product and formula, ordinary interpolation bound, and endpoint/full-normal conventions. * [High Newton radical contraction](research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md), SHA256 1faa5d2e02edf0a1462cc43b243e0ab4403bf56e9f1af0befb6b492441d9dd03: exact both-parity split and the radical Fourier bound (7). Only written mathematics, source-text reads, and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, or compilation was run. Adopted notes and public manuscripts were unchanged.

title: Endpoint connection constants and a finite-level bulk overlap
text:
# Endpoint connection constants and a finite-level bulk overlap Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The original microscopic endpoint values have explicit connection constants. Their derivation uses the terminating endpoint recurrence, an exact hypergeometric generating function, and a growing overlap with the original finite-level recurrence. No interchange of a fixed-index limit and a bulk limit is used. The leading value oscillates in \(\log N\) at nonzero real endpoint parameter. At parameter zero its two modes coalesce into a logarithm. The theorem supplies the value-derived part of the actual normal comparison; it does not identify a separately interpolated normal with that derivative. ## 1. Original data and statement Set \[ 	heta=\pi/N,\quad s_r=2\sin(r	heta),\quad S_k=\prod_{r=1}^k s_r,\quad c(r)=2\cos((2r+1)	heta),\quad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N), \] \[ e_k(Z)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{r<k}(c(r)-Z),\qquad K_N(Z,w)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e_k(Z)e_k(w),\qquad F_{j,N}(\alpha)=K_N(c(j),w_N(\alpha)). 	ag{1} \] These are ordinary original polynomials, including their high Newton sector. Throughout the asymptotic theorem, \(\alpha\) is real and \(|\alpha|\le A<\infty\). Put \[ 
u=\alpha/\pi,\qquad a=	frac12+i
u/2,\qquad b=1-a,\qquad p=ab=	frac14(1+
u^2). 	ag{2} \] For real \(
u
e0\), define \[ k_\pm(
u)=  rac{\Gamma(\pm i
u)} {\Gamma(1/2\pm i
u/2)^4},\qquad C_0(
u)=k_++k_-,\qquad C_1(
u)=i
u(k_+-k_-). 	ag{3} \] Both \(C_0,C_1\) have removable values at zero and are even analytic functions on a complex neighborhood of any fixed compact real \(
u\)-interval. Their values there are \[ C_0(0)= rac{2(\gamma_{\!E}+4\log2)}{\pi^2},\qquad C_1(0)= rac2{\pi^2}. 	ag{4} \] For \(s>0\), use the real logarithm in \[ g_\alpha(s)= rac1s\left\{ C_0(
u)\cos(
u\log s) +C_1(
u) rac{\sin(
u\log s)}{
u}ight\},\qquad S_N(x)= rac{N}{\pi}\sin(\pi x). 	ag{5} \] The sine quotient is interpreted by its value \(\log s\) at zero. Equivalently, away from \(
u=0\), \[ g_\alpha(s)=k_+s^{-1+i
u}+k_-s^{-1-i
u}. 	ag{6} \] **Theorem.** Fix a closed interval \(I\Subset(0,1/2)\). There is \(\epsilon>0\), depending only on \(A\) and a buffered choice of \(I\), such that, uniformly at its physical nodes, \[ F_{j,N}(\alpha)=g_\alpha(S_N(j/N))+O(N^{-1-\epsilon}), 	ag{7} \] \[ N(F_{j,N}-F_{j-1,N}) =\left.\partial_x g_\alpha(S_N(x))ight|_{x=j/N} +O(N^{-1-\epsilon}). 	ag{8} \] The constants are uniform for real \(|\alpha|\le A\). More generally, let \(f_N(x,\alpha)\) be any exact value interpolation on a fixed larger bulk interval and a fixed complex \(x\)-neighborhood, with a uniform polynomial analytic bound: \[ f_N(j/N,\alpha)=F_{j,N}(\alpha),\qquad |f_N|\le C N^P. 	ag{9} \] For every fixed \(r\ge0\), on the smaller real interval, \[ \partial_x^r f_N(x,\alpha) =\partial_x^r g_\alpha(S_N(x))+O_r(N^{-1-\epsilon}), 	ag{10} \] after reducing \(\epsilon\) once. No small-error assertion on a fixed complex \(x\)-strip is made. The proof of (10) uses strips of width comparable to \(1/\log N\). The adopted two-channel theorem, as used in the pinned structural source, supplies an interpolation satisfying (9). The conclusions are independent of which such interpolation is chosen. ## 2. The universal endpoint recurrence and its generating function At a physical index \(j\), the Newton sum (1) terminates at \(k=j\). For each fixed \(j\), direct sine-product limits give \[ F_{j,N}(\alpha)\longrightarrow v_j(\alpha):= {}_4F_3\!\left( egin{matrix}-j,j+1,a,b\1,1,1\end{matrix};1ight) =\sum_{k=0}^j  rac{(-j)_k(j+1)_k(a)_k(b)_k}{(k!)^4}. 	ag{11} \] Indeed \[ e_k(c(j))\longrightarrow  rac{(-1)^k(-j)_k(j+1)_k}{(k!)^2},\qquad e_k(w_N(\alpha))\longrightarrow  rac{(-1)^k(a)_k(b)_k}{(k!)^2}. \] Only a fixed finite sum is involved in (11). The exact original recurrence is \[ F_{j+1,N}=(1+d_{j,N})F_{j,N} +q_{j,N}(F_{j,N}-F_{j-1,N}), \] \[ q_{j,N}= rac{C_N(j)}{A_N(j)},\qquad d_{j,N}= rac{c(0)-w_N(\alpha)}{A_N(j)},\qquad A_N(j)= rac{s_{j+1}^4}{s_{2j+1}s_{2j+2}},\quad C_N(j)= rac{s_j^4}{s_{2j}s_{2j+1}}. 	ag{12} \] At zero use \(C_N(0)=0\). Its fixed-index limits are \[ q_j^0= rac{j^3}{(j+1)^3},\qquad d_j^0=- rac{2p(2j+1)}{(j+1)^3}. 	ag{13} \] Thus \[ (j+1)^3v_{j+1} =\{(j+1)^3+j^3-2p(2j+1)\}v_j-j^3v_{j-1}, \quad v_0=1,\quad v_1=1-2p. 	ag{14} \] This conclusion could also be obtained directly from the terminating sum, but (12) fixes its original normalization. The generating identity needed for the connection problem is \[  oxed{\quad V(z):=\sum_{j\ge0}v_j z^j ={}_2F_1(a,a;1;z)\,{}_2F_1(b,b;1;z) =(1-z)^{2a-1}{}_2F_1(a,a;1;z)^2 . \quad} 	ag{15} \] Here all functions start with their analytic branches at \(z=0\). We verify the identity rather than invoke an identification of orthogonal polynomials. Write \(D=z\partial_z\). Equation (14) is equivalent to \[ [D^3-z\{2D^3+3D^2+(3-4p)D+1-2p\} +z^2(D+1)^3]V=0. 	ag{16} \] For example, the left shift contributes \(D^3V\), and the last shift contributes \(z^2(D+1)^3V\). Conversely its coefficient recurrence determines every analytic coefficient from \(v_0\). For an explicit check of the proposed right side, let \(k=a-1/2\), \(f={}_2F_1(a,a;1;z)\), and \(h=(1-z)^k f\). The hypergeometric equation gives \[ z(1-z)h''+(1-2z)h' -\left\{	frac14+ rac{k^2}{1-z}ight\}h=0. 	ag{17} \] If \(h''+Ph'+Qh=0\), direct differentiation of \(h^2\) gives \[ (h^2)'''+3P(h^2)'' +(P'+4Q+2P^2)(h^2)' +(2Q'+4PQ)h^2=0. 	ag{18} \] In (17), \[ P= rac{1-2z}{z(1-z)},\qquad Q=- rac1{4z(1-z)}- rac{k^2}{z(1-z)^2}. \] Multiplying (18) by \(z^3(1-z)^2\) yields coefficients \[  egin{array}{c|c} \partial_z^3&z^3(1-z)^2\ \partial_z^2&3z^2(1-z)(1-2z)\ \partial_z&z+(4p-8)z^2+7z^3\ 1&-(1-2p)z+z^2 \end{array} \] because \(p=1/4-k^2\). These are exactly (16) in ordinary derivatives. The constant coefficient is one. Uniqueness of its analytic coefficient recurrence proves the final expression in (15). The middle expression follows from Euler's transformation \({}_2F_1(b,b;1;z)=(1-z)^{2a-1}{}_2F_1(a,a;1;z)\); alternatively the same substitution into the second-order equation, with its value and derivative at zero, proves that transformation. ## 3. Connection constants, coefficient bounds, and coalescence Put \(\zeta=1-z\). Away from \(
u=0\), in a small slit neighborhood of \(z=1\), the connection formula is \[ {}_2F_1(a,a;1;z) =A_
u\,{}_2F_1(a,a;2a;\zeta) +B_
u\,\zeta^{-i
u}{}_2F_1(b,b;2b;\zeta), \] \[ A_
u= rac{\Gamma(-i
u)}{\Gamma(b)^2},\qquad B_
u= rac{\Gamma(i
u)}{\Gamma(a)^2}. 	ag{19} \] Here is a direct normalization argument for these constants. For \(0<\Re a<1\), Euler's integral gives \[ {}_2F_1(a,a;1;z)=  rac1{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(1-a)} \int_0^1u^{a-1}(1-u)^{-a}(1-zu)^{-a}\,du. 	ag{20} \] Its expansion at zero proves the integral by the beta integral. The two functions in (19) solve the same differential equation and have distinct local exponents when \(2a-1
e0\) is not an integer. For \(\Re a<1/2\), evaluation of (20) at \(z=1\) is another beta integral and gives \(\Gamma(1-2a)/\Gamma(1-a)^2\) for the regular coefficient. For \(\Re a>1/2\), rescaling \(1-u=(1-z)v\) in its singular part gives \(\Gamma(2a-1)/\Gamma(a)^2\) for the singular coefficient. These coefficients are meromorphic in \(a\). Analytic continuation of the two local solutions and their Wronskian proves (19) throughout a neighborhood of the compact real \(
u\)-interval, except its displayed removable coalescence. This argument also fixes the branches inherited from \(z=0\). Substitution in (15) shows that its only leading nonanalytic terms at one are \[ A_
u^2(1-z)^{i
u} +B_
u^2(1-z)^{-i
u}. 	ag{21} \] The cross term is analytic at one. Both analytic multipliers in (19) have value one there. We give the uniform coefficient estimate used below. Choose a small fixed \(0<\sigma<1/4\). Uniformly for \(
u\) on a fixed compact real interval, \[ v_j=g_\alpha(j)+O_A(j^{-2+\sigma}),\qquad v_j-v_{j-1} =g_\alpha(j)-g_\alpha(j-1)+O_A(j^{-3+\sigma}). 	ag{22} \] To justify the coefficient transfer first away from zero, recall the exact identity \[ [z^j](1-z)^\lambda = rac{\Gamma(j-\lambda)} {\Gamma(-\lambda)\Gamma(j+1)}. 	ag{23} \] For \(\lambda\) in compact subsets with \(\Re\lambda>-1\), the beta integral for the ratio of gamma functions, followed by the substitution \(v=j(1-u)\), gives \[  rac{\Gamma(j-\lambda)}{\Gamma(j+1)} =j^{-1-\lambda}\{1+O(j^{-1})\}. 	ag{24} \] The bound is uniform on those compact sets; splitting the integral at \(v=j^{1/3}\), Taylor expansion on the first part and its exponential tail proves the stated error. Analytic continuation interprets (23) at its removable integer parameters. For clarity, the local remainder transfer needs no global convergence of the series at one. After subtracting (21) and the constant cross term, the remainder is \(O(|1-z|^{1-\sigma})\), uniformly on a compact parameter set with \(|\Im
u|<\sigma\) avoiding zero. It is analytic in a disk larger than the unit disk slit along \([1,\infty)\). Deform the coefficient contour to a circle of radius \(1/j\) about one and two fixed-angle rays \(1+t e^{\pm i\varphi}\), \(0<\varphi<\pi/2\), followed by fixed outer arcs.
