The theorem is a statement about the complete original clock contraction conditional on the undercolor. It does not replace that undercolor by an optimizer or alter its subsequent physical sum. ## 4. The actual residue period and its Gaussian normalization This asymptotic also applies to a specified exact cycle, without choosing a cycle from a critical point. Let \(G_N(z)\) be the nonzero sine-factorial interpolation of the direct source, normalized by \(G_N(a)=S_a\) for integers \(0\le a<N\). Define \[ I_{\sigma,N}(h)= \frac{\exp\{\sigma\pi i(U+2j-1+1/N)h\}} {G_N(h-v)G_N(u-h+v)} . \tag{13} \] It agrees with the summand of (2) at every allowed integer. Choose small positively oriented circles about \(h=v,\ldots,v+u\), containing no other integer or interpolation pole, and let \(\Gamma_N\) be their oriented sum. Then \[ C_{\sigma,N} =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma_N} I_{\sigma,N}(h)\pi\cot(\pi h)\,dh. \tag{14} \] This follows directly from the residues, including the two endpoint residues. The Fourier-character choice in (13) is specified explicitly; it equals the literal summand on every residue. It is not being imposed on an unrelated exterior continuation. For real physical parameters \(0<U,\ 0<j<j+U<1\), put \[ R_\sigma=\frac U2-\frac{\sigma i}{2\pi} \log\frac{s(j+U)}{s(j)},\qquad H_\sigma=V+R_\sigma . \tag{15} \] This is the canonical clock critical point already derived from the original source. The corrected clock action, before evaluating it there, is \[ F_\sigma(R)=-\mathcal J(R)-\mathcal J(U-R) +\sigma\pi i(V+R)(U+2j-1). \tag{16} \] The prior primitive calibration, or its elementary specialization after subtracting the two unchanged outer factorials, gives \[ F_\sigma'(R_\sigma)=0,\quad F_\sigma(R_\sigma)=W_\sigma,\quad F_\sigma''(R_\sigma) =-\frac{2\pi s(U)} {s(R_\sigma)s(U-R_\sigma)} . \tag{17} \] The Hessian is negative real on this physical domain, since \(U-R_\sigma=\overline{R_\sigma}\). It has no zero on the continued regular clock chart. The exact factorial interpolation, at \(h=N(V+R)\), has the local summand expansion \[ I_{\sigma,N}(N(V+R)) =\frac1N \frac{e^{\sigma\pi i(V+R)}} {\sqrt{s(R)s(U-R)}} e^{NF_\sigma(R)}\{1+O(N^{-1})\}. \tag{18} \] It is uniform and holomorphic near the critical point. The square roots use the same factorial logarithms. The lattice measure is \(N\,dR\). Consequently its normalized one-dimensional Gaussian model has leading amplitude \[ \begin{split} A_{\rm G} &=\frac{e^{\sigma\pi iH_\sigma}} {\sqrt{s(R_\sigma)s(U-R_\sigma)}} \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{-F_\sigma''(R_\sigma)}}\\ &=\frac{e^{\sigma\pi iH_\sigma}}{\sqrt{s(U)}} =A_\sigma . \end{split} \tag{19} \] The Gaussian root is positive at physical real parameters and then continued. The last equality uses (15): \(e^{\sigma\pi iR_\sigma} =e^{\sigma\pi iU/2}\sqrt{s(j+U)/s(j)}\). There is also a direct real-lattice base point fixing this Gaussian coefficient. Set \(j_0=(1-U)/2\). The exact normalized Fourier lift in (2), without any further change of phase, is then \(a_{\sigma,N}=e^{\sigma\pi i/N}\). Writing \(r=h-v\), the complete sum is \[ C_{\sigma,N}(u,v;j_0) =\sum_{r=0}^{u} \frac{e^{\sigma\pi i(V+r/N)}}{S_rS_{u-r}} . \tag{19a} \] The support is the real integer interval \(h=v,\ldots,v+u\), including both endpoints. This slice belongs to the exact undercolor continuation; it is itself a physical undercolor when \((N-u)/2\) is integral. Centering the phase in (19a) puts every summand in the half-plane \[ \operatorname{Re} e^{-\sigma\pi i(V+U/2)}C_{\sigma,N}(u,v;j_0) \ge \cos(\pi U/2)\sum_{r=0}^{u}\frac1{S_rS_{u-r}}>0. \tag{19b} \] No cancellation is possible at this base point. More precisely, on \(0<R<U\) its real entropy is \[ E_U(R)=-\mathcal J(R)-\mathcal J(U-R),\qquad E_U''(R)= -\frac{\pi\sin(\pi U)} {\sin(\pi R)\sin(\pi(U-R))}<0 . \tag{19c} \] It extends continuously to \([0,U]\), is symmetric about \(U/2\), and has its unique maximum there. Uniformly for \(U\) in a compact subset of \((0,1)\), there is a strict entropy gap outside any fixed sufficiently small neighborhood of \(U/2\). The same factorial splitting used for (9), with the crude Stirling remainder and a bounded sum-to-integral error for \(g\), gives \[ \log S_k=N\mathcal J(k/N)+O(\log N), \qquad 0\le k\le u\le(1-\epsilon)N . \tag{19d} \] At \(k=0\) this is immediate; the estimate for \(k\ge1\) is uniform down to \(k=1\). Thus all summands outside that neighborhood, including both endpoints, are exponentially smaller than the central contribution, up to a fixed polynomial factor. Inside the neighborhood, (9) gives the density in (18) with real \(R\). Rescale \(r-u/2\) by \(\sqrt N\). Strict concavity supplies an integrable Gaussian bound, and the resulting Gaussian Riemann sums converge with either parity of \(u\). Consequently the actual lattice sum, with its positive orientation, satisfies \[ C_{\sigma,N}(u,v;j_0) =N^{-1/2}e^{NE_U(U/2)} \frac{e^{\sigma\pi i(V+U/2)}}{\sqrt{s(U)}} \{1+o(1)\}. \tag{19e} \] The error is uniform on those compact \(U\)-sets and over all allowed \(v\). The coefficient is one by this ordinary lattice Laplace argument, not by a freely chosen square root or cycle orientation. Formula (11) continues the marked selected expansion from this base slice throughout (4); its proof by the exact product provides the uniform complex estimates, without an assumption about transport of individual thimbles. Equations (11), (14), and (19) prove that the **actual finite residue period** has this selected Gaussian symbol with coefficient one. There is no unknown local multiplier to be supplied from a nonvanishing conjecture. This conclusion is stronger than existence of a stationary point or a nonzero pointwise density: the exact period itself has the relative expansion (11). It does not assert an independently proved one-thimble homology decomposition of \(\Gamma_N\). The proof evaluates the whole period algebraically by (3), so possible endpoint or Fourier-sector effects have already been included. Equality of its leading coefficient with (19) must not be used to discard such sectors in a different coupled exterior period. ## 5. The full physical row, with its Cartan scalar retained For the complete row also restrict \(V\) and \(U+V\) to compact subsets of \((0,1)\). The exact clock source multiplies (2) by its remaining factors: \[ \mathcal R_{\sigma,N}(u,v;j) =\kappa^\sigma\frac{S_{u+v}}{S_v} e^{-\sigma\pi i d j}C_{\sigma,N}, \qquad \kappa=q^{d^2/2}. \tag{20} \] This follows from its original factor \(N/(S_{d-u-v}S_v)\) by exact reflection. At \(j=J/N\), (20) is the literal physical crossing coefficient, with over-input \(u+v\), over-output \(v\), under-input \(J\), and transfer \(u\). At complex \(j\) it is the specified continuation of that same finite product and Cartan mark. Let \(G_\sigma(U,V,j)\) be the physical action (27a) of the joint clock note. Explicitly, \[ \begin{split} G_\sigma ={}&\mathcal J(U+V)+\mathcal J(j+U) -\mathcal J(V)-\mathcal J(j)-\mathcal J(U)\\ &+\sigma\pi i[-j-V+2Vj-U/2+U(j+V)+U^2/2]. \end{split} \tag{21} \] Then \[ \mathcal R_{\sigma,N} =\kappa^\sigma N^{-1/2}\mathcal A_\sigma e^{NG_\sigma} \exp\left\{ \sum_{r=1}^p \frac{B_{2r}\mathcal D_{2r-1}} {(2r)!\,N^{2r-1}} +O(N^{-2p-1})\right\}, \tag{22} \] where \[ \begin{split} \mathcal A_\sigma &=e^{\sigma\pi i(j+V+U/2)} \exp\left\{\frac{ \ell(U+V)+\ell(j+U)-\ell(V)-\ell(j)-\ell(U)}2\right\},\\ \mathcal D_m &=\ell^{(m)}(U+V)+\ell^{(m)}(j+U) -\ell^{(m)}(V)-\ell^{(m)}(j)-\ell^{(m)}(U). \end{split} \tag{23} \] The proof is multiplication of (11) by the exact factors (20), using (9). In particular \(e^{-\sigma\pi i d j}=e^{-N\sigma\pi i j} e^{\sigma\pi i j}\); its finite shift accounts for the \(j\) in the amplitude. All logarithmic correction coefficients in (22) are independent of the crossing sign, while the full phases and Cartan scalar retain that sign. The amplitude in (23) is nonzero. Thus the entire original local row has a uniform relative symbol, not merely a one-sided modulus estimate. Its fixed undercolor derivatives are controlled on smaller complex compacts. This derivative control does not assert that each derivative value is nonzero. ## 6. Composition and the remaining short-component problem For any fixed braid, the exact joint clock theorem first fixes a conserved physical flow and then gives independent clock intervals (2) at all its crossings. The products (3) may therefore be performed simultaneously, with the original cut, pivots, and exterior scalar unchanged. If those conditional physical colors range in a compact set satisfying the local hypotheses at every crossing, multiplication of (22) gives a uniform all-orders expansion for the product of the complete rows. The leading amplitudes multiply and are nonzero. This holds for any fixed number of signed crossings, including any fixed short signed component; the constants may depend on that component and on the chosen compact set. The remaining operation is the coherent sum or integral over physical flows with the prescribed boundary observation. Its neighboring factors share those variables. The theorem supplies no lower bound for that exterior pairing, no automatic localization to the compact set, and no estimate for physical endpoint strata. In particular termwise relative errors cannot be summed as relative errors of a potentially cancelling whole period. What has now been established unconditionally is the actual local clock contraction's selected nonzero amplitude, full relative expansion, specified residue-period normalization, and Gaussian coefficient one. The general partial filling theorem still requires the geometric source pairing and complementary estimates for the remaining original physical-flow period.

title: An exact contour for the complete-meridian trace
text:
# An exact contour for the complete-meridian trace Research note, 2 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. The finite trace at the complete meridian contains first derivatives at double roots. Those derivatives make a direct Fourier expansion slightly different from an ordinary sampling formula: the coefficient of the positive Fourier mode of charge $\ell$ is proportional to $\ell$. Summing these modes gives a rational kernel with double poles. This note derives that kernel directly from the original finite trace, including the vertical endpoint term. It also gives a version after removing outer grid points, and a criterion under which all charges higher than one are controlled on a single contour. The contour identity is exact for every signed integer crossing power. The existence of a contour with the required global phase bound for all fixed small powers is a separate analytic problem. ## 1. The original finite trace at the complete meridian Let $N\geq3$, $d=N-1$, $q=e^{\pi i/N}$, and $\eta=(-1)^d$. For an even trigonometric polynomial $f(t)=f^\sharp(-2\cos t)$, write \[ \mathcal D_{n,N}[f]=\phi(R^n f^\sharp),\qquad C_{N,n}=q^{nd^2/4},\qquad 	au_j= rac{2\pi}{N}\left( rac d2-jight), \quad 0\leq j<N. 	ag{1} \] The polynomial $f^\sharp$ may have arbitrary degree. The functional $\phi$ means the full closing functional in $\mathbb C[z]/(P_N)$, where $P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2$ and $T_N$ is the ordinary Chebyshev polynomial, including its first normal derivatives. Define the odd entire function \[ g(t)=\sin t\,f(t)\exp\left( rac{inN}{4\pi}t^2ight). 	ag{2} \] **Proposition 1.** The exact complete-meridian trace is \[  oxed{\displaystyle \mathcal D_{n,N}[f]=\eta C_{N,n}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}g'(	au_j).} 	ag{3} \] In particular, (3) is a derivative sampling formula, not a sum of function values at the distinct roots of the pair algebra. *Proof.* The original moving-meridian trace, keeping $f^\sharp$ fixed, is \[ \mathcal D_{n,\sigma,N}[f] = rac{\eta N C_{N,n}(\sigma)}{\sin(2\pi\sigma)} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} g\left(	au_j+ rac{2\pi\sigma}{N}ight), \qquad C_{N,n}(\sigma)=q^{n(d^2/4-\sigma^2/2)}. 	ag{4} \] This is the finite identity in [the Fourier trace calculation](../papers/circle-tree-volume/fourier-trace.tex). The grid in (1) is symmetric and $g$ is odd, so the numerator sum vanishes at $\sigma=0$. Its first derivative is $(2\pi/N)\sum_jg'(	au_j)$. Since $\sin(2\pi\sigma)=2\pi\sigma+O(\sigma^3)$, the removable value of (4) is (3). The derivative of $C_{N,n}(\sigma)$ gives no extra term. The removable value of the original finite trace is exactly its Hermite trace; no roots or normal directions have been dropped. $\square$ For later estimates, the summand is explicitly \[ g'(t)=\left\{\cos t\,f(t)+\sin t\,f'(t) + rac{inN}{2\pi}t\sin t\,f(t)ight\} \exp\left( rac{inN}{4\pi}t^2ight). 	ag{5} \] When $N$ is odd, the single grid point $	au=0$ contributes $g'(0)=f(0)$, with its original crossing scalar. The two points $	au$ and $-	au$ associated with a double root give its full value-and-derivative contribution. ## 2. Summing every positive Fourier charge For a positive real number $y$, define \[ W_N(t)= rac{e^{-iNt}}{(1-\eta e^{-iNt})^2}. 	ag{6} \] Its poles lie on the real physical grid. In the lower half-plane, \[ W_N(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} \ell\eta^{\ell-1}e^{-i\ell Nt}. 	ag{7} \] This series is absolutely and locally uniformly convergent there. **Proposition 2.** For every $y>0$, the complete trace is \[  oxed{ egin{aligned} \mathcal D_{n,N}[f] ={}&- rac{N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi i} \int_{-\pi-iy}^{\pi-iy}g(t)W_N(t)\,dt\ &+ rac{\eta N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi} \int_{-y}^{y}  rac{g(\pi+iv)}{4\cosh^2(Nv/2)}\,dv . \end{aligned}} 	ag{8} \] The horizontal integral is directed from left to right. The second line is the exact contribution from the vertical sides of the original rectangle. It is not an error term until it has been estimated for the particular source. *Proof.* The grid kernel \[ K_N(t)= rac{iNe^{iNt}}{e^{iNt}-\eta} \] has residue one at every point of the grid. The positively oriented rectangle with corners $\pm\pi\pm iy$ encloses exactly the $N$ points in (1). Applying the residue theorem to $K_Ng'$ and integrating by parts on the closed contour gives \[ \mathcal D_{n,N}[f] =- rac{\eta C_{N,n}}{2\pi i}\oint K_N'(t)g(t)\,dt, \qquad K_N'(t)= rac{N^2\eta e^{iNt}}{(e^{iNt}-\eta)^2}. 	ag{9} \] The derivative $K_N'$ is even, and $g$ is odd. Reflecting the upper horizontal side by $t\mapsto-t$, with its boundary orientation, therefore makes it equal to the lower horizontal contribution. On the lower side, \[ K_N'(t)=N^2\eta W_N(t), \] which gives the first line of (8). On either vertical side $t=\pm\pi+iv$, one has $e^{iNt}=-\eta e^{-Nv}$ and hence \[ K_N'(\pm\pi+iv)=- rac{N^2}{4\cosh^2(Nv/2)}. 	ag{10} \] The right side is directed upward and the left side downward. Oddness gives $g(-\pi+iv)=-g(\pi-iv)$. Combining both sides, and then replacing $v$ by $-v$ in one term, gives the second line of (8), with the sign shown there. $\square$ The factor $\ell$ in (7) is essential: it is the Fourier expression of the first normal derivatives. Using a simple-pole kernel in its place would give a different finite functional. ## 3. Removing outer grid points before contour deformation It is often easier to estimate the outer part of the original finite sum directly. This can be done without changing the contour identity for its remaining part. Choose an integer $m$ with $0\leq m<N/2$, and set \[ a_N=\pi- rac{2\pi m}{N}>0. \] Then $e^{iNa_N}=-\eta$, and $\pm a_N$ lie halfway between consecutive physical grid points. Define the retained trace \[ \mathcal D_{n,N}^{\,a_N}[f] =\eta C_{N,n}\sum_{|	au_j|<a_N}g'(	au_j). 	ag{11} \] The removed contribution is literally the sum of (5) over the complementary grid points. In particular, normal derivatives are retained on both sides of this decomposition. **Corollary 3.** For every $y>0$, \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal D_{n,N}^{\,a_N}[f] ={}&- rac{N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi i} \int_{-a_N-iy}^{a_N-iy}g(t)W_N(t)\,dt\ &+ rac{\eta N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi} \int_{-y}^{y}  rac{g(a_N+iv)}{4\cosh^2(Nv/2)}\,dv . \end{aligned} 	ag{12} \] *Proof.* Repeat the proof of Proposition 2 with vertical sides $\pm a_N$. The enclosed residues are exactly the terms in (11), and (10) still holds because $e^{iNa_N}=-\eta$. $\square$ Given a desired limiting cutoff $0<a<\pi$, one can choose these midpoint boundaries with $a_N=a+O(N^{-1})$. There is no moving parameter or infinite family of endpoint connectors in (12). For example, suppose the removed grid terms satisfy \[ |f(	au_j)|+|f'(	au_j)| \leq CN^A e^{N(M-\delta)} \qquad (|	au_j|\geq a_N) 	ag{13} \] for a fixed $\delta>0$. Equation (5) then bounds their total contribution by $C(1+|n|)N^{A+2}e^{N(M-\delta)}$. A bound on values alone is not substituted for (13). ## 4. A freely deformable lower contour Let $\Gamma_N$ be any piecewise smooth path from $-a_N-iy$ to $a_N-iy$ that stays in the open lower half-plane and is homotopic to the straight segment there. The integrand $gW_N$ is holomorphic throughout that half-plane. Therefore the horizontal integral in (12) can be replaced exactly by the integral over $\Gamma_N$. The vertical endpoint current remains unchanged. This permits a useful separation of choices. The endpoint height $y$ can be small enough to preserve an already proved endpoint gap. Only the interior of $\Gamma_N$ needs to descend to the critical point. All the deformations concern one holomorphic rational integrand, rather than an infinite list of Fourier modes. If $-\operatorname{Im}t\geq h>0$, then \[ W_N(t)=e^{-iNt} igl(1+E_N(t) igr),\qquad |E_N(t)|\leq  rac{2e^{-Nh}+e^{-2Nh}}{(1-e^{-Nh})^2}. 	ag{14} \] For all sufficiently large $N$, the right side is at most $10e^{-Nh}$. Thus, if $\Gamma_N$ has length at most $CN^A$ and \[ |g(t)e^{-iNt}|\leq CN^A e^{NM}\qquad(t\in\Gamma_N), 	ag{15} \] then the contribution from every charge $\ell\geq2$, already summed together, is bounded by \[ CN^{A'}e^{N(M-h)}. 	ag{16} \] The estimate is conditional on the bound along the entire contour. The existence of a local saddle expansion alone does not imply (15). ## 5. The actual endpoint current The endpoint term in (12) has its own finite estimate. Suppose that for $|v|\leq y$, \[ |f(a_N+iv)|\leq CN^A\exp N(E+Bv^2), 	ag{17} \] where $E,B$ are independent of $N$. Since \[ \left|\exp rac{inN}{4\pi}(a_N+iv)^2ight| =\exp\left(- rac{nNa_N}{2\pi}vight),\qquad  rac1{4\cosh^2(Nv/2)}\leq e^{-N|v|}, \] the absolute value of the endpoint term is at most \[ CN^{A+2}(1+y) \exp N\left\{E+By^2+ \left( rac{|n|a_N}{2\pi}-1ight)_+yight\}. 	ag{18} \] Here $x_+=\max\{x,0\}$. The factor $\sin(a_N+iv)$ is uniformly bounded when $y$ stays in a fixed compact interval. If $E<M$, then a sufficiently small fixed $y>0$ makes the exponent in (18) strictly less than $M$, for every fixed $n$. The interior contour may subsequently be moved farther into the lower half-plane. One can replace the quadratic term in (17) by any established local modulus of continuity. The quadratic form is convenient, but the endpoint argument needs only that its cost tends to zero with $y$. ## 6. What is sufficient for a fixed small-power asymptotic The exact identity reduces the analytic problem to ordinary steepest descent with two explicitly retained errors. To state this precisely, suppose a fixed crossing power $n$ and a family $f_N$ satisfy the following conditions. 1. The outer grid terms obey (13). 2. The endpoint current has a strict gap as in (18). 3. There is a family of lower contours $\Gamma_N$, of bounded length and a fixed positive distance from the real axis, on which (15) holds and has a strict gap outside a neighborhood of one critical point $t_*$. In that neighborhood, \[ f_N(t)=N^\alpha a(t)e^{N\Psi(t)}(1+O(N^{-1})), \] with a uniform holomorphic error, $a(t_*)
e0$, and \[ \Phi(t)=\Psi(t)+ rac{in}{4\pi}t^2-it, \qquad \Phi'(t_*)=0,\quad\Phi''(t_*)
e0, \quad \operatorname{Re}\Phi(t_*)=M. \] 4. The local contour crosses the saddle along a direction of strict quadratic decrease, and $\sin t_*
e0$. Then ordinary one-variable saddle integration applied to (12) gives \[ \mathcal D_{n,N}[f_N] =C_{N,n}N^{\alpha+3/2}A_* e^{N\Phi(t_*)}(1+O(N^{-1})),\qquad A_*
e0. 	ag{19} \] The contour orientation and the continued square root of the Hessian fix $A_*$. The rational correction in (14), the endpoint current, and the removed finite grid terms are exponentially smaller. For the one-edge source with $\alpha=-3/2$, the resulting terminal polynomial has a nonzero leading amplitude of order $N^0$. The role of the rational kernel is precise. Once a contour with (15) exists, there is no additional infinite-charge theorem to prove. Constructing and estimating that contour uniformly in the free boundary variable remains necessary. This note does not infer it from the finite trace identity. ## 7. Finite numerical check of signs and normal terms Run the finite verification with ```sh python3 experiments/audit_complete_trace_rational_contour.py ``` The script requires `mpmath`. The identities (8) and (12) were compared directly with their derivative sums in 120 cases at 60 decimal digits for $N\in\{3,4,5,8\}$, $n\in\{-3,0,1,2,3\}$, and $f(t)\in\{1,\cos(2t),\cos((N+2)t)\}$, using $y=0.17$, both for the full grid and after removing its outermost pair. The largest relative discrepancy, measured with denominator $1+|\mathcal D|$, was $5.4	imes10^{-47}$. The high-frequency examples test the absence of a degree restriction. The case $n=0$ also checks the cancellation between the horizontal and vertical parts when the exact trace vanishes. These are numerical sign checks. The proof of the identity is the residue and integration-by-parts calculation in Section 2.

title: An exact formula for the canonical factorial
text: # An exact formula for the canonical factorial This note evaluates the logarithmic derivative of the canonical factorial as a finite sum. Integrating that sum gives an exact formula in the lower half-plane, including its additive constant. In particular, its behavior at large negative imaginary part is determined by the original gamma product; no unspecified periodic factor remains. The result concerns the interpolation used in [`papers/conway-asymptotics/factorial.tex`](../papers/conway-asymptotics/factorial.tex). It is not by itself an estimate for a quantum sum or a proof that a correction contour can be discarded. ## 1. Definition and statement Fix an integer $N\geq2$. For $-1<\Re z<N$, define \[ G_N(z)=\left(\frac{2\pi}{N}\right)^z\Gamma(z+1) \prod_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{\Gamma(Nm+z+1)}{\Gamma(Nm-z)(Nm)^{2z+1}}. \tag{1} \] Powers of positive numbers use their real logarithms. The product is locally normally convergent, is nonzero in this strip, and has $G_N(0)=1$. Its logarithm is chosen to be zero at $z=0$. These facts also follow directly from the product: its $m$-th logarithmic factor is \[ -\frac{z(z+1)(2z+1)}{6N^2m^2}+O(m^{-3}). \tag{2} \] The shift relation \[ G_N(z+1)=2\sin\frac{\pi(z+1)}N\,G_N(z) \tag{3} \] continues $G_N$ to a nonzero holomorphic function on $\Im z<0$. There is a unique logarithm there agreeing with the logarithm of (1) on the overlap. Write this logarithm as $g_N$. **Theorem.** The logarithmic derivative is the finite sum \[ g_N'(z)=\frac{\pi}{N^2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (z-k)\cot\frac{\pi(z-k)}N. \tag{4} \] Terms at $z=k$ have their removable values. Formula (4) holds on the original strip and by continuation wherever both sides are regular. For $\Im t<0$, put \[ L(t)=\frac{i\pi t^2}{2} +t\Log(1-e^{-2\pi it}) +\frac{i}{2\pi}\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{-2\pi it}). \tag{5} \] Here $\Log(1-w)=-\sum_{j\geq1}w^j/j$ and $\operatorname{Li}_2(w)=\sum_{j\geq1}w^j/j^2$ for $|w|<1$. Thus the branches in (5) are specified without analytic continuation across a cut. For every $\Im x<0$, \[ \boxed{ g_N(Nx)=\frac12\log N-\frac{i\pi N}{12} +\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}L\left(x-\frac{k}{N}\right).} \tag{6} \] The remainder form of the same identity is \[ \begin{split} g_N(Nx)={}&\frac{i\pi N x^2}{2} -\frac{i\pi(N-1)x}{2}+\frac12\log N\\ &+i\pi\left(\frac{N}{12}-\frac14+\frac{1}{12N}\right) +E_N(x). \tag{7} \end{split} \] Writing $w=e^{-2\pi ix}$ and $\zeta_N=e^{2\pi i/N}$, the remainder is exactly \[ \boxed{ E_N(x)=x\Log(1-w^N) -\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}k\Log(1-w\zeta_N^k) +\frac{i}{2\pi N}\operatorname{Li}_2(w^N).} \tag{8} \] Every logarithm and dilogarithm on the right is analytic in the disk $|w|<1$. The factor $x\Log(1-w^N)$ is displayed separately; $x$ is still the coordinate on the covering half-plane. If $r=|w|<1$, one explicit bound is \[ |E_N(x)|\leq \left(|x|+\frac{1}{2\pi N}\right)\frac{r^N}{1-r^N} +\frac{N-1}{2}\frac{r}{1-r}. \tag{9} \] For fixed $N$, (9) gives the stated quadratic asymptotic, with error $O_N((1+|x|)e^{2\pi\Im x})$, as $\Im x\to-\infty$ in any fixed vertical strip. The explicit bound (9), rather than this shorthand, also applies when $x$ and $N$ vary simultaneously. ## 2. Finite evaluation of the logarithmic derivative Let $\psi=\Gamma'/\Gamma$. Logarithmic differentiation of the locally normally convergent product gives \[ g_N'(z)=\log\frac{2\pi}{N}+\psi(z+1) +\sum_{m\geq1}\bigl[ \psi(Nm+z+1)+\psi(Nm-z)-2\log(Nm)\bigr]. \tag{10} \] All manipulations below may first be made away from the isolated poles of the individual digamma terms. The resulting identities extend across their removable singularities. Set \[ a_j=\frac{z+1+j}{N},\qquad b_j=\frac{-z+j}{N}, \qquad 0\leq j<N. \tag{11} \] The Gauss multiplication identity, differentiated once, says \[ \psi(Nv)=\log N+\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\psi(v+j/N). \tag{12} \] Consequently the part of the sum in (10) with $1\leq m\leq K$ is \[ \frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\bigl[T_K(a_j)+T_K(b_j)\bigr] -2\log\Gamma(K+1), \tag{13} \] where the functional equation of the digamma function gives the exact finite identity \[ T_K(a):=\sum_{m=1}^K\psi(m+a) =(K+a)\psi(K+a+1)-a\psi(a+1)-K. \tag{14} \] For example, subtracting the expression at $K-1$ from that at $K$ gives $\psi(K+a)$, and the expression at $K=0$ vanishes. For $a$ in a compact set, \[ T_K(a)=K\log K-K+a\log K+a+\frac12-a\psi(a+1)+O(K^{-1}). \tag{15} \] Also \[ \frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(a_j+b_j)=1. \] Substitution of (15) into (13), followed by Stirling's formula for $\Gamma(K+1)$, therefore gives the limit \[ 2-\log(2\pi) -\frac1N\sum_j\bigl[a_j\psi(a_j+1)+b_j\psi(b_j+1)\bigr] =-\log(2\pi) -\frac1N\sum_j\bigl[a_j\psi(a_j)+b_j\psi(b_j)\bigr]. \tag{16} \] The constants $2$ cancel because $a\psi(a+1)=a\psi(a)+1$. The error tends locally uniformly to zero. Equations (10) and (16) give \[ g_N'(z)=\psi(z+1)-\log N -\frac1N\sum_j\bigl[a_j\psi(a_j)+b_j\psi(b_j)\bigr]. \tag{17} \] The pairing $b_{N-1-j}=1-a_j$ and the reflection identity \[ \psi(1-a)-\psi(a)=\pi\cot(\pi a) \] transform the summand into \[ a\psi(a)+(1-a)\psi(1-a) =\psi(a)+(1-a)\pi\cot(\pi a). \] Applying (12) once more cancels $\psi(z+1)-\log N$ in (17). Thus \[ g_N'(z)=-\frac\pi N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(1-a_j)\cot(\pi a_j). \tag{18} \] With $k=N-1-j$, one has $a_j=1+(z-k)/N$; (18) is exactly (4). This argument starts from (1), rather than from a difference equation, so it determines the derivative of the specified interpolation. ## 3. Integration and the constant Direct differentiation of the convergent series in (5) gives \[ L'(t)=i\pi t\frac{1+e^{-2\pi it}}{1-e^{-2\pi it}} =\pi t\cot(\pi t). \tag{19} \] The derivative with respect to $x$ of the sum in (6) is therefore $N g_N'(Nx)$. Their difference is constant on the lower half-plane. To determine it, take $x\to0$ from below. For $0<r<1$, the boundary value from below has \[ \Log(1-e^{2\pi ir})=\log(2\sin\pi r)+i\pi(r-1/2). \] The elementary Fourier identity \[ \Re\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi ir}) =\pi^2(r^2-r+1/6) \tag{20} \] then gives \[ \begin{split} \Im L(-r)&=\pi/12,\\ \Re L(-r)&=-r\log(2\sin\pi r) -\frac1{2\pi}\Im\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi ir}). \tag{21} \end{split} \] Identity (20) can be obtained by integrating the imaginary part of $-\Log(1-e^{2\pi ir})=\sum_{m\geq1}e^{2\pi imr}/m$, first with an Abel factor less than one. The integration constant is $\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\pi^2/6$. All dilogarithm boundary series converge absolutely. At $r=0$, the term $t\Log(1-e^{-2\pi it})$ tends to zero, so $L(0)=i\pi/12$ in this limiting sense. In the sum over $r=k/N$, the imaginary parts of the dilogarithms in the second line of (21) cancel in the pairs $k,N-k$. The same pairing gives \[ \sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{k}{N}\log(2\sin\pi k/N) =\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\log(2\sin\pi k/N) =\frac12\log N, \tag{22} \] where the last equality follows by evaluating $\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\zeta_N^k)=N$ and taking absolute values. It follows that \[ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}L(-k/N)=-\frac12\log N+\frac{i\pi N}{12}. \tag{23} \] Since $g_N(0)=0$, equation (23) fixes the constant in (6). ## 4. Disk expression and the lower end Summing the quadratic terms in (6) uses \[ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{k}{N}=\frac{N-1}{2},\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{k^2}{N^2} =\frac{(N-1)(2N-1)}{6N}. \] These sums give the polynomial and constant in (7). The remainder before resummation is \[ E_N(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left[ \left(x-\frac{k}{N}\right)\Log(1-w\zeta_N^k) +\frac{i}{2\pi}\operatorname{Li}_2(w\zeta_N^k) \right]. \tag{24} \] Absolute convergence in the disk proves the root-of-unity identities \[ \sum_k\Log(1-w\zeta_N^k)=\Log(1-w^N),\qquad \sum_k\operatorname{Li}_2(w\zeta_N^k) =\frac1N\operatorname{Li}_2(w^N). \tag{25} \] There is no additive logarithmic ambiguity: both sides of the first identity vanish at $w=0$. Substitution gives (8). The elementary series bounds \[ |\Log(1-v)|\leq\frac{|v|}{1-|v|},\qquad |\operatorname{Li}_2(v)|\leq\frac{|v|}{1-|v|} \] and $\sum k/N=(N-1)/2$ prove (9). One may equivalently exponentiate (7) and (8): \[ \begin{split} G_N(Nx)={}&\sqrt N\exp\left\{ \frac{i\pi N x^2}{2}-\frac{i\pi(N-1)x}{2} +i\pi\left(\frac{N}{12}-\frac14+\frac1{12N}\right)\right\}\\ &\cdot\exp\{x\Log(1-w^N)\} \prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\exp\left\{-\frac{k}{N}\Log(1-w\zeta_N^k)\right\} \exp\left\{\frac{i}{2\pi N}\operatorname{Li}_2(w^N)\right\}. \tag{26} \end{split} \] The finite product on the second line, excluding the displayed factor containing $x$, is a nonzero holomorphic function of $w$ at $w=0$, with value one. Thus (26) records exactly which factor still depends on the logarithmic covering coordinate. Applications to a source containing several factorials must combine these factors with the original quadratic phases before concluding that the source descends to a function of $w$. ## 5. Numerical reproduction The standalone script [`experiments/check_exact_cyclotomic_factorial.py`](../experiments/check_exact_cyclotomic_factorial.py) checks the finite formula against truncated versions of the original gamma product and its logarithmic derivative. It also checks the lattice normalization, shift, reflection, equality of (6) and (8), and the explicit bound (9). Run ```sh python3 experiments/check_exact_cyclotomic_factorial.py --output repro/results/research-exact-cyclotomic-factorial.json ``` The saved values are in [`repro/results/research-exact-cyclotomic-factorial.json`](../repro/results/research-exact-cyclotomic-factorial.json). These finite-precision calculations are diagnostics; the proof is the finite digamma calculation and the determination of its constant above. ## 6. Relation to the existing cyclic dilogarithm The weighted finite product in (26) is the inverse of the cyclic dilogarithm \[ D_N(w;\zeta_N)=\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-w\zeta_N^k)^{k/N}, \qquad D_N(0;\zeta_N)=1, \] with its local branches fixed at zero. This is an established function; see equation (9) and Section 1.2 of Garoufalidis and Kashaev, [*Evaluation of state integrals at rational points*, version 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1411.6062v2). That paper also treats formulas at roots of unity in Section 1.4. This attribution concerns the known finite product. The proof above derives the specified Gamma interpolation, its constant and its logarithmic covering factor directly. Its application here is to the original finite source and the precise contour correction in [the adjacent-pair translation calculation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_adjacent_pair_cyclotomic_gauge.md).

title: A selected small-activity saddle of the actual factorial coupon
text: # A selected small-activity saddle of the actual factorial coupon Private written proof, 18 November 2026. The residual last-head coupon in U has an actual nonzero complex asymptotic on a small open sector. Its finite polynomial is represented by its original constant-term circle. A direct Taylor-cap estimate and a single saddle on that circle give the coefficient, including the binomial half-density. No complex occupation interpolation or assumed saddle occurrence is used. This evaluates the coupon factor only. Its convolution with the quotient, turnover, resolvent, and original source remains as in U. In particular it does not select a geometric contribution to that larger period. The sole complete direct U is pinned below. It identifies the actual coupon and its source interfaces. All finite recurrences, contour identities, estimates, and saddle calculations are proved here. ## 1. The literal polynomial, including its top row Set \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad c_0=2\pi i,\quad Q=e^{c_0/N},\quad f_a=\prod_{j=1}^a(1-Q^j),\quad f_0=1. \tag{1} \] U's retained coupon is \(ZG^{-1}\), where \(Zw_a=(-1)^aw_a\) and \(Gw_a=f_aw_a\). In the original binomial coherent convention its exact kernel is \[ \boxed{\quad H_N(s)=\sum_{a=0}^d\binom da\frac{(-s)^a}{f_a}, \qquad s=wz. \quad}\tag{2} \] There is no omitted overall factor in (2). The factors outside this coupon in U's opposite-source interface remain outside it. Let \(D_s=s\partial_s\) and \(\mathcal Q_sH(s)=H(Qs)\). Consecutive coefficients in (2) give \[ \boxed{\quad [D_s(1-\mathcal Q_s)+s(d-D_s)]H_N=0,\qquad H_N(0)=1 . \quad}\tag{3} \] Indeed, for \(1\le a\le d\), \(a(1-Q^a)h_a=-(N-a)h_{a-1}\). The potential degree-\(N\) term on the right also vanishes: \(d-D_s\) kills the degree-\(d\) coefficient. Thus the physical upper endpoint has been used, not deleted. The associated exponentiated principal row, with \(H_N\) formally proportional to \(e^{N\Psi(s)}\) and \(y=s\Psi'(s)\), is \[ y(1-e^{c_0y})+s(1-y)=0. \tag{4} \] It includes the whole component \(y=1\), for every \(s\). We will not divide this component out. The actual contour analysis below selects a small branch \(y\sim\sqrt{s/c_0}\), away from it. ## 2. An exact circle and a controlled finite Euler cap Define the finite polynomial \[ E_N(t)=\sum_{a=0}^d\frac{t^a}{f_a}. \] Its exact coefficient recurrence is \[ E_N(Qt)=(1-t)E_N(t)+\frac{t^N}{N}, \qquad f_d=N. \tag{5} \] Consequently the original coupon has the exact constant-term period \[ \boxed{\quad H_N(s)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint (1+z)^d E_N(-s/z)\,\frac{dz}{z}. \quad}\tag{6} \] Any positively oriented circle about zero gives the same value. This is a finite Laurent-polynomial identity. In particular the forcing and finite cap in (5) are still present. We next prove a local relative approximation for this actual finite \(E_N\). Put \[ L_N(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{t^j}{j(1-Q^j)},\qquad P_N(t)=e^{L_N(t)}. \tag{7} \] The degree-\(d\) Taylor polynomial of \(P_N\) is exactly \(E_N\). To see this, the coefficients below degree \(N\) in \[ L_N(Qt)-L_N(t)=-\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}t^j/j \] equal those of \(\log(1-t)\). Hence \(P_N(Qt)=(1-t)P_N(t)+O(t^N)\) as formal series. Its constant coefficient is one, and the recurrence determines its next \(N-1\) coefficients to be \(1/f_a\). For \(1\le j<N\), \[ |1-Q^j|\ge4\min(j,N-j)/N. \tag{8} \] It follows that, for \(0<R\le1/4\), \[ \sup_{|t|\le R}|L_N(t)|\le CNR \tag{9} \] with an absolute constant \(C\). For \(j\le N/2\), sum \(NR^j/(4j^2)\). For \(j>N/2\), the bound from (8) is at most a constant times \(NR^{N/2}\sum_{k\le N/2}1/k\), which is bounded by \(CNR\) uniformly in \(N\). This proves (9). Choose a sufficiently small fixed \(\rho>0\), and apply Cauchy's coefficient estimate on \(|t|=2\rho\). Since \(E_N\) is the exact Taylor cap, \[ \sup_{|t|\le\rho}|E_N(t)-P_N(t)| \le2^{1-N}e^{2CN\rho}, \qquad \inf_{|t|\le\rho}|P_N(t)|\ge e^{-CN\rho}. \] Taking \(\rho\) so that \(3C\rho<\frac12\log2\) gives \[ \boxed{\quad E_N(t)=P_N(t)(1+O(e^{-\delta N})),\quad |t|\le\rho, \quad}\tag{10} \] for some \(\delta>0\). This is a relative estimate of the actual finite polynomial, not an infinite-series replacement of it. It also proves that \(E_N\) is zero-free there for large \(N\). On a possibly smaller disk, with logarithms continued from zero, \[ L_N(t)=-\frac{N}{c_0}\operatorname{Li}_2(t) -\frac12\log(1-t)+O(N^{-1}). \tag{11} \] For completeness, split the sum at \(j=N/2\). On the lower half, \[ \frac1{1-e^{h j}}=-\frac1{h j}+\frac12+O(|h|j), \qquad h=c_0/N, \] uniformly; the remainder after multiplication by \(t^j/j\) sums to \(O(N^{-1})\). The upper half is exponentially small by (8). The corresponding tails of the dilogarithm and logarithm series are exponentially small too. This proves (11). Cauchy estimates on a larger small disk give every fixed \(t\)-derivative of its remainder and of (10). Combining (10)--(11) yields the actual local finite-cap estimate \[ \boxed{\quad E_N(t)=(1-t)^{-1/2} \exp[-N\operatorname{Li}_2(t)/c_0]\,(1+O(N^{-1})). \quad}\tag{12} \] All branches and the unit factor in this formula come from \(t=0\). ## 3. A single saddle on the original circle Choose a number \(0<\vartheta<\pi/2\). There exists \(a_*>0\) such that the following construction holds on \[ \mathcal A=\{a:0<|a|<a_*,\ |\arg a|<\vartheta\}, \qquad s=c_0a^2. \tag{13} \] This is an unambiguous chosen square-root sector in \(s\). All asymptotic estimates below are uniform on compact subsets of \(\mathcal A\), which stay away from \(a=0\). If \(\vartheta>\pi/4\), this includes sufficiently small positive real \(s\): its selected root is \(a=e^{-i\pi/4}\sqrt{s/(2\pi)}\). In (6) use the phase and amplitude \[ \Phi_s(z)=\log(1+z)-\operatorname{Li}_2(-s/z)/c_0,\qquad A_s(z)=(1+z)^{-1}(1+s/z)^{-1/2}. \tag{14} \] These have their small branches on the circles used below. Write \(z_*(a)=a\,v(a)\). The critical equation is \[ z\partial_z\Phi_s(z) =\frac{z}{1+z}-\frac1{c_0}\log(1+s/z)=0. \tag{15} \] After division by \(a\), its left side becomes \[ \frac{v}{1+av}-\frac{\log(1+c_0a/v)}{c_0a}. \] At \(a=0\) this is \(v-v^{-1}\), whose derivative at \(v=1\) is two. The analytic implicit-function theorem therefore gives a unique analytic \(v(a)=1+O(a)\) near this branch. Use exactly the circle \[ z=z_*(a)e^{i\theta}, \qquad -\pi\le\theta\le\pi. \tag{16} \] For sufficiently small \(a_*\), it satisfies \(|z|<1/2\) and \(|s/z|<\rho\). Thus the finite-cap estimate (12) is valid everywhere on this original constant-term circle. No endpoint or other residue has been crossed. There is a strict global maximum of the real part of the phase on this circle at \(\theta=0\). Indeed, uniformly in a fixed complex \(\theta\)-strip, \[ \Phi_s(z_*(a)e^{i\theta})=2a\cos\theta+R(a,\theta), \qquad \partial_\theta^jR=O(|a|^2) \tag{17} \] for every fixed \(j\). This follows by expanding (14) and using \(v(a)=1+O(a)\). The exact critical equation implies \(\partial_\theta R(a,0)=0\). Consequently, for real \(|\theta|\le\pi\), \[ |R(a,\theta)-R(a,0)|\le C|a|^2\theta^2. \] Since \(\Re a\ge|a|\cos\vartheta\), reducing \(a_*\) if necessary gives \[ \boxed{\quad \Re[\Phi_s(z_*e^{i\theta})-\Phi_s(z_*)] \le-c|a|\theta^2. \quad}\tag{18} \] This proves uniqueness of the contributing circle maximum. It also controls the region opposite the chosen saddle and every other part of this actual circle. Their contributions have not been dismissed solely from the formal characteristic equation; no estimate for points off this circle is asserted. Put \[ \Psi(s)=\Phi_s(z_*),\qquad B(s)=(z\partial_z)^2\Phi_s(z_*)=2a+O(a^2). \tag{19} \] Then the second \(\theta\)-derivative is \(-B(s)\), and \(\Re B(s)>0\) after reducing the sector radius. The square root is fixed by \(B(s)\sim2a\) on the positive \(a\)-axis, then continued analytically. ## 4. The nonzero coefficient On the circle (16), (6) and (12) give \[ H_N(s)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{N\Phi_s(z_*e^{i\theta})} A_s(z_*e^{i\theta})(1+O(N^{-1}))\,d\theta. \tag{20} \] The relative error is holomorphic and uniformly controlled there. The exponentially small Taylor-cap error in (10) gives an exponentially small relative contribution after integration: (18) bounds its absolute size by a constant times \(e^{N\Re\Psi(s)-\delta N}\). A direct Gaussian calculation in (20) now gives \[ \boxed{\quad H_N(s)= \frac{e^{N\Psi(s)}}{\sqrt{2\pi N B(s)}}\, A_s(z_*)\,(1+O(N^{-1})). \quad}\tag{21} \] Here are the needed error details. On a compact subset of (13), split the circle at \(|\theta|=N^{-2/5}\). Relative to \(e^{N\Re\Psi}\), the complement is \(O(e^{-cN^{1/5}})\) by (18). On the inner interval expand the analytic phase through its cubic term and the amplitude through its linear term. Their odd Gaussian terms integrate to zero on the symmetric interval. The remaining errors are bounded by Gaussian moments of \(N\theta^4\), \(N^2\theta^6\), and \(\theta^2\), giving relative \(O(N^{-1})\). The analytic \(O(N^{-1})\) error in (20) has the same bound. Extending the Gaussian to the real line costs an exponentially small error. Finally \(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-NB\theta^2/2}d\theta =\sqrt{2\pi/(NB)}\), first for positive \(B\) and then by holomorphic continuation with \(\Re B>0\). This proves (21) uniformly on such compact sets. Cauchy estimates give all fixed derivatives of its normalized error on smaller sectors. The coefficient has a useful exact expression in the selected occupation variable \[ y(s)=\frac{z_*}{1+z_*}=a+O(a^2). \] Equation (15) fixes the logarithmic sheet \[ \log(1+s/z_*)=c_0y,\qquad -s/z_*=1-e^{c_0y}. \] Therefore \[ \begin{split} \Psi(s)&=-\log(1-y) -\operatorname{Li}_2(1-e^{c_0y})/c_0,\\ B(s)&=y(1-y)+(1-e^{-c_0y})/c_0,\\ A_s(z_*)&=(1-y)e^{-c_0y/2}. \end{split}\tag{22} \] The critical relation also gives \[ s=\frac{y(e^{c_0y}-1)}{1-y},\qquad s\Psi'(s)=y. \tag{23} \] Writing \(A=e^{c_0y}=1+s/z_*\), the first line of (22) is \(\Psi=-\operatorname{Li}_2(1-A)/c_0-\log(1-y)\). Its integration constant is fixed by \(\Psi\to0\) as \(a\to0\) on the chosen sector. This calibrates the actual coupon action only. The division by \(1-y\) is used only on this small selected branch, where \(|y|<1/2\). It is not a deletion of the \(y=1\) component of the exact row (3)--(4). In particular the actual coupon asymptotic is \[ \boxed{\displaystyle H_N(s)= \frac{(1-y)e^{-c_0y/2}} {\sqrt{2\pi N\,[\,y(1-y)+(1-e^{-c_0y})/c_0\,]}}\, e^{N\Psi(s)}(1+O(N^{-1})). }\tag{24} \] Every displayed factor is nonzero on a sufficiently small chosen sector away from zero. Thus \(H_N\) itself is nonzero there for all sufficiently large \(N\), uniformly on each compact subset. This is a selected coefficient of the literal finite coupon period, not merely a formal solution of (4). ## 5. Source and normal scope Formula (2) is exactly the kernel of the retained \(ZG^{-1}\) coupon in U. Pulling (24) back by \(s=wz\) gives an actual local coherent-kernel asymptotic wherever \(wz\) lies in this sector. The original binomial dual, the sign \(Z\), and the degree \(d=N-1\) are all responsible for factors in (14),(22),(24); none was absorbed into an unspecified amplitude. There is a source-incidence restriction as well. In U's full turnover formula, the residual last-head coupon corresponds to the original donor, not automatically to a recipient coherent identity kernel. Its contraction with the upper column must therefore be retained. Formula (24) is the bare coupon kernel; it is not substituted for that different composed matrix row. At fixed quantum root this coupon is independent of the meridian \(M\). Its meridian-normal burden in the full source therefore lies in the other interfaces and in any prescribed \(M\)-dependent arguments. Fixed derivatives of (24) may be used for such arguments while they remain in compact subsets of the proved domain. This is not a computation of the whole opposite-source first jet. Nor is the root reflection used in U differentiated in the quantum parameter. Off the root, the reflected donor diagonal contains its full finite products and is not automatically the simplified coupon (2). No ordinary quantum-normal identification is inferred from the present fixed-root saddle proof. The upper-cap component, the finite Euler forcing, and the source complements have not been discarded. The first two are accounted for by the exact polynomial identities and the actual circle estimate. Complements belonging to other factors or to a larger paired-source contour remain as prescribed in U. The result does not show that a loxodromic geometric source frame has \(wz\) in this sector, or that the product of this coupon with the upper resolvent and quotient has a nonzero geometric period. ## Complete proof direct * U: notes/research_upper_euler_column_resolvent_chart.md, SHA256 14b9686f569f224b95df928f25f81456b339a019dd5800148ba30676c91fbce1. The complete direct was freshly read nontruncated in the immediately preceding active author sequence and retained unchanged here. Every used implication was checked. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. Frozen and public files were not changed.

title: A faithful boundary packet for the first actual beta move
text: # A faithful boundary packet for the first actual beta move Written proof, 23 November 2026. The retained cyclic factorial in the first actual nine-cell beta move can be removed with zero error on a faithful boundary packet. For a positive crossing this packet is one complete middle-degree row; for a negative crossing it is one complete middle-degree column. Explicit continuants reconstruct the whole original Hopf box, including every repeated-root normal, from that packet. Reconstruction is part of the assertion. The ratio-free array alone is not asserted to be the original crossing. After reconstruction the boxes can be substituted in any fixed literal Conway construction, with its original turns, marked closing, pivots and external scalar lines. This does not require a nonzero knot invariant or a semisimple quotient. The algebraic reconstruction works at every level \(N\ge2\). Its literal charged nine-cell application has the existing odd-level scope \(N>2\). No positive gluing formula, tame reconstruction norm, geometric source coefficient, or volume lower bound is proved. ## 1. The complete physical algebra and its source Put \[ N\ge2,\qquad d=N-1,\qquad q=e^{\pi i/N},\qquad Q=q^2,\qquad x=-q^{-1}=q^d,\qquad F_j=(Q;Q)_j. \tag{1} \] All physical head indices lie in \(0,\ldots,d\). Square brackets mean reduction to that set; physical total degree below is an ordinary integer, not a residue. Let \(V\) have its original balanced basis. The generators are \[ E|a\rangle=(Q^{-a}-1)|a-1\rangle,\quad F|a\rangle=(1-Q^{a+1})|a+1\rangle,\quad K|a\rangle=xQ^{-a}|a\rangle, \] with outside-basis arrows omitted. The original pair Casimir and full commutant algebra of [P] are \[ E_t=E_1K_2+E_2,\qquad F_t=F_1+K_1^{-1}F_2,\qquad K_t=K_1K_2, \qquad \Omega=F_tE_t+qK_t+q^{-1}K_t^{-1}, \] \[ H_N=\mathbb C[z]/P_N(z),\qquad P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2=\prod_{j=0}^d(z-c_j),\qquad c_j=q^{2j+1}+q^{-2j-1}. \tag{2} \] Here the \(F_t,F_1,F_2\) in the coproduct denote quantum-group arrows, not the scalar factorials \(F_j\) of (1). The physical representation \[ f\longmapsto f(\Omega) \tag{3} \] identifies \(H_N\) with the entire two-head \(E_t,F_t,K_t\) commutant. An endomorphism commuting with those three operators is called a two-head Hopf box below. These are the actual operators, including the derivative channels at double roots of \(P_N\). Here normals mean the Casimir directions \(f'(c)\) at those double roots. All parameters stay at (1); no moving meridian family or quantum-parameter jet is asserted. Let \[ W_d=\operatorname{span}\{e_j=|j,d-j\rangle:0\le j\le d\}, \qquad A=\Omega|_{W_d}. \tag{4} \] By [P,H], \(A\) is complex symmetric and irreducible tridiagonal: \[ A_{jj}=a_j,\qquad A_{j,j+1}=A_{j+1,j}=b_j=-(1-Q^{j+1})^2. \tag{5} \] Every \(b_j\) is nonzero. Its characteristic and minimal polynomial are both \(P_N\). Thus restriction of (3) to \(W_d\) remains faithful. No eigenvector diagonalization is used below. The original fixed-root closing is \[ \phi(f)=\frac1N\operatorname{Tr}_{V\otimes V} [(I\otimes g)f(\Omega)] =(-1)^dN^2[z^d]\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}f =(f(A))_{0d}, \qquad g=K^{1-N}. \tag{6} \] This endpoint identity is for a complete Hopf box. It is not asserted for an arbitrary matrix inserted into the pivotal trace. The actual turn \(J\) is the full linear involution on \(H_N\), with its original cups and caps. In the normalized Newton basis \[ e_r^{\rm N}(z)=s_r^{-2}\prod_{h<r}(c_h-z),\qquad s_r=\prod_{h=1}^r2\sin(\pi h/N),\qquad s_0=1, \tag{7} \] it obeys \(Je_r^{\rm N}=e_{d-r}^{\rm N}\). The two original rows are \[ \lambda_0(f)=f(c_0),\qquad \phi(f)=\lambda_0(Jf). \tag{8} \] Any separately recorded framing, peripheral or closing multiplier is retained outside these identities. ## 2. Two faithful observations and their explicit inverses For a matrix \(Y\) on \(W_d\), define its first-row and last-column data \[ \rho_+(Y)=(Y_{0j})_{j=0}^d,\qquad \rho_-(Y)=(Y_{id})_{i=0}^d. \tag{9} \] Both observations are defined on every matrix, without a Hopf condition. Their restrictions to \(\mathbb C[A]\) are isomorphisms onto \(\mathbb C^N\). Here is an explicit proof and inverse. Define the monic continuants \[ p_0(z)=1,\qquad p_1(z)=z-a_0,\qquad p_{j+1}(z)=(z-a_j)p_j(z)-b_{j-1}^2p_{j-1}(z), \tag{10} \] and \[ B_0=1,\qquad B_j=\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}b_h=(-1)^jF_j^2,\qquad u_j(z)=p_j(z)/B_j. \tag{11} \] The recurrence is used up to \(j=d-1\). Every denominator is nonzero. Induction in (10), applying the tridiagonal matrix to \(e_j\), gives \[ p_j(A)e_0=B_je_j. \tag{12} \] Indeed it holds for \(j=0,1\). If it holds at \(j,j-1\), the \(e_{j-1}\) terms cancel, and the remaining term is \(B_jb_je_{j+1}=B_{j+1}e_{j+1}\). Since \(A\) is symmetric, (12) also gives \[ e_0^{\mathsf T}u_j(A)=e_j^{\mathsf T}. \tag{13} \] All transposes in this proof are bilinear transposes, without conjugation. Consequently the first-row inverse is the polynomial \[ I_+(w)=\sum_{j=0}^dw_ju_j(z)\quad\bmod P_N. \tag{14} \] Its degree is at most \(d\), and its first physical row is exactly \(w\). Uniqueness follows either from (12) or because the \(u_j\) have distinct degrees \(j\) and nonzero leading coefficients. For the opposite endpoint reverse the coefficients: \[ \widehat a_j=a_{d-j},\qquad \widehat b_j=b_{d-1-j}. \tag{15} \] Let \(\widehat p_j,\widehat B_j,\widehat u_j\) be given by (10),(11) with these coefficients. The same induction gives \[ \widehat u_j(A)e_d=e_{d-j},\qquad I_-(v)=\sum_{i=0}^dv_i\widehat u_{d-i}(z). \tag{16} \] Thus \(I_-(v)(A)e_d=v\), with all output entries retained. Define full physical completions of arbitrary middle-degree matrices by \[ \mathcal P_+(Y)=I_+(\rho_+(Y))(\Omega),\qquad \mathcal P_-(Y)=I_-(\rho_-(Y))(\Omega). \tag{17} \] They are linear maps into the full commutant algebra. They fix every \(f(\Omega)\), since their selected row or column agrees with it. Equivalently, their restrictions back to \(W_d\) are retractions onto \(\mathbb C[A]\). Formula (17) also specifies all other physical degrees; they are not filled by arbitrary matrices. These observations are faithful to normals. If all observed entries of \(f(A)\) vanish, (14) or (16) forces \(f=0\) in \(H_N\). In particular no nonzero double-root derivative direction is discarded. This conclusion uses the full minimal polynomial, not values only at the distinct \(c_j\). The original cup, in contrast, is an eigenvector: \(f(\Omega)p=f(c_0)p\). That one column does not replace (9). ## 3. The actual nine-cell port maps For the charged-array application suppose now that \(N>2\) is odd. Write the strict signed crossings of [R] as \(M_\sigma^0\), where \[ R_+=\kappa M_+^0,\qquad R_-=\kappa^{-1}M_-^0,\qquad \kappa=q^{d^2/2}. \tag{18} \] The \(R_\pm\) are the full original physical crossings and are inverses. All fractional powers mean the original specified exponentials. Both \(M_\sigma^0\) are complete Hopf boxes preserving integer degree. Use the original eight boundary face indices and their four differences \[ k_m=\alpha_{m,-}-\alpha_{m,+}+h_m,\qquad f_m(k)=s_{0m}^{[k-1]}s_{m5}^{[-k]},\qquad 1\le m\le4. \tag{19} \] The \(h_m\) are the original charges; the \(s_{ab}\) are the specified nonzero decoration roots. They are not new adjustable normalizers. Keep the literal scalar \(C_N(\mathbf s)\), and put \[ \varphi_+=3(h_1-1)/2,\qquad \varphi_-=0. \tag{20} \] These are the original sector conventions of [R]. The exact positive port map is \[ \mathcal E_+(M)_\alpha =C_NQ^{\varphi_+}s_{05}^dN^2Qx^{b-u} \prod_{m=1}^4f_m(k_m)\,M_{v,u;a,b}, \] \[ u=[-k_1],\quad v=[-k_2],\quad a=[k_3-1],\quad b=[k_4-1]. \tag{21} \] The negative port map is instead \[ \mathcal E_-(M)_\alpha =C_NQ^{\varphi_-}s_{05}^dN^2x^{b-e} \prod_{m=1}^4f_m(k_m)\,M_{c,e;a,b}, \] \[ c=[-k_1],\quad e=[-k_4],\quad a=[k_2-1],\quad b=[k_3-1]. \tag{22} \] The different index placement and the extra positive \(Q\) are retained. Equations (21),(22) are the literal maps of [R,(17),(18)]. For middle-degree output \((i,d-i)\) and input \((j,d-j)\), define \[ \mathbf k_+(i,j)=([i+1],[-i],[j+1],[-j]),\qquad \mathbf k_-(i,j)=([-i],[j+1],[-j],[i+1]). \tag{23} \] Their complete nonzero port scalars are \[ e_{+,ij}=C_NQ^{\varphi_+}s_{05}^dN^2Qx^{i-j} \prod_mf_m(k_{+,m}(i,j)), \] \[ e_{-,ij}=C_NQ^{\varphi_-}s_{05}^dN^2x^{i-j} \prod_mf_m(k_{-,m}(i,j)). \tag{24} \] On the regular decoration domain each is a unit. For any boundary array let its paired-fiber average at \(\mathbf k\) mean \(N^{-4}\) times the sum over all face indices satisfying (19). There are exactly \(N^4\) such indices. In particular (21),(22) give \[ \left\langle\mathcal E_\sigma(M)\right\rangle_{\mathbf k_\sigma(i,j)} =e_{\sigma,ij}M_{i,d-i;j,d-j}. \tag{25} \] Thus division by the actual \(e_{\sigma,ij}\), after this specified average, is the port inverse used here. No norm bound for that inverse is asserted. ## 4. Delete the ratio on the faithful packet The first beta identity in [R,(30)--(32)] has a distinguished quotient \[ \frac{\overline W_{0235}(K+L)} {\overline W_{0235}(K+L-k_2)}. \tag{26} \] For reference its five remaining internal indices can be called \(u,v,\tau,s,z\in\mathbb Z/N\), with \[ K=u+v+1,\qquad L=1-k_1+s+z,\qquad \Xi_0=u(1+\tau)+v(1+s)+(1+\tau)(1+s) +z-k_1+(3h_1-1)/2. \tag{27} \] Besides (26), its base-sector internal weight is precisely \[ \mathfrak n\mathfrak f_{01235}Q^{\Xi_0} \frac{W_{1234}(u)W_{1245}(v)W_{2345}(\tau) W_{0134}(s)W_{0145}(z)} {\overline W_{1235}(K)\overline W_{0135}(L) \overline W_{0345}(k_4+\tau+v+z)}. \tag{28} \] This is the literal beta image of the boundary coefficient in (21),(22), with every boundary multiplier still attached. In particular \(\mathfrak n,\mathfrak f_{01235},C_N\), the sector phases and the \(f_m\) factors are not reset to one. Factors already present in (21),(22) are not multiplied a second time. For the negative or another transported sector retain its original extra boundary phase once, as prescribed in [R, Section 6]. The bar on \(W\) is a label, not complex conjugation. In normalized Fermat coordinates its recurrence is \[ \frac{\overline W(n+1)}{\overline W(n)} =\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha Q^n},\qquad \alpha^N+\beta^N=1,\qquad \alpha\beta\ne0. \tag{29} \] All roots are the original jointly marked roots. Their products are periodic. Explicitly \(W(n)=\prod_{h=1}^{[n]}\beta/(1-\alpha Q^h)\) and \(\overline W(n)=\prod_{h=0}^{[n]-1}\beta/(1-\alpha Q^h)\), with both empty products equal to one; scalar decoration factors remain in (28). In the present quotient put \[ m=[-k_2],\quad r_0=u+v+s+z+2,\quad t=\alpha_{0235}Q^{r_0}. \tag{30} \] Since \(K+L=r_0-k_1\) modulo \(N\), (29) gives exactly \[ \frac{\overline W_{0235}(K+L)} {\overline W_{0235}(K+L-k_2)} =R_m(tQ^{-k_1}),\qquad R_m(Z)=\beta_{0235}^{-m}(Z;Q)_m. \tag{31} \] In particular it equals one whenever \(k_2=0\), for every internal tuple. This does not identify the internal \(r_0\) with a boundary index. Define the ratio-free beta coefficient by replacing only (26) by one in this literal finite beta sum. Retain all of (27),(28), all original port factors and the same paired-fiber average. Denote the resulting paired coefficient by \(\mathfrak b_\sigma^\flat(\mathbf k)\). This is a specified finite tensor operation, not a new invariant. Equivalently it is the paired average of the literal beta array with that single quotient deleted. Only these paired coefficients are needed. Before deletion the corresponding coefficient is \(\langle\mathcal E_\sigma(M_\sigma^0)\rangle_{\mathbf k}\): this is the actual finite beta identity of [R]. That identity retains arbitrary exterior coefficients, and hence applies coefficientwise to these paired coefficients. Since (26) is identically one at \(k_2=0\), \[ \mathfrak b_\sigma^\flat(\mathbf k) =\left\langle\mathcal E_\sigma(M_\sigma^0)\right\rangle_{\mathbf k} \quad\text{if }k_2=0. \tag{32} \] No cancellation or sign estimate has been used in this equality. Pull the ratio-free coefficients back to a middle-degree matrix: \[ (Y_\sigma^\flat)_{ij} =e_{\sigma,ij}^{-1} \mathfrak b_\sigma^\flat(\mathbf k_\sigma(i,j)). \tag{33} \] For the positive sign, \(\mathbf k_+(0,j)=(1,0,[j+1],[-j])\). For the negative sign, \(\mathbf k_-(i,d)=([-i],0,1,[i+1])\). Equations (25),(32),(33) therefore prove the entire row and column identities \[ \rho_+(Y_+^\flat)=\rho_+(M_+^0|_{W_d}),\qquad \rho_-(Y_-^\flat)=\rho_-(M_-^0|_{W_d}). \tag{34} \] There are \(N\) observations in each identity, not a single cup value. ## 5. Exact reconstructed boxes and arbitrary Conway assembly **Theorem.** On the regular marked decoration domain, at every odd \(N>2\), the literal ratio-free beta packets satisfy \[ \boxed{\qquad \mathcal P_+(Y_+^\flat)=M_+^0,\qquad \mathcal P_-(Y_-^\flat)=M_-^0. \qquad} \tag{35} \] Consequently the full original signed crossings are \[ \boxed{\qquad R_+=\kappa\mathcal P_+(Y_+^\flat),\qquad R_-=\kappa^{-1}\mathcal P_-(Y_-^\flat). \qquad} \tag{36} \] **Proof.** By (34), each reconstructed box and its original Hopf box have identical faithful data (9). The uniqueness established in (12)--(17) proves equality in \(H_N\), hence on the full physical pair. The scalar factors in (18) prove (36). This argument includes every normal at every repeated root. \(\square\) For clarity, (35) is not an equality \(Y_\sigma^\flat=M_\sigma^0|_{W_d}\). Unobserved rows or columns can change upon deletion. Reconstruction is the explicit kernel (17), and is retained once at every replaced crossing. Now take any fixed literal Conway expression with signed crossing leaves, products in \(H_N\), genuine turns \(J\), and its original closing row. Replace each signed leaf by the corresponding right side of (36). Induction over the expression shows that every open subtree packet is unchanged: this is true at the leaves by (36), preserved by the same product, and preserved by the same linear turn. Applying the same original closing therefore gives exactly the same scalar. Pivots, framing and peripheral lines retain their original positions and values. No equality for a modified non-Hopf array is inserted in place of (6). Integer twist leaves can be reconstructed internally and multiplied before substitution into the original expression. Thus arbitrary fixed short powers and all other prescribed powers are included as finite identities at each level. There is no large-twist hypothesis here. This is an exact source adapter, not a statement about their asymptotics. If reconstruction is moved to an exterior covector, its full bilinear dual must be moved there. It is not removed by a metric change or by replacing that covector with an endpoint row. The same rule applies to the inverse port factors (24). Individual ray-modified crossing patterns need their actual transported co-source from [R]; (36) concerns the original complete crossings, not a new endpoint closing for those individual patterns. ## 6. Norms and the unchanged degree-four minimum The sparse original signed data help identify the cost still present. By [H, Section 3], the first middle-degree row of \(R_+\) has only its last entry nonzero, equal to \(\kappa x^{-d}\). Inverting this row identity gives \[ R_-e_d=\kappa^{-1}x^d e_0. \tag{37} \] Indeed \(e_0^{\mathsf T}R_+=\kappa x^{-d}e_d^{\mathsf T}\) implies \(e_d^{\mathsf T}R_-=\kappa^{-1}x^d e_0^{\mathsf T}\); symmetry supplies (37). Thus both selected data vectors in (36), with their full Cartan factors restored, have Euclidean norm one. The other observed beta entries vanish by the full signed finite sum. They are not independent positive summands. In the Newton norm from (7), the complete original packets are [C] \[ R_\pm=\kappa^{\pm1} \sum_{r=0}^d(-q)^{\pm r}e_r^{\rm N},\qquad \|R_\pm\|_{\rm N}=\sqrt N. \tag{38} \] Accordingly the inverse on these particular actual data has norm ratio \(\sqrt N\) into this specified packet norm. This is not an operator bound for (17) on arbitrary data, a physical Hilbert--Schmidt bound, or a bound for changing the metric of further gluing. The continuant and port kernels retain their entire physical cost and complex phase. There is also a precise consequence for the degree-four source minimum of [C]. Keep the same literal compiler, Newton metric, vertices, local tensors \(T_v\), original root row and budgets \[ b_v=16\max(1,\|T_v\|_{\rm HS}),\qquad B_{\rm tot}=\prod_vb_v. \tag{39} \] If a prescribed leaf packet is replaced by its exactly reconstructed beta expression, the resulting element of \(H_N\) is the same leaf. Hence every \(T_v\), every \(b_v\), and every normalized recursion \(\Phi_v\) is unchanged. On the identical product of unit balls the objective remains pointwise \[ E_N(x)=|Lx_{v_0}|^2+ \sum_v\|\Phi_v((x_c)_c)-x_v\|^2. \tag{40} \] Its gradient, minimum and [C]'s value \((197/196)B_{\rm tot}^2\min E_N\) are therefore exactly unchanged, including at zeros. This does not assign old budgets to a new enlarged network of ratio-free variables and reconstruction gates. The gain proved here is zero-error removal of the retained ratio on a faithful full-normal packet, followed by exact original-source assembly. General interpolation, cyclic-row reconstruction and the existence of algebra projections are existing tools. Their application to this actual beta quotient and its two signed port placements is the source-specific content. The reconstruction kernel still carries coherent complexity. No geometric trial, positivity, subexponential full inverse, or volume lower bound follows. ## Complete inputs and closest coverage The complete matching texts used for the proof are: - [R] [Full-Psi ray crossings and the original nine-cell boundary](research_full_psi_ray_crossings_and_nine_cell_boundary.md), 588 lines, SHA-256 495a2fde1ed1d7ca0707f060208121bddb2673be21ff3bcb9bac737420ac2d24. - [P] [Full physical pair commutant and marked trace](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_pair_casimir_commutant_and_rotated_trace.md), 331 lines, SHA-256 00ab946b3eddb61256bdbd8ec487789a15991a80e1a28b4eee53bbb4a00f7666. - [H] [Complete Casimir--Hermite packets](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_complete_casimir_hermite_packet.md), 321 lines, SHA-256 a4e96738a3a093d963fe13cc03585085951fa8699a506ade4e2e7a47c17b3f4c. - [C] [Strongly convex minimum for the complete Conway source](research_convex_normalized_conway_source.md), 329 lines, SHA-256 6b89b4c6a67ef7a32cc41a5966c650f32de65d284ae7b70d94a71bddba21df3c. R supplies the literal port maps, complete finite beta identity and its co-source scope. P supplies the full algebra, physical tridiagonal block, genuine turn and original closing. H supplies the existing continuants and sparse signed row; the reconstruction proof is written out above. C fixes the Newton normalization and the exact compiler used in (38)--(40). No additional eigenframe or Gram inverse is assumed. Two complete closest comparisons were read for coverage: - [Source-preserving commutant projection and window repair](research_source_preserving_commutant_projection_and_window_repair.md), 543 lines, SHA-256 ff75410cfbba220c17bfd8153f27f901f21f1d98077b186945ebe502f24032e2. - [Original crossing in the coupled flag Euler exchange](research_actual_crossing_flag_euler_exchange.md), 287 lines, SHA-256 784a76132cf8116ec8afc5807e6bd98bb51178beb7f959b7ce3ab42e56eab6b5. The first constructs a different lowering-commutant projection calibrated to one source functional, rather than the faithful beta completion (17). The second transports the full retained coupon in coupled flags; it does not perform its elimination on a faithful row or column. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used.

title: A filled cover cannot make its short meridian geometrically long
text: # A filled cover cannot make its short meridian geometrically long 25 November 2026. Research proof. The proposed cover shortcut has a necessary filling-compatibility condition. It prevents using an unbranched cover to turn a fixed short filling into a long one while retaining multiplication of the completed hyperbolic volume by the covering degree. This is a check on that route, not a quantum descent statement or a restriction of the finite-exception target. Let \(X\) be a complete hyperbolic drilled exterior, and let \(Y=X(s)\) denote some prescribed fillings along primitive slopes \(s_i\). Suppose \(p:Y'\to Y\) is a finite unbranched cover of degree \(D\). Drill every preimage of each filling core to obtain \(X'\to X\). Equip \(X'\) with the pullback of the complete drilled metric on \(X\). For a horotorus \(T_i\), let \(T'_{ij}\to T_i\) have degree \(d_{ij}\), and define normalized slope length by \[ \mathcal L_T(s)=\frac{\operatorname{length}_T(s)} {\sqrt{\operatorname{area}(T)}}. \] Changing the size of the horotorus does not change this ratio. The primitive filling meridian \(s'_{ij}\) upstairs maps to \(\pm s_i\), rather than to a higher multiple. Indeed each component of the inverse image of the filled solid torus is an unbranched solid- torus cover. A meridian disk downstairs lifts to disks mapped homeomorphically to it, since the disk is simply connected. Their boundaries are the primitive upstairs meridians. Equivalently, the boundary subgroup contains \(s_i\), the kernel of the map from the boundary fundamental group to that of the solid torus. The lifted flat metric gives \[ \operatorname{area}(T'_{ij})=d_{ij}\operatorname{area}(T_i), \qquad \operatorname{length}(s'_{ij})=\operatorname{length}(s_i), \qquad \boxed{\mathcal L(s'_{ij})=\mathcal L(s_i)/\sqrt{d_{ij}}.} \] In particular the normalized length does not increase. If all the preimage filling cores are retained, \(\sum_jd_{ij}=D\) for each \(i\). For the simultaneous parameter \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-2}=\sum_i\mathcal L(s_i)^{-2}\), this gives \[ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{tot}}(X') =\mathcal L_{\mathrm{tot}}(X)/\sqrt D. \] A cover of the unfilled exterior can instead have primitive lifted slope mapping to \(ks_i\), \(k>1\). Its normalized length is \(k\mathcal L(s_i)/\sqrt{d_{ij}}\), but that filling map cannot extend unbranched across the core: its meridian has degree \(k\). A branched completion does not supply the unbranched completed-volume law used by the proposed descent. This distinction does not rule out a different drilling construction or a separately proved branched quantum identity. The [earlier cover analysis](regge_period_covers_and_a_curves.md) gives peripheral isogenies, the marked regulator degree and quantum parameter changes. It does not impose the filled-meridian condition above. The proof here is disk lifting and flat area scaling; no invariant identity is imported. The original source lower bound remains unproved.

title: Quantitative reconstruction of the canonical finite charge source
text: # Quantitative reconstruction of the canonical finite charge source Private written proof, 16 November 2026. Two consecutive blocks of lattice charge observations recover the canonical polarized charge function, including its first-normal blocks. For the actual cosine source, its exact charge reflection reduces this to one full block of \(N\) samples. The recovery has polynomial cost on bounded real charge sets and an explicit, sharp exponential cost in a complex direction. It is different from reconstructing a contour-polarized family. The known small-charge initializer does not provide this full unit charge block with the required uniform error. The signed period difference and its discrete Fourier transform already occur in [the actual charge equation, §§12–13](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_current_free_aw_crossing_transport.md#12-the-physical-charge-equation-has-two-channels). The [Fourier–Hermite Gram](../papers/filling-bounds/README.md) gives polynomially conditioned physical-jet coordinates, and the [one-sided angular projection](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_one_sided_hermite_projection.md) changes angular representatives. The additional result below is a continuous-charge reconstruction with quantitative error bounds, using the canonical finite charge normal form. ## 1. The actual charge space and its two sample blocks Fix \(N\ge2\), \(D=N-1\), \(\eta=(-1)^D\), and \(m=\lfloor N/2\rfloor\). Use \(y=1-\chi\) and \[ \lambda_a=\pi(D-2a),\qquad 0\le a\le D. \tag{1} \] The canonical polarized observation of an original boundary class \(f\in\mathcal A_N\) is \[ F_\sigma(y)=\phi_N\!\left(f\exp_{\mathcal A_N} (\sigma iNyL_N)\right), \qquad \sigma\in\{+1,-1\}. \tag{2} \] The complete finite normal form proved in the polarization source is \[ F_\sigma(y)= \sum_{a=0}^{m-1}(u_a+yv_a)e^{\sigma i\lambda_a y} +\mathbf1_{N\ {\rm odd}}u_*. \tag{3} \] All coefficients depend linearly on the full original values and first normals of \(f\). No normal is omitted: the coefficients of \(y e^{\sigma i\lambda_a y}\) recover the values, and the other coefficients then recover the first normals. The odd simple node contributes only \(u_*\). For the cosine observation \[ F(y)=\phi_N(f\mathcal C_{N,1-y}), \tag{4} \] its positive and negative generalized frequencies give exactly \[ F_\sigma=(2\Pi_\sigma+\Pi_0)F. \tag{5} \] Here \(\Pi_\sigma\) retains the frequencies \(\sigma\lambda_a\), \(0\le a<m\), together with their linear polynomial factors, and \(\Pi_0\) retains the odd constant. This is the actual canonical coupon projection. Both (3) and (4) belong to the larger space \[ \mathcal B_N= \left\{\sum_{a=0}^{D}(U_a+yV_a)e^{i\lambda_a y}\right\}. \tag{6} \] Its dimension is \(2N\). Every \(F\in\mathcal B_N\) obeys \[ B(y):=\eta F(y+1)-F(y)=\sum_aV_a e^{i\lambda_a y}, \qquad A(y):=F(y)-yB(y)=\sum_aU_a e^{i\lambda_a y}. \tag{7} \] Indeed \(e^{i\lambda_a}=\eta\). Thus the first difference in (7) retains the normal channel; replacing it by signed periodicity would lose that channel. Set \(y_j=j/N\), \(0\le j<N\), and retain the \(2N\) samples \[ d_j=F(y_j),\qquad d_{j+N}=F(y_j+1). \tag{8} \] They are the original charge lattice \(\chi=1-j/N\), over two consecutive blocks. Define \[ B_j=\eta d_{j+N}-d_j,\qquad A_j=d_j-y_jB_j. \tag{9} \] Ordinary finite Fourier orthogonality gives the explicit inverse \[ V_a=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{-i\lambda_a y_j}B_j, \qquad U_a=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{-i\lambda_a y_j}A_j. \tag{10} \] For example, \(e^{-i\pi Dy}B(y)=\sum_aV_ae^{-2\pi iay}\); the \(N\) frequencies are distinct modulo \(N\). This proves (10), and also proves that (8) determines the whole of (6). There is no division by an unknown source scalar. For the actual cosine source there is a stronger reconstruction. Its normal form is even in \(y\), and (7) gives the exact relation \[ F(y+1)+F(y-1)=2\eta F(y). \tag{10a} \] Consequently the first block alone determines the second: \[ d_N=\eta d_0,\qquad d_{N+j}=2\eta d_j-d_{N-j}\quad(1\le j<N). \tag{10b} \] Equivalently these are the full-quotient Chebyshev relations \(T_{N+j}(-z/2)+T_{N-j}(-z/2)=2\eta T_j(-z/2)\), since \(T_N(-z/2)=\eta\) in \(\mathcal A_N\). They preserve the first normals. Substitution into (9) gives \[ \begin{aligned} &B_0=0,\qquad A_0=d_0,\\ &B_j=d_j-\eta d_{N-j},\qquad A_j=(1-y_j)d_j+\eta y_jd_{N-j}\quad(1\le j<N). \end{aligned} \tag{10c} \] Equations (10), (10c), and (5) reconstruct the canonical polarized observation from the \(N\) original cosine observations at \(\chi=1-j/N\), \(0\le j<N\). Charge zero is already determined by charge one. This does not assert a signed-period law for the normal blocks: the nonzero difference \(B_j\) is still retained. ## 2. Exact interpolation and its complex error bound Define the finite kernels \[ K_{\sigma,N}(z)= 2\sum_{a=0}^{m-1}e^{\sigma i\lambda_a z} +\mathbf1_{N\ {\rm odd}}. \tag{11} \] Their total coefficient weight is \(2m+\mathbf1_{N\ {\rm odd}}=N\). Substituting (9) into (10) and applying (5) proves \[ \boxed{\quad F_\sigma(y)=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}K_{\sigma,N}(y-y_j) \bigl[(1+y_j-y)d_j+\eta(y-y_j)d_{j+N}\bigr] -\mathbf1_{N\ {\rm odd}}\frac yN\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}B_j. \quad} \tag{12} \] This formula reconstructs the polarized observation from the cosine observations (8), not merely from already polarized data. The factor two in (11) is absent at the odd simple frequency. The final term projects away the linear zero-frequency coefficient. It is zero for the exact cosine data, since their odd zero-frequency block is constant. Keeping it in (12) makes the reconstruction land in the canonical space even for noisy data. If the supplied data are instead those of (3), the analogous direct reconstruction replaces the factor two by one; it retains the odd constant once. Let \(\widehat d\) be arbitrary approximate samples with \[ \max_{0\le j<2N}|\widehat d_j-d_j|\le\delta_N. \tag{13} \] Apply the right side of (12) to these data and call its output \(\widehat F_\sigma\). Since \(0\le y_j<1\) and \(0<\lambda_a\le\pi D\) for \(a<m\), \[ |K_{\sigma,N}(y-y_j)| \le N e^{\pi D(-\sigma\Im y)_+}, \qquad |1+y_j-y|+|y-y_j|\le3+2|y|. \tag{14} \] Here \(r_+=\max(r,0)\). At even levels these inequalities immediately bound the reconstruction. At odd levels separate the nonzero frequencies, of total weight \(N-1\), from the corrected constant. The latter is \(N^{-1}\sum_j A_j\), whose error is at most \(3\delta_N\). Thus at either parity \[ \boxed{\quad |\widehat F_\sigma(y)-F_\sigma(y)| \le N(3+2|y|)\delta_N e^{\pi D(-\sigma\Im y)_+}. \quad} \tag{15} \] The same bound holds for the direct reconstruction from polarized samples. Equations (9)–(10) also give the separate coefficient bounds \[ |\Delta V_a|\le2\delta_N,\qquad |\Delta U_a|\le3\delta_N. \tag{16} \] All formulas hold at both parities, including \(N=2\). They hold with coefficients in any normed vector space, by the same triangle inequalities; in particular ordinary free-boundary parameters and fixed derivatives may be retained. For the actual cosine source, suppose instead that only its first block is approximated, with error at most \(\delta_N\). Construct \(A_j,B_j\) by (10c) before applying (10) and (5). Their errors satisfy \[ |\Delta B_j|\le2\delta_N,\qquad |\Delta A_j|\le\delta_N, \tag{16a} \] because the two coefficients of \(A_j\) have absolute values \(1-y_j,y_j\). The Fourier coefficients have the same bounds. The projection in (5) has total coefficient weight \(N\), so \[ \boxed{\quad |\Delta F_\sigma(y)|\le N(1+2|y|)\delta_N e^{\pi D(-\sigma\Im y)_+}. \quad} \tag{16b} \] At odd levels \(\eta=1\) and \(\sum_jB_j=0\) follows from \(j\leftrightarrow N-j\), even for the approximate first block. Thus no artificial linear zero-frequency term enters this single-block reconstruction. The real sample block may start at any real \(y_0\): apply the same argument to \(F(y_0+z)\). This translation preserves the frequency subspaces and their projection, so (15) then has \(3+2|y-y_0|\) in place of \(3+2|y|\). Only the location, not the length, of the required doubled block has changed. This translated assertion uses two blocks; the one-block reduction (10c) uses the original reflection center \(y=0\). For \(s\) selected variables, use the tensor product of (12). It reconstructs the original \(s\)-variable canonical polarized observation from \((2N)^s\) cosine lattice samples, retaining all mixed normal data. If their uniform error is \(\delta_N\), then \[ |\Delta F_{\boldsymbol\sigma}(\mathbf y)| \le N^s\delta_N\prod_{v=1}^s(3+2|y_v|) \exp\!\left[\pi D\sum_{v=1}^s(-\sigma_v\Im y_v)_+\right]. \tag{17} \] This follows either by multiplying the exact interpolation weights and summing their absolute values, or by successive operator norms from (15). It does not assume independent physical contractions. In charge variables the exponential cost is \(\pi D\sum_v(\sigma_v\Im\chi_v)_+\). For the actual tensor cosine source, its separate charge reflection permits (10c) in every coordinate. Only \(N^s\) samples in \(\{\chi_v=1-j_v/N:0\le j_v<N\}\) are then required, and (17) improves to \[ |\Delta F_{\boldsymbol\sigma}(\mathbf y)| \le N^s\delta_N\prod_{v=1}^s(1+2|y_v|) \exp\!\left[\pi D\sum_v(-\sigma_v\Im y_v)_+\right]. \tag{17a} \] This estimate retains every mixed first normal. The first block in this assertion is the full unit-charge cube, not a fixed small subinterval of it. ## 3. What the bounds transfer, and what they cost On a fixed compact target set, suppose the approximate samples have the actual uniform error \[ \delta_N\le C N^p e^{N(M-\gamma)}. \tag{18} \] Then (17) proves the concrete reconstruction error estimate \[ |\Delta F_{\boldsymbol\sigma}(\mathbf y)| \le C' N^{p+s} \exp N\left[M-\gamma+ \pi\sum_v(-\sigma_v\Im y_v)_+\right]. \tag{19} \] Thus comparison with a proposed target action \(S(\mathbf y)\) has a strict relative error gap whenever \[ \gamma>M+\pi\sum_v(-\sigma_v\Im y_v)_+ -\Re S(\mathbf y) \tag{20} \] uniformly on that set. The reconstructed approximate function is specified by (12); identifying its asymptotic action is a separate calculation. Formula (19) does not assume that interpolating a lattice leading term automatically produces \(e^{NS}\). Nor does it supply the sample error (18). For an actual heat preimage with real base power \(b_v\), target power \(n_v\), and target angle \(t_v^*\), substitute \[ \chi_{0,v}=1-\frac{(n_v-b_v)t_v^*}{2\pi},\qquad y_{0,v}=\frac{(n_v-b_v)t_v^*}{2\pi} \tag{21} \] into (19). Formula (21) follows also by subtracting the original primitive equations at powers \(\mathbf b\) and \(\mathbf n\), at the same angle: \(P_{\mathbf b}=P_{\mathbf n} +i(\mathbf n-\mathbf b)\mathbf t^*/2\), coordinatewise. Its explicit directional cost is \[ \pi\sum_v(-\sigma_v\Im y_{0,v})_+ =\pi\sum_v(\sigma_v\Im\chi_{0,v})_+ =\frac12\sum_v[-\sigma_v(n_v-b_v)\Im t_v^*]_+. \tag{22} \] For instance a uniform absolute sample error \(e^{-N\gamma}\) is still exponentially small after this reconstruction if \(\gamma\) exceeds (22). Any subsequent heat integral retains its own marked Gaussian and tail estimates; these are not included in (22). This is a quantitative prerequisite, not coverage of the preimages by the known small-charge samples. The exponential factor in (15) cannot be removed from a uniform reconstruction theorem. Take the actual cosine-space element \(F(y)=\cos(\pi Dy)\). Its real lattice samples have modulus at most one, whereas (5) gives \[ F_\sigma(y)=e^{\sigma i\pi Dy},\qquad |F_\sigma(y)|=e^{\pi D(-\sigma\Im y)} \quad\hbox{if }-\sigma\Im y>0. \tag{23} \] This is a member of the faithful finite source space, so the exponential rate in (15) is sharp.
