# Actual fixed-width Gauss coherent boundaries from the complete input sum Private written proof, 18 November 2026. The original ordinary-binomial input of the actual Gauss first row can be summed before taking any asymptotic limit. At every fixed width this gives two scalar coefficient integrals. Their original circles select a nonzero branch on a specified small input sector. The competing vacuum in the wider boundary is retained and estimated on the entire circle. This is an actual coherent boundary theorem. It does not apply a binomial transform to an error estimate for a monomial kernel, and it does not yet propagate the coherent boundary to nonzero output activities. The smaller sector below is essential for the proof. ## 1. Literal matrix row and its two coefficient integrals Use the notation and actual matrices of the complete direct W: \[ c_0=2\pi i,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad d=N-1,\quad x=-q^{-1},\quad f_a=(Q;Q)_a. 	ag{1} \] Fix a number \(r\ge2\) of tail heads, put \(s=r-1,\ p=r-2\), and restrict to integer degree \(T\le d\), where \[ \sigma_N=(T+1)/N\in I\Subset(1/2,1),\qquad 	au=T/N,\quad C=Q^{-T-1},\quad K_{r,T}=x^rQ^{-T}. 	ag{2} \] The original simplex basis is \[ | etaangle=| eta_1,\ldots, eta_s,T-| eta|angle, \qquad  eta_i\ge0,\quad | eta|\le T. \] Write \(A=A_N^{(r)}\) for W's actual operator and retain its vacuum entry exactly: \[ a_{00}^{(r)}=(-1)^d N K_{r,T}^d v_r,\qquad v_r=V_0^{(r)},\qquad V_a^{(r)}=\sum_{n=a}^T Q^{n(n+r-1)} {T rack n}_Q{T-a rack n-a}_Q. 	ag{3} \] W proves \(v_r
e0\) for all sufficiently large \(N\), uniformly in (2). Set \(G_r(t)=\sum_{a=0}^T(V_a^{(r)}/v_r)t^a\). The matrix \(A\) is symmetric in this original bilinear basis. Indeed the literal root head actions give \(E^t=x^{-1}KF,\ F^t=xEK^{-1}\); the ordered coproduct gives the same identities for a total on any interval. The Cartan factors cancel in \((F^nE^n)^t\), so each term of W's ordered formula \[ A=(-1)^dN\sum_{n=0}^d(-1)^nq^{n^2}F^nE^nK^{d-n}/f_n^2 \] is symmetric on fixed degree. W's first-column formula consequently gives the exact first row \[  rac{A_{\mathbf0, eta}}{a_{00}^{(r)}} = rac{V_{| eta|}^{(r)}}{v_r} \prod_{i=1}^s c_i^{ eta_i}, \qquad c_i=x^{r-i}. 	ag{4} \] Symmetry here is only a finite matrix identity; it is not a positive pairing or a replacement of the right coherent dual. Retain that dual literally. On \(z_r
e0\), put \[ \xi_i=c_i z_i/z_r,\qquad c_T(z)=\sum_{| eta|\le T}  inom d{T-| eta|}\prod_{i=1}^s inom d{ eta_i} z_r^{T-| eta|}\prod_{i=1}^s z_i^{ eta_i}| etaangle. 	ag{5} \] Define the normalized coherent boundary \[ \mathcal C_{r,N,T}(\xi)=  rac{\langle\mathbf0|A c_T(z)angle} {a_{00}^{(r)}z_r^T inom dT}. 	ag{6} \] Every factorial dual and every physical cap in (5) is present. The finite ordinary-binomial polynomial \[ \mathcal B_{r,N,T}(z)=  inom dT^{-1}[u^T](1+u)^d\prod_{i=1}^s(1+u z_i)^d 	ag{7} \] gives the exact identity \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal C_{r,N,T}(\xi)= \operatorname{CT}_t\,G_r(t) \mathcal B_{r,N,T}(\xi_1/t,\ldots,\xi_s/t). \quad} 	ag{8} \] To check it, the coefficient of \(z^ eta\) in (7) is \( inom dT^{-1} inom d{T-| eta|}\prod_i inom d{ eta_i}\). The \(t\)-constant term pairs this coefficient only with \(V_{| eta|}^{(r)}/v_r\). This proves (8) for the entire finite sum. In particular all inactive magnetic indices have already been summed; no small-slope approximation is used to obtain (8). ## 2. The complete multivariate binomial coefficient circle There is a fixed small polydisk \(|z_i|<\epsilon\), uniform in (2), on which (7) has the actual asymptotic \[ \mathcal B_{r,N,T}(z)=e^{N S_B(z;	au)} A_B(z;	au)(1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{9} \] The error is holomorphic, with fixed derivatives on smaller polydisks. All functions in this assertion keep \(	au=T/N\) exactly, not \(\sigma_N\). Here are the phase, amplitude and complete-circle proof. Let \(u=u(z)\) be the analytic solution near \(b=	au/(1-	au)\) of \[  rac{u}{1+u}+\sum_{i=1}^s rac{uz_i}{1+uz_i}=	au. 	ag{10} \] The derivative in \(\log u\) at \(z=0\) is \(	au(1-	au)>0\), uniformly. Put \[  egin{split} S_B(z;	au)&=\log(1+u)+\sum_i\log(1+uz_i)-	au\log u\ &\hspace{12mm}+	au\log	au+(1-	au)\log(1-	au),\ D_B(z;	au)&= rac{u}{(1+u)^2} +\sum_i rac{uz_i}{(1+uz_i)^2},\ A_B(z;	au)&=  rac{\sqrt{	au/(1-	au)}} {(1+u)\prod_i(1+uz_i)\sqrt{D_B(z;	au)}}. \end{split} 	ag{11} \] All logarithms and the Gaussian square root are continued from \(z=0\). Thus \(S_B(0)=0,\ A_B(0)=1\), and \[ \partial_{z_i}S_B(0)=b. 	ag{12} \] Use the actual coefficient circle \(u=u(z)e^{i	heta}\) in (7). It is a positive circle about zero; changing its complex radius is allowed because the coefficient integrand has no other poles. At \(z=0\), the real phase loss is \[ \log rac{|1+b e^{i	heta}|}{1+b} =	frac12\log\left(1-  rac{4b}{(1+b)^2}\sin^2(	heta/2)ight) \le -c(1-\cos	heta). 	ag{13} \] The compact range of \(	au>1/2\) keeps \(b\) bounded above and a positive distance from \(1\), so the logarithm can be differentiated on this circle without a zero. Its possible winding changes only the imaginary lift; the original coefficient integrand is single-valued. For small complex \(z\), the saddle condition (10) makes the first \(	heta\)-derivative vanish at zero. The difference from the phase at \(z=0\) has uniformly small second derivative on the circle. Near zero this preserves the quadratic bound in (13); away from zero its uniform smallness preserves the fixed gap. Thus the whole circle, including its complement, has a unique real maximum at the chosen saddle after the polydisk is shrunk. The coefficient integrand, written with \(N\) in the exponent, has amplitude \([(1+u)\prod_i(1+uz_i)]^{-1}\). Taylor expansion on the central arc with the bound (13) therefore gives \[ [u^T](1+u)^d\prod_i(1+uz_i)^d = rac{e^{N[S_B-	au\log	au-(1-	au)\log(1-	au)]}} {\sqrt{2\pi N D_B}\,(1+u)\prod_i(1+uz_i)} (1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{14} \] The coefficient of this Gaussian is one: it is the original positively oriented circle and the square root is positive at \(z=0\). Finally \[  inom{N-1}T=  rac{\sqrt{(1-	au)/	au}}{\sqrt{2\pi N}}\, e^{-N[	au\log	au+(1-	au)\log(1-	au)]} (1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{15} \] Division proves (9)--(11), including every \(d=N-1\) amplitude factor. The uniform holomorphic error and its derivatives follow by working on a slightly larger polydisk first. In particular (9) also gives the absolute bound \[ |\mathcal B_{r,N,T}(z)|\le C e^{N\Re S_B(z;	au)} 	ag{16} \] throughout a smaller whole polydisk. ## 3. The outer saddle and the honest input sector For clarity distinguish the constants \[ a=2/c_0,\qquad b=	au/(1-	au),\qquad b_C=C^{-1}-1. 	ag{17} \] The scalar boundary data supplied by W are \(\phi(t;C), A_G(t;C)\) and \(Y_B(t;C)\), with \(\phi(0)=0,\ \phi'(0)=a\). Define \[ W(t;C)= rac{C^{-1}-Y_B(t;C)}t,\qquad A_r^\partial(t;C)=  rac{p!\,A_G(t;C)W(t;C)^p}{(a b_C)^p}. 	ag{18} \] On a sufficiently small punctured disk \(W\) has no zeros. W proves both the whole-disk competing bound \[ |G_r(t)|\le C_r(1+e^{N\Re\phi(t;C)}) 	ag{19} \] and, on compact sets with \(\Re\phi(t;C)>0\), \[ G_r(t)=N^{-p}e^{N\phi(t;C)} A_r^\partial(t;C)(1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{20} \] The vacuum summand in (19) cannot be removed on the entire circle. Choose a bounded open domain of complex shapes \(\vartheta=(\vartheta_1,\ldots,\vartheta_s)\) with \(\sum_i\vartheta_i=1\), with openness relative to that affine hyperplane. Work uniformly on its compact subsets; zero coordinates are allowed. Use the input coordinates \[ \xi_i= rac{\vartheta_i a_*^2}{a b},\qquad 0<|a_*|<a_0,\qquad |\arg a_*|<	heta_0<\pi/3. 	ag{21} \] The shapes and the square-root choice describe a genuine open input sector when \(\sum_i\xi_i
e0\). Estimates below are uniform on compact subsets of this punctured sector and the shape domain. They do not assert a uniform limit when \(N|a_*|\) stays bounded. Let \[ F(t)=\phi(t;C)+S_B(\xi_1/t,\ldots,\xi_s/t;	au). 	ag{22} \] After setting \(t=(a_*/a)v\), its leading expression is \(a_*(v+v^{-1})+O(a_*^2)\). The equation \(D_tF=0\) consequently has a unique analytic solution near \(v=1\): \[  egin{split} t_*&=(a_*/a)(1+O(a_*)),\ \Psi(\xi;C,	au)&=F(t_*)=2a_*+O(a_*^2),\ \mathcal H&=D_t^2F(t_*)=2a_*+O(a_*^2). \end{split} 	ag{23} \] Here and below \(D_t=t\partial_t\). The implicit derivative after dividing the saddle equation by \(a_*\) is \(2\) at \(v=1\). Thus these are actual analytic functions, not just formal expansions. Their estimates are uniform for the stated compact shape set. Use the original constant-term circle \(t=t_*e^{i	heta}\). Both \(t\) and all \(\xi_i/t\) remain inside the disks of (9),(19). On this circle the combined phase satisfies \[ \Re[F(t_*e^{i	heta})-F(t_*)] \le-[2\Re a_*-C|a_*|^2](1-\cos	heta). 	ag{24} \] Indeed its leading expression is \(2a_*\cos	heta\). The periodic analytic remainder has second derivative \(O(|a_*|^2)\), and its first derivative at zero is zero because \(t_*\) is the exact saddle. Integration of that derivative bound on \([-\pi,\pi]\) gives (24). There is a separate estimate for the vacuum part of (19): \[ \max_	heta\Re S_B(\xi/t_*e^{-i	heta};	au) \le |a_*|+C|a_*|^2. 	ag{25} \] By contrast \(\Re\Psi=2\Re a_*+O(|a_*|^2)\). Therefore (21) and a sufficiently small \(a_0\) give \[ \Re\Psi-\max_	heta\Re S_B(\xi/t_*e^{-i	heta};	au) \ge 	frac12(2\cos	heta_0-1)|a_*|>0. 	ag{26} \] This is why the sector is restricted to \(	heta_0<\pi/3\). The envelope allowed by (19),(16) has leading maximum \(\max(|a_*|,2\Re a_*)\); a sector approaching \(\pi/2\) would not establish (26). Choose a fixed small central arc about \(	heta=0\). On that arc \(\Re\phi(t_*e^{i	heta};C)>0\), uniformly on every compact subset of (21), so (20) applies with holomorphic relative error. On the complementary arc, (19),(16),(24),(26) bound the whole integrand by the sum of two exponentials with a strict gap below \(\Re\Psi\). Relative to the central amplitude this remains exponentially small despite the factor \(N^p\). This estimates every competing boundary branch and all finite caps through the actual polynomials in (8). ## 4. Actual coherent boundary and its normalization On the central arc substitute (9),(20) into (8). Taylor expansion at the exact saddle, followed by (24)--(26), gives \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal C_{r,N,T}(\xi)= N^{-p} rac{e^{N\Psi(\xi;C,	au)}}{\sqrt{2\pi N\mathcal H}}\, A_r^\partial(t_*;C) A_B(\xi_1/t_*,\ldots,\xi_s/t_*;	au) (1+O(N^{-1})). \quad} 	ag{27} \] The Gaussian square root is continued from positive real \(a_*\); \(\mathcal H=2a_*+O(a_*^2)\) has positive real part on a sufficiently small sector. Its coefficient is one, because the positive circle in (8) passes once through the selected saddle and the full complement was just bounded. All displayed amplitude factors are nonzero. Fixed input and shape derivatives follow on smaller compact sets by Cauchy; the sector coordinate is locally invertible for \(a_*
e0\). In particular the original, unnormalized boundary is \[  oxed{ egin{split} \langle\mathbf0|A_N^{(r)}c_T(z)angle ={}&a_{00}^{(r)}z_r^T inom dT\, N^{-p} rac{e^{N\Psi}}{\sqrt{2\pi N\mathcal H}}\, A_r^\partial(t_*;C)A_B(\xi/t_*;	au)\ &\hspace{32mm}\cdot(1+O(N^{-1})). \end{split}} 	ag{28} \] Neither the width-dependent vacuum normalization nor the physical phases \(c_i=x^{r-i}\), nor the homogeneous character \(z_r^T\), nor the binomial factor has been omitted. The normalized action is calibrated by \(\Psi	o0\) as \(a_*	o0\), while (27) is only a punctured-sector asymptotic. The exact expression (8) remains valid in the microscopic region where this Gaussian approximation is not uniform. The selected input sector is all-width and allows bounded complex shapes without requiring each \(\xi_i\) to have a nonzero phase slope. Its proof used the full original input sum, not a termwise transform of the monomial approximation. This distinction is material: inactive Cauchy interfaces can create an extensive phase even when the corresponding monomial phase is constant. The output in (28) is still the literal vacuum row. A theorem for nonzero output activities would need propagation of this coherent initializer with the exact binomial-conjugated input operators and their retained endpoints. No such propagation is asserted here. Nor does (28) estimate the exterior braid, turnover, inverse Cartan factor or closed source in the original opposite kernel. The proof is at fixed \(q_N,M=1\) and physical integer \(T\); it gives no meridian normal, complex-degree interpolation or geometric-cycle coefficient. ## 5. Complete direct and protocol The sole complete proof direct is: * **W:** [research_fixed_width_gauss_boundary_branches.md](research_fixed_width_gauss_boundary_branches.md), 427 lines, SHA256 cdcb82d2bd48948ff45baaec65a71f639607e10a9bc12acff344e34ae972d404. W supplies the actual first column and vacuum normalization, the marked phase/amplitude, and the whole-disk competing bound. The matrix transpose, exact ordinary-binomial contraction, its inner coefficient saddle and the complete outer-circle selection are proved here. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations are used; frozen and public files are unchanged. Author freeze protocol: the entire matching final was freshly reread nontruncated. The sole complete direct W was freshly read in full in this author sequence and retained unchanged. Every used implication was checked, and both hashes were renewed. Independent matching review and parent adoption remain separate.

title: Actual fixed-width Gauss coherent kernels from reverse propagation
text:
# Actual fixed-width Gauss coherent kernels from reverse propagation Private written proof, 18 November 2026. The complete ordinary-binomial first row in B initializes reverse suffix-Casimir propagation. At the fixed root both apparent inverse Euler factors in the binomial-conjugated generators are exactly short clock-rotation integrals. This permits an analytic estimate of the actual low output coefficients, followed by recovery of the entire finite cap. The resulting full coherent kernel has a nonzero amplitude and a nondegenerate mixed phase on the specified small input sectors. This proof does not transform the relative error of a monomial kernel. The input sum is paid first, and the new error estimate is propagated with its literal binomial weights. ## 1. Actual kernel and coherent initialization Use the root conventions \[ c_0=2\pi i,\quad Q=e^{c_0/N},\quad q=e^{c_0/(2N)},\quad x=-q^{-1},\quad d=N-1,\quad \epsilon=N^{-1},\quad h=c_0/N. 	ag{1} \] Fix \(r\ge2,\ s=r-1,\ p=r-2\) and integer degree \(T\le d\), with \[ \sigma=(T+1)/N\in I\Subset(1/2,1),\quad C=e^{-c_0\sigma}=Q^{-T-1},\quad 	au=T/N=\sigma-\epsilon, \quad c_i=x^{r-i}. 	ag{2} \] The actual matrix \(A=A_N^{(r)}\), the simplex basis \(|\alphaangle=|\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_s,T-|\alpha|angle\), and its nonzero vacuum \(a_{00}^{(r)}\) are those of the complete directs M and B. Retain these finite objects exactly. Write \[ b_ eta= inom d{T-| eta|}\prod_{i=1}^s inom d{ eta_i}, \qquad b_{\mathbf0}= inom dT. 	ag{3} \] Our normalized full coherent kernel is \[ U_N(ho,\xi)= \sum_{\substack{|\alpha|\le T\| eta|\le T}}  rac{A_{\alpha eta}}{a_{00}^{(r)}} c^{-\alpha- eta}ho^\alpha\xi^ eta  rac{b_ eta}{b_{\mathbf0}}. 	ag{4} \] For the original monomial output and ordinary-binomial coherent input, \[ v(w)A c_T(z)= a_{00}^{(r)}(w_rz_r)^T inom dT\, U_N(ho,\xi),\qquad ho_i=c_iw_i/w_r,\quad \xi_i=c_iz_i/z_r. 	ag{5} \] All caps and physical phases in (4),(5) remain. Choose an input polydisk \(D\) with compact closure, with successively larger polydisks inside B's punctured sector, avoiding each coordinate \(\xi_i=0\). The sector has bounded shapes and \[ a_*^2=a\,b\,\sum_i\xi_i,\quad a=2/c_0,\quad b=	au/(1-	au),\qquad |\arg a_*|<	heta_0<\pi/3. 	ag{6} \] Choose the same branches on the larger domains, uniformly for (2). The avoidance of coordinate zero is used only for analytic coefficients of the dehomogenized operator rows; it is a genuine nonempty open subdomain of B's chart. B proves the actual boundary asymptotic, with all complementary terms estimated, \[ U_N(0,\xi)=N^{-p-1/2} e^{N\Psi(\xi;C,	au)} B_\partial(\xi;C,	au) (1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{7} \] Its explicit unit is \[ B_\partial= (2\pi\mathcal H)^{-1/2} A_r^\partial(t_*;C) A_B(\xi/t_*;	au). 	ag{8} \] Here \(t_*\) is the actual outer saddle, \(\Psi=\phi(t_*;C)+S_B(\xi/t_*;	au)\), and all functions are exactly those of B. In particular its Gaussian coefficient is one. For the propagation parameter keep \(\sigma\) exact and put \[ \psi(\xi;\sigma)=\Psi(\xi;e^{-c_0\sigma},\sigma),\qquad B_0(\xi;\sigma)= B_\partial(\xi;e^{-c_0\sigma},\sigma) \exp[-\partial_	au\Psi(\xi;e^{-c_0\sigma},\sigma)]. 	ag{9} \] The derivative in (9) keeps \(C,\xi\) fixed. These functions are analytic on the chosen input domain. Taylor expansion in the exact \(	au=\sigma-\epsilon\), on a slightly larger domain, turns (7) into \[ N^{p+1/2}U_N(0,\xi) =e^{N\psi(\xi;\sigma)}B_0(\xi;\sigma) (1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{10} \] Thus the \(N-1\) degree correction is retained in the initialized amplitude. No derivative of a root asymptotic in \(M\) or \(q\) is involved. ## 2. The exact binomial generators are local clock arcs For a single head let \[ R_v(z)=\sum_{a=0}^d inom da v_a z^a,\qquad D=z\partial_z. \] Using the actual zero endpoint arrows, direct coefficient comparison gives \[  egin{split} R_{Ev}&=z^{-1} rac{D}{N-D}(Q^{-D}-1)R_v,\ R_{Fv}&=z rac{d-D}{D+1}(1-Q^{D+1})R_v,\ R_{Kv}&=xQ^{-D}R_v. \end{split} 	ag{11} \] Their displayed order is part of the identity. For example \( inom d{a-1}/ inom da=a/(N-a)\), while \( inom d{a+1}/ inom da=(d-a)/(a+1)\). At this fixed root \(e^{hN}=1\). Hence both quotients in (11) have the following exact integral forms: \[  oxed{ egin{split} \widehat E&= h z^{-1}D\int_0^1 e^{c_0t}Q^{-tD}\,dt,\ \widehat F&= -h z(d-D)\int_0^1 e^{ht}Q^{tD}\,dt,\ \widehat K&=xQ^{-D}. \end{split}} 	ag{12} \] Indeed \[  rac{Q^{-D}-1}{N-D} =h\int_0^1e^{ht(N-D)}dt,\qquad  rac{1-Q^{D+1}}{D+1} =-h\int_0^1e^{ht(D+1)}dt. 	ag{13} \] These identities hold on every physical monomial, including both endpoints. They are not estimates obtained by replacing an inverse Euler operator by its principal value. Every clock rotation in (12) moves an argument by \(O(N^{-1})\). Apply (12) separately to the heads and use the original ordered coproduct. The binomial-conjugated suffix Casimirs \(\widehat\Omega_i\), for the intervals \([i,r]\), are exact operators on the weighted input polynomials. Dehomogenization is literal: \[ D_r=T-\sum_{i<r}D_i,\qquad Q^{tD_r}=Q^{tT}\prod_{i<r}Q^{-tD_i}. 	ag{14} \] All scalar \(Q^{tT}\) and all intermediate degree changes in ordered products are retained. Multiplication by \(z_i/z_j\) becomes the actual ratio \(c_j\xi_i/(c_i\xi_j)\). On the chosen nonzero-coordinate polydisks every resulting coefficient is analytic and bounded. More specifically, each such Casimir is a finite sum of terms \[ \int_{[0,1]^k} a_{
u,N}(\xi,t)\, N^{-|
u|}\partial_\xi^
u f(\Phi_{N,t}\xi)\,dt,\qquad |
u|\le2. 	ag{15} \] The coefficients, and their fixed derivatives on smaller domains, are uniformly bounded and analytic in \(\epsilon\) at zero, with \(\sigma\) on its stated compact real interval. \(\Phi_{N,t}\) is a diagonal clock rotation; its displacement is bounded by \(C\epsilon\), uniformly on the compact integration cube. Formula (15) follows by multiplying the literal expressions (12); derivatives of their coefficients contribute terms of lower order. There is no unbounded radial integration or discarded cap in (15). ## 3. Reverse finite triangular propagation Use the exact suffix notation of M: \[ \Omega_i=\Omega_{[i,r]},\qquad D_i=\Omega_i-K_i^{-1}\Omega_{i+1}. \] The expansion with its original operator order is \[ D_i=K_t[F_iE_i+q(K_i-K_i^{-1})] +F_iE_t+K_i^{-1}F_tE_iK_t. 	ag{16} \] For an output index \(\alpha\), put \(k_i(\alpha)=xQ^{-\alpha_i}\). The only term in \(D_i|\alphaangle\) that raises low degree \(|\alpha|\) is \[ a_i^+(\alpha)|\alpha+e_iangle,\qquad a_i^+(\alpha)= (1-Q^{\alpha_i+1})(Q^{-T+|\alpha|}-1). 	ag{17} \] Every other column \(\gamma\) has \(|\gamma|\le|\alpha|\). This includes all diagonal and degree-preserving transfers; neither endpoint is dropped. The original matrices \(A,\Omega_i\) are symmetric. Transpose the exact column equation in M, then use the literal binomial map on its input variable. If \(U_\alpha(\xi)=[ho^\alpha]U_N\), the result is \[  egin{split} c_i a_i^+(\alpha)U_{\alpha+e_i} ={}&[\widehat\Omega_i-k_i(\alpha)^{-1} \widehat\Omega_{i+1}]U_\alpha\ &-\sum_{|\gamma|\le|\alpha|} (D_i)_{\gamma\alpha}c^{\gamma-\alpha}U_\gamma . \end{split} 	ag{18} \] This is an exact row of the actual finite matrix. Every choice of predecessor is compatible because they come from the same matrix, not from an assumed integrable approximate system. Choose \(\delta>0\) small depending on \(I\) and the input domains. For \(|\alpha|\le\delta N\), \[ |a_i^+(\alpha)|\ge c(\alpha_i+1)/N. 	ag{19} \] The corresponding highest term in the output generating equation is \[  rac{c_i}{ho_i}(1-T_i)(CT_{m all}-1)U_N, \qquad T_i:ho_i\mapsto Qho_i. 	ag{20} \] For the new degree-\(n\) coefficient \(v_\gamma\) of a logarithm divided by \(N\), its diagonal multiplier is therefore \[ c_iN(1-Q^{\gamma_i})(CQ^n-1), \qquad |\,\cdot\,|\ge c\gamma_i. 	ag{21} \] Other terms involve lower output degrees, as in (18). Apparent negative powers in (20) have the exact endpoint differences that make the complete row analytic. ## 4. Uniform analytic low-degree estimate and the whole cap Here is the analytic argument for (18), including the new second input derivatives in (15). It proves an actual kernel estimate, not just existence of a formal principal solution. By (10) the exact boundary is a unit on the enlarged input domain for large \(N\). Expand the formal output logarithm \[ V_N=N^{-1}\log[N^{p+1/2}U_N] 	ag{22} \] there, starting with that boundary branch, and first retain output degree at most \(k_N=\lfloor\delta Nfloor\). The division in (21) is bounded by a constant times \(1/\gamma_i\). Multinomial majorants, with \(z=\sum_i|ho_i|\), turn these divisions into the usual \(1/n\) at output degree \(n\). Use a nonnegative scalar variable \(y\) to majorize input displacements inside the larger input polydisk. Enlarge constants to dominate every coefficient and every arc in (15), and put \[ \varphi_\epsilon(y) =e^{L\epsilon}(1+y)-1. 	ag{23} \] An \(O(\epsilon)\) clock arc is dominated by this map. Its scaled first difference is dominated by \(L(1+y)F'(\varphi_\epsilon(y))\) for a positive analytic majorant \(F\). The following elementary inequality pays the additional derivatives: \[ \epsilon F''(y) \preccurlyeq C F'(\varphi_\epsilon(y)). 	ag{24} \] Indeed the Taylor expansion of \(F'(y+a)\), with nonnegative coefficients, contains \(aF''(y)\), and \(\varphi_\epsilon(y)-y\) coefficientwise dominates \(c\epsilon\). The same argument handles any of the finitely many input coordinate directions after increasing \(L,C\). Conjugating (15) by \(e^{NV}\) gives analytic combinations of first input derivatives of \(V\), clock increments \(N\Delta V\), and \(\epsilon\) times second input derivatives of \(V\). For example two scaled derivatives give a product of two first derivatives plus \(\epsilon\partial^2V\). Thus (24) is exactly the missing derivative budget, rather than an estimate on an unscaled second derivative. Pad a degree-\(n\) input majorant by \(\varphi_{n\epsilon}\). Enlarge \(L\) once to include the combined displacements of every arc and the extra Taylor translation in a whole application of (15). That complete application then consumes one padding step when an output degree is raised. In a product of previously available coefficients, its required padding is bounded by the new total degree: \(\max(n_j+1)\le\sum n_j+1\). Boundary factors have degree zero and obey the same rule. Taking \(\delta\) smaller ensures that all these padded domains remain inside the enlarged input sector. This also controls a bounded continuum of arc parameters; integration over its fixed cube only changes the majorant constant. For completeness a positive implicit first-order majorant can be chosen in the form \[  egin{split} U_z=B(y)\{& 1+U+(1+U_y)^2+ e^{B(y)((1+y)U_y+zU_z)}\ &+zU_z+zU_z^2 e^{B(y)((1+y)U_y+zU_z)}\}, \qquad U(y,0)=U_0(y). \end{split} 	ag{25} \] Here \(B,U_0\) are fixed nonnegative analytic series dominating the boundary logarithm and the finitely many operator coefficients. The squared input gradient accounts for (15). Every dependence on the unknown \(U_z\) has a factor \(z\), so (25) can be solved for \(U_z=\mathscr H(y,z,U,U_y)\) on a neighborhood of the initial line. An actual analytic solution follows from its characteristic ordinary differential equations \[ \dot y=-\mathscr H_P,\qquad \dot U=\mathscr H-P\mathscr H_P,\qquad \dot P=\mathscr H_y+\mathscr H_U P . 	ag{26} \] The initial projection has derivative one. Analytic ODE existence and the inverse function theorem give a common small bidisk. Its coefficient recursion is nonnegative and dominates the exact degree-by-degree recursion (18),(21), with the padding just proved. Thus the entire low logarithm has a uniform analytic bound. The same construction controls errors. Subtract two conjugated rows. An exponential difference factors as its increment difference times a bounded analytic multiplier. A second-derivative difference is \(\epsilon\partial^2\) of the error and is treated by (24). After removal of the diagonal (21), the positive linear error majorant has the form \[ E_z=B_1(E+E_y)+zB_2E_z+\epsilon^jB_3,\qquad E(y,0)=\epsilon^jE_0(y). 	ag{27} \] All coefficients are bounded analytic series on smaller domains. Invert \(1-zB_2\) and use the linear instance of (26). Its solution is \(\epsilon^j\) times a uniformly bounded analytic function. This gives stability for \(j=1,2\), without a high-degree clock inverse or an uncontrolled analytic-radius loss. The full finite cap is recovered separately. M supplies an \(e^{C_1N}\) bound on the actual matrix coefficients divided by \(a_{00}^{(r)}\). Multiplying by the finitely many binomial factors, summing the polynomially many physical indices and evaluating on the fixed input polydisk preserves an \(e^{C_2N}\) bound. The harmless \(N^{p+1/2}\) normalization is included in it. The exponential of the bounded low logarithm has the same type of bound on a fixed output polydisk and agrees with the actual polynomial through degree \(k_N\). Cauchy's estimate for their remaining coefficients gives, on a smaller output polydisk, \[ C(k_N+1)^{s-1}e^{C_3N}  rac{(r_0/R_0)^{k_N+1}}{(1-r_0/R_0)^s}. 	ag{28} \] Choose \(r_0/R_0\) after \(\delta\). This makes (28) exponentially smaller than \(e^{N\Re V_N}\), whose reciprocal has an \(e^{C_4N}\) bound from the low logarithm. Consequently the actual kernel is a unit on the resulting output-input domain, and its full logarithm obeys the same estimates. All original coefficients above the low band have been retained in this step. ## 5. Phase, transport and the actual relative estimate The principal equations are obtained from the exact rows (18) by the following unambiguous substitution: on the output put \(T_i=e^{c_0ho_iS_{ho_i}}\); in the weighted input use the principal symbols of (11), with the homogeneous last momentum \(\sigma-\sum_i\xi_iS_{\xi_i}\). Keep the displayed order until this commuting principal substitution is made. Initialize \[ S(0,\xi;\sigma)=\psi(\xi;\sigma). 	ag{29} \] This defines the selected system; it is not an arbitrary Casimir branch. The estimates of Section 4 construct its analytic compatible solution as follows. Every fixed output coefficient of the exact low logarithm has a limiting recursion from (21), with nonzero diagonal proportional to its new index. Starting with (29), this determines it uniquely. The uniform analytic majorant makes these limits a convergent analytic function \(S\), uniformly in the stated real parameter interval. Compatibility of all the rows is inherited from their exact finite identities. This argument also gives the coefficientwise analytic dependence on \(C\). Substitution of \(e^{NS}\) into the exact equations leaves a conjugated residual \(O(\epsilon)\), including the \(\epsilon\partial_\xi^2S\) terms and every physical half-shift. The bound is uniform on smaller domains by Cauchy. Equation (27) with \(j=1\) proves \(V_N-S=O(\epsilon)\). The uniformly bounded functions \(N(V_N-S)\) now have coefficient limits determined by the linear first transport recursion, with boundary \(\log B_0\). Uniqueness at each new output coefficient and the analytic majorant give a compatible analytic function \(\alpha(ho,\xi;\sigma)\). Its constant exponential is fixed by (9), not freely chosen. Inserting \(S+\epsilon\alpha\) cancels the first two orders of every exact row. Taylor expansion of their short arcs and scaled derivatives has uniform \(O(\epsilon^2)\) remainder on smaller domains; the order-two operators in (15) cause no difficulty because \(S,\alpha\) have uniform analytic derivative bounds there. The boundary error is \(O(\epsilon^2)\) by (10). Apply (27) with \(j=2\), then (28), to obtain \[  oxed{\quad U_N(ho,\xi)=N^{-p-1/2} e^{N S(ho,\xi;\sigma)} \mathcal A(ho,\xi;\sigma)(1+O(N^{-1})), \qquad \mathcal A=e^\alpha
e0. \quad} 	ag{30} \] Every fixed output and input derivative follows on smaller domains. This is uniform analyticity in those variables. It does not claim a uniform complex-\(C\) neighborhood merely from the normal-family argument on the physical real arc. ## 6. The initialized full mixed rank The phase in (30) has a nondegenerate full mixed Hessian, which can be checked explicitly at the output axis. All quantities in this section are principal quantities with \(C=e^{-c_0\sigma}\); the actual \(	au=\sigma-\epsilon\) correction already belongs to (9) and the transport. Use B's two saddles at \(	au=\sigma\), called \(t,u\), and set \[ p_i= rac{u\xi_i}{t+u\xi_i},\quad P=\sum_{i=1}^s p_i=t\phi'(t;C),\quad p_r=\sigma-P,\quad u= rac{p_r}{1-p_r}. 	ag{31} \] These are the boundary input occupation momenta, by differentiation of its actual stationary phase. Put \[ A_i=e^{-c_0p_i},\quad R=e^{-c_0p_r} = rac{C Y_B(t)}{1-t},\quad D_*=- rac{(1-t)^2R(R-1)}{t c_0(C-1)C}. 	ag{32} \] For a weighted head the principal symbols from (11) are \[ E=z^{-1} rac{p}{1-p}(e^{-c_0p}-1),\quad F=z rac{1-p}{p}(1-e^{c_0p}),\quad K=-e^{-c_0p}. 	ag{33} \] At the boundary, (31) turns these, for \(i<r\), into \[ E_i= rac{c_i^0u}{t z_r}(A_i-1),\qquad F_i= rac{t z_r}{c_i^0u}(1-A_i^{-1}),\qquad c_i^0=(-1)^{r-i}. 	ag{34} \] The last head has the same formulas with \(t=1,c_r^0=1\). In the ordered suffix coproduct the alternating signs telescope. Writing \(B_i=\prod_{k=i}^r A_k\), direct multiplication gives \[ \Omega_i=c_i^0\left[  rac{(1-t)^2R-1-t^2}{t} - rac{(1-t)^2R(R-1)}{t B_i}ight]. 	ag{35} \] For \(i=r\) this is \(-2\), as it must be. At output vacuum the diagonal part of (16) is \(O(\epsilon)\). The leading coefficient in its raising row is \(-c_0(C-1)c_i^0\), while its right side is \(\Omega_i+\Omega_{i+1}\). Since \(B_1=C\), (35) gives \[  oxed{\quad S_{ho_i}(0,\xi)= D_*\left(\prod_{k=1}^i A_k-\prod_{k=1}^{i-1}A_kight). \quad} 	ag{36} \] This fixes the physical signs as well as the branch. Let \(Y=Y_B(t)\). Summing (36), and using \(e^{-c_0P}=(1-t)/Y\), gives \[ \sum_i S_{ho_i}(0,\xi) =F(P)= rac{(CY-1+t)(Y+t-1)}{t c_0(C-1)}. 	ag{37} \] The boundary quadratic in B gives \[ Y=1+t- rac{C+1}{C-1}t^2+O(t^3),\qquad P= rac2{c_0}t+O(t^2). \] Consequently \[ F(P)= rac2{c_0} + rac{C+1}{2(C-1)}P+O(P^2),\qquad F'(0)
e0 	ag{38} \] uniformly in the strict upper chamber. For fixed nonzero small \(P\), variations of the \(p_i\) with \(\sum p_i=P\) give rank \(s-1\) in the prefix-product differences in (36): the cumulative sums recover each prefix product, whose logarithmic derivatives are triangular and nonzero. Their output sum is zero. Equation (38) supplies the remaining radial rank. Hence the map \(p\mapsto(S_{ho_i})_i\) is invertible for sufficiently small nonzero \(P\) with bounded ratios \(p_i/P\). Finally the actual input map in these variables is \[ \xi_i=k(P) rac{p_i}{1-p_i},\qquad k(P)=t(P)/u(P)= rac{P}{ab}(1+O(P)), \quad a=2/c_0,\quad b=\sigma/(1-\sigma). 	ag{39} \] Its Jacobian determinant is exactly \[ k(P)^s\prod_i(1-p_i)^{-2} \left[1+ rac{k'(P)}{k(P)} \sum_i p_i(1-p_i)ight] =2\left( rac{P}{ab}ight)^s(1+O(P)). 	ag{40} \] It is nonzero on the chosen small balanced input domains. Combining (36)--(40) proves \[ \det S_{ho\xi}(0,\xi)
e0. 	ag{41} \] After shrinking the output neighborhood this remains nonzero. The local canonical nondegeneracy is therefore initialized by the actual contracted boundary, rather than assumed for the suffix system. ## 7. Original normalization and scope Combining (5) and (30) gives the actual full kernel \[ v(w)A_N^{(r)}c_T(z)= a_{00}^{(r)}(w_rz_r)^T inom dT\, N^{-p-1/2}e^{N S(ho,\xi;\sigma)} \mathcal A(ho,\xi;\sigma)(1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{42} \] It includes the complete physical matrix, its true binomial input, its width-dependent vacuum normalization and every finite cap. The \(N-1\) scalar and clock corrections are included in (9),(12) and the transport. The inactive monomial input directions have not been treated as independent Bessel saddles. This is a fixed-root, physical-integer-degree theorem on a specified small input sector and a small output neighborhood of the vacuum. It does not estimate the exterior braid/turnover factors of the original opposite kernel, its inverse Cartan coupon, its meridian normal or its closed source. It does not identify this local chart with a chosen geometric representation or continue the degree to a nonreal total moment. Those are distinct composition and source questions. title: Actual fixed-width Gauss monomial kernels on initialized sectors
text:
# Actual fixed-width Gauss monomial kernels on initialized sectors Private written proof, 18 November 2026. The exact suffix-Casimir equations propagate the actual initialized column to a full monomial kernel at any fixed width. The initial output domain is a separated winning sector of W, not a disk about the vacuum. A finite input-degree estimate, with an explicit output-shift budget, pays the entire remaining input cap. Compatibility of the transport equations is obtained from the actual finite solutions. The ordinary-binomial input is not transformed in this theorem. Inactive input phase slopes vanish. Its Cauchy interfaces can therefore carry new exponential phases, and cannot be replaced by repetitions of the two-head Bessel saddle. ## 1. Original finite matrices and the initialized domain Use \[ c_0=2\pi i,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad x=-q^{-1},\quad d=N-1,\quad f_n=(Q;Q)_n. 	ag{1} \] Fix \(r\ge2\), put \(s=r-1,\ p=r-2\), and restrict the actual \(r\)-head space to degree \(0\le T\le d\). Write its basis as \[ | etaangle=| eta_1,\ldots, eta_s,T-| eta|angle, \qquad  eta\in{\mathbb Z}_{\ge0}^s,\quad | eta|\le T. \] The chamber and exact clocks are \[ \sigma_N=(T+1)/N\in I\Subset(1/2,1),\quad C=Q^{-T-1},\quad K_{r,T}=x^rQ^{-T},\quad c_i=x^{r-i}. 	ag{2} \] The single-head actions are \[ Ew_a=(Q^{-a}-1)w_{a-1},\quad Fw_a=(1-Q^{a+1})w_{a+1},\quad Kw_a=xQ^{-a}w_a, \] with the actual zero endpoint arrows. The ordered totals satisfy \(E_{AB}=E_AK_B+E_B\), \(F_{AB}=F_A+K_A^{-1}F_B\). G's literal Gauss operator is \[ A_N^{(r)}=(-1)^dN\sum_{n=0}^d  rac{(-1)^nq^{n^2}}{f_n^2}F^nE^nK^{d-n}. 	ag{3} \] It is a polynomial in the total \(K,\Omega\). Every consecutive partial Casimir commutes with (3), by its centrality on the corresponding interval and the ordered coproduct. These matrices are symmetric in the original bilinear basis. Indeed on one head \(E^t=x^{-1}KF\), \(F^t=xEK^{-1}\). The coproduct gives the same identities for any interval. Hence \((FE)^t=KFEK^{-1}=FE\), and every interval Casimir is symmetric. Equation (3), or its Casimir-polynomial form in G, is consequently symmetric on each fixed degree. Let \(a_{00}^{(r)}=(A_N^{(r)})_{\mathbf0,\mathbf0}\). W proves that it is nonzero for all large \(N\) in (2). Retain it exactly, and define the full monomial kernel \[ {\cal K}_N(ho,\zeta) =\sum_{|\alpha|,| eta|\le T}  rac{(A_N^{(r)})_{\alpha eta}}{a_{00}^{(r)}} \prod_{i=1}^s c_i^{-\alpha_i- eta_i} ho^\alpha\zeta^ eta. 	ag{4} \] Its original homogeneous factors are \[ v_{\mathbf w}A_N^{(r)} \sum_ eta \left(\prod_{i=1}^s z_i^{ eta_i}ight)z_r^{T-| eta|} |\, eta,T-| eta|\,angle =a_{00}^{(r)}(w_rz_r)^T{\cal K}_N(ho,\zeta), \quad ho_i=c_iw_i/w_r,\quad \zeta_i=c_iz_i/z_r. 	ag{5} \] The input on the left is monomial; it has no inserted binomial weights. First shrink W's seed disk to lie inside the output disk of L's two-head analytic phase. Choose a winning index \(j\) and a small simply connected output polydisk \(D\), with a larger polydisk \(D^+\), on which W's coordinates are distinct, nonzero, and \[ \Re\phi(ho_j;C)\ge\eta,\qquad \Re\phi(ho_j;C)\ge \max_{i
e j}\{0,\Re\phi(ho_i;C)\}+\eta. 	ag{6} \] Assume the same inequalities with a smaller fixed gap hold on a neighborhood of \(\overline {D^+}\), uniformly for the chosen compact parameter arc in (2). Such polydisks exist by W. Its exact boundary theorem gives \[ N^p{\cal K}_N(ho,0) =e^{N\phi(ho_j;C)}{\cal A}_{m in}(ho;C) (1+O(N^{-1})), 	ag{7} \] with holomorphic relative error and fixed derivatives, where \[ {\cal A}_{m in} = rac{ho_j^p}{\prod_{i
e j}(ho_j-ho_i)}  rac{p!\,A_G(ho_j;C)W(ho_j;C)^p} {[a(C^{-1}-1)]^p}, \quad a=2/c_0,\quad W(t;C)= rac{C^{-1}-Y_B(t;C)}t. 	ag{8} \] Here \(\phi,A_G,Y_B\) are the actual two-head functions specified in W and L. Every factor in (8) is a unit on the chosen domain. The losing boundary branches remain inside the actual left side of (7); W estimates their full complement. ## 2. An exact triangular system at every width For \(1\le i\le s\), write \(\Omega_i=\Omega_{[i,r]}\), \(K_i=xQ^{-J_i}\), and \(\Omega_{r}=-2I\). The consecutive totals on \([i+1,r]\) are denoted \(E_t,F_t,K_t\). Define \[ D_i=\Omega_i-K_i^{-1}\Omega_{i+1}. \] Direct expansion, with the displayed operator order, gives \[ D_i=K_t[F_iE_i+q(K_i-K_i^{-1})] +F_iE_t+K_i^{-1}F_tE_iK_t. 	ag{9} \] For a physical input \( eta\), put \(k_i( eta)=xQ^{- eta_i}\). Since \(\Omega_{i+1}\) preserves \( eta_i\), the actual two commutators give the exact column identity \[ A_ND_i| etaangle =[\Omega_i-k_i( eta)^{-1}\Omega_{i+1}]A_N| etaangle. 	ag{10} \] There is just one term of \(D_i| etaangle\) which increases \(| eta|\): \[ a_i^+( eta)| eta+e_iangle,\qquad a_i^+( eta)=(1-Q^{ eta_i+1})(Q^{- eta_r}-1), \quad  eta_r=T-| eta|. 	ag{11} \] It comes from the last-head summand of \(F_iE_t\), so there is no additional tail clock. The other terms of \(F_iE_t\) preserve \(| eta|\); the last-head recipient of \(F_tE_iK_t\) lowers it, and its other recipients preserve it. The first term of (9) is diagonal. Thus every other input column in (10) has degree at most \(| eta|\). Formula (10) determines the column \( eta+e_i\) from columns of lower input degree. Different choices of a predecessor are compatible because these are identities of the same actual matrix. All endpoint zeros in (9)--(11) are retained. Choose a fixed small \(\delta>0\). For \(| eta|\le\delta N\), \[ |a_i^+( eta)|\ge c( eta_i+1)/N. 	ag{12} \] The first factor has this lower bound on the short root arc, while the second stays away from zero by (2). There is a useful generating version of its highest-input term. Let \(T_i f(\zeta)=f(\zeta_1,\ldots,Q\zeta_i,\ldots)\) and \(T_{m all}=\prod_iT_i\). The term (11), in (4), is \[  rac{c_i}{\zeta_i}(1-T_i)(CT_{m all}-1){\cal K}_N. 	ag{13} \] The numerator is divisible by \(\zeta_i\). On the formal logarithm \(V_N=N^{-1}\log(N^p{\cal K}_N)\), the coefficient of a new input multi-index \(\gamma\), \(|\gamma|=n\), has exact linear factor \[ c_iN(1-Q^{\gamma_i})(CQ^n-1),\qquad \gamma_i>0. 	ag{14} \] Its modulus is comparable to \(\gamma_i\) for \(n\le\delta N\). All other terms use lower input degree, with finite output clock shifts. This follows either by expanding (13), whose input increments have no constant term, or by taking the logarithm of (10). There is no extracted-vacuum term in these full-kernel equations. Reindexing an input lowering or transfer pairs each negative input monomial with its vanishing zero-occupation clock difference. The potential degree-\(T+1\) raising term in (13) is killed by \(CQ^{T+1}-1=0\). Thus all normalized exponentials below are differences of the logarithm at nearby clock arguments, rather than an uncontrolled quotient of a separately extracted column by the whole kernel. ## 3. Actual analytic estimates with an output-shift budget We record the estimate in sufficient detail to distinguish it from formal multi-variable Cauchy data. Initially \(V_N\) is a formal input series whose coefficients are holomorphic on \(D^+\); the constant coefficient is the calibrated logarithm of (7). All output operators in (10) have a fixed finite shift alphabet, depending only on \(r\). In homogeneous coordinates their actions are obtained from \[ E_i=w_i^{-1}(T_i^{-1}-1),\quad F_i=w_i(1-QT_i),\quad K_i=xT_i^{-1}. 	ag{15} \] After setting \(w_r=1\) and keeping total degree \(T\), their coefficients are analytic on \(D^+\) and their shifts are \(ho\mapsto Q^
uho\), with integer vectors \(
u\) in a fixed finite set. Factors \(Q^{\pm T}=Q^{\mp1}C^{\mp1}\) are kept exact. No large coefficient depending on an unscaled occupation is introduced. Expand output coefficients about the center of \(D^+\), and majorize absolute Taylor coefficients by a positive scalar variable \(y\), which dominates the sum of coordinate displacements. There is a constant \(L_r\) such that each output shift is majorized by \[ \varphi_h(y)=e^{L_rh}(1+y)-1,\qquad h=1/N. 	ag{16} \] For a positive analytic majorant \(F\), the integral of the derivative along the short rotation also gives \[ N\,|f(Q^
uho)-f(ho)| \preccurlyeq L_r(1+y)F'(\varphi_h(y)). 	ag{17} \] Here \(\preccurlyeq\) refers to absolute Taylor coefficient domination, with constants enlarged for the fixed alphabet. One can verify (17) directly by differentiating \(f(e^{t
u}ho)\) and majorizing its Taylor series on \(|t|\le |c_0|/N\). Use the input majorant variable \(z=\zeta_1+\cdots+\zeta_s\). An input coefficient of total degree \(n\) is bounded by the coefficient of \(z^n\), with its multinomial factor \(n!/\gamma!\). Under this convention division by (14) is bounded by a constant times division by \(n\): indeed \(\gamma_i n!/\gamma!=n(n-1)!/(\gamma-e_i)!\). Attach to each degree-\(n\) coefficient the output padding \(\varphi_{nh}(y)\). A subsequent output shift consumes one further step. In a product with input degrees \(n_1,\ldots,n_k\), every shifted factor fits inside the degree budget because \[ \max_\ell(n_\ell+1)\le\sum_\ell n_\ell+1. 	ag{18} \] The same inequality includes arbitrarily many degree-zero boundary factors. Analytic coefficient majorants may also be evaluated at the enlarged argument. Choose \(\delta\) so that every \(\varphi_{nh}\), \(n\le\delta N+1\), stays within the enlarged winning domain. This is where the fixed gap in (6) is used. We spell out a convergent positive majorant for the resulting logarithmic induction. After removing the exact coefficient (14), output increments are bounded by a constant times \((1+y)U_y\), and input increments by a constant times \(zU_z\). The finite coefficients in (9),(15) have a positive analytic majorant \(B(y)\). Input terms preserving degree carry at least one input variable after removable division. Their linear differences are bounded by \(B(y)zU_z\). A product of two such differences is bounded by \(B(y)zU_z^2\), multiplied by an exponential of \(B(y)zU_z\). For the linear double differences the coefficient bound \(n/N\le\delta\) reduces \(N^{-1}n^2\) to a constant times \(n\). All output terms are bounded by an exponential of the output increment and the input increment. Thus, with positive constants enlarged, one may use \[  egin{split} U_z=B(y)\{&1+U+U_y+zU_z\ &+\exp[B(y)((1+y)U_y+zU_z)]\ &+zU_z^2\exp[B(y)zU_z]\},\qquad U(y,0)=U_0(y). \end{split}	ag{19} \] Here \(U_0\) dominates the calibrated boundary logarithm on a larger output domain. The estimates above, with (18), prove coefficientwise domination by induction on total input degree; they do not require that output derivatives be bounded by a fixed number independently of their order. Equation (19) is analytic with a genuine local solution. Its right side has derivative \(O(z)\) with respect to the unknown \(U_z\). Solve for \(U_z=H(y,z,U,U_y)\) by positive analytic iteration on a bounded polydisk. Integrate its characteristic system \[ \dot y=-H_P,\quad \dot U=H-PH_P,\quad \dot P=H_y+H_U P. 	ag{20} \] The initial projection derivative is one. Uniform analytic Picard iteration for a small fixed complex time, followed by its analytic inverse, constructs the solution. All coefficients are nonnegative, since the implicit iteration and input-degree recursion are positive. This proves convergence, and bounds the degree-\(n\) logarithmic coefficient by a fixed geometric sequence on a smaller output domain, with the padding (16). The constants are uniform in \(N,T\); no resonance beyond the low band is inverted. The same argument gives stability. Subtract two logarithmic rows with uniformly bounded positive backgrounds. Factor each exponential difference by the increment difference. After the normal term (14) has been removed, the new majorant is linear: \[ E_z=B_1(y,z)(E+E_y)+zB_2(y,z)E_z+\varepsilon^kB_3(y,z), \quad E(y,0)=O(\varepsilon^k),\quad \varepsilon=1/N. 	ag{21} \] The coefficients are fixed positive analytic functions on smaller domains. The output padding remains (18). Invert \(1-zB_2\) and use (20) in its linear form. It follows that the low logarithmic error is \(O(\varepsilon^k)\), uniformly on a still smaller output domain and input polydisk. This estimate applies in particular for \(k=1,2\). There is no omitted finite tail. All entries of the original total \(E,F,K^{\pm1}\) have uniformly bounded operator norms at fixed width. As in L, \(e^{-cN}\le |f_n|\le e^{cN}\). Equations (3) and W's nonzero normalization give an \(e^{cN}\) bound for every coefficient of \(N^p{\cal K}_N\). On any fixed bounded output domain, summing its finite output monomials changes only \(c\). Let \(V_N^{[k]}\) retain input degrees at most \(k_N=\lfloor\delta Nfloor\). Then \(e^{NV_N^{[k]}}\) and \(N^p{\cal K}_N\) agree through that input degree. Both are bounded by \(e^{cN}\) on a fixed comparison domain. Cauchy's coefficient estimate in \(s\) input variables gives a tail bounded by \[ C(k_N+1)^{s-1}e^{cN}(\varrho/R)^{k_N+1} /(1-\varrho/R)^s. 	ag{22} \] The inverse of \(e^{NV_N^{[k]}}\) costs at most \(e^{c'N}\). Choose the fixed final input radius \(\varrho\) sufficiently small after \(\delta\). Then (22) is exponentially relative. This proves actual zero-freeness and whole-cap recovery on the chosen output sector times that input polydisk. ## 4. Phase, compatible transport, and the actual kernel Let \(S_2(u,v;C)\) be L's initialized two-head phase. The principal solution on the winning branch is \[ S(ho,\zeta;C)=S_2(ho_j,\zeta_j;C). 	ag{23} \] This can be checked in every suffix row, not merely the total Casimir. In the monomial principal symbols \[ e_i=w_i^{-1}(e^{-c_0t_i}-1),\quad f_i=w_i(1-e^{c_0t_i}),\quad k_i=-e^{-c_0t_i}, \] every inactive momentum \(t_i\) is zero. Its head has \(e_i=f_i=0,k_i=-1\). A suffix containing only such heads and the last head has constant Casimir. A suffix containing the active head reduces to a scalar sign times the active two-head Casimir. If there are \(h\) inactive heads between \(j\) and \(r\), rescaling its first coordinate by \((-1)^h\) produces precisely the active two-head coproduct. The leading value of \(c_j=x^{r-j}\) in (4) supplies this sign. Thus L's two-head Hamiltonian identity proves all principal rows. The exact \(x\) half shifts and \(Q^T=Q^{-1}C^{-1}\) remain for transport. For clarity compatibility of the transport is not assumed. The principal substitution (23) has residual \(O(N^{-1})\) in all normalized logarithmic rows, and its boundary differs from the actual logarithm by \(O(N^{-1})\), by (7). The stability estimate (21), followed by (22), gives \[ V_N-S=O(N^{-1}). 	ag{24} \] Consequently \(W_N=N(V_N-S)\) is a uniformly bounded holomorphic family on smaller domains. At each limiting clock \(C\) in the compact arc, take integer degrees tending to it. Cauchy bounds on Taylor coefficients and a diagonal subsequence give a uniformly convergent subsequence on smaller polydisks. Its analytic limit \(\alpha\) satisfies every first-order transport row, obtained by expanding the exact shifts in (9),(10),(13), and \[ \alpha(ho,0)=\log{\cal A}_{m in}(ho;C). 	ag{25} \] At the initial input face the normal coefficient in the \(i\)-th row is a nonzero scalar multiple of \(c_0(C-1)\partial_{\zeta_i}\). More generally its formal input-degree recursion is the limit of (14), so it determines each next coefficient uniquely from the lower input degrees. Thus the limit is unique and the transport rows are compatible. Their coefficients and this recursion depend analytically on \(C\); the Cauchy bounds just obtained are uniform on its compact arc. This constructs a uniformly analytic transport solution without assuming a globally noncharacteristic multi-time system. Uniform analyticity here is in the output and input variables. Analytic coefficient dependence on \(C\) follows from the recursion; the real-arc limit argument does not assert a uniform complex-\(C\) neighborhood. Equivalently \(\alpha\) is specified completely by (25) and the coefficient of \(N^{-1}\) in the exact logarithmic equations (9),(10),(13), with \(q=e^{c_0/(2N)}\), \(x=-e^{-c_0/(2N)}\), \(Q^T=Q^{-1}C^{-1}\) before expansion. This definition retains every subprincipal clock and the \(T=N\sigma_N-1\) offset. It leaves no freely chosen amplitude. Substitute \(S+\alpha/N\) into the finite equations. Taylor expansion of their fixed shift alphabet on larger polydisks gives an analytic residual \(O(N^{-2})\), since the principal and all transport rows vanish. The boundary error is \(O(N^{-2})\) by (7). Applying (21) with \(k=2\), then recovering the entire cap by (22), proves the actual result \[  oxed{\quad {\cal K}_N(ho,\zeta) =N^{-p}e^{NS_2(ho_j,\zeta_j;C)} {\cal A}_r(ho,\zeta;C)(1+O(N^{-1})), \qquad {\cal A}_r=e^\alpha . \quad}	ag{26} \] The amplitude is an analytic unit and equals (8) at \(\zeta=0\). The relative error and all fixed output/input derivatives have the same estimate on smaller domains. All losing branches of the initialized column and every finite input coefficient were included in the proof. No positivity or tame spectral frame was used. ## 5. Why the ordinary-binomial input remains a separate step Equation (26) is a full matrix kernel in its stated monomial polarization. It has only one active principal input slope: \[ S_{\zeta_i}(ho,0)=0\quad(i
e j). 	ag{27} \] Thus L's nonzero-slope coefficient circle does not apply in all input variables. The distinction is substantive. Already the finite identity kernel in one such variable has \[ \sum_{a=0}^d(ho\zeta)^a = rac{1-(ho\zeta)^N}{1-ho\zeta}; \] on a small product disk its principal phase is zero, while its literal binomial input is \(\sum_a inom da(ho\eta)^a=(1+ho\eta)^d\). Its exponential phase is recovered at the Cauchy interface, not from a nonzero small-circle slope. An \(O(N^{-1})\) monomial relative estimate alone does not justify that further transform. The inactive dependence of \({\cal A}_r\), whose initial row (8) contains explicit Cauchy factors, is therefore retained in full. No pole is selected or deleted here. A later binomial theorem would have to keep those interfaces, their caps and competing branches on the actual extraction cycles. Finally the original factors in (5), the exact \(a_{00}^{(r)}\), and G's surrounding quotient braid, top Cartan and turnover remain unchanged. Fixed real occupation sectors do not establish a chart for a loxodromic geometric total moment. No meridian normal, geometric-source coefficient, or closed-source lower bound is asserted. ## Complete proof directs * G: notes/research_opposite_kernel_forced_cyclic_normalization.md, SHA256 42e6d6c3a5039859c241a2832de56301eff49d749db86d67868f3534c89aaaaa. * W: notes/research_fixed_width_gauss_boundary_branches.md, SHA256 cdcb82d2bd48948ff45baaec65a71f639607e10a9bc12acff344e34ae972d404. * L: notes/research_actual_gauss_coherent_goursat_kernel.md, SHA256 37ade960cb7938372b7854b00aebc1df82e648144f850fcd4a356f68a00159e1.
