For real \(w>2\), multiplying the rational amplitudes by \(w+1\) gives a uniformly bounded holomorphic family, bounded away from zero at the saddle. The physical tails have at most polynomial loss from \(w-c_a\), uniformly after the same multiplication. This proves the stated uniformity. Evenness in \(u\) ensures holomorphy in the ordinary color disk; Cauchy's formula applied to the normalized error proves its ordinary derivative claims. In particular an angular derivative vanishing at \(u=0\) has not been substituted for an ordinary outside normal. \(\square\) ## 4. Uniform physical defects and exterior pair colors **Theorem 3.** On a smaller fixed disk \(|\zeta+2|<r_n\), uniformly over every distinct physical node, \[ D_{n,N}(c_a;\zeta) =-\epsilon_NN^{-2}b_n^{\rm e/o}(c_a;\zeta) e^{N\mathcal S_n(\zeta)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{21} \] The normalized error has all fixed ordinary outside-color derivatives \(O(N^{-1})\). The coefficients in (21) are uniformly bounded above and away from zero, so the actual defect values are nonzero for all sufficiently large levels. *Proof.* Use the exact pole cancellation in the [physical normal-defect packet](research_physical_normal_defect_packet.md). If \(I^{\rm tail}\) interpolates the omitted source values and zero on all retained nodes, the omitted Cauchy sum is \(NI^{\rm tail}/Q_N\). At an outside physical node the exact identity is \[ D_{n,N}(c_a;\zeta) =\frac{\partial_wh_{n,N}(c_a;\zeta) -\partial_wI^{\rm tail}_{n,N}(c_a;\zeta)} {Q_N'(c_a)} -\frac{\mathcal J_{n,N}(c_a;\zeta)}N. \tag{22} \] At an inside node it is \(D=-(\mathcal J+\mathcal T)/N\). The first term in (22), and the inside tail, have a fixed gap by (15) and the polynomial cardinal differentiation bounds. Those bounds commute with ordinary outside derivatives. The odd simple node is inside and uses its ramified residue, not an original first normal. The contour packet for \(\mathcal J(c_a;\zeta)\) is uniform over all \(c_a\in[-2,2]\). Its horizontal Cauchy denominators are uniformly separated; on the midpoint vertical sides they cost at most \(O(N)\), already absorbed by the strict gap. At the perturbed saddle \(c_a+2\cos t_n(\zeta)\) stays uniformly away from zero. The proof of Theorem 2 therefore gives \(\mathcal J(c_a;\zeta)= \epsilon_NN^{-1}b_n^{\rm e/o}(c_a;\zeta) e^{N\mathcal S_n(\zeta)}(1+O(N^{-1}))\). Substitute in the exact identities to obtain (21). Uniform holomorphy and a smaller outside disk give the normalized derivative conclusion. \(\square\) There is also a local consequence at each actual unit-charge positive pair of fixed integer powers \(n,p\ge3\). Let \(t_*\) be its angle at the power-\(n\) vertex. The independent [pair-to-half-charge theorem](research_pair_half_charge_action_gap.md) places \(t_*\) strictly outside the half-charge rectangle and gives \(\Re S_n(t_*;-2)>\Re\mathcal S_n(-2)\). These strict inequalities persist for \(t\) near \(t_*\) and \(\zeta\) near \(-2\). The exact exterior residue formula therefore yields, with some fixed \(\delta>0\), \[ \begin{split} D_{n,N}(-2\cos t;\zeta) &=\frac{h_{n,N}(-2\cos t;\zeta)}{Q_N(-2\cos t)} (1+O(N^{-1/2}e^{-\delta N}))\\ &=\epsilon_NN^{-3/2}\chi_{\rm e/o}(t) \widehat a_e(t,\zeta)e^{NS_n(t;\zeta)}(1+O(N^{-1})),\\ \chi_{\rm e}(t)&=1,\qquad \chi_{\rm o}(t)=\frac{i}{2\sin(t/2)}. \end{split} \tag{23} \] All fixed ordinary derivatives in both colors are retained, in the differentiated holomorphic sense. The original crossing carrier \(C_{N,n}=\exp\{\pi in(N-1)^2/(4N)\}\) was omitted in (18) and is restored exactly once in an original trace. At odd levels the top-degree correction is still present. With \(\ell_{n,N}(\zeta)=[w^m]I_{n,N}(w;\zeta)\), \[ \phi_N[R^nK_N(\,\cdot\,,\zeta)e_m] =C_{N,n}(-1)^mN\ell_{n,N}(\zeta),\qquad N\ell_{n,N}(\zeta) =\lim_{w\to+\infty}w\,\mathcal O_{n,N}(w;\zeta). \tag{24} \] Thus this endpoint also has the nonzero packet obtained from (20), with coefficient \(b_{n,\infty}^{\rm o}(\zeta)\). Formula (24) is the original odd rank-one term, not a missing physical first normal. These results provide a free-outside source packet and the whole-contour and omitted-row estimates needed for composition. They do not justify replacing a coherent shared-index transform by its finite-order physical-row expansion. The remaining joint cycle and its possible cancellations require their own estimate. ## 5. Whole outside-period decay, with a complex strip The complete half-charge contour also gives an upper bound on the whole outside period. This assertion concerns the exact observation and the exact defect values; it does not continue the local relative expansion (20) to distant outside colors. **Theorem 4.** For each fixed integer \(n\ge3\) there are \(c,B,h_*>0\) such that, for every fixed ordinary derivative order \(k\), some \(C_k,A_k\) satisfy \[ \begin{split} &(w+1)\left|\partial_\zeta^k \mathcal O_{n,N}(w;\zeta)\right| +\max_a\left|\partial_\zeta^k D_{n,N}(c_a;\zeta)\right|\\ &\hspace{10mm}\le C_kN^{A_k} \exp N\{M_n-c(1-\cos u)+Bv^2\},\\ &\qquad \zeta=-2\cos(u+iv),\quad -\pi\le u\le\pi,\quad |v|\le h_*,\quad w>2. \end{split} \tag{25} \] The constants are independent of the physical row and of the level parity. The odd top trace in (24), and each of its fixed ordinary outside derivatives, obeys the same upper exponent. *Proof.* Keep the complete half-charge rectangle of height \(H_0\). After the exact folding of its horizontal sides, choose a small fixed neighborhood of the unique saddle on the lower side. Its closure lies in the domain of the free-edge theorem. On this neighborhood the [whole-period edge estimate](research_pair_free_boundary_kernel.md#7-whole-outside-period-decay-and-a-complex-strip) gives, including all fixed ordinary outside derivatives, \[ |K_N(-2\cos t,-2\cos(u+iv))| \le CN^A\exp N\{\Re\psi(t,0) -\kappa(1-\cos u)+B_0v^2\}. \tag{26} \] The original crossing and the lower sine or cosine denominator add exactly the terms which turn \(\Re\psi(t,0)\) into \(\Re S_n(t;-2)\), up to bounded factors. This real part is at most \(M_n\) on the complete horizontal side. The denominator's nonconstant term is retained and uniformly bounded there. Consequently the contribution of this saddle neighborhood has the upper exponent in (25), with \(c\le\kappa\) and \(B\ge B_0\). No assumption about the location of a saddle for distant \(u\) is made. Every other horizontal piece, each vertical connector, and the original omitted physical rows have a complete-outside gap. Let \(\delta>0\) be a common lower bound for that gap, after removing the small saddle neighborhood. Equations (10) and (15) bound these pieces, for arbitrary real \(u\), by \[ CN^A\exp N\{M_n-\delta+|v|\}. \tag{27} \] Their ordinary outside derivatives have the same exponent by (10) and (11). Shrink the strip so that \(|v|\le\delta/4\), and choose \(c\le\delta/8\). Since \(1-\cos u\le2\), \[ M_n-\delta+|v| \le M_n-\frac{3\delta}{4} < M_n-c(1-\cos u). \tag{28} \] Thus these full error sectors retain the angular loss as well. This use of a fixed gap is why no individual angular decay of every omitted normal row is required. For the observation, all Cauchy factors have the polynomial uniform bounds used in Theorem 2, after multiplication by \(w+1\). For a physical defect row, use its exact inside or outside identity (22). The saddle Cauchy factors are uniformly bounded over the entire real physical interval. The midpoint vertical factors cost only powers of \(N\). Its additional regular first-normal and tail-interpolant terms satisfy (27) by (11), (14), and the fixed polynomial collocation bounds. This proves (25), with every physical row included. All derivatives here act on the ordinary polynomial color \(\zeta\). On the saddle neighborhood this is part of (26); on the complement it follows from the proved polynomial bounds, including at \(\zeta=\pm2\). In particular no division by \(\sin u\) or loss of an endpoint normal is used. Finally multiply the exact finite observation (18) by \(w\) and let \(w\to+\infty\) in the bound (25). Formula (24) transfers the result to the original odd top term. The original crossing carrier has unit modulus. This proves the theorem. \(\square\) The inequalities in (25) are upper bounds for genuine source observations, with an independently proved local nonzero packet from Theorems 2–3. They leave the signed shared-wire closure and its global cycle coefficient open.

title: A full-degree generating section with its original source normalization
text:
# A full-degree generating section with its original source normalization 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The centered Conway basis has a generating polynomial whose finite quantum-difference equation includes the exact characteristic-polynomial forcing. At every physical Casimir node it factors into finite products. This gives a nonzero dilogarithmic approximation on the entire open unit disk, uniformly through both ends of the physical index range. The same approximation retains the actual first Casimir normals. Their proof uses an exact cyclic primitive with a necessary central correction, rather than differentiation of values interpolated between the physical nodes. An explicit analytic section is exponentially accurate in all these physical Hermite coordinates. A separate small-disk estimate reaches fixed off-spectrum Casimir labels too. Neither statement identifies the original closing of a general assembled short component. ## 1. The actual generating polynomial and its terminal equation Use the full algebra and centered basis of [the Fourier compiler](research_centered_fourier_conway_compiler.md): \[ N\ge2,\quad d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad p=Q^{-1},\quad \eta=(-1)^d,\quad P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2 . \] The quotient \(\mathcal H_N=\mathbb C[z]/P_N\) retains first derivatives at double roots. Its physical nodes are \[ c_j=q^{2j+1}+q^{-2j-1},\qquad 0\le j\le d. \] The centered basis satisfies \[ f_a=N^{-1/2}R^+p_a(z),\qquad p_0=1, \] where \(R^+\) is the original invertible positive crossing and \[ zp_a=(p^{a+1}-1)p_{a+1}+2q^{-1}p^ap_a+(p^a-1)p_{a-1} \quad(0\le a<d). 	ag{1} \] Here \(p_{-1}=0\); the symbol \(p\) without an index is the root \(Q^{-1}\), not one of the polynomials. Each \(p_a\) has degree \(a\). Define \[ G_N(t;z)=\sum_{a=0}^{d}p_a(z)t^a,\qquad D_N(t)=1-\eta t^N=1+(-1)^Nt^N . 	ag{2} \] Every coefficient in (2) is an ordinary polynomial in \(z\). For completeness, the terminal relation in (1) has the following ordinary-polynomial normalization. Put \[ \mathcal P_a=(-1)^a(p;p)_a p_a\quad(0\le a\le d). \] These are monic. Define the next monic polynomial by the terminal recurrence, rather than by a vanishing factorial: \[ \mathcal P_{m term} =(z-2q^{-1}p^d)\mathcal P_d-(1-p^d)^2\mathcal P_{d-1}. \] The actual endpoint identity for multiplication by \(z\) in the centered basis shows \(\mathcal P_{m term}=0\) in \(\mathcal H_N\). Its degree is \(N\) and its leading coefficient is one. It is therefore exactly \(P_N\). Also \((p;p)_d=N\), by factoring \(u^N-1\) at \(u=1\). Consequently summing (1), including its terminal remainder, gives \[  oxed{\quad (1+q^{-1}t)^2G_N(pt;z)-(1+zt+t^2)G_N(t;z) = rac{(-1)^N}{N}P_N(z)t^N . \quad} 	ag{3} \] Indeed the coefficient of \(t^{a+1}\), for \(a<d\), is (1); the last coefficient is \[ (2q^{-1}p^d-z)p_d+(p^d-1)p_{d-1} =- rac{P_N(z)}{(-1)^dN}. 	ag{4} \] No polynomial \(p_N\) has been defined by division by zero. Let \(b(t,z)=1+zt+t^2\). If \(z=w+w^{-1}\), factoring the finite products proves the exact cyclic norm identity \[  oxed{\quad \prod_{k=0}^{N-1} rac{b(p^kt,z)}{(1+q^{-1}p^kt)^2} =1- rac{(-1)^NP_N(z)t^N}{D_N(t)^2}. \quad} 	ag{5} \] Both sides are polynomial identities after denominators are cleared, so no choice of \(w\) is needed in the assertion. In the full nonreduced algebra \(\mathcal H_N\), this norm is one wherever \(D_N(t)
e0\). Off that algebraic relation, the forcing in (3) remains. It cannot be replaced by a homogeneous eigenfunction equation at an arbitrary geometric Casimir value. There is a precise local section ambiguity, also in the nonreduced algebra. In \(\mathcal H_N[[t]]\), the polynomial \(G_N\) is a formal unit with constant coefficient one and satisfies \[ G_N(pt)= rac{b(t,z)}{(1+q^{-1}t)^2}G_N(t). 	ag{5a} \] If \(F\) is any other formal unit solution with \(F(0)=1\), then \(F/G_N\) is invariant under \(t\mapsto pt\). Comparison of coefficients, using that \(p\) is primitive, proves \[ F/G_N\in1+t^N\mathcal H_N[[t^N]]. 	ag{5b} \] Conversely every such factor gives another normalized solution. Multiplication by this group is free and transitive on the normalized solutions. This is the local section torsor meant here. No semisimple quotient or general Hilbert 90 theorem is used. There is also an explicit finite-product analytic cochain. Set \(a(t,z)=b(t,z)/(1+q^{-1}t)^2\), and anchor all logarithms at zero: \[ \mathcal E_N(t,z)= \exp\!\left\{ rac1N\sum_{k=0}^{d}k\log a(p^kt,z)ight\}. 	ag{5c} \] Reindexing the finite sum proves \[  rac{\mathcal E_N(pt,z)}{\mathcal E_N(t,z)} = rac{a(t,z)}{\operatorname{Norm}(a)(t,z)^{1/N}}, 	ag{5d} \] with the anchored norm root. On \(\mathcal H_N\) it is a normalized solution, so (5b) applies. Off shell, (5) implies that its logarithmic coefficients through degree \(N-1\) still equal those of \(G_N\). Hence \(\mathcal E_N-G_N\in(t^N)\), coefficientwise in \(z\), on its Taylor domain. Its branch divisors are the explicitly displayed zeros and poles of the finitely many \(a(p^kt,z)\). ## 2. Exact factorization at every physical node Write \(a_l(t)=1+q^{-1}Q^lt\), with integer \(l\). Then \(D_N(t)=\prod_{l=1}^N a_l(t)\). **Proposition 1.** For every \(0\le j\le d\), \[  oxed{\quad G_N(t;c_j)=D_N(t)  rac{\prod_{l=-j+1}^{0}a_l(t)} {\prod_{l=1}^{j+1}a_l(t)} . \quad} 	ag{6} \] The displayed quotient has its removable values at the canceled factors. It is an ordinary polynomial of degree \(d\), with constant coefficient one. All its zeros lie on \[ t^N=\eta . 	ag{7} \] **Proof.** The denominator in (6) consists of distinct factors of \(D_N\), so cancellation gives a polynomial of degree \(N-(j+1)+j=d\). Its constant coefficient is one. Since \(a_l(pt)=a_{l-1}(t)\), its shift ratio is \[  rac{a_{-j}(t)a_{j+1}(t)}{a_0(t)^2} = rac{1+c_jt+t^2}{(1+q^{-1}t)^2}. 	ag{8} \] Thus it satisfies (3) at \(z=c_j\). In degrees \(1,\ldots,d\), the coefficient recursion has nonzero factors \(p^a-1\). The constant coefficient therefore determines the degree-\(d\) solution uniquely. This proves (6). Every remaining numerator factor is one of the factors of \(D_N\), possibly repeated, proving (7). \(\square\) It follows that \(G_N(t)\) is a unit of the complete algebra \(\mathcal H_N\) for \(D_N(t)
e0\): its value at every spectral root is nonzero. This statement uses the ordinary unit criterion in each local factor \(\mathbb C[\epsilon]/\epsilon^m\); it does not discard its nilpotent coordinate. ## 3. A uniform phase and amplitude on the physical unit disk For \(|t|<1\) and \(z\) in a neighborhood of \([-2,2]\), define the analytic branches \[ A(t,z)=b(t,z)^{-1/2},\qquad \Phi(t,z)=- rac1{2\pi i}\int_0^t  rac{\log b(u,z)-2\log(1+u)}u\,du . 	ag{9} \] They are normalized by \(A(0,z)=1,\Phi(0,z)=0\). For any fixed closed subdisk, a common complex neighborhood of \([-2,2]\) suffices. The integrand at zero is removable. At \(z=w+w^{-1}\), this is equivalently \[ \Phi(t,z)= rac{ \operatorname{Li}_2(-wt)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-w^{-1}t) -2\operatorname{Li}_2(-t)}{2\pi i}, 	ag{10} \] where the analytic branches in (9), not a new cut, determine (10). **Proposition 2.** For every \(0<ho<1\), uniformly for all physical indices and levels, \[ G_N(t;c_j)=D_N(t)A(t,c_j)e^{N\Phi(t,c_j)} (1+O_ho(N^{-1})), \qquad |t|\leho . 	ag{11} \] The relative error is holomorphic in \(t\), and its fixed \(t\)-derivatives are \(O(N^{-1})\) on smaller disks. **Proof.** Put \(u_j=(j+1/2)/N\), and set \(F(v)=\log(1+te^{2\pi iv})\), using its branch at \(t=0\). All its required real-\(v\) derivatives are uniformly bounded for \(|t|\leho<1\). The numerator product in (6) samples midpoints on \([-j/N,0]\); the denominator samples midpoints on \([0,(j+1)/N]\). Composite midpoint summation, followed by moving the two outer endpoints by \(1/(2N)\), gives \[ \log rac{G_N(t;c_j)}{D_N(t)} =N\!\left(\int_{-u_j}^0F(v)\,dv-\int_0^{u_j}F(v)\,dvight) - rac{F(-u_j)+F(u_j)}2+O_ho(N^{-1}). 	ag{12} \] The midpoint error is bounded by a constant times \((j+1)/N^2\le1/N\). The endpoint Taylor errors are also \(O(1/N)\). This includes \(j=0,d\); no interior-index restriction is used. The integral in (12) is \(\Phi(t,c_j)\), and the two endpoint terms give \(\log A(t,c_j)\). Exponentiation proves (11). Cauchy's formula on nested disks gives the derivative statement. \(\square\) ## 4. The actual first normal and its central correction The value formula alone cannot be differentiated in the discrete index \(j\). Instead differentiate the actual polynomial \(G_N(t;z)\) in its Casimir variable \(z\). Fix a double node \(c_j=2\cos	heta_j\), where \(	heta_j=(2j+1)\pi/N\); thus \(\sin	heta_j
e0\). Set \[ H_j(t)= rac{\partial_zG_N(t;c_j)}{G_N(t;c_j)},\qquad R_j(t)= rac{t}{b(t,c_j)}. 	ag{13} \] These are rational functions. Differentiating (3), and using \(P_N'(c_j)=0\), gives \[ H_j(pt)-H_j(t)=R_j(t). 	ag{14} \] The differentiated cyclic norm identity (5) gives \(\sum_{k=0}^{d}R_j(p^kt)=0\). **Proposition 3.** The actual logarithmic derivative is \[  oxed{\quad H_j(t)= rac1N\sum_{k=0}^{d}kR_j(p^kt) -\eta\, rac{d-2j}{2i\sin	heta_j}\,  rac{t^N}{D_N(t)} . \quad} 	ag{15} \] In particular the central function of \(t^N\) is retained. **Proof.** Let \(H_{m part}=N^{-1}\sum kR_j(p^kt)\). Reindexing this finite sum and using its zero cyclic average proves (14) for \(H_{m part}\). Thus \(H_j-H_{m part}\) is invariant under \(t\mapsto pt\). All its poles lie on (7). It vanishes at zero and is bounded at infinity: \(G_N(t;c_j)\) has degree exactly \(d\), while its Casimir derivative has degree at most \(d\). At \(t_*=-q^{-1}\), formula (6) shows \(G_N(t_*;c_j)
e0\), because the factor \(a_1\) is canceled and is not restored by the numerator. Hence the invariant difference has at most a simple pole there. Cyclic invariance implies the same at every point of (7). Multiplication by \(D_N\) now gives an invariant polynomial of degree at most \(N\), vanishing at zero. Consequently the difference is \(C t^N/D_N\). Write \(w=e^{i	heta_j}=qQ^j\). At \(t_*\), only terms \(k=j,d-j\) in \(H_{m part}\) can have a pole. Their residues in \(R_j(p^kt)\) are, respectively, \(-q^{-1}/(w-w^{-1})\) and \(q^{-1}/(w-w^{-1})\). Therefore \[ \operatorname{Res}_{t=t_*}H_{m part} = rac{q^{-1}(d-2j)}{N(w-w^{-1})},\qquad \operatorname{Res}_{t=t_*} rac{t^N}{D_N(t)} = rac{\eta q^{-1}}N . 	ag{16} \] Canceling this pole fixes \(C=-\eta(d-2j)/(w-w^{-1})\), proving (15). \(\square\) There is a useful equivalent finite sum. Choose the representative \(0\le j<d/2\) of a double node and set \[ s_j=2i\sin	heta_j,\qquad F_l(t)= rac{q^{-1}Q^lt}{1+q^{-1}Q^lt}. \] Then \[ H_j(t)= rac1{s_j} \sum_{l=j+2}^{N-j}F_l(t). 	ag{16a} \] Indeed \(R_j=(F_{j+1}-F_{-j})/s_j\). Cyclic reindexing of the weighted sum in (15) gives \[ H_{m part}= rac1{s_j}\left[ \sum_{l=j+2}^{N-j}F_l- rac{d-2j}{N} \sum_{l=1}^NF_light]. \] Since \(\sum_{l=1}^NF_l=tD_N'/D_N=-\eta Nt^N/D_N\), its last term cancels the central correction exactly. This is a cancellation proved with the central term present, not permission to omit that term in the primitive. **Theorem 4.** Define the actual relative error near the physical nodes by \[ \epsilon_N(t,z)=  rac{G_N(t;z)}{D_N(t)A(t,z)e^{N\Phi(t,z)}}-1 . 	ag{17} \] For every \(ho<1\), its complete physical Hermite data obey \[ |\epsilon_N(t,c_j)|\le C_ho/N,\qquad |\partial_z\epsilon_N(t,c_j)|\le C_ho/N \quad(c_j\ \hbox{double}),\qquad |t|\leho . 	ag{18} \] Only the value is required at the odd simple node \(-2\). Fixed \(t\)-derivatives have the same bounds on smaller disks. **Proof.** The value estimate is Proposition 2. To estimate (15), expand \[ R_j(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}r_nt^n,\qquad r_n=(-1)^{n-1} rac{\sin(n	heta_j)}{\sin	heta_j}. 	ag{19} \] For all real physical nodes, \(|r_n|\le n\). At double nodes \(r_{\ell N}=0\). Finite Fourier summation in \(H_{m part}\) therefore gives coefficient \(r_n/(p^n-1)\) when \(N
mid n\) and zero otherwise. For \(n\le N/2\), the Bernoulli expansion, uniformly away from its next pole, gives \[  rac{r_n}{p^n-1} =- rac{r_n}{(2\pi i/N)n}- rac{r_n}2 +O(n^2/N). 	ag{20} \] Every Taylor coefficient of the actual \(H_j\) has bound \(CN^2\): formula (16a) has at most \(N\) summands with coefficient modulus one, and \(|\sin	heta_j|\ge2/N\). Thus its tail above \(N/2\) costs at most a polynomial in \(N\) times \(ho^{N/2}\). The leading terms in (20) have the same tail bound, since \(|r_n|\le n\). The central term starts at degree \(N\) and has coefficient bounded by \(CN^2\), consistent with this estimate. Summing (20) and these tails proves \[ H_j(t)=N\Phi_z(t,c_j) - rac{t}{2b(t,c_j)}+O_ho(N^{-1}). 	ag{22} \] Here \(\Phi_z=-(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_0^tdu/b(u,z)\), directly from (9), and \(A_z/A=-t/(2b)\). Taking the logarithmic derivative of (17) at the actual double node now proves the second estimate in (18). No value-only interpolation was differentiated. Holomorphy in \(t\) and Cauchy estimates prove the remaining assertions. \(\square\) The theorem is a relative estimate in the full physical Hermite coordinates. It is not a uniform estimate in the Newton packet norm, whose conversion can amplify componentwise errors. ## 5. Original source normalizations The functional \(\psi(g)=\phi((R^+)^2g)/N\) satisfies \(\psi(p_ap_b)=\delta_{ab}\). Hence, exactly, \[ \psi(G_N(t))=1. 	ag{23} \] This is the fixed source normalization of the section, not an unknown knot value. With \(x=-q^{-1}\), define the actual open packet \[ \mathcal F_N(t)= rac{R^+G_N(t)}{\sqrt N} =\sum_{a=0}^{d}f_at^a . \] The two original closure rows of the centered compiler give \[  oxed{\quad \phi(\mathcal F_N(t)) = rac{\kappa^{-1}D_N(t)}{\sqrt N(1-xt)},\qquad m(\mathcal F_N(t)) = rac{\kappa D_N(t)}{\sqrt N(1-x^{-1}t)}. \quad} 	ag{24} \] Both formulas have their removable polynomial values at a canceled factor. In particular neither closing vanishes off (7). Their scalar rate on fixed interior disks is zero; no hyperbolic volume has been assigned to these normalizing packets. ## 6. An exponentially accurate section and its off-spectrum germ The exact low-degree logarithm supplies a zero-free analytic section. Let \(S_n(z)=2T_n(z/2)\), and set \[ \ell_{N,n}(z)=  rac{(-1)^{n+1}(S_n(z)-2q^{-n})}{n(p^n-1)} \quad(1\le n<N),\qquad U_N(t,z)=\exp\!\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\ell_{N,n}(z)t^night). 	ag{25} \] The forcing in (3) starts at degree \(N\), so the formal logarithm of \(G_N\) through degree \(N-1\) is exactly the exponent in (25). Thus \(G_N-U_N\) is divisible by \(t^N\), coefficientwise as a formal series of ordinary polynomials in \(z\). On the full physical Hermite coordinates one has the stronger estimate \[  oxed{\quad \left| rac{G_N(t;c_j)}{U_N(t,c_j)}-1ight| +\left|\left.\partial_z\! \left( rac{G_N(t;z)}{U_N(t,z)}ight)ight|_{z=c_j}ight| \le C_ho N^2ho^N,\qquad |t|\leho<1 , \quad} 	ag{25a} \] where the derivative is required only at double nodes. For a simple node only the first summand occurs. To prove this, use the logarithm of \(G_N(t;c_j)\) equal to zero at \(t=0\). Proposition 1 puts every zero on the unit circle and there are exactly \(d\) zeros with multiplicity. Its degree-\(n\) logarithmic coefficient therefore has magnitude at most \(d/n\). After the first \(N-1\) matching coefficients, its tail on the disk has bound \(C_hoho^N\). At a double node, (16a) bounds every Taylor coefficient of \(G_z/G\) by \(CN^2\). Its first \(N-1\) coefficients also agree with \(\partial_z\log U_N\); the remaining tail is at most \(C_ho N^2ho^N\). Exponentiation and logarithmic differentiation prove (25a). Fixed \(t\)-derivatives remain exponentially small on smaller disks. There is also a safe common germ at arbitrary fixed Casimir labels. It is useful to state its size limitation explicitly. For every fixed compact set \(\Lambda\) of Casimir labels and every prescribed \(c>0\), there is \(r>0\) such that \[ G_N(t;z)=U_N(t,z)(1+O(e^{-cN})), \qquad z\in\Lambda,\quad |t|\le r. 	ag{26} \] One may enlarge \(\Lambda\) before choosing \(r\); fixed derivatives then have the same exponential bound on smaller compact sets. In particular this is a nonzero section for sufficiently large \(N\), including off-spectrum \(z\). Here are quantitative reasons for (26). On an enlarged compact \(\Lambda\), the monic recurrence bounds \(|\mathcal P_a(z)|\le C^a\). The elementary sine-product bound \[ e^{-C_0N}\le |(p;p)_a|\le e^{C_0N}\quad(0\le a<N) 	ag{27} \] then gives \(|p_a(z)|\le e^{C_1N}\). For the lower bound in (27), use \(2\sin(\pi k/N)\ge4\min(k,N-k)/N\), discard factors at least one, and compare the remaining sum of logarithms with \(\int_1^m\log u\,du\). Its total negative part is \(O(N)\). Also \(|S_n(z)|\le C_2^n\) on that compact. On a sufficiently small fixed circle \(|t|=R\), (25) has \(|\log U_N|\le C_3N\): split \(n\le N/2\), where \(|p^n-1|\ge c_0n/N\), from its complementary range, where \(|p^n-1|\ge c_0(N-n)/N\). Consequently \(G_N-U_N\) has supremum at most \(e^{C_4N}\) on that circle. Its zero of order at least \(N\) gives \[ |G_N-U_N|\le e^{C_4N}(|t|/R)^N \quad(|t|<R). 	ag{28} \] On a smaller fixed disk \(|U_N^{-1}|\le e^{C_5N}\). Choose \(r/R\) so small that (28) after this multiplication is at most \(e^{-cN}\). This proves (26), with Cauchy estimates on nested parameter domains proving the derivative statement. For clarity, the coefficient expansion on \(n\le N/2\) is \[ \ell_{N,n}(z)=(-1)^n\left[  rac{N(S_n(z)-2)}{2\pi i n^2}+ rac{S_n(z)}{2n}ight] +O(C_\Lambda^n/N). 	ag{28a} \] It follows by expanding \((e^{-2\pi in/N}-1)^{-1}\) and \(q^{-n}=e^{-\pi in/N}\) on \(|2\pi n/N|\le\pi\). On \(C_\Lambda|t|<1/2\) the error sums to \(O(N^{-1})\). The complementary coefficients, bounded as above, have exponentially small sums there. The two displayed main series are \(N\Phi\) and \(\log A\), respectively. Thus \[ U_N(t,z)=A(t,z)e^{N\Phi(t,z)}(1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{29} \] The leading phase and nonzero amplitude are therefore those in (9). Keeping the full explicit exponent (25), rather than just (29), supplies the exponential accuracy. A fixed geometric Casimir label can be included in \(\Lambda\); no assertion places its required geometric generating coordinate inside the disk in (26). ## 7. Exact assembly with nonnegative powers The local ambiguity (5b) is harmless in one specified full source construction. It is not a rule for deleting an arbitrary intermediate boundary component. Take a finite original Conway compiler tree in the centered basis. Compress genuine turns into edge parities, so the gluing on each internal edge is either \(\delta_{ab}\) or \(\delta_{a+b,d}\). Keep each signed input, unit and final marked closing as its own vertex, with all recorded scalars. On a tree, choose vertex reversals recursively so that every edge becomes anti-diagonal: if its original parity is \(e_{vw}\), set \[ s_w=1+e_{vw}+s_v\pmod2 	ag{30} \] after choosing one root reversal. Simultaneously reversing every incident index turns a trivalent tensor \(C\) into \( ar C\). At one-valent inputs and closing vertices it explicitly reverses the given finite vector. Thus all arrays and source rows remain known. For a vertex \(v\), form its finite generating polynomial \[ V_v((t_e)_{e
i v}) =\sum_{0\le a_e\le d} T_v((a_e)_{e
i v}) \prod_{e
i v}t_e^{a_e}. 	ag{31} \] The original scalar is exactly \[  oxed{\quad [\,\prod_e t_e^d\,]\prod_v V_v . \quad} 	ag{32} \] Indeed each edge receives two nonnegative powers, and the selected coefficient enforces their sum to be \(d\), precisely its anti-diagonal contraction. It follows that any vertex may be replaced by a nonnegative-power formal series agreeing with it modulo the ideal generated by the incident \(t_e^N\). Expand the difference of the two full products by changing one vertex at a time. Every term then has exponent at least \(N>d\) in one edge variable; the other factors have no negative powers, so it cannot contribute to (32). In particular the exact trivalent polynomial is \[ V_C(t_1,t_2,t_3) =N^{-1/2}\psi\!\left( R^+G_N(t_1;z)G_N(t_2;z)G_N(t_3;z)ight). 	ag{33} \] This is the original \(C\), not an ordinary untwisted polynomial linearization. Replacing its leg sections by \(U_N\) from (25) preserves all coefficients through degree \(d\) in each variable, and hence the complete source (32), exactly. The analytic cochain \(\mathcal E_N\) in (5c) is another eligible leg replacement. This uses equality of the coefficients as full algebra elements, not merely their values at distinct spectral roots. The same assertion applies to the corresponding coefficient-conjugate sections at a \( ar C\) vertex. More generally the factors in (5b) change no such assembled source: their difference from one starts in degree \(N\) in that leg. Their coefficients may lie in the full algebra; applying the specified \(\psi\) or \(\phi\) does not reduce the leg degree. Thus this central ambiguity acts trivially on this full coefficient functional. The order matters. First reverse the finite tensors, then choose nonnegative-power extensions of the resulting arrays. Applying \(t^dG(1/t)\) to an already untruncated section introduces negative powers and invalidates the ideal argument. Nor is (32) a statement about arbitrary factors in a meridian or a quantum normal parameter. For analytic sections it has the original small Taylor-circle cycle. A later deformation toward a geometric saddle must still track every pole, branch and contributing cycle. Sectorial terms such as \(t_e^N\log t_e\) are not Taylor sections and are not covered. Nor is a factor in \((t_e/t_f)^N\) covered unless its complete expansion has nonnegative powers in every edge variable. ## 8. Scope and complete proof source The exact forced equation, norm identity, physical factorization, and source rows concern the original full finite algebra. The first-normal estimate retains its nilpotent directions. The parameter \(t\) here generates the centered label; it is not the moving cap-resolvent coordinate or a peripheral meridian. These statements do not provide an asymptotic for the triple generating period \(\psi(R^+G_N(t_1)G_N(t_2)G_N(t_3))\), nor prove a nonzero coefficient after arbitrary signed short-component assembly. The uniform physical Hermite estimate and the small off-spectrum germ must not be promoted to an uncontrolled larger spectral chart, Newton-norm approximation, or source-normal volume certificate. The sole complete proof direct was read at its matching pin: | Source | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Centered source compiler](research_centered_fourier_conway_compiler.md) | 0edbabe42280d70e4d5dcbcb55b188a3e773c14b99fbd212eb0fe8c5b176a413 | The complete [Jacobi generating-unit note](research_actual_jacobi_generating_unit.md), [physical-angle crossing transport](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_current_free_aw_crossing_transport.md), the [arbitrary-power source compiler](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_arbitrary_power_source_compilation.md), and [finite Fourier-band theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_newton_interpolation_finite_fourier_band.md) were read for coverage. They already supply local analytic units, source-aware difference transport and exact finite Fourier representations. Their estimates are not imported here. The Jacobi unit theorem excludes its full-degree endpoint; the estimates above use the actual full-\(N\) polynomial and prove its complete first normal on the entire physical unit disk. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. No mathematical program, numerical iteration, test, build, git operation or earlier-final edit was performed.

title: Exact unit-turn identities for a full microscopic endpoint kernel
text: # Exact unit-turn identities for a full microscopic endpoint kernel Private written calculation, 16 November 2026. The original unit-leaf coupon map has an exact all-degree formula. For a full endpoint kernel it is a finite root-of-unity hypergeometric sum, equivalently a canonical multiplication in the endpoint variable. Its complementary fixed-index limit has a beta-integral expression. None of these identities supplies a uniform bound through growing Newton indices. In particular this note does not permit turning a marked leaf in the adopted full-product forest theorem. ## 1. Original operators and the full triangular formula Use \[ N\ge2,\quad D=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\quad\kappa=q^{D^2/2}, \] \[ s_j=2\sin(j\pi/N),\quad S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j s_h,\quad S_0=1,\quad c_h=2\cos((2h+1)\pi/N), \] \[ P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2,\qquad e_j(Z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{h<j}(c_h-Z),\qquad K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{D}e_j(w)e_j(Z). \tag{1} \] All operator equalities below are in the original full algebra \(\mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[Z]/(P_N)\), with \(\phi_N(e_i e_j)=\mathbf1_{i+j=D}\) and \(Te_j=e_{D-j}\). The ordinary representative of a class is its remainder of degree at most \(D\), denoted \(\operatorname{can}\). For \(\sigma=\pm1\), retain the original signed crossing and define \[ U_\sigma=\kappa^\sigma T R^{-\sigma}T. \tag{2} \] The original turn relation gives \[ T(R^\sigma P)=R^{-\sigma}U_\sigma P. \tag{3} \] For every \(0\le k\le D\), multiplication preserves the terminal Newton flag \(\operatorname{span}\{e_{D-k},\ldots,e_D\}\), because \(Ze_j=c_je_j-s_{j+1}^2e_{j+1}\), with its last raised term zero in the algebra. Thus \(U_\sigma\) preserves degree at most \(k\). No radical or half-degree restriction is needed for this assertion. The full multiplication matrix of \(R\) in the original basis is \[ M_{ij}=\kappa(-1)^i q^{i(j+1)} \frac{S_i}{S_jS_{i-j}}\quad(i\ge j); \tag{4} \] the negative crossing has its coefficient-conjugate matrix. Frobenius self-adjointness gives \(J M^{-\sigma}J=(M^{-\sigma})^{\mathsf T}\), where \(J\) reverses the basis. Consequently, for every degree at most \(D\), \[ [e_r]U_\sigma\left(\sum_{s=0}^D p_s e_s\right) =\sum_{s=r}^D p_s(-1)^s q^{-\sigma s(r+1)} \frac{S_s}{S_rS_{s-r}}. \tag{5} \] All factorial indices are below \(N\); no singular specialization has been used. This is the same triangular identity as in the low-degree leaf source, now applied to its full valid matrix range. For the full endpoint kernel put \[ U_\sigma K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{r=0}^D a_{r,N}^{\sigma}(w)e_r(Z). \] Then exactly \[ \boxed{\quad a_{r,N}^{\sigma}(w)= \sum_{s=r}^{D}(-1)^s q^{-\sigma s(r+1)} \frac{S_s}{S_rS_{s-r}}\,e_s(w). \quad} \tag{6} \] For real \(w\), the two signs are coefficient-conjugate. The extreme coefficient satisfies \[ a_{D,N}^{\sigma}(w)=e_D(w). \tag{7} \] Indeed the single term has multiplier \((-1)^Dq^{-\sigma D(D+1)}=1\). This does not control the intermediate coefficients. ## 2. Literal finite hypergeometric forms For a scalar \(v\ne0\) write \(w=v+v^{-1}\) and use \((z;Q)_s=\prod_{h=0}^{s-1}(1-zQ^h)\). Directly from (1), \[ e_s(w)=(-1)^s q^s \frac{(qv;Q)_s(q/v;Q)_s}{(Q;Q)_s^2}. \tag{8} \] The identity follows by multiplying \((1-q^{2h+1}v)(1-q^{2h+1}/v)=q^{2h+1}(c_h-w)\) and \(1-Q^h=-iq^h s_h\). Set \[ A_r(v)=\frac{(qv;Q)_r(q/v;Q)_r}{(Q;Q)_r^2},\quad M=D-r,\quad a=qvQ^r,\quad b=qv^{-1}Q^r,\quad c=Q^{r+1}. \tag{9} \] Then (6) becomes the following exact finite sums: \[ \boxed{\begin{split} a_{r,N}^{+}(w) &=q^{-r^2}A_r(v) \sum_{\ell=0}^{M} \frac{(a;Q)_\ell(b;Q)_\ell} {(c;Q)_\ell(Q;Q)_\ell}\,Q^{-r\ell},\\ a_{r,N}^{-}(w) &=q^{r^2+2r}A_r(v) \sum_{\ell=0}^{M} \frac{(a;Q)_\ell(b;Q)_\ell} {(c;Q)_\ell(Q;Q)_\ell}\,Q^\ell . \end{split}} \tag{10} \] To verify the phases, use \[ {s\brack r}_{Q}=q^{r(s-r)}\frac{S_s}{S_rS_{s-r}} \] in (6), substitute (8), and set \(s=r+\ell\). The positive-sign phase is \(q^{-r^2}Q^{-r\ell}\); the negative-sign phase is \(q^{r^2+2r}Q^\ell\). Splitting the finite Pochhammer products at \(r\) gives (10). In the first sum \(c/(ab)=Q^{-r}\), but its upper limit is literally \(M=N-1-r\). The factor \((c;Q)_\ell\) remains nonzero through that limit and vanishes at the next index. Similarly \((Q;Q)_\ell\) is nonzero throughout the displayed range. There is no convergent infinite series here. In particular an infinite \(q\)-Gauss identity cannot be substituted for (10). ## 3. An ordinary resolvent and the endpoint-side adapter The Frobenius representative of ordinary degree-\(D\) evaluation is \[ \boxed{\quad \delta_w(Z):=(TK_N(w,\cdot))(Z) =\frac{P_N(Z)-P_N(w)}{\eta N^2(Z-w)}. \quad} \tag{11} \] The right side is an ordinary polynomial, including at \(Z=w\). Indeed its leading coefficient is \(1/(\eta N^2)\), so its trace is one. Multiplication by \(Z-w\) leaves the constant \(-P_N(w)/(\eta N^2)\) modulo \(P_N\). For any ordinary polynomial \(f\) of degree at most \(D\), write \(f(Z)=f(w)+(Z-w)q(Z)\), with \(\deg q<D\). Since \(\phi_N(q)=0\), this proves \(\phi_N(\delta_w f)=f(w)\). The same equality follows from the dual Newton expansion \(\sum_s e_s(w)e_{D-s}(Z)\), proving (11). Transposing the multiplication matrix in (4) also gives \[ \boxed{\quad a_{r,N}^{\sigma}(w) =\kappa^\sigma [\operatorname{can}(R^{-\sigma}e_r)](w), \qquad (U_\sigma^{(Z)}K_N)(w,Z) =\kappa^\sigma [\operatorname{can}_w(R(w)^{-\sigma}K_N(w,Z))]. \quad} \tag{12} \] The right side is the specified ordinary polynomial obtained after the indicated canonical multiplication, then evaluated at the ordinary endpoint \(w\). It is not the unreduced product \(\kappa^\sigma R(w)^{-\sigma}K_N(w,Z)\) off the physical spectrum. Equation (12) is a derived adapter, not permission to quotient an arbitrary original free boundary factor. At a physical \(Z=c_j\), this reads \[ (U_\sigma K_N(w,\cdot))(c_j) =\kappa^\sigma [\operatorname{can}(R^{-\sigma}F_{j,N})](w), \qquad F_{j,N}(Z)=K_N(c_j,Z). \tag{13} \] Thus the remaining estimate is an actual oscillatory finite crossing functional. Bounds for an arbitrary multiplication operator or for each term of (6) do not estimate it with the needed polynomial cost. ## 4. A complementary fixed-index anchor Now put \(w=w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N)\), with real \(\alpha\) in a fixed compact interval, and write \[ E_{i,N}(\alpha)=(-1)^i e_i(w_N(\alpha)),\qquad \mathsf E_m(\alpha)= \frac{(a_0)_m(b_0)_m}{(m!)^2},\quad a_0=\tfrac12+i\alpha/(2\pi),\quad b_0=\overline{a_0}. \tag{14} \] For a fixed nonnegative integer \(m\), set \(r=D-m\). Sine reflection in (6) gives exactly, for either sign, \[ a_{D-m,N}^{\sigma}(w_N(\alpha)) =\eta(-1)^m\sum_{\ell=0}^{m} (-1)^\ell q^{-\sigma m(\ell+1)} \frac{S_m}{S_\ell S_{m-\ell}}\, E_{N-1-\ell,N}(\alpha). \tag{15} \] For the phase, write \(s=N-1-\ell\) in (6). Since \((-1)^s e_s(w)=E_s\), \[ q^{-\sigma(N-1-\ell)(N-m)} =\eta(-1)^{m+\ell}q^{-\sigma m(\ell+1)}. \] The factorial quotient is \(S_m/(S_\ell S_{m-\ell})\). The adopted two-ended endpoint calculation gives, for each fixed \(\ell\), \[ E_{N-1-\ell,N}(\alpha)\longrightarrow \frac{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)} {\pi^2(\ell+1)^2\mathsf E_{\ell+1}(\alpha)}. \tag{16} \] Its complementary identity retains the entire upper Newton end; no low-index approximation is used in (16). As \(N\to\infty\), the finite sum (15) therefore gives \[ \boxed{\quad \eta(-1)^m a_{D-m,N}^{\sigma}(w_N(\alpha)) \longrightarrow \frac{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)}{\pi^2} \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 (1-tu)^m(1-t)^{a_0-1}(1-u)^{b_0-1}\,dt\,du . \quad} \tag{17} \] The convergence is uniform on compact real parameter intervals. To verify the integral, the beta identity gives exactly \[ \frac1{(\ell+1)^2\mathsf E_{\ell+1}(\alpha)} =\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 (tu)^\ell(1-t)^{a_0-1}(1-u)^{b_0-1}\,dt\,du . \tag{18} \] Indeed its two beta factors are \(\Gamma(\ell+1)\Gamma(a_0)/\Gamma(\ell+1+a_0)\) and the analogous \(b_0\) factor. The sine binomial in (15) tends to \(\binom m\ell\); summing its alternating finite powers gives \((1-tu)^m\). For real \(\alpha\), the absolute value of the integral in (17) is at most \[ \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 (1-t)^{-1/2}(1-u)^{-1/2}\,dt\,du=4. \tag{19} \] This bounds the limiting anchor uniformly in \(m\). At \(\alpha=0\) the integrand is positive. No positivity is asserted for other real parameters. The quantifiers remain important: (17) is proved for each fixed \(m\), followed by \(N\to\infty\). Its bounded limiting expression does not prove a uniform finite-\(N\) estimate when \(m\) grows, and does not control the whole Newton reconstruction or its real spectral norm. Both signs have the same fixed-index limit after the displayed exact phase is retained. ## 5. Scope and direct sources The question left open is a polynomial real-interval bound for the whole \(U_\sigma K_N(w_N(\alpha),Z)\), including all its physical normals, uniformly in the level. The naive triangular bound can be exponential at full degree. Equations (10)--(13) identify the exact finite cancellation that would have to replace it. Equation (17) supplies only one endpoint anchor. In particular no marked-leaf operation is added to a reduction certificate here. No whole-source or filled-action bound follows, and no infinite root-of-unity hypergeometric summation is used. The complete direct sources were read at their unchanged pins, with the used implications and hashes checked: * [Original unit-leaf operator](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_low_degree_charged_leaf_reduction.md), SHA256 80df78ceafaa97182aebc6831651921f7f8040e1356ee07a3d0d3fbadd02846a: original crossing matrix, full turn relation, Frobenius transpose, and canonical-representative convention. * [Both endpoint Newton limits](research_endpoint_normal_two_ended_limit.md), SHA256 1e72bffbd0718fec2ae61c7a91dbb93bcd1506a8ca3db28f030cc8fcb2400e93: exact complementary product identity and locally uniform fixed upper-index limit used in (16). Only written algebra, text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or build was run. Adopted notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: A polynomial bound for one full microscopic endpoint under a unit turn
text: # A polynomial bound for one full microscopic endpoint under a unit turn Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The original signed unit-leaf operator sends one full microscopic endpoint kernel to a polynomially bounded ordinary representative on the entire real spectral interval. The proof uses its exact forced Askey--Wilson equation and retains the complete first spectral normals. It does not bound that operator on arbitrary polynomials or on products of endpoint kernels. ## 1. Statement and original normalization Put \[ N\ge2,\quad D=N-1,\quad \theta=\pi/N,\quad q=e^{i\theta},\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\quad \kappa=q^{D^2/2}, \] \[ s_j=2\sin(j\theta),\quad S_j=\prod_{\ell=1}^j s_\ell,\quad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\theta), \] \[ e_j(Z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{a<j}(c_a-Z),\quad P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2,\quad K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^D e_j(w)e_j(Z). \tag{1} \] The algebra is \(\mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[Z]/(P_N)\), with its original Frobenius functional, physical turn, and crossing: \[ \phi_N(e_i e_j)=\mathbf1_{i+j=D},\qquad Te_j=e_{D-j},\qquad U_\sigma=\kappa^\sigma T R^{-\sigma}T,\quad \sigma=\pm1. \tag{2} \] Products in this algebra are represented by their ordinary remainders of degree at most \(D\), denoted \(\operatorname{can}\). This convention is essential at an ordinary free endpoint. For \(A<\infty\), define \[ w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N),\qquad F_{N,\sigma,\alpha}(Z) =(U_\sigma^{(Z)}K_N)(w_N(\alpha),Z),\qquad |\alpha|\le A. \tag{3} \] Here \(\alpha\) may be complex. **Theorem 1.** There are finite constants \(C_A,p_A\), independent of \(N,\sigma,\alpha\), such that \[ \boxed{\quad \sup_{Z\in[-2,2]}|F_{N,\sigma,\alpha}(Z)|\le C_A N^{p_A}. \quad} \tag{4} \] For every fixed pair of nonnegative integers \(a,b\), the same conclusion holds for \(\partial_\alpha^a\partial_Z^bF\), with a possibly larger constant and power. In particular every physical value and every first spectral normal is retained, at both parities. The powers in (4) are deliberately not optimized. They may depend on the fixed parameter bound \(A\). No assertion concerns a parameter bound growing with \(N\). ## 2. Stable full-Hermite interpolation and the two initial jets For an ordinary polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(D\), write \[ p(-2\cos t)=\sum_{|m|\le D}b_m e^{imt},\qquad b_{-m}=b_m, \qquad \tau_j=(D-2j)\pi/N,\quad 0\le j<N. \tag{5} \] Then \(-2\cos\tau_j=c_j\) and \(e^{iN\tau_j}=\eta\). Let \(v_j=p(c_j)\) and \(d_j=\partial_t[p(-2\cos t)]_{t=\tau_j}\), and set \[ V_m=N^{-1}\sum_jv_j e^{-im\tau_j},\qquad W_m=N^{-1}\sum_j(d_j/i)e^{-im\tau_j}. \] The finite Fourier orthogonality gives, for \(1\le m<N\), \[ V_m=b_m+\eta b_{m-N},\qquad W_m=m b_m+(m-N)\eta b_{m-N}, \] \[ b_m=\frac{W_m+(N-m)V_m}{N},\qquad b_0=V_0. \tag{6} \] Consequently the canonical full-Hermite polynomial determined by compatible data obeys \[ \sum_{|m|\le D}|b_m| \le (2N-1)\max_j|v_j|+2\max_j|d_j|. \tag{7} \] Compatibility means the values agree at the paired angular lifts and the angular derivatives have opposite signs. The odd simple node has \(t=0\) and derivative zero by evenness; no spectral normal is imposed there. Thus (6)--(7) apply at every level, including \(N=2\). If \(p\) is this representative, then \[ |p(w_N(\alpha))|\le e^A\sum_{|m|\le D}|b_m|. \tag{8} \] Indeed \(w_N(\alpha)=-2\cos(\pi+i\alpha/N)\), and \(|e^{im(\pi+i\alpha/N)}|\le e^A\). The original crossing satisfies \[ |R^\sigma(c_j)|=1,\qquad \left|\partial_t R^\sigma(-2\cos t)|_{\tau_j}\right| \le N/2. \tag{9} \] These are the original Gaussian values and first normals, not values of a chosen off-spectrum exponential. Equivalently, at a double root, \[ (R^\sigma)'(c_j)/R^\sigma(c_j) =i\sigma\,\frac{N-2j-1}{4\sin((2j+1)\theta)}. \tag{10} \] The odd simple value also has modulus one. Let \[ Q_N(Z)=\partial_wK_N(c_0,Z). \] The full normal source proves \[ \|Q_N\|_{[-2,2]}\le N^4/4. \tag{11} \] Ordinary Markov on \([-2,2]\) therefore bounds \(Q_N'\) by \(C N^6\), and the angular derivative of \(Q_N(-2\cos t)\) by the same coarse power. Equations (7)--(10), applied to the full data of the products, give \[ \|\operatorname{can}(R^{-\sigma})\|_{\mathrm{Fourier},1} \le C N,\qquad \|\operatorname{can}(R^{-\sigma}Q_N)\|_{\mathrm{Fourier},1} \le C N^6. \tag{12} \] Multiplication retains its actual product-rule normals. The exact endpoint-side adapter is \[ F_{N,\sigma,\alpha}(Z) =\kappa^\sigma [\operatorname{can}_w(R(w)^{-\sigma}K_N(w,Z))] _{w=w_N(\alpha)}. \tag{13} \] Since \(K_N(c_0,w)=1\), differentiating this finite polynomial identity in \(Z\) gives both anchors: \[ |F(c_0)|\le C_A N,\qquad |F'(c_0)|\le C_A N^6. \tag{14} \] The second anchor uses (11); it is not inferred from the first anchor or from a value-only row recurrence. ## 3. The exact forced equation Let \(C\) denote multiplication by \(Z\) and put \(J=TCT\). Because crossing multiplication commutes with \(C\), \[ J U_\sigma=U_\sigma J. \tag{15} \] The exact ordinary reproducer \[ TK_N(w,\cdot) =\frac{P_N(Z)-P_N(w)}{\eta N^2(Z-w)} \] implies in the full algebra \[ (w-J)K_N(w,\cdot)=\eta P_N(w)e_D/N^2. \] Also \(U_\sigma e_D=\kappa^\sigma R^\sigma\), from \(T(R^{-\sigma})=R^\sigma\). Hence \[ \boxed{\quad (w-J)F=\eta P_N(w)\kappa^\sigma R^\sigma/N^2. \quad} \tag{16} \] Every expression in (16) has its canonical ordinary representative. For the index variable \(r\), put \[ c(r)=2\cos((2r+1)\theta),\qquad A(r)=\frac{s_{r+1}^4}{s_{2r+1}s_{2r+2}},\qquad C(r)=\frac{s_r^4}{s_{2r}s_{2r+1}}. \tag{17} \] The removable values are \(C(0)=C'(0)=0\). The original off-grid kernel difference identity identifies the action of \(J\) on every canonical polynomial: \[ (JF)(c(r))=(c_0+A(r)+C(r))F(c(r)) -A(r)F(c(r+1))-C(r)F(c(r-1)). \tag{18} \] One can check the identification on \(K_N(w,\cdot)\): its coefficients \(e_j(w)\) span the polynomial space, and its exact source is precisely the preceding reproducer equation. Thus (16)--(18) are ordinary rational identities in \(r\), not merely equations for the values. Set \(J_N=\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor\). Only rows \(0\le j<J_N\) will be used. They are all regular. At even levels \(J_N\) is the last double root; at odd levels it is the last distinct root, which is simple. We never use the singular next row at even levels. Write \(h_j=F(c_j)\), and in this range define \[ q_j=C(j)/A(j),\quad d_j=(c_0-w)/A(j),\quad f_j=\frac{\eta P_N(w)\kappa^\sigma R^\sigma(c_j)} {N^2 A(j)}. \tag{19} \] Equation (16) becomes exactly \[ h_{j+1}=(1+q_j+d_j)h_j-q_jh_{j-1}+f_j. \tag{20} \] At \(j=0\), the \(q_0h_{-1}\) term is absent. ## 4. Polynomial propagation through the entire value grid For all regular positive rows, \[ q_j= \left(\frac{\sin(j\theta)}{\sin((j+1)\theta)}\right)^3 \frac{\cos((j+1)\theta)}{\cos(j\theta)} \in(0,1),\qquad q_0=0. \tag{21} \] Both ratios are in \((0,1)\), since \((j+1)\theta<\pi/2\). Also \[ A(j)\ge\frac{16}{\pi^2}\frac{(j+1)^2}{N^2}. \tag{22} \] Indeed \(s_{j+1}\ge4(j+1)/N\), whereas \(s_{2j+1}s_{2j+2}\le16\pi^2(j+1)^2/N^2\). For bounded complex \(\alpha\), \[ |c_0-w_N(\alpha)|\le C_A/N^2,\qquad P_N(w_N(\alpha))=2\cosh\alpha+2. \tag{23} \] Consequently \[ |d_j|+|f_j|\le C_A/(j+1)^2. \tag{24} \] For \(j\ge1\), balance the difference rather than diagonalizing the transfer: \[ X_j=\binom{h_j}{(j+1)(h_j-h_{j-1})}. \] Writing \(r=j+1\), its exact step is \[ X_{j+1}= \begin{pmatrix} 1+d_j&q_j/r\\ (r+1)d_j&(1+1/r)q_j \end{pmatrix}X_j+\binom{f_j}{(r+1)f_j}. \tag{25} \] For the maximum row-sum norm, (21),(24) imply \[ \|M_j\|\le1+B_A/(j+1),\qquad \left\|\binom{f_j}{(j+2)f_j}\right\| \le B_A/(j+1). \tag{26} \] Here \(B_A\) is a fixed finite constant. In particular every forward product obeys \[ \|M_{k-1}\cdots M_j\| \le \exp\!\left(B_A\sum_{\ell=j}^{k-1}\frac1{\ell+1}\right) \le C_A N^{B_A}. \tag{27} \] No lower bound on a transfer determinant or on \(h_j\) is used. At the first row \(h_1=(1+d_0)h_0+f_0\). The anchor (14) therefore bounds \(X_1\) polynomially. Variation of constants in (25), with at most \(N\) terms and (27), proves \[ \max_{0\le j\le J_N}|h_j| \le C_A N^{p_A^{(0)}}. \tag{28} \] For \(N=2\) there is only the anchor value. This also explains why a coalescing final pair or the odd simple root causes no instability: the proof reaches it from regular rows. ## 5. The original spectral normals Use the index derivative \[ y_j=c'(j)F'(c_j),\qquad c'(j)=-4\theta\sin((2j+1)\theta). \tag{29} \] Differentiate the ordinary identity (20), with \(q,d,f\) regarded as their functions of \(r\). At each regular row, \[ y_{j+1}=(1+q_j+d_j)y_j-q_jy_{j-1}+g_j, \] \[ g_j=(q_j'+d_j')h_j-q_j'h_{j-1}+f_j'. \tag{30} \] Primes on these coefficients mean the index derivative, not a spectral derivative. The source derivative in \(f_j'\) is the derivative of the actual canonical \(R^\sigma(c(r))\). By (9), \(|\partial_rR^\sigma(c(r))|_{r=j}\le\pi\). All coefficient derivatives in (30) have a uniform polynomial bound in \(N\). For clarity, a coarse bound sufficient here is \[ |q_j'|+|d_j'|+|f_j'|\le C_A N^{10}. \tag{31} \] For \(j\ge1\), every nonzero sine in (17) is at least \(2/N\) in absolute value. Differentiation costs at most a factor \(C/N\) in each numerator or denominator sine; the quotient rule, (22), and (23) therefore give (31). At zero, remove \(C(0)\) first; \(C'(0)=q'(0)=0\), while the other denominators are nonzero. The same bound holds. This elementary estimate intentionally ignores cancellations. The anchor \(y_0=c'(0)F'(c_0)\) is polynomial by (14). The derivative of the first row gives \[ y_1=(1+d_0)y_0+d_0'h_0+f_0', \tag{32} \] since \(q_0=q_0'=0\). Thus \(y_1\) is polynomial also. To propagate only the required double-root normals, use (30) through the row preceding the last double root. Balancing \((y_j,(j+1)(y_j-y_{j-1}))\) gives exactly the same matrices \(M_j\) as in (25). The added vector is \((g_j,(j+2)g_j)\), which is polynomial by (28),(31). Forward variation of constants and (27) now give \[ \max_{\text{double }c_j}|y_j| \le C_A N^{p_A^{(1)}}. \tag{33} \] There is no inverse fundamental-matrix estimate in this argument. At a double root, \[ |c'(j)|\ge8\pi/N^2. \tag{34} \] Therefore every \(F'(c_j)\) is polynomially bounded. At the odd simple node its value was already included in (28); no normal there is needed or supplied by this argument. The lone \(N=2\) normal is the initial anchor itself. Insert these values and normals into (7). This proves the real interval bound (4). Markov supplies every fixed ordinary spectral derivative. Finally \(F\) is entire in \(\alpha\); repeating (4) on \(|\alpha|\le A+1\) and applying Cauchy's formula supplies every fixed \(\alpha\)-derivative, jointly with the spectral derivatives. This proves Theorem 1. ## 6. Exact source consequence and limits For a leaf with original power \(\sigma=\pm1\) and precisely the one full endpoint factor in (3), its original contraction is \[ \phi_N^{(Z)} [R^\sigma(Z)K_N(w_N(\alpha),Z)K_N(Z,X)] =T(R^\sigma K_{w_N(\alpha)})(X) =R^{-\sigma}(X)F_{N,\sigma,\alpha}(X) \quad\text{in }\mathcal A_N. \tag{35} \] At a traced neighbor this changes its power by \(-\sigma\) and inserts the polynomially bounded full coupon \(F\). All its other factors and joint normal operations remain. At a free neighbor the product on the right must first be taken in its canonical ordinary representative. The actual Gaussian physical jets and (7) show that this representative is polynomially bounded too. The argument establishes one such turn, including all physical jets. It does not identify \(F\) with a product of microscopic endpoint kernels, and gives no closure theorem for repeated turns after branching. In particular it does not assert a polynomial norm for \(U_\sigma\) on every polynomial with polynomial real norm. A product input has a different forced equation; it is not covered merely because each factor satisfies (16). No scalar lower bound, filled-action estimate, or whole-current gap follows from (4). The archived exact unit-turn note already gives the full triangular matrix, finite hypergeometric sums, and adapter (13). The archived all-color normal theorem supplies the original difference equation and the nontrivial endpoint normal bound (11). The added result here is the polynomial full-grid propagation for the exact forced problem, and its single-factor leaf consequence. Both complete direct sources were read at these versions, with the directly used implications and hashes checked: * [Exact full endpoint unit-turn identities](research_full_endpoint_unit_turn_identities.md), SHA256 e2f69aaff28080b9dd9e11365ce18d68a9d738667917204714556681c50789e8: original operators, Frobenius reproducer, turn normalization and the endpoint-side canonical adapter. * [Full physical normal source](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_all_color_path_normal_bound.md), SHA256 08f8932c2cdee4c7afadbb4db3cd85480603f8adb4c936ce29a5517b2d4799c7: off-grid difference identity, Gaussian values and normals, removable first row, and the real-interval \(Q_N\) estimate. Only written mathematics, source-text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical test or build was run. Existing private notes and public manuscripts were unchanged.

title: Boundary reduction for a global full sharp-source maximum
status: Global full-fiber maxima: ordinary positivity and no diagonals
text: # Boundary reduction for a global full sharp-source maximum The variational theorem concerns the entire original flow fiber with freely varying spectra. It does not assert finite-coefficient asymptotics, phase alignment or a volume bound. ## 1. Original fiber and explicit hypotheses Fix an original simple-white certified plat. Its white sphere is a simple triangulation, the protected faces u,v are adjacent along the marked MAIN edge, and a port pairs two shaded triangles across a MATCHING edge. Keep every original incidence, including the protected zeros. Let P be the FULL nonnegative transport fiber: each port supplies1, each ordinary face demands1, and each protected face demands0. No LEFT/CROSS/RIGHT label inequalities are imposed on P. A local vector q=(X,B,C,Y) with sum1 is written mu=B, nu=1-C, xi=X, zeta=Y=nu-mu-xi. The actual complete geometric flow qG belongs to P. It has positive load on EVERY ordinary incidence, zero on protected incidences, and both middle loads strictly less than1/2. Its two literal triangle allocations are positive on every ordinary triangle corner. Each port has at least one ordinary outer incidence: the two protected faces are joined by a MAIN edge, not by its outer MATCHING edge. Therefore qG_x+qG_y>0 at every port. (1) For 0<=delta<=1/2 define h_delta on the FULL interval by the original [sharp functional](research_global_sharp_coefficient_limsup_majorant.md) h_delta(q)=int_0^mu log|alpha_delta| +int_nu^1 log|alpha_delta| +inf_(x>0){int_mu^nu log Lambda_delta(t;x,1)dt -xi log x}, (2) alpha_delta=4[cos^2(pi delta)-sin^2(pi t)]. Here Lambda=beta rho, with beta(t)=4 sin^2(pi t) and rho the exact [positive eta-word root](research_positive_eta_word_transfer.md), eta=cos^2(pi delta)/sin^2(pi t). Endpoint values are the continuous ones. In particular h_(1/2)=0 for ALL q. At delta=0, h_0 is the [continuous full-kernel endpoint entropy](actual_fejer_full_kernel_entropy_identity_reduction.md). On CROSS (B,C<=1/2), h_0(q)=max_(a+b=q) [Ctri(a)+Ctri(b)], (3) where the two original triangle rows have supply1/2 and their indicated middle loads B,C. This is the exact latent split of the original port, not independently reassigned angles. The all-CROSS geometric allocation has [total endpoint entropy Phi_D>0](actual_fejer_unique_geometric_maximizer.md). Consider a GLOBAL maximum of sum_e h_(delta_e)(q_e), with q in P and independent real delta_e in[0,1/2]. Alternatively maximize over the closed non-CROSS union, but assume the maximum being studied has value at least Phi_D and at least one STRICT non-CROSS middle load greater than1/2. Such a port keeps the geometric segment below in that union for all sufficiently small perturbations. No analogous claim is made for a seam-only non-CROSS boundary maximum. The statements use the sharp continuum functional directly. Where it is used as an upper functional for the actual source, this theorem does not supply a new coefficient-identification or cap-uniform N limit. ## 2. Fixed-load spectral exclusions First, a positive-length port at strict 0<delta<1/2 cannot have an endpoint at either simple alpha pole. Write the poles as p=1/2-delta and p'=1/2+delta. Moving an endpoint pole into the active interval increases the two outside integrals by |s|log(1/|s|)+O(|s|). If both endpoints are poles, necessarily mu=p,nu=p'; decreasing delta moves both inside and gives twice this gain. All other outside-integral changes are O(|s|). The tilted tail changes only O(|s|), uniformly in the tilt: with eta=cos^2(pi delta)/sin^2(pi t), 0<=partial_(log eta)log rho_eta(x)<=1/2, and partial_delta log eta is bounded on every strict delta compact. Taking a common infimum preserves that Lipschitz estimate, also for closed outer loads. Thus an arbitrarily small feasible spectral change increases (2). This excludes positive-length pole endpoints without assuming face stationarity or concavity in the row variables. Second, at delta=0 a positive-length nonterminal one-sided interval cannot maximize in its free spectrum. For a lower interval nu<1/2, put z=sin^2(pi delta) and L_z=Lambda_z/alpha_z, with z small enough that alpha stays positive on the interval. Directly from the positive root, -partial_z log Lambda_z <=1/[2(1-z)], partial_z log L_z >=1/[2(1-z)]. The first inequality follows by bounding its square-root denominator below by 4xy(1-z); it remains valid at a monomial tilt. Hence, uniformly in every outer tilt and after the same infimum, h_delta(q)-h_0(q)>=-(nu-mu)log(1-z)/2>0. (4) Reflection proves the upper one-sided case. Thus every positive-length delta=0 port at a maximum lies in CROSS, allowing its seams for now. Finally classify a positive-length delta=1/2 port at fixed loads. The sharp entropy dominates its monomer action because J*>=0. If 0<mu<nu<1, choose a positive k=cos(pi delta) smaller than the minimum of sin(pi t) on that fixed interval. The entire active interval is then after the small lower pole and before its reflection, and its actual monomer action is int_mu^nu -log[1-k^2/sin^2(pi t)]dt>0. (5) Thus every interval with both endpoints strictly inside(0,1) is excluded at the cap, uniformly over its closed outer split. Write I_k(0,a) for the initial monomer integral of log[sin^2/|k^2-sin^2|]. If mu=0 and 1/2<nu<1, the exact total and reflection identities give I_k(0,nu)=-I_k(0,1-nu)>0 (6) for sufficiently small k, because the latter initial interval has negative monomer action by its regular positive suffix formula. Exact reflection treats nu=1 and 0<mu<1/2. For mu=0,0<nu<1/2 and BOTH outer loads positive, the [protected-middle cap lemma](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_protected_middle_spectral_cap_exclusion.md) gives, at small positive k=cos(pi delta), h_delta>=2 min(xi,nu-xi)log(1+k) -(2/pi)k^2 cot(pi nu)>0. (7) The half-terminal extension has no baseline cost, and a full interval [0,1] has the same positive chord bound for strict outer loads. Exact reflection covers the protected output. Consequently a cap maximum with positive length can only have a monomial outer split and be [0,nu], 0<nu<=1/2; its reflected interval; or the whole interval[0,1]. (8) Every other fixed-load cap candidate has an available positive value at another spectrum, while the cap value is zero. This classification does not yet eliminate the zeros at (8). ## 3. One geometric segment, with source spectra retained or retuned Use the EXACT full-fiber segment q(eps)=(1-eps)q+eps qG. (9) It preserves every ordinary target, protected zero and row supply. It activates every zero ORDINARY incidence. It is not required to preserve an old LEFT/CROSS/RIGHT label at a boundary: the full source fiber has no such imposed labels. If a strict non-CROSS port was specified, its strict inequality persists for small eps. For a non-diagonal strict-spectrum port, keep delta fixed. The [ordinary-zero barrier table](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_sharp_spectral_ordinary_zero_barrier.md) and exact reflection give nonnegative eps log(1/eps) coefficients, strictly positive if an ordinary zero incidence is activated. Upper rows equal1/2 are regular units at a strict spectrum; there is no half-label inequality in this full fiber. At the full two-terminal interval mu=0,nu=1, write mu=eps B and 1-nu=eps C. With strict base outer loads use xi=xi0+eps dot_xi, 0<xi0<1; the two-end calculation gives B+C. At the x-zero corner instead use xi=eps X, and its coefficient is 2(B+C+X). Outer reflection is identical. These exhaust the positive-length full-row zero patterns. All other changes are O(eps). For a delta=0 CROSS port choose an attaining split in (3), and mix its two triangle rows with the actual geometric triangle rows. Their sum is EXACTLY the local vector in (9). The optimized h_0 at that vector is at least the entropy of this mixed split. Each triangle has a nonnegative closed-corner singular coefficient, strictly positive at every activated zero ordinary corner. Thus an ordinary zero in the port gives a positive gain. At a seam nu=1/2 the output triangle is the pure-middle vertex, and its contribution is 2 dot_nu eps log(1/eps)+O(eps), dot_nu>0. (10) The input triangle has no negative singular contribution. The mu=1/2 seam is reflected and gives -2 dot_mu>0. This uses an actual latent complete split inside the FULL endpoint polynomial. It makes no infeasible fixed-pattern retagging or terminal KKT assertion. For a diagonal mu=nu=a, retune its spectrum. At a in(0,1), (1) opens a positive interval; placing a simple pole inside it gives W eps log(1/eps)+O(eps), or 2W at a=1/2, uniformly in the outer split. At a=0 or1 use cos(pi delta_eps)=eps^2; its cost is at worst O(eps^2). These are the [free-spectral retuning estimates](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_free_spectral_diagonal_retuning.md). For a cap port from (8), the [cap-corner lemma](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_spectral_cap_corner_activation.md) gives the needed ordinary-zero gain. At [0,nu0] with nu0<1/2 and x load zero, choose cos^2(pi delta_eps)=eps K. Its singular coefficient is B+X, where B=dot_mu and X=dot_xi. It is positive if either zero incidence is ordinary. At a flat half-terminal monomial interval [0,1/2], the base value is zero for EVERY spectrum. Retune its base to delta=0 and use the actual latent CROSS split above. Its output triangle is the pure-middle vertex, so (10) gives a strictly positive gain because qG_c<1/2. This remains true when the input middle and the zero outer incidence are both protected. Thus the half-terminal monomial is excluded at every initial spectrum, not only at the cap. Exact reflection excludes the upper half-terminal monomial as well. At the flat full terminal interval, retune to a fixed strict delta and use the corresponding corner table. A full [0,1] monomial interval has three zero incidences, at least one ordinary, so its gain is strict. If both zeros of a half-interval cap corner are protected, keep the cap value zero. That port has no ordinary zero to activate. Reflected and outer-exchanged cases use the same exact source symmetries. All spectra are independent, so these choices can be made simultaneously without altering (9). There are only finitely many ports. Every listed singular coefficient is nonnegative; every strict gain dominates all O(eps) terms. Thus global maximality implies: * every non-diagonal port has positive load on every ordinary incidence; * no interior diagonal remains; * no positive-length delta=0 port lies on a CROSS seam; * no half-terminal monomial remains at any spectrum; * every remaining positive-length cap port has its two zero incidences both protected, and is a monomial corner [0,nu] with 0<nu<1/2, or its exact reflection. This conclusion is for a global free-spectrum maximum. No such simultaneous retuning is inferred at a local fixed-spectrum maximum. ## 4. Endpoint diagonals form an impossible closed component Only diagonals at a=0 or1 can now remain. Let D be their ports and F their occupied middle faces. Such a row sends its entire supply1 to one ordinary face. Protected demand0 excludes a protected occupied face, and demand1 makes the map D->F injective. Therefore |D|=|F|. Every face in F is saturated by its diagonal row. By section3 every ordinary incidence of a non-diagonal row is positive. Thus no non-diagonal row can even be incident to F: N(F)=D in the full supported bipartite incidence graph B. Evaluate the same demands with qG. The faces F require |F|=|D|, and only D can supply them. All supplies of D are therefore used inside F. Because qG is strictly positive on every ordinary incidence, no D row has an arc to an ordinary face outside F. Hence D union F is a union of connected components of B. The original graph B is connected. Delete u,v from the simple white triangulated sphere: the remaining white graph is connected. The [elementary connectivity argument](actual_original_boundary_transverse_rank.md) reroutes a path through the cyclic link of u, and then through the link of v with u deleted, which is a connected path or cycle. Every remaining white edge belongs to an original port quartet, so it induces a two-step path through that port in B. Every port has an ordinary incidence. These facts connect all vertices of B without creating any new source adjacency. Consequently nonempty D would mean all ports are diagonal. Their total sharp entropy is zero. This contradicts the feasible geometric value Phi_D>0 for an unrestricted full-fiber maximum. In the strict non-CROSS variant, the comparison must instead assume the studied maximum has positive value (as is automatic for any candidate at or above Phi_D). The all-geometric point need not lie in that restricted set, so its value is not silently used as a feasible NC lower bound. Thus D is empty under these stated value hypotheses. No actual identity smoothing or cover is needed for this tight-cut argument. ## 5. What the reduction proves, and what remains An unrestricted global full sharp maximum on this original certified fiber has no diagonal and has positive load on every ordinary incidence. Positive-length strict-spectrum ports have no endpoint at a pole; delta=0 ports are strict CROSS. The only cap ports left by this argument are monomial intervals [0,nu], 0<nu<1/2, and their exact reflections, whose parent middle and one outer incidence are both the original protected faces. Half-terminal monomials at any spectrum have been excluded by their cost-free retuning to delta=0. Those two zero incidences form the actual marked MAIN edge uv in one shaded triangle. The edge has two incident triangles, and they belong to distinct ports since ports pair across MATCHING edges. Thus at most two such positive-length cap ports remain, adjacent to the mark. This count does not identify their geometry, phase, or contribution. The same boundary reduction holds for a competing maximum of value at least Phi_D over the closed non-CROSS union if at least one STRICT non-CROSS port is present. A seam-only constrained maximum requires its own documented argument; it is not covered by a feasible qG segment here. Ordinary positivity is not an all-boundary theorem. Protected zero faces remain, the possible marked cap corners remain, and the full spectral/filling phase still has to be controlled. No finite positive ordinary multipliers, terminal geometric interpretation at a cap, new developing representation, bound by Phi_D, or quantum period conclusion is asserted at those residual cap configurations. All arguments here concern the sharp continuum functional. They use the exact original row/face constraints, both unused products, the normalized eta word and the separately proved endpoint entropy. They do not replace a signed polynomial by a new positive model or interchange a shrinking spectral scale with N. Any later use for the original finite source must retain its exact scalar zeros and the independently proved coefficient upper/identification statements. ## Scope No lower coefficient limit or volume comparison follows from this activation argument. The finite-multiplier conclusion is proved in the separate stationary addendum.

# Finite shared multipliers and the stationary branches after full-fiber activation The stationary classification gives neither separate weighted local maximality nor strong duality. Phase compatibility, cap geometry and volume comparison remain separate. ## 1. The original maximum and its remaining degrees Use precisely the original simple-white certified diagram, protected pair, full transport fiber and independent real spectra of [full-fiber boundary activation theorem](research_full_fiber_sharp_boundary_activation.md). Each original port has supply one; each ordinary face has demand one; the two protected faces have demand zero. No LEFT/CROSS/RIGHT label inequality is imposed. For one port write \[ q=(\xi,\mu,1-
u,
u-\mu-\xi) \quad	ext{in the order }(x,b,c,y). 	ag{1} \] The theorem applies to an unrestricted global maximum. It also applies to a competing maximum of value at least \(\Phi_D\) in the closed non-CROSS union, provided at least one middle load is strictly greater than \(1/2\). That strict margin persists in a neighborhood, so every sufficiently small variation within the full transport fiber is still admissible for this restricted problem. No seam-only NC maximum is included. The boundary reduction has already proved: * all ordinary incidences have positive load and every port has positive interval length; * at \(0<\delta<1/2\), neither interval endpoint is an alpha zero; * every \(\delta=0\) port is strict CROSS; * half-terminal monomial intervals are absent at every spectrum; * a remaining cap \(\delta=1/2\) is a monomial interval \([0,
u]\), \(0<
u<1/2\), or its reflection, with its parent middle and one outer incidence both protected. There are at most two, adjacent to the original marked MAIN edge. Keep these protected coordinates fixed at zero. The maximum is in the relative interior of the resulting original transport polytope. The relative-interior assertion is about actual incidence coordinates, not an enlarged triangle or fractional-cover flow. ## 2. Fixed-spectrum smoothness and finite common weights Put \[  egin{aligned} \alpha_\delta(t)&=4 igl[\cos^2(\pi\delta)-\sin^2(\pi t) igr],\  eta(t)&=4\sin^2(\pi t),\qquad \eta_\delta(t)= rac{\cos^2(\pi\delta)}{\sin^2(\pi t)},\ \Lambda_\delta(t;x,y)&=  rac{ eta(t)}2 \left[x+y+\sqrt{(x-y)^2+4\eta_\delta(t)xy}ight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{2} \] The original sharp functional is \[ h_\delta(q)= \int_0^\mu\log|\alpha_\delta(t)|\,dt+ \int_
u^1\log|\alpha_\delta(t)|\,dt+ \inf_{\ell\in\mathbb R} \left\{\int_\mu^
u\log\Lambda_\delta(t;e^\ell,1)\,dt -\xi\ellight\}. 	ag{3} \] Both unused integrals and their normalization remain present. If both outer incidences are ordinary, their loads are positive. Thus \(0<\xi<
u-\mu\). For \(\delta<1/2\) the integrated logarithmic root has a unique finite minimizing tilt. Indeed \[ \partial_\ell^2\log\Lambda_\delta(t;e^\ell,1) = rac{\eta_\delta(t)\cosh(\ell/2)} {4 igl(\sinh^2(\ell/2)+\eta_\delta(t) igr)^{3/2}}>0, 	ag{4} \] and its first derivative ranges from zero to one. The integrated first derivative therefore ranges from zero to \(
u-\mu\). At a protected start zero or stop one, the first derivative is bounded by one and the second derivative is integrable; on compact tilt sets it is \(O(t)\) or \(O(1-t)\) at the corresponding endpoint. The implicit function theorem consequently gives a smooth finite tilt in the free degree coordinates. Every movable row is strictly inside \((0,1)\). At strict spectrum it also avoids the two alpha zeros, so differentiating the outside integrals in that row is regular. Their possible interior logarithmic zeros do not affect this degree smoothness. At \(\delta=0\), the strict CROSS inequalities keep both movable endpoints away from the central zero. A protected endpoint is fixed and is not differentiated. Thus (3) is \(C^1\) on the relevant relative open face. If an outer incidence is protected, specialize the exact monomer first: its forced outer degree leaves \(\Lambda_\delta(t;0,y)= eta(t)y\), or its reflection. The same row argument proves smoothness on this protected face without taking a finite tilt of a zero weight. Both outer incidences cannot be protected, because their MATCHING edge differs from the marked MAIN edge. Finally, at the cap the full sharp functional is identically zero for every degree vector. It is smooth on its protected-coordinate face as well. Let \(A\) be the original finite row/face constraint matrix after protected incidences are removed. The differential of the total fixed-spectrum entropy annihilates \(\ker A\): every sufficiently small positive and negative tangent displacement is admissible. Elementary row-space orthogonality gives finite real row and face multipliers. Redundant balance equations cause no difficulty. Choose the sign of the ordinary face multiplier \(\lambda_f\) so that \[ L_f=e^{-\lambda_f}>0,\qquad \mathcal F_e(q_e)=h_{\delta_e}(q_e) +\sum_{f	ext{ at }e}q_{ef}\log L_f. 	ag{5} \] Here \(\mathcal F_e\) is stationary on the local row simplex. The row multiplier drops out because the local supply is fixed. The same finite \(L_f\) occurs at every original incidence of \(f\). At protected faces use the literal value zero only after specializing their zero coordinates; no expression \(0\log0\) or infinite multiplier is used. This is equality stationarity in degree variables. It is not local maximality of an individual weighted coupon. In particular no independent optimization of local rows or interchange of a shared infimum and maximum has been used. ## 3. The exact row equations and branch derivatives At a port let \(x,b,c,y\) now denote its common face weights. A protected one is zero in the literal specialized formula. If both outer weights are positive, outer stationarity in (5) sets the minimizing tilt to \(\ell=\log(x/y)\). Homogeneity and \(\int_0^1\log|\alpha_\delta|=0\) then give the stationary local Lagrangian in the exact form \[ F(\mu,
u;\delta)=\mu\log b+(1-
u)\log c+ \int_\mu^
u\log\mathcal L_\delta(t;x,y)\,dt, \qquad \mathcal L_\delta= rac{\Lambda_\delta}{|\alpha_\delta|}. 	ag{6} \] Omit a protected-middle term, whose degree is fixed at zero. The same formula follows directly from the monomer when one outer weight is zero. Every ordinary middle row is free locally, including a row equal to \(1/2\). Therefore \[ \mathcal L_\delta(\mu)=b\quad(b>0),\qquad \mathcal L_\delta(
u)=c\quad(c>0). 	ag{7} \] A protected input has \(\mu=0\), and a protected output has \(
u=1\), with no corresponding derivative equation. The spectra are independent of every row/face constraint. At a strict spectral maximum the derivative of (3), with the degrees held fixed, is zero. At an already stationary tilt and rows, it equals the derivative of (6) or any of its stationary branch primitives: the tilt and row derivatives cancel. This does not differentiate along an assumed shared feasible family of separately optimized rows. For precision retain the absolutely normalized primitives from [original LEFT spectral envelope and normalized primitives](actual_global_left_weighted_spectral_envelope.md). Write \[ A=x+y>0,\quad P=xy\ge0,\quad z=\sin^2(\pi\delta),\quad D=A^2-4Pz>0,\quad p=	frac12-\delta. 	ag{8} \] On the lower half, \(\mathcal L\) increases from zero to infinity on \((0,p)\), then decreases from infinity to \[ q_{\mathrm{end}}= rac{A+\sqrt D}{2z} 	ag{9} \] on \((p,1/2]\). If the row solving \(\mathcal L(r)=q\) is before the pole, its normalized half-cofactor action is \(Q_q\). If it is after the pole, denote the action by \(J_q\). Both use the same definition \[ r\log q+\int_0^r\log|\alpha_\delta|\,dt+ \int_r^{1/2}\log\Lambda_\delta(t;x,y)\,dt. 	ag{10} \] on their respective row branch. The original derivative formulas are \[  egin{aligned} E_q&=A+2qz+2\sqrt z\sqrt{qA+P+q^2z},& Q_q'&=-\log(E_q/\sqrt D),\ T_q&=2qz-A+2\sqrt z\sqrt{q^2z-qA+P},& J_q'&=-\log(T_q/\sqrt D). \end{aligned} 	ag{11} \] Primes mean differentiation in \(\delta\) at fixed face weights. These constants are those of the original outside integrals, not an unfixed primitive. For example the post-pole derivative is fixed by \(r	o1/2\), where the half-alpha integral has derivative zero and \(T_q	o\sqrt D\). At a protected input the exact limiting primitive is \(Q_0\), with \(E_0=A+2\sqrt{zP}\). In particular \(Q_q'<0\), except when \(q=P=0\); and \(J_q'<0\) at every strict post-pole row. At the terminal post-pole row the latter derivative is zero. These conclusions include the exact monomer specialization \(P=0\). ## 4. Strict spectral CROSS and half seams cannot remain First suppose \(\mu<1/2<
u\). Reflect the upper half by \(t\mapsto1-t\). The full interval (3) has exactly its original two half-cofactor Legendre expressions with one common outer tilt.
