A maximum principle for the geometric cosine phases
text: # A maximum principle for the geometric cosine phases Research note, 3 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts and running certificate inputs are unchanged. The cosine phases of a positive path satisfy a simple maximum principle. It gives a short proof of the spectral half-plane bound and, more usefully for pair activation, an upper bound for each real angle in terms of its own charge. The latter removes a large part of the parameter region considered in the existing support tests. The argument uses the already proved positive charge family and height bound. It does not use the spectral half-plane theorem as an input. Thus it provides an alternative proof of that theorem without changing its current file or the inputs of any running verification. ## 1. The geometric equations Use the finite positive paths of the [fractional-charge theorem](research_positive_path_fractional_charge_cube.md): all selected integer powers satisfy \(n_v\ge3\), all charges satisfy \(0\le\chi_v\le1\), and at least one outside endpoint is complete. At a positive-charge vertex write \[ t_v=a_v-iH_v,\qquad 0<a_v<\pi,\qquad 0<H_v<H_*:=\frac{23}{20}. \tag{1} \] Zero-charge vertices and complete outside endpoints have \(t_v=0\). For an incidence \(vw\), its return on the original geometric branch is \[ r_{vw}=k_{vw}+ig_{vw} =\operatorname{arsinh}\!\left( \tan(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)\right). \tag{2} \] At an active vertex \(k_{vw}>0\). Its two real period equations are \[ \sum_{w\sim v}k_{vw}=\frac{n_vH_v}{2},\qquad \sum_{w\sim v}g_{vw}=\frac{n_va_v}{2}-\pi\chi_v . \tag{3} \] The sums have the original incidence degrees; an absent edge contributes nothing. The branch in (2) has positive real part and imaginary part in \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\). Put \[ B_v=\frac{\sinh H_v}{\sin a_v},\qquad \beta_v=\arg\cos(t_v/2). \tag{4} \] For an active vertex both numbers are positive. Direct trigonometric identities give \[ \arg\tan(t_v/2)=-\arctan B_v,\qquad \tan\beta_v =\tanh(H_v/2)\tan(a_v/2) =B_v\,\frac{1-\cos a_v}{1+\cosh H_v}<B_v. \tag{5} \] Set \(\beta_v=0\) at complete vertices. We will use the elementary strict bound \[ \cosh H_*<\frac74. \tag{6} \] For completeness, the positive series for \(\cosh x\) gives \[ \cosh x\le1+\frac{x^2}{2} +\frac{x^4}{24(1-x^2/30)} \quad(0\le x<\sqrt{30}). \] At \(x=23/20\), the right side is \(31889123/18353600\), whose difference from \(7/4\) is \(229677/18353600>0\). ## 2. The maximum cosine phase **Theorem 1.** Throughout this charge family, \[ \tan^2\beta_v<\frac9{11}<\frac{100}{121} \quad\text{at every active vertex. In particular}\quad 0<\beta_v<\frac{\pi}{4}. \tag{7} \] *Proof.* If there are no active vertices the assertion is vacuous. Otherwise choose a vertex \(v\) where \(\beta_v\) is largest. Every neighbor has \[ \beta_w\le\beta_v<\arctan B_v. \tag{8} \] Thus each product in (2) has strictly negative argument, while its real part remains positive. The same sign holds for \(g_{vw}\): indeed \[ \sinh(k+ig)=\sinh k\cos g+i\cosh k\sin g \] on the specified branch. The second period equation therefore gives \[ a_v<\frac{2\pi\chi_v}{n_v}\le\frac{2\pi}{3}. \tag{9} \] Consequently \[ \tan^2\beta_v =\tanh^2(H_v/2)\tan^2(a_v/2) <3\,\frac{\cosh H_*-1}{\cosh H_*+1} <3\,\frac{3}{11}=\frac9{11}. \tag{10} \] Every other cosine phase is at most this maximum. The final comparison in (7) has exact difference \(1/121\). \(\square\) The maximizer of the cosine phase need not maximize height or real angle. No such additional assertion is used. ## 3. A local angle bound in terms of the charge The maximum principle gives a bound at every vertex, not just at the maximizer. Let \[ b=\frac{10}{11},\qquad m_b(B)=\frac{b-B}{1+bB},\qquad \kappa_b=\frac{\sqrt{1+b^2}-1}{\sqrt{1+b^2}+1}. \tag{11} \] **Theorem 2.** Every active vertex satisfies \[ a_v\le\frac{2\pi\chi_v}{n_v}+\kappa_b\sin a_v <\frac{2\pi\chi_v}{n_v}+\frac3{20}\sin a_v, \qquad a_v<\frac{40\pi}{17n_v}\chi_v. \tag{12} \] *Proof.* Fix \(v\), and write \(a,H,B,n,\chi\) for its data. By (7), all neighboring phases are less than \(\arctan b\). If \(B\ge b\), every return has nonpositive imaginary part, so \(a\le2\pi\chi/n\), which implies (12). Suppose \(0<B<b\). The argument \(\varphi\) of each product in (2) is at most \(\arctan b-\arctan B\). If \(\varphi\le0\) then \(g\le0\). If \(\varphi>0\), the same identity for \(\sinh(k+ig)\) gives \[ \tan g=\tanh k\,\tan\varphi,\qquad g\le k\tan\varphi\le k\,m_b(B). \tag{13} \] Thus this last upper bound holds in both cases. Summing it and using both equations (3) yields \[ a-\frac{2\pi\chi}{n}\le Hm_b(B) \le \sin a\,\frac{B(b-B)}{1+bB}. \tag{14} \] The second inequality uses \(H\le\sinh H=B\sin a\). The maximum of \(B(b-B)/(1+bB)\) on \(0\le B\le b\) is \(\kappa_b\). Differentiation gives its unique interior maximizer \((\sqrt{1+b^2}-1)/b\). For \(b=10/11\), \[ \kappa_b=\frac{\sqrt{221}-11}{\sqrt{221}+11}<\frac3{20}, \quad\text{since}\quad 221\cdot17^2=63869<64009=23^2\cdot11^2. \tag{15} \] This proves the first two bounds in (12). Finally \(\sin a\le a\) gives \(17a/20<2\pi\chi/n\). \(\square\) Using only \(\beta<\pi/4\), the same proof gives the weaker constant \(3-2\sqrt2\) in place of \(3/20\). The rational refinement (15) uses the quantitative maximum principle (7). ## 4. The spectral half-plane as a consequence **Corollary 3.** Every geometric free color in the stated charge family satisfies \[ \Re(-2\cos t_v)<\frac74. \tag{16} \] *Proof.* Complete vertices give the value \(-2\). At an active vertex with \(a\le2\pi/3\), \[ -2\cos a\cosh H\le\cosh H<\frac74. \tag{17} \] If \(a>2\pi/3\), the proof of Theorem 2 shows \(B<b\). Since \(\sin a<\sqrt3/2\), (12) gives \[ a<\frac{2\pi}{3}+\frac{3\sqrt3}{40}, \qquad \cos a>-\frac{49}{80}. \tag{18} \] The cosine estimate follows from \(\cos(2\pi/3+u)\ge-1/2-\sqrt3\,u/2\). Also \[ \sinh H=B\sin a<\frac{5\sqrt3}{11}, \qquad \cosh H<\frac{14}{11}. \tag{19} \] Consequently \[ \Re(-2\cos t)<\frac{343}{220}<\frac74. \tag{20} \] This proves the assertion in both angle ranges. \(\square\) This recovers the conclusion of the [geometric half-plane theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_geometric_spectral_half_plane.md). In particular, for \(N\ge16\), its physical Jacobi matrices obey \[ c_0-\Re w>\frac14-\frac{\pi^2}{N^2}>\frac15, \qquad \|(\mathcal J_j-wI)^{-1}\|\le5, \tag{21} \] with the same original boundary forcing and first-normal qualifications as in the [Jacobi boundary problem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_physical_jacobi_charge_boundary.md). ## 5. Reducing the pair-height search region Consider the two power-three vertices in [simultaneous pair activation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_path_pair_activation_gap.md). They have the same charge \(\chi\), and let \(H\) be their larger height. If the scaled height estimate fails, then \(\chi\le50H/59\). Theorem 2 applies to both vertices, even to the one with smaller height, and gives \[ a_v,a_w<\frac{2000\pi}{3009}H <\frac{209}{100}H . \tag{22} \] The last strict comparison follows already from \(\pi<22/7\). For example, throughout \(H\le1/2\) both angles are less than \(209/200\). This removes the large-angle part of the old sector-only search region by an analytic argument. More precisely, the angle at the maximum-height endpoint lies in \[ \arcsin\!\left(\frac{\sinh H}{\sqrt3}\right) \le a\le \min\left\{ \pi-\arcsin\!\left(\frac{\sinh H}{\sqrt3}\right), \frac{2000\pi}{3009}H, \arccos\!\left(-\frac{7}{8\cosh H}\right) \right\}. \tag{23} \] The closed inequalities deliberately enlarge the strict geometric domain. The first two sector bounds are existing results; the last two are consequences of (22) and (16). For the affine height estimate, put \[ \chi_{\max}(H)= \min\left\{1,\frac{40}{37}\left(H-\frac{37}{200}\right)\right\}. \tag{24} \] A failure of that estimate implies \(\chi\le\chi_{\max}(H)\). In addition to the sector and spectral restrictions in (23), Theorem 2 then gives the stronger implicit bound \[ a-\frac3{20}\sin a <\frac{2\pi}{3}\chi_{\max}(H). \tag{25} \] The function on the left is strictly increasing. Its unique inverse, or any rigorously larger elementary bound, may therefore be used to restrict a subsequent support verification. The neighboring cosine domains can also be reduced: writing \(c=x+iy=\cos(t_w/2)\), Theorem 1 and Corollary 3 give \[ 0\le y\le\frac{10}{11}x,\qquad x^2-y^2>\frac1{16}. \tag{26} \] The value \(c=1\) at a complete neighbor satisfies these conditions. An absent incidence has return zero and must be included separately; it is not represented by a cosine satisfying (26). Intersecting the old cosine domains with (26) introduces new boundary pieces, so the old arc-only support verification cannot be reused without checking those pieces. These are reductions of the domain containing the actual geometric solution. They do not assert the old support inequalities at all points of their larger rectangles. No running certificate has been changed, and neither the full pair-height estimate nor the integrated pair-energy gap follows until the remaining support bounds are proved. ## 6. A stronger angle restriction at larger heights When \(\sinh H\ge b=10/11\), the signs in the local return equation give a further reduction. Define \[ d(H)=\frac{\sinh H-b}{1+b\sinh H}\ge0. \tag{27} \] **Proposition 4.** At an active vertex of power \(n\), charge \(\chi\) and height \(H\ge\operatorname{arsinh}b\), \[ a\le\frac{2\pi\chi}{n} -\frac2n\arctan\!\left( d(H)\tanh\frac{nH}{2}\right). \tag{28} \] The following implicit bound is at least as strong: \[ a\le\frac{2\pi\chi}{n} -\frac2n\arctan\!\left[ \frac{\sinh H-b\sin a}{\sin a+b\sinh H} \tanh\frac{nH}{2}\right]. \tag{29} \] *Proof.* Since \(B=\sinh H/\sin a\ge\sinh H\ge b\), every product in (2) has nonpositive argument. In fact, its argument \(\varphi\) satisfies \[ -\varphi\ge\arctan B-\arctan b,\qquad \tan(-\varphi)\ge d_B:=\frac{B-b}{1+bB}\ge d(H). \tag{30} \] Here \(0\le-\varphi<\pi/2\). The identity used in (13), with the opposite sign, therefore gives \[ -g\ge f_{d_B}(k),\qquad f_d(k):=\arctan(d\tanh k). \tag{31} \] For \(d\ge0\), this is an increasing concave function on \([0,\infty)\), with \(f_d(0)=0\). Directly, \[ f_d''(k)= -\frac{2d(1+d^2)\tanh k\,\operatorname{sech}^2k} {(1+d^2\tanh^2k)^2}\le0. \tag{32} \] For any nonnegative \(k_i\) with sum \(S\), concavity gives \(f_d(k_i)\ge(k_i/S)f_d(S)\) when \(S>0\). Consequently \[ \sum_i(-g_i)\ge f_{d_B}\!\left(\sum_i k_i\right) \ge f_{d(H)}(nH/2). \tag{33} \] Insert the imaginary period equation (3) to obtain (28). Keeping \(d_B=(\sinh H-b\sin a)/(\sin a+b\sinh H)\) gives (29). An absent incidence contributes zero to both sums, so the same argument applies to terminal vertices. \(\square\) The whole affine search range has \(H\ge37/40>10/11\), hence \(\sinh H>b\). A failure of the affine height estimate must therefore satisfy, at its maximum-height endpoint, \[ a\le\frac{2\pi}{3}\chi_{\max}(H) -\frac23\arctan\!\left(d(H)\tanh\frac{3H}{2}\right), \tag{34} \] in addition to the earlier restrictions. The explicit right side is a rigorous bound; using the stronger implicit inequality (29) would require retaining its dependence on \(a\) in the verifier. Neither inequality estimates the real return sum by itself. They reduce the parameter domain of the remaining support problem and do not replace that problem by a claimed height theorem. ## 7. A sharper bound for the maximum cosine phase The negative return phases at a maximizing vertex give more than their sign. Retaining their sizes improves (7) to a bound that removes some of the largest possible neighboring returns. **Theorem 5.** Throughout the positive charge family of Section 1, \[ \tan^2\beta_v<\frac12. \tag{35} \] *Proof.* Choose a vertex attaining the positive maximum of \(\beta\), and omit its subscript. Put \[ \tau=\tanh(H/2),\qquad b_*=\tan\beta,\qquad q=\tau^2,\qquad B_*=b_*^2. \tag{36} \] The letters \(B_*,b_*\) in this proof denote squared phase and phase, not the return ratio \(B=\sinh H/\sin a\) from (4). Equation (5) gives \(b_*=\tau\tan(a/2)\). Because every neighboring cosine phase is at most \(\beta\), the negative argument of each product in (2) is at least \(\arctan B-\beta\). Its tangent simplifies exactly: \[ \tan(\arctan B-\beta) =\frac{B-b_*}{1+Bb_*} =\tanh(H/2)\cot(a/2)=\frac{\tau^2}{b_*}. \tag{37} \] Apply the concavity argument (31)--(33), now with \(d=\tau^2/b_*\), to all incidences at this vertex. Both period equations give \[ \frac{na}{2} +\arctan\!\left(\frac{\tau^2}{b_*}\tanh\frac{nH}{2}\right) \le\pi\chi\le\pi. \tag{38} \] The left side increases with \(n>0\). Since \(n\ge3\), the triple-angle identity for the hyperbolic tangent yields \[ 3\arctan(b_*/\tau) +\arctan\!\left( \frac{\tau^3(3+\tau^2)}{b_*(1+3\tau^2)}\right)\le\pi. \tag{39} \] Suppose \(B_*\ge1/2\). The previous maximum principle and (6) give \[ \frac{B_*}{3}\le q<\frac3{11},\qquad \frac12\le B_*<\frac9{11}<1. \tag{40} \] The first inequality follows from \(a<2\pi/3\). In particular \(3\arctan(b_*/\tau)\) lies in \((\pi/2,\pi]\). The other angle in (39) is positive and less than \(\pi/2\). Consequently (39) is equivalent to the tangent inequality \[ \frac{\tau^3(3+\tau^2)}{b_*(1+3\tau^2)} \le \frac{b_*(3\tau^2-b_*^2)} {\tau(3b_*^2-\tau^2)}. \tag{41} \] All denominators are positive on (40). Multiplying out, (41) requires \[ \begin{split} P(q,B_*):={}&q^4+3(1-B_*)q^3 +3B_*(1-B_*)q-B_*^2\ge0. \end{split} \tag{42} \] This polynomial is strictly increasing in \(q>0\) for \(0<B_*<1\), and strictly decreasing in \(B_*\ge1/2\): \[ \begin{split} P_q&=4q^3+9(1-B_*)q^2+3B_*(1-B_*)>0,\\ P_{B_*}&=-3q^3+3(1-2B_*)q-2B_*<0. \end{split} \tag{43} \] But \[ P(q,B_*)\le P(3/11,1/2)=-\frac{139}{14641}<0, \tag{44} \] contradicting (42). The maximal phase therefore satisfies (35), as do all other phases. \(\square\) The proof also covers a terminal vertex: it uses the actual sum of returns, and concavity is valid for one or more nonnegative terms. No assumption that the two returns have equal real parts is made. Theorem 2 can now be applied with \(b=1/\sqrt2\). Its optimal constant is \[ \kappa_b=\frac{\sqrt6-2}{\sqrt6+2}<\frac19, \tag{45} \] where the strict comparison is \(8\sqrt6<20\). Thus every positive vertex satisfies \[ a<\frac{2\pi\chi}{n}+\frac19\sin a,\qquad a<\frac{9\pi}{4n}\chi. \tag{46} \] For a failed scaled pair estimate this gives the particularly simple restriction \[ a_v,a_w<\frac{75\pi}{118}H<2H. \tag{47} \] Here \(75(22/7)/118=825/413<2\). Proposition 4 likewise holds with \(b=1/\sqrt2\). For later support estimates, the neighboring cosine now lies in the quarter ellipse (5) intersected with \[ 0\le y\le x/\sqrt2. \tag{48} \] This conclusion is independent of the current support certificates. It is a stronger restriction on the actual geometric solution, not an assertion that the previous support inequalities hold throughout their larger domains. ## 8. A single arc suffices for the smaller cosine domain For a height cap \(C>0\), let \(D_C\) be the quarter ellipse from the pair-activation note, and put \[ D_C^\sharp=D_C\cap\{x+iy:0\le y\le x/\sqrt2\},\qquad \vartheta_C=\arctan\!\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\coth(C/2)\right). \tag{49} \] Theorem 5 puts every neighboring geometric cosine in this domain. The complete cosine \(1\) and the zero return used for an absent incidence are included. **Proposition 6.** Fix \(A=\tan((a-iH)/2)\) with \(0<a<\pi\), \(H>0\), and a real support slope \(s\le0\). Then \[ \begin{split} &\max_{c\in D_C^\sharp} \{\Re\operatorname{arsinh}(Ac) -s\Im\operatorname{arsinh}(Ac)\}\\ &\quad= \max\left\{0,\ \max_{0\le\vartheta\le\vartheta_C} \left[\Re\operatorname{arsinh}(Ac_C(\vartheta)) -s\Im\operatorname{arsinh}(Ac_C(\vartheta))\right] \right\},\\ &\hspace{30mm} c_C(\vartheta)=\cosh(C/2)\cos\vartheta +i\sinh(C/2)\sin\vartheta . \end{split} \tag{50} \] All branches are the original right-half-plane branches. *Proof.* The domain is star-shaped about zero. On any ray \(c=r e^{i\beta}\) in the domain, write \(\varphi=\arg(Ae^{i\beta})\). It lies strictly between \(-\pi/2\) and \(\pi/2\). Apart from a positive real factor, the radial derivative of the support function has argument \[ \arctan s+\delta(r),\qquad \delta(r)=\varphi-\frac12\arg(1+r^2A^2e^{2i\beta}). \tag{51} \] If \(\varphi\ge0\), then \(0\le\delta(r)\le\varphi\), so this derivative has positive real part. If \(\varphi<0\), \(\delta(r)\) increases from \(\varphi\) toward zero: its derivative is \(-r\Im(A^2e^{2i\beta})/|1+r^2A^2e^{2i\beta}|^2>0\). The angle in (51) stays in \((-\pi,0]\). Its cosine can therefore change sign only from negative to positive. The support function on the ray has no strict interior maximum; its maximum is at zero or at the outer endpoint. The outer endpoints form precisely the ellipse arc in (50). The relation \(y/x\le1/\sqrt2\) is equivalent there to \(\vartheta\le\vartheta_C\). Taking the maximum over rays proves the formula. \(\square\) Thus both support terms for pair activation can be bounded using one arc and the value zero, even in the affine regime. The old three-piece sector boundary need not be retained if this smaller phase domain is used instead. This observation gives a simpler candidate for a new verification; it does not certify its support inequalities by itself.

title: Global injectivity of positive marked logarithmic gluing
text: # Global injectivity of positive marked logarithmic gluing Research proof, 22 November 2026. Positive ideal shapes give a global uniqueness statement for a fixed logarithmic gluing system. The proof compares two configurations in the product of shape strips; their joining segment need not satisfy any gluing equation. It also proves that the inverse is holomorphic on the realized image. No existence or source-cycle assertion is included. ## 1. The positive shape coordinates and the real constraint matrix Let \[ \mathcal S=\{x\in\mathbb C:0<\operatorname{Im}x<\pi\}, \qquad z=e^x, \qquad v(x)=-\operatorname{Log}(1-e^x). \tag{1} \] The logarithm in (1) is principal. Since \(z\) is in the upper half-plane, \(1-z\) is in the lower half-plane, so this defines one holomorphic function on the entire convex strip. In particular, \[ 0<\operatorname{Im}v(x)<\pi,\qquad v'(x)=\frac{e^x}{1-e^x},\qquad \operatorname{Im}v'(x) =\frac{\operatorname{Im}(e^x)}{|1-e^x|^2}>0. \tag{2} \] For \(t\ge1\), apply \(v\) separately to the coordinates of \(x\in\mathcal S^t\). Let \(A,B\) be real \(t\)-by-\(t\) matrices satisfying \[ R=(A\ B),\qquad \operatorname{rank}R=t, \qquad AB^{\mathsf T}=BA^{\mathsf T}. \tag{3} \] Define the holomorphic logarithmic constraint map \[ F_R(x)=Ax+Bv(x). \tag{4} \] Neither block in (3) is required to be invertible. Use the complex bilinear alternating form \[ \Omega((a,b),(c,d))=a^{\mathsf T}d-b^{\mathsf T}c \quad\text{on }\mathbb C^{2t}. \tag{5} \] The real kernel of \(R\) is Lagrangian for this form. Indeed it is the image of the rank-\(t\) matrix \(\binom{-B^{\mathsf T}}{A^{\mathsf T}}\): multiplication by \(R\) gives zero, and the pairing of two of its columns is zero by (3). Its complexification is therefore isotropic and is closed under complex conjugation. ## 2. A strict comparison for any two positive configurations For \(x,x'\in\mathcal S^t\), write \(\Delta x=x-x'\) and \(\Delta v=v(x)-v(x')\). Convexity of the strip and the fundamental theorem of calculus give \[ \Delta v_j=\Delta x_j\int_0^1 v'(x'_j+s\Delta x_j)\,ds. \tag{6} \] Consequently \[ \operatorname{Im}\sum_j\overline{\Delta x_j}\Delta v_j =\sum_j|\Delta x_j|^2 \int_0^1\operatorname{Im}v'(x'_j+s\Delta x_j)\,ds >0\quad\text{if }x\ne x'. \tag{7} \] The points of the segment in (6) are used only to evaluate the one-variable function (1). No gluing condition is imposed there. **Theorem.** Under (3), \(F_R\) is injective on \(\mathcal S^t\). Its complex Jacobian is invertible everywhere. Hence it is a biholomorphism onto the open realized image \(F_R(\mathcal S^t)\). Suppose first that \(F_R(x)=F_R(x')\). Then \(w=(\Delta x,\Delta v)\) and \(\overline w\) lie in the complexification of the real Lagrangian kernel in Section 1. Thus \[ 0=\Omega(\overline w,w) =2\mathrm i\operatorname{Im} \sum_j\overline{\Delta x_j}\Delta v_j. \tag{8} \] By (7), this forces \(x=x'\), proving injectivity. At any point the complex Jacobian is \[ J_R(x)=A+B\operatorname{diag}(v'(x_j)). \tag{9} \] If \(J_R(x)a=0\), the vector \(w=(a,\operatorname{diag}(v'(x_j))a)\) belongs to the same complexified Lagrangian kernel. Its pairing with its conjugate is \[ 0=\Omega(\overline w,w) =2\mathrm i\sum_j\operatorname{Im}v'(x_j)|a_j|^2. \tag{10} \] Equation (2) forces \(a=0\). This proves (9) is invertible. The holomorphic inverse-function theorem supplies local inverses; injectivity makes them agree on every overlap. Their union is the single holomorphic inverse on the realized image. This proves all assertions of the theorem. ## 3. Actual edge rows and arbitrary primitive filling directions Consider an actual oriented ideal triangulation with \(t\) tetrahedra and \(c\) torus ideal-vertex links, with positively ordered shapes. Retain every face identification, edge occurrence and marked primitive peripheral path. In the convention (1), the incidence argument in [M] gives \(t-c\) independent real edge rows. Their peripheral symplectic quotient has dimension \(2c\); different cusps pair to zero, and each cusp's primitive meridian and longitude have nonzero intersection pairing. Append one row \[ \gamma_i=a_i\mu_i+b_i\lambda_i, \qquad (a_i,b_i)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, \tag{11} \] at each cusp. These rows are independent modulo the edge rows and pair to zero. The complete \(t\)-row system therefore satisfies (3), as proved locally in [M]. This rank and isotropy argument is incidence-theoretic and does not depend on the shape values. For integral coprime \((a_i,b_i)\), (11) is the original primitive path; real coefficients give the corresponding real polarization. Fix the actual affine logarithmic target, including all edge windings, peripheral signs, and constants introduced by the quad convention. The equations are then precisely \[ F_R(x)=q. \tag{12} \] The theorem gives at most one positive assignment satisfying this fixed target, across all positive components, and a nonsingular Jacobian at every such assignment. No completeness hypothesis is needed for this uniqueness and transversality step. In particular one may keep a meridian row at every unfilled cusp and choose \(\mu_i+p_i\lambda_i\) at every designated filled cusp, with arbitrary fixed real \(p_i\). Mixed signs and \(p_i=0\) cause no exception. For an actual integral filling the similarity-log equation has its prescribed primitive target, for example \[ U_i+p_iV_i=-2\pi\mathrm i. \tag{13} \] The logs in (13) are the actual continued similarity logs, with their original primitive basis. They are not uncentered SL eigenlogs or equations only modulo \(2\pi\mathrm i\). Deleting dependent edge rows does not lose constraints: their linear relations and constants must agree in the full marked system. If they did not agree, that target would have no solution. Quad changes likewise transform both the rows and their affine constants. The theorem does not compare different logarithmic lifts of one exponentiated equation. One useful consequence concerns continuation along the same fixed primitive slopes, with the right sides of (13) varying continuously. No two positive solutions at a fixed target can collide, and no Jacobian can become singular at an interior positive point. A continuation remaining in a compact subset of \(\mathcal S^t\) extends past a finite endpoint by compactness and (9). This does not prove that such compact containment or continuation exists. ## 4. Algebraic multipliers at a realized target Suppose now that \(A,B\) have integer entries and that all \(\gamma_i=e^{q_i}\) are nonzero algebraic numbers. Exponentiating (12) gives the square rational system \[ G_i(z):=\prod_j z_j^{A_{ij}}(1-z_j)^{-B_{ij}} =\gamma_i,\quad 1\le i\le t. \tag{14} \] Work on \(\prod_jz_j(1-z_j)\ne0\). At a realized positive solution, \[ D_zG=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_i)J_R(x) \operatorname{diag}(z_j^{-1}) \tag{15} \] is invertible. Thus this is an isolated nonsingular algebraic solution and all its shapes are algebraic. Here is also a direct field argument. Over a number field containing the \(\gamma_i\), differentiate (14) in the finitely generated field generated by the \(z_j\). Equation (15) forces every \(dz_j\) to vanish. In characteristic zero the dimension of these differentials is the transcendence degree, so that field is a finite algebraic extension. Other positive solutions of (14) can have different logarithmic targets \(q+2\pi\mathrm i k\). They are not identified by this corollary. Global uniqueness is the fixed-log statement (12). ## 5. Relation to the earlier results and the remaining boundary [M] proves the all-cusp marked incidence and local polarized Jacobian theorem. [E] proves global comparison, fixed-slope uniqueness and positive-region elimination for its explicit original eight-tetrahedron edge blocks. The argument (6)--(10) gives a global comparison directly in the product of ideal-shape strips, for any real Lagrangian constraint matrix. It does not require the original wire or peripheral image to be convex. Polarized rigidity and geometric variational principles are established subjects; no historical novelty claim is made here. Uniqueness does not supply a positive point. Already for \(t=1\), \(A=1,B=-1\), the target \(q=-\log8\) would imply \(z(1-z)=1/8\), whose two roots are real. There is no positive solution. Nor is the realized image asserted convex or the map to \(\mathbb C^t\) asserted proper. A hyperbolic filling need not be represented by a positive assignment on this same fixed triangulation and log lift. The result does not construct a cone path, prove primitive metric completion from multiplier equations, identify a quantum source critical scheme, or select the coefficient of its original cycle. The original closing, normal data, and noncancellation estimates remain separate. No finite-exception or volume-limit theorem follows. ## Complete proof sources * M: [Marked multicusp rigidity](../papers/marked-fillings/README.md), 261 lines, SHA-256 f882d2c7d1f723590391d3cc03dcd9bba7a12d13c2e006c6dea570e1b4af1b42. * E: [Positive edge global monotonicity](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md), 678 lines, SHA-256 da5129c7110190035eedb8249d4004dd06b5a7555e78d948234d8de50fa17500.

title: Global logarithmic phases on the proper-return domains
text:
# Global logarithmic phases on the proper-return domains Private written proof, 15 November 2026. The proper-return strip of the original positive primitive equations supports a single global Newton label and value phase. The domain for two disjoint proper subproducts is contractible, and all seven multiplication factorial arguments have fixed global logarithms and primitives calibrated from the original strict real gate. The same statement holds for both signed crossing gates, with their existing integer Fourier characters retained. These functions pull back to an arbitrary-degree vertex and any binary resolution with allocated integer crossing powers. The resulting phases telescope to the original angular action, independently of the resolution. This is a global statement about logarithmic marks and actions. It does not determine a Fourier coefficient of the complete lattice kernel or an intersection coefficient of the original finite cycle. **Theorem.** The domains \(\mathcal E,\mathcal D\) and \(\mathcal V_{d,n}\) defined below are contractible. The globally normalized phases satisfy the multiplication, crossing and complementary identities (23), (32) and (38). Every allocated proper-subproduct resolution on \(\mathcal V_{d,n}\) therefore has the same marked action (39). The original crossing characters and finite pairing are retained. ## 1. The universal proper-return domain Put \[ \mathcal T=\{t\in\mathbb C:|\Re t|<\pi,\ \Im t<0\}, \qquad H=-\Im t,\qquad a=	an(t/2), \] \[ \mathcal S_t=\{R\in\mathbb C: 0<\Re(R\overline t)<\pi H\},\qquad \mathcal E=\{(t,R):t\in\mathcal T,\ R\in\mathcal S_t\}. 	ag{1} \] This is an open domain in \(\mathbb C^2\). It is contractible. Indeed every return has unique real coordinates \[ R=-\pi i u+i t v,\qquad 0<u<1,\quad v\in\mathbb R, 	ag{2} \] because \(\Re(R\overline t)=\pi Hu\) and \(H>0\). Thus (2) is a homeomorphism \(\mathcal E\simeq\mathcal T	imes(0,1)	imes\mathbb R\). It is used for topology, not as a holomorphic coordinate change. Use the original prefix functions \[ \mathcal N_R=a\cosh R+i\sinh R,\qquad \mathcal D_R=a\cosh R-i\sinh R,\qquad Y_R=\mathcal N_R/\mathcal D_R,\qquad Q_R=\mathcal N_R\mathcal D_R. 	ag{3} \] Here \(Q_R\) is not the root of unity. The source prefix identities give the zeros of \(\mathcal N_R,\mathcal D_R\) respectively at \[ R=it/2+\pi i k,\qquad R=-it/2+\pi i k,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z. 	ag{4} \] The zeros of \(\sinh R\) are \(\pi i k\). Every value in these lists has real pairing \(-\pi kH\), outside the strict interval in (1). Also \(a
e0\) and \(1+a^2
e0\) on \(\mathcal T\). Consequently all these factors are holomorphic units on \(\mathcal E\). Every holomorphic unit on a simply connected domain has a holomorphic logarithm: integrate its closed logarithmic derivative and fix one value. Define the global label \(X(t,R)\) by \[ e^{2\pi iX(t,R)}=Y_R,\qquad X(t,-\pi i/2)=1/2. 	ag{5} \] The second condition is consistent for all \(t\), because \(Y_{-\pi i/2}=-1\) identically. It fixes the logarithm globally. In particular \(\sin(\pi X)
e0\). The unit \[ \chi_R=\mathcal D_R e^{\pi iX(t,R)} 	ag{6} \] is a specified square root of \(Q_R\), with \(\chi_{-\pi i/2}=-i\). Exact algebra gives \[ \sin(\pi X(t,R))= rac{\sinh R}{\chi_R}, \qquad X_R= rac{a}{\pi Q_R},\qquad X_t=- rac{(1+a^2)\sinh R\cosh R}{2\pi Q_R}. 	ag{7} \] Thus \(X_R\) never vanishes. The unit \(2\sin(\pi X)\) has a global logarithm \(\mathcal K\), normalized to be real on \(t=-iH,\ R=-iho,\ 0<ho<\pi\). There the label lies in \((0,1)\), as verified in (19). The one-form \(\mathcal K\,dX\) is closed, so it has a global primitive \(\mathcal J(t,R)\), normalized by \[ d\mathcal J=\mathcal K\,dX,\qquad \mathcal J(t,-\pi i/2)=J(1/2)=0. 	ag{7a} \] The normalization is consistent because \(X=1/2\) on that line. This primitive agrees with the original \(J(x)=\int_0^x\log(2\sin\pi s)\,ds\) on the real slice. There is a global logarithm \(\mathcal L(t,R)=\Log[\sin(t/2)/\sinh R]\), normalized to be real when \(t=-iH,\ R=-iho,\ 0<ho<\pi\). On that slice the ratio is \(\sinh(H/2)/\sinho>0\). The one-form \[ \omega=2\mathcal L(t,R)\,dX- rac R\pi\,dt 	ag{8} \] is closed. To check this directly, use \(\mathcal L_t=1/(2a)\), \(\mathcal L_R=-\coth R\) and (7): \[ 2\mathcal L_tX_R-2\mathcal L_RX_t+ rac1\pi = rac{1-(1+a^2)\cosh^2R}{\pi Q_R}+ rac1\pi=0. 	ag{9} \] Contractibility therefore gives a unique holomorphic primitive \(\mathcal B\), normalized by \[ d\mathcal B=\omega,\qquad \mathcal B(t,-\pi i/2)=it/2. 	ag{10} \] Along the indicated line \(dX=0\), so (8) gives \(i\,dt/2\); the normalization is consistent. This is the original value phase, globally lifted to \(\mathcal E\). On the strict initial chart it agrees with \[ B(x,c)=\int_0^x\Log(2\cos(2\pi s)-c)\,ds-2J(x), \quad c=-2\cos t,\quad x=X(t,R). 	ag{11} \] Indeed the source derivatives are \(B_t=-R/\pi\) and \[ B_x=\Log rac{2\cos(2\pi x)-c}{4\sin^2\pi x} =2\Log rac{\sin(t/2)}{\sinh R}, 	ag{12} \] with their real logarithms on the purely imaginary slice. Its source normalization \(B(1/2,c)=it/2\) is (10). Thus (8)--(10) continue the specified phase, without an undetermined additive constant. ## 2. Two proper subproducts and their seven primitives Define \[ \mathcal D=\{(t,\alpha, eta): t\in\mathcal T,\ \Re(\alpha\overline t)>0,\ \Re( eta\overline t)>0,\ \Re((\alpha+ eta)\overline t)<\pi H\}. 	ag{13} \] In (2), write \(\alpha=-\pi i u_1+itv_1\) and \( eta=-\pi i u_2+itv_2\). Then \[ u_1,u_2>0,\qquad u_1+u_2<1,\qquad v_1,v_2\in\mathbb R. 	ag{14} \] This identifies \(\mathcal D\) topologically with \(\mathcal T\), an open triangle and \(\mathbb R^2\). It is contractible. Put \(\gamma=\alpha+ eta\) and \[ x=X(t,\alpha),\qquad y=X(t, eta),\qquad z=X(t,\gamma). 	ag{15} \] Every one of \[ x,\ y,\ z,\ x+y,\ z-x,\ z-y,\ x+y-z 	ag{16} \] avoids the integers throughout \(\mathcal D\). Besides (7), the exact identities are \[  egin{split} \sin\pi(x+y)&= rac{a\sinh\gamma}{\chi_\alpha\chi_ eta},\ \sin\pi(z-x)&= rac{a\sinh eta}{\chi_\gamma\chi_\alpha},\ \sin\pi(z-y)&= rac{a\sinh\alpha}{\chi_\gamma\chi_ eta},\ \sin\pi(x+y-z)&=  rac{(1+a^2)\sinh\alpha\,\sinh eta\,\sinh\gamma} {\chi_\alpha\chi_ eta\chi_\gamma}. \end{split} 	ag{17} \] They follow by expanding the numerators using (3) and (6). All factors on the right are units by Section 1. The global marks have an actual strict real calibration slice: \[ t=-iH,\qquad \alpha=-iho_1,\quad eta=-iho_2, \qquad ho_1,ho_2>0,\quadho_1+ho_2<\pi. 	ag{18} \] To verify this, set \(A=	anh(H/2)\in(0,1)\). On the slice \[ \chi_{-iho}=-i\sqrt{A^2\cos^2ho+\sin^2ho},\qquad  rac{d}{dho}X(-iH,-iho) = rac{A}{\pi(A^2\cos^2ho+\sin^2ho)}>0. 	ag{19} \] This label increases from zero to one and obeys \(X(-iH,-i(\pi-ho))=1-X(-iH,-iho)\). Hence \(x+y<1\) and \(z>\max(x,y)\). All four sines in (17) are positive on (18). Since \(-1<x+y-z<1\), its positive sine implies \(x+y-z>0\). Thus \[ 0<x,y,\qquad \max(x,y)<z<x+y<1. 	ag{20} \] For each argument \(\ell\) in (16), the unit \(2\sin(\pi\ell)\) has a global logarithm normalized to its real logarithm on (18). The one-form \[ \Log(2\sin\pi\ell)\,d\ell 	ag{21} \] is closed: its exterior derivative is \(\pi\cot(\pi\ell)\,d\ell\wedge d\ell=0\). It therefore has a global primitive \(J_\ell\), fixed by the original \(J(\ell)\) at any one point of (18). These primitives agree with the source \(J\)'s on the entire slice, and are their unique continuations on \(\mathcal D\). Define the globally marked multiplication action \[ \mathcal M= J_{x+y}+J_z-J_x-J_y-J_{z-x}-J_{z-y}-J_{x+y-z}. 	ag{22} \] Then the exact global critical-value identity is \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal M(t,\alpha, eta)= \mathcal B(t,\alpha)+\mathcal B(t, eta) -\mathcal B(t,\alpha+ eta). \quad} 	ag{23} \] For a direct verification of its differential, (17) gives \[  rac{\sin\pi(x+y)\sin\pi(z-x)} {\sin\pi x\sin\pi(x+y-z)} = rac{\sin^2(t/2)}{\sinh^2\alpha}, 	ag{24} \] the analogous identity with \( eta\), and \[  rac{\sin\pi z\sin\pi(x+y-z)} {\sin\pi(z-x)\sin\pi(z-y)} = rac{\sinh^2\gamma}{\sin^2(t/2)}. 	ag{25} \] The calibrated logarithms turn these into exact logarithmic identities, since the possible integer discrepancies are constant and zero on (18). Hence \[ d\mathcal M= 2\mathcal L(t,\alpha)\,dx+ 2\mathcal L(t, eta)\,dy- 2\mathcal L(t,\gamma)\,dz. 	ag{26} \] This is the differential of the right side of (23), because the \(dt\) terms cancel by \(\gamma=\alpha+ eta\). Its additive constant is zero by the original strict multiplication identity, on (18). ## 3. Both signed crossings with their original Fourier marks For \(\sigma=\pm1\), use the same contractible domain \(\mathcal E\), and set \[ R_{m in}=R,\qquad R_{m out}=R-i\sigma t/2,\qquad y=X(t,R_{m in}),\quad x=X(t,R_{m out}). 	ag{27} \] Translation by \(-i\sigma t/2\) preserves \(\mathcal S_t\). Both individual sines are units, and \[ \sin\pi(x-y)=  rac{a\,\sinh(-i\sigma t/2)} {\chi_{R_{m out}}\chi_{R_{m in}}}
e0. 	ag{28} \] Thus all three crossing factorial primitives have global marks on \(\mathcal E\). Here is a strict real crossing point in this domain, fixing their calibration: \[ H_*=\operatorname{arsinh}1,\quad t_*=\sigma\pi/2-iH_*,\quad a_*=(\sigma-i)/\sqrt2, \] \[ R_{{m in},*}=\sigma H_*/2-i\pi/4,\qquad R_{{m out},*}=-i\pi/2,\qquad y_*=1/4,\quad x_*=1/2. 	ag{29} \] Both pairings equal \(\pi H_*/2\), and (27) holds. The global label lift in (5) gives exactly these labels. To see the input mark without an integer reset, use \[ t_s=s\sigma\pi/2-iH_*,\qquad R_{m out}=-i\pi/2,\qquad R_{m in}=R_{m out}+i\sigma t_s/2,\quad 0\le s\le1. 	ag{30} \] Along this path \(Y_{m out}=-1\) and \(Y_{m in}=(-\cos t_s)^{-\sigma}\). Its continuous argument decreases from \(\pi\) to \(\pi/2\). The input label at the endpoint is \(1/4\); the output stays \(1/2\). The initial input is connected to \(R=-\pi i/2\) by the horizontal segment at \(t=-iH_*\); its label has real part \(1/2\). Along (30), \(1/4\leq\Re y\leq1/2\), so its individual primitive remains the original analytic \(J\) in \(0<\Re y<1\). The same path gives the original logarithm in (12): at its input \(\sin(t/2)/\sinh R_{m in}=ia\), continued from a positive value to \((1+i\sigma)/\sqrt2\). Thus this is the old strict crossing mark. The additive value-phase constant also agrees with the source. At fixed \(t=t_*\), let the real label decrease from \(1/2\) to \(1/4\), and use \(R=\operatorname{artanh}(a_*	an\pi x)\), continued from \(R=-\pi i/2\). Its elementary logarithm gives \[ 0\leq\sigma\Re R\leq H_*/2,\qquad -\pi/2\leq\Im R\leq-\pi/4. 	ag{30a} \] For example the real-part bound follows by maximizing \( rac14\log[(1+\sqrt2\lambda+\lambda^2)/ (1-\sqrt2\lambda+\lambda^2)]\) for \(\lambda\geq1\); its maximum at \(\lambda=1\) is \(H_*/2\). The imaginary-part bounds follow from the arguments of \(1\pm a_*\lambda\). Therefore this whole return path lies in \(\mathcal S_{t_*}\), since its pairing is between \(\pi H_*/4\) and \(3\pi H_*/4\). Starting from the common normalization at \(x=1/2\), it continues exactly the source \(B(x,-2\cos t_*)\) to \(x=1/4\). There is no additional additive constant at (29). Normalize the three crossing primitives at (29), and put \[ \mathcal F_\sigma =J_x-J_y-J_{x-y} +\sigma i\pi(1/2+x+xy). 	ag{31} \] The individually occurring \(J_x,J_y\) are the pullbacks of the same global individual-label primitive in Section 1; the difference argument is calibrated at \(x-y=1/4\). The source crossing comparison extends globally to \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal B(t,R_{m in})-\mathcal B(t,R_{m out}) +\sigma i\left( rac\pi4+ rac{t^2}{4\pi}ight) =\mathcal F_\sigma-2\pi i\sigma x. \quad} 	ag{32} \] Indeed the pinned crossing identity proves it on a neighborhood of (29). Its strict gate parametrization is regular there: the explicit relation, obtained by substituting (27) into (3), \[ -2\cos t=2-4\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)e^{i\sigma\pi(x-y)} 	ag{33} \] has nonzero \(t\)-derivative and nonzero \(x\)-derivative there, and \(X_R
e0\). All functions in (32), with their just-specified marks, are holomorphic on the connected \(\mathcal E\). The identity theorem proves (32) throughout. Equivalently its differential and its value at (29) give the same continuation. The linear term \(-2\pi i\sigma x\) is retained. On the original integer output \(I=Nx+\delta_I\), its exponential is \(e^{-2\pi i\sigma I}=1\); its offset contribution is also one for every actual integer \(\delta_I\). Off the integer grid it changes the Fourier character and cannot be deleted. ## 4. Arbitrary degree, allocated powers, and the final pairing Fix a degree \(d\ge2\) and the actual signed integer total power \(n\). Consider the open primitive return domain \[ \mathcal V_{d,n}= \left\{(t,r_1,\ldots,r_d):  egin{array}{l} t\in\mathcal T,\quad \Re(r_e\overline t)>0\ 	ext{for all }e,\ \sum_er_e-int/2=-\pi i \end{array}ight\}. 	ag{34} \] It is an open domain in the complex affine constraint bundle. Writing \(r_e=-\pi i u_e+itv_e\) identifies it topologically with \[ \mathcal T	imes \{u_e>0:\sum_eu_e=1\}	imes \{v_e\in\mathbb R:\sum_ev_e=n/2\}. 	ag{35} \] It is contractible. For any nonempty proper subset \(A\) and any allocated integer power \(n_A\), put \[ R_A=\sum_{e\in A}r_e-i n_A t/2. 	ag{36} \] The allocation term \(-i n_A t/2\) has zero real pairing with \(t\), and \[ \Re(R_A\overline t) =\pi H\sum_{e\in A}u_e\in(0,\pi H). 	ag{37} \] Thus every allocated prefix pulls back the same global functions of Section 1. At a multiplication gate with disjoint nonempty \(A,B\) and proper union, allocated powers add and \(R_{A\cup B}=R_A+R_B\); its map lands in \(\mathcal D\). At a signed crossing on a proper prefix, \(n_A\) increases by \(\sigma\) and (27) applies. Hence every finite binary proper-subproduct resolution, with any such allocated integer crossing layers, has globally fixed factorial logs and actions on (34). The same subset with the same allocated power always has the same label; reassociation does not reset that label. The final complementary pairing has its own exact lift. For \(R\in\mathcal S_t\), also \(-\pi i-R\in\mathcal S_t\). From (3), \(Y_{-\pi i-R}=Y_R^{-1}\), and calibration gives \[ X(t,-\pi i-R)=1-X(t,R),\qquad \mathcal B(t,-\pi i-R)=it-\mathcal B(t,R). 	ag{38} \] For the second identity, \(\sinh(-\pi i-R)=\sinh R\), so the logarithms in (8) agree by calibration; differentiating the sum gives \(i\,dt\), with the stated constant at \(R=-\pi i/2\). Summing (23) and (32) over the gate tree cancels every internal value phase. If the last factor is reserved for the complementary pairing, (38) gives the remaining vertex action \[  oxed{\quad \sum_{e=1}^d\mathcal B(t,r_e) + rac{int^2}{4\pi}-it+ rac{i\pi n}{4}. \quad} 	ag{39} \] Here the left side of each crossing identity (32) is used; in factorial coordinates this is exactly the sum of the globally marked \(\mathcal F_\sigma\)'s minus \(2\pi i\sum_g\sigma_gx_{{m out},g}\), and the multiplication actions (22). Signed inverse layers cancel with their literal signs; only their total \(n\) occurs in (39). The value does not depend on the binary tree or the distribution of its crossing powers. Formula (39) is the original angular vertex action and its known scalar phase. The finite source still uses \(\phi_N(e_i e_j)=\mathbf1_{i+j=N-1}\); its reversal has the exact offset \(-1\), not a changed finite pairing. The finite crossing carriers and their subleading scalars are those of the pinned spectral adapter. The global action identity does not replace them by their limits. The positive primitive theorem places every actual selected vertex with positive incident edges in (34). The functions above therefore pull back to any such finite original network. This does not require the network's geometric realization locus itself to be contractible: the marked functions are already defined on the ambient product of the domains (34). Degree-one traces have no proper-prefix chart here. The degree-two zero-power case retains its exact complementary delta pairing without adding a fictitious strict gate. The condition in (34) is the primitive return equation, not the whole inverse-period contour. On the latter the return sum is generally \(\xi-\pi i\) with real \(\xi
e0\); the final complement is then \(\xi-\pi i-R\), for which (38) does not apply. Thus this theorem gives coherent phases on the primitive locus and does not carry that existing descent contour into Newton variables. ## 5. What global phase transport implies about coefficients The theorem fixes logarithmic marks, additive action constants, and the original crossing Fourier characters throughout the proper-return domains. It removes path ambiguity in those data. It does not place every factorial argument in its original strip: the positive-star construction has a real negative argument, and the exact chamber atlas retains its level-dependent wall factors. At a chosen point, compare these globally marked primitives with a chamber's canonical \(J_+\) or \(J_-\). The difference is an explicitly retained integer-affine Fourier character, as in the atlas. Its integer coefficients are constant on any connected chart where the corresponding branch comparison is defined. Contractibility does not say that this character is zero. In particular, the support test cannot use the wall polynomial alone. Already on the original strict signed-crossing triangle all wall factors are one, whereas (32) has the nonzero character \(-2\pi i\sigma x\). That character belongs to the original lattice lift, not to a missing wall term. A coefficient test must retain both the lattice kernel and the wall factors with the fixed action above. Even a nonzero coefficient of a specified local expansion of those complete factors does not compute the original relative-cycle intersection. The finite supported residue cycle, its endpoint currents, and its deformed boundary terms still require control. No full scalar noncancellation, new knot class, or extension of the volume theorem is asserted. ## Direct sources * [Positive primitive prefixes](research_positive_primitive_prefix_regularity.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{a01b55a71d133aadff4aac0929e50de03e1059991d6874e81646c770eb5604a6}\): the actual proper-return strip, numerator/denominator divisors, all seven sine exclusions, crossing translations and original proper-subproduct resolution. * [Spectral--Newton adapters](research_newton_spectral_legendre_adapters.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{34c0e2e1114488c6ac82a5dffbdbd8a4a8d85e7fbba252de91833dc8d697e303}\): original value-phase derivatives and constants, strict gate calibration, crossing Fourier character, exact final pairing, carrier and whole-source telescoping. * [Factorial chamber atlas](research_newton_factorial_chamber_atlas.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{34d6e0e4e82a98bf8e6063558ecafdedb0a58d6229fbe462e7e4bfff48f4db4c}\): source-preserving wall factors and the distinction between their constant coefficient and the premarked geometric character. * [Positive star real wall](research_positive_star_real_factorial_wall.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{8e58d9a8a430ed3f54277e1c960d68bf42486d6879f64c03df953936708f32af}\): the stated limitation on inferring an original factorial strip from positive primitive geometry. Only written proofs, source-text reads and file hashes are used. No mathematical code, numerical evaluation, tests or compilation are used.

title: A global closed-domain coefficient majorant from the original full tail
status: Uniform original-source upper bound on the full closed domain
text: # A global closed-domain coefficient majorant from the original full tail The global majorant is an upper bound. It does not give a lower coefficient limit or select a phase or cycle. ## 1. Exact treatment of the final spectral cap Retain the original full interval 0<=i<=j<=d=N-1 and r=j-i. Write theta=pi/N, kappa=cos(pi delta), 0<=delta<=1/2, and lambda_N=cos(theta)+cos(2pi delta), eta_a=lambda_N/[cos(theta)-cos((2a-1)theta)]. The actual coefficient of x^k b^i c^(d-j)y^(r-k), 0<=k<=r, is a_N=(prod_(a<i)alpha_a(delta))(prod_(a>j)alpha_a(delta)) [x^k y^(r-k)]K_(i,j), up to the recorded common unit sign. Thus its total degree is d. In particular CROSS is one full-interval K, not a difference of separately estimated central cofactors. Put s_a=2sin(pi a/N). The exact recurrence is K_(i,i)=1, K_(i,i+1)=s_(i+1)^2(x+y), K_(i,a)=s_a^2(x+y)K_(i,a-1) +s_a s_(a-1)alpha_(a-1)xy K_(i,a-2), a>=i+2. Dividing by prod_(i<h<=a)s_h^2 gives second coefficient alpha_(a-1)/(s_a s_(a-1))=eta_a-1: the exact identity is alpha_(a-1)+s_a s_(a-1)=2lambda_N. The row range avoids s_0. Every used denominator, i+2<=a<=j<=d, is positive. The exact normalized tail Q=K_(i,j)/prod_(i<a<=j)s_a^2 has the two-letter word expansion: the coefficient of each x^k y^(r-k) is a polynomial in lambda_N with NONNEGATIVE coefficients. Thus, even on the last cap where lambda_N<0, |[x^k y^(r-k)]Q(lambda_N)| <=[x^k y^(r-k)]Q(|lambda_N|). (1) This is the actual eta-word expansion, not an absolute-value substitution in the original signed two-step recurrence. Define a real effective spectral parameter by cos(2pi delta_eff)=|lambda_N|-cos(theta). For N>=3 its right side lies in[-1,1], and its eta parameters are exactly the positive ones in (1). If k_eff=cos(pi delta_eff), then k_eff^2=kappa^2 if lambda_N>=0, k_eff^2=1-cos(theta)-kappa^2 if lambda_N<0. (2) The negative case implies kappa^2<(1-cos theta)/2. Hence uniformly |k_eff-kappa|<=sqrt(1-cos theta)=O(1/N). (3) The original unused alpha_r(delta) factors are NOT changed to delta_eff. If any of them, or the retained A_rest factor, vanishes, the coefficient is zero and automatically satisfies the upper bound. ## 2. Uniform fixed-tilt bounds on the full compact parameter set For any fixed T<infinity, all l in[-T,T], every original row interval, and all real delta in[0,1/2], the full-interval fixed-block proof gives N^(-1)log K_(i,j)(exp(l),1;delta_eff) <=int_(i/N)^(j/N) log Lambda_(delta_eff)(t;exp(l),1)dt+o(1), (4) uniformly. Here are the inputs that remain valid at the cap. Divide K by prod_(i<h<=a)s_h instead of its square. The exact signed transfer is T_a=[[s_a(x+y),alpha_(a-1)(delta_eff)xy],[1,0]], a>=i+2, with initial values 1 and s_(i+1)(x+y). Its entries are uniformly bounded on the whole row range and the fixed tilt interval. Its frozen limiting matrix has spectral radius rho=(x+y)sin(pi t) +sqrt((x-y)^2 sin^2(pi t)+4xy k_eff^2), and both eigenvalue magnitudes are at most rho. On [eta,1-eta], rho has a uniform positive lower bound. Cayley--Hamilton therefore bounds the m-th power by C(m+1)rho^m with uniform C, INCLUDING the repeated-root case x=y,k_eff=0; no eigenbasis inverse is used. For each fixed m, an actual m-row block differs uniformly by o(1) from its frozen block. Multiply these block bounds, then let N grow, m grow, and eta decrease to zero in that order. The factor C(m+1) costs log(C(m+1))/m per row. The bounded transfers on the two endpoint intervals cost O(eta N), and their omitted logarithmic integrals cost O(eta log(1/eta)N). Restoring prod s_a by its uniform sine-log upper sum gives (4), with Lambda=2sin(pi t)rho. Uniformly in l and delta, c_T sin^2(pi t)<=Lambda_delta(t;exp(l),1)<=C_T, so the missing endpoint integrals are uniformly small. The proof includes the defective balanced root at the final spectral cap. The integral in (4) is jointly continuous on the full compact set of endpoints, delta and l in[-T,T]: on every interior t interval this is ordinary continuity, and the displayed integrable lower bound controls both endpoints uniformly. Equation (3) consequently allows delta_eff to be replaced by delta in that integral at cost o(1), uniformly in all these variables. Equivalently regard the integral as a continuous function of kappa in[0,1], so no inverse-cosine derivative near an endpoint is needed. The original unused products satisfy the full uniform UPPER Riemann estimate N^(-1)log |prod_(a<i)alpha_a(delta) prod_(a>j)alpha_a(delta)| <= B_delta(i/N,j/N)+o(1), B_delta(mu,nu)=int_0^mu log|alpha_delta(t)|dt +int_nu^1 log|alpha_delta(t)|dt. (5) The same truncation proof covers all real delta, including merging cosine zeros and every sampled zero. The two cosine logarithms have uniformly integrable singularities. Moving a mesh endpoint by one row changes the corresponding integral by o(1) uniformly; a missing sampled zero is never assigned a finite lower logarithm. For the exact original coefficient a_N(k,i,d-j,r-k), equations(1)--(5) and finite Cauchy extraction give, uniformly for l in[-T,T], N^(-1)log|a_N| <=B_delta(mu,nu)+Phi_delta(mu,nu,l)-xi l+o(1), (6) Phi_delta=int_mu^nu log Lambda_delta(t;exp(l),1)dt, mu=i/N, nu=j/N, xi=k/N. No coefficient positivity is asserted on the negative lambda_N cap; the exact domination (1) is what supplies (6) there. Both parities and all original scalar modes/zeros are retained in the coefficient. ## 3. Uniform truncation of the outer Legendre infimum Let w=nu-mu and 0<=xi<=w. Factor the limiting tail root as Lambda_delta(t;exp(l),1)=4sin^2(pi t) rho_eta(exp(l),1), rho_eta(x,y)=[x+y+sqrt((x-y)^2+4eta xy)]/2, eta=kappa^2/sin^2(pi t). With a=exp(-|l|), the elementary square-root inequality gives 1<=rho_eta(exp(l),1)/max(exp(l),1) =[1+a+sqrt((1-a)^2+4eta a)]/2 <=1+sqrt(eta a). (7) Thus log rho_eta=max(0,l)+r_delta(t,l), where 0<=r_delta(t,l) <=log(1+exp(-|l|/2)/sin(pi t)). (8) Set R_T=int_0^1 log(1+exp(-T/2)/sin(pi t))dt. It tends to0. An explicit bound, using sin(pi t)>=2min(t,1-t), is R_T <=(1+a_T)log(1+a_T)-a_T log a_T, a_T=exp(-T/2). (9) Subtract the l-independent sine integral from Phi-xi l. Its remaining value is (w-xi)l+int r for l>=0 and -xi l+int r for l<=0. If l>T, its value is at least(w-xi)T, while the value at T is at most (w-xi)T+R_T. The same comparison holds at -T for l<-T. Therefore 0<=inf_(|l|<=T)(Phi-xi l)-inf_(l in R)(Phi-xi l)<=R_T, (10) UNIFORMLY in every closed row interval, xi, and delta. It includes w=0, xi=0,w, delta=1/2 and exact protected endpoints. There is no uniform-minimizer assumption and no concavity in mu or nu. ## 4. Continuity and the global coefficient LIMSUP Define on the FULL closed parameter domain H_delta(mu,nu,xi)=B_delta(mu,nu) +inf_l[Phi_delta(mu,nu,l)-xi l]. (11) B is continuous, by the same uniform integrability as (5). For each finite T the truncated minimum is continuous: its integrand is jointly continuous on a compact parameter set, and the difference of two minima is bounded by the uniform difference of their functions. Equation(10) then makes H a uniform limit of continuous functions. In particular H is continuous and finite on the entire closed domain. Given epsilon>0 choose T with R_T<epsilon, use (6) uniformly on that fixed tilt interval, and minimize there. Equations(10)--(11) prove limsup_(N->infinity) sup_(all i,j,k,delta) [N^(-1)log|a_N|-H_delta(i/N,j/N,k/N)]<=0. (12) This is a GLOBAL uniform coefficient upper bound, including the final spectral cap, all closed outer degrees, diagonal and terminal intervals, both level parities, and sampled zeros. Zero coefficients have logarithm minus infinity. No lower rate or every-level equality is inferred. If normalized degrees are taken over d=N-1, they sum to1 exactly and give mu=q_b,nu=1-q_c,xi=q_x. The N-normalized parameters in (12) differ by O(1/N). Uniform continuity of H on its full compact domain absorbs that difference uniformly. No finite protected target or seam support is changed. ## 5. The original shared-source upper problem is now compact For a fixed actual diagram D with R ports, use the original incidence flow polytope: each port supplies1, each ordinary face demands1, and the two original protected faces demand0. Assume it is nonempty, as it is in the certified geometric class. If it is empty, every finite source coefficient is identically zero and no finite maximum is needed. Define M_D=max_(q in this polytope, delta in[0,1/2]^R) sum_e H_(delta_e)(q_b,1-q_c,q_x). (13) The maximum exists by continuity. The number of original finite degree arrays is polynomial in N at fixed R. Apply (12) to every local factor and the triangle inequality to the ONE original marked coefficient. For its actual raw full numerator S_N, sup_(delta in[0,1/2]^R)|S_N(delta)| <=exp{N[M_D+o(1)]}. (14) All signs and omitted-half phases are still in S_N; (14) bounds their absolute sum rather than asserting they align. Only the upper passage from finite arrays to limiting flows is used. There is no lattice lower approximation, equality of rates, or separate optimization of local weighted norms in place of the shared target. The former boundary-UNIFORM coefficient-majorant burden is removed by (12), but the boundary-GEOMETRY and global phase questions remain. In particular neither M_D<=Phi_D nor a contributing full period is proved here. The [full-fiber boundary reduction](research_full_fiber_sharp_boundary_activation.md) and [stationary classification](research_full_fiber_sharp_stationary_classification.md) apply to this compact upper problem at their stated scopes. The global phase comparison still needs its own quantitative estimate. This proof uses no numerical audit. ## Dependencies and internal verification scope The [original four-state source](research_original_one_sided_four_state_transfer.md) supplies the exact full-interval coefficient and unused-row factors. The [positive eta-word identity](research_positive_eta_word_transfer.md) gives the polynomial domination in section1. The [global CROSS proof](../papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/README.md) supplies the antecedent fixed-block argument; section2 extends it explicitly through the cap on the full row range. The [full-fiber stationary classification](research_full_fiber_sharp_stationary_classification.md) is a downstream consequence together with the separate boundary lemmas; it is not a premise of the coefficient upper bound. No coefficient lower bound, positivity at the cap, phase alignment, complete-volume comparison or full-period estimate follows from this upper bound.

title: The full interior phase of an actual weighted crossing
text: # The full interior phase of an actual weighted crossing 24 November 2026. Research note. Written proof. Earlier finals and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The whole physical crossing Gaussian extends beyond small real boundary weights. Its entire strict interior phase is determined by one quadratic root and one explicit action comparison. The amplitude is not globally concave; eliminating two occupation variables reveals the required one-dimensional shape instead. An unbounded ordering cone of physical head weights lies in this phase. On that cone the complete original Green source, including its carry, has a strict exponential norm gap from the crossing. All statements use the weighted physical metric directly and retain the exact phase. They do not estimate an original closed knot scalar. ## 1. The actual weighted matrix Use the complete physical source of [G,W]. Put \[ q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad d=N-1,\quad x=-q^{-1}, \quad\kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad s_r=\prod_{h=1}^r2\sin(\pi h/N),\quad s_0=1 . \tag{1} \] The balanced physical basis is orthonormal. For real head weights \(\rho=(\rho_a,\rho_b,\rho_c,\rho_e)\), set \[ R^\pm_\rho=W_{\rm out}R^\pm W_{\rm in}^{-1},\quad W_{\rm in}|a,b\rangle=e^{\rho_a a+\rho_b b}|a,b\rangle,\quad W_{\rm out}|c,e\rangle=e^{\rho_c c+\rho_e e}|c,e\rangle . \tag{2} \] For the positive crossing the exact nonzero entries are \[ (R^+_\rho)_{(b+k,j);(j+k,b)} =\chi_N(j,b,k)e^{N\lambda\cdot z} \frac{s_{b+k}s_{j+k}}{s_ks_bs_j}, \quad z=(u,v,t)=(j,b,k)/N, \tag{3} \] where \(j,b,k\ge0\), \(j+k,b+k\le d\), and \[ \chi_N=\kappa x^{-b-j}Q^{jb}(-i)^k q^{\,k(b+j)+k(k+1)/2},\qquad \lambda=(\rho_e-\rho_a,\rho_c-\rho_b,\rho_c-\rho_a). \tag{4} \] In particular \(|\chi_N|=1\). There is one term per entry. The negative crossing is the exact flip-conjugate of the positive one, with \(\rho\) replaced by \(\rho^\leftrightarrow=(\rho_b,\rho_a,\rho_e,\rho_c)\), as in [G]. Write \(\lambda_-(\rho)=\lambda(\rho^\leftrightarrow)\). Define the continuous amplitude profile \[ h(y)=\int_0^y\log(2\sin\pi r)\,dr,\quad \mathcal D=\{u,v,t\ge0:\ u+t\le1,\ v+t\le1\}, \] \[ S(u,v,t)=h(u+t)+h(v+t)-h(u)-h(v)-h(t),\qquad S_\lambda=S+\lambda_u u+\lambda_v v+\lambda_t t . \tag{5} \] [W] proves its norm rate on every compact real weight set, including factorial endpoints. We now determine all its global maximizers. ## 2. Eliminate the two side occupations exactly For fixed \(0<t<1\), each of the \(u,v\) problems is strictly concave with derivatives tending to opposite infinities at its two endpoints. Its unique solution is \[ u_\lambda(t)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Arg} (e^{-\lambda_u}-e^{-\pi it}),\qquad v_\lambda(t)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Arg} (e^{-\lambda_v}-e^{-\pi it}), \tag{6} \] with argument in \((0,\pi)\). Both belong to \((0,1-t)\). These are [W]'s exact inner optima in the coordinates of [G]. Put \[ F_\lambda(t)=S_\lambda(u_\lambda(t),v_\lambda(t),t),\quad A=\cosh\lambda_u,\quad B=\cosh\lambda_v,\quad E=e^{\,2\lambda_t-\lambda_u-\lambda_v}. \tag{7} \] The continuous endpoint values are \[ F_\lambda(0)=B_\lambda:=(\lambda_u)_++(\lambda_v)_+, \qquad F_\lambda(1)=\lambda_t . \tag{8} \] For \(c=\cos\pi t\), direct differentiation gives \[ F_\lambda'(t) =\frac12\log\frac{E(1-c^2)}{(A-c)(B-c)},\qquad F_\lambda'(1-)=-\infty , \tag{9} \] \[ F_\lambda''(t)=\frac{\pi}{2\sin\pi t} \left(\frac{Ac-1}{A-c}+\frac{Bc-1}{B-c}\right). \tag{10} \] To verify (9), the inner equation is \(\sin\pi(u+t)=e^{-\lambda_u}\sin\pi u\), and hence \(\sin\pi(u+t)=e^{-\lambda_u/2}\sin\pi t/ \sqrt{2(A-c)}\). Substitute this and its \(v\) counterpart in the envelope derivative of (5). Differentiating gives (10). For \(A>1\), the function \((Ac-1)/(A-c)\) increases strictly with \(c\), since its derivative is \((A^2-1)/(A-c)^2\). It therefore decreases strictly with \(t\). For \(A=1\) it is identically \(-1\) in the interior. Consequently: * If both side weights are nonzero, \(F_\lambda''\) changes sign exactly once, from positive to negative. * If either side weight is zero, \(F_\lambda''<0\) everywhere in \((0,1)\). Thus there is at most one interior local maximum. Every such maximum is nondegenerate. In the first case a stationary point at the inflection has negative third derivative and is not a local maximum. ## 3. One quadratic and one action comparison classify the phase Set \[ \alpha=|\lambda_u|,\quad\beta=|\lambda_v|,\quad a=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2},\quad b=\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}, E_c=\sinh^2 a . \tag{11} \] The following square identity is useful for every \(-1<c<1\): \[ \frac{(A-c)(B-c)}{1-c^2} =E_c+\frac{(\cosh(a)c-\cosh(b))^2}{1-c^2}. \tag{12} \] It follows by expansion using \(A+B=2\cosh(a)\cosh(b)\). If \(\alpha\beta>0\), the minimum is attained at \(c=\cosh(b)/\cosh(a)\in(0,1)\); if precisely one side weight is zero, the infimum is the limit at \(c=1\). If both vanish, that infimum is zero. Equations (9)--(12) show that an interior local maximum exists exactly when \(E>E_c\). For both nonzero side weights, \(F_\lambda'\) tends to \(-\infty\) at both endpoints and has one maximum; for one zero side weight it is strictly decreasing. The zero-weight pair has \(F_\lambda'(0+)=+\infty\). These observations also verify the threshold at equality. When \(E>E_c\), define \[ \Delta=(A+B)^2-4(1+E)(AB-E),\qquad c_*=\frac{A+B-\sqrt{\Delta}}{2(1+E)},\quad t_*=\frac1\pi\arccos c_* . \tag{13} \] Here \(\Delta>0\), \(-1<c_*<1\), and \(t_*\) is the unique interior local maximum. The stationary equation is exactly \[ (1+E)c^2-(A+B)c+AB-E=0. \tag{14} \] If a side weight vanishes, clearing factors introduces a possible root \(c=1\); it is an endpoint and is not selected in (13). When both side weights vanish, (13) gives \(c_*=(1-E)/(1+E)\). The full strict interior phase is the explicit open set \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal I=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^3: E>E_c,\quad F_\lambda(t_*)>B_\lambda\}. \quad} \tag{15} \] For \(\lambda\in\mathcal I\), the unique global maximizer is \[ z_\lambda=(u_\lambda(t_*),v_\lambda(t_*),t_*),\qquad M_\lambda=S_\lambda(z_\lambda),\qquad H_\lambda=-S''(z_\lambda)>0 . \tag{16} \] Indeed side boundaries at \(0<t<1\) are strictly below (6). The endpoint \(t=1\) is never a global maximum, by (9). The remaining competitor is (8), and there is only one interior local maximum. Its full Hessian is negative definite: its inner \(u,v\) block is negative diagonal, and the Schur complement is \(F_\lambda''(t_*)<0\). If (15) fails, the global value is \(B_\lambda\), except that an existing interior maximum can tie it at equality. Global concavity would be an incorrect shortcut. At \(u=v=t=1/8\), one has \[ \frac1\pi S''= \begin{pmatrix}-\sqrt2&0&1\\0&-\sqrt2&1\\ 1&1&1-\sqrt2\end{pmatrix}. \tag{17} \] Its Schur complement in the last coordinate is \(+1\). The phase classification uses the reduced profile, not global concavity of the three-variable action. ## 4. A whole weighted Gaussian on every compact interior phase Let \(K\Subset\mathcal I\) be any fixed compact set. Its centers stay in a fixed compact subset of the interior of \(\mathcal D\); \(H_\lambda\) is uniformly positive definite. Uniqueness and compactness give a strict uniform action loss outside a fixed neighborhood of these centers. Put \[ a(z)=\left[ \frac{\sin\pi(u+t)\sin\pi(v+t)} {\sin\pi u\sin\pi v\sin\pi t}\right]^{1/2}, \qquad a_\lambda=a(z_\lambda)>0 . \tag{18} \] Use the same finite Taylor prescription as [G, (15)] to define real polynomials \(P_{\lambda,r}\), with \(P_{\lambda,0}=1\) and degree at most \(3r\), now at \(z_\lambda\). For a fixed integer \(J\ge0\), on the exact support (3) set \[ (\mathcal G^+_{N,J,\rho})_{(b+k,j);(j+k,b)} =\chi_N(j,b,k)\frac{a_\lambda e^{NM_\lambda}}{\sqrt{2N}}\, e^{-y^{\mathsf T}H_\lambda y/2} \sum_{r=0}^J N^{-r/2}P_{\lambda,r}(y), \quad y=\frac{(j,b,k)-Nz_\lambda}{\sqrt N}. \tag{19} \] It is zero off that support. For the negative sign use the exact flip-conjugation, with \(\lambda=\lambda_-(\rho)\). **Theorem.** Uniformly for the induced tilt in \(K\), at all sufficiently large integer levels and with no parity restriction, \[ \frac{\|R^\pm_\rho-\mathcal G^\pm_{N,J,\rho}\|_{\rm HS}} {\|R^\pm_\rho\|_{\rm HS}} \le C_{K,J}N^{-(J+1)/2}, \tag{20} \] \[ \|R^\pm_\rho\|_{\rm HS}^2 =\sqrt N\,\frac{\pi^{3/2}a_\lambda^2} {2\sqrt{\det H_\lambda}}\, e^{2NM_\lambda}(1+O_K(N^{-1})). \tag{21} \] These norms are measured directly in the stated weighted arrays. **Proof.** The sine-factorial expansion and its finite Euler--Maclaurin remainder in [G, (13)--(16)] are uniform on every fixed interior compact. At the centers (16) they give the same Gaussian-polynomial entry error, bounded by \[ C_{K,J}\frac{e^{NM_\lambda}}{\sqrt N} N^{-(J+1)/2}(1+|y|^{C_{K,J}})e^{-c_K|y|^2}. \tag{22} \] Its squared lattice sum is at most \(C_{K,J}\sqrt N e^{2NM_\lambda}N^{-J-1}\). The remainder inside the fixed neighborhood is Gaussian bounded; outside it the strict uniform action loss and [W]'s endpoint-uniform factorial bound make it exponentially smaller. A ball of \(O(\sqrt N)\) indices gives the matching lower norm. This proves (20) on the entire physical matrix. The leading Gaussian integral gives (21); the first correction is odd and its lattice sum is exponentially small, exactly as in [G]. The negative sign follows from the exact source identity. \(\square\) The relevant full packet space is the exact weighted image \(W_{\rm out}\mathcal A_NW_{\rm in}^{-1}\). Physical orthogonal projection onto this image preserves (20), since the actual crossing belongs to it. Every repeated-root normal remains; no spectral-value quotient is used. An application retains both incident interface factors in this metric. At coexistence \(F_\lambda(t_*)=B_\lambda\), the complete action gap to the boundary is absent. Exact \(k=0\) matrix entries can have that boundary action, while (19) is centered at \(t_*>0\). The theorem therefore makes no all-order single-bulk-Gaussian claim on this phase boundary. Its constants are uniform on fixed compact subsets of \(\mathcal I\), not on its unbounded entirety. ## 5. An unbounded cone with a complete original source gap There is a simple unbounded sufficient region for (15): \[ \lambda_t\ge B_\lambda . \tag{23} \] For every finite set of side weights, (9) gives an interior value strictly greater than \(F_\lambda(1)=\lambda_t\). If (23) holds, the global maximum is consequently strictly greater than both boundary values, so it belongs to \(\mathcal I\). In physical head weights the positive sufficient cone is exactly \[ \mathcal C_+=\{\rho:\max(\rho_a,\rho_e) \le\min(\rho_b,\rho_c)\}, \tag{24} \] since \(\lambda_t-B_\lambda=\min(\rho_b,\rho_c)-\max(\rho_a,\rho_e)\). For the negative crossing the reversed cone is \(\mathcal C_-=\{\rho:\max(\rho_b,\rho_c) \le\min(\rho_a,\rho_e)\}\). Let \(L^\pm_\rho\) be [W]'s actual complete Green source in these same metrics. It contains both ground terms and the original degree-\(N\) carry. Its exact rate for either operator or Hilbert--Schmidt norm is \[ \log\|L^\pm_\rho\|=N\delta(\rho)+O_K(\log N),\qquad \delta(\rho)=\max\{0,\max(\rho_c,\rho_e)-\min(\rho_a,\rho_b)\}. \tag{25} \] On \(\mathcal C_+\), \(\delta=\lambda_t=\rho_c-\rho_a\); on \(\mathcal C_-\), \(\delta=(\lambda_-)_t=\rho_e-\rho_b\). The interior maximum is strictly greater than this value. Thus for every compact \(K_\sigma\subset\mathcal C_\sigma\) there is \(\eta_{K_\sigma}>0\) such that \[ \boxed{\qquad \frac{\|L^\sigma_\rho\|}{\|R^\sigma_\rho\|} \le N^{C_{K_\sigma}}e^{-N\eta_{K_\sigma}}, \qquad \rho\in K_\sigma,\quad \sigma\in\{+,-\}. \qquad} \tag{26} \] This holds separately for operator and Hilbert--Schmidt norms. It follows from (21), [W]'s operator/HS rate equality, and (25). The carry has not been deleted. No uniform positive gap on the whole unbounded cone is claimed. ## Scope and complete sources [W] already proves the exact global three-variable rate and its one-dimensional reduction, but does not assert arbitrary-weight uniqueness. [G] already proves every fixed Gaussian correction order in a small real tilt chamber. The addition here is the global critical-point classification, its full strict-interior weighted Gaussian phase, and the explicit unbounded sufficient cones for the complete source gap. No new general Laplace method or sine-factorial expansion is claimed. The estimates do not identify a geometric metric for an arbitrary short component, match full boundary marginals, or supply a relative error for a prescribed closed scalar. The original turns, caps, source normalization and exterior still enter any such composition. There is no new volume lower bound or finite-exception theorem. | Label | Complete text | Lines | SHA-256 | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | | G | [Whole physical crossing Gaussian](research_full_physical_crossing_gaussian_packet.md) | 306 | 7f1b9932f88aa549bc55088b6f056f5a362548bc51c9fdd7c6b00469e725f531 | | W | [Weighted crossing and complete source](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/weighted_crossing_source_gap.md) | 244 | a6a6411a780c904493db4fca3b5536f902aa5be8b6ef7cfb880a4f57509f436c | Both complete matching texts were read. Only written mathematics, text reads and metadata operations were used.
