title: The integral clock coupling and its finite Gaussian transform
text: # The integral clock coupling and its finite Gaussian transform Written deduction, 15 November 2026. We use the complete original singleton incidence sum, including every closing degree and pivotal phase. For a braid whose closure is a knot, its quadratic phase has an integral normal form governed by the Alexander polynomial at \(-1\). This gives an exact Fourier reduction at every level. No coprimality assumption, numerical calculation, or change of the closing functional is used. The nonzero Gaussian coefficients obtained below have polynomial size. This controls those coefficients, not the coherent sum in which they occur. In particular it supplies no volume lower bound. ## 1. The original lattice and its midpoint map Let the signed braid have \(b\) heads and \(c\) crossings, with knot closure \(K\). Put \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), and \(S_a=\prod_{r=1}^a2\sin(\pi r/N)\), with \(S_0=1\). Use the physical signs \(\sigma_j\) of the joint-phase source. At crossing \(j\), the overstrand goes from \(u_j+v_j\) to \(v_j\), and the understrand goes from \(J_j\) to \(J_j+u_j\). Its four incidences are \[ (d-u_j-v_j,\ u_j-h_j+v_j,\ h_j-v_j,\ v_j). \tag{1} \] The closing row on head \(i\) is \((d-a_i,a_i)\). The linear wire conservation equations are precisely those in the joint-phase note, Section 2. Let \(P\) be their integral solution lattice in the physical variables \(u,v,a\), without the inequalities. Every \(J_j\) is its actual integral prefix function. Define \[ \mathcal M:P\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^c, \qquad \mathcal M_j(p)=u_j+2J_j. \tag{2} \] Thus \(\mathcal M_j\) is the sum of the two understrand degrees. The homogeneous incidence lattice is integrally isomorphic to \(P\oplus\mathbb Z^c\), the second factor consisting of the clocks \(h_j\). Indeed (1) and the closing pairs reconstruct all incidence variations; conversely \(v_j=n_{j3}\), \(h_j=n_{j2}+n_{j3}\), \(u_j=n_{j1}+n_{j2}\), and the closing indices recover the inverse. There is no divisibility condition in this change of coordinates. The affine source fiber has the integral base point with all physical degrees and clocks zero. Its first incidence in each event is \(d\), and all its other incidences are zero. Consequently every source state is this base point plus a unique element of \(P\oplus\mathbb Z^c\). The inequalities \(0\le n_e\le d\) still specify exactly which such elements occur. The full variable-dependent phase is \[ \Phi_N(p,h)= \sum_j\sigma_jh_j\mathcal M_j(p) +\sum_j(N+\sigma_j)h_j -d\sum_j\sigma_jJ_j(p)-2\sum_{i=2}^b a_i(p). \tag{3} \] In particular its quadratic part is a pairing of clocks with physical flows. It has no clock--clock or physical--physical term. ## 2. An integral exact sequence Write \(y\in\mathbb Z^b\) for the initial head degrees and \(t_j=\mathcal M_j(p)\). At a positive crossing on adjacent heads, the checked output degrees are \[ \binom{t-J}{I+2J-t} =M_+\binom I J+v_+t, \quad M_+=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}, \quad v_+=\binom1{-1}. \tag{4} \] For a negative crossing the input order is \((J,I)\), and the output is \[ \binom{I+2J-t}{t-J} =M_-\binom J I+v_-t, \quad M_-=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=M_+^{-1}, \quad v_-=-v_+. \tag{5} \] These are direct consequences of transfer conservation and \(u=t-2J\); they do not impose a new coloring on the source. Embed these matrices and vectors at each crossing's two heads and put \[ B=M_c\cdots M_1,\qquad D_j=M_c\cdots M_{j+1}v_j. \tag{6} \] Every matrix preserves the sum of the head degrees. Write \(\mathbb Z_0^b=\{y:\sum_i y_i=0\}\). Closing the braid gives the integral identification \[ P=\{(y,t)\in\mathbb Z^b\oplus\mathbb Z^c: (I-B)y=Dt\}, \qquad \mathcal M(y,t)=t. \tag{7} \] The inverse follows the crossings in order, using \(u=t-2J\). The columns of \(D\) span \(\mathbb Z_0^b\). To check this integrally, \(\operatorname{im}(M_j-I)\subset\mathbb Z v_j\). It follows that \(D_j-v_j\) is an integral combination of the later raw vectors \(v_{j+1},\ldots,v_c\). Descending induction therefore proves that the propagated and raw columns have the same integral span. The raw vectors are signed adjacent simple roots. The graph of the adjacent heads occurring in a knot braid is connected: otherwise its braid permutation would preserve two nonempty sets, whereas that permutation is one cycle. The simple roots on this connected graph span \(\mathbb Z_0^b\). Consequently (7) gives the exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\ker(I-B)\longrightarrow P \xrightarrow{\mathcal M}\mathbb Z^c \xrightarrow{\ t\mapsto[Dt]\ } \mathbb Z_0^b/(I-B)\mathbb Z^b\longrightarrow0. \tag{8} \] This also proves \(\operatorname{rank}P=c+1\): the map \((I-B,-D):\mathbb Z^{b+c}\to\mathbb Z_0^b\) is surjective. ## 3. The Alexander group in the cokernel Conjugate the head coordinates by \(E=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,-1,\ldots)\). The local matrices in (4)--(5) become, respectively, the inverse and the value at \(t=-1\) of the unreduced Burau block \[ T(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1-t&t\\1&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{9} \] Thus \(EBE^{-1}\) is the Burau matrix at \(-1\) for the braid with crossing signs reversed, using the same product convention. Its closure is the mirror of \(K\); this does not change \(|\Delta_K(-1)|\). Here is the minor argument, including the issue at even braid width. Over \(R=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]\), the unreduced braid matrix \(\mathcal B(t)\) fixes the column \(\mathbf1\) and the row \(v(t)=(1,t,\ldots,t^{b-1})\). At \(t=1\) it is the permutation of a single cycle, so \(I-\mathcal B(t)\) has rank \(b-1\) over \(\mathbb Q(t)\). Its adjugate is therefore \[ \operatorname{adj}(I-\mathcal B(t)) =f(t)\,\mathbf1\,v(t),\qquad f(t)\in R. \tag{10} \] The coefficient is Laurent polynomial because the first entry of both null vectors is one. All deleted minors are consequently \(f(t)\) times a signed Laurent unit. To identify \(f\), use the braid presentation \(\langle x_1,\ldots,x_b:\beta(x_i)=x_i\rangle\) of the mirror knot group. The Artin automorphism preserves \(x_1\cdots x_b\); one of these relations follows from the other \(b-1\). Abelian Fox differentiation gives \(\mathcal B(t)-I\), up to the transpose and Laurent basis changes fixed by the action convention. The boundary map of the infinite cyclic cover is \((t-1)\mathbf1^T\). Its kernel is free with basis \(e_i-e_b\), \(i<b\). Expressing the remaining relation boundaries in this basis amounts to deleting one generator coordinate from the Fox matrix. The resulting square matrix presents the Alexander module; its determinant is the Alexander polynomial up to a Laurent unit. This is one of the minors in (10). Hence \(f(t)\) is \(\Delta_K(t)\), with the mirror convention, up to such a unit. At \(t=1\) a deleted minor of the single-cycle permutation matrix has value \(\pm1\). Thus \(f(-1)\equiv f(1)\pmod2\) is odd and nonzero. In particular \(I-B\) has rank \(b-1\). Its right kernel is the primitive alternating vector \(\varepsilon=(1,-1,\ldots)^T\), and its left kernel is \(\mathbf1^T\). Deleting one output coordinate identifies \(\mathbb Z_0^b\) with \(\mathbb Z^{b-1}\). The maximal minors of the resulting \((b-1)\)-by-\(b\) matrix are precisely the specialized cofactors; each has absolute value \(|f(-1)|\). Their greatest common divisor is the index of its image. Therefore \[ \left|\mathbb Z_0^b/(I-B)\mathbb Z^b\right| =|\Delta_K(-1)|. \tag{11} \] No division by \(1+t+\cdots+t^{b-1}\) occurs. In particular the argument remains valid when \(b\) is even. This is an integral cokernel statement, rather than a specialization of a rational rank computation. The finite group, not only its order, has an Alexander description. The column dependence of \(I-B\) has coefficients \(\varepsilon_i=\pm1\). After deleting one output coordinate, any one input column is therefore an integral combination of the other columns. Deleting it leaves exactly the same image lattice. The resulting square matrix is the specialized Alexander presentation above, up to integral basis changes and possibly a transpose. A square matrix and its transpose have the same integer Smith factors. Consequently, as an abstract finite abelian group, \[ \operatorname{coker}\mathcal M\cong \mathcal A_K/(t+1)\mathcal A_K, \tag{11a} \] where \(\mathcal A_K\) is the Alexander module. The mirror convention replaces \(t\) by \(t^{-1}\), which has the same specialization at \(-1\). This is an abstract isomorphism; no canonical identification with a transposed presentation is asserted. Combining (8)--(11), the midpoint map has rank \(c\), a primitive rank-one kernel, and a finite cokernel of odd order. Let its nonzero Smith factors be \(s_1\mid\cdots\mid s_c\), all positive. Then \[ \prod_{j=1}^c s_j=|\Delta_K(-1)|. \tag{12} \] Their nonunit members are independent of the braid presentation by (11a); the number of unit factors changes with the number of crossings. For \(b=1,c=0\), the braid is empty. The same assertions use the empty product one, \(P=\mathbb Z\), and the zero midpoint map. ## 4. Integral hyperbolic form of the actual phase The kernel generator with initial heads \(\varepsilon\) has \(a_1=1\). Therefore \(P=\ker(a_1)\oplus\mathbb Z\varepsilon\), and the image of \(\mathcal M|_{\ker(a_1)}\) is the full image of \(\mathcal M\). Choose its Smith bases on this complement. Changing the physical basis and making the dual integral change in the clocks, with their signs \(\sigma_j\) absorbed, transforms the quadratic term in (3) into \(\sum_j s_j x_jy_j\). Choose the remaining physical coordinate \(z\) to be the primitive kernel direction with initial heads \(\varepsilon\); with this choice, \(z=a_1\) exactly. All these changes are unimodular on the integral incidence lattice. Thus the complete phase, including its linear terms, is exactly \[ \Phi_N=\sum_{j=1}^c (s_jx_jy_j+\alpha_{j,N}x_j+\beta_{j,N}y_j) +\gamma_Nz. \tag{13} \] The displayed coefficients are the transformed integer linear coefficients of (3), and are affine functions of \(N\). No phase has been absorbed into an unspecified normalization. Equivalently, the symmetric quadratic matrix is integrally congruent to \(\bigoplus_j\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&s_j\\s_j&0\end{smallmatrix}\right) \oplus(0)\). Its rank is \(2c\). The linear term along the free direction can be read without finding the other Smith coordinates: \[ \gamma_N=-d\sum_j\sigma_jJ_j(\varepsilon) -2\sum_{i=2}^b\varepsilon_i. \tag{14} \] Indeed the zero-midpoint transport fixes \(\varepsilon\) at every horizontal slice, and its clocks do not vary. If crossing \(j\) uses heads \(i_j,i_j+1\), then \(\sigma_jJ_j(\varepsilon)=-(-1)^{i_j-1}\). Consequently \[ \gamma_N=(N-1)\sum_j(-1)^{i_j-1} +2\mathbf1_{b\ {\rm even}}. \tag{15} \] This is one explicit place where the prescribed closing pivots enter the Fourier support. Dropping them changes the finite transform. ## 5. The complete finite Gaussian transform Put \(m=2N\), \(e_m(t)=e^{2\pi it/m}\), and \(G_m=(\mathbb Z/m)^{2c+1}\), in the coordinates \((x,y,z)\) of (13). This phase is periodic modulo \(m\). Define its normalized Fourier coefficients by \[ g_N(k)=m^{-(2c+1)}\sum_{w\in G_m} e_m(\Phi_N(w)-k\cdot w). \tag{16} \] For \(r_j=\gcd(m,s_j)=\gcd(N,s_j)\), these coefficients vanish unless \[ k_z\equiv\gamma_N\pmod m,\qquad k_{x_j}\equiv\alpha_{j,N}\pmod{r_j},\qquad k_{y_j}\equiv\beta_{j,N}\pmod{r_j}. \tag{17} \] On exactly this affine set, choose any solution \(y_j^*\) of \(s_jy_j^*\equiv k_{x_j}-\alpha_{j,N}\pmod m\). Then the exact coefficient is \[ g_N(k)=\prod_{j=1}^c\frac{r_j}{m}\, e_m\!\left(\sum_j(\beta_{j,N}-k_{y_j})y_j^*\right). \tag{18} \] The expression is independent of the choices of \(y_j^*\). For proof, the sum in \(z\) gives the first condition in (17). Summing in \(x_j\) gives zero unless \(s_jy_j+\alpha_{j,N}-k_{x_j}\equiv0\). That congruence has \(r_j\) solutions when the second condition holds. They differ by \(m/r_j\); summing their remaining characters gives zero unless the third condition holds, and otherwise gives \((r_j/m)e_m((\beta_{j,N}-k_{y_j})y_j^*)\). Multiplication proves (18). This argument also covers even and composite \(N\). In particular, every admitted coefficient is nonzero, with \[ |g_N(k)|=\frac{\prod_j\gcd(N,s_j)}{(2N)^c},\qquad (2N)^{-c}\le |g_N(k)|\le |\Delta_K(-1)|(2N)^{-c}. \tag{19} \] There are \(m^{2c}/\prod_j r_j^2\) admitted frequencies. If \(N\) is coprime to \(\Delta_K(-1)\), the only support restriction is the one marked hyperplane \(k_z=\gamma_N\), and every coefficient there has modulus \((2N)^{-c}\). No assertion of positivity of its phase is made. ## 6. Exact reduction of the original closing evaluation Let \(\mathcal W_N\subset\mathbb Z^{2c+1}\) be the coordinates of the actual feasible incidence states and define \[ a_N(w)=\prod_eS_{n_e(w)}^{-1}\quad(w\in\mathcal W_N), \qquad Z_N(k)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W_N}a_N(w)e_m(k\cdot w). \tag{20} \] Every \(a_N(w)\) is positive. Distinct feasible states stay distinct modulo \(m\): if their coordinate difference were \(m v\), their incidence difference would be \(m\) times a nonzero integral vector, whereas each incidence lies between zero and \(N-1<m\). Thus zero extension to \(G_m\) introduces no aliases. Fourier inversion of (16) now gives the original source exactly: \[ \boxed{\quad K_N=\mathcal C_N\sum_{k\text{ satisfying }(17)}g_N(k)Z_N(k), \qquad \mathcal C_N=\chi_N\kappa^{\sum_j\sigma_j} \eta^{b-1}N^{c+b-1}. \quad} \tag{21} \] Here \(\kappa=q^{d^2/2}\), \(\eta=q^{-d^2}\), and \(\chi_N\) are the original factors. The positive value \(Z_N(0)\) is the absolute incidence partition whose exponent is the proved concave angle optimization. It is not substituted for the right side of (21). Its Fourier evaluations at other frequencies can have phases and zeros, and the coefficients (18) also have their specified phases. ### Removing the free direction by the actual marked cut The adopted [marked-cut theorem](research_incidence_marked_cut_observability.md) gives a further exact reduction. If the incidence sum is weighted by \(t^{a_1}\), its value is \[ F_N(\mathbf1)\,\frac{1+t+\cdots+t^{N-1}}N. \tag{22} \] This follows from scalarity of the complete pivotal partial trace. In particular, for every \(0\le r<N\), the sum over all remaining coordinates at \(a_1=r\) equals \(F_N(\mathbf1)/N\). This is an identity of complete sums; it is not applied to a fixed clock sector or to a multivariable fugacity deformation of the exterior. Our chosen Smith complement makes \(a_1=z\). For any prescribed integer \(r\) in this range, define the positive slice and its Fourier evaluations by \[ Z_N^r(k_x,k_y)= \sum_{(x,y,r)\in\mathcal W_N} a_N(x,y,r)e_m(k_x\cdot x+k_y\cdot y). \tag{23} \] Let \(g_N^0(k_x,k_y)\) be the normalized Fourier transform on \((\mathbb Z/m)^{2c}\) of (13) restricted to \(z=0\). Its coefficients are exactly (18), subject only to the two congruences for each pair in (17). The radical congruence is absent. At \(z=r\) the additional phase is exactly \(e_m(\gamma_Nr)\); the pair phase is unchanged. Fourier inversion on this slice, followed by (22), gives \[ \boxed{\quad K_N=N\mathcal C_N e_m(\gamma_Nr) \sum_{k_x,k_y}g_N^0(k_x,k_y)Z_N^r(k_x,k_y). \quad} \tag{24} \] All original inequalities and every closing pivot remain in this formula. The same injection modulo \(m\) proves that the slice has no aliases. No unknown scalar was divided out, so (24) also holds when the original invariant vanishes. The choice \(r=r_N\) may depend on the level; in particular one may choose a central physical degree instead of the boundary degree zero. No contributing geometric saddle is inferred for such a chosen slice. The unweighted \(Z_N^r(0)\) is a different positive partition from \(Z_N(0)\). For \(r=0\), the condition pins a boundary face and can force further zero coordinates. The number \(2c\) is the rank of the ambient integral and Fourier lattice; a feasible slice need not have that dimension. The unsliced angle maximum cannot be assigned to an arbitrary prescribed central or boundary slice. There is, however, an exact choice preserving that positive exponent. Since \(Z_N(0)=\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}Z_N^r(0)\), choose \(r_N\) attaining the largest positive slice. Then \[ \frac{Z_N(0)}N\le Z_N^{r_N}(0)\le Z_N(0). \tag{25} \] The already proved exponent of \(Z_N(0)\), namely the maximum of the concave absolute incidence action, is therefore also the exponent of this adaptively chosen positive slice. The choice uses positive weights alone, not the unknown invariant. It need not be a prescribed central slice or contain the selected complex geometric point. Equation (25) is not a lower bound for the coherent sum in (24). What (24) removes exactly is the permanent free direction of the quadratic phase, using the actual marked cut at any allowed degree. The older feedback theorem already gives a finite Fourier realization of the understrand coupling. The additional content here is its integral normal form on the complete conserved-flow lattice, the Alexander-controlled torsion, the explicit closing character, and the nonzero polynomial size of every admitted Gaussian coefficient. Smith reduction, the Burau--Alexander relation, and finite Fourier orthogonality themselves are classical methods, not novelty claims. For coverage of the Burau--Alexander relation see Anthony Conway, [Burau maps and twisted Alexander polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.06678). Its abstract was checked for coverage; none of its proofs is a premise of the integral argument above. The result applies to every fixed knot braid, hence also to a braid obtained after any fixed short partial filling that gives a knot. It proves no uniform asymptotic stability under that operation. The closed Markov identity in the direct source shows why the phases in (21) remain necessary: complete nonzero-clock sectors can cancel exactly even though their absolute weights have positive exponential rate. The Gaussian factors cannot be exponentially small on their support; the remaining question is the noncancellation of their prescribed coherent contraction. No nonzero geometric coefficient or volume limit is inferred here. ## Direct source versions | Source | SHA-256 | | --- | --- | | research_joint_clock_phase_equations.md, Sections 2--4 | 71393aa353909dfa2dd19b078b1d3fccdf8561520aa071b7537e4bbfc50bb867 | | research_incidence_cycle_difference_equations.md, Sections 1--3 | 8d9b4231b2f3a8795b857f361b2054d50a727392457a378a12adb4fe0430e618 | | closed_braid_period_line.md, Section 5 | cdb5cd8402f17d975a923951d156a6092a9cb5291e8348035fb81623d80f8529 | | actual_clock_feedback_normal_form.md, Sections 1--3 | f58a4dfd06615ecace95959e58474837f7eb50ef7f01a3c00d517d3938cb06bf | | research_charged_source_angle_optimization.md, Sections 1--3 | 45b21fabb9cb65512bc3e576eb3d659b6fe14c3dcd90b4164bfdb12b8cedea64 | | research_charged_variational_markov_loss.md, Sections 2--3 | 5c7e01c1c93d3b399e81b93d2dfff99efea05653c010593d86e1a07a14c11ccb | | research_incidence_marked_cut_observability.md, Section 1 | c0b9f010a8ab4b69b96bbcb0a32a6b8dad6ed8c39fca1029834f2ba74c13cbfc |

title: Exact difference equations for the complete incidence sum
text:
# Exact difference equations for the complete incidence sum Private written deduction, 14 November 2026. This note concerns the original finite sum, with all phases retained. The additional variables introduced below record its coefficients; they are not identified with meridian or longitude eigenvalues. There are two useful statements. First, alternating cycles in the event--anchor incidence graph give exact difference equations without boundary remainders, even at the prescribed root of unity. Second, these equations determine every coefficient of the finite generating polynomial from one coefficient. This is rigidity of the coefficient array. Evaluation of that array can still vanish by cancellation. ## 1. The finite polynomial and its quadratic phase Let \(G\) be the bipartite multigraph whose vertices are the events and anchors of the original source. Its edges are their distinct incidences. Write \(E\) for this edge set and \(C\) for its unsigned incidence matrix. Parallel edges are retained. Put \[ q=e^{\pi i/N},\qquad d=N-1,\qquad \mathcal F_d=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}:Cn=d\mathbf1\}, \qquad S_j=\prod_{r=1}^j2\sin(\pi r/N),\quad S_0=1. 	ag{1} \] Every coordinate of a feasible \(n\) is at most \(d\). We assume \(\mathcal F_d
e\varnothing\). The case of empty support gives the zero polynomial throughout. Use one event per crossing, together with the original closing events. The complete source formula and its joint-phase calculation give, after taking out a specified scalar independent of \(n\), \[ w_N(n)= rac{q^{\Phi_N(n)}}{\prod_{e\in E}S_{n_e}}, \qquad \Phi_N(n)= rac12 n^{\mathsf T}Hn+Na^{\mathsf T}n+b^{\mathsf T}n. 	ag{2} \] Here \(H\) is a fixed symmetric integral matrix with even diagonal; \(a,b\) are fixed integral vectors. Their entries come from the crossing signs, the order of undercrossings, and the closing pivots. They do not depend on the level. An additive constant in \(\Phi_N\) belongs to the extracted scalar. For precision, the joint-phase formula uses linear functions \(h_j,u_j,v_j,J_j\) of the incidences at each crossing. They are, respectively, its auxiliary clock, understrand transfer, overstrand output, and the accumulated understrand input. If \(\alpha_i\) is the closing index on head \(i\), the complete exponent is \[ \Phi_N= \sum_j\sigma_j h_j(u_j+2J_j) +N\sum_j(h_j-\sigma_jJ_j) +\sum_j\sigma_j(h_j+J_j)-2\sum_{i>1}\alpha_i. 	ag{3} \] Thus (2) follows with \[  egin{split} H&=\sum_j\sigma_j\{ h_j\otimes(u_j+2J_j)+(u_j+2J_j)\otimes h_j\},\ a&=\sum_j(h_j-\sigma_jJ_j),\ b&=\sum_j\sigma_j(h_j+J_j)-2\sum_{i>1}\alpha_i. \end{split} 	ag{4} \] In (4), a linear function denotes its integral coefficient vector. The proof of (3), including its boundary factors, belongs to [the joint-phase calculation](research_joint_clock_phase_equations.md). The arguments below also apply to any specified phase of the form (2). Introduce independent nonzero complex variables \(z_e\), and define \[ F_N(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathcal F_d}w_N(n)z^n, \qquad z^n=\prod_e z_e^{n_e}. 	ag{5} \] The original scalar is its prescribed external factor times \(F_N(\mathbf1)\). No normalization by that value is used. Each coefficient in (5) is nonzero, since \(S_j>0\) for \(0\le j<N\). Let \(T_e\) act by replacing \(z_e\) with \(qz_e\), fixing the other variables. These operators commute with one another and satisfy \(T_ez_e=qz_eT_e\). On a monomial \(z^n\), \(T_e\) has eigenvalue \(q^{n_e}\). Define \[ s(T_e)= rac{T_e-T_e^{-1}}{i}, \qquad s(n)= rac{q^n-q^{-n}}{i}=2\sin(\pi n/N). 	ag{6} \] The conservation equations in (1) give the exact operator identities \[ \left(\prod_{e
i v}T_e-q^dight)F_N=0 \quad\hbox{for every event or anchor }v. 	ag{7} \] ## 2. Alternating cycles give equations with no boundary remainder A simple cycle in a bipartite multigraph has even length. Give its successive edges alternating signs \(+1,-1\), and give all other edges value zero. Denote the resulting vector by \(c\). It satisfies \(Cc=0\). A two-edge cycle between parallel incidences is allowed. Write \(c_+\) and \(c_-\) for its positive and negative edge sets, and put \[ \ell_c= rac12c^{\mathsf T}Hc+b^{\mathsf T}c\in\mathbb Z. 	ag{8} \] **Theorem 1.** The original generating polynomial satisfies \[  oxed{\left[ \prod_{e\in c_+}s(T_e) - z^c(-1)^{a^{\mathsf T}c}q^{\ell_c} \left(\prod_eT_e^{(Hc)_e}ight) \prod_{e\in c_-}s(T_e) ight]F_N=0.} 	ag{9} \] The multiplication by \(z^c\) is on the left of the shift operators, as displayed. Negative powers are interpreted in the Laurent polynomial ring. *Proof.* For \(m,m+c\in\mathcal F_d\), factorial cancellation gives \[ \left(\prod_{e\in c_+}s(m_e+1)ight)w_N(m+c) = q^{\Phi_N(m+c)-\Phi_N(m)} \left(\prod_{e\in c_-}s(m_e)ight)w_N(m). 	ag{10} \] The phase difference is exactly \[ \Phi_N(m+c)-\Phi_N(m) =(Hc)^{\mathsf T}m+Na^{\mathsf T}c+\ell_c. 	ag{11} \] Since \(q^N=-1\), this is the coefficient relation in (9). It remains to check the boundary of the finite support. On the left of (9), a term with \(n_e=0\) for any \(e\in c_+\) vanishes because \(s(0)=0\). Every remaining term has \(m=n-c\ge0\) and \(Cm=d\mathbf1\), and so has an allowed partner in (10). On the right, a term with \(m_e=0\) for some \(e\in c_-\) vanishes for the same reason. Every remaining term has \(n=m+c\ge0\) and \(Cn=d\mathbf1\). The row sums ensure all its coordinates are at most \(d\); there is no additional upper boundary. This pairs every nonzero term. No value of a sine factorial at \(N\), no division by a vanishing factor, and no cyclic extension of the index set is needed. \(\square\) There are only finitely many simple cycles for a fixed graph, so (7) and (9) form a finite system whose number of generators does not grow with \(N\). This is a system in the auxiliary variables \(z_e\); it is not yet a recurrence in the color or a peripheral quantum \(A\)-polynomial. ## 3. Rigidity of the finite coefficient array **Theorem 2.** Among polynomials supported in \(\mathcal F_d\), the solutions of all the cycle equations (9) form a one-dimensional complex vector space, spanned by \(F_N\). *Proof.* First, any two feasible integral flows are joined by simple alternating cycle moves through feasible integral flows. To see this, orient every edge of the bipartite graph from its event to its anchor. For two flows \(n,n'\), the difference \(n'-n\) has zero signed divergence. Direct its positive entries with that orientation and its negative entries against it. At each vertex, total incoming multiplicity equals total outgoing multiplicity. A nonempty such directed multigraph contains a directed simple cycle. Its corresponding alternating vector \(c\) is sign-compatible with \(n'-n\). Thus \(n+c\ge0\), its margins are unchanged, and its integral distance from \(n'\) is strictly smaller. Repeating finishes after finitely many moves. Now let \(G(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathcal F_d}g(n)z^n\) satisfy (9). For adjacent feasible flows \(m,m+c\), comparison of the coefficient of \(z^{m+c}\) gives (10) with \(g\) in place of \(w_N\). All sine factors in that relation lie at indices \(1,\ldots,d\) and are nonzero. Therefore \[  rac{g(m+c)}{w_N(m+c)} = rac{g(m)}{w_N(m)}. 	ag{12} \] Connectivity makes the ratio constant on the entire support. The polynomial \(F_N\) itself satisfies the equations by Theorem 1 and is nonzero. This proves the assertion. \(\square\) The support condition is essential. The shift equations alone, on an unrestricted space of functions at a root of unity, do not give this uniqueness conclusion. Also, (12) does not show \(F_N(\mathbf1)
e0\). A linear functional on a one-dimensional space of coefficient arrays can annihilate its generator. The original closing evaluation still requires its own estimate. ## 4. The associated algebraic equations There is a direct classical algebraic system behind (9). Replace the commuting shift symbols \(T_e\) by nonzero variables \(y_e\), and take the level limit of their scalar coefficients. Thus \(q^{\ell_c}	o1\) and \(q^d	o-1\). The result is \[ \prod_{e
i v}y_e=-1,\qquad \prod_{e\in c_+}(y_e-y_e^{-1}) = (-1)^{a^{\mathsf T}c}z^c y^{Hc} \prod_{e\in c_-}(y_e-y_e^{-1}). 	ag{13} \] The factors \(i\) cancel because a cycle has equally many positive and negative edges. These are Laurent polynomial equations over \(\mathbb Q\). Their equations and degrees depend on the fixed diagram, not on \(N\). On the regular open set \(y_e-y_e^{-1}
e0\), cycles multiply according to addition in \(\ker_{\mathbb Z}C\). A lattice basis of cycles consequently suffices for (13) on that open set. At the excluded divisors the uncancelled equations must be retained. To verify the stationary meaning rather than infer it formally, choose local logarithms \(y_e=e^{\pi i x_e}\) with \(Cx=\mathbf1\). On a regular simply connected chart choose an analytic primitive \(\mathcal J'(x)=\log(2\sin\pi x)\), normalized to \(\mathcal J=J\) on an interval in \((0,1)\), where \(J(t)=\int_0^t\log(2\sin\pi u)\,du\). The local action is \[ \mathcal S(x;z)= -\sum_e\mathcal J(x_e) +\pi i\left( rac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+a^{\mathsf T}xight) +\sum_e x_e\log z_e. 	ag{14} \] Its real restriction at \(z_e=1\) has the same real part as the concave angle expression in the complete-source note. Direct differentiation gives \[ \exp(D_c\mathcal S) = (-1)^{a^{\mathsf T}c}z^cy^{Hc} \prod_e(2\sin\pi x_e)^{-c_e}. 	ag{15} \] Thus (13) is precisely the exponentiated stationary equation \(\exp(D_c\mathcal S)=1\). At a chosen solution, this means \(D_c\mathcal S\in2\pi i\mathbb Z\), not automatically zero. Those integers are additive on the cycle lattice. For completeness they can be represented by an integer vector \(r\in\mathbb Z^E\). Indeed \(\ker_{\mathbb Z}C\) is primitive: its quotient in \(\mathbb Z^E\) is the subgroup \(\operatorname{im}_{\mathbb Z}C\) of a free abelian group, and is therefore free. Hence every integer functional on the kernel extends to \(\mathbb Z^E\). Replacing (14) by \(\mathcal S-2\pi i\,r^{\mathsf T}x\) makes all its tangent derivatives vanish at that solution. This is the usual integer Fourier ambiguity, retained explicitly here. The equations \(\prod_{e
i v}y_e=-1\) fix \(Cx\) only modulo even integers. The actual source uses the lift \(Cx=\mathbf1\) and the specified finite support. Neither that lift nor the contribution of a stationary point is selected by (13) alone. ## 5. What this contributes to the geometric comparison Equations (9) act on the exact original sum before a semiclassical approximation. Equations (13) are a fixed algebraic object obtained from them, and (14)--(15) check its relation to the angle action and full quadratic phase. This makes the geometric comparison a comparison of explicit equations rather than an assertion that concavity must imply knot-group relations. The joint-phase note supplies a further comparison: its independent clock equations eliminate rationally, and the remaining regular equations have the original physical crossing differential. The earlier marked-braid notes already identify that physical correspondence with meridian representations. This avoids treating the classical representation comparison as a newly discovered general theorem. It does not turn coefficient rigidity into a nonzero contribution under the original evaluation. Theorems 1--2 prove no volume limit or finite-exception theorem. The general use of hypergeometric state sums and difference equations is established territory. Coverage references include [Garoufalidis--Lê, *The colored Jones function is q-holonomic*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0309214) and [Garoufalidis, *On the characteristic and deformation varieties of a knot*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0306230). No proof from those papers is used above. The derivation here checks the precise finite root-of-unity support, its boundary cancellations, and the actual prescribed phase; it makes no novelty claim for the general difference-equation method. ## Direct source versions | Source | SHA-256 | | --- | --- | | research_charged_source_angle_optimization.md, Sections 1--3 | 45b21fabb9cb65512bc3e576eb3d659b6fe14c3dcd90b4164bfdb12b8cedea64 | | research_joint_clock_phase_equations.md, Sections 2--5 | 71393aa353909dfa2dd19b078b1d3fccdf8561520aa071b7537e4bbfc50bb867 | Both written source implications were read in these versions. No numerical results or executions are used in these proofs.

title: The exact marked-cut restriction of the incidence polynomial
text:
# The exact marked-cut restriction of the incidence polynomial Private written proof, 15 November 2026. The incidence cycle equations determine the full coefficient array from one coefficient. This note computes a particular observation of that array using the original closing operator. For every complete braid intertwiner, its restriction to the marked closing fugacity is the original scalar times a universal geometric sum. This gives an exact transport with uniformly bounded comparison factors, but also forced zeros at distance of order \(1/N\) from the prescribed evaluation. All derivatives along this line still contain the same unknown original scalar. No numerical calculation, mathematical code, or saved numerical result is used. The conclusion concerns an auxiliary closing fugacity, not the meridian variable of the reduced ADO period. ## 1. The actual closing line Fix \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), and \(Q=q^2\). Use the original incidence polynomial of [the cycle-equation theorem](research_incidence_cycle_difference_equations.md): \[ F_N(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathcal F_d}w_N(n)z^n, \qquad w_N(n)= rac{q^{\Phi_N(n)}}{\prod_eS_{n_e}},\qquad S_a=\prod_{r=1}^a2\sin(\pi r/N),\quad S_0=1. 	ag{1} \] Every incidence remains distinct. The complete quadratic phase, including all closing pivots, is the phase in that theorem. The original invariant is \(\gamma_NF_N(\mathbf1)\), where \(\gamma_N
e0\) is its specified external factor, independent of the incidence state. It is not defined by division by the invariant. At the unpivoted marked closing event the two incidence charges are \((d-a_1,a_1)\). Let \(e_*\) be the second incidence, carrying the transmitted physical degree \(a_1\). Define the actual one-variable restriction \[ f_N(t)=F_N(z_e=1\ (e
e e_*),\ z_{e_*}=t), \qquad D_N(t)= rac1N\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}t^a. 	ag{2} \] The marked incidence can be parallel to another incidence; it is not merged with it. All other fugacities are set to their prescribed values. **Theorem.** For every complete signed braid with its original closing, \[  oxed{f_N(t)=F_N(\mathbf1)D_N(t).} 	ag{3} \] This is a polynomial identity, including when \(F_N(\mathbf1)=0\). It remains true after any fixed signed tangle insertion assembled into such an original intertwiner. The statement is about the complete assembled operator, not an individual clock sector or an arbitrary degree-changing coupon. **Proof.** Let \(W_N\) be that operator on \(b\) original heads, and let \(g\) be the actual pivotal matrix. The whole-source formula is \[ K_N= rac{\chi_N}{N} \operatorname{Tr}[(I\otimes g^{\otimes(b-1)})W_N]. 	ag{4} \] The specified scalar \(\chi_N
e0\) includes the exterior normalization. The original partial trace \[ C_N=\operatorname{Tr}_{2,\ldots,b} [(I\otimes g^{\otimes(b-1)})W_N] 	ag{5} \] is a Hopf endomorphism of the remaining head. The finite proof in [the prescribed-cut theorem](research_rivin_jones_prescribed_cut_and_hermite_recovery.md), Section 2, applies: cyclicity of the tail trace and the actual coproduct make \(C_N\) commute with the first-head generators. The Cartan eigenvalues are distinct and the adjacent raising/lowering arrows are nonzero. Thus \(C_N=c_NI\). This also holds for one head. Let \(A_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t,\ldots,t^d)\). The alias-free incidence expansion of (4), with this diagonal insertion on the first head, multiplies every term by precisely \(t^{a_1}\). It does not change its support or its coefficient normalization. Therefore \[ \gamma_N f_N(t) = rac{\chi_N}{N}\operatorname{Tr}(A_tC_N) =\chi_Nc_ND_N(t). 	ag{6} \] At \(t=1\), (4) gives \(\gamma_NF_N(\mathbf1)=\chi_Nc_N\). Canceling only the known nonzero \(\gamma_N\) proves (3). The argument never divides by \(c_N\) or the knot invariant. \(\square\) The use of scalarity is legitimate before this one-parameter insertion: the complete original \(W_N\) is an intertwiner. If other incidence fugacities are left arbitrary, the resulting operator need not be an intertwiner. In particular, (3) does not assert that \(D_N(t)\) divides the full multivariable polynomial. ## 2. Exact transport and its source The polynomial \(D_N\) has the whole expression \[ D_N(t)= rac{1-t^N}{N(1-t)},\qquad D_N(1)=1. 	ag{7} \] Its two exact shift laws give \[  oxed{(1-Qt)f_N(Qt)=(1-t)f_N(t),} 	ag{8} \] and \[  oxed{(1-qt)f_N(qt)-(1-t)f_N(t) = rac{2t^N}{N}F_N(\mathbf1).} 	ag{9} \] These follow by using \(Q^N=1\) and \(q^N=-1\) in (7). There are no omitted endpoint terms. The right side of (9) contains the unknown prescribed scalar itself. Thus (9) is not an affine source equation with independently known forcing, of the type used in [the affine quantum-A period theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/affine_quantum_a_period.md). There is nevertheless a useful uniformly bounded transport to the midpoint between adjacent \(Q\)-orbit points: \[ f_N(q)= rac{2F_N(\mathbf1)}{N(1-q)},\qquad  rac2\pi|F_N(\mathbf1)|\le |f_N(q)|\le |F_N(\mathbf1)|. 	ag{10} \] Indeed the magnitude of the coefficient is \(1/[N\sin(\pi/(2N))]\); the inequalities \(2x/\pi\le\sin x\le x\) on \([0,\pi/2]\) prove (10). The exact identity and both inequalities remain valid if the scalar vanishes. They move the same unknown observation without an exponential normalization cost; they supply no absolute lower bound. Among polynomials of degree at most \(d\), equation (8) itself has the one-dimensional solution space spanned by \(D_N\). In fact, if \(f(t)=\sum_{a=0}^df_at^a\), comparing its coefficient at \(t^a\), \(1\le a<N\), gives \((Q^a-1)(f_a-f_{a-1})=0\), so all coefficients coincide. The coefficients at zero and \(N\) give identities. This shows explicitly how a rigid restricted equation can still leave its original closing multiplier undetermined. ## 3. Forced zero locus and the exact scalar connection If \(F_N(\mathbf1)
e0\), the zeros of \(f_N\) are exactly the simple points \[ t=Q^j,\qquad 1\le j<N. 	ag{11} \] If \(F_N(\mathbf1)=0\), the entire restriction is zero. In either case all the nontrivial \(Q\)-orbit evaluations vanish. The closest forced zeros have distance \(2\sin(\pi/N)\) from \(1\). Hence even a nonzero original scalar does not produce an \(N\)-independent zero-free complex neighborhood of the prescribed point in this actual source direction. For fixed derivative order \(r\ge0\), the logarithmic moments are exactly \[ \left.(t\partial_t)^r f_N(t)ight|_{t=1} = rac1N\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}a^r\,F_N(\mathbf1), 	ag{12} \] where the \(r=0\) sum is \(N\). Thus even the entire germ on this line vanishes when the original scalar vanishes. It cannot provide an independent nonzero pointing for that scalar. On its nonzero locus the exact logarithmic derivative is \[ \partial_t f_N(t)=a_N(t)f_N(t),\qquad a_N(t)= rac1{1-t}- rac{Nt^{N-1}}{1-t^N}. 	ag{13} \] At \(t=1\) the apparent singularity is removable, with value \((N-1)/2\). At every point in (11), \(a_N\) has a simple pole of residue one. No holomorphic first-order scalar connection on a fixed neighborhood of \(1\) can transport a nonzero \(f_N\) for all sufficiently large \(N\): a nonzero solution of such a scalar equation has no zeros in its connected domain. Equation (13) identifies the required moving singularities explicitly. The microscopic behavior is equally explicit. Uniformly for \(s\) in each fixed compact complex set, \[ D_N(e^{s/N})= rac{e^s-1}{s}+O(N^{-1}), 	ag{14} \] with the removable value one at \(s=0\). This follows by expanding \(N(e^{s/N}-1)=s(1+O(N^{-1}))\), keeping the removable factor at zero. Thus the nearby zeros belong to the actual source profile; they are not an artifact of a norm estimate. ## 4. Relation to period rigidity and the remaining estimate The earlier [general flow fusion](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_general_flow_fusion.md), Section 2, already gives the full-block geometric sum and its even/odd root values. What is added here is its universal occurrence after the entire intertwiner has been closed, as the exact restriction of the new incidence polynomial. The statement is independent of braid width, crossing signs and the chosen fixed short insertion. The cycle theorem's normalized coefficient array is still unique. Restriction (2) takes its one-dimensional solution line to \(\mathbb C D_N\) with multiplier \(F_N(\mathbf1)\); that restriction can be zero only if the actual prescribed observation is zero. This makes no alternative choice of a source or an array. It identifies the additional scalar whose estimate coefficient rigidity does not supply. This agrees with the distinction in [the closed-braid period line](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/closed_braid_period_line.md), Section 2: an invertible intertwiner frame and its evaluated cut are different objects. It also agrees with the function-level source distinction in [the global period audit](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/global_period_rigidity_function_audit.md). Those general distinctions alone did not give (3) or (10). The fixed-presentation hypothesis in [whole-period cyclotomic rigidity](whole_period_cyclotomic_rigidity.md) is relevant to (7). Its degree in \(t\) grows with \(N\), but retaining the power coordinate \(w=t^N\) gives the fixed whole expression \((1-w)/(N(1-t))\). Its value at \(t=w=1\) must be taken on that power graph, with the removable germ retained. Dividing out this known whole factor leaves exactly the constant \(F_N(\mathbf1)\), not a new computation of it. Nor is this auxiliary \(t\) automatically the meridian parameter of an actual quantum-A equation. Consequently (10) is an exact controlled transport of the prescribed observation, and (11)--(13) obstruct a particular zero-free scalar transport argument. Neither proves or disproves nonvanishing of the original invariant at any level. A phase-sensitive lower bound in a transverse source direction, or a nonzero geometric projection of the actual closing, is still required for the finite-exception target. ## Direct written source versions All directly used implications were read at these SHA-256 versions. | Source | SHA-256 | | --- | --- | | `research_incidence_cycle_difference_equations.md` | `8d9b4231b2f3a8795b857f361b2054d50a727392457a378a12adb4fe0430e618` | | `actual_global_charged_bridge_flow.md` | `b444e487eab3ec0a56c40b22584837cefcbe374a137b0beeaa185116c2a81d8c` | | `research_rivin_jones_prescribed_cut_and_hermite_recovery.md` | `1b0e105ffb67b2b8552f5fddc5f0a3ac009e9795b33e27599ac4726ebd74079e` | | `closed_braid_period_line.md` | `cdb5cd8402f17d975a923951d156a6092a9cb5291e8348035fb81623d80f8529` | | `affine_quantum_a_period.md` | `ea09b1967caa38c3b4c81cf01ee4a265142d874a37dd390be2cfbb59150f6819` | | `global_period_rigidity_function_audit.md` | `d9cd5f85648be196cb803c2890848f7d5d38057f58e778a26ce5c377ffd8fd84` | | `whole_period_cyclotomic_rigidity.md` | `587d7d39e13769159e8bc0c8fee4d45820216773797d7f0ef8776f875d720210` | | `actual_general_flow_fusion.md` | `708929d138a1cdcadc74cfde2f7e0a6857f3a0cad63dfffa6de419a4098d65aa` |

title: The two selected angles of a positive internal pair
text: # The two selected angles of a positive internal pair Research proof, 3 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. Consider two consecutive selected vertices, with one complete outside endpoint attached to each of them. This note proves that both selected angles have real part less than \(\pi/2\), throughout the charge cube, when both crossing powers are integers at least three. The proof uses the coupled period equations. Separate height bounds would not imply this conclusion. The result concerns geometry. It does not assert an asymptotic for a complete-end kernel at a complex selected angle, or a nonzero coefficient in the finite two-vertex source. ## 1. The family and the first possible boundary point Let the powers be \(n,p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge3}\), and let the charges belong to \([0,1]^2\). The [fractional-charge theorem](research_positive_path_fractional_charge_cube.md) gives the continuous positive geometric family. At an active vertex write its angle as \[ t=a-iH,\qquad 0<a<\pi,\quad 0<H<23/20. \tag{1} \] At a zero-charge or complete endpoint the angle is zero. The bounds we need from the [maximum-phase theorem](research_geometric_phase_maximum_principle.md) are \[ \cosh H<7/4,\qquad a<\frac{9\pi}{4n}\chi . \tag{2} \] The original return from this vertex to a neighbor of angle \(u\) is \[ r(t,u)=\operatorname{asinh}\bigl(\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2)\bigr)=k+ig. \tag{3} \] Its branch has \(k>0\) and \(-\pi/2<g<\pi/2\) when the first vertex is active. There are two incidences, one to a complete endpoint. Their returns satisfy \[ k_0+k_1=\frac{nH}{2},\qquad g_0+g_1=\frac{na}{2}-\pi\chi . \tag{4} \] **Theorem 1.** Throughout this charge cube, both selected angles satisfy \[ 0\le \Re t<\pi/2. \tag{5} \] It suffices to exclude a first point with \(a=\pi/2\). Indeed, join the complete point to any prescribed charge by the straight charge segment. Along this segment the geometric solution is continuous. At a first such point the other selected angle still has real part at most \(\pi/2\). A vertex of power at least five cannot be the first one, by (2). At the proposed first point put \[ z=\tan(t/2)=\operatorname{sech}H-i\tanh H=e^{-i\omega}, \qquad \omega=\arctan(\sinh H). \tag{6} \] Let \(C=\cos(u/2)\) for the other selected endpoint. Its real angle is at most \(\pi/2\), and its height is less than \(23/20\). Therefore \[ \Re C^2\ge\frac12,\qquad 0\le\arg C<\arctan(23/40). \tag{7} \] The first inequality follows from \(\Re C^2=(1+\cos(\Re u)\cosh(-\Im u))/2\). For the second, use \(\tan\arg C=\tan(\Re u/2)\tanh(-\Im u/2)\). The complete-end return \(r_0=\operatorname{asinh}z\) has the exact components \[ k_0=\operatorname{asinh}\sqrt{\operatorname{sech}H}, \qquad g_0=-\arctan\bigl(\sqrt2\sinh(H/2)\bigr). \tag{8} \] These formulas follow by squaring \(\sinh(k_0+ig_0)=z\), with the positive real and negative imaginary branches. They agree at \(H=0\) and retain those branches for \(H>0\). For the other return, \(\sinh r_1=zC\) implies \[ \tan g_1=\tanh k_1\,\tan(\arg C-\omega). \tag{9} \] Consequently \(g_1\) lies strictly between \(0\) and \(\arg C-\omega\), unless the latter is zero, in which case \(g_1=0\). ## 2. A vertex of power four cannot reach the boundary Suppose \(n=4\). By (2) and (8), \[ k_0>\operatorname{asinh}(3/4)=\log2>2/3. \tag{10} \] The real period equation gives \(2H>k_0\), hence \(H>1/3\). Since \(\sqrt2>7/5\), \[ \omega+|g_0| >\arctan(1/3)+\arctan(7/30) =\arctan(51/83)>\arctan(23/40)>\arg C. \tag{11} \] If \(\arg C\le\omega\), (9) gives \(g_1\le0\). Otherwise it gives \(g_1<\arg C-\omega<|g_0|\). In either case \(g_0+g_1<0\). But at \(a=\pi/2\), the imaginary period equation for power four is \(g_0+g_1=\pi(1-\chi)\ge0\). This is a contradiction. ## 3. A vertex of power three cannot reach the boundary Suppose \(n=3\). First, \[ H>1/2. \tag{12} \] Otherwise \[ \cosh H\,\sinh^2(3/4) <\frac87\left(\frac78\right)^2<1, \] so \(k_0>3/4\ge3H/2\), contradicting (4). The elementary bounds used here follow directly from the positive Taylor series: \(\cosh(1/2)\le53/47<8/7\) and \(\sinh(3/4)\le24/29<7/8\). Equations (8) and (12) now give \[ \omega+|g_0|> \arctan(1/2)+\arctan(7/20) =\arctan(34/33)>\pi/4. \tag{13} \] Put \[ k_*=\frac{3H}{2}-k_0=k_1,\qquad g_*=-\frac{\pi}{4}-g_0. \tag{14} \] Since \(\chi\le1\), the imaginary equation in (4) gives \(g_1\ge g_*\). By (13), \(g_*+\omega>0\). Equation (9) also gives \(0<g_1+\omega<\pi/2\), since both \(\omega\) and \(\arg C\) belong to \([0,\pi/2)\), with \(\omega>0\). For fixed \(k>0\), the correct real-square identity is \[ \Re\!\left[\bigl(e^{i\omega}\sinh(k+ig)\bigr)^2\right] =\frac12\left\{ \cos(2\omega)\bigl(\cosh(2k)\cos(2g)-1\bigr) -\sin(2\omega)\sinh(2k)\sin(2g)\right\}. \tag{15} \] Its monotonicity must be checked on the actual first-quadrant arc, rather than inferred from \(g+\omega>0\). Write \(e^{i\omega}\sinh(k+ig)=X(g)+iY(g)\). For \(-\pi/2<g<\pi/2\), direct differentiation gives \[ X'=-\tanh k\,Y-\frac{\sin\omega\cos g}{\cosh k}, \qquad Y'=\tanh k\,X+\frac{\cos\omega\cos g}{\cosh k}. \tag{16} \] Thus \(X'<0\) and \(Y'>0\) wherever \(X>0\) and \(Y\ge0\). In particular \(X^2-Y^2\) strictly decreases along that arc. The arc is an interval in \(g\): its inequalities are \[ -\tan\omega\,\tanh k\le\tan g <\cot\omega\,\tanh k. \] Put \(C_*=e^{i\omega}\sinh(k_*+ig_*)\). The complete-return identity \(\sinh r_0=e^{-i\omega}\), together with (8), simplifies this expression to \[ C_*=2\sinh H-\frac{\cosh(3H/2)}{\sqrt2} +i\left(\frac{\sinh(3H/2)}{\sqrt2}-1\right). \tag{17} \] For the calculation, put \(h=H/2\) and use \[ e^{i\omega}\sinh r_0=1,\qquad e^{i\omega}\cosh r_0 =\frac{\sqrt2(\cosh h+i\sinh h)}{\cosh H}. \] In the expansion of \(e^{i\omega}\sinh(3H/2-i\pi/4-r_0)\), the first product is \[ \frac{(\sinh(3h)-i\cosh(3h))(\cosh h+i\sinh h)} {\cosh(2h)} =2\sinh H-i. \] Subtracting \((\cosh(3h)-i\sinh(3h))/\sqrt2\) gives (17). No exponentiated period equation is substituted. Let \(X=\sqrt2\sinh(H/2)\). Then \(0<X<1\), because \(X^2=\cosh H-1<3/4\), and (17) gives the polynomial identity \[ \frac12-\Re C_*^2 =S(X):=4X^5-4X^4+8X^3-8X^2+X+1. \tag{18} \] The polynomial is strictly positive on \([0,1]\). For an explicit rational verification, its degree-five Bernstein coefficients on the two indicated intervals are | Interval for \(X\) | Bernstein coefficients | |---|---| | \([0,1/2]\) | \(1,\ 11/10,\ 1,\ 4/5,\ 11/20,\ 3/8\) | | \([1/2,1]\) | \(3/8,\ 1/5,\ 1/10,\ 1/5,\ 7/10,\ 2\) | Here the coefficients multiply \(\binom5j y^j(1-y)^{5-j}\), after the affine change from the stated interval to \(0\le y\le1\). Each basis function is nonnegative, and their sum is one. It remains to compare the actual first-quadrant point \(C\) with \(C_*\). This requires two height ranges. Set \[ H_c=\frac23\operatorname{asinh}\sqrt2 . \] One has \(1/2<H_c<1\): use \(\sinh(3/4)<7/8<\sqrt2<3/2<\sinh(3/2)\). For every height under consideration, and also at \(H_c\), the real part in (17) is positive. Indeed \[ \Re C_*=\frac{\sqrt{1+X^2/2}}{\sqrt2} (4X-2X^2-1), \qquad 7/20<X<1, \] and the concave quadratic in parentheses is positive on \([7/20,1]\). At \(H_c\), the upper bound \(X<1\) follows, for example, from \(\cosh H_c<\cosh1\le17/11<2\). If \(H\ge H_c\), (17) also gives \(\Im C_*\ge0\). Both \(C_*\) and the actual \(C\) therefore lie on the first-quadrant arc for \(k=k_*\). Since \(g_1\ge g_*\), (16) gives \(\Re C^2\le\Re C_*^2<1/2\), by (18). If \(H<H_c\), \(C_*\) lies below that arc, so the preceding comparison cannot be used. The maximum of \(X(g)^2-Y(g)^2\) on the first-quadrant arc occurs at \(Y=0\). Solving that condition gives its value \[ R_0(H)= \frac{\sinh^2k_*(H)\cosh^2k_*(H)} {\sinh^2k_*(H)+\operatorname{sech}^2H}. \] Here \(k_*(H)=3H/2-k_0(H)>0\) at the proposed point. It increases strictly with \(H\), since \(k_0(H)\) decreases. The function \[ R(x,c)=\frac{x(1+x)}{x+c} \quad\text{satisfies}\quad \partial_xR=\frac{x^2+2cx+c}{(x+c)^2}>0,\qquad \partial_cR=-\frac{x(1+x)}{(x+c)^2}<0 \] for \(x,c>0\). Thus \(R_0(H)\) increases with \(H\), on the interval from the proposed height to \(H_c\). At \(H_c\), \(k_*>0\) and (17) gives \(\Im C_*=0\), so \[ \Re C^2\le R_0(H)<R_0(H_c) =\Re C_*(H_c)^2<1/2 . \] The final strict bound is again (18) and its positive Bernstein coefficients. Both height ranges contradict (7). The power-three first point is impossible as well. This proves Theorem 1. ## 4. Scope and reproducibility The argument uses the original two incidences at each selected vertex, including its complete outside end. It does not apply to an arbitrary interior vertex of a longer selected path. It also uses the integer alternatives \(n=3\), \(n=4\), and \(n\ge5\); no assertion for every noninteger power between three and five is made. The bound places the two selected angles in a smaller regular region for subsequent contour work. It does not by itself prove \(\Re\psi(t,0)>-\Im t\), nor does it control the endpoint and alias terms in a finite-source contour. The exact polynomial identities, Bernstein coefficients and scalar comparisons are checked by [the accompanying script](../experiments/check_internal_pair_angle_bound.py): ~~~sh python3 experiments/check_internal_pair_angle_bound.py ~~~

title: The original quantum source for positive internal pairs
text:
# The original quantum source for positive internal pairs Research proof, updated 4 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. For an internal pair with powers \(n,p\ge3\), the complete outside kernels now have an independently normalized complex phase. This allows one to retain those kernels as whole factors. The exact remaining contour has three variables: the shared Newton index and the two trace angles. No separate asymptotic for either one-vertex Fourier source is required. Sections 1–5 give a contour reduction for every pair of powers at least three. Sections 6–7 complete the estimate when both powers are at least seven. In that range the original two-boundary source has a nonzero geometric leading coefficient at every sufficiently large level, with a uniform expansion near the complete boundary colors. The proof retains the original first-normal traces and their endpoint terms. This is a theorem for a specified partially filled three-edge circle-tree exterior. It does not establish stability under every short partial filling, arbitrary tangle composition, or finitely many exceptional assignments per template. ## 1. The original source and the complete-end normalization Let \(\phi_N,R_N,e_j\) be the original trace, crossing and Newton polynomials, including the first normal at each double physical root. Put \[  egin{split} L&=\lfloor(N-1)/2floor,\qquad \eta=(-1)^{N-1},\ K_N(t,r)&=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos r),\ \mathcal L_N(t)&=\sum_{j=0}^L e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2),\ \mathcal P_{n,p,N} &=\phi_N^{(t)}\phi_N^{(r)} [R_N(t)^nR_N(r)^pK_N(t,0)K_N(t,r)K_N(r,0)] . \end{split} 	ag{1} \] The outside colors in this note are exactly complete. Denote the original geometric rate by \(M_{n,p}\). The [complete-pair energy theorem](research_radical_path_sector_gap.md#6-a-uniform-estimate-for-every-positive-pair-of-powers-at-least-three) gives \[ M_{n,p}>2M_\infty+ rac1{100},\qquad M_\infty= rac{4G}{\pi}. 	ag{2} \] For complex \(t\) in any compact subset of \[ \Re(-2\cos t)<2, 	ag{3} \] the [last-row normalization](research_last_physical_row_riccati.md) and the [even low-kernel comparison](research_even_complete_low_kernel.md) give, through both level parities, \[ \mathcal L_N(t)= \exp\{N\Psi(t)+O(\log N)\},\qquad \Psi(t)=\psi(t,0). 	ag{4} \] Here the error is a holomorphic logarithm with all fixed derivatives bounded by \(O(\log N)\) on smaller compact sets. The branch is fixed by the original first physical row. Equivalently, with \(w=-2\cos t\), \[ \Psi(t)= rac2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2} \operatorname{arsinh} \left( rac{\sqrt{2-w}}2\cot yight)\,dy . 	ag{5} \] The square root and inverse hyperbolic sine are their branches in the right half-plane. Formula (5) fixes \(\Psi(0)=M_\infty\) and is holomorphic on (3). This input is stronger than a formal stationary phase identity: it estimates the actual finite low-index polynomial on the contours used below. ## 2. Uniform removal of the original real tails Use the continuous real Newton entropy \[ V_t(x)=L_{\cos}(x+t/(2\pi))+L_{\cos}(x-t/(2\pi))-2J(x), \quad L_{\cos}(s)=\int_0^s\log|2\cos\pi y|\,dy , 	ag{6} \] for real \(0\le t\le\pi\) and \(0\le x\le1/2\). Write \(m(t)=\max_x V_t(x)\). The [real Newton theorem](research_three_crossing_real_period_newton_bound.md) proves \[  egin{gathered} |e_j(-2\cos t)|\le C N^A e^{NV_t(j/N)},\ 0\le V_t(x)\le V_0(x),\quad V_0(0)=V_0(1/2)=0,\quad m(0)=M_\infty/2,\quad m(t)\longrightarrow0\quad(t	o\pi). \end{gathered} 	ag{7} \] All constants may be enlarged to cover the finitely many small levels. Let \(\mathcal P^{m all\,low}_{n,p,N}\) be (1) with all three edges restricted to their literal indices \(0,\ldots,L\). **Proposition 1.** For every fixed \(n,p\ge3\), \[ |\mathcal P_{n,p,N}-\mathcal P^{m all\,low}_{n,p,N}| \le C N^A e^{2NM_\infty}. 	ag{8} \] One may choose fixed cuts \(0<\alpha< eta<1/2\) and \(0<T<\pi\) such that retaining only \[ \alpha\le j/N\le eta,\qquad |t_a|<T_N,\qquad |r_b|<T_N, \quad T_N=T+O(N^{-1}) 	ag{9} \] in the shared index and the two original physical traces changes the source by at most \[ C N^A e^{N(2M_\infty+1/200)} <C N^A e^{N(M_{n,p}-1/200)}. 	ag{10} \] The physical cut can be chosen as \(T_N=\pi-2\pi m_N/N\), so \(e^{iNT_N}=-\eta\); it lies strictly between grid angles. The shared-index contour boundaries obey \(N\alpha_N,N eta_N\in\mathbb Z+1/2\). Thus no pole lies on a cut and no half-residue is introduced. The odd simple node at angle zero is retained with its original value contribution. Every first normal remains on the side of the cut to which its original physical root belongs. *Proof.* Each radical edge has polynomial norm on the real color square, with polynomial bounds for its fixed ordinary normals, by the [radical Fourier theorem](research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md#7-fourier-bounds-for-the-original-radical-polynomials). Every full or low edge has real-square norm at most \(C N^A e^{NM_\infty}\), by (7). Expand the difference of the products of three edges. Each term has at least one radical and at most two exponentially sized factors. Applying the original two Hermite traces and fixed powers of the crossing costs only powers of \(N\). This proves (8). For a fixed low shared index \(j\), the complete two-trace integrand before applying the crossings is \[ e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos r)\mathcal L_N(t)\mathcal L_N(r). 	ag{11} \] Its norm on the real color square is at most a polynomial times \(e^{N(2V_0(j/N)+2M_\infty)}\). Hence the omitted shared indices have rate at most \(2M_\infty+2\sup_{x
otin[\alpha, eta]}V_0(x)\). If instead \(|t|\ge T\), then uniformly over all low \(j\) and all real \(r\), \[  egin{split} |e_j(-2\cos t)|&\le C N^A e^{Nm(T)},\ |\mathcal L_N(t)|&\le C N^A e^{N(m(T)+m(0))},\ |e_j(-2\cos r)|&\le C N^A e^{Nm(0)},\ |\mathcal L_N(r)|&\le C N^A e^{2Nm(0)} . \end{split} 	ag{12} \] Their product has rate \(2m(T)+2M_\infty\). The same estimate holds with \(t,r\) exchanged. These are bounds on entire real color rectangles for the polynomial (11). Apply Markov's inequality in each variable on those rectangles before restricting to physical nodes. Every required first or mixed first normal has the same exponential bound and only a polynomial additional factor. The crossing and trace have polynomial physical Hermite norm for each fixed power. Thus the bounds also apply to the original sums of values and normals; no assertion about a derivative is inferred from sampled values alone. Choose the cuts so that \[ 2\sup_{[0,\alpha]\cup[ eta,1/2]}V_0<1/200,\qquad 2m(T)<1/200 . 	ag{13} \] Their existence follows from (7). Integer rounding and the midpoint angular cuts preserve the strict inequalities for all sufficiently large \(N\). There are only polynomially many original terms. Equations (8), (12), and (13) prove (10). The cuts may be enlarged to include the selected geometric point; this only decreases the removed tails. \(\square\) ## 3. A compact contour with the original trace kernels Write the geometric point as \[ z_*=(x_*,t_*,r_*),\qquad Y=\Im x_*>0,\quad H_t=-\Im t_*>0,\quad H_r=-\Im r_*>0 . 	ag{14} \] It has \(0<\Re x_*<1/4\) and \(0<\Re t_*,\Re r_*<\pi/2\). Increase \(T\), if needed, so \(T>\pi/2\). Choose even positive smooth functions \(h_t,h_r\) on \([-T,T]\). They equal \(H_t,H_r\) respectively near the corresponding positive critical angle, and their graphs \[ \Gamma_t:\ t=	au-ih_t(	au),\qquad \Gamma_r:\ r=\sigma-ih_r(\sigma) 	ag{15} \] lie in (3). Such paths always exist: for \(|	au|\le\pi/2\) there is no height restriction from (3), while for \(\pi/2<|	au|<\pi\) it suffices to take \[ h_t(	au)<\operatorname{arcosh}(-1/\cos	au). 	ag{16} \] Their endpoint heights may be made arbitrarily small and positive.
