For large \(N\), \(c_0-\Re w\ge\gamma/2\), so \[ \Re d_r\ge(\gamma b_0/2)Q_rQ_{r+1}. \tag{11} \] For \(\Re u\ge0\), \[ \Re\frac{u}{1+u} \ge\frac{\Re u}{1+\Re u}. \tag{12} \] Applying (12) to the form \(u_{r+1}=d_r+q_ru_r/(1+u_r)\) of (2), and using (8), proves the induction: \[ \Re u_{r+1} \ge \Re d_r+\frac{cQ_{r+1}}{1+cQ_r} \ge cQ_{r+1}. \tag{13} \] Thus the needed lower bound comes from the original row solution. No dominant mode is prescribed as a boundary condition. ## 3. Transport down to a square-root distance from the endpoint Write \(\lambda_r=\lambda(r/N,w)\). On this closed tail, including the limit \(x=1/2\), the explicit formula (4) gives \[ |\lambda_r-1|\le C Q_r,\qquad \Re\lambda_r\ge1+c_1Q_r,\qquad |\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_r|\le C/N. \tag{14} \] For example, \((\lambda(x,w)-1)/(\cos(\pi x)/\sin^3(\pi x))\) extends continuously at \(x=1/2\) with value \(\sqrt{2-w}\). Its real part stays strictly positive on the compact domain. The local recurrence defect is uniformly bounded by \[ \left|1+d_r+q_r(1-\lambda_r^{-1})-\lambda_{r+1}\right| \le C/N. \tag{15} \] There is no endpoint singularity hidden in this assertion. The identity \[ \frac1{A_r}= \frac{\sin((2r+1)\theta)\cos((r+1)\theta)} {2\sin^3((r+1)\theta)} \tag{16} \] shows that \(d_r-(2-w)\cot^2(r\theta)=O(N^{-1})\), uniformly to the last row. Moreover \[ |q_r-1|\,|1-\lambda_r^{-1}| =\frac{|Q_{r+1}-Q_r|}{Q_r}|1-\lambda_r^{-1}| \le C/N. \] Together with (14) and \(\lambda_r=1+(2-w)\cot^2(r\theta)+(1-\lambda_r^{-1})\), this proves (15). Let \(e_r=|\rho_r-\lambda_r|\). Subtracting the exact and approximate recurrences, then using (10) and (14), yields \[ e_{r+1}\le \frac{q_r}{|\rho_r\lambda_r|}e_r+C/N \le (1-c_2h_r/N)e_r+C/N . \tag{17} \] Choose the positive constant \(c_2\) small enough that the displayed factor is nonnegative. At \(r_0\), the bulk theorem gives \(e_{r_0}=O(N^{-1})\). An induction with the barrier \(C_2/h_r\), where \(C_2\ge C/c_2\), proves \[ e_r\le C_2/h_r. \tag{18} \] For the induction, \(h_{r+1}=h_r-1\), and the right side of (17) at the proposed barrier is at most \(C_2/h_r\), hence at most \(C_2/h_{r+1}\). We use (18) only while \(h_r\ge\sqrt N\). Because both ratios lie in \(\Re z\ge1\), the line segment between them stays in that half-plane, and \[ |\Log\rho_r-\Log\lambda_r|\le e_r. \tag{19} \] Summing (18)--(19) over these rows costs \(O(\log N)\). ## 4. The final square-root layer Choose \(k_N\) so that \(\sqrt N\le h_{k_N}<\sqrt N+1\). Equations (14) and (18) imply \[ |u_{k_N}|\le C/\sqrt N,\qquad |u_{k_N}|/Q_{k_N}\le C. \tag{20} \] Since \(\Re u_r\ge0\), the exact recurrence and (8) imply \[ \frac{|u_{r+1}|}{Q_{r+1}} \le\frac{|u_r|}{Q_r}+\frac{|d_r|}{Q_{r+1}} \le\frac{|u_r|}{Q_r}+C Q_r . \tag{21} \] There are \(O(\sqrt N)\) remaining rows, and \(\sum_{r=k_N}^{J_N}Q_r=O(1)\) by (9). Thus \[ |u_r|\le C Q_r,\qquad \sum_{r=k_N}^{J_N} (|\Log\rho_r|+|\Log\lambda_r|)=O(1). \tag{22} \] For the logarithms use the integral from \(1\) to \(1+u_r\), which lies in \(\Re z\ge1\). The same argument applies to \(\lambda_r\). The absolute theorem in the linked note already supplies the normalization through \(r_0\), with error \(O(\log N)\). The function \(\Log\lambda(x,w)\) has bounded first derivative on \([1/5,1/2]\), uniformly on (5). Its remaining Riemann-sum error is \(O(1)\). Combining this fact with (19)--(22) proves (6). The proof also permits every earlier stopping row. Finally apply the same proof on a slightly larger compact free-color set and use Cauchy's formula for the holomorphic logarithmic error. This proves the derivative assertion. ## 5. The actual complete-end kernel at odd levels Define the holomorphic function \[ \Psi(w)=\int_0^{1/2}\Log\lambda(x,w)\,dx . \tag{23} \] The integrable logarithmic singularity at \(x=0\) is the one handled by the absolute normalization theorem. The integral is holomorphic on \(\Re w<2\). On the original geometric branch \[ w=-2\cos t,\qquad \Psi(w)=\psi(t,0). \tag{24} \] This is the normalized phase identity in the physical-row note: the opposite endpoint of its integral is \(\psi(\pi,t)=0\). **Corollary 2.** If \(N\) is odd, then on every fixed compact subset of \(\Re w<2\), \[ K_N(w,-2)=\exp\{N\Psi(w)+E_N(w)\},\qquad |\partial_w^\ell E_N(w)|\le C_\ell\log N \tag{25} \] for every fixed \(\ell\ge0\) and all sufficiently large odd \(N\). In particular the factor \(e^{E_N}\) is holomorphic and nonzero, and its modulus is bounded above and below by fixed powers of \(N\). Indeed \(c_{J_N}=-2\) at odd levels, so symmetry of the original kernel gives \(K_N(w,-2)=F_{J_N,N}(w)\) exactly. The difference between the integral in (6) and (23), multiplied by \(N\), is \(O(N^{-1})\): the omitted interval has length \(1/(2N)\) and \(\Log\lambda(x,w)=O(1/2-x)\) there. This proves (25). At even levels Theorem 1 applies to the actual last row \(c_{J_N}=-2\cos(\pi/N)\). It is not an estimate of \(K_N(w,-2)\). An extrapolation in the physical-row label or a claim about its first-normal correction is not used. The logarithmic derivative bounds in (25) have a useful local consequence. On a fixed complex neighborhood, the nonzero factor changes by \(1+O((\log N)/\sqrt N)\) over a bounded Gaussian window of radius \(N^{-1/2}\). Thus it can be kept as an \(N\)-dependent nonzero amplitude in a local saddle calculation. A full-source lower bound still needs an original contributing cycle and a bound on its complement; neither follows merely from (25). ## 6. Reproducing the finite checks The checker below evaluates the defining finite Newton rows, rather than generating them from the recurrence it tests. It checks both parities, the exact coefficient identities, the propagated lower barrier, and the odd-level equality with the original complete-end kernel. Its reported scaled asymptotic errors are diagnostics; the uniform estimates are proved above. ~~~sh python3 experiments/check_last_physical_row_riccati.py ~~~ The [saved record](../repro/results/research-last-physical-row-riccati.json) includes the checker and proof dependencies.

title: The literal charged tetrahedron inverse and three-face bubble
text: # The literal charged tetrahedron inverse and three-face bubble Private written proof, 17 November 2026. We reconstruct the inversion and bubble in Kashaev's 1994 definitions [K], including their finite normalization sums. Neither the printed inversion identity nor CG duality is used as a proof premise. This is the charged face-state identity at odd level, not yet the original marked-source adapter for deleting a free vertex. ## 1. The specified functions and regular data Let \(N>2\) be odd, \(\omega\) a primitive \(N\)-th root, and interpret \(1/2\) modulo \(N\), as in [K]. All finite indices are in \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). Choose nonzero roots \[ P=x_p,\quad Q=x_q,\quad R=x_r,\quad B=x_{pq},\quad C=x_{qr},\quad H=x_{pqr}, \] \[ B^N=P^N+Q^N,\qquad C^N=Q^N+R^N,\qquad H^N=P^N+Q^N+R^N. \tag{1} \] Thus the three individual central parameters and all the partial sums displayed in (1) are nonzero. We work on a lifted regular parameter domain with fixed choices of these roots. Put \[ \langle U,V\rangle=\frac{U^N-V^N}{N(U-V)},\qquad \langle U\rangle=U^{N-1}, \] \[ \kappa_*= \frac{\langle B,Q\rangle^{1/2}\langle H,R\rangle^{1/2} \langle C,R\rangle^{1/2}} {\langle H,C\rangle^{1/2}}. \tag{2} \] The same square-root choices in (2) are used in both normalizations below. None of its brackets vanishes under (1). Independently changing the sign of only one normalization is not permitted. For \(x^N+y^N=z^N\) with \(xyz\ne0\), define the periodic sequence \[ W(x,y,z;k)=\prod_{j=1}^{[k]}\frac{y}{z-x\omega^j}, \qquad w(x,y,z;i,j)=W(x,y,z;i-j)\omega^{j^2/2}. \tag{3} \] The cyclic product is one, so the recurrence extends (3) consistently to every integer. Also write \[ v(u;k)=\prod_{j=1}^{k}(1-u\omega^j)^{-1}\quad(0\le k<N),\qquad f(u,v\mid z)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{v(u;k)}{v(v;k)}z^k, \qquad z^N=\frac{1-u^N}{1-v^N}. \tag{4} \] In (4) the letter \(v\) inside \(f\) is a parameter; \(v(u;k)\) is the displayed one-argument product. Extend that product to all integers by \(v(u;k+1)=v(u;k)/(1-u\omega^{k+1})\). Then \(v(u;k+N)=v(u;k)/(1-u^N)\); the summand in (4), rather than either product separately, is cyclic. Set \[ u=\frac RH,\quad v=\frac{R}{\omega C},\quad z=\frac{BC}{HQ},\qquad \rho=\kappa_* f(u,v\mid z),\qquad \bar\rho=\kappa_* f(\omega v,u/\omega\mid z^{-1}). \tag{5} \] These are exactly [K, (1.25),(1.29)], including the three numerator square roots in (2). The bar is a label, not complex conjugation. The literal two matrices are [K, (1.24),(1.28)]: \[ \mathcal R^{\gamma,\delta}_{\alpha,\beta} =\frac{\rho}{C^{N-1}}\, \omega^{\alpha\delta} w(HQ,PR,BC;\gamma,\alpha)\, \delta_{\beta,\gamma+\delta}, \] \[ \overline{\mathcal R}^{\alpha,\beta}_{\gamma,\delta} =\frac{\bar\rho}{B^{N-1}}\, \frac{\delta_{\beta,\gamma+\delta}} {\omega^{\alpha\delta} w(HQ/\omega,PR,BC;\gamma,\alpha)}. \tag{6} \] Every denominator in these finite definitions is nonzero on (1). The apparently additional denominators used in the calculations below are nonzero there as well: in particular \((HQ)^N-(BC)^N=-P^NR^N\), and \(H^N-C^N=P^N\). ## 2. The complete finite normalization product We prove the identity needed for (5) without importing a transformation formula for \(f\). Temporarily use arbitrary regular \(u,v,z\) satisfying (4), and put \[ a_k=\frac{v(u;k)}{v(v;k)}z^k,\qquad b_k=\frac{v(\omega v;k)}{v(u/\omega;k)}z^{-k},\qquad C_0=(1-\omega v)(1-u). \] The two sequences are periodic. Direct cancellation of their products gives, including the cyclic seam, \[ b_k=\frac{g_k}{a_k},\qquad g_k=\frac{C_0}{(1-v\omega^{k+1})(1-u\omega^k)}. \tag{7} \] Regroup the product of their two sums by \(n=j-k\). For \(1\le n<N\), their recurrence gives \[ \frac{a_{k+n}}{a_k}g_k =C_0z^n \frac{\prod_{j=2}^{n}(1-v\omega^{k+j})} {\prod_{j=0}^{n}(1-u\omega^{k+j})}. \tag{8} \] Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\prod_{j=n+1}^{N-1}(1-u\omega^{k+j})\). The denominator becomes \(1-u^N\). The numerator is a polynomial in \(\omega^k\) of degree \(N-2\), with constant coefficient one. Summing over \(k\) kills every nonconstant monomial. Thus \[ \sum_k\frac{a_{k+n}}{a_k}g_k =\frac{NC_0z^n}{1-u^N}\qquad(1\le n<N). \tag{9} \] For \(n=0\), partial fractions and the finite geometric-root sum give \[ \sum_k g_k =\frac{NC_0}{\omega v-u} \left(\frac{\omega v}{1-v^N} -\frac{u}{1-u^N}\right). \tag{10} \] Here \(\sum_k(1-t\omega^k)^{-1}=N/(1-t^N)\), obtained by multiplying by \(1-t^N\) and summing the finite geometric series. Combining (9),(10), and using (4), proves \[ \begin{split} f(u,v\mid z)f(\omega v,u/\omega\mid z^{-1}) &=\frac{NC_0}{1-u^N} \left\{\frac{\omega v z^N-u}{\omega v-u} +\frac{z-z^N}{1-z}\right\}\\ &=\frac{N(1-\omega v)(1-u)(1-z^N)(\omega vz-u)} {(1-u^N)(1-z)(\omega v-u)}. \tag{11} \end{split} \] This proof first uses the displayed nonzero denominators; the identity also extends wherever its literal finite sides are regular. No such extension is needed for the parameters in (5). For those parameters, substitution of (1) gives explicitly \[ \kappa_*^2= \frac{B^NQ^N(H-C)} {N^2(B-Q)(H-R)(C-R)}, \] \[ f(u,v\mid z)f(\omega v,u/\omega\mid z^{-1}) = -\frac{NP^NR^N(C-R)(H-R)(B-Q)} {B^NQ^N(HQ-BC)(H-C)}. \] Consequently the full normalization, including its sign, is \[ \rho\bar\rho =\frac{(PR)^N}{N(BC-HQ)}. \tag{12} \] ## 3. Raw \(w\) orthogonality and the actual inverse We now multiply the two matrices (6). Their Kronecker symbols first give \(\beta=\beta'\). In \((\overline{\mathcal R}\mathcal R)^{\alpha,\beta} _{\alpha',\beta'}\), put \(n=[\alpha'-\alpha]\), \(k=\gamma-\alpha\), and, for this calculation only, \(x=HQ,y=PR,z=BC\). Apart from an index-dependent phase independent of \(k\), the remaining sum is \[ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\omega^{-nk} \frac{W(x,y,z;k-n)}{W(x/\omega,y,z;k)}. \tag{13} \] For \(1\le n<N\), the ratio in (13) is exactly \[ \frac{z-x}{y^n}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(z-x\omega^{k-j}). \tag{14} \] It is a polynomial in \(\omega^k\) of degree \(n-1\). After the factor \(\omega^{-nk}\), none of its powers is divisible by \(N\); hence (13) is zero. For \(n=0\), the ratio is \((z-x)/(z-x\omega^k)\), so (13) equals \[ \frac{Nz^{N-1}(z-x)}{y^N}. \tag{15} \] The phase omitted in describing (13) is one when \(n=0\). Multiplying (15) by the prefactor \(\rho\bar\rho/(B^{N-1}C^{N-1})\), and using (12), gives one. Thus \[ \overline{\mathcal R}\mathcal R=I,\qquad \mathcal R\overline{\mathcal R}=I. \tag{16} \] The second equality follows because the matrices are finite square matrices. This establishes the actual inverse with its primary normalization, rather than naming a matrix “dual” and assuming (16). ## 4. Charged tensors, the face contraction, and the third trace On the face-index space let \(Z|j\rangle=\omega^j|j\rangle\), \(X|j\rangle=|j+1\rangle\), and \(Y=\omega^{1/2}XZ\). In the same branches as above, the primary charged tensor and its opposite-orientation tensor are \[ T(a,c)= \omega^{ac/2}C^{N-1} Y_1^{-a}Z_1^{-c}\mathcal R Z_1^cZ_2^{-a}, \] \[ \bar T(a,c)= \omega^{-ac/2}B^{N-1} Z_2^{-a}Z_1^c\overline{\mathcal R}Z_1^{-c}Y_1^{-a}. \tag{17} \] The first line is [K, (3.1)]. To check the second against the conjugation definition (3.2), let \(\mathsf C|j\rangle=|-j\rangle\). Then \(\mathsf C Z\mathsf C=Z^{-1}\) and \(\mathsf C Y\mathsf C=Y^{-1}\). Conjugating the finite product at indices \((-i,-j)\) changes \(w(x,y,z;-i,-j)\) to \(1/w(x/\omega,y,z;i,j)\), with the roots of the conjugate parameters chosen compatibly. For its scalar, replacing \(k\) by \(-k\) in the periodic summand gives \[ f_{\omega^{-1}}(u,v\mid z) =f_\omega(v/\omega,u/\omega\mid z^{-1}). \] Applied to (5) with the conjugated root of unity, this is precisely \(\bar\rho\). The same square-root choices are continued from a compatible real parameter anchor. These finite identities give (17), including its scalar \(B^{N-1}\), from the primary definition. They do not choose independent normalization roots after contraction. Write the tetrahedral edge charges as \(c_{ij}\). The four vertex sums \(1/2\) imply \[ c_{01}=c_{23}=a,\qquad c_{12}=c_{03}=c,\qquad c_{02}=c_{13}=\tfrac12-a-c. \tag{18} \] Since \(N\) is odd these deductions and halves are legitimate. The primary inverse-pair conditions are \[ c_{13}+c'_{13}=1,\qquad c_{01}+c'_{01}=0. \] By (18) they are exactly \(a'=-a,c'=-c\). Now (17),(16) cancel without commuting any unpaired clock past a shear: \[ T(a,c)\bar T(-a,-c) =B^{N-1}C^{N-1}I =\langle s_{02}\rangle\langle s_{13}\rangle I. \tag{19} \] The reverse product has the same value. In the primary face ordering, the inputs are \((\alpha_3,\alpha_1)\), and the outputs are \((\alpha_2,\alpha_0)\). Thus gluing faces \(0,2\) is exactly (19), leaving identity factors on faces \(1,3\). Gluing the two copies of face \(1\) is the ordinary coordinate pairing \(\delta_{\alpha_1,\alpha'_1}\). Its partial trace is therefore \[ \sum_{\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2}T_u(s,c,\alpha) \bar T_u(s,c',\alpha') =N\langle s_{13}\rangle\langle s_{02}\rangle \delta_{\alpha_3,\alpha'_3}. \tag{20} \] There is no additional pivot in this **face-index** trace. This is a conclusion from the literal charges and matrices, not an assertion about a physical quantum-group cap. ## 5. The retained edge weights and the marked-link route The three glued faces in (20) meet at vertex \(3\). Equation (18) gives total charges \[ c_{03}+c'_{03}=0,\qquad c_{23}+c'_{23}=0,\qquad c_{13}+c'_{13}=1. \] Thus the charged-link rule in [K, (4.3)] routes the link through \(0\!-\!3\!-\!2\); it does not erase an unmarked isolated vertex. For the corresponding link move, the boundary edge \(02\) is required to be initially non-link, and the detour is replaced by \(0\!-\!2\). This is a boundary routing condition, not a conclusion from local charges in an arbitrary exterior. The removed internal non-link edge \(13\) has weight \(\langle s_{13}\rangle^{-1}\). The local total on \(02\) is one before removal, so its exterior charge is zero and it becomes a link edge afterwards; its old non-link weight is \(\langle s_{02}\rangle^{-1}\). These two factors cancel the decoration factors in (20). The factor \(N\) is then canceled by the relative vertex measure: the primary normalization \(N^{2-K}\) has one extra factor \(N^{-1}\) before removal of this vertex. All other boundary data are retained. Accordingly the normalized local identity is valid with arbitrary exterior tensors under exactly this routing and these charge data. It can be differentiated in regular continuous decoration parameters while retaining the displayed factors. This does not differentiate the level off its root or specify an original meridian-normal family. ## 6. Scope and proof inputs This reconstructs the primary charged face-state bubble by finite algebra. It proves neither that the original \(P,S\) free vertices already carry the required charged link detours nor that their local tetrahedra have this face-module assignment. In particular, a physical wire represented by a *pair* of face indices is not the single face traced in (20). The original marked quantum-group cap, its pivot and its cut matrix cannot be inserted or removed by reinterpreting that trace. A global adapter must transport the actual boundary state, all charge and root data, and the retained source currents. Singular decoration limits are not covered by the regular calculation above. The sole direct source is R. M. Kashaev, *Quantum Dilogarithm as a 6j-Symbol*, [hep-th/9411147v2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9411147v2). Only its explicit finite definitions and charge/edge-weight conventions are inputs to the argument above. Its pentagon, inversion, bubble and global invariance assertions are not assumed. Equations (1.25) and (1.29) specify the relevant finite conventions.

title: Literal crossing amplitudes on complex slit charts
text:
# Literal crossing amplitudes on complex slit charts Private written proof, 18 November 2026. The exact root-factorial interpolant has a uniform nonzero local amplitude on a larger domain than its original vertical strip. The domain includes every nonreal scaled factorial length. Applied to the literal balanced signed crossing, this gives its actual five-factor amplitude without a coherent occupation sum or a change of the physical imaginary quantum ray. The hypothesis is that all the affine factorial lengths lie in one compact part of the stated slit domain. Existence of such a simultaneous logarithmic chart at a geometric representation is not proved here. Neither an interpolation nor its nonzero amplitude selects the original finite support cycle. The complete proof directs are I, the exact factorial interpolant; V, its moving-period version; and B, the literal balanced crossing. Their pins appear below. ## 1. The same marked factorial on a larger domain Put \[ \mathcal D=\mathbb C\setminus ((-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty)),\qquad h_N=2\pi i/N,\quad q_N=e^{h_N/2},\quad Q_N=e^{h_N}, \qquad N\ge2 . 	ag{1} \] The domain \(\mathcal D\) is simply connected. For example \(z\mapsto z/(1-z)\) maps it to the plane slit along the nonpositive real ray. All logarithms below are continued from the interval \(0<z<1\) in this domain. Keep I's exact function, with positive-base powers marked by their real logarithms: \[ G_N(\zeta)= (2\pi/N)^\zeta\Gamma(\zeta+1) \prod_{k\ge1}  rac{\Gamma(Nk+\zeta+1)} {\Gamma(Nk-\zeta)(Nk)^{2\zeta+1}}, \qquad \widehat F_N(\zeta)= e^{\,\pi i\zeta(\zeta+1)/(2N)-\pi i\zeta/2}G_N(\zeta). 	ag{2} \] This is the original section, not another solution of its difference equation. Its exact identities are \[ \widehat F_N(\zeta+1) =(1-Q_N^{\zeta+1})\widehat F_N(\zeta),\qquad \widehat F_N(0)=1,\qquad \widehat F_N(n)=(Q_N;Q_N)_n\quad(0\le n<N). 	ag{3} \] In particular every original finite factorial is unchanged. For every compact \(K\Subset\mathcal D\), (2) evaluated at \(\zeta=Nz\) is holomorphic and nonzero on a neighborhood of \(K\). Indeed none of \[ Nz+1,\qquad N(k+z)+1,\qquad N(k-z) 	ag{4} \] is a Gamma pole there. Each possible pole would require a real \(z\le0\) or \(z\ge1\). For large \(k\) the logarithm of the product factor is \(O_{N,K}(k^{-2})\), by the same cancelled Gamma-ratio expansion as in I. Its derivatives converge normally too. Thus the product continues the original function to this whole domain. The simply connected domain fixes its logarithm by the original positive interval. Define the analytic functions on \(\mathcal D\) \[ J(z)=\int_0^z\Log(2\sin\pi t)\,dt,\qquad \mathcal H(z)=J(z)+ rac{\pi i}{2}(z^2-z), 	ag{5} \] \[ \mathcal L(z)=\mathcal H'(z) =\Log(2\sin\pi z)+\pi i(z-	frac12),\qquad a(z)=\exp\!\left\{ 	frac12\Log(2\sin\pi z)+	frac{\pi i z}{2}ight\}. 	ag{6} \] The endpoint in (5) is its integrable logarithmic endpoint on the original interval, followed by analytic continuation. These marks give \[ e^{\mathcal L(z)}=1-e^{2\pi i z},\qquad a(z)^2=i(1-e^{2\pi i z}). 	ag{7} \] They do not reset either logarithm or square root. Equivalently \(\mathcal H\) is the continued branch of \((\operatorname{Li}_2(1)-\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{2\pi iz})) /(2\pi i)\). ## 2. Uniform asymptotics and bounded endpoint shifts Uniformly on every \(K\Subset\mathcal D\), \[ \Log G_N(Nz) =NJ(z)+	frac12\Log(2N\sin\pi z) + rac{\pi\cot\pi z}{12N}+O_K(N^{-3}). 	ag{8} \] All fixed holomorphic derivatives have the same remainder bound on a smaller compact set. Here is why the strip proof extends without a new summation argument. For the finitely many small \(k\), the numbers \(z,k+z,k-z\), with \(z\in K\), avoid zero and the negative real ray. Compactness puts them in sectors \(|\arg w|\le\pi-\delta_K\), with moduli bounded below. For the remaining \(k\), the arguments in (4) lie in a fixed smaller sector around the positive real axis and have size comparable to \(Nk\). The uniform Gamma expansion used and justified in I therefore has remainder \(O_K(N^{-3})\) for the initial term and \(O_K(N^{-3}k^{-3})\) for the \(k\)-th product term. To make its enlarged sector scope explicit, the Euler remainder after \(1/(12w)\), initially on \(\Re w>0\), can be integrated by parts twice. It is a fixed multiple of \(w^{-3}\) plus a fixed multiple of \(\int_0^\infty\widetilde B_4(t)(w+t)^{-4}\,dt\), where \(\widetilde B_4\) is the bounded periodic fourth Bernoulli polynomial. This integral is holomorphic on the plane slit along the nonpositive real ray, so the same formula continues there. If \(|\arg w|\le\pi-\delta\), splitting the integral at \(2|w|\) bounds its absolute value by \(C_\delta|w|^{-3}\): on the first interval \(|w+t|\ge c_\delta|w|\), and on the tail \(|w+t|\ge t/2\). This proves precisely the sector bound needed above, including arguments with negative real part. In detail that product logarithm is \[ N\phi_k(z)+	frac12\Log(1-z^2/k^2) + rac1{12N}\left( rac1{k+z}- rac1{k-z}ight) +O_K(N^{-3}k^{-3}), 	ag{9} \] \[ \phi_k(z)=(k+z)\Log(1+z/k) -(k-z)\Log(1-z/k)-2z. \] The finite small-\(k\) constants can be enlarged to give the single summable remainder in (9). All its logarithms have their continuation from the original strip. The sums of the displayed terms converge normally. Their sine-product and cotangent identities hold on the original strip by I and hence on \(\mathcal D\) by analytic continuation. Summing (9), including the initial Gamma factor, proves (8). The proof uses the actual product, not continuation of an asymptotic identity without a remainder bound. It follows that \[ \widehat F_N(Nz)= N^{1/2}a(z)e^{N\mathcal H(z)} \exp\!\left\{ rac{\pi\cot\pi z}{12N}+O_K(N^{-3})ight\}. 	ag{10} \] For a bounded complex shift \(\gamma\), Taylor expansion on a slightly larger compact subset of \(\mathcal D\) gives \[  oxed{\quad \widehat F_N(Nz+\gamma)= N^{1/2}a(z)e^{\gamma\mathcal L(z)} e^{N\mathcal H(z)}(1+O(N^{-1})). \quad} 	ag{11} \] The bound is uniform for \(z\) and \(\gamma\) in fixed compacts, with every fixed derivative on smaller compacts. The leading amplitude is a holomorphic unit, bounded above and below there. This includes bounded affine offsets which depend on \(N\), such as the offset in \(\lfloor N/2floor\). No convergence of those offsets is needed for the uniform assertion. More generally, for a fixed finite list and integer signs \(\varepsilon_
u\), \[ \prod_
u\widehat F_N(Nz_
u+\gamma_
u)^{\varepsilon_
u} =N^{ rac12\sum_
u\varepsilon_

u [a(z_
u)e^{\gamma_
u\mathcal L(z_
u)}]^{\varepsilon_
u} \exp\!\left\{N\sum_
u\varepsilon_

u)ight\} (1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{12} \] Every \(z_
u\) must remain in the same fixed compact subset of \(\mathcal D\). Cancellations in a later sum are not estimated by (12). ## 3. The literal two signed balanced coefficients Use B's equal-color factorial basis, with \(d=N-1\), \[ x=-M/q_N,\qquad D e_{a,b}=x^{-a-b}Q_N^{ab}e_{a,b},\qquad \kappa=q_N^{H^2/2},\quad q_N^H=x. 	ag{13} \] The last equality uses the original marked logarithm, \(\log x=(N-1)\log q_N+\log M\). The common Cartan scalar \(\kappa\) is retained. On the finite head, \[ E e_a=(MQ_N^{-a}-M^{-1})e_{a-1},\qquad F e_b=(1-Q_N^{b+1})e_{b+1}, 	ag{14} \] with the actual zero extreme arrows. Let \(P\) be the flip. The checked crossings, in their actual order, are \[ R_+=\kappa P D \sum_{n=0}^{d} rac{(-1)^nq_N^{n^2}}{(Q_N;Q_N)_n} E_1^nF_2^n , \] \[ R_-=\kappa^{-1} \sum_{n=0}^{d} rac{q_N^n}{(Q_N;Q_N)_n} E_1^nF_2^n\,D^{-1}P. 	ag{15} \] There is no cyclic wrap or added high occupation. Choose the logarithm of \(M\) near one and set \[ \alpha=-2\log M/h_N,\qquad Q_N^\alpha=M^{-2}. 	ag{16} \] For positive crossing input \((a,b)\), the output is \((b+n,a-n)\), with \(0\le n\le\min(a,d-b)\). Its exact interpolated coefficient is \[  oxed{\quad R_+(a,b,n)=m_+(a,b,n;M)  rac{\widehat F_N(b+n)\widehat F_N(a+\alpha)} {\widehat F_N(b)\widehat F_N(n) \widehat F_N(a-n+\alpha)},\quad} 	ag{17} \] \[ m_+=\kappa\,(-1)^nq_N^{n^2}x^{-a-b} Q_N^{(a-n)(b+n)} M^n Q_N^{-n(2a-n+1)/2}. 	ag{18} \] For negative crossing input \((a,b)\), the output is \((b-n,a+n)\), with \(0\le n\le\min(b,d-a)\). Its exact interpolated coefficient is \[  oxed{\quad R_-(a,b,n)=m_-(a,b,n;M)  rac{\widehat F_N(a+n)\widehat F_N(b+\alpha)} {\widehat F_N(a)\widehat F_N(n) \widehat F_N(b-n+\alpha)},\quad} 	ag{19} \] \[ m_-=\kappa^{-1}q_N^n x^{a+b}Q_N^{-ab} M^nQ_N^{-n(2b-n+1)/2}. 	ag{20} \] Off the integer lattice, \((-1)^n\) in (18) means the fixed interpolation \(e^{\pi i n}\); all other powers use the displayed original logarithms. To verify (17), cancel the finite \(F_2^n\) product against \((Q_N;Q_N)_n\), giving the Gaussian coefficient \({b+n rack n}_{Q_N}\). The remaining color product is exactly \[ \prod_{j=a-n+1}^{a}(MQ_N^{-j}-M^{-1}) =M^nQ_N^{-n(2a-n+1)/2}  rac{\widehat F_N(a+\alpha)} {\widehat F_N(a-n+\alpha)} 	ag{21} \] by (3). The Cartan diagonal acts on \((a-n,b+n)\). For (19), the flip first gives \((b,a)\), its inverse Cartan scalar is \(x^{a+b}Q_N^{-ab}\), and the inverse series in (15) has coefficient \(q_N^n\). The same calculation proves (19)--(20). At a common zero in an endpoint ratio, equality means the whole finite product (21) before specialization. No negative factorial is assigned to a forbidden physical state. Thus the five leading lengths, before division by \(N\), are \[  egin{array}{c|c|c} &	ext{numerator}&	ext{denominator}\ \hline +&b+n,\ a&b,\ n,\ a-n\ -&a+n,\ b&a,\ n,\ b-n . \end{array} 	ag{22} \] The color shift \(\alpha\) is a bounded endpoint shift when \(|M-1|=O(N^{-1})\). Applying (12) proves an actual nonzero \(N^{-1/2}\) local amplitude for each crossing on every common compact chart satisfying (22) in \(\mathcal D\). For example, with \(a=NA,b=NB,n=NC\), the positive factorial phase is \[ \mathcal H(B+C)+\mathcal H(A)-\mathcal H(B) -\mathcal H(C)-\mathcal H(A-C). 	ag{23} \] Its amplitude is the corresponding ratio of the five \(a(\cdot)\)'s, times \(e^{\alpha[\mathcal L(A)-\mathcal L(A-C)]}\). The known scalar (18) remains exact and contributes its marked polynomial exponential to the full action. All original pivot, framing and other peripheral multipliers of a word must likewise be retained, not replaced by one. ## 4. Physical meridian normals and genuine quantum normals The estimates are joint in bounded \(\alpha\), on larger compacts before differentiation. Since \(\partial_M=-2(h_NM)^{-1}\partial_\alpha\), each fixed meridian normal has polynomial \(N\)-cost. This differentiates the entire scalar in (18) or (20), including \(\kappa\). It does not differentiate a specialized color product as if its meridian dependence had disappeared. Moving-quantum coefficient normals can also be retained. Fix \(N\) and all original indices, let \[ q=q_Ne^\epsilon,\qquad P= rac{\pi i}{\log q}, 	ag{24} \] and use V's same Gamma product \(\widehat F_P\), not a root reflection with a moving endpoint. In (15)--(21) replace the quantum parameters by these actual generic ones, keep \(d=N-1\) fixed, and use \(\alpha(P)=-2\log M/(2\log q)\). The finite product identities remain exact as analytic coefficient identities. If the original finite-color normal ties \(M\) to \(q\), that relation must be substituted before differentiation. A fixed-\(M\) auxiliary coefficient germ is not relabeled as that entire representation family. The sector argument of Section 2 works uniformly for \(P\) in a sufficiently small relative complex neighborhood of \(N\), with every scaled argument divided by \(P\). At fixed indices its logarithmic \(P\)-derivative is bounded on these compacts: differentiating \(P J(\zeta/P)\) gives \(J(y)-yJ'(y)\), and the remainder is differentiated on a larger relative disk. For fixed \(M\), the bounded color shift causes only bounded additional terms. Since \(P'(\epsilon)=O(N^2)\), every factorial ratio and exact monomial has logarithmic \(\epsilon\)-derivative \(O(N^2)\). For \(\kappa\) this follows directly from \(\log\kappa=(\log x)^2/(2\log q)\), with \(\log x=\pi i-\log q+\log M\). Consequently, for all sufficiently large \(N\), there is a disk \(|\epsilon|\le c/N^2\) on which the full local coefficient divided by its root value is bounded above and below by fixed constants. Cauchy's formula gives, for every fixed \(j\), \[ \left|\partial_\epsilon^jR_\pm ig|_{\epsilon=0}ight| \le C_jN^{2j}|R_\pm|_{\epsilon=0}. 	ag{25} \] Here all five lengths lie in the compact slit chart, so the root coefficient is nonzero. Fixed physical endpoint factorials outside this interior hypothesis require V's separate endpoint bounds; (25) does not silently include them. The fixed-\(M\) convention in (24) and the fixed endpoint \(d=N-1\) are part of this assertion. The same proof includes a specified original parameter path \(M(\epsilon)\) with \(M(0)=e^{-h_N\alpha_0/2}\), bounded \(\alpha_0\), and \(\log M(\epsilon)-\log M(0)=O(N\epsilon)\) holomorphically on a slightly larger disk, with its Cauchy derivative bounds. Then \(\alpha(\epsilon)\) remains bounded and \(\partial_\epsilon\alpha=O(N^2)\); its extra logarithmic derivative has the same cost as in (25). In particular the ordinary color relation \(M=-q^N\), based at \(M=1\), is covered. All its parameter derivatives, rather than a root-only reflection formula, must be taken. ## 5. The source cycle and the outstanding chart condition For a literal finite word, replace only its original factorial products by (2), retaining the original affine matching lattice. I's sum of small product cotangent circles about the supported integer points is then an exact period of that same finite sum. Equations (17)--(22) identify its local signed summands; they do not replace its support by independent head intervals. There are no extra coherent input/output occupation sums here. Five-shape regularity says that certain exponentiated clocks avoid zero and one. It alone does not put all their compatible affine logarithmic lengths in \(\mathcal D\). On real exterior lengths the actual interpolant can have finite-level zeros or poles; no uniform nonzero amplitude on a neighborhood containing them follows from this note. Any whole-ratio cancellation must be verified before changing that conclusion. Even on a paid common chart, the original cotangent cycles, physical support walls, and residual framing direction remain. No contributing contour, framing-fiber period, geometric coefficient, or scalar lower bound is asserted. This is an explicit adapter for the existing factorial interpolation, not a novelty claim for Gamma asymptotics. ## Complete proof-source pins * I: notes/exact_factorial_interpolation_and_complex_contours.md, SHA256 1f34f65437dfe0bfb4062a7a74840beae1676353cf13bb8a86f8849a8a36bc72. * V: notes/actual_moving_period_factorial_normals.md, SHA256 8fa02b96eaf532ad6b242216e7161b1cfc64a6e6a968563a3da9e5c07f660cd1. * B: notes/balanced_verma_coherent_braiding.md, SHA256 0203bdd7dbb36a4f8deb1c310b3445608e53d10922049447da8eecec4f87d1c4. I supplies the exact marked product, the summable Gamma remainder and original finite residue cycle. V supplies its actual moving-period section and fixed-index convention. B supplies the balanced signed finite matrices and their unchanged common Cartan line. The enlarged sector argument, bounded-shift amplitude, five-factor identities and normal bounds are written above. Only written mathematics and source-text operations were used. Frozen/public files are unchanged.

title: A common slit chart for the actual factorial crossing source

# A common slit chart for the actual factorial crossing source Private written proof, 18 November 2026. Every finite collection of literal crossing factorial clocks can be put off the unit circle by an arbitrarily small complex change of a regular selected-flag frame. No factor clock in the required list is constant on the full framing orbit. This follows from an irreducible prefix-minor calculation, and does not require faithfulness of the representation. Integral wire-logarithm repair then puts all the normalized factorial lengths in one common slit domain. For complete geometric holonomy, the change can be made arbitrarily close to the regular midpoint frame. An exact complex-binomial cut selects its cut position in the principal stationary scheme, while retaining the original unmarked scalar. Its exponential total-variation cost can be made arbitrarily small, and is recorded rather than omitted. This is a chart and source-presentation theorem. It does not deform the finite state cycle to this point or estimate a full coherent kernel. ## 1. Actual clocks and the statement Keep a fixed finite braid whose closure is one knot, its actual signed crossings, pivotal closures, framing and factorial basis. Use the classical correspondence of M and the weighted principal source of S. At a positive crossing, with input clocks \(A,B\) and transfer \(C\), the output clocks are \(BC,A/C\). At a negative crossing they are \(B/C,AC\). The complete color is \(M=1\), with classical \(x=-1\). The five leading factorial lengths at a positive crossing are \[ (b+n,\ a;\ b,\ n,\ a-n)/N, 	ag{1} \] and at a negative crossing they are \[ (a+n,\ b;\ a,\ n,\ b-n)/N. 	ag{2} \] The semicolon separates numerator from denominator factors. Their exponentials are respectively \[ (BC,A;\ B,C,A/C),\qquad (AC,B;\ A,C,B/C). 	ag{3} \] Thus each is a wire occupation clock or a transfer clock. These are the actual five-factor lists, not independent octahedral coordinates. For example M's positive finite product is \[  rac{F_{b+n}}{F_bF_n}(Qx^2/A;Q)_n. \] At the physical color \(Qx^2=1\), reversing its last product gives \[ (Q^{-a};Q)_n =(-1)^nQ^{-an+n(n-1)/2} rac{F_a}{F_{a-n}}, 	ag{4} \] which proves (1) without deleting its monomial factor. The negative formula is the same reversal with \(a,b\) interchanged. All Cartan, sign and pivotal factors remain. At nearby color, write \(\alpha=-2\log M/h\), \(h=\log Q\); the reversed endpoints are \(a+\alpha,a-n+\alpha\), or \(b+\alpha,b-n+\alpha\). Their leading clocks are \(A/M^2,A/(CM^2)\), or \(B/M^2,B/(CM^2)\). Fixed Weyl offsets remain in the finite factors. Let \[ \mathcal D=\mathbb C\setminus  igl((-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty) igr). 	ag{5} \] Fix any selected-flag representation with noncentral strand meridians, and any nonempty regular chart of its finite actual braid correspondence. The theorem is that, in every complex neighborhood in that chart, there is a frame and a compatible set of wire logarithms for which every length in (1)--(2) lies in \(\mathcal D\). Each length in fact has nonzero imaginary part. The lengths lie in compact subsets of \(\mathcal D\) on a sufficiently small common neighborhood. For a complete hyperbolic knot, G supplies the required regular midpoint chart. In that case the cut logarithm can be retained near \(\pi i\), and the source cost in Section 5 can be made smaller than \(\exp(\varepsilon N)\) for every prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). The chart theorem for noncentral representations below uses no faithfulness or cusp-lattice assumption; G is used only to start arbitrarily close to that particular geometric midpoint. ## 2. Every nonscalar prefix has an irreducible minor Normalize the selected flag to the vector \(w=(1,0)^t\). Write \[ \alpha_t=(1,t),\qquad v_{t,s}=(1-ts,s)^t,\qquad F(t,s)=(v_{t,s},w-v_{t,s}),\qquad s
e0. 	ag{6} \] Then \(\alpha_t(v_{t,s})=1\), and \(\alpha_t\) is the first row of \(F^{-1}\). These are the original framing coordinates \(F(r,s)\) with \(r=1-ts\). In particular this is the full two-dimensional selected-flag frame chart, not a fixed-\(s\) slice. For a determinant-one matrix \(P= egin{pmatrix}a&b\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), put \[ w_P(t,s)=\alpha_tPv_{t,s} =a+ct+s igl[b+(d-a)t-ct^2 igr]. 	ag{7} \] The map \(P\mapsto w_P\) is linear and injective: its coefficients recover \(a,c,b,d-a\). If \(P\) is nonscalar, \(w_P\) is an irreducible nonconstant polynomial in \(\mathbb C[t,s]\). Indeed set \(A(t)=a+ct\), \(B(t)=b+(d-a)t-ct^2\). If \(c
e0\), \[ B(-a/c)=-1/c, 	ag{8} \] by \(ad-bc=1\). Thus \(A,B\) are relatively prime. If \(c=0\), then \(a
e0\), so \(A\) is a unit, and \(B\) can vanish identically only when \(P\) is scalar. In both cases the primitive polynomial \(A+sB\) has degree one in \(s\) over \(\mathbb C(t)\) and is irreducible there; clearing polynomial contents proves irreducibility over \(\mathbb C[t,s]\). For scalar \(P=\pm I\), instead \(w_P=\pm1\). Finally, \[ w_P=\lambda w_Q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P=\lambda Q,\quad\lambda=\pm1 	ag{9} \] for determinant-one matrices. Hence distinct projective nonscalar matrices give nonassociate irreducible prefix polynomials. These polynomial statements are made before restricting to \(s
e0\) or to the regular braid chart. An identity on any of those nonempty complex opens would be the same rational-function identity, so localizing the chart does not invalidate the argument. ## 3. No required occupation or transfer clock is constant At any braid stage let \(H_1,\ldots,H_b\) be M's unframed strand matrices, and \(P_j=H_j\cdots H_1\), \(P_0=I\). They are determinant-one matrices; \(H_j\) is minus the corresponding actual meridian and is noncentral. M's exact Gauss inverse gives \[ K_j= rac{w_{P_j}}{w_{P_{j-1}}},\qquad A_j=x\, rac{w_{P_{j-1}}}{w_{P_j}}. 	ag{10} \] If \(A_j\) were constant, injectivity in (9) would give \(P_j=\pm P_{j-1}\), and therefore \(H_j=\pm I\), a contradiction. This includes input and output wire clocks at every stage. Consider an adjacent crossing at positions \(j,j+1\), and abbreviate the four prefix matrices by \(P_0,P_1,P_2,P'_1\). Here \(P_0\) means the prefix immediately before these positions, not necessarily the identity. The prefix \(P_2\) is preserved by M's actual Hurwitz correspondence. The positive transfer formula is \[ C= rac{w_{P_0}w_{P_2}}{w_{P_1}w_{P'_1}}, 	ag{11} \] and for the inverse crossing it is the reciprocal of (11). For example \(K'_j=K_{j+1}/C\) in the positive map and \(K'_j=K_{j+1}C\) in the inverse map, which proves both formulas directly from (10). Suppose (11) were a nonzero constant. If \(P_1\) is nonscalar, its irreducible polynomial \(w_{P_1}\) must divide \(w_{P_0}w_{P_2}\). Equations (7)--(9) then force \(P_1=\pm P_0\) or \(P_1=\pm P_2\). Both are impossible: the intervening strand matrix is a noncentral meridian. If \(P_1\) is scalar, both \(P_0\) and \(P_2\) are nonscalar for the same reason. The left side of the cleared identity has two irreducible factors, counted with multiplicity, whereas the right side has at most one. This is again impossible. Thus every transfer clock is nonconstant. It follows that every function in (3) is nonconstant on the full selected-flag frame orbit. Multiplying a function by a fixed nonzero color constant or taking its inverse preserves this conclusion. Consequently there are no identically unit-modulus functions in the required factor-clock list. This assertion is about these actual clocks; it does not assert multiplicative independence of them or of arbitrary monomials in wire clocks. On a sufficiently small connected complex neighborhood in the regular chart all these finitely many clocks are holomorphic and nonzero. For a nonconstant such function the set \(|C|=1\) has empty interior: otherwise restriction to complex lines and the one-variable maximum principle would make it constant on an open set, hence everywhere. It is closed in the neighborhood. The complement of the finite union of these sets is therefore open and dense. Choose a frame there. This proves simultaneous off-unit modulus, arbitrarily close to any initially supplied regular frame. ## 4. Exact wire-logarithm compatibility There is no assumption that independently chosen logarithms already obey additive state conservation. Here is an integral repair. View the oriented knot diagram as the directed crossing graph: edges are wire arcs and each crossing has two incoming and two outgoing arcs. Let \(L\) be its integer incidence matrix, with incoming coefficient \(+1\) and outgoing coefficient \(-1\). Its multiplicative conservation law is the actual one \(A_aA_b=A_cA_d\). Choose any logarithms \(\zeta_e\) of the wire clocks. Then \[ L\zeta=2\pi i\,k,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z^V, \qquad \sum_v k_v=0. 	ag{12} \] The graph is connected because the closure is one knot. Its incidence matrix has integer image exactly the vectors of total sum zero. For a direct proof, choose a spanning tree and remove its leaves successively. At a leaf prescribe the unique incident tree-edge integer to cancel the current integer at that leaf, then transfer the remaining integer to its neighbor. The last vertex has integer zero by the total-sum condition. This constructs \(m\in\mathbb Z^E\) with \(Lm=-k\). Hence \[ \widetilde\zeta=\zeta+2\pi i\,m,\qquad L\widetilde\zeta=0 	ag{13} \] without changing any multiplicative clock. The repair can preserve the chosen cut logarithm. The oriented one-component knot traverses the crossing graph as an Euler circuit, so the cut edge is not an undirected bridge. Choose the spanning tree without that edge. The same leaf elimination then has \(m_{m cut}=0\). Loops of the graph cause no difficulty: their incidence columns are zero, and they are not used in the tree. Define a positive transfer logarithm by \(
u=\widetilde\zeta_c-\widetilde\zeta_b\), so conservation gives also \(
u=\widetilde\zeta_a-\widetilde\zeta_d\). For a negative crossing use \(
u=\widetilde\zeta_b-\widetilde\zeta_c =\widetilde\zeta_d-\widetilde\zeta_a\). These are exactly the additive relations behind (1)--(2), and their exponentials are the prescribed transfers. Every normalized factor length is now its appropriate logarithm divided by \(2\pi i\). For every such clock \(Z\), \[ \Im\left( rac{\log Z}{2\pi i}ight) =- rac{\log|Z|}{2\pi}
e0. 	ag{14} \] This is independent of the integer logarithm lift. All required lengths therefore belong to \(\mathcal D\) simultaneously, with the exact additive conservation and transfer relations retained. Finite integer shifts of the lifts need not be individually small. At the chosen point there are finitely many lengths. Shrinking the common neighborhood keeps each in a compact subset of \(\mathcal D\). All fixed \(O(N^{-1})\) Weyl offsets remain in slightly larger compact subsets for sufficiently large \(N\). Nearby color endpoints from Section 1 are included by continuity. This is local uniformity for a fixed source/frame, not a denominator bound uniform over a degenerating family of diagrams. ## 5. Exact complex-binomial selection and its recorded cost Put \(d=N-1\), \(c_0=2\pi i\), and set \(	heta=\widetilde\zeta_{m cut}/c_0\). Since the cut clock is off-unit, \(\Im	heta
e0\), in particular \(	heta
e0,1\). Use the literal diagonal probe \[ P_{N,	heta}=\sum_{a=0}^{d}  inom da	heta^a(1-	heta)^{d-a}T_a. 	ag{15} \] The binomial theorem gives \(\operatorname{Tr}P_{N,	heta}=1\) for every complex \(	heta\). The actual scalar endomorphism identity in S therefore gives \[ \operatorname{Tr}(P_{N,	heta}C_N)=F_N 	ag{16} \] with every original crossing, pivot, framing and support wall. For a marked cut endomorphism \(C\), retain instead the exact current \[ \operatorname{Tr}((P_{N,	heta}-T_0)C) =\operatorname{Tr}(B_{N,	heta}[C,\mathcal E]),\qquad B_{N,	heta}=-\sum_{r<d}  rac{\sum_{a>r} inom da	heta^a(1-	heta)^{d-a}} {M Q^{-r-1}-M^{-1}}E_{r+1,r}. 	ag{17} \] Direct multiplication telescopes the commutator to \(P_{N,	heta}-T_0\). Thus no marked-source equality is inferred from (16). For \(u=ha\) the exact consecutive weight ratio is \[  rac{	heta}{1-	heta} rac{c_0-h-u}{u+h}. 	ag{18} \] With the logarithms continued consistently near the selected \(	heta\), the principal normalized boundary action is \[ g_	heta(u)=c_0\left[ -z\log z-(1-z)\log(1-z) +z\log	heta+(1-z)\log(1-	heta)ight], \qquad z=u/c_0. 	ag{19} \] It is the action in S plus the exact linear logarithm of the change of binomial weights. On these matching sheets \[ g_	heta(c_0	heta)=g_	heta'(c_0	heta)=0,\qquad g_	heta''(c_0	heta)=- rac1{c_0	heta(1-	heta)}. 	ag{20} \] Other sheets retain their additive Fourier characters. The exponentiated cut row is \[  rac{p_{m out}}{p_{m in}} = rac{1-	heta}{	heta} rac{u}{c_0-u}. 	ag{21} \] The ordered-coproduct ideal calculation in S uses only the internal rows and the unit cut factors. It still forces \(p_{m out}=p_{m in}\). Hence (21) is equivalent, in that localized graph ring, to \(u=c_0	heta\). Conversely a full braid fixed point at that logarithmic cut value satisfies the weighted principal rows. Our chosen framed representation is therefore a regular principal stationary point of this exact source presentation. This remains an exponentiated-row statement with its log lifts. The price of the complex probe is exact: \[ \sum_a\left| inom da	heta^a(1-	heta)^{d-a}ight| =R_	heta^d,\qquad R_	heta=|	heta|+|1-	heta|. 	ag{22} \] At \(M=1\) the denominators have moduli \(2|\sin(\pi(r+1)/N)|\ge4/N\). For \(|M-1|\le1/(4N)\), their changes are less than \(3|M-1|\le3/(4N)\), so their moduli remain at least \(3/N\). On that disk (17) has operator norm at most \((N/3)R_	heta^d\) in the stated factorial basis. All fixed meridian derivatives have the corresponding polynomial factor on a smaller disk by the Cauchy formula; the exponential factor is retained. For complete geometric holonomy start at G's regular midpoint \(A_{m cut}=-1\). The off-unit frames of Section 3 are dense arbitrarily close to it. Preserve the branch of the cut logarithm near \(\pi i\) in Section 4. Then \(	heta\) is arbitrarily close to \(1/2\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), continuity and \(R_{1/2}=1\) permit the choice \[ \log R_	heta<\varepsilon. 	ag{23} \] Thus this source cost is at most \(e^{\varepsilon d}\), with an actual fixed choice of frame and \(	heta\); it is not declared polynomial or zero. Internal transfer and head walls remain. No uniform slit-chart margin as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) is asserted. No contributing deformation of the original finite cycle has been constructed by changing its exact trace-one probe. ## 6. Scope and complete sources The theorem supplies a common scalar factorial slit chart and an exact source presentation having its geometric point as a regular principal critical point. It does not prove the scalar factorial amplitude theorem itself, a uniform full coherent-kernel phase, an integration contour reaching this point, an \(r\)-centralizer period, or a nonzero geometric coefficient. The construction also does not replace actual support inequalities by analytic clocks. * M: notes/marked_braid_holonomy.md, SHA256 eff47c757d0e44bda0c396c094315b8e1fce11f1fc2d6445d636c6d2d3a46c4f. * S: notes/research_soft_binomial_cut_stationary_source.md, SHA256 667cb1eb70b770552de05e6f95f518016852b2c0aecdc874c3dff167fccb3d8b. * G: notes/research_midpoint_geometric_braid_frame.md, SHA256 9b9756929ac16b9413744ab376ac74718ecbaac645ab0440e3e3a835349b8e30. The three complete sources were freshly read nontruncated in this author sequence. Their used implications are checked separately from the polynomial irreducibility, transfer-factor, integer-lift and complex-probe calculations proved here. title: A literal two-cell subdivision of the marked Hamiltonian wire
text:
# A literal two-cell subdivision of the marked Hamiltonian wire Private written proof, 17 November 2026. A two-tetrahedron ball with its actual link edge has the paired-boundary tensor \(Z^{-1}/N\). Its composition with the normalized joining tensor \(NZ\) is the identity. We prove this in both endpoint orders, retaining the original fixed cut \(E_{00}\), the face permutation maps, and all edge and vertex measures. No free-vertex deletion or global geometric-period assertion is used. ## 1. The ball, its orders, and its two charge assignments Let \(N>2\) be odd, \(d=N-1\), \(q\) primitive, and \(\epsilon=1/2\) in \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). All indices and charges are cyclic. Choose four distinct vertex decorations and compatible nonzero roots \(s_{ij}^N=z_i-z_j\), with \(s_{ji}=-s_{ij}\). Normalization roots are the shared ones of [B]. Start with order \[ (0,1,2,3)=(\mathsf P,L,\mathsf S,R). 	ag{1} \] Glue a positive and a negative tetrahedron, preserving vertex labels, on faces \(0\) and \(2\). These two faces form a disk. The result is a ball; its sole interior edge is \(13=LR\). Declare that edge to be the link. Its boundary is the union of two two-triangle disks, with material vertices \(L\) and \(R\). At the \(L\) disk the triangles are glued along \(\mathsf P-L-\mathsf S\); at the \(R\) disk along \(\mathsf P-R-\mathsf S\). Their common boundary consists of two distinct \(\mathsf P\mathsf S\) edges. Each material vertex is interior to its port disk, although all four vertices are on the boundary of the ball. Write a tetrahedral charge triple as \((a,b,c)\) on opposite pairs \(01|23,02|13,03|12\), with \(a+b+c=\epsilon\). Use the same triple on the two cells, choosing either \[  egin{array}{c|c|c|c} &	ext{triple in (1)}& (h_L,h_R)&	ext{triple in }(\mathsf P,L,R,\mathsf S)\ \hline \mathrm I&(0,0,\epsilon)&(1,0)&(0,\epsilon,0)\ \mathrm {II}&(\epsilon,0,0)&(0,1)&(\epsilon,0,0). \end{array} 	ag{2} \] Here \(h_L,h_R\) are the total charges on \(L\mathsf S\) and \(R\mathsf S\). The totals on \(\mathsf PL,\mathsf PR\) are \(1-h_L,1-h_R\), respectively. The interior link edge has total charge zero. Each of the two boundary \(\mathsf P\mathsf S\) occurrences has charge zero. These statements follow by listing the opposite pairs in (2). The final column is the order with the poles extreme. It exchanges slots \(2,3\) in (1), reverses each cell orientation, and changes the glued faces to \(0,3\). In particular either orientation of the material wire relative to \(L<R\) is covered by (2). This exchange will be proved on the actual tensors below. Put \[ x=s_{03}s_{12},\qquad y=s_{01}s_{23},\qquad z=s_{02}s_{13},\qquad x^N+y^N=z^N, \] \[ W(t)=\prod_{j=1}^{[t]} rac{y}{z-xq^j},\qquad  ar W(t)=\prod_{j=1}^{[t]} rac{y}{z-xq^{j-1}}. 	ag{3} \] Both products are periodic and nonzero. The literal normalization proved in [B] is \[ ho arho= rac{y^N}{N(z-x)}. 	ag{4} \] The bar labels the opposite tensor, not a Hermitian adjoint. ## 2. The complete finite contraction Use the face slots \((\alpha, eta,\gamma,\delta)=(\alpha_3,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_0)\). The explicit kernels of [S, (3)] are \[  egin{split} T(a,c)_{\alpha eta}^{\gamma\delta} &=ho q^{c(\gamma-\alpha)+\alpha\delta+ac/2+\alpha^2/2} W(\gamma-a-\alpha)\delta_{ eta,\gamma+\delta},\  ar T(a',c')_{\gamma\delta}^{\alpha' eta'} &= arho q^{c'(\gamma-\alpha')-\alpha'\delta-a'c'/2-\alpha'^2/2}  ar W(\gamma+a'-\alpha')^{-1}\delta_{ eta',\gamma+\delta}. \end{split} 	ag{5} \] For all the old and reordered charges in (2), \(ac=0\). Thus these entries also agree exactly with the 1994 operator convention of [B], whose general conversion is recorded in [S, (22)]. The ball tensor in order (1) is \[ Q_{\alpha eta}^{\alpha' eta'} =\sum_{\gamma,\delta} T(a,c)_{\alpha eta}^{\gamma\delta}  ar T(a',c')_{\gamma\delta}^{\alpha' eta'}. 	ag{6} \] The deltas give \( eta= eta'\), leaving one sum. A useful exact sum, including \(m=0,d\), is \[ \sum_tq^{(m+1)t} rac{W(t)}{ ar W(t-m)} =N y^{m-N}(z-x)(-x)^{d-m}q^{m(m+1)/2}, \qquad 0\le m<N. 	ag{7} \] Indeed \[  rac{W(t)}{ ar W(t-m)} = rac{y^m(z-x)}{\prod_{j=0}^m(z-xq^{t-j})}. \] Complete its denominator to the full cyclic product \(y^N\). The complementary numerator has degree \(d-m\) in \(q^t\). After multiplication by \(q^{(m+1)t}\), only its top term survives. Its coefficient is \((-x)^{d-m}q^{m(m+1)/2}\), since \(\sum_{j=1}^{d}j=0\) modulo the odd \(N\). This proves (7) without a limiting or generic-rank argument. Let \(n=[\alpha'-\alpha]\), and put \(r=-y/x\). For case I take \(t=\gamma-\alpha\). The phase left in (6) is \[ (n+1)t-n eta-n(n+1)/2. \] Use (7) with \(m=n\), then (4). For case II take \(t=\gamma-\alpha-\epsilon\). Its phase is \[ nt-n eta-n(n-1)/2, \] and its ratio is \(W(t)/ ar W(t+1-n)\). Use (7) with \(m=[n-1]\). The exact results are \[ Q_{\alpha eta}^{\alpha' eta'}= x^d q^{-n eta}\delta_{ eta, eta'}  egin{cases} r^n,&\mathrm I,\ r^{[n-1]},&\mathrm {II}. \end{cases} 	ag{8} \] No power of \(N\) or decoration factor has been suppressed. Before the order exchange this is a difference-to-diagonal array; it is not yet the paired physical wire. ## 3. The actual paired face permutation We use the primary face tensor [K, (3.6)], but prove the needed paired permutation rather than invoking the printed symmetry. For regular representations \(p,q_0\), let \(P_0=x_p,Q_0=x_{q_0},D_0=x_{q_0^{-1}p}\), choosing \(x_{p^{-1}q_0}=-D_0\). Write \[ \phi(p,q_0)=  rac{\langle P_0,D_0angle^{1/2}} {N\langle Q_0,-D_0angle^{1/2}} f\left(0, rac{P_0}{qD_0}\,\middle|- rac{D_0}{Q_0}ight), \quad F_{uv}(p,q_0)=\phi(p,q_0)q^{uv}, \quad F^{uv}(p,q_0)= rac{q^{-uv}}{N\phi(p,q_0)}. 	ag{9} \] Here the brackets and finite \(f\) are precisely those of [B]. The scalar is a unit. To see this directly, the cyclic summand recurrence at first argument zero gives \[ f(0,v\mid qz)= rac{z-1}{qvz}f(0,v\mid z). \] At (9), \(v,z
e0\) and \(z^N
e1\). A zero would therefore annihilate all \(N\) Fourier coefficients of the nonzero cyclic summand, which is impossible. The bracket factors are units as well. Consequently the displayed upper and lower \(F\)'s are literal bilinear inverses. For the old tetrahedron use the primary roots \[ (P_0,Q_0,R_0,B_0,C_0,H_0) =(s_{01},s_{12},s_{23},s_{02},s_{13},s_{03}). \] After exchange \(23\) they are \((P_0,C_0,-R_0,H_0,Q_0,B_0)\); its Fermat triple is \((z,-y,x)\). Denote its scalars by \(ho_{m new}, arho_{m new}\). The exact cyclic product identities \[ W_{m old}(n) ar W_{m new}(-n)=q^{-n(n+1)/2},\qquad  ar W_{m old}(n)W_{m new}(-n)=q^{-n(n-1)/2} 	ag{10} \] follow by taking successive ratios and checking \(n=0\). They include the cyclic endpoints. For clarity, the full scalar in the positive-cell permutation is \[ \Theta=  rac{ho_{m old}\phi(q_0,q_0r_0)} { arho_{m new}\phi(pq_0,pq_0r_0)}. \] Using the 1994 kernels, direct summation gives \[  egin{split} &\sum_{ eta,\delta} T^{94}_{\alpha eta}{}^{\gamma\delta}(a,c) F_{\delta D}(q_0,q_0r_0)F^{ eta B}(pq_0,pq_0r_0)\ &\hspace{12mm}= \Theta q^{a/4}  ar T^{94}_{m new,\alpha D}{}^{\gamma B} (a,\epsilon-a-c). \end{split} 	ag{11} \] The Fourier sum imposes \(B=\alpha+D\); (10) supplies the remaining product and quadratic phase. The negative mate has the inverse placements \(F^{\delta D'},F_{ eta'B'}\), scalar \[  ar\Theta=  rac{ arho_{m old}\phi(pq_0,pq_0r_0)} {ho_{m new}\phi(q_0,q_0r_0)} \] and phase \(q^{-a'/4}\). Its new charges are \((a',\epsilon-a'-c')\), by the second identity in (10). These equations are obtained from the finite kernels; neither \(\Theta=1\) nor a published permutation theorem is assumed. The two internal \(F\)'s cancel on the shared face \(0\). Moreover (4) for the new triple gives \[ \Theta ar\Theta=  rac{y^N/[N(z-x)]}{(-y)^N/[N(x-z)]}=1. 	ag{12} \] In both cases (2), \(a=a'\), so the two phases in (11) cancel. All old and new \(ac\)'s are zero. Thus the raw two-cell tensor in the pole-extreme order equals exactly the paired transform of (8) on its remaining face \(1\): \[ Q^F_{\alpha\alpha';BB'}= \sum_{ eta, eta'}Q_{\alpha eta}^{\alpha' eta'} F^{ eta B}(pq_0,pq_0r_0)F_{ eta'B'}(pq_0,pq_0r_0). \] The scalar \(\phi\) cancels, and \[  rac1N\sum_ eta q^{ eta(B'-B-n)}=\delta_{B'-B,n}. 	ag{13} \] This is an actual paired face operation. It is not an arbitrary physical Fourier change of the cut index. ## 4. The boundary adapters and the exact physical word Use the common poles \(\mathsf P,\mathsf S\) and root pairs \[ (a_L,b_L)=(s_{01},s_{12}),\qquad (a_R,b_R)=(s_{03},-s_{23}). \] Thus \(x=a_Rb_L\) and \(r=a_Lb_R/(a_Rb_L)\). For either port set \[ f_
u(k)=a_
u^{[k-1]}b_
u^{[-k]},\qquad \mathcal A_
u(j)=q^{jk_
u}f_
u(k_
u),\quad 
u=L,R. 	ag{14} \] Specify the ordered boundary faces by \[ k_L=\alpha'-\alpha+h_L,\qquad k_R=B-B'+h_R. \] The opposite order at the two ports is part of the boundary map. On (13), \(k_L+k_R=1\). The full endpoint-inclusive identities are \[  egin{array}{ll} f_L([n+1])f_R([-n])=x^d r^n,&\mathrm I,\ f_L(n)f_R([1-n])=x^d r^{[n-1]},&\mathrm {II}. \end{array} 	ag{15} \] For case I the endpoint \(n=d\) uses \(f_L(0)=a_L^d\) and \(f_R(1)=b_R^d\); all other entries are the geometric progression. For case II the endpoints \(n=0,1\) give respectively \((a_Lb_R)^d\) and \(x^d\); the remaining entries give the displayed progression. Thus no cyclic carry was dropped. Equations (8),(13),(15), followed by the finite Fourier expression for \(\delta_{k_L+k_R,1}\), prove the all-boundary identity \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal Q_{m collar} = rac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}q^{-j} \mathcal A_L(j)\mathcal A_R(j). \quad} 	ag{16} \] The paired adapters are the actual functions of [A]. Their inverse on their rank-\(N\) images proves that the physical two-leg tensor is \[ K= rac1N Z^{-1}, \qquad Z_{ij}=q^i\delta_{ij}. 	ag{17} \] In particular it is symmetric under exchanging the physical ends. The two charge recipes, not symmetry alone, prove its use in either order relative to an oriented material wire. ## 5. Sewing, the material-vertex measure, and the fixed cut Two oppositely ordered port disks with common roots \(a,b\) and complementary charges obey the exact bilinear identity [A] \[ \sum_{\alpha_-,\alpha_+} \mathcal A_h(\alpha_-,\alpha_+;i) \mathcal A_{1-h}(\alpha_+,\alpha_-;j) =N^2(ab)^d q^i\delta_{ij}. 	ag{18} \] In this gluing the material port vertex becomes one interior vertex, and its two edges to the poles become non-link edges. Their actual factors are \(N^{-1}\), \(a^{-d}\), and \(b^{-d}\). Therefore the normalized joining tensor is exactly \[ S=NZ. 	ag{19} \] The collar has no interior vertex and its only interior edge is the link edge \(LR\); it contributes no additional non-link weight. The two boundary pole-edge occurrences remain boundary data. Inserting the collar in an old port identification replaces one interior material vertex by two. The corresponding old factor \(S\) is replaced by two sewings and the literal ball (17): \[ SK=KS=I,\qquad SKS=S. 	ag{20} \] Thus the change of vertex count, the two sets of non-link edge weights, every decoration factor, and the original wire clock are all accounted for. This is an equality of boundary tensors. It holds against arbitrary exterior tensors on the specified paired images, including the actual crossing arrays of [S]. An arbitrary row on the full face-pair space is restricted to that image by its exact projector; no Hermitian row is substituted. The literal planar cut is \(E_{00}\), as proved in [A]. Since \(K\) and \(S\) are diagonal, \[ [K,E_{00}]=[S,E_{00}]=0,\qquad SKS E_{00}=S E_{00}=N E_{00}. 	ag{21} \] The cut can be placed on either side of the inserted neutral collar without changing its index or replacing it by a uniform state. In the face-pair realization its transported representative is \[ \mathcal E_

u\), including its \(f_
u^{-1}\), is the one of [A]. For an oriented crossing diagram one may choose \(h=1\) on incoming crossing ports and \(h=0\) on outgoing ports. There are two of each, so the boundary sum is two, as required by [S, (8)]. Every joined wire has complementary charges. Recipe I or II in (2) selects the incoming and outgoing ends independently of their global vertex order. Consequently any finite number of these specified wire subdivisions preserves the finite paired-boundary contraction and its prescribed cut by repeated use of (20),(21). This statement concerns the stated port gluing; it does not assert a separate identification of a proposed whole triangulation. All identities are finite holomorphic equalities on the same regular root domain, so their decoration derivatives retain the normalizations and inverse rows. No off-root level deformation, original meridian-normal adapter, positivity, or scalar lower bound follows. In particular the calculation supplies a material wire-resolution interface, not the further Hamiltonian detours through \(\mathsf P,\mathsf S\), a free-vertex deletion, or a pushforward of a selected geometric integration cycle. ## Complete direct proof sources - [K] Kashaev, *Quantum Dilogarithm as a 6j-Symbol*, hep-th/9411147v2, complete 13-page primary text; only its literal definitions and charge/weight conventions are used.
