The quotient is entire and even: (16) makes its numerator vanish to order at least two at every zero of \(c\). For the convergence through those zeros, choose a larger circle avoiding them. Division on that circle gives the \(O(N^{-1})\) bound, the maximum principle carries it inside, and Cauchy's formula gives the derivatives. For real \(\alpha
e0\), (18) is strictly positive, because \(D\) is real and \(c^2-1>0\). Thus the carry is not zero. In particular \(F_+F_-
e1\) as ordinary functions, whereas their classes modulo \(P\) are inverse. Pointwise multiplication of limiting crossing values would miss this explicit order-one source correction. ## 6. The actual crossed Frobenius kernel Put \(\eta=(-1)^d\). The original reverse Newton kernel satisfies \[ B_N(z,w)=\sum_{i=0}^d e_i(z)e_{d-i}(w) = rac\eta{N^2} rac{P_N(z)-P_N(w)}{z-w}. 	ag{19} \] For completeness, use \(z e_i=c_i e_i-s_{i+1}^2 e_{i+1}\) for \(i<d\), the top identity \((z-c_d)e_d=\eta P_N/N^2\), and \(c_{d-i}=c_i\), \(s_{N-i}=s_i\). All interior terms in \((z-w)B_N\) telescope. The original Frobenius identity in section 1 also gives \(\phi_{N,z}[B_N(z,w)f(z)]=f(w)\) for canonical \(f\). For \(r=r_{N,\sigma}\), its canonical multiplication kernel is \[ C_{r,N}(z,w)=\operatorname{can}_z[r(z)B_N(z,w)] = rac\eta{N^2}  rac{P_N(z)r(w)-P_N(w)r(z)}{z-w}. 	ag{20} \] The expression is canonical in both variables. Subtracting it from \(r(z)B_N\) leaves a multiple of \(P_N(z)\), which proves (20), and \(\phi_{N,z}[C_{r,N}(z,w)f(z)] =\operatorname{can}(rf)(w)\). Its full microscopic limit is \[ \eta C_{r_{N,\sigma},N}(w_N(\alpha),w_N( eta)) \longrightarrow  rac{P(\alpha)F_\sigma( eta)-P( eta)F_\sigma(\alpha)} {\alpha^2- eta^2}. 	ag{21} \] The error is \(O_A(N^{-1})\), including every fixed mixed holomorphic derivative on bounded bidisks. Indeed \(N^2(w_N(\alpha)-w_N( eta))/(\alpha^2- eta^2) =\operatorname{sinhc}((\alpha+ eta)/(2N)) \operatorname{sinhc}((\alpha- eta)/(2N))=1+O_A(N^{-2})\). Every numerator is even in each variable and antisymmetric under their exchange, so division by \(\alpha^2- eta^2\) is removable. Buffered Cauchy estimates preserve the error in (6): write each even function as an entire function of \(u=\alpha^2\), and use its divided difference at \(u,v= eta^2\). This is the integral of its first derivative on the segment from \(u\) to \(v\); a larger disk controls that derivative. Another buffered Cauchy estimate gives all mixed derivatives. These are original atomic multiplication and inverse-pair gluing data. No estimate for iterated canonical reductions, whole-kernel contractions, escaping Newton mass, or the original closing after an arbitrary fixed short component follows. Such estimates are required before interchanging this limit with arbitrary Conway compositions or turns. ## Complete sources and coverage The entire matching texts were read; [K], [N], and [W] are proof inputs. [G] concerns a different coherent boundary source with an affine Gamma extension, not this microscopic crossing multiplier. [T] already shows why a local germ estimate does not control the complementary source after a genuine turn. title: The exact middle-weight turn and its positive boundary Gram
text:
# The exact middle-weight turn and its positive boundary Gram 21 November 2026. Research note. Earlier final notes and public manuscripts remain unchanged. The faithful middle-weight model has an explicit triangular change of coordinates: it is the transpose of the already known Newton crossing, with its common scalar removed. This identifies the genuine turn with a finite Euler kernel. Its four boundary rows and columns collapse by finite binomial identities, including the exact rows for both original closings. The turn also has a direct positive factorization: its product with index reversal is precisely the inverse of its boundary Gram. The cyclic intertwiner itself is already present in the canonical-graph calculation. The purpose here is to identify it with the cyclic-column matrix of the middle-weight model and derive the resulting turn kernel and endpoint factors. No geometric contour or volume estimate follows from the change of coordinates alone. ## 1. The physical block and the known intertwiner Fix \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), and \[ x=-q^{-1},\qquad \kappa=q^{d^2/2},\qquad F_r=(Q;Q)_r,\qquad s_r=\prod_{j=1}^r2\sin(\pi j/N),\qquad F_0=s_0=1. \] Write \[ (z;Q)_m=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(1-zQ^j),\qquad 
u_r=(-1)^rQ^{r(r+1)/2},\qquad {r rack a}_Q= rac{F_r}{F_aF_{r-a}}\quad(0\le a\le r<N). \] All these factorial denominators are nonzero. The physical middle space has the ordered basis \[ v_a=|a,d-aangle,\qquad 0\le a\le d. \] Let \(A=\Omega_d\) be its original pair Casimir. The actual balanced single-head generators and coproduct are \[ E|aangle=(Q^{-a}-1)|a-1angle,\quad F|aangle=(1-Q^{a+1})|a+1angle,\quad K|aangle=xQ^{-a}|aangle, \] \[ E_t=E_1K_2+E_2,\qquad F_t=F_1+K_1^{-1}F_2,\qquad K_t=K_1K_2,\qquad \Omega=F_tE_t+qK_t+q^{-1}K_t^{-1}. 	ag{1} \] Missing endpoint arrows are zero. On the middle weight \(K_t=1\). Expanding (1) gives the symmetric tridiagonal matrix \[ A_{a+1,a}=A_{a,a+1}=-(1-Q^{a+1})^2, \] \[ A_{aa}=c_0-q(1-Q^a)^2-q^{-1}(1-Q^{a+1})^2 =4qQ^a-q(1+Q)Q^{2a},\qquad c_0=q+q^{-1}. 	ag{2} \] For example, the two return paths in \(F_tE_t\) contribute \(xQ(1-Q^a)^2=-q(1-Q^a)^2\) and \(x^{-1}Q^{-1}(1-Q^{a+1})^2=-q^{-1}(1-Q^{a+1})^2\). The two adjacent paths give the first formula in (2). Thus this is the physical Casimir of the middle-weight model, in the same coordinates as the existing canonical-graph identity. Put \[ c_r=q^{2r+1}+q^{-2r-1},\qquad b_r(z)=s_r^{-2}\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}(c_j-z). \] The full boundary algebra is \(H_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2)\), where \(T_N\) is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. It includes every first derivative at its double roots. Its cyclic-column matrix and Newton multiplication matrix are \[ C=[b_0(A)v_0\ \cdots\ b_d(A)v_0],\qquad Z_{m Newt}e_r=c_re_r-s_{r+1}^2e_{r+1}, 	ag{3} \] with the last raised term zero. Here \(e_r\) denotes a standard coordinate vector; the columns of \(C\) are written in the physical basis \(v_a\). **Proposition 1.** The cyclic-column matrix is \[  oxed{\quad C_{ar}=
u_a(-q)^{r-a}{r rack a}_Q =(-1)^rq^{r(a+1)} rac{s_r}{s_as_{r-a}} \quad(0\le a\le r\le d), \quad} 	ag{4} \] and is zero for \(a>r\). Consequently \[ C=\kappa^{-1}T_1^{\mathsf T},\qquad C^{-1}=\overline C,\qquad C_{dd}=1, 	ag{5} \] where \(T_1\) is the original Newton crossing matrix, including its scalar \(\kappa\). **Proof.** The symmetric physical block (2) and the full intertwiner \[ A\,T_1^{\mathsf T}=T_1^{\mathsf T}Z_{m Newt} 	ag{6} \] are the existing canonical-graph identity, Section 4. We check the coordinate identification and endpoints explicitly. The proposed matrix in (4) has \(Ce_0=v_0\). Its three interior entry ratios are \[  rac{C_{a-1,r}}{C_{ar}} =qQ^{-a} rac{1-Q^a}{1-Q^{r-a+1}},\qquad  rac{C_{a+1,r}}{C_{ar}} =qQ^a rac{1-Q^{r-a}}{1-Q^{a+1}}, \] \[  rac{C_{a,r+1}}{C_{ar}} =-q rac{1-Q^{r+1}}{1-Q^{r-a+1}}. 	ag{7} \] These follow directly by canceling factorials. For an entry \(0\le a\le r\), clear the denominators in \(AC=CZ_{m Newt}\). Writing \(u=Q^a\), \(t=Q^{r-a+1}\), and dividing by \(q\) leaves \[  egin{split} 0={}&[4u-(1+Q)u^2-Q^{-1}ut-(ut)^{-1}](1-t)\ &-u^{-1}(1-u)^3 -u(1-Qu)(1-t/Q)(1-t) +(ut)^{-1}(1-ut)^3. \end{split} 	ag{8} \] Indeed the second and last terms together are \[ (1-t)[(ut)^{-1}-3u+u^2(1+t)], \] after which (8) factors to zero. Zero off-diagonal coefficients retain this verification at \(a=0\), at \(a=r\), and at \(r=d\), except for the one cleared zero denominator \(a=0,r=d\). At that corner \(C_{1d}/C_{0d}=x\), and \[ A_{00}-x(1-Q)^2=c_0=c_d, \] which is the required entry. For \(a=r+1\), equality reduces to \(
u_{r+1}=-Q^{r+1}
u_r\); entries with \(a>r+1\) vanish on both sides. This proves (6) without deleting any endpoint. The true cyclic-column matrix in (3) also intertwines \(A\) and \(Z_{m Newt}\), and has first column \(v_0\). The Newton recurrence determines all successive columns, because \(s_{r+1}
e0\) for \(r<d\). Thus (4) is exactly (3). The alternative expression in (4) uses \({r rack a}_Q=q^{a(r-a)}s_r/(s_as_{r-a})\). It identifies the transpose of the known Newton crossing, as stated in (5). The finite Pascal inverse is \[ (C^{-1})_{ar} =
u_r^{-1}q^{r-a}Q^{(r-a)(r-a-1)/2}{r rack a}_Q. 	ag{9} \] Multiplication verifies (9) by the finite binomial identity \(\sum_{h=0}^{m}(-1)^hQ^{h(h-1)/2}{m rack h}_Q =(1;Q)_m\), which is zero for \(1\le m<N\). Using \(\overline{{r rack a}_Q} =Q^{-a(r-a)}{r rack a}_Q\), (9) equals \(\overline C\). Finally \(
u_d=1\), proving \(C_{dd}=1\). \(\square\) ## 2. Exact closings and a finite Euler form For a whole Hopf box \(f(A)\), put \(y=f(A)v_0=C\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is its complete Newton coefficient vector. The original marked cap and Frobenius closing are particularly simple: \[  oxed{\quad m^{m pkt}(y)=\sum_{a=0}^d x^ay_a,\qquad \phi^{m pkt}(y)=y_d. \quad} 	ag{10} \] For the first identity, multiply (4) by \(x^a=(-q)^{-a}\) and sum in \(a\). The \(r\)-th result is \[ (-q)^r\sum_{a=0}^r(-1)^aQ^{a(a-1)/2}{r rack a}_Q =\mathbf1_{r=0}. \] Thus \((x^a)_aC=e_0^{\mathsf T}\). The second identity follows from triangularity and \(C_{dd}=1\): \(e_d^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}=e_d^{\mathsf T}\). These are exactly the two reconstructed original rows. Every recorded external framing or normalization line remains unchanged. Let \(P_{m rev}v_a=v_{d-a}\). The genuine packet turn is \[ \mathcal J=C P_{m rev}C^{-1}. 	ag{11} \] There is an explicit finite Euler realization of (11), rather than an unspecified change of frame. Define the strict weighted shift \[ \mathsf Lv_r=(1-Q^r)v_{r-1},\qquad \mathsf Lv_0=0, \] \[ V_Q(B)=\sum_{h=0}^d rac{B^h}{F_h},\qquad P_Q(B)=\sum_{h=0}^d  rac{(-1)^hQ^{h(h-1)/2}B^h}{F_h}. \] For \(B^N=0\), these two polynomials are inverses. Formula (4) gives \[ C=D_
u V_Q(-q\mathsf L),\qquad  oxed{\quad \mathcal J=D_
u V_Q(-q\mathsf L)\, P_{m rev}\,P_Q(-q\mathsf L)D_
u^{-1}. \quad} 	ag{12} \] Here \(D_
u=\operatorname{diag}(
u_a)\); no endpoint phase is dropped. If a strict unit shift is preferred, set \(\mathsf Sv_r=v_{r-1}\) for \(r\ge1\), \(\mathsf Sv_0=0\), and \(D_F=\operatorname{diag}(F_r)\). Then \(\mathsf L=D_F^{-1}\mathsf SD_F\). These factorial frames must remain in the corresponding Euler coefficient periods. ## 3. A single finite kernel for the turn **Proposition 2.** Every entry of the physical middle turn is \[  oxed{\quad \mathcal J_{ab}=(-q)^{d-a-b} \sum_{t=0}^{\min(d-a,b)} (-1)^tQ^{t(t-1)/2-(a+b)t} {a+t rack a}_Q{b rack t}_Q . \quad} 	ag{13} \] **Proof.** In the product \(CP_{m rev}\overline C\), set \(t=d-r\), where \(r\) is the column index of the first factor. Its range is exactly \(0\le t\le\min(d-a,b)\). Use \[ {d-t rack a}_Q =
u_a^{-1}Q^{-at}{a+t rack a}_Q, 	ag{14} \] which follows by reflecting the \(a\) numerator factors through \(Q^N=1\). Also \(\overline{{b rack t}_Q}=Q^{-t(b-t)}{b rack t}_Q\). The remaining phase in the summand is \[ (-q)^{d-a-b}
u_t^{-1}Q^{-at-t(b-t)} =(-q)^{d-a-b}(-1)^t Q^{t(t-1)/2-(a+b)t}. \] This proves (13). Every factorial index is below \(N\); the formula is a finite sum, not a specialization of an infinite summation. \(\square\) ## 4. All four endpoint collapses The finite kernel has exact endpoint values \[  oxed{ egin{aligned} \mathcal J_{a0}&=(-q)^{d-a},& \mathcal J_{db}&=(-q)^{-b},\ \mathcal J_{ad}&=(-q)^{-a}F_{d-a},& \mathcal J_{0b}&=(-q)^{d-b}
u_b^{-1}F_b . \end{aligned}} 	ag{15} \] The first two have just the \(t=0\) term in (13). At \(a=0\), the finite binomial theorem gives \[ \sum_{t=0}^b(-1)^tQ^{t(t-1)/2-bt}{b rack t}_Q =(Q^{-b};Q)_b=
u_b^{-1}F_b. \] For \(b=d\), first use \({d rack t}_Q=
u_t^{-1}\); the remaining sum is \(\sum_{t=0}^{d-a}Q^{-at}{a+t rack a}_Q\). Put \(m=d-a\). Reflection gives \[ {a+t rack a}_Q =(-1)^tQ^{-mt+t(t-1)/2}{m rack t}_Q. \] Because \(a+m=d\), the sum becomes \[ \sum_{t=0}^{m}(-1)^tQ^{t(t+1)/2}{m rack t}_Q =(Q;Q)_m=F_m. \] This proves the last two identities without an infinite-series argument or a missing endpoint. In particular the output-index-\(d\) row in (15) is exactly the marked-cap row in (10), as required by \(\phi^{m pkt}\mathcal J=m^{m pkt}\). One factual norm consequence in the physical Euclidean basis is \[ \|\mathcal Je_0\|^2=\|e_d^{\mathsf T}\mathcal J\|^2=N,\qquad \|\mathcal Je_d\|^2=\|e_0^{\mathsf T}\mathcal J\|^2 =\sum_{r=0}^d|F_r|^2. 	ag{16} \] Thus the physical kernel contains the full sine-factorial weights; it is not a flat Fourier matrix. Equation (16) is not a bound for a whole knot or for a received geometric packet. ## 5. A positive factor of the actual turn Abbreviate \(P=P_{m rev}\). The full Frobenius symmetry of multiplication gives \(T_1^{\mathsf T}=PT_1P\). Equations (5) therefore imply \[ PCP=C^{\mathsf T}. 	ag{17} \] This is also a direct identity of the finite entries (4). Together with \(C^{-1}=\overline C\), it gives the positive factor \[  oxed{\quad H:=\mathcal JP=CP\overline CP=CC^*>0,\qquad \mathcal J=HP. \quad} 	ag{18} \] The matrix is Hermitian positive definite, rather than merely a positive formal symbol. Its inverse is the correctly transported boundary Gram: \[ G_{\mathcal M}=(C^{-1})^*C^{-1} =C^{\mathsf T}\overline C=H^{-1}, \qquad \|y\|_{G_{\mathcal M}}=\|C^{-1}y\|_2. 	ag{19} \] Moreover \[ PHP=H^{-1},\qquad \det H=1,\qquad H^{-1/2}\mathcal JH^{1/2}=P. 	ag{20} \] Indeed (17) gives \(PHP=C^{\mathsf T}\overline C=H^{-1}\). The determinant is \(|\det C|^2=\prod_a|
u_a|^2=1\). The unique positive square root satisfies \(PH^{1/2}P=H^{-1/2}\), by squaring and uniqueness; substituting this identity in \(\mathcal J=HP\) proves the last formula. The antidiagonal turn entries have no remaining internal phase: \[  oxed{\quad H_{aa}=\mathcal J_{a,d-a} =\sum_{r=a}^d |C_{ar}|^2 =\sum_{r=a}^d \left( rac{s_r}{s_as_{r-a}}ight)^2>0 . \quad} 	ag{21} \] This follows from \(H=CC^*\) and (4); it can also be read from the phase cancellation under the reflection (17). In particular \(H_{00}=N\) and \(H_{dd}=1\). Positive definiteness in (18) does not assert that every entry of \(H\), or every entry of \(\mathcal J\), is real and nonnegative. The metric (19) is exactly the original Euclidean Newton metric expressed on the middle weight. It gives \[ \mathcal J^*G_{\mathcal M}\mathcal J=G_{\mathcal M}. 	ag{22} \] Both source rows in (10) have exactly unit dual norm: their products with \(C\) are \(e_0^{\mathsf T}\) and \(e_d^{\mathsf T}\). Thus \(H^{-1/2}\) supplies a concrete orthonormal coordinate change for the actual turn and the complete retained source packet. No unknown closed period defines this Gram. There is no assertion that it is diagonal or has polynomial condition number in the flat physical coordinates. If every packet, gate and root row is transported by \(C\), using \(G_{\mathcal M}\) and its tensor-product metric, this is an isometric change of the original Newton problem. In particular, if \(M\) denotes the bilinear Newton product, its transported map is \(C M(C^{-1}\otimes C^{-1})\), and a source row becomes \(\ell C^{-1}\). Their Hilbert--Schmidt norms, normalization budgets, residual energy and exact minimized value are unchanged when measured in the transported metrics. The positive energy is therefore the previous Newton energy in different coordinates, not a new growth estimate. The flat-coordinate factorial norms in (16) cannot be added as new source or volume contributions. ## 6. The remaining analytic duty The packet model is faithful to all repeated-root normals. The turn in (11)--(15) is the actual fixed-root turn, and (10) retains both original source rows. Its Newton version is unitary reversal; its physical version includes the explicit Euler and factorial frames. No bound for their changes of norm is inferred from that reversal. The previously proved modular relation already reduces redundant twist/turn words. The regular-bend calculation already specifies the actual parameter-dependent cups and caps. Neither should be replaced by a new convention here. In particular, differentiating a generic quantum parameter requires its actual bend family; these fixed-root formulas alone do not give such derivatives. What remains for the geometric application is to transport the complete marked contour through (12) or (13), including the strict shift endpoints and factorial frames, and prove the required estimate for the resulting actual packet and prescribed closing. An isolated endpoint norm or the finite sum does not prove that the selected geometric contribution survives an arbitrary short component. Individual non-Hopf face factors still act as full middle-block matrices, in their original order. Only a whole Hopf box is identified with its polynomial packet. The source rows in (10) are not an extension of the all-array averaged physical trace to arbitrary inserted matrices. The turn studied here acts on cyclic middle-weight packets. A recoupling matrix in a highest-weight multiplicity frame is a different typed operator until its boundary and source adapters have been supplied. ## Complete proof sources and coverage All three complete proof texts were read at matching pins. title: A regular midpoint frame for complete knot holonomy
text: # A regular midpoint frame for complete knot holonomy Private written proof, 18 November 2026. The actual braid coordinates admit a regular geometric frame with cut position exactly \(A_{\rm cut}=-1\). This holds for every complete hyperbolic knot holonomy and every fixed finite braid word, using the five-shape crossing chart of M below. It strengthens the generic-frame statement by fixing the midpoint position in advance. The obstruction to this choice would be a group element acting as half of the primitive meridian translation. The complete cusp lattice excludes it. The remaining frame parameter can then be chosen from a finite predetermined rational grid. This is a statement about the actual classical braid chart. It neither identifies the integration cycle of the binomial cut nor proves that a geometric contribution survives in the invariant. ## 1. Cusp normalization and the midpoint meridian Let \(\rho_0\) be the complete faithful projective holonomy of a hyperbolic knot complement. Choose its oriented peripheral basis \((\mu,\lambda)\). Normalize the cusp fixed point to \(\infty\), and the meridian translation to one. Then \[ \rho_0(\mu)=J_1,\qquad \rho_0(\lambda)=J_\tau,\qquad J_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Im\tau>0. \tag{1} \] Here the full stabilizer of this cusp point is \[ \operatorname{Stab}_{\rho_0(\pi_1)}(\infty) =\{J_{m+n\tau}:m,n\in\mathbb Z\} \quad\hbox{in }\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C). \tag{2} \] Equation (2) uses the full peripheral group of an embedded complete torus cusp, not a proper sublattice. Indeed a lift of that cusp is a horoball whose deck stabilizer is the fundamental group of its torus quotient. Taking the horoball far enough out identifies this stabilizer with the full parabolic fixed-point stabilizer. The meridian is primitive in that torus lattice. Consequently \(J_{1/2}\) is not the image of any group word: \(m+n\tau=1/2\) forces \(n=0\) and then an impossible integer \(m=1/2\). For \(s\ne0\), use the change of projective frame \[ F(r,s)=\begin{pmatrix}r&1-r\\s&-s\end{pmatrix},\qquad F(r,s)^{-1}= \begin{pmatrix}1&(1-r)/s\\1&-r/s\end{pmatrix}. \tag{3} \] It sends the selected flag \((1,1)\) to \(\infty\), and \[ F(r,s)^{-1}J_1F(r,s) =\begin{pmatrix}1+s&-s\\s&1-s\end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} \] At \(s=-2\), the actual convention of M is \(G=-\mu\), \(x=-1\), so the cut coordinates are \[ \mu_{\rm cut}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}, \quad K=1,\quad e=-2,\quad f=2,\quad A_{\rm cut}=x/K=-1,\quad p_{\rm new}=1. \tag{5} \] The last equality follows directly from M's physical relation \(f=(1-A)/p_{\rm new}\). Thus (5) is the actual midpoint position and selected flag, with a noncentral complete meridian. ## 2. A prefix minor cannot vanish throughout this slice Let \(P\) be any determinant-one matrix representing the projective image of a group word, and write \[ P=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}. \] The letter \(d\) in this section is a matrix entry, not a quantum dimension. Multiplication of (3) gives \[ (F^{-1}PF)_{11} =\frac cs r(1-r)+(a-d)r+d+bs . \tag{6} \] For fixed nonzero \(s\), this polynomial is identically zero in \(r\) precisely when \[ c=0,\qquad a=d,\qquad d+bs=0. \] The determinant then gives \(d^2=1\), so this case is exactly \[ P=\pm J_{-1/s}. \tag{7} \] At \(s=-2\), (7) contradicts (2). Therefore every such prefix minor has at most two exceptional values of \(r\). Signs of determinant-one lifts do not affect this argument: both the zero condition and (2) are projective statements. This is the reason for the midpoint choice. A general fixed slice \(s\) can fail this test if \(-1/s\) is an actual peripheral translation. ## 3. The other finite braid-chart conditions Keep any fixed finite braid presentation and the actual holonomy-braiding convention of M. At each stage its strand meridians are conjugates of the knot meridian. Every ordered prefix \(P_j=H_j\cdots H_1\), with \(H_j=-\mu_j\), is up to its central sign the image of a group word. The same is true at intermediate braid stages by the explicit Wirtinger rule. Thus Section 2 applies simultaneously to all prefix minors. For clarity the remaining nonvanishing conditions can also be checked on this fixed slice. Put \[ v_r=\begin{pmatrix}r\\s\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_r=(1,(1-r)/s),\qquad \alpha_r(v_r)=1. \tag{8} \] They are the first column of \(F\) and first row of \(F^{-1}\). Each varies injectively in its affine projective-line chart. Once the prefix minors are nonzero, the Gauss inverse of M has \[ e_j=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \alpha_r\hbox{ is a left eigenline of }H_j, \tag{9} \] \[ f_j=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ v_r\hbox{ is an eigenline of } P_{j-1}^{-1}P_j . \tag{10} \] Here the matrices on the right are in the unframed normalization of (1); their framed representatives are used on the left. One can verify these tests directly. If \(P_{j-1}=(p_{uv})\), the lower Gauss factor is \[ B_-(P_{j-1})=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-p_{21}&p_{11}\end{pmatrix}. \] The upper-right entry of \(B_-(P_{j-1})H_jB_-(P_{j-1})^{-1}\) is \((H_j)_{12}/p_{11}\). Its vanishing says that the first dual basis row is a left eigenline, proving (9) after undoing \(F\). The lower-left entry vanishes precisely when \(P_{j-1}e_1\) is an eigenvector of \(H_j\), or equivalently when \(e_1\) is an eigenvector of \(P_{j-1}^{-1}H_jP_{j-1}=P_{j-1}^{-1}P_j\). This proves (10). Each matrix in (9)--(10) is a noncentral parabolic: the second is a conjugate of the corresponding meridian. It has a unique projective eigenline. Consequently each condition excludes at most one value of \(r\). There are only finitely many stages and strands. Choose one \(r\) outside all their exceptional values. Then all \(K_j,e_j,f_j\) are nonzero, and the actual positive and negative crossing denominators are nonzero. In the complete case \(x^2=1\), the physical identity \[ e_jf_j=\frac{(1-A_j)(1-x^2/A_j)}x \] also excludes \(A_j=1\), both before and after every crossing. The transfer shape \(C\ne1\) follows from the nonzero product \(e_1f_2\), or its negative-crossing counterpart. M's five ordered crossing shapes consequently avoid both zero and one. This proves regularity in that five-shape chart; it is not a claim that a four-term subdivision has no pinched crossing. ## 4. A finite rational choice and bounded frame Let \(p\) count the prefix minors tested above, and let \(q_+\), \(q_-\) count the eigenline tests (9), (10). There are at most \[ B=2p+q_++q_- \] bad complex numbers \(r\). One of the \(B+1\) predetermined rational values \[ r_k=\frac{k}{B+2},\qquad 1\le k\le B+1 \tag{11} \] therefore works. In particular it can be chosen in \((0,1)\). At \(s=-2\), the ordinary Euclidean matrix norms satisfy \[ \|F(r,-2)\|\le3,\qquad \|F(r,-2)^{-1}\|\le3/2 . \tag{12} \] These follow by bounding their Frobenius norms in (3). The normalization of the complete cusp in (1) has already been made; (12) does not bound the original cusp-normalizing conjugation or the entries of every other holonomy. If the unframed matrices lie in a coefficient field \(k\), this choice of frame uses only rational coefficients and preserves that field. No degree bound for \(k\) is asserted. The finite count does not give a uniform lower bound on all chart denominators over a degenerating family of knot holonomies. For each fixed complete representation they are finitely many nonzero numbers, which is sufficient for an open neighborhood. ## 5. A selected-flag deformation through the same midpoint There is an explicit local extension beyond the complete meridian. Work on any augmented holomorphic representation family near \(\rho_0\), with chosen meridian eigenvalue \(M^{-1}\) and eigenflag. A local frame sends that flag to \(\infty\), putting the meridian in upper triangular form. Its off-diagonal entry is a unit at completion, so a diagonal change normalizes it to one. Thus it has the form \[ J_M=\begin{pmatrix}M^{-1}&1\\0&M\end{pmatrix}. \] Keep a good rational \(r\) from (11), and define \[ s(M,r)=-2M-(M^{-1}-M)r,\qquad F_M=F(r,s(M,r)). \tag{13} \] The function \(s\) is nonzero near \(M=1\). Direct multiplication gives \[ F_M^{-1}J_MF_M =\begin{pmatrix}-M&M+M^{-1}\\-2M&2M+M^{-1}\end{pmatrix}. \tag{14} \] It is independent of \(r\), its selected eigenvector is \((1,1)\), and the actual cut symbols with \(x=-M\) are \[ K=M,\qquad e=-(M+M^{-1}),\qquad f=2,\qquad A_{\rm cut}=-1,\qquad p_{\rm new}=1. \tag{15} \] These agree with the literal symbol formulas of M. Every other prefix minor and crossing denominator that was nonzero at \(\rho_0\) remains nonzero on a sufficiently small neighborhood of the augmented family. The matrices \(F_M\) and their inverses remain bounded there. The existence and parametrization of that augmented family are not proved by this change of frame. The assertion is that whenever the marked family is supplied, (13) puts it in this same actual midpoint chart. No square-root choice or change of the selected peripheral eigenflag is hidden. ## 6. Consequences and the remaining quantum question The complete geometric representation has a regular point in the actual source's classical chart with \(A_{\rm cut}=-1\), and this choice persists on a marked nearby deformation. Thus midpoint framing is not excluded by a generic chart divisor, for any fixed finite braid of a hyperbolic knot. No alternating or long-twist hypothesis is used. The parameter \(r\) has not been integrated out. At fixed cut meridian, varying it is the residual peripheral centralizer action. A binomial cut also changes the boundary phase and its stationary equations. Its concentration near the middle occupation does not, by itself, identify its critical scheme or its original relative integration cycle with this classical slice. The normal residue and the off-divisor source remain different data. In particular this lemma gives no nonzero geometric cycle coefficient or scalar lower bound, and proves no new volume-conjecture filling case. It supplies the regular classical target for the source comparison. ## Coverage and complete proof-source pins Existence of diagrammatic solutions associated with representations has substantial prior coverage, including [Cho--Yoon--Zickert, *On the Hikami--Inoue conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11841). Their stated cluster-coordinate criterion retains a boundary-parabolic lift obstruction. The present calculation uses projective group words in the actual five-shape crossing chart and does not identify that chart with their cluster variables or discard their lift condition. The recent [arc-faithful braid statement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13305) concerns nondegenerate four-term octahedral shapes after rewording. Neither paper's proof is used here. No novelty claim is made for general representation-associated critical-point existence. * M: notes/marked_braid_holonomy.md, SHA256 eff47c757d0e44bda0c396c094315b8e1fce11f1fc2d6445d636c6d2d3a46c4f. * I: notes/research_fixed_interior_cut_source.md, SHA256 93b2887527e0b5c9cb93f4da77702c996f0524e0a93f0c0032909345efdbd1b2. M supplies the actual rational crossing/holonomy map, Gauss inverse, selected-flag convention and five-shape chart. I fixes the interpretation of midpoint cut position. All matrix calculations, the fixed-slice exclusion, finite-grid choice and local deformation are proved above. The complete unchanged M and I were read in the author sequence, their used implications checked and matching hashes renewed. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. Frozen and public files are unchanged.

title: Mixed whole-CROSS and regular-window phase losses
status: Whole CROSS and supported windows in one cycle bound
text: # Mixed whole-CROSS and regular-window phase losses The cycle-packing conclusion is conditional on the stated hypotheses. A product formula for the complete capacity is not assumed. ## 1. The whole-CROSS polynomial, with both parities retained Put \(d=N-1\), \(\theta=\pi/N\), \(u=-4\sin^2(\pi\delta)\), and \[ a_r=4\cos^2((r+\tfrac12)\theta),\qquad s_r=2\sin(r\theta),\qquad A=x+y,\quad P=xy. \] All variables are the original four face variables of a port. Fix their zero pattern, require \(A>0\), and let the positive entries range in a fixed positive compact set. A zero variable stays exactly zero. In particular this includes protected middle and protected outer patterns allowed by the original marked source. It excludes two zero outer faces. Write \[ P_N^\times(x,b,c,y;u)=(-1)^dH_{V_N,\mathrm{CROSS}}(x,b,c,y;u). \tag{1} \] The sign in (1) is part of the actual numerator convention; it has modulus one and is restored when taking products of raw coupons. The [exact factorization](../papers/filling-bounds/README.md), at the same level \(N\), uses \[ \begin{aligned} R_0(b;u)&=1,\\ R_j(b;u)&=b^j\prod_{r<j}(a_r+u) +s_j^2 A R_{j-1}(b;u) +s_js_{j-1}(a_{j-1}+u)P R_{j-2}(b;u). \end{aligned}\tag{2} \] The last summand is omitted at \(j=1\). For even \(N=2m\), set \(D_b=R_{m-1}(b;u)\) and \(E_b=(a_{m-1}+u)R_{m-2}(b;u)\). Then \[ P_N^\times=s_m^2 A D_bD_c +s_ms_{m-1}P(D_bE_c+E_bD_c). \tag{3} \] For odd \(N=2m+1\), put \(G_b=R_m(b;u)\) and keep \(D_b=R_{m-1}(b;u)\). The formula is \[ P_N^\times=G_bG_c+u s_ms_{m+1}P D_bD_c. \tag{4} \] The second term of (4) is the original path which skips the central row; its unused factor \(u\) remains. These are polynomial identities, also when a diagonal or central factor vanishes. Every central summand contains one cofactor from each of the \(b\)- and \(c\)-sides. No decomposition into separately optimized face variables is made. Define the positive endpoint value \[ B_N(L)=P_N^\times(L;0)>0. \tag{5} \] The zero-spectral recurrence has nonnegative coefficients. Positivity in (5) follows from the first summand of (3), or from \(G_b(0)G_c(0)\) in (4), since \(A>0\). ## 2. A finite majorant and the whole-port angular loss The cofactor interpolation theorem gives, coefficient by coefficient, \[ |R_j(u)|_{\mathrm{coef}} \le C\log(N+1)R_j(0),\qquad -4\le u\le0, \quad 0\le j\le\lfloor d/2\rfloor. \tag{6} \] Together with the exact central comparisons in that theorem, it implies \[ |P_N^\times(L e^{i\vartheta};u)| \le M_N^\times(L):=C_0\log^2(N+1)B_N(L) \tag{7} \] for every face phase and every real \(\delta\). The constant can be chosen uniformly over the fixed radius compact and all sufficiently large levels of both parities. Protected zero variables need no assigned phase. Here are the central comparisons explicitly. At even levels, \[ D_b(0)\ge s_{m-1}^2 A R_{m-2}(b;0),\qquad P\le A^2/4. \tag{8} \] Thus \(P D_b(0)R_{m-2}(c;0)\), and its reflection, are bounded by a uniform multiple of \(A D_b(0)D_c(0)\), already a positive summand of \(B_N\). At odd levels, \[ G_b(0)\ge s_m^2 A D_b(0),\qquad P D_b(0)D_c(0)\le\frac{1}{4s_m^4}G_b(0)G_c(0). \tag{9} \] The factors \(s_m,s_{m-1},s_{m+1}\) used here are bounded away from zero at large \(N\). The remaining factors \(|u|\) and \(|a_{m-1}+u|\) in (3)–(4) are bounded on the real spectral interval. This proves (7) without discarding the odd skipped-central term or dividing by a possibly zero diagonal. For the supported incidences define the distance to common phase by \[ d_\times(\vartheta) =\min_{\varphi\in\mathbb T} \max_{f\in\operatorname{supp}(x,b,c,y)} |\vartheta_f-\varphi|_{\mathbb T}. \tag{10} \] Incidences are retained separately if two arguments happen to be the same original face. For every fixed \(\eta>0\), there are \(c>0\), \(C_1\ge1\), and \(N_0\) such that \[ |P_N^\times(L e^{i\vartheta};u)| \le C_1e^{-cN}M_N^\times(L) \quad\text{whenever }d_\times(\vartheta)\ge\eta, \tag{11} \] uniformly for all real \(\delta\) and \(N\ge N_0\). To prove this, choose any positive outer incidence \(p\), which exists because \(A>0\). Taking \(\varphi=\vartheta_p\) in (10) shows that some supported incidence has circular distance at least \(\eta\) from \(p\). If it is \(b\), the supported phases of \((x,b,y)\) are separated; if it is \(c\), those of \((x,c,y)\) are separated. If it is the other outer incidence, both sides are separated. The selected side therefore has at least two positive entries. The [actual cofactor angular theorem](../papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/README.md) gives \[ |R_j(\text{phased side};u)| \le C N^K e^{-\gamma N}R_j(\text{positive side};0) \tag{12} \] for each terminal cofactor on that side. Indeed all terminal indices in (3)–(4) equal \(J\) or \(J-1\), with \(J=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\). Apply (6) to the other side and (8)–(9) to each of the finitely many central summands. This bounds the left side of (11) by \(CN^{K'}e^{-\gamma N}B_N(L)\); absorb the polynomial into, for example, \(e^{-\gamma N/2}\). A cofactor with one positive face is a monomial, but cannot be the selected mismatched side. It consequently causes no exception to this argument. If the whole port has only one supported phase, the condition in (11) is empty. Thus a whole CROSS port has alignment label zero at every supported incidence. This is a whole-port conclusion from the exact central factorization, not an assumption that the two cofactor phases can be chosen independently. ## 3. Endpoint normalization and its rate Let \(Q(x,b,y)\) denote the original absolute complete triangle potential at \(\delta=0\), with homogeneity degree \(1/2\). Then, on the fixed radius compact and fixed zero pattern, \[ \log B_N(L)=N\{Q(x,b,y)+Q(x,c,y)\}+O(\log N). \tag{13} \] In particular the exact majorant in (7) has a polynomial upper bound \[ M_N^\times(L)\le C N^K \exp\!\left[N\{Q(x,b,y)+Q(x,c,y)\}\right]. \tag{14} \] This polynomial normalization is not needed for (11), but identifies its source-rate interface without an unspecified exponential scalar. For completeness, (13) follows from the existing endpoint cofactor packets with a quantitative product estimate. For \(b>0\), including exactly one zero outer weight, the [interior-start packet](../papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/README.md) has its starting saddle in a fixed compact subset of \((0,1/2)\). The finite prefix diagonal is bounded away from zero before that saddle, and the positive tail root is bounded away from zero from there to the terminal row. Their logarithms have uniform bounded derivatives on these intervals. The finite-row shift is bounded, and the finite tail root differs from its limiting root by \(O(N^{-1})\). Elementary Euler–Maclaurin estimates therefore give \(N\phi_N(t_N)=NQ(x,b,y)+O(1)\). The packet amplitude is a bounded unit times \(\sqrt N\); hence \(\log R_{J-k}(b;0)=NQ(x,b,y)+O(\log N)\), for fixed \(k\). For \(b=0\) and \(xy>0\), the [protected-middle packet](../papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/README.md) is a bounded nonzero amplitude times \(\prod_{j=1}^n s_j\lambda_{j,+}\). The positive \(\lambda_{j,+}\) is uniformly bounded away from zero even at the lower endpoint and differs from a smooth limiting root by \(O(N^{-1})\). Its logarithmic sum has bounded Riemann error. The remaining sine product has only the endpoint logarithm: comparison with \(\log t\) gives Riemann error \(O(\log N)\). The [absolute marked-action identity](../papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/README.md) identifies the resulting integral with the same \(Q(0;x,y)\). Finally, if \(b=0\) and exactly one outer weight is positive, (2) is the literal monomial \[ R_n(0;0)=(x+y)^n\prod_{j=1}^n s_j^2, \qquad Q(x,0,y)=\tfrac12\log(x+y). \tag{15} \] The half-sine product again contributes only \(O(\log N)\). These cases exhaust the allowed support patterns on either cofactor side. Apply their estimates to (3) at \(u=0\), using (8) for the upper comparison and its positive first term for the lower comparison. At odd levels (4) at zero is exactly \(G_b(0)G_c(0)\). This proves (13). ## 4. Mixed cycles on the one original face torus Take a fixed original source and one radius \(L_f>0\) per ordinary face. Protected face variables are specialized to zero before coefficient extraction. Select a set \(J\) of ports consisting of either: - whole CROSS coupons satisfying the hypotheses above, with majorant \(\mathcal E_{e,N}=M_{e,N}^\times\) and zero incidence labels; - literal regular moving windows satisfying the [four-positive theorem](research_regular_spectral_window_phase_exclusion.md) or the [one-protected-outer theorem](research_protected_outer_window_phase_exclusion.md), with \(\mathcal E_{e,N}=E_{e,N}\) and their actual endpoint-sign labels. - fixed-start \(b=0\) or reflected fixed-stop \(c=0\) windows satisfying the [protected-middle theorem](research_protected_middle_window_phase_exclusion.md), again with their literal positive envelopes and only their three supported incidences. Their hypotheses require both outer weights and the other middle weight positive. Each selected port now has the two bounds \[ |P_{e,N}|\le\mathcal E_{e,N},\qquad |P_{e,N}|\le C_e e^{-c_eN}\mathcal E_{e,N} \quad\text{if }d_e\ge\eta, \tag{16} \] where \(d_e\) is distance to its supported alignment. For CROSS this is (10); for a window subtract its prescribed \(0/\pi\) incidence labels before minimizing over a common phase. All constants are obtained at the same fixed threshold \(\eta\). Use the original supported incidence multigraph, retaining repeated incidences. For a nonempty finite collection \(\mathcal C\) of odd-label cycles, put \(\eta=\pi/(4r_{\max})\) and let \[ \kappa_{\mathcal C}= \max\left\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}\lambda_C: \lambda_C\ge0,\quad \sum_{C\ni e}\lambda_C\le c_e\ \text{for every }e\in J\right\}. \tag{17} \] The [fractional cycle-packing proof](research_regular_window_cycle_packing.md) uses only (16), so applies unchanged. CROSS vertices can carry paths between moving-window vertices, including across a protected middle whose zero incidence is absent. A cycle containing only CROSS vertices has even label and supplies no such obstruction. At unselected ports let \(M_{e,N}\) be any certified phase-uniform majorants for their actual polynomials. For the unchanged original target exponents \(t_f(N)\), Cauchy extraction on the one shared torus gives \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \left|\left[\prod_f z_f^{t_f(N)}\right] \prod_e P_{e,N}(z)\right| \le C e^{-\kappa_{\mathcal C}N} \frac{\prod_{e\in J}\mathcal E_{e,N}(L) \prod_{e\notin J}M_{e,N}(L)} {\prod_f L_f^{t_f(N)}}.} \tag{18} \] Raw numerator signs, any external source character and all additional source prefactors retain their actual moduli. There is no new power of \(N\), a changed face target, or an independent radius per incidence in (18). ## 5. Scope of the rate criterion The whole-CROSS contribution to the logarithmic majorant in (18) is exactly \(Q(x,b,y)+Q(x,c,y)\) by (13). The moving-window contribution is its own original positive envelope. They are not identified with each other. If the normalized logarithmic limsup of the entire positive quotient in (18) is \(B_L\), its actual shared coefficient has upper rate \(B_L-\kappa_{\mathcal C}\). Thus \[ B_L-\kappa_{\mathcal C}<\Phi_D, \tag{19} \] is a conditional strict source-rate certificate whenever the original complete rate \(\Phi_D\) is known. No uniform margin in (19), no exhaustive window cover, and no universal bound by \(\Phi_D\) have been proved here. A family of polynomially many pieces still needs the uniform finite-level errors and constants specified in the cycle-packing criterion. Compatible phase systems, uncovered irregular windows, and the remaining source sectors require their own estimates. The statement here is for real spectral variables; a complex-strip version must also budget the unconditional Bernstein growth of all noncontracting factors. The finite central identities and cofactor angular theorem used above have their own original-source audits. This note composes their proved estimates analytically; it makes no claim to a new physical-matrix or asymptotic numerical audit.

title: Concavity of the mixed Newton wire and filling phase
text: # Concavity of the mixed Newton wire and filling phase Research proof, 3 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. The phase obtained by retaining one Newton index has a useful concavity region that does not depend on the filling power. It applies before the shared wire is summed out. In particular, it does not require the full bare kernel to have a geometric asymptotic at a large complex angle. The theorem below concerns the explicit holomorphic phase. It gives a strict maximum and quantitative boundary gaps on a specified convex contour domain. An application to an exact finite source must still justify its local interpolation and control the rest of its integration cycle. ## 1. The phase and its regular factorial domain Use the original sine-factorial primitive \(J\), normalized by \[ J'(z)=\Log(2\sin\pi z),\qquad J(0)=0. \tag{1} \] Its branch is holomorphic on \(0<\Re z<1\) and agrees with the real logarithm on \(0<z<1\). The original Newton phase and the complete-end edge phase satisfy \[ \begin{split} b(x,t)&=-J(1/2-x+t/(2\pi)) -J(1/2-x-t/(2\pi))-2J(x),\\ \psi(t,0)&=-4J(1/4+t/(4\pi)) -4J(1/4-t/(4\pi)). \end{split} \tag{2} \] The second equality has the original normalization \(\psi(0,0)=M_\infty=4G/\pi\). Differentiating it gives \(\psi_t(t,0)=-\pi^{-1}\operatorname{arsinh}(\tan(t/2))\) on the branch through zero. For a real power \(n\), retain the mixed phase \[ \mathcal F_n(x,t) =b(x,t)+\psi(t,0)+\frac{int^2}{4\pi}-it. \tag{3} \] Here \(x\) is the Newton index divided by the level, and \(t\) is the original angular variable at the selected vertex. The last two terms are the original crossing and unit-charge terms. Put \[ s=\frac12-\frac{t}{2\pi},\qquad x=a+iY,\quad s=b+iS,\qquad 0\le Y\le S. \tag{4} \] The letter \(b\) without arguments in (4) denotes \(\Re s\); the Newton phase is always written \(b(x,t)\). For \(0<a<b<1/2\), all three Newton factorial arguments \(x,s-x,1-s-x\) have real parts strictly between zero and one. The same holds for the arguments of the complete-end phase in (2). Reflection and duplication of the sine primitive give \[ J(1-z)=-J(z),\qquad J(z)=2J(z/2)+2J(1/2+z/2). \tag{5} \] Both identities follow by differentiating and fixing the constant on the real interval. Analytic continuation in their regular strips retains these constants. Consequently the part of (3) preceding the filling terms is \[ \mathcal H(x,s) =J(s+x)-J(s-x)-2J(x)+2J(s)-8J(s/2). \tag{6} \] ## 2. A convex domain with strictly negative real Hessian For \(h\ge0\), define \[ \alpha(h)=\frac1{2\pi} \arccos(\operatorname{sech}(2\pi h)). \tag{7} \] Thus \(0\le\alpha(h)<1/4\). At fixed heights \(Y,S\), let \[ \mathcal P_{Y,S} =\{(a,b):\alpha(Y)<a<b<1/2,\ \alpha(S)<b\}. \tag{8} \] This is a convex open polygon. Its inequalities are independent of the real power \(n\). **Theorem 1.** For every \(0\le Y\le S\) and every real \(n\), the function \[ (a,b)\longmapsto \Re\mathcal F_n(a+iY,\ \pi-2\pi(b+iS)) \tag{9} \] has strictly negative Hessian on \(\mathcal P_{Y,S}\). *Proof.* Define four real quantities, with the indicated complex arguments retained: \[ \begin{split} u&=\Re\cot\pi(s+x),& v&=\Re\cot\pi(s-x),\\ w&=\Re\cot\pi x,& d&=\Re\csc\pi s. \end{split} \tag{10} \] Differentiating (6) twice, and using \(\cot(z/2)-\cot z=\csc z\), gives the negative real Hessian \[ \mathsf H =\pi \begin{pmatrix} v+2w-u&-v-u\\ -v-u&v+2d-u \end{pmatrix}. \tag{11} \] The filling terms in (3) have affine real parts on a contour of fixed \(Y,S\), so they make no contribution to this matrix. The inequalities \(0<a<b<1/2\) imply \(v,w,d>0\). If \(a+b\ge1/2\), then \(u\le0\), and (11) is the sum of the positive diagonal matrix \(2\pi\operatorname{diag}(w,d)\) and two positive semidefinite rank-one matrices. Suppose instead that \(a+b<1/2\), so \(u>0\). For \(0<r<1/2\) and \(h\ge0\), write \[ C(r,h)=\Re\cot\pi(r+ih) =\frac{\sin(2\pi r)} {\cosh(2\pi h)-\cos(2\pi r)}. \tag{12} \] It decreases as \(h\) increases. Its derivative in \(r\) is \[ C_r(r,h)= \frac{2\pi\{\cos(2\pi r)\cosh(2\pi h)-1\}} {\{\cosh(2\pi h)-\cos(2\pi r)\}^2}. \tag{13} \] In particular \(C_r(r,h)<0\) when \(r>\alpha(h)\). Once this condition holds, it continues to hold as \(r\) increases within \((0,1/2)\). Starting at \((a,Y)\), first increase the real argument to \(a+b\), and then increase the height to \(Y+S\). Equations (8), (12), and (13) give \(u<w\). Starting instead at \((b,S)\) gives \(u<\Re\cot\pi s\). Finally \[ d-\Re\cot\pi s=\Re\tan(\pi s/2)>0, \tag{14} \] so \(u<d\). The strict last inequality follows from \(0<\Re s<1/2\). Now (11) becomes \[ \mathsf H =\pi(v+u) \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix} +2\pi\operatorname{diag}(w-u,d-u), \tag{15} \] which is positive definite. This proves the theorem. \(\square\) ## 3. An explicit coercive bound on compact domains Put \(u_+=\max(u,0)\). The proof gives the pointwise matrix bound \[ \mathsf H\ \succeq 2\pi\min\{w-u_+,d-u_+\}\,I. \tag{16} \] Both entries inside the minimum are strictly positive on (8). Let \(Q\) be a compact convex subset of that polygon, and set \[ \mu_Q=\inf_Q\min\{w-u_+,d-u_+\}>0. \tag{17} \] This constant is defined by elementary trigonometric functions on a compact set. Any explicit lower bound for it can be substituted in the following estimate. **Corollary 2.** Suppose the holomorphic phase (3) has a critical point \((x_*,t_*)\) on the fixed-height contour over \(Q\). Write \(x_*=a_*+iY\) and \(s_*=1/2-t_*/(2\pi)=b_*+iS\). Then for every \((a,b)\in Q\), \[ \Re\mathcal F_n(a+iY,\pi-2\pi(b+iS)) \le \Re\mathcal F_n(x_*,t_*) -\pi\mu_Q\bigl((a-a_*)^2+(b-b_*)^2\bigr). \tag{18} \] In particular the critical point is the unique real maximum on this contour domain. A boundary set at Euclidean distance at least \(\delta\) from \((a_*,b_*)\) loses at least \(\pi\mu_Q\delta^2\) in its exponential rate. *Proof.* The real gradient vanishes at the holomorphic critical point. Integrate (16) along the segment from it to \((a,b)\), which lies in \(Q\) by convexity. \(\square\) The ordinary angular distance satisfies \(b-b_*=-(\Re t-\Re t_*)/(2\pi)\); this supplies the precise conversion from (18) to angular coordinates. ## 4. Two selected vertices and their shared wire For powers \(n,p\), the mixed phase of the internal pair is \[ \mathcal A_{n,p}(x,t,r)= \mathcal F_n(x,t)+\mathcal F_p(x,r). \tag{19} \] Thus the one shared Newton index is retained in both terms. Fix heights \(Y,S_1,S_2\) with \(0\le Y\le\min(S_1,S_2)\), and write \[ x=a+iY,\qquad \frac12-\frac{t}{2\pi}=b_1+iS_1,\qquad \frac12-\frac{r}{2\pi}=b_2+iS_2. \tag{20} \] The common real domain is the convex polyhedron \[ \alpha(Y)<a<b_i<1/2,\qquad \alpha(S_i)<b_i\quad(i=1,2). \tag{21} \] **Corollary 3.** The real part of (19) has strictly negative Hessian on (21), for every real \(n,p\). On a compact convex subset \(Q\), let \(\mu_i>0\) be the infimum in (17) for its projection to \((a,b_i)\). If a holomorphic critical point lies on this fixed-height contour, then \[ \begin{split} \Re\mathcal A_{n,p} \le \Re\mathcal A_{n,p,*} -\pi\bigl[ (\mu_1+\mu_2)(a-a_*)^2 +\mu_1(b_1-b_{1,*})^2 +\mu_2(b_2-b_{2,*})^2\bigr]. \end{split} \tag{22} \] *Proof.* Add the two Hessian bounds (16), each pulled back to its own two coordinates. Their sum is strictly positive in all three real directions. Integrate along a segment in the convex domain as in Corollary 2. \(\square\) All factorial arguments remain in their regular strips on (21). This controls the central mixed phase and its real contour faces. It does not yet control indices outside that domain, the other Fourier periods, first-normal remainders, or the interpolation error for the actual coefficient functions. In particular, the exact Fourier identity \(\mathcal P_{n,p,N}=N\int W_{n,N}(x)W_{p,N}(x)\,dx\) still needs estimates on the complementary part of its full period before (22) can be used to prove its leading coefficient.

title: The complete value from a fixed number of nearby ordinary-color jets
text:
# The complete value from a fixed number of nearby ordinary-color jets Private written proof, 23 November 2026. A single final row of an actual color recurrence reconstructs the original complete value from quantum derivatives of only \(d\) colors strictly below \(N\). The number of derivatives is fixed by the operator, and the observation row has polynomial norm. No full color orbit, cyclotomic candidate or arithmetic coefficient hypothesis is needed for this local observation. The input jets can have unknown exponential size. This is a reduction of the actual data and their observation cost, not a geometric lower bound or a new short-filling volume theorem. ## 1. Original source and the terminal divisor Use the actual \(Q\)-only reduced color functions \(\mathcal C_r(Q)\) and a specified all-level recurrence of [M]: \[ P=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_j(Q,Y)T^j,\qquad TY=QYT,\qquad d\ge1, \] \[ \sum_{j=0}^{d}a_j(Q,Q^m)\mathcal C_{m+j}(Q)=0, \qquad m\ge1,\qquad a_d
e0. 	ag{1} \] The fixed coefficients are Laurent polynomials after one recorded denominator clearing. Complex coefficients are allowed. The actual reduced, zero-framed closing is \[ Q_N=e^{2\pi i/N},\qquad K_N=\mathcal C_N(Q_N). 	ag{2} \] In [O]'s half-root convention \(q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\), the same ordinary root value is \(\mathcal C_r(Q_N)=C_r(q_N)\). Every original crossing phase, pivot and framing stays in these color functions; no closed scalar is used to normalize the row. In the Laurent ring factor the leading coefficient maximally as \[ a_d(Q,Y)=(1-Q^dY)^\mu b_d(Q,Y),\qquad B(Q)=b_d(Q,Q^{-d}). 	ag{3} \] Here \(\mu\ge0\) is finite and \(B
e0\). Indeed the substitution \(Z=Q^dY\) identifies this Laurent ring with \(\mathbb C[Q^{\pm1},Z^{\pm1}]\); evaluation at \(Z=1\) has kernel generated by \(1-Z\). Maximality proves \(B
e0\). In particular \(\mu\) is at most the \(Y\)-exponent span of \(a_d\). Put \[ v=\operatorname{ord}_{Q=1}B(Q)\ge0. 	ag{4} \] All these quantities are fixed by the recorded operator. ## 2. Exact observation and polynomial stability At fixed \(N>d\) vary the quantum parameter by \[ Q=Q_N(1+\zeta/N). 	ag{5} \] The color dimensions are held fixed during differentiation. Define the actual below-complete quantum jets and the known row coefficients by \[ J_{j,\ell,N}=[\zeta^\ell]\, \mathcal C_{N-d+j}\!\left(Q_N(1+\zeta/N)ight), \quad 0\le j<d,\quad 0\le\ell\le\mu, \] \[ A_{j,r,N}=[\zeta^r]\, a_j\!\left(Q_N(1+\zeta/N), [Q_N(1+\zeta/N)]^{N-d}ight). 	ag{6} \] These are honest derivatives of integral-color functions at fixed color, including their off-root pivot and framing. They are not fixed-\(Q_N\) meridian derivatives of the root ADO state. **Theorem.** For every sufficiently large \(N\), \[  oxed{\quad K_N= rac{(-1)^{\mu+1}}{B(Q_N)} \sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\mu} A_{j,\mu-\ell,N}J_{j,\ell,N}. \quad} 	ag{7} \] The total absolute row weight satisfies \[  rac1{|B(Q_N)|} \sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\mu}|A_{j,\mu-\ell,N}| \le C N^v . 	ag{8} \] Thus only \(d(\mu+1)\) scalar jets are supplied, and every color \(N-d,\ldots,N-1\) is strictly between zero and \(N\). There is no parity or primality restriction. For arbitrary approximate data \(\widetilde J_{j,\ell,N}\), define \(G_N\) by the same explicit row (7). Then \[  oxed{\quad |G_N-K_N|\le C N^v \max_{j,\ell}|\widetilde J_{j,\ell,N}-J_{j,\ell,N}|. \quad} 	ag{9} \] The approximations need not be coefficients of a common lifted section. The assertion compares them with the specified actual jets. Constants may depend on the knot, its fixed filling, and the chosen fixed recurrence. No uniform bound over growing words is asserted. ## 3. Proof of the exact row and its cost Use row \(m=N-d\) in the generic identity (1), before root evaluation. At its leading entry, \[ a_d(Q,Q^{N-d})=(1-Q^N)^\mu b_d(Q,Q^{N-d}). 	ag{10} \] Under (5), \(Q_N^N=1\) gives \[ 1-Q^N=1-(1+\zeta/N)^N=-\zeta+O(\zeta^2). 	ag{11} \] The coefficient of \(\zeta\) is exactly \(-1\) at every level. Also \(Q_N^{N-d}=Q_N^{-d}\), so the last factor in (10) has value exactly \(B(Q_N)\). For all sufficiently large \(N\) that value is nonzero. The coefficient of \(\zeta^\mu\) in the last term of (1) is therefore \[ (-1)^\mu B(Q_N)K_N. 	ag{12} \] No positive-order jet of the complete color occurs in (12). The other terms give the convolution in (7), including all lower ordinary-color jets. This proves (7) with its displayed sign. For the quantitative claim, a monomial \(Q^aY^b\) in any fixed \(a_j\) becomes \(Q^{E_N}\), where \(E_N=a+b(N-d)=O(N)\). Its scaled Taylor coefficient is \[ [\zeta^r]Q^{E_N} =Q_N^{E_N} inom{E_N}{r}N^{-r}. 	ag{13} \] For each fixed \(r\le\mu\), this is bounded independently of \(N\), also for negative integral \(E_N\). Finite sums prove \(|A_{j,r,N}|\le C\). Write \(B(Q)=(Q-1)^vB_0(Q)\), \(B_0(1)
e0\). Laurent polynomials are holomorphic at one, so \[ |B(Q_N)|\ge c|Q_N-1|^v\ge c'N^{-v} 	ag{14} \] for all sufficiently large \(N\). Here \(|Q_N-1|=2\sin(\pi/N)\ge4/N\). Equations (13)--(14) prove (8), and the triangle inequality proves (9). No companion-product inversion or algebraic-number estimate is used. The earlier root-normal coordinate is retained if desired: \[ \delta=1-Q^N=1-(1+\zeta/N)^N,\qquad \zeta=N[(1-\delta)^{1/N}-1]. 	ag{15} \] Both substitutions have uniformly bounded fixed Taylor coefficients, with linear coefficient \(-1\). Their triangular fixed-depth jet changes and inverses are uniformly bounded. The gain in (7) is the selection of a fixed nearby color block, not a coordinate relabeling. ## 4. What is now isolated, and prior coverage The ordinary root estimate [O] is uniform throughout \(1\le r<N\). For a fixed \(b\)-strand knot presentation it gives \[ |\mathcal C_r(Q_N)|\le\sin(\pi/N)^{1-b} \le(N/2)^{b-1}. 	ag{16} \] If \(\mu=0\), (7)--(8) consequently imply \(|K_N|\le C N^{v+b-1}\). More generally the \(\ell=0\) part of (7) is polynomially bounded. Any positive exponential size in this row must therefore enter through the finitely many \(\ell\ge1\) quantum jets. Equation (16) alone does not bound those derivatives. The stronger necessary boundary-column condition is already proved in [P, Section 2]: positive complete growth forces \(a_j(Q,Q^{-j})\equiv0\) for every \(j\), equivalently the actual Laurent operator has a retained right factor \(1-Y\), up to sign. It is prior coverage, not an addition here. The full ordinary-orbit reconstruction [J] already gives a polynomial row from quantum jets in all noncomplete residue classes, using genuine high colors up to \(HN-1\). Formula (7) instead uses one recurrence row and only \(d\) colors below \(N\); its derivative depth depends on the terminal factor of that specified recurrence. This is different input from the earlier quantitative Mellin theorem. That theorem controls error from an approximate whole source equation, its prefix and pole lattice. Here those hypotheses are replaced by approximations to the actual near-\(N\) jets themselves. Their construction and geometric asymptotics are not supplied. The row is complex and signed: large packet norm does not give a lower bound for its observed sum. No nonzero geometric coefficient or volume theorem follows. All four complete matching texts were read. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. Frozen and public files are unchanged. | Role | Complete source | SHA-256 | | --- | --- | --- | | M, input, 212 lines | [Actual color recurrence and Mellin source](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/mellin_cyclotomic_jet_uniqueness.md) | bf9fc91f4a4795b67b164b2828ebe5109f59fcb97adc2664846a98ee690090f2 | | O, input, 254 lines | [Original ordinary-color bound](ordinary_color_plancherel_bound_audit.md) | 1c8b95921af8da7063d92af35cfcc15756b276fb9c85639fb2ffc3def1f922f0 | | J, coverage, 348 lines | [Full ordinary-orbit jet reconstruction](research_ordinary_orbit_jet_reconstruction.md) | 6c9c3089b93204ae6b7045265ece6deac1552563de806dae3810392c239c028d | | P, coverage, 537 lines | [Peripheral normal source](peripheral_normal_period.md) | 1f2baaedd082b9b8f0b6634c9b2948f4b06c8a31d0869e7a490f66fc13a08964 |

title: Adjacent graph fillings controlled by degree and crossing power
text: # Adjacent graph fillings controlled by degree and crossing power Research proof, 4 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. The original finite source has a nonzero geometric contribution on any fixed graph of same-index edges if \[ n_v^2+d_v^2\ge4096 \quad\hbox{at every selected vertex }v. \tag{1} \] Here \(d_v\) is the actual incidence degree, with loops counted twice, and \(n_v\) is the original fixed integer crossing power. Signs may differ and zero powers are allowed. Selected vertices may be adjacent; all vertices may be selected. No edge is duplicated to increase a degree. This is a theorem for the specified original finite source. An arbitrary graph is not thereby identified with a knot presentation. For an original marked circle-tree realization, the positive shapes and original period equations below supply the analytic input to its separate marked-completion theorem. ## 1. The exact source and the conclusion Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a fixed finite undirected graph, allowing loops and repeated edges. Choose a nonempty selected set \(I\); no selected vertex is isolated. Unselected angles are initially zero. Use the full original Newton kernel and Hermite trace \[ \begin{split} K_N(t,u)&=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos u),\\ Z_{\Gamma,I,N} &=\left(\prod_{v\in I}\phi_N^{(w_v)}\right) \left[\prod_{v\in I}R(w_v)^{n_v} \prod_{\{v,w\}\in E}K_N(t_v,t_w)\right], \qquad w_v=-2\cos t_v . \end{split} \tag{2} \] Every product is formed before taking the trace in its variable. All double-root first normals and the odd simple-root term are retained. A loop contributes \(K_N(t_v,t_v)\) once. Put \(m=|I|\), \(e=|E|\), \(R_v=(n_v^2+d_v^2)^{1/2}\), and \[ \Phi_{\boldsymbol\chi}(\mathbf t) =\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E}\psi(t_v,t_w) +\sum_{v\in I} \left(\frac{in_vt_v^2}{4\pi}-i\chi_vt_v\right). \tag{3} \] The edge phase has its original normalization \(\psi(0,0)=M_\infty=4G/\pi\) and \(\psi_t(t,u)=-\operatorname{asinh}(\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2))/\pi\). The charge cube in (3) is used only to compare stationary actions; no quantum source at nonintegral charge is assumed. **Theorem 1.** Assume (1). The whole cube \(\boldsymbol\chi\in[0,1]^I\) has a unique critical point in \(|t_v|\le1/10\), continuing from the complete point. Its original edge shapes are positive. At unit charges write \(t^*=\mathbf t(\mathbf1)\), \(\Phi=\Phi_{\mathbf1}\), \(M=\Re\Phi(t^*)\), and \(\mathcal H=-\Phi''(t^*)\). Along all sufficiently large integer levels, at both parities, \[ \begin{split} Z_{\Gamma,I,N} &=\varepsilon_N N^{3(m-e)/2} \mathcal A\,e^{N\Phi(t^*)}(1+O(N^{-1})),\\ \varepsilon_N &=\prod_{v\in I} \exp\!\left(\frac{\pi i n_v(N-1)^2}{4N}\right),\\ \mathcal A &=\left(\frac{i}{\pi}\right)^m(2\pi)^{m/2} \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{v\in I}\sin t_v^* \prod_{\{v,w\}\in E}a_e(t_v^*,t_w^*)} {\sqrt{\det\mathcal H}}\ne0 . \end{split} \tag{4} \] The Gaussian branch is the one on complex symmetric matrices with positive definite real part. The expansion has every fixed inverse-power order. It continues to a fixed small complex neighborhood of all complete outside colors, with all fixed ordinary spectral derivatives. The constants and first valid level may depend on the fixed graph and powers. The explicit geometric and comparison bounds below do not depend on graph size. In particular every selected vertex of actual degree at least \(64\) permits any fixed integer power, including zero, even next to other selected vertices. ## 2. Unit-charge contraction weighted by the actual degree For one incidence define the removable holomorphic function \[ f(t,u)=\frac{2\operatorname{asinh}(\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2))}{t}-1. \tag{5} \] On \(|t|,|u|\le1/5\), elementary disk estimates give \[ \begin{split} |\tan(t/2)-t/2|&\le |t|^3/16, &|\tan(t/2)|&\le(51/100)|t|,\\ |\cos(u/2)-1|&\le |u|^2/7, &|\cos(u/2)|&\le101/100,\\ |\operatorname{asinh}z-z|&\le |z|^3/5 &&(|z|\le11/100). \end{split} \tag{6} \] For completeness, on the disk of radius \(1/10\), \(|\tan z|\le(51/50)|z|\) follows from \(|\sin z|\le\sinh|z|\) and \(|\cos z|\ge2-\cosh|z|\). Integrating \(\tan^2z\) gives the first bound. The positive cosh series gives the cosine bounds. Finally integrate the binomial derivative bound \[ |(1+z^2)^{-1/2}-1| \le\frac{|z|^2}{2(1-(11/100)^2)^{3/2}}. \] The asinh argument in (5) has magnitude at most \((51/100)(1/5)(101/100)<11/100\). Consequently \[ |f(t,u)| \le\left[\frac18+\frac25 \left(\frac{51}{100}\frac{101}{100}\right)^3\right]|t|^2 +\frac{51}{350}|u|^2 <\frac13\max(|t|,|u|)^2 . \tag{7} \] Set \(r=1/10\), \(\epsilon=1/300\), and \(C_v(\mathbf t)=\sum_{w\sim v}(1+f(t_v,t_w))\), with one summand per incidence. On the polydisk \(|t_v|\le r\), \[ |C_v-d_v|\le d_v\epsilon,\qquad \sum_w|\partial_{t_w}C_v|\le\frac4{15}d_v. \tag{8} \] For the derivative apply Cauchy's inequality in each incidence argument, using (7) on the doubled disk. Each partial derivative is at most \(4r/3\). A loop adds both derivatives, exactly as its two incidences require. The stationary equations are precisely \[ t_v=\mathcal T_v(\mathbf t) =\frac{2\pi\chi_v}{n_v+iC_v(\mathbf t)}. \tag{9} \] By (1) and (8), \[ \begin{split} |n_v+iC_v|&\ge(1-\epsilon)R_v,\\ |\mathcal T_v|&\le\frac{825}{8372}<\frac1{10},\\ \|D\mathcal T\|_\infty &\le\frac{16500}{625807}<\frac1{32}. \end{split} \tag{10} \] These rational bounds use \(R_v\ge64\), \(d_v\le R_v\), and \(\pi<22/7\). Banach's theorem proves uniqueness and holomorphic local dependence on the charge parameters. Write \(C_v=A_v+iB_v\). Since \(A_v\ge(299/300)d_v>0\), \[ \begin{split} H_v:=-\Im t_v &=\frac{2\pi\chi_v A_v} {(n_v-B_v)^2+A_v^2},\\ 0<H_v&<\frac{32}{5}\frac{\chi_vd_v}{R_v^2} \le\frac{\chi_v}{10} \quad(\chi_v>0),\\ t_v&=0\quad(\chi_v=0). \end{split} \tag{11} \] The coefficient before \(d_v/R_v^2\) is at most \(567600/89401<32/5\). For a subset \(S\subseteq I\), set its charges to zero. The exact stationary derivative \(\partial_{\chi_v}\Re\Phi_{\boldsymbol\chi}=\Im t_v=-H_v\) then gives \[ 0\le M(\boldsymbol\chi^S)-M(\boldsymbol\chi) \le\frac{16}{5}\sum_{v\in S}\frac{d_v\chi_v^2}{R_v^2} \le\frac1{1280}\sum_{v\in S}d_v. \tag{12} \] The edge shapes are those continued from completeness. For \(|t_v|\le1/10\), \(|\tan(t_v/2)|\le51/1000\). Thus for each edge the branch \(q_e=\sqrt{1+\tan^2(t_v/2)+\tan^2(t_w/2)}\) has real part greater than \(99/100\), while the Euclidean norm of the two real tangent parts is less than \(1/10\). The [positive-edge criterion](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md) therefore proves positivity of all original edge shapes. The continuation (9) fixes the original logarithmic periods, including at zero powers and without a complete outside vertex. ## 3. Refined edge estimates on the actual contour heights The retained contour uses the larger real range \[ |\Re t|,|\Re u|\le\pi/2,\qquad |\Im t|,|\Im u|\le1/10 . \tag{13} \] Write \(w=\tan(t/2)\), \(z=\tan(u/2)\) and \[ K(t,u)=-2\pi\psi''(t,u) =\frac1s\begin{pmatrix}1+w^2&-wz\\-wz&1+z^2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad s^2=1+w^2+z^2. \tag{14} \] The branch continues from \(s=1\). On (13), \(|w|,|z|\le1\) and \(|\Im w|,|\Im z|\le1/10\). Also \(|\partial_{\Im t}\tan(t/2)|\le1\). Here is a direct quantitative comparison with real angles. Put \(A=|w|^2\), \(B=|z|^2\). Differentiating (14) gives \[ \|\partial_wK\|_F^2 \le\frac{A(1+A+2B)^2+(2B+A)(1+B)^2}{|s|^6} \le\frac{2}{(24/25)^3}<\left(\frac85\right)^2. \tag{15} \] Indeed \(|s|^2\ge(24/25)(1+A+B)\), and \[ \begin{split} 2(1+A+B)^3 &-\{A(1+A+2B)^2+(2B+A)(1+B)^2\}\\ &=A^3+2A^2B+4A^2+AB^2+6AB+4A+2B^2+4B+2\ge0. \end{split} \] The same estimate holds for \(\partial_zK\). Integrating the two vertical parameter changes gives \(\|K(t,u)-K(\Re t,\Re u)\|_2\le8/25\). At real angles the two eigenvalues of (14) are \(s\) and \(1/s\), with \(1\le s\le\sqrt3\). Since \(1/\sqrt3>4/7\) and \(\sqrt3<7/4\), we obtain \[ \Re K\succeq\frac14 I,\qquad \|\Re K\|_2<\frac{21}{10},\qquad \|\Im K\|_2\le\frac8{25}. \tag{16} \] These estimates hold for either sign of each angle and height. Sum (16) over the actual edges and extend selected vectors by zero at outside vertices. For real vectors \(a,b\), set \(A_2=\sum_vd_va_v^2\), \(B_2=\sum_vd_vb_v^2\). The same inequalities hold in this degree-weighted norm, by Cauchy--Schwarz over incidences. Loops use the same coordinate twice and are already included. ## 4. Every original mixed trace current has a gap Choose the largest physical midpoint \(T_N\le\pi/2\). For all sufficiently large \(N\), \(T_N\ge3/2\). Apply the exact Hermite rectangle identity at each retained selected variable, with lower height \(-H_v\). For a vertical coordinate use the side \(\sigma_vT_N\), where \(\sigma_v=\operatorname{sgn}(n_v)\) for \(n_v\ne0\) and \(\sigma_v=1\) for \(n_v=0\). The exact side-reflection factor \(\sigma_v\) is retained. For a nonempty set \(S\) of vertical coordinates, write \(t-t^*=a+ib\). Then \(b_v=0\) outside \(S\), while \[ |a_v|>7/5,\qquad 0\le b_v\le1/5,\qquad n_va_vb_v\ge0 \quad(v\in S). \tag{17} \] The last inequality follows from \(|t_v^*|<1/10<T_N\); it does not require a sign assertion for \(\Re t_v^*\), and it includes \(n_v=0\). Let \(\mathcal E_S\) be the actual exponential modulus of the mixed current. Its vertical trace penalty is \(-|h_v|\), so \(\mathcal E_S\le\Re\Phi(t)\). Taylor's formula at the full complex critical point, keeping the chirp exactly, gives \[ \begin{split} \mathcal E_S-M &\le\frac1{4\pi} \left[-\frac14A_2+\frac{21}{10}B_2 +\frac{16}{25}\sqrt{A_2B_2}\right] -\frac1{2\pi}\sum_vn_va_vb_v\\ &\le-\frac{A_2}{32\pi}+\frac{3B_2}{4\pi} -\frac1{2\pi}\sum_vn_va_vb_v\\ &<-\frac1{32\pi}\sum_{v\in S}d_v <-\frac1{110}\sum_{v\in S}d_v. \end{split} \tag{18} \] The Young inequality used here is \((16/25)\sqrt{AB}\le A/8+(512/625)B\), and \(21/10+512/625<3\). The final loss follows from \(49/800-3/100=1/32\). The straight segment from \(t^*\) to every mixed point stays in (13), so all averaged Hessian estimates used in (18) are valid. No favorable chirp is needed at a zero-power vertex. The [full wide-kernel theorem](research_bare_kernel_thin_rectangle.md#6-the-full-rectangle-through-real-angle-pi-over-two) turns (18) into a bound for each actual finite mixed integrand. The exact trace identity is applied to the whole incident product, including loops, and carries all first normals. No independent edge contour or discarded alias is introduced. ## 5. Removing original physical rows before the contour Partition the original derivative-sampling trace by its set \(S\) of vertices whose physical angles lie outside \((-T_N,T_N)\). For a nonempty \(S\), keep its literal crossing values and normals, and deform only the remaining traces at the stationary point whose charges on \(S\) are zero. The [centered incidence estimates](research_path_mixed_trace_currents.md#8-a-stronger-centered-loss-for-a-removed-incidence) give a loss \(21/200\) at each removed incidence. They hold on the full retained box, including all fixed ordinary derivatives. When both endpoints of an edge are removed, their two losses are both retained. The strict reserve in those estimates allows the \(O(N^{-1})\) midpoint shift below \(\pi/2\). A loop at a removed vertex likewise has both losses. Equivalently, Markov's inequality can be applied to its diagonal polynomial, whose degree is at most \(2(N-1)\). After centering, the remaining upper phase is exactly (3) with the removed vertices fixed at zero. The actual degrees retain their incidences to these newly complete vertices. Equation (12) therefore proves \[ \operatorname{rate}(S) \le M(\mathbf1)-\left(\frac{21}{200}-\frac1{1280}\right) \sum_{v\in S}d_v < M(\mathbf1)-\frac1{10}\sum_{v\in S}d_v. \tag{19} \] All crossing values on the physical real grid have modulus one, and their first normals cost only powers of \(N\) for the fixed integer powers. At zero power that crossing normal vanishes. Every mixed ordinary derivative of the fixed incident products also has only polynomial cost. These comparisons retain all physical rows at both level parities. ## 6. The nonzero coefficient and the source scope On the all-horizontal rectangle the real Hessian satisfies \[ \Re[-\Phi''(t)] \succeq\frac1{8\pi} \operatorname{diag}(d_v)>0. \tag{20} \] The real phase is therefore strictly concave, with its unique maximum at \(t^*\). Every fixed complement of its neighborhood has a strict gap. The full wide-kernel expansion supplies the actual nonzero local edge amplitudes. Each horizontal trace has exact prefactor \(iN^2C_{N,n_v}/\pi\) and rational kernel \[ \frac{e^{-iNt_v}} {(1-(-1)^{N-1}e^{-iNt_v})^2}. \tag{21} \] All unit-charge heights in (11) are strictly positive for the fixed graph and powers. Hence the leading Fourier term in (21) has coefficient exactly one, and all its higher charges are exponentially smaller on this same contour. There is no coupon coefficient \(1/2\): the source (2) has no coupon. The product of edge amplitudes and \(\sin t_v^*\) is nonzero. The latter factors cannot vanish because \(H_v>0\) and \(|t_v^*|<1/10\). Equation (20) gives a nonzero complex Gaussian determinant. The powers of \(N\) are \(2m\) from the traces, \(-3e/2\) from the edges and \(-m/2\) from the Gaussian, giving (4). Bounds (18)--(19) prevent the rest of the original source from canceling this term. Higher local expansion orders follow from the same uniform holomorphic kernel expansion. The outside continuation is an estimate on an actual complex neighborhood, not continuation of a bound at one boundary value. Allow each unselected angle to vary in a sufficiently small closed disk \(|u_w|\le r_0<1/10\). The same incidence estimates (7)--(10) apply with these angles fixed; thus the selected critical point is jointly holomorphic, stays in \(|t_v|<1/10\), and has strictly positive depth by (11). On each retained contour every selected and outside argument is in the wide kernel box. The Hessian comparison (16) still applies after putting the displacement zero at the outside vertices. For an edge meeting a removed physical row, the complex selected endpoint in the centered incidence lemma may equally be an unselected outside angle. Its bound is exactly \(\Re\psi(0,u_w)-21/200\), with every fixed ordinary derivative. Edges with two removed ends use the two-endpoint version. Thus (19) holds with these actual complex outside parameters and the corresponding continued stationary action. The charge comparison (12) remains valid: \(A_v=\Re C_v>0\) also for these complex fixed outside angles. No estimate is inferred merely from the complete value. The same exact trace and normal bookkeeping is recorded for the complementary power-degree regime in [the network source theorem](research_degree_controlled_network_source.md). All inequalities have strict reserves. For the fixed graph and powers, the unit-charge depths have a positive lower bound on a smaller compact outside polydisk, so all Fourier-charge errors remain exponentially small there. The resulting phase, amplitude and normalized remainder are holomorphic and separately even in every outside angle, by the exact source symmetry and uniqueness of the small stationary branch. They therefore descend to holomorphic functions of the ordinary colors \(-2\cos u_w\) near \(-2\). Cauchy's formula on smaller ordinary-color disks gives every fixed normal, including at the ramified complete angle. It does not assert that a derivative of a nonzero amplitude is itself nonzero. The [exact scalar checker](../experiments/check_network_degree_power_source.py) verifies the disk, contraction, matrix and current constants, including the polynomial identity behind (15). Its [saved record](../repro/results/research-network-degree-power-source.json) records the proof and source dependencies. No numerical pattern or norm-to-overlap assumption enters the proof. This criterion extends the isolated high-degree mechanism to adjacent selected vertices in the original finite source. It does not identify arbitrary graphs with knot invariants, combine different edge kernels, or settle all assignments having a vertex that fails (1). ## 7. The original marked circle-tree consequence Suppose now that the graph, page order, disk frames and carriers come from the original ordered circle-tree exterior. Retain its original meridians, disk longitudes, main components and marked annular interfaces. For the actual integer filling coefficients \(p_v\), impose \[ n_v=\eta_v-2p_v,\qquad n_v^2+d_v^2\ge4096, \qquad\hbox{primitive filled curve } \mu_v+p_v\lambda_v^{\mathrm{disk}}. \tag{22} \] No change of peripheral basis is made, including when \(n_v=0\). The positive shapes from Section 2 and the continued unit-charge equations are precisely \[ n_vt_v^*+2i\sum_{w\sim v}r_{vw}(t^*)=2\pi,\qquad \Im t_v^*<0. \tag{23} \] Their logarithmic lifts are fixed along the actual small solution on the whole charge cube. The [positive-point marked-completion theorem](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md) therefore applies to this original marked presentation. If \(Y(\mathbf p)\) is its partial exterior, every main cusp and every unselected auxiliary cusp remains complete, and \(\operatorname{Vol}Y(\mathbf p)=2\pi M\). The edge constants in (3) are included in this absolute equality. **Corollary 2.** If all auxiliary vertices are filled, the original strand tracing gives one main component and no internal closed component, and (22) holds, then the resulting knot satisfies the original full-level Kashaev volume identity \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N} \log|\langle K\rangle_N| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K). \tag{24} \] The leading coefficient is nonzero by (4), with the original carrier and zero-framing unit factors retained. This consequence uses the original circle-tree source identification and literal component tests. It attaches no knot interpretation to an arbitrary graph in Theorem 1, and it does not assert finite exceptions for templates having selected vertices outside (22). ## 8. Mixing the degree and power regimes at adjacent vertices The hypotheses of the two network theorems can also be combined vertex by vertex, with a larger degree-power threshold at vertices of the second type. This is a new mixed statement, not an inference from the two separate theorems. **Theorem 3.** In the exact graph source (2), suppose each selected vertex is assigned one of the following types: \[ \begin{array}{ll} P:& |n_v|\ge\max(8,4d_v),\\ D:& R_v=\sqrt{n_v^2+d_v^2}\ge512. \end{array} \tag{25} \] Then the nonzero original source expansion (4), at both parities and to every fixed order, holds. Its complex outside-color continuation and all ordinary normals hold as well. The original marked circle-tree conclusion of Section 7 holds with (25) in place of (22)'s size condition. Degrees are always the original incidence degrees. In particular a high-degree vertex with any fixed power, including zero, can be adjacent to vertices satisfying the first condition. No topology is changed to meet (25). **A hybrid contraction.** Use the product domain \[ \mathcal B_v= \begin{cases} \{t:|\Re t|\le1,\ |\Im t|\le1/3\},&v\text{ of type }P,\\ \{t:|t|\le1/40\},&v\text{ of type }D. \end{cases} \tag{26} \] Every incidence is in the first, larger box. On this box the one-edge estimates in Section 2 of [the power-dominated network proof](research_degree_controlled_network_source.md) give \(|K_{vv}-1|<2/5\), \(|K_{vv}|+|K_{vw}|<86/45\), \(|\tan(t/2)|<3/5\), and \(|\Im\tan(t/2)|<1/4\). Define the removable quotient \[ C_v=\sum_{w\sim v}\int_0^1 K_{vv}(\sigma t_v,t_w)\,d\sigma, \qquad |C_v-d_v|<\frac25d_v. \tag{27} \] This is the same \(C_v=2\sum r_{vw}/t_v\) as in (9). For a derivative bound, the polynomial calculation (15), now using \(|\Im\tan(t/2)|<1/4\), gives \(\|\partial_w K\|_F^2\le2/(3/4)^3<(9/4)^2\). Also \[ |\partial_t\tan(t/2)| =\frac1{\cosh\Im t+\cos\Re t}<\frac23, \] since \(\cos1>1/2\). Hence \(\|\partial_t K\|_F<3/2\). The two derivatives of an incidence in (27) are bounded by \(3/4\) and \(3/2\), respectively, so \[ \sum_w|\partial_{t_w}C_v|<\frac94d_v. \tag{28} \] For a loop both derivatives are included in each of its two incidences. This is also the correct row count for the original period equation and its Hessian. At a \(P\) vertex use the direct-return map \(2\pi\chi_v/n_v-(2i/n_v)\sum r_{vw}\). The cited proof maps into the interior of its box and bounds its Jacobian row by \(43/90\), independently of the neighbor types. At a \(D\) vertex use the quotient map (9). Equations (27)--(28) give \[ \begin{split} |n_v+iC_v|&>\frac35 R_v,\\ |\mathcal T_v|&<\frac{55}{2688}<\frac1{40},\\ \sum_w|\partial_{t_w}\mathcal T_v| &<\frac{25\pi}{2R_v} \le\frac{550}{7168}<\frac1{12}. \end{split} \tag{29} \] Thus the hybrid map is a contraction on (26), for every \(\boldsymbol\chi\in[0,1]^I\). Both formulas solve exactly the same original period equations, not modified vertex equations. They also give holomorphic dependence in a neighborhood of the charge cube. Zero charge gives zero angle; positive charge gives strictly positive depth because \(\Re C_v>3d_v/5\). The \(P\)-vertex estimates remain \(|t_v|<9/10\), \(H_v<3/10\), and \(H_v\le U_{|n_v|,d_v}\chi_v\), with \(U_{|n_v|,d_v}/(2d_v)<3/40\). At a \(D\) vertex, besides \(|t_v|<1/40\), \[ H_v\le\frac{70\pi}{9}\frac{d_v}{R_v^2}\chi_v, \qquad \frac{35\pi}{9R_v^2}<\frac3{40}. \tag{30} \] Consequently completing any selected subset costs less than \((3/40)\sum d_v\) in stationary real action. Positivity of all original edge shapes follows on the larger box just as in the cited network proof: the sum of the two squared imaginary tangent parts is less than \(1/8\), so the positive-edge criterion holds. Continuation from zero fixes all original logarithmic periods. **A stronger wide-rectangle Hessian bound.** On \(|\Re t|,|\Re u|\le\pi/2\), \(|\Im t|,|\Im u|\le3/10\), one has \[ \Re K\succ\frac13 I, \qquad \|\Re K\|_2,\ \|\Im K\|_2<\frac{10}{3}. \tag{31} \] Here is a direct proof. Put \(w=\tan(t/2),z=\tan(u/2)\), \(X=(\Re w,\Re z)\), \(Y=(\Im w,\Im z)\), \(x=|X|^2\le2\), \(y=|Y|^2<9/50\), and \(\alpha=\Re\sqrt{1+w^2+z^2}>0\). The exact determinant/trace formula in [the edge-Hessian proof](research_edge_hessian_and_phase_response.md) gives \[ \lambda_{\min}(\Re K) \ge\frac{\alpha^2-\{\Im(w\bar z)\}^2} {\alpha(|s|^2+1)} \ge\frac{(41/50)\sqrt{1+x}}{2+x+9/50}> \frac13. \tag{32} \] Indeed \(\alpha^2\ge1+x-y\), \(\{\Im(w\bar z)\}^2=xy-(X\cdot Y)^2\), \(\alpha^2\le1+x\), and \(|s|^2\le1+x+y\). The last one-variable ratio has a single interior maximum; its values at \(x=0,2\) exceed \(1/3\). At \(x=2\) it suffices that \(\sqrt3>209/123\), which follows by squaring.
