At the endpoints the continued phase has \[ F(0;t,0)=0,\qquad F(1/2;t,0)=it/2 . \tag{13} \] The second equality uses \(J_+(-t/(2\pi))=-J(t/(2\pi))-it/2\). The real endpoint rates are therefore \(0\) and \(H/2\). The complete-edge gap gives \(\Re\psi(t,0)>H+1/500\), uniformly on \(\mathcal T\). ## 3. The reflected contour controls the lower lattice alias For fixed \(x\in(0,1/2)\) and \(0\le v\le h(x)\), define \[ D_x(v)=\Re F(x-iv;t,0)-\Re F(x+iv;t,0). \tag{14} \] The complete factor \(b(y,0)\) cancels in this difference. **Lemma 3.** One has \(D_x(v)<2\pi v\) for \(v>0\). *Proof.* Write \(\cos t=c+id\), where \(c,d>0\), and put \[ R_v=\cos(2\pi x)\cosh(2\pi v)+c,\qquad B_v=\sin(2\pi x)\sinh(2\pi v). \tag{15} \] Differentiating (14), the sine-denominator arguments cancel and give \[ D_x'(v)=\arg\{R_v+i(d+B_v)\} +\arg\{R_v+i(d-B_v)\}. \tag{16} \] Both arguments start in \((0,\pi)\) and are continued from \(v=0\). There is no zero in the range under consideration by (12). The first argument always belongs to \((0,\pi)\). If the second remains at most \(\pi\), their sum is less than \(2\pi\). Otherwise \(R_v<0\), \(B_v>d\), and its continued argument is \(\pi+\arctan((B_v-d)/(-R_v))\). The first argument is then \(\pi-\arctan((B_v+d)/(-R_v))\), so their sum is again strictly less than \(2\pi\). There is no additional winding: for \(x\le1/4\) the real part \(R_v\) is positive; for \(x>1/4\) both the real and imaginary parts of \(R_v+i(d-B_v)\) decrease with \(v\). Since \(D_x(0)=0\), integration proves the claim. \(\square\) Consequently the lower reflected ray, after its exact cotangent penalty, satisfies \[ \Re F(x-ih(x);t,0)-2\pi h(x) <\Re F(x+ih(x);t,0)\le\Re\psi(t,0). \tag{17} \] The upper nonconstant cotangent term has the additional penalty \(2\pi h(x)>0\). These strict inequalities give uniform gaps on every compact subarc, uniformly for \(t\in\mathcal T\). ## 4. The original finite contour and both endpoint sectors Choose fixed \(0<\alpha<\beta<1/2\), sufficiently close to \(0\) and \(1/2\), respectively. By (13), continuity, and compactness, the two short endpoint arcs, the two vertical connectors between the ray and its reflection at these cuts, and the omitted real intervals all have rate strictly below \(\Re\psi(t,0)\). The cuts contain the selected saddle for every \(t\in\mathcal T\). Move them by \(O(N^{-1})\) to half-grid lines; all strict gaps persist. Use the exact factorial interpolation \[ B_N(y,t)=\frac{N} {G_N(N(1/2-y+t/(2\pi))-1/2) G_N(N(1/2-y-t/(2\pi))-1/2)G_N(Ny)^2}. \tag{18} \] This sampling equality is an ordinary entire identity in \(t\), not merely equality of physical jets. Indeed the [exact factorial reflection identity](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/exact_factorial_interpolation_and_complex_contours.md) \(G_N(z)G_N(N-1-z)=N\) holds identically. Applying the integer shift identity to the two factors in this product gives \[ B_N(j/N,t)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{\ell=0}^{j-1} \{2\cos((2\ell+1)\pi/N)+2\cos t\} =e_j(-2\cos t). \] In particular \(B_N(0,t)=1\) exactly, for arbitrary complex \(t\). The defining Gamma product makes (18) holomorphic on the region between these two truncated rays: the reciprocal-factorial zeros at negative integer arguments create no poles, and the first positive factorial zeros lie outside the region. The [uniform factorial bounds](research_uniform_factorial_and_boundary_decay.md) apply on the entire contour. When \(\Re(1/2-y-t/(2\pi))<0\), its imaginary part is positive throughout this region, by (12). Use the upper continuation and the exact identity \[ \frac1{G_N(Nw-1/2)} =\frac{e^{-i\pi Nw}}N(1+e^{2\pi iNw})G_N(-Nw-1/2). \tag{19} \] Both terms are included. Their sum is bounded by the continued phase in (2); no value is assigned by discarding a Newton zero. Near the saddle all factorial real parts are positive. The usual full factorial expansion there is \[ B_N(y,t)B_N(y,0)= \frac{e^{NF(y;t,0)}}{4N^2\sin^2(\pi y)} (1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{20} \] For any prescribed further order, apply the sectorial Stirling formula through that order to each Gamma factor in the defining product. On this compact saddle neighborhood the arguments \(Nw\) and \(N(k\pm w)\) stay in fixed sectors away from the negative real axis and zero. The remainder after the \(N^{-(2q-1)}\) term is bounded by \(C_qN^{-(2q+1)}k^{-(2q+1)}\) for the \(k\)-th product factor. It is summable, while the finitely many initial factors have the same uniform sectorial bound. This extends (20) to every fixed order. Only the exact upper bounds, not this relative expansion, are used on the remaining contour and its reflected factorial faces. Enclose exactly the retained integers by \(\pi N\cot(\pi Ny)\). On the upper and lower rays this equals \(\mp i\pi N+O(N e^{-2\pi N|\Im y|})\). Equations (17) and (13) bound every nonconstant term and every vertical current below the selected rate. The two constant horizontal terms combine to \(+N\) times the oriented principal wire integral; Cauchy deformation between the rays introduces only the already bounded endpoint connectors. Lemma 2 supplies its unique strict maximum and nonzero Gaussian coefficient. Thus the actual retained sum has (3). For completeness the omitted original low indices satisfy, uniformly up to both endpoints, \[ |e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2)| \le N^C\exp\{N\Re F(j/N;t,0)\}. \tag{21} \] This follows directly from the same midpoint factorial bounds, now keeping \(G_N(Nj/N)\) exact at \(j=0\). Replacing \(J(x+1/(2N))\) by \(J(x)\) costs \(O(\log N)\) in the exponent uniformly for \(0\le x\le1/2\). The zero or half-integer final factorial argument is covered by the midpoint estimate. Hence (21) covers both possible final low indices, and the endpoint gaps prove the omitted finite sums are exponentially smaller. ## 5. A fixed complex outside neighborhood and the full kernel All contour and tail inequalities just proved are strict on compact sets. The real upper exponent of the exact reciprocal factorial is continuous across zero and across either side of the negative real axis. Therefore the same bounds persist uniformly for \(t\) in a slightly larger complex neighborhood and \(|u|<\epsilon\), after decreasing \(\epsilon>0\). For the real omitted indices this uses the continuous factorial upper exponent, not an analytic continuation of their errors from \(u=0\). On the retained contour the outside factorial arguments have positive real part if \(\epsilon\) is small enough. The selected saddle moves holomorphically. Locally deform the principal ray through this saddle; outside a fixed small saddle neighborhood all gaps persist, and inside it the nonzero quadratic derivative (7) gives the ordinary holomorphic Gaussian expansion. This proves (3) for \(L_N(t,u)\), uniformly with every fixed inverse-power order. The exact contour and normalized errors are holomorphic, so Cauchy estimates retain fixed derivatives on smaller neighborhoods. Finally the [original radical Fourier estimate](research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md#7-fourier-bounds-for-the-original-radical-polynomials) and its polynomial degree give \[ |K_N(t,u)-L_N(t,u)| \le N^2 e^{(N-1)(|\Im t|+|\Im u|)}. \tag{22} \] By the complete-edge gap and continuity, \(\Re\psi(t,u)>|\Im t|+|\Im u|+c\) on a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood, for some \(c>0\). Thus (22) is exponentially small relative to the packet, with all fixed derivatives after shrinking the neighborhoods. This establishes Theorem 1 for the full original kernel. In particular the extension preserves the outside ordinary normal: even holomorphy in \(u\) descends through \(-2\cos u=-2+u^2+O(u^4)\). No joint-cycle lower bound is asserted. The conclusion supplies an independently normalized free-boundary edge factor for a subsequent original trace or Fourier contraction. For a fixed integer pair, the selected charge-cube image is compact. Its nonzero angles satisfy (1), while its zero angles have neighborhoods covered by the [thin-rectangle kernel theorem](research_bare_kernel_thin_rectangle.md). A finite cover therefore supplies one common outside neighborhood for this fixed pair's entire charge cube. This conclusion still concerns the individual edge kernel. ## 6. Independent finite normalization record The [focused checker](../experiments/check_pair_free_boundary_kernel.py) verifies (9) and the derivative identities symbolically. It compares the finite Barnes-product factorial interpolation with original Newton products and ordinary normals at genuinely complex selected and outside angles, through both parities. Its separate comparisons of the full and low finite sums with (3) are normalization diagnostics, not the proof of a uniform asymptotic. The [saved record](../repro/results/research-pair-free-boundary-kernel.json) includes the script, direct dependency, and proof hashes. ## 7. Whole outside-period decay and a complex strip The same actual contours give a bound useful before a subsequent trace or Fourier contraction. This requires a global factorial estimate, not merely positivity of the finite physical samples. **Theorem 4.** After shrinking \(V\) around \(\mathcal T\), there are constants \(c,B,h_0>0\) and \(C,A_0<\infty\) such that \[ |K_N(t,u+iv)|\le C N^{A_0} \exp N\{\Re\psi(t,0)-c(1-\cos u)+Bv^2\}, \quad -\pi\le u\le\pi,\quad |v|\le h_0,\quad t\in V . \tag{23} \] All fixed selected-variable and outside-angle derivatives obey the same bound after increasing the polynomial power and shrinking the parameter neighborhoods. This includes fixed ordinary outside-color normals at the complete point and throughout the real color interval. *Proof of the real-period bound.* Keep the finite cuts and the upper and lower contours of Section 4. Every retained contour point satisfies \(\alpha/2<\Re y<(1/2+\beta)/2<1/2\) and a uniform height bound. The exact [factorial boundary inequality](research_uniform_factorial_and_boundary_decay.md#4-decay-in-the-real-boundary-angle) therefore gives a common \(c_1>0\) with \[ |B_N(y,u)|\le \frac{C}{N} \exp N\{\Re b(y,0)-c_1(1-\cos u)\}, \qquad -\pi\le u\le\pi . \tag{24} \] This inequality holds on both rays and on every connector. For all these real \(u\), the shifted factorial real parts stay in a fixed subinterval of \((-1,1)\). If a shifted argument is negative, its exact reciprocal reflection retains both exponential terms, as in (19). The real upper exponent uses the side approached by that argument; its boundary values agree at the negative real axis. Thus (24) remains valid at its zeros and on its reflected sectors. Multiply (24) by the old bound for \(B_N(y,t)\). Every principal contour integral, every cotangent alias and every vertical current from Section 4 keeps its old exponent, with the additional loss \(c_1(1-\cos u)\). In particular this argument bounds the principal integral even when its saddle moves far from the complete one. For the omitted original low indices, the exact positive Fourier expansion of the [low Newton polynomials](research_zero_power_internal_boundary_theorem.md#2-positive-laurent-coefficients-and-angular-decrease) implies \[ |e_j(-2\cos u)|\le e_j(-2),\qquad 2j<N,\quad u\in\mathbb R. \tag{25} \] The condition includes the final low index at both parities. Their old finite-tail gap therefore remains valid throughout the real outside period. The radical bound (22) likewise has its old strict gap when \(u\) is real. If \(\delta>0\) is the smaller of these gaps, choose \(c_2\le\min(c_1,\delta/4)\). Since \(1-\cos u\le2\), these two error sectors also satisfy \[ |K_N(t,u)|\le C N^{A_0} e^{N\{\Re\psi(t,0)-c_2(1-\cos u)\}} . \tag{26} \] This proves the real-period assertion with the original factorial currents and the full radical included. *Proof of the strip bound.* Near \(u=0\), Theorem 1 and the original phase derivative give \[ \psi(t,z)-\psi(t,0)=-\frac{\cos(t/2)}{4\pi}z^2+O(z^4). \tag{27} \] The real part of \(\cos(t/2)\) is bounded below by a positive constant on the chosen compact \(t\)-domain. Young's inequality for the mixed \(uv\) term in (27), followed by decreasing the neighborhood, gives \[ \Re\{\psi(t,u+iv)-\psi(t,0)\} \le-\kappa u^2+B_0v^2 \tag{28} \] for some \(\kappa>0\). The nonzero bounded amplitude and relative error in (3) prove (23) on this local neighborhood. For the complementary real angles use the actual finite Laurent degree. Put \(f_N(z)=e^{-N\psi(t,0)}K_N(t,z)\), of angular degree at most \(D=N-1\). The function \(Z^D f_N(z)\), \(Z=e^{iz}\), is a polynomial in \(Z\). The subharmonic Poisson bound in the disk, applied to (26), and the analogous reciprocal polynomial for the other half-plane give \[ \log|f_N(u+iv)|\le \log(CN^{A_0})+D|v| -c_2N\{1-e^{-|v|}\cos u\} \le\log(CN^{A_0})+ N\{-c_2(1-\cos u)+(1+c_2)|v|\}. \tag{29} \] Equivalently, apply the maximum principle to the polynomial \(Z^Df_N(z)\) multiplied by \(e^{-c_2NZ}\): its boundary modulus is at most \(CN^{A_0}e^{-c_2N}\). This proves (29) directly even in the presence of zeros. Outside a fixed smaller interval about zero, \(1-\cos u\) has a positive lower bound. Choose \(h_0>0\) small enough that the last linear cost in (29) is absorbed by half of this angular loss. Combining with (28) proves (23), for \(c\le\min(c_2/2,2\kappa)\) and \(B\ge B_0\). This step uses the finite polynomial on the whole circle, not an analytic continuation of a pointwise asymptotic. Finally, apply Cauchy's formula to the holomorphic normalized function \(e^{-N\psi(t,0)}K_N(t,z)\). Fixed \(t\)-derivatives may use fixed smaller neighborhoods; angle derivatives use circles of radius \(1/N\), on which the exponent in (23) changes by \(O(1)\). Thus only polynomial factors in \(N\) are lost. For ordinary outside-color derivatives use color circles of radius \(O(N^{-2})\): the inverse cosine changes by \(O(N^{-1})\) uniformly on this compact strip, including its two quadratic branch points. The even finite polynomial is single-valued in the color there. Cauchy's formula again costs only powers of \(N\). The selected ordinary normal follows on \(V\) from \(\sin t\ne0\), or from the thin theorem in a neighborhood of a zero charge. \(\square\) The constants in (23) can likewise be made common over the fixed pair's charge cube by the finite cover already described. On its thin neighborhoods of zero charge, apply (24) to the existing thin theorem's finite wire contours; their endpoint and alias gaps, the same low-index positivity, and their radical gap give (26). The local thin packet and (29) then give the identical strip argument there. This supplies the edge estimate and its exact observation normals needed in a composition argument. It does not provide the missing joint trace-cycle coefficient. Evenness and the real coefficients of the original Newton polynomials give the conjugate statements at mirrored selected angles, with the conjugated phase and the same absolute bounds.

title: The pair color lies beyond the half-charge observation contour
text: # The pair color lies beyond the half-charge observation contour Research proof, 3 November 2026. Frozen manuscripts are unchanged. The actual angle at either vertex of a positive complete-ended internal pair lies strictly below and to the right of the corresponding half-charge leaf saddle. Its half-charge action is strictly larger. Both statements follow from the original logarithmic periods and elementary bounds for a single analytic derivative. They do not assume a nonzero coefficient for the filled pair. This supplies the geometric comparison needed to evaluate the [proved half-charge Cauchy observation](research_complete_source_pick_observation.md) at an actual pair color. The exact Cauchy residue and interpolation remainder must still be kept when making that source substitution. ## 1. Original periods and the half-charge reference Fix integer powers \(n,p\ge3\), with unit charges at the two selected vertices and one complete outside endpoint at each. Write their positive angles as \(t=a-iH\) and \(u\). The proved [pair angle bound](research_internal_pair_angle_bound.md), [complete-edge height bound](research_internal_pair_complete_edge_gap.md), and [cosine maximum principle](research_positive_path_real_wire_order.md) give \[ 0<a<\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad 0<H<\frac{107}{100},\qquad |\cos(u/2)|<1. \tag{1} \] The two original returns at \(t\) are \[ r_0(t)=\operatorname{asinh}\tan(t/2),\qquad r_1(t,u)=\operatorname{asinh}\{\tan(t/2)\cos(u/2)\}=k+ig, \quad k>0,\quad |g|<\pi/2. \tag{2} \] Their logarithmic filling equation is \[ nt+2i\{r_0(t)+r_1(t,u)\}=2\pi. \tag{3} \] All branches are the selected ones continued from completeness. Put \[ f_n(z)=nz+2ir_0(z),\qquad S_n(z)=\Psi(z)+\frac{inz^2}{4\pi}-\frac{iz}{2}, \quad \Psi(z)=\psi(z,0). \tag{4} \] The original complete constant is retained in \(\Psi\). In particular \[ S_n'(z)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\{f_n(z)-\pi\},\qquad f_n'(z)=n+i\sec(z/2). \tag{5} \] Let \(t_0=a_0-iH_0\) be the half-charge saddle \[ f_n(t_0)=\pi,\qquad 0<a_0<\pi/3,\quad 0<H_0<2/5,\qquad M_n=\Re S_n(t_0). \tag{6} \] Its existence, uniqueness, branches, and actual observation coefficient are proved in Sections 5–6 of the linked half-charge note. No geometric or source coefficient is selected by an exponentiated equation here. ## 2. Two elementary cones **Lemma 1.** The original internal return in (2) satisfies \[ 0<k<\pi/2+g . \tag{7} \] *Proof.* On (1), \[ |\tan(t/2)|^2 =\frac{\cosh H-\cos a}{\cosh H+\cos a}<1. \] Together with \(|\cos(u/2)|<1\), this gives \[ \sinh^2 k+\sin^2g =|\sinh r_1|^2<1. \tag{8} \] If \(g\le0\), put \(v=\pi/2+g\in(0,\pi/2]\). Then \(\sinh k<\sin v\), so \(k<\operatorname{asinh}(\sin v)<v\). The last strict inequality follows from \(\operatorname{asinh}x<x\) for \(x>0\) and \(\sin v\le v\). If \(g>0\), use \(k<\operatorname{asinh}1<1<\pi/2+g\). This proves (7). \(\square\) **Lemma 2.** Throughout the rectangle \[ 0<a<\pi/2,\qquad 0<H<107/100,\qquad z=a-iH, \] one has \[ \frac67<\Re\sec(z/2)<\frac{10}{7},\qquad 0<-\Im\sec(z/2)<\frac12. \tag{9} \] Consequently, writing \(f_n'(z)=A(z)+iB(z)\), \[ n<A(z)<n+\frac12,\qquad \frac67<B(z)<\frac{10}{7}. \tag{10} \] *Proof.* Set \(c=\cos(a/2)\) and \(v=\sinh(H/2)\). Then \[ \Re\sec(z/2)=\frac{c\sqrt{1+v^2}}{c^2+v^2},\qquad -\Im\sec(z/2)=\frac{\sin(a/2)v}{c^2+v^2}. \tag{11} \] Here \(c>1/\sqrt2\). A geometric majorant for the positive cosh series gives \[ \cosh(H/2)<\cosh(11/20) \le 1+\frac{(11/20)^2}{2\{1-(11/20)^2/12\}} =\frac{5405}{4679}<\frac76. \tag{12} \] The majorant bounds each ratio after the quadratic term by \((11/20)^2/12\). Hence \(v^2<13/36<1/2<c^2\). The first expression in (11), at fixed \(v\), decreases with \(c\) because its derivative has the sign of \(v^2-c^2\). It is therefore at least \(1/\sqrt{1+v^2}>6/7\). It is at most \(1/c<\sqrt2<10/7\): after multiplication by the positive denominators this uses \(c^2(\sqrt{1+v^2}-1)\le v^2\). Finally \(c^2+v^2\ge2cv\), so the second expression in (11) is at most \(\tan(a/2)/2<1/2\). All its factors are positive. This proves (9) and (10). \(\square\) ## 3. Position and a quantitative action gap **Theorem 3.** For the actual pair angle \(t\), put \[ t-t_0=d-ih . \] Then \[ d>0,\qquad h>0, \tag{13} \] and the half-charge actions obey \[ \boxed{\quad \Re S_n(t)-M_n >\frac{d^2}{98\pi}+\frac{3h^2}{14\pi}>0 . \quad} \tag{14} \] The corresponding statement holds at the other vertex with power \(p\). *Proof.* By the exact logarithmic equation (3), \[ f_n(t)-f_n(t_0) =\pi+2g-2ik=R-iK,\qquad R=2(\pi/2+g),\quad K=2k. \tag{15} \] Lemma 1 gives \(0<K<R\). The straight segment from \(t_0\) to \(t\) lies in the rectangle of Lemma 2. Put \[ \overline A+i\overline B =\int_0^1 f_n'(t_0+s(t-t_0))\,ds. \] The bar here means an average, not complex conjugation. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[ d=\frac{\overline A R-\overline B K} {\overline A^2+\overline B^2}>0,\qquad h=\frac{\overline B R+\overline A K} {\overline A^2+\overline B^2}>0 . \tag{16} \] For the first sign use \(\overline A>n\ge3>10/7>\overline B\) and \(K<R\). Moreover \[ \frac hd>\frac{\overline B}{\overline A} >\frac{6}{7(n+1/2)}. \tag{17} \] Since \(S_n'(t_0)=0\), integrating (5) twice gives the exact identity \[ S_n(t)-S_n(t_0)=\frac{i(d-ih)^2}{2\pi} \int_0^1(1-s)f_n'(t_0+s(t-t_0))\,ds. \tag{18} \] Write the last integral as \(\widetilde A+i\widetilde B\). From (10), \(\widetilde A>n/2\) and \(3/7<\widetilde B<5/7\). Taking real parts of (18) and using (17) therefore gives \[ \begin{split} \Re\{S_n(t)-S_n(t_0)\} &=\frac{2\widetilde A dh+ \widetilde B(h^2-d^2)}{2\pi}\\ &>\frac{n-5/2}{14\pi(n+1/2)}\,d^2 +\frac{3}{14\pi}\,h^2\\ &\ge\frac{d^2}{98\pi}+\frac{3h^2}{14\pi}, \end{split} \tag{19} \] where the final comparison uses \(n\ge3\). This proves the theorem. \(\square\) For each fixed pair the right side of (14) is a fixed positive number. By continuity, a smaller positive gap persists on a fixed complex neighborhood of its selected angle. No uniform positive gap as the powers tend to infinity is asserted. The position statement is also exactly the one needed by the Cauchy observation contour. Its angular rectangle has real ends tending to \(\pm\pi/2\) and imaginary heights \(\pm H_0\). The two preimages \(t,-t\) of the pair color \(-2\cos t\) lie strictly outside that rectangle, because \(H>H_0\). They remain separated from it on a fixed neighborhood. There are no further preimages in that angular period. Thus an exact residue formula for evaluation at this color uses its exterior case, not the case where the evaluation pole is enclosed and cancels the direct term. These statements compare a specified original pair angle with a specified original-source observation action. They do not identify the coefficient of the full signed pair contraction. In particular the complementary-time observations, the shared wire, and all ordinary boundary normals must still be retained in that contraction. ## 4. The actual local normal defect at even levels Here is the source consequence, using the exact residue formula and exterior observation packet proved independently in [the observation note, equation (34) and Corollary 4](research_complete_source_pick_observation.md#complex-colors-and-the-exact-normal-defect). At \(N=2m\), put \(Q(w)=2T_m(w/2)\), let \[ h_{n,N}(w) =e^{inN\arccos(-w/2)^2/(4\pi)}\mathcal L_N(w), \] and let \(\mathcal I_{n,N}\) be its ordinary value interpolant of degree less than \(m\) at the distinct physical roots. The holomorphic normal defect is \[ \mathscr D_{n,N}(w) =\frac{h_{n,N}(w)-\mathcal I_{n,N}(w)}{Q(w)}. \tag{20} \] It retains the actual first normals through \(h'_{n,N}(c_a)-\mathcal I'_{n,N}(c_a) =Q'(c_a)\mathscr D_{n,N}(c_a)\). The original crossing scalar multiplies both sides when restored. For every fixed pair in Theorem 3, there are a fixed complex neighborhood of its angle \(t\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[ \begin{split} \mathscr D_{n,N}(-2\cos z) &=\frac{h_{n,N}(-2\cos z)}{Q(-2\cos z)} \left(1+O(N^{-1/2}e^{-\delta N})\right)\\ &=(-1)^m N^{-3/2}a_e(z,0)e^{NS_n(z)} \left(1+O(N^{-1})\right)\ne0 \end{split} \tag{21} \] for all large even levels. All fixed ordinary complex-color derivatives have the corresponding differentiated holomorphic expansions on smaller neighborhoods. Indeed Theorem 3 places the color outside the exact observation rectangle, so the exterior residue formula applies. That formula gives \(\mathcal I_{n,N}/Q=O(N^{-2}e^{NM_n})\), whereas the complete-edge packet and the exact cosine denominator give the direct term \(N^{-3/2}a_e e^{NS_n}\), with the parity scalar in (21). The strict action gap (14), reduced slightly on the neighborhood, gives the first relative error in (21). This proves the application; it was not an input to the geometric argument in Sections 1–3. Thus a nonzero local source is proved, including its ordinary normal directions. The remaining whole signed pair contraction still requires the rest of its contour to be controlled.

title: A homogeneous Bargmann kernel for the physical Krein pairing
text:
# A homogeneous Bargmann kernel for the physical Krein pairing Written research proof, 23 November 2026. The physical Hermitian pairing has an exact double-Gaussian realization with one homogeneous binomial kernel. The actual factorial frame is conformal for this pairing, with scalar \(N\) per head. Its paired gluing therefore requires neither an incomplete-exponential approximation nor an unknown factorial-frame metric. Original exterior rows and both cap types remain. The form is indefinite. Its explicit nonzero kernel symbol is not a noncancellation theorem for an arbitrary marked closing. In particular, the physical operator, coefficient-form matrix, and Gaussian Riesz operator are distinguished throughout. ## 1. Original finite coefficients and Gaussian moments Fix \(N\geq2\), \(d=N-1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(Q=q^2\), and \(x=-q^{-1}\). On the original balanced head put \[ F_a=(Q;Q)_a,\quad G_F=\operatorname{diag}(F_a),\qquad H_N=q^{-1}Z^{-1}R_d,\quad H_N|aangle=qQ^a|d-aangle . 	ag{1} \] Here \(Z|aangle=Q^a|aangle\), \(R_d|aangle=|d-aangle\), and \(0\leq a\leq d\). Thus \(H_N^\dagger=H_N\), \(H_N^2=I\). Use exactly the finite Gaussian calculus of [B]: \[  egin{gathered} P_u(z)=\sum_{a=0}^d u_az^a,\qquad d\mu_N(z)= rac N\pi e^{-N|z|^2}\,d^2z,\qquad h_a= rac{a!}{N^a},\ \int z^a ar z^{\,b}\,d\mu_N(z)=\delta_{ab}h_a,\qquad \mathcal K_A(z,w)=\sum_{a,b=0}^d z^aA_{ab} rac{(Nw)^b}{b!}. \end{gathered} 	ag{2} \] Angular integration and one elementary gamma integral prove the moment identity. Finite kernels compose with this measure and have trace integral \(\operatorname{Tr}A\). The identity kernel is \(E_d(Nzw)\), \(E_d(s)=\sum_{a=0}^d s^a/a!\), retaining its full cutoff. ## 2. Exact paired integral Let \(h=\operatorname{diag}(h_a)\). The Gaussian Riesz operator of the coefficient form \(u^\dagger H_Nv\) is \(h^{-1}H_N\). Its exact kernel is \[  oxed{\quad \mathscr K_N(z,w):=\mathcal K_{h^{-1}H_N}(z,w) =q rac{N^d}{d!}(z+Qw)^d .\quad} 	ag{3} \] Indeed column \(b\) has its sole nonzero entry in row \(d-b\), giving coefficient \(qQ^bN^d/[(d-b)!b!]\). The ordinary binomial theorem proves (3), including both endpoints. All its scalars remain. For arbitrary full coefficient vectors \(u,v\), \[  oxed{\quad u^\dagger H_Nv= \iint\overline{P_u(z)}\,\mathscr K_N(z, ar w)P_v(w) \,d\mu_N(z)d\mu_N(w).\quad} 	ag{4} \] The first integral pairs a row index with \( ar u_a h_a\); the second pairs \((N ar w)^b/b!\) with \(v_b\). Their result is \(u^\dagger h(h^{-1}H_N)v\). All sums are finite, so the double Gaussian integral is absolutely convergent without asymptotic assumptions. The kernel is Hermitian in the paired variables, since \( ar qQ^{-d}=q\). For clarity, the operator \(H_N\) itself has a different kernel: \[ \mathcal K_{H_N}(z,w)=qz^dE_d(QNw/z). 	ag{5} \] Its apparent singularity is removable by the finite sum. A cutoff transition in (5) is not an obstruction to (4), which uses (3). Also \((h^{-1}H_N)^2\) has diagonal entries \(1/(h_ah_{d-a})\); the Gaussian Riesz operator is not an involution. Only the coefficient-form matrix \(H_N\) squares to the identity. ## 3. The actual factorial congruence and row transport There is an exact phased complement, stronger than a modulus identity: \[ F_a\overline{F_{d-a}}=N,\qquad  oxed{\quad G_F^\dagger H_NG_F=NH_N.\quad} 	ag{6} \] Indeed \(F_d=N\), and its factors from \(a+1\) through \(d\) are the factors \(1-Q^{-j}\), \(1\leq j\leq d-a\), in reverse order. Thus \(F_d/F_a=\overline{F_{d-a}}\). Inserting this in each anti-diagonal entry proves the second formula. On \(r\) heads put \(G=G_F^{\otimes r}\) and \(\mathscr H_r=H_N^{\otimes r}\). Then \[ (Gu)^\dagger\mathscr H_r(Gv)=N^r u^\dagger\mathscr H_rv. 	ag{7} \] The right side is the tensor product of the paired integrals (4), with the displayed \(N^r\). This is precisely the factorial frame used in [B], with all phases rather than only its singular values. For \(T=G^{-1}AG\), any already proved identity \(A^\dagger\mathscr H_rA=\mathscr H_r\) therefore implies \(T^\dagger\mathscr H_rT=\mathscr H_r\). This applies to the unreduced signed physical words of [H]. It does not identify the reduced word of [B] with such an isometry after a head is eliminated. Congruence is not similarity. The actual physical operator \(H_N\), written in factorial coordinates, is \[ G_F^{-1}H_NG_F|aangle =qQ^a rac{|F_a|^2}{N}|d-aangle . 	ag{8} \] It is neither the coefficient-form matrix \(H_N\) nor the Gaussian Riesz matrix \(h^{-1}H_N\). No positive condition-number estimate for the factorial frame follows from (6). Every original bilinear row \(\lambda\) has the explicit coefficient form-dual vector \(z_\lambda=\mathscr H_r\lambda^\dagger\), so that \(\lambda y=z_\lambda^\dagger\mathscr H_ry\). In factorial coordinates \(y=Gu\), the actual row is \(\eta=\lambda G\). Its corresponding vector satisfies \[ v_\eta=\mathscr H_r\eta^\dagger=N^rG^{-1}z_\lambda, \qquad \lambda y=v_\eta^\dagger\mathscr H_ru . 	ag{9} \] Equations (4),(9) preserve an arbitrary original exterior. The original Cartan-weighted traces and first meridian derivative in [B] are applied by linearity to the same coefficient identities. They are not replaced by a squared norm or an independently selected row. ## 4. Literal ordinary and marked cap functions Set \[ c(z)_a= rac{(N ar z)^a}{a!},\qquad \mathcal F_N(t)=\sum_{a=0}^d F_a rac{t^a}{a!},\qquad B_N(z,w)=\sum_{a=0}^d inom da q^{a^2}z^aw^{d-a}. 	ag{10} \] These are specified full finite packets and polynomials. The unrestricted marked row is \(\ell_m|a,bangle=x^b/N^2\) [H]. Hence \[  oxed{\quad \ell_m(G_Fc(z)\otimes G_Fc(w)) =N^{-2}\mathcal F_N(N ar z)\mathcal F_N(Nx ar w). \quad} 	ag{11} \] The ordinary cap is \(\ell_o|a,bangle=x^a\delta_{a+b,d}/N\). Using \(F_aF_{d-a}=N(-1)^aQ^{a(a+1)/2}\) gives \[ \ell_o(G_Fc(z)\otimes G_Fc(w)) = rac{N^d}{d!}B_N( ar z, ar w). 	ag{12} \] Indeed \(x^a(-1)^aQ^{a(a+1)/2}=q^{a^2}\). Only when the actual assembled source forces this pair to integer degree \(d\) may the marked row be replaced by its restriction \(\ell_{m,d}\). For that restriction the exact formula is \[ \ell_{m,d}(G_Fc(z)\otimes G_Fc(w)) = rac{x^dN^{d-1}}{d!}B_N(Q ar z, ar w). 	ag{13} \] Its extra phase is \(q^{2a}=Q^a\). Equation (13) is not a formula for the unrestricted row on an arbitrary exterior; (11) is. These cap functions retain a known finite Gaussian chirp: \[ B_N(z,w)=\exp\!\left[ rac{\pi i}{N}(z\partial_z)^2ight](z+w)^d, \qquad \mathcal F_N'(t)=\mathcal F_N(t)-Q\mathcal F_N(Qt),\quad \mathcal F_N(0)=1 . 	ag{14} \] The first equality is a finite diagonal operation on degrees through \(d\). The second follows from \(F_{a+1}=(1-Q^{a+1})F_a\); the potential top term is zero because \(1-Q^N=0\). No reflection rule for a separated ray moment is being assumed. The original cup, pivots, framing/peripheral lines, and the full marked row remain in (9) or (11); none becomes (3) by a choice of metric. ## 5. Local symbol and exact coefficient-dual packet inversion For independent complex arguments let \(L_N=z+Qw\) and \(L=z+w\). The only zero divisor of (3) is \(L_N=0\), of order \(d\). On a fixed compact chart where \(L
e0\), choose a local logarithm. Stirling's formula and the first quantum shift give uniformly \[ \mathscr K_N(z,w)=N^{-1/2}  rac{\exp(2\pi i w/L)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,L} \exp\{N(1+\Log L)\}(1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{15} \] Indeed \(N^d/d!=e^N/\sqrt{2\pi N}(1+O(N^{-1}))\), and \(N\Log L_N=N\Log L+2\pi i w/L+O(N^{-1})\). The exact phase \(q\) and shift \(Q\) remain in (3); the shift produces the nonzero finite amplitude factor in (15). There is also an exact action on coefficient polynomials, without any incomplete-exponential estimate: \[  oxed{\qquad P_{H_Nu}(z)=qz^dP_u(Q/z).\qquad} 	ag{16} \] It is a polynomial even at zero. If a supplied actual coefficient packet has a relative expansion \(P_{u_N}(w)=c_NN^aA(w)e^{N\phi(w)}(1+O(N^{-1}))\) on a fixed neighborhood of \(f
e0\), then on a corresponding neighborhood of \(f^{-1}\), (16) gives \[ P_{H_Nu_N}(z)=c_NN^a rac{qA(Q/z)}z \exp\{N[\Log z+\phi(Q/z)]\}(1+O(N^{-1})). 	ag{17} \] The relative error is merely pulled back. The amplitude is nonzero if the input amplitude is. Formula (17) concerns the coefficient \(H_N\)-action or the specified coefficient form-dual packet. It does not replace the physical similarity (8) or the Gaussian Riesz operator by that action. At principal order the occupation transforms as \(z\partial_z[\Log z+\phi(1/z)]=1-w\phi'(w)\), \(w=1/z\). Thus the lower resolved point \((f,0)\) of [B] is paired with an upper occupation, with its distinct logarithmic mark retained. The form kernel is regular at the associated matched seam: complexify the Gaussian variables to \((z,\zeta,w,\omega)\). Its principal seam phase is \(\Log(z+\omega)-z\zeta-w\omega\), giving \[ \zeta=w= rac1{z+\omega},\qquad \zeta z+w\omega=1 . 	ag{18} \] This is the Gaussian FORM-dual seam: its left row coordinates are \((\zeta,z)\). It is different from (17), whose coefficient-action output has polynomial coordinate \(z_{m out}\). The two maps are not identified by their common occupation reflection. For the lower right point \((w,\omega)=(f,0)\), this gives \((\zeta,z)=(f,f^{-1})\) and kernel linear form \(f^{-1}
e0\). The mixed kernel derivative is \(-1/(z+\omega)^2
e0\). This verifies a nonzero local seam symbol on these matched charts, uniformly for \(f\) in compact subsets of \(\mathbb C^*\). It does not prove that the actual marked exterior is that dual packet, that a full composed stationary Hessian is nondegenerate, or that complementary regions have smaller rate. All finite integrals above remain whole; no source-current component or integration region has been discarded. The caps (11)--(13) still require their actual phase analysis in a general short component. No scalar lower bound follows from the indefinite form or local ellipticity alone. ## Complete proof sources and coverage - [B] [Actual reduced word Bargmann source period](research_reduced_word_bargmann_source_period.md), 565 lines, SHA-256 `abbe118e89f2d80f82f4bcd591a71dc193fda852cd488262461d07b262696655`. - [H] [Common physical tensor Krein form](research_physical_tensor_krein_crossing_form.md), 286 lines, SHA-256 `610b5ac7d889429163ec230e9d644d174d38382733dbad57826fce66cec8e348`. The complete [common-spin first-jet dual](research_reduced_common_spin_first_jet_dual.md), 387 lines, SHA-256 `1ba0870e39871de7cf7b53a041e5c47d133dc8ee3755aa8b99df71ae810b9f6f`, and [compact coherent source calculus](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/compact_coherent_source_period.md), 469 lines, SHA-256 `8c6c3277367a4aa6c69269da635139d5f881f3d3d0d894e04dd97028d76537e4`, are coverage only. Coherent kernels and their resolutions are established methods. The proof above specifies the physical indefinite pairing, its exact factorial congruence, and its unchanged original boundary.

title: The marked edge cover with some boundary angles fixed at zero
text:
# The marked edge cover with some boundary angles fixed at zero Research note, 15 November 2026. The original circle-tree face construction has one square root for each tree edge. When some auxiliary boundary angles are fixed at zero, different edges can acquire the same radicand. The restricted cover can then be reducible. This note identifies its component through the marked complete structure, proves that its regular complex charts are connected, and checks that the original face maps are rational on this component. The conclusion concerns an explicit family of representations of the original augmented exterior. It does not assert that every hyperbolic short partial filling occurs in that family. A path in this family need not preserve filling slopes, positive tetrahedra, logarithmic periods, or the coefficient of a cycle in the quantum source. ## 1. The restricted cover and its components Let \(\mathcal T=(V,E)\) be an original ordered circle tree with at least one edge. Retain its page orders, disk frames, half-twist carriers, and primitive peripheral curves, as in Sections 2--3 of the [circle-tree geometry manuscript](../papers/circle-tree-geometry/main.tex). Choose a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq V\), and write \(U=V\setminus S\). The selected variables are \(a_v=	an(t_v/2)\), for \(v\in S\); set \(a_u=0\) for \(u\in U\). The equations are \[ q_e^2=1+a_v^2+a_w^2,\qquad e=vw\in E. 	ag{1} \] At the marked complete point \(o\), every \(a_v=0\) and every \(q_e=1\). Fixing \(a_U=0\) will be called the complete-parameter slice. Away from the positive metric domain, this terminology specifies parameters and peripheral multipliers, not a complete hyperbolic metric. Partition the edges into \(E_S\), with both endpoints selected; \(E_U\), with neither endpoint selected; and boundary edges, with one endpoint in each set. For \(v\in S\), let \(k_v\) be its number of boundary edges, and put \(B=\{v\in S:k_v>0\}\). Choose one reference boundary edge \(e_v\) at each \(v\in B\). Set \[ f_e=1+a_v^2+a_w^2\quad(e=vw\in E_S), \qquad g_v=1+a_v^2\quad(v\in S). 	ag{2} \] **Theorem 1.** The reduced affine cover (1) has \[ 2^{\,|E_U|+\sum_{v\in B}(k_v-1)} 	ag{3} \] irreducible components. Each has degree \[ 2^{\,|E_S|+|B|} 	ag{4} \] over the selected parameter space. On the open set where every \(q_e
e0\), they are disjoint, and their labels are exactly \[ q_e=\sigma_e\quad(e\in E_U),\qquad q_e=\epsilon_e q_{e_v} \quad(e
e e_v	ext{ a boundary edge at }v), 	ag{5} \] where every displayed sign is independently \(1\) or \(-1\). The marked component \(X_S\), through \(o\), has every sign in (5) equal to \(+1\). Thus (5) with these signs is an exact sheet test on this open set. The absolute signs of the remaining independent roots are not additional component labels. **Proof.** Work over \(R=\mathbb C[a_v:v\in S]\). Each internal polynomial \(f_e\) is irreducible: its homogenization is the rank-three quadratic form \(z^2+a_v^2+a_w^2\), whereas a product of two linear forms has rank at most two. Distinct tree edges give distinct primes. For each \(v\in B\), the prime \(a_v-i\) divides \(g_v\) to order one, divides no other \(g_w\), and divides no internal \(f_e\). Consequently the classes \[ \{f_e:e\in E_S\}\cup\{g_v:v\in B\} 	ag{6} \] are independent in \(\operatorname{Frac}(R)^*/ \operatorname{Frac}(R)^{*2}\): take valuations first at the internal primes and then at \(a_v-i\). Independent square classes give a field extension of degree \(2^{|E_S|+|B|}\). One elementary justification is induction: in a multiquadratic extension, an element whose square belongs to the base field is an eigenvector for every sign automorphism. Expanding it in the root-monomial basis shows that it is a base-field multiple of one root monomial. Thus a new base-field radicand becomes a square only if its class is generated by the preceding ones. It follows that \[ R[r_e,s_v:e\in E_S,\ v\in B]/ (r_e^2-f_e,\ s_v^2-g_v) 	ag{7} \] is a domain. Indeed it is free over \(R\) in the root monomials, and these monomials are independent in that extension field. On \(q_e
e0\), the untouched roots have the constant signs in (5), and each quotient of two boundary roots at the same vertex has square one. Splitting by these signs leaves exactly (7), with the corresponding units inverted. This proves the disjoint decomposition and both counts. For completeness, the full algebra in (1) is free over \(R\) by successively adjoining monic quadratics. Its generic algebra is a product of the fields just described. Hence it is reduced: a nilpotent would vanish generically and so would be \(R\)-torsion, contrary to freeness. Its minimal components all dominate the base: a nonzero element of \(R\) is a non-zero-divisor in this reduced finite algebra and cannot lie in a minimal prime. The closures of the components above are therefore all the components. Their degrees sum to \(2^{|E|}\). Different closures can meet when a shared boundary root vanishes, so the disjointness assertion was restricted to \(q_e
e0\). At \(o\), all signs are \(+1\), as claimed. \(\square\) ## 2. A regular open set and its connectedness On \(X_S\) use the following convenient open set: \[ \mathcal R_S= \left\{\prod_{v\in S}(1+a_v^2) \prod_{e\in E}q_e(q_e^2+1)
e0ight\}. 	ag{8} \] This deliberately excludes the ramification locus \(q_e=0\), even where an individual face expression might extend. It contains \(o\). Its base is the complement of the hypersurfaces \[ g_v=0\ (v\in S),\quad f_e=0,\ f_e+1=0\ (e\in E_S),\quad g_v+1=0\ (v\in B). 	ag{9} \] The map to that base is an unramified cover with all the independent sign changes in (6) as deck transformations. **Proposition 2.** The complex manifold \(\mathcal R_S\) is path connected. Removing any further proper algebraic divisor from it leaves a path-connected set. In particular any two surviving regular points can be joined without crossing that divisor. **Proof.** The base in (9) is path connected. On the complex line through any two allowed points, none of its defining polynomials is identically zero, since it is nonzero at those points. There are only finitely many forbidden values on that line, and a path can detour around them in its complex parameter plane. A small loop about a generic smooth point of \(f_e=0\) changes the sign of \(r_e\) alone. Such a point can be chosen away from all the other hypersurfaces in (9). Likewise a loop about a generic point of \(a_v=i\) changes the sign of \(s_v\) alone. If an internal edge touches \(v\), its radicand there is \(a_w^2\), so it is nonzero at a generic point of this divisor. The preceding loops generate every deck sign. Conjugating them by base paths permits all these sign changes at any one base point. Thus a lifted path between two base points can be followed by loops that correct its endpoint sheet. This proves connectedness of \(\mathcal R_S\). Finally cover a path in \(\mathcal R_S\) by finitely many complex coordinate balls. A proper algebraic divisor has empty interior in this connected manifold: otherwise a local defining holomorphic function, and hence the divisor, would contain the whole component. Choose intermediate points outside the divisor in the successive ball overlaps. In each ball, the complex line between its two chosen points is not contained in the divisor. Its intersections with the divisor are discrete; only finitely many lie near the compact line segment under consideration. Detour around them inside the ball. The resulting concatenated path proves the last assertion. \(\square\) This argument also proves that the independent absolute root signs are connected by complex continuation. It does not prove that they can be changed within the positive tetrahedron domain. ## 3. The original face maps, not only their multipliers Fix an edge with \(a=a_v\), \(b=a_w\), and \(q=q_e\). The coordinates in Section 3 of the geometry manuscript become \[  egin{gathered} E= rac{q+i}{q-i},\qquad H_v= rac{q-a}{q+a},\qquad H_w= rac{q-b}{q+b},\ R= rac{1+b^2}{q^2+1},\qquad R_1=1-R= rac{1+a^2}{q^2+1},\ Z_v= rac{q+a}{q-i},\qquad Z_w= rac{q+b}{q-i},\qquad Q_v= rac{1+ia}{1-ia}. \end{gathered} 	ag{10} \] Here \(R\) is a face-coordinate ratio; it is unrelated to the ring in the proof of Theorem 1. No square root in addition to those in (1) has been introduced. All denominators in (10) are units on (8). For the apex denominators, the exact factorizations are \[  egin{aligned} (q-a)(q+a)&=1+b^2,&(q-b)(q+b)&=1+a^2,\ Z_w-R_1&= rac{(q+b)(b+i)}{q^2+1},& Z_w-ER_1&= rac{(q+b)(b-i)}{(q-i)^2}. \end{aligned} 	ag{11} \] In particular the second apices in the two projection copies simplify to \((b-i)/(q-i)\) and \((b+i)/(q+i)\), respectively. The original eight tetrahedron shapes are \[ (A,B,-1/A,-1/B),\qquad(C,D,-1/C,-1/D), 	ag{12} \] where, as in Section 1 of the [positive edge note](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md), \[ A= rac{q+a}{b-i},\quad C= rac{q-a}{b-i},\quad B=- rac{q-b}{a+i},\quad D=- rac{q+b}{a+i}. 	ag{13} \] They are finite and nonzero on (8). None is \(1\) or \(-1\): an equality of one of the four ratios to either value says that \(q\) is a signed sum of \(a,b,i\); substituting in \(q^2=1+a^2+b^2\) forces one of \(a\pm i,b\pm i\) to vanish. Thus every shape in (12) avoids \(0,1,\infty\). The original ordered face triples are consequently distinct. No positivity is asserted. For clarity, the literal white matrices are \[  egin{aligned} W_0&= egin{pmatrix}1&0\0&E\end{pmatrix},& W_1&= egin{pmatrix}1&E-1\0&E\end{pmatrix},\ W_2&= egin{pmatrix}E-R&R(1-E)\E-1&1-ER\end{pmatrix},& W_3&= egin{pmatrix}R&0\1-E&ER\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} 	ag{14} \] The pure shaded map and the two maps used on the odd disk seam are \[ S_0= egin{pmatrix}0&-ER\1&-1-E\end{pmatrix},\quad A_0= egin{pmatrix}R&-R\1&ER-1-E\end{pmatrix},\quad B_0= egin{pmatrix}R/E-1-1/E&R\-1&R\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{15} \] The manuscript identifies each of these with its ordered face map, including the actual half-twist permutation. Their determinants are units on (8): those of (14) are, respectively, \(E,E,E(1-R)^2,ER^2\), and those of (15) are \(ER,ER(R-1),R(R-1)/E\). Across pages, the doubled disk-side triangle ratios are \((-Q_v^{-1},-Q_v,-Q_v^{-1})\) on the incoming boundary and \((-Q_v,-Q_v^{-1},-Q_v)\) on the outgoing boundary. They depend only on the shared vertex parameter. Normalizing one ordered triangle then matches the full other triangle. The map between two ordered distinct triples is rational in their coordinates. Consequently every page identification and every finite product or inverse used to develop the original cut is rational in \((a,q)\). Apparent poles caused by an affine vertex moving to infinity can be handled by homogeneous coordinates; they do not require a new field extension. **Proposition 3.** On \(\mathcal R_S\), these maps give a rational \(\mathrm{PGL}_2\) representation family of the original marked augmented exterior. Its image has the same irreducible Zariski closure as the marked complete germ with \(a_U=0\). **Proof.** Near \(o\), the original cut construction, the full page ratio table, and the pure and odd edge-return identities establish the representation of that exterior. This includes the original peripheral paths, rather than just their eigenvalues. Every group relation is a rational identity in the face matrices on the integral component \(X_S\). An identity holding on the complete open analytic germ therefore holds in its function field. One elementary way to check this last step is to take the field norm of a putatively nonzero rational difference to \(\mathbb C(a_S)\). Its norm is nonzero, but would vanish on an open base polydisk, a contradiction. Regularity of the face maps extends the identity throughout (8). The same argument applies to any polynomial relation among the resulting representation coordinates. Hence a relation holds on the complete germ if and only if it holds on the whole rational image. The closure of a rational image of an integral variety is irreducible, which proves the assertion. It also applies after passing to conjugacy invariants. It does not identify this closure with every component of the full representation or character variety. \(\square\) All assertions here are projective. Choosing determinant-one matrix representatives over the function field could require square roots of their determinants; none is needed for Proposition 3. The actual primitive words also give \[ e^{V_v}=Q_v^2,\qquad e^{U_v}=Q_v^{-\eta_v} \prod_{e
i v} rac{q_e+a_v}{q_e-a_v}. 	ag{16} \] Here \(\eta_v\in\{-1,0,1\}\) is the retained half-twist carrier. At \(v\in U\), both multipliers are one. The main meridian remains parabolic: in a local marked frame \(W_0^{-1}W_1\) is translation by \(E-1
e0\). These are representation statements. The completeness of a positive metric, and the winding integers in its primitive periods, require the additional argument in the [marked completion note](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md). ## 4. Avoiding critical points of the primitive-period map There is also a useful regularity divisor that can be removed without disconnecting the marked component. Fix arbitrary integers \(n_v\), \(v\in S\). In any local logarithmic chart put \[ t_v=-i\log Q_v,\qquad r_{v,e}= rac12\log rac{q_e+a_v}{q_e-a_v},\qquad F_v=\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}- rac{i n_v}{2}t_v. 	ag{17} \] Choose the initial logarithms to vanish at \(o\). The derivatives of (17) are independent of additive logarithmic periods. Direct differentiation of (1) gives \[  rac{\partial r_{v,e}}{\partial t_v} = rac{1+a_v^2}{2q_e},\qquad  rac{\partial r_{v,e}}{\partial t_w} =- rac{a_va_w}{2q_e}\quad(e=vw). 	ag{18} \] Thus the selected Jacobian \(J_n=(\partial F_v/\partial t_w)\) is rational, with \[ (J_n)_{vv}=\sum_{e
i v} rac{1+a_v^2}{2q_e}- rac{i n_v}{2}, \qquad (J_n)_{vw}= egin{cases} -a_va_w/(2q_{vw}),&vw\in E_S,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases} 	ag{19} \] At \(o\), it is diagonal with entries \((d_v-i n_v)/2\), where \(d_v\ge1\) is the original tree degree. It is therefore nonsingular for every integer choice of \(n\). **Corollary 4.** Every point of \(\mathcal R_S\) with \(\det J_n
e0\) can be connected to \(o\) through points having that same property. Along such a path the actual primitive multipliers admit continued logarithms, and the selected map (17) has a local inverse at every point. **Proof.** The determinant is a nonzero rational function, regular on (8), since its value at \(o\) is nonzero. Apply Proposition 2 after deleting its zero divisor. The factors in (16) are nonzero on (8), so they have logarithms along any parameterized interval. The holomorphic inverse function theorem applies to (19) locally. \(\square\) This path does not in general hold \(F_v\) constant. In particular it is not a path of solutions of the fixed primitive filling equations \(F_v=-\pi i\). Its endpoint logarithms can differ from independently prescribed endpoint logarithms by integral periods. Corollary 4 does not discard that difference. ## 5. What this resolves for short partial fillings For a proposed short partial filling, the first question is whether its marked discrete faithful representation has a lift to the original coordinates (1). If such a lift is supplied, (5) tests whether it lies on the marked complete component. If it also satisfies (8) and the Jacobian condition, the preceding results provide a path of regular marked representation and period charts from completeness to that lift. The complex path can pass through tetrahedra with negative or zero imaginary shape, provided the shapes themselves stay nondegenerate. There is no proof here that every hyperbolic short partial filling has such a lift. There is also no assertion that a regular path preserves the original integration cycle or prevents cancellation of its geometric contribution. Those are separate from the algebraic component and period-map regularity proved above. On the positive domain, the stronger metric and full-period conclusions already follow from the marked completion theorem; this note adds complex continuation outside that domain without extending those metric conclusions. The independent-square-class argument for unrestricted edge parameters already appears in Section 7 of [the all-circle characteristic note](../papers/meridian-expansions/README.md). The additional issue here is the repeated roots created by fixing \(a_U=0\), their marked component, and the regular continuation of the literal original face construction. No new general claim about multiquadratic extensions is intended. ## Source versions and directly used statements The written derivation uses the following frozen versions. No numerical calculation or software experiment enters the proof. * `papers/circle-tree-geometry/main.tex`, SHA256 `2404285044d7efb8376b3fdeaa3a6da6f2d36bc29da6a7e176f09f8230339301`: Sections 2--3 identify the marked cut, original page order, rational face maps, pure and odd returns, and the primitive meridian/longitude words; Section 6 identifies the marked main parabolic meridian. * `notes/research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md`, SHA256 `da5129c7110190035eedb8249d4004dd06b5a7555e78d948234d8de50fa17500`: Section 1 supplies the eight original rational shape expressions. Its positivity and uniqueness conclusions are not extended here. * `notes/research_positive_point_marked_completion.md`, SHA256 `28de22f081e24629ea6d26ad05213301a9bcf5d17d3ae7d00cc9c675a8218887`: Sections 1--3 distinguish the positive contraction from a fixed-slope path and record the original apex denominators; Section 5 supplies the distinction between multiplier logarithms and full primitive periods. Its completion theorem is used only to delimit the stronger conclusions already available in the positive domain. * `notes/actual_all_circle_geometric_characteristic.md`, SHA256 `34d530b896d660852878e7cb585bbec87f6091d3d9d9f395858f2c487aac98bb`: Section 7, equations (R9)--(R11), is the coverage comparison for the unrestricted independent-square-class argument. The proof above establishes the restricted tangent-coordinate statements directly.

title: The partial endpoint Green estimate and its retained boundary packet
text: # The partial endpoint Green estimate and its retained boundary packet Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The exact truncation defect has the real product rate, uniformly even at its zeros. Backward propagation on a fixed physical bulk interval preserves that rate for the forced part of the error, including first normals. The estimate also retains an off-grid boundary packet and the defect of the chosen baseline. Neither of those terms is identified with the last Newton product. An exact ideal-multiple example shows why matching physical jets and thin-strip moderateness do not determine the error. This is not an obstruction to a sharper estimate for the specifically normalized common baseline, and does not provide a filled-leaf scalar seed. ## 1. The ordinary truncation and its physical window Put \[ h=N^{-1},\quad \theta=\pi/N,\quad D=N-1,\quad c_a=2\cos((2a+1)\theta),\quad s_a=2\sin(a\theta), \] \[ S_k=\prod_{a=1}^k s_a,\qquad e_k(C)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{a<k}(c_a-C),\qquad w=2\cosh(\alpha/N), \] \[ c_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi h),\quad t_N(x)=\pi-2\pi x-\pi h,\quad k_0=\lceil N/2\rceil. \tag{1} \] The parameter \(\alpha\) ranges over an arbitrary fixed bounded complex disk; larger disks are used for derivatives. Fix \(0<\delta<1/2\), let \(L=\lfloor\delta N\rfloor\), \(K=k_0+L<D\) for large \(N\), and define \[ H_K(C)=\sum_{a=0}^K e_a(w)e_a(C),\qquad u_N(x)=H_K(c_N(x)). \tag{2} \] The ordinary original operator, denoted by \(\mathscr J_N\) on functions of \(x\), is \[ \mathscr J_N F=(c_0+A_N+B_N)F-A_NF(x+h)-B_NF(x-h), \] \[ A_N(x)=\frac{s_{Nx+1}^4}{s_{2Nx+1}s_{2Nx+2}},\qquad B_N(x)=\frac{s_{Nx}^4}{s_{2Nx}s_{2Nx+1}}. \tag{3} \] On polynomials in \(C\) it is the ordinary lift of \(J=TCT\), with lowering rule \(Je_a=c_ae_a-s_a^2e_{a-1}\). Therefore \[ \boxed{\quad R_N(x):=(\mathscr J_N-w)u_N(x) =s_{K+1}^2e_{K+1}(w)e_K(c_N(x)). \quad} \tag{4} \] Indeed \((c_a-w)e_a(w)=s_{a+1}^2e_{a+1}(w)\), so every coefficient except the last cancels in the finite sum. Equation (4) is ordinary, before any quotient reduction or differentiation. Fix a closed interval \(I=[a,b]\) with a larger fixed real buffer inside \((0,1/2)\), such that throughout that buffer, for large \(N\), \[ 0<t_-\le t_N(x)\le t_+<2\pi\delta. \tag{5} \] At every physical node \(x=j/N\) in this window, \(H_K\) and the full kernel \(K_N(w,C)\) have exactly the same value and first spectral normal. The omitted Newton terms contain both occurrences of each such physical root. This also follows from the exact physical termination in the scalar-compatibility source. The window is strictly in the bulk, so no extra spectral normal is introduced at an odd simple endpoint. ## 2. A uniform product estimate, including its zeros Define the continuous real rate \[ J_\delta(t)=-\int_0^\delta \log\left|\frac{\sin^2(t/2)-\sin^2(\pi v)} {\cos^2(\pi v)}\right|\,dv . \tag{6} \] The logarithmic singularity is integrable. On (5), for every fixed pair of nonnegative derivative orders \(a_1,b_1\), \[ \boxed{\quad |\partial_\alpha^{a_1}\partial_x^{b_1}R_N(x)| \le C N^p e^{-N J_\delta(t_N(x))},\qquad x\in I. \quad} \tag{7} \] The constants can depend on the interval, cutoff and derivative orders. The estimate is uniform at product zeros and at both level parities. It is an upper bound, not a nonzero product asymptotic. Here is a proof with the needed zero control. Let \(Q_N\) be the monic distinct-node polynomial. The exact product formulas give \[ R_N=(c_K-w)\beta_N Q_N(c_N(x)) \prod_{l=0}^{L-1}\rho_{l,N}, \tag{8} \] where \[ \rho_{l,N}(\alpha,t)= \frac{[\cos^2 A_l+\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))] [\sin^2(t/2)-\sin^2 A_l]}{\cos^4 B_l}, \] \[ (A_l,B_l)= \begin{cases} ((l+\tfrac12)\theta,(l+1)\theta),&N\text{ even},\\ ((l+1)\theta,(l+\tfrac32)\theta),&N\text{ odd}, \end{cases} \] \[ \beta_N= \begin{cases} \cosh(\alpha/2)/(2N^2),&N\text{ even},\\ \cosh(\alpha/2)\cosh(\alpha/(2N)) /(4N^2\cos^4(\theta/2)),&N\text{ odd}. \end{cases} \tag{9} \] On every disk \(|z-x|\le r/N\), with fixed \(r\), the factors \(c_K-w\), \(N^2\beta_N\), and \(Q_N(c_N(z))\) are bounded. For the last assertion use \(Q_N(c_N(z))=-a_N(z)\sin(\pi Nz)\), with \(a_N=2\) at even levels and \(a_N=4\cos(\pi z+\pi/(2N))\) at odd levels. The cosine factors in (9) are uniform units. Their logarithmic sums are smooth Riemann sums; the microscopic parameter changes their logarithm by \(O(N^{-1})\) in total. For the numerator use \[ \sin^2(t/2)-\sin^2 A_l =\sin(t/2+A_l)\sin(t/2-A_l). \tag{10} \] The first sine is a uniform unit on the buffered real window. In the second, write \(\sin y=y(\sin y/y)\). Its second factor is a uniform analytic unit. The remaining product has, up to \((\pi/N)^L\), the form \(\prod_{l<L}(\xi-l-\omega)\), where \(\Re\xi\) is a distance \(cN\) from both ends of the index interval and \(|\Im\xi|+|\omega|\) is bounded. Splitting at the nearest integer and comparing the two sides with \(\prod_{k\le m}(k+C)\) bounds this product by the corresponding two factorials times a fixed power of \(N\). Stirling's elementary logarithmic estimate gives \[ \log\left|\prod_{l<L}\rho_{l,N}(\alpha,t_N(z))\right| \le -N J_\delta(t_N(x))+C\log N, \qquad |z-x|\le r/N. \tag{11} \] The bounded shifts and the floor in \(L\) change the estimate by \(O(\log N)\). A factor arbitrarily near zero can only improve this upper estimate; no lower bound on its distance from zero was used. The factorial comparison also covers complex distances of size \(O(N^{-1})\) from the real zero. This proves (11) uniformly on the indicated disks. Combining it with (8), then using Cauchy's formula on smaller disks and larger parameter disks, proves (7). In particular fixed \(x\)-derivatives cost only additional powers of \(N\). On the window (5), direct differentiation gives \[ J_\delta'(t)=-\frac1{2\pi} \log\frac{\tan(\pi\delta)+\tan(t/2)} {\tan(\pi\delta)-\tan(t/2)}<0. \tag{12} \] One obtains (12) by substituting \(y=\tan(\pi v)\) in the principal-value integral for the derivative of (6). All arguments in the displayed logarithm are positive because \(t<2\pi\delta\). Also \(J_\delta(t)>0\) there: at \(t=2\pi\delta\), every nonzero ratio inside (6) is less than one, and (12) increases the rate as \(t\) decreases. Thus \(J_\delta(t_N(x))\) is increasing with \(x\). ## 3. Exact backward Green propagation with first normals Let \(H_N(x,\alpha)\) be any holomorphic baseline on the buffered bulk neighborhood, and retain its actual ordinary defect \[ r_H=(\mathscr J_N-w)H_N,\qquad E_N=u_N-H_N. \tag{13} \] No bound or normalization of \(H_N\) is implicit here. For a holomorphic scalar \(F\), define \[ X_F(x)=\binom{F(x)}{N(F(x)-F(x-h))},\qquad Z_F(x)=\binom{X_F(x)}{\partial_xX_F(x)}. \tag{14} \] Primes below differentiate the ordinary coefficient functions. Put \[ q_N=B_N/A_N,\quad d_N=(c_0-w)/A_N,\quad T_N=\begin{pmatrix}1+d_N&q_N/N\\Nd_N&q_N\end{pmatrix}, \] \[ b_N=A_N^{-1}\binom1N,\qquad \mathcal T_N=\begin{pmatrix}T_N&0\\T_N'&T_N\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathcal R_N(r)=\binom{b_Nr}{b_N'r+b_Nr'}. \tag{15} \] Solving (3) for the forward value and differentiating gives exactly \[ Z_F(x+h)=\mathcal T_N(x)Z_F(x) -\mathcal R_N((\mathscr J_N-w)F)(x). \tag{16} \] This includes coefficient derivatives and the independent normal state. It does not infer a normal equation from values alone. On the fixed buffered bulk domain, \[ A_N=\tan^2(\pi x)+O(h),\quad q_N=1+O(h),\quad d_N=O(h^2),\quad T_N=I+O(h),\quad T_N'=O(h). \tag{17} \] These follow directly from (3), uniformly for bounded complex \(\alpha\); the same estimates hold on a fixed smaller complex neighborhood. In particular \(\mathcal T_N^{\pm1}=I+O(h)\), and \[ \|\mathcal R_N(r)\| \le CN(|r|+|r'|). \tag{18} \] Choose any fractional grid \(x_j=(j+\vartheta)/N\), \(0\le\vartheta<1\), and indices \(j\le b_N^*\) with their row points in \(I\) and all neighboring arguments inside its buffer. The symbol \(b_N^*\) is an index, distinct from the vector \(b_N\) in (15). Let \(\Phi_{j,k}\) be the fundamental propagator of (16)'s homogeneous matrix, with \(\Phi_{k,k}=I\), and use inverse products when \(j<k\). Uniformly on this fixed real interval, \[ \|\Phi_{j,k}\|\le C. \tag{19} \] Indeed there are at most \(CN\) factors of norm \(1+Ch\). Backward variation of constants is the ordinary exact identity \[ \boxed{\quad Z_{E_N}(x_j)=\Phi_{j,b_N^*}Z_{E_N}(x_{b_N^*}) +\sum_{l=j}^{b_N^*-1}\Phi_{j,l+1} \mathcal R_N(R_N-r_H)(x_l). \quad} \tag{20} \] In particular (7), (12), and (18)--(19) give \[ \boxed{\quad \|Z_{E_N}(x_j)\| \le C\|Z_{E_N}(x_{b_N^*})\| +CN^p e^{-N J_\delta(t_N(x_j))} +CN\sum_{l=j}^{b_N^*-1}(|r_H(x_l)|+|r_H'(x_l)|). \quad} \tag{21} \] The right boundary packet contains both adjacent scalar values and both adjacent first derivatives, as encoded in (14). It is actual data for the same fractional grid. It is not replaced by a packet on the physical grid or by an incoming rate at the left boundary. All constants are uniform in \(\vartheta\). For an exact homogeneous baseline the last term is zero. For a baseline whose defect and its first derivative are bounded by \(N^p e^{-\kappa N}\), it is at most another polynomial times \(e^{-\kappa N}\). Neither case deletes the boundary term. Since \(c_N'\) is a uniform unit in this bulk, the same estimate controls first spectral normals with the stated polynomial losses. Parameter derivatives obey the analogous differentiated identity, or Cauchy estimates when the supplied packets are uniformly holomorphic on larger parameter sets. In particular, for the specifically constructed baseline \(A_N^0\) of the common-baseline source, the missing datum has the literal form \[ \mathfrak b_N^\delta(\vartheta) =Z_{u_N-A_N^0}(x_{b,N}(\vartheta)),\qquad x_{b,N}(\vartheta)=\frac{\lfloor Nb-\vartheta\rfloor+\vartheta}{N}. \tag{21a} \] At a specified target \(x_0\), choosing \(\delta=\delta_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)\) leaves the concrete obligations to bound (21a) and the last sum in (21) by a polynomial times \(e^{-NJ_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)}\), uniformly in \(\vartheta\). The \(O(N^{-1})\) angle offset changes this rate only by a bounded factor on the fixed bulk arc. Initializing the modified differential equation at a far-right physical row fixes its two-component state at that row. It does not supply this sharper bound at the adjacent fractional grids, or for the derivative part of (21a). The currently proved exponential compatibility estimate has no such optimized constant. ## 4. What changing the cutoff controls Fix \(0<\delta_1<\delta_2<1/2\) and a real buffered arc with \(0<t<2\pi\delta_1\). The two partial polynomials have the same physical full jets on that arc. Their exact difference is the finite Newton band between the two cutoffs. The product proof in section 2 is uniform for every intermediate cutoff. For \(\delta>t/(2\pi)\), the ratio \[ \frac{\sin^2(\pi\delta)-\sin^2(t/2)} {\cos^2(\pi\delta)} \] increases from zero to infinity. Hence \(J_\delta(t)\), as a function of \(\delta\), increases to its unique maximum and then decreases. Its minimum on \([\delta_1,\delta_2]\) is at an endpoint. Summing the \(O(N)\) exact terms and using the same small disks proves, for every fixed derivative order, \[ |\partial_\alpha^{a_1}\partial_x^{b_1} (u_N^{\delta_2}-u_N^{\delta_1})(x)| \le CN^p\exp\{-N\min(J_{\delta_1}(t_N(x)), J_{\delta_2}(t_N(x)))\}. \tag{22} \] The maximizing cutoff satisfies \(\sin^2(\pi\delta_*(t))=(1+\sin^2(t/2))/2\), giving the previously proved \(J_*(t)\). Formula (22) bounds cutoff variation. It does not bound the component common to these partial polynomials relative to a separately normalized baseline. In particular it does not identify the error in (21) with \(e^{-NJ_*(t)}\). ## 5. An exact alias ambiguity and its limited implication The full physical relation is \[ P_N(C)=2T_N(C/2)+2,\qquad P_N(c_N(x))=4\sin^2(\pi Nx). \tag{23} \] Its composition in (23) is \(h\)-periodic, so it commutes with (3). Consequently \(\mathscr J_N(P_NF)=P_N\mathscr J_NF\) as an ordinary identity, with the removable polynomial interpretation. At \(\alpha=i\pi\), one has \(w=c_0\), and the full kernel and every partial polynomial in (2) are exactly \(1\). For any fixed \(c>0\), however, \[ \widetilde H_N(x) =1+e^{-cN}\sin^2(\pi Nx) \tag{24} \] is another exact homogeneous solution of \((\mathscr J_N-c_0)\widetilde H_N=0\). It has exactly the same full physical jets. In ordinary spectral terms the difference is \(e^{-cN}P_N(C)/4\). It has zero first normal at every double root and zero value at the odd simple root. On every fixed bulk strip of height \(H<c/(2\pi)\), (24) is uniformly bounded. At real midpoint rows its difference from the partial polynomial is exactly \(e^{-cN}\), while the truncation defect (4) is identically zero. Choosing \(c<\min_{x\in I}J_\delta(t_N(x))\) for large \(N\) also rules out a universal \(N^p e^{-NJ_\delta}\) comparison with every such moderate homogeneous representative. This example proves only that physical jets, thin-strip moderateness, and the truncation forcing do not fix the off-grid normalization. It does not contradict the specifically normalized common baseline, nor exclude an improved boundary estimate for that baseline on a larger domain. In fact its modified-flow construction preserves the constant solution at \(\alpha=i\pi\): the initial coefficient matrix kills \((1,0)^t\), and every flow iteration retains that property. Thus (24) is not that constructed baseline. In the original closed trace the ideal multiple is invisible, with any shared polynomial spectator and its full normals retained. Splitting that trace into exterior and interface currents must keep their cancellation; one separate current is not invariant under this ambiguity. The unresolved estimate is therefore a source-specific bound on the boundary packet and baseline defect in (21), at the required action. Neither the optimized real product rate nor this Green identity supplies that estimate or a nonzero filled-leaf term. ## 6. Coverage and direct sources The ordinary finite truncation identity and its both-parity product are prior results. The additional statement here is their uniform real zero-inclusive forcing bound, the explicit backward full-normal Green budget, and the normalization diagnostic. A targeted source search found the earlier coarse holomorphic iteration and a lower bound on its complex forcing, but no statement of (21). The following complete sources were read at unchanged pins, with their used implications checked: * [Ordinary truncation and both-parity lowering product](research_endpoint_low_high_exponential_cancellation.md), SHA256 594bd802439d08e3dfe32f6cfa1027d291b36c502061dc7723fd0a8734527f5d. * [Exact partial scalar and original physical jets](research_microscopic_endpoint_bulk_scalar_compatibility.md), SHA256 2b8713ed16b66f5faa004403ac1d032021eee0a6f8f38082481d002c672c0b2e. * [Common baseline and optimized real product diagnostic](research_unturned_endpoint_complex_baseline_and_window.md), SHA256 9d233d9bb11c2842e62d5523f97e9621a3bd22532e3b527ceaab8125782c1cc1. Only written mathematics, source-text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build or compilation was run. Frozen notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: The original trace on a path with large signed powers
text:
# The original trace on a path with large signed powers Research note, 3 November 2026. For every fixed finite positive path with crossing powers at least twenty, all the mixed vertical terms of a central trace rectangle have a strict gap below the selected geometric action. The gap comes from one inequality at each vertex where a vertical term occurs. Its constants do not depend on the length of the path. Sections 4--6 compare every complementary original row and every mixed current with the selected action when the signed powers have absolute value at least sixty-four. The [full thin-box kernel theorem](research_bare_kernel_thin_rectangle.md) supplies the required uniform bound and nonzero expansion. Section 7 retains one outside angle and proves its whole-period and complex-strip estimates. Sections 8--9 give the stronger local comparisons used for powers seven and eight in the [full path-source theorem](research_uniform_path_trace_assembly.md#7-the-source-theorem-at-powers-seven-and-eight). The proved wide-kernel bound now supplies their finite-source input. ## 1. The phase and the selected point Let \(I\) be the selected vertices of an original finite circle path. Complete outside endpoints, when present, have angle zero. Write \(d_v\in\{1,2\}\) for each selected vertex's original degree, including incidences to those outside endpoints. Put \[ \Psi(\mathbf t)=\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E}\psi(t_v,t_w),\qquad \Phi(\mathbf t)=\Psi(\mathbf t)+ \sum_{v\in I}\left( rac{i n_vt_v^2}{4\pi}-it_vight), 	ag{1} \] where \(\psi\) is the original complete edge phase. Every \(n_v\) is an integer at least twenty. The selected geometric critical point is denoted by \[ t_v^*=	heta_v-iH_v,\qquad \mathcal M=\Re\Phi(\mathbf t^*). 	ag{2} \] The [edge-response theorem](research_edge_hessian_and_phase_response.md), Section 7, proves \[ 0<	heta_v< rac{7\pi}{3n_v},\qquad 0<H_v< rac{21d_v}{16n_v}< rac13 . 	ag{3} \] It also proves, throughout \(\mathcal B=\{t:|\Re t|\le1,\ |\Im t|\le1/3\}\), \[ K(t,u)=-2\pi\psi''(t,u),\qquad \Re K(t,u)\succeq rac15 I . 	ag{4} \] Here and below real parts of complex symmetric matrices mean their entrywise real parts, which are their Hermitian parts. There is a useful upper bound on the same box: \[ \|K(t,u)\|_2<2. 	ag{5} \] Indeed, with \(w=	an(t/2)\), \(z=	an(u/2)\), and \(s=\sqrt{1+w^2+z^2}\), the exact matrix is \[ K= rac1s  egin{pmatrix}1+w^2&-wz\-wz&1+z^2\end{pmatrix}. \] The bounds already proved on \(\mathcal B\) give \(|w|,|z|<3/5\) and \(\Re(s^2)>7/8\). Its absolute row and column sums are less than \((43/25)/\sqrt{7/8}<2\), proving (5). ## 2. Every mixed face is below the same critical value Fix \(T=19/20\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq I\), consider the following product of segments: \[  egin{cases} t_v=x_v-iH_v,\quad -T\le x_v\le T,&v
otin S,\ t_v=T+ih_v,\quad -H_v\le h_v\le H_v,&v\in S. \end{cases} 	ag{6} \] The vertices in \(S\) are those at which the vertical term of the exact trace identity is used. Its exponential modulus, including its trace kernels, is \[ \mathcal E_S(\mathbf t)= \Re\!\left(\Psi(\mathbf t)+ \sum_v rac{i n_vt_v^2}{4\pi}ight) -\sum_{v
otin S}H_v-\sum_{v\in S}|h_v|. 	ag{7} \] **Theorem 1.** For every subset \(S\) and every point of (6), \[ \mathcal E_S(\mathbf t) \le\mathcal M- rac{|S|}{400}. 	ag{8} \] In particular this estimate applies simultaneously to all nonempty mixed-current subsets of an arbitrarily long fixed path. The powers may have unrelated magnitudes. **Proof.** First, \(\mathcal E_S\le\Re\Phi\). At a horizontal vertex the charge term \(\Re(-it_v)=-H_v\) is precisely the term in (7). At a vertical vertex it is \(h_v\), which is at least \(-|h_v|\). Write \[ \mathbf t-\mathbf t^*=\mathbf a+i\mathbf b. \] Then \(b_v=0\) outside \(S\), while on \(S\) \[ a_v=T-	heta_v> rac7{12},\qquad 0\le b_v=h_v+H_v\le2H_v. 	ag{9} \] The first inequality follows from (3), \(n_v\ge20\), and \(\pi<22/7\). The segment from \(\mathbf t^*\) to \(\mathbf t\) stays in the convex box \(\mathcal B^I\). Let \(K_G\) be the sum of the edge matrices embedded in the selected vertex coordinates. Define its weighted average along that segment by \[ \overline K_G= 2\int_0^1(1-s)K_G(\mathbf t^*+ s(\mathbf a+i\mathbf b))\,ds =A+iB . 	ag{10} \] Extend all vectors by zero at complete outside endpoints. Equations (4)--(5) imply, with \(A_2=\sum_vd_va_v^2\) and \(B_2=\sum_vd_vb_v^2\), \[ a^TAa\ge A_2/5,\qquad |b^TAb|\le2B_2,\qquad |a^TBb|\le2\sqrt{A_2B_2}. 	ag{11} \] The last bound follows first on each edge and then from Cauchy--Schwarz over edges. These inequalities therefore have no factor depending on path length. Taylor's formula at the full complex critical point, with the quadratic filling term kept exactly, gives \[ \Re\Phi(\mathbf t)-\mathcal M =- rac1{4\pi}  igl(a^TAa-b^TAb-2a^TBb igr) - rac1{2\pi}\sum_vn_va_vb_v. 	ag{12} \] The elementary inequality \(4\sqrt{A_2B_2}\le A_2/10+40B_2\) now yields \[ \Re\Phi(\mathbf t)-\mathcal M \le- rac{A_2}{40\pi} + rac{42B_2}{4\pi} - rac1{2\pi}\sum_{v\in S}n_va_vb_v. 	ag{13} \] The last term has the favorable sign because the vertical side in (6) is the positive real side of the rectangle. For \(v\in S\), (3) and \(d_v\le2\) give \[ n_va_v\ge rac{19n_v}{20}- rac{7\pi}{3}, \qquad 42b_v< rac{441}{2n_v}. \] For every \(n\ge20\), \[  rac{19n^2}{20}- rac{7\pi n}{3}- rac{441}{2}>0. 	ag{14} \] For a rational verification, replace \(7\pi/3\) by \(22/3\). The resulting expression equals \(77/6>0\) at \(n=20\) and increases thereafter. Thus \(n_va_v\ge42b_v\ge21d_vb_v\). The last two terms of (13) consequently have nonpositive sum. Using (9), \[ \Re\Phi(\mathbf t) \le\mathcal M- rac1{40\pi} \sum_{v\in S}d_v(T-	heta_v)^2 <\mathcal M- rac{|S|}{400}. \] Indeed \(49/(5760\pi)>1/400\), for example by \(\pi<22/7\). This proves (8). \(\square\) The same argument works with midpoint cutoffs \(T_N\le T\) and \(T_N=T+O(N^{-1})\), giving a gap \( |S|/401\) for all sufficiently large levels. This weakened constant is only to absorb the finite-grid rounding. ## 3. Why these are the actual Hermite currents Put \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\) and retain the original crossing unit \(C_{N,n}\) from the [exact complete trace formula](research_exact_complete_trace_contour.md). Choose \(T_N\) to be the largest midpoint between consecutive physical angles that is no greater than \(T\). Then \(T_N\le T\), \(0\le T-T_N<2\pi/N\), and \(e^{iNT_N}=-\eta\). For an even polynomial spectator \(f(t)\), the retained trace is exactly \[  egin{split} \mathcal D_{n,N}^{T_N}[f] ={}&- rac{N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi i} \int_{-T_N-iH}^{T_N-iH} \sin t\,f(t)e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)}  rac{e^{-iNt}}{(1-\eta e^{-iNt})^2}\,dt\ &+ rac{\eta N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi} \int_{-H}^{H}  rac{\sin(T_N+ih)\,f(T_N+ih) e^{inN(T_N+ih)^2/(4\pi)}} {4\cosh^2(Nh/2)}\,dh . \end{split} 	ag{15} \] The original value and first derivative at every retained double root, and the simple odd-level root, are all included. The two vertical sides have already been combined into the positive real side in the second line. This uses the spectator's evenness, not a change of the source. Apply (15) at every selected vertex to the exact product of original edge kernels \[ \prod_{\{v,w\}\in E}K_N(t_v,t_w). 	ag{16} \] Each kernel is even in each angle, so the identity remains applicable when other variables have already been moved. The expansion has one term for every subset \(S\subseteq I\), with exactly the domains (6). It introduces no independent edge variables and no missing derivatives at shared edges. The horizontal rational kernel has modulus bounded by a fixed multiple of \(e^{-NH_v}\), and its leading term is \(e^{-iNt_v}\). The vertical factor obeys exactly \[  rac1{4\cosh^2(Nh_v/2)} \le e^{-N|h_v|}. 	ag{17} \] Thus (7) is precisely the exponential upper functional for these terms, provided the edge kernels obey \[ |K_N(t,u)|\le C N^A e^{N\Re\psi(t,u)} \quad	ext{uniformly on }\mathcal B^2. 	ag{18} \] Under (18), Theorem 1 makes every nonempty mixed term exponentially smaller than the selected contribution, at all level parities. Their number \(2^{|I|}-1\) is fixed before \(N	o\infty\). For the empty subset, (4) gives strict horizontal concavity on the entire retained rectangle and its unique maximum at \(\mathbf t^*\). The summed higher Fourier charges are smaller by \(\exp(-N\min_v H_v)\). A uniform nonzero kernel asymptotic near that saddle, together with (18), then gives a nonzero Gaussian coefficient for the retained trace. No separate charge-by-charge certificate is needed. ## 4. A centered bound for the original complementary rows Write \(e_j(t)=e_j(-2\cos t)\) in this section, and keep all \(0\le j<N\) in the original kernel \(K_N(t,u)=\sum_j e_j(t)e_j(u)\). Set \(\gamma=1/200\) and \[ \Omega=\{z:|\Re z|\le19/20,\ |\Im z|\le1/200\}. 	ag{19} \] **Lemma 2.** Uniformly for \(z\in\Omega\) and real \(9/10\le|u|\le\pi\), \[ |K_N(u,z)| \le C N^A e^{N[\Re\psi(0,z)-\gamma(1-\cos u)]}. 	ag{20} \] For two real angles one also has \[ |K_N(u,v)|\le C N^A e^{N[M_\infty-\gamma(1-\cos u)-\gamma(1-\cos v)]}, \qquad M_\infty=\psi(0,0). 	ag{21} \] The first derivative in either removed spectral variable, or the mixed first derivative in both, obeys the same bounds at polynomial cost if each angular loss is replaced by the constant \(\gamma(1-\cos(9/10))\) and the removed angles satisfy \(|u|,|v|\ge9/10\). **Proof of (20).** We separate the original wire indices into \(j/N\in[1/8,1/3]\), the rest of the lower half, and the upper half. This separation is only an estimate of the exact kernel. For a central index and \(|r|\le19/20\), every factor of \(e_j(r)\) is positive. Its exact logarithmic second derivative is \[ -\partial_z^2\log e_j(z) = rac14\sum_{
u<j} \left[ \sec^2\!\left( rac{(2
u+1)\pi/N+z}{2}ight) +\sec^2\!\left( rac{(2
u+1)\pi/N-z}{2}ight) ight]. 	ag{22} \] On a vertical line the modulus of each squared secant is no larger than its value at real part \(r\). The sum at real part \(r\) is a midpoint sum of a convex function. Hence its value is at most \[  rac N{4\pi} \left[	an\!\left( rac{\pi j}{N}+ rac r2ight) +	an\!\left( rac{\pi j}{N}- rac r2ight)ight]. \] The bracket increases with \(j/N\) and \(|r|\). At \(j/N=1/3,\ |r|=19/20\), its first tangent is \(\cot(\pi/6-19/40)<21\) and its second is less than one. Integrating (22) twice vertically, with zero initial real derivative, proves the finite inequality \[ |e_j(r+ih)|\le e_j(r)e^{Nh^2}. 	ag{23} \] For example \(\pi>157/50\) proves the cotangent bound; the resulting coefficient \(22/(8\pi)\) is less than one. The [real Newton estimate](research_three_crossing_real_period_newton_bound.md) gives, uniformly on this central wire, \[ |e_j(u)|\le C N^A e_j(0) e^{-N(1-\cos u)/20}. 	ag{24} \] Indeed the coefficient there is at least \(\sin(\pi/4)/(4\pi)>1/20\). Put \(A_r(y)=V_0(y)+V_r(y)\), with the real Newton entropy \(V_r\) defined in that note. Its maximum on the lower half is attained uniquely at \[ y_*(r)= rac1{2\pi} \arccos\! rac{1-\cos r}{3+\cos r}, \qquad  rac15<y_*(r)\le rac14, 	ag{25} \] and equals the original edge phase \(\psi(0,r)\). The latter identity is the real stationary formula in the original edge calculation; its value at \(r=0\) is \(M_\infty\), fixing the additive constant. Uniform logarithmic factorial errors therefore bound the positive central sum \(\sum e_j(0)e_j(r)\) by \(C N^A e^{N\psi(0,r)}\). The phase is real on the real square. From (4), its real part increases vertically from \(r\): \(\Re\psi(0,r+ih)\ge\psi(0,r)\).
