A more effective joint contour must retain the direct phase in (25), its Cauchy diagonal and the original grouped currents; the argument does not exclude such a contour. ## 6. Reproduction Run the [focused checker](../experiments/check_physical_normal_defect_packet.py): ~~~sh python3 experiments/check_physical_normal_defect_packet.py ~~~ It computes the first normals from the literal Newton products, including the terms whose values vanish, and compares them with ordinary collocation at both parities. It also records the normalized defect at every physical row for several finite levels. Those ratios check the phase and coefficient; the proof of a uniform physical-row asymptotic remains Sections 2–3 above. The fixed-neighborhood extension and the transform bound are proved in Section 5; no growing-order derivative test is substituted for that contour proof. The [saved record](../repro/results/research-physical-normal-defect-packet.json) separates exact finite identities from convergence diagnostics and includes the input hashes.

title: Coherent full-normal traces of physical row products
text:
# Coherent full-normal traces of physical row products Private written proof, 17 November 2026. The positive coefficient contour for a product of physical value rows also controls its original boundary normals. The source-exact Jacobi derivative replaces each normal by a polynomial cofactor and the Ward endpoint coupon. The coupon has a cut, which is retained below. Its jump is polynomial, and the entire uncharged cut lies strictly below the positive coefficient saddle. This proves a polynomial relative upper bound for every mixed first normal, uniformly over all physical rows with a fixed support margin. In a strict bulk degree chart the leading mixed normal is nonzero. A single holomorphic scalar packet then approximates all those physical jets with exponential accuracy. No charged closing, arbitrary-height continuation, or complete network lower bound follows from this local packet. ## 1. Original source and statements Let \(N\ge3\), \(D=N-1\), \(J=\lfloor D/2floor\), and \[ 	heta=\pi/N,\qquad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)	heta),\qquad P_N(C)=2T_N(C/2)+2,\qquad \eta=(-1)^D. 	ag{1} \] The \(N\) indices of the roots of \(P_N\) include their multiplicities. The original trace is \[ \phi_N(f)=\eta N^2[C^D]\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}f. 	ag{2} \] Put \[ F_j(C)=K_N(c_j,C),\qquad G_j(C)=\left.\partial_wK_N(w,C)ight|_{w=c_j}. 	ag{3} \] The normal \(G_j\) is prescribed only at a double physical node. At the odd simple node \(j=J\), only the value is used. Fix \(m\ge3\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and physical indices satisfying \[ k=\sum_{i=1}^m j_i-D\ge\varepsilon N. 	ag{4} \] Write \[ \Gamma_{\mathbf j}=\phi_N\Bigl(\prod_iF_{j_i}\Bigr)>0,\qquad \Gamma_{\mathbf j,I} =\phi_N\Bigl(\prod_{i\in I}G_{j_i} \prod_{i
otin I}F_{j_i}\Bigr), 	ag{5} \] where \(I\) contains only double-node indices. The positive coefficient theorem supplies its actual saddle \(ho=ho_{\mathbf j,N}\), with \[ 0<a\leho\le b<1/4,\qquad V_N\asymp N. 	ag{6} \] All constants in (6) depend only on \(m,\varepsilon\). Set \[ R=ho^{-1},\qquad C_-=c_0-R,\qquad C_+=c_0+R,\qquad M_{\mathbf j}(R)=  rac{\prod_iF_{j_i}(C_-)}{|P_N(C_-)|}. 	ag{7} \] For large \(N\), \(C_-<-2\), with a fixed margin. The exact coefficient normalization gives \[ \Gamma_{\mathbf j} = rac{N^2R\,M_{\mathbf j}(R)} {\sqrt{2\pi V_N}} igl(1+O(N^{-1}) igr). 	ag{8} \] **Theorem 1 (all physical rows).** There are constants \(B,C\), depending only on \(m,\varepsilon\), such that \[ |\Gamma_{\mathbf j,I}| \le C N^B\Gamma_{\mathbf j}. 	ag{9} \] This is uniform in every physical row, both parities, and every allowed subset \(I\). It includes \(j=0\), even last normals, and odd simple values. For the leading coefficient, define on \(0<x<1/2,\ C<2\) \[ g(x,C)=-  rac{2\operatorname{arsinh}  igl(	frac12\sqrt{2-C}\cot(\pi x) igr)} {4\pi\sin(2\pi x)}. 	ag{10} \] The square root and inverse hyperbolic sine have their positive real branches here. **Theorem 2 (bulk normal coefficients).** In addition to (4), suppose that \(j_i/N\) for \(i\in I\) stays in a fixed compact subinterval of \((0,1/2)\). Then \[  rac{\Gamma_{\mathbf j,I}}{\Gamma_{\mathbf j}} =N^{|I|} \left\{\prod_{i\in I}g(j_i/N,C_-) +O\!\left( rac{\log N}{N}ight)ight\}. 	ag{11} \] The error is uniform; the unselected value rows may still approach either endpoint or the fold. Each selected factor in (10) is negative and bounded away from zero. Thus (11) has a nonzero leading coefficient, with sign \((-1)^{|I|}\). Here is the scalar assertion needed to distinguish coherent normal data from separate normal estimates. Let \[ \mathcal B\Subset \{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):0<x_i<1/2,\ \sum_i x_i>1\} 	ag{12} \] be a real compact set, and let \[  oldsymbol\Gamma_N(w_1,\ldots,w_m) =\phi_N\Bigl(\prod_iK_N(w_i,C)\Bigr). 	ag{13} \] **Theorem 3 (one scalar packet on each bulk chart).** A finite cover of \(\mathcal B\) by real product neighborhoods has the following property. On a fixed complex neighborhood of each such product there is a holomorphic scalar \(\mathcal W_N(\mathbf x)\) and constants \(B,\gamma>0\) such that, at every physical tuple in that product, \[ \left| \left[\prod_{i\in I}  rac{1}{C_N'(x_i)}\partial_{x_i}ight] \mathcal W_N(\mathbf x)\Big|_{\mathbf x=\mathbf j/N} -\Gamma_{\mathbf j,I}ight| \le C N^B e^{-\gamma N}\Gamma_{\mathbf j}, \quad C_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+	heta). 	ag{14} \] This includes \(I=\varnothing\) and all \(2^m\) mixed first jets. Equivalently \(\mathcal W_N\), expressed in the local external spectral coordinates \(w_i=C_N(x_i)\), is a single scalar approximation to (13) and those derivatives. The physical error exponent in Theorem 3 comes only from the omitted coefficient-circle arc and the paid cut, minus the explicitly bounded reference-radius loss. The analytic normal-connection rate sets the available thin complex neighborhood, but does not enter that physical error exponent. The charts are strict bulk charts. The theorem does not prescribe fold normals, compare charts on a tall complex continuation, or compare its gaps with a charged-closing loss. ## 2. The exact normal representative and its cut Use the actual common-shift Jacobi determinant, with \(c_0\) held fixed: \[ F_j^\epsilon(C)=  rac{\det(\mathcal J_j(\epsilon)-CI)} {\prod_{r<j}A(r+\epsilon)},\qquad R_j(C)=\left.\partial_\epsilon F_j^\epsilon(C)ight|_0. 	ag{15} \] Set \(R_0=0\). Its spectral eigenvalues exceed \(c_0\); write \(r_{j,b}=\lambda_{j,b}-c_0>0\). In particular \[ F_j(c_0-z)=\prod_{b=1}^j(1+z/r_{j,b}). 	ag{16} \] For \(j\ge1\) in the double-node range, the pinned source gives \[  egin{split} c'(j)G_j(C)={}&c'(0)F_j(C)Q_0(C)+R_j(C)\ &+ rac{c'(0)P_N(C)}{N^2s_1^2} F_j(C)[(\mathcal J_j-CI)^{-1}]_{00}, \end{split} 	ag{17} \] where \(Q_0=G_0\), \(s_1=2\sin	heta\), and \[ c'(j)=-4	heta\sin((2j+1)	heta). 	ag{18} \] At \(j=0\), the endpoint is simply \(G_0=Q_0\). The last factor in (17), after multiplication by \(F_j\), is a polynomial cofactor. Thus there are no genuine Jacobi-resolvent poles in this expression. Let \(\widetilde Q_N\) be the actual even Ward representative of \(Q_0\), descended to \(\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus[2,\infty)\). Define \[ \widehat G_j(C)=  rac{c'(0)F_j(C)\widetilde Q_N(C)+R_j(C)}{c'(j)}. 	ag{19} \] For \(j=0\) this is \(\widetilde Q_N\). It has the value and required first inner-\(C\) normal of the original \(G_j\) at every physical inner node. Consequently products in (5) may use (19) inside their original trace, with the complete product rule. This uses the full physical ideal, including the simple odd node; it is not an equality between free off-grid polynomials. The uniform source bounds are \[ |c'(j)|^{-1}\le C N^2,\qquad \|\mathcal J_j'\|\le6\pi N^3,\qquad |A'/A|\le4\pi. 	ag{20} \] On every fixed-height physical angular rectangle, \[ |\widetilde Q_N|\le C N^2(1+\log N). 	ag{21} \] The compact spectral circles and their two banks below are contained in such rectangles on the original branch. The jump in (21) is explicit. Write \(\sigma=(-1)^N=-\eta\) and \(\ell_N(t)=D/2-t/(2	heta)\). The Ward function \(V_N\) satisfies \[ \widetilde Q_N(-2\cos t) = rac{\eta V_N(t)+c_0}{4\sin^2	heta},\qquad V_N(t+2\pi)-V_N(t) =-2\sigma N\sin	heta\cot(\pi\ell_N(t)). 	ag{22} \] For \(C=2\cosh h\), \(h\ge0\), the upper spectral bank is \(t_+=\pi+ih\), and the lower bank may be written \(t_-=-\pi+ih\), using the evenness of \(V_N\). Since \(\ell_N(t_-)=N-	frac12-iNh/(2\pi)\), (22) gives \[  oxed{\quad \widetilde Q_{N,+}(2\cosh h) -\widetilde Q_{N,-}(2\cosh h) = rac{iN}{2\sin	heta}	anh(Nh/2). \quad} 	ag{23} \] This sign uses upper minus lower bank. Both the jump and each bank have polynomial size. At \(C=2\) the two banks meet and the jump vanishes. Let \[ \mathcal P_I(C)= \prod_{i\in I}\widehat G_{j_i}(C) \prod_{i
otin I}F_{j_i}(C). 	ag{24} \] Start from small contours around the physical spectrum, where (19) has the exact source data, and enlarge them to the circle \(|C-c_0|=R\), cut at its right intersection. Cauchy's theorem gives the exact identity \[ \Gamma_{\mathbf j,I}= rac{\eta N^2}{2\pi i} \left\{ \int_{\mathcal C_R} rac{\mathcal P_I(C)}{P_N(C)}\,dC +\int_2^{C_+}  rac{\mathcal P_{I,+}(C)-\mathcal P_{I,-}(C)} {P_N(C)}\,dC ight\}. 	ag{25} \] The outer circle is counterclockwise with its original slit branches. The upper cut bank runs from \(2\) to \(C_+\), and the lower bank returns. The shrinking cap at \(2\) contributes zero: the numerator is bounded there and \(P_N(2)=4\). No cut term has been deleted. ## 3. Cofactor omissions preserve the circle gap Diagonalizing the real symmetric matrix \(\mathcal J_j-c_0I\) gives \[ R_j(c_0-z)=  rac{\displaystyle\sum_b d_{j,b} \prod_{a
e b}(r_{j,a}+z)} {\prod_{r<j}A(r)} -\left(\sum_{r<j}A'(r)/A(r)ight)F_j(c_0-z), \qquad |d_{j,b}|\le\|\mathcal J_j'\|. 	ag{26} \] This formula is valid also at repeated eigenvalues: choose any orthonormal eigenbasis and take the diagonal entries of \(\mathcal J_j'\). It is a polynomial identity. On \(z=Re^{i\vartheta}\), division by \(F_j(C_-)\) turns each full factor into \((r+Re^{i\vartheta})/(r+R)\), of modulus at most one. Omission of one factor costs at most \((r+R)^{-1}\le R^{-1}\). The sum in (26), (20), and the Ward bound (21) show that every fixed normal product has only a polynomial loss. This argument does not require an upper bound on a Jacobi eigenvalue. More importantly, the denominator alone gives a strict gap. Put \(d_a=c_0-c_a\ge0\). A fixed positive fraction of the \(d_a\)'s lie in \([1,2]\), and \(R^{-1}\in[a,b]\). Consequently \[  rac{|P_N(C_-)|}{|P_N(c_0-Re^{i\vartheta})|} =\prod_a  rac{1-ho d_a}{|1-ho d_ae^{-i\vartheta}|} \le \exp\{-cN\sin^2(\vartheta/2)\}. 	ag{27} \] Indeed each of those geometric factors equals \(\{1+4u(1-u)^{-2}\sin^2(\vartheta/2)\}^{-1/2}\), with \(u=ho d_a\) bounded away from zero and one. Omitting numerator factors leaves all of (27) available. Thus \[ \left| rac{\mathcal P_I(c_0-Re^{i\vartheta})} {P_N(c_0-Re^{i\vartheta})}ight| \le C N^B M_{\mathbf j}(R) e^{-cN\sin^2(\vartheta/2)}. 	ag{28} \] This includes the two one-sided limits at the cut. The circle integral is at most \(C N^{B-1/2}M_{\mathbf j}(R)\). ## 4. The whole uncharged cut has a strict gap The original slit profile is \[ \Psi_x(C)= 2\int_0^x\operatorname{arsinh}  igl(	frac12\sqrt{2-C}\cot(\pi s) igr)\,ds, \qquad 0\le x\le1/2. 	ag{29} \] The all-row source theorem gives \[ N^{-1}\log|F_j(C)|=\Re\Psi_{j/N}(C)+o(1) 	ag{30} \] uniformly over all physical rows on each compact slit set. Only this uniform \(o(1)\) is used on the slit. On half-plane compacts the stronger error is \(O(\log N/N)\). For \(C=2\cosh h\) on the upper bank, define \[ B_x(h)=\Re\Psi_x(2\cosh h+i0) =2\int_0^{\min(x,\pi^{-1}\arctan(\sinh(h/2)))} \operatorname{arcosh}  igl(\sinh(h/2)\cot(\pi s) igr)\,ds. 	ag{31} \] The real part in (29) converges continuously to (31), uniformly in \(x\in[0,1/2]\) and bounded \(h\). To see this directly, split the integral at a small positive \(s\); away from zero continuity is uniform, and near zero a uniform bound \(C(1+|\log s|)\) has an arbitrarily small integral. This also treats the moving threshold of the inverse hyperbolic cosine. For \(h>0\), differentiating (31) has no boundary term because its integrand vanishes at the moving endpoint. The substitution \(v=\sin(\pi s)\) gives \[ B_x'(h)= rac1\pi \arcsin\!\left(\min\{\coth(h/2)\sin(\pi x),1\}ight) \ge x. 	ag{32} \] In particular \(B_{1/2}(h)=h/2\). For \(x_i=j_i/N\), set \[ \mathcal A_{\mathbf x}(h) =\sum_iB_{x_i}(h)-h. 	ag{33} \] By (4), for large \(N\), \[ \mathcal A_{\mathbf x}'(h) \ge\sum_i x_i-1\ge\varepsilon/2. 	ag{34} \] Thus the cut action is increasing. This statement concerns the uncharged product; it has no extra filling factor. Here is a rigorous bound on the finite source along the cut, including zeros of determinants. For real \(C\), all roots of \(F_j\) are real, so for fixed \(\delta>0\) \[ |F_j(C)|\le|F_j(C+i\delta)|. 	ag{35} \] Every omitted-factor term in (26) satisfies \[ \left|\prod_{a
e b}(\lambda_{j,a}-C)ight| \le\delta^{-1} \prod_a|\lambda_{j,a}-C-i\delta|. 	ag{36} \] Equations (20)--(23), (26), and (36) therefore imply, uniformly on the whole finite cut, \[ |\mathcal P_{I,+}(C)-\mathcal P_{I,-}(C)| \le C_\delta N^B\prod_i|F_{j_i}(C+i\delta)|. 	ag{37} \] For \(I=\varnothing\) the left side is zero. Fix \(\delta\) first, use (30), then use the uniform continuity following (31). Since \[ P_N(2\cosh h) =e^{Nh}(1+e^{-Nh})^2\ge e^{Nh}, 	ag{38} \] for any fixed tolerance \(	au>0\) we obtain \[ \left| rac{\mathcal P_{I,+}(2\cosh h) -\mathcal P_{I,-}(2\cosh h)} {P_N(2\cosh h)}ight| \le C_	au N^B e^{N\{\mathcal A_{\mathbf x}(h)+	au\}}, \quad 0\le h\le h_{+,N}, 	ag{39} \] where \(h_{+,N}=\operatorname{arcosh}(C_+/2)\). No estimate by the inverse of \(F_j(C)\) on the cut has been used. It remains to compare its endpoint with the actual saddle. Put \(h_{-,N}=\operatorname{arcosh}(-C_-/2)\). The allowed \(R\)'s form a compact subinterval of \((4,\infty)\); since \(c_0	o2\), there is a fixed \(\Delta>0\) such that \[ h_{+,N}-h_{-,N}\ge\Delta. 	ag{40} \] The numerator cannot erase this denominator gap. Indeed, with \(R_\delta=\sqrt{R^2+\delta^2}\), (16) gives \[ |F_j(C_++i\delta)| \le F_j(c_0-R_\delta) \le F_j(C_-)(R_\delta/R)^j. 	ag{41} \] The last exponent costs \(O(N\delta^2)\), uniformly in all indices. Apply (30) at \(C_++i\delta\), then take the boundary limit using (31). It follows, uniformly over the tuples and allowed radii, that \[ \sum_i B_{x_i}(h_{+,N}) \le N^{-1}\log\prod_iF_{j_i}(C_-)+o(1). 	ag{42} \] For full precision in (42), any desired positive tolerance is first obtained by fixing a sufficiently small \(\delta\); the remaining \(o(1)\) is then supplied by (30). This is sufficient with the fixed gap in (40). Also \[ \log|P_N(C_-)|=Nh_{-,N}+O(1) 	ag{43} \] uniformly, at both parities. Equations (34), (40)--(43), with tolerances smaller than \(\Delta/4\), prove \[ \left|\int_2^{C_+}  rac{\mathcal P_{I,+}-\mathcal P_{I,-}}{P_N}\,dCight| \le C N^B M_{\mathbf j}(R)e^{-\gamma_0N} 	ag{44} \] for a fixed \(\gamma_0>0\). The finite cut length is uniformly bounded. The argument includes \(h=0\), every root threshold, and every physical row. Combining (25), (28), (44), and (8) proves Theorem 1. ## 5. The leading bulk normal insertion On a fixed bulk degree interval and a buffered compact negative spectral neighborhood containing all \(C_-\), the pinned slit-normal connection gives one holomorphic unit \(A_N(x,C)\) with \[  egin{split} A_N(j/N,C)&=F_j(C)(1+O(e^{-\kappa N})),\ \partial_xA_N(j/N,C) -C_N'(j/N)\widehat G_j(C) &=F_j(C)O(e^{-\kappa N}),\ \log A_N(x,C)-N\Psi_x(C)&=O(\log N). \end{split} 	ag{45} \] The construction uses an actual physical anchor. These bounds hold on larger fixed domains before differentiation. Cauchy's formula in \(x\) and \(C\) gives \[ N^{-1} rac{\widehat G_j(C)}{F_j(C)} =g(j/N,C)+O(\log N/N), 	ag{46} \] with all fixed \(C\)-derivatives. Here \(C_N'(x)=-4\pi\sin(2\pi x+	heta)\); replacing it by \(-4\pi\sin(2\pi x)\) costs \(O(N^{-1})\). This proves precisely (10), including its sign. Restrict (25) to a fixed small arc about \(\vartheta=0\). The rest of the circle and the entire cut have exponential gaps by (28),(44). On that arc the normalized insertion \[ a_N(C)=N^{-|I|} \prod_{i\in I} rac{\widehat G_{j_i}(C)} {F_{j_i}(C)} 	ag{47} \] is holomorphic with uniformly bounded fixed derivatives. There are no roots of \(F_j\) in this negative neighborhood. The scalar coefficient Fourier integral from the positive source has zero linear term at \(ho\), variance \(V_N\), and cumulants of every fixed order \(O(N)\). Its modulus has (27). Multiplication by a holomorphic insertion with bounded first two derivatives gives \[  rac{	ext{inserted circle integral}} {	ext{value circle integral}} =a_N(C_-)+O(N^{-1}). 	ag{48} \] For completeness, on \(|\vartheta|\le N^{-2/5}\) expand the insertion through its linear term and the centered characteristic function through its cubic term. Each single odd term integrates to zero on the symmetric interval. The remaining errors are bounded by \(C(V_N^{-1}+N V_N^{-2}+N^2V_N^{-3})=O(N^{-1})\). Outside that interval (27) is negligible. The analytic map \(C=c_0-Re^{i\vartheta}\) has uniformly bounded derivatives, so these estimates apply to (47). The polynomial global normal bound makes the discarded arc and cut negligible also after normalization. Equations (46)--(48) prove (11). ## 6. An exponentially accurate common scalar packet We use the exact scalar correction from Section 6 of the pinned slit-normal connection. On a sufficiently thin fixed degree neighborhood, it gives a holomorphic function \(\mathfrak F_N(x,C)\) satisfying, identically in \(C\) on the buffered negative spectral domain, \[ \mathfrak F_N(j/N,C)=F_j(C),\qquad \partial_x\mathfrak F_N(j/N,C) =C_N'(j/N)\widehat G_j(C). 	ag{48a} \] This is the finite \(\operatorname{sinc}^2\) correction of the two normalized errors in (45); its scalar construction preserves both jets at every other degree node as well. It obeys a polynomial normalized own-profile bound on the present half-plane compact. The exponential rate \(\kappa\) in (45) limits the thickness allowed for that bound. It does not create an error in (48a). We give a uniform fixed-chart contour rather than letting it depend nonholomorphically on the external variables. Choose a reference real tuple in (12), a nearby physical tuple at each \(N\), and its exact saddle \(ho_{0,N}\). Write \(R_{0,N}=ho_{0,N}^{-1}\). Take one small symmetric arc \[ \gamma_{0,N}:\quad C=c_0-R_{0,N}e^{i\vartheta},\qquad |\vartheta|\le\vartheta_0, 	ag{49} \] oriented counterclockwise as part of that circle. Choose \(\vartheta_0>0\) small enough that all these arcs and fixed neighborhoods lie in the negative spectral domain used in (45). Define \[ \mathcal W_N(\mathbf x)=  rac{\eta N^2}{2\pi i} \int_{\gamma_{0,N}}  rac{\prod_i\mathfrak F_N(x_i,C)}{P_N(C)}\,dC. 	ag{50} \] This is one jointly holomorphic scalar. The external coordinate change \(w_i=C_N(x_i)\) is univalent on sufficiently small bulk neighborhoods. We verify that the same arc works for an entire fixed real product neighborhood. Jacobi matrices of successive sizes are nested principal matrices. Interlacing and the increasing function \(r\mapstoho r/(1+ho r)\in[0,1]\) show that increasing one \(j_i\) by one changes its Bernoulli mean by a number in \([0,1]\). The target integer \(k\) changes by one. On a slightly enlarged compact \(ho\)-interval, \(\mu_N'(ho)\asymp N\). Therefore the exact saddle satisfies the uniform lattice Lipschitz estimate \[ |ho_{\mathbf j,N}-ho_{\mathbf j',N}| \le  rac{C}{N}\sum_i|j_i-j_i'|. 	ag{51} \] All comparisons stay within the fixed support margin. For the source-specific coefficient function \(H\), set \(\mathcal F(ho)=\log H(ho)-k\logho\). At its saddle \(\mathcal F'=0\), and \(\mathcal F''=O(N)\) on the relevant compact interval (use the mean and variance formulas). Thus, if \(|\mathbf j/N-\mathbf x^0|\le\delta\), \[ 0\le\mathcal F(ho_{0,N}) -\mathcal F(ho_{\mathbf j,N}) \le C N\delta^2+O(N^{-1}). 	ag{52} \] Equivalently the value mass \(R M_{\mathbf j}(R)\) at the reference radius is at most \(e^{CN\delta^2+O(1)}\) times its mass at the actual saddle. The elementary identity behind this equivalence is \(R M_{\mathbf j}(R)=a_{\mathbf j}H(ho)ho^{-k}\). The bounds (28),(44) apply to any radius in the enlarged compact interval, regardless of whether it is the current tuple's saddle. At the reference radius let \[ g_{m arc}=c\sin^2(\vartheta_0/2),\qquad g_{m cut}=\gamma_0, 	ag{53} \] where \(c\) is the uniform constant in (28) and \(\gamma_0\) is the cut gap in (44). Choose \(\delta>0\) after these constants and after \(\vartheta_0\), so that the loss \(C\delta^2\) in (52) is smaller than half of \(\min(g_{m arc},g_{m cut})\). At a physical tuple, differentiating (50) in any subset of its distinct external variables replaces the corresponding \(\mathfrak F_N\)'s by \((C_N')^{-1}\partial_x\mathfrak F_N\). Equation (48a) identifies the resulting integrand exactly with (24) on the retained arc. This holds simultaneously for every mixed subset \(I\). Thus the physical comparison error consists precisely of the omitted circle arc and the entire cut in (25). They are exponentially small by the preceding paragraph. Finally (8) compares the mass to \(\Gamma_{\mathbf j}\). Any fixed positive \[ \gamma< \min(g_{m arc},g_{m cut})-C\delta^2 	ag{54} \] is allowed after adjusting the polynomial prefactor. This proves (14) for every subset \(I\). A finite cover of the compact set in (12) completes Theorem 3. The argument constructs the scalar packet with exact source-compatible arc jets, rather than assigning independent normal functions to value estimates. The rate \(\kappa\) from (45) enters only the available complex strip and its normalized holomorphic bound; it is absent from (54). No off-grid approximation to the canonical polynomial (13), or comparison of (54) with a subsequent charged-closing loss, is asserted. ## 7. Scope and complete direct sources The all-row estimate (9) controls the original mixed boundary normals before any further signed observation. The cut in (25) is part of the proof, not a discarded ideal multiple. A crossing representative has an exponentially large jump on this same cut; its additional action is not covered by (34) or (44). The packet (50) covers only its stated bulk physical tuples. It does not replace the whole original grid, cancel exterior currents, or provide a lower bound after an arbitrary crossing. Its common mixed jets remove a local normal-compatibility ambiguity, with an explicit source-preserving contour and retained correction. The complete direct texts and their used implications were read at these pins: * [Positive coefficient saddle for physical products](research_physical_products_positive_coefficient_saddle.md), SHA256 e82fea1f786383a1cfe4529573805adf5fc75a77e433e38ea609024bdeed7824: exact positive coefficient, all-row compact saddle, denominator characteristic gap, and local central limit. * [Physical Jacobi charge boundary](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_physical_jacobi_charge_boundary.md), SHA256 530425b0c4504f2512954438465deb6d9a6e322fa58c641b6c678161baae6583: actual determinant, common-shift cofactor identity, uniform row bounds, and full-inner-trace normal substitution. * [Odd Ward logarithmic factorial](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_odd_ward_logarithmic_factorial.md), SHA256 63ae4693846f00a9b843b98b423959964a8ccb3a72dc8ee0fc1ac36b69f3d4b8: even full-jet endpoint representative, physical-rectangle bound, and exact angular monodromy. * [Physical-row slit-plane bound](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_mixed_next_first_short_edge_slit_plane_bound.md), SHA256 efe1c1c89bb01f5a0aca9468917595926648780bca265f73000ede095f432e7b: uniform all-row profile, its original normalization, and the stronger half-plane logarithmic remainder. * [Actual slit normal connection](research_physical_row_slit_normal_connection.md), SHA256 a5084adb4ff25cb08020e5f9485bd1aaea5b49468c6ab0af311ebc1c0c504d99: one actually anchored scalar mode with exponential value and independent-normal agreement, and its exact scalar full-jet correction on thin bulk degree charts. Only written mathematics, text reads and metadata hashes were used. No mathematical programs, tests, numerical evaluations, or builds were run. Frozen notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: One positive coefficient for any fixed number of physical rows
text: # One positive coefficient for any fixed number of physical rows Private written proof, 17 November 2026. The original trace of a product of physical value rows has an exact one-variable coefficient representation. Its generating function is a product of linear factors and reciprocal linear factors, all with positive coefficients. Exponential tilting therefore turns the trace into the probability that a sum of Bernoulli and geometric random variables equals a prescribed integer. This representation gives a uniform nonzero leading coefficient for any fixed number of rows, including rows at the midpoint. It also evaluates every fixed-degree polynomial inserted into that trace. It does not estimate a crossing power or an inserted boundary derivative: their degrees or coefficients depend on the level. ## 1. Exact coefficient representation Let \(N\ge3\), \(D=N-1\), \(J=\lfloor D/2\rfloor\), and put \[ c_a=2\cos((2a+1)\pi/N),\qquad P_N(C)=2T_N(C/2)+2,\qquad \eta=(-1)^D. \] Here \(T_N\) is the Chebyshev polynomial, so \(P_N\) is monic of degree \(N\). The indices \(a=0,\ldots,N-1\) list its roots with their full multiplicities. Define \[ d_a=c_0-c_a\ge0,\qquad \phi_N(f)=\eta N^2[C^D]\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}f. \tag{1} \] The trace is applied to the canonical remainder even when the ordinary degree of \(f\) is larger than \(D\). The physical row \(F_j(C)=K_N(c_j,C)\), \(0\le j\le J\), has ordinary degree \(j\) and \(F_j(c_0)=1\). The positive Jacobi recurrence in the first direct source realizes it as \[ F_j(C)=\frac{\det(\mathcal J_j-CI)} {\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}A_r},\qquad \mathcal J_j>c_0I. \tag{2} \] Let \(r_{j,1},\ldots,r_{j,j}>0\) be the eigenvalues of \(\mathcal J_j-c_0I\), with multiplicity. Since \(F_j(c_0)=1\), \[ F_j(c_0-z)=\prod_{b=1}^{j}(1+z/r_{j,b}). \tag{3} \] An empty product is one, so (3) also covers \(j=0\). Fix \(m\) physical indices \(j_1,\ldots,j_m\). Set \[ s=\sum_i j_i,\qquad k=s-D,\qquad a_{\mathbf j}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\prod_{b=1}^{j_i}r_{j_i,b}^{-1}, \] \[ H_{\mathbf j,N}(x)= \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{m}\prod_{b=1}^{j_i} (1+r_{j_i,b}x)} {\displaystyle\prod_{a=0}^{N-1}(1-d_ax)} . \tag{4} \] All Taylor coefficients of \(H\) are positive. For \(N\ge3\) at least one \(d_a\) is positive, so every nonnegative coefficient is strictly positive. **Proposition 1.** With the convention that a negative Taylor coefficient is zero, \[ \Gamma_{\mathbf j}^{(m)} :=\phi_N\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}F_{j_i}\right) =N^2a_{\mathbf j}[x^k]H_{\mathbf j,N}(x). \tag{5} \] Consequently this trace is positive exactly when \(s\ge D\). When \(s=D\), its exact value is \(N^2a_{\mathbf j}\). **Proof.** Polynomial division gives \[ [C^D]\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}f=[C^{-1}]\,f(C)/P_N(C), \tag{6} \] where the right side is the Laurent coefficient at infinity. The polynomial quotient contributes no \(C^{-1}\) term. The substitution \(C=c_0-z\) changes that coefficient's sign. Also \[ P_N(c_0-z)=(-1)^N\prod_a(z-d_a). \] The two signs and \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\) cancel. By (3), the required coefficient is therefore \(N^2a_{\mathbf j}\) times the coefficient of \(z^{-1}\) in \[ z^{s-N} \frac{\prod_{i,b}(1+r_{j_i,b}/z)} {\prod_a(1-d_a/z)}. \] Putting \(x=1/z\) proves (5). This calculation retains every double root of \(P_N\); it has not replaced the trace by a sum of values at distinct roots. \(\square\) ## 2. The exact probability distribution Suppose \(k>0\), and write \(d_{\max}=\max_a d_a\). For \(0<\rho<d_{\max}^{-1}\), take mutually independent random variables as follows: * one Bernoulli variable for each \(r=r_{j_i,b}\), with success probability \(v_r=\rho r/(1+\rho r)\); * one geometric variable for each \(d=d_a\), with probabilities \(\mathbb P(Y_d=n)=(1-u_d)u_d^n\), \(n\ge0\), where \(u_d=\rho d\). A factor with \(d=0\) gives the zero variable. Let \(S_\rho\) be their sum. Its probability generating function is \[ \mathbb E z^{S_\rho}=\frac{H(\rho z)}{H(\rho)}. \tag{7} \] Its mean and variance are \[ \mu_N(\rho)=\sum_r\frac{\rho r}{1+\rho r} +\sum_a\frac{\rho d_a}{1-\rho d_a}, \] \[ V_N(\rho)=\sum_r\frac{\rho r}{(1+\rho r)^2} +\sum_a\frac{\rho d_a}{(1-\rho d_a)^2} =\rho\mu_N'(\rho). \tag{8} \] The mean is strictly increasing from zero to infinity. Thus there is exactly one \(\rho=\rho_{\mathbf j,N}\) satisfying \[ \mu_N(\rho)=k. \tag{9} \] Equations (5) and (7) give the exact identity \[ \Gamma_{\mathbf j}^{(m)} =N^2a_{\mathbf j}H(\rho)\rho^{-k} \mathbb P(S_\rho=k). \tag{10} \] In particular the saddle in (9) is selected by the original finite source, without a choice of logarithmic branch. ## 3. Uniform control up to the midpoint Fix \(m\ge3\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). Consider every physical tuple with \[ \sum_i j_i-D\ge\varepsilon N. \tag{11} \] There are constants \(0<a<b<1/4\) and \(0<c<C<\infty\), depending only on \(m,\varepsilon\), such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\), \[ a\le\rho_{\mathbf j,N}\le b,\qquad cN\le V_N(\rho_{\mathbf j,N})\le CN . \tag{12} \] No bound keeping \(j_i/N\) away from \(1/2\) is needed. To prove the lower bound on \(\rho\), first control the number of large Jacobi eigenvalues. For each fixed \(0<\delta<1/2\), the coefficients \[ A_r=\frac{(2\sin((r+1)\pi/N))^4} {2\sin((2r+1)\pi/N)\,2\sin((2r+2)\pi/N)},\qquad C_r=\frac{(2\sin(r\pi/N))^4} {2\sin(2r\pi/N)\,2\sin((2r+1)\pi/N)} \tag{13} \] are uniformly bounded for \(r\le(1/2-\delta)N\), with \(C_0=0\). For small arguments this follows from \(\sin t\asymp t\); elsewhere the displayed denominators stay away from their upper endpoint zero. The diagonal of \(\mathcal J_j-c_0I\) is \(A_r+C_r\), and its off-diagonal entries are \(-\sqrt{A_rC_{r+1}}\). Delete the last at most \(\delta N+2\) rows and columns of this matrix. The remaining principal matrix has norm at most a constant \(R_\delta\), by the bound on its row sums. Eigenvalue interlacing therefore implies that at most \(\delta N+2\) of its original eigenvalues exceed \(R_\delta\). The same statement is immediate if \(j\) was already below the cutoff. Since \(d_a<4\), the mean in (8), for \(0<\rho<1/4\), is at most \[ \mu_N(\rho) \le m(\delta N+2)+\frac{mN}{2}R_\delta\rho +\frac{4N\rho}{1-4\rho}. \tag{14} \] Choose \(\delta\) so that \(m\delta<\varepsilon/4\), then choose \(a>0\) small enough. For large \(N\), the right side at \(\rho=a\) is less than \(\varepsilon N\). Equations (9) and (11) imply \(\rho>a\). For the upper bound, the \(N\) equally spaced angular roots of \(P_N\), including multiplicity, imply that for each fixed small \(\xi>0\), at least \(c_*\sqrt{\xi}\,N\) of the numbers \(d_a\) lie in \([4-\xi,4)\), for large \(N\). Here \(c_*>0\) is an absolute constant. The counting assertion follows from \(2+2\cos t=4-t^2+O(t^4)\) near the maximum. Thus, as \(b\uparrow1/4\), the geometric part alone has \(\mu_N(b)/N\) arbitrarily large, uniformly for large \(N\): take \(\xi\) comparable with \(1-4b\) in that count. Choose a fixed \(b<1/4\) for which this mean exceeds \(mN/2\). Since \(k\le mN/2\), monotonicity gives \(\rho<b\). Finally a fixed positive fraction of the \(d_a\) lie in \([1,2]\). For \(\rho\in[a,b]\), their geometric variances are bounded below by a positive constant. All geometric variances are bounded above by \(4b/(1-4b)^2\), and each Bernoulli variance is at most \(1/4\). This proves (12). ## 4. A uniform leading coefficient **Theorem 2.** Fix \(m,\varepsilon\) as in (11). Uniformly over all such tuples and both parities, \[ \Gamma_{\mathbf j}^{(m)} =\frac{N^2a_{\mathbf j}H(\rho)\rho^{-k}} {\sqrt{2\pi V_N(\rho)}}\,(1+O(N^{-1})). \tag{15} \] The displayed leading factor is strictly positive. Moreover, for every fixed integer \(h\), \[ \frac{[x^{k+h}]H}{[x^k]H} =\rho^{-h}(1+O_h(N^{-1})). \tag{16} \] The constants are uniform for \(h\) in any fixed finite set. **Proof.** Fourier inversion applies to the integer-valued variable in (7). At the saddle \(\mathbb E S_\rho=k\). The geometric factors with \(d_a\in[1,2]\) give \[ \left|\mathbb E e^{i\theta(S_\rho-k)}\right| \le \exp(-cN\sin^2(\theta/2)),\qquad -\pi\le\theta\le\pi. \tag{17} \] Indeed each of their uncentered factors has modulus \[ \frac{1-u}{|1-ue^{i\theta}|} =\left(1+\frac{4u}{(1-u)^2}\sin^2(\theta/2)\right)^{-1/2}, \] where \(u\) is uniformly separated from zero and one. All remaining factors have modulus at most one. The sum of the absolute cumulant bounds of each fixed order is \(O(N)\). For the geometric factors this uses \(u\le4b<1\). For Bernoulli factors it holds uniformly for all success probabilities, regardless of the size of a Jacobi eigenvalue. Consequently, on a fixed small interval, \[ \log\mathbb E e^{i\theta(S_\rho-k)} =-\tfrac12V_N\theta^2-\tfrac{i}{6}\kappa_3\theta^3 +O(N\theta^4), \qquad |\kappa_3|\le CN. \tag{18} \] Outside \(|\theta|\le N^{-2/5}\), (17) makes the integral exponentially small compared with \(N^{-1/2}\). Inside, expand the cubic exponential and \(e^{-ih\theta}\). Their first odd terms integrate to zero on this symmetric interval. After Gaussian integration, the relative errors are bounded by constant multiples of \[ N/V_N^2+N^2/V_N^3+(1+h^2)/V_N=O_h(N^{-1}). \] The discarded Gaussian tails are exponentially small. Hence, uniformly for bounded \(h\), \[ \mathbb P(S_\rho=k+h) =(2\pi V_N)^{-1/2}(1+O_h(N^{-1})). \tag{19} \] Equation (10) proves (15). Applying (7) to \(k+h\) and \(k\) and taking their ratio proves (16). \(\square\) The proof is an elementary local central-limit argument for this particular finite product. No asymptotic independence is assumed; the independence in (7) is an exact representation. ## 5. Fixed-degree observations in the original trace Let \(q(C)\) be any fixed polynomial. Formula (6) gives exactly \[ \frac{\phi_N(q(C)\prod_i F_{j_i}(C))} {\Gamma_{\mathbf j}^{(m)}} =\frac{[x^k]\{H(x)q(c_0-x^{-1})\}}{[x^k]H(x)} . \tag{20} \] The numerator uses only finitely many adjacent coefficients of \(H\). Their ratios are given by (16). Thus \[ \frac{\phi_N(q(C)\prod_i F_{j_i}(C))} {\Gamma_{\mathbf j}^{(m)}} =q(c_0-\rho^{-1})+O_q(N^{-1}). \tag{21} \] This holds uniformly on (11); no derivative at a repeated root has been dropped in taking the trace. It also holds uniformly for polynomials of bounded degree with bounded coefficients. If \(|q(c_0-\rho^{-1})|\ge\delta>0\), the observed trace has a nonzero leading coefficient and the same exponential rate as \(\Gamma_{\mathbf j}^{(m)}\). The qualifier about bounded degree is essential. The original crossing \(R^p\), even for fixed \(p\), is represented in the finite algebra by a polynomial whose degree grows with \(N\). The Fourier cancellations in that trace are not covered by (16) or (21). Likewise replacing a physical value row by its independent boundary derivative changes the positive factorization used in (3). ## 6. Complete direct sources and scope The complete direct sources used here are: * [The physical Jacobi equation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_physical_jacobi_charge_boundary.md), SHA256 530425b0c4504f2512954438465deb6d9a6e322fa58c641b6c678161baae6583: the exact physical recurrence, determinant formula, strict location of its eigenvalues, and normalization \(F_j(c_0)=1\). * [The full physical product](research_physical_row_full_product_normal_support.md), SHA256 708d22248526c75b0d8b26cc9a07c63d8471b07d200b9e9947059ca8145b2efd: the original Frobenius trace, canonical remainder, physical row range, and repeated-root conventions. The positivity and degree support of the unobserved product trace were already known from the positive Newton multiplication table. The contribution here is its single positive coefficient, the uniform scalar saddle including midpoint rows, its explicit probability normalization, and the bounded-degree observation estimate. No identification with the volume of a partially filled knot complement or lower bound for its complete crossed source is asserted. Only written mathematics, source reads, and metadata hashes were used. No mathematical programs, tests, numerical evaluations, or builds were run. Frozen manuscripts and public documents remain unchanged.

title: Alternating physical-row linearization and odd-turn quadratic phases
text: # Alternating physical-row linearization and odd-turn quadratic phases Private written proof, 17 November 2026. The ordinary product of two original physical rows has strictly alternating linearization coefficients throughout its full triangle support, provided its degree stays in the physical-row range. A finite positive recursion proves the signs and computes every coefficient. An odd signed turn removes precisely the alternating signs, retaining a sum with positive amplitudes and the original quadratic phases. Above this degree range, an expansion in physical value rows alone is impossible. The original normal rows supply the missing degrees and have the retained Jordan action. No cancellation or lower bound for the resulting quadratic sum is inferred. ## 1. Original rows and monic normalization Use \[ N\ge2,\quad D=N-1,\quad J=\lfloor D/2\rfloor,\quad \theta=\pi/N,\quad q=e^{i\theta},\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\quad \kappa=q^{D^2/2}, \] \[ s_r=2\sin(r\theta),\quad S_r=\prod_{a=1}^r s_a,\quad S_0=1, \quad c_r=2\cos((2r+1)\theta), \] \[ P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2,\quad e_r(Z)=S_r^{-2}\prod_{a<r}(c_a-Z),\quad K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{r=0}^{D}e_r(w)e_r(Z). \tag{1} \] All canonical operators are in the original full algebra \(\mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[Z]/(P_N)\). Its physical turn satisfies \(Te_r=e_{D-r}\), and \[ V_n=\kappa^nTR^{-n}T,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z. \tag{2} \] Write \[ F_j(Z)=K_N(c_j,Z),\qquad 0\le j\le J. \tag{3} \] These polynomials have degree exactly \(j\), with \(F_0=1\). Their original recurrence, for \(0\le r<J\), is \[ A_rF_{r+1}=(c_0+A_r+C_r-Z)F_r-C_rF_{r-1}, \tag{4} \] \[ A_r=\frac{s_{r+1}^4}{s_{2r+1}s_{2r+2}},\qquad C_r=\frac{s_r^4}{s_{2r}s_{2r+1}}\ (r\ge1),\qquad C_0=0. \tag{5} \] The term containing \(F_{-1}\) is absent. Every displayed denominator in this range is nonzero, and \(A_r>0\), \(C_r>0\) when \(r\ge1\). Put \[ H_0=1,\qquad H_j=\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}A_r =\frac{S_j^4}{S_{2j}}>0,\qquad p_j=(-1)^jH_jF_j . \tag{6} \] The factorial formula follows by multiplying (5); \(2j<N\) for all \(j\le J\). Thus \(p_j\) is monic and \[ p_0=1,\quad p_1=Z-b_0,\quad p_{r+1}=(Z-b_r)p_r-a_rp_{r-1}, \tag{7} \] Only indices at most \(J\) are used; the \(p_1\) identity applies when \(J\ge1\). \[ b_r=c_0+A_r+C_r,\qquad a_r=A_{r-1}C_r\ (r\ge1),\qquad a_0=0 . \tag{8} \] ## 2. Strict monotonicity before the physical fold Only \(b_0,\ldots,b_{J-1}\) and \(a_0,\ldots,a_{J-1}\) will be used. When \(N\le4\), \(J\le1\), so all products in the theorem below have a constant factor. For the nontrivial range assume \(N\ge5\). **Lemma 1.** The two sequences in (8) are strictly increasing over their stated ranges. **Proof.** The sine addition formulas give \[ b_r=\frac8{c_0+c_r} =\frac2{\cos(r\theta)\cos((r+1)\theta)} . \tag{9} \] For example, with \(u=r\theta\), use \[ \frac{\sin^3(u+\theta)}{\cos(u+\theta)} +\frac{\sin^3u}{\cos u} =\tan(u+\theta)+\tan u -\tfrac12\{\sin(2u+2\theta)+\sin2u\} \] in (5). This gives \(A_r+C_r=8/(c_0+c_r)-c_0\); at \(r=0\), the expression has the stated removable value. The denominators in (9) are positive before the fold, and \(c_r\) strictly decreases. Hence \(b_r\) strictly increases. For \(r\ge1\), exactly \[ a_r=\frac{s_r^8}{s_{2r-1}s_{2r}^2s_{2r+1}} =\frac{(1-x_r)^3}{(1+x_r)(d-x_r^2)},\qquad x_r=\cos(2r\theta),\quad d=\cos^2\theta . \tag{10} \] For \(1\le r\le J-1\), \[ -\cos2\theta\le x_r\le\cos2\theta<\cos\theta. \tag{11} \] Here \(\cos2\theta>0\). The denominators in (10) are positive on this interval. The logarithmic derivative of its right-hand function \(a(x)\) is \[ \frac{a'(x)}{a(x)} =\frac{2\{2x^2+(1-d)x-2d\}} {(1-x^2)(d-x^2)}. \tag{12} \] The numerator's quadratic is convex. At the two ends \(x=\pm(2d-1)=\pm\cos2\theta\), its values are respectively \[ (6d-1)(d-1),\qquad (10d-3)(d-1). \tag{13} \] Both are negative because \(N\ge5\) gives \(1/2<d<1\). Convexity makes the numerator strictly negative on (11). Since \(x_r\) strictly decreases with \(r\), \(a_r\) strictly increases. Finally \(a_0=0<a_1\) whenever the latter is required. This proves the lemma. \(\square\) No recurrence at or beyond the singular physical end has been imposed in this argument. ## 3. A finite positive product recursion We give the algebraic mechanism explicitly. It applies to the monic recurrence (7), with no orthogonality or literature linearization theorem as an additional premise. For \(1\le m\le n\), \(m+n\le J\), define \[ D_{m,n}=p_mp_n-p_{m-1}p_{n+1}. \tag{14} \] The recurrence gives, for \(m\ge2\), \[ \begin{split} D_{m,n}={}&(b_n-b_{m-1})p_{m-1}p_n +(a_n-a_{m-1})p_{m-1}p_{n-1}\\ &+a_{m-1}D_{m-1,n-1}, \end{split} \tag{15} \] with the exact starting identity \[ D_{1,n}=(b_n-b_0)p_n+a_np_{n-1}. \tag{16} \] To verify (15), expand \(p_m\) and \(p_{n+1}\) by (7). The \(Z\)-terms cancel. Add and subtract \(a_{m-1}p_{m-1}p_{n-1}\); what remains is precisely the last difference in (15). Let \(g_{m,n;\ell}\) be the coefficients in \[ p_mp_n=\sum_\ell g_{m,n;\ell}p_\ell . \tag{17} \] The following is one explicit finite formula by recursion: \[ g_{0,n;\ell}=\mathbf1_{\ell=n}, \tag{18} \] \[ \begin{split} g_{m,n;\ell}={}&g_{m-1,n+1;\ell}\\ &+\sum_{r=0}^{m-1} \left(\prod_{h=1}^{r}a_{m-h}\right) \bigl\{ (b_{n-r}-b_{m-r-1})g_{m-r-1,n-r;\ell}\\ &\hspace{42mm} +(a_{n-r}-a_{m-r-1})g_{m-r-1,n-r-1;\ell} \bigr\}, \qquad 1\le m\le n,\quad m+n\le J . \end{split} \tag{19} \] An empty product is one; exchange \(m,n\) if necessary. Every coefficient on the right has smaller first index and uses valid physical indices. Thus (18)--(19) is a terminating finite prescription. Substituting the explicit sine coefficients (8)--(10) gives the exact rational coefficient at every level. Unrolling the recursion is a finite sum of products of its positive weights. It introduces no singular factorial or infinite series. **Proposition 2.** The coefficients in (17) obey \[ g_{m,n;\ell}>0\quad\text{if }|m-n|\le\ell\le m+n, \qquad g_{m,n;\ell}=0\quad\text{otherwise}, \tag{20} \] including the one-term convention when one index is zero. **Proof.** Unroll (15) down to (16) and add \(p_{m-1}p_{n+1}\). This proves the polynomial identity (19), hence its coefficients. Induct on \(m\), taking \(m\le n\). Lemma 1 makes every difference in braces strictly positive: its larger index exceeds its smaller index by \(n-m+1\). All other multipliers are positive. The first term in (19) has no support below \(n-m+2\). The first and second products in each brace have no support below \(n-m+1\) and \(n-m\), respectively, by induction. None has degree above \(m+n\). Hence no coefficient outside the asserted range occurs. For strict positivity inside that range, the \(r=0\) first product has positive coefficients on \([n-m+1,n+m-1]\); the second has positive coefficients on \([n-m,n+m-2]\). For \(m=1\) these are the individual indices \(n\) and \(n-1\). Together they cover the entire range except its top index \(n+m\), whose coefficient is one because the product is monic, also supplied by the first term in (19). This proves (20). \(\square\) ## 4. Alternating signs and the original odd turn **Theorem 3.** For all original physical indices \(j,k\) with \(j+k\le J\), exactly as ordinary polynomials, \[ \boxed{\quad F_jF_k=\sum_{\ell=|j-k|}^{j+k} (-1)^{j+k-\ell}\mathsf A_{jk\ell,N}F_\ell,\qquad \mathsf A_{jk\ell,N} =\frac{H_\ell}{H_jH_k}g_{j,k;\ell}>0 . \quad} \tag{21} \] The factorial normalization is \(H_r=S_r^4/S_{2r}\), and (18)--(19) specifies every coefficient by a finite positive recursion. The formulas hold at both parities. For \(j=k=1\) they recover \[ \mathsf A_{112}=\frac{c_0^4}{(c_0^2-1)(c_0^2-2)},\quad \mathsf A_{111}=\frac4{c_0^2-2},\quad \mathsf A_{110}=\frac1{c_0^2-1}. \tag{22} \] **Proof.** Substitute \(p_r=(-1)^rH_rF_r\) in (17) and apply Proposition 2. The special case follows from (8)--(10), or the first recurrence step (16). The degree is at most \(J<N\), so no canonical reduction or hidden quotient equality is used. \(\square\) For completeness, the exact physical-row turn law is \[ V_nF_\ell=(-1)^{n\ell} q^{-n\ell(\ell+1)}F_\ell . \tag{23} \] Indeed \[ TF_\ell=\delta_{c_\ell} =\frac{P_N(Z)}{\eta N^2(Z-c_\ell)} \tag{24} \] and multiplication by any polynomial \(r\) on this vector is \(r(c_\ell)\). Thus \(V_nF_\ell\) is a scalar multiple of \(F_\ell\). The full triangular matrix of the original unit turn with sign \(\sigma\in\{1,-1\}\) has degree-\(\ell\) diagonal \((-1)^\ell q^{-\sigma\ell(\ell+1)}\); comparison of leading coefficients and then integer powers proves (23). Divisibility by the full relation in (24) retains every normal. Combining (21) and (23), for every odd signed integer \(n\), \[ \boxed{\quad V_n(F_jF_k)=(-1)^{j+k} \sum_{\ell=|j-k|}^{j+k} \mathsf A_{jk\ell,N}\, q^{-n\ell(\ell+1)}F_\ell . \quad} \tag{25} \] For even \(n\), the summand also has the sign \((-1)^\ell\). All quadratic phases in (25) are original. Positive amplitudes are not a declaration that their coherent sum is positive, zero-free, or of a specified geometric action. ## 5. The high-degree boundary and its full normal channels For physical \(j,k\le J\), always \(j+k\le2J\le D\). Consequently, if \(j+k>J\), the product has degree \(j+k\) even in its canonical representative. Every linear combination of the physical rows \(F_0,\ldots,F_J\) has degree at most \(J\). An \(F\)-only linearization is therefore impossible in this range. Canonical reduction cannot repair it. At each double physical node retain \[ G_j(Z)=\partial_wK_N(c_j,Z). \tag{26} \] Its degree is exactly \(D-j\). In fact \(e_k'(c_j)=0\) once \(k>D-j\), because both occurrences \(j,D-j\) of the node are then present in the Newton product. At \(k=D-j\) only the first occurrence is present, so its derivative is nonzero. Therefore \[ \{F_j:0\le j\le J\} \ \cup\ \{G_j:c_j\text{ is double}\} \tag{27} \] has exactly one nonzero polynomial of each degree \(0,\ldots,D\) and is a basis of the full algebra. At odd levels the final simple row has no added \(G_j\). Its retained signed-turn action is \[ \boxed{\quad V_nG_j=\lambda_{n,j}G_j +\kappa^n(R^{-n})'(c_j)F_j,\qquad \lambda_{n,j}=(-1)^{nj}q^{-nj(j+1)} , \quad} \tag{28} \] where the prime is the original spectral first normal. To verify it, differentiate the ordinary reproducer before specializing a double node. Since \(P_N(c_j)=P_N'(c_j)=0\), \[ TG_j=\frac{P_N(Z)}{\eta N^2(Z-c_j)^2}. \tag{29} \] Multiplication by \(r\) on (29) gives \(r(c_j)\) times (29), plus \(r'(c_j)\delta_{c_j}\), modulo the full relation. Apply \(T\), with \(r=R^{-n}\), to obtain (28). The original normal is not replaced by a derivative of a chosen off-grid phase. Equations (27)--(29) locate the additional channels required above the range of Theorem 3. No sign assertion for their product coefficients is made here. In particular an odd turn there must retain its triangular normal coupling, not merely the scalar phase in (23). ## Scope and direct sources The theorem is a general local composition identity for actual physical rows, with unrestricted indices in its stated low-degree range. It supplies a larger coherent class than phase-positive Laurent polynomials: the odd-turn expression (25) has positive amplitudes with an explicit quadratic phase. Bounding that sum after further original products, turns and closing remains a separate problem. No nonzero knot scalar or general filling asymptotic follows from the sign theorem alone. The two complete direct texts were read, their directly used identities checked, and their pins verified: * [Physical Jacobi charge boundary](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_physical_jacobi_charge_boundary.md), SHA256 530425b0c4504f2512954438465deb6d9a6e322fa58c641b6c678161baae6583: exact row recurrence, normalization and valid physical index range. * [Exact signed-turn identities](research_full_endpoint_unit_turn_identities.md), SHA256 e2f69aaff28080b9dd9e11365ce18d68a9d738667917204714556681c50789e8: full canonical algebra, triangular signed turn and ordinary reproducer. The positivity proof and finite coefficient recursion are derived above. No named orthogonal-polynomial positivity theorem, numerical evaluation, mathematical program, test or compilation is used. Adopted notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: Exact moderate analytic interpolation of physical row degree
text:
# Exact moderate analytic interpolation of physical row degree Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The original physical rows admit an exact analytic interpolation in their degree on any fixed interval strictly between the endpoint and the fold. Its size has the original row action, with polynomial loss. The construction uses the attracting original Riccati equation, an exponentially accurate discrete primitive, and a localized cardinal correction. It does not substitute the off-grid full kernel. The complex height is fixed independently of the level and is bounded explicitly in terms of the contraction and analytic radii below. There is one interpolant on the whole degree interval, so subdivision does not introduce mismatched internal connector functions. The two outer connectors retain their original action cost. No estimate at the filled action, or permission to discard those connectors, follows. The tail-weight extension below also interpolates the literal terminating consumed-normal coefficient, retaining its action \(-J_\delta\) and its checkerboard character. It uses a finite prefix and an explicitly bounded error up to the actual physical stop; no infinite off-grid tail is substituted. ## 1. Original rows, domains, and canonical action Put \(N\ge3\), \(	heta=\pi/N\), and \[ c_j=2\cos((2j+1)	heta),\qquad F_{j,N}(Z)=K_N(c_j,Z),\qquad 0\le j\le\lfloor(N-1)/2floor . 	ag{1} \] These are the literal physical rows, ordinary polynomials of degree \(j\) in \(Z\). Their normalization is \(F_{0,N}=1\). Fix \[ 0<a<b<	frac12,\qquad \mathcal W=\{Z:\Re Z\le2-\gamma,\ |Z|\le R\}, \quad \gamma>0,\ R<\infty . 	ag{2} \] An empty \(\mathcal W\) can be omitted. All exterior derivative statements use a larger bounded convex open domain \(\mathcal V\) whose closure is in \(\{\Re Z<2\}\) and which contains a fixed neighborhood of \(\mathcal W\). When needed, take one more such enlargement. Every constant below is uniform on its stated closed exterior domain. The root-location theorem gives \[ F_{j,N}(Z)=\prod_{
u=1}^j  rac{r_{j,
u}-Z}{r_{j,
u}-c_0}, \qquad r_{j,
u}>2. 	ag{3} \] Thus every anchor used below is a holomorphic unit on \(\mathcal V\), with the unique logarithm obtained by summing the logarithms of these right-half-plane factors. It is real for real \(Z<2\). In particular, anchoring at a physical row does not introduce an arbitrary logarithm or an unproved nonvanishing assertion. For real \(0<x<1/2\), put \[ p(x,Z)=2+(2-Z)\cot^2(\pi x),\qquad \lambda(x,Z)= rac{p+\sqrt{p^2-4}}2 , 	ag{4} \] where the root is positive for real \(Z<2\). On the exterior domain in (2), \(\Re p>2\), the branch is a unit, and \(\Re\lambda>1\). On a sufficiently small fixed complex neighborhood of any enlarged real degree interval inside \((0,1/2)\), these assertions persist uniformly. Use its continued logarithm. Define the canonical action by \[ \Psi(x,Z)=\int_0^x\operatorname{Log}\lambda(u,Z)\,du. 	ag{5} \] The integral first follows the positive real axis and then continues inside that simply connected degree neighborhood. It converges at zero: \[ \operatorname{Log}\lambda(x,Z) =\operatorname{Log}(2-Z)-2\log(\pi x)+O(x^2). 	ag{6} \] The original row Riccati theorem, with precisely this normalization, proves \[ \log F_{j,N}(Z)=N\Psi(j/N,Z)+O(\log N) 	ag{7} \] uniformly on compact degree intervals below \(1/2\), with every fixed exterior derivative. This is the original edge action \(\psi(\pi-2\pi x,u)\) when \(Z=-2\cos u\), calibrated by \(\psi(\pi,u)=0\). The half-offset in the actual physical angle can instead be retained; on the present bulk interval it changes (7) only by a bounded analytic factor. ## 2. An analytic attracting ratio with exponential nodal accuracy The exact recurrence is \[ ho_{j+1,N}=\mathscr R_{N,j/N,Z}(ho_{j,N}),\qquad ho_{j,N}=F_{j,N}/F_{j-1,N}, 	ag{8} \] where \[  egin{split} A_N(x)&= rac{[2\sin(\pi x+	heta)]^4} {4\sin(2\pi x+	heta)\sin(2\pi x+2	heta)},\ C_N(x)&= rac{[2\sin(\pi x)]^4} {4\sin(2\pi x)\sin(2\pi x+	heta)},\ q_N(x)&=C_N(x)/A_N(x),\qquad d_N(x,Z)=(c_0-Z)/A_N(x),\ \mathscr R_{N,x,Z}(z)&=1+d_N(x,Z)+q_N(x)(1-z^{-1}). \end{split} 	ag{9} \] The symbol \(q_N(x)\) here is the Riccati coefficient, not the cyclotomic root. On each fixed enlarged degree neighborhood, \[ A_N=	an^2(\pi x)+O(N^{-1}),\quad q_N=1+O(N^{-1}),\quad d_N=(2-Z)\cot^2(\pi x)+O(N^{-1}). 	ag{10} \] All these are uniform holomorphic estimates. Here are precise choices of the constants needed later. Choose \(d>0\) with \([a-4d,b+4d]\subset(0,1/2)\). Shrink a fixed complex thickening of that interval until, on it and the larger exterior domain, \(\Re p>2\) and \(\Re\lambda\ge1+3\kappa\) for some \(\kappa>0\). For all large \(N\), arrange also \(|q_N|\le1+\kappa\). On each disk \(|z-\lambda(x,Z)|\le\kappa\), the maps in (9) have Lipschitz constant \[ \vartheta= rac{1+\kappa}{(1+2\kappa)^2}<1. 	ag{11} \] Taylor's formula and (10) give a constant \(D_0\) such that \[ |\mathscr R_{N,x,Z}(\lambda(x,Z)) -\lambda(x+N^{-1},Z)|\le D_0/N. 	ag{12} \] Put \(K_0=D_0/(1-\vartheta)\). After increasing the level threshold, the moving disks of radius \(K_0/N\) are invariant: a point in the disk centered at \(\lambda(x,Z)\) maps into the disk centered at \(\lambda(x+N^{-1},Z)\). Fix \(0<\sigma<d\), let \(m_N=\lfloor\sigma Nfloor\), and define \(R_N(x,Z)\) by starting with \(\lambda(x-m_N/N,Z)\) and applying in order the \(m_N\) maps with degree arguments \[ x-m_N/N,\ x-(m_N-1)/N,\ldots,x-1/N. 	ag{13} \] Reserve a fixed complex buffer for all these shifts. The construction is holomorphic, and \[ |R_N-\lambda|\le K_0/N,\qquad \Re R_N>1+2\kappa. 	ag{14} \] It applies on a fixed neighborhood of \([a-d,b+d]\). At a physical degree \(x=j/N\), the actual ratio at the starting index \(j-m_N\) is \(O(N^{-1})\) from its chosen root by the original bulk Riccati theorem. The larger moving disks of radius \(\kappa\) are also invariant for large \(N\), since \(\vartheta\kappa+D_0/N<\kappa\). The actual initial ratio lies in these disks; its \(O(N^{-1})\) constant need not be bounded by \(K_0\). Contracting the two initial values through (13) proves \[ |R_N(j/N,Z)-ho_{j,N}(Z)| \le C N^{-1}\vartheta^{m_N}. 	ag{15} \] This comparison uses the normalized original solution, not merely the existence of a formal characteristic root. The index \(j-m_N\) remains in a fixed bulk interval, so the cited estimate applies uniformly. The same estimate on larger exterior domains supplies all fixed exterior derivatives by Cauchy. Put \(l_N=\operatorname{Log}R_N\), using its right-half-plane logarithm. On a fixed complex neighborhood it is uniformly bounded, holomorphic, and \[ l_N=\operatorname{Log}\lambda+O(N^{-1}). 	ag{16} \] Choose a radius \(r>0\) so that every degree point used next has its closed \(r\)-disk in that neighborhood, including the shift buffer already reserved. For a constant \(M\), \[ |l_N^{(k)}|\le M k!r^{-k}. 	ag{17} \] ## 3. An exponentially accurate analytic discrete primitive Let \(j_0=\lceil Naceil\), \(x_0=j_0/N\), and put \(p_N=\lfloor\pi rN/2floor\). For sufficiently large \(N\) define \[  egin{split} \mathcal A_N(x,Z)={}&N\int_{x_0}^x l_N(u,Z)\,du + rac{l_N(x,Z)-l_N(x_0,Z)}2\ &+\sum_{k=1}^{p_N-1}  rac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!\,N^{2k-1}} [l_N^{(2k-1)}(x,Z)-l_N^{(2k-1)}(x_0,Z)],\ \widehat F_N(x,Z)={}&F_{j_0,N}(Z)\exp\mathcal A_N(x,Z). \end{split} 	ag{18} \] The integral is the analytic primitive on the degree rectangle. Thus \(\widehat F_N\) is a holomorphic unit, with its anchor and logarithm fixed by (3). We give the growing-order remainder explicitly. The bound \(\sup|B_{2p}(\{\cdot\})|\le4(2p)!/(2\pi)^{2p}\), the Euler--Maclaurin formula for a right-endpoint sum, and (17) give \[ \left|\mathcal A_N(j/N,Z)- \sum_{h=j_0+1}^j l_N(h/N,Z)ight| \le C N\, rac{(2p_N)!}{(2\pi rN)^{2p_N}}. 	ag{19} \] For clarity, apply the formula through its \(p_N\)-th endpoint term and add the bound for that term when omitting it in (18). It has the same or a smaller upper bound. The real interval of integration has bounded length; \(Z\) can be complex throughout. Since \(2p_N\le\pi rN\), the elementary inequality \((2p_N)!\le(2p_N)^{2p_N}\) makes the right side exponentially small. For all sufficiently large \(N\), it is at most \(C\exp(-\kappa_{m EM}N)\), where one may take \[ \kappa_{m EM}=\pi r\log2/4. 	ag{20} \] This uses growing-order derivative bounds on a fixed complex neighborhood; a fixed-order expansion would not suffice. Equations (15) and (19), summed over at most \(N\) ratios, imply \[ \left| rac{F_{j,N}(Z)}{\widehat F_N(j/N,Z)}-1ight| \le C e^{-\kappa_0N}, \quad j_0\le j\le j_1:=\lfloor Nbfloor, 	ag{21} \] with, for example, \[ \kappa_0=\min\{\sigma|\log\vartheta|/2,\ \kappa_{m EM}\}>0. 	ag{22} \] Constants and level thresholds absorb bounded prefactors. The primitive also has a uniform complex growth bound. The terms in (18) after the half-endpoint correction sum to \(O(N^{-1})\): by (17), successive upper bounds have ratio at most \(1/4\) up to \(p_N\), after increasing the threshold if necessary. Consequently (16) yields, uniformly for \(x,y\) in a fixed smaller degree rectangle, \[ \log rac{\widehat F_N(x,Z)}{\widehat F_N(y,Z)} =N[\Psi(x,Z)-\Psi(y,Z)]+O(1). 	ag{23} \] The logarithm here is the difference of the defined primitives. Using (7) at \(x_0\) gives \[ \log\widehat F_N(x,Z)=N\Psi(x,Z)+O(\log N),\qquad N^{-C}e^{N\Re\Psi(x,Z)} \le|\widehat F_N(x,Z)|\le N^Ce^{N\Re\Psi(x,Z)}. 	ag{24} \] Enlarging a constant covers the omitted bounded factors. ## 4. One exact interpolant on the whole interval Let \(L\) bound \(|\partial_x\Psi|\) on the degree rectangle and larger exterior domain used in (23). The following construction does not require \(b-a\) to be small. Put \[ A=\max\{1,4L^2/\kappa_0\},\qquad H\le\min\left\{ rac r4,\  rac{\kappa_0}{16(\pi+L)},\ \sqrt{ rac{\kappa_0}{16A}}ight\},\qquad H>0, 	ag{25} \] shrinking \(H\) further if necessary to stay in the reserved degree rectangle. Let \(\operatorname{sinc}z=\sin(\pi z)/(\pi z)\) with its removable value at zero, and define \[  egin{split} \delta_{j,N}(Z)&=F_{j,N}(Z)-\widehat F_N(j/N,Z),\ \mathfrak F_N(x,Z)&=\widehat F_N(x,Z) +\sum_{j=j_0}^{j_1}\delta_{j,N}(Z) \operatorname{sinc}(Nx-j) \exp[-AN(x-j/N)^2]. \end{split} 	ag{26} \] This is a finite analytic formula. In particular \[ \mathfrak F_N(j/N,Z)=F_{j,N}(Z) \quad(j_0\le j\le j_1) 	ag{27} \] as an identity of holomorphic functions of \(Z\). Every exterior normal at those rows is therefore exact. We prove the uniform relative bound, which is the reason for the Gaussian localizer. Write \(x=X+iY\). The identity \(\operatorname{sinc}z= rac12\int_{-1}^1e^{i\pi zu}\,du\) gives \[ |\operatorname{sinc}(Nx-j)|\le e^{\pi N|Y|}. 	ag{28} \] Equation (23) bounds the ratio of the surrogate at a node to its value at \(x\) by \(C\exp\{NL(|X-j/N|+|Y|)\}\). Also \[ \left|\exp[-AN(x-j/N)^2]ight| =\exp[-AN(X-j/N)^2+ANY^2]. 	ag{29} \] Combining these with (21), summing at most \(N\) terms, and using \(Ld-Ad^2\le L^2/(4A)\) proves \[ \left| rac{\mathfrak F_N}{\widehat F_N}-1ight| \le CN\exp\left\{-N\left[ \kappa_0- rac{L^2}{4A}-(\pi+L)|Y|-AY^2ight]ight\}. 	ag{30} \] The choices (25) make the three losses at most \(3\kappa_0/16\). Thus, uniformly on \(|\Im x|\le H\), and on a small fixed real enlargement of \([a,b]\) contained in the degree rectangle, \[ \left| rac{\mathfrak F_N}{\widehat F_N}-1ight| \le C e^{-\kappa_0N/2}. 	ag{31} \] Increasing the threshold makes this smaller than \(1/2\). The exact interpolant is a holomorphic unit there, and (24) holds with \(\mathfrak F_N\) in place of \(\widehat F_N\). On smaller degree and exterior domains, Cauchy's formula gives the same exponential conclusion, with a possibly smaller positive exponent, for every fixed derivative of the relative error. This includes exterior spectral normals. Derivatives of the unnormalized function also differentiate its original action; they are not asserted to have an \(N\)-independent prefactor. The real enlargement accommodates cutoffs at half-integer degree, such as \((j_0-1/2)/N\) and \((j_1+1/2)/N\). The estimate uses the Lipschitz bound for \(\Psi\) on that enlarged rectangle and is otherwise unchanged. ## 5. The actual terminating tail amplitude The same correction method also applies to the original consumed-normal tail weight, with its true exponentially decreasing action. This gives an amplitude for the actual row sum, rather than only for its incident kernel rows. Fix \(0<\delta<1/2\), and now require \[ 0<a<b<	frac12-\delta,\qquad |\alpha|\le A_\alpha<\pi. 	ag{32} \] Put \(m=\lfloor N/2floor\), \(L_N=\lfloor\delta Nfloor\), \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\), and \(	au(x)=\pi-2\pi x-\pi/N\). The original omitted coefficient is \(\omega_{j,N,L_N}(\alpha)=\eta(-1)^j\gamma_{j,N}(\alpha)\). Its exact finite lowering formula is \[ \gamma_{j,N}(\alpha) =T_{0,N}(\alpha,	au(j/N)) \sum_{\ell=L_N+1}^{p_j} \prod_{r=0}^{\ell-1}ho_{r,N}(\alpha,	au(j/N)), \qquad p_j=m-1-j. 	ag{33} \] Define \[ (u_r,v_r)=  egin{cases} ((r+	frac12)\pi/N,(r+1)\pi/N),&N\ {m even},\ ((r+1)\pi/N,(r+	frac32)\pi/N),&N\ {m odd}, \end{cases} \] \[ ho_{r,N}(\alpha,t)=  rac{[\cos^2u_r+\sinh^2(\alpha/(2N))] [\sin^2(t/2)-\sin^2u_r]}{\cos^4v_r}, 	ag{34} \] \[ T_{0,N}(\alpha,t)=  egin{cases} N^{-1}\cosh(\alpha/2)\sin t,&N\ {m even},\ \displaystyle  rac{\cosh(\alpha/2)\cosh(\alpha/(2N))} {N\cos^4(\pi/(2N))}\sin t\sin(t/2),&N\ {m odd}. \end{cases} 	ag{35} \] These formulas, including the upper stop \(p_j\), are the actual full-normal tail identity from the pinned outer-row source. The original normal has already differentiated the omitted radical; only the values of the remaining spectator are sampled by (33). Choose \(0<\sigma_\gamma<1/2-\delta-b\), and put \(k_N=\lfloor\sigma_\gamma Nfloor\). Define the finite analytic prefix \[ \widehat\Gamma_N(x,\alpha)=T_{0,N}(\alpha,	au(x)) \sum_{\ell=L_N+1}^{L_N+k_N} \prod_{r=0}^{\ell-1}ho_{r,N}(\alpha,	au(x)). 	ag{36} \] For all sufficiently large \(N\), this prefix ends before every actual stop \(p_j\) with \(j/N\in[a,b]\). Here is the uniform tail estimate with that stop retained. At a physical row, \(r<p_j\) implies that both relevant cosines stay bounded away from zero, uniformly for \(j/N\ge a\). Using \(\sin^2(	au(j/N)/2)=\cos^2(\pi(j+1/2)/N)\), the ratio in (34) differs by \(O(N^{-1})\), uniformly through this entire physical range, from \[ ho(u,x)=1- rac{\sin^2(\pi x)}{\cos^2(\pi u)}, \qquad u=r/N,\quad x=j/N. 	ag{37} \] In that range the limiting ratio is nonnegative up to an \(O(N^{-1})\) endpoint change and is at most \(1-\sin^2(\pi a)\). Consequently there is a fixed \(q<1\) such that all the actual ratios through the stop obey \(|ho_{r,N}|\le q\). This remains uniform for bounded complex \(\alpha\): its contribution to (34) is \(O(N^{-2})\). This estimate is only used up to the original stop. On a fixed sufficiently small complex degree neighborhood of \([a,b]\), the prefix ratios with \(r\le L_N+k_N\) are units, and also have modulus at most \(q<1\), after enlarging \(q\) and shrinking the neighborhood. Indeed \(\delta+\sigma_\gamma<1/2-b\) leaves a strict margin in (37). Factor the first product out of (36), writing \[ \widehat\Gamma_N=T_{0,N} \left(\prod_{r=0}^{L_N}ho_{r,N}ight)G_N. 	ag{38} \] The remaining finite sum satisfies \[ G_N(x,\alpha) = rac1{1-ho(\delta,x)}+O(N^{-1})+O(q^{k_N}). 	ag{39} \] For a direct proof, freeze each subsequent ratio at \(ho(\delta,x)\). Its error after \(s\) steps is \(O((s+1)/N)\). A telescoping product estimate bounds the error of a product of \(s\) such factors by \(C(s+1)^2q^{s-1}/N\). Their sum is \(O(N^{-1})\), and the tail of the frozen geometric series is \(O(q^{k_N})\). All estimates are holomorphic and uniform on the chosen neighborhood. In particular \(G_N\) is a unit bounded above and below. The factors \(T_{0,N}\) are also units there after removing \(N^{-1}\): \(\sin	au\) and the odd factor \(\sin(	au/2)\) stay nonzero, and \(\cosh(\alpha/2)\) has no zero on the compact disk in (32). Comparing the remaining actual sum from \(L_N+k_N+1\) through its literal \(p_j\) with the first product, the bound \(q<1\) therefore proves \[ \left| rac{\gamma_{j,N}(\alpha)} {\widehat\Gamma_N(j/N,\alpha)}-1ight| \le Cq^{k_N} \le C e^{-\kappa_\gamma N},\qquad \kappa_\gamma=\sigma_\gamma|\log q|/2>0 . 	ag{40} \] No infinite off-grid tail was substituted for the finite source. Define the real-normalized analytic phase \[ \Xi_\delta(x)=\int_0^\delta \log\left(1- rac{\sin^2(\pi x)}{\cos^2(\pi u)}ight)\,du =-J_\delta(x). 	ag{41} \] All factors in this integral are positive on the real rectangle under consideration and have units on its chosen complex thickening. Uniform Riemann sums for the logarithm of (34), including both parity offsets and \(L_N-\delta N=O(1)\), now give \[ \log\widehat\Gamma_N(x,\alpha) =N\Xi_\delta(x)-\log N+O(1). 	ag{42} \] The bounded term has a canonical analytic branch obtained from (35), (38), and (39); only its bounded real part is needed here. In particular the ratio of values at two degree points is bounded by \(C\exp\{N L_\gamma|x-y|\}\) along paths in the rectangle, with \(L_\gamma\) any bound for \(|\Xi_\delta'|\), and with the path length in place of the distance if necessary. Choose a fixed analytic buffer \(r_\gamma>0\) inside the degree neighborhood just constructed. Apply exactly (26)--(31), with \(\widehat F_N,\delta_{j,N},\kappa_0,L,r\) replaced by \(\widehat\Gamma_N,\gamma_{j,N}-\widehat\Gamma_N(j/N), \kappa_\gamma,L_\gamma,r_\gamma\). This produces one analytic \(\mathfrak G_N(x,\alpha)\), exact at all the physical degree nodes in \([a,b]\), with \[ \mathfrak G_N(j/N,\alpha)=\gamma_{j,N}(\alpha),\qquad |\mathfrak G_N|\le C N^{-1}e^{N\Re\Xi_\delta(x)} 	ag{43} \] on the quantitative fixed strip given by (25) with those replacements. Its relative error from the finite prefix is exponentially small, including fixed \(\alpha\) derivatives on smaller disks. The lower bound of the same order also holds there for large \(N\). ## 6. What this permits in the original finite sum For any \(Z\) in the stated domain and any holomorphic spectator \(f(x,Z)\), the exact finite sum with these rows is \[ \sum_{j=j_0}^{j_1} F_{j,N}(Z)f(j/N,Z) = rac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma  rac{2\pi iN}{e^{2\pi iNx}-1} \mathfrak F_N(x,Z)f(x,Z)\,dx . 	ag{44} \] Here \(\Gamma\) is any positively oriented contour in the constructed strip enclosing exactly the displayed degree nodes and no other kernel pole. The residue of the displayed kernel at each node is one. Products of finitely many rows at the same consumed-normal index may be interpolated by the product of their \(\mathfrak F_N\)'s; the exterior variables and every shared spectator remain independent. Their actions add, their polynomial costs multiply, and all sampled mixed exterior normals are still exact. The exact Gaussian crossing and any integer alias may be kept in \(f\). For \(n
e0\), on the Fresnel ray \(x=e^{i\,\operatorname{sgn}(n) \pi/4}r\), \[ |e^{i\pi nNx^2}|=e^{-\pi|n|Nr^2}. 	ag{45} \] Such a ray can only be used where it lies in the constructed strip; no continuation to unbounded height is asserted. In particular the availability of a fixed height in (25) is not permission to rotate an entire macroscopic ray beyond that height. Equation (45) concerns only the displayed quadratic factor; all original linear characters, half-offsets, and scalar carriers stay in \(f\). For any fixed admissible path \(\Gamma_1\) in the strip, away from the kernel poles, the literal integral in (44) is bounded by its length times the supremum of \[ C N^C\left| rac{N}{e^{2\pi iNx}-1}ight| \exp\{N\Re\Psi(x,Z)\}\,|f(x,Z)|. 	ag{46} \] With several incident rows, replace \(\Psi\) by their sum. Thus the interpolation does not add an extensive spectral-band action to the original row phase. On fixed horizontal heights the kernel has its explicit geometric-series alias bound; on cutoff segments at half-integer degree its denominator is \(e^{-2\pi N\Im x}+1\). Those original kernel and Gaussian factors have not been omitted. There is only one function (26) across the entire degree interval. If a contour is subdivided, the artificial common faces cancel exactly with opposite orientations, including all spectators. The two external endpoint connectors do not cancel for this reason. They retain the value of (46) on their actual paths. Nor does the construction estimate a spectator which has not itself been bounded. In particular, full traces whose other colors leave the exterior domain (2) cannot silently be replaced by a norm on that domain. Finally the interval stays away from both \(x=0\) and \(x=1/2\). The contraction, analytic radius, and height can deteriorate as those boundaries are approached. The present theorem does not supply a uniform endpoint-to-fold interpolation, a filled-action bound for the outer connectors, a joint relative-cycle transport, or a nonzero geometric coefficient. It supplies an exact moderate bulk interpolation with explicit height and decay budgets, which was not provided by the physical-row asymptotic alone. Use the minimum of the row and tail strip heights when combining their interpolants. In the narrower degree interval (32), the actual single-tail row sum can be placed in the same formula by replacing the interpolated amplitude by \[ \eta e^{i\pi Nx}\mathfrak G_N(x,\alpha) \prod_e\mathfrak F_N(x,Z_e)\,f(x,\mathbf Z). 	ag{47} \] At \(x=j/N\), this is exactly \(\omega_{j,N,L_N}(\alpha)\prod_eF_{j,N}(Z_e)f(j/N,\mathbf Z)\). The factor \(e^{i\pi Nx}\), the original Gaussian in \(f\), and the residue kernel are retained; integer alias changes must preserve their sampled product. Its noncharacter amplitude has the actual bound \[ C N^C\exp N\Re\left\{-J_\delta(x) +\sum_e\Psi(x,Z_e)ight\}. 	ag{48} \] This also preserves every exterior mixed normal at the sampled rows. Extra shared endpoint coupons, other coupled traces, and arbitrary spectators stay in \(f\); no estimate for them follows from (48). A free color tending to \(2\) is outside the fixed half-plane gap (2). The left endpoint \(x=0\) and the terminating tail boundary \(x=1/2-\delta\) are likewise outside the uniform strip construction. Thus (47)--(48) do not complete the original paired vertical/current boundary estimate. ## 7. Direct-source readbacks All three complete direct sources were read and their used statements checked at the following versions: * [Physical-row Riccati transport](research_physical_row_riccati_transport.md), SHA256 a9d5719e4a3129ad999e511037d87d0a31b70546db7ec24558277739e58bbf4a: exact recurrence, physical-ratio attraction on a larger complex exterior domain, canonical logarithms, absolute normalization, and original phase identification. * [Original Racah root location](actual_matching_edge_racah_root_location.md), SHA256 f84b82d7924a0c92ca803bc4834bcb0f18f63cedebf2bd072d41d0545a9f5793: literal physical-row polynomial, roots strictly above two, and its normalized canonical logarithm. * [Actual omitted endpoint rows](research_endpoint_outer_row_decay.md), SHA256 85e708606a44cbbbc45a82db0685fcb1d35215c89470ccdc7408790305e55e30: exact both-parity lowering products, the true terminating stop, consumed-normal functional, and its original graph placement. The growing-order Euler--Maclaurin bound and the exact correction are proved above. Only written mathematics, source text reads and hashes were used; no mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or compilation was run. Frozen notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: Positive physical-row charge transport and endpoint-window stability

# Positive physical-row charge transport and endpoint-window stability Private written proof, 16 November 2026. An original kernel evaluated at a physical color of index \(a\) has a positive Fourier law supported on \([-a,a]\). Inside a surviving full trace, this is an exact positive convolution of the original charge parameter. Its coefficient mass costs \(O(a\log(N/a))\), and its charge shifts cost \(a/N\). This gives a quantitative endpoint-window stability lemma for any supplied uniform charged descendant estimate. It does not supply that estimate or an arbitrary-short-filling theorem. ## 1. The actual physical row and its positive law Put \(D=N-1\), \(J=\lfloor D/2floor\), \(	heta=\pi/N\), \(\eta=(-1)^D\), and \[ c_a=2\cos((2a+1)	heta),\quad s_j=2\sin(j	heta),\quad S_j=\prod_{h=1}^j s_h,\quad e_j(z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{h<j}(c_h-z). 	ag{1} \] Retain the ordinary kernel \(K_N(w,z)=\sum_{j=0}^D e_j(w)e_j(z)\) and the original physical row \[ F_{a,N}(z)=K_N(c_a,z),\qquad 0\le a\le J. \] The endpoint source proves the exact formula and root location \[ F_{a,N}(z)= \sum_{k=0}^a  rac{S_{a+k}}{S_{a-k}S_k^4}\prod_{h<k}(c_h-z) =\prod_{
u=1}^a  rac{r_{a,
u}-z}{r_{a,
u}-c_0}, \qquad r_{a,
u}>2. 	ag{2} \] An empty product is one. Define \(M_{a,N}=F_{a,N}(-2)\). For independent variables \(X_
u\in\{-1,0,1\}\) with \[ \Pr(X_
u=0)= rac{r_{a,
u}}{r_{a,
u}+2},\qquad \Pr(X_
u=1)=\Pr(X_
u=-1)= rac1{r_{a,
u}+2}, \quad K_a=\sum_{
u=1}^aX_
u, 	ag{3} \] one has the exact entire angular identity \[  oxed{\quad F_{a,N}(-2\cos t)=M_{a,N}\,\mathbb E(e^{iK_at}) =M_{a,N}\,\mathbb E(\cos K_at). \quad} 	ag{4} \] Indeed each normalized factor in (2) is \((r_{a,
u}+e^{it}+e^{-it})/(r_{a,
u}+2)\). This is a finite probability law, not a new inner product or a probabilistic assumption on the quantum source. It is symmetric, supported on \([-a,a]\), and \[ \mathbb E K_a=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}K_a =\sum_{
u=1}^a rac2{r_{a,
u}+2}\le a/2. 	ag{5} \] Equivalently \(F_{a,N}(-2\cos t)=\sum_{k=0}^a eta_{a,k}\cos(kt)\) with \( eta_{a,k}\ge0\) and \(\sum_k eta_{a,k}=M_{a,N}\). Products of physical rows convolve these laws; their masses multiply and their support bounds add. Let \(\mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[z]/(2T_N(z/2)+2)\). Its original closing is \(\phi_N(f)=\eta N^2[z^D]\operatorname{rem}_{\,2T_N(z/2)+2}f\). The canonical coupon \(\mathcal C_{N,\chi}\) has the full Hermite data of \(\cos(N(1-\chi)t)\) at \(z=-2\cos t\), with value one at the odd simple node. Equation (4) implies, in this full physical algebra, \[  oxed{\quad F_{a,N}\mathcal C_{N,\chi} =M_{a,N}\,\mathbb E\mathcal C_{N,\chi-K_a/N}. \quad} 	ag{6} \] To verify every normal, multiply (4) by \(\cos(N(1-\chi)t)\). Symmetry of \(K_a\) turns the product into \(\mathbb E\cos((N(1-\chi)+K_a)t)\). This entire angular identity can be differentiated and divided by \(2\sin t\) at every positive physical angle. At the odd simple node \(t=0\), both sides have value \(M_{a,N}\). These are all the physical data. Thus (6) holds for every complex \(\chi\), retaining the original full normal. It is not asserted as an ordinary polynomial identity for arbitrary complex charge. ## 2. A uniform coefficient-mass bound For \(a=0\), \(M_{0,N}=1\). For \(1\le a\le J\), \[  oxed{\quad 1\le M_{a,N} \le(a+1)\left[ rac{\pi^2e^4}{4} \left( rac Naight)^2ight]^a . \quad} 	ag{7} \] In particular, if \(C_0=\pi e^2/2\), \[ \log M_{a,N}\le\log(a+1)+2a\log(C_0N/a). 	ag{8} \] *Proof.* The terms of (2) at \(-2\) are nonnegative. For \(k\le a\le N/2\), use \[ S_{a+k}/S_{a-k} \le(2\pi/N)^{2k} rac{(a+k)!}{(a-k)!}, \quad S_k\ge(4/N)^k k!,\quad \prod_{h<k}(c_h+2)\le4^k. \] The \(k\)-th term is at most \[ \left( rac{\pi^2N^2}{16}ight)^k  rac{(a+k)!}{(a-k)!(k!)^4} \le  rac{[(\pi^2/4)N^2a^2]^k}{(k!)^4}. 	ag{9} \] The final upper sequence increases for \(0\le k\le a\): the ratio of consecutive terms is at least \(\pi^2N^2/(4a^2)\ge\pi^2>1\). The inequality \(a!\ge(a/e)^a\), obtained by integrating \(\log x\), bounds its last term by the power in (7). Summing \(a+1\) terms proves the result. The lower bound follows already from the \(k=0\) term. \(\square\) The root product also gives \[ \sup_{z\in[-2,2]}|F_{a,N}(z)|=M_{a,N}. 	ag{10} \] All fixed spectral derivatives on this interval cost at most a fixed power of \(a+1\), by the polynomial Markov estimate used in the endpoint source. This is consistent with (6), which already retains the normals exactly. For \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and \(a\le\varepsilon N\), monotonicity of \(x\log(C_0/x)\) on this interval gives \[ M_{a,N}\le N\exp\{N h(\varepsilon)\},\qquad h(\varepsilon)=2\varepsilon\log(C_0/\varepsilon) \longrightarrow0. 	ag{11} \] Consequently any uniform \(a=o(N)\) window has subexponential mass and charge support \(o(1)\). A statement at one descendant charge alone is not made uniform by this observation. ## 3. Exact transport of a shared graph source Fix a finite original circle tree, a nonempty traced set \(S\), and a set \(U\subseteq S\) of evaluated physical vertices. Let \(Y=S\setminus U\). Set \(z_v=c_{a_v}\) for \(v\in U\). Every original edge is retained. Every untraced outside color is complete, \(z_b=-2\), for the estimates below. The algebraic formula also permits free outside colors, with their literal row polynomials left unevaluated. Let \(A_N(\mathbf z)\) be any joint polynomial spectator, including any additional fixed coupons. Write \(A_{N,\mathbf a}\) for its evaluation at \(U\). Keep the original crossing elements \(R_{n_w}\), their scalar carriers, and the original full trace at every \(w\in Y\). At a survivor define the entire shared cut-row product \[ p_w(z)=\prod_{\substack{v\in U\vw\in E}}F_{a_v,N}(z), \quad M_w=p_w(-2),\quad A_w=\sum_{\substack{v\in U\vw\in E}}a_v. 	ag{12} \] By (4), \(p_w(-2\cos t)=M_w\mathbb E(e^{iK_wt})\), with a symmetric law supported on \([-A_w,A_w]\). These finite auxiliary laws may be taken independent for different surviving vertices. Let \(G'\) retain only edges with neither endpoint in \(U\). Denote its actual full traced source with spectator \(A_{N,\mathbf a}\) by \(Z_{G',N}^{A_{N,\mathbf a}}(\mathbf n_Y, oldsymbol\chi_Y)\). This includes all original surviving kernels and other insertions. Define the literal evaluated-edge factor \[ D_U(\mathbf a)= \prod_{\substack{vw\in E\v,w\in U}}K_N(c_{a_v},c_{a_w}) \prod_{\substack{vb\in E\v\in U,\ b
otin S}}F_{a_v,N}(-2). 	ag{13} \] For free outside colors, replace the corresponding factors in the second product by \(F_{a_v,N}(z_b)\); do not assign them a charge or a trace. Let \(\mathscr R_U(\mathbf a)\) be the original surviving contraction with these evaluated colors, including all factors (12)--(13), but with the evaluated vertices' crossing values kept separately. Applying (6) at each survivor gives exactly \[  oxed{\quad \mathscr R_U(\mathbf a)=D_U(\mathbf a) \left(\prod_{w\in Y}M_wight) \mathbb E\!\left[ Z_{G',N}^{A_{N,\mathbf a}} (\mathbf n_Y, oldsymbol\chi_Y-\mathbf K/N)ight]. \quad} 	ag{14} \] There is no independence assumption on the graph spectator.
