Eliminating a positive filled region preserves the comparison Divide the vertices of an incident-edge network into interior vertices \(S\), whose powers and charges are fixed, and boundary vertices \(B\), whose angles are allowed to vary. Assume every boundary vertex is incident to an included edge. Whenever the interior equations have a positive solution, define the boundary response by \[ \mathcal R_b(\mathbf t_B) =\sum_{e
i b}r_{b,e}(\mathbf t_S(\mathbf t_B), \mathbf t_B). 	ag{32} \] Theorem 3 makes the interior solution unique. Its nonsingular Jacobian makes it holomorphic locally. These local solutions agree on overlaps, so (32) is a well-defined holomorphic response on its realized positive domain. **Corollary 4.** For any two different boundary assignments in that domain, \[ \Re\sum_{b\in B} \delta\mathcal R_b\,\overline{\delta t_b}>0. 	ag{33} \] The local derivative \(\mathcal R'\) is complex symmetric and has positive definite real part. **Proof.** Sum (23) over the original edges for the two interior solutions. At each interior vertex, \(\delta R_v=i n_v\delta t_v/2\), so the real part of its contribution is zero. The remaining terms give (33). If any boundary angle differs, at least one incident edge configuration differs, making the comparison strict. For the infinitesimal assertion, order the variables as interior followed by boundary. The derivative of the interior equations and boundary response before elimination is a complex symmetric matrix \[ H_{m all}=  egin{pmatrix}A&B_0\B_0^T&D\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Re H_{m all}>0. 	ag{34} \] Here \(A\) includes the interior terms \(-i\operatorname{diag}(n_v)/2\). Implicit differentiation gives the Schur complement \[ \mathcal R'=D-B_0^TA^{-1}B_0. 	ag{35} \] For any nonzero boundary vector \(y\), put \(x=-A^{-1}B_0y\). Direct multiplication gives \[ \Re\left[y^*(D-B_0^TA^{-1}B_0)yight] =\Re\left[  egin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix}^{\!*} H_{m all}  egin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix}ight]>0. 	ag{36} \] The Schur complement is symmetric, proving the assertion. \(\square\) An original boundary carrier contributes a purely imaginary real-coefficient multiple of its own angle to the peripheral period. Adding this term preserves (33) and the positive real part in (35). Each original carrier is added once, rather than once for each block incident to its circle. Consequently any number of positive regions can be eliminated and then joined through their original shared boundary angles: their monotonicity comparisons add, and further real signed filling powers contribute zero real energy. This is a closure property of the actual geometric period equations. It does not assert a corresponding closure theorem for the quantum integration cycles, estimates on other critical points, or nonvanishing leading coefficients. ## 7. Continuation and its remaining obstruction At the complete point, with all outside angles zero and all charges zero, \(R_v=0\) and the Jacobian of (27) is \[  rac12\operatorname{diag}(d_v-i n_v), 	ag{37} \] where \(d_v\) is the original degree. It is invertible. Thus any fixed real powers admit a unique positive solution for sufficiently small cone charges. More generally, follow a continuous prescribed charge path through positive solutions. Theorem 3 rules out both an interior collision of solutions and a singular Jacobian. If the solutions stay in a compact subset of the positive domain, the implicit-function theorem extends them past any finite endpoint of the charge interval. Therefore a maximal positive continuation can stop only by leaving every compact subset of that domain. In the disk coordinates this means approaching a boundary \(|\zeta_e|=1\) or \(|\xi_e|=1\), possibly with divergent logarithmic coordinates or degenerate peripheral data. There are immediate necessary range conditions. From (21) and (27), \[ |c_v|< rac{d_v+|n_v|}{2}. 	ag{38} \] Indeed, \(\pi|c_v|\le|\Im R_v|+|n_v|\,|\Re t_v|/2\), and each incident meridian increment has imaginary part strictly smaller than \(\pi/2\). At unit charge (38) gives \(d_v+|n_v|>2\). This condition is sufficient in the isolated-vertex theorem. No sufficiency for a connected selected set is claimed here. The comparison (23) concerns the positive geometric branch. Other critical points of the complexified original source can lie outside this positive domain or on different logarithmic lifts. Neither Theorem 3 nor the continuation statement compares their critical values. The global relative-cycle and endpoint requirements in [the persistence theorem](research_dominant_saddle_transport.md) therefore remain to be proved separately. ## 8. Related variational results Existence and uniqueness through geometric variational principles have substantial precedent. Bobenko and Springborn, [*Variational principles for circle patterns and Koebe's theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0203250), Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **356** (2004), 659--689, establish existence and uniqueness results for circle patterns with prescribed intersection angles. Rivin's [*Combinatorial optimization in geometry*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9907032) provides related optimization background, including applications to hyperbolic structures on three-manifolds. The statements proved here retain the original complex primitive periods and arbitrary real filling powers, and include the boundary response after eliminating a filled region. Their proofs are the explicit shape identities and monotonicity calculations above. This brief coverage check does not establish a novelty claim or identify these statements with a theorem in either cited work.

title: The volume of a positive edge and its primitive action
text:
# The volume of a positive edge and its primitive action For every positive configuration of the eight original edge tetrahedra, their volume is \[  oxed{\quad V_e(t,u)=2\pi\Re\psi(t,u) -2\{\Im t\,\Im r_t+\Im u\,\Im r_u\}. \quad} 	ag{1} \] Here \(\psi\) is the original edge phase, normalized at completeness, and \(r_t,r_u\) are its original marked meridian increments. The identity holds throughout the positive edge domain. It is not restricted to a filling path. At a positive solution of the primitive filling equations, the correction terms combine exactly with the quadratic crossing terms and the linear filling charges. Thus the stationary action has the absolute volume normalization, without a separate integration along a common-charge cone path. One must still establish that the positive cells with the prescribed marking realize the intended filled manifold. This calculation does not replace that geometric assembly, nor does it establish a quantum asymptotic. ## 1. The original shapes and branches Use the [positive edge domain](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md) and its strip coordinates \(P,Q\). Write \[ f(P)=\arctan(	anh P),\qquad P=x+iy,\qquad f(P)=\alpha+i eta, 	ag{2} \] with \(|y|,|\alpha|<\pi/4\), and use the analogous notation for \(Q\). The branches are fixed at \(P=Q=0\). The positive domain is biholomorphic to the product of two unit disks, so the original closed holomorphic period form has a single-valued primitive there. We choose that primitive as \[ d\psi=- rac1\pi(r_t\,dt+r_u\,du),\qquad \psi(0,0)= rac{4G}{\pi}, 	ag{3} \] where \(G=D(i)\) is Catalan's constant and \(D\) is the Bloch--Wigner dilogarithm. The ordered original shapes are \[ (A,B,-1/A,-1/B),\qquad (C,D_0,-1/C,-1/D_0). 	ag{4} \] The symbol \(D_0\) denotes a tetrahedron shape; \(D(z)\) always denotes its volume function. The exact coordinate expressions are \[  egin{array}{ll} C=i e^{-2P},& B=i e^{2if(P)}=(C-1)/(C+1),\[2mm] A=i e^{2Q},& D_0=i e^{2if(Q)}=(A+1)/(1-A). \end{array} 	ag{5} \] They are obtained from the original ordered cross ratios in [the corner geometry note](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_square_corner_flat_geometry.md), Section 1. Every shape in (4) lies in the upper half-plane. The two groups associated to \(P\) and \(Q\) are interleaved between the original octahedra; regrouping their volumes does not change their face attachments. ## 2. A differential calculation for four tetrahedra The Bloch--Wigner function can be defined locally by \[ D(z)=\Im\operatorname{Li}_2(z)+\log|z|\arg(1-z). 	ag{6} \] The expression is single valued after continuation. Differentiating, using \(d\operatorname{Li}_2(z)=-\log(1-z)\,dz/z\), gives \[ dD(z)=\log|z|\,d\arg(1-z)-\log|1-z|\,d\arg z. 	ag{7} \] The inversion identity \(D(1/z)=-D(z)\) follows either from (6) or by differentiating its two sides using (7) and fixing the constant at \(z=i\), where complex conjugation gives the required sign. Put \[ H(z)=D(z)-D(-z). 	ag{8} \] Then \(D(z)+D(-1/z)=H(z)\). If \(w=(z-1)/(z+1)\), subtraction in (7) gives \[ dH(z)=\log|z|\,d\arg w-\log|w|\,d\arg z. 	ag{9} \] The same transformation sends \(w\) to \(-1/z\). Hence \[ dH(w)=dH(z). 	ag{10} \] Only derivatives of arguments occur, so these equations require no arbitrary argument constant. For the \(P\)-group in (4), take \(z=C\), \(w=B\). Its volume is \[ V_P=D(C)+D(-1/C)+D(B)+D(-1/B)=H(C)+H(B). 	ag{11} \] The strip coordinates give \[ \log|C|=-2x,\quad d\arg C=-2\,dy,\qquad \log|B|=-2 eta,\quad d\arg B=2\,d\alpha. 	ag{12} \] Equations (9)--(12) therefore imply \[ dV_P=-8(x\,d\alpha+ eta\,dy). 	ag{13} \] For the \(Q\)-group, take \(z=A\) and \(w=(A-1)/(A+1)=-1/D_0\). Since \(H(-1/z)=H(z)\), its volume is again \(H(z)+H(w)\). Now \[ \log|A|=2x,\quad d\arg A=2\,dy,\qquad \log|D_0|=-2 eta,\quad d\arg D_0=2\,d\alpha. 	ag{14} \] Substitution in (9), with \(w=-1/D_0\), gives the same formula: \[ dV_Q=-8(x\,d\alpha+ eta\,dy). 	ag{15} \] At the origin, each group consists of four shapes equal to \(i\) and has volume \(4G\). Let \(E(\alpha,y)\) be the normalized square energy from [the convex variation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_filling_convex_variation.md), so \(dE=x\,d\alpha+ eta\,dy\) and \(E(0,0)=0\). The calculation proves the useful absolute identity \[ V_P=4G-8E_P,\qquad V_Q=4G-8E_Q. 	ag{16} \] In particular the strict convexity of \(E\) is precisely strict concavity of the corresponding four-tetrahedron volume in these angle coordinates. ## 3. Converting to primitive boundary coordinates Write \[ t=s_t+ih_t,\quad u=s_u+ih_u,\qquad r_t=k_t+ig_t,\quad r_u=k_u+ig_u. 	ag{17} \] The exact linear period identities give \[ 4\,d(E_P+E_Q) =k_t\,ds_t+k_u\,ds_u+h_t\,dg_t+h_u\,dg_u. 	ag{18} \] Consequently (13) and (15) imply \[ dV_e=-2(k_t\,ds_t+k_u\,ds_u +h_t\,dg_t+h_u\,dg_u). 	ag{19} \] On the other hand, (3) gives \[ 2\pi\,d\Re\psi =-2(k_t\,ds_t+k_u\,ds_u-g_t\,dh_t-g_u\,dh_u). 	ag{20} \] Subtracting \(2\,d(h_tg_t+h_ug_u)\) produces (19). At completeness \(h_t=h_u=0\), \(V_e=8G\), and \(2\pi\psi(0,0)=8G\). The positive domain is connected. This proves (1), including its absolute additive constant. Thus the formula uses the original volume of eight ordered tetrahedra. In particular one cannot replace \(D(-1/z)\) by \(D(z)\) away from special configurations. The difference \(H(z)=D(z)-D(-z)\) in (8) is what makes the calculation valid on the full domain. ## 4. A stationary action on an arbitrary selected region Let \(S\) be any finite selected set in an original circle tree, and include each original edge incident to \(S\) exactly once. Boundary variables at unselected ends are denoted \(u_b\). Assume all these edge configurations are positive, with their original branch and marking. Define \[ \Psi(\mathbf t,\mathbf u)=\sum_e\psi(t_{v(e)},t_{w(e)}), 	ag{21} \] where a boundary endpoint uses its \(u_b\). For each selected vertex take a real crossing power \(n_v\) and a real filling charge \(c_v\), and impose the original logarithmic equations \[ \sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e} = rac{i n_v}{2}t_v-\pi i c_v. 	ag{22} \] Equivalently, \(\Psi_{t_v}+in_vt_v/(2\pi)=ic_v\). Let \[ \mathcal S= \Psi+ rac{i}{4\pi}\sum_{v\in S}n_vt_v^2 -i\sum_{v\in S}c_vt_v. 	ag{23} \] This is evaluated at a solution of (22); no assertion about its quantum coefficient is part of the notation. **Theorem.** The sum \(V_{m cells}\) of the original positive tetrahedron volumes satisfies \[ V_{m cells} =2\pi\Re\mathcal S -2\sum_{b
otin S}\Im u_b \sum_{\substack{e
i b\e	ext{ included}}} \Im r_{b,e}. 	ag{24} \] In particular, when the outside angles are complete, \[ V_{m cells}=2\pi\Re\mathcal S. 	ag{25} \] **Proof.** Sum (1) over the included edges. At a selected vertex put \(s_v=\Re t_v\) and \(h_v=\Im t_v\). The imaginary part of (22) gives \[ \sum_{e
i v}\Im r_{v,e} =n_vs_v/2-\pi c_v. 	ag{26} \] Its contribution to the correction in (1) is therefore \[ -n_vs_vh_v+2\pi c_vh_v =2\pi\Re\left\{ rac{in_vt_v^2}{4\pi}-ic_vt_vight\}. 	ag{27} \] Boundary incidences give the remaining terms of (24). No limiting operation is used. \(\square\) All original carrier conventions remain in force: \(n_v=\eta_v-2p_v\) when the power comes from the original integral filling coefficient \(p_v\) and carrier \(\eta_v\). Equation (23) uses that \(n_v\) once. It does not introduce another carrier term per incident edge. ## 5. The geometric and analytic obligations left by this identity The result calibrates the action whenever the specified positive configuration is available. If its original face attachments and primitive peripheral curves realize a complete filling, the cell volume in (25) is the hyperbolic volume of that filled manifold: the tetrahedron interiors partition its nonsingular part, and the filled cores have volume zero. This is an implication with the geometric realization stated as a hypothesis. For example, the [negative-corridor criterion](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md) gives a positive primitive solution at unit charges when all selected crossing magnitudes are at least four, independently of the path length. Formula (25) now gives its absolute cell-volume anchor directly. The existence of a common-charge cone path is not needed for that calculation. The separate [pointwise marked-completion theorem](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md) verifies the face assembly, full primitive periods and solid-torus completion for every positive critical point with the required strict core signs. It therefore supplies the actual marked hyperbolic-volume interpretation for this corridor class. Neither this identity nor existence and uniqueness of the positive solution supplies the coefficient of its saddle in the original root-of-unity period. The whole-source estimate and noncancellation problem remain separate. ## 6. An explicit holomorphic primitive The period normalization can also be checked without integrating along a selected path. On the full strip \(|\Im P|<\pi/4\), define \[ F(P)= rac{\pi P}{4} + rac{i}{4}\left\{ \operatorname{Li}_2(-i e^{-2P}) -\operatorname{Li}_2(i e^{-2P})ight\} - rac G2. 	ag{28} \] The two dilogarithm arguments lie respectively in the lower and upper half-planes, so they avoid the principal cut \([1,\infty)\). Differentiation gives \[ F'(P)= rac\pi4+ rac i2 \log rac{1+i e^{-2P}}{1-i e^{-2P}} =\arctan(	anh P)=f(P). 	ag{29} \] The branch identity is fixed at \(P=0\) and continued on the strip. Also \(F(0)=0\), because \(\operatorname{Li}_2(i)-\operatorname{Li}_2(-i)=2iG\). The original edge phase therefore has the explicit expression \[  oxed{\quad \psi(t,u)= rac1\pi\left[ 4G-2(P+Q)\{f(P)+f(Q)\}+4\{F(P)+F(Q)\} ight]. \quad} 	ag{30} \] To verify it, use the exact strip identities \[ t=2\{f(P)+f(Q)\},\quad u=-2i(P-Q),\quad r_t=P+Q,\quad r_u=i\{f(Q)-f(P)\}. 	ag{31} \] Differentiating (30) gives (3), and its complete value is \(4G/\pi\). Thus (30) is the same original branch used in (1). It provides a separate expression for numerical or symbolic checks of the volume identity. ## 7. Reproducing the finite comparisons The separate [checker](../experiments/check_positive_edge_volume_identity.py) compares the eight original Bloch--Wigner volumes with (1) and the explicit primitive (30), including points well outside the small complete chart. At selected points it also integrates the original meridian differential independently. It includes stationary boundary-correction checks for (24). .venv/bin/python experiments/check_positive_edge_volume_identity.py \ --precision 120 --output /tmp/positive-edge-volume-replay.json The [saved replay](../repro/results/research-positive-edge-volume-identity-root.json) contains 24 edge comparisons, eight independently integrated period comparisons, and four stationary correction comparisons. Its script SHA256 is 1ab9a944c378fbc3fdd99c0aa48c23656b9d1487ed30816dffb5b270892ac98a. These finite comparisons check the conventions; the differential proof above establishes the identities on the entire domain. ## 8. A quantitative comparison for other primitive charges The volume identity also gives a comparison on the entire closed angle domain, without constructing a filling path for the competing charges. Keep a fixed selected region, the original real powers \(n_v\), zero outside angles, and the original edge-angle relations. Assume there is an interior solution at unit charges with \(t_v^*=s_v^*+ih_v^*\), where \(h_v^*<0\). The pointwise completion theorem supplies its marked hyperbolic interpretation when \(n_v=\eta_v-2p_v\) for the original integral slopes. For every included edge use the two square coordinates of (16). Collect them in the real vector \[ X=(A_{P,e},y_{P,e},A_{Q,e},y_{Q,e})_e,\qquad \mathcal E(X)=4\sum_e(E_{P,e}+E_{Q,e}). 	ag{32} \] The coordinates retain a shared real angle \(s_v\) at each vertex. They obey \[ \sum_{e
i v}g_{v,e}- rac{n_v}{2}s_v=-\pi c_v \quad(v\in S),\qquad s_b=0\quad(b
otin S). 	ag{33} \] Here the charges \(c_v\) are allowed to be any real numbers. The comparison also allows closed squares, and does not require matching the imaginary angles of the competing cells. This larger domain is useful for an upper bound. Define its continuous volume function by \[ V_{m ang}(X)=8G\,|E_{m inc}|-2\mathcal E(X). 	ag{34} \] On positive configurations it is the sum of the original eight tetrahedron volumes, by (16). Equation (34) defines its continuous extension to the closed squares. Let \(X^*\) be the unit-charge solution, and put \[ \delta=\min_
u\{\pi/4-|X_
u^*|\}>0,\qquad \kappa= rac{\delta}{\pi}\sin^2\delta. 	ag{35} \] **Theorem 2.** Every closed-square assignment satisfying the same real matching equations and (33) obeys \[  oxed{\quad V_{m ang}(X) \le V_{m ang}(X^*)+ 2\pi\sum_{v\in S}h_v^*(c_v-1) -2\kappa\|X-X^*\|_2^2 . \quad} 	ag{36} \] In particular, if all \(c_v\ge1\), any increase in a charge has a strict volume cost. With the actual core lengths \(\ell_v=-2h_v^*\), this cost is at least \(\pi\sum_v\ell_v(c_v-1)\). **Proof.** At the unit solution, (18) and the real parts of the primitive equations give \[  egin{split} d\mathcal E_{X^*}(X-X^*) &=\sum_{v\in S}h_v^* \left(\sum_{e
i v}\Delta g_{v,e} - rac{n_v}{2}\Delta s_vight)\ &=-\pi\sum_{v\in S}h_v^*(c_v-1). \end{split} 	ag{37} \] The outside terms vanish: their real angles stay zero, and their imaginary angles at \(X^*\) are zero. This calculation keeps every incidence of the original region. For clarity, the explicit quadratic remainder in the supporting inequality follows from the square Hessian \[ E''(A,y)= rac1{\sqrt{1-\sin^2(2A)\sin^2(2y)}}  egin{pmatrix} \cos(2y)/\cos(2A)&-\sin(2A)\sin(2y)\ -\sin(2A)\sin(2y)&\cos(2A)/\cos(2y) \end{pmatrix}. 	ag{38} \] Its determinant is one. On \(\lvert Avert,\lvert yvert\le\pi/4-\delta/2\), its trace is at most \(2/\sin^2\delta\), so \(E''\ge(\sin^2\delta/2)I\). Write \(D=X-X^*\). Every coordinate of \(D\) has magnitude at most \(\pi/2\). For \(0\le r\le r_0=\delta/\pi\), the segment \(X^*+rD\) lies in the smaller square just used. Hence \(\mathcal E''\ge2\sin^2\delta\,I\) on this initial segment. Convexity holds on the rest of the segment. The integral form of the supporting-plane remainder therefore gives \[  egin{split} \mathcal E(X)-\mathcal E(X^*) -d\mathcal E_{X^*}D &\ge2\sin^2\delta\,(r_0-r_0^2/2)\|D\|_2^2\ &\ge\kappa\|D\|_2^2. \end{split} 	ag{39} \] For a boundary endpoint, apply the inequality first along the open segment and pass to its endpoint using continuity of the square energy. Combining (34), (37) and (39) proves (36). \(\square\) If a competitor is itself an actual positive critical point for the charges \(\mathbf c\), the earlier volume identity gives \[ \Re\mathcal S_{\mathbf c} \le \Re\mathcal S_{\mathbf1} -\sum_v |h_v^*|(c_v-1) - rac{\kappa}{\pi}\|X-X^*\|_2^2 \qquad(\mathbf c\ge\mathbf1). 	ag{40} \] This compares the normalized original actions, including their additive constants. Every nontrivial integer charge vector with \(c_v\ge1\) therefore has a gap of at least \(\min_v|h_v^*|\) in its real action. At unit charges, (36) also bounds every point outside a fixed angle neighborhood strictly below the geometric volume. The compared configurations have the same original edge relations. They change only the primitive filling charges. This is not a bound for arbitrary shifted internal edge equations or for a different tetrahedral subdivision. In particular it does not apply to the [wrong-edge alias face counterexample](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/positive_geometric_alias_volume_counterexample.md). The earlier [Legendre contour construction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/general_legendre_rivin_contour.md) already separates positive peripheral competitors from those other faces. The explicit core-length bound (36) supplies that comparison here in the original circle-tree coordinates. No quantum contour has been changed in this argument. To use (40) for the finite source, its competing contributions must first be represented in these original positive cells, with their amplitudes and boundary terms retained. The volume comparison does not establish that representation or the coefficient of the geometric contribution. ## 9. The signed identity on regular continuations Positivity was needed to interpret every tetrahedron volume as positive and to obtain the convex comparison above. It is not needed for the differential identity itself. This distinction allows a comparison of other regular critical values on the same marked source branch. Consider any regular analytic continuation of the original edge from its complete configuration. All shape parameters and face maps are retained in their original order. The continuation avoids zero, one and infinity for every tetrahedron shape, as well as the singularities of the original face charts. Continue the angle logs, the meridian logs and \(\psi\) along this path. They are not reset to principal values at its endpoint. Define \[ V_e^{m sgn}= D(A)+D(B)+D(-1/A)+D(-1/B) +D(C)+D(D_0)+D(-1/C)+D(-1/D_0). 	ag{41} \] Here the Bloch--Wigner function assigns its usual signed volume; some terms may be negative or zero. **Proposition 3.** On every such continued branch, \[ V_e^{m sgn}=2\pi\Re\psi -2\{\Im t\,\Im r_t+\Im u\,\Im r_u\}. 	ag{42} \] **Proof.** The differential (7), inversion identity and calculation (9)--(10) hold without a half-plane restriction. Locally along the continuation choose the continued logarithms \[ C=i e^{-2P},\qquad A=i e^{2Q},\qquad B=i e^{2if(P)},\qquad D_0=i e^{2if(Q)}. 	ag{43} \] The rational relations (5) and the period identities (31) continue from the complete point. The functions denoted by \(f(P)\) and \(f(Q)\) in (43) are the continued branches, not new principal inverse tangents. Thus (12)--(15) and (18)--(20) remain identities of real differentials in each local chart. In particular \[ dV_e^{m sgn} =d\!\left[2\pi\Re\psi -2(\Im t\,\Im r_t+\Im u\,\Im r_u)ight]. 	ag{44} \] The two sides agree at completeness. Integration along the specified path proves (42). Overlapping logarithmic charts use the same continued periods. A winding change in an individual term of (42) is therefore not an independent normalization freedom. The argument also applies when a shape crosses the real axis away from zero and one, since the Bloch--Wigner function and its differential extend there. \(\square\) One loop makes the role of the boundary correction explicit. Keep \(Q\) fixed and wind once around \(P_0=i\pi/4\), avoiding that point and every other chart singularity. Since \(f'(P)=\operatorname{sech}(2P)\) has residue \(1/(2i)\) there, the continued quantities satisfy \[ \Delta f(P)=\pi,\qquad \Delta F(P)=\pi(P-P_0),\qquad \Delta\psi=2P-2Q-4P_0. 	ag{44a} \] The middle identity follows by integrating \(f\,dP\) by parts and evaluating the residue of \(P f'(P)\). The real part of \(\psi\) generally changes. But \(\Delta r_u=-i\pi\), \(\Delta t=2\pi\), and \(\Im u=-2\Re(P-Q)\). These changes cancel exactly in (42), as the unchanged signed shape volume requires. Sum this identity on an original circle tree, along one common regular network continuation from completeness. Suppose the outside angles remain zero and the selected equations are \[ \sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e} = rac{i n_v}{2}t_v-\pi i c_v,\qquad c_v\in\mathbb Z. 	ag{45} \] The same algebra as (26)--(27), without a sign assumption on the shapes, proves \[ \sum_e V_e^{m sgn}=2\pi\Re\mathcal S_{\mathbf c}. 	ag{46} \] In (46) every original edge is included. Complete edges outside the selected region contribute their original constant \(8G\). There is a direct representation interpretation when the filled peripheral matrices have distinct fixed points. In addition to the regularity above, assume \[ e^{2it_v}
e1\quad(v\in S),\qquad n_v=\eta_v-2p_v,\quad p_v\in\mathbb Z. 	ag{47} \] The original rational face identities give an equivariant development of the same cut triangulation and a representation of its exterior group. This is an algebraic face-cocycle construction; it does not require positive developed tetrahedra. The original peripheral matrix words still have multipliers \[ U_v=2\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}-i\eta_vt_v,\qquad V_v=2it_v. 	ag{48} \] Equation (47) makes the longitude semisimple with two distinct fixed points. The original cusp decoration is a common retained fixed point of the longitude and meridian. Since the meridian also commutes with the longitude, it fixes the other point as well. The retained common flag is essential here: commutation alone in \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)\) would permit an interchange of the two fixed points when the longitude has multiplier \(-1\). By (45), \(U_v+p_vV_v=-2\pi i c_v\), so their primitive filling product has multiplier one and fixes both points. It is the identity in \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)\), not merely a matrix with a unit eigenvalue. Thus the representation descends to the original marked filling \(M=Y(\mathbf p)\). The original oriented ideal chain computes the signed sum in (46). It computes the representation volume on the filling as well: replace the old cusp map by the equivariant axis map, using a face-compatible conical homotopy whose boundary volume tends to zero, then extend the same boundary triangulation over the filling solid torus with its vertices on that axis. Every added tetrahedron has zero volume. The details and the \(O(Y^{-2})\) boundary estimate are proved in [the peripheral representation-volume calculation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/general_peripheral_representation_volume_bound.md), Section 2, and [the filling-chain normalization](general_source_regulator_hyperbolic_equality.md), Section 6. The original chain and peripheral curves are the ones used here; no new regulator constant is chosen. Consequently, when \(M\) is hyperbolic, the proved [representation-volume inequality](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/general_peripheral_representation_volume_bound.md) gives \[ |2\pi\Re\mathcal S_{\mathbf c}| =|\operatorname{Vol}(ho)| \le\operatorname{Vol}(M). 	ag{49} \] This is a bound for the specified regular continued critical values, with their full original logarithmic branches. It gives neither a strict gap nor the coefficient of a critical point in the quantum period. The hypotheses matter. A singular face chart, an escaping decoration, or a selected longitude with multiplier one is not disposed of by this argument. In the last case, the exponentiated filling relation alone need not kill a nontrivial unipotent matrix. Nor has every term obtained by a different quantum interpolation been identified with a regular continuation in (41)--(48). Those comparisons and the original relative integration cycle remain part of the source theorem. The [action-comparison checker](../experiments/check_circle_tree_action_comparisons.py) compares the quantitative supporting inequality at 24 angle assignments, the signed identity at four configurations outside the positive domain, and the logarithmic loop (44a) by direct contour integration. The [saved record](../repro/results/research-circle-tree-action-comparisons-root.json) uses 110-digit arithmetic; its input critical points are stored to forty significant digits in the separate corridor record. Those finite checks verify the formulas and branch conventions, not the general representation-volume theorem. python3 experiments/check_circle_tree_action_comparisons.py \ --precision 110 --output /tmp/circle-tree-action-comparisons.json

title: A positive two-state transfer for the actual spectral tail
status: Exact positive tail transfer; regular local saddle
text: # A positive two-state transfer for the actual spectral tail 31 October 2026. This exact model of the normalized tail includes the negative coefficients of its usual two-term recurrence. It gives compact-interior Perron and outer-angular estimates, not an exponentially accurate interpolation in both endpoint rows or a global sign-cancellation theorem. ## 1. Exact normalization and word expansion Use the original one-sided tail from the [relative-energy theorem](../papers/casimir-source-asymptotics/README.md). For fixed actual rows \(0\le i\le j\), let \(r=j-i\), \(\theta=\pi/N\), and $$ s_a=2\sin(a\theta),\qquad \lambda=\cos\theta+\cos(2\pi\delta),\qquad \eta_a=\frac{\lambda}{\cos\theta-\cos((2a-1)\theta)}. $$ The denominator occurs only at \(a\ge i+2\), so no zero row denominator is used. Put $$ Q_r=\frac{K_{i,j}}{\prod_{a=i+1}^j s_a^2},\qquad Q_0=1,\quad Q_1=x+y,\quad Q_l=(x+y)Q_{l-1}+(\eta_{i+l}-1)xyQ_{l-2}.\tag{1} $$ For \(r\ge1\), initialize \((X_1,Y_1)=(x,y)\), and set $$ \begin{pmatrix}X_l\\Y_l\end{pmatrix} =M_l\begin{pmatrix}X_{l-1}\\Y_{l-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad M_l=\begin{pmatrix}x&\eta_{i+l}x\\y&y\end{pmatrix}, \qquad 2\le l\le r.\tag{2} $$ Then \(Q_l=X_l+Y_l\) exactly: \(Y_{l-1}=yQ_{l-2}\), and summing (2) gives (1). Equivalently, $$ Q_r=\sum_{w\in\{x,y\}^r}x^{\#x(w)}y^{\#y(w)} \prod_{l=2}^r\eta_{i+l}^{\mathbf1_{\{w_{l-1}=y,\ w_l=x\}}}. \tag{3} $$ The initial state contains no transition weight. The empty word gives \(Q_0=1\). This proof retains every actual row parameter. For real \(\lambda\ge0\), all word weights are nonnegative even if \(\eta_a-1<0\). No claim of positivity is made for the original unused prefix/suffix factors or for negative \(\lambda\) in the final spectral cap. The energy Cauchy theorem treats that cap separately without this positivity. ## 2. Uniform angular contraction in the relative outer phase Suppose every entry of the real matrices (2) lies in \([m,M]\), with \(0<m\le M<\infty\). This holds uniformly when \(x,y\) range in a compact positive set, \(\delta\) stays a fixed distance below \(1/2\), and all rows \((i+l)/N\) stay in a compact subinterval of \((0,1/2)\). For phases \(\vartheta_x,\vartheta_y\), the matrix is obtained by multiplying its two rows by their respective phases. In each entry of a two-step product, the two intermediate states contribute positive weights \(A,B\in[m^2,M^2]\) and relative phase \(\vartheta=\vartheta_x-\vartheta_y\). Therefore $$ \begin{aligned} |Ae^{i\vartheta}+B|^2 &=(A+B)^2-4AB\sin^2(\vartheta/2),\\ \frac{4AB}{(A+B)^2}&\ge(m/M)^4. \end{aligned}\tag{4} $$ Set \(\kappa=(m/M)^4\). Pair consecutive transfer matrices, apply (4) entrywise, and then multiply nonnegative majorants. The unpaired transfer and initial vector obey ordinary triangle inequalities. This gives the exact bound $$ |Q_r(xe^{i\vartheta_x},ye^{i\vartheta_y})| \le\exp\!\left[-\frac\kappa2 \left\lfloor\frac{r-1}{2}\right\rfloor \sin^2\!\frac{\vartheta_x-\vartheta_y}{2}\right]Q_r(x,y). \tag{5} $$ Thus a macroscopic interval has a uniform exponential outer-angular gap away from equal phases. Equal phases are an essential exception: \(Q_r(e^{i\vartheta}x,e^{i\vartheta}y)=e^{ir\vartheta}Q_r(x,y)\). There is no independent contraction in both frequencies. If either outer weight is zero, the surviving polynomial is a monomial and the relative angular statement is vacuous. At \(\lambda=0\) strict matrix positivity also fails; (5) is not extended there by assumption. ## 3. A compact-interior relative Perron product Fix a compact positive set of outer weights, a compact real spectral set with \(\delta<1/2\), and constants \(\epsilon>0\) such that $$ \epsilon\le i/N<j/N\le1/2-\epsilon,\qquad (j-i)/N\ge\epsilon. \tag{6} $$ For all sufficiently large \(N\), the matrices (2) are uniformly strictly positive, bounded, and vary by \(O(N^{-1})\) per row. Their Perron roots are $$ \rho_l=\frac{x+y+\sqrt{(x-y)^2+4\eta_{i+l}xy}}2.\tag{7} $$ The square root, \(\rho_l\), and the Perron eigenspaces extend analytically to one fixed small complex neighborhood of the compact parameter set. The second eigenvalue may vanish. Nevertheless the discriminant stays nonzero and the modulus of its ratio to \(\rho_l\) is bounded by some \(a<1\), also on a sufficiently small complex neighborhood. No division by the second eigenvalue is used. Choose right and left eigenvectors \(v_l,u_l\), normalized by \(\mathbf1^Tv_l=1\) and \(u_l^Tv_l=1\). With \(z=(x,y)^T\), define $$ A_{i,j,N}=(\mathbf1^Tv_r)(u_2^Tz) \prod_{l=3}^r(u_l^Tv_{l-1}).\tag{8} $$ The empty products retain their usual meanings. Uniformly under (6), $$ Q_r=A_{i,j,N}\prod_{l=2}^r\rho_l\,[1+O(N^{-1})].\tag{9} $$ Here \(A_{i,j,N}\) is a nonvanishing analytic factor bounded above and below uniformly, on a smaller fixed complex neighborhood. Indeed each \(u_l^Tv_{l-1}=1+O(N^{-1})\), while the initial and terminal factors are positive units on the real compact set. For a proof, use the two instantaneous eigenvectors as a moving basis. After dividing each matrix by \(\rho_l\), successive changes of basis have diagonal entries \(1+O(N^{-1})\) and off-diagonal entries \(O(N^{-1})\). The second coordinate contracts by at most \(a+O(N^{-1})\). Its initial contribution feeds the first coordinate by a geometric sum of size \(O(N^{-1})\). Thereafter the generated second coordinate is \(O(N^{-1})\) of the first, so its feedback is \(O(N^{-2})\) per step, with total \(O(N^{-1})\). The terminal second-coordinate error has the same size. The diagonal main factors are exactly those in (8). These estimates also hold uniformly for the complex neighborhood, and Cauchy gives the corresponding fixed-parameter derivative estimates on a smaller neighborhood. The original tail is still \(K_{i,j}=(\prod s_a^2)Q_r\). In the limit \(t=(i+l)/N\), multiplication of (7) by \(4\sin^2(\pi t)\) gives exactly $$ 2\sin(\pi t)\left[(x+y)\sin(\pi t)+ \sqrt{(x-y)^2\sin^2(\pi t)+4xy\cos^2(\pi\delta)}\right],\tag{10} $$ the original sharp weighted tail root. Thus no new scalar normalization or absolute recurrence has entered. ## 4. A regular outer-coefficient saddle In the regime (6), let \(k/r\) stay in a compact subinterval of \((0,1)\), and set \(y=1\). There is a unique positive tilt \(x=e^{\ell_N}\) with $$ \partial_\ell\log Q_r(e^\ell,1)\big|_{\ell_N}=k.\tag{11} $$ These tilts lie in a fixed compact interval. To see this directly from (3), condition on all states except one. The conditional ratio of an \(x\) state to a \(y\) state equals \(e^\ell\) times at most two transition ratios, which are uniformly bounded above and below. Small or large fixed \(\ell\) therefore puts the expected \(x\) fraction uniformly near zero or one. Positivity of every word makes the mean strictly increasing. At compact tilts the variance \(V_N=\partial_\ell^2\log Q_r\) satisfies \(cN\le V_N\le CN\). For the lower bound condition on all odd positions: the even states become independent Bernoulli variables with probabilities bounded away from zero and one. Conditional variance and the law of total variance give a constant times \(r\). For the upper bound and all higher fixed cumulants, (9) provides an analytic logarithm on a uniform complex tilt neighborhood, with derivatives \(O(N)\). Cauchy coefficient extraction, (5), and the Taylor expansion of that analytic logarithm now give $$ [x^ky^{r-k}]Q_r(x,y) =\frac{Q_r(e^{\ell_N},1)e^{-k\ell_N}} {\sqrt{2\pi V_N}}[1+O(N^{-1})].\tag{12} $$ For precision, outside a fixed small angular interval (5) is exponentially small. Inside it, the variance lower bound and bounded higher derivatives give Gaussian decay. On the shrinking central interval the cubic term is odd and imaginary and integrates to zero; the quartic and squared cubic terms contribute relative \(O(N^{-1})\). All constants are uniform on the stated strict compact sets. Formula (12) is a coefficient theorem for the actual tail, not for a separately chosen positive comparison polynomial. ## 5. Original factors and the remaining magnetic problem A complete original one-sided coefficient includes the omitted-half factor, all unused prefix and suffix rows, and \(\prod s_a^2\). They must multiply (9) or (12) exactly. On a strict sign chamber the unused-row signs form the recorded lattice character. The omitted-half factor retains its two oscillatory modes and can vanish densely; it is not a nonzero analytic amplitude that may be divided out on a fixed spectral disk. These results control the outer relative frequency and give a relative \(O(N^{-1})\) regular coefficient approximation. They do not give an exponentially accurate analytic interpolation in \(i/N,j/N,k/N\). The [literal four-state transfer](research_original_one_sided_four_state_transfer.md) and [analytic switch theorem](research_analytic_switching_suppression.md) now provide a separate route for the middle frequencies: the [regular-window theorem](research_regular_spectral_window_phase_exclusion.md) proves exponential loss outside the exact local alignment, retaining both gauge boundary terms and every unused factor. On an inconsistent shared sign system it improves the original Cauchy bound relative to the window envelope. Compatible phase systems, irregular windows and comparison of that envelope with complete volume remain open. Polynomial relative errors or smooth integration by parts alone would not prove that exponential loss. The exact recurrence/source interface is checked by the [finite original-coefficient audit](../experiments/audit_actual_one_sided_relative_spectral_energy.py). The new word, contraction and regular saddle arguments above are analytical; no large-level numerical profile is used as their proof.

title: A quantitative gradient gap for positive logarithmic gluing
text:
# A quantitative gradient gap for positive logarithmic gluing Research proof, 23 November 2026. A realized positive marked gluing system has a full-gradient bound on its entire positive logarithmic chart. The bound uses curvature only near its solution. It excludes escape of the selected logarithmic coordinates to infinity in finite normalized descent time. Finite flat-angle or cut-boundary exits remain possible and are retained. This is a classical no-infinite-coordinate-escape statement. It does not identify an original quantum period with this chart or establish the no-ends hypothesis for its relative cycle. ## 1. Positive coordinates and the marked constraint Let \(t\geq1\), and put \[ \mathcal S=\{x\in\mathbb C:0<\Im x<\pi\},\qquad z=e^x,\qquad v(x)=-\operatorname{Log}(1-e^x). 	ag{1} \] The logarithm is principal. Apply \(v\) coordinatewise on \(\mathcal S^t\). On this convex product, \[ \Im v'(x)= rac{\Im(e^x)}{|1-e^x|^2}>0. 	ag{2} \] Let \(A,B\) be real \(t\)-by-\(t\) matrices with \[ \operatorname{rank}(A\ B)=t,\qquad AB^{\mathsf T}=BA^{\mathsf T}, \qquad F_R(x)=Ax+Bv(x). 	ag{3} \] Keep one specified affine logarithmic target \(c\). In an actual ideal triangulation these are the independent edge rows and one marked primitive peripheral row per cusp of [G]. Every edge winding, quad constant and peripheral logarithmic lift belongs to \(c\). We assume a positive solution is supplied, not merely that the exponentiated equations have a solution. ## 2. Positive quad selection removes the invertible-block restriction Here is the transversal argument of [Q] in convention (1). Since \[ (A+iB)(A+iB)^*=AA^{\mathsf T}+BB^{\mathsf T}>0, 	ag{4} \] the column expansion of \(\det(A+iB)\) has a nonzero term choosing one of \(A_j,B_j\) in each column. For every selected \(A_j\), make the positive cyclic quad change \[ z'_j= rac1{1-z_j},\qquad (x'_j,v'_j)=(v_j,i\pi-x_j-v_j). 	ag{5} \] Both new coordinates are the principal positive logs of their stated quad types. The functions \(1/(1-z)\) and \(z/(1-z)\) map the upper half-plane to itself, so \(0<\Im(x+v)<\pi\). Exponentiating and checking these arguments proves (5) on the entire positive domain. For the rotated columns, substitution gives \[ A'_j=B_j-A_j,\qquad B'_j=-A_j,\qquad c'=c-i\pi\sum_{j\ \mathrm{rotated}}A_j . 	ag{6} \] Other columns are unchanged. The new \(B'\) is the chosen nonzero transversal up to column signs. The linear part of (5) is real symplectic, so the rank and isotropy conditions (3) persist. The marked target is transformed by (6), not reset modulo \(2\pi i\). This choice depends only on the rows, not on a later solution or on the quantum level. Drop primes henceforth. Now \(B\) is invertible and \[ P=B^{-1}A=P^{\mathsf T}\in M_t(\mathbb R),\qquad u=B^{-1}c,\qquad S(x)=\sum_{j=1}^t\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{x_j}) +	frac12x^{\mathsf T}Px-u^{\mathsf T}x, \quad 
abla S=B^{-1}(F_R(x)-c). 	ag{7} \] The dilogarithm is its principal upper-half-plane branch, whose derivative in \(x\) is \(v(x)\). Let \(x_*\in\mathcal S^t\) denote the supplied solution in these selected coordinates. The sign and normalization in (7) agree with the positive classical potential [Q, (4)]. Explicitly its alternative coordinate is \(y=\operatorname{Log}(1-1/z)=i\pi-x-v\). Thus \(A_y=A-B\), \(B_y=-B\), \(c_y=c-i\pi B\mathbf1\), and \(B_y^{-1}A_y=I-P\), \(B_y^{-1}c_y=-u+i\pi\mathbf1\). Substitution in that displayed potential gives exactly (7). No claim identifying its additive constant with an unsupplied quantum-source transformation is needed below. ## 3. Curvature near the solution controls the full chart Choose \(r>0\) so that the closed Euclidean ball \(\overline{B(x_*,r)}\) is contained in \(\mathcal S^t\), and put \[ m=\min_{\substack{y\in\overline{B(x_*,r)}\1\leq j\leq t}} \Im v'(y_j)>0. 	ag{8} \] For example take \(r\) smaller than half the distance of every \(\Im x_{*,j}\) from \(0,\pi\). The numerator in (2) then has a positive lower bound and its denominator a finite upper bound on this ball. All norms below are Euclidean. **Theorem.** For every \(x\in\mathcal S^t\), \[  oxed{\quad \|
abla S(x)\|\geq m\min(\|x-x_*\|,r). \quad} 	ag{9} \] In particular the full gradient is bounded away from zero outside the ball, including at every escaping sequence in this chart. **Proof.** Set \(d=x-x_*\). The joining segment remains positive. As in the secant comparison of [G], \[ \Im igl(d^*
abla S(x) igr) =\sum_j|d_j|^2\int_0^1\Im v'(x_{*,j}+sd_j)\,ds. 	ag{10} \] Here \(
abla S(x_*)=0\), and the contribution \(d^*Pd\) is real. Every integrand is positive. On the first \(\min(1,r/\|d\|)\) portion of the segment each is at least \(m\). Consequently, for \(d
e0\), \[ \Im igl(d^*
abla S(x) igr) \geq m\|d\|\min(\|d\|,r). 	ag{11} \] Cauchy--Schwarz and division by \(\|d\|\) prove (9). At \(d=0\) the assertion is immediate. \(\square\) This also gives \(\|F_R(x)-c\|\geq mr/\|B^{-1}\|\) outside the ball. Thus approximate full fixed-log gluing cannot escape within the positive chart. Neither a representation-volume theorem nor control of a weighted residual at infinity is required for this restricted conclusion. The constants can be uniform in families. Suppose real symmetric \(P_a\) and targets \(u_a\) have supplied critical points \(x_{*,a}\) in a compact subset of \(\mathcal S^t\). A common positive radius \(r\) makes the union of the closed balls have compact closure in \(\mathcal S^t\), and (2) supplies a common \(m>0\) there. The proof gives (9) for every member, without a bound on its filling coefficients in \(P_a\). For varying constraint rows, use a specified common invertible quad chart wherever that family has one. No unrecorded transition between different selected charts is included in the assertion. ## 4. Growing phase and finite descent time For the growing classical exponential and its height, use \[ e^{NS(x)/(2\pi i)},\qquad h(x)=\Re rac{S(x)}{2\pi i}= rac{\Im S(x)}{2\pi}, \qquad \|
abla_{\mathbb R}h\|= rac{\|
abla S\|}{2\pi}. 	ag{12} \] At fixed parameters, consider the normalized lowering flow away from the critical point, \[  rac{dx}{ds}=- rac{
abla_{\mathbb R}h}{ \|
abla_{\mathbb R}h\|^2}, \qquad  rac{dh}{ds}=-1. 	ag{13} \] Outside \(B(x_*,r)\) its speed is at most \(2\pi/(mr)\). For any trajectory remaining in the positive chart, its distance from the center therefore satisfies \[ \|x(s)-x_*\| \leq\max(r,\|x(0)-x_*\|)+ rac{2\pi s}{mr}. 	ag{14} \] Indeed every excursion outside the ball starts either at the initial point or on its radius-\(r\) sphere; its total outside time is at most \(s\). Inside the ball the distance is already at most \(r\). Thus no selected logarithmic coordinate can diverge in finite normalized descent time, equivalently during a finite height drop. These bounds are uniform for the families just described. They do not construct a continuation of an arbitrary target path. ## 5. Boundary and source scope The flow may reach a finite flat-angle or logarithmic cut boundary, or approach the critical point, where the normalized field is singular. No such exit is removed. A positive quad rotation can send an old \(z	o0\) end to \(z'	o1\); hence boundedness of the selected logs is not a quad-invariant exclusion of ideal degenerations. All finite \(0,1,\infty\) interpretations and the corresponding boundary currents remain to be treated in the actual coordinates and with their marks. The Legendre contour of [L] already has a calibrated volume maximum, controlled radial homotopies and explicit alias bulk translations. The estimate here concerns instead the full principal gradient over the entire positive product, using only a local curvature constant. It settles the infinite-coordinate part of a normalized-flow check while that flow stays in this specified positive chart. It proves neither a boundary-action gap nor absence of relative-cycle handles from cuts, finite boundaries or other logarithmic charts. In particular no original Kashaev source, cap, normal direction or relative current has been replaced. A source-preserving passage to this positive polarization and control of its actual boundary terms remain necessary. There is no selected-cycle, scalar lower-bound or finite-exception conclusion. ## Complete sources and coverage - [G] [Global positive marked log gluing](research_global_positive_log_gluing.md), 226 lines, SHA-256 `8b712324fb10211e2b5f253c934bac1f0270a719645b7cad6493a85437c2286f`: the actual marked incidence interpretation and secant comparison. The quantitative estimate is proved above. - [Q] [Positive quad selection and classical torus](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/positive_quad_chart_and_actual_torus_signature.md), 213 lines, SHA-256 `eee291f797da0d19c327612ab6fd46a6fa13fd5b270880c0c05c138242e3d93f`: quad-transversal coverage and the exact positive classical potential. Its linear selection argument is supplied above in convention (1). [L] [Global Legendre contour](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/general_legendre_rivin_contour.md), 421 lines, SHA-256 `b51be11036b05fbccd586c2d0a4505559631870357cf128dd256dcc87e26970b`, is complete coverage, not an additional premise of (9)--(14). No claim of historical novelty is made for positive symplectic gluing or monotonicity. Only written mathematics and source-text operations are used; no frozen file is changed.

title: A positive Mellin realization of the original Conway gluing
text:
# A positive Mellin realization of the original Conway gluing Private written proof, 23 November 2026. The original full Frobenius pairing is a Mellin residue of a positive real measure. This identity is valid for arbitrary ordinary polynomial products, so it retains the actual Conway multiplication, turns and normal channels. A normalized positive integral also approximates the squared original closing with an explicit error uniform in the level. Its regularization parameter can be chosen from local source budgets, without evaluating or dividing by the closed invariant. These are finite-source identities and estimates. No geometric growth estimate for the positive integral, or finite-exception theorem, follows. ## 1. Original source and the pure positive measure Fix \(N\ge2\), and put \(D=N-1\), \(\eta=(-1)^D\). Use the actual pair algebra, canonical representative and original cylindrical row: \[ P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2,\qquad H_N=\mathbb C[z]/(P_N),\qquad \phi_N(h)=\eta N^2[z^D]\operatorname{rem}_{P_N}h . 	ag{1} \] Here \(T_N\) is the ordinary Chebyshev polynomial. The monic \(P_N\) has roots \(c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N)\), counted with multiplicity. The original double roots and odd-level simple root are retained. On \(x>2\), write \[ w=w(x)= rac{x+\sqrt{x^2-4}}2>1,\qquad x=w+w^{-1}. \] Then \(P_N(x)=w^N+2+w^{-N}>0\). Define the pure positive measure \[ d
u_N(x)= rac{dx}{P_N(x)},\qquad x>2. 	ag{2} \] This is not the Ward current: its density has no hyperbolic-tangent factor. Its source identification will instead be the exact residue in the next section. Every actual finite Conway packet has a canonical polynomial of degree at most \(D\). All prescribed external scalar factors may be included in that packet. Thus write its original scalar closing as \(K_N=\phi_N(f_N)\), without changing its normalization. For the other original Conway row \(\lambda_0(f)=f(c_0)\), use the actual turn \(T e_i=e_{D-i}\). The exact identity \(\phi_N(Tf)=\lambda_0(f)\) puts it in the same form. This retains the full original packet and its prescribed closing. ## 2. Exact regularized gluing at every polynomial degree For any ordinary polynomial \(h\), initially define \[ I_N(s;h)=\int_2^\infty x^{-s} rac{h(x)}{P_N(x)}\,dx, \qquad \Re s>\deg h-N+1. 	ag{3} \] The zero polynomial causes no exception. The logarithm of the positive real \(x\) fixes \(x^{-s}\). **Theorem 1.** This integral continues meromorphically to \(\Re s>-1\), and \[  oxed{\qquad \phi_N(h)=\eta N^2\operatorname*{Res}_{s=0}I_N(s;h). \qquad} 	ag{4} \] The residue in (4) depends only on the class of \(h\) in \(H_N\), with no bound on its ordinary degree. In particular \(\phi_N(fg)\) is the original full bilinear gluing. **Proof.** Divide \(h=P_Nq+r\), where \(\deg r<N\), and let \(a=[x^D]r\). Write \(q=\sum_k q_kx^k\). Direct integration gives the continuation \[ I_N(s;h)= \sum_k q_k rac{2^{k+1-s}}{s-k-1} +a rac{2^{-s}}s +\int_2^\infty x^{-s} \left\{ rac{r(x)}{P_N(x)}- rac a xight\}dx. 	ag{5} \] The last integrand is \(O_{N,h}(x^{-2-\Re s})\) at infinity and has no singularity at \(2\), since \(P_N(2)=4\). It is holomorphic for \(\Re s>-1\), locally uniformly with the needed logarithmic derivatives in \(s\). None of the polynomial terms has a pole at zero. The residue is therefore \(a\), proving (4). In particular every ordinary multiple of \(P_N\) has zero residue. \(\square\) Equation (4) retains the full first normals, rather than only the distinct-root values. For example, its original physical form is \[ \phi_N(h)=\eta\sum_{c\ {m double}} \{(4-c^2)h'(c)-ch(c)\} +\mathbf1_{N\ {m odd}}h(-2). 	ag{6} \] This is the same coefficient functional (1), as established by the actual source calculus. There is no new normal at the odd simple node. Consequently every finite original tensor contraction may replace each Frobenius contraction by (4), leaving its polynomial kernels and crossing coupons unchanged. With one variable per contracted algebra copy, the resulting iterated Mellin residues reproduce the original contraction. To justify the statement directly, expand its finite multivariate polynomial numerator into monomials. In a sufficiently far right half-plane in every \(s\)-variable all integrals converge absolutely. Formula (5), applied coefficientwise, continues them; their iterated residues commute and extract precisely the original quotient coefficients. Arbitrary free spectators remain coefficients. Thus unreduced trivalent products are allowed in this exact identity. This is a bilinear regularized gluing, not a positive inner product at the residue. Positivity of (2) does not make (6) positive. ## 3. A positive approximation to the squared original closing For this section \(f\) is its **canonical** polynomial, \(\deg f\le D\). Set \[ M=\max_{-2\le x\le2}|f(x)|,\qquad K=\phi_N(f), \qquad C_N=3+	frac12\log N. \] For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), define \[ \mathcal A_{N,\varepsilon}(f)= N^4\varepsilon\int_2^\infty (x/2)^{-\varepsilon}x^{-(N-1)}|f(x)|^2\,d
u_N(x). 	ag{7} \] This converges and is nonnegative; it is positive if \(f
e0\). **Theorem 2.** Uniformly for every \(N\ge2\), every canonical \(f\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[  oxed{\quad 0\le\mathcal A_{N,\varepsilon}(f)\le N^4M^2,\qquad \left|\mathcal A_{N,\varepsilon}(f)-|K|^2ight| \le\varepsilon N^4M^2C_N. \quad} 	ag{8} \] No nonzero-source or relative-precision hypothesis is imposed. **Proof.** If \(f=0\), all assertions hold. Otherwise write \(a_D=[z^D]f\) and \(H(\zeta)=\zeta^D f(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})\). This is a polynomial, including when \(\deg f<D\). On the unit circle its modulus is at most \(M\); hence the maximum principle gives \(|H|\le M\) on the closed disk and \(H(0)=a_D\). Each Taylor coefficient has modulus at most \(M\). Therefore, for \(x\ge3\), \[ |H(1/w)-a_D|\le rac{M}{w-1}\le rac{2M}{x}. 	ag{9} \] The last inequality follows directly from the displayed formula for \(w(x)\). Together with \(|H|,|a_D|\le M\), this proves \[ \int_2^\infty \left||H(1/w)|^2-|a_D|^2ight| rac{dx}{x} \le M^2\left\{\log(3/2)+ rac43ight\}<2M^2. 	ag{10} \] Since \(f(x)=w^DH(1/w)\), (7) is exactly \[ \mathcal A_{N,\varepsilon}(f)=N^4\varepsilon \int_2^\infty (x/2)^{-\varepsilon} R_N(x)|H(1/w)|^2 rac{dx}{x}, \] \[ R_N(x)= rac{(1+w^{-2})^{-(N-2)}}{(1+w^{-N})^2}. 	ag{11} \] We have \(0<R_N\le1\). Also \(w^{-N}\le w^{-2}\) and \[ 1-R_N\le (N-2)w^{-2}+2w^{-N} \le Nw^{-2}\le rac{4N}{x^2}. \] Splitting at \(2\sqrt N\) gives \[ \int_2^\infty(1-R_N(x)) rac{dx}{x} \le	frac12\log N+	frac12. 	ag{12} \] The weight in (11) obeys \[ \varepsilon\int_2^\infty(x/2)^{-\varepsilon} rac{dx}{x}=1. 	ag{13} \] Thus (11) immediately gives the upper bound in (8). Subtract \(N^4|a_D|^2=|K|^2\) using (13). In the resulting integral use (10), (12), and \((x/2)^{-\varepsilon}\le1\). Its absolute value is at most \[ \varepsilon N^4M^2 \{2+	frac12\log N+	frac12\} \le\varepsilon N^4M^2C_N. \] This proves (8). The positive density and a nonzero polynomial give strict positivity when \(f
e0\). \(\square\) The rightmost possible pole gives an equivalent exact normalization: \[ |\phi_N(f)|^2=N^4\operatorname*{Res}_{s=N-1} \int_2^\infty x^{-s}|f(x)|^2\,d
u_N(x). 	ag{14} \] Its residue is \(|a_D|^2\); it is zero if \(\deg f<D\). For continuation the numerator means the ordinary polynomial \(f(z)\overline{f( ar z)}\), restricted to real \(x\). The estimate (8), rather than just this coefficient identity, controls the positive integral at a specified finite regularization parameter. ## 4. Source-only budgets and the unchanged volume target Put \(M_N=\max_{[-2,2]}|f_N|\). Any supplied \(B_N\ge\max(1,M_N)\) gives the explicit choice \[ \varepsilon_N= rac1{N^6B_N^2C_N},\qquad \left|\mathcal A_{N,\varepsilon_N}(f_N)-|K_N|^2ight| \le N^{-2}. 	ag{15} \] Such a budget need not use the closed coefficient. In the original Newton basis \[ e_i(z)=S_i^{-2}\prod_{j<i}(c_j-z),\qquad S_i=\prod_{r=1}^i2\sin(\pi r/N),\quad S_0=1, \] we have \(|e_i(x)|\le4^i/S_i^2\) on \([-2,2]\). If a known local tensor budget gives \(L_N\ge\|f_N\|_{m Newton}\), take \[ B_N=\max\left(1,L_N\sum_{i=0}^{D} rac{4^i}{S_i^2}ight). 	ag{16} \] For completeness, products of recorded leaf norms and gate Hilbert--Schmidt norm bounds supply \(L_N\) by induction: the norm of each contracted output is at most the gate norm times the product of its input norms. The actual turn is unitary in the Newton metric. Known external scalar factors are included in this budget. No closed invariant is required as an input, and no efficient algorithm is claimed. For every fixed positive number \(V\), (15) implies the equivalence \[ \lim_{N	o\infty} rac{2\pi}{N}\log|K_N|=V \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lim_{N	o\infty} rac\pi N \log\mathcal A_{N,\varepsilon_N}(f_N)=V. 	ag{17} \] Use \(\log0=-\infty\). If either limit is \(V>0\), its positive quantity grows exponentially and dominates the absolute error \(N^{-2}\). The ratio of the two quantities in (15) then tends to one, proving the other limit. Positivity of \(V\) is essential here. The finite-\(\varepsilon\) expression is a controlled approximation to the original squared source, not a substituted knot invariant. The canonical requirement in Theorem 2 is essential; Theorem 1 has no such degree restriction. Full original channels and arbitrary fixed short components remain allowed. A geometric estimate of the positive integral in (17), with its actual packet and chosen parameter, is still unproved. No Casson--Rivin growth or finite-exception case is asserted. ## Complete source and coverage readbacks All complete matching texts below were read. The residue realization, uniform estimate and budget argument above use only written proofs. | Role | Complete text | Lines | SHA-256 | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | | Input | [Original dualizing residue](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_actual_source_dualizing_residue.md) | 408 | 806f8e4530736632830a15cff19f4c0f72e659fa6280d48005c4184a6ffc9afb | | Input | [Full Conway boundary algebra](research_conway_full_boundary_quotient_gram.md) | 463 | debe56dbad8151b90d44d0fccbf0dcf33dafb780370e01c8acdadbd2939dc077 | | Coverage | [Positive Ward measure](research_positive_ward_measure_and_coherent_cauchy_tail.md) | 492 | 18d2aa9142806d0acd744abbbb412843acd35bf18015b8c6fc73b23428a75096 | | Coverage | [Cyclotomic Mellin residue](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/cyclotomic_mellin_residue.md) | 215 | 918cbf22fcfd6c5b156e133dd6f6f8c4dca75e6c0d7b1d70063a6ee5c172aff3 | | Coverage | [Cauchy metric checkpoint](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/cauchy_metric_route_checkpoint.md) | 425 | 063766ead607758a71c40eebf07c4ae964a487bdbda65c29da52b6512bedb70a | The Ward measure has its additional hyperbolic-tangent factor and an existing full indefinite cut pairing. The cyclotomic Mellin residue uses the ordinary-color generating variable. Neither is identified with (2)--(5). Cheap Cauchy boundaries alone already have extensive coverage; they do not supply the estimate (8) or geometric growth here. No mathematical program, numerical test, build, git operation or edit to a previous final or public manuscript was performed.

title: Positive path solutions throughout the fractional-charge cube
text:
# Positive path solutions throughout the fractional-charge cube Research note, 3 November 2026. Fix a finite path and its original integer crossing powers, all at least three. The unit-charge positive solution extends uniquely when each filling charge is allowed to vary independently between zero and one. A zero charge makes that vertex complete and separates the positive-charge components. No lower bound on a nonzero charge is required in the statement. The proof has two inputs already established in the repository. The [integer corridor theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md), Theorem 15 and its mirror, supplies the unit-charge solutions. The [fractional-charge height bound](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_path_height_bound.md#5-the-same-bound-during-a-positive-fractional-charge-deformation) bounds every positive solution which already exists. That bound alone does not give existence. Here we prove the missing closedness argument: no angle endpoint, zero height, open square side, or square corner can be reached while all charges stay positive. The integer-power hypothesis is retained. The proof does not interpolate the crossing powers through nonintegers, and it does not assert a quantum asymptotic. ## 1. The path, equations and conclusion Let the selected vertices form a nonempty finite path, with original degrees at most two. At least one end is attached to a complete outside vertex. Retain every original edge, including its prescribed carrier and primitive marking. At a selected vertex fix an integer \(n_v\ge3\), and let its charge be \(\lambda_v\in[0,1]\). At an outside vertex set \(t=0\). The sought angles and their original edge returns are \[ t_v=a_v-iH_v,\qquad r_{v,e}=k_{v,e}+ig_{v,e} =\operatorname{arsinh}\! \left(	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)ight) \quad(e=\{v,w\}). 	ag{1} \] The branch is the original positive branch, with \(-\pi/2<\Im r<\pi/2\) in its interior. The full logarithmic equations, rather than just their exponentials, are \[ \sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}= rac{in_v}{2}t_v-\pi i\lambda_v. 	ag{2} \] Their real and imaginary parts are \[ \sum_{e
i v}k_{v,e}= rac{n_vH_v}{2},\qquad \sum_{e
i v}g_{v,e}- rac{n_v a_v}{2}=-\pi\lambda_v. 	ag{3} \] For clarity, positivity can be stated in either of the equivalent coordinate systems proved in [the positive-edge theorem](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md) and [the convex variation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_filling_convex_variation.md). In tangent coordinates \(z_v=	an(t_v/2)\), it is \[ \Re\sqrt{1+z_v^2+z_w^2}> \sqrt{(\Re z_v)^2+(\Re z_w)^2}. 	ag{4} \] In real angle coordinates, the two squares on an oriented edge have coordinates \[  egin{split} A_P=a_v/4-g_{w,e}/2,&\qquad A_Q=a_v/4+g_{w,e}/2,\ y_P=g_{v,e}/2+a_w/4,&\qquad y_Q=g_{v,e}/2-a_w/4. \end{split} 	ag{5} \] They lie in the open square \((-\pi/4,\pi/4)^2\). The equivalent edge inequalities are \[ |a_v|+2|g_{w,e}|<\pi,\qquad |a_w|+2|g_{v,e}|<\pi. 	ag{6} \] The square energy \(E\), with \(E(0,0)=0\), has derivatives \[ E_A= rac12\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(2A)\cos(2y)), \qquad E_y= rac12\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(2y)\cos(2A)). 	ag{7} \] The total energy is \(\mathcal E=4\sum_e(E_{P,e}+E_{Q,e})\). Outside incidences are retained as variables; their stationarity equations impose complete outside angles. **Theorem 1.** For every charge vector \(\lambda\in(0,1]^{V}\), equations (1)--(2) have a unique positive solution in the original variational domain. It satisfies \[ 0<a_v<\pi,\qquad 0<H_v<23/20 \quad(v\in V). 	ag{8} \] It is the unique closed constrained minimum of \(\mathcal E\). The minimum and its real angle coordinates depend continuously on the entire cube \([0,1]^V\), and real analytically wherever all charges are positive. At a zero charge the unique solution has \(t_v=0\) and \(r_{v,e}=0\) at every incidence of that vertex. The remaining positive-charge components have the solutions just described, with these zero-charge vertices treated as complete boundaries. Every original edge remains present. This theorem concerns the positive logarithmic equations and their convex minima. At unit charges, or at a Boolean face where every nonzero charge is one, the existing [pointwise marked-completion theorem](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md) applies. No additional topological completion statement for fractional charges is needed or claimed here. ## 2. Strict feasibility and local continuation For every Boolean vector \(\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{V}\), make its zero-charge vertices complete. Each remaining selected component is a path with a complete outside end. Solve it by the unit-charge corridor theorem and its mirror. Joining these solutions retains every original edge. At a zero-charge vertex, \(\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(0)\cos(t_w/2))=0\), so both equations in (3) hold there. A complete edge has two interior squares. Thus these finitely many assignments \(X^\epsilon\) are strictly feasible in the common real angle domain. Their convex combination with weights \[ p_\epsilon(\lambda)= \prod_v\lambda_v^{\epsilon_v}(1-\lambda_v)^{1-\epsilon_v} 	ag{9} \] is strictly feasible at the charge \(\lambda\). Indeed the constraints in (3) are affine in the real coordinates and in \(\lambda\), and the marginal mean of \(\epsilon_v\) is \(\lambda_v\). The edge inequalities define a convex domain. Since the finite list \(X^\epsilon\) lies in its interior, all these convex combinations stay a fixed positive distance from every square side. The closed feasible sets are compact and nonempty, so a constrained minimum exists at every charge. At an interior critical point this minimum is unique and locally real analytic in \(\lambda\). One can see the required nondegeneracy directly from (7). With \(\Delta=1-\sin^2(2A)\sin^2(2y)>0\), the square Hessian is \[ 
abla^2E=  rac1{\sqrt\Delta}  egin{pmatrix} \cos(2y)/\cos(2A)&-\sin(2A)\sin(2y)\ -\sin(2A)\sin(2y)&\cos(2A)/\cos(2y) \end{pmatrix}. 	ag{10} \] It has determinant one and positive diagonal entries. The map from vertex/incidence coordinates to all square coordinates is injective. Therefore the total Hessian is positive definite on the real variable space, and in particular on the tangent space of the constraints. Those constraints have independent rows: the variable \(a_v\) has coefficient \(-n_v/2\) in its own row and occurs in no other constraint. The bordered critical-point system is consequently invertible. The implicit function theorem gives local analytic continuation. The unit-charge solution has the signs in (8). They persist locally. To prove existence for an arbitrary positive target charge it remains to show that this positive solution cannot reach a boundary along the segment joining the unit vector to that target. ## 3. Compact limits have bounded returns and square gradients Consider a convergent sequence of charge vectors whose entries lie in a fixed interval \([\lambda_0,1]\), \(\lambda_0>0\), and positive solutions with \(0<a_v<\pi\), \(H_v>0\). The fractional-charge height theorem gives \(H_v<23/20\). After passage to a subsequence, all \(a_v,H_v\) converge in \([0,\pi]	imes[0,23/20]\). For every selected incidence the argument of the inverse hyperbolic sine in (1) has positive real part. Explicitly, write \[ 	an(t_v/2)=  rac{\sin a_v-i\sinh H_v}{\cos a_v+\cosh H_v}. 	ag{11} \] Both real summands in the product with \(\cos(t_w/2)=\cos(a_w/2)\cosh(H_w/2) +i\sin(a_w/2)\sinh(H_w/2)\) are nonnegative, and the first is strictly positive. Consequently \(k_{v,e}>0\). Equation (3) gives \[ 0<k_{v,e}\le n_vH_v/2\le23n_v/40. 	ag{12} \] Also \(|g_{v,e}|<\pi/2\). The returns therefore remain bounded. The four square gradients on an edge are linear combinations of its two returns and two imaginary angles, by equations (3) and (6) of the corridor note. Hence all square gradients remain bounded as well. A square cannot converge to an open side: in (7), the derivative normal to that side diverges if the other coordinate stays in the open interval. At a square corner, a convergent gradient is a finite subgradient of the closed convex energy. To check this without a compactness theorem for minimizers, take the limit in \[ E(Y)\ge E(X_j)+
abla E(X_j)\cdot(Y-X_j) 	ag{13} \] for any fixed point \(Y\) of the closed square. Thus a corner limit satisfies precisely the finite corner subgradient conditions already used in the corridor theorem. The constraints and the linear stationarity equations also pass to the limit. ## 4. Neither an angle endpoint nor a zero height can occur The arguments in this section concern a possible limit from Section 3. The complete outside vertices remain fixed. First, the pair \((a_v,H_v)=(\pi,0)\) is impossible. If it occurred, \(|	an(t_v/2)|\) would tend to infinity. The bounded return (12) implies that \(	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)=\sinh r_{v,e}\) stays bounded on each incident edge. Therefore \(\cos(t_w/2)\) tends to zero. In the closed parameter rectangle this means \((a_w,H_w)=(\pi,0)\). This conclusion propagates along the finite selected path to a complete outside vertex, where \(\cos(0)=1\), a contradiction. The pair \((a_v,H_v)=(0,0)\) is also impossible. Here \(	an(t_v/2)\) tends to zero and every neighboring cosine is bounded. All its returns tend to zero. Equation (3) would then give \(\lambda_v=0\), contrary to \(\lambda_v\ge\lambda_0\). Suppose next that \(a_v=0\) and \(H_v>0\). Put \(B=23/40\). On an incident edge the argument in (1) is \(z=x-iy\), where \[ 0\le x\le rac{H_v}{2}\sinh B,\qquad 0\le y\le\sinh B. 	ag{14} \] For \(y<1\), integration of the derivative of \(\operatorname{arsinh}\) along the horizontal segment from \(-iy\) to \(x-iy\) gives \[ 0\le\Re\operatorname{arsinh}(x-iy) \le rac{x}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}. 	ag{15} \] Indeed \(\Re(1+(s-iy)^2)=1+s^2-y^2\ge1-y^2\), so the derivative's modulus is at most \(1/\sqrt{1-y^2}\). The rational Taylor estimate \(\cosh(23/20)<7/4\), written in [the energy comparison](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_edge_cut_energy_comparison.md), §7, gives \(\sinh^2B<3/8\). Since the degree is at most two, (14)--(15) imply \[ \sum_{e
i v}k_{v,e} \le H_v rac{\sinh B}{\sqrt{1-\sinh^2B}} <H_v\sqrt{3/5}< rac32H_v. 	ag{16} \] This contradicts (3), because \(n_v\ge3\). Now suppose \(H_v=0\) with \(0<a_v<\pi\). Every incidence has \(k_{v,e}=0\), by (3) and nonnegativity of the limiting real returns. If a neighbor had \(a_w<\pi\), the argument \(	an(a_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)\) would have positive real part, so \(k_{v,e}>0\). Thus every neighbor would have \(a_w=\pi\). The case \((\pi,0)\) has already been excluded, so \(H_w>0\). Then \(\cos(t_w/2)=i\sinh(H_w/2)\), and the selected return has strictly positive imaginary part. But the closed edge inequality \(a_w+2|g_{v,e}|\le\pi\) forces \(g_{v,e}=0\). This is a contradiction. It remains to exclude \(a_v=\pi,\ H_v>0\). If a selected neighbor had \(0<a_w<\pi\), then \(\cos(t_v/2)=i\sinh(H_v/2)\) and \(\Re	an(t_w/2)>0\). The argument defining \(r_{w,e}\) would have positive imaginary part, hence \(g_{w,e}>0\). The closed edge inequality at \(v\) instead forces \(g_{w,e}=0\). Every selected neighbor must therefore also have angle \(\pi\); angle zero has already been excluded. On an edge to such a selected neighbor, \(	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2)\) is positive real, so \(g_{v,e}=0\). On an edge to a complete outside vertex its limiting argument is \(-i\coth(H_v/2)\), whose right-half-plane inverse-sine limit has imaginary part \(-\pi/2\). Thus every incidence at \(v\) has \(g_{v,e}\le0\). On the other hand, (3) requires \[ \sum_{e
i v}g_{v,e} =n_v\pi/2-\pi\lambda_v\ge\pi/2>0, 	ag{17} \] again a contradiction. All selected limit angles consequently satisfy \(0<a_v<\pi\) and \(H_v>0\). Their return arguments have positive real part, so the original branches remain regular. ## 5. Every unit-charge corner test remains necessary Only square corners could still prevent an interior limit. We give the charge comparison explicitly, since feasibility alone would not exclude them. Mirror the positive-power configuration to the negative-power convention of the corridor note. This sends \(t\) to \(-\overline t\) and \(r\) to \(-\overline r\), leaving the imaginary returns \(g\) and positive angle magnitudes unchanged. Orient a corner from its negative-incidence endpoint \(v\) to its positive-incidence endpoint \(w\), and put \(	heta=a_v,\ \phi=a_w\), \(m=n_v,\ p=n_w\). The corner incidences are \[ g_{v,e}=-(\pi-\phi)/2,\qquad g_{w,e}=+(\pi-	heta)/2. 	ag{18} \] If the endpoint has another incidence, its value is \[  egin{split} g_{v,\mathrm{other}} &= rac{m	heta-\pi-\phi}{2}+\pi(1-\lambda_v),\ g_{w,\mathrm{other}} &= rac{p\phi-3\pi+	heta}{2}+\pi(1-\lambda_w). \end{split} 	ag{19} \] At a terminal the corresponding expression is zero. Thus each other incidence is at least its value in the unit-charge formula with the same corner angles. The real stationarity equations, and all the directed-incidence inequalities involving the heights, are unchanged. Here is the complete list of necessary reductions used in the unit proof. Equation references in the first column refer to the [corridor note](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md). | Step of the unit proof | Conditions still necessary at the fractional-charge limit | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | Proposition 3 and Corollary 4 | The two patterns (19) of that note; \(0<	heta,\phi<\pi\); the negative endpoint has \(	heta>\pi/2\). | These use the square corner subgradient, strict negative mirrored heights and the unchanged companion square. | | Theorem 6, equations (48)--(55) | A negative endpoint of magnitude \(m\ge4\) is impossible. | Its other incidence is at least \((m	heta-\pi-\phi)/2>0\). The old upper bound \(m	heta\le\pi+\phi+2g_{v,\mathrm{other}}\), followed by the unchanged outgoing estimate, gives the same contradiction \(m	heta<4	heta\). | | Proposition 8, equations (70)--(73) | For the remaining negative magnitude three, \(\phi>\pi/2\), and the positive magnitude is \(p\le6\). | When \(\phi\le\pi/2\), (19) gives the same lower bound \(g_{v,\mathrm{other}}\ge3(	heta-\pi/2)/2\). At the positive endpoint \(p\phi\le3\pi-	heta+2g_{w,\mathrm{other}}<4\pi-	heta\). Terminal bounds only become stronger. | | Proposition 9, equations (74)--(78) | \(	heta>2\pi/3\), and the negative endpoint has a strictly positive other incidence. | The real-period estimate \(6X>C_6\) does not contain a charge. Formula (19) gives the same positive lower bound afterward; a terminal or complete outside incidence is excluded as before. | | Theorem 13, equations (87)--(96) | Put \(x=\pi-	heta,\ y=\pi-\phi\). Then \(0<x<\pi/3\), \(0<y<4x/3\), \(p y>(p-3)\pi-x\), and \(pX-H_c\ge C_p\). Only \(p=4,5\) remain. | The negative outgoing bound is still \(R<	an((3x-y)/2)\), because the actual other incidence is larger. The positive angle bound is weaker than the fractional equation, and the real-period condition is identical. The same algebra excludes \(p=3,6\). | For the last step define, exactly as in the corner certificate, \[  egin{split} X&=	frac12\operatorname{arsinh}(\cot x\sin y),& H_c&=	frac12\operatorname{arsinh}(\cot y\sin x),\ R&= rac{\sqrt{1-\cos^2x\cos^2y}}{\cos x(1+\cos y)},& \Lambda&=x+py-(p-3)\pi,\ C_p&=	frac12\{p\operatorname{arsinh}(1/p) +\operatorname{arsinh}p\}. \end{split} 	ag{20} \] The letter \(H_c\) here is the companion-square quantity, not a vertex height. The surviving conditions are exactly \[  egin{gathered} y<4x/3,\qquad \Lambda>0,\qquad pX-H_c\ge C_p,\ R<	an((3x-y)/2),\ \Lambda<\pi\ \Longrightarrow\ 2H_c/p<\sin y\,	an(\Lambda/2). \end{gathered} 	ag{21} \] Only the last implication needs a further charge check. Equation (19) at the positive endpoint reads \[ g_{w,\mathrm{other}} =(\pi-\Lambda)/2+\pi(1-\lambda_w). 	ag{22} \] If \(\Lambda<\pi\), this incidence is positive. The other neighbor's angle is at most \(\pi-2g_{w,\mathrm{other}} =\Lambda-2\pi(1-\lambda_w)\le\Lambda\). The unchanged outgoing and real-period inequalities therefore imply the last line of (21). If the endpoint is terminal, equation (22) instead gives \(\Lambda=\pi+2\pi(1-\lambda_w)\ge\pi\); that conditional test is correctly not invoked. The angle bounds place \((x/\pi,y/\pi)\) in the same two closed rectangles: \[  egin{array}{c|cc} p&x/\pi&y/\pi\ \hline 4&[3/19,1/3]&[1/6,4/9]\ 5&[6/23,1/3]&[1/3,4/9]. \end{array} 	ag{23} \] The existing [rational corner verifier](../experiments/verify_negative_three_corner_exclusion.py) and its [saved certificate](../repro/results/research-negative-three-corner-exclusion.json) exclude (21) on all of these rectangles. Its 94 terminal rectangles for \(p=4\) and 10 for \(p=5\) are unchanged: the fractional equations have only strengthened the necessary conditions. Therefore the limiting configuration has no corner. ## 6. Completing the continuation and adding zero charges Fix a target vector with every charge positive, and join it to the unit vector by a straight segment. Let \(\mathcal U\) be the set of segment parameters admitting a positive solution with the strict signs in (8). It contains the unit endpoint. Section 2 makes it relatively open. Take any convergent sequence of parameters in \(\mathcal U\). All their charges have a common positive lower bound. Section 3 gives a compact limiting assignment with bounded square subgradients. Section 4 excludes every angle endpoint and zero height. There are no open square sides, and Section 5 excludes all corners. Thus the limit is interior and has the required strict signs. Its stationarity equations pass to the limit, so it is a positive solution at the limiting parameter. The height theorem applies again and gives the strict bound \(H_v<23/20\). Hence \(\mathcal U\) is also relatively closed. Connectedness of the segment proves existence at its target. The interior stationary solution is the global constrained minimum by convexity. It is unique: any distinct closed feasible point can be joined to it by a segment whose interior is in the open angle domain, where the energy is strictly convex. The stationary first variation is zero along that segment, so the other point cannot have the same minimum energy. This also proves uniqueness of the continued branch. Now allow zero charges. Make every zero-charge vertex complete and solve each remaining positive-charge component by the result just proved. Each component has at least one complete boundary vertex. Join them with the original edges. At a zero-charge vertex all its returns are zero, so (2), the matching conditions, and the stationarity equations are exact. Every square is interior, including squares on complete edges. The same convex argument identifies this assignment as the unique closed minimum. Finally, continuity at the cube faces follows directly from the variational problem. For a sequence \(\lambda_j	o\lambda\), take a convergent subsequence of its minimizing real coordinates. Its limit is feasible at \(\lambda\). If \(Z\) is any feasible point there and \(Y\) is the strictly feasible point from (9), then \(Z_\epsilon=(1-\epsilon)Z+\epsilon Y\) is interior.
