The coordinate correction \[ \delta a_v= rac{2\pi}{n_v} (\lambda_{j,v}-\lambda_v), \qquad \delta g_{v,e}=0 	ag{24} \] makes its constraints exactly those at \(\lambda_j\). For fixed \(\epsilon>0\) this correction stays in the open angle domain for all sufficiently large \(j\). The minimum at \(\lambda_j\) has no larger energy than this competitor. Pass first to the limit in \(j\), then let \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). The limiting point minimizes at \(\lambda\), and hence equals its unique minimum. Every subsequence has that limit, proving continuity on the full cube. The interior analytic dependence was established in Section 2. This completes the proof of Theorem 1. The result supplies a genuine family of positive stationary solutions for varying charges, with the original powers fixed. It does not prove that a corresponding quantum saddle has a nonzero coefficient. That remains an analytic question about the original finite source. ## 7. Differentiating the energy along the actual charge family Let \(F(\lambda)\) be the minimum in Theorem 1. The new existence statement justifies integration along actual stationary solutions, without assuming that intermediate charges remain geometric. That assumption has now been proved. **Corollary 2.** The minimum is differentiable on the charge cube, with one-sided derivatives on its faces, and \[  rac{\partial F}{\partial\lambda_v} =\pi H_v(\lambda). 	ag{25} \] For any piecewise continuously differentiable path \(\lambda(s)\) in the cube, \[ F(\lambda(1))-F(\lambda(0)) =\pi\int_0^1\sum_v H_v(\lambda(s))\lambda'_v(s)\,ds. 	ag{26} \] In particular the simultaneous activation of a fixed pair \(v,w\), with all other charges fixed at one, has the exact cost \[  rac{F(\mathbf1)-F(\lambda^{v=w=0})}{\pi} =\int_0^1 igl(H_v(\lambda_v=\lambda_w=s) +H_w(\lambda_v=\lambda_w=s) igr)\,ds. 	ag{27} \] The unchanged entries of the charge vector are suppressed in the notation on the right. *Proof.* All cube minima are interior square assignments. Continuity on the compact cube and the nondegeneracy in (10) therefore allow the critical-point equations to be solved in an open neighborhood of any one of its points, even when some charges are zero. The real angle coordinates and the energy have analytic local extensions there; positivity signs need not persist outside the cube. Write the \(v\)-th real constraint as \(C_v=\sum g_{v,e}-n_v a_v/2=-\pi\lambda_v\). The energy differential at a stationary point is \(\sum_v h_v\,dC_v\), where \(h_v=-H_v\). This follows directly from the edge differential: its coefficient of \(da_v\) is \(\sum k_{v,e}=-n_vh_v/2\), and its coefficient of each \(dg_{v,e}\) is \(h_v\). Hence \(dF=-\pi\sum_vh_v\,d\lambda_v\), proving (25). The chain rule proves (26), and the straight activation path gives (27). \(\square\) The height bound also gives monotonicity in each charge and \[ |F(\lambda')-F(\lambda)| \le rac{23\pi}{20}\|\lambda'-\lambda\|_1. 	ag{28} \] The single-activation budget and the resulting large-power edge comparison were already proved by endpoint supporting planes in [the energy comparison](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_edge_cut_energy_comparison.md), §7; they are not new consequences being claimed here. What is newly available is the exact integral (27) through the entire stationary family. The remaining uniform \(3,3\) insertion comparison asks whether that integral is always less than \(4G/\pi\). The separate upper bound \(23/20\) for each height does not establish this two-vertex inequality. ## 8. A uniform relation between angle and height The height bound can be strengthened by retaining the real angle. This is useful when estimating an old path component attached to an activated pair: its boundary angle and height cannot range independently over the full height rectangle. **Theorem 3.** At every vertex with positive charge in Theorem 1, \[  rac{\sinh H_v}{\sin a_v}<\sqrt3,\qquad H_v<\operatorname{arsinh}(\sqrt3\sin a_v). 	ag{29} \] Equivalently, the original tangent coordinate satisfies \[ - rac{\pi}{3} <\arg	an(t_v/2)<0. 	ag{30} \] Complete vertices are excluded from the ratio in (29), since their numerator and denominator both vanish. *Proof.* For each positive-charge vertex put \(R_v=\sinh H_v/\sin a_v\), and choose a vertex where \(R_v\) is largest. Write its angle and height as \(a,H\). If one of its incidences has \(g_{v,e}>0\), its neighbor must have positive charge. Formula (11) and the sign of the imaginary part of the principal inverse hyperbolic sine give \[ R_v<	an(a_w/2)	anh(H_w/2) =R_w\, rac{1-\cos a_w}{1+\cosh H_w}<R_w. 	ag{31} \] This contradicts the choice of \(v\). A complete neighbor instead has a strictly negative return imaginary part at \(v\). Thus every incidence at the maximizing vertex is nonpositive, and its charge equation yields \[ a\le rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{n_v} \le rac{2\pi}{3}. 	ag{32} \] Suppose \(R_v\ge\sqrt3\). Set \(C=\cosh H\). The height bound and the rational estimate in Section 4 give \(1<C<7/4\), and \[ \sin^2a\le rac{\sinh^2H}{3}< rac{11}{16}. 	ag{33} \] On the interval \([\pi/2,2\pi/3]\), however, \(\sin^2a\ge3/4\). Hence (32)--(33) imply \(a<\pi/2\). It follows that \[ \cos a\ge\sqrt{ rac{4-C^2}{3}},\qquad C+\cos a\ge C+\sqrt{ rac{4-C^2}{3}}\ge2. 	ag{34} \] The last inequality holds for \(1\le C\le2\): after squaring its nonnegative sides it is equivalent to \((C-1)(C-2)\le0\). Therefore \[ |	an(t_v/2)|^2 = rac{\sin^2a+\sinh^2H}{(C+\cos a)^2} \le rac{\sinh^2H}{3}. 	ag{35} \] Every neighbor, including a complete one, satisfies \[ |\cos(t_w/2)|^2 = rac{\cosh H_w+\cos a_w}{2}< rac{11}{8}. \] Since \(|\sinh(k+ig)|^2=\sinh^2k+\sin^2g\), each real return at \(v\) is at most \(\operatorname{arsinh}(\sqrt{11/24}\sinh H)\). The real period equation and the degree bound would consequently require \[  rac{3H}{4} \le\operatorname{arsinh} \left(\sqrt{ rac{11}{24}}\sinh Hight). 	ag{36} \] This is impossible for \(0<H\le23/20\). Indeed the function \(\sinh(3H/4)/\sinh H\) is strictly decreasing. Its logarithmic derivative is \((3/4)\coth(3H/4)-\coth H<0\), because \(u\coth u\) is strictly increasing for \(u>0\). At the upper endpoint, \[ 24\sinh^2(69/80)>11\sinh^2(23/20). 	ag{37} \] For an entirely rational verification, put \(x=69/80\), \(y=23/20\). The positive Taylor series give \[ \sinh x>x+ rac{x^3}{6},\qquad \sinh y\le y+ rac{y^3}{6(1-y^2/20)}< rac{10}{7}. \] The geometric bound on the latter tail uses the fact that the successive ratios after \(y^3/6\) are at most \(y^2/20<1\). Finally, \[ 24\left(x+ rac{x^3}{6}ight)^2 -11\left( rac{10}{7}ight)^2 = rac{683309192723}{6422528000000}>0. 	ag{38} \] Thus (37) holds, contradicting (36). The maximizing ratio is less than \(\sqrt3\), proving (29) at every active vertex. Formula (11) gives \(-\Im	an(t_v/2)/\Re	an(t_v/2)=R_v\), which proves (30). \(\square\) The rational comparisons in (37)--(38) are reproduced by [the tangent-sector checker](../experiments/check_positive_path_tangent_sector.py); its [saved results](../repro/results/research-positive-path-tangent-sector.json) use exact fractions throughout. This theorem constrains the geometric deformation. It does not assert a bound on an original quantum sum or settle the simultaneous-pair integral in (27).

title: Partial cone charges on positive paths
text:
# Partial cone charges on positive paths Research note, 3 November 2026. For a finite original path with every crossing power at least eight, the stationary equations have a unique solution in one fixed complex box for every vector of cone charges between zero and one. The proof is a contraction of the exact return map. It does not require a variational existence theorem at each intermediate charge. The imaginary part of each angle is bounded by its own charge times an explicit constant of order \(d_v/n_v^2\). Integrating these bounds gives a change-of-action estimate supported only on the vertices whose charges change. The constants do not depend on path length or on the charges at other vertices. These are statements about the original analytic phase and its marked period equations. No finite quantum invariant at a nonintegral cone charge is assumed, and no coefficient of the original quantum integration cycle is inferred. ## 1. Exact equations and their common domain Let \(I\) be the selected vertices of a finite original path. At least one endpoint meets a complete outside vertex. All original degrees, including complete outside incidences, satisfy \(1\le d_v\le2\). Fix integers \(n_v\ge8\). Outside angles are zero. For an oriented incidence \((v,e)\), with \(e=\{v,w\}\), put \[ r_{v,e}(t)=\operatorname{arsinh}  igl(	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2) igr). 	ag{1} \] The branches are those continued from zero. The phase is \[ \Phi_\lambda(t)=\sum_{e=\{v,w\}}\psi(t_v,t_w) +\sum_{v\in I} rac{i n_vt_v^2}{4\pi} -i\sum_{v\in I}\lambda_vt_v. 	ag{2} \] Every original edge incident to \(I\) is included once. Extra complete edges, if retained, add a constant only. Since \(\psi_{t_v}=-r_{v,e}/\pi\), the exact stationary equations are \[ n_vt_v+2i\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}(t)=2\pi\lambda_v. 	ag{3} \] These use the original powers and full logarithmic charges. Use the box \[ \mathcal B=\{z:|\Re z|\le1,\ |\Im z|\le1/3\}. 	ag{4} \] Section 7 of [the edge-response note](research_edge_hessian_and_phase_response.md) proves the elementary estimates \[ |	an(z/2)|<3/5,\qquad |\Im	an(z/2)|<1/4, \qquad \Re[-2\pi\psi''(z,u)]\succeq	frac15 I 	ag{5} \] for \(z,u\in\mathcal B\). These are analytic edge estimates, not an assumed quantum asymptotic on this larger box. Write the normalized edge Hessian as \[ K(z,u)= rac1s  egin{pmatrix}1+w^2&-wv\-wv&1+v^2\end{pmatrix}, \quad w=	an(z/2),\quad v=	an(u/2),\quad s=\sqrt{1+w^2+v^2}. 	ag{6} \] On the box, \(\Re(s^2)>7/8\). Hence \(|s|,\Re s>9/10\), and the square root is on the complete sheet throughout. ## 2. The exact return map is a contraction **Theorem 1.** For every real charge vector \(\lambda\in[-1,1]^I\), equations (3) have exactly one solution \(t(\lambda)\) in \(\mathcal B^I\). The solution is in its interior and extends holomorphically to a neighborhood of this charge cube of width independent of the path and its powers. For \(\lambda\in[0,1]^I\), each coordinate has \[ \lambda_v=0\ \Longrightarrow\ t_v=0,\qquad \lambda_v>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \Re t_v>0,\quad \Im t_v<0. 	ag{7} \] The edge configurations are positive. At \(\lambda=\mathbf1\) this is the selected marked geometric solution already established for the original filling. **Proof.** Rewrite (3) as the fixed-point equation \[ \mathcal T_v(t)= rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{n_v} - rac{2i}{n_v}\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}(t). 	ag{8} \] First we verify that \(\mathcal T\) preserves the box. For \(z,u\in\mathcal B\), elementary trigonometric bounds give \[ |\cos(u/2)|<41/40,\qquad |\Im\cos(u/2)|< (12/25)(17/100)=51/625. 	ag{9} \] Here \(\sin(1/2)<12/25\), \(\sinh(1/6)<17/100\) and \(\cosh(1/6)<41/40\); their Taylor bounds were recorded in the edge-response note. If \(Z=	an(z/2)\cos(u/2)\), then \[ |Z|<123/200,\qquad |\Im Z|<  rac35 rac{51}{625}+ rac14 rac{41}{40} < rac13. 	ag{10} \] In particular \(|Z|<1\), so the branch of \(\operatorname{arsinh}Z\) is regular on the entire box. For \(r=\operatorname{arsinh}Z=A+iB\), its principal branch has \(|B|<\pi/2\), and \[ |\Re r|\le\operatorname{arsinh}|Z|<123/200,\qquad |\Im r|<\arcsin(1/3)<7/20. 	ag{11} \] Indeed \(|Z|^2=\sinh^2 A+\sin^2 B\) and \(\Im Z=\cosh A\sin B\). The last numerical inequality follows from \(\sin(7/20)>7/20-(7/20)^3/6>1/3\). Since \(d_v/n_v\le1/4\), equations (8)--(11) imply \[ |\Re\mathcal T_v|< \pi/4+7/40<1,\qquad |\Im\mathcal T_v|<123/400<1/3. 	ag{12} \] These are strict bounds independent of the number of vertices. For contraction, differentiate the returns: \[ \partial_{t_v}r_{v,e}=	frac12K_{vv},\qquad \partial_{t_w}r_{v,e}=	frac12K_{vw}. 	ag{13} \] From (5)--(6), \[ |K_{vv}|+|K_{vw}| < rac{1+9/25+9/25}{9/10}= rac{86}{45}. 	ag{14} \] The maximum row sum of the complex Jacobian of \(\mathcal T\) is therefore at most \[  rac{d_v}{n_v} rac{86}{45} \le rac{43}{90}< rac12. 	ag{15} \] Complete outside variables are fixed and add no Jacobian columns. Integrating the derivative on a straight segment in the convex box proves this Lipschitz bound for the complex supremum norm. The closed finite product box is complete, so Banach's theorem gives a unique fixed point. The estimates also give holomorphic dependence uniformly in path length. For example, allow each \(\lambda_v\) to have distance less than \(1/100\) from \([-1,1]\). The two right sides of (12) then increase by at most \(\pi/400\), and still lie strictly inside the box. The derivative bound (15) is unchanged. Iteration from zero consists of holomorphic functions of the charges, and converges uniformly on compact subsets. Its limit is therefore holomorphic on this neighborhood. For the signs, define the removable quotient \[ Q_v(t)=\sum_{e
i v} rac{r_{v,e}(t)}{t_v} = rac12\sum_{e
i v} \int_0^1K_{vv}(\sigma t_v,t_w)\,d\sigma . 	ag{16} \] The last equality is the complex fundamental theorem of calculus, since \(r_{v,e}(0,t_w)=0\). The segment stays in the same box. We will use the slightly stronger centered estimate \[ |K_{vv}-1|<2/5. 	ag{17} \] To verify it, the exact expression (6) gives \[ K_{vv}-1= rac{s w^2-v^2}{s(s+1)}. \] Using \(|w|,|v|<3/5\), \(|s|>9/10\) and \(|s+1|\ge1+\Re s>19/10\) gives \[ |K_{vv}-1| < rac{9}{25} rac{1+10/9}{19/10}= rac25. \] Consequently \[ |Q_v-d_v/2|<d_v/5. 	ag{18} \] In particular \(\Re Q_v>3d_v/10>0\) and \(|\Im Q_v|<d_v/5\). The stationary equation factors exactly as \[ t_v= rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{n_v+2iQ_v}. 	ag{19} \] The denominator has positive real and positive imaginary parts. Formula (7) follows, including the exact zero coordinate when \(\lambda_v=0\). The edge Hessians have positive real part by (5). The original positive-edge theorem identifies this with positivity of the eight original tetrahedra on the continued branch. At unit charges, Proposition 5 of the edge-response note places the already selected geometric solution inside the same box. Uniqueness of the fixed point identifies the two solutions, retaining their original full logarithmic periods. \(\square\) The theorem also provides a path to a partial-charge solution by scaling its charges from zero. This path is defined by (3), not by silently rescaling the powers. Coordinates of zero charge stay exactly zero along it. ## 3. Componentwise heights and action loss For positive charges write \(t_v=	heta_v-iH_v\). For \(n\ge8\) and \(d\in\{1,2\}\), define \[ L_{n,d}=  rac{6\pi d/5}{(n+2d/5)^2+(3d/5)^2}, \qquad U_{n,d}=  rac{14\pi d/5}{(n-2d/5)^2+(7d/5)^2}. 	ag{20} \] **Theorem 2.** Throughout \([0,1]^I\), \[ L_{n_v,d_v}\lambda_v\le H_v(\lambda) \le U_{n_v,d_v}\lambda_v. 	ag{21} \] For \(\lambda_v>0\), both estimates may be made strict. In particular \[ U_{n,d}\le rac{35\pi}{373}< rac3{10}, \qquad U_{n,d}\le rac{280\pi}{81} rac{d}{n^2}. 	ag{22} \] Let \(S(\lambda)=\Phi_\lambda(t(\lambda))\) and \(M(\lambda)=\Re S(\lambda)\). If \(0\le\lambda\le\mu\le1\) coordinatewise, then \[  oxed{\displaystyle  rac12\sum_v L_{n_v,d_v}(\mu_v^2-\lambda_v^2) \ \le M(\lambda)-M(\mu)\le\  rac12\sum_v U_{n_v,d_v}(\mu_v^2-\lambda_v^2).} 	ag{23} \] Only changed charges contribute. For arbitrary \(\lambda,\mu\in[0,1]^I\), one has \[ |M(\lambda)-M(\mu)| \le rac12\sum_v U_{n_v,d_v}|\mu_v^2-\lambda_v^2|. 	ag{24} \] **Proof.** Write \(Q_v=A+iB\). Equation (19) gives \[ H_v= rac{4\pi\lambda_v A}{(n_v-2B)^2+4A^2}, \qquad 3d_v/10<A<7d_v/10,\quad |B|<d_v/5. 	ag{25} \] On this rectangle, the displayed expression increases with both \(A\) and \(B\): for the first monotonicity one uses \(2A<n_v-2B\), which follows from \(n_v>9d_v/5\). Its opposite corners give precisely (20)--(21). The maximum of \(U_{n,d}\) for \(n\ge8\), \(d=1,2\) is \(U_{8,2}=35\pi/373<3/10\). Also \(n-2d/5\ge9n/10\), which proves the second bound in (22) after dropping the other positive denominator term. Differentiating the stationary action introduces no derivative of \(t(\lambda)\), because its full gradient vanishes. Thus \[ \partial_{\lambda_v}S=-it_v,\qquad \partial_{\lambda_v}M=-H_v . 	ag{26} \] Integrate (21) along the straight segment from \(\lambda\) to \(\mu\). At each coordinate, \(\int_0^1[\lambda_v+s(\mu_v-\lambda_v)] (\mu_v-\lambda_v)\,ds=(\mu_v^2-\lambda_v^2)/2\). This proves (23). Varying coordinates one at a time and using the triangle inequality gives (24). \(\square\) For example, turning a set \(A\) of unit charges down to zero increases the real stationary action by an amount between \( rac12\sum_{v\in A}L_{n_v,d_v}\) and \( rac12\sum_{v\in A}U_{n_v,d_v}\), whatever the charges at the other vertices. The latter is at most \(35\pi|A|/746<3|A|/20\). At the all-zero vector every angle is zero, so the action there is the sum of the complete edge phases. No change of peripheral basis or of the original powers occurs. ## 4. Signed powers and filling every auxiliary vertex The contraction does not use a complete outside endpoint, nor the positivity of the powers. These restrictions in the initial statement can be removed without changing its constants. **Corollary 3.** Let \(Y\) be an original ordered circle-tree exterior whose underlying graph is a nontrivial finite path. Select any nonempty set \(I\) of its auxiliary vertices, possibly every vertex. At each selected vertex choose its original power \[ n_v=\eta_v-2p_v,\qquad p_v\in\mathbb Z,\qquad |n_v|\ge8, 	ag{27} \] with its fixed carrier \(\eta_v\). Unselected angles are zero. There is a unique solution in \(\mathcal B^I\) for every \(\lambda\in[-1,1]^I\), with the same uniform holomorphic extension as in Theorem 1. For nonnegative charges, \[ \lambda_v=0\Longrightarrow t_v=0,\qquad \lambda_v>0\Longrightarrow \operatorname{sgn}(\Re t_v)=\operatorname{sgn}(n_v), \quad\Im t_v<0. 	ag{28} \] The height and action bounds (20)--(24) hold with \(n_v\) replaced by \(|n_v|\). At unit charges, these positive original cells determine the smooth Dehn filling along the original slopes \(\mu_v+p_v\lambda_v^{m disk}\). Here \(\lambda_v^{m disk}\) denotes the original disk longitude, to distinguish it from the cone charge. Every main cusp and every unselected auxiliary cusp remains complete. If all constant edge terms of \(Y\) are included in (2), its absolute volume is \(2\pi M(\mathbf1)\). The original component test still determines whether the main link is a knot. **Proof.** The box estimates (12) and the contraction estimate (15) use only \(d_v/|n_v|\). They do not use the existence of a boundary vertex. Hence they apply verbatim to this graph. In (19), the denominator still has positive imaginary part, while its real part \(n_v-2\Im Q_v\) has the sign of \(n_v\). This proves (28). Its real-part magnitude lies between \(|n_v|-2d_v/5\) and \(|n_v|+2d_v/5\), so the same maximization and minimization in (25) prove the unchanged bounds. The continuation from zero charges stays on the same box chart, and every original edge remains positive by (5). At unit charges, (3) is exactly \[ \sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e} = rac{i n_v}{2}t_v-\pi i. \] Together with \(\Im t_v<0\), these are precisely the hypotheses of Theorem 1 in [the marked completion theorem](research_positive_point_marked_completion.md). That theorem allows any selected set, including all auxiliary vertices; it does not require a complete outside end. It supplies the original primitive filling and its absolute action-volume identity, with every carrier and marked disk retained. This proves the geometric assertions directly, without using the earlier positive-path existence theorem. \(\square\) For later estimates one also has, for \(\lambda_v\ge0\), \[ |t_v|\le rac{2\pi\lambda_v}{|n_v|-2d_v/5}. 	ag{29} \] When \(|n_v|\ge64\), the loss from increasing a unit charge at that vertex is bounded by \[  rac12U_{|n_v|,d_v} < rac{35\pi d_v}{99856}< rac{d_v}{800}. 	ag{30} \] Indeed \(|n_v|-2d_v/5\ge64-4/5=316/5\), and dropping the other denominator term in (20) gives the first bound. The second follows, for example, from \(\pi<22/7\). In this range (29)--(30) also give \[ |\Re t_v|< rac1{10},\qquad 0<H_v< rac1{200} 	ag{31} \] at unit charges. These bounds remain independent of path length and of all other powers. ## 5. What the charge estimate does not distinguish The edge phase is even separately in each angle on this complete chart. Flipping \(\lambda_v\) and \(t_v\) simultaneously therefore preserves (3), leaves every other angle unchanged, and preserves the stationary action. Uniqueness in Theorem 1 proves that these are the corresponding selected solutions. Consequently \(S(\lambda)\) is even in each charge separately. Thus (23) compares charge magnitudes and zeroed charges; it does not supply a strict gap between the different choices of signs of unit charges. Those contributions still require the original finite trace, with its orientations and coefficients. Likewise, the bounds above do not estimate a high Newton-index tail or a mixed boundary current of the finite quantum source. They supply the marked phase and an explicit action budget for such a comparison. An upper bound for another contour piece must still be proved from its own exact finite-source expression.

title: The original wire saddle stays in its factorial chamber on every positive path
text: # The original wire saddle stays in its factorial chamber on every positive path Research proof, 3 November 2026. This uses the coupled original period equations, not merely separate bounds on the endpoint angles. It proves the real wire order throughout the positive path charge cube for every integer power at least three. The conclusion places the geometric critical points in the original regular factorial chamber. It does not assert that the geometric saddle dominates the full finite kernel or that its coefficient in a general source is nonzero. ## 1. Inputs and a cosine maximum principle Take the finite positive paths of the [fractional-charge theorem](research_positive_path_fractional_charge_cube.md): selected powers \(n_v\ge3\), charges \(0\le\chi_v\le1\), original incidence degrees at most two, and the stated complete outside endpoints. At an active vertex write \[ t_v=\vartheta_v-iH_v,\qquad 0<\vartheta_v<\pi,\quad H_v>0. \tag{1} \] At zero-charge and complete vertices, \(t_v=0\). The original return and both period equations are \[ \begin{split} r_{vu}&=k_{vu}+ig_{vu} =\operatorname{asinh}\bigl(\tan(t_v/2)\cos(t_u/2)\bigr),\\ \sum_{u\sim v}k_{vu}&=\frac{n_vH_v}{2},& \sum_{u\sim v}g_{vu}&=\frac{n_v\vartheta_v}{2}-\pi\chi_v . \end{split} \tag{2} \] At an active endpoint, \(k_{vu}>0\) and \(-\pi/2<g_{vu}<\pi/2\). The [cosine-phase maximum principle](research_geometric_phase_maximum_principle.md) supplies \[ \beta_v:=\arg\cos(t_v/2)\in(0,\pi/4), \qquad \beta_v=0\ \hbox{at a complete vertex}. \tag{3} \] Only the strict qualitative bound in (3) is needed below. **Lemma 1.** Every active vertex satisfies \[ |\cos(t_v/2)|<1. \tag{4} \] *Proof.* If (4) failed, choose an active vertex at which \(C=|\cos(t_v/2)|\ge1\) is maximal over all selected and complete vertices. Every neighbor then has \(|\cos(t_u/2)|\le C\), so \[ |\sinh r_{vu}| =|\tan(t_v/2)\cos(t_u/2)| \le|\sin(t_v/2)|. \tag{5} \] Since \(|\sinh(k+ig)|^2=\sinh^2k+\sin^2g\), this gives \(k_{vu}\le\operatorname{asinh}|\sin(t_v/2)|\). Put \(t_v=\vartheta-iH\). The supposition \(C\ge1\) implies \[ \cosh H+\cos\vartheta\ge2,\qquad |\sin(t_v/2)|^2=\frac{\cosh H-\cos\vartheta}{2} \le2\sinh^2(H/2). \tag{6} \] But for every \(H>0\), \[ \operatorname{asinh}\bigl(\sqrt2\sinh(H/2)\bigr)<\frac{3H}{4}. \tag{7} \] Indeed \(\sinh(3H/4)>(3/2)\sinh(H/2)> \sqrt2\sinh(H/2)\); the first inequality follows from the strict increase of \(\sinh x/x\) on \(x>0\). The degree bound and (5)--(7) would give \(\sum k_{vu}<3H/2\), contradicting (2) and \(n_v\ge3\). This proves (4). \(\square\) This maximum principle itself uses neither the quantitative height bound nor the charges' upper bound. It uses the original real period equation, degree at most two, and the positivity of the real returns. At complete vertices the cosine modulus is exactly one. ## 2. The selected wire lies in the upper quarter strip For an edge \(vu\), put \[ A=\cos^2(t_v/2),\qquad B=\cos^2(t_u/2),\qquad k=\frac{AB}{A+B},\qquad x=\frac1\pi\arcsin\sqrt{k}. \tag{8} \] These are the selected branches continued from the complete edge, where \(A=B=1\) and \(x=1/4\). By (3), \(A,B\) have positive real part and nonnegative imaginary part. By Lemma 1 their moduli are at most one, strictly less than one at an active endpoint. For an edge with an active endpoint, \(k\) has positive real and positive imaginary parts, so the branch in (8) has \(0<\Re x<1/2\) and \(\Im x>0\). **Lemma 2.** Every edge with an active endpoint satisfies \[ 0<\Re k<\frac12,\qquad 0<\Re x<\frac14,\qquad \Re x>\alpha(\Im x),\quad \alpha(y)=\frac{\arccos(\operatorname{sech}(2\pi y))}{2\pi}. \tag{9} \] *Proof.* Write \[ 1/A=r e^{-i\alpha},\qquad 1/B=s e^{-i\beta}, \quad r,s\ge1,\quad 0\le\alpha,\beta<\pi/2. \tag{10} \] The function \(|r e^{-i\alpha}+s e^{-i\beta}-1|^2\) is strictly increasing in either radius for \(r,s\ge1\): half its \(r\)-derivative is \(r+s\cos(\alpha-\beta)-\cos\alpha>0\), and similarly for \(s\). At \(r=s=1\), subtracting one from this function gives \[ 2\bigl[(1-\cos\alpha)(1-\cos\beta)+\sin\alpha\sin\beta\bigr]\ge0. \tag{11} \] At least one radius is strictly greater than one. Thus, with \(Z=1/A+1/B\), one has \(|Z-1|>1\). Equivalently \(|Z|^2>2\Re Z\), so \(\Re k=\Re(1/Z)<1/2\). Its positivity was already noted after (8). Now \(\cos(2\pi x)=1-2k\). Taking real parts shows \[ 0<\cos(2\pi\Re x)\cosh(2\pi\Im x)<1. \tag{12} \] The first inequality implies \(\Re x<1/4\); the second is exactly the last inequality in (9). \(\square\) For an all-complete edge, \(x=1/4\); it is a constant part of the geometric configuration. The selected square root \[ q=\cot(\pi x),\qquad q^2=1+\tan^2(t_v/2)+\tan^2(t_u/2) \tag{13} \] is the original one. Equation (13) follows from (8) and is continued from \(q=1\). ## 3. The coupled equations force the real wire order **Theorem 3.** On every edge of the original positive path, throughout its whole charge cube, \[ \boxed{\quad \Re x< \min\left\{\frac12-\frac{\Re t_v}{2\pi}, \frac12-\frac{\Re t_u}{2\pi}\right\}. \quad} \tag{14} \] *Proof.* It suffices to prove the inequality at one endpoint \(v\). It is automatic when that endpoint is complete. Suppose it fails at an active endpoint. Use radian coordinates \[ T=t_v/2=a-ih,\qquad W=\pi x=A_0+iY, \qquad A_0\ge\pi/2-a . \tag{15} \] Here \(0<a<\pi/2\), \(h>0\), and Lemma 2 gives \(0<A_0<\pi/4,\ Y>0\). In particular \(a>\pi/4\). The upper-right-quadrant property gives \(\Re(A\bar B)>0\), hence \(|A+B|>|B|\), in the notation of (8). Consequently \[ |\sin^2W|=|k|<|A|=|\cos^2T|. \tag{16} \] In (16) the two sides are \(\sin^2A_0+\sinh^2Y\) and \(\cos^2a+\sinh^2h\). Since \(A_0\ge\pi/2-a\), their real trigonometric terms have the opposite weak order. It follows that \(Y<h\). The original return satisfies the exact identity \[ e^{2r_{vu}} =\frac{q+\tan T}{q-\tan T} =\frac{\cos(W-T)}{\cos(W+T)}. \tag{17} \] For the first equality use \(\sinh r_{vu}=\tan T\cos(t_u/2)\) and \(\cosh r_{vu}=q\cos(t_u/2)\). The latter square-root sign is fixed at completeness and continues on the positive charge cube; neither side vanishes there. The second equality uses \(q=\cot W\). Thus (17) retains the original return. In (15), \(0<a-A_0<\pi/2\) and \(Y+h>0\), so \[ 0<\arg\cos(W-T) =\arctan\bigl(\tan(a-A_0)\tanh(Y+h)\bigr) <a-A_0 . \tag{18} \] Also \(\pi/2\le A_0+a<3\pi/4\) and \(Y-h<0\). The denominator in (17) therefore has nonpositive real and strictly positive imaginary parts: \[ \pi/2\le\arg\cos(W+T)<\pi . \tag{19} \] The argument of their quotient belongs to \((-\pi,0)\). Since the original return has \(2g_{vu}\in(-\pi,\pi)\), there is no additional \(2\pi\) ambiguity in (17). Equations (18)--(19) yield the strict estimate \[ g_{vu}<\frac{a-A_0-\pi/2}{2} \le a-\pi/2<0. \tag{20} \] Put \(B_v=\sinh H_v/\sin\vartheta_v\) and \(\omega=\arctan B_v\). The argument of \(\tan T\cos(t_u/2)\) is \(\beta_u-\omega\). Its real part is positive, since it equals \(\sinh k_{vu}\cos g_{vu}\). When its argument is negative, the exact relation \[ \tan g_{vu} =\tanh k_{vu}\tan(\beta_u-\omega) \tag{21} \] shows that \(g_{vu}>\beta_u-\omega\ge-\omega\). Thus (20) implies \[ \omega>\pi/2-a . \tag{22} \] There can be only one further incidence at \(v\). Its return imaginary part, or zero if the incidence is absent, must satisfy the original period equation. By (20), \[ g_{\rm other} =n_va-\pi\chi_v-g_{vu} >(n_v-1)a-\pi/2 \ge2a-\pi/2>0. \tag{23} \] A terminal vertex is already impossible. Otherwise let \(w\) be the other neighbor. The positive version of (21) gives \[ 0<g_{\rm other}<\beta_w-\omega . \tag{24} \] Combining (22)--(24) forces \[ \beta_w>2a-\pi/2+\omega>a>\pi/4, \tag{25} \] contradicting (3). This excludes the failure in (15) and proves (14) at both endpoints. \(\square\) Only \(n_v\ge3,\ \chi_v\le1\) and the original degree bound were used in (23). In particular the contradiction does not replace the actual charge by one or alter an attaching degree. ## 4. What this proves about the original phase For an active edge put \(s_v=1/2-t_v/(2\pi)=b_v+iS_v\), and similarly at \(u\). Equations (9), (14), and the geometric spectral half-plane give \[ Y,S_v,S_u\ge0,\qquad \alpha(Y)<\Re x<b_v,b_u,\qquad \alpha(S_v)<b_v,\quad\alpha(S_u)<b_u. \tag{26} \] For the last two inequalities use \(\cos(2\pi b_v)\cosh(2\pi S_v)=\Re(-2\cos t_v)/2<1\). All original factorial arguments \[ x,\quad s_v-x,\quad1-s_v-x \tag{27} \] and their \(u\)-counterparts have real parts strictly between zero and one. Thus the selected wire branch stays in the original regular factorial chart along the entire charge cube. The zero logarithmic lift of its stationary equation, fixed at completeness, continues in this chart. For fixed endpoint angles the real part of the principal wire phase \(b(x,t_v)+b(x,t_u)\), on its fixed-height line, is strictly concave on \(\alpha(Y)<\Re x<\min(b_v,b_u)\). Indeed, with the quantities in the [mixed-phase calculation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_mixed_phase_height_extension_and_wire_order.md), each incidence has \(v>0,w>0,u<w\). Its negative \(x\)-second derivative is \(\pi(v+2w-u)>0\). The geometric critical wire is therefore the unique maximum on this central interval, with a positive curvature bound on compact subintervals. For an internal two-vertex piece with complete outer ends, the complete-end-compensated mixed phase consequently has its actual positive-charge critical point inside the concavity domain of Proposition 1 in the linked note, without requiring any height ordering. This gives strict horizontal concavity of that mixed phase on its stated convex domain. Zero-charge faces are understood by continuity and the direct nondegenerate Hessian at completeness. A general interior vertex has no extra complete-end term; this conclusion does not insert one there. The earlier exact \(A=1,B=3/10+3i/5\) wire-order counterexample obeys the separate endpoint bounds but was not an integer-filled path. Theorem 3 explains precisely why the coupled equations exclude such a failure on the actual family. Finally, regularity and a strict central maximum do not control the rest of the finite source. The [all-three bare-kernel obstruction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_bare_kernel_power_three_obstruction.md) still exhibits larger endpoint sectors before the original trace contracts them. No assertion about those sectors, global mixed currents, or the nonzero full-source saddle coefficient follows solely from (14) or (26).

title: A compact descent contour from the original primitive periods
text:
# A compact descent contour from the original primitive periods Private written proof, 15 November 2026. Suppose a fixed short partial filling has a positive solution in the original circle-tree edge decomposition. Its primitive-period map has a canonical inverse on a real slice. The entire real slice need not be in its image. Nevertheless the original convex angle energy constructs a bounded, star-shaped inverse domain around the solution, with a constant strict action loss on its boundary. This is a theorem about the actual classical source action and its peripheral marking. It does not identify this contour with the original finite quantum cycle. ## 1. Fixed original data and the compact angle problem Fix an original ordered circle tree, a nonempty selected set \(S\) of size \(k\), and every edge incident to \(S\), counted once. Write \(m\) for the number of included edges. Every selected vertex has positive original degree. Fix the full complex angles at the outside endpoints, the original real signed crossing powers \(n_v\), and the primitive unit charges. In a physical integral filling, \(n_v=\eta_v-2p_v\), with the original carrier \(\eta_v\). Use the canonical positive edge branches of [the global monotonicity theorem](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md). At an endpoint write \[ t_v=s_v+i h_v,\qquad r_{v,e}=k_{v,e}+i g_{v,e}. 	ag{1} \] Before matching imaginary angles, use one \(h_{v,e}\) per incidence. For an oriented edge \(e=(v,w)\), its two positive square factors have coordinates \[  egin{aligned} A_P&=s_v/4-g_{w,e}/2,& A_Q&=s_v/4+g_{w,e}/2,\ y_P&=g_{v,e}/2+s_w/4,& y_Q&=g_{v,e}/2-s_w/4. \end{aligned} 	ag{2} \] Each coordinate lies in \((-\pi/4,\pi/4)\). Equivalently, \[ |s_v|+2|g_{w,e}|<\pi,\qquad |s_w|+2|g_{v,e}|<\pi. 	ag{3} \] The outside \(s_b,h_b\) are prescribed. The selected constraints are \[ \sum_{e
i v}g_{v,e}- rac{n_v}{2}s_v=-\pi \qquad(v\in S). 	ag{4} \] Let \(\mathcal P\) be this open feasible polytope in the selected \(s_v\) and all incidence \(g_{v,e}\), and let \(\overline{\mathcal P}\) be its closure. Boundaries and interiors below are relative to its affine constraint space. We assume that the original primitive equations have a positive solution \(t^0\); in particular \(\mathcal P\) is nonempty. There is no zero-dimensional case under these hypotheses. The \(k\) constraints (4) are independent, since each contains incidence variables belonging to its own selected vertex. The affine space has dimension \((k+2m)-k=2m>0\). Its projection to the selected \(s\) coordinates is surjective: any infinitesimal change of \(s_v\) can be offset in one incidence variable at that vertex. Strict feasibility therefore gives the full local \(k\)-dimensional period problem. The empty selected set is excluded throughout. For one square let \[  egin{aligned} x(A,y)&=	frac12\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(2A)\cos(2y)),\ B(A,y)&=	frac12\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(2y)\cos(2A)),\ dE_\square&=x\,dA+B\,dy,\qquad E_\square(0,0)=0. \end{aligned} 	ag{5} \] These are real single-valued functions on the open square. The existing variational theorem proves that \(E_\square\) is strictly convex, extends continuously to its closed square, and has the edge identity \[ 4\,dE_e=k_{v,e}\,ds_v+k_{w,e}\,ds_w +h_{v,e}\,dg_{v,e}+h_{w,e}\,dg_{w,e}, \qquad E_e=E_{\square,P}+E_{\square,Q}. 	ag{6} \] Define the original energy, with the outside imaginary angles retained, \[ \mathcal E=4\sum_eE_e- \sum_{b
otin S}h_b\sum_{e
i b}g_{b,e}. 	ag{7} \] It is continuous on the compact polytope, strictly convex in its interior. Let \(z_0\) denote the angle assignment of \(t^0\). The original variational theorem says that \(z_0\) is its unique global minimum, including against boundary assignments. ## 2. The exact real-period image and its boundary completion For \(\xi\in\mathbb R^k\), introduce only a linear tilt: \[ \mathcal E_\xi(z)=\mathcal E(z)-\sum_{v\in S}\xi_v s_v(z), \qquad z_\xi=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\overline{\mathcal P}} \mathcal E_\xi. 	ag{8} \] The minimizer is unique for every \(\xi\). Here the existing boundary proof applies unchanged: a square on an open side has inward energy derivative \(-\infty\), while an interior square or a corner has a finite derivative along a line to a strictly feasible assignment. Adding the linear term in (8) cannot remove that contradiction. Thus every square factor of a boundary minimizer is either interior or a corner. Uniqueness follows from strict convexity along a segment between distinct minimizers; if the only differing factors join adjacent corners, their midpoint would instead be an excluded open-side minimizer. Existence follows from compactness. The map \(\xi\mapsto z_\xi\) is continuous on all of \(\mathbb R^k\). Indeed, for \(\xi_j	o\xi\), any convergent subsequence of the compact minimizers minimizes \(\mathcal E_\xi\) by passage to the minimum inequality. Uniqueness identifies its limit with \(z_\xi\), proving continuity of the whole sequence. Define the actual period map and its real image by \[ P_v(t)=\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}(t)- rac{i n_v}{2}t_v, \qquad J= rac{\partial P}{\partial t}, \qquad \Xi=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^k:z_\xi\in\mathcal P\}. 	ag{9} \] **Proposition 1.** The set \(\Xi\) is open and contains zero. It is exactly the set of \(\xi\) for which the original positive domain, with its fixed outside angles, contains a solution of \[ P(t)=\xi-\pi i\mathbf1. 	ag{10} \] That solution \(t(\xi)\) is unique and real analytic. At any finite boundary point \(\xi_*\in\partial\Xi\), the completed assignment \(z_{\xi_*}\) has at least one corner factor and no open-side factor. Every approach from \(\Xi\) converges to that same angle assignment. The reconstructed complex angles can diverge at a corner; their boundedness is not asserted. **Proof.** Attach multipliers \(h_v\) to (4). Stationarity of (8) in the incidence variables gives \(h_{v,e}=h_v\) at selected vertices and \(h_{b,e}=h_b\) at outside vertices. Stationarity in \(s_v\) gives \[ \sum_{e
i v}k_{v,e}+n_vh_v/2=\xi_v. 	ag{11} \] Together with (4), these are exactly (10). Conversely a positive solution gives an interior stationary point and hence the unique global minimizer of (8). The original edge monotonicity gives \(\operatorname{Re}J>0\), with \(J\) complex symmetric. It is therefore invertible. The implicit-function theorem gives openness and real analyticity; global uniqueness also follows directly from strict monotonicity. If a finite boundary point had an interior minimizer, this same theorem would put a neighborhood in \(\Xi\). It must therefore have a corner, by the preceding boundary exclusion. Continuity of the unique closed minimizer proves the asserted limit. \(\square\) Thus (8) gives an exact global description of the image slice by a fixed compact convex problem. It does not assert that \(\Xi\) is all of \(\mathbb R^k\), convex, or star shaped. Finite image boundaries are possible corner degenerations of the original cells. ## 3. The calibrated action equals a constant minus the angle energy Let \(M_\infty=\psi(0,0)\), with the original edge normalization, and retain the primitive-charge action \[ F(t)=\sum_{e=vw}\psi(t_v,t_w) + rac{i}{4\pi}\sum_{v\in S}n_vt_v^2 -i\sum_{v\in S}t_v. 	ag{12} \] The outside arguments are the fixed original boundary angles. As in the original trace calculation, \[ F_t=- rac{P+\pi i\mathbf1}{\pi}. 	ag{13} \] **Proposition 2.** At every point of \(\Xi\), with the canonical positive logarithms, \[  oxed{\quad \operatorname{Re}F(t(\xi)) =mM_\infty- rac{\mathcal E(z_\xi)}\pi. \quad} 	ag{14} \] The constant is the same on all components of \(\Xi\). **Proof.** On one positive edge, \(\psi_{t_v}=-r_{v,e}/\pi\). Hence \[ d(\pi\operatorname{Re}\psi) =\sum_{j=v,w}(-k_{j,e}\,ds_j+g_{j,e}\,dh_j). \] Combining this with (6) gives the exact identity \[ \pi\operatorname{Re}\psi+4E_e -g_{v,e}h_v-g_{w,e}h_w=\pi M_\infty. 	ag{15} \] Its differential vanishes. The positive edge domain is the connected two-disk domain of the original coordinate theorem, and its complete value fixes the displayed constant. Thus this is a global identity on that positive domain, not a choice of a constant on an inverse period component. At an interior minimizer, all imaginary angles match. Sum (15) and subtract the outside term in (7). Equation (4) gives \[ \mathcal E=\pi mM_\infty-\pi\operatorname{Re}\sum_e\psi +\sum_{v\in S}h_v(n_vs_v/2-\pi). \] Since \(\operatorname{Re}(i n_vt_v^2/(4\pi))=-n_vs_vh_v/(2\pi)\) and \(\operatorname{Re}(-it_v)=h_v\), this is exactly (14). \(\square\) In particular \(t^0\) is the unique global maximum of \(\operatorname{Re}F\) on the entire inverse-period slice, not only on its component containing \(t^0\). For the differential form of the result, define the finite convex conjugate \[ \mathcal C(\xi)=\max_{z\in\overline{\mathcal P}} \{\xi\cdot s(z)-\mathcal E(z)\}. 	ag{16} \] Uniqueness and continuity of the maximizer imply \(\mathcal C\in C^1(\mathbb R^k)\), with \(
abla\mathcal C=s(z_\xi)\). This follows directly by sandwiching its difference quotient between the two maximizing linear forms. On \(\Xi\) it is real analytic and \[ 
abla^2\mathcal C= rac{\partial s}{\partial\xi} =\operatorname{Re}(J^{-1})>0, \qquad \operatorname{Re}(J^{-1}) =J^{-*}(\operatorname{Re}J)J^{-1}. 	ag{17} \] Here the real part is the Hermitian part, equal to the entrywise real part for these symmetric matrices. Along a ray inside \(\Xi\), \[  rac{d}{dr}\mathcal E(z_{r\omega}) =r\,\omega^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{Re}(J^{-1})\omega>0 \qquad(r>0,\ |\omega|=1), 	ag{18} \] and the action derivative is minus this expression divided by \(\pi\). Equivalently its exact loss is \[ \operatorname{Re}F(t^0)-\operatorname{Re}F(t(\xi)) = rac{\mathcal C(0)-\mathcal C(\xi) +\xi\cdot
abla\mathcal C(\xi)}\pi. 	ag{19} \] ## 4. A bounded star-shaped domain with a strict boundary gap The compact angle problem supplies a positive number \[ \Delta=\min_{z\in\partial\mathcal P}\mathcal E(z) -\mathcal E(z_0)>0. 	ag{20} \] Strict positivity follows from continuity and the unique interior minimum. This is a boundary-energy quantity in the specified original polytope; no computable lower bound is assumed. **Theorem 3.** For every \(0<\delta<\Delta\), the set \[ \Omega_\delta= \{\xi\in\mathbb R^k: \mathcal E(z_\xi)<\mathcal E(z_0)+\delta\} 	ag{21} \] is a bounded open strictly star-shaped domain with smooth boundary. Its closure lies in \(\Xi\). Every ray has a unique boundary radius \(ho_\delta(\omega)>0\), depending smoothly on its direction. Its inverse image \[ \Gamma_\delta=t(\Omega_\delta) 	ag{22} \] is an embedded real \(k\)-dimensional contour with compact closure in the original positive domain. It has its unique action maximum at \(t^0\), and \[ \operatorname{Re}F ig|_{\partial\Gamma_\delta} =\operatorname{Re}F(t^0)-\delta/\pi. 	ag{23} \] **Proof.** The closed angle sublevel \(K_\delta=\{z:\mathcal E(z)\le\mathcal E(z_0)+\delta\}\) is compact and contained in \(\mathcal P\). Thus every minimizer occurring in (21), or at equality, is interior and reconstructs a regular matched positive point. The inverse-period parameters of those minimizers are bounded. To see this without assuming properness of the whole period map, choose one incidence at each selected vertex and reconstruct its imaginary angle using (5) and the original square formulas. These are smooth on the compact set \(K_\delta\). At every interior minimizer all incidences give the same angle. Formula (11) then expresses its \(\xi\) as bounded smooth functions of that compact angle data. Consequently the set defined by the weak inequality in (21) is bounded and closed, hence compact and contained in \(\Xi\). There is also global monotonicity along each parameter ray, including after a possible exit from \(\Xi\). For \(0\le r_1<r_2\), the two minimum inequalities from (8) imply \[ \omega\cdot(s_2-s_1)\ge0,\qquad r_1\omega\cdot(s_2-s_1) \le\mathcal E(z_{r_2\omega})-\mathcal E(z_{r_1\omega}) \le r_2\omega\cdot(s_2-s_1). 	ag{24} \] Thus the energy cannot decrease along the ray. Before the level in (21) is reached, the minimizer is interior and (18) makes it strictly increasing for \(r>0\). The ray must reach that level at a finite radius: otherwise its parameters would lie in the bounded weak sublevel just proved. Continuity and strict increase give exactly one first radius. There is no later equality interval: the first level point lies in the open set \(\Xi\), so (18) gives an immediate strict increase there, followed by the nondecrease in (24). At that radius the radial derivative in (18) is positive. The implicit function theorem therefore makes \(ho_\delta\) smooth; for \(k=1\) this means the two positive endpoint radii. This proves all assertions about \(\Omega_\delta\). Injectivity and nonsingularity of the period map prove the embedding in (22). Compactness of its closure follows from the same reconstruction on \(K_\delta\). Finally (14) gives (23) and the unique maximum. \(\square\) At the center the real phase curvature in \(\xi\) coordinates is \(-\operatorname{Re}(J(t^0)^{-1})/\pi\), which is negative definite. On each compact annulus of this contour the action has a positive gap. If the original core signs satisfy \(\operatorname{Im}t_v^0<0\), then sufficiently small \(\delta\) makes the entire closed contour lie in the lower poly-half-plane: compact angle sublevels shrink to their unique minimizer as \(\delta\downarrow0\). All these finite-contour assertions persist for sufficiently small complex changes of the prescribed outside angles. On a compact closed contour, the holomorphic inverse-function theorem applies uniformly to (10); the continued contour and critical point retain, for example, half of the strict boundary gap in (23). The statement uses the same continued primitive logarithms, not newly selected endpoint branches. ## 5. What this does not prove about the original finite source Finite boundary points of the full image \(\Xi\) are accounted for by its unique corner minimizers. If \(|\xi|	o\infty\), a sequence of interior minimizers cannot remain in a compact subset of \(\mathcal P\), by (11). Neither fact asserts that the full inverse slice is a proper integration cycle with integrable ends. Indeed \(\mathcal E\) is bounded on the closed polytope, so (14) by itself does not make the action tend to \(-\infty\) along an infinite end. Theorem 3 avoids this issue by constructing a finite compact collar. For the original finite source, one must still match its boundary to the actual trace endpoints, control the connecting faces and vertical currents, and justify the complete edge-kernel asymptotics on the deformation. Its being a descent contour for the calibrated classical phase does not supply those facts or its relative homology coefficient. The original lattice modes and peripheral scalar factors are unchanged. This limitation is substantive even inside positive edge charts. The [actual full-wire obstruction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_all_three_edgewise_contour_obstruction.md) proves that on positive all-three path fillings the full individual wire kernel can have a strictly larger rate than its geometric packet. Its dominant endpoint products can then vanish after the original adjacent Hermite traces. Thus neither an edgewise smaller remainder nor a competing rate for the whole contraction follows from the positive classical contour; the full source must be treated coherently. The [local coefficient theorem](research_primitive_filling_local_gaussian_unit.md) supplies a nonzero primitive Gaussian coefficient when its regular chart conditions hold. Together, the two results give a local block and a compact classical contour with a strict boundary action gap. They still do not identify the entire selected scalar with that block, exclude cancellation from the remaining source, or cover a short hyperbolic filling outside the original positive decomposition. ## Pinned direct sources * `notes/research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md`, SHA256 `da5129c7110190035eedb8249d4004dd06b5a7555e78d948234d8de50fa17500`: the full positive two-disk coordinates, canonical branches, exact meridian increments, global strict monotonicity and accretive primitive-period Jacobian for arbitrary real signed powers. * `notes/research_positive_filling_convex_variation.md`, SHA256 `2777b2bcb149d64a79757ba64ccb16be5438cf37ce820ad50c5f532afd8fc6c0`: the square energy, exact differential (6), original angle constraints and boundary term, compact continuous extension, exclusion of open sides and uniqueness of the closed minimizer. The present proof adds real-period tilts, the global calibrated action identity and compact inverse-period contours. * `notes/research_primitive_filling_local_gaussian_unit.md`, SHA256 `daff63f379f9a037fc69f67503b69eef6a749e305592f10a10644dc155779b92`: the original primitive-charge action and its exact finite trace normalization, and the separate local Gaussian-unit statement. * `notes/research_all_three_edgewise_contour_obstruction.md`, SHA256 `39008a1b4a95ec5b21caeea7a4abaa7972795050b82a1415ce8aef7dcdd495b0`: the actual positive-chart full-wire obstruction and exact adjacent endpoint cancellation used solely to delimit the source conclusion. Only written proofs and source-text reads enter this note. No mathematical code, numerical calculation, test or compilation was run, and no frozen manuscript or other note was edited.

title: Completing a positive primitive solution with its original marking
text:
# Completing a positive primitive solution with its original marking A positive solution of the original circle-tree filling equations, with negative imaginary boundary angles at the selected circles, already determines the actual marked hyperbolic filling. A path of solutions with fixed slopes is not needed for this conclusion. The proof uses a different path for a specific purpose: it contracts the positive tangent coordinates to the complete structure while keeping each selected longitude loxodromic. That path identifies the full logarithmic periods of the original peripheral curves. The primitive filling equations are imposed only at its endpoint. The local tube completion then gives the original smooth filling. This extends the geometric argument in Section 6 of the [circle-tree geometry manuscript](../papers/circle-tree-geometry/main.tex), with its original cut cells, page order and primitive curves. No manuscript is modified here. ## 1. Statement and conventions Let \(Y\) be an original ordered circle-tree exterior with at least one edge, as defined by the marked cut construction in that manuscript. Retain every original half-twist carrier, disk frame, page order, main component and auxiliary cusp. At an auxiliary vertex \(v\), the primitive basis is \((\mu_v,\lambda_v)\), where \(\lambda_v\) is the original disk longitude. Choose selected vertices \(S\), original integer filling coefficients \(p_v\), and carriers \(\eta_v\), and put \[ n_v=\eta_v-2p_v. 	ag{1} \] The outside angles are zero. For a selected vertex use a complex angle \(t_v\) on the canonical branch \(|\Re t_v|<\pi\). For an edge \(e=\{v,w\}\), put \[ a_v=	an(t_v/2),\quad a_w=	an(t_w/2),\qquad q_e^2=1+a_v^2+a_w^2. 	ag{2} \] The positive branch is the one characterized by \[ \Re q_e> \sqrt{(\Re a_v)^2+(\Re a_w)^2}. 	ag{3} \] This is exactly positivity of the eight original ordered tetrahedra, as proved in [the positive edge theorem](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md). Define the original returns by \[ r_{v,e} =\operatorname{arsinh}  igl(	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2) igr), 	ag{4} \] on the same canonical positive branch. **Theorem 1.** Suppose (3) holds at every original edge, \(\Im t_v<0\) for \(v\in S\), and the full logarithmic equations are \[ \sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e} = rac{i n_v}{2}t_v-\pi i \qquad(v\in S). 	ag{5} \] Then the original cells glue to a hyperbolic metric on \(Y\) whose completion is the smooth Dehn filling along the original primitive curves \(\mu_v+p_v\lambda_v\). Every main cusp and every unselected auxiliary cusp is complete. The filled core at \(v\) has length \(-2\Im t_v>0\). Let \(\Psi=\sum_e\psi(t_v,t_w)\) include every original edge, including complete edges outside the selected region. Then \[ \operatorname{Vol}Y(\mathbf p) =2\pi\Re\left\{ \Psi+ rac{i}{4\pi}\sum_{v\in S}n_vt_v^2 -i\sum_{v\in S}t_v ight\}. 	ag{6} \] This is a geometric statement. It does not assert that an original quantum source has this exponential rate. ## 2. A positive path used to fix branches We give the contraction explicitly. On one edge set \[ X=(\Re a_v)^2+(\Re a_w)^2,\quad Y_0=(\Im a_v)^2+(\Im a_w)^2,\quad Z=\Re a_v\Im a_v+\Re a_w\Im a_w,\quad D_0^2=XY_0-Z^2. 	ag{7} \] Writing \(q=P+iQ\), the identity \(q^2=1+a_v^2+a_w^2\) gives \[ X-D_0^2=(P^2-X)(X+Q^2). 	ag{8} \] For \(X>0\), positivity (3) is equivalent to \(D_0^2<X\), with the square root chosen to have positive real part. Conversely this strict inequality excludes a nonpositive real value of \(q^2\): such a value would have \(Z=0\) and \(Y_0\ge1+X\), contradicting \(D_0^2<X\). When \(X=0\), positivity is exactly \(Y_0<1\). Therefore \[ a_v(ho)=ho a_v,\qquad 0\leho\le1 	ag{9} \] preserves every positive edge simultaneously. For \(X>0\) its criterion is \(ho^4D_0^2<ho^2X\); for \(X=0\) it is \(ho^2Y_0<1\). The angle branch is \[ t_v(ho)=2\arctan(ho a_v). 	ag{10} \] The positive domain excludes the inverse-tangent cuts \(a_v\in i[1,\infty)\cup-i[1,\infty)\). For example, if \(\Re a_v=0\), \(|\Im a_v|\ge1\), and \(\Re a_w
e0\), then \(D_0^2\ge X\); if both real parts are zero, then \(Y_0\ge1\). Thus (10) is the continuous canonical branch throughout the contraction. The sign of \(\Im	an(t/2)\) is the sign of \(\Im t\) in the canonical strip. Also the principal inverse tangent takes the lower half-plane, with its excluded cut removed, to negative imaginary part. It follows that \[ \Im t_v(ho)<0\qquad (v\in S,\ 0<ho\le1). 	ag{11} \] All outside angles stay zero. The path generally does not satisfy (5), and is not being called a fixed-slope cone path. ## 3. The original gluing is regular on this whole path The original face coordinates on an edge are rational functions of \(a=a_v\), \(b=a_w\), and \(q=q_e\). In particular \[ E= rac{q+i}{q-i},\quad R= rac{1+b^2}{q^2+1},\quad R_1=1-R= rac{1+a^2}{q^2+1},\quad Z_1= rac{q+b}{q-i}. 	ag{12} \] On the positive domain, \(\Re q>0\), so \(q,q\pm i
e0\). Moreover \(\Re(q\pm a),\Re(q\pm b)>0\), hence these factors are nonzero. The excluded inverse-tangent cuts give \(a\pm i
e0\) and \(b\pm i
e0\). Thus \(E,R,R_1\) are nonzero. The further apex denominators factor as \[ Z_1-R_1= rac{(q+b)(b+i)}{q^2+1},\qquad Z_1-E R_1= rac{(q+b)(b-i)}{(q-i)^2}, 	ag{13} \] and are nonzero, as are the expressions obtained by interchanging the endpoints. Every face triple remains distinct because the original tetrahedra are positive. Consequently all original face maps are nonsingular on (9). The original incoming and outgoing doubled disk triangles have the complex edge ratios in equation \(\mathrm{ctg:pants}\) of the manuscript. They depend only on the shared angle through \(Q_v=e^{it_v}\), including the complex shears. The ordered page gluing therefore remains the same full face identification. The pure and odd edge-return matrix identities in equations \(\mathrm{ctg:pure	ext{-}returns}\) and \(\mathrm{ctg:odd	ext{-}returns}\) are rational identities in these regular variables. They continue on the entire path. In the fixed topological triangulation, every edge product is therefore one. Its sum of positive dihedral angles is continuous, is an integral multiple of \(2\pi\), and equals \(2\pi\) at the complete endpoint. It remains \(2\pi\). Thus the abstract glued tetrahedra give a nonsingular oriented hyperbolic metric at every finite point of the original exterior. This does not require that a deformed projection half-ball remain convex or that its development be globally injective. ## 4. Complete main and outside cusps The main meridians are the original corner words \(W_{j-1}^{-1}W_j\), or their transported inverses. Their multipliers at the corner flags are identically one. They remain nonidentity on the full positive domain. For example \[ W_0^{-1}W_1:z\longmapsto z+(E-1), \qquad E-1= rac{2i}{q-i}
e0. 	ag{14} \] The other consecutive white maps cannot coincide projectively: the \(W_1,W_2\) pair has respectively zero and nonzero lower-left entries; the \(W_2,W_3\) pair has respectively nonzero and zero upper-right entries, since \(R(E-1)
e0\); and the \(W_3,W_0\) pair again has nonzero and zero lower-left entries. Thus all these marked main meridians are nontrivial parabolics. Every commuting peripheral transformation is a translation in the same fixed-flag affine chart. The horospherical triangles form a nonsingular similarity structure on the compact topological cusp torus. With translation holonomy its Euclidean metric descends and is complete, so the corresponding main end is an ordinary complete cusp. At an unselected auxiliary vertex, \(t_v=0\) and \(r_{v,e}=0\) for every incident edge. Its two peripheral multipliers are one. Its similarity holonomy is therefore translational as well, and the same compact-link argument proves completeness. A zero translation for an individual peripheral generator cannot cause a degeneracy: the complete flat link has an injective translation lattice. ## 5. The full logarithms at a selected end The actual primitive words of the manuscript give affine multipliers with continued logarithms \[ U_v=2\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}-i\eta_vt_v =-2\pi\Psi_{t_v}-i\eta_vt_v,\qquad V_v=2it_v. 	ag{15} \] These are initially logarithms of multipliers. We now verify that they are the full periods of the original primitive paths, including their winding integers. For \(0<ho\le1\), equation (11) gives \(\Re V_v=-2\Im t_v>0\). Send the original selected ideal flag to infinity. The longitude has a nonunit affine multiplier, so the abelian peripheral holonomy has a second common fixed point \(q_v\) in this affine chart. Its similarity development misses \(q_v\). Indeed the vector field \((z-q_v)\partial_z\) is invariant under the peripheral affine holonomy. Its pullback by the similarity development therefore descends to the compact link torus. Every zero would have index \(+1\), because the similarity development is locally orientation-preserving. The sum of indices is the Euler characteristic zero. Thus there are no zeros. On the simply connected link cover one may consequently set \[ f_v=\log(\operatorname{dev}_v-q_v). 	ag{16} \] Its derivative is everywhere nonsingular. The metric \(|df_v|^2\) descends to a smooth Euclidean metric on the compact torus and is complete. Its lifted developing map \(f_v\) covers the Euclidean plane; since that plane is simply connected, it is a diffeomorphism. The two generator periods therefore form an injective real rank-two lattice. Let \(P_{\mu_v},P_{\lambda_v}\) be these periods along the original oriented primitive curves. Their exponentials are the multipliers computed in (15), so \[ P_{\mu_v}-U_v,\quad P_{\lambda_v}-V_v \in2\pi i\mathbb Z. 	ag{17} \] The integers are continuous along \(0<ho\le1\). The link is nonsingular, its selected flag and original paths are retained, and the nonunit multiplier never disappears. To fix the integers, use a continuous affine frame near \(ho=0\), and write the longitude as \(z\mapsto a(ho)z+b(ho)\). At completeness \(a(0)=1\) and \(b(0)
e0\), because the original primitive longitude is a nonzero translation on the complete Euclidean torus. Its second fixed point is \[ q_v= rac{b}{1-a}, 	ag{18} \] which tends to infinity as \(ho\downarrow0\). The original generator paths pass through finitely many link triangles. Their affine images and Euclidean lengths remain bounded, say by \(B\) and \(L\), near completeness. Hence \[ |P_\gamma(ho)| \le rac{L}{|q_v(ho)|-B} \longrightarrow0. 	ag{19} \] Also \(U_v,V_v	o0\). Thus both integers in (17) vanish near zero, and then along the entire path. The endpoint values in (15) are exactly the original full primitive periods. This argument used the positive unfilled contraction, not the filling equation at intermediate parameters. ## 6. The endpoint solid torus At the endpoint, (1) and (5) give \[ U_v+p_vV_v=-2\pi i. 	ag{20} \] In the affine chart sending the two fixed points to zero and infinity, write upper-half-space coordinates as \((z,y)\), put \(r=y/|z|\), and use \[ \varrho=\operatorname{arsinh}(1/r),\qquad 	heta=\Im f_v,\qquad X=\Re f_v+	frac12\log(1+r^2). 	ag{21} \] Direct substitution into \(y^{-2}(|dz|^2+dy^2)\) gives \[ d\varrho^2+\cosh^2\varrho\,dX^2 +\sinh^2\varrho\,d	heta^2. 	ag{22} \] The original ideal end contains all sufficiently high vertical rays over its finitely many similarity triangles. Those triangles miss the second fixed point, and their quotient is compact. Thus the end contains a full punctured tube \(0<\varrho<\varrho_0\) in (21). The original primitive curve \(\mu_v+p_v\lambda_v\) has zero real period and angular period exactly \(-2\pi\). Its complementary curve is the original \(\lambda_v\), since the change of primitive basis has determinant one. Its positive real period is \[ \ell_v=\Re V_v=-2\Im t_v>0. 	ag{23} \] Adding the axis \(\varrho=0\) therefore gives a smooth solid torus with the prescribed primitive meridian, not a multiple cover or an unspecified slope. Its core length is \(\ell_v\). After performing this completion at every selected end, the remaining cusp ends are complete and the middle is compact. The resulting smooth metric is complete and has finite volume on the original marked filling \(Y(\mathbf p)\). Its universal local development covers simply connected hyperbolic space and is an isometry. This proves the geometric assertion of Theorem 1. Finally the original tetrahedron interiors partition the metric away from their faces and the completed cores, all of which have measure zero. Their volume sum is therefore the actual hyperbolic volume. The [pointwise volume identity](research_positive_edge_volume_identity.md) gives (6), including its absolute additive constant. ## 7. The explicit negative-corridor class **Corollary 2.** In an original circle tree, select a connected path with at least one outside end, with original selected degrees one or two. Fix negative crossing powers \(n_v=-b_v\), with \[ b_v\ge3\qquad(v\in S), 	ag{24} \] and retain the original carrier parity and integral slopes. Then the selected filling, with all other auxiliary cusps left complete, has its original marked hyperbolic structure. Its volume is given by (6). **Proof.** The [negative-corridor variational theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md), Theorem 15, gives an interior positive solution of (5) at unit charges. It also proves \(\Im t_v<0\). Theorem 1 applies. \(\square\) The threshold in (24) is independent of the number of selected vertices. The last two corner cases in the variational proof use an exact rational interval certificate; its full domain and reproducible bounds are given there. The original slopes and carrier conventions are unchanged. This is a geometric conclusion and does not supply a quantum asymptotic. If the phase includes only edges incident to the selected path, add \(8G=2v_{m oct}\) for each omitted complete original edge to the right side of (6). Several nonadjacent selected paths may be treated simultaneously: their incident edge sets are disjoint, even when they share an outside vertex. At that vertex the angle is zero, so all original interface maps and complete periods match in their recorded order. The full logarithmic period Jacobian at an interior solution is nonsingular: the real part of the return Jacobian is positive definite, whereas the crossing contribution is purely imaginary on the diagonal. Hence the implicit function theorem also gives the marked boundary deformation germ near this complete outside point, with all selected primitive periods fixed at (20). Positivity and the core length signs persist locally. No new meridian or longitude is chosen in this continuation. The theorem does not resolve arbitrary coefficients two and three in a negative corridor. The [exact rational normal form](research_definite_rational_corridor_normal_form.md) still retains those coefficients, boundary shifts and rotations. Nor does the geometric theorem establish saddle survival in the original finite quantum source. Those remain separate problems, and no cofinite assignment statement follows from this corollary. ## 8. Reproducing the original-coordinate checks The separate [checker](../experiments/check_positive_corridor_completion.py) solves sixteen original primitive systems in the explicit corridor class. It checks the logarithmic filling residuals, the core signs, the full rational face denominators and positive tetrahedron shapes along the tangent-radial contraction. It also compares the direct tetrahedron volumes with the calibrated stationary action. .venv/bin/python experiments/check_positive_corridor_completion.py \ --precision 110 --output /tmp/positive-corridor-completion-replay.json The [saved replay](../repro/results/research-positive-corridor-completion-root.json) records 900 positive edge checks along those contractions, at 110 decimal digits. Its script SHA256 is 1041957cc7a3ee5fb21133db3d92e6a1d789ec8266d8b4d005aafb11814e2b64. These are finite checks of the formulas and conventions. The marked topological completion and the uniform theorem are supplied by the written proof above.

# Proper Newton prefixes at a positive primitive filling Private written proof, 15 November 2026. At a positive solution of the original primitive filling equations, every proper group of incident edges has a nonzero period component in a fixed real direction. This excludes all algebraic divisors of the intermediate Newton labels, independently of the signed powers assigned to the group. A binary resolution that leaves one incident factor for the final complementary pairing therefore has no algebraically singular multiplication or single-crossing gate. This does not place the labels in the strips required by the original factorial asymptotics. It does not determine a coefficient in the original quantum integration cycle. ## 1. Comparing one endpoint with its complete value For an original positive edge use the canonical angles \(t,u\), returns \(r_t,r_u\), and coordinates \[ a=	an(t/2),\qquad b=	an(u/2),\qquad q^2=1+a^2+b^2. 	ag{1} \] The pinned positive-edge theorem gives the exact criterion \[ \Re q>\sqrt{(\Re a)^2+(\Re b)^2}, 	ag{2} \] and the global comparison \[ \Re\{\delta r_t\,\overline{\delta t} +\delta r_u\,\overline{\delta u}\}>0 	ag{3} \] for any two distinct positive configurations. Their joining segment need not remain positive. Its canonical branches satisfy \[ |\Re t|,|\Re u|<\pi,\qquad |\Im r_t|,|\Im r_u|<\pi/2. 	ag{4} \] **Lemma 1.** If \((t,u)\) is positive, so is \((0,u)\). If \(t
e0\), \[ \Re(r_t\overline t)>0. 	ag{5} \] **Proof.** Positivity excludes \(b\in i[1,\infty)\cup-i[1,\infty)\). Write \(b=x+iy\), and choose \(q_0=\sqrt{1+b^2}\) with positive real part. For \(x
e0\), the radicand is not a nonpositive real number, and \[ (\Re q_0)^2-x^2 = rac{|1+b^2|+1-|b|^2}{2}>0. 	ag{6} \] If \(|b|^2\le1\), positivity of the expression is immediate, with equality requiring the excluded values \(b=\pm i\). If \(|b|^2>1\), it follows from \[ |1+b^2|^2-(|b|^2-1)^2=4x^2>0. \] For \(x=0\), the excluded cuts give \(|y|<1\), so \(q_0=\sqrt{1-y^2}>0\). Hence \(\Re q_0>|\Re b|\) in all cases. This is criterion (2) at \((0,u)\). Its canonical first return is zero. Apply (3) to \((t,u)\) and \((0,u)\): the second angle is unchanged, and the first changes nontrivially. This gives (5). \(\square\) ## 2. A strip containing every proper prefix Fix a selected vertex of the original circle tree, and count its incident factors individually. Write its angle as \(t\), its returns as \(r_e\), and its real signed power as \(n\). Assume all its incident edges are positive and that its full marked period is \[ \sum_e r_e- rac{int}{2}=-\pi i. 	ag{7} \] For physical surgery \(n=\eta-2p\), with the original carrier \(\eta\). There is no new existence assertion here. We have \(t
e0\), since otherwise all its returns vanish and (7) fails. Lemma 1 makes every number \[ \ell_e=\Re(r_e\overline t) 	ag{8} \] strictly positive. Pairing (7) with \(\overline t\) gives \[ \sum_e\ell_e=-\pi\Im t. 	ag{9} \] Thus \(H=-\Im t>0\) follows from the stated hypotheses. For a nonempty proper edge subset \(A\) and any real allocation \(n_A\), put \[ R_A=\sum_{e\in A}r_e- rac{i n_A t}{2}. 	ag{10} \] An integer \(n_A\) is the actual signed number of crossing layers assigned to that partial product. **Theorem 2.** Every such prefix lies in the open convex strip \[ \mathcal S_t=\{R:0<\Re(R\overline t)<\pi H\}. 	ag{11} \] Consequently, for every integer \(k\), \[ R_A
e\pi i k,\qquad R_A
e it/2+\pi i k,\qquad R_A
e-it/2+\pi i k. 	ag{12} \] **Proof.** The allocation term in (10) has zero real pairing with \(t\). Therefore \[ \Re(R_A\overline t)=\sum_{e\in A}\ell_e. 	ag{13} \] The sum is positive and omits at least one positive term in (9). This proves (11). Each value excluded in (12) has real pairing \(-\pi kH\), outside the strict interval in (11). \(\square\) This is independent of the powers' signs and magnitudes, the number of incident factors, and the chosen binary tree. The proof uses the actual canonical returns, not arbitrary logarithms of eigenvalues. ## 3. Newton labels and multiplication divisors Keep \(a=	an(t/2)\). The positive canonical domain gives \(a
e0\) and \(1+a^2
e0\). Define \[ N(R)=a\cosh R+i\sinh R,\qquad D(R)=a\cosh R-i\sinh R,\qquad Y(R)=N(R)/D(R). 	ag{14} \] The original prefix dictionary in the pinned spectral-adapter note is \[ e^{2\pi i x_A}=Y(R_A),\qquad 	an(\pi x_A)=	anh(R_A)/a. 	ag{15} \] The exponential formula remains meaningful when the tangent formula has a pole. The label retains its continued logarithmic lift. The zeros of \(N\) and \(D\) are respectively \(R=it/2\pmod{\pi i}\) and \(R=-it/2\pmod{\pi i}\). This follows by exponentiating \(a=	an(t/2)\). Also \(Y(R)=1\) exactly when \(\sinh R=0\). Theorem 2 gives \[ Y(R_A)\in\mathbb C^*,\qquad \sin(\pi x_A)
e0. 	ag{16} \] The strip \(\mathcal S_t\) is simply connected, so its nonvanishing holomorphic function \(Y\) has a holomorphic logarithm. One prescribed value fixes that logarithm; other choices shift \(x_A\) by an integer. For \(c=-2\cos t\) and \(C(x)=2\cos(2\pi x)\), direct substitution also gives \[ C(x_A)-c=  rac{4a^2} {(1+a^2)(a^2\cosh^2R_A+\sinh^2R_A)}
e0. 	ag{17} \] The denominator is \((1+a^2)N(R_A)D(R_A)\). Thus there is no additional spectral-node collision. Consider a product with disjoint nonempty subsets \(A,B\), whose union is still proper. Allocated powers add, so its output return is \(R_A+R_B\). Denote its labels by \(x,y,z\). The seven arguments of the original multiplication factorials are \[ x,\ y,\ z,\ x+y,\ z-x,\ z-y,\ x+y-z. 	ag{18} \] **Corollary 3.** None of the seven sines of the arguments (18) vanishes at the stated positive primitive point. **Proof.** The individual prefix sines are nonzero by (16). For two returns \(\alpha, eta\), direct multiplication gives \[ N(\alpha)N( eta)-D(\alpha)D( eta) =2ia\sinh(\alpha+ eta), 	ag{19} \] \[  egin{split} &N(\alpha)N( eta)D(\alpha+ eta) -D(\alpha)D( eta)N(\alpha+ eta)\ &\hspace{12mm}=2i(1+a^2)\sinh\alpha\,\sinh eta\, \sinh(\alpha+ eta). \end{split} 	ag{20} \] All denominator factors are nonzero. Equation (19) excludes \(e^{2\pi i(x+y)}=1\); (20) excludes \(e^{2\pi i(x+y-z)}=1\). Finally, \[ Y(R)= rac{(a+i)e^{2R}+a-i}{(a-i)e^{2R}+a+i} 	ag{21} \] is a Möbius function of \(e^{2R}\), with determinant \(4ia
e0\). Hence \(Y(\alpha+ eta)=Y(\alpha)\) would force \(e^{2 eta}=1\), and \(Y(\alpha+ eta)=Y( eta)\) would force \(e^{2\alpha}=1\). Both are excluded by Theorem 2. These are the divisors for \(z-x\) and \(z-y\). \(\square\) ## 4. Signed crossings and a regular algebraic resolution A single crossing of sign \(\sigma=\pm1\) changes a proper-prefix return by \[ R\longmapsto R-i\sigma t/2. 	ag{22} \] Both returns remain in \(\mathcal S_t\), so their input and output label sines are nonzero. The sine of their difference is also nonzero: equality of their clocks would, by (21), force \(e^{-i\sigma t}=1\), contrary to \(\Im t<0\). For an integer physical crossing power, any selected vertex of degree at least two has a direct algebraically regular resolution. Leave one incident factor for the final complementary Frobenius pairing. Multiply the other factors by any binary tree, apply the required signed crossing layers, and perform that pairing. Every gate prefix has a nonempty proper edge set, so all the preceding exclusions apply. The degree-two zero-power expression has no gate to check. Distributing crossing layers among other proper subproducts gives the same divisor exclusions. These are exact operations in the full original Newton algebra. Multiplication is associative and commutative; crossing powers are literal multiplications by \(R^n\); signed powers fuse exactly. The final pairing remains \(\phi_N(e_i e_j)=\mathbf1_{i+j=N-1}\), including all repeated-node normal data. No factors or normals are discarded. The rational fiber Hessians displayed in the spectral-adapter note are consequently finite and nonzero at these labels. Every sine in their formulas is among those just checked, their exponential factors are units, and \((2-c)/4=1/(1+a^2)
e0\). This is an algebraic statement about those formulas, not a factorial asymptotic outside its proved domain. ## 5. Remaining analytic and endpoint questions The complete edge set, with its full power, has return \(-\pi i\) on the boundary of (11). It is handled by the complementary pairing, not as a strict multiplication gate. A degree-one vertex has no nonempty proper subset, so this theorem supplies no degree-one endpoint chart. The theorem removes genuine algebraic prefix resonance as an additional obstruction at an existing positive primitive point. It does not prove that every hyperbolic partial filling has such a positive point. There is a separate analytic question. When \(\Re t
e0\), the strip (11) is oblique and its boundary generally has a non-real image under (14). A holomorphic logarithm on (11) does not by itself place the real parts of all arguments (18), or the crossing arguments, between zero and one. The continued primitive and its integer Fourier characters must still be matched to a domain where the original factorial interpolation has the required asymptotics. No label is reset here. Even a valid factorial comparison and local Morse equivalence do not determine the geometric block's coefficient in the original finite cycle. Endpoints, other Fourier modes and the full coherent contraction remain. No new volume limit or knot family is asserted. ## Direct sources * notes/research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md, SHA256 da5129c7110190035eedb8249d4004dd06b5a7555e78d948234d8de50fa17500: canonical branches, inverse-tangent cut exclusion, positivity, global comparison, and full marked primitive periods. * notes/research_newton_spectral_legendre_adapters.md, SHA256 34c0e2e1114488c6ac82a5dffbdbd8a4a8d85e7fbba252de91833dc8d697e303: original prefix dictionary and crossing increment, multiplication and crossing generating families, and their fiber Hessians. * notes/research_corner_newton_source_transport.md, SHA256 24a7f6f721d0a925405424d9a8aba1ac9db8ce7e90ddb937b2a317e10f98b345: full Newton algebra, signed layers and transpose convention, exact crossing transport, and original integer cycles. * notes/actual_positive_newton_multiplication.md, SHA256 543b5be6035ecec349ce8e78ee47085345ceefe4fc51e5f2005b802d999805bb: original multiplication factorials, complementary pairing and associativity in the full repeated-root algebra. Only written reasoning, source-text reads and file hashes were used. No mathematical code, numerical evaluation, tests or compilation were run. Frozen and public files were not changed.

title: Full physical fold windows on a positive product chart
text: # Full physical fold windows on a positive product chart Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The common product baseline can be normalized through the simultaneous complete fold using the actual three-fifths kernel theorem. This supplies the missing nearby physical values and independent first normals, with exponentially small normalized errors. The comparison uses the canonical kernel only on a small complete bidisk. Outside that bidisk it uses the actual physical-row bounds, rather than an off-grid bound for the canonical kernel. An exact two-line repair then includes a whole fixed fold window. A closed contour around both angular lifts, with its factor one-half, retains every double spectral normal and the odd simple value. No evenness of the repaired representative or equality of arbitrary free-color functions is asserted. Exterior sides and real interfaces remain. ## 1. Original data and the common baseline Use the original normalization \[ N\ge2,\quad h=N^{-1},\quad \eta=(-1)^{N-1},\quad X_j=(j+\tfrac12)h,\quad C(X)=2\cos(2\pi X),\quad t(X)=\pi-2\pi X,\quad P_N(z)=2T_N(z/2)+2, \tag{1} \] and \(K_N(z,w)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e_k(z)e_k(w)\). Put \(J_N=\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor\). Its distinct physical rows are \[ c_a=C(X_a),\qquad F_a(w)=K_N(c_a,w),\qquad 0\le a\le J_N. \tag{2} \] For \(a\le\lfloor(N-2)/2\rfloor\), the original independent normal is \(G_a(w)=\partial_zK_N(c_a,w)\). Retain the pinned pole-free representative \(\widehat G_a(w)\). It has exactly the value and required first spectral normal of \(G_a\) at every physical second endpoint. It is holomorphic on \(\mathbb C\setminus[2,\infty)\); it is not the canonical normal polynomial at an arbitrary untraced endpoint. Fix a positive pair and its product domains from the pinned product gluing theorem. Shrink to buffered inner angular domains \(\mathcal U_t,\mathcal U_u\) containing zero and the target. They are bounded and connected, lie in the original angular strips, and retain the single original phase \(\psi(t,u)\). All compact estimates below are taken with fixed larger buffers in those domains. The baseline of that theorem is denoted by \(H_N(t,u)\); it is already phase normalized: \[ U_N(t,u)=e^{N\psi(t,u)}H_N(t,u),\qquad \sup_K|H_N|\le e^{o_K(N)}. \tag{3} \] The baseline is holomorphic through \((0,0)\), but this fact alone does not prescribe any fold data. Choose the common positive real seed intervals used to construct \(H_N\) inside a sufficiently small complete disk. More precisely, choose fixed numbers \[ 0<\rho_0<\rho_1<R<3/5 \tag{4} \] such that the closed \(R\)-disk lies inside both buffered inner angular domains. The two positive real seed intervals lie in \((0,\rho_0)\), with fixed positive length and all required buffers. These choices are possible because the product domains contain a neighborhood of zero. The common baseline theorem then gives exponentially small errors in its two original bulk row families, as holomorphic functions of the other parameter. ## 2. Actual complete-disk comparison The pinned three-fifths theorem concerns the full canonical polynomial: \[ K_N(-2\cos t,-2\cos u) =N^{-3/2}a(t,u)e^{N\psi(t,u)} (1+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-1})), \qquad a(t,u)\ne0. \tag{5} \] It holds on a neighborhood of the closed three-fifths bidisk, at both parities and with all fixed ordinary spectral derivatives, including the ramification at \(t=0\) or \(u=0\).
