title: The local primitive-filling coefficient is an algebraic unit
text:
# The local primitive-filling coefficient is an algebraic unit Private written proof, 15 November 2026. The original circle-tree source determines a particularly simple divisor for its local primitive-charge Gaussian coefficient. On its regular marked chart, that coefficient has no zero except a selected zero-angle factor. This rules out all-order cancellation *inside that local Morse block*. It does not identify the coefficient with which the original finite source selects the block. ## 1. The original boundary source and the local chart Let \(\mathcal T=(V,E)\) be an original ordered circle tree with at least one edge, and let \(\varnothing
e S\subseteq V\) be a set of filled vertices. Write \(k=|S|\), let \(E_S\) contain every edge with at least one endpoint in \(S\), and put \(m=|E_S|\). The set need not be connected. For \(v\in S\), let \(d_v\) be its original tree degree. For \(w
otin S\), put \(d_S(w)=\#\{vw\in E:v\in S\}\). Retain every original signed crossing power \(n_v\), including its carrier. At complete main color and levels \(N\ge3\), define \[ K_N(t,u)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e_j(-2\cos t)e_j(-2\cos u), \qquad \mathcal D_{n,N}f=\phi_N(R^nf). 	ag{1} \] The exact boundary polynomial of the filled region is \[ Z_{S,N}(\mathbf u)= \left(\prod_{v\in S}\mathcal D_{n_v,N}^{(v)}ight) \prod_{e=vw\in E_S}K_N(t_v,t_w), \qquad t_w=u_w\quad(w
otin S). 	ag{2} \] The raw product is reduced only by the actual vertex traces. In particular (2) includes their first Hermite normals. It follows directly by leaving the outside vertex factors open in the original finite contraction \(\mathrm{cta:exact	ext{-}source}\). Use tangent and edge coordinates \[ a_v=	an(t_v/2),\qquad q_e^2=1+a_v^2+a_w^2. 	ag{3} \] Choose the component and continued logarithms marked at \(a=0,q_e=1\). The regular open conditions used below are \[ 1+a_v^2
e0\quad(v\in V),\qquad q_e(q_e^2+1)
e0\quad(e\in E_S). 	ag{4} \] On the complete-parameter slice \(a_{V\setminus S}=0\), this is the incident-edge restriction of the regular cover in [the partial-boundary component note](research_partial_boundary_edge_cover_component.md). One may instead fix regular outside angles and retain the same local marked formulas. No arbitrary representation is asserted to admit these coordinates. Let \(\psi(t_v,t_w)\) be the original continued edge action and set \[  egin{aligned} \Psi(\mathbf t,\mathbf u)&=\sum_{e\in E_S}\psi(t_v,t_w),\ F(\mathbf t,\mathbf u)&=\Psi(\mathbf t,\mathbf u) + rac{i}{4\pi}\sum_{v\in S}n_vt_v^2-i\sum_{v\in S}t_v,\ r_{v,e}&= rac12\log rac{q_e+a_v}{q_e-a_v},\qquad \mathcal P_v=\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e}- rac{i n_v}{2}t_v,\qquad J=\left( rac{\partial\mathcal P_v}{\partial t_w}ight)_{v,w\in S}. \end{aligned} 	ag{5} \] The logarithms are continued, not replaced by principal values at the endpoint. The derivative identity \(\psi_{t_v}=-r_{v,e}/\pi\) gives \[ F_{t_v}=- rac{\mathcal P_v+\pi i}{\pi},\qquad -F_{\mathbf t\mathbf t}=J/\pi. 	ag{6} \] Thus the primitive filling equations are exactly the stationary equations \(\mathcal P_v=-\pi i\). The selected Jacobian is the actual primitive-period Jacobian, with the outside angles fixed. ## 2. Simplifying the original edge half-density The canonical factorial interpolation of the original Newton sum has wire phase \(B_e(x;t,u)=b(x,t)+b(x,u)\). Its branch at completeness has \(x_*=1/4\). The original stationary equation is \[ \cos(2\pi x_*)= rac{1-\cos t\cos u}{2+\cos t+\cos u} = rac{q_e^2-1}{q_e^2+1}. 	ag{7} \] Consequently \(\cot(\pi x_*)=q_e\) on the marked logarithmic lift. Write \(a=	an(t/2)\), \(b=	an(u/2)\), and \(q=q_e\). Then \[ \sin^2(\pi x_*)= rac1{1+q^2},\qquad -B_{e,xx}(x_*;t,u) = rac{2\pi q(1+q^2)^2}{(1+a^2)(1+b^2)}. 	ag{8} \] For the second equality, substitute (7) into the original formula \[ B_{e,xx}=-2\pi\sum_{\xi=t,u} \left\{ rac{\sin(2\pi x)}{\cos(2\pi x)+\cos\xi} +\cot(\pi x)ight\}. \] The two fractions become \(q(1+a^2)/(1+b^2)\) and its endpoint interchange. Their sum with \(2q\) is \(q(1+q^2)^2/((1+a^2)(1+b^2))\). All quantities in (8) are nonzero on (4). The original sine factors in the factorial interpolation are also nonzero there: at the saddle their possible additional zeros are \(q\pm a=0\) or \(q\pm b=0\), whereas \((q-a)(q+a)=1+b^2\) and \((q-b)(q+b)=1+a^2\). Thus its local formal Gaussian coefficients continue on the marked logarithmic and half-density covers. This is continuation of formal coefficients; it is not an extension of a finite-sum asymptotic domain. The original leading edge coefficient is \[ \alpha_e=  rac{\sqrt{2\pi}} {4\sin^2(\pi x_*)\sqrt{-B_{e,xx}(x_*;t,u)}}. \] Its square therefore simplifies exactly to \[  oxed{\alpha_e^2=  rac{(1+a_v^2)(1+a_w^2)}{16q_e}.} 	ag{9} \] The marked square root has \(\alpha_e(0,0)=1/4\). In particular the edge coefficient is a unit on (4), without a positivity premise. ## 3. The full Hermite trace fixes the primitive-charge prefactor Put \(\mathfrak q_N=e^{\pi i/N}\), \(\eta=(-1)^{N-1}\), and \(C_{N,n}=\mathfrak q_N^{n(N-1)^2/4}\). The exact complete trace for an arbitrary-degree even polynomial \(f(t)\) is \[ \mathcal D_{n,N}f=\eta C_{N,n}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}g'(	au_j), \quad g(t)=\sin t\,f(t)e^{inNt^2/(4\pi)}, \quad 	au_j= rac{\pi(N-1-2j)}N. 	ag{10} \] After pairing the upper and lower horizontal sides, its exact lower contour contribution is \[ - rac{N^2C_{N,n}}{\pi i} \int g(t)W_N(t)\,dt, \qquad W_N(t)= rac{e^{-iNt}}{(1-\eta e^{-iNt})^2} =\sum_{\ell\ge1}\ell\eta^{\ell-1}e^{-i\ell Nt}. 	ag{11} \] The exact vertical endpoint current is retained separately in the source identity. Formula (11) has unit coefficient for charge one at both parities. It is the double-pole kernel of the full Hermite trace, not an ordinary value-sampling trace. Apply (11) in every selected variable of (2), and take the charge-one term in each horizontal kernel. For its *local formal Gaussian block* at a specified stationary point \(\mathbf t_*\), the wire factors contribute \(N^{-3m/2}\prod_e\alpha_e\), and the angle Gaussian contributes \((2\pi/N)^{k/2}/\sqrt{\det(-F'')}\). Including all trace factors gives \[ \mathfrak G_{S,N}= \left(\prod_{v\in S}C_{N,n_v}ight) N^{3(k-m)/2}e^{NF(\mathbf t_*,\mathbf u)} \left(A_0+N^{-1}A_1+\cdotsight), 	ag{12} \] where \[ A_0=\left(- rac1{\pi i}ight)^k(2\pi)^{k/2}  rac{\prod_{e\in E_S}\alpha_e\, \prod_{v\in S}\sin t_{*,v}} {\sqrt{\det[-F''(\mathbf t_*,\mathbf u)]}}. 	ag{13} \] The square roots include the continued local contour orientation. Equation (12) defines the local formal block; it is deliberately not an asserted asymptotic expansion of \(Z_{S,N}\). When \(S\) is connected with \(b\) boundary edges, \(m=k-1+b\), so the power in (12) is \(-3(b-1)/2\), agreeing with the original boundary source normalization. The finite turn scalars and the final writhe factor remain those of \(\mathrm{cta:exact	ext{-}source}\). At complete main color the edge factors \(H_N/W_j\), \(H_N\), and turn scalars equal one; the remaining writhe and displayed \(C_{N,n_v}\) factors are nonzero phases. None is absorbed by division by an unknown invariant. ## 4. The explicit local coefficient theorem **Theorem.** Suppose a point on (4), with the retained logarithmic marks, satisfies \(\mathcal P_v=-\pi i\) for all \(v\in S\), \(\det J
e0\), and \(a_v
e0\) for every selected vertex. The original local primitive-charge block (12) has nonzero leading coefficient. More precisely, \[  oxed{ A_0^2= rac{(-8)^k}{16^m}\,  rac{ \displaystyle\prod_{v\in S}a_v^2(1+a_v^2)^{d_v-2} \displaystyle\prod_{w
otin S}(1+a_w^2)^{d_S(w)} }{ \displaystyle\left(\prod_{e\in E_S}q_eight)\det J }.} 	ag{14} \] The square is a rational unit on that regular primitive critical chart. The coefficient itself is a unit on its retained half-density cover. No restriction on the sizes or signs of the fixed \(n_v\) is required for this local statement. **Proof.** Square (13), use (6), and retain the complex signs: \[ \left(- rac1{\pi i}ight)^{2k}(2\pi)^k\pi^k=(-2)^k. \] Now substitute (9) and \(\sin^2t_v=4a_v^2/(1+a_v^2)^2\). Each incident edge supplies one factor \(1+a_v^2\) at its endpoint. The selected exponent is therefore \(d_v-2\), and the outside exponent is \(d_S(w)\). This gives (14). All its numerator and denominator factors are units under the stated hypotheses, including when \(d_v=1\). \(\square\) On a supplied positive geometric filling with the original core condition \(\operatorname{Im}t_v<0\), the selected zero-angle exclusion follows automatically. The theorem does not establish that an arbitrary hyperbolic short filling admits this chart, a positive decomposition, or the nonsingular Jacobian condition. ## 5. Formal exactness and the remaining source map For clarity, at an isolated holomorphic Morse point the complete local stationary series detects formal twisted exactness. Choose local Morse coordinates with phase \(F_*-\sum y_i^2/2\), put \(h=N^{-1}\), and include the coordinate Jacobian in a top density \(f(y,h)\,dy\). The normalized Gaussian functional is \[ \mathcal E(f)= \left.\exp\left( rac h2\sum_i\partial_{y_i}^2ight) f(y,h)ight|_{y=0}. 	ag{15} \] It is well defined coefficientwise for holomorphic germs formal in \(h\). Integration by parts gives \(\mathcal E((h\partial_{y_i}-y_i)b)=0\). Conversely, split the constant coefficient of \(f\) as its value at zero plus \(\sum_i y_i b_i\). Replacing \(y_i b_i\) by \(h\partial_{y_i}b_i\) modulo these currents and repeating in successive powers of \(h\) gives \[ \ker\mathcal E= \sum_i(h\partial_{y_i}-y_i)\mathcal O_y[[h]]. 	ag{16} \] Thus the local top twisted de Rham quotient is the rank-one \(\mathbb C[[h]]\) module detected by (15). This statement is formal; it asserts neither convergence of the current primitives nor an equality of analytic global relative periods. By (14), the local density in (12) has a nonzero class in this quotient, already at leading order. Odd-moment cancellation cannot annihilate its entire Gaussian series. The source's zero-charge sector illustrates why the trace still matters: (10) is a total derivative, so its zero Fourier mode has zero local stationary series to every order. The factor \(\ell\) in (11) records exactly this cancellation. A positive edge amplitude before taking the trace does not remove it. Finally, neither (14) nor (16) makes the original finite source a faithful pairing on this local quotient. The selected source still contains the wire lattice modes, all endpoint currents, the other angular charges, the prescribed exterior, and its actual closing. No source-compatible map identifying its geometric contribution with (12) has been proved here. All-order vanishing of a *selected scalar* therefore cannot be used to infer that this already nonzero local class is exact. That inference would first need the missing comparison with the original relative cycle. The explicit divisor (14) separates the local question from that remaining comparison. ## Pinned sources and directly used statements All derivations above are written algebra and formal Gaussian reduction. No mathematical code or numerical experiment was used. * `papers/circle-tree-volume/finite-bounds.tex`, SHA256 `e4cf66544703af6d9a78208deae971c4d9f4367ba4b2ad660694ee489ef67ea1`: the full original vertex contraction, Newton pairing, physical turn factors, reduced cut, and final framing normalization. * `papers/circle-tree-volume/edge-packet.tex`, SHA256 `53eb6dbfbda3ca639db35911ed50947c29655840337f9d1f1ce909d435013dbb`: the canonical factorial interpolation, original wire stationary equation and curvature, calibrated edge action, and normalized leading edge coefficient. Its finite-sum domain is not enlarged. * `notes/research_exact_complete_trace_contour.md`, SHA256 `a63c66e8078457fa84e8044dc876beca36126348e816de9c6997d2a2610474e8`: the all-degree derivative trace, both-parity double-pole kernel, exact paired horizontal prefactor and retained endpoint current. * `notes/research_partial_boundary_edge_cover_component.md`, SHA256 `f3fdc37ee25b537680a96747ff40a746054b44ecb3bdd09f5fe246f5d29e762d`: the marked component and regular edge coordinates, literal peripheral multipliers, continued logarithmic primitive equations, and their rational selected Jacobian. Its limitations on inclusion, logarithmic continuation and cycle survival are retained here.

title: A uniform bound for one cap in its moment norm
status: Uniform finite norm bound; both parities
text: # A uniform bound for one cap in its moment norm A cap is the part of the finite source at a crossing region next to the marked strand. Two adjacent face variables there are prescribed to be zero; the other two carry the original coefficient targets. After all other variables have been extracted, the cap acts as a linear functional on a finite list of coefficients. This note proves that its norm grows at most polynomially with the level, uniformly as its real spectral parameter varies between \(-2\) and \(2\). The inner product uses a full moment matrix, so it retains the mixed terms between different coefficients. The theorem holds at both level parities. To turn it into a bound by hyperbolic volume, one would also have to bound the norm of the remaining coefficients. That is a separate problem; the last section explains why the present estimate alone does not solve it. ## 1. Original coefficients and the assertion Let \(N\ge2\), and define \[ d=N-1,\qquad M=\lfloor N/2\rfloor-1,\qquad \theta=\frac{\pi}{N},\qquad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\theta),\qquad s_j=2\sin(j\theta),\qquad S_j=\prod_{r=1}^j s_r. \tag{1} \] Empty products are one. The original protected left coefficient, including every unused spectral row, is \[ v_j(\sigma)=(-1)^jS_j^2\prod_{r=j+1}^{d}(\sigma-c_r), \qquad 0\le j\le M. \tag{2} \] Put \[ U_0=\csc^2(\theta/2),\qquad b_k=\prod_{r=1}^k\frac{\sin(r\theta)}{\sin((r+1/2)\theta)}, \qquad h_k=b_k^2,\qquad H=(h_{i+j})_{0\le i,j\le M},\qquad g_j(\sigma)=\frac{(-1)^jv_j(\sigma)}{U_0}. \tag{3} \] Thus \(H=H_0\circ H_0\), where \(H_0=(b_{i+j})\) and the circle denotes entrywise multiplication. This is the coupled Gram matrix, not an unrestricted tensor-product Gram matrix. It is positive definite by the exact positive moment construction recalled below. **Theorem.** For every \(N\ge2\) and every real \(\sigma\in[-2,2]\), \[ \boxed{\qquad \kappa_N(\sigma):=g(\sigma)^T H^{-1}g(\sigma) \le e^{210}N^5 . \qquad} \tag{4} \] The constants are deliberately coarse. The proof retains \[ 2M=N-2\quad(N\ \text{even}),\qquad 2M=N-3\quad(N\ \text{odd}). \tag{5} \] In particular it does not ask for a nonexistent moment of order \(N\). The case \(N=2\) is immediate: \(M=0\), \(H=(1)\), \(g_0(\sigma)=\sigma/2\), and \(\kappa_2(\sigma)\le1\). The rest of the proof assumes \(N\ge3\). ## 2. A sine-Cauchy Gram matrix Introduce a comparison matrix \[ C_{ij}=\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin((i+j+1)\theta)} =\frac{N\sin\theta}{\pi} \int_0^\infty\frac{t^{i+j}}{1+t^N}\,dt . \tag{6} \] The integral follows by substituting \(y=t^N\) in the elementary beta integral. It is finite because \(i+j\le2M\le N-2\). Consequently \(C\) is positive definite. Its measure is a probability measure and has density at least \(1/\pi\) on \([0,1]\): here \(N\sin(\pi/N)\ge2\) and \(1+t^N\le2\). For a polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(M\), expansion in the shifted Legendre polynomials gives \[ \max_{0\le t\le1}|p(t)|^2 \le (M+1)^2\int_0^1|p(t)|^2\,dt. \tag{7} \] Indeed the shifted polynomial of degree \(r\) has squared norm \(1/(2r+1)\) and absolute value at most one on this interval; Cauchy--Schwarz sums \(\sum_{r=0}^M(2r+1)=(M+1)^2\). This proof applies to complex coefficients. In particular evaluation at zero, as a functional on the \(C\) norm, satisfies \[ (C^{-1})_{00}\le\pi(M+1)^2 . \tag{8} \] Let \(A\) be the real lower bidiagonal matrix \[ A_{jj}=c_j,\qquad A_{j,j-1}=s_j^2\quad(1\le j\le M). \tag{9} \] It satisfies the exact matrix identity \[ AC=CA^T. \tag{10} \] To check this, put \(k=i+j\). For \(k\ge1\) the difference of the two entries is \[ (c_i-c_j)\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin((k+1)\theta)} +(s_i^2-s_j^2)\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin(k\theta)}=0. \tag{11} \] The equality uses \(c_i-c_j=-4\sin((k+1)\theta)\sin((i-j)\theta)\) and \(s_i^2-s_j^2=4\sin(k\theta)\sin((i-j)\theta)\). At \(i=j=0\) both sides agree directly; no division by \(\sin0\) is used. Thus \(A\) is self-adjoint for the inner product with matrix \(C^{-1}\). Equivalently \(C^{-1/2}AC^{1/2}\) is a real symmetric matrix. Its eigenvalues are the distinct numbers \(c_0,\ldots,c_M\). The full spectral polynomial, with its original repeated roots, is \[ \chi_N(z)=\prod_{r=0}^{d}(z-c_r) =2\bigl(T_N(z/2)+1\bigr). \tag{12} \] Here \(T_N(\cos a)=\cos(Na)\). For real \(z\in[-2,2]\), \[ |\chi_N'(z)|\le N^2. \tag{13} \] For example, differentiating gives \(\chi_N'(z)=N U_{N-1}(z/2)\); the geometric-sum formula for \(\sin(Na)/\sin a\) gives \(|U_{N-1}|\le N\), including its endpoint limits. The original coefficient recurrence is \[ (\sigma-c_j)g_j=s_j^2g_{j-1}\quad(j\ge1),\qquad (\sigma-c_0)g_0=\chi_N(\sigma)/U_0. \tag{14} \] For a fixed \(\sigma\), let \[ q_\sigma(z)=\frac{\chi_N(\sigma)-\chi_N(z)}{\sigma-z}, \tag{15} \] interpreted as a polynomial divided difference. Since \(\chi_N(A)=0\), equation (14), first away from its finitely many nodes and then by polynomial continuation, gives \[ g(\sigma)=U_0^{-1}q_\sigma(A)e_0. \tag{16} \] For every eigenvalue \(c_j\) of \(A\), the mean-value bound (13) implies \[ |q_\sigma(c_j)|\le N^2 \qquad(-2\le\sigma\le2). \tag{17} \] This includes \(\sigma=c_j\); there is no resolvent singularity in (15). The finite-dimensional spectral theorem in the \(C^{-1}\) inner product therefore yields \[ \begin{aligned} g(\sigma)^T C^{-1}g(\sigma) &\le \frac{N^4}{U_0^2}(C^{-1})_{00}\\ &\le\frac{\pi^5}{16}(M+1)^2. \end{aligned} \tag{18} \] The last step uses \(U_0\ge4N^2/\pi^2\). This estimate is for the complete source vector \(g\), not for its two separated spectral factors. ## 3. A quantitative lower density for the original coupled measure The exact beta-product construction of the protected moments has the following form. Let \(T_1,T_2\) be independent \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1/2)\) variables. Independently, for \(k\ge1\) and \(\ell=1,2\), take \[ A_{k,\ell}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(kN-1/2,1/2),\qquad B_{k,\ell}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(kN+1,1/2),\qquad G=\prod_{k\ge1}\prod_{\ell=1}^2\frac{B_{k,\ell}}{A_{k,\ell}}, \qquad X=T_1T_2G. \tag{19} \] All factors are independent. The product is defined by the convergent series of logarithms. The beta integral and Euler's sine product give \[ \mathbb E X^j=h_j\qquad(0\le j\le d). \tag{20} \] These are precisely the original cap moments. To recall why the infinite product is legitimate, a beta ratio pair has logarithmic mean and variance of order \((kN)^{-2}\). Its real moments on compact subsets of \(-1<s<N-1/2\) have logarithms of the same summable order. The log series converges in \(L^2\), and a slightly larger positive moment gives uniform integrability at each integer \(j\le d\). Thus (20) follows from finite products, not from an unproved interchange of an infinite product and an integral. This is the original positive-moment theorem; the estimates below quantify its density. Here are explicit bounds sufficient for that purpose. If \(Y_a\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,1/2)\) and \(f(a)=\mathbb E\log Y_a\), then \[ f(a)=-\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-at}}{1+e^{-t/2}}\,dt,\qquad 0<f'(a)=\operatorname{Var}(\log Y_a)\le a^{-2}, \qquad |f(a)|\le a^{-1}. \tag{21} \] These formulas follow by differentiating the beta integral, or by expanding the usual difference of the two logarithmic gamma derivatives as a convergent integral. The displayed estimates follow immediately from the integral and its derivative. Since \(kN-1/2\ge5kN/6\), (21) gives for each ratio in (19) \[ 0\le\mathbb E\log(B_{k,\ell}/A_{k,\ell}) \le\frac{3}{(kN)^2},\qquad \operatorname{Var}\log(B_{k,\ell}/A_{k,\ell}) \le\frac{3}{(kN)^2}. \tag{22} \] Summing and using \(\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}<2\) gives \[ 0\le\mathbb E\log G\le12N^{-2},\qquad \operatorname{Var}\log G\le12N^{-2}. \tag{23} \] Remove just one inverse-beta factor and put \(G_*=A_{1,1}G\). The variable \(G_*\) is independent of \(A_{1,1},T_1,T_2\). Its logarithmic variance is at most that of \(G\), and its logarithmic mean lies between \(-1/(N-1/2)\) and \(12/N^2\). Chebyshev's inequality, with displacement \(8/N\) from the respective means, proves \[ \mathbb P(|\log G|\le24/N)\ge3/4,\qquad \mathbb P(|\log G_*|\le24/N)\ge3/4. \tag{24} \] For example the failure probability is at most \(12/64<1/4\), and the absolute mean is at most \(4/N\). We now prove the density bound \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{d\mu_N}{dt}(t)\ge \frac{e^{-200}}{N^2} \begin{cases} 1,&0<t\le1,\\ t^{-N-1/2},&t\ge1, \end{cases} \quad} \tag{25} \] where \(\mu_N\) is the law of \(X\). Densities and their inequalities may be read almost everywhere, which suffices for all ensuing integrals. First, the product \(Y=T_1T_2\) has density \[ f_Y(y)=\frac14\int_y^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{1-x}\sqrt{x-y}} \ge\frac{\pi}{4}\qquad(0<y<1). \tag{26} \] The last integral without \(1/\sqrt x\) is \(\pi\), and \(1/\sqrt x\ge1\). For \(0<t\le e^{-24/N}\), condition on the first event in (24). Then \(t/G\le1\), \(G^{-1}\ge e^{-24/N}\ge e^{-8}\), and \[ f_X(t)\ge (3\pi/16)e^{-8}. \tag{27} \] For the remaining \(t\), write \(X=R/A_{1,1}\), where \(R=T_1T_2G_*\). Since the \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1/2)\) density is at least \(1/2\), each event \[ e^{-60/N}\le T_\ell\le e^{-50/N} \tag{28} \] has probability at least \(5e^{-20}/N\). Together with the second event in (24), these independent events have probability at least \((75/4)e^{-40}N^{-2}\) and imply \[ e^{-144/N}\le R\le e^{-76/N}. \tag{29} \] Set \(a=N-1/2\). The conditional density of \(R/A_{1,1}\) at \(t>R\) is \[ \frac{R^a}{B(a,1/2)}\,t^{-a-1}(1-R/t)^{-1/2}. \tag{30} \] Here \(B(a,1/2)\le B(1,1/2)=2\). If \(t\ge e^{-24/N}\), all values of \(R\) in (29) satisfy \(R<t\) and \(R^a\ge e^{-144}\). Equations (29)--(30) therefore give \[ f_X(t)\ge\frac{75}{8}\, e^{-184}N^{-2}t^{-N-1/2}. \tag{31} \] For \(t\le1\) the last power is at least one. The bounds (27),(31) imply (25), with ample room in the numerical constant. The different tail powers in (6) and (25) are essential. There is no assertion that \(\mu_N\) pointwise dominates a constant multiple of the sine-Cauchy measure on the whole half-line. ## 4. The finite-degree tail comparison We first record an elementary weighted inequality. If \(q\) has degree at most \(M\) and \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}\), then \[ \int_0^1 |q(t)|^2t^\alpha\,dt \le2\sqrt2(M+1) \int_0^1 |q(t)|^2t^{\alpha+1/2}\,dt. \tag{32} \] For \(\alpha=0\), put \(\delta=1/[2(M+1)^2]\). Inequality (7) shows that the interval \([0,\delta]\) contains at most half the unweighted squared norm. The remaining half lies where \(t^{1/2}\ge\sqrt\delta\), proving (32). For \(\alpha=1\), write \(A_r=\int_0^1|q(t)|^2t^r\,dt\). The same argument first gives \(A_1\ge A_0/[4(M+1)^2]\); hence (7) implies \(\|q\|_\infty^2\le4(M+1)^4A_1\). It follows that \[ \int_0^\delta t|q(t)|^2\,dt \le \frac{\delta^2}{2}\|q\|_\infty^2 \le \frac12 A_1 . \tag{33} \] Again the remaining half has the extra weight at least \(\sqrt\delta\). This proves (32) also for complex coefficients. For a polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(M\), define its reversal \(q(t)=t^M p(t^{-1})\). Substitution \(t=1/x\) shows \[ \begin{aligned} \int_1^\infty |p(x)|^2x^{-N}\,dx &=\int_0^1|q(t)|^2t^{N-2M-2}\,dt,\\ \int_1^\infty |p(x)|^2x^{-N-1/2}\,dx &=\int_0^1|q(t)|^2t^{N-2M-3/2}\,dt . \end{aligned} \tag{34} \] The first exponent is exactly \(0\) at even levels and \(1\) at odd levels. Therefore (32) compares precisely these two tails. Since \(N\sin\theta/\pi\le1\), equations (6),(25),(32)--(34) yield, for every coefficient vector \(p\), \[ \begin{aligned} p^*Cp &\le \int_0^1|p(t)|^2\,dt +\int_1^\infty|p(t)|^2t^{-N}\,dt\\ &\le 2\sqrt2(M+1)e^{200}N^2\,p^*Hp . \end{aligned} \tag{35} \] Thus the required finite-dimensional matrix comparison is \[ H\succeq \frac{e^{-200}}{2\sqrt2(M+1)N^2}\,C . \tag{36} \] This is a comparison of quadratic forms on the original finite cutoff. The proof explicitly uses that cutoff to compensate for the tail discrepancy; entrywise moment comparisons would not prove (36). ## 5. The coupled bound and its precise source implication Inverting the positive matrices in (36) and applying (18) gives \[ \begin{aligned} \kappa_N(\sigma) &\le 2\sqrt2(M+1)e^{200}N^2 \frac{\pi^5}{16}(M+1)^2\\ &\le \frac{\sqrt2\,\pi^5}{64}\,e^{200}N^5 <e^{210}N^5 . \end{aligned} \tag{37} \] This proves (4) for both parities and every real spectral value, including repeated nodes and the odd simple endpoint. No separation into the two one-factor spectral functionals is used. To state the actual coefficient consequence, retain the original spectator targets and write the resulting homogeneous polynomial as \[ B(x,c)=\sum_{k=0}^d B_kx^kc^{d-k},\qquad a_j=(-1)^jB_{d-j}\quad(0\le j\le M). \tag{38} \] The original protected contraction and its exact coupled energy are \[ [x^dc^d]H_L(x,0,c,0;\sigma)B(x,c) =U_0\sum_{j=0}^M g_j(\sigma)a_j,\qquad \mathcal E_N(B)=a^*Ha. \tag{39} \] Finite-dimensional Cauchy--Schwarz with (4) now proves \[ \sup_{\sigma\in[-2,2]} \left|[x^dc^d]H_L(x,0,c,0;\sigma)B(x,c)\right|^2 \le e^{210}N^5U_0^2\,\mathcal E_N(B). \tag{40} \] This is a polynomial comparison with the same interference-retaining energy that occurs at \(\sigma=2\). All exterior coefficients are retained; they are not replaced by independent absolute local bounds. The energy can itself exceed a positive endpoint comparison exponentially, as the existing cap-moment obstruction proves. Consequently (40) is not a bound by the drilled action, a strict full-minus-central estimate, or a filling-volume theorem. It does remove a specific spectral obstruction: controlling the actual coupled energy would suffice uniformly over the entire real cap spectrum at polynomial cost. Derivative or first-normal estimates are not asserted here; any passage through the finite Hermite functional must retain its separate hypotheses and factors. ## 6. Dependencies and finite checks The original coefficient (2) and its normalization are recorded in the protected sharp-scalar derivation and in the frozen spectral-moment projection note. The positive law (19)--(20) is the existing theorem in [An exact positive moment form for the original flat-cap coefficients](research_flat_cap_positive_moment_form.md), not a new assertion of positivity. Its single-factor metric and the noninvariance of the monomial-diagonal subspace are also explained in [Actual continuant recurrences and an explicit positive cap tensor metric](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_cap_demand_continuant_jacobi_interface.md). The present proof instead uses the sine-Cauchy matrix (6), the self-adjoint recurrence (10), and the finite-degree comparison (36). The accompanying exact finite checker compares the original unused-row products, the direct matrix polynomial (16), and the symmetry identity (10), at representative levels of both parities. Those checks are checks of finite identities. The density and weighted-integral arguments above, rather than a numerical spectrum scan, prove the uniform theorem.

title: Regular stop-window exclusion with a protected input middle
status: Fixed-start protected-middle phase gap and exact reflection
text:
# Regular stop-window exclusion with a protected input middle 31 October 2026. **research local theorem.** This keeps the original specialization \(b=0\) exactly, hence the start row is \(i=0\). It assumes a strict regular maximum only for the stop. There is no regular start maximum, inverse zero-face weight, or inverse initial-row gauge. The conclusion is a phase loss relative to the original window envelope, not a comparison with complete volume. The reflected protected-output case is proved by an exact finite row reflection in §6. No double-zero specialization is included. ## 1. The exact fixed-start source Use \(N\ge3\), \(d=N-1\), \(	heta=\pi/N\), \(\sigma=-2\cos(2\pi\delta)\), and \[ s_r=2\sin(r	heta),\quad \alpha_r=2\cos((2r+1)	heta)-\sigma,\quad  eta_r=s_r^2,\quad \gamma_r=s_rs_{r-1}\alpha_{r-1}. \] Let \(A=x+y\), \(P=xy\), and retain the original continuant \[ K_{0,0}=1,\quad K_{0,1}= eta_1A,\qquad K_{0,r}= eta_rA K_{0,r-1}+\gamma_rP K_{0,r-2}. 	ag{1} \] The [literal source expansion](research_original_one_sided_four_state_transfer.md) has the factor \(b^i\). Since every exponent is nonnegative, specializing \(b=0\) selects exactly \(i=0\): \[ (-1)^dH_{V,\mathrm{LEFT}}(x,0,c,y) =A_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha \sum_{j=0}^{M}c^{d-j} \prod_{j<r\le M}\alpha_r\,K_{0,j}(x,y), \quad M=\lfloor N/2floor-1,\quad A_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha=\prod_{r=M+1}^{d}\alpha_r. 	ag{2} \] For the full numerator use \(M=d\), the empty omitted product, and \(H_V\) instead of \(H_{V,\mathrm{LEFT}}\). The start-at-zero diagonal term \(j=0\) is present in (2). It lies outside the regular stop window considered below; it has not been discarded from the full source. Let \(I=[
u_-,
u_+]\Subset(0,1)\) be a fixed stop window. In the half-row case take \(I\Subset(0,1/2)\). Write \(q_-\le j\le q_+\) for all integers in \(NI\). Restrict the sum in (2) to these rows and call the resulting raw polynomial \(W_N\). Let \(E_N\) be the same sum with positive face moduli and absolute values of every unused scalar factor. Throughout, \(x_0,y_0,c_0\) range over a fixed positive compact set, and \(\delta\) over a compact subset of \((0,1/2)\). The window stays away from the two zeros \(1/2\pm\delta\) of \[ \alpha(t)=4[\cos^2(\pi t)-\sin^2(\pi\delta)]. \] All compactness assumptions are uniform on the chosen parameter chart. ## 2. An exact positive seed, including the initial singular rows For \(r\ge2\), put \[ \eta_r=1+ rac{\alpha_{r-1}}{s_rs_{r-1}} = rac{\cos	heta+\cos(2\pi\delta)} {\cos	heta-\cos((2r-1)	heta)},\qquad M_r= egin{pmatrix}x&\eta_rx\y&y\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{3} \] For all sufficiently large \(N\), every \(\eta_r\), \(2\le r\le d\), is positive. They need not be uniformly bounded near the initial row. The following identities use them exactly: \[  egin{aligned} Z_1&= eta_1(x,y)^T,\ Z_r&= eta_rM_rZ_{r-1},\qquad r\ge2,\ Z_r&=G_r(K_{0,r},K_{0,r-1})^T,\qquad G_r= egin{pmatrix}1&- eta_ry\0& eta_ry\end{pmatrix},\ \mathbf1^TZ_r&=K_{0,r}. \end{aligned}	ag{4} \] At \(r=1\), (4) follows from \(K_{0,1}= eta_1(x+y)\). Thereafter it is the exact gauge identity \(G_rC_rG_{r-1}^{-1}= eta_rM_r\), where \[ C_r= egin{pmatrix} eta_r(x+y)&\gamma_rxy\1&0\end{pmatrix}. \] No \(G_0^{-1}\) occurs. Equivalently, (4) is the exact positive word expansion beginning with \((x,y)\), rather than an invented initial asymptotic amplitude. At complex face phases, entrywise absolute values satisfy \[ |Z_r(x_0e^{i\vartheta_x},y_0e^{i\vartheta_y})| \le Z_r(x_0,y_0). 	ag{5} \] This uses only positivity of the exact \(\eta_r\), not a bound on their size. In particular \(|K_{0,r}(x,y)|\le K_{0,r}(x_0,y_0)\). On any regular row interval, both \(G_r,G_r^{-1}\) are bounded, so the norm of the original active state is bounded by a constant times the positive \(K_{0,r}\). The same holds after further active propagation: it is still the exact state in (4), with the full initial seed retained. Choose once a macroscopic bulk interval strictly between \(0\) and the left endpoint of \(I\). On this interval the entries of \(M_r\) lie in one fixed positive compact set. Apply the [two-step word contraction](research_positive_eta_word_transfer.md) only there, and ordinary entrywise majorants before and after it. For any fixed separation of the outer relative phase, \[ |K_{0,j}(x,y)|\le e^{-\kappa_1N}K_{0,j}(x_0,y_0) \quad	ext{for every }j\in NI. 	ag{6} \] The early unbounded \(\eta_r\)'s introduce no loss: they occur identically in the positive majorant. Summation proves the window estimate in this outer-mismatch case. ## 3. Stop-action differences do not require a start-rate formula The limiting positive active root is \[ \Lambda_+(t)=2\sin(\pi t) \left[(x_0+y_0)\sin(\pi t) +\sqrt{(x_0-y_0)^2\sin^2(\pi t) +4x_0y_0\cos^2(\pi\delta)}ight], \quad L_\delta(t)=\Lambda_+(t)/|\alpha(t)|. 	ag{7} \] Choose a reference point \(
u_0\in I\) and define the stop primitive \[ F_{\mathrm{stop}}(
u) =(1-
u)\log c_0+\int_{
u_0}^{
u}\log L_\delta(t)\,dt. 	ag{8} \] Changing the lower limit to zero adds a constant; that normalization is unnecessary here. Assume (8) has a uniformly strict interior maximum \(
u_*\), with a fixed positive gap to both window boundaries. This is the only endpoint-maximum hypothesis. Here is a uniform relative estimate valid for the exact initial seed. Let \(u_r>0\) be positive left Perron vectors of \(M_r(x_0,y_0)\), chosen smoothly and with a fixed normalization on a regular neighborhood of \(I\), and let \(ho_r\) be their Perron roots. Their components are bounded above and below, and \(u_r/u_{r-1}=1+O(N^{-1})\) componentwise. Since the state \(Z_{r-1}\) is positive, (4) gives \[ u_r^TZ_r= eta_rho_r u_r^TZ_{r-1}. \] Comparing \(u_r^TZ_{r-1}\) with \(u_{r-1}^TZ_{r-1}\) and multiplying over any subinterval of that neighborhood yields \[ \log rac{K_{0,j}(x_0,y_0)}{K_{0,q}(x_0,y_0)} =\sum_{r=q+1}^{j}\log( eta_rho_r)+O(1). 	ag{9} \] For \(j<q\) use the reversed scalar ratio. The error is uniform for all such rows and all \(N\), independent of the magnitude or direction of the earlier positive seed. No matrix inverse or secondary-root inverse is used. Smooth Riemann comparison replaces the sum by \(N\int_{q/N}^{j/N}\log\Lambda_+(t)\,dt+O(1)\). Factor out the unused product above \(q_+\) and \(A_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha\) exactly. If this common product vanishes, both \(W_N\) and \(E_N\) vanish. Otherwise, for positive summands \(T_j=c_0^{d-j}\prod_{j<r\le M}|\alpha_r|\,K_{0,j}(x_0,y_0)\), their nonzero ratios obey \[ \log(T_j/T_q) =N[F_{\mathrm{stop}}(j/N)-F_{\mathrm{stop}}(q/N)]+O(1). 	ag{10} \] Only the varying unused factors in the pole-free stop window enter this estimate. Thus each boundary summand is exponentially below the positive window sum. No absolute estimate for a potentially tiny common scalar, no regular starting row, and no start saddle has been assumed. ## 4. Only the stop switch is gauged Put \(A_{q_--1}=(K_{0,q_--1},K_{0,q_--2})^T\) and use the exact stop matrices \[ T_r^{\mathrm{stop}} = egin{pmatrix}c\alpha_r&w_r\0&C_r\end{pmatrix}, \qquad w_r=e_1^TC_r=( eta_r(x+y),\gamma_rxy). 	ag{11} \] If \(V_N\) is the off-diagonal block of their ordered product over \(q_-\le r\le q_+\), the original window is exactly \[ W_N=(-1)^dA_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha c^{d-M} \left(\prod_{q_+<r\le M}c\alpha_right) V_N A_{q_--1}. 	ag{12} \] The stop at \(j\) includes \(C_j\), giving \(K_{0,j}\), not a shifted continuant. Equation (12) contains the complete original seed at row zero. Let \(s_
u=\arg\alpha(
u_*)\in\{0,\pi\}\). The supported alignment is \[ \vartheta_x=\vartheta_y=\vartheta_c+s_
u \pmod{2\pi}. 	ag{13} \] There is no phase for \(b=0\). At the maximum of (8), \(c_0|\alpha(
u_*)|=\Lambda_+(
u_*)\). The positive root is strictly larger in modulus than the secondary root on the strict compact chart. Shrink the window, retaining its interior maximum and boundary gap, so that \(c_0|\alpha(t)|\) stays strictly above that secondary modulus throughout it. Away from (13), either the outer relative phase has a fixed separation, already covered by (6), or it is small and the scalar phase \(\vartheta_c+s_
u\) is separated from the common outer phase. At exactly equal outer phases a constant unitary diagonal change of basis makes \(C_r\) that common phase times its real companion. The scalar therefore misses the Perron root by phase and the secondary root by modulus. A sufficiently small outer-phase perturbation preserves this full Sylvester separation. Analyticity in the scaled row variable extends it to one fixed complex neighborhood of the stop window. Apply the [analytic switch theorem](research_analytic_switching_suppression.md) only to (11). It retains \[ V_N=H_{\mathrm{end}}(C_{q_+}\cdots C_{q_-}) -\left(\prod_{r=q_-}^{q_+}c\alpha_right)H_{\mathrm{start}} +\sum_j\left(\prod_{r=j+1}^{q_+}c\alpha_right) R_j(C_{j-1}\cdots C_{q_-}), \quad \|R_j\|\le Ce^{-\kappa_2N}. 	ag{14} \] Multiply each term by the actual seed in (12). Equation (5), the regular \(G\)-bounds, and (4) bound the first endpoint by a constant times \(K_{0,q_+}(x_0,y_0)\), and the second by a constant times \(K_{0,q_--1}(x_0,y_0)\), with their exact after-products. These are the two stop-boundary summands, within one mesh step. Their fixed loss follows from (10). For a residual insertion at \(j\), the same argument bounds its active input by \(CK_{0,j-1}(x_0,y_0)\). On the stop window the ratio \(K_{0,j}/K_{0,j-1}\) is bounded above and below by positive constants, directly from the positive matrix update in (4). Hence the residual is bounded by \(Ce^{-\kappa_2N}\) times the original positive stop summand at \(j\). There are only \(O(N)\) insertions. Both boundary terms and the residual are thus exponentially below the positive window envelope. Restoring all exact common factors gives, for every fixed distance \(\varepsilon>0\) from (13), \[  oxed{|W_N|\le C e^{-\kappa N}E_N.}	ag{15} \] Constants are uniform on the stated compact chart. Sampled zeros in common unused factors and either parity's raw prefactor remain exact. ## 5. The protected target and supported incidence graph The original \(b\)-face target is zero. Nonnegative polynomial exponents make the substitution \(b=0\) exactly its constant-term restriction, also when that face occurs at other ports. No new integration variable or phase is assigned to it. These ports supply the same two local inequalities used by the [cycle-packing criterion](research_regular_window_cycle_packing.md): the unconditional positive-envelope bound and (15). Use the three supported incidences \((x,y,c)\), with labels \((0,0,s_
u/\pi)\). All repeated incidences, shared ordinary radii, original targets, and external source characters remain as in that criterion. The local result itself gives no comparison with \(\Phi_D\). ## 6. Exact reflection and the protected output For every finite level and every spectral value, \[ \alpha_{d-r}=\alpha_r,\qquad  eta_{N-r}= eta_r,\qquad K_{i,j}(x,y)=K_{d-j,d-i}(x,y). 	ag{16} \] For the last identity reverse a monomer/dimer tiling of the interval \(i+1,\ldots,j\). A monomer at \(r\), of weight \( eta_r(x+y)\), goes to \(N-r\). A dimer ending at \(r\), of weight \(s_rs_{r-1}\alpha_{r-1}xy\), goes to one ending at \(N+1-r\); its weight is unchanged because \(s_{N-r}=s_r\) and \(\alpha_{N-r}=\alpha_{r-1}\). The reversed interval is \(d-j+1,\ldots,d-i\). This proves (16), including empty intervals, without a physical-turn or unrecorded duality. In the full original path expansion, the substitution \[ (i,j,b,c)\longmapsto(d-j,d-i,c,b) \] preserves every monomial, unused row factor and the raw sign. This is an internal local polynomial identity, not a relabeling of shared source faces. Hence the \(c=0\) specialization, which forces \(j=d\), is the exact reflection of the \(b=0\) specialization. A regular start window reflects to a regular stop window, with the explicit mesh shift \(j'/N=1-N^{-1}-i/N\). Such an \(O(N^{-1})\) boundary shift is covered by the same boundary-gap and one-row comparisons above. The genuine RIGHT half-row sector has \(i\ge\lceil N/2ceil\). Under reflection this is precisely \(j'\le\lfloor N/2floor-1=M\), at both parities. Thus (15) applies to protected-output FULL and RIGHT windows, with supported alignment \(\vartheta_x=\vartheta_y=\vartheta_b+\arg\alpha(\mu_*)\). The output-zero incidence is absent. This is an exact source reflection, not an assertion that a general turned operator is multiplicative. Both outer weights must remain positive, and the other middle must remain positive. No double-zero extension, irregular stop/start maximum, spectral cap, or pole-touching window is included. The theorem controls these specified source windows only; global window coverage and the complete-volume comparison remain separate. The conclusion retains every strict-window and positive-supported-weight hypothesis stated above.

title: Regular-window phase exclusion with one protected outer face
text:
# Regular-window phase exclusion with one protected outer face 31 October 2026. **research local theorem.** This is the exact scalar-active extension of the [regular-window phase theorem](research_regular_spectral_window_phase_exclusion.md). It treats \(y=0\) and \(x,b,c
e0\), with their moduli uniformly positive. It does not cover a zero middle weight or two zero outer weights. Its conclusion is relative to the original positive window envelope, not a comparison with hyperbolic volume. ## 1. The literal protected specialization has three states Use \(N\ge3\), \(d=N-1\), \(\sigma=-2\cos(2\pi\delta)\), and \[ \alpha_r=2\cos rac{(2r+1)\pi}{N}-\sigma, \qquad  eta_r=4\sin^2 rac{\pi r}{N},\qquad a_r= eta_rx. 	ag{1} \] Setting the original outer variable \(y\) equal to zero removes exactly the dimer terms of the original continuant. Thus, for every \(i\le j\), \[ K_{i,j}(x,0)=x^{j-i}\prod_{r=i+1}^{j} eta_r, \qquad K_{i,i}=1. 	ag{2} \] This is a polynomial specialization, not a limiting estimate involving an inverse power of \(y\). Set \((B_{-1},R_{-1},Z_{-1})=(1,0,0)\). The exact recurrence is \[  egin{aligned} B_r&=b\alpha_rB_{r-1},\ R_r&=B_{r-1}+a_rR_{r-1},\ Z_r&=R_r+c\alpha_rZ_{r-1}. \end{aligned}	ag{3} \] Equivalently, \[  egin{pmatrix}B_r\R_r\Z_r\end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix} b\alpha_r&0&0\1&a_r&0\1&a_r&c\alpha_r \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix}B_{r-1}\R_{r-1}\Z_{r-1}\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{4} \] The direct before-to-after entry \(1\) retains the path \(i=j\). Induction gives \[ Z_M=\sum_{0\le i\le j\le M} b^ic^{M-j}\prod_{r<i}\alpha_r\prod_{j<r\le M}\alpha_r K_{i,j}(x,0). 	ag{5} \] For the original LEFT half-row source take \(M=\lfloor N/2floor-1\) and \(A_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha=\prod_{r=M+1}^{d}\alpha_r\). The raw source is \[ (-1)^dH_{V,\mathrm{LEFT}}(x,b,c,0) =A_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha c^{d-M}Z_M. 	ag{6} \] For the full numerator take \(M=d\) and the empty omitted product: \((-1)^dH_V(x,b,c,0)=Z_d\). These are the same source normalization and sign as in the [four-state identity](research_original_one_sided_four_state_transfer.md). All omitted-half modes and sampled zeros remain exact. ## 2. Strict regular windows and their three-phase alignment Let \(x_0,b_0,c_0\) range over a fixed positive compact set and \(\delta\) over a compact subset of \((0,1/2)\). Put \[ \alpha(t)=4[\cos^2(\pi t)-\sin^2(\pi\delta)],\qquad L_\delta(t)= rac{4x_0\sin^2(\pi t)}{|\alpha(t)|}. \] Choose fixed disjoint row windows \(I_\mu<I_
u\) inside \((0,1)\), both staying away from \(1/2\pm\delta\). In the half-row case they lie inside \((0,1/2)\). Assume \[ F(\mu,
u)=\mu\log b_0+(1-
u)\log c_0 +\int_{\mu}^{
u}\log L_\delta(t)\,dt, 	ag{7} \] has a uniformly strict interior maximum \((\mu_*,
u_*)\) on those windows. The logarithmic poles in the integral are interpreted integrably. The maximum stays a fixed distance from each boundary, and the boundary values of each separated endpoint action have a fixed strict loss. This last formulation makes the required uniformity explicit. Restrict (5) to all integers \(i\in NI_\mu\), \(j\in NI_
u\), and multiply by the exact prefactor in (6). Call the resulting raw polynomial \(W_N\). Let \(E_N\) be the same window sum using \(x_0,b_0,c_0\), absolute values of unused \(\alpha\)'s and of the omitted product, and the positive monomer product (2). The windows are disjoint, so the diagonal path is outside this restricted piece, while (4) retains it in the full source. Write \(x=x_0e^{i\vartheta_x}\), and similarly for \(b,c\). Define \[ s_\mu=\arg\alpha(\mu_*),\qquad s_
u=\arg\alpha(
u_*),\qquad s_\mu,s_
u\in\{0,\pi\}. \] The exact local alignment is \[ \vartheta_x=\vartheta_b+s_\mu =\vartheta_c+s_
u\pmod{2\pi}. 	ag{8} \] There is no phase assigned to the zero variable \(y\). In a LEFT straddling window \(s_\mu=0\), \(s_
u=\pi\), so (8) is \(\vartheta_x=\vartheta_b=\vartheta_c-\pi\). For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), there are uniform \(C,\kappa>0\) and \(N_0\) such that \[  oxed{|W_N|\le Ce^{-\kappa N}E_N}	ag{9} \] whenever the supported phase triple stays at least \(\varepsilon\) from (8). The distance can be the minimum over the common phase of the maximum of the three circular errors, or the equivalent maximum of the two relative-phase errors. ## 3. Exact start and stop switches Write \(p_-\le i\le p_+<q_-\le j\le q_+\) for the integer windows. The start and stop matrices are the scalar-block matrices \[ T_r^{\mathrm{start}}=  egin{pmatrix}a_r&1\0&b\alpha_r\end{pmatrix}, \qquad T_r^{\mathrm{stop}}=  egin{pmatrix}c\alpha_r&a_r\0&a_r\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{10} \] Let \(U_N,V_N\) be their respective off-diagonal product entries. Then \[  egin{aligned} W_N={}&(-1)^dA_{\mathrm{rest}}^\alpha c^{d-M} \left(\prod_{q_+<r\le M}c\alpha_right)V_N \left(\prod_{p_+<r<q_-}a_right)U_N \left(\prod_{r<p_-}b\alpha_right). \end{aligned}	ag{11} \] A start at \(i\) inserts \(1\), and the stop at \(j\) includes the active step \(a_j\). Thus (11) contains exactly (2), not a shifted path. There is no extra factor of \(N\) or auxiliary normalization. ## 4. Scalar separation and both boundary terms If (8) fails by a fixed amount, at least one supported middle phase mismatches \(\vartheta_x\) by a fixed amount. On its window, \(a_r\) and the relevant middle scalar have strictly positive moduli bounded above and below. For two such moduli \(u,v\ge m_*>0\), \[ |ue^{i\phi}-ve^{i\psi}| \ge2m_*\left|\sin rac{\phi-\psi}{2}ight|. 	ag{12} \] The exact coefficients are analytic in the scaled row variable, with \[ \alpha_h(t)=4\cos^2(\pi(t+h/2))-4\sin^2(\pi\delta), \qquad a(t)=4x\sin^2(\pi t),\qquad h=N^{-1}. \] The scalar gap (12) therefore extends to a fixed complex neighborhood of the selected window, uniformly for large \(N\). This is the full Sylvester hypothesis in the [analytic switching theorem](research_analytic_switching_suppression.md). No secondary eigenvalue, positive two-state gauge or outer-relative-phase estimate is involved. Apply that theorem to the mismatched matrix in (10). Keep both pure endpoint terms and the residual switch sum. The residual coupling is \(O(e^{-cN})\); it remains multiplied by the original scalar products. Here those active products concatenate exactly: \[ K_{v,w}(x,0)K_{u,v}(x,0)=K_{u,w}(x,0). 	ag{13} \] Their absolute values are exactly the corresponding positive products. To compare with \(E_N\), first factor out all common unused products outside the two windows. These may include sampled zeros in the full-row case, and the omitted-half product may also vanish. If a common factor vanishes, both sides of (9) vanish. Otherwise the same estimate applies to the remaining variable products, with no bound on an inverse common factor. The variable \(\alpha\)'s stay away from zero, while \( eta\) stays positive on the active compact interval. Their logarithmic Riemann sums give uniform rate differences equal to the differences of (7), with \(O(\log N)\) errors. Each gauge endpoint term places the relevant start or stop at a window boundary, up to one mesh step. Strict endpoint maximality and separation of the two endpoint actions give a fixed exponential loss relative to the positive interior window sum. Both endpoint terms are retained. For the residual, (13) reassembles the active products exactly; the one-row factors and their reciprocals on the selected windows are uniformly bounded. Each insertion is therefore bounded by its \(e^{-cN}\) residual factor times a constant multiple of an original positive switch summand, up to one mesh shift. Summing polynomially many locations costs only a polynomial factor. Absorb it in a smaller exponential constant and restore all common factors. This proves (9). ## 5. Protected targets and the shared phase graph In the original marked coefficient the protected face has target zero. All polynomial exponents are nonnegative, so specializing that variable to zero is exactly the required constant-term restriction. No phase or Cauchy integration variable is supplied for that face. Consequently these ports may be combined with the four-positive ports in the [cycle-packing criterion](research_regular_window_cycle_packing.md). Use just the three supported incidences \((x,b,c)\), with labels \((0,s_\mu/\pi,s_
u/\pi)\). The local loss and the unconditional positive-envelope bound have exactly the forms needed there. The circular telescoping, fractional packing and original shared-target Cauchy arguments are unchanged. The case \(x=0\), \(y,b,c
e0\), follows by exchanging the two outer variables in the literal recurrence. Neither case permits a forced zero middle, two zero outers, a boundary maximum or a window touching a pole. No universal packing capacity, envelope margin or filled-volume theorem is inferred from this extension. The finite dictionary is an algebraic specialization of the already four-state and restricted-window identities, whose existing audits include a zero outer weight. The exponential estimate above is analytical; no additional finite-level test is claimed as its proof.

title: Calibrated transport and the actual q-Hahn normal amplitude
text:
# Calibrated transport and the actual q-Hahn normal amplitude Written proof, 24 November 2026. The actual paired q-Hahn normal has a nonzero leading amplitude on each fixed strict physical compact when its scaled channel separation is sufficiently small. The allowed separation is a fixed positive number depending on that compact. This improves the shrinking-window upper bound to an amplitude theorem for the original generic derivative. The proof uses its two exact source equations, an analytic inverse with a controlled remainder, and one small original physical prefix. A convergent closed-walk expansion computes the prefix trace and fixes the normalization constant. No boundary uniformity is inferred from an interior compact estimate. The conclusion is a local packet theorem, not a lower bound for the original closed knot source. ## 1. The source and the leading coefficient Let \(N\ge3\), \(h=N^{-1}\), \(d=N-1\), \(q_0=e^{\pi i/N}\). Take actual integers \[ 0\le j<l,\qquad j+l=d,\qquad s=l-j,\qquad \xi=j/N. 	ag{1} \] For \(q=q_0e^\epsilon\) set \[ Q=q^2,\quad B=Q^{-N},\quad x=q^d,\quad t=N	au,\quad u=N
u,\quad T=Q^t,\quad U=Q^u. 	ag{2} \] All powers use \(\log q=\pi i/N+\epsilon\). The actual generic source is \[ C_m(q;t,u)=x^u\sum_{k=0}^m  rac{(Q^{-m};Q)_k(B^2Q^{m+1};Q)_k(U^{-1};Q)_kQ^k} {(BQ;Q)_k(T^{-1};Q)_k(Q;Q)_k}, \quad (a;Q)_k=\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}(1-aQ^r). 	ag{3} \] Retain its original divided derivative \[ w_{j,l}= rac{D C_j(q_0;t,u)-D C_l(q_0;t,u)} {-2N\Delta_j},\qquad D=q\partial_q,\quad \Delta_j=q_0^{2j+1}-q_0^{-2j-1},\quad R_{N,j}(	au,
u)= rac{w_{j,l}}{C_j(q_0;t,u)}. 	ag{4} \] The derivative fixes \(N,t,u\). Both generic highest-weight-\(d\) columns, including the large partner, remain in this definition. Write \[ {\cal P}=\{(	au,
u)\in\mathbb C^2: 	frac12<\Re	au<1,\quad 0<\Re
u<\Re	au\}. 	ag{5} \] The following quantities are limiting coefficient functions, not a complex interpolation of the finite integer channel: \[  egin{gathered} \sigma=e^{\pi i	au},\quad c=\cos(\pi	au),\quad z=e^{\pi i(	au-2
u)},\quad b_\xi=\sin(\pi\xi),\quad d_\xi=\cos(\pi\xi),\ W_\xi=1-2cz+d_\xi^2z^2,\quad V=1-2cz+z^2,\ Y_\xi= rac{(b_\xi z+i\sqrt{W_\xi})^2}{V},\qquad H_\xi=-4ib_\xi\sqrt{W_\xi}/z . \end{gathered} 	ag{6} \] For real \(0<\xi\le1/2\), [J,P] prove that \(W_\xi,V\) do not vanish on \({\cal P}\). The square root is their source branch, positive at real centers \(
u=	au/2\). Define the normalized primitive \[ {\cal F}_\xi(	au,
u) =\int_0^1 rac{
u}{H_\xi(	au,	heta
u)}\,d	heta . 	ag{7} \] The integrand has a regular limit at \(	heta=0\). Section 5 proves its holomorphy and both transport derivatives. At the folded endpoint it simplifies to the explicit unit \[ {\cal F}_{1/2}={\cal F}_0 = rac{\sqrt{1-2cz}+i\sigma}{8\pi c}. 	ag{8} \] The subscript \(0\) in \({\cal F}_0\) denotes the folded formula. **Theorem.** For every compact \(K\Subset{\cal P}\), there is a fixed \(\delta_K>0\) such that, uniformly over the actual pairs (1) with \(1\le s\le\delta_KN\), as \(N	o\infty\), \[  oxed{\quad w_{j,l}(N	au,N
u) =N{\cal F}_{\xi}(	au,
u)\, C_j(q_0;N	au,N
u)(1+o_K(1)). \quad} 	ag{9} \] The relative error tends to zero with every fixed holomorphic derivative on smaller compacts. After decreasing \(\delta_K\), \({\cal F}_\xi\) is uniformly separated from zero on \(K\). In particular, for large \(N\), the actual normal is nonzero there and \[ c_KN\le |R_{N,j}|\le C_KN,\qquad  rac1N igl(\log|w_{j,l}|-\log|C_j(q_0)| igr) =O_K(\log N/N). 	ag{10} \] The constants and the allowed positive scaled window depend on \(K\). For every prescribed \(S_N=o(N)\), (9) consequently gives, uniformly for all actual \(s\le S_N\) on each fixed physical compact, \[ w_{j,l}=N{\cal F}_0 C_j(q_0)(1+o(1)). 	ag{11} \] This includes Gaussian and logarithmically enlarged Gaussian windows. No rate for the \(o(1)\) is asserted. ## 2. A common generic magnetic operator and actual confluence For \(X=U^{-1}\), let \(\mathscr T f(X)=f(QX)\), and put \[  egin{split} a(X)&=(1-X^{-1})(BQ-(TX)^{-1}),\ b(X)&=(B^{-1}-Q/X)(1-(TX)^{-1}),\ {\cal L}&=a(X)(\mathscr T-I)+b(X)(\mathscr T^{-1}-I) +(B^{-1}+BQ)I . \end{split} 	ag{12} \] This operator preserves polynomials. Its apparent negative powers cancel on constants and linear polynomials; higher monomials have no negative powers. On \(P_k(X)=(X;Q)_k\) it has the exact action \[ {\cal L}P_k=\Lambda_kP_k+\eta_kP_{k-1},\quad \Lambda_k=B^{-1}Q^{-k}+BQ^{k+1},\quad \eta_k=(B^{-1}-Q^k)(1-Q^{k-1}/T)(1-Q^{-k}). 	ag{13} \] For \(k\ge1\), subtract the leading term. The remainder has degree at most \(k-1\) and vanishes at \(1,Q^{-1},\ldots,Q^{2-k}\). At \(X=Q^{1-k}\), only the \(\mathscr T^{-1}\) term remains, with \(P_k(X/Q)/P_{k-1}(X)=1-Q^{-k}\). This proves the lower coefficient; constants are immediate. Comparing consecutive coefficients in (3) now gives \({\cal L}(x^{-u}C_m)=\Lambda_m(x^{-u}C_m)\), with the same finite coefficient ratio as [C]. The physical common operator and its eigenvalue are \[ \Omega_q=q^{-1}x^u{\cal L}x^{-u},\qquad \lambda_m(q)=q^{-1}\Lambda_m =q^{2N-1-2m}+q^{-2N+1+2m}. 	ag{14} \] At the root, \(\lambda_j=\lambda_l\) and \(C_j=C_l\) by [C]. Also \(D(\lambda_j-\lambda_l)(q_0)=-2N\Delta_j\). Differentiate their two common operator equations and subtract. The operator derivative cancels against their vanishing root difference. The actual divisor in (4) therefore gives \[ (\Omega_{q_0}-\lambda_j)w_{j,l}=C_j . 	ag{15} \] There is no additional scalar in this forcing. At the root the magnetic equation for the original ordinary column is \[ A_+C(	au,
u+h)+A_-C(	au,
u-h)+(D_h-\lambda_j)C=0, 	ag{16} \] \[ A_+=(U-T)(1-QU)/T,\quad A_-=(U-QT)(1-U)/(QT),\quad D_h=(U/T)[2(q_0^{-1}+q_0T)-(q_0+q_0^{-1})U]. \] Here \(Q=Q_0\). The shift \(X\mapsto QX\) is \(u\mapsto u-1\); conjugating (12) by \(x^u\), with \(x=-q_0^{-1}\), gives precisely these coefficients and checks the physical \(q^{-1}\) in (14). ## 3. The second generic shift and the normalized equations The coproduct shift is also generic and common to both partners. The equivalent finite Newton form in [C] is \(C_m=x^uH_m(U,V)/D_m(UV)\), \(V=Q^{t-u}\), \(D_m(T)=\prod_{r<m}(T-Q^r)\). Its numerator is a linear combination, with coefficients depending only on \(Q,B\), of \[ B_a(U,V)=V^a\prod_{r<a}(U-Q^r)\prod_{r<m-a}(V-Q^r). 	ag{17} \] Each basis term satisfies the polynomial identity \[ (1-Q^{-m}UV)B_a =(1-U)B_a(U/Q,V)+U(1-V)B_a(U,V/Q). 	ag{18} \] Its two shifted ratios are \(Q^{-a}(U-Q^a)/(U-1)\) and \(Q^{-m}(V-Q^{m-a})/(V-1)\); the weighted sum is \(1-Q^{-m}UV\). Replace \(V\) by \(QV\), and use \(D_m(QT)/D_m(T)=(1-QT)/(1-Q^{1-m}T)\). This proves exactly \[ (1-QT)C_m(t+1,u) =x(1-U)C_m(t,u-1)+(U-QT)C_m(t,u). 	ag{19} \] No restriction to the small channel or to the root entered the argument. Subtract the partners, differentiate their root collision, and divide by the actual gap. The derivatives of the common coefficients again cancel. Thus \(w\) satisfies the homogeneous version of (19), with its root coefficients. For \(C=C_j(q_0;N	au,N
u)\), define \[ p_\pm=A_\pm C(	au,
u\pm h)/C,\quad p_	au=(1-QT)C(	au+h,
u)/C,\quad p_b=x(1-U)C(	au,
u-h)/C . 	ag{20} \] The full physical theorem makes these holomorphic on fixed compacts for large \(N\). Dividing (15),(19) by the ordinary column gives the source-exact normalized equations \[  egin{split} p_+[R(
u+h)-R]+p_-[R(
u-h)-R]&=1,\ p_	au[R(	au+h,
u)-R]&=p_b[R(	au,
u-h)-R]. \end{split} 	ag{21} \] The suppressed first coordinate in the first line is \(	au\). ## 4. An exponentially effective analytic inverse Fix a real channel interval \(\Xi=[3/8,1/2]\). The ordinary amplitude [J,P] gives, uniformly for \(\xi\in\Xi\) and with all fixed derivatives on physical compacts, \[ p_+-p_-=H_\xi+O(h),\qquad p_b/p_	au=r_\xi+O(h),\qquad r_\xi= rac{(U-1)Y_\xi^{-1}} {(U-1)Y_\xi^{-1}+U-T}. 	ag{22} \] Indeed \(A=(U-T)(1-U)/T=-V/z^2\), so \(A(Y_\xi-Y_\xi^{-1})=-4ib_\xi\sqrt{W_\xi}/z=H_\xi\). The limiting coproduct coefficient is nonzero by the simple second characteristic in [J,P]. Thus \(p_	au\), \(p_+-p_-\), and the triangular multiplication matrix below have bounded inverses, uniformly on fixed compacts and \(\xi\in\Xi\). Put \(Z_
u=h\partial_
u R\), \(Z_	au=h\partial_	au R\). For analytic functions let \[ {\cal A}_\pm f=\int_0^1 f(	au,
u\pm th)\,dt,\qquad {\cal A}_	au f=\int_0^1 f(	au+th,
u)\,dt . 	ag{23} \] The fundamental theorem of calculus converts (21) exactly into \[ (p_+{\cal A}_+-p_-{\cal A}_-)Z_
u=1,\qquad p_b{\cal A}_-Z_
u+p_	au{\cal A}_	au Z_	au=0. 	ag{24} \] Write this as \((M_N+E_N)Z=(1,0)^T\), where \[ M_N= egin{pmatrix}p_+-p_-&0\p_b&p_	au\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{25} \] Every entry of \(E_N\) is a bounded multiplier times an averaging operator minus the identity. All its coefficient bounds are uniform on the fixed buffered compacts just specified. Here the analytic inverse must suppress an exponentially growing initial bound, not merely a polynomial one. Fix an inner compact and an outer neighborhood at distance \(ho>0\) in the maximum coordinate norm, both inside \({\cal P}\). Use \(m=\lfloor aNfloor\) nested neighborhoods with successive distances \(ho/m\). Cauchy's estimate and shifts of length at most \(h\) give \[ \|({\cal A}-I)f\|_{m inner} \le rac{Ch}{ho/m-h}\|f\|_{m next}. 	ag{26} \] For \({\cal B}_N=M_N^{-1}E_N\), choose a fixed \(a>0\) sufficiently small. Its norm at each such step is then at most a fixed \(q_*<1/2\), since \(m h\le a<ho\). Products of these estimates apply also to variable coefficients: \[ \|{\cal B}_N^r f\|_{K_0}\le q_*^r\|f\|_{K_r}, \qquad 0\le r\le m. 	ag{27} \] The neighborhoods and the outer coefficient bounds are fixed before the subdivision; no derivative constant growing with \(m\) is omitted. On a further fixed outer compact, [U] gives \[ \|R\|\le C N^A\exp(C s^2/N),\qquad s\le\eta N. 	ag{28} \] Cauchy's estimate gives the same exponential bound, times a polynomial, for \(Z\) on the outer neighborhood in (26). For \(s\le\delta N\), choose \(\delta>0\) small enough that \(C\delta^2\) is less than half the exponential decay rate of \(q_*^m\). Also take \(\delta<\eta\) and small enough that the actual \(\xi\) lies in \(\Xi\). The exact finite Neumann identity, with \(v_N=M_N^{-1}(1,0)^T\), is \[ Z=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(-{\cal B}_N)^r v_N +(-{\cal B}_N)^m Z . 	ag{29} \] The geometric sum is bounded. By (27),(28), the remainder tends to zero exponentially, uniformly in the allowed channels. Therefore \(Z=O(1)\) on the inner compact. Run this bound on a slightly larger inner neighborhood. In the exact identity \(Z=v_N-{\cal B}_NZ\), a single ordinary fixed-distance Cauchy estimate now makes the second term \(O(h)\). Consequently \[ h\partial_
u R=H_\xi^{-1}+O(h),\qquad h\partial_	au R=-r_\xi/H_\xi+O(h). 	ag{30} \] All fixed derivatives follow by buffering and Cauchy's formula. For any prescribed finite collection of connecting paths and compacts, one positive \(\delta\) can be chosen for their union. ## 5. The closed primitive and its folded normalization The one-form \[ \omega_\xi=H_\xi^{-1}\,d
u -r_\xi H_\xi^{-1}\,d	au 	ag{31} \] is closed. One source-based verification uses the ordinary action \(\Phi_\xi\) in [J,P]. Its two characteristic equations are \[ A(e^{\Phi_
u}+e^{-\Phi_
u})+D-\mu_\xi=0,\quad (1-T)e^{\Phi_	au}=(U-1)e^{-\Phi_
u}+U-T,\quad \mu_\xi=2\cos(2\pi\xi), 	ag{32} \] where \(D=2U(1+T-U)/T\). For \(\xi<1/2\), differentiating their analytic coefficient functions with respect to \(\mu_\xi\) gives precisely the two coefficients of (31). Hence \(\omega_\xi=\partial_{\mu_\xi}(d\Phi_\xi)\) is closed. The formulas in (6),(22) extend regularly to \(\xi=1/2\), so closedness holds there by continuity as well. This differentiates the limiting action, not a finite complex channel. The normalization in (7) is justified at the boundary explicitly. At \(
u=0\), \(z=\sigma\), \(W_\xi=-b_\xi^2\sigma^2\), and the source branch is \(\sqrt{W_\xi}=-ib_\xi\sigma\). This follows first along real physical \(	au,
u\), where the square root has positive real part, and then by continuation in the strip \(1/2<\Re	au<1\). Thus \[ H_\xi(	au,0)=-4b_\xi^2=\mu_\xi-2,\qquad r_\xi(	au,
u)\longrightarrow0\quad(
u\longrightarrow0). 	ag{33} \] For the second limit, \(Y_\xi^{-1} =V/(b_\xi z+i\sqrt{W_\xi})^2\) vanishes at \(
u=0\); its denominator is nonzero, while \(U-T	o1-T
e0\). The coefficients extend holomorphically across this boundary locally, and the \(	au\) coefficient of (31) is zero there. Closedness therefore gives \[ {\cal F}_{\xi,
u}=H_\xi^{-1},\qquad {\cal F}_{\xi,	au}=-r_\xi/H_\xi,\qquad {\cal F}_\xi(	au,0)=0 . 	ag{34} \] The integral (7) is along a segment inside \({\cal P}\) except its regular endpoint; it proves holomorphy and continuous analytic dependence on the real parameter \(\xi\), up to the fold. At \(\xi=1/2\), direct differentiation shows that (8) has these two derivatives and its boundary value is zero. For the \(	au\) derivative one may check \[ {\cal F}_{0,
u}= rac{i z}{4\sqrt W},\qquad {\cal F}_{0,	au}=  rac{i(\sqrt W+i\sigma)^2}{16c^2\sigma\sqrt W}, \quad W=1-2cz. 	ag{35} \] The identities \(2c(z-\sigma)=-(\sqrt W-i\sigma)(\sqrt W+i\sigma)\) and \(2c(z-i\sqrt W)=-(\sqrt W+i\sigma)(\sqrt W+i\sigma^{-1})\) give \(r_{1/2}=-(\sqrt W+i\sigma)^2/(4c^2\sigma z)\), which verifies the second transport derivative. ## 6. One original physical prefix calibrates the constant Fix \(	au_*=3/4\), a sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\), and the interior anchor \(p_0=(	au_*,\varepsilon_0)\). Let \(t_N\) be the nearest integer to \(3N/4\), and \(u_N=\lfloor\varepsilon_0Nfloor\). For \(s\le\delta N\) and a small fixed \(\delta\), \(l\le t_N\le d\) for large \(N\). These are complete original physical slices. The root Casimir matrix on degree \(t_N\) is symmetric tridiagonal with entries from (16): \[ D_{N,r}= rac{U_r}{T_N} [2(q_0^{-1}+q_0T_N)-(q_0+q_0^{-1})U_r],\quad A_{N,r}=(U_r-T_N)(1-Q_0U_r)/T_N, 	ag{36} \] \(U_r=Q_0^r\), \(T_N=Q_0^{t_N}\). Let \(J_{[u]}\) be its leading \(u\)-by-\(u\) prefix. For \(f_0(z)=1\), \(f_u(z)=\det(zI-J_{[u]})/(A_{N,0}\cdots A_{N,u-1})\), the actual source identity in [G] is \[ C_{j,u}=f_u(c_j),\qquad w_{j,u}=f_u'(c_j),\qquad R_{N,j}(t_N/N,u/N)= \operatorname{Tr}(c_jI-J_{[u]})^{-1}, \quad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N). 	ag{37} \] Indeed the two generic columns are the same normalized forward solution at \(\lambda_j(q),\lambda_l(q)\). Their common matrix derivative cancels at confluence, with exactly the eigenvalue-gap derivative in (4). The ordinary scalar normalization \(C_m(q;t,0)=1\) is unchanged. For \(r\le u_N\), (36) gives \[ D_{N,r}=2+O(\varepsilon_0+h),\quad A_{N,r}=O(\varepsilon_0+h),\quad \|E_N\|\le C(\varepsilon_0+h),\qquad E_N=J_{[u_N]}-2I. 	ag{38} \] The norm follows from tridiagonal row and column sums, without a dimension factor. Choose \(\varepsilon_0\) so this norm is less than one for large \(N\). Uniformly for \(\xi\in\Xi\), \(c_j=\mu_\xi+O(h)\) and \(|c_j-2|\ge3\). Thus the resolvent in (37) has the uniformly convergent expansion \[  rac1N\operatorname{Tr}(c_jI-J_{[u_N]})^{-1} =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}  rac{N^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}E_N^k}{(c_j-2)^{k+1}} . 	ag{39} \] Its tails are bounded by a fixed geometric series, since \(u_N/N\le\varepsilon_0\). We compute its limit directly. At \(v=r/N\) the limiting coefficients are \[ A(v)= rac{(e^{2\pi iv}-T_*)(1-e^{2\pi iv})}{T_*},\quad D(v)= rac{2e^{2\pi iv}(1+T_*-e^{2\pi iv})}{T_*},\quad T_*=e^{2\pi i	au_*}. 	ag{40} \] For every fixed \(k\), the diagonal of \(E_N^k\) is a finite sum over closed length-\(k\) walks with steps \(-1,0,1\). Away from the at most \(2k\) boundary rows, coefficients in each walk differ from their value frozen at \(r/N\) by \(O_k(h)\). The boundary rows contribute \(O_k(h)\) after division by \(N\). Consequently the Riemann sums give \[  rac1N\operatorname{Tr}E_N^k\ \longrightarrow\ \int_0^{\varepsilon_0} \operatorname{CT}_\zeta [D(v)-2+A(v)(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})]^k\,dv . 	ag{41} \] Here \(\operatorname{CT}\) denotes the Laurent constant coefficient. The convergence is uniform in \(\xi\in\Xi\); the matrix coefficients do not depend on \(\xi\), and \(c_j-\mu_\xi=O(h)\) uniformly. Choose \(\varepsilon_0\) still smaller if needed so the absolute sum of the three limiting coefficients is also less than one. The same geometric domination then applies to the limiting series. This justifies first taking the limit for finitely many \(k\) and then letting the geometric tail decrease. The sum of (41), with the denominators in (39), is \[ \int_0^{\varepsilon_0} \operatorname{CT}_\zeta  rac{dv}{\mu_\xi-D(v)-A(v)(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})} =\int_0^{\varepsilon_0} rac{dv}{H_\xi(	au_*,v)} ={\cal F}_\xi(p_0). 	ag{42} \] For the first equality, expand the denominator geometrically. Only even powers of \(\zeta+\zeta^{-1}\) contribute, with constant coefficient \( inom{2k}{k}\). The resulting expression is \[  rac1{\mu_\xi-D} \left(1- rac{4A^2}{(\mu_\xi-D)^2}ight)^{-1/2}. 	ag{43} \] Its branch at \(v=0\) is \(1/(\mu_\xi-2)\), negative real. The characteristic (32) gives \(H_\xi^2=(\mu_\xi-D)^2-4A^2\), with the same value \(H_\xi(	au_*,0)=\mu_\xi-2\). The uniformly gapped small prefix keeps both branches regular, so (43) is exactly \(1/H_\xi\), with the original selected sign. Equations (39)--(43) prove the actual anchor limit \[ R_{N,j}(t_N/N,u_N/N)/N ={\cal F}_\xi(p_0)+o(1), 	ag{44} \] uniformly for the channel family, at one fixed positive \(\varepsilon_0\). No limit of interior estimates toward \(
u=0\) is used to calibrate the finite source. ## 7. Closing the local amplitude and its precise scope Given the target compact \(K\), choose a buffered compact containing its paths to \(p_0\). Apply section 4 there and choose the resulting positive \(\delta_K\) once. Integrating (30),(34) gives \[ R_{N,j}/N={\cal F}_\xi+a_{N,j}+O_K(h) 	ag{45} \] on that compact, where \(a_{N,j}\) is constant in \(	au,
u\). The moving physical anchor in (44) is \(O(h)\) from \(p_0\); (30) bounds the corresponding change in \(R/N\) by \(O(h)\). Thus (44) fixes \(a_{N,j}=o(1)\), uniformly. The folded coefficient (8) is nowhere zero on \({\cal P}\). If \(\sqrt{1-2cz}+i\sigma=0\), squaring gives \(z=\sigma\), because \(2c\sigma=1+\sigma^2\) and \(c
e0\). Then \(e^{-2\pi i
u}=1\), contrary to \(0<\Re
u<\Re	au<1\). Continuous dependence in (7) therefore makes \({\cal F}_\xi\) uniformly nonzero on \(K\) when \(\xi\) is sufficiently close to \(1/2\). Decrease \(\delta_K\) accordingly. Equation (45) now proves (9),(10); buffered Cauchy estimates give every fixed derivative of their relative errors. Using the ordinary amplitude from [J,P] yields the explicit form \[ w_{j,l}=N^{1/2}{\cal F}_{\xi} B_{\xi}e^{N\Phi_{\xi}}(1+o_K(1)). 	ag{46} \] The actual discrete \(\xi=j/N\) remains in the action and amplitude. For \(s=o(N)\), \({\cal F}_\xi	o{\cal F}_0\), giving (11). Replacing the ordinary action by its folded value is not asserted in this relative formula. The allowed fixed scaled window depends on the chosen complex compact. This is not an amplitude theorem for arbitrary macroscopic separations on the entire tube with one uniform window. It does not continue the finite channel to a complex parameter, place every short-filled geometric boundary packet in this domain, estimate the complete contracted coupon, or identify a contributing geometric coefficient under the original closing. No additional knot-volume case or finite-exception theorem follows without those remaining source estimates.
