title: Radial charge compactness and the sharp corner alternative
text:
# Radial charge compactness and the sharp corner alternative Private written proof, 15 November 2026. A positive unit-charge solution with complete outside angles gives uniform bounds on every height, real return and square covector at every positive solution with common charge \(0<\chi\le1\). The bounds do not assume that those positive solutions form a connected charge interval. Any first loss of positivity at a positive charge must therefore have a finite corner limit satisfying the sharp gradient-limit equality, rather than only the weaker corner subgradient inequality. This does not exclude that corner event. In particular it does not prove that existence at charge one implies existence at every smaller charge. The original finite quantum cycle is not changed or estimated. ## 1. Original graph, branches and constants Take a finite graph of the original positive edge blocks, with the incidence-counted peripheral sums of the pinned period theorem. An original ordered circle tree is a special case. Let \(S
e\varnothing\) be its selected vertices, and include each edge incident to \(S\) once. Each selected vertex has positive original degree. A loop contributes two endpoint incidences to its vertex. The graph extension uses these same block formulas and sums; it asserts no new topological realization for an arbitrary graph. Prescribe real powers \(n_v\), and put every outside angle equal to zero. For the original integer filling data the relation \(n_v=\eta_v-2p_v\), including its marking, stays fixed. The radial equations are \[ R_v(t)- rac{i n_v}{2}t_v=-\pi i\chi,\qquad R_v=\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e},\qquad 0\le\chi\le1. 	ag{1} \] All returns and angles use the canonical branches continued from completeness. In particular, \[ r_{v,e}=\operatorname{arsinh}  igl(	an(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2) igr),\qquad |\operatorname{Re}t_v|<\pi,\quad |\operatorname{Im}r_{v,e}|<\pi/2 	ag{2} \] at a positive edge \(e=(v,w)\). Assume there is a positive solution at \(\chi=1\), and denote its real angle assignment by \(z_1\). Write \[ t_v=s_v-iH_v,\qquad h_v=\operatorname{Im}t_v=-H_v,\qquad r_{v,e}=k_{v,e}+i g_{v,e}. 	ag{3} \] The sign \(H_v>0\) at a positive solution with \(\chi>0\) is proved below, not included in the definition of positivity. For each oriented edge the square coordinates and covectors are \[  egin{aligned} A_P&=s_v/4-g_{w,e}/2,&A_Q&=s_v/4+g_{w,e}/2,\ y_P&=g_{v,e}/2+s_w/4,&y_Q&=g_{v,e}/2-s_w/4, \end{aligned} 	ag{4} \] \[ x=E_A=	frac12\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(2A)\cos(2y)),\qquad B=E_y=	frac12\operatorname{arsinh}(	an(2y)\cos(2A)). 	ag{5} \] The square energy is normalized by \(E(0,0)=0\). The pinned convex theorem gives its positive definite Hessian in \((-\pi/4,\pi/4)^2\), continuous extension to the closed square, and constant boundary value \(G_{m Cat}/2\). Consequently \[ 0\le E(A,y)\le G_{m Cat}/2. 	ag{6} \] Let \(e_G\) be the number of included edges, and set \[  egin{split} \alpha&=\min_{	ext{all square coordinates at }z_1} \left( rac{\pi}{4}-|	ext{coordinate}|ight)>0,\ E_{\max}&=4e_GG_{m Cat}=\pi e_GM_\infty,\qquad M_\infty=4G_{m Cat}/\pi,\ H_*&=E_{\max}/\alpha,\ K_*&=\max\left\{3H_*, \operatorname{arsinh} igl(\cosh(H_*/2) igr)ight\},\ L_*&=K_*/2+H_*/4. \end{split} 	ag{7} \] These are finite constants determined by the supplied positive unit point and original graph. No numerical value of them is needed. ## 2. The closed minimizers at every radial charge Let \(X\) be the ambient open angle body, with outside \(s_b=0\), defined by \[ |s_v|+2|g_{w,e}|<\pi,\qquad |s_w|+2|g_{v,e}|<\pi. 	ag{8} \] Its closure \(\overline X\) uses weak inequalities. It is compact: every selected vertex has an incidence, all selected real angles are bounded by \(\pi\), and every incidence is bounded by \(\pi/2\). Define the row maps and total energy by \[ ho_v(z)=\sum_{e
i v}g_{v,e}-n_vs_v/2,\qquad \mathcal E(z)=4\sum_e(E_{P,e}+E_{Q,e}). 	ag{9} \] There is no outside work term, because the full outside angles are zero. The edge-square map is injective, so \(\mathcal E\) has positive definite Hessian on \(X\), and \[ 0\le\mathcal E\le E_{\max} \quad\hbox{on }\overline X. 	ag{10} \] For \(0\le\chi\le1\), put \[ \overline{\mathcal P}_\chi =\{z\in\overline X:ho_v(z)=-\pi\chi\ (v\in S)\}. 	ag{11} \] The test assignment \(\chi z_1\) means scaling all selected \(s_v\) and all incidence variables, including outside incidences. Since the fixed outside real angles are zero, every square coordinate scales by \(\chi\), and \[ ho_v(\chi z_1)=-\pi\chi,\qquad 	ext{each square margin at }\chi z_1	ext{ is at least }\alpha. 	ag{12} \] Thus strict feasibility is uniform even at \(\chi=0\). This is a primal test assignment, not a claim that geometric angles or periods scale to another solution. The existing convex theorem gives a unique closed minimizer \(z_\chi\) of \(\mathcal E\) on (11), for every \(\chi\in[0,1]\). It has no open-side square; it may have corners. The map \(\chi\mapsto z_\chi\) is continuous on \([0,1]\). Here is a direct proof of the last assertion. A sequence of minimizers has convergent subsequences in \(\overline X\), and any limit at \(\chi_0\) is feasible there. Given a comparison \(z\) feasible at \(\chi_0\), first replace it by \[ z^\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)z+\varepsilon\chi_0z_1\in X. 	ag{13} \] For \(\chi_j	o\chi_0\), the assignment \(z^\varepsilon+(\chi_j-\chi_0)z_1\) stays in \(X\) for large \(j\) and has the exact rows at \(\chi_j\). Pass to the minimum inequality and then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). The limiting minimizer is optimal at \(\chi_0\), hence equals its unique \(z_{\chi_0}\). By the original variational theorem, \(z_\chi\in X\) if and only if the original equations (1) have a positive solution. Define \[ I=\{\chi\in[0,1]:z_\chi\in X\}. 	ag{14} \] It is relatively open and contains neighborhoods of both zero and one. At zero the minimizer is the complete assignment \(z_0=0\). The original complete Jacobian is \(	frac12\operatorname{diag}(d_v-i n_v)\), so it is invertible; the positive solution for small real \(\chi\) has \[ t_v(\chi)=- rac{2\pi i}{d_v-i n_v}\chi+O(\chi^2). 	ag{15} \] At one, and at any other positive solution, the original period Jacobian is nonsingular. Neither this fact nor (12)--(14) asserts that \(I\) is connected. ## 3. Uniform height and return bounds on the whole positive set **Theorem 1.** At every positive solution with \(\chi\in I\cap(0,1]\), independently of its component in \(I\), \[ 0<H_v,\qquad \sum_{v\in S}H_v\le H_*, \qquad |k_{v,e}|\le K_*, \qquad |x_P|,|x_Q|,|B_P|,|B_Q|\le L_*. 	ag{16} \] All outside returns and heights are zero. **Proof.** The proper-prefix positivity lemma gives, for each selected endpoint of a positive edge, \[ \ell_{v,e}=\operatorname{Re}(r_{v,e}\overline{t_v})>0 \quad(t_v
e0). 	ag{17} \] It is an edge statement, so it also applies individually to both incidences of a loop. If \(t_v=0\), every return at that vertex is zero by (2), contrary to (1) with \(\chi>0\). Pairing (1) with \(\overline{t_v}\) therefore gives \[ \sum_{e
i v}\ell_{v,e}=\pi\chi H_v>0. 	ag{18} \] In particular \(H_v>0\). At the positive solution the full ambient gradient identity is \[ d\mathcal E(z_\chi) =-\sum_{v\in S}H_v\,dho_v. 	ag{19} \] This includes the outside incidence directions: their gradient coefficients are their prescribed outside imaginary angles, zero. Choose one selected endpoint incidence at each vertex. Starting from \(\chi z_1\), decrease the chosen \(g\) at each selected vertex by \(\alpha\), and leave all other coordinates unchanged. Call the result \(y_\chi\). Each square coordinate changes by at most \(\alpha/2\). Perturbations at opposite endpoints affect its \(A\) and \(y\) coordinates separately, including when the edge is a loop. Thus (12) gives a strict margin at least \(\alpha/2\), and \[ ho_v(y_\chi)=-\pi\chi-\alpha. 	ag{20} \] This point need not satisfy the original radial charge rows. It is an admitted comparison in the ambient angle body. The supporting inequality at \(z_\chi\), (19), and (10) yield \[ \alpha\sum_{v\in S}H_v \le\mathcal E(y_\chi)-\mathcal E(z_\chi) \le E_{\max}. 	ag{21} \] This proves the uniform height bound. For a selected incidence, (3), (17) and (18) give \[ s_vk_{v,e}=\ell_{v,e}+H_vg_{v,e},\qquad 0<\ell_{v,e}\le\pi\chi H_v,\qquad |g_{v,e}|<\pi/2. 	ag{22} \] If \(|s_v|\ge\pi/2\), it follows that \[ |k_{v,e}|\le3H_v\le3H_*. 	ag{23} \] If \(|s_v|\le\pi/2\), the exact identities \[ |	an((s_v-iH_v)/2)|^2 = rac{\cosh H_v-\cos s_v}{\cosh H_v+\cos s_v}\le1, \qquad |\cos(t_w/2)|^2 = rac{\cosh H_w+\cos s_w}{2}\le\cosh^2(H_*/2) 	ag{24} \] hold, with \(H_w=0\) for an outside endpoint. Formula (2) then implies \(|\sinh r_{v,e}|\le\cosh(H_*/2)\). Since \[ |\sinh(k+i g)|^2=\sinh^2 k+\sin^2 g, 	ag{25} \] we obtain the other bound in the definition of \(K_*\). At an outside endpoint \(t_b=0\), (2) gives \(r_{b,e}=0\). Finally the original edge identities give \[ x_P=k_{v,e}/2-h_w/4,\qquad x_Q=k_{v,e}/2+h_w/4,\qquad B_P=h_v/4+k_{w,e}/2,\qquad B_Q=h_v/4-k_{w,e}/2. 	ag{26} \] The preceding bounds imply the claimed \(L_*\). \(\square\) There is also a direct bound on every original tetrahedron modulus. The four generating shapes are \[ i e^{r_{v,e}}e^{-it_w/2},\quad i e^{-r_{v,e}}e^{-it_w/2},\quad i e^{it_v/2}e^{-r_{w,e}},\quad i e^{it_v/2}e^{r_{w,e}}, 	ag{27} \] and the other four are their negative reciprocals. Every shape \(Z\) therefore obeys \[ e^{-(K_*+H_*/2)}\le |Z|\le e^{K_*+H_*/2}. 	ag{28} \] Approach to the real axis, including the value one, is not excluded by this annulus bound. ## 4. Every limiting alternative, including the zero endpoint **Theorem 2.** Let \(\chi_j\in I\cap(0,1]\) tend to \(\chi_*\in[0,1]\). 1. The primal assignments converge to the unique closed minimizer \(z_{\chi_*}\). The finitely many heights, returns and square covectors admit a jointly convergent subsequence with the bounds (16). 2. If \(\chi_*=0\), all these coordinates tend to their complete values. In particular \(t_v,r_{v,e},x_P,B_P,x_Q,B_Q	o0\). 3. If \(\chi_*>0\) and \(z_{\chi_*}\in X\), it is the original positive solution at \(\chi_*\), and the period implicit-function theorem extends it through that parameter. 4. Otherwise at least one square is a corner and no square is on an open side. At every corner \((A,y)=(\varepsilon_A\pi/4,\varepsilon_y\pi/4)\), each limiting covector satisfies \[ U=\varepsilon_Ax>0,\qquad V=\varepsilon_yB>0,\qquad \sinh(2U)\sinh(2V)=1. 	ag{29} \] All original affine rows, endpoint matching relations and real period equations remain valid in the limit, with those covectors. **Proof.** Primal convergence follows from Section 2, and Theorem 1 gives the stated subsequential compactness. At zero, \[ 0\le\mathcal E(z_{\chi_j})\le\mathcal E(\chi_jz_1)\longrightarrow0. 	ag{30} \] The unique zero of the nonnegative square sum is the complete angle assignment, since its square-coordinate map is injective. Thus every square coordinate tends to zero, where its inverse and gradient (5) are continuous. Equations (26) and the original edge-coordinate identities give all the claimed complete limits. An interior limit reconstructs the original matched positive solution by the convex variation theorem. Its nonsingular complex period Jacobian gives the extension in part 3. An open-side limit would contradict the bounded covectors: for example, if \(A	o\varepsilon_A\pi/4\) and \(|y|\le\pi/4-\epsilon\), then (5) makes \(|x|	o\infty\). The other three open sides are identical. Hence a boundary limit has a corner. At an interior square the exact algebraic identity is \[ \sinh(2x)\sinh(2B)=\sin(2A)\sin(2y). 	ag{31} \] Also \(x\) has the sign of \(A\), and \(B\) has the sign of \(y\). At a corner the right side tends to \(\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_y\). The finite covector limit therefore has \(U,V\ge0\) and \(\sinh(2U)\sinh(2V)=1\), forcing both to be positive. This proves (29) with equality. For clarity, the matching and real-period relations being passed to the limit are \[ h_{v,e}=2(B_P+B_Q)=h_v,\qquad h_{w,e}=-2(x_P-x_Q)=h_w,\qquad k_{v,e}=x_P+x_Q,\qquad k_{w,e}=B_P-B_Q, 	ag{32} \] \[ ho_v=-\pi\chi,\qquad \sum_{e
i v}k_{v,e}+n_vh_v/2=0. 	ag{33} \] They are finite linear identities, so they survive subsequential limits without choosing new logarithmic branches. \(\square\) **Corollary 3 (no zero-height limit at positive charge).** For every \(0<\chi_0\le1\), there is a constant \(h_0>0\) such that \[ H_v(\chi)\ge h_0 \qquad(v\in S,\ \chi\in I\cap[\chi_0,1]). 	ag{33a} \] This does not require a complete outside neighbor in every selected component. In particular, uniformly on this set, \[ |\sin t_v|\ge\sinh h_0,\qquad |\sin(t_v/2)|\ge\sinh(h_0/2),\qquad |\cos(t_v/2)|\ge\sinh(h_0/2). 	ag{33b} \] **Proof.** If (33a) failed, choose a sequence as in Theorem 2, with \(\chi_*\ge\chi_0\), and a vertex \(v\) whose height tends to zero. Pass to a joint limit of all bounded coordinates. Prefix pairings are nonnegative in the limit and sum to \(\pi\chi_*H_v=0\), so \[ s_vk_{v,e}=0 \quad\hbox{for every incidence at }v. 	ag{33c} \] All limiting \(H_w\) are nonnegative, all \(|s_w|\le\pi\), and all returns stay in the closed range \(|g_{w,e}|\le\pi/2\). Use the exact original identity in a form that has no division: \[ \sinh r_{v,e}\,\cos(t_v/2) =\sin(t_v/2)\cos(t_w/2). 	ag{33d} \] It holds before the limit by (2), and every factor is bounded by Theorem 1. Thus it passes to the limit even at an angular endpoint; no inverse-hyperbolic branch is extended across a cut. If \(s_v=0\), then \(t_v=0\), and (33d) gives \(\sinh r_{v,e}=0\) at every incidence. The closed canonical range forces \(r_{v,e}=0\). Equation (1) would then have zero left side and nonzero right side, a contradiction. If \(0<|s_v|<\pi\), (33c) gives \(k_{v,e}=0\). Taking real parts of (33d) forces \[ 0=\operatorname{Re}\cos(t_w/2) =\cos(s_w/2)\cosh(H_w/2), 	ag{33e} \] since \(\sin(s_v/2)
e0\). Hence \(|s_w|=\pi\) at every neighbor. The weak edge inequality then gives \(g_{v,e}=0\), so \(r_{v,e}=0\). The full identity (33d) now gives \(\cos(t_w/2)=0\), hence \(H_w=0\) as well. Apply (33d) at this neighboring endpoint \(w\): its cosine is zero and its sine is \(1\) or \(-1\), so \(\cos(t_v/2)=0\). This contradicts \(0<|s_v|<\pi\). The same argument includes a loop. The only remaining zero-height possibility is therefore \[ s_v=\pi\ \hbox{or}\ -\pi. 	ag{33f} \] At such an endpoint (33d) forces \(\cos(t_w/2)=0\) at every neighbor: \(|s_w|=\pi\) and \(H_w=0\). This propagates along all edges of the selected component. A complete outside neighbor would contradict it immediately, since its cosine is one. If the propagated component has no outside neighbor, it is a whole connected component of the included graph. Every vertex in it has \(|s|=\pi,H=0\). Every incidence is zero by the weak inequalities. Consequently both square factors of every edge are corners. If the component has \(e_C\) edges, its energy is exactly \(4e_CG_{m Cat}\). Replace only this component of \(z_{\chi_*}\) by the corresponding component of \(\chi_*z_1\). There is no outside edge to change. The replacement has the same charge rows and is strictly interior by (12). Every square energy is strictly less than \(G_{m Cat}/2\): the boundary energy is constant, while strict convexity excludes that maximum in the interior. Thus the replacement strictly lowers the energy of this component. Its edge count is positive because every selected vertex has positive degree. This contradicts the minimizing property of \(z_{\chi_*}\). All zero-height alternatives have been excluded. Compactness and the finiteness of \(S\) prove a uniform \(h_0\) in (33a). Finally \[ |\sin(s-iH)|^2=\sin^2s+\sinh^2H,\qquad |\cos(s-iH)|^2=\cos^2s+\sinh^2H 	ag{33g} \] give (33b), also at half angles. \(\square\) The lower bound prevents these sine and half-angle observation factors from vanishing even along a corner approach at positive charge. It does not prevent square corners or make their Hessians nonsingular, and it is not a lower bound on the original scalar. The general corner KKT condition permits \(\sinh(2U)\sinh(2V)\ge1\). Theorem 2 requires equality at a corner reached from actual positive radial solutions. An arbitrary corner certificate with strict inequality is therefore not a counterexample to radial continuation from a positive unit point. Conversely, equality does not itself exclude a corner. The square Hessian can have a collapsing and a diverging eigenvalue there, so interior nonsingularity does not justify continuation through it. Thus the component of \(I\) containing one can fail to reach zero only through the specific finite boundary system (29), (32), (33). The component containing zero also exists by (15). This note does not prove that the two components coincide, or that any intervening corner event actually occurs. It gives a necessary boundary system, not a sufficient criterion for such an event. ## 5. The comparison at an existing positive charge vector For completeness, the supporting-plane comparison has a direct extension independent of radial continuation. Suppose an original positive solution with baseline charge vector \( oldsymbol\chi\), \(\chi_v>0\), is already given. Complete outside data are not required for this paragraph; retain their full linear work in the energy. Put \(H_v=-\operatorname{Im}t_v>0\). The prefix comparison or vertex reflection gives this strict sign with \(\pi\chi_vH_v\) in place of (18). With the Bregman remainder based at this solution, \[ D_{ oldsymbol\chi}(z) =\mathcal E(z)-\mathcal E(z_{ oldsymbol\chi}) -d\mathcal E(z_{ oldsymbol\chi}) (z-z_{ oldsymbol\chi}), 	ag{34} \] the exact ambient formula is \[ \mathcal E(z)-\mathcal E(z_{ oldsymbol\chi}) =D_{ oldsymbol\chi}(z) +\pi\sum_v H_v(c_v-\chi_v) \quad\hbox{when }ho_v(z)=-\pi c_v. 	ag{35} \] The minimum \(\delta_{ oldsymbol\chi}\) of this remainder on the ambient angle boundary is strictly positive by the same compact strict-convexity argument as in the adopted split-current gap. For a nonempty deleted set \(C\), suppose \(|n_v|/2\ge\chi_v\) there, and suppose an admitted deleted weak assignment has surviving charges \(|c'_w|\ge\chi_w\). Reflect negative surviving charges as in that theorem, set each removed \(s_v=\operatorname{sgn}(n_v)\pi\), and set all restored incidences to zero. The exact edge-boundary energy gives \[  oxed{\quad M_{ oldsymbol\chi}-M_{m del} \ge rac{\delta_{ oldsymbol\chi}}{\pi} +\sum_{v\in C}H_v\left( rac{|n_v|}{2}-\chi_vight) +\sum_{w\in S\setminus C}H_w(|c'_w|-\chi_w)>0 . \quad} 	ag{36} \] The actions include the charge term \(-i\sum c_vt_v\). Their normalization follows from the same original edge identity as in the split-current theorem. Isolated surviving vertices retain their rows and the bound \(|s_w|\le\pi\); empty deleted assignment sets are not assigned an action. Formula (36) compares actions at an existing positive baseline. It neither constructs that baseline at another charge nor changes a charge in the original finite source. ## Direct sources and scope The five pinned source proofs were read in full. * [Original convex variation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_filling_convex_variation.md), SHA256 2777b2bcb149d64a79757ba64ccb16be5438cf37ce820ad50c5f532afd8fc6c0: square energy, injective coordinates, continuous extension, closed minimizer uniqueness, and original charged variational rows. * [Global original periods](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md), SHA256 da5129c7110190035eedb8249d4004dd06b5a7555e78d948234d8de50fa17500: exact return and shape formulas, canonical branch ranges, original finite-network extension, uniqueness and period Jacobian. * [Positive proper prefixes](research_positive_primitive_prefix_regularity.md), SHA256 a01b55a71d133aadff4aac0929e50de03e1059991d6874e81646c770eb5604a6: strict individual pairing with the endpoint angle; its proof is independent of the value of the later prescribed positive charge. * [Corner KKT conditions](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_filling_corner_kkt.md), SHA256 6c70541966289535c95cd223050ca68e1748b076a2bb3021f941f2744df26a71: constant square-boundary energy and the distinction between sharp gradient limits and the full corner subdifferential. * [Split-current action gap](research_split_current_convex_action_gap.md), SHA256 8e42b3e549cebd45fa301ae3c41858ab2def475fa072985a49f5bc639ee204dc: ambient Bregman boundary gap, signed-charge reflection, exact deleted-edge calibration and source scope of the final comparison. The new compactness estimate removes divergent heights, returns and square covectors as possible failures on this radial positive set. It also excludes zero-height limits on closed positive-charge intervals. The sharp equality-corner system remains. No general no-corner theorem, volume theorem, quantum contour transport or nonzero geometric coefficient is asserted. Only written proofs, source-text reads and file hashes were used. No mathematical code, numerical evaluation, test or compilation was run. Frozen notes, manuscripts and public documents were unchanged.

title: Two-square radial limits and a regular lifted primitive system
text:
# Two-square radial limits and a regular lifted primitive system Private written proof, 16 November 2026. For a proper selected subset of an original circle tree, finite two-square degenerations along a positive radial approach have a restricted form. At a charge strictly between zero and one they are internal matching edges, their endpoint real angles are zero, and both endpoints have another strictly positive original edge. The original period equations are nonsingular at every such limit after retaining a vanishing edge square root as an independent variable. This includes the square-root fold, not only the regular imaginary square-root values. The classification uses integer original powers, a common radial charge, complete outside angles, and a supplied positive unit-charge solution. The resulting local implicit-function theorem permits independent nearby complex charges, but it does not assert this classification for limits of arbitrary charge paths. Nor does it complete a cone metric at a two-square corner or select a quantum cycle. ## 1. Original data and the admitted limit Let \(G\) be a finite connected original ordered circle tree with at least one edge, and let \(\varnothing
e S\subsetneq V(G)\). Include every edge incident to \(S\), once. Outside angles are complete: \(t_b=0\). Fix the actual integer powers and their original marking, \[ n_v=\eta_v-2p_v\in\mathbb Z,\qquad v\in S. 	ag{1} \] No change of these powers, carriers or peripheral curves will be made. Write the original radial equations as \[ \mathcal P_v(t)=\sum_{e
i v}r_{v,e} - rac{i n_vt_v}{2}=-\pi i\chi, \qquad 0<\chi\le1. 	ag{2} \] Assume a positive solution at \(\chi=1\). Let \(I\) be the positive radial set of the pinned compactness theorem. It is not assumed connected. Consider a sequence \(\chi_j\in I\cap(0,1]\) approaching a limit with at least one corner square. We use the complete normalization of the original returns. At each endpoint put \[ t_v=s_v-iH_v,\qquad r_{v,e}=k_{v,e}+ig_{v,e}. 	ag{3} \] The radial theorem gives a jointly convergent subsequence of all these coordinates and their square covectors. Throughout this note their unadorned symbols denote that limit. It has \[ 0<\chi_*<1,\quad H_v>0\ (v\in S),\quad |s_v|\le\pi,\quad |g_{v,e}|\le\pi/2. 	ag{4} \] Outside \(s_b,H_b,r_{b,e}\) are zero. The strict inequalities in the charge follow from the complete limit at zero and the unique strictly positive closed minimizer at one. The uniform positive height bound holds on every closed positive-charge interval, so every selected height in (4) is strictly positive. There are no open-side squares. Each boundary square is a finite sharp corner, with its signed covectors \(U,V>0\) satisfying \(\sinh(2U)\sinh(2V)=1\). All original affine rows survive: \[ \sum_{e
i v}k_{v,e}= rac{n_vH_v}{2},\qquad \sum_{e
i v}g_{v,e}- rac{n_vs_v}{2}=-\pi\chi_*. 	ag{5} \] These conclusions are applied only to a limit of actual positive solutions, not to an arbitrary corner KKT certificate. For an ordered edge \(e=(v,w)\), the square coordinates are \[  egin{aligned} A_P&=s_v/4-g_{w,e}/2,& A_Q&=s_v/4+g_{w,e}/2,\ y_P&=g_{v,e}/2+s_w/4,& y_Q&=g_{v,e}/2-s_w/4. \end{aligned} 	ag{6} \] Thus the weak edge inequalities are \[ |s_v|+2|g_{w,e}|\le\pi,\qquad |s_w|+2|g_{v,e}|\le\pi. 	ag{7} \] The original tangent and square-root coordinates and return identities are \[ a_v=	an(t_v/2),\quad a_w=	an(t_w/2),\quad q_e^2=1+a_v^2+a_w^2, 	ag{8} \] \[  egin{aligned} e^{r_{v,e}}&=\cos(t_w/2)(q_e+a_v),& e^{-r_{v,e}}&=\cos(t_w/2)(q_e-a_v),\ \sinh r_{v,e}&=a_v\cos(t_w/2),& \cosh r_{v,e}&=q_e\cos(t_w/2). \end{aligned} 	ag{9} \] The symmetric identities hold at \(w\). The square root is the one continued along the supplied positive sequence. Positive heights keep every selected half-angle cosine nonzero; outside cosines equal one. Bounded angles and returns therefore allow (8)--(9) to pass to the limit, with no inverse-function branch reset. ## 2. Real angular endpoints cannot occur **Lemma 1.** Every selected endpoint in the limit satisfies \[ |s_v|<\pi. 	ag{10} \] **Proof.** Suppose \(s_v=\varepsilon\pi\), where \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\). By (7), \(g_{w,e}=0\) on every adjacent endpoint. Thus \(A_P=A_Q=\varepsilon\pi/4\). Since neither square can lie on an open side, both \(y_P,y_Q\) are endpoints of their intervals. Formula (6) implies \[ s_w\in\{0,\pi,-\pi\},\qquad  egin{cases} g_{v,e}\in\{-\pi/2,\pi/2\},&s_w=0,\ g_{v,e}=0,&|s_w|=\pi. \end{cases} 	ag{11} \] At \(v\) the exact half-angle values are \[ a_v=-i\coth(H_v/2),\qquad \cos(t_v/2)=\varepsilon i\sinh(H_v/2). 	ag{12} \] First let \(s_w=0\), allowing a complete outside endpoint. The sinh identity in (9) is a negative imaginary number of modulus strictly greater than one. Hence \[ g_{v,e}=-\pi/2. 	ag{13} \] Meanwhile \(g_{w,e}=0\) makes \(\cosh r_{w,e}\) strictly positive real. By its cosh identity, \(q_e=-\varepsilon iQ\) for some \(Q>0\). The other cosh identity now reads \[ -i\sinh k_{v,e} =-\varepsilon iQ\cosh(H_w/2). 	ag{14} \] Consequently \(k_{v,e}\) is nonzero with sign \(\varepsilon\). Next suppose \(s_w=\delta\pi\). Both returns have imaginary part zero. Their positive real coshes in (9), and \(\cos(t_w/2)=\delta i\sinh(H_w/2)\), force \(\delta=\varepsilon\). Thus opposite signed angular endpoints cannot be adjacent. The sinh identity at \(v\) gives \[ \sinh k_{v,e} =\varepsilon\coth(H_v/2)\sinh(H_w/2), 	ag{15} \] again nonzero with sign \(\varepsilon\). Consider a maximal connected component of vertices with \(s=\varepsilon\pi\). Every adjacent vertex outside this component has real angle zero. At every vertex in the component all its real returns have sign \(\varepsilon\), so (5) gives \(\operatorname{sgn}n_v=\varepsilon\). In particular integrality gives \(|n_v|\ge1\). The component is contained in \(S\). Connectedness of \(G\) and properness of \(S\) provide a component vertex \(v\) with at least one neighbor outside it. Let \(d_0(v)\ge1\) be the number of its zero-real-angle neighbors. Equations (11), (13) and the imaginary row in (5) give the exact equality \[ 2\chi_*=|n_v|+d_0(v)\ge2. 	ag{16} \] This contradicts \(\chi_*<1\). \(\square\) The integer-power restriction is substantive in this proof: \(|n_v|\ge1\) need not hold for arbitrary real powers. The endpoint argument only needs each relevant limiting charge to be below one; it does not itself require them to be equal. The common radial charge will be used in Theorem 3 to exclude a degree-one endpoint of a two-square edge. Equation (16) does not contradict a charge at or above one. **Corollary 2.** For every \(\chi_0>0\) there is \(\epsilon>0\), depending on the fixed data and supplied unit solution, such that all positive radial solutions satisfy \[ |s_v|\le\pi-\epsilon \qquad(v\in S,\ \chi\in I\cap[\chi_0,1]). 	ag{17} \] **Proof.** Otherwise choose a sequence approaching an angular endpoint. The radial compactness theorem gives a finite limit with positive heights. If its charge is one, its primal assignment is the supplied positive minimizer; an interior limit at any other charge is also positive. A corner limit at a charge in \((0,1)\) contradicts Lemma 1. These exhaust the possibilities. \(\square\) ## 3. The complete two-square subgraph Call an edge *two-square* if both of its square factors are corners at the admitted limit. Denote the set of these edges by \(T\). **Theorem 3.** The following statements hold. 1. Every edge \(e=(v,w)\in T\) has both endpoints in \(S\), with \[ s_v=s_w=0,\qquad g_{v,e}=g_{w,e}=-\pi/2. 	ag{18} \] Writing \(A_v=	anh(H_v/2)\) and \(A_w=	anh(H_w/2)\), \[ 0<A_v,A_w<1,\quad a_v=-iA_v,\quad a_w=-iA_w,\quad q_e=iQ_e,\quad Q_e^2=A_v^2+A_w^2-1\ge0. 	ag{19} \] In particular \(|Q_e|<\min(A_v,A_w)<1\). 2. The edges in \(T\) form a matching. If \(T
e\varnothing\), then \(\chi_*>1/2\). Both endpoints of each edge in \(T\) have another original edge, and every such other edge is strictly positive. 3. Every included edge outside \(T\) is positive or a regular single-square corner. On a two-square edge the factors \[ a_v\pm i,\ a_w\pm i,\ q_e\pm a_v,\ q_e\pm a_w,\ q_e\pm i 	ag{20} \] are all nonzero. The only possible square-root ramification is \(q_e=0\). It is not excluded. **Proof.** A finite sharp corner places its disk coordinate on the unit circle away from \(1,-1,i,-i\). If both disk coordinates \(\zeta,\xi\) are on that circle, their finite tangent coordinates satisfy \[ q= rac{1+\zeta\xi}{1-\zeta\xi},\quad a= rac{\zeta+\xi}{1-\zeta\xi},\quad b= rac{\zeta-\xi}{i(1-\zeta\xi)}. 	ag{21} \] Here \(\zeta\xi
e1\). Indeed finite \(q\), supplied by (8), and \((q+1)(1-\zeta\xi)=2\) exclude that value. Formula (21) then makes \(q,a,b\) purely imaginary. In the closed canonical angular strip a purely imaginary tangent has real angle zero or \(\pm\pi\). Lemma 1 leaves only zero. Thus the endpoint tangents have the form in (19). At any selected vertex with \(s_v=0\), every incidence obeys \[ \Im\sinh r_{v,e} =-A_v\cos(s_w/2)\cosh(H_w/2)<0, 	ag{22} \] since all neighboring real angles are strictly between \(-\pi\) and \(\pi\), including outside angles zero. As \(\Im\sinh(k+ig)=\cosh k\sin g\), the canonical closed range implies \[ g_{v,e}<0 \quad\hbox{on every incidence at }v. 	ag{23} \] For a two-square edge, (6) with \(s_v=s_w=0\) requires both \(|g_{v,e}|=|g_{w,e}|=\pi/2\); (23) fixes the signs in (18). Equations (8) and (21) give (19). An outside endpoint would have \(A_w=0\), contradicting \(A_v^2+A_w^2\ge1\). The strict bound on \(|Q_e|\) follows because both \(A_v,A_w<1\). It also proves all the nonvanishings in (20). At a vertex incident to \(d_T(v)\) two-square edges, the imaginary row has no carrier term because \(s_v=0\). Therefore (18), (23) give \[ \chi_*\ge d_T(v)/2. 	ag{24} \] Since \(\chi_*<1\), one has \(d_T(v)\le1\), proving the matching assertion. For any edge of this matching at least one endpoint has another original edge: otherwise connectedness would make the whole original tree this two-vertex edge, contrary to proper selection. Its additional strictly negative incidence in (23) implies \(\chi_*>1/2\). A degree-one endpoint at the other end would force \(\chi_*=1/2\) by its own row. The common radial charge therefore excludes that leaf also. It remains to check the stronger assertion that the other edges are positive. Let such an edge meet \(v\), with \(a_v=-iA_v,\ 0<A_v<1\). If \(b=a_w\) has nonzero real part \(x\), the exact positive-edge criterion uses \[ X=(\Re a_v)^2+(\Re b)^2=x^2,\qquad D_0^2=\{\Im(a_v\overline b)\}^2=A_v^2x^2<X. 	ag{25} \] It is therefore strictly positive on the limiting branch, whose square root has nonnegative real part. The strict inequality makes that real part positive. If \(\Re b=0\), Lemma 1 gives \(s_w=0\); put \(b=-iA_w\), allowing \(A_w=0\) outside. When \(A_v^2+A_w^2<1\) the edge is strictly positive by the other case of the same criterion. Otherwise (9) gives \[ |\sinh r_{v,e}|=  rac{A_v}{\sqrt{1-A_w^2}}\ge1, 	ag{26} \] a negative imaginary value. Hence \(g_{v,e}=-\pi/2\), and the symmetric identity gives \(g_{w,e}=-\pi/2\). Both squares would be corners. This is a second matching edge at \(v\), a contradiction. Finally there are no open-side squares, and every finite sharp single corner is regular by the pinned corner classification. This proves all alternatives in part 3. \(\square\) The theorem does not rule out a two-square edge. It identifies the entire such subgraph at the limit and the positive edges attached to it. In particular, it distinguishes a finite regular imaginary root \(q_e
e0\) from the genuine fold \(q_e=0\), rather than discarding the latter. ## 4. Coercivity after omitting the fold edges For a nonfold edge the derivative of its original return pair is \[ J_e= rac1{2q_e}  egin{pmatrix} 1+a_v^2&-a_va_w\ -a_va_w&1+a_w^2 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \det J_e=1/4. 	ag{27} \] Its Hermitian part is positive definite on a positive edge. At a regular single-square corner it is nonnegative of rank one, and its real kernel line has two nonzero coordinates. The latter statement means a zero endpoint variation forces the other endpoint variation to vanish. On a nonfold two-square edge, (19) gives instead \[ J_e= rac1{2iQ_e}  egin{pmatrix} 1-A_v^2&A_vA_w\ A_vA_w&1-A_w^2 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \Re J_e=0. 	ag{28} \] Here \(\Re\) denotes the Hermitian part; for these symmetric matrices it equals the entrywise real part. Let \(F=\{e\in T:q_e=0\}\). For each remaining included edge, let \(\iota_e\) insert a selected variation into its two endpoint slots, using zero at an outside endpoint. Define \[ J_{m rest} =\sum_{e
otin F}\iota_e^T J_e\iota_e - rac i2\operatorname{diag}(n_v). 	ag{29} \] **Lemma 4.** At the admitted limit, \[ \Re J_{m rest}>0. 	ag{30} \] In particular, if there are no fold edges, the ordinary selected primitive Jacobian is nonsingular, even when \(T
e\varnothing\). **Proof.** All included Hermitian forms in (29) are nonnegative. A vector in their joint kernel vanishes at every selected endpoint incident to a positive edge. Theorem 3 therefore pins both endpoints of every two-square edge, including every omitted fold edge. Extend the vector by zero outside \(S\). Along a single-square corner edge zero propagates to the other endpoint. A positive edge pins both endpoints; the endpoints of a two-square edge are already pinned. Follow an original graph path from any selected vertex to an outside vertex. These three facts propagate zero along it, so the entire vector is zero. The proof applies to complex variations as well, since each real kernel line is complexified and every Hermitian form is nonnegative. \(\square\) ## 5. The original equations in a regular lifted fold chart At an edge \(e=(v,w)\in F\), abbreviate \[ A=A_v,\qquad B=A_w,\qquad A,B>0,\quad A^2+B^2=1. 	ag{31} \] Retain \(q_e\) as an independent complex variable and impose \[ f_e(t,q_e)=q_e^2-1-	an^2(t_v/2)-	an^2(t_w/2)=0. 	ag{32} \] For nonfold edges use their locally holomorphic square roots with the given limiting values. At a fold use the holomorphic returns \[  egin{aligned} \widehat r_{v,e}(t,q_e) &=\log\{\cos(t_w/2)(q_e+	an(t_v/2))\},\ \widehat r_{w,e}(t,q_e) &=\log\{\cos(t_v/2)(q_e+	an(t_w/2))\}. \end{aligned} 	ag{33} \] All logarithm arguments are nonzero near the limit by (20). Choose their branches to have the original limiting values \(-i\pi/2\). These values follow directly from (9), (18), and \(A^2+B^2=1\): both arguments in (33) equal \(-i\). On (32), (33) are exactly the original continued returns, including their logarithmic lifts. The supplied positive sequence lies in these branches when sufficiently close. The full lifted system consists of \(|S|+|F|\) equations in the same number of unknowns \((t_v)_{v\in S},(q_e)_{e\in F}\): \[  egin{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{e
i v}\widehat r_{v,e} - rac{i n_vt_v}{2}=-\pi i c_v,&v\in S,\ f_e(t,q_e)=0,&e\in F. \end{cases} 	ag{34} \] On nonfold edges the hat denotes the ordinary original return. The base charge is \(c_v=\chi_*\) for all \(v\). **Theorem 5.** The Jacobian of (34) with respect to \((t,q_F)\) is invertible at the admitted limit. Thus there is a unique local holomorphic solution of the lifted original primitive equations for all complex charge vectors \(c\) sufficiently near \(\chi_*\mathbf1\), with the prescribed limiting values and logarithmic branches. **Proof.** We compute each fold block with the other variables fixed. At \(q=0,a_v=-iA,a_w=-iB\), \[ df_e=iAB(B\,dt_v+A\,dt_w). 	ag{35} \] The angular derivative and \(q\) column of its return pair in (33) are respectively \[ C_e=  egin{pmatrix} iB^2/(2A)&iB/2\ iA/2&iA^2/(2B) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \partial_q  inom{\widehat r_{v,e}}{\widehat r_{w,e}} = inom{i/A}{i/B} = rac{i}{AB} inom{B}{A}. 	ag{36} \] For example, \(\partial_{t_v}\log(q+a_v)=(1+a_v^2)/(2(q+a_v))\) and \(\partial_{t_w}\log\cos(t_w/2)=-a_w/2\), giving the first row. Formula (35) is the direct derivative of (32). Let \((w,
u)\) be in the kernel of the full Jacobian. For each fold define the real selected vector \(\ell_e\) supported at \(v,w\), with entries \(B,A\). The constraint equations imply \[ \ell_e^T w=0. 	ag{37} \] On the two endpoint slots this says \(w=(A,-B)z\) for some complex \(z\), and direct multiplication in (36) gives \(C_e(A,-B)^T=0\). Thus every fold's angular derivative vanishes on the constrained tangent vector. Let \(L\) have columns \(\ell_e\), and put \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1/(A_eB_e))\). The remaining linearized primitive equations reduce exactly to \[ J_{m rest}w+iLD
u=0,\qquad L^Tw=0. 	ag{38} \] Since \(L\) is real, the second relation also gives \(w^*L=0\). Multiply the first relation by \(w^*\), take real parts and use Lemma 4. It follows that \(w=0\). Then \(LD
u=0\). The fold edges form a matching, so the columns of \(L\) have disjoint nonempty supports and are linearly independent. Every diagonal entry of \(D\) is nonzero; hence \(
u=0\). The square Jacobian is injective and therefore invertible. The holomorphic implicit-function theorem proves the assertion. \(\square\) The fold is regular in this lifted system even though \(q\) cannot be a holomorphic function of two unconstrained endpoint angles there. The projection of the charge-parametrized solution to the angle coordinates need not be locally invertible. Neither \(\det J_e\) away from zero nor interior nonsingularity alone would justify Theorem 5; its proof uses the additional constraint and the positive edges forced by the original radial rows. In particular this theorem does not assert a nondegenerate scalar phase Hessian in the lifted variables. A fold tangent may have \(dt=0\) and \(dq_e
e0\); the angular critical one-form alone does not detect that direction in the same manner as the full primitive-period map. For the actual filling marking the full periods along the local solution are still \[ U_v=2\sum_{e
i v}\widehat r_{v,e}-i\eta_vt_v,\qquad V_v=2it_v,\qquad U_v+p_vV_v=-2\pi i c_v. 	ag{39} \] This identity follows from (1) and (34), with the original local logarithms. It makes no integer change to a return, carrier or peripheral row. ## 6. Consequences and limits of the statement For the supplied positive radial approach, every finite corner alternative now has a regular local system of original primitive equations: ordinary angle coordinates suffice when no \(q_e\) vanishes, and the finitely many matching square roots give the lifted coordinates in Theorem 5 otherwise. Close terms of the approaching sequence lie on that unique local branch by the implicit-function theorem. This is local analytic control of the specified limit. It does not show that the positive radial set is connected, that a continued branch still consists of positive original cells, or that a completed cone metric exists at a two-square limit. In particular the previously proved uniform-end and marked-metric continuation theorems have regular single-square hypotheses; those theorems are not invoked at the two-square edges here. A metric attachment, volume calibration there, and transport of the original relative quantum cycle require additional arguments. The classification is not asserted for arbitrary independent charge approaches or arbitrary noninteger powers. Independent charge variation occurs only after the common-charge integral limit has been classified and its lifted Jacobian proved invertible. No new class of short fillings satisfying the original volume identity is claimed. ## Direct sources The following four source texts were read in full, with their directly used identities checked at the pinned versions. * [Radial compactness and sharp corners](research_radial_charge_compactness_and_corners.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{744d36368876f255df6e2b1f2ca15dd23e805d5d5a39b009f6983fec2c6243ec}\): unique closed minimizers, the zero and unit endpoints, bounded actual returns/covectors, no open-side limits, sharp corner equalities, and uniform positive heights. * [Original positive edge periods](research_positive_edge_global_monotonicity.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{da5129c7110190035eedb8249d4004dd06b5a7555e78d948234d8de50fa17500}\): exact tangent/disk formulas, canonical logarithmic ranges and return identities, the strict positive-edge criterion, and the original carrier and full peripheral periods. * [Original square-corner geometry](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_square_corner_flat_geometry.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{511c2c93d61482664cf62ed3b146c0af19ffbb149fa8772a4d1eb5ca7026eed0}\): finite sharp disk limits, regular single-square corners, and the distinct two-square singular products, including \(q=0\). * [Regular corner period assembly](research_regular_corner_period_assembly.md), SHA256 \(	exttt{7d551e90d04b7c45232074109581bf2a807569259f98ad81e00855bec7f51ce5}\): the literal edge Jacobian, positive and rank-one corner Hermitian forms, nonzero kernel gains and original incidence assembly. The new zero-Hermitian two-square blocks and the fold augmentation are proved above, not attributed to that theorem. Only written mathematics, source-text reads and file hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical computation, test or compilation was run. Frozen sources, manuscripts and public documents were unchanged.

title: Bounding radical edge contributions by the pieces of a path
text: # Bounding radical edge contributions by the pieces of a path Research proof, 3 November 2026. The high Newton sector can be estimated after its exact contraction, without evaluating its individual polynomials on a complex geometric contour. On a path, the contracted source separates into pieces with physical boundary values. Existing bounds over the whole boundary period control many of these pieces. This gives two conclusions proved below. For paths whose selected powers have magnitude at least sixty-four, every nonempty radical matching has a uniform strict rate gap. For the internal pair of powers \(3,3\), its entire radical contribution also has a strict gap, established by an elementary comparison of convex energies. The latter result does not estimate the remaining low-sector trace. ## 1. What remains after a radical matching is contracted Use the original kernel, trace, crossing, and radical decomposition from [the exact contraction theorem](research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md). Write \(m_N=\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), \[ K_N=K_N^{\rm low}+H_N^{\rm rad},\qquad W_{ab}=\sum_r b_{ra}b_{rb},\qquad \sum_{a,b}|W_{ab}|\le4m_N^3. \tag{1} \] Every original crossing value \(R(c_a)^n\) has modulus one, including for negative powers. Let \(\Gamma\) be an original finite path. Its selected vertices carry the original traces and fixed crossing powers. Any unselected endpoints are ordinary boundary variables. Choose a matching \(M\) of edges whose two endpoints are selected, and put \(S=V(M)\). Consider the exact term in which edges in \(M\) carry \(H_N^{\rm rad}\) and all other edges carry the full kernel \(K_N\). Call this term \(\mathscr T_{M,N}\). These are the terms, with signs, in the inverse expansion \[ Z_K-Z_{\rm low} =\sum_{M\ne\varnothing}(-1)^{|M|+1}\mathscr T_{M,N}. \tag{2} \] Delete only the edges in \(M\). At their endpoints replace the traces by the physical values \(c_{a_v}\). Every other edge remains. Denote the resulting path components by \(C\), and their original source polynomials by \(F_{C,N}\). In this notation the crossing values at \(S\) are kept outside \(F_{C,N}\). An isolated evaluated vertex contributes one. A component with one edge and no traced vertex contributes the bare kernel. **Proposition 1.** The matching term is exactly \[ \mathscr T_{M,N} =\sum_{\mathbf a} \prod_{\{v,w\}\in M}W_{a_va_w} \prod_{v\in S}R(c_{a_v})^{n_v} \prod_C F_{C,N}(\mathbf c_{\partial C}), \qquad 0\le a_v<m_N. \tag{3} \] The boundary arguments of each component include its prescribed original outside boundaries as well as the physical values at \(S\). **Proof.** The joint-spectator version of the radical contraction theorem replaces each matching edge by \(W\). Every other edge touching \(S\) becomes \(K_N(c_a,w)\) or \(K_N(c_a,c_b)\). After the matching edges have been removed, the remaining products and traces lie in disjoint components of the path, so they factor. This proves (3), with all original first normals and boundary polynomial dependence retained. \(\square\) In particular, the edge between two neighboring matched pairs is still present. Its factor \(K_N(c_a,c_b)\) can have exponential size. It is a bare-edge component in (3), with complete-boundary rate \(M_\infty=4G/\pi\), where \(G\) is Catalan's constant. It must not be counted as a polynomial cost or replaced by one. ## 2. The rate comparison supplied by whole-boundary estimates Write \(c_a=-2\cos u_a\), with \(u_a=\pi-(2a+1)\pi/N\in[0,\pi]\). Suppose every component in (3) has a proved bound \[ \sup_{\mathbf u\in[-\pi,\pi]^{\partial C}} |F_{C,N}(\mathbf u)| \le A_C N^{b_C}e^{N\mu_C}, \tag{4} \] where \(\mu_C\) is its complete-boundary geometric rate. For an isolated evaluated vertex take \(\mu_C=0\). **Theorem 2.** Under (4), \[ |\mathscr T_{M,N}| \le (4m_N^3)^{|M|} \left(\prod_C A_C\right)N^{\sum_C b_C} e^{N\sum_C\mu_C}. \tag{5} \] The estimate is uniform over the original real outside boundaries. **Proof.** Use (4) inside (3), the unit moduli of the crossing values, and (1) separately on each disjoint pair of colors. \(\square\) There is an exact geometric interpretation of the rate in (5). Let \(\lambda^S\) set the charges at \(S\) to zero and keep all other selected charges equal to one. Suppose the complete geometries of the components and the original positive stationary solution exist with the stated marking. Reinsert the matching edges as complete edges. Their endpoints have angle zero, so their zero-charge equations hold, and each inserted edge adds \(M_\infty\) to the absolute stationary action. Consequently \[ \sum_C\mu_C =M_\Gamma(\lambda^S)-|M|M_\infty. \tag{6} \] This is the same complete-edge accounting as in [the edge-cut energy identity](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_edge_cut_energy_comparison.md). Thus, if the desired full rate is \(M_\Gamma(\mathbf1)\), the sufficient strict comparison is \[ M_\Gamma(\lambda^S)-M_\Gamma(\mathbf1)<|M|M_\infty. \tag{7} \] Together, (4) and (7) give an actual upper bound on the whole coherent radical term. The argument never substitutes the larger product of absolute individual-color contributions for a remaining trace. For fixed \(\Gamma\) there are finitely many matchings, so strict gaps for all of them also bound their sum in (2). The hypothesis (4) is already available for the bare edge, the proved single-vertex two-boundary sources, and the other original pieces with proved whole-boundary estimates. It is not presently established for every connected cluster of short powers. ## 3. A strict radical gap for the proved long paths **Corollary 3.** Suppose every selected power satisfies \(|n_v|\ge64\), with independently chosen signs. Then every nonempty matching obeys \[ |\mathscr T_{M,N}| \le C_MN^{a_M} \exp N\!\left[ M_\Gamma(\mathbf1) -|M|\left(M_\infty-\frac1{200}\right)\right]. \tag{8} \] Here complete outside boundaries are used to define \(M_\Gamma(\mathbf1)\); the upper bound holds uniformly over their real boundary periods when those endpoints are left free. **Proof.** Every component after the cut is a long path with one or two boundary endpoints, a bare edge, or a constant factor. The one- and two-boundary estimates in [the path trace theorem](research_uniform_path_trace_assembly.md), Section 5, prove (4). The complete geometries and charge comparison are supplied by [the signed partial-charge theorem](research_positive_path_partial_charge_bounds.md), Corollary 3. In its notation, \[ M_\Gamma(\lambda^S)-M_\Gamma(\mathbf1) <\sum_{v\in S}\frac{d_v}{800} \le\frac{|M|}{200}, \tag{9} \] since \(|S|=2|M|\) and each original degree is at most two. Combine (5), (6), and (9). All graph sizes and powers are fixed before the level tends to infinity. \(\square\) When a component has a proved nonzero complete-boundary asymptotic, its whole-boundary bound also implies \[ \sup_{\mathbf u}|F_{C,N}(\mathbf u)| \le C_CN^{d_C}|F_{C,N}(\mathbf0)| \tag{10} \] for all sufficiently large \(N\). This uses the nonzero leading coefficient as well as the common exponential rate. It is not asserted at a small level where the complete value might vanish. ## 4. The radical contribution of an internal pair of powers three Consider the original two-boundary source \[ P_N(s,u)=\mathcal D_{3,N}^{(t)}\mathcal D_{3,N}^{(r)} [K_N(s,t)K_N(t,r)K_N(r,u)]. \tag{11} \] Only the middle edge has both endpoints traced. Replace that edge by \(H_N^{\rm rad}\) and call the result \(P_N^{\rm rad}\). The two pieces in (3) are bare edges. The full real-angle bound in [the centered kernel estimate](research_path_mixed_trace_currents.md), equation (21), therefore gives \[ |P_N^{\rm rad}(s,u)|\le CN^a \exp N\!\left[ 2M_\infty-\frac{(1-\cos s)+(1-\cos u)}{200}\right] \qquad(s,u\in[-\pi,\pi]). \tag{12} \] The losses in the two internal physical angles may be dropped when summing the bounded Gram weights. The outside losses remain. Let \(M_{3,3}\) be the complete-boundary geometric rate of (11). The positive solution exists by the integer corridor theorem in [the variational path proof](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md), Theorem 15, after mirroring its negative-power convention. **Theorem 4.** One has \[ M_{3,3}>2M_\infty+\frac1{100}. \tag{13} \] Consequently the entire radical term in (11) has a strict exponential gap below its geometric rate. This also holds for the mirrored pair \(-3,-3\). **Proof.** Use the square energy \(E(A,y)\), normalized to vanish at zero, from the convex filling variation. It is even in each coordinate and satisfies \[ E_A=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}(\tan(2A)\cos(2y)), \qquad E_y=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}(\tan(2y)\cos(2A)). \tag{14} \] The total energy is four times the sum of the two square energies on every edge. Its minimum \(F\) satisfies \[ F=\pi(3M_\infty-M_{3,3}). \tag{15} \] This is the absolute energy identity, with all three original edges included. Choose a feasible trial with real angle \(s_v=\pi/2\) at both selected vertices, imaginary return \(g_{v,e}=-\pi/8\) at each of their two incidences, and \(s=g=0\) at the two outside endpoints. Each selected constraint is \(\sum_e g_{v,e}-3s_v/2=-\pi\). All edge inequalities are strict. The middle edge has square pairs \((3\pi/16,\pi/16)\) and \((\pi/16,-3\pi/16)\). Each attaching edge has two copies of \((\pi/8,-\pi/16)\), up to the square symmetries. By symmetry of \(E\), \[ F\le8E(3\pi/16,\pi/16)+16E(\pi/8,\pi/16). \tag{16} \] For \(0\le A,y<\pi/4\), equation (14) implies \(E(A,y)\le E(A,0)+E(0,y)\). Write \(E_0(A)=E(A,0)\). Since \(\operatorname{arsinh}(\tan x)'=\sec x\) on this interval, integration twice gives \[ E_0(A)=\frac14\int_0^{2A}(2A-t)\sec t\,dt. \tag{17} \] The function \(\sec t\) is convex. Bound it above by its linear interpolants on \([0,A]\) and \([A,2A]\), and integrate these two affine functions exactly. This yields \[ E_0(A)\le\frac{A^2}{24} (5+6\sec A+\sec(2A)). \tag{18} \] Combining (16)--(18), \[ F\le24E_0(\pi/16) +16E_0(\pi/8)+8E_0(3\pi/16). \tag{19} \] The following elementary rational upper bounds suffice: \[ \sec\frac\pi{16}<\frac{51}{50},\quad \sec\frac\pi8<\frac{13}{12},\quad \sec\frac\pi4<\frac{10}{7},\quad \sec\frac{3\pi}{16}<\frac{121}{100},\quad \sec\frac{3\pi}8<\frac{21}{8}. \tag{20} \] Here is one way to check all five without approximate trigonometry. For \(0\le x\le33/28\), \[ \cos x\ge p_6(x):=1-\frac{x^2}{2} +\frac{x^4}{24}-\frac{x^6}{720}. \] The alternating Taylor remainder has the stated sign, and \(p_6\) is decreasing on this interval. Substitute the respective upper arguments \(11/56,11/28,11/14,33/56,33/28\), using \(\pi<22/7\). Direct rational arithmetic gives lower bounds strictly larger than the reciprocals in (20). Substituting (20) and \(\pi<22/7\) in (19) gives \[ F<\frac{9283241}{2634240}<\frac{18}{5}. \tag{21} \] Finally, the alternating series defining Catalan's constant gives \[ G>1-\frac19+\frac1{25}-\frac1{49}. \] These rational bounds imply \[ \frac{4G-18/5}{\pi} >\frac{4(1-1/9+1/25-1/49)-18/5}{22/7} =\frac{187}{17325}>\frac1{100}. \tag{22} \] Use \(\pi M_\infty=4G\) in (15) to conclude (13). Conjugation gives the mirrored statement. \(\square\) The seven rational inequalities in (20)--(22) are reproduced by [the exact-fraction checker](../experiments/check_three_pair_radical_energy_gap.py): ```sh python3 experiments/check_three_pair_radical_energy_gap.py ``` Its [saved result](../repro/results/research-three-pair-radical-energy-gap.json) records the exact positive margins. The checker verifies these scalar inequalities; the feasible-angle construction, variational identity, and quantum radical bound are the written arguments above. The strict gap persists on a sufficiently small complex neighborhood of \(s=u=0\). Indeed \(P_N^{\rm rad}\) has degree at most \(N-1\) in each outside spectral variable; the elementary Laurent polynomial bound extends (12) with added exponent \(N(|\Im s|+|\Im u|)\). The positive geometric critical point and its action continue holomorphically nearby. Shrinking the neighborhood preserves a fixed portion of the gap in (13). This observation controls the radical error in a prospective local two-boundary theorem; it does not prove that theorem's remaining low-sector asymptotic. ## 5. Why ordinary-color bounds do not settle the remaining pieces The colors \(c_a\) above are physical values of an auxiliary pair Casimir. The main strands still carry their original complete root color. The ordinary-color comparison in [the representation audit](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_ordinary_color_comparison_audit.md) instead specializes the main knot color and uses the one-component quotient argument to replace all its strands by an ordinary color. Those hypotheses do not follow from fixing auxiliary Casimir values. In particular, a general bound (4) cannot be imported from that ordinary-color theorem. Nor do the existing bounds for the normal determinant at each color establish it: they permit exponential cancellation between different physical colors. For arbitrary short path components, their complete-boundary rate and their whole-boundary upper bound must still be compared within the original source. The results above remove this issue for the explicitly identified components and for the radical sector of the internal \(3,3\) pair, while leaving its low-sector problem visible. ## 6. A uniform estimate for every positive pair of powers at least three The energy comparison for the pair \(3,3\) extends to every pair of real powers \(n,p\ge3\). The complete outside endpoints are essential in the following proof of interiority. A pair embedded in a longer selected path has different boundary conditions, and this argument does not establish the corresponding comparison there. **Theorem 5.** Consider two consecutive selected vertices, each joined at its other end to a complete outside vertex. Give the selected vertices real powers \(n,p\ge3\) and unit charges. Their convex filling problem has its unique minimum in the interior of every edge square. It therefore determines the unique positive stationary solution with the original logarithmic normalization. Its complete-boundary rate satisfies \[ M_{n,p}>2M_\infty+\frac1{100}. \tag{23} \] For integer \(n,p\ge3\), let \[ P_{n,p,N}(s,u)= \mathcal D_{n,N}^{(t)}\mathcal D_{p,N}^{(r)} [K_N(s,t)K_N(t,r)K_N(r,u)]. \tag{24} \] Its middle-edge radical term obeys \[ |P_{n,p,N}^{\rm rad}(s,u)| \le CN^a\exp N\!\left[ M_{n,p}-\frac1{100} -\frac{(1-\cos s)+(1-\cos u)}{200}\right] \quad(s,u\in[-\pi,\pi]). \tag{25} \] The same conclusions hold for the mirrored pair \(-n,-p\). The real-power statement concerns the geometric variational problem; the finite quantum statement here uses integer crossing powers. **Proof of interiority.** Work first with the negative-power convention of the [variational corridor proof](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_negative_corridor_variational_bounds.md). Its strict-feasibility and corner arguments in Propositions 1--3 use real inequalities \(b_v\ge2\), without rounding a power to an integer. They therefore apply to \(b_v=n,b_w=p\). Alternatively, strict feasibility follows directly by reversing the signs of the real angles in the trial constructed below. These arguments give a unique minimum, exclude open sides, and show that the two outside edges are interior. Their selected incidences are strictly negative. Every selected real return and dual height is also strictly negative. Suppose the middle edge had a corner. Orient it so that \(v\) has the negative corner incidence, and write \(\theta=-s_v\), \(\phi=-s_w\). The corner classification gives \(\theta>\pi/2\), \(0<\phi<\pi\), and \[ g_{v,e}=-\frac{\pi-\phi}{2},\qquad g_{w,e}=\frac{\pi-\theta}{2}. \tag{26} \] Write \(g_v^{\rm out},g_w^{\rm out}<0\) for the incidences on the outside edges. The two imaginary period equations read \[ n\theta=\pi+\phi+2g_v^{\rm out}<\pi+\phi,\qquad p\phi=3\pi-\theta+2g_w^{\rm out}<3\pi-\theta. \tag{27} \] The first equation and \(n\ge3\) imply \[ \frac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\frac{2\pi}{n} \le\frac{2\pi}{3}, \qquad \phi>n\theta-\pi>\frac{\pi}{2}. \tag{28} \] The second equation then gives \(p<5\). For completeness, the remaining corner contradiction uses only real inequalities, not the integrality of either power. Let \(X>0,H>0\) be the magnitudes of the relevant covectors of the companion interior square, and \(U,V>0\) those of the corner. The corner subgradient and companion-square formulas, as in equations (74)--(77) of the corridor proof, give \[ \begin{split} \sinh(2X)&=(-\cot\theta)\sin\phi,\\ u_w&=X-U>0,\qquad -k_{w,e}=V+H,\\ V&\ge V_0(U):= \tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}(\operatorname{csch}(2U)). \end{split} \tag{29} \] Here \(u_w=-h_w/2\). The real period equation at \(w\), including its strictly negative outside return, implies \[ V+H<p(X-U)<6(X-U). \tag{30} \] Consequently \[ 6X>6U+V_0(U)\ge C_6:=\frac{6\operatorname{arsinh}(1/6) +\operatorname{arsinh}6}{2} >\frac32\log3. \tag{31} \] The minimum occurs at \(\sinh(2U)=1/6\), by differentiation. For the last strict inequality, use \(\operatorname{arsinh}6>\log12\), \(6\operatorname{arsinh}(1/6)>6/7>5/6\), and \(\log(9/4)\le5/6\). On the other hand, (28)--(29) give \[ X\le\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}(1/\sqrt3) =\tfrac14\log3, \tag{32} \] contradicting (31). Thus there is no corner. The variational reconstruction gives the unique positive primitive solution. Mirroring returns to the positive-power convention. **Proof of the energy bound.** Put \[ b=\frac{\pi}{16},\qquad s_v=\frac{3\pi}{2n},\quad s_w=\frac{3\pi}{2p}, \qquad a=\frac{s_v}{4},\quad c=\frac{s_w}{4}. \tag{33} \] Set each of the four selected incidences equal to \(-\pi/8\), and both outside incidences and angles equal to zero. Then \(\sum g_{v,e}-ns_v/2=-\pi\), and likewise at \(w\). Moreover \(0<a,c\le2b\), so every edge inequality is strict. The total energy of this trial is \[ F_{\rm trial}(a,c)= 8E(a,b)+8E(c,b) +4\{E(a+b,c-b)+E(a-b,c+b)\}. \tag{34} \] The first two terms are at most \(16E(2b,b)\), since \(E_A\ge0\) for nonnegative coordinates. The expression in braces is convex jointly in \(a,c\) on \([0,2b]^2\). Every point of this rectangle is a convex combination of its four corners, so its value is at most the largest corner value. Evenness and coordinate symmetry of \(E\) give those values as \[ \begin{array}{c|c} (a,c)&E(a+b,c-b)+E(a-b,c+b)\\ \hline (0,0)&2E(b,b)\\ (2b,0),(0,2b)&E(3b,b)+E(b,b)\\ (2b,2b)&2E(3b,b). \end{array} \tag{35} \] Because \(E(b,b)\le E(3b,b)\), the last entry is the largest. Thus the actual minimum satisfies \[ F_{n,p}\le F_{\rm trial}(a,c) \le16E(\pi/8,\pi/16)+8E(3\pi/16,\pi/16) <\frac{18}{5}. \tag{36} \] The last inequality is exactly the rational estimate (16)--(21); no further numerical estimate is needed. The interiority just proved permits the absolute energy identity \(F_{n,p}=\pi(3M_\infty-M_{n,p})\). Equation (22) now proves (23). **Proof of the quantum consequence.** The exact radical contraction evaluates both crossing factors at physical colors. Their moduli are one for every integer \(n,p\). Thus the same bare-edge estimate used in (12) gives that inequality with \(P_N^{\rm rad}\) replaced by \(P_{n,p,N}^{\rm rad}\). Combining it with (23) proves (25). Conjugation gives the same-sign negative pair. \(\square\) This theorem removes the radical sector for every internal two-vertex source (24) with same-sign magnitudes at least three. It does not establish its low-sector asymptotic, a nonzero coefficient for its geometric contribution, or a bound for an arbitrary longer cluster of short powers. Those are separate questions about the original finite trace. ## 7. The middle Newton polynomials on the whole real period The cutoff in the low kernel also has a simple exact Fourier description. Set \[ m=\lfloor N/2\rfloor,\qquad L=N-1-m,\qquad \theta=\pi/N,\qquad s_1=2\sin\theta. \tag{37} \] The original polynomial \(e_L\) is the last one retained in \(K_N^{\rm low}\). It is not a radical element at either parity. **Lemma 6.** For every \(N\ge2\) and every complex \(t\), \[ e_L(-2\cos t)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac1N\sum_{k=-L}^L e^{ikt}, &N\text{ odd},\\[2mm] \displaystyle\frac4{Ns_1}\sum_{k=-L}^L \cos(k\theta)e^{ikt},&N\text{ even}. \end{cases} \tag{38} \] Consequently \[ \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|e_L(-2\cos t)| \le \begin{cases} 1,&N\text{ odd},\\ N,&N\text{ even}. \end{cases} \tag{39} \] All angular derivatives of fixed order cost at most the additional factor \(L^r\). All ordinary derivatives in the spectral variable \(z\in[-2,2]\) also have polynomial bounds, including at \(z=-2\). *Proof.* Use the full physical angular grid \[ t_j=\frac{\pi(N-1-2j)}N,\qquad 0\le j<N. \tag{40} \] At odd \(N=2m+1\), the Newton product vanishes at every distinct physical node except \(z=-2\). At that node \(e_m(-2)=1\). Indeed \(S_m^2=N\), and the numerator \(\prod_{a=0}^{m-1}(c_a+2)\) is \(N\). The latter equality also follows by differentiating \[ 2T_N(z/2)+2=(z+2)\prod_{a=0}^{m-1}(z-c_a)^2 \] at \(-2\): its derivative there is \(N^2\), and all factors \(c_a+2\) are positive. Thus the values on (40) are one at \(t=0\) and zero at the other \(N-1\) points. The polynomial in \(-2\cos t\) has frequencies \(-m,\ldots,m\). The unique Fourier interpolant on these \(N\) points is the first line of (38). At even \(N=2m\), the only nonzero physical value is at \(c_{m-1}=-2\cos\theta\), represented twice in (40), at \(t=\pm\theta\). The exact value is \[ e_{m-1}(c_{m-1}) =\frac{S_{N-2}}{S_{m-1}^2} =\frac{N/s_1}{N/2}=\frac2{s_1}. \tag{41} \] The product evaluation is the one used in the [middle-normal calculation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_bare_kernel_power_three_obstruction.md#6-the-midpoint-forcing-after-the-original-internal-pair-trace), equations (38)--(41). Discrete Fourier inversion on (40) therefore gives coefficient \(4\cos(k\theta)/(Ns_1)\). The possible Nyquist coefficient vanishes because \(\cos(m\theta)=0\). The remaining frequencies are exactly \(-L,\ldots,L\), proving the second line. Since both sides are trigonometric polynomials, the equalities hold for complex \(t\) as well. Every coefficient displayed in (38) is nonnegative. At even levels their sum is \[ \frac4{Ns_1}\sum_{k=-m+1}^{m-1}\cos(k\theta) =\frac1{N\sin^2(\theta/2)}\le N, \tag{42} \] using \(\sin(\pi/(2N))\ge1/N\). The odd sum is one. This proves (39) and the angular derivative bound. For ordinary spectral derivatives, apply Markov's inequality directly to \(e_L(z)\) on \([-2,2]\), whose degree is \(L\). There is no division by \(\sin t\), so the bound includes the parabolic endpoints. \(\square\) The next polynomial \(e_{L+1}\) belongs to the radical sector. The [radical Fourier estimate](research_high_newton_radical_contraction.md) gives \[ \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|e_{L+1}(-2\cos t)| \le\sqrt{N-1}. \tag{43} \] The two bounds concern the actual finite polynomials with their normals. They do not give geometric-rate estimates on a fixed complex internal contour. Such an estimate for the low kernel is explicitly false at some actual all-three path configurations. The [finite identity checker](../experiments/check_middle_newton_fourier_formula.py) compares (38) with the defining Newton product at levels \(2\) through \(18\), including every physical value and first ordinary normal and several complex angles. Its [saved record](../repro/results/research-middle-newton-fourier-formula.json) contains 493 comparisons at 100 decimal digits. These verify the finite normalizations; the proof for all levels is the Fourier inversion above. ## 8. Contracting several cutoff forcings before estimating them Orient any nonempty set \(F\) of selected edges of the original path. On each \(e=(v,w)\in F\), replace its kernel by the literal right side of the low-kernel difference equation: \[ J_{e,N}(z_v,z_w) =-s_{L+1}^2 e_L(z_v)e_{L+1}(z_w). \tag{44} \] Leave every other edge equal to its full original kernel, and take all the original crossing traces. Denote this finite source by \(\mathscr J_{F,N}\). The edges of \(F\) need not form a matching. This definition specifies a product of actual cutoff forcings; it does not assert that applying arbitrary difference operators to a network produces only these terms. Delete the edges of \(F\), replace their endpoints \(S=V(F)\) by free physical boundary variables, and let \(C\) denote the remaining components. An uncut edge between two vertices of \(S\) stays present. Let \(F_{C,N}\) be the original source of each such component, excluding the crossings at the evaluated vertices. **Proposition 7.** For fixed powers and a fixed path, \[ |\mathscr J_{F,N}| \le C_{\Gamma,\mathbf n,F}N^{a_{\Gamma,F}} \prod_C \sup_{\mathbf u\in[-\pi,\pi]^{\partial C}} |F_{C,N}(\mathbf u)|. \tag{45} \] This estimate is uniform in every real original outside angle. Every fixed collection of ordinary outside derivatives satisfies the same estimate with a possibly larger polynomial factor. Each component on the right has at most \(|I|-2\) traced vertices. *Proof.* At a vertex \(v\in S\), collect its incident factors from (44) into \(Q_v(z)\). Its degree is at most \(2(N-1)\), since the original degree of \(v\) is at most two. Equations (39) and (43) give \(\|Q_v\|_{[-2,2]}\le N^2\); Markov's inequality gives \(\|Q_v'\|_{[-2,2]}\le2N^4\). The factors \(s_{L+1}^2\) have absolute value at most four. Apply the full physical residue formula to \(\phi_N(R^{n_v}Q_v f)\). At a double physical root \(c\), its contribution is exactly \[ \eta\bigl[ (4-c^2)(R^{n_v}Q_v)'(c)-cR^{n_v}(c)Q_v(c) \bigr]f(c) +\eta(4-c^2)R^{n_v}(c)Q_v(c)f'(c). \tag{46} \] At the odd simple root \(-2\), the contribution is \(R^{n_v}(-2)Q_v(-2)f(-2)\), with no derivative. The original crossing has unit modulus at physical roots and \[ |(R^{n_v})'(c)|\le C_{n_v}N^2 \tag{47} \] at the double roots. This follows from the exact crossing-normal formula and the sine chord bound; it is valid for each fixed signed integer power. Thus all coefficients in (46), and their total absolute sum over the at most \(N\) roots, are bounded by powers of \(N\). No normal has been removed. After performing these functionals at every \(v\in S\), the remaining traces factor into the original components \(C\). Each removed vertex has at most one uncut incidence. Accordingly each differentiation in (46) is a first ordinary derivative in one component's boundary variable. Several such derivatives can act on the same component, but they are in its distinct boundary variables. Its original boundary polynomial has degree at most \(N-1\) in each one. Applying Markov's inequality successively bounds all these mixed derivatives by its whole-real-boundary supremum at polynomial cost. This proves (45). There are at least two removed traced vertices, since \(F\ne \varnothing\). Every component therefore has at most \(|I|-2\) traced vertices. For ordinary derivatives at the original outside boundary, use the same polynomial estimate after obtaining (45). \(\square\) If these smaller sources have their whole-boundary upper bounds \(\|F_{C,N}\|\le A_CN^{b_C}e^{N\mu_C}\), then (45) gives rate \(\sum_C\mu_C\). For positive paths, the [all-edge-subset comparison](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_positive_path_pair_activation_gap.md#5-removing-any-set-of-selected-edges) identifies this rate as \[ \sum_C\mu_C =M_\Gamma(\lambda^S)-|F|M_\infty <M_\Gamma(\mathbf1)-\frac{|F|}{1000}. \tag{48} \] The last strict bound remains conditional on the two support certificates specified in that note. Once those inequalities are established, it applies to every fixed literal forcing (44), not only to the two-vertex calculation in the earlier midpoint note. ## 9. What this does and does not supply in an induction Suppose whole-real-boundary upper bounds at the complete geometric rate are known for every original path source with fewer than \(m\) traced vertices. Under the geometric comparison just specified, all nonempty radical matching terms of an \(m\)-vertex path, and all terms (44), have a strict gap below its geometric rate. Their bounds consume only sources with at most \(m-2\) traced vertices. They require no nonzero leading coefficient in those shorter sources. Let \(Z_{\Gamma,N}^{\rm low}\) replace precisely the edges joining selected vertices by \(K_N^{\rm low}\); edges to the original outside boundary remain full. The exact radical expansion and the induction hypothesis give \[ \sup_{\mathbf u\in[-\pi,\pi]^{\partial\Gamma}} |Z_{\Gamma,N}(\mathbf u)-Z_{\Gamma,N}^{\rm low}(\mathbf u)| \le C N^a e^{N(M_\Gamma(\mathbf1)-1/1000)}. \tag{49} \] Hence an upper bound at rate \(M_\Gamma(\mathbf1)\) for the original \(m\)-vertex source is equivalent to the same upper bound for its joint low-sector source, up to polynomial factors. At complete boundary values a nonzero leading geometric asymptotic for either source transfers to the other unchanged. The remainder in (49) is an ordinary polynomial of degree at most \(N-1\) in each original boundary variable. Chebyshev expansion therefore extends (49) to complex outside angles at the additional rate \[ \sum_j|\Im u_j|. \tag{50} \] Fixed ordinary derivatives cost further powers of \(N\). This is sufficient to preserve a strict gap on a sufficiently small fixed boundary neighborhood; it is not a free geometric-rate bound on a large complex internal domain. The remaining induction step is the joint low-sector contour. The [unsummed phase theorem](research_unsummed_network_phase_coercivity.md) supplies a nondegenerate local geometric contour. It does not identify every complementary current with (44) or with a radical matching. The [exact facet rule](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_factorial_core_contour_compiler.md) lists where general factorial currents are supported, but gives no reduction of all of them to shorter physical-boundary sources. Moreover, a geometric upper bound for the individual low kernels is false on some actual positive all-three paths, by [the low-kernel obstruction](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_bare_kernel_power_three_obstruction.md#5-removing-the-radical-still-leaves-a-larger-cutoff-current). Summing each vertex first does not solve that issue either: [the traced three-crossing vertex](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_traced_three_vertex_endpoint.md) has a larger endpoint term near such configurations. Thus the missing assertion is specific: a contour identity for the joint low source whose main geometric term has its original nonzero coefficient, and whose entire complementary part either has a proved direct gap or reduces to the shorter sources bounded above. None of the preceding upper bounds alone provides that identity or its coefficient.

title: Real-meridian transport and one form for every meridian jet
