title: A positive variational formula for an actual source on a tree
text: # A positive variational formula for an actual source on a tree 20 November 2026. Research note; the public manuscripts remain frozen. A scalar contraction on a tree is the infimum of a product of positive local norms, after allowing full matrix changes of basis on its internal edges. The same statement holds for the norm of a vector-valued output. There is no replacement of the original closing functional in this formula. That functional is one of the tensors being optimized. The infimum is generally approached by increasingly singular changes of basis. Existence of the formula therefore gives neither a geometric minimizer nor a volume asymptotic. A second result gives a useful way to certify near optimality: on a fixed tree, matching the full reduced density matrices across every edge approximately forces the contraction norm to be close to the product of the local norms. The estimate is independent of the dimensions of the edge spaces. Matching only their diagonal entries is insufficient. These facts apply to the complete Conway compiler. They also apply directly to the actual all-main-color energy, by treating multiplication of the original physical braid operators as a tree of linear maps. The latter application retains the main-color cap projector and does not identify that energy with an auxiliary-color or unfilled covariance norm. ## 1. Tensors, pairings, and the permitted gauges Let \(\mathcal T\) be a finite connected tree, with vertex set \(V\) and internal edge set \(E\). At each edge \(e\), fix a finite-dimensional complex coordinate space \(H_e\), with its Euclidean Hermitian norm. Choose one endpoint as its positive end. A tensor at that end has an \(H_e\) factor; the tensor at the other end has an \(H_e^*\) factor. The edge contraction is the complex bilinear evaluation pairing. One distinguished vertex may also have an uncontracted output in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space \(F\). All other tensor factors are contracted along the tree. Denote the resulting output by \[ Y=\operatorname{Contr}(T_v:v\in V)\in F. \tag{1} \] The scalar case is \(F=\mathbb C\). Each local tensor has its ordinary coefficient Hilbert--Schmidt norm, denoted by \(\|T_v\|\). The dual coordinate factors have the corresponding Euclidean norm. An edge gauge is an invertible matrix \(g_e\in\mathrm{GL}(H_e)\). It acts by \(g_e\) at the positive end and by \(g_e^{-\mathsf T}\) at the negative end. These two actions preserve the bilinear evaluation. Consequently the gauged tensors \(T_v(g)\) have exactly the same output \(Y\), with its complex phases. Define \[ \mathcal C(T)=\inf_{g_e\in\mathrm{GL}(H_e)} \prod_{v\in V}\|T_v(g)\|. \tag{2} \] Every matrix and norm in this definition is specified before the output is evaluated. No factor contains a division by \(Y\). The original source must be included among the tensors. For example, a linear closing row is a one-leg tensor at the root. Leaving it out and optimizing an open network is a different problem. A retained external scalar can be put into that root tensor or kept as its known absolute multiplier. ## 2. The exact variational identity **Theorem 1.** For every network in Section 1, including a zero output, \[ \boxed{\mathcal C(T)=\|Y\|.} \tag{3} \] There is no dimension factor in (3). **Proof.** Contracting a leaf vector into its neighbor has operator norm at most the norm of that vector. Repeated Cauchy--Schwarz along the tree therefore gives \[ \|Y\|\le\prod_v\|T_v(g)\| \tag{4} \] for every gauge. This proves one inequality in (3). The bilinear functional associated with a vector has the same Euclidean norm as that vector; complex conjugation in its Riesz vector changes no norm. In particular no norm of an unnormalized Bell vector is inserted in (4). For the reverse inequality, use induction on the number of vertices. For one vertex, its tensor is precisely the output, and the assertion is immediate. Otherwise choose a leaf different from the output vertex. If its vector is zero, every product in (2) and the output are zero. Suppose its vector is nonzero. By interchanging the two edge conventions if necessary, regard it as a vector \(a\in H_e\). Choose an invertible edge gauge sending \(a\) to the first unit vector \(e_0\). Write the transformed neighboring tensor as \[ \sum_i e_i^*\otimes A_i. \] The remaining factors in \(A_i\) can include the output space \(F\). The reduced tree obtained by contracting the leaf has neighboring tensor \(A_0\), and its output is still \(Y\). Apply the further gauge \(D_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t,\ldots,t)\) at the leaf end of this edge, with \(t\to+\infty\). The leaf remains \(e_0\), of norm one; its neighbor becomes \[ e_0^*\otimes A_0+t^{-1}\sum_{i>0}e_i^*\otimes A_i. \] Its norm tends to \(\|A_0\|\). Fix any gauges on the other edges before taking this limit. Their actions commute with this edge action, so the limiting product is exactly the corresponding product for the reduced tree. Taking its infimum proves \(\mathcal C(T)\le\mathcal C(T_{\rm reduced})\). Induction and (4) give (3). If \(A_0=0\), the same limit gives zero; thus this argument also covers a zero output without a continuity assumption on the infimum. \(\square\) This proof is an exact contraction argument, rather than an assertion that a metric chosen from the unknown answer exists. It also explains why unbounded condition numbers are permitted in (2). The diagonal matrices \(D_t\) used in the proof become singular in the limit. The tree hypothesis concerns the contraction graph used in this theorem. A physical diagram with cycles may be compiled into a tree by bundling all live indices into a larger matrix index. The resulting gauge acts on that whole bundled space. It is not then a product of gauges on the original individual physical wires. ## 3. Positive matrices and geodesic convexity Full complex gauges can be replaced by positive Hermitian matrices. Indeed write \(g_e=U_eP_e\), where \(U_e\) is unitary and \(P_e>0\). At the two ends, the actions are \[ U_eP_e,\qquad \overline U_eP_e^{-\mathsf T}. \] The two unitary factors do not change their local tensor norms. Removing all of them shows that positive gauges have the same infimum. It is convenient to use \(H_e=P_e^2=g_e^*g_e>0\) as variable. The squared local norm is \[ \|T_v\|_H^2= \left\langle T_v, \left(\bigotimes_{e\text{ positive at }v}H_e\right) \otimes \left(\bigotimes_{e\text{ negative at }v}\overline H_e^{-1}\right) \otimes I_F\,T_v\right\rangle. \tag{5} \] The \(I_F\) factor is present only at the output vertex. Assume for this paragraph that each local tensor is nonzero. The objective is \[ L(H)=\sum_v\log\|T_v\|_H. \tag{6} \] **Proposition 2.** The function (6) is convex along simultaneous positive-matrix geodesics \[ H_e(t)=H_e(0)^{1/2}\exp(tX_e)H_e(0)^{1/2}, \qquad X_e=X_e^*. \tag{7} \] **Proof.** In (5), pull the fixed factors \(H_e(0)^{1/2}\), or their conjugate inverses, into the tensor. Diagonalize each Hermitian \(X_e\). On a negative end the corresponding generator is \(-\overline X_e\). The remaining tensor factors act on different legs and commute. Thus the squared norm at a vertex has the form \[ \sum_\alpha c_\alpha e^{t\ell_\alpha}, \qquad c_\alpha\ge0, \] with real \(\ell_\alpha\). The second derivative of its logarithm is the variance of these real numbers for their normalized positive weights. It is nonnegative. Sum the resulting convex functions and divide by two. \(\square\) Convexity does not assert attainment. Even when \(Y\ne0\), the minimizing matrices can escape to infinity in the positive cone. Restricting (2) to diagonal gauges, prescribed tensor-product gauges, or a bounded condition number generally gives only an upper bound on \(\|Y\|\). ## 4. A dimension-independent certificate from full edge marginals There is a local condition which certifies that a specified set of gauges is already close to the infimum. It uses full reduced density matrices, including their off-diagonal entries. Fix gauges and suppose all gauged local tensors are nonzero. Normalize them to unit vectors \(\tau_v=T_v(g)/\|T_v(g)\|\). For an internal edge, let \(\rho_{v,e}\) be the reduced density matrix of \(\tau_v\) on that coordinate factor; trace over all its other factors, including \(F\) when appropriate. Each density matrix is positive with trace one. Because the contraction is bilinear, the two endpoint matrices are compared with a transpose: \[ \delta_e=\|\rho_{v,e}-\rho_{w,e}^{\mathsf T}\|_1, \qquad \delta=\max_e\delta_e. \tag{8} \] Here \(\|\cdot\|_1\) is the trace norm. Transposition leaves this norm unchanged, so (8) is independent of the chosen endpoint order. **Theorem 3.** Let \(m=|V|\ge2\), put \(S=\sum_{e\in E}\delta_e\), and write \([a]_+=\max(a,0)\). Then \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{\|Y\|}{\prod_v\|T_v(g)\|} \ge[1-4m\sqrt S-5mS]_+. \quad} \tag{9} \] The estimate has no dependence on any edge dimension. **Proof.** Work first with the normalized local tensors. For a density matrix put \(L(\rho)=1-\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)\). Two elementary properties control the errors without a dependence on tree depth. For a bipartite density matrix, \[ L(\rho_{AB})\le L(\rho_A)+L(\rho_B). \tag{10} \] Indeed the commuting swaps \(F_A,F_B\) on two copies satisfy \((I-F_A)(I-F_B)\ge0\). Taking its trace against \(\rho_{AB}\otimes\rho_{AB}\) gives (10). Also \[ |L(\rho)-L(\sigma)| \le\|\rho-\sigma\|_1\|\rho+\sigma\|_{\rm op} \le2\|\rho-\sigma\|_1. \tag{11} \] Orient the tree toward its output vertex. A nonroot vertex tensor is pure on its parent leg and all its child legs together. Their two reduced density matrices have the same nonzero eigenvalues, by the singular-value decomposition. Its parent-leg linear entropy is therefore at most the sum of its child-leg linear entropies, by repeated use of (10). At a leaf that entropy is zero. Across each edge, (11) costs at most \(2\delta_e\). Induction from the leaves shows that the linear entropy on every half-edge is at most \(2S\). The output space at the root causes no change: the root is not used for a parent-leg induction. Choose a top unit eigenvector \(a_{v,e}\) of each half-edge density matrix, and let \(\eta_{v,e}=1-\lambda_{\max}(\rho_{v,e})\). Since \(\operatorname{tr}\rho^2\le\lambda_{\max}(\rho)\), \(\eta_{v,e}\le2S\). The tensor product of these rank-one projectors at a vertex has probability \[ p_v\ge1-\sum_{e\ni v}\eta_{v,e} \ge1-2\deg(v)S. \tag{12} \] The projectors act on different legs and commute, so this is the elementary union bound for their complementary projections. Suppose temporarily that \(S<1/(16m^2)\), so every \(p_v\) is positive. Normalize the projected vertex tensor, and call the result \(\varphi_v\). At a nonroot it is a product of its chosen half-edge vectors, with the scalar phase fixed by the projection of \(\tau_v\). At the root it is their product tensored with a unit output vector in \(F\), again with that phase retained. Consequently \[ \|\tau_v-\varphi_v\|^2=2-2\sqrt{p_v} \le2(1-p_v)\le4\deg(v)S. \tag{13} \] The vectors at the ends of an edge are nearly paired. Write \(\rho=\rho_{v,e}\), \(\sigma=\rho_{w,e}^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(P,Q\) be their top rank-one eigenprojections. A trace-zero Hermitian matrix tested against a projection has absolute trace at most half its trace norm; its positive and negative parts have equal trace. Hence \[ 1-\eta_{v,e}-\delta_e/2\le\operatorname{tr}(P\sigma) \le\operatorname{tr}(PQ)+\eta_{w,e}. \] The last inequality splits \(\sigma\) into its top eigenspace and its positive remainder of trace \(\eta_{w,e}\). The bilinear edge overlap \(t_e=|a_{v,e}^{\mathsf T}a_{w,e}|\) therefore satisfies \[ t_e^2\ge1-\tfrac92 S. \tag{14} \] The product network \((\varphi_v)\) has output norm \(\prod_e t_e\), at least \(1-\tfrac92(m-1)S\): use \(\sqrt{1-a}\ge1-a\) and multiply the resulting bounds. The tree Cauchy estimate (4) and a multilinear telescoping sum give \[ \begin{split} \|\operatorname{Contr}(\tau_v)\| &\ge1-\tfrac92(m-1)S-\sum_v\|\tau_v-\varphi_v\|\\ &\ge1-\tfrac92(m-1)S-2\sqrt{2m(m-1)S}. \end{split} \tag{15} \] Here \(\sum_v\deg(v)=2(m-1)\) and Cauchy--Schwarz were used. This proves the weaker lower bound (9) when \(S<1/(16m^2)\). If \(S\ge1/(16m^2)\), its bracket is nonpositive, so (9) follows from nonnegativity of a norm. Restoring the local norms proves the assertion. \(\square\) In particular, for a fixed tree and a sequence of levels, the condition \(\delta_N\to0\) implies \[ \frac{\|Y_N\|}{\prod_v\|T_{v,N}(g_N)\|}\longrightarrow1. \tag{16} \] This criterion involves only local tensors, their prescribed gauges, and their reduced density matrices. It does not assume a lower bound for the unknown output. It also handles growing trees: since \(S\le(m-1)\delta\), the condition \(\delta=o(m^{-3})\) suffices for the ratio in (16) to tend to one. No optimal numerical constants or dependence on \(m\) are claimed. The same matrices are the full gauge derivative. Vary one edge gauge by \(g_e(s)=e^{sX}g_e\), with \(X=X^*\). Direct differentiation gives \[ \left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}\sum_v\log\|T_v(g(s))\| =\operatorname{tr}X (\rho_{v,e}-\rho_{w,e}^{\mathsf T}). \tag{17} \] Exact full matrix balance is therefore the stationary condition. On a tree it saturates (4). A pure leaf marginal then forces its neighbor to factor across that edge; removing it propagates this factorization. Thus a finite exactly balanced gauge is a restrictive condition. The limits used in Theorem 1 need not provide such a finite gauge. Diagonal or classical moment balance is weaker. On a single edge, the unit vectors \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) and \((1,-1)/\sqrt2\) have the same diagonal probabilities but zero bilinear pairing. Their full density matrices, compared as in (8), differ. Theorem 3 cannot be invoked after discarding that difference. ## 5. The actual Conway source and the actual main-color energy The complete Conway compiler in [Orthogonal boundary packets under Conway composition](research_conway_full_boundary_quotient_gram.md) uses the full Newton boundary space, the actual multiplication tensor, the actual turn, arbitrary full leaf packets, and the original closing row. Its expression graph, with that row included, is a tree of the kind above. Theorem 1 therefore gives an exact positive variational formula for its original scalar. All repeated-root derivative channels and the original leaf phases remain in the tensors. There is also a direct application to the whole main-color energy, without using a complete-color Conway space for ordinary main colors. Fix a braid on \(b\) strands and use the original \(N\)-dimensional physical modules at each of its \(N\) main-color orbit points. Set \[ A_N=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N\operatorname{End}(V_{j,N}^{\otimes b}), \qquad \dim A_N=N^{2b+1}. \tag{18} \] Equip this space with its coordinate Hilbert--Schmidt norm. Each signed crossing of the fixed word supplies one known vector in \(A_N\). Componentwise matrix multiplication supplies a fixed bilinear tensor. Compile the word as any finite multiplication tree. Its output is the tuple of the original physical braid operators. At the root use the explicit linear map which takes the prescribed \((0,0)\) partial pivotal trace in each color, with its zero-framing factor. Thus the uncontracted output is exactly \[ Y_N=(c_1,\ldots,c_N). \tag{19} \] The map is given by the original pivot matrices and selected cut entry; it is not defined from the evaluated numbers \(c_j\). The [main-color cap-projection theorem](research_main_color_cap_projection_energy.md) proves, with precisely these original conventions, \[ \|Y_N\|^2=E_N=|K_N|^2+R_N, \qquad 0\le R_N\le(N-1)(N/2)^{2b-2}. \tag{20} \] In particular all the cap coherence in that theorem remains inside the root tensor in the present construction. It has not been replaced by an independent product window or an identity projector. For this concrete tree, Theorem 1 says \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{\pi}{N}\log E_N =\inf_{H_e>0}\frac{2\pi}{N} \sum_v\log\|T_{v,N}\|_H. \quad} \tag{21} \] The left side is finite: the ordinary trivial main color is one. The internal gauges in (21) are full matrices on the bundled space (18). The claim does not make the original physical crossing diagram acyclic, or make these gauges tensor products of single-wire metrics. The diagonal physical-gauge hierarchy in [the weighted plat-energy note](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_weighted_fourier_plat_energy.md) is a useful restricted upper-bound problem. The equality here uses the full edge matrix gauges of a compiled tree. Restricting those gauges again would require a separate argument for equality. ## 6. A concrete geometric certificate and the remaining theorem Suppose the original knot is hyperbolic and its complement volume is \(V>0\). A sufficient certificate for its volume identity is now: 1. Specify positive full edge metrics for the actual tree in (18)--(19), independently of the unknown output. 2. Prove that their full marginal defects (8) tend to zero. 3. Prove that their local norm objective tends to the geometric value: \[ \frac{2\pi}{N}\sum_v\log\|T_{v,N}\|_{H_N}\longrightarrow V. \] Equivalently, if \(F_N=\prod_v\|T_{v,N}\|_{H_N} =\exp(NV/(2\pi)+o(N))\) and \(S_N=\sum_e\delta_{e,N}\to0\) for this fixed tree, Theorem 3 gives (16). These statements imply \(\pi N^{-1}\log E_N\to V\). The polynomial remainder in (20) then gives the original Kashaev volume identity. Eventual nonvanishing is a consequence, rather than a premise. This replaces a global closing-angle estimate by a local full-matrix balance certificate. It does not show that the classical angle equations already provide that certificate. Their scalar or diagonal balance must still be connected to the full matrices in (8), including their phases. The local Gaussian covariance of actual crossing kernels is one possible input to such a construction; no such global construction is proved here. Nor may an infimum and a large-level limit simply be interchanged in (21). Candidate geometric metrics give upper bounds on the infimum. Theorem 3 supplies a lower comparison only when their full defects are controlled. Unknown escaping metric sequences are otherwise still allowed. For the finite-exception problem, the certificate would have to survive every required fixed short partial filling. Its constants can depend on that fixed partial assignment; the filling coefficients remain fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity. One must prove the certificate for all sufficiently long remaining assignments that give hyperbolic knots, and repeat it on the finitely many short-coordinate branches. Theorem 1 is valid on every such branch, but does not supply its geometric metrics. Exact reductions which leave a fixed hyperbolic core in an infinite assignment fiber still require a volume proof for that core. The variational reformulation does not remove that obligation. ## Direct texts and proof scope The linear-algebra proofs above are self-contained. The following complete texts were read for the actual-source applications and comparison with the existing gauge construction: | Direct text | SHA-256 | |---|---| | [Complete Conway compiler](research_conway_full_boundary_quotient_gram.md) | `debe56dbad8151b90d44d0fccbf0dcf33dafb780370e01c8acdadbd2939dc077` | | [Actual main-color cap projection](research_main_color_cap_projection_energy.md) | `79856f4581e099a1e8a16cdd76ab4578377070e2b3dbaa1a7bed1d5dbb358968` | | [Weighted physical-source gauges](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_weighted_fourier_plat_energy.md) | `69757cb8ab3b857b690d9da8d3d7a46e4a42df4f0ab47a6bb85816aa9efc38b2` | No mathematical program, numerical test, build, git operation, or public document change was used. The capacity identity is elementary tensor linear algebra, not a novelty claim about general tensor scaling. Its purpose here is an exact formulation for the original source and the dimension-independent full-marginal certificate, with the remaining geometric construction stated explicitly.

title: Integrating a shared microscopic current in the actual endpoint modes
text: # Integrating a shared microscopic current in the actual endpoint modes Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The original microscopic current integrates one common real parameter at all incidences of its removed vertex. On buffered physical windows, its exact full-jet representatives admit a uniform integrated estimate sharper than the supremum of their separate endpoint factors. The gain is logarithmic. A nonzero integrated coefficient for every incidence number at least three, and a surviving zero-frequency term for two incidences, preclude an exponential improvement from this local integration alone. These are local source statements. The actual remaining traces, outside rows, interfaces and connecting contours are retained. No whole-current rate or nonzero original closing is inferred. ## 1. The original current and its local representatives Fix an integer \(n\), a real \(A>0\), and an incidence number \(d\ge1\), all independent of \(N\). Put \[ \eta=(-1)^{N-1},\quad C_{N,n}=e^{\pi i n(N-1)^2/(4N)},\quad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N),\quad C_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi/N). \tag{1} \] The exact original unit-charge current is \[ V_{n,1}^{A/N}[f] =\int_0^{A/N}\rho_{N,n,1}(h)f(2\cosh h)\,dh, \] \[ \rho_{N,n,1}(h)= \frac{i\eta N^2C_{N,n}}{2\pi} \frac{\sinh h\,e^{inN(\pi^2-h^2)/(4\pi)} \sinh(nNh/2)} {\cosh^2(Nh/2)}. \tag{2} \] With the common variable \(\alpha=Nh\), define \[ \Theta_{N,n}=\frac{i\eta C_{N,n}e^{inN\pi/4}}{2\pi},\qquad q_{N,n}(\alpha)= N\sinh(\alpha/N)\frac{\sinh(n\alpha/2)}{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)} e^{-in\alpha^2/(4\pi N)}. \tag{3} \] Then \(\rho(h)\,dh=\Theta_{N,n}q_{N,n}(\alpha)\,d\alpha\) exactly. In particular \(|\Theta_{N,n}|=1/(2\pi)\). There is no discarded crossing phase or denominator alias. For \(n=0\), every integral below is exactly zero. For each incidence \(i\), choose the actual sharp baseline and one designated-half representative \(H_{i,N}^{\sigma_i}(x_i,\alpha)\) of the endpoint kernel \(K_N(w_N(\alpha),C_N(x_i))\). Use fixed nested real windows with buffers inside \(0<\Re x_i<1/2\), any prescribed finite heights, and a compact part of the designated half \(\sigma_i\Im x_i\ge0\). All estimates hold on smaller buffers. No fold or endpoint extension is needed here. The pinned actual connection and repair theorems give, for real \(0\le\alpha\le A\), uniformly on these domains, \[ H_{i,N}^{\sigma_i}(x_i,\alpha) =g_\alpha(Ns_i)+O_{\mathrm{hol},x_i}(N^{-1-\epsilon}), \qquad s_i=\frac{\sin(\pi x_i)}{\pi}, \tag{4} \] for some \(\epsilon>0\). Every fixed spatial derivative has this error. The value \(\epsilon\) may be decreased for the finite set of windows. The logarithm of \(s_i\) is its continuation from positive real \(s_i\), and is bounded on the chosen compacts. Here \[ \mathfrak k_\pm(\alpha)= \frac{\Gamma(\pm i\alpha/\pi)} {\Gamma(1/2\pm i\alpha/(2\pi))^4},\qquad g_\alpha(Ns)= \frac{\mathfrak k_+(\alpha)e^{i\alpha\log(Ns)/\pi} +\mathfrak k_-(\alpha)e^{-i\alpha\log(Ns)/\pi}}{Ns}. \tag{5} \] The combined expression is removable at \(\alpha=0\). No endpoint-parameter derivative estimate for the error in (4) is assumed or used. Define the integrated local representative \[ \mathcal J_{N,n,d}(\mathbf x)= \Theta_{N,n}\int_0^A q_{N,n}(\alpha) \prod_{i=1}^dH_{i,N}^{\sigma_i}(x_i,\alpha)\,d\alpha . \tag{6} \] The same \(\alpha\) occurs in all \(d\) factors. Its actual polynomial counterpart is \[ \mathcal Q_{N,n,d}(\mathbf Z)= \int_0^{A/N}\rho_{N,n,1}(h) \prod_{i=1}^dK_N(2\cosh h,Z_i)\,dh. \tag{7} \] At every covered physical grid tuple, (6) and (7) have exactly the same values and mixed first spectral normals. This follows from the exact individual repairs, their product rule, and differentiation under a finite integral. Identifying several \(Z_i\)'s is also allowed: the ordinary product rule retains the one full normal of that shared color. An additional joint spectator independent of \(\alpha\) remains inside its subsequent original trace. ## 2. Uniform integrated upper bounds Put \(L=\log N/\pi\), and consider sufficiently large \(N\). **Theorem 1.** For every fixed spatial multi-index \(\beta\), \[ |\partial_{\mathbf x}^{\beta}\mathcal J_{N,n,d}| \le C_\beta N^{-d} \begin{cases} L^{-1},&d=1,\\ 1,&d=2,\\ L^{d-3},&d\ge3. \end{cases} \tag{8} \] The constants are uniform on the prescribed buffered compacts and at both parities. They may depend on \(n,A,d\) and the domains. The same theorem holds with any or all representatives replaced by their actual baselines. *Proof.* Factor the density as \[ q_{N,n}(\alpha)=\alpha^2b_{N,n}(\alpha),\qquad b_{N,n}(0)=n/2. \tag{9} \] On a fixed complex neighborhood of \([0,A]\), small enough to avoid the zeros of \(\cosh(\alpha/2)\), these are holomorphic with uniformly bounded derivatives, and \[ b_{N,n}\longrightarrow b_n(\alpha)=\frac{\sinh(n\alpha/2)} {\alpha\cosh^2(\alpha/2)} \quad\hbox{uniformly with every fixed derivative.} \tag{10} \] The value at zero is removable. Let \(\ell_i=\log s_i/\pi\). The Gamma residues are \(\mathfrak k_+=-i/(\pi\alpha)+O(1)\) and \(\mathfrak k_-=i/(\pi\alpha)+O(1)\). Consequently there are holomorphic, uniformly bounded coefficients \(a_i,b_i\), with all fixed derivatives on slightly smaller domains, such that exactly \[ Ns_i\,g_\alpha(Ns_i) =a_i(\alpha)\frac{\sin(L\alpha)}{\alpha} +b_i(\alpha)\cos(L\alpha), \qquad a_i(0)=2/\pi . \tag{11} \] Explicitly, \[ a_i=i\alpha[ \mathfrak k_+e^{i\ell_i\alpha} -\mathfrak k_-e^{-i\ell_i\alpha}],\qquad b_i=\mathfrak k_+e^{i\ell_i\alpha} +\mathfrak k_-e^{-i\ell_i\alpha}. \tag{12} \] Their apparent singularities at zero cancel. Choose the complex parameter neighborhood smaller if necessary to avoid all other Gamma singularities. No large-\(N\) parameter derivative is involved. Expanding the product in (11), the terms with \(j\) sine-over-parameter factors have integrals of the form \[ \int_0^A \alpha^{2-j}F_{j,N}(\alpha,\mathbf x) \sin^j(L\alpha)\cos^{d-j}(L\alpha)\,d\alpha, \tag{13} \] where the finite family of \(F_{j,N}\)'s and their fixed derivatives are uniformly bounded. For \(j\le2\), their absolute integrals are bounded. For \(j\ge4\), split at \(1/L\), use \(|\sin(L\alpha)|\le\min(L\alpha,1)\), and integrate to obtain \(O(L^{j-3})\). For \(j=3\), the trigonometric polynomial \(\sin^3 u\cos^{d-3}u\) is a finite sum of nonzero sine harmonics. Write \(F_{3,N}(\alpha)=F_{3,N}(0)+\alpha G_{3,N}(\alpha)\). The \(G\)-term has bounded absolute integral. Each remaining integral \(\int_0^A\sin(kL\alpha)\,d\alpha/\alpha\) is uniformly bounded: after rescaling, its tail is bounded by integration by parts. This proves (8) for \(d\ge2\). When \(d=1\), (13) consists of a sine with smooth coefficient \(\alpha F_{1,N}\), and a cosine with smooth coefficient \(\alpha^2F_{0,N}\). One integration by parts gives \(O(L^{-1})\), including its endpoint at \(A\); both coefficients vanish at zero. Finally (4), the coalesced bound \(|g_\alpha(Ns_i)|\le CL/N\), and the product rule show that replacing the Gamma product by the actual product costs \[ O_\beta(N^{-d-\epsilon}L^{d-1}). \tag{14} \] This is smaller than every scale in (8). The same argument applies to every fixed spatial derivative: differentiating (11)--(13) changes only uniformly bounded coefficient functions. The pinned repair estimates supply the corresponding actual derivative error in (14). \(\square\) ## 3. The retained endpoint, zero-frequency term and small-parameter layer The upper bound is not an exponential improvement. Its leading terms can be specified without discarding the endpoint \(A\). For \(d=1\), twice integrating the two individual exponentials gives \[ \begin{split} \mathcal J_{N,n,1}(x) =\frac{\Theta_{N,n}}{Ns}\frac{q_{N,n}(A)}{iL} \bigl[ \mathfrak k_+(A)e^{iA(L+\ell)} -\mathfrak k_-(A)e^{-iA(L+\ell)} \bigr]+O_{\mathrm{hol},x}(N^{-1}L^{-2}). \end{split} \tag{15} \] Indeed \(q_{N,n}\mathfrak k_\pm e^{\pm i\ell\alpha}\) are smooth with uniformly bounded derivatives and have value zero at \(\alpha=0\). Their second integration by parts has bounded endpoint and integral remainders. Equation (14) is absorbed in the error of (15). The displayed endpoint coefficient may oscillate or vanish; no lower bound is assigned to it. For \(d=2\), let \[ q_n(\alpha)=\alpha\frac{\sinh(n\alpha/2)}{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)}, \] \[ B_{n,A}(s_1,s_2)= \int_0^A q_n(\alpha)\mathfrak k_+(\alpha)\mathfrak k_-(\alpha) \left[e^{i\alpha\log(s_1/s_2)/\pi} +e^{-i\alpha\log(s_1/s_2)/\pi}\right]\,d\alpha . \tag{16} \] The integrand is removable at zero. Then \[ \mathcal J_{N,n,2} =\frac{\Theta_{N,n}}{N^2s_1s_2} [B_{n,A}(s_1,s_2)+O_{\mathrm{hol},\mathbf x}(L^{-1})]. \tag{17} \] The two equal-sign modal products have frequencies \(\pm2L\). Their coefficients, including \(q_{N,n}\), are smooth at zero, so integration by parts bounds them by \(O(L^{-1})\). The opposite-sign products have frequency zero in \(L\) and give (16). Replacing \(q_{N,n}\) by \(q_n\) costs \(O(N^{-1})\); (14) is also smaller than the displayed error. If \(s_1=s_2>0\) and \(n\ne0\), then \[ B_{n,A}(s_1,s_1) =2\int_0^Aq_n(\alpha)|\mathfrak k_+(\alpha)|^2\,d\alpha \tag{18} \] is nonzero and has the sign of \(n\). This is one coefficient identity for the whole two-incidence operator, not a positivity claim for its later closing. **Theorem 2.** For every \(d\ge3\), uniformly on the same spatial compacts and with every fixed spatial derivative, \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{N^d}{\Theta_{N,n}L^{d-3}}\mathcal J_{N,n,d} \longrightarrow \frac{n}{2}\left(\frac2\pi\right)^d \frac{\mathcal C_d}{\prod_i s_i}, \quad} \tag{19} \] where \[ \mathcal C_3=\pi/4,\qquad \mathcal C_d=\int_0^\infty t^{2-d}\sin^d t\,dt>0 \quad(d\ge4). \tag{20} \] For \(n\ne0\) the limit is nowhere zero on these compacts. *Proof.* Suppose first \(d\ge4\). Only the term \(j=d\) of (13) can contribute after division by \(L^{d-3}\). Each term with \(j<d\) tends to zero by the bounds just proved. In the remaining term set \(t=L\alpha\). Its normalized integrand is \[ {\bf1}_{t\le AL}\,t^{2-d}\sin^d t\, b_{N,n}(t/L)\prod_i a_i(t/L). \tag{21} \] The absolute majorant \(C t^{2-d}|\sin t|^d\) is integrable for \(d\ge4\), both at zero and infinity. The coefficient tends uniformly on compact \(t\)-intervals to \((n/2)(2/\pi)^d\). Dominated convergence proves (19). It applies after every fixed spatial derivative as well, using the coefficient bounds; the actual error (14), divided by \(N^{-d}L^{d-3}\), is \(O(N^{-\epsilon}L^2)\). For \(d=3\), all \(j<3\) trigonometric polynomials in (13) have nonzero frequencies only, since their total degree is odd. Their coefficients are smooth at zero; integration by parts gives \(O(L^{-1})\). For the remaining term put \(F_N=b_{N,n}\prod_i a_i\), so \(F_N(0)=(n/2)(2/\pi)^3\). The difference \([F_N(\alpha)-F_N(0)]/\alpha\) has uniformly bounded first derivative and hence contributes \(O(L^{-1})\). The constant term is \[ F_N(0)\int_0^{AL}\frac{\sin^3 t}{t}\,dt \longrightarrow F_N(0)\pi/4. \tag{22} \] For completeness, integration by parts gives a uniform \(O(R^{-1})\) tail for each \(\sin(kt)/t\). Its integral is \(\pi/2\) for \(k>0\): exponential damping gives \(\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon t}\sin(kt)\,dt/t =\arctan(k/\varepsilon)\), and the same tail estimate removes the damping. Now \(\sin^3t=(3\sin t-\sin3t)/4\), proving (22). This is conditional Dirichlet convergence, not absolute dominated convergence. The argument and actual error bound apply to spatial derivatives too. For even \(d\ge4\), positivity in (20) is immediate. For odd \(d\ge5\), pair successive intervals of length \(\pi\). Each pair is the integral of \(\sin^d u>0\), \(0<u<\pi\), times \((2k\pi+u)^{2-d}-((2k+1)\pi+u)^{2-d}>0\). Absolute convergence permits these pairings. Thus \(\mathcal C_d>0\). \(\square\) ## 4. Exact source placement and limits of the estimate Equations (6)--(7) are a local representation of the original current at one removed vertex, with arbitrary fixed incidence number. The crossing power \(n=0\) makes this removed current zero; it places no restriction on powers at surviving vertices. The cut height \(A/N\) is retained exactly, including the term (15). Changing \(A\) or joining adjacent height pieces is a different decomposition whose endpoint terms must be added with their original orientations. At each surviving traced color, the pinned one-sided construction expresses the original physical-window trace as its two exterior half-contours plus its real interface. Integrating that exact identity in \(\alpha\) commutes with all finite traces and contour integrals. The integrated interface keeps its sharp exponential bound because \(\int_0^A|q_{N,n}(\alpha)|\,d\alpha\le C\). All original vertical half-sides, rational aliases and physical rows outside the windows remain. The common surviving spectator has not been removed or assigned a norm bound here. Thus the nonzero limit (19) is a local integrated multiplier; it is not a nonzero coefficient for the original scalar. Nor do (8)--(19) bound the ordinary canonical polynomial at off-grid colors. Its exact local full jets are represented by (6), and that is the scope of the estimate. Several current vertices may have edges between them. Their factors \(K_N(w_N(\alpha),w_N(\beta))\), or other parameter-dependent joint sources, are additional shared amplitudes. This proof does not omit them or silently extend (19) to them. Likewise it supplies no bound for a subsequent outer turn. For a parent's fixed height \(H>0\), the full current ranges over \(0\le\alpha\le NH\); the theorem concerns its bounded microscopic segment only. The supremum bound for \(d\) separate factors is \(O(N^{-d}(\log N)^d)\). Integrating their actual common parameter improves this to (8), while (17)--(20) show why the improvement cannot generally be exponential in \(N\). Shared signs create a zero-frequency sector, and the coalescing layer \(\alpha\asymp1/\log N\) has a nonzero integrated coefficient. Any strict parent-action comparison still requires the complete source and its retained currents. ## 5. Coverage and direct sources The full-current note already supplies the exact integration and finite charge convolution. The grouped Ward-current matching formula and the vertical cotangent regrouping identity concern different current representations; their complete texts were checked for overlap. Neither supplies the shared Gamma-mode integral above. They are coverage pointers, not proof dependencies. The following complete direct sources were read at these hashes, with their used normalization, actual-connection and full-jet implications checked: * [Original full-period current](research_full_period_current_charge_convolution.md), SHA256 3f74b9824ecbf0b71a79b17959c7208f650103f95932192cfba87c7a7aa05595. * [Actual tall Gamma connection](research_endpoint_nonreal_insertion_lower_bound.md), SHA256 ab3b4687b53c2168d22342c0e822b243a563f716d2a7a0de18d87c372546d7d0. * [Exact one-sided full-jet window assembly](research_sharp_endpoint_one_sided_window_assembly.md), SHA256 163d4cf2fc98648c0739152dbb463f2ad8f19d58b34b31d9184469847e60e541. Only written mathematics and source-text/hash reads were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or build was run. Previously adopted notes and public manuscripts were unchanged.

title: Sharp CROSS-degree domination and a uniform original seam gap
status: All-spectrum CROSS domination, explicit seam gap and filled-period negligibility
text: # Sharp CROSS-degree domination and a uniform original seam gap 31 October 2026. The comparison is between the explicitly defined sharp functionals. It does not turn a coefficient limsup into a coefficient limit. The global coefficient upper theorem supplies the finite source consequence at both parities and all spectral boundaries. ## 1. The full closed-domain functional Use the original local degree order q=(q_x,q_b,q_c,q_y), q>=0 and sum q=1, and put mu=q_b, nu=1-q_c, xi=q_x, 0<=xi<=nu-mu. The CROSS degree closure is 0<=mu<=1/2<=nu<=1. (1) This is a condition on the original four degrees. It does not assign a finite coefficient to a new path label at a seam. For 0<=delta<=1/2 use exactly the full sharp functional in the global coefficient theorem: alpha_delta(t)=2cos(2pi t)+2cos(2pi delta), Lambda_delta(t;x,y)=2sin(pi t) *[(x+y)sin(pi t) +sqrt((x-y)^2 sin^2(pi t)+4xy cos^2(pi delta))], B_delta(mu,nu)=int_0^mu log|alpha_delta(t)|dt +int_nu^1 log|alpha_delta(t)|dt, H_delta(q)=B_delta(mu,nu) +inf_(l in R){int_mu^nu log Lambda_delta(t;exp(l),1)dt-xi*l}. (2) All integrals include their actual unused rows. The logarithmic singularities are integrable. H is continuous on the entire closed simplex and spectral interval by the proved uniform tilt-clipping argument, including xi=0,nu-mu, diagonal rows, protected coordinates, and delta=1/2. **Theorem.** On (1), for every real spectrum, H_delta(q)<=H_0(q)=h(q), (3) where h is the original continuous complete-endpoint coefficient entropy. In fact H_delta(q) is nonincreasing as delta goes from0 to1/2 for each fixed CROSS degree vector q. No sampled finite product is divided by a zero, and no coefficient lower asymptotic is used. ## 2. The unused products are maximized at the complete spectrum Set f(t)=log|2cos(pi t)|, as a locally integrable, even, one-periodic function. Its value is a decreasing function of dist(t,Z) in[0,1/2]. For 0<=a<=1/2 define J_delta(a)=int_0^a log|alpha_delta(t)|dt. The exact factorization alpha_delta(t)=4cos(pi(t+delta))cos(pi(t-delta)) and evenness of f give, with NO extra constant or factor two, J_delta(a)=int_(delta-a)^(delta+a) f(t)dt. (4) For fixed a this moving integral is absolutely continuous in delta, because f is locally L1. Almost everywhere, partial_delta J_delta(a)=f(delta+a)-f(delta-a). (5) If a,delta belong to[0,1/2], dist(delta+a,Z)=min(delta+a,1-delta-a) >=|delta-a|=dist(delta-a,Z). The first inequality follows separately from delta+a>=|delta-a| and 1-delta-a>=|delta-a|, the latter being equivalent to 1>=2max(delta,a). Thus (5)<=0 almost everywhere. Absolute continuity retains this sign through the logarithmic singularity at delta+a=1/2. Consequently J_delta(a)<=J_0(a), (6) and, more generally, J_delta(a) is nonincreasing in delta. If a=0 it is zero. If a=1/2 it is the full-period integral of f, also zero, independent of delta. For 0<a<1/2 the derivative is strictly negative almost everywhere in0<delta<1/2, but strictness is not needed below. On the CROSS domain, alpha_delta(1-t)=alpha_delta(t) and both unused endpoint lengths are at most1/2. Therefore B_delta(mu,nu)=J_delta(mu)+J_delta(1-nu) <=J_0(mu)+J_0(1-nu)=B_0(mu,nu). (7) This is where the CROSS degree hypothesis is used. A one-sided row instead gives a difference of two lower-half prefix integrals; (7) does not imply the same comparison there. ## 3. The tail comparison and the exact endpoint normalization For every finite real l and every0<t<1, the displayed positive root in (2) is nonincreasing in delta, since cos^2(pi delta) decreases. Thus log Lambda_delta(t;exp(l),1)<=log Lambda_0(t;exp(l),1). Integrate over the same original interval and subtract xi*l. The inequality holds for EVERY finite tilt, so it also holds after the two infima over l. Combining with (7) proves H_delta<=H_0. The same argument between any two ordered spectra proves monotonicity. Integrable endpoint bounds justify each integral; alternatively the already proved closed continuity passes from interior row endpoints. No finite minimizing tilt is assumed when an outer degree is zero or at its full value. For completeness H_0 in (3) is the actual endpoint entropy, not another normalization. Put tau=1-nu. Symmetry about1/2 splits the tail integral into [mu,1/2] and [tau,1/2]. The identity int_0^(1/2)log alpha_0(t)dt=0 converts each corresponding prefix term J_0(a) into minus the alpha integral over its active half. Hence H_0(q)=inf_l{Phi_mu(l)+Phi_tau(l)-xi*l}, Phi_a(l)=int_a^(1/2) log[Lambda_0(t;exp(l),1)/alpha_0(t)]dt. (8) The integrand is exactly the source-normalized endpoint function l/2+log tan(pi t)+asinh(tan(pi t)cosh(l/2)). Its half-interval Legendre entropy is the proved triangle entropy Ctri(alpha)=V(2pi alpha)/(2pi), with alpha summing to1/2. The infimum in (8) equals the maximum of the sum of the two such entropies over xi_1+xi_2=xi and 0<=xi_1<=1/2-mu,0<=xi_2<=1/2-tau. Indeed every split is bounded above by its value at a common tilt. At a finite minimizing tilt choose xi_a=Phi_a'(l); this attains equality in both half infima. The closed endpoint/outer cases follow by continuity of H_0 and of the triangle entropies and their closed split interval. This is only one-dimensional outer Legendre convolution, not concavity or duality in the row endpoints. It gives exactly the published h(q) on CROSS closure, including both terminal seams and the pure-middle corner. ## 4. A strict gap for all seam-only original shared data Fix an original simple-white certified marked plat D. Let Q_D be its actual compact incidence-flow polytope: each port supplies1, each ordinary face demands1, and both original protected faces demand0. Let Phi_D=Vol(Y_D)/(2pi). The proved endpoint theorem and unique geometric maximum give max_(q in Q_D) sum_e h(q_e)=Phi_D, q_geom is the unique maximizer, q_geom,e,b<1/2 and q_geom,e,c<1/2 at EVERY port. (9) These assertions retain the actual original marked packing and matching. They are not claims about a freely chosen incidence graph. Define the closed seam-only subset Sigma_D={q in Q_D: all q_e,b,q_e,c<=1/2, and at least one equals1/2}. (10) If it is empty, no seam-only candidate exists. There is an explicit fixed-diagram gap when it is nonempty. Put a_D=min_e{1/2-q_geom,e,b, 1/2-q_geom,e,c}>0, gamma_D=(pi/2) a_D^2. (11) Here and below ||q-q_geom|| is the Euclidean norm on ALL original incidence coordinates, namely the square root of sum_e sum_(f=x,b,c,y)(q_(e,f)-q_geom,(e,f))^2. A shared face's separate port incidences remain separate coordinates; protected coordinates are fixed at zero. No norm on the vector of distinct global face sums is used. To prove (11) is a valid gap, recall the exact triangle entropy Ctri(alpha)=sum_j f(alpha_j), sum_j alpha_j=1/2, where f(t)=[Lob(pi t)+Lob(pi/2-pi t)]/pi, f''(t)=-2pi/sin(2pi t)<=-2pi, 0<t<1/2. Here Lob is the Lobachevsky function in the endpoint triangle theorem. Its continuous endpoint values extend the resulting strong-concavity inequality to the CLOSED triangle simplex. The sum over both latent triangles of every CROSS port is therefore 2pi-strongly concave in the Euclidean latent incidence norm. The actual linear projection to q sums the two outer entries and retains each middle entry separately; its squared operator norm is at most2. Given two feasible q vectors, choose their maximizing latent allocations. Their convex mixture is feasible for the mixture of the original q vectors. Applying the latent strong-concavity inequality and ||P v||^2<=2||v||^2 shows that F(q)=sum_e h(q_e) is pi-strongly concave on the entire closed original CROSS fiber. This argument also covers a protected monomial half, which has no free latent coordinate. For any q in that fiber and0<t<1, maximality at q_geom gives Phi_D>=F((1-t)q_geom+t q) >=(1-t)Phi_D+t F(q)+(pi/2)t(1-t)||q-q_geom||^2. Divide by t and let t decrease to0. No boundary gradient is needed: F(q)<=Phi_D-(pi/2)||q-q_geom||^2. (11a) Every seam q has at least one middle coordinate equal to1/2, hence ||q-q_geom||>=a_D. Equations (11)--(11a) give its entropy gap directly, without an uncomputed seam maximization. The constant uses the exact normalization Phi_D=Vol(Y_D)/(2pi), and is not uniform over diagrams. Apply (3) portwise. Uniformly over ALL original spectra, max_(q in Sigma_D, delta in[0,1/2]^R) sum_e H_(delta_e)(q_e)<=Phi_D-gamma_D. (12) In particular a maximum of the sharp functional on the closed non-CROSS union {q: some q_e,b>=1/2 or q_e,c>=1/2} with value at least Phi_D MUST have a strictly overloaded middle >1/2. Its possible seam-only alternative is excluded. This supplies that hypothesis for the existing restricted-non-CROSS activation and stationary reductions; it does not settle the remaining strictly overloaded, phase-inconsistent candidates. There is moreover a UNIFORM fixed-diagram overload margin eta_D>0: q in Q_D, max_middle(q)>=1/2, sum_e H_(delta_e)(q_e)>=Phi_D => max_middle(q)>=1/2+eta_D. (12a) To prove this, the set of pairs (q,delta) satisfying the two premises is closed in a compact space. If it is empty the conclusion is vacuous. Otherwise none of its points has max_middle(q)=1/2, since such a q lies in Sigma_D and contradicts (12). The continuous positive function max_middle(q)-1/2 therefore has a positive minimum on this set. This also handles an empty Sigma_D: then equality max_middle=1/2 is already excluded by the flow constraints themselves. Equivalently, a sequence of high-valued candidates whose maximal middle decreases to1/2 would have a seam-only limit, contradicting (12). No lower coefficient rate is used in this compactness argument. Thus the strict-overload qualifier in the existing high-value restricted non-CROSS reductions is automatic, with a margin uniform over their candidate maxima for this one fixed D. ## 5. Uniform finite-source consequence near the entire seam set Joint continuity of sum H on Q_D times the compact spectral cube makes (12) stable on a fixed neighborhood. There is rho_D>0 such that dist_infinity(q,Sigma_D)<=rho_D => sum_e H_(delta_e)(q_e)<=Phi_D-gamma_D/2 (13) for every q in Q_D and every real spectral vector. This neighborhood may include actual LEFT or RIGHT degree vectors slightly beyond the seams; no finite path label is changed. If Sigma_D is empty, compactness instead gives an empty sufficiently small neighborhood of the seam conditions, and there is no such contribution to bound. For each N let a_(e,N)(n_e;delta_e) be the ACTUAL local coefficient, with the original total degree d=N-1, unused products and raw phases. Sum over any set of original target arrays n whose EXACT normalized flow q=n/d lies in the neighborhood (13). The global uniform coefficient LIMSUP majorant and the polynomial number of arrays at fixed D give limsup_(N->infinity) N^(-1)log sup_(delta in[0,1/2]^R) sum_(such arrays n) prod_e |a_(e,N)(n_e;delta_e)| <=Phi_D-gamma_D/2. (14) Empty sums have logarithm minus infinity. In particular the actual signed sum over those arrays is eventually bounded by exp{N(Phi_D-gamma_D/3)}. This includes both parities, composite levels, all protected/row/spectral boundaries and sampled spectral zeros. The d-normalized target is unchanged; no lower approximation of a limiting flow or every-level coefficient limit is required. A degree-array restriction chosen independently of the spectral variables still produces an original spectral polynomial of degree at most d in each variable. Thus the existing cosine-Bernstein and whole-domain three-integration-by-parts transfer applies to this restricted source: its fixed thin-strip and entire weighted Fourier/Hermite period have a strict gap below Phi_D. All original scalar characters and endpoint currents remain. This concerns only the stated seam neighborhood; it is not a bound on the whole non-CROSS period. There is a direct interface with the actual filled volume. Denote this whole seam-neighborhood period by I_seam and the original whole all-CROSS period by I_cross, with the SAME original Fourier/Hermite normalization. After retaining a smaller fixed gap kappa_D>0, the transfer just used gives |I_seam|<=C_D prod_e(1+|n_e|)^3 exp{N(Phi_D-kappa_D)}, n_e=epsilon_e-2p_e. (15) The [entire all-CROSS theorem](general_all_cross_long_filling_volume.md) gives an eventually nonzero period and its relative asymptotic, with lim_(N->infinity) N^(-1)log|I_cross| =Vol(the actual smooth filled exterior)/(2pi) =Phi_D-O_D(sum_e |n_e|^(-2)). (16) The prescribed half twists, primitive fillings and actual final-diagram normalization are exactly those of that theorem. Choose a fixed-diagram threshold T(D) above its geometric and analytic thresholds and large enough that the loss in (16) is less than kappa_D/2 whenever every |p_e|>T(D). For each independently signed vector p fixed BEFORE N tends to infinity, equations (15)--(16) then imply I_seam/I_cross=O_p(exp(-c_D N)), c_D>0, (17) for example with any fixed c_D<kappa_D/2 after enlarging the vector-dependent starting level. Both level parities and composite levels are retained. No bound on ratios of the twist magnitudes is imposed, and no joint growing-twist/level estimate is asserted. Any common recorded framing/component character or common nonzero normalization factor cancels in (17); it has not been replaced by a new marked normalization. Equation (17) proves only negligibility of the specified seam remainder. It does not give equality of the FULL invariant with all-CROSS: the macroscopic, strictly overloaded non-CROSS contribution remains to be controlled. The nonzero all-CROSS contribution is the cited theorem, not a new lower-period claim from the present coefficient upper bound. ## 6. Dependencies The [global coefficient majorant](research_global_sharp_coefficient_limsup_majorant.md) supplies (2), closed continuity and the uniform original coefficient upper bound. Section 3 above and the [closed half-block theorem](actual_fejer_half_block_entropy.md) supply the normalized half/triangle identity. The [full endpoint entropy](actual_fejer_full_kernel_entropy_identity_reduction.md) and [unique geometric maximum](actual_fejer_unique_geometric_maximizer.md) give the original endpoint function and (9). The [whole-domain Fourier lemma](actual_global_diagonal_spectral_sector_gap.md), section 4, applies to the restricted polynomial in section 5. The [full-fiber activation](research_full_fiber_sharp_boundary_activation.md) and [stationary classification](research_full_fiber_sharp_stationary_classification.md) are downstream applications of the uniform overload statement (12a), not premises of the direct CROSS comparison or seam gap. No numerical audit or coefficient lower limit is used. The comparison covers only CROSS degrees and the resulting seam neighborhood; macroscopic strictly overloaded phase-inconsistent candidates remain outside the conclusion. In particular (17) is not a full-invariant volume theorem.

title: Sharp one-sided endpoint representatives on a physical window
text: # Sharp one-sided endpoint representatives on a physical window Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The reflected sharp normal connection can be inserted into the exact one-sided Hermite repair. This gives local representatives of the original full physical jets whose real interface has any prescribed rate below \(J_*\) at the target point. The common baseline is bounded at every fixed target height. The original crossing, shared spectators, and all exterior contour sides remain in the exact trace. No bound for their closing is asserted. ## 1. The local sharp baseline Set \(h=N^{-1}\), \(\eta_N=(-1)^{N-1}\), and \[ C_N(x)=2\cos(2\pi x+\pi h),\qquad x_j=jh,\qquad w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha h),\qquad B_{i,N}(x)=K_N(w_N(\alpha_i),C_N(x)). \tag{1} \] Fix \(x_0\in(0,1/2)\), a finite number \(r\ge1\) of factors, and parameter rectangles \[ |\Re\alpha_i|\le A,\qquad |\Im\alpha_i|\le\pi-\epsilon, \qquad A<\infty,\quad 0<\epsilon<\pi. \tag{2} \] Larger rectangles of the same kind are reserved for derivatives. Fix any positive loss \(\ell<J_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)\), and put \[ \gamma=J_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)-\ell>0,\qquad \delta=\frac1\pi\arcsin\frac{\sin(\pi x_0)}{\sqrt2}, \] \[ I_\delta(X)=\int_0^\delta \log\frac{\sin^2(\pi X)-\sin^2(\pi u)} {\sin^2(\pi u)}\,du. \tag{3} \] Losses at least \(J_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)\) follow from any smaller positive loss. The sharp identity is \(I_\delta(x_0)=J_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)\), with normalization \[ J_*(t)=\frac1\pi\int_t^\pi \operatorname{asinh}(\sin(s/2))\,ds. \] Choose nested real intervals about \(x_0\), with fixed positive buffers inside \((0,1/2)\), so small that \[ \min_{\text{largest real buffer}}I_\delta \ge\gamma. \tag{4} \] Let \(I\) be the inner interval. Prescribe any fixed finite upper and lower heights, and a larger buffered rectangle over these intervals. The reflected connection theorem supplies one scalar \(V_{i,N}\) on this rectangle for each factor, with polynomial norm and polynomial bounds for every fixed spatial and parameter derivative. It is the specified two-value-normalized sine-factor combination, with the same cutoff on the entire rectangle. At all physical nodes of \(I\), its actual errors \[ e_{i,j}=B_{i,N}(x_j)-V_{i,N}(x_j),\qquad d_{i,j}=B_{i,N}'(x_j)-V_{i,N}'(x_j) \tag{5} \] satisfy \[ |\partial_{\boldsymbol\alpha}^{\beta} e_{i,j}| +|\partial_{\boldsymbol\alpha}^{\beta} d_{i,j}| \le C_\beta N^{p_\beta}e^{-N\gamma}. \tag{6} \] The prime in (5) is the actual angular derivative, hence \(B_{i,N}'(x_j)=C_N'(x_j)\partial_CK_N(w_N(\alpha_i),c_j)\). This use of both channels is the new input; it does not infer the derivative from a values-only approximation. ## 2. Exact repair without a designated-height loss Let \(\mathcal W_N=\{j:x_j\in I\}\), or any consecutive subwindow. For \(\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}\) set \[ L_j^\sigma(x)=e^{\sigma2\pi i(x-x_j)/h} \operatorname{sinc}^2((x-x_j)/h), \qquad \operatorname{sinc}z=\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}, \] \[ C_{i,N}^\sigma(x)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal W_N} \left[e_{i,j} +\left(d_{i,j}-\frac{\sigma2\pi i}{h}e_{i,j}\right)(x-x_j)\right] L_j^\sigma(x), \qquad H_{i,N}^\sigma=V_{i,N}+C_{i,N}^\sigma. \tag{7} \] At its own node \(L_j^\sigma=1\) and \((L_j^\sigma)'=\sigma2\pi i/h\); at every other node it has a double zero. Therefore, exactly on the chosen window, \[ H_{i,N}^\sigma(x_j)=B_{i,N}(x_j),\qquad (H_{i,N}^\sigma)'(x_j)=B_{i,N}'(x_j). \tag{8} \] Since \(C_N'\) is a unit on the real buffer, these are precisely the original values and first spectral normals. The Fourier support of \(L_j^+\) is \([0,2/h]\), and that of \(L_j^-\) is \([-2/h,0]\); their absolute coefficient masses are one. On the designated half-plane \(\sigma\Im x\ge0\), every fixed spatial derivative costs only a power of \(N\). There are \(O(N)\) summands, and \(x-x_j\) is bounded on the prescribed rectangle. Thus (6) gives, including its boundary, \[ \boxed{\quad |\partial_x^k\partial_{\boldsymbol\alpha}^{\beta}C_{i,N}^\sigma(x)| \le C N^p e^{-N\gamma}, \qquad \sigma\Im x\ge0. \quad} \tag{9} \] The exponent is not reduced to absorb polynomial factors. On an opposite collar \(|\Im x|\le d\), the corresponding bound is \(CN^p e^{-N(\gamma-4\pi d)}\). In particular a fixed collar with \(4\pi d<\gamma\) is allowed, but no bound on the entire opposite half-rectangle is inferred. The same statements hold for fixed original endpoint spectral derivatives, with additional polynomial factors: the source families are even in each \(\alpha_i\), and the local \(\alpha_i^2\)-to-\(w_N(\alpha_i)\) coordinate has derivative \(N^{-2}(1+O(N^{-2}))\). ## 3. The sharp real interface and shared products Retain the full grid kernel \[ D_h(x)=(\pi/h)^2\csc^2(\pi x/h). \tag{10} \] For one factor, write \(z=x-x_j\), \(k_h=2\pi i/h\). The exact interface is \[ \begin{split} D_h(C_{i,N}^+-C_{i,N}^-) =\sum_{j\in\mathcal W_N}\frac1{z^2} \bigl\{& [e_{i,j}+(d_{i,j}-k_he_{i,j})z]e^{k_hz}\\ &-[e_{i,j}+(d_{i,j}+k_he_{i,j})z]e^{-k_hz}\bigr\}. \end{split} \tag{11} \] Each singularity at its own \(z=0\) is removable, with value \(4\pi i d_{i,j}/h\). For real \(z\), Taylor expansion on \(|z|\le h\) and the direct formula on \(|z|\ge h\) bound each term by \(C(h^{-2}|e_{i,j}|+h^{-1}|d_{i,j}|)\). Consequently, on the whole real window, \[ \boxed{\qquad |D_h(C_{i,N}^+-C_{i,N}^-)|\le CN^p e^{-N\gamma}. \qquad} \tag{12} \] This is the explicit weighted Hermite identity of the previous window construction with the new sharp error data. It retains every alias of \(D_h\). For factors sharing one spectral variable, define \[ P_N^\sigma=\prod_{i=1}^r H_{i,N}^\sigma,\qquad P_N^0=\prod_{i=1}^rV_{i,N}. \tag{13} \] \(P_N^+\) and \(P_N^-\) each have exactly the original shared value and first normal at every covered node, by the ordinary product rule. Telescoping products gives \[ |P_N^\sigma-P_N^0|\le CN^p e^{-N\gamma} \quad(\sigma\Im x\ge0), \qquad |D_h(P_N^+-P_N^-)|\le CN^p e^{-N\gamma} \quad(x\text{ real}). \tag{14} \] For the second estimate write the product difference as a sum with exactly one factor \(H_i^+-H_i^-=C_i^+-C_i^-\), apply (12) to that factor, and retain the other polynomially bounded real factors. Fixed endpoint-parameter derivatives have the same bound by the product rule. There is no multiplication of the exponential rate by the number of factors. ## 4. Exact placement in the original full-normal trace Write the consecutive window as \(j_0\le j\le j_1\), and choose midpoints \[ a_N=(j_0-\tfrac12)h,\qquad b_N=(j_1+\tfrac12)h. \tag{15} \] Choose exterior half-contours in the prescribed rectangle. The lower contour \(E_-\) runs down the left side, across the bottom, and up the right side; the upper contour \(E_+\) runs up the right side, across the top, and down the left side. Both vertical half-sides in each contour are retained. For a fixed original signed power \(n\), use its actual carrier and angular crossing \[ \tau_N(x)=\pi-2\pi x-\pi h,\qquad E_{N,n}(x)= e^{\pi i n(N-1)^2/(4N)}e^{inN\tau_N(x)^2/(4\pi)}. \tag{16} \] Let \(A_N(C;\mathbf y)\) be the complete remaining joint spectator, holomorphic on neighborhoods of the two closed half-rectangles bounded by these contours and the real window, with other traces still unapplied. Put \[ g_\sigma(x)=\sin(2\pi x+\pi h)\, P_N^\sigma(x)E_{N,n}(x)A_N(C_N(x);\mathbf y). \tag{17} \] The original restricted full Hermite trace is exactly \[ \boxed{\quad -\frac{\eta_N}{2\pi^2 i} \left\{\int_{E_-}D_hg_-\,dx+\int_{E_+}D_hg_+\,dx +\int_{a_N}^{b_N}D_h(g_+-g_-)\,dx\right\}. \quad} \tag{18} \] Indeed, for \(g(x)=\sin(2\pi x+\pi h)f(C_N(x))\), \[ g'(x_j)=-\pi\{(4-c_j^2)f'(c_j)-c_jf(c_j)\}. \tag{19} \] The residue of \(D_hg\) is \(g'(x_j)\). Equations (8) and (13) preserve this complete residue, including the derivative of the crossing and the shared spectator. Closing the upper half-contour along the real path from \(a_N\) to \(b_N\) and the lower one in the opposite direction gives (18). Their interface difference has no grid poles. Its pointwise real bound is \[ \boxed{\quad |D_h(g_+-g_-)(x)| \le CN^p e^{-N\gamma} |\sin(2\pi x+\pi h)E_{N,n}(x)A_N(C_N(x);\mathbf y)|. \quad} \tag{20} \] The spectator remains inside this estimate. No growth bound for it, nor a bound for the integrated closing, is supplied. The exterior integrals in (18), all their aliases, and every physical row outside the window remain. For several traced colors the same replacements are coefficientwise in the other variables and may be made before their closings. Ordinary mixed differentiation preserves all shared first normals. An edge coupling two such colors remains in the joint spectator; it is not split into independent factors or estimated here. ## 5. Scope and direct sources The previous one-sided window theorem already supplied the repair, interface identity, and full contour normalization. The additional consequence is that their error exponent can now be chosen arbitrarily close to \(J_*(\pi-2\pi x_0)\) on a sufficiently small fixed window, while the common scalar remains moderate at the prescribed heights. It uses the new reflected full-normal baseline, not the old modified-flow baseline. In particular no estimate of the old baseline's fractional-grid Green boundary packet is needed or asserted. The exterior-current problem, spectator action comparison, and nonzero saddle coefficient are unchanged by the exact construction above. Both complete direct sources were read at their final matching pins, and all directly used physical-jet, repair, and contour implications were rechecked: * [Reflected sharp physical normal connection](research_reflected_endpoint_sharp_normal_connection.md), SHA256 a8a379d7b492d7d2487de3c1397408478f66242f153ac0cab8eb3d224f226916. * [One-sided endpoint window construction](research_unturned_endpoint_complex_baseline_and_window.md), SHA256 9d233d9bb11c2842e62d5523f97e9621a3bd22532e3b527ceaab8125782c1cc1. Only written mathematics and source-text/hash reads were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test, build or compilation was run. Existing adopted and public notes are unchanged.

title: Sharp physical Grams and a positive history sum for the actual coproduct
text: # Sharp physical Grams and a positive history sum for the actual coproduct 24 November 2026. Research proof. Earlier finals and manuscripts are unchanged. The actual cyclic-source coproduct has a canonical positive invariant Gram. Its optimal distortion in the original physical metric has an explicit sharp exponential rate. A positive sum of squared power norms has a stronger asymptotic with its prefactor, and determines the norms of every cyclic spectral projector exactly. The rate is a regular ideal bipyramid value. It is a metric and projector rate, not a knot-volume rate. ## 1. The original source family and the statement Fix an integer \(b\ge1\), independently of \(N\ge2\). Put \[ d=N-1,\quad q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad Q=q^2,\quad \gamma=(-1)^{N+1},\quad x=-q^{-1},\quad s_a=\prod_{h=1}^a2\sin(\pi h/N),\quad s_0=1. \tag{1} \] Give the balanced physical basis \(w_0,\ldots,w_d\) its ordinary orthonormal metric, and use the tensor-product metric on \(b\) heads. Stars, operator norms and unnormalized Hilbert--Schmidt norms below refer to this physical metric. Use [B]'s regular complete-color source chart, at \(M=1\): \[ E_iw_a=(Q^{-a}-1)w_{a-1}\ (a>0),\qquad E_iw_0=\mu_iw_d,\qquad K_iw_a=xQ^{-a}w_a. \tag{2} \] Choose the fixed source line \[ |\mu|=1/N,\qquad \mu_i=\gamma^{1-i}\mu,\qquad X_i=E_iK_{i+1}\cdots K_b,\quad E_{\rm tot}=\sum_{i=1}^bX_i,\quad K_{\rm tot}=\prod_{i=1}^bK_i. \tag{3} \] The coproduct is the literal one in [M]. The source freedom in [B] preserves the whole original selected knot operator on this line. That statement retains its crossings, pivots, framing and external normalization. It does not permit resetting an intermediate exterior. No off-meridian extension of this root-level construction is asserted. Since \(\prod_{a=1}^d(Q^{-a}-1)=\gamma N\), direct multiplication gives \[ X_iX_j=QX_jX_i\ (i<j),\qquad X_i^N=cI,\quad c=\gamma^bN\mu,\quad |c|=1. \tag{4} \] Indeed \(E_i^N=\gamma N\mu_iI\) and \(K_i^N=\gamma I\). The root multinomial identity therefore gives \[ E_{\rm tot}^N=bcI. \quad\text{Choose }e^N=bc,\qquad T=E_{\rm tot}/e. \quad T^N=I,\quad |e|=b^{1/N},\quad K_{\rm tot}T=QT K_{\rm tot}. \tag{5} \] Every choice of the root \(e\) is allowed. Define \[ \mathcal A_N=\max_{0\le k<N}\|T^k\|_{\rm op},\qquad J_{\rm av}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(T^k)^*T^k,\qquad \mathcal H_N=\operatorname{Tr}J_{\rm av} =\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\|T^k\|_{\rm HS}^2. \tag{6} \] These are specified from the actual coproduct, without a knot value. For a positive Hermitian Gram \(J\), write \(\kappa(J)=\lambda_{\max}(J)/\lambda_{\min}(J)\). Let \(\mathcal J_N\) be the Grams satisfying both \(T^*JT=J\) and \(K_{\rm tot}^*JK_{\rm tot}=J\). Put \[ n=2b+1,\quad \delta=\pi/n,\quad h(u)=\int_0^u\log(2\sin\pi v)\,dv,\quad M_b=-n h(1/n)>0, \tag{7} \] \[ C_b= \frac{2^{1-b}b^{-4b/n}\sin\delta} {\sqrt n\,\sin(2\delta)^b}. \tag{8} \] **Theorem.** The class \(\mathcal J_N\) contains \(J_{\rm av}\), and \[ \mathcal A_N\le\inf_{J\in\mathcal J_N}\sqrt{\kappa(J)} \le\sqrt N\,\mathcal A_N. \tag{9} \] The same inequalities hold when only \(T\)-invariance is required. Through all integer levels, \[ \log\mathcal A_N=NM_b+O_b(\log N),\qquad \log\inf_{J\in\mathcal J_N}\sqrt{\kappa(J)} =NM_b+O_b(\log N). \tag{10} \] Moreover the positive history sum has the asymptotic \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal H_N=C_bN e^{2NM_b}(1+O_b(N^{-1})).\quad} \tag{11} \] For the actual spectral projectors \[ P_j=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}Q^{-jk}T^k,\qquad 0\le j<N, \tag{12} \] one has the exact identities and their common asymptotic \[ J_{\rm av}=N\sum_jP_j^*P_j,\qquad \|P_j\|_{\rm HS}^2=\mathcal H_N/N^2 =\frac{C_b}{N}e^{2NM_b}(1+O_b(N^{-1})). \tag{13} \] The finite identities hold at every \(N\ge2\); the asymptotics have fixed \(b\) and no parity restriction. They are independent of the phases of \(\mu,e\). ## 2. Exact physical power entries, including every wrap For \(0\le k<N\), the finite quantum multinomial formula is \[ E_{\rm tot}^k= \sum_{\substack{k_1+\cdots+k_b=k\\k_i\ge0}} \frac{(Q;Q)_k}{\prod_i(Q;Q)_{k_i}}\, X_b^{k_b}\cdots X_1^{k_1}. \tag{14} \] It follows by induction from (4), with the displayed descending order. All factorial denominators are nonzero. For the \(N\)-th power, every mixed coefficient vanishes because its numerator contains \(1-Q^N\) and its denominators do not. The remaining pure terms prove (5). On an input \(w_{\boldsymbol a}\), set \(r_i=[a_i-k_i]_N\), with residues in \(0,\ldots,d\). The \(K\) dressings have unit modulus. On one head, exactly \[ |\langle r|E_i^{\,u}|a\rangle|=s_a/s_r,\qquad r=[a-u]_N,\quad 0\le u<N. \tag{15} \] Without a wrap this is the consecutive sine product. With a wrap, \(a<u\), its modulus is \(s_a|\mu_i|\,s_d/s_r=s_a/s_r\), since \(s_d=N\). There is at most one wrap in (15). For fixed input and output, each \(k_i\) is determined modulo \(N\); its required range \(0\le k_i\le k<N\) determines it uniquely. Thus (14) has at most one term at any specified matrix entry. Its nonzero modulus is exactly \[ |\langle\boldsymbol r|T^k|\boldsymbol a\rangle| =b^{-k/N}s_k\prod_{i=1}^b\frac{s_{a_i}}{s_{k_i}s_{r_i}}. \tag{16} \] The full complex coefficient remains (14) applied to the literal matrices (2); no phase has been removed from an original contraction. Absolute values in (16) are used for norms and the positive sum (6). The history sum is parametrized once by \[ 0\le a_i<N,\quad k_i\ge0,\quad k:=\sum_i k_i<N. \tag{17} \] There is no transfer-path multiplicity or lattice-index factor. ## 3. A global maximum on the full wrapped support Use scaled variables \(u_i=k_i/N\), \(t=\sum_i u_i\le1\), and \(a_i/N=y_i\). On each wrap sector put \(z_i=y_i-u_i\) without a wrap and \(z_i=y_i-u_i+1\) with a wrap. The endpoint-uniform sine estimate in [G] gives the logarithm of (16) as \(NS+O_b(\log N)\), uniformly on (17), where \[ S=h(t)-\sum_i h(u_i)+\sum_i\{h(y_i)-h(z_i)\}. \tag{18} \] The factor \(b^{-t}\) is bounded above and below and is kept in the amplitude below. The sector actions extend continuously to their closed supports, using \(h(0)=h(1)=0\). Fix \(0<u<1\). In the sector without a wrap, \(D_u(y)=h(y)-h(y-u)\), \(u\le y\le1\), is strictly concave: \[ D_u''(y)= -\frac{\pi\sin(\pi u)} {\sin(\pi y)\sin(\pi(y-u))}<0. \tag{19} \] Its unique maximum is at \(y=(1+u)/2\), with value \(-2h((1-u)/2)\), by \(h(1-v)=-h(v)\). In the wrapped sector, \(0\le y\le u\), its value is instead \(h(y)+h(u-y)\). This is strictly convex in the interior, with second derivative \(\pi\sin(\pi u)/ [\sin(\pi y)\sin(\pi(u-y))]\). Its maximal value is \(h(u)\) at the endpoints. The difference of the two sector maxima is \[ -2h((1-u)/2)-h(u)=-2h(u/2)>0. \tag{20} \] Here \(h(u)=2h(u/2)-2h((1-u)/2)\), proved by differentiation; \(h\) is strictly negative on \((0,1/2)\). After maximizing every \(y_i\), (18) becomes \(h(t)-2\sum_i h(u_i/2)\). Strict convexity of \(h\) on \([0,1/2]\) makes the transfers equal at fixed \(t\). The remaining one-variable function is \[ F_b(t)=h(t)-2b h(t/(2b)),\qquad F_b'(t)=\log\frac{\sin(\pi t)}{\sin(\pi t/(2b))}. \tag{21} \] The sine-difference formula gives its unique maximum at \[ t_*=\frac{2b}{n},\quad u_{i,*}=\frac2n,\quad y_{i,*}=\frac12+\frac1n,\quad z_{i,*}=\frac12-\frac1n, \qquad F_b(t_*)=M_b. \tag{22} \] For example \(F_b''<0\) follows because \(v\cot v\) strictly decreases on \((0,\pi)\). The one-variable endpoint values and continuity cover \(t=0,1\). Equality in the preceding optimizations at this maximum is unique. In particular the maximum has no wraps, all factorial lengths are strict interior points, and every closed wrap sector is separated from it by a positive action gap. There are only polynomially many entries for fixed \(b\). An operator norm lies between a maximal entry and \(N^b\) times it. The uniform estimate in (18), followed by rounding (22) on its strict interior lattice, proves the first part of (10). For geometric calibration, let \(\Lambda(\theta)=-\int_0^\theta\log(2\sin v)\,dv\). Then \(2\pi M_b=2n\Lambda(\pi/n)\). The regular ideal \(n\)-gonal bipyramid splits about its axis into \(n\) tetrahedra of angles \((2\pi/n,\pi/2-\pi/n,\pi/2-\pi/n)\). The duplication identity for \(\Lambda\) gives volume \(2\Lambda(\pi/n)\) for each. This is the familiar bipyramid value; its occurrence as the sharp physical Gram rate is the assertion here. ## 4. A canonical invariant Gram attains the sharp rate For any \(J>0\) with \(T^*JT=J\), every power is \(J\)-unitary. Converting its two norms gives \(\|T^k\|_{\rm op}\le\sqrt{\kappa(J)}\). This proves the lower bound in (9), without a spectral-basis assumption. Since \(T^N=I\), shifting the sum in (6) shows \(T^*J_{\rm av}T=J_{\rm av}\). Also \[ I\le J_{\rm av}\le N\mathcal A_N^2 I. \tag{23} \] The physical unitary \(K_{\rm tot}\) conjugates \(T^k\) to \(Q^kT^k\); the phase cancels in each summand of \(J_{\rm av}\). Thus \(K_{\rm tot}^*J_{\rm av}K_{\rm tot}=J_{\rm av}\). This proves existence and the upper bound in (9), and completes (10). The optimum is asserted at exponential scale, not as an exact finite-level condition number for \(J_{\rm av}\). ## 5. The positive history sum and its prefactor Near (22), no term wraps. In the \(2b\) variables \((\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol y)\), let \(H=-S''\) at the maximum. Put \(\alpha=\pi\cot\delta\), \(\beta=\pi\tan\delta\). Differentiation of (18) gives \[ H_{uu}=\alpha\boldsymbol1\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T} +\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}I,\quad H_{uy}=-\beta I,\quad H_{yy}=2\beta I. \tag{24} \] Eliminating the \(y\) block leaves \((\alpha/2)(I+2\boldsymbol1\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T})\). Therefore \(H>0\) and \[ \det H=n\pi^{2b}. \tag{25} \] The interior sine-product expansion proved in [G] yields for (16) \[ (2N)^{(1-b)/2}b^{-t}A(\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol y) e^{NS}(1+O_b(N^{-1})),\qquad A^2=\sin(\pi t)\prod_i \frac{\sin(\pi y_i)}{\sin(\pi u_i)\sin(\pi z_i)}. \tag{26} \] At the maximum \(A_*^2=\sin\delta/\sin(2\delta)^b\). The grid in (17) has mesh \(1/N\) in each of its \(2b\) coordinates. Summing the squared leading Gaussian consequently gives \[ N^{2b}(2N)^{1-b}N^{-b} \frac{\pi^b}{\sqrt{\det H}}\, b^{-2t_*}A_*^2 e^{2NM_b} =C_bN e^{2NM_b}. \tag{27} \] There is no hidden factor from a residue class or a wrap. Here is an error justification at the asserted relative order. On a fixed interior neighborhood use the all-order expansion [G, (13)] in (16). Taylor expansion at (22), in rescaled coordinates of mesh \(N^{-1/2}\), gives its squared density as a Gaussian times \(1+N^{-1/2}p_1+O(N^{-1})(1+|v|^L)\), with a Gaussian-polynomial remainder on a shrinking central neighborhood. The first polynomial is odd. Gaussian-polynomial mesh sums have exponentially small sum-to-integral errors uniformly in their fractional centers, by periodization and the Gaussian Fourier integral as in [G]. The odd term therefore contributes no algebraic first correction. Negative local curvature controls the intermediate tail; the strict global maximum, wrap gap and endpoint-uniform factorial estimate control all other terms exponentially. The proof of [G, (16)] applies with \(2b\) variables and this density. It yields the relative \(O_b(N^{-1})\) error in (11), through both parities. ## 6. Orthogonal powers and corrected spectral packets Conjugation by the physical unitary \(K_{\rm tot}\) is unitary on matrix Hilbert--Schmidt space. Its eigenvalues on \(T^k\) are \(Q^k\). Hence the \(N\) powers in (6) are exactly pairwise orthogonal. The polynomial identity \(T^N=I\) has simple roots, so (12) gives its complete spectral projectors. Conjugation by \(K_{\rm tot}\) cycles their eigenspaces; they all have rank \(N^{b-1}\). Hilbert--Schmidt orthogonality of powers proves the norm identity in (13). Finite Fourier orthogonality also proves \(N\sum_jP_j^*P_j=J_{\rm av}\) exactly. Thus this canonical positive Gram orthogonalizes the actual spectral packets, with their physical sizes and history sum explicitly known. At \(b=1\) there is also an exact normalization check. Writing \(B_N=\sum_{a=0}^d s_a^{-2}\), (15) and reflection give \(\mathcal H_N=(\sum_a s_a^2)(\sum_a s_a^{-2})=N^2B_N^2\). Formula (8) gives \(C_1=1/\sqrt3\), consistently with (11). ## 7. What this supplies to the original source The theorem computes a positive history sum and a sharp invariant-metric rate for an actual coproduct, including every wrapped physical entry. It does not make the original pivotal tail functional a norm. The original \(g=K^{1-N}\), marked projection, neighboring crossings, and all their transported interfaces must remain when using this Gram. The source freedom invoked in Section 1 concerns the whole assembled selected knot operator; it does not identify arbitrary local sectors. The intermediate tensor-product Casimir and multiplicity channels are not replaced by one-head scalar eigenvalues. Already at \(b=1\) this positive metric rate is nonzero, although a normalized unknot cut has value one. Therefore neither (11) nor (13) is a Kashaev nonvanishing statement, a selected geometric coefficient, or a hyperbolic-volume lower bound. General short-component propagation and the finite-exception volume assertion remain open. [C] already proves conditioning lower bounds for a different actual cyclic Wall operator. [F] already gives sharp positive angle costs for actual divided fusion in its source-fixed factorial metric. The addition here is the matching upper and lower optimal distortion rate in the original physical metric, together with (11)--(13) for this cyclic-source coproduct. No novelty is claimed for finite-group averaging, quantum multinomials, or the bipyramid volume formula. ## Complete inputs and coverage All five complete matching texts were read. Only written mathematics and text/hash operations were used. title: A single spectral representative on short physical windows
