title: A whole-interval upper rate for turned microscopic endpoint products
text:
# A whole-interval upper rate for turned microscopic endpoint products Private written proof, 16 November 2026. The exact divided-difference product module, including its polynomial channel gauge and forced recovery, gives a regular finite physical recurrence. Its full value/normal transfer has the terminal maximal characteristic rate. The original fixed-row initialization can itself have that rate. Keeping both costs gives a uniform upper bound of twice the terminal integral for every fixed ordinary endpoint product. This is an upper bound, not a nonzero coefficient or a filled-action comparison. The conclusion for one unit turn is subexponential stability of the whole product. It does not say that its image is another endpoint product, or that arbitrary repeated tree elimination stays in this class. ## 1. Original source and statement Use the original normalizations \[ q=e^{\pi i/N},\quad D=N-1,\quad \eta=(-1)^D,\quad \kappa=q^{D^2/2},\quad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\pi/N), \] \[ P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2,\qquad \mathcal A_N=\mathbb C[Z]/(P_N),\qquad e_j(Z)=S_j^{-2}\prod_{a<j}(c_a-Z), \] \[ S_j=\prod_{a=1}^j2\sin(a\pi/N),\quad Te_j=e_{D-j},\quad K_N(w,Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{D}e_j(w)e_j(Z),\quad \phi_N(e_i e_j)=\mathbf1_{i+j=D}. 	ag{1} \] The symbol \(T_N\) denotes Chebyshev's polynomial; \(T\) is the original physical turn, and \(R\) the original crossing. Put \[ C f=Zf\pmod {P_N},\quad J=TCT,\quad V_n=\kappa^nTR^{-n}T,\quad D_n=V_nCV_{-n}, \] \[ Q_0(Z)=\partial_wK_N(c_0,Z),\qquad G_n=T(R^{-n}),\qquad H_n=T(R^{-n}Q_0). 	ag{2} \] All canonical real norms below are on the ordinary interval \([-2,2]\). Parameters \(w_i\) remain ordinary variables before their indicated substitution; no exterior quotient is imposed. For fixed \(n
e0\), let \(	au_{\ell,n}(u)\), \(1\le\ell\le|n|\), be the distinct physical terminal shift roots on \(0<u<1/2\). Each retains its algebraic multiplicity two. Define \[ L_n(u)=\max_\ell\log|	au_{\ell,n}(u)|,\qquad \mathcal I_n=\int_0^{1/2}L_n(u)\,du,\qquad \mathcal I_0=0. 	ag{3} \] The whole-terminal source proves that this improper integral is finite, \(L_n\ge0\), and \(L_1=L_{-1}=0\). **Theorem 1.** Fix integers \(r\ge1,n\), and a finite \(A\). For \(|\alpha_i|\le A\), set \[ w_i=2\cosh(\alpha_i/N),\qquad B_{ oldsymbol\alpha,N} =\operatorname{can}\prod_{i=1}^rK_N(w_i,Z). 	ag{4} \] Then \[  oxed{\quad \limsup_{N	o\infty} rac1N \log\left(1+\sup_{|\alpha_i|\le A} \|V_nB_{ oldsymbol\alpha,N}\|_{\mathbb R}ight) \le2\mathcal I_n . \quad} 	ag{5} \] The same bound holds after any fixed number of spectral \(Z\) derivatives and parameter \(\alpha_i\) derivatives. In particular all original physical first normals are retained. For \(n=\pm1\), (5) is an actual subexponential bound on the whole turned product. No polynomial bound is asserted. A useful quantitative version for \(n
e0\) is the following. For every sufficiently small fixed \(\epsilon>0\), there are constants, uniform over (4), such that \[  egin{split} 1+\|V_nB_{ oldsymbol\alpha,N}\|_{\mathbb R} \le{}& C_{\epsilon}N^{p_\epsilon} (1+\|G_n\|_{\mathbb R}+\|H_n\|_{\mathbb R})\ &{}	imes\exp\left\{ N\int_\epsilon^{1/2-\epsilon}L_n(u)\,du +C_{n,r,A}N\epsilon\log(e/\epsilon) +C_\epsilon N^{1-1/(66r)}ight\}. \end{split} 	ag{6} \] The constant multiplying the endpoint loss is independent of \(\epsilon\). The other constants can depend on the fixed interior interval. This separation specifies the order of limits. ## 2. Polynomial inputs and the actual fixed-row initialization The two-half-plane source proves that every fixed ordinary product in (4) has polynomial real norm, uniformly on bounded complex parameter sets, including both parities. Its proof also supplies the single-kernel bound on any larger fixed parameter polydisk. It uses the actual physical row/root bound and retains the full high complement. The six ordinary channels of the product module are \[ (f_i,\mathcal D f_i,\mathcal S f_i, \mathcal S\mathcal D f_i,P_N,1), \qquad f_i=K_N(w_i,Z). 	ag{7} \] Here the half-shift mean and divided difference have the exact definitions in the module source. On the real interval their two arguments are \(2\cos(	heta\pm\pi/N)\), both in \([-2,2]\). The fundamental theorem of calculus on the interval between these arguments, with its removable coincident-point limit, gives \[ \|\mathcal S f\|_{\mathbb R}\le\|f\|_{\mathbb R},\qquad \|\mathcal D f\|_{\mathbb R}\le\|f'\|_{\mathbb R}. 	ag{8} \] Markov's inequality thus bounds all channels (7) polynomially. The same is true for their fixed tensor products and their polynomial gauges \((Z-2)^a\), \(0\le a\le2r\). Their ordinary degrees are \(O_r(N)\). Canonical reduction preserves their physical values and first normals; Markov and the stable full-Hermite reconstruction therefore keep their canonical real norms polynomial. All these estimates are uniform for bounded complex \( oldsymbol\alpha\). We need actual turned initial data for these channels. They are not assumed polynomial after turning. **Lemma 2.** Fix \(M,n\). If \(p_N\) is any canonical polynomial, then, for all \(0\le j\le M\), \[ |(V_np_N)(c_j)|+|(V_np_N)'(c_j)| \le C_{M,n}N^{b_{M,n}}\|p_N\|_{\mathbb R} (\|G_n\|_{\mathbb R}+\|H_n\|_{\mathbb R}). 	ag{9} \] For a polynomially bounded family of inputs, these data have upper exponential rate at most \(\mathcal I_n\). *Proof.* Write \[ F_j(Z)=K_N(c_j,Z),\qquad Q_j(Z)=\partial_wK_N(c_j,Z). 	ag{10} \] The exact physical first-variable recurrence and its index derivative, as recorded in the whole-terminal source, imply in the full algebra \[ F_j=F_j(C)1,\qquad Q_j=a_{j,N}(C)Q_0+b_{j,N}(C)1. 	ag{11} \] In (11), the first \(F_j\) on the right is its ordinary degree-\(j\) row polynomial. The polynomials \(a_{j,N},b_{j,N}\) have degrees bounded in terms of \(j\) alone, and coefficients bounded by a fixed power of \(N\). Here is the recurrence justification of this slightly stronger form of the fixed-row estimate. Put \[ s_t=2\sin(t\pi/N),\quad A(t)= rac{s_{t+1}^4}{s_{2t+1}s_{2t+2}},\quad B(t)= rac{s_t^4}{s_{2t}s_{2t+1}}. 	ag{12} \] Starting with \(F_0=1\), the value equation is \[ F_{j+1}=\left(1+ rac{B(j)}{A(j)} + rac{c_0-C}{A(j)}ight)F_j - rac{B(j)}{A(j)}F_{j-1}. 	ag{13} \] The previous row is absent at \(j=0\). Differentiate the original ordinary index equation, with unknown \(c'(j)Q_j\), where \(c(t)=2\cos((2t+1)\pi/N)\). It has the same homogeneous part, terms involving coefficient derivatives and \(F_j,F_{j-1}\), and a scalar multiple of \(P_N(C)\). The last term is zero in the full algebra. The removable identities \(B(0)=B'(0)=0\) leave no previous normal at the first row. Starting from \(Q_0\) therefore gives (11) by induction. Every inverse sine and every \(1/c'(j)\) involved at these fixed rows is polynomial in \(N\); the degrees and coefficient assertions follow. For large \(N\), all these fixed rows are double nodes. Since \(T\) is self-adjoint for the original Frobenius pairing, \(TC=JT\), and multiplication by \(R^{-n}\) commutes with \(C\), \[ T(R^{-n}F_j)=F_j(J)G_n,\qquad T(R^{-n}Q_j)=a_{j,N}(J)H_n+b_{j,N}(J)G_n. 	ag{14} \] The original kernel evaluation gives exactly \[  egin{split} (V_np_N)(c_j) &=\kappa^n\phi_N ig(F_j(J)G_n\,p_N ig),\ (V_np_N)'(c_j) &=\kappa^n\phi_N ig( [a_{j,N}(J)H_n+b_{j,N}(J)G_n]p_N ig). \end{split} 	ag{15} \] Every product and its product-rule normal is inside this trace. In particular the normal term is \(H_n\), not \(V_nQ_0\). The operator source proves \(\|J\|_{\mathbb R}\le34N^3\). For canonical \(f,p\), Markov followed by full-Hermite reconstruction and the trace norm gives \[ |\phi_N(fp)|\le C N^5 \|f\|_{\mathbb R}\|p\|_{\mathbb R}. 	ag{16} \] This is the same full-normal product estimate as in the whole-terminal anchor corollary. Equations (11),(14)--(16) prove (9). The whole-terminal upper theorem then gives the stated rate. \(\square\) The scaled angular derivatives \(c_N'(j/N)(V_np_N)'(c_j)\), where \(c_N(u)=2\cos(2\pi u+\pi/N)\), obey the same estimate. Thus Lemma 2 initializes every fixed window of every actual channel in (7), its gauge, and the original product, uniformly in the endpoint parameters. ## 3. The exact gauged and recovered physical systems Retain all matrices and polynomial gauges of the divided- difference module. Put \[ R_*=6^r,\qquad k=33r,\qquad \mathcal F=V_n\operatorname{can}\mathcal W,\qquad Y=V_nB_{ oldsymbol\alpha,N}. 	ag{17} \] Here \(\mathcal W\) is the \(R_*\)-vector of gauged ordinary tensor channels. Its product component, denoted \(\mathcal F_*\) after turning, has gauge exponent \(r\). The exact equations are \[ \{d(D_n)(J-c_0)I_{R_*}-(q-q^{-1})^2E(D_n)\}\mathcal F=0, \qquad (D_n-2)^rY=\mathcal F_*. 	ag{18} \] They are full-algebra identities. Their ordinary residuals are \(P_N\) multiples; they need not vanish off-grid. The module proves \[ \deg d=k,\quad \deg E_{ab}\le k,\quad d(Z)\longrightarrow(Z-2)^k, 	ag{19} \] with uniformly bounded cleared coefficients for (4). Their dependence on \(N^{-1}\) has bounded analytic expansions near zero on each bounded complex parameter set. This follows also directly from the displayed finite formulas: the apparent quotients \((w_i-c_0)/(q-q^{-1})^2\) are removable and bounded, and the source coefficient is \(O(N^{-2})\). Fix \(n=\sigma m
e0\), \(m=|n|\), and set \[ M=km+1,\qquad \ell=rm. 	ag{20} \] The two equations in (18) have physical shift orders \(M\) and \(\ell\), respectively, in each direction. For completeness their extreme phases and coefficients are as follows. If \(d_k\) is the leading coefficient of \(d\), the first equation has extremes \[  egin{split} a_+(j)&=-d_k q^{-\sigma[k(2j+1)+mk^2]} \prod_{h=0}^{km} A(j+h)\ I_{R_*},\ a_-(j)&=-d_k q^{ \sigma[k(2j+1)-mk^2]} \prod_{h=0}^{km} B(j-h)\ I_{R_*}. \end{split} 	ag{21} \] For recovery they are \[  egin{split} b_+(j)&=q^{-\sigma[r(2j+1)+mr^2]} \prod_{h=0}^{rm-1}A(j+h),\ b_-(j)&=q^{ \sigma[r(2j+1)-mr^2]} \prod_{h=0}^{rm-1}B(j-h). \end{split} 	ag{22} \] Indeed the exact extremes of \(D_n\) are \[ q^{-\sigma(2j+m+1)}\prod_{h=0}^{m-1}A(j+h),\qquad q^{\sigma(2j-m+1)}\prod_{h=0}^{m-1}B(j-h). 	ag{23} \] Multiply \(k\) or \(r\) shifted copies to obtain (21)--(22). The final \(J\) in (21) contributes its minus sign and the last \(A\) or \(B\). All lower powers and the entire correction \((q-q^{-1})^2E(D_n)\) have order at most \(km=M-1\); none changes (21). The leading coefficient \(d_k\) tends to \(1\), so no small scalar is introduced there. On a buffered compact interval \(I\subset(0,1/2)\), divide by the forward extremes and form the companions \(\mathsf A_W(u)\), of dimension \(2MR_*\), and \(\mathsf A_Y(u)\), of dimension \(2\ell\). Their windows at row \(j\) are, respectively, \[ X_j^W=(\mathcal F(c_{j-M}),\ldots,\mathcal F(c_{j+M-1})), \qquad X_j^Y=(Y(c_{j-\ell}),\ldots,Y(c_{j+\ell-1})). 	ag{24} \] Let \(\mathsf B(u)\) have only its final row nonzero. It selects \(\mathcal F_*(c_j)\), the product component in the current, central row of the \(W\) window, with coefficient \(b_+(Nu)^{-1}\). It has size \(2\ell\) by \(2MR_*\). All three matrices and their first \(u\) derivatives are uniformly bounded on the fixed buffered interval. Write \(Z_j^W,Z_j^Y\) for the same windows of derivatives with respect to \(u\), evaluated at their shifted grid arguments. The exact coupled system is \[  egin{pmatrix}X^W\Z^W\X^Y\Z^Y\end{pmatrix}_{j+1} =  egin{pmatrix} \mathsf A_W&0&0&0\ \mathsf A_W'&\mathsf A_W&0&0\ \mathsf B&0&\mathsf A_Y&0\ \mathsf B'&\mathsf B&\mathsf A_Y'&\mathsf A_Y \end{pmatrix}_{u=j/N}  egin{pmatrix}X^W\Z^W\X^Y\Z^Y\end{pmatrix}_{j}. 	ag{25} \] Primes in (25) mean scaled-coordinate coefficient derivatives. The windows have their actual unequal sizes. In particular no zero padding or dummy zero characteristic roots occur. To justify the normal equations, apply the ordinary physical operators to the canonical polynomials before evaluating. The exact residual identity \[ P_N(c_N(u))=4\sin^2(\pi Nu) 	ag{26} \] annihilates both the residual value and its first \(u\) derivative at every indicated grid row. This gives (25) with all coefficient derivatives and all recovery forcing. It does not assert an off-grid homogeneous equation. ## 4. Compact transfer with the multiple roots retained Let \(x=2\cos(2\pi u)\), and let \(x_n(u,t),y(u,t)\) be the exact limiting symbols of \(D_n,J\), with \(t\) the physical shift variable. The principal \(W\) equation is \[ (x_n-2)^k(y-2)I_{R_*}; 	ag{27} \] the recovery equation has principal symbol \((x_n-2)^r\). The terminal characteristic source and bulk theorem show that \(x_n-2\), after clearing its \(t^{-m}\), has precisely the \(m\) separated roots \(	au_{\ell,n}\), each double. Also, with \(a(u)=	an^2(\pi u)\), \[ y-2=-a(u)t^{-1}(t-1)^2. 	ag{28} \] The root \(1\) is not terminal. At \(t=1\), one has \(y=2\) and \(x_n=2+(-1)^n(x-2)
e2\), as follows from the ordered twist recurrence at \(y=2\) and its two initial values \(x_0=x,\ x_1=4-x\). Thus the scalar \(W\) companion has terminal blocks of length \(2k=66r\) and one block of length two at \(1\). After a fixed permutation, its principal matrix is a direct sum of \(R_*\) copies of this scalar companion. The recovery companion has terminal blocks of length \(2r\). The repetition of channels does not concatenate those Jordan chains. All distinct roots are separated, nonzero, and analytic locally on the buffered interval. Their frames and frame derivatives can be chosen uniformly bounded there. Here are explicit quantitative details for the multiple-root step. A scalar companion has a confluent Vandermonde frame whose chain at a root \(t\) consists of \[ v(t),v'(t),\ldots,v^{(s-1)}(t)/(s-1)!, \qquad v(t)=(1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1})^{\mathsf T}. 	ag{29} \] It gives a Jordan block with diagonal \(t\) and superdiagonal one. Separation and the nonzero leading coefficient give uniformly bounded frames, inverses and derivatives on each fixed compact interval; finitely many overlapping frames suffice if one does not choose a global analytic labeling. Set \[ \vartheta=N^{-1/(66r)}. 	ag{30} \] Scale each chain of length \(s\le66r\) by \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\vartheta,\ldots,\vartheta^{s-1})\). Its superdiagonal becomes \(\vartheta\), and the condition cost of all these scalings is at most \(\vartheta^{-(66r-1)}\). The finite-\(N\) diagonal companions differ from their principal companions by \(O(N^{-1})\), uniformly with fixed derivatives on the buffered interval. In the scaled frame this error, and the change of frame over one row, are therefore \(O(N^{-1}\vartheta^{-(66r-1)})=O(\vartheta)\). For the four blocks of (25), make the additional constant grade scaling \[ (1,N,N,N^2). 	ag{31} \] All nonzero off-diagonal blocks in (25) go from a lower grade to a higher one. Each grade-one coupling thus gains at least \(N^{-1}\), and the direct first-to-fourth coupling gains \(N^{-2}\). Even a general bounded coupling between different Jordan chains consequently costs at most \[ C N^{-1}\vartheta^{-(66r-1)} =C\vartheta. 	ag{32} \] This includes the actual source forcing and both derivative couplings. It avoids treating a squared recovery equation as a single unrelated high-multiplicity scalar equation. The transformed one-step norm is at most \[ \max\{1,\max_\ell|	au_{\ell,n}(u)|\} +C_I\vartheta. 	ag{33} \] Since \(L_n\ge0\), its logarithm is at most \(L_n(u)+C_I\vartheta\). The total frame condition at the two ends costs at most \(C_I N^{\,2+(66r-1)/(66r)}\); increasing a polynomial power also covers a finite change of local frame. Products of (33), followed by the Lipschitz Riemann-sum estimate for \(L_n\) on \(I\), prove the compact bound \[ \|\mathcal T_{j_2,j_1}\| \le C_I N^{p_I} \exp\left\{N\int_{j_1/N}^{j_2/N}L_n(u)\,du +C_I N^{1-1/(66r)}ight\}. 	ag{34} \] It bounds every forward prefix, using the integral over the whole interval if convenient. The estimate involves the maximal modulus, not an assumed selected-branch coefficient. ## 5. The two endpoint strips and the unequal final windows Put \(J_N=\lfloor(N-1)/2floor\). The joint state (25) starts at \(j=M\). Its \(W\) window uses only the fixed rows \(0,\ldots,2M-1\); the \(Y\) window uses a subset of these. By (8)--(9), its norm is at most \[ C N^b(\|G_n\|_{\mathbb R}+\|H_n\|_{\mathbb R}). 	ag{35} \] The fact that \(M\) is large is harmless: \(n,r\) are fixed. For all joint centers \[ M\le j\le J_N-M,\qquad d_j=\min\{j-M+1,J_N-M-j+1\}\ge1, 	ag{36} \] every coefficient and first derivative in (25) is bounded by \[ C_{n,r,A}(N/d_j)^B. 	ag{37} \] We give the coefficient check because a factor \(N^B\) per step would be insufficient. The original \(D_n\) is built by a fixed number of products of \(J\) and spectral multiplication. In a coefficient of the \(W\) operator, every \(A(t),B(t)\) occurs with \[ j-M+1\le t\le j+M-1. 	ag{38} \] This follows by counting the shift before the last factor in each ordered product. The final \(J\) in the highest term attains the upper endpoint \(j+km=j+M-1\); all other terms stay within it. Recovery uses the smaller range with \(M\) replaced by \(\ell\). Thus every coefficient row in (38) lies between \(1\) and \(J_N-1\), at distance at least \(d_j\) from the corresponding singular boundary. Every nonzero denominator sine in (12) then has modulus at least \(c\,d_j/N\). Also \(\sin((t+1)\pi/N)\ge c\,d_j/N\). One may use \[ |A(t)|+|B(t)|\le C(N/d_j)^2,\qquad |A(t)^{-1}|\le C(N/d_j)^4. 	ag{39} \] First derivatives with respect to \(u=t/N\) cost only further inverse sines, hence further powers of \(N/d_j\). The cleared coefficients \(d,E\) are uniformly bounded fixed-degree polynomials. Their leading coefficient \(d_k\) is uniformly a unit. Equations (21)--(22) therefore bound the normalized row coefficients and their derivatives by (37). This also bounds the recovery selector and its derivative. There is no additional standalone power of \(N\) at each row. Take the two strips of length \(\epsilon N+O_{n,r}(1)\). On either strip, products of (37) are bounded by \[ C^K\prod_{a=1}^{K}(N/a)^B \le\exp\{C K\log(eN/K)\} \le\exp\{C N\epsilon\log(e/\epsilon)+O(\log N)\}. 	ag{40} \] The constants in this estimate do not depend on \(\epsilon\). Partial products obey the same bound. The final joint center \(j=J_N-M\) generates the \(W\) value at \(J_N\), but generates \(Y\) only through \(J_N-M+\ell\). This discrepancy must not be ignored. Continue only the exact recovery equation and its first normal equation for \[ J_N-M+1\le j\le J_N-\ell . 	ag{41} \] There are \(M-\ell\) such additional steps, a fixed number. All required \(\mathcal F_*(c_j)\) and its angular normal are already available from the completed \(W\) propagation. The coefficients in these last recovery rows are at most a polynomial in \(N\), by the same sine-distance argument with \(\ell\). They multiply the bound already obtained, with only a further polynomial cost. Their last output is the actual \(Y(c_{J_N})\). At odd \(N\), \(c_{J_N}=-2\) is the simple node; its angular derivative is zero and no spectral normal there is required. At even \(N\), the last node is double and its first normal is retained. All coefficient evaluations remain at most \(J_N-1\); no singular next row was invoked. ## 6. Whole-interval assembly and derivatives Apply (40) to the left strip, (34) to the fixed intervening compact interval, and (40) to the right strip. Then use the finite recovery completion (41). Since \(L_n\ge0\), the same total bound controls every intermediate value and scaled angular normal. Replacing either compact endpoint by a neighboring grid point changes its exponent by \(O_\epsilon(1)\). Together with (35), this bounds every physical value and required angular first normal of \(Y\) by the right side of (6). The ordinary canonical polynomial is recovered with the stable full-Hermite inequality \[ \|Y\|_{\mathbb R}\le(2N-1)\max_{m physical}|Y| +2\max_{m angular}|\partial_tY(-2\cos t)|. 	ag{42} \] Here \(t=\pi-2\pi u-\pi/N\), so its angular derivative is \(-1/(2\pi)\) times the scaled derivative used in (25). The paired lifts and odd simple node therefore give exactly the data required by (42). This proves (6). For fixed \(\epsilon\), the whole-terminal upper theorem gives an initial limsup of at most \(\mathcal I_n\). Divide the logarithm of (6) by \(N\), take the upper limit, and only then send \(\epsilon\) to zero. The endpoint loss tends to zero and the improper characteristic integral converges. This proves (5) for \(n
e0\). For \(n=0\), \(V_0=I\), and the polynomial input bound already proves (5). All estimates were uniform on arbitrary fixed bounded complex parameter polydisks. Cauchy's formula on a slightly larger such polydisk gives the same exponential rate for every fixed parameter derivative. Ordinary Markov inequalities for the degree-\(D\) output add only polynomial factors for fixed spectral derivatives. This establishes the derivative assertion without discarding any original normal channel. The proof pays two independent upper budgets: the actual fixed-row source initialization, bounded by \(\mathcal I_n\), and subsequent maximal-characteristic transport, bounded by \(\mathcal I_n\). Nothing here shows that both budgets are attained or that either can be removed. The characteristic determinant alone would not justify even this conclusion without (9), the regular extreme coefficients, and the forced recovery. ## 7. Direct sources and scope All five complete direct sources have been read at the following pins, with the used implications checked: * [Exact product module](research_endpoint_product_divided_difference_module.md), SHA256 8a1b215aa6034365d4faa84130381d6a78a17383c03ecf6c6b48a77b6c4e3093: six ordinary channels, aliases, polynomial gauge, degree \(33r\), cleared matrices, original turn and forced recovery. * [Whole-terminal upper bound](research_whole_terminal_characteristic_upper_bound.md), SHA256 ee91f066e0e5b0eb60e4076ba2a2090e1439787c57caf6eaaa09341138d05176: actual \(G_n,H_n\) initialization and rates, fixed-row original equations, full-Hermite and coherent trace bounds, integrability and nonnegativity of \(L_n\). * [Physical bulk transfer](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_terminal_twist_bulk_transfer_bound.md), SHA256 fca96865315f21dc9961be89061cc6c3a292b2b563e7ded756e86c3438ef5bde: exact signed physical operators and extremes, ideal residuals, separated double terminal roots and the value/normal transfer convention. * [Original finite-band operators](research_unit_turn_finite_band_branching_operator.md), SHA256 31d9f574c7dc3aaac07e4eb50c131b3328be46b3c2a2ef46f9dae7f0c4ddb9cb: full algebra and Frobenius transport, ordered twist recurrence, and the polynomial \(J\) norm. * [Whole endpoint products](research_endpoint_two_half_plane_relative_source.md), SHA256 985fa3331379c3877734f28773d314b667ee87fa63314a5ef4513a3fe128d194: uniform polynomial real norm for fixed ordinary microscopic endpoint products on bounded complex parameter sets. No selected-branch lower coefficient, volume gap, arbitrary tree closure, or equality with a terminal source is claimed. All crossing phases, tensor channels and first normals were retained before taking upper bounds. Only written mathematics and source-text/hash reads were used. No mathematical program, numerical experiment, test or build was run. Adopted notes and public manuscripts are unchanged.

title: Finitely many exceptional assignments for a two-circle template
text: # Finitely many exceptional assignments for a two-circle template Research consequence, 2 November 2026. This note applies the proved terminal-filling theorem to a tree consisting of one edge. It does not prove the finite-exception statement for arbitrary trees or Conway templates. The frozen manuscripts are unchanged. ## 1. The knot family and the claim Use the physical tangle conventions of the [circle-tree geometry paper](../papers/circle-tree-geometry/main.tex). Let \(R\) be the elementary crossing, \(T\) the prescribed quarter-turn, and \(C\) cylindrical closure. The one-edge tree has the closure \[ K(a,b)=C\bigl(R^aT(R^b)\bigr). \] Fix the original endpoint marking, disk frames, and carrier parities. Thus \(a=\eta_1-2p_1\) and \(b=\eta_2-2p_2\), with fixed \(\eta_1,\eta_2\in\{-1,0,1\}\) and \(p_1,p_2\in\mathbb Z\). Restrict attention to assignments whose closure is a hyperbolic knot. The parameters count assignments; no identification of distinct assignments representing the same knot is made. **Corollary.** There is a finite number \(B_*\), depending on this fixed marked template, such that every hyperbolic knot \(K(a,b)\) with \[ \max\{|a|,|b|\}\ge B_* \] satisfies the original Kashaev volume identity \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{N}\log|\langle K(a,b)\rangle_N| =\operatorname{Vol}(S^3\setminus K(a,b)). \] The twists are fixed before \(N\) tends to infinity, and the limit is through all integer levels. Consequently only finitely many original filling assignments in this two-parameter family remain untreated. The corollary does not claim that the remaining assignments violate the volume identity. ## 2. The three elementary powers have no hyperbolic descendants For the zero power, \(T(R^0)\) is the cup-cap tangle, rather than the through identity. It changes the cylindrical closure into the cap closure: \[ K(a,0)\simeq D(R^a). \] Here \(D\) denotes the cap closure. Each crossing can be pulled to an end cap and removed as a curl. The resulting unframed knot is the unknot. The precise cap identities and the retained components are proved in [the tangle reduction paper](../papers/conway-reductions/closures.tex). A quarter-turn of a single crossing gives the inverse crossing in the original vertical frame: \[ T(R)=R^{-1},\qquad T(R^{-1})=R. \] This is a local equality of the two one-crossing diagrams with their ordered endpoints. It is also reflected by the exact turned crossing identities \(\mathcal H_1=R^{-1}\) and \(\mathcal H_{-1}=R\) in [the finite transform calculation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_terminal_powers_qbinomial.md). Therefore \[ K(a,1)\simeq C(R^{a-1}),\qquad K(a,-1)\simeq C(R^{a+1}). \] The latter closures are two-strand torus links. When they have one component, they are unknots or torus knots and are not hyperbolic. The elementary group argument excluding these knots is included in the tangle reduction paper. Its closed-turn and cyclicity isotopies, proved in [the collar calculation](../papers/conway-reductions/moves.tex), also give \[ C(R^aT(R^b))\simeq C(T(R^a)R^b) \simeq C(R^bT(R^a)). \] They retain the physical rotations and crossing signs. Thus the same conclusion holds when \(a\in\{0,1,-1\}\). It follows that every hyperbolic knot in this family has \[ |a|\ge2,\qquad |b|\ge2. \] This is a statement about the actual knot diagrams. A vanishing or small exponential rate of a polynomial would not by itself establish the required topological exclusion. ## 3. Closing the finitely many short-coordinate families Let \(B_0\ge3\) be an integer threshold for the all-long theorem on this fixed one-edge template. It proves the identity whenever both \(|a|\ge B_0\) and \(|b|\ge B_0\), with the allowed fixed parities. For each allowed fixed integer \(c\) with \(2\le|c|<B_0\), the [terminal-filling theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_verified_terminal_fillings_and_long_remainder.md) applies with the first vertex fixed at \(a=c\). It supplies a finite threshold \(B_{1,c}\) for the other power. The same theorem with the second vertex fixed supplies \(B_{2,c}\). Both vertices are original terminal vertices, so this use does not require a theorem about a vertex that becomes terminal after a previous short filling. Choose an integer \[ B_*\ge\max\left(B_0, \{B_{1,c}:2\le|c|<B_0\}, \{B_{2,c}:2\le|c|<B_0\}\right), \] where only the allowed parity values are included. These are finite sets. No uniform bound for all fixed terminal powers is needed. Suppose \(K(a,b)\) is hyperbolic and \(\max\{|a|,|b|\}\ge B_*\). Section 2 excludes the powers \(0,\pm1\). If both powers have magnitude at least \(B_0\), the original all-long theorem applies. Otherwise exactly one power is in the finite range \(2\le|c|<B_0\), while the other has magnitude at least \(B_*\). The corresponding terminal-filling theorem applies. This proves the corollary. All unresolved assignments lie in the finite square \(|a|<B_*, |b|<B_*\). The affine maps from \(p_1,p_2\) to \(a,b\) are injective, so the corresponding set of original surgery assignments is finite as well. ## 4. Why this does not yet extend to arbitrary trees The later [isolated-vertex theorem](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_isolated_vertex_coverage_and_assembly.md) now estimates every original vertex with degree \(d_v\) and fixed power \(n_v\) satisfying \(d_v+|n_v|>2\), with all its boundary variables retained. Its assembly theorem permits any independent set of such fixed vertices before independently long remaining fillings. Thus isolated internal short powers are no longer the missing case. Arbitrary connected sets of adjacent short fillings still need a joint boundary estimate. Several specific connected families have been proved, but the finite-branching argument for arbitrary templates requires a theorem at every partial assignment it reaches. It must also retain the original parameter fibers in zero-power and cap reductions: a finite untreated set of reduced knots can have infinitely many original assignments. The one-edge corollary is therefore a completed special case of the finite-exception target, rather than its general proof.

title: The two-ended microscopic kernel with its original normal channels
text: # The two-ended microscopic kernel with its original normal channels Private written proof, 23 November 2026. The original Newton kernel has an entire limit when both colors lie at distance of order \(N^{-2}\) from \(2\). Both ends of its finite Newton sum survive. The low end gives the Wilson polynomial at a fixed physical index; the complementary end vanishes at that value but contributes to its true first normal. The error is \(O(N^{-1})\), with every fixed holomorphic parameter derivative. This concerns the canonical ordinary kernel, without replacing it by a moderate representative. It supplies neither an orthogonality transform with the original cap nor an estimate of a closed knot source. ## 1. The original kernel and the limiting series Let \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(\theta=\pi/N\), and set \[ s_m=2\sin(m\theta),\quad S_k=\prod_{m=1}^k s_m,\quad S_0=1, \qquad c_j=2\cos((2j+1)\theta), \] \[ e_k(Z)=S_k^{-2}\prod_{j<k}(c_j-Z),\qquad K_N(Z,W)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}e_k(Z)e_k(W),\qquad P_N(Z)=2T_N(Z/2)+2=\prod_{j=0}^{d}(Z-c_j). \tag{1} \] The repeated roots in \(P_N\) retain the original first normals. At odd levels the additional root \(-2\) is simple. Define \[ w_N(\alpha)=2\cosh(\alpha/N),\qquad E_{k,N}(\alpha)=(-1)^k e_k(w_N(\alpha)), \] \[ \mathsf E_k(\alpha)= \frac{(\tfrac12+i\alpha/(2\pi))_k (\tfrac12-i\alpha/(2\pi))_k}{(k!)^2},\qquad \mathsf H_m(\alpha)= \frac{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)}{\pi^2m^2\mathsf E_m(\alpha)} \quad(m\ge1). \tag{2} \] Here \(\mathsf E_0=1\). Every \(\mathsf H_m\) means its entire continuation: the zeros of \(\mathsf E_m\) are the simple zeros \(\alpha=\pm i(2r+1)\pi\), \(0\le r<m\), whereas the numerator has a double zero at each of them. Both families are even. **Theorem.** The series \[ \boxed{\quad \mathcal K(\alpha,\beta)= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathsf E_k(\alpha)\mathsf E_k(\beta) +\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\mathsf H_m(\alpha)\mathsf H_m(\beta) \quad} \tag{3} \] converge normally on every compact complex bidisk. They define an entire symmetric function, even in each variable. For every fixed \(A<\infty\) and nonnegative integers \(a,b\), \[ \sup_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le A} \left|\partial_\alpha^a\partial_\beta^b \{K_N(w_N(\alpha),w_N(\beta))-\mathcal K(\alpha,\beta)\}\right| \le \frac{C_{A,a,b}}{N}. \tag{4} \] The estimate holds for all sufficiently large \(N\), through both parities. For real parameters (3) is a positive Gram kernel; this does not change the original bilinear closing functional. ## 2. Exact complementary coefficients and uniform tails The sine product and the full physical polynomial give exactly \[ S_{N-1}=N,\qquad P_N(w_N(\alpha))=4\cosh^2(\alpha/2), \] \[ E_{N-m,N}(\alpha)= \frac{4\cosh^2(\alpha/2)}{N^2s_m^2E_{m,N}(\alpha)} \qquad(1\le m<N). \tag{5} \] Indeed the last \(m\) roots of \(P_N\) are the first \(m\) roots in reverse order, and \(S_{N-m}=N/S_{m-1}\). Cancellation in the full product proves (5); at zeros it is the removable identity. We recall, and justify, the uniform bound \[ |E_{i,N}(\alpha)|\le \frac{C_A}{\min(i,N-i)} \qquad(1\le i<N,\ |\alpha|\le A). \tag{6} \] At zero parameter, for \(i\le N/2\), \[ E_{i,N}(0)=\prod_{r<i} \left\{\frac{\sin((r+\tfrac12)\theta)} {\sin((r+1)\theta)}\right\}^{\!2} \asymp\left\{\frac{(1/2)_i}{i!}\right\}^{\!2} \asymp\frac1{i+1}. \tag{7} \] The first comparison has absolute constants: for \(f(v)=\sin v/v\), the product of its half-step ratios lies between \(1\) and \(1/f(i\theta)\le\pi/2\). The second is the elementary central-binomial, or Wallis, bound. Formula (5), \(s_m\ge4m/N\) for \(m\le N/2\), and the lower bound in (7) give the other half of (6) at \(\alpha=0\). For complex \(|\alpha|\le A\), \[ |w_N(\alpha)-2|\le2\cosh(A/N)-2, \] \[ \frac{|e_i(w_N(\alpha))|}{|e_i(2)|} \le\prod_{r<i}\left(1+ \frac{2\cosh(A/N)-2}{2-c_r}\right) \le\frac{P_N(w_N(A))}{P_N(2)}=\cosh^2(A/2). \tag{8} \] All \(2-c_r\) are positive. This proves (6), without discarding the repeated roots or either end of the Newton list. ## 3. A sharper unit comparison on a linear range Write \(\operatorname{sinc}z=\sin z/z\) and \(\operatorname{sinhc}z=\sinh z/z\), with removable values one. The exact difference of cosines gives \[ E_{i,N}(\alpha)=\mathsf E_i(\alpha)U_{i,N}(\alpha), \] \[ U_{i,N}(\alpha)=\prod_{r=0}^{i-1} \frac{\operatorname{sinhc}((\alpha+i(2r+1)\pi)/(2N)) \operatorname{sinhc}((\alpha-i(2r+1)\pi)/(2N))} {\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(r+1)/N)^2}. \tag{9} \] This factorization is valid at zeros of \(\mathsf E_i\). For \(i\le N/4\), all displayed factors are units on a fixed bounded \(\alpha\)-disk once \(N\) is sufficiently large. We claim \[ |U_{i,N}^{\ \pm1}-1|\le C_A\frac{i^2}{N^2} \qquad(1\le i\le N/4,\ |\alpha|\le A). \tag{10} \] Here is the cancellation that gives the linear-range estimate. Put \(v_r=(r+1/2)\pi/N\), \(h=\pi/(2N)\), and \(a=\alpha/(2N)\). At \(\alpha=0\), a continuous logarithm gives \[ \log U_{i,N}(0)=2\sum_{r<i} \{\log\operatorname{sinc}v_r -\log\operatorname{sinc}(v_r+h)\} =O(i^2/N^2). \tag{11} \] Indeed \((\log\operatorname{sinc})'(v)=O(v)\) on a fixed neighborhood of \([0,\pi/4]\). Let \(g(z)=\log\operatorname{sinhc}z\), with \(g(0)=0\), on a fixed zero-free disk containing all \(a\pm iv_r\). It is even. The function \(g(a+iv_r)+g(a-iv_r)-2g(iv_r)\) is even in \(a\), vanishes at zero, and is \(O_A(N^{-2})\) by its uniformly bounded second derivative. Summing over \(r<i\) and using (11) gives \(|\log U_{i,N}(\alpha)|\le C_Ai^2/N^2\). This logarithm is bounded on the entire stated range; exponentiating both signs proves (10). It need not tend to zero at \(i=N/4\). Combining (5) and (9) gives the entire identity \[ E_{N-m,N}(\alpha)=\mathsf H_m(\alpha) \operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/N)^{-2}U_{m,N}(\alpha)^{-1}. \tag{12} \] It follows first off the zeros and then at them by continuation. For each fixed index, (9) and (12) give respectively the limits \(\mathsf E_i\) and \(\mathsf H_m\), uniformly on compact disks. Passing (6) to these limits proves \[ \sup_{|\alpha|\le A} (|\mathsf E_m(\alpha)|+|\mathsf H_m(\alpha)|) \le C_A/m\qquad(m\ge1). \tag{13} \] In particular both series in (3) converge normally, including all their apparently singular parameter values. ## 4. Summing the two ends and retaining derivatives Let \(L=\lfloor N/4\rfloor\). Split the canonical finite sum into \(0\le i\le L\), \(i=N-m\) with \(1\le m\le L\), and the remaining middle. There is no overlap for large \(N\). Since the two signs \((-1)^i\) cancel in every same-index product, these are products of the \(E_{i,N}\) defined above. For \(1\le i\le L\), (9)--(10) and (13) give \[ |E_{i,N}(\alpha)E_{i,N}(\beta) -\mathsf E_i(\alpha)\mathsf E_i(\beta)| \le \frac{C_A}{i^2}\frac{i^2}{N^2}=\frac{C_A}{N^2}. \tag{14} \] The index-zero terms agree exactly. The high products obey the same bound by (12), since \(\operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/N)^{-2}-1=O(m^2/N^2)\). Summing these errors costs \(O_A(N^{-1})\). By (6), the middle sum is bounded by \(C_A\sum_{L<i<N-L}\min(i,N-i)^{-2}=O_A(N^{-1})\). Both infinite tails after \(L\) are \(O_A(N^{-1})\) by (13). This proves (4) for \(a=b=0\). Prove it on a larger bidisk and apply Cauchy's formula to obtain every stated mixed derivative, with the same rate. The Gram assertion follows directly from (3), whose two coefficient families are real at real parameters. ## 5. The fixed-index value and its true first normal Put \[ \mathscr K(r,\alpha)=\mathcal K(\alpha,i\pi(2r+1)). \] For every fixed integer \(j\ge0\), \[ \mathscr K(j,\alpha)= {}_4F_3\!\left(\begin{matrix}-j,j+1, \tfrac12+i\alpha/(2\pi),\tfrac12-i\alpha/(2\pi)\\ 1,1,1\end{matrix};1\right). \tag{15} \] In fact \(\mathsf E_k(i\pi(2j+1))=0\) for \(k>j\), while every \(\mathsf H_m(i\pi(2j+1))=0\). This is the normalized Wilson value \(W_j((\alpha/(2\pi))^2;1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2)/(j!)^3\). The complementary series cannot be discarded before differentiation. Termwise differentiation is allowed by normal convergence, and \[ \left.\partial_r\mathsf H_m(i\pi(2r+1))\right|_{r=j} =\begin{cases} 0,&m\le j,\\ \displaystyle(-1)^{j+1} \frac{((m-1)!)^2}{(m-j-1)!(m+j)!},&m>j. \end{cases} \tag{16} \] To check this, substitute \(\mathsf E_m(i\pi(2r+1))=(-r)_m(r+1)_m/(m!)^2\) and \(\cosh^2(i\pi(2r+1)/2)=\sin^2\pi r\) in (2). For \(m>j\), the factor \(\mathsf E_m(i\pi(2r+1))\) has one simple zero, of derivative \((-1)^{j+1}(m-j-1)!(m+j)!/(m!)^2\); for \(m\le j\) it is nonzero. Writing \(c_N(r)=2\cos((2r+1)\pi/N)\), (4) and the chain rule give \[ \boxed{\quad \frac{\partial_Z K_N(c_j,w_N(\alpha))}{N^2} =-\frac{\partial_r\mathscr K(j,\alpha)}{4\pi^2(2j+1)} +O_{A,j}(N^{-1}). \quad} \tag{17} \] Indeed \(N^2c_N'(j)=-4\pi^2(2j+1)+O_j(N^{-2})\). Every fixed \(\alpha\)-derivative retains the estimate. For fixed \(j\), this is its original double-root normal at all sufficiently large levels; no normal at the moving odd simple node has been introduced. At \(j=0\), differentiation of the low series gives \(-\sum_{m\ge1}\mathsf E_m(\alpha)/m\); (16) gives \(-\sum_{m\ge1}\mathsf H_m(\alpha)/m\) for the high series. Consequently the earlier endpoint function is \[ \mathcal Q(\alpha)=\frac1{4\pi^2} \sum_{m\ge1}\frac{\mathsf E_m(\alpha)+\mathsf H_m(\alpha)}m, \qquad N^{-2}\partial_ZK_N(c_0,w_N(\alpha)) =\mathcal Q(\alpha)+O_A(N^{-1}). \tag{18} \] Thus its previous \(O(N^{-1/2})\) rate improves to \(O(N^{-1})\), including every fixed parameter derivative. Both series in (18) are positive for real \(\alpha\). ## 6. Source scope and complete coverage For the original ordinary Askey--Wilson operator, write \[ (\mathcal L f)(c_N(r))=(c_0+A_N(r)+C_N(r))f(c_N(r)) -A_N(r)f(c_N(r+1))-C_N(r)f(c_N(r-1)), \] where \(A_N(r)=s_{r+1}^4/(s_{2r+1}s_{2r+2})\), \(C_N(r)=s_r^4/(s_{2r}s_{2r+1})\), and \(s_r=2\sin(\pi r/N)\). Combined expressions are continued through their apparent poles. The exact full kernel obeys \[ wK_N(z,w)-\mathcal L_zK_N(z,w) =\frac{(-1)^{N-1}}{N^2}P_N(w)e_{N-1}(z). \tag{19} \] The endpoint first normal of its right side, at \(z=c_0\) and \(w=w_N(\alpha)\), is \(4\cosh^2(\alpha/2)/(N^2s_1^2)\to\cosh^2(\alpha/2)/\pi^2\). This source is retained. We have not identified (3) with a standard homogeneous Wilson function or imported a Wilson orthogonality theorem. The Wilson name in (15) uses only its defining terminating formula. The estimates concern bounded microscopic parameters and fixed physical indices. They are not uniform over all \(j\) of order \(N\), arbitrary outer turns, or original cap contractions after a general short word. Neither Gram positivity nor the nonzero endpoint normal changes the original closing into an adjoint norm or proves a geometric coefficient. The earlier two-ended result treated one endpoint normal; its uniform coefficient bound and exact unit factorization are retained here. The connection note treated values and their growing bulk overlap. The shared-current note explicitly retained doubly microscopic edges as additional joint amplitudes. None supplies the full limit (3)--(4). title: The original factorial amplitude through a two-square fold
text: # The original factorial amplitude through a two-square fold Private written proof, 16 November 2026. At every two-square edge classified by the radial primitive theorem, both original same-index halfwire factorials are holomorphic units on one neighborhood independent of the level. They have a uniform all-order expansion with the retained original phase \(b_0\) and a nonzero leading amplitude. This includes the square-root fold \(q=0\). The proof fixes the phase constant and logarithmic marking, rather than inferring an asymptotic expansion from finite-level holomorphy. This result concerns the factors at the classified two-square edges. It does not assert a single-phase expansion for unrelated incidences, replace a free cardinal boundary by a factorial, or determine the coefficient of the local Morse disk in the original relative cycle. ## 1. A centered factorial expansion with a fixed constant Write \[ \Omega=\mathbb C\setminus\bigl((-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty)\bigr). \tag{1} \] This domain is simply connected: \(u\mapsto u/(1-u)\) identifies it with the plane cut along the nonpositive real axis. Let \[ J'(u)=\Log(2\sin\pi u),\qquad J(1/2)=0, \tag{2} \] where the logarithm is real on \(0<u<1\). This is the original sine primitive, since \(\int_0^{1/2}\log(2\sin\pi u)\,du=0\). Its reflection identities are \[ J(1-u)=-J(u),\qquad J^{(2r)}(1/2)=0\quad(r\ge1). \tag{3} \] In particular its restrictions to the upper and lower half-planes are the marked branches of the archived half-plane expansions. Use the original normalized gamma-product factorial \(G_N\), \(N\ge2\). Its exact logarithmic derivative and divisor are \[ \frac{G_N'(w)}{G_N(w)} =\frac{\pi}{N^2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(w-k) \cot\frac{\pi(w-k)}N,\qquad \operatorname{ord}_{w=k}G_N(w)=\lfloor k/N\rfloor . \tag{4} \] There are no other divisors. Terms with \(w=k\), \(0\le k<N\), are removable. Put \[ H_N(u)=G_N(Nu-1/2). \tag{5} \] Every divisor of (5) lies on one of the two removed real rays. Thus \(H_N\) has a holomorphic logarithm on \(\Omega\). Its exact normalization is \[ H_N(1/2)=\sqrt N>0. \tag{6} \] Indeed (4) gives \(G_N'(N-1-w)/G_N(N-1-w)=G_N'(w)/G_N(w)\); hence \(G_N(w)G_N(N-1-w)\) is constant. At \(w=0\) it is \(\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}2\sin(\pi j/N)=N\). Positivity of the defining gamma product on \(-1<w<N\) fixes the sign in (6). Choose \(\log H_N(1/2)=\tfrac12\log N\). **Lemma 1.** For every compact \(K\Subset\Omega\) and integer \(R\ge0\), \[ \log H_N(u)=\tfrac12\log N+NJ(u) +\sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{B_{2r}(1/2)}{(2r)!\,N^{2r-1}}J^{(2r)}(u) +O_{K,R}(N^{-2R-1}). \tag{7} \] The remainder is holomorphic and has the same order under every fixed derivative on smaller compact sets. Here \(B_m(z)\) are the Bernoulli polynomials and an empty sum is zero. **Proof.** Equation (4) gives the literal midpoint sum \[ \frac d{du}\log H_N(u) =\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}F_u((k+1/2)/N), \qquad F_u(s)=\pi(u-s)\cot\pi(u-s). \tag{8} \] For \(u\) in a compact subset of \(\Omega\), \(0\le s\le1\), this function and all its fixed derivatives are uniformly bounded. The apparent singularity at \(u=s\) is removable; every other possible pole would place \(u\) on a removed ray. The leading integral is \[ \int_0^1F_u(s)\,ds=J'(u). \tag{9} \] Its derivative is \(F_u(0)-F_u(1)=\pi\cot\pi u=J''(u)\). At \(u=1/2\), integration by parts gives \[ \int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\pi v\cot\pi v\,dv =-2\int_0^{1/2}\log(\sin\pi v)\,dv=\log2, \] which fixes (9). The elementary log-sine integral here follows from reflection and the sine double-angle formula. Midpoint Euler--Maclaurin, with enough remainder terms, gives \[ \frac d{du}\log H_N(u) =NJ'(u)+\sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{B_{2r}(1/2)}{(2r)!\,N^{2r-1}}J^{(2r+1)}(u) +O_{K,R}(N^{-2R-1}). \tag{10} \] The endpoint derivative difference used here is \[ \partial_s^{2r-1}F_u(1)-\partial_s^{2r-1}F_u(0) =J^{(2r+1)}(u). \tag{11} \] The odd Bernoulli polynomials at \(1/2\) vanish. Formula (10) can, for example, be obtained by retaining one further even term and absorbing it and its uniformly bounded remainder at the stated order. Join \(K\) to \(1/2\) by paths of uniformly bounded length in a larger compact subset of \(\Omega\). Such paths exist by a finite cover and connectedness of the domain. Integrating (10), then using (3) and (6), proves (7), including its constant. Cauchy estimates on a slightly larger compact set give the derivative assertion. No asymptotic error was continued from another domain. \(\square\) The usual uncentered version follows by replacing \(u\) in (7) by \(u+1/(2N)\). Bernoulli translation gives \[ \log G_N(Nu)=\tfrac12\log N+NJ(u)+\tfrac12J'(u) +\sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{B_{2r}}{(2r)!\,N^{2r-1}}J^{(2r)}(u) +O_{K,R}(N^{-2R-1}), \tag{12} \] where \(B_{2r}=B_{2r}(0)\). To justify the indicated remainder, first retain sufficiently many terms in (7) and in its Taylor expansion. The identities \(B_m(1)=B_m(0)\) for \(m\ne1\) and \(B_m(0)=0\) for odd \(m>1\) cancel the intervening even inverse powers. The logarithm in (12) is the one induced by (5); on the original real interval it is the actual real logarithm. ## 2. A common exact unit neighborhood At a classified two-square edge write \[ t=-iH,\quad u=-iK,\quad A=\tanh(H/2),\quad B=\tanh(K/2),\quad q=iQ,\quad Q^2=A^2+B^2-1\ge0, \quad |Q|<\min(A,B)<1. \tag{13} \] These are the actual limiting data of the pinned radial theorem; in particular \(H,K>0\). The retained stationary wire is \[ x_*=\frac12-\frac{i}{\pi}\operatorname{artanh}Q. \tag{14} \] Use \(D=N-1\) and the literal source factor \[ B_N(x,t)= \frac{N}{G_N(Nz_+-1/2)G_N(Nz_--1/2)G_N(Nx)^2}, \qquad z_\pm=\frac12-x\pm\frac{t}{2\pi}. \tag{15} \] At (13)--(14), \[ z_+=\frac{i}{\pi}\{\operatorname{artanh}Q-H/2\}, \qquad z_-=\frac{i}{\pi}\{\operatorname{artanh}Q+H/2\}. \tag{16} \] The first lies strictly below the real axis and the second strictly above it. The same assertion holds with \(H\) replaced by \(K\). **Theorem 2.** A neighborhood \(\mathcal U\) of \((x_*,t,u)\), independent of \(N\ge2\), exists on which \(B_N(x,t)\) and \(B_N(x,u)\) are holomorphic and nonzero. It can be chosen so that all their normalized arguments \(x,z_+,z_-\) lie in fixed compact subsets of \(\Omega\). The assertions hold simultaneously for every edge of a finite classified two-square matching, including every \(Q=0\). **Proof.** Shrink a relatively compact neighborhood so that \(1/4<\Re x<3/4\) and the two signs in (16) are separated from zero, for each endpoint. Then the shifted arguments in (15) are nonreal at every level and have no divisor by (4). Also \(-1<\Re(Nx)<N\), so \(G_N(Nx)\) is a unit. The strict inequalities are independent of \(N\). They also give the compact subsets of \(\Omega\). Intersect the finitely many neighborhoods for the matching. \(\square\) For precision, the corresponding reversed factor \(B_N(D/N-x,t)\) is an exact unit on a possibly smaller common neighborhood as well. Its shifted arguments are \(N(x-1/2\pm t/(2\pi))+1/2\), still strictly nonreal; its unshifted argument is \(N(1-x)-1\), whose real part lies strictly between \(-1\) and \(N\) for all \(N\ge2\). This does not identify its different asymptotic phase with \(b_0\). ## 3. Agreement with the retained geometric logarithms The domain membership at the target alone does not determine a previously continued logarithmic marking. Here the actual positive approach and its allowed tangent contraction fix it. **Lemma 3.** At each edge in Theorem 2, the primitive obtained by using (2) in \[ b_{\rm can}(x,t)=-J(z_+)-J(z_-)-2J(x) \tag{17} \] is exactly the retained original \(b_0(x,t)\) germ, including its additive constant and its logarithmic derivatives. **Proof.** Let \((a_j,b_j)\) be its positive approach, tending to \((-iA,-iB)\). The pinned positive-wire theorem proves that \[ (\lambda a_j,\lambda b_j),\qquad 0\le\lambda\le1, \tag{18} \] stays positive. Its original stationary branch has \(\Re q_j(\lambda)>0\), \(x_j(0)=1/4\). Thus continuation along (18) gives precisely the original marked phase, from completeness. Put \(\lambda_0=(A^2+B^2)^{-1/2}\le1\). The limiting root is nonnegative real on \([0,\lambda_0]\), with \[ q_\lambda^2=1-\lambda^2(A^2+B^2), \tag{19} \] and for \(\lambda>\lambda_0\) is the imaginary root whose sign is that of \(Q\). If \(Q=0\), this latter interval is empty. The principal square roots along (18) converge uniformly to this continuous path. For \(Q\ne0\), the sign of their imaginary parts is eventually the sign of \(Q\); at the single zero of (19), continuity of the square root gives the same conclusion. The inverse cotangent has no singularity on this compact path, which avoids \(q=\pm i\), so the wires converge uniformly too. The limiting endpoint angle is \[ t_\lambda=-2i\operatorname{artanh}(\lambda A). \tag{20} \] Before \(\lambda_0\), \(x_\lambda\) is real in \([1/4,1/2]\). For \(0<\lambda\le\lambda_0\), the two arguments \(z_\pm\) therefore have opposite nonzero imaginary parts, with nonnegative real parts. At \(\lambda=0\) all three arguments equal \(1/4\). After \(\lambda_0\), write \(q_\lambda=iQ_\lambda\). Then \[ Q_\lambda^2=\lambda^2(A^2+B^2)-1,\qquad |Q_\lambda|<\lambda A,\quad |Q_\lambda|<\lambda B, \tag{21} \] because \(\lambda A,\lambda B<1\). Formula (16), with these contracted values, again places \(z_+\) strictly below and \(z_-\) strictly above the axis. The wire has real part \(1/2\). Consequently each entire limiting argument path is a compact subset of \(\Omega\). Uniform convergence implies that the late actual positive paths (18) stay in this same domain. Along them the logarithm (2) is the original one, since it agrees at their common complete starting point. Its primitive constants agree there as well. Passing to the limit proves (17), and continuation to the small independent-variable neighborhood proves equality of the full germs. This argument does not assume that the radial charge path is connected, or deform fixed primitive equations along (18). \(\square\) ## 4. The actual local amplitude **Theorem 4.** Uniformly on compact subsets of the neighborhood in Theorem 2, with all fixed holomorphic derivatives after the displayed phase and prefactor are extracted, \[ \boxed{\quad B_N(x,t)=\frac{e^{Nb_0(x,t)}}{2N\sin\pi x} \exp\left\{\sum_{r=1}^{R}\frac{C_r(x,t)}{N^{2r-1}} +O(N^{-2R-1})\right\},\quad} \tag{22} \] for every \(R\ge0\), where \[ C_r(x,t)=- \frac{B_{2r}(1/2)\{J^{(2r)}(z_+)+J^{(2r)}(z_-)\} +2B_{2r}J^{(2r)}(x)}{(2r)!}. \tag{23} \] In particular \(2N\sin(\pi x)e^{-Nb_0}B_N\to1\) holomorphically, and the leading amplitude is a unit through the fold. **Proof.** Apply (7) to the two shifted factors in (15), and (12) to its two unshifted factors. The four half-logarithms give \(2\log N\); subtracting them from the numerator \(\log N\) leaves \(-\log N\). The two unshifted half-logarithms of the sine give \(-J'(x)=-\Log(2\sin\pi x)\). The action and all remaining terms are exactly (17), (23). Lemma 3 identifies the action with the retained \(b_0\). The uniform remainder and derivative statements follow from Lemma 1. \(\square\) For the two endpoints of one affected edge this gives \[ B_N(x,t)B_N(x,u) =\frac{e^{N\{b_0(x,t)+b_0(x,u)\}}}{4N^2\sin^2\pi x} (1+O_{\rm hol}(N^{-1})). \tag{24} \] At its stationary limit the leading coefficient is explicitly \[ \frac1{4\sin^2\pi x_*}=\frac{1-Q^2}{4}>0. \tag{25} \] It equals \(1/4\) at a fold. For a finite matching the products of (22)--(25) hold simultaneously, with their original shared angular variables. Compact families of the stated regular data have uniform constants after taking a finite cover; no height or regularity margin is claimed outside such compact families. There is thus no Stokes or logarithmic wall obstruction to this specific local factorial amplitude. The proof does not delete exponentially small terms of the exact factorial as a source identity: (22) is an asymptotic expansion of that exact function. The full unsummed Hessian theorem supplies nonzero coordinate Jacobians through a fold, so these affected factors introduce no additional zero under its local Morse change of variables. The other factors of the original source remain in place: unrelated halfwires, the full-Hermite angular kernels, both charged cosine terms, all constants and spectators, and any genuine free cardinal ends. A nonzero local factorial density does not establish the coefficient of the geometric exponential sector in their prescribed integral. In particular neither a global contour coefficient nor a metric completion at a two-square limit follows. ## Direct sources and coverage * [Exact canonical factorial](research_exact_cyclotomic_factorial.md), SHA256 0f989261f53747266ac62dba40ca7548138012b266521e98a03bd94b450c657b: the original gamma product, normalization and exact finite logarithmic derivative. The complete written text was reread. * [Exact factorial divisors](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_factorial_rectangle_divisor_criterion.md), SHA256 462b8c22c73f73b12152bca96cf6636708dcf153c2cbc2751458454827b3ddf8: all-level divisor orders and the distinction between a unit and a pole-free interpolation. The complete text was reread. * [Positive wire product domain](research_positive_wire_product_contour.md), SHA256 5646f2d6b2a8dfa2d8c49662d17f19f3743fc4efcaf3c3685c6a899975a4c230: actual tangent contraction, inverse-cotangent marking and exact halfwire conventions. The complete text was reread. * [Radial two-square primitive lift](research_radial_two_square_primitive_lift.md), SHA256 21d9af750653621cc82bd73373a99a138210fc4cdb10407faabcb209505df9ad: the supplied radial-limit hypotheses and classification (13). The unchanged complete author and peer-source readbacks are retained. * [Full unsummed fold phase](research_unsummed_two_square_morse_lift.md), SHA256 82ad7a75e6ab2857bbebb2f003f7e182ab1f26da1cf425f579106cdad11d15dd: the retained \(b_0\) marking, full Hessian result and exact-source limitations. The complete text was reread. The archived [uniform half-plane expansion](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_factorial_uniform_halfplane_continuation.md) and [lower-half continuation](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_lower_half_factorial_continuation.md) already establish factorial asymptotics away from real walls. Both complete texts were read for coverage. The proof here uses (4) directly to fix all centered constants on one slit domain; its source-specific addition is the contraction proof of the retained phase and the actual unit/amplitude at every classified two-square edge. Only written mathematics, source-text reads and hashes were used. No mathematical program, numerical evaluation, test or compilation was run. Frozen notes, manuscripts and public documents were unchanged.

title: Uniform factorial bounds and decay in a free boundary angle
text: # Uniform factorial bounds and decay in a free boundary angle Research proof, 2 November 2026. This note gives upper bounds on the exact Newton interpolation, including the places where a factorial argument crosses zero. It also proves a decrease of the real phase in the remaining boundary angle. These are inputs to a contour argument, not a proof that any particular contour represents the dominant contribution. ## 1. A midpoint estimate that includes zero Let $G_N$ be the canonical factorial in [the factorial continuation note](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/research_terminal_reflected_factorials.md), and let $J$ denote the primitive of $\log(2\sin\pi w)$ continued from $0<w<1$. Fix $0<\delta<1$ and a finite $H>0$. **Lemma 1.** There is a constant $C=C(\delta,H)>1$ such that, for all $N\ge3$ and all $w$ with $0\le\Re w\le1-\delta$, $|\Im w|\le H$, \[ C^{-1}\sqrt N\,e^{N\Re J(w)} \le |G_N(Nw-1/2)| \le C\sqrt N\,e^{N\Re J(w)}. \tag{1} \] At $w=0$, set $J(0)=0$. The estimate includes that point. **Proof.** Substitute $z=Nw-1/2$ into the defining Gamma product: \[ G_N(Nw-1/2)= (2\pi/N)^{Nw-1/2}\Gamma(Nw+1/2) \prod_{a\ge1} \frac{\Gamma(N(a+w)+1/2)} {\Gamma(N(a-w)+1/2)(Na)^{2Nw}}. \tag{2} \] Keep the first Gamma factor exact. For $z$ in the closed right half-plane, define \[ Q(z)=\Gamma(z+1/2)e^z z^{-z},\qquad Q(0)=\sqrt\pi, \] using the principal logarithm. Its absolute value is bounded above and bounded away from zero on that half-plane. On its intersection with a fixed disk this follows by continuity, nonvanishing of Gamma, and $z\log z\to0$. Outside a sufficiently large disk, the sectorial midpoint Stirling expansion gives $Q(z)=\sqrt{2\pi}(1+O(1/|z|))$ uniformly for $|\arg z|\le\pi/2$. In every other factor of (2), the real parts of $a\pm w$ are at least $\delta$. Apply the same Stirling expansion there. Its first corrections occur in the difference \[ -\frac1{24N}\sum_{a\ge1} \left(\frac1{a+w}-\frac1{a-w}\right), \] which is uniformly convergent because its terms are $O(a^{-2})$. The remainders are bounded by a uniformly summable $O(N^{-3}a^{-3})$ sequence, with the finitely many initial terms absorbed into a constant depending on $\delta,H$. The resulting error in the logarithm of the product is $O_{\delta,H}(1/N)$. The leading logarithm is $NJ(w)$: differentiating its convergent series gives Euler's product for $\log(2\sin\pi w)$, and the value at zero fixes the integration constant. The remaining constant is $\sqrt{N/(2\pi)}\,Q(Nw)$. Its modulus is between two positive multiples of $\sqrt N$. This proves (1), including $w=0$. The argument uses only the defining Gamma product and the usual [sectorial Stirling expansion](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.11). $\square$ ## 2. Reciprocal bounds across the negative real axis For $\Re w<0$, choose $J_+(w)$ above the negative real axis and $J_-(w)$ below it. Their real boundary values on the axis agree. The exact identity from the continuation note is \[ \frac1{G_N(Nw-1/2)} =\frac{2\cos(\pi Nw)}N G_N(-Nw-1/2). \tag{3} \] On the upper side, $J_+(w)=-J(-w)+i\pi w$ and $2\cos(\pi Nw)=e^{-i\pi Nw}(1+e^{2\pi iNw})$. The factor in parentheses has modulus at most two. On the lower side use the conjugate sign. Lemma 1 therefore implies the following uniform upper estimate: \[ \left|\frac1{G_N(Nw-1/2)}\right| \le C N^{-1/2}e^{-N\Re J_{\rm side}(w)}, \quad -1+\delta\le\Re w\le1-\delta, \quad |\Im w|\le H. \tag{4} \] For nonnegative real part, $J_{\rm side}$ is the ordinary continued branch and (4) follows directly from (1). At negative real arguments, (3) proves the bound with both cosine terms retained. Reciprocal factorial zeros do not cause an exception: the left side can vanish, and (4) is an upper bound. Thus (4) does not require staying a fixed distance from the negative real axis or from zero. ## 3. The exact Newton interpolation Put $d=N-1$ and \[ B_N(x,t)= \frac{G_N(d/2+Nt/(2\pi))G_N(d/2-Nt/(2\pi))} {G_N(d/2-Nx+Nt/(2\pi))G_N(d/2-Nx-Nt/(2\pi))G_N(Nx)^2}. \] The numerator is exactly $N$, by $G_N(z)G_N(d-z)=N$. At every integer $k$ with $0\le k<N$, this is the original Newton polynomial $e_k(-2\cos t)$ when $x=k/N$. Let $x$ range over a compact rectangle $0<\alpha\le\Re x\le\beta<1/2$, $|\Im x|\le H_x$. Let $t$ range over a bounded complex set on which the real parts of \[ w_+=\frac12-x+\frac{t}{2\pi},\qquad w_-=\frac12-x-\frac{t}{2\pi} \] stay in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]$ for some $\delta>0$. Apply (4) to $w_\pm$ and (1) to $x+1/(2N)$; the finitely many small levels can be handled by increasing the constant. Since $x$ stays away from zero and one, $N[J(x+1/(2N))-J(x)]$ is uniformly bounded. It follows that \[ |B_N(x,t)|\le\frac{C}{N}\exp\{N\mathfrak b(x,t)\}, \qquad \mathfrak b(x,t)= -\Re J_{\rm side}(w_+)-\Re J_{\rm side}(w_-)-2\Re J(x). \tag{5} \] The estimate includes all moving-zero faces and their intersections. On a contour where the chosen branches are holomorphic, $\mathfrak b(x,t)=\Re b(x,t)$. Elsewhere (5) specifies the real upper exponent directly, using the side approached by each argument. One must use those same branches in a certificate for a contour face. For a real boundary angle $u\in[-\pi,\pi]$, the conditions on $w_\pm$ hold uniformly on the entire rectangle in $x$. Thus (5) also supplies an exact bound on the second boundary factor throughout the whole real angular period. ## 4. Decay in the real boundary angle **Lemma 2.** Write $x=\xi+ih$, where $0<\xi<1/2$. For $-\pi\le u\le\pi$ one has \[ \mathfrak b(x,u)-\mathfrak b(x,0) \le-\frac{\sin(2\pi\xi)}{4\pi\cosh^2(\pi h)} (1-\cos u). \tag{6} \] **Proof.** Evenness reduces to $0\le u\le\pi$. Away from zeros, differentiation of the continued primitive gives \[ \partial_u\mathfrak b(x,u) =\frac1{4\pi}\log\frac{A}{B}, \] \[ A=\cos^2(\pi\xi+u/2)+\sinh^2(\pi h),\qquad B=\cos^2(\pi\xi-u/2)+\sinh^2(\pi h). \] Here $B-A=\sin(2\pi\xi)\sin u\ge0$ and $B\le\cosh^2(\pi h)$. Hence \[ \partial_u\mathfrak b(x,u) \le-\frac{\sin(2\pi\xi)\sin u}{4\pi\cosh^2(\pi h)}. \] Integrating proves (6). When $h=0$, an interior zero of $A$ gives an integrable logarithmic singularity. Apply the argument on the two sides of that point and pass to the continuous primitive; no bound on the pointwise logarithm at the zero is required. $\square$ In particular, on the fixed wire rectangle there is $c>0$ such that \[ |B_N(x,u)|\le\frac{C}{N} \exp\!\left[N\{\mathfrak b(x,0)-c(1-\cos u)\}\right] \qquad(-\pi\le u\le\pi). \tag{7} \] This applies to positive and negative wire heights and to every intermediate height on a connecting surface. If a complete contour argument bounds the remaining factors at the selected rate when $u=0$, (7) supplies the extra real-boundary loss on the same contour. It does not supply the missing contour argument or its nonzero leading coefficient. Its role is to make that argument usable after the terminal tangle is glued to another tangle.

title: Uniform full-dilogarithm ray moments and finite transfer inverses
text: # Uniform full-dilogarithm ray moments and finite transfer inverses Fix the full function and its marked negative ray from [F]. The ray moments have size comparable to \(N^{-1}\), uniformly over every physical degree, for all sufficiently large levels. The top degree has an additional endpoint contribution, which is retained below. The resulting finite nilpotent transfer and its inverse have subexponential operator bounds. No lower bound for a closed scalar observation is inferred. ## 1. The original moments and the uniform profile Let \(N\ge2\), \(d=N-1\), \(\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}\), and \(Q=\exp(2\pi i/N)\). The signed ray part of the literal moment functional [F, Section 4a] is \[ j_{\epsilon,a} =-\frac{\epsilon(-1)^{N-a}}{2\pi i} \int_0^1\Psi_\epsilon(\log r+i\epsilon\pi) r^{N-a-1}\,dr, \qquad 0\le a<N. \tag{1} \] Thus the original coefficient is its shifted-circle contribution plus (1). This sign convention retains the minus sign of the radial part of the full moment functional. Put \[ b=N-a,\qquad \phi(r)=-\frac{\operatorname{Li}_2(-r)}{2\pi},\qquad c=\frac{\log2}{2\pi},\qquad c_0=\frac1{2\pi}. \tag{2} \] The uniform assertion is \[ \begin{split} I_{\epsilon,b,N} &:={\int_0^1\Psi_\epsilon(\log r+i\epsilon\pi)r^{b-1}\,dr}\\ &=\frac{\sqrt2\,e^{i\epsilon N\pi/24}}{b+i\epsilon Nc} -\frac{\mathbf1_{b=1}}{i\epsilon Nc_0} +O(N^{-3/2}),\qquad 1\le b\le N. \tag{3} \end{split} \] The error is uniform in the integer \(b\) and in \(\epsilon\). In particular there are constants \(c_*,C_*>0\) and \(N_0\) such that \[ \frac{c_*}{N}\le |j_{\epsilon,a}|\le\frac{C_*}{N} \quad(N\ge N_0,\ 0\le a<N). \tag{4} \] No assertion excluding coefficient zeros at the finitely many smaller levels is made. ### The actual quantum remainder The full-strip estimate [F,(7a)] and its stated logarithmic derivative estimate give, on this particular ray, \[ \Psi_\epsilon(\log r+i\epsilon\pi) =\sqrt{1+r}\,e^{i\epsilon N\phi(r)}(1+e_{\epsilon,N}(r)), \qquad \sup_{r>0}\bigl(|e_{\epsilon,N}|+|r e'_{\epsilon,N}|\bigr) \le C/N. \tag{5} \] The derivative bound follows by Cauchy's estimate on a smaller fixed logarithmic strip. The same chosen function and branch occur in (1) and (5). Also [F,(13b)] gives the exact identity \[ |\Psi_\epsilon(\log r+i\epsilon\pi)|=\sqrt{1+r}. \tag{6} \] We use no uniform ordinary derivative of \(e_{\epsilon,N}\) at zero. Indeed, split the error in replacing the integrand in (1) by the leading expression in (5) at \(r_0=N^{-2}\). On \([0,r_0]\), (5) or (6) bounds its integral by \(C N^{-2}\), uniformly for \(b\ge1\). On \([r_0,1]\) set \(A_b(r)=r^{b-1}\sqrt{1+r}\,e_{\epsilon,N}(r)\). Its supremum is \(O(N^{-1})\), and \[ \int_{r_0}^1|A_b'(r)|\,dr\le C\log N/N. \tag{7} \] The derivative of \(r^{b-1}\) has integral at most one; the only logarithmic loss is \(\int_{r_0}^1dr/(Nr)\) from (5). Now \[ \phi'(r)=\frac{\log(1+r)}{2\pi r},\qquad c\le\phi'(r)\le c_0\quad(0\le r\le1), \tag{8} \] and \(\phi''\) is bounded, with removable values at zero. One integration by parts against \(e^{i\epsilon N\phi}\), using (7)--(8), bounds the upper-interval error by \(C\log N/N^2\). Consequently \[ I_{\epsilon,b,N} =\int_0^1 r^{b-1}\sqrt{1+r}\,e^{i\epsilon N\phi(r)}dr +O(\log N/N^2), \tag{9} \] uniformly in every physical degree. This retains both original endpoints; it is not a replacement of the full moment by a bare circle coefficient. ### The two ranges of physical degrees First let \(1\le b\le\sqrt N\), and write \(a_b(r)=r^{b-1}\sqrt{1+r}\). Its endpoint first derivatives and the \(L^1\) norm of its second derivative are \(O(b)\). For \(b=1,2\) this is checked directly; for \(b\ge3\), the largest term has integral \((b-1)(b-2)\int_0^1r^{b-3}dr=b-1\). The other terms are bounded in the same way. The derivatives of \(\phi\) through third order are bounded on this interval, and \(\phi'\) is bounded away from zero. Two integrations by parts give \[ \int_0^1a_b(r)e^{i\epsilon N\phi(r)}dr =\frac{\sqrt2 e^{i\epsilon N\pi/24}}{i\epsilon Nc} -\frac{\mathbf1_{b=1}}{i\epsilon Nc_0} +O(b/N^2). \tag{10} \] Here \(\phi(0)=0\), \(\phi(1)=\pi/24\), and \(a_b(0)=\mathbf1_{b=1}\). Replacing the first denominator in (10) by \(b+i\epsilon Nc\) changes it by \(O(b/N^2)\). This proves (3) in the first range. For \(b>\sqrt N\), set \[ \delta=(b-1)/N,\qquad \Phi(r)=\delta\log r+i\epsilon\phi(r),\qquad A(r)=\sqrt{1+r}. \] Since \(\Phi'=\delta/r+i\epsilon\phi'\) never vanishes on the positive interval, integration by parts gives the endpoint term \[ \frac{\sqrt2 e^{i\epsilon N\pi/24}}{b-1+i\epsilon Nc} \] and remainder \[ -\frac1N\int_0^1e^{N\Phi(r)} \left(\frac{A(r)}{\Phi'(r)}\right)'dr. \tag{11} \] The endpoint at zero vanishes. On \([1/2,1]\), the differentiated factor in (11) is uniformly bounded, so this part is \(O(1/(Nb))\). On \((0,1/2]\), use \(|\Phi'|\ge\delta/r\) to bound that factor by \(C\delta^{-2}\). Its integral is bounded by \(C\delta^{-2}2^{-b}/(Nb)\), which is smaller than \(N^{-3/2}\) in the stated range. Finally replacing \(b-1\) by \(b\) in the endpoint denominator costs \(O(N^{-2})\). Together with (9), this proves (3) for all \(b\). For \(b\ge2\), the modulus of the displayed main term in (3) is at least \(\sqrt2/(N\sqrt{1+c^2})\). For \(b=1\), the lower triangle bound, multiplied by \(N\), tends to \[ \sqrt2/c-1/c_0>0. \] The upper bounds are uniform as well. The error in (3) is smaller than these bounds at all sufficiently large levels, proving (4). ## 2. Exact finite normalization and the endpoint seam Define the nonzero common phase and scale \[ \zeta_{\epsilon,N} =-\frac{\epsilon(-1)^N\sqrt2}{2\pi i} e^{i\epsilon N\pi/24},\qquad h_a=\frac{N(-1)^a}{\zeta_{\epsilon,N}}j_{\epsilon,a}. \tag{12} \] Its modulus is \(\sqrt2/(2\pi)\), independent of level. For \(0\le a\le d-1\), equation (3) gives \[ h_a=\frac1{1-a/N+i\epsilon c}+O(N^{-1/2}). \tag{13} \] Consequently \(|h_0|\) is bounded above and below, all \(h_a\) are bounded, and \[ |h_a-h_{a-1}|\le C N^{-1/2}\quad(1\le a<d),\qquad |h_d-h_{d-1}|\le C. \tag{14} \] The last difference is deliberately separate. It contains the \(b=1\) contribution in (3), including its level-dependent phase. It is not set to zero or estimated by the first bound in (14). Let \(T\) act on any finite-dimensional Hilbert space, with \(\|T\|_2\le1\) and \(T^N=0\). Put \[ \mathcal J_{\epsilon,N}(T)=\sum_{a=0}^d j_{\epsilon,a}T^a, \qquad H(S)=\sum_{a=0}^d h_aS^a. \] Then exactly \[ \mathcal J_{\epsilon,N}(T) =\frac{\zeta_{\epsilon,N}}N H(-T). \tag{15} \] For all sufficiently large \(N\), these maps are invertible and \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \|\mathcal J_{\epsilon,N}(T)\|_2\le C, \qquad \|\mathcal J_{\epsilon,N}(T)^{-1}\|_2 \le C N e^{C\sqrt N}.} \tag{16} \] To prove the inverse bound, work modulo \(S^N=0\). The exact identity \[ (1-S)H(S)=h_0\left(1+\sum_{a=1}^d b_aS^a\right), \qquad b_a=(h_a-h_{a-1})/h_0 \tag{17} \] has \(|b_a|\le\eta_N=C/\sqrt N\) for \(a<d\), and \(|b_d|\le C\). For \(B_<(S)=\sum_{a=1}^{d-1}b_aS^a\), the coefficient of degree \(n\ge1\) in \((1+B_<)^{-1}\) is bounded by \[ \sum_{k=1}^n {n-1\choose k-1}\eta_N^k =\eta_N(1+\eta_N)^{n-1}. \tag{18} \] This counts the ordered positive compositions of \(n\); all series are finite modulo \(S^N\). The last seam contributes exactly \(-b_dS^d\) to the inverse, because its product with every positive power of \(S\) vanishes. Thus the sum of absolute coefficients of the inverse in (17) is at most \(C(1+\eta_N)^d+C\le C e^{C\sqrt N}\). Multiplication by \(1-S\), whose norm is at most two, proves the inverse estimate in (16). The direct bound follows from (4) by summing \(N\) coefficients. This proof does not assume normality or diagonalizability of \(T\). ## 3. Actual atom scope The original unit-color transfers in [F, Section 5] have precisely \(\|T\|\le1\), \(T^N=0\). Their unit geometric phases are retained by replacing \(T\) by the corresponding unit multiple. In particular the original \(u\)-ray is \(\mathcal J_{-,N}(Q^{-1}T)\), while the \(v\)-ray is \(\mathcal J_{+,N}(T)\). Formula (15) keeps the additional \((-1)^a\) phase explicitly rather than dropping it. The original reciprocal-factorial ray diagonal has entries \(Q^{-a}j_{-,a}\), and the reflected factorial ray diagonal has entries \(NQ^{d-a}j_{+,d-a}\). By (4), for all sufficiently large levels their norms and inverse norms satisfy respectively \[ \|D_{\rm rec}\|\le C/N,\quad \|D_{\rm rec}^{-1}\|\le CN, \qquad \|D_{\rm fac}\|+\|D_{\rm fac}^{-1}\|\le C. \tag{19} \] These are the literal factors and index reflection of [F,(15)]. Any fixed composable product of these ray maps and fixed unitary maps therefore has norm and inverse norm at most \(N^M e^{C\sqrt N}\), with constants depending on the fixed product. The assertion is about those invertible atomic maps. Original cups, projections, marked covectors and subsequent contractions remain their specified maps; (16)--(19) give no lower bound for their scalar observation. Mixed circle/ray patterns may still retain exponential source factors. The estimates concern the full function's selected moments at radius one and the original nilpotent finite atoms. They do not identify a negative-ray chain with a geometric thimble, prove an off-root identity, or extend an odd-level tetrahedral state to even levels. ## Complete direct source - [F] [Full-dilogarithm coefficient cycles](https://github.com/sashakolpakov/murakamis_dream/blob/19d5b911bc409486f0e72b51a876a6a2bc70ee02/notes/actual_modular_dilog_circle_and_boundary_source.md), SHA256 48649230d0552bac1a38c8d31a784e1ad4102172ed73916fdfc275aa9775dd7e. The entire proof was read. The fixed full function, uniform full-strip remainder and logarithmic derivatives, exact ray modulus, and original atomic reflection formulas are used. The entire underlying defining-integral proof in `literature_state_volume.md` was also read; its unchanged hash is ae6117e059081c1cbd298ac65690294a6209a5b2d79b5b84ea5758789bd34946. No mathematical program or numerical experiment was used.

title: Uniform confluence depth for the original generic fusion source
